title: Learning through Discernment: when a small language model learns from user feedback on the job, and when it decays
description:
arXiv:2611.23716v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Small language models on devices could keep improving by learning, overnight, from their own daily work. Without a true outcome, however, something must decide which attempts are worth learning from, and both the model's own judgment and the user's reaction can be wrong. We study a small model (Qwen3 0.6B and 1.7B) with a LoRA adapter, fine-tuned each night on the attempts a judge accepts, over 127 lives of up to a year on WebShop and $\tau^2$-bench. We compare the true outcome, the user's stated verdict and the model's own judgment with a separate, frozen "feedback sense" that reads the user's reaction, built in three versions. Judging itself, the model improved and then decayed, over a year and whatever its adapter. A sense that took polite give-ups for success collapsed 3 of 5 lives; one built for discernment, which first asks whether the user gave a clear verdict, kept 4 of 5 near the oracle for two weeks, then faded on clean but scarce lessons, to the level of self-judging by day 60. When the user cannot see the outcome ($\tau^2$-bench), the sense read reactions correctly, yet 80% of its lessons were failures the customer had thanked. Across 97 lives, the share of failed attempts among the lessons predicted the outcome (Spearman $\rho$ = -0.81). In our experiments, learning from users held up only where the judge kept failures out and the user could see the outcome; lopsided lessons may also narrow the model.

title: Introducing Vercel Security Review
description:
Today, we are launching Vercel Security Review in public beta.

Security Review is a new capability in Vercel Agent, alongside Code Review and Investigation. Once enabled, it scans for vulnerabilities on every push to a team's connected GitHub repositories.

Findings appear as comments on pull requests, are listed in the Security dashboard, and are available via CLI. With your permission, Vercel Agent can also validate and push fixes for findings.

How it works

Security reviews are triggered by GitHub push events, including direct pushes to your production branch. In monorepos, reviews are scoped to the project's root directory. Here is how it works:

  1. You push code to a GitHub repository connected to a Vercel project.

  2. As soon as the push lands, Security Review scans the changed code for vulnerabilities like missing authorization checks or exposed secrets.

  3. Findings are posted to the Security dashboard. On private and internal repositories, Security Review also adds a GitHub check to the commit and comments on the pull request.

  4. You can fix findings by clicking Fix with Vercel Agent in the dashboard, or use the CLI to pull findings and have your own coding agent implement changes.

  5. When subsequent security reviews no longer detect a finding, it is marked as no longer detected in the dashboard, and the GitHub comment is closed.

Each review compares the push against a base and covers only what changed. For deployments, the base is the branch’s previous deployment, so the agent reviews the change against what’s already running. Because it only scans the diff, Security Review finishes in seconds and can run on every preview and production deployment.

What the agent checks

The agent reads the diff along with the surrounding code, traces how the changed code can be reached, checks for existing protections, and rechecks each finding before reporting it. That process is how it catches logic flaws like missing authorization checks, which pattern-matching scanners miss.

Each review also applies your team’s security policies, which you can write in plain language and apply to specific projects or across your team. For example, a policy can require any endpoint that returns customer data to check that the requester owns it. You can also manage policies with the Vercel CLI, using vercel security policy.

How findings are tracked

Each new finding is checked against ones that have already been reported, so the same issue isn’t flagged twice. Every finding is tied to the deployment where it first appeared and changes are followed from there. That means that when a vulnerable change from a pull request is merged into your production branch, the finding is flagged in production as well.

When a later review no longer detects the issue in an environment, the agent marks the finding as no longer detected there.

Acting on findings

Every finding explains the vulnerability and how to fix it, with links to the commit and deployment where it first appeared.

Findings are listed in the Vulnerability view in the Security dashboard, where you can ask Vercel Agent to validate and commit fixes. Findings are also available via CLI, so you can fix vulnerabilities with your own coding agent.

Each new finding generates an audit log event, which Enterprise teams can send to their SIEM through Audit Log Drains.

Here is a demo of sample findings in the dashboard:

Fixing vulnerabilities with Vercel Agent

When Vercel Agent can fix a finding, you will see the option to click Fix with Vercel Agent on the finding page in the dashboard. After you click, the agent confirms the vulnerability still exists, then makes the smallest change that fixes it and updates the tests.

Say a developer pushes a change to an invoice download endpoint, and the lookup doesn't check which organization the invoice belongs to. Within seconds, Security Review flags that any signed-in user could download another organization's invoice by changing its ID. Vercel Agent's fix scopes the lookup to the user's organization:

Fixing vulnerabilities with your own coding agent

You can point your coding agent or other systems at the Vercel CLI to pull and fix vulnerabilities:

Findings in the dashboard also give you the ability to copy details as Markdown or JSON, making it easy to paste them into an agent conversation.

Every code change needs security review

Frontier AI models are making vulnerabilities far easier to find and exploit. Last month, researchers turned two decade-old flaws in PHP core into working remote code execution exploits with relatively little effort.

At the same time, agents are writing more of the code teams ship, and each handles security review its own way, or in many cases, not at all.

With Vercel Security Review, you can scan every push on every project for vulnerabilities by default, using the security policies you set.

What's next

Security Review starts with code pushed to GitHub. Next, we're bringing it to deployments from the Vercel CLI and v0, and to repositories that don't deploy on Vercel. We're also working on suggested fixes you can apply directly from the pull request.

Get started

Vercel Security Review is available today in public beta for Pro and Enterprise teams.

To get started, enable Security Review in Vercel Agent Settings. You can choose to run Security Review on all projects, or only the ones you choose. To learn more, read the Changelog entry and the Security Review documentation.

Security Review is billed at the Vercel Agent rate, with model tokens at the provider's rate and no markup, plus $0.25 per million tokens.

Security reviews are free until November 10, 2026. Fixes made with Vercel Agent are billed at the rate above.

title: Optimizing Rust Lock-Free MPMC for Latency Reduction
description:
💡 Originally published on Bijak Technology Enterprise Journal with full interactive parameter benchmarks.

In large-scale event-driven clusters processing millions of messages per second, relying on synchronization primitives like std::sync::Mutex or RwLock introduces fatal systemic bottlenecks. When thousands of threads contend for the same mutex, kernel-level context switching and cache line bouncing inflate p99 tail latency to hundreds of milliseconds. Modern distributed systems require lock-free concurrency engineering that leverages atomic CPU instructions directly to maintain memory state consistency without engaging OS thread schedulers.

To understand how this mitigation operates in a real-world topology, let's examine the event processing architecture flowing from NATS JetStream to Tokio worker pools through the following diagram:

flowchart TD
 A[NATS JetStream Server] -->|TCP / Zero-Copy Stream| B(Tokio Reactor Core)
 B --> C{Crossbeam MPMC Ring Buffer}
 C -->|Lock-Free Pop| D[Worker Thread 1]
 C -->|Lock-Free Pop| E[Worker Thread 2]
 C -->|Lock-Free Pop| F[Worker Thread N]
 D --> G[(Database / Sink)]
 E --> G
 F --> G

Implementing MPMC Queue with Crossbeam & Atomic Operations in Rust

The most effective approach to eliminate mutex overhead is utilizing atomic-backed ring buffers (AtomicUsize) using the crossbeam-queue crate or custom implementations. Below is an asynchronous message processing module integrating NATS subscribers with zero-copy deserialization and a lock-free queue in Rust:

use crossbeam_queue::SegQueue;
use std::sync::Arc;
use tokio::task;
use bytes::Bytes;

#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct EventPayload {
 pub id: u64,
 pub data: Bytes,
}

pub struct EngineSupervisor {
 queue: Arc<SegQueue<EventPayload>>,
 worker_count: usize,
}

impl EngineSupervisor {
 pub fn new(worker_count: usize) -> Self {
 Self {
 queue: Arc::new(SegQueue::new()),
 worker_count,
 }
 }

 pub fn push_event(&self, payload: EventPayload) {
 self.queue.push(payload);
 }

 pub async fn spawn_workers(&self) {
 for worker_id in 0..self.worker_count {
 let q = Arc::clone(&self.queue);
 task::spawn(async move {
 loop {
 if let Some(event) = q.pop() {
 process_payload(worker_id, event).await;
 } else {
 tokio::task::yield_now().await;
 }
 }
 });
 }
 }
}

async fn process_payload(worker_id: usize, event: EventPayload) {
 println!("Worker {} processing event ID: {}", worker_id, event.id);
}

Performance Benchmark: Traditional Mutex vs Rust Lock-Free MPMC

To quantify the effectiveness of this architecture, heavy load testing was conducted in a private cluster environment. Metrics focus on throughput (RPS), average latency (p50), and extreme tail latency (p99) under a load of 500,000 concurrent requests. As a foundation for high-performance infrastructure, similar architectures are frequently paired with networking optimizations such as those found in Traefik v3 API gateway architecture setups to maintain efficient communication pipelines.

Evaluation Metric Traditional Arc<Mutex<VecDeque>> Rust Lock-Free MPMC Queue Improvement / Reduction
Throughput (RPS) 142,500 req/sec 689,200 req/sec +383.6%
p50 Latency 4.2 ms 0.35 ms -91.6%
p99 Tail Latency 128.4 ms 2.1 ms -98.3%
CPU Context Switches 45,200 /sec 1,150 /sec -97.4%

Architectural Conclusion and Infrastructure Recommendations

Eliminating tail latency in enterprise event stream systems cannot be achieved solely by scaling physical CPU capacity. It requires low-level synchronization pattern overhauls toward lock-free data structures that minimize cache misses and preserve data pipeline integrity via NATS JetStream and Rust asynchronous runtime integration. To run such compute-intensive workloads optimally, ensure you utilize infrastructure supporting strict resource isolation like High-Performance VPS solutions from infrastruktur Hostinger KVM VPS.

title: Mock an e-commerce backend for your React app in 5 minutes
description:
You're building the frontend for a store. The design is ready, but the backend isn't, and you're tired of hardcoding const products = [...] in a file.

In this tutorial we'll build a small React product page against a free mock REST API, with no backend, no API key and no signup. By the end you'll have:

  • a product list with search and pagination
  • each product's category and reviews loaded in the same request
  • a "create product" form that shows real validation errors
  • a way to test your loading and error states on demand

Disclosure: I built DevSeed API, the mock API used here. It's free, and I'd love feedback on it.

1. Look at the data

Every endpoint is a plain GET you can open in the browser:

https://www.devseedapi.com/api/v1/ecommerce/products?limit=2

{
  "success": true,
  "data": [
    { "id": "p1", "name": "Wireless Mouse", "price": 29.99, "categoryId": "c1", "createdAt": "2026-03-02T10:00:00Z" },
    { "id": "p2", "name": "Mechanical Keyboard", "price": 79.99, "categoryId": "c1", "createdAt": "2026-03-02T10:10:00Z" }
  ],
  "meta": { "total": 120, "page": 1, "limit": 2, "totalPages": 60 }
}

The e-commerce set also has categories, reviews, orders, cart and coupons, and there are user and SaaS datasets too. Every list endpoint supports the same query params:

What Example
Pagination ?page=2&limit=10
Search ?search=mouse
Exact filter ?categoryId=c1
Range filter ?minPrice=20&maxPrice=50
Sort ?sortBy=price&order=asc
Related data ?include=category,reviews

They combine, so ?search=mouse&maxPrice=50&sortBy=price&order=asc returns the mouse-related products under $50, cheapest first.

2. Load related data in one request

This is the part most mock APIs skip. On a real product page you need the product's category and its reviews, and you don't want to fire three requests and join them yourself.

GET https://www.devseedapi.com/api/v1/ecommerce/products/p1?include=category,reviews

{
  "success": true,
  "data": {
    "id": "p1",
    "name": "Wireless Mouse",
    "price": 29.99,
    "categoryId": "c1",
    "category": { "id": "c1", "name": "Computer Accessories" },
    "reviews": [
      { "id": 101, "productId": "p1", "userId": "u1", "rating": 5, "comment": "Excellent mouse!" },
      { "id": 163, "productId": "p1", "userId": "u70", "rating": 5, "comment": "Exactly as described." }
    ]
  }
}

(Trimmed a little for space.) include works on list endpoints too, which is what we'll use next.

3. A product list with search and pagination

Set up a React app (npm create vite@latest shop -- --template react) and add a small hook:

// useProducts.js
import { useEffect, useState } from "react"

const API = "https://www.devseedapi.com/api/v1/ecommerce"

const LOADING = { status: "loading", products: [], meta: null, error: null }

export function useProducts({ search, page, simulate = {} }) {
  // One string describing the request; a new value means a new fetch.
  const key = JSON.stringify({ search, page, ...simulate })
  const [result, setResult] = useState({ key: null })

  useEffect(() => {
    const controller = new AbortController()
    const params = new URLSearchParams({ limit: 8, include: "category,reviews", ...JSON.parse(key) })

    fetch(`${API}/products?${params}`, { signal: controller.signal })
      .then(async res => {
        const body = await res.json()
        if (!res.ok) throw new Error(body.message ?? `HTTP ${res.status}`)
        setResult({ key, status: "success", products: body.data, meta: body.meta, error: null })
      })
      .catch(err => {
        if (err.name !== "AbortError") {
          setResult({ key, status: "error", products: [], meta: null, error: err.message })
        }
      })

    return () => controller.abort()
  }, [key])

  // Until the response for the current request arrives, we're loading.
  return result.key === key ? result : LOADING
}

And the page:

// ProductList.jsx
import { useState } from "react"
import { useProducts } from "./useProducts"

const average = reviews =>
  reviews.length ? (reviews.reduce((sum, r) => sum + r.rating, 0) / reviews.length).toFixed(1) : "–"

export default function ProductList() {
  const [search, setSearch] = useState("")
  const [page, setPage] = useState(1)
  const { status, products, meta, error } = useProducts({ search, page })

  return (
    <div>
      <input
        placeholder="Search products"
        value={search}
        onChange={e => { setSearch(e.target.value); setPage(1) }}
      />

      {status === "loading" && <p>Loading…</p>}
      {status === "error" && <p role="alert">Couldn't load products: {error}</p>}

      <ul>
        {products.map(p => (
          <li key={p.id}>
            <strong>{p.name}</strong> · ${p.price} · {p.category?.name} · ★ {average(p.reviews)} ({p.reviews.length})
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>

      {meta && (
        <nav>
          <button disabled={page <= 1} onClick={() => setPage(page - 1)}>Previous</button>
          <span> Page {meta.page} of {meta.totalPages} </span>
          <button disabled={page >= meta.totalPages} onClick={() => setPage(page + 1)}>Next</button>
        </nav>
      )}
    </div>
  )
}

Each product arrives with its category and reviews already attached, so there's no second round of requests. meta.totalPages drives the pagination buttons.

4. A create form with real validation errors

Mock APIs usually accept anything you POST, so your error handling never gets exercised. Here, writes are validated like a real API but never stored: the response shows the record that would have been created.

Send a bad body:

curl -X POST https://www.devseedapi.com/api/v1/ecommerce/products \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name":"Desk Lamp","price":"cheap"}'

{
  "success": false,
  "message": "Validation failed",
  "errors": [
    { "field": "price", "message": "must be a number" },
    { "field": "categoryId", "message": "is required" }
  ]
}

That's a 422. It even checks references: "categoryId": "c999" fails with no categories record with id "c999". A valid body returns 201 with a new id and a Location header.

A form that maps those errors onto fields:

// NewProductForm.jsx
import { useState } from "react"

const API = "https://www.devseedapi.com/api/v1/ecommerce"

export default function NewProductForm() {
  const [form, setForm] = useState({ name: "", price: "", categoryId: "c1" })
  const [fieldErrors, setFieldErrors] = useState({})
  const [created, setCreated] = useState(null)

  async function handleSubmit(e) {
    e.preventDefault()
    setFieldErrors({})
    setCreated(null)

    const res = await fetch(`${API}/products`, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
      body: JSON.stringify({ ...form, price: form.price === "" ? undefined : Number(form.price) }),
    })
    const body = await res.json()

    if (res.status === 422) {
      setFieldErrors(Object.fromEntries(body.errors.map(err => [err.field, err.message])))
    } else if (res.ok) {
      setCreated(body.data)
    }
  }

  const field = name => (
    <label>
      {name}
      <input value={form[name]} onChange={e => setForm({ ...form, [name]: e.target.value })} />
      {fieldErrors[name] && <small style={{ color: "crimson" }}>{fieldErrors[name]}</small>}
    </label>
  )

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
      {field("name")}
      {field("price")}
      {field("categoryId")}
      <button>Create</button>
      {created && <p>Created {created.name} with id {created.id}</p>}
    </form>
  )
}

Leave the price empty or type a category that doesn't exist, and you'll see the server's message under the right field. PUT, PATCH and DELETE on /products/:id work the same way.

5. Test your loading and error states

The happy path is easy. The states that break in production are the slow request and the failed one, and they're hard to trigger against a real backend. Three query params do it:

Param Effect
delay=2000 waits 2 seconds before responding
error=503 always responds with that status
errorRate=30 fails 30% of requests with a 500

Our hook already passes extra params through, so:

// See the spinner for 2 seconds
useProducts({ search, page, simulate: { delay: 2000 } })

// See the error state
useProducts({ search, page, simulate: { error: 503 } })

// Flaky network: does a retry button or a stale list still look right?
useProducts({ search, page, simulate: { errorRate: 30 } })

The error=503 case returns { "success": false, "message": "Simulated API Error" } with a 503 status, so the component shows "Couldn't load products: Simulated API Error". This is also handy for Storybook stories and Playwright/Cypress tests of your error UI.

Swapping in the real backend later

When your backend is ready, change API to point at it. If your real API uses the same ideas (page/limit, a meta object, field-level 422 errors), the components barely change. If it doesn't, the mock gives you a concrete contract to discuss with your backend team.

A few honest limits: writes are never saved, so a POST won't appear in the next GET. The data is the same for everyone, and there's a rate limit of 200 requests per 15 minutes per client.

Wrap-up

We built a product list with search, pagination and related data in a single request, a form that handles real validation errors, and a way to test loading and failure states, all against a free API with no setup.

  • Docs and a live console for every endpoint: https://www.devseedapi.com/docs/ecommerce/products
  • Source: https://github.com/gayashanacd/dev-seed-api

If there's a dataset you'd want next (social media, fintech, edtech…), or something that annoyed you, tell me here. It takes under a minute, and it decides what gets built next.

title: PhysScope: Agentic Multimodal Physics Reasoning with Grounded Visual Memory
description:
arXiv:2611.23010v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can correctly interpret physics diagrams yet apply constraints outside the states or conditions in which they hold, causing premise errors to propagate through subsequent calculations. We introduce PhysScope, an inference-time visual harness that supports self-correction of these scope mismatches without updating model weights. PhysScope enables the model to link physical scopes directly to its visual observations and explicitly constructs derived views to support reasoning. The harness imposes explicit constraints on state distinctions, conditions, and physical scopes during model reasoning, and checks agent-proposed revisions against sources and scopes. Accepted revisions invalidate registered dependents, thereby maintaining scope-aware working memory. On PhysAlign, PhysScope achieves higher solving scores than direct solving across all six evaluated VLMs. With Gemini-3.8-flash, it outperforms Canvas-CoT by 9.34 percentage points and substantially improves solving accuracy on the out-of-distribution (OOD) PhysUniBench benchmark. Ablation studies support explicit scope management and dependency maintenance as design principles for multimodal physics reasoning agents.

title: Grounding Radiology Reports in 3D Chest CT: Results of the ReXGrounding Challenge
description:
arXiv:2611.23862v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Segmenting each reported finding in a radiology scan would allow findings to be measured and tracked over time and let AI systems generate reports that are verifiable, but so far AI models have performed poorly at this task. To advance this task, we organized the ReXGrounding Challenge at MICCAI 2026, the first challenge dedicated to it. Given a non-contrast chest CT scan and the set of findings from its report, participants trained models to produce the corresponding set of 3D segmentations. The challenge used 2,992 training and 200 validation scans from the ReXGroundingCT dataset, and evaluated methods on a held-out test set of 300 scans with 582 findings, exhaustively annotated by board-certified radiologists. In total, 48 teams from 15 countries made 760 submissions, and the best method reached a Dice of 0.375 and a hit rate of 0.77, matching agreement between two independent radiologist groups (Dice 0.32, hit rate 0.76, on a 50-scan subset). On the 100 scans of the pre-challenge benchmark, the winner reached a Dice of 0.390, against 0.285 for VoxTell, the best model before the challenge, which five of the six best teams fine-tuned. Non-focal findings remained far harder to segment than focal ones, instance F1 stayed below inter-reader agreement (0.34 vs. 0.47), and models sometimes segmented the right abnormality in the wrong location. Top methods thus match radiologist agreement in Dice, but non-focal findings, findings with multiple instances, and adherence to the anatomical location described in the text remain open problems.

title: CADMAGEDDON: High-Fidelity CAD Reconstruction with Local Inference
description:
arXiv:2611.22563v2 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: CAD practitioners often work with proprietary parts that they are unwilling to share with external services. For individuals and small companies, bringing this work in-house also requires computational resources they can afford. We introduce CADMAGEDDON, an open-source agent that reconstructs editable CAD from meshes and can run locally on single-GPU systems and current-generation laptops. The method decomposes this complex task into a chain of simple visual decisions about what to construct and what to correct. Geometric tools support precise construction, allowing the agent to focus on visual reasoning. Using the mid-sized Qwen3.8-27B model, CADMAGEDDON outperforms prior approaches, including systems based on frontier models, in reconstruction quality on all the main benchmarks. CADMAGEDDON integrates with FreeCAD, bringing its reconstructions into practitioners' existing CAD workflows. Code: https://github.com/kulibinai/cadmageddon

title: How We Used Seven AI Agents to Ship a PoC in 72 Hours
description:
Our engineering team recently participated in a 72-hour development challenge organized by the innovation unit of a global electronics company.

The assignment was to build a working application using New York City's publicly available building-energy data. Each participating company had to define its own product, users, and implementation approach.

We delivered a live proof of concept (PoC) that analyzes energy consumption across approximately 30,000 commercial buildings, identifies underperforming properties, and generates recommendations with estimated improvement costs and payback periods.

The project involved six people, including four engineers, a business analyst, and a UX designer. Three engineers worked throughout the build, with a fourth joining on the final day.

Seven AI agents handled implementation, code review, and fixes within a workflow we had already been developing at MEV.

By the end of the challenge, the team had merged approximately 127 pull requests, spent around 107 human working hours, and deployed an application with a basic infrastructure cost of $45 per month.

The project received first place in the organizer's code-quality and AI-integration assessments.

Here's how we organized the development process, where the agents were useful, and which decisions remained with the engineers.

Defining a product before writing code

The initial brief provided access to data collected under New York City's Local Law 84, which requires certain buildings to report their annual energy consumption.

The dataset contained information on approximately 30,000 buildings.

It could support several types of applications, from individual building-performance dashboards to portfolio-level energy analysis.

We spent the first morning defining one specific user.

Our target was a Building Performance Analyst responsible for energy performance across a portfolio of commercial properties.

This person needs to identify underperforming buildings, investigate potential improvements, and present recommendations to management.

That user definition shaped the application.

A basic dashboard showing energy consumption would provide useful information, but the analyst also needed to explain why a particular building deserved attention and what improvements might cost.

We therefore focused on three capabilities:

  • Compare a building's energy performance against similar properties.
  • Generate improvement recommendations with estimated costs and payback periods.
  • Allow users to ask questions about building data in natural language.

While the business analyst and UX designer worked through the user journey, engineers prepared the infrastructure and development environment.

By limiting the application to one primary user, we could test the complete flow from raw data to a recommendation within the challenge's time limit.

How we organized seven AI agents

Our development process used seven specialized AI agents running through Claude Code.

Each agent had a specific responsibility. Their behavior was defined in written specifications stored alongside the application code and maintained under version control.

The agents operated as part of the MEV Innovation Lab Delivery System, an internal workflow that coordinates AI-assisted implementation, reviews, and fixes.

The core sequence looked like this:

GitHub Issue
     |
     v
Architect Agent
     |
     v
Engineer reviews and approves plan
     |
     v
Builder Agent
     |
     v
Review and specialized checks
     |
     v
Fixer Agent
     |
     v
Engineer approves final changes
     |
     v
Merge and deployment

The workflow included an architect, builder, reviewer, and fixer, along with specialized checks for security, design, and release readiness.

An engineer could start the chain with a command referencing an existing ticket:

/dev <ticket-number>

The agents then processed the task through planning, implementation, review, and correction.

This reduced the amount of manual coordination required between individual development steps.

Human approval remained part of the workflow

We established two mandatory human approval points.

The first came after the architect agent prepared an implementation plan. An engineer reviewed the proposed scope and approach before allowing the agents to generate code.

The second came after the automated review and correction stages. An engineer examined the final changes before approving the merge.

The agents handled much of the work between those points.

We also ran review chains locally before opening pull requests. Reviewer and security agents identified issues and categorized findings by severity, from P0 through P4.

That gave engineers a set of findings to evaluate rather than requiring them to discover every potential issue manually.

The implementation and review stages were automated, while responsibility for architecture and accepting code remained with the engineering team.

Preparing the delivery pipeline before the first ticket

The agents needed an environment where their output could be integrated and tested quickly.

We prepared hosting on DigitalOcean and configured GitHub Issues to work directly with the agent workflow.

Deployment was automated. After changes were merged, the application deployed without a separate manual release process.

Database migrations used a separate job triggered after the relevant merge.

This preparation mattered because frequent code changes were expected. During a 72-hour build, manual deployments and repeated environment setup would consume time needed for implementation and verification.

We also kept the agent specifications in version control.

That allowed the team to maintain the workflow definitions alongside the code being developed.

What did AI code review save?

The team merged approximately 127 pull requests during the challenge.

Based on an estimate of at least 30 minutes for conventional human review per pull request, we calculated that the automated review chain replaced close to 60 hours of manual review effort.

This is an estimate based on review volume and assumed review time, rather than a measured reduction in the project's elapsed delivery time.

Human approval still happened before merging.

The benefit was that engineers could review changes after automated agents had already examined the implementation, identified potential problems, and attempted corrections.

The team could then concentrate on the issues that needed engineering judgment.

Our engineering manager, Ivan Makarov, estimated that roughly 90% of the team's time went into planning and testing.

That included identifying edge cases and preparing tests before giving implementation tasks to the agents.

AI-generated code could handle an expected workflow quickly. The engineers had to account for missing fields, unexpected inputs, and interactions between application components.

For this project, the ability to specify and evaluate the work was as important as generating the code.

The difficult work remained in the architecture

The application had to process approximately 300 MB of New York City building-energy records.

Loading that data without losing records or overwhelming the application required attention to ingestion and database behavior.

Performance mattered because users needed to move around a map and compare buildings interactively.

The calculations used to rank individual buildings against comparable properties had to return results quickly enough to support that workflow.

Each senior engineer owned a vertical part of the application, including the associated architectural decisions.

That ownership reduced handoffs when implementation revealed problems requiring immediate decisions.

For example, the engineers designed the application's behavior for cases when the external AI provider was unavailable.

If the model API failed or returned a rate-limit error, the map and building comparisons remained usable. The recommendation area displayed a notice instead of causing the entire page to fail.

The team also prepared database migration controls to support repeatable deployments.

These were engineering decisions made alongside implementation, rather than tasks delegated entirely to coding agents.

Reducing model calls with a three-stage recommendation process

The application uses AI to suggest energy-efficiency improvements for individual buildings.

Sending every request directly to an LLM with the entire dataset would create unnecessary model usage.

We designed the recommendation workflow in three stages.

Stage 1: Identify comparable buildings

The application uses statistical analysis to find buildings with similar characteristics.

This establishes the context needed to interpret a property's energy performance.

Stage 2: Retrieve relevant improvement options

The system consults a stored library of energy-efficiency measures to identify suitable improvements.

For the PoC, we loaded three upgrade options drawn from US Department of Energy guidance.

The application architecture supports a larger library, but populating hundreds of measures was outside the challenge scope.

Stage 3: Generate the recommendation

Only the final stage calls Claude.

The model receives the selected building context and relevant improvement options, then generates a recommendation adapted to the property.

This limits the role of the LLM to the part of the workflow where language generation adds value.

Statistical comparison and retrieval happen before the model request.

The approach also reduces the amount of information the model needs to process for each recommendation.

Keeping the infrastructure cost at $45 per month

The PoC ran on a small DigitalOcean setup.

Our reported monthly infrastructure breakdown was:

Component Monthly cost
API hosting $25
Database migration service $5
Database $15
Total $45

This figure represents the basic application infrastructure used for the PoC.

Development costs were separate. Four engineers used Claude Code subscriptions priced at $200 per month each.

The $45 monthly figure should also be understood in the context of the PoC's workload and configuration. A production application with substantial traffic, a larger data pipeline, and greater AI usage would require a separate cost assessment.

We also implemented a subscription billing structure using Stripe.

The application had two subscription tiers, with the user's plan checked before each AI request.

The pricing was provisional, but the workflow demonstrated how AI consumption could be controlled by subscription limits.

Model calls were logged with information that allowed us to trace the prompt version, generated recommendation, and associated cost.

That provides a starting point for monitoring AI usage and investigating output behavior.

What we deliberately left out

A three-day delivery window forced us to decide which capabilities were essential to demonstrating the product.

We made several scope decisions early.

One city was enough

The dataset already contained approximately 30,000 New York City buildings.

Adding another city would have increased integration and data-processing work without contributing much additional evidence that the core application functioned.

We concentrated on the available dataset.

Three improvement measures were enough for the recommendation engine

The longer-term design anticipated a library containing hundreds of building-efficiency measures.

For the PoC, we used three options to test the complete process: retrieve relevant measures, analyze a building, and produce an improvement recommendation.

Adding more options would mostly have increased content preparation work.

Existing UI components were sufficient

We used existing interface components instead of investing time in custom interface development.

The UX work focused on making the analyst's workflow usable and connecting the screens to the underlying functionality.

Those choices allowed the team to complete a working application while keeping the scope aligned with the challenge.

Can this AI-agent workflow scale beyond a 72-hour PoC?

The workflow used in this project was a deliberately simplified version of our broader agent-assisted engineering process.

Its underlying pattern can be applied to longer projects: divide work into defined tasks, use specialized agents, automate verification, and require engineers to approve plans and final changes.

However, the exact configuration from this experiment would need to evolve for a larger, long-running application.

A mature project introduces additional requirements around context management, test coverage, dependencies between tasks, review depth, and changes to existing code.

The seven-agent setup demonstrated that a small senior team could coordinate a high volume of implementation work within a limited period.

It did not establish that every project can be delivered with the same team size, review process, infrastructure, or timeline.

Similarly, the completed application was a working PoC with functioning deployment, data processing, recommendations, and billing integration. Further scaling and production-readiness work would be required before serving substantial commercial traffic.

What we learned from the 72-hour build

The experiment gave us a useful measure of how agent-assisted engineering can work when the delivery process has already been established.

The result was a live application analyzing approximately 30,000 buildings, developed over three days with about 107 hours of human effort and approximately 127 merged pull requests.

The agent workflow reduced the amount of implementation and preliminary review work engineers had to perform manually.

Much of the human effort went into defining the product, designing the architecture, identifying edge cases, testing the application, and approving the results.

Several decisions contributed to the delivery speed: one well-defined user, a limited feature set, an existing agent workflow, automated deployment, and senior engineers who could take ownership of entire application components.

We now apply these principles through the MEV Innovation Lab, where engineering teams build and validate early product concepts, test technical feasibility, and develop working proofs of concept.

The seven agent specifications used for this experiment are also publicly available through MEV's GitHub resources.

The 72-hour build demonstrated what this approach could deliver under tightly controlled scope and with an experienced team. The next engineering challenge is adapting the workflow to larger codebases, longer development cycles, and the quality requirements of sustained production use.

This article is based on the MEV engineering team's 72-hour development challenge and the AI-agent workflow used during the project.

title: OICycle: Observe, Infer, and Intervene Cycle for Belief-State Learning in Longitudinal Clinical Decision Making
description:
arXiv:2611.22826v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Clinical care is a closed loop: clinicians observe partial evidence, infer the patient's state, and intervene, and each intervention determines what is observed next. This makes clinical decision making a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), in which a belief over a latent patient state must be updated from irregular, multimodal, and incomplete records. Yet most deep clinical models predict from a single snapshot or from coarsely aggregated history, while POMDP-based clinical methods need hand-specified discrete state spaces and transition models that real electronic health records cannot supply. We introduce OICycle (Observe, Infer, and Intervene Cycle), which learns a stochastic belief state directly from retrospective trajectories. At every episode, a learned recurrent operator fuses a sample of the previous belief with the new multimodal observations and the intervention that produced them. The resulting Gaussian belief is trained to predict clinicians' next interventions, the time to the next episode, and next-episode mortality. To enable reproducible evaluation, we release a benchmark derived from MIMIC-IV, MIMIC-IV-Note, and MIMIC-CXR that organizes 72,075 hospital admissions (5.4M laboratory, microbiology, radiology, prescription, and note records) into temporally ordered therapeutic--diagnostic episodes. Compared with an otherwise identical history-free model, OICycle improves next-intervention adaptive recall from 0.253 to 0.347, time-to-next-episode macro-F1 from 0.293 to 0.351, and next-episode mortality macro-F1 from 0.585 to 0.649. Analysis shows that the learned belief encodes intervention type and trajectory position and evolves smoothly across episodes, and that the benefit of history is concentrated in interventions whose ordering depends on prior findings.
