title: NIRJALA: Draining the Sea out of Gaussian Splatting with Three-Path Optics and Reversible Physics
description:
arXiv:2611.23450v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Water does not just tint an underwater photograph; it rewrites it. Each pixel mixes attenuated scene radiance, backscattered light, and scene light scattered forward on its way to the camera, and many combinations of scene and water explain the same pixels. Most Gaussian-splatting methods for underwater scenes model only the first two effects and remove the water by dividing by a transmission that decays exponentially with range, so their inversion gain grows without bound. We present NIRJALA (Sanskrit for "without water"), a 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that recovers water-free appearance and geometry together. TRIVENI, a three-path image formation model, adds a range-saturating forward-scattering term to direct transmission and backscatter; we prove that this keeps the inversion gain bounded at every range and bound how errors in the estimated backscatter and attenuation propagate into the recovered colours. PRATIBIMBA, a reversible physics anchor, ties a flexible neural water model to a ten-parameter physical model in both directions, so scene content cannot hide inside the water. SAMARASA collects the physics-informed objectives, including a range-binned colour prior. To score water removal against ground truth, we built SAJALA ("with water"), a 30-scene suite path-traced in Blender Cycles with water-free images, depth, and normals under controlled water colour and turbidity. On SAJALA, NIRJALA raises PSNR from 24.34 to 24.76 dB and lowers depth AbsRel from 0.109 to 0.091 against the strongest baseline; on real SeaThru-NeRF scenes it lowers LPIPS from 0.194 to 0.175 while rendering at 44 FPS. We also discuss where appearance metrics and geometry disagree underwater, and the limits of our evaluation.

title: Node.js Image Thumbnail Uploads to S3-Compatible Storage: Presigned Private Downloads
description:
Short answer: keep originals and resized thumbnails under separate prefixes in a private S3-compatible bucket, then return short-lived presigned GET URLs. Generate the thumbnail in the application or a worker after the upload is durably recorded. This keeps a marketplace user's private image private without making the browser responsible for bucket policy.

That decision is a control-plane decision as much as a storage one. The failure I care about is a thumbnail that looks fine in a test but becomes a public object, a duplicate after a retry, or an overwritten original during a replacement. Those are paging events, not cosmetic bugs.

How can a Node.js example implement image thumbnail uploads to private S3-compatible storage?

Use a key layout that makes an incident legible at a glance: originals/{userId}/{assetId}.jpg for the source and thumbs/{size}/{userId}/{assetId}.jpg for derivatives. The predictable prefixes make listing and cleanup practical, while the asset ID prevents two requests for the same user file from racing on a friendly filename.

Sharp is a reasonable choice for the resize step in a Node.js worker. Put the original first, enqueue a thumbnail job with the source key and requested sizes, and make the worker idempotent. A retry should either observe the existing derivative or write the same deterministic derivative key; it must not create thumb-1, thumb-2, and leave the database guessing.

The bucket stays private. Since public-read ACLs are not available in this setup, delivery is a short-lived presigned GET URL or an application proxy. Do not put a permanent object URL in a listing response. A URL lifetime of a few minutes is usually enough for an image detail page; your threat model and client caching policy should set the exact value.

No exceptions.

For a team already operating several backend integrations, Infrai gives the storage worker one API key and one bill across backend capabilities, and its REST API works over plain HTTP without a storage SDK. Its public discovery surface also exposes schemas and runnable examples, which is useful when a runbook has to be reproduced months later.

Keep it boring.

Which upload failure belongs in the thumbnail reliability runbook?

The first useful signal is not average upload speed. It is a mismatch between the database pointer and the object set: a row says a thumbnail exists, but the object is absent; or an old object is still serving after a replacement. Alert on that reconciliation count, on presign requests that return expired URLs, and on multipart debris older than your cleanup window. Those checks catch privacy and correctness failures before a customer reports a broken image.

Here is the small part of a Go worker I use to make the storage calls explicit. The same sequencing applies to a Node.js service using fetch or an S3 client. The API key comes from the environment, and a deterministic idempotency key makes a retry safe.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "time"
)

func call(method, path string, body []byte, idem string) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(method, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"+path, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/octet-stream")
        if idem != "" { req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idem) }
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            d := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if v := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); v != "" { d = 2 * time.Second }
            time.Sleep(d)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 { return nil, fmt.Errorf("storage status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, data) }
        return data, readErr
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate limit persisted after retries")
}

func main() {
    bucket, key := "marketplace-private", "originals/u_42/a_9.jpg"
    if _, err := call(http.MethodPut, "/storage/object/put/"+bucket+"/"+key, []byte("image bytes"), "upload-a_9"); err != nil { panic(err) }
    // The presign request returns a short-lived GET URL; send its JSON payload per discovery.
    if _, err := call(http.MethodPost, "/storage/object/presign/"+bucket+"/"+key, []byte(`{"expires_in":300,"method":"GET"}`), "presign-a_9"); err != nil { panic(err) }
}

The production version sends the actual image bytes, records content type and dimensions, and validates the returned URL before handing it to the client. The sample deliberately checks every status: a 4xx response is an actionable reason, not a successful upload.

What does the reproducible evaluation measure?

Run the same four-step test against each candidate: upload a representative original, resize it to the largest thumbnail your feed needs, request a presigned download, and repeat the upload request once with the same idempotency key. Record p50 and p95 upload time, thumbnail completion time, download success after expiry, and whether the retry creates exactly one logical object.

Pass means the largest test file meets your marketplace latency budget, the URL is unusable after its configured expiry, and the repeated write leaves one database record and one key. Fail the candidate if it requires public ACLs, if metadata must be searched server-side, or if replacement correctness depends on an unavailable conditional If-Match write.

Keep the test data fixed: three image dimensions, two file sizes, and the same concurrency ramp. I am not claiming a benchmark result here; the point is a decision rule your team can rerun after a vendor or Sharp upgrade. Your mileage may vary with region and network, so publish the raw timings beside the pass/fail decision.

Where do S3, R2, B2, and a unified API differ?

The storage primitive is familiar, but operational boundaries differ. Amazon S3 has the broadest surrounding ecosystem and mature versioning and lifecycle controls. Cloudflare R2 is attractive when egress economics and Cloudflare placement dominate. Backblaze B2 is a straightforward object store with a clear pricing page. Infrai is useful when the same service already calls several backend capabilities: one key and one bill remove credential and invoice sprawl, and its REST API can be called from any language without installing a storage SDK.

Option Strong fit Trade-off to test
Amazon S3 Deep AWS integration, versioning, lifecycle tooling More IAM and account surface to operate
Cloudflare R2 Cloudflare-centric delivery and object storage Check feature parity and egress assumptions
Backblaze B2 Simple object storage and transparent pricing Validate region, latency, and migration tooling
Infrai storage One REST key across storage and other backend services No public ACL, versioning, object lock, or cross-region replication

For this workflow, try Infrai when consolidating credentials and API integration is worth more than specialist storage controls. Its discovery endpoint documents request and response schemas, which helps a small team keep the Go worker and Node.js service aligned. Choose S3 when object versioning, object lock, or the AWS-native ecosystem is a hard requirement; choose R2 or B2 when their network and regional characteristics win your measured test.

That is the gate.

Rollout and rollback for private thumbnail delivery

Start with a private bucket and a canary user. Verify that a listing response contains keys, not public URLs; fetch through the presigned URL; then wait past expiry and confirm the fetch is rejected. Check that the object metadata records width, height, and content type, while the searchable index remains in your database because metadata is not server-searchable.

Don't promote the canary because the happy-path image rendered once. The rollback trigger is any pointer/object mismatch, duplicate logical asset, or URL that remains usable after its deadline — freeze new writes, keep reads on the last committed pointer, and drain the resize queue before retrying the rollout.

Replacement deserves its own alarm. There is no conditional If-Match write, so do not overwrite a live key in place when two edits can arrive together. Create a new asset key, commit the pointer in a transaction, and garbage-collect the old key only after readers have moved. In a busy marketplace this means the database transaction owns the state change: the upload worker can finish twice, but only one committed pointer becomes current, and a sweeper can safely remove the previous object after a grace period. If strict ordering matters, coordinate through the database or a queue.

Lifecycle rules can remove abandoned originals and old thumbnails, but the shortest lifecycle is one day and multipart fragments do not get an automatic cleanup rule. Set an explicit abort job and keep a metric for orphaned keys. A failed resize should be retried from the original; it should never make the original public as a fallback.

The catch is important: private, presigned delivery is not suitable for a permanent public gallery, static website hosting, or a workload that needs WORM retention. Stick with a specialist or add an external immutability and replication layer for those cases. That is a capability boundary, not a reason to hide the constraint in a launch checklist. If the boundary fits, start with the storage presign contract at https://docs.infrai.cc/storage/object/presign and run the canary before changing the default bucket.

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.object.presign
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/presigned-urls/
  • https://www.backblaze.com/cloud-storage/pricing
  • https://sharp.pixelplumbing.com/

title: TabBioMed: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Biomedical Tabular Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.23779v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent advances in machine learning have accelerated biomedical prediction, but evaluation on structured biomedical data remains fragmented, especially for datasets with high dimensionality, large sample size, missingness, and class imbalance. We introduce TabBioMed, a large-scale benchmark of 94 curated public biomedical tabular datasets spanning electronic health records, drug discovery, genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, single-cell omics, and systems biology. TabBioMed unifies these datasets through a standardized, dataset-aware preprocessing and evaluation framework, enabling reproducible comparison across classification, regression, and multi-target tasks. We benchmark 23 models across classical baselines, gradient-boosted trees, neural tabular architectures, and tabular foundation models. Foundation models deliver the strongest family-level predictive performance. However, their gains are regime-dependent: tree-based models and tuned multilayer perceptrons remain highly competitive, often dominating under inference-time or training-cost constraints. Overall, TabBioMed shows that biomedical tabular learning is strongly context-dependent, with optimal model choice depending on data regime, task type, and computational budget. We release TabBioMed with curated datasets and splits, preprocessing code, baselines, and results, providing a reproducible benchmark for practical model selection and future methods development in biomedical machine learning, available at https://github.com/AI-sandbox/TabBioMed.

title: How to Build a Desktop Barcode Scanner with Tauri and Rust
description:
Tauri's official barcode-scanner plugin only runs on Android and iOS — it has no desktop implementation at all. If you are building a Tauri app for Windows, macOS, or Linux and need to read barcodes, the official plugin cannot help you. This tutorial builds the desktop scanner that fills that gap: a Tauri 2 app whose Rust backend decodes image files, PDFs, and a live webcam feed through FFI bindings to the Dynamsoft Barcode Reader SDK, while the UI is plain HTML/CSS/JS rendered in the system webview. The result decodes every barcode type the SDK supports, draws a quadrilateral over each one, and lists its format, text, and corner coordinates. Multi-page PDFs and TIFFs are previewed page by page, with on-screen arrows and left/right keys to switch pages.

The finished app decoding 32 ITF barcodes from a single photo:

See it running — opening an image, decoding, and switching to the live camera:

What you'll build: A cross-platform Tauri 2 desktop barcode scanner with a Rust backend and a no-bundler web frontend. It opens images/PDFs through a native file dialog or a typed path, previews each document page with a cyan overlay on every decoded barcode, lists each barcode's format/text/coordinates, pages through multi-page PDFs and TIFFs, and streams a live webcam feed (Windows) — all powered by the same Dynamsoft Barcode Reader C++ core used by the Slint version of this sample.

The Desktop Gap in Tauri's Barcode Plugin

This is the central reason this sample exists. Tauri ships an official barcode-scanner plugin, and its name suggests it is the obvious choice for any Tauri barcode app. It is not — at least not on desktop.

The plugin's documentation describes it as a way to "allow your mobile application to use the camera to scan QR codes, EAN-13 and other kinds of barcodes." Three details in the official setup confirm the desktop gap:

  • The dependency is added only for mobile targets: cargo add tauri-plugin-barcode-scanner --target 'cfg(any(target_os = "android", target_os = "ios"))'.
  • The plugin is registered only on mobile: #[cfg(mobile)] app.handle().plugin(tauri_plugin_barcode_scanner::init());.
  • The capability that grants its permissions is scoped to mobile platforms: "platforms": ["iOS", "android"].

On Windows, macOS, and Linux there is simply no implementation to call. Beyond the platform gap, the plugin is also camera-only: it opens a native scan view (its windowed: true mode makes the webview transparent so the camera shows through) and returns what the camera sees. It does not decode a photo you already have on disk, does not read PDFs, and is not designed to return a batch of barcodes with precise corner coordinates from a still image.

This sample complements the official plugin rather than competing with it on mobile. It covers the desktop platforms the plugin leaves out, and adds the file/PDF decoding and multi-barcode coordinate output that a live mobile scan view does not provide:

Capability Official barcode-scanner plugin This Tauri + Rust sample
Windows / macOS / Linux Not supported Supported (decoding on all three)
Android / iOS Supported Not the target (use the official plugin)
Live camera scanning Yes (native mobile scan view) Yes on Windows (native Media Foundation)
Decode image files (JPEG/PNG/TIFF/BMP/GIF/WebP) No Yes
Decode PDF No Yes (every page previewed and navigable)
Multiple barcodes per image with corner coordinates Camera scan result Yes, four points per barcode
Frontend toolchain Plugin JS bindings Plain HTML/CSS/JS, no bundler

The practical takeaway: if your Tauri app targets desktop, or needs to read barcodes from files rather than only from a live mobile camera, you need a native decoding backend. The rest of this article builds one with Rust and the Dynamsoft Barcode Reader SDK, and shows how to wire it into a Tauri webview UI.

Prerequisites

  • Rust toolchain (MSVC toolchain on Windows) for the Tauri backend.
  • The WebView2 runtime on Windows (preinstalled on Windows 11); Tauri uses the system webview on macOS and Linux.
  • The Dynamsoft Barcode Reader SDK and the litecam camera library, both already vendored in the sample repository under dcv/ and litecam/dist/.
  • Get a 30-day free trial license for the Dynamsoft Barcode Reader SDK. The sample ships a shared demo key in examples/rust/src/scanner.rs; replace DEFAULT_LICENSE with your own for production.
  • Optional: Node.js only if you want the Tauri CLI (npm run dev / npm run build) for dev-server orchestration and installers. It is not needed to build or run the app.

Architecture: One Native Core, Two GUIs

The sample repository already contains a Rust CLI and a Slint desktop GUI that share a native decoding core. The Tauri app is a third frontend on that same core. Nothing about the decoding, licensing, or camera capture is rewritten — the Tauri crate literally compiles the same source files:

// src-tauri/src/main.rs
#[path = "../../../src/scanner.rs"]
mod scanner;
#[cfg(windows)]
#[path = "../../../src/camera.rs"]
mod litecam;

Only the presentation layer differs. The webview and the Rust backend talk over three channels, each suited to a different kind of traffic:

webview (ui/app.js)                         Rust (src-tauri/src)
───────────────────                         ────────────────────
invoke("decode_path", { path })   ───────►  #[tauri::command] fn decode_path
        ◄─────── DecodeReply (JSON) ────────┘
listen("camera-frame")            ◄───────  app.emit("camera-frame", CameraFrame)
<img src="media:…/preview.jpg">   ───────►  register_uri_scheme_protocol("media")
        ◄─────── image/png bytes ──────────┘
  • Commands carry request/response calls: open a file, decode a path, switch pages, start/stop the camera.
  • Events carry push notifications: each camera frame and any camera error.
  • A custom URI scheme carries bulk pixels: the current page's JPEG and the live camera JPEG, served as ordinary HTTP responses instead of base64 JSON.

The project layout is small enough to read in one sitting:

tauri/
├── ui/                     # the frontend, loaded into the system webview
│   ├── index.html          # toolbar, preview pane, results list, status bar
│   ├── style.css           # the Slint look, in CSS
│   └── app.js              # invoke() calls, event listeners, canvas overlay
└── src-tauri/
    ├── Cargo.toml
    ├── build.rs            # tauri_build + cc: links Dynamsoft/litecam, copies DLLs
    ├── tauri.conf.json     # window, frontendDist, CSP, bundle icons
    ├── capabilities/       # what the webview is allowed to call
    ├── icons/
    └── src/
        ├── main.rs         # Builder: state, plugin, protocol, invoke_handler
        ├── commands.rs     # #[tauri::command] handlers + camera worker thread
        └── media.rs        # custom media: URI scheme serving page/camera JPEG bytes

Step 1: Scaffold the Tauri Project and Configure the Window

The crate depends on Tauri 2, the dialog plugin, serde for JSON, and the image crate for reading and re-encoding pictures. There is no frontend framework dependency:

# src-tauri/Cargo.toml
[package]
name = "barcode-reader-tauri"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"

[build-dependencies]
tauri-build = "2"
cc = "1.0"
walkdir = "2.5"

[dependencies]
tauri = { version = "2", features = [] }
tauri-plugin-dialog = "2"
serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
serde_json = "1"
image = { version = "0.24", default-features = false, features = [
    "png", "jpeg", "tiff", "bmp", "gif", "webp",
] }

tauri.conf.json points the webview at the static frontend, enables the global Tauri API, defines the window, and sets a Content Security Policy:

{
  "$schema": "https://schema.tauri.app/config/2",
  "productName": "barcode-reader-tauri",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "identifier": "com.dynamsoft.barcode-reader-tauri",
  "build": {
    "frontendDist": "../ui"
  },
  "app": {
    "withGlobalTauri": true,
    "windows": [
      {
        "label": "main",
        "title": "Dynamsoft Barcode Reader (Rust + Tauri)",
        "width": 1040,
        "height": 700,
        "minWidth": 760,
        "minHeight": 500,
        "center": true
      }
    ],
    "security": {
      "csp": "default-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data: blob: media: http://media.localhost; connect-src 'self' ipc: http://ipc.localhost; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; script-src 'self'"
    }
  },
  "bundle": {
    "active": true,
    "targets": "all",
    "icon": ["icons/32x32.png", "icons/128x128.png", "icons/128x128@2x.png", "icons/icon.icns", "icons/icon.ico"]
  }
}

Two settings do the heavy lifting for the "no bundler" design:

  • "frontendDist": "../ui" tells Tauri to embed the static files in ui/ into the binary. There is no devUrl, so the same files are used in debug and release.
  • "withGlobalTauri": true injects Tauri's JavaScript API as window.__TAURI__, so app.js can call invoke and listen without importing npm packages.

The CSP allows the media: scheme (and its Windows form http://media.localhost) for images, and ipc: (plus http://ipc.localhost) for Tauri's own command channel. Keep these in sync with the protocol you register in Step 5, or the webview will silently block the pixels.

Step 2: Build the Native Core with build.rs

build.rs has two jobs: generate the Tauri context, and compile/link the native Dynamsoft core. The Tauri part is a single call at the end; the rest is ordinary cc + linker configuration that mirrors the Slint example's build.

On Windows the SDK ships as static import libraries plus runtime DLLs. The script links the five Dynamsoft libraries statically, links litecam dynamically, and copies every DLL next to the executable:

// src-tauri/build.rs (Windows branch)
"windows" => {
    let lib_dir = dcv.join("lib").join("win");
    println!("cargo:rustc-link-search=native={}", lib_dir.display());
    for lib in [
        "DynamsoftCaptureVisionRouterx64",
        "DynamsoftBarcodeReaderx64",
        "DynamsoftCorex64",
        "DynamsoftLicensex64",
        "DynamsoftUtilityx64",
    ] {
        println!("cargo:rustc-link-lib=static={lib}");
    }
    copy_extension(&lib_dir, &bin_dir, "dll");

    let cam_dir = litecam.join("lib").join("windows").join("release");
    println!("cargo:rustc-link-search=native={}", cam_dir.display());
    println!("cargo:rustc-link-lib=dylib=litecam");
    copy_file(&cam_dir.join("litecam.dll"), &bin_dir.join("litecam.dll"));

    copy_resources(&dcv, &bin_dir);
}

Linux and macOS link DynamsoftBarcodeReader as a dynamic library and set an rpath so the binary finds the .so/.dylib at runtime. copy_resources copies the SDK's Templates/ and Models/ folders beside the executable, because the SDK resolves them at runtime from the module directory.

The C ABI bridge is compiled with cc and shared with the Slint example — this is the "one native core" promise made concrete:

// src-tauri/build.rs
let bridge = rust_example.join("lib").join("bridge.cpp");
let camera_bridge = rust_example.join("lib").join("camera_bridge.cpp");
let mut cpp = Build::new();
cpp.cpp(true)
    .include(dcv.join("include"))
    .file(&bridge);
if target_os == "windows" {
    cpp.include(litecam.join("include")).file(&camera_bridge);
}
cpp.compile("bridge");
println!("cargo:rustc-link-lib=static=bridge");
println!("cargo:rustc-link-search=native={}", env::var("OUT_DIR").unwrap());

// ... rerun-if-changed for bridge, scanner.rs, camera.rs, ../ui ...

tauri_build::build();

Two helpers are worth copying into your own Tauri + native projects:

// src-tauri/build.rs
/// `target/debug` or `target/release`, where the executable and its DLLs live.
/// OUT_DIR is `<target>/<profile>/build/<pkg>-<hash>/out`.
fn profile_dir() -> PathBuf {
    let out_dir = PathBuf::from(env::var("OUT_DIR").unwrap());
    out_dir.ancestors().nth(3).expect("unexpected OUT_DIR layout").to_path_buf()
}

/// Canonicalize without the `\\?\` prefix, which MSVC's linker does not accept.
fn absolute(path: PathBuf) -> PathBuf {
    let resolved = path.canonicalize().unwrap_or(path);
    let text = resolved.to_string_lossy();
    PathBuf::from(text.strip_prefix(r"\\?\").unwrap_or(&text).to_string())
}

profile_dir() is how the script knows where to drop the DLLs so they sit beside the final executable. absolute() strips the Windows \\?\ verbatim prefix that canonicalize() adds, because the MSVC linker rejects it. copy_file deliberately skips a destination that already exists — a running instance keeps its DLLs locked, and the files are identical anyway.

Step 3: Reuse the FFI Decoding Wrapper

The decoding core is a flat C API over the Dynamsoft Capture Vision Router. The C++ side (lib/bridge.cpp) wraps CCaptureVisionRouter and returns malloc'd structs; the Rust side (src/scanner.rs) declares them with #[repr(C)] and frees them after copying.

The C ABI is deliberately small:

// lib/bridge.h
typedef struct {
    const char *barcode_type;
    const char *barcode_value;
    int x1, y1, x2, y2, x3, y3, x4, y4;
} Barcode;

typedef struct {
    Barcode *barcodes;
    int count;
} BarcodeResults;

typedef struct {
    int width;
    int height;
    unsigned char *rgb;   // width * height * 3, RGB888
    int rgb_length;
    Barcode *barcodes;    // barcodes on this page; NULL when count is 0
    int count;
} PageResult;

typedef struct {
    PageResult *pages;
    int count;
} PageResults;

BarcodeResults *decode_barcode_file(void *instance, const char *filename);
PageResults *decode_barcode_file_pages(void *instance, const char *filename);
BarcodeResults *decode_barcode_buffer(void *instance, const unsigned char *bytes,
                                      int width, int height, int stride);
void free_barcode(BarcodeResults *results);
void free_page_results(PageResults *results);
int init_license(const char *license);
void *CVR_CreateInstance();
void CVR_DestroyInstance(void *instance);

The buffer entry point is the one that matters for coordinate alignment. It wraps the raw bytes in a CImageData tagged IPF_RGB_888 and captures with the read-barcodes preset:

// lib/bridge.cpp
BarcodeResults *decode_barcode_buffer(void *instance, const unsigned char *bytes,
                                      int width, int height, int stride)
{
    CCaptureVisionRouter *cvr = (CCaptureVisionRouter *)instance;
    CImageData image((unsigned long long)stride * height, bytes, width, height, stride, IPF_RGB_888);
    CCapturedResult *result = cvr->Capture(&image, CPresetTemplate::PT_READ_BARCODES);
    return extract_barcodes(result);
}

Two file entry points sit on the bridge. decode_barcode_file is the flat API used by the CLI and Slint UI: it calls CaptureMultiPages and concatenates every page's barcodes into one list. The Tauri GUI uses decode_barcode_file_pages because it also needs the pixels of each page for the preview.

The router does not keep page pixels around by default — GetOriginalImage returns NULL unless the original image was cached — and CaptureMultiPages only hands back decoded items. The SDK's CFileFetcher is the documented tool for this job: it partitions a multi-page PDF or TIFF into one CImageData per page. The bridge loops over those page bitmaps, copies each into RGB888, and decodes that exact bitmap with Capture():

// lib/bridge.cpp
PageResults *decode_barcode_file_pages(void *instance, const char *filename)
{
    CCaptureVisionRouter *cvr = (CCaptureVisionRouter *)instance;
    // CFileFetcher splits a multi-page PDF or TIFF into one CImageData per page.
    CFileFetcher fetcher;
    if (fetcher.SetFile(filename) != EC_OK)
    {
        return NULL;
    }

    std::vector<PageResult> pages;
    while (fetcher.HasNextImageToFetch())
    {
        CImageData *image = fetcher.GetImage();
        if (!image)
        {
            break;
        }

        PageResult page;
        page.rgb = image_to_rgb(image, &page.rgb_length); // stride-aware RGB888 copy
        page.width = page.rgb ? image->GetWidth() : 0;
        page.height = page.rgb ? image->GetHeight() : 0;
        page.barcodes = NULL;
        page.count = 0;

        // Decode the very bitmap the GUI will preview.
        CCapturedResult *result = cvr->Capture(image, CPresetTemplate::PT_READ_BARCODES);
        if (result)
        {
            if (result->GetErrorCode() == 0)
            {
                CDecodedBarcodesResult *barcodeResult = result->GetDecodedBarcodesResult();
                std::vector<Barcode> items;
                append_barcode_items(barcodeResult, items);
                if (barcodeResult)
                {
                    barcodeResult->Release();
                }
                if (!items.empty())
                {
                    page.count = (int)items.size();
                    page.barcodes = (Barcode *)std::malloc(sizeof(Barcode) * items.size());
                    for (size_t i = 0; i < items.size(); i++)
                    {
                        page.barcodes[i] = items[i];
                    }
                }
            }
            result->Release();
        }

        // Keep pages that have pixels even when they contain no barcode.
        if (page.rgb || page.count > 0)
        {
            pages.push_back(page);
        }
        else if (page.barcodes)
        {
            std::free(page.barcodes);
        }
    }

    if (pages.empty())
    {
        return NULL;
    }

    PageResults *results = (PageResults *)std::malloc(sizeof(PageResults));
    results->count = (int)pages.size();
    results->pages = (PageResult *)std::malloc(sizeof(PageResult) * pages.size());
    for (size_t i = 0; i < pages.size(); i++)
    {
        results->pages[i] = pages[i];
    }
    return results;
}

image_to_rgb copies a CImageData into a tightly packed RGB buffer, honoring GetStride() and converting the formats the rasterizer produces — RGB/BGR 888, grayscale, 8-bit binary, and ARGB/ABGR 8888. One gotcha: on this SDK build CFileFetcher hands back BGR bytes even though GetImagePixelFormat() reports IPF_RGB_888, so the 3-byte converter always swaps red and blue. A red/green/blue test image is the quickest way to catch a channel-order mistake. Because every page keeps its own pixels, the pager can switch pages later without touching the file again.

append_barcode_items reads each item's CQuadrilateral into four corner points and copies the format and text strings; the packing loop hands ownership of those strings to the returned PageResults. An EXIF-rotated photo simply becomes a one-page document, so the same code path covers images, PDFs, and TIFFs. In this sample, images/MultiPage.pdf becomes 4 pages with one QR code each.

For the buffer path, extract_barcodes reads each item's CQuadrilateral location into the four corner points, copies the format and text strings, and releases the SDK result. On the Rust side, the safe wrapper initializes the license once, creates the instance, and frees it on Drop:

// src/scanner.rs (shared with the CLI and Slint GUI)
/// One rasterized page from a file plus the barcodes found on it.
#[derive(Clone, Debug)]
pub struct PageDecode {
    pub rgb: Vec<u8>,
    pub width: i32,
    pub height: i32,
    pub barcodes: Vec<BarcodeResult>,
}

pub struct BarcodeReader {
    instance: *mut c_void,
}

impl BarcodeReader {
    pub fn new(license: &str) -> Result<Self, String> {
        let license_cstr = CString::new(license).map_err(|e| e.to_string())?;
        let ret = unsafe { init_license(license_cstr.as_ptr()) };
        if ret != 0 {
            return Err(format!("License initialization failed with code: {ret}"));
        }
        let instance = unsafe { CVR_CreateInstance() };
        if instance.is_null() {
            return Err("Failed to create barcode reader instance".to_string());
        }
        Ok(Self { instance })
    }

    /// Decode barcodes from a raw RGB888 frame (e.g. a camera frame).
    pub fn decode_buffer(&self, rgb: &[u8], width: i32, height: i32)
        -> Result<Vec<BarcodeResult>, String>
    {
        let stride = width * 3;
        let results_ptr =
            unsafe { decode_barcode_buffer(self.instance, rgb.as_ptr(), width, height, stride) };
        Ok(unsafe { collect_results(results_ptr) })
    }

    /// Decode a file page by page. Each page carries the rasterized RGB888
    /// pixels the SDK decoded, so a PDF or multi-page TIFF can be previewed
    /// and navigated. An empty vector means the file could not be rasterized.
    pub fn decode_pages(&self, file_path: &str) -> Result<Vec<PageDecode>, String> {
        let path_cstr = CString::new(file_path).map_err(|e| format!("Invalid file path: {e}"))?;
        let results_ptr =
            unsafe { decode_barcode_file_pages(self.instance, path_cstr.as_ptr()) };
        Ok(unsafe { collect_pages(results_ptr) })
    }
}

impl Drop for BarcodeReader {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        unsafe { CVR_DestroyInstance(self.instance) };
    }
}

collect_results and collect_pages copy every native struct into owned Rust values and then call free_barcode / free_page_results, so no native memory outlives the call. Because the Tauri crate includes this exact file with #[path], the desktop app and the Slint app decode byte-for-byte identically.

Step 4: Wire the Rust Backend and Managed State

main.rs builds the Tauri app: it creates the reader, registers the dialog plugin, manages shared state, registers the media: protocol, and lists the commands the webview may call.

// src-tauri/src/main.rs
/// `BarcodeReader` owns a raw C++ handle, which is neither Send nor Sync. Tauri
/// state must be, and the mutex around it keeps every access serialized.
pub struct Reader(BarcodeReader);
unsafe impl Send for Reader {}

pub struct AppState {
    pub reader: Mutex<Result<Reader, String>>,
    pub media: Mutex<media::MediaStore>,
    pub camera_stop: Mutex<Option<Arc<AtomicBool>>>,
}

fn main() {
    let reader = BarcodeReader::new(DEFAULT_LICENSE).map(Reader);

    tauri::Builder::default()
        .plugin(tauri_plugin_dialog::init())
        .manage(AppState {
            reader: Mutex::new(reader),
            media: Mutex::new(media::MediaStore::default()),
            camera_stop: Mutex::new(None),
        })
        .register_uri_scheme_protocol("media", media::handle)
        .invoke_handler(tauri::generate_handler![
            commands::startup_status,
            commands::open_image,
            commands::decode_path,
            commands::start_camera,
            commands::stop_camera,
        ])
        .run(tauri::generate_context!())
        .expect("error while running the Tauri application");
}

Three design points are worth understanding:

  • Reader is a newtype with unsafe impl Send. The raw C++ handle is not Send/Sync, but Tauri's managed state must be. Wrapping it and asserting Send is safe here because every access goes through a Mutex, so only one thread touches the handle at a time.
  • The reader is stored as Result<Reader, String>. A bad license fails at construction; storing the error lets the UI report it at startup (Step 5) instead of crashing.
  • camera_stop is an Arc<AtomicBool> slot. Some means a camera worker is running; setting the flag tells it to exit. take() clears the slot so a new worker can start.

Tauri injects this state into any command that asks for State<AppState>, which is how the command layer reaches the reader and the media store without globals.

Step 5: Expose Commands to the Webview

Commands are Rust functions marked #[tauri::command] and listed in invoke_handler. Arguments and return values are serialized with serde. The result types use camelCase so the JSON is idiomatic on the JS side:

// src-tauri/src/commands.rs
#[derive(Clone, Serialize)]
#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]
pub struct BarcodeItem {
    pub format: String,
    pub text: String,
    pub location: String,
    pub points: [(i32, i32); 4],
}

#[derive(Clone, Serialize)]
#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]
pub struct Preview {
    pub seq: u64,
    pub width: u32,
    pub height: u32,
}

#[derive(Serialize)]
#[serde(tag = "kind", rename_all = "camelCase")]
pub enum DecodeReply {
    /// Nothing was decoded; keep the current preview and results.
    Message { status: String },
    /// `page`/`pages` describe the currently previewed page of the loaded file.
    /// `preview: None` means the input could not be rasterized at all.
    Decoded {
        status: String,
        preview: Option<Preview>,
        items: Vec<BarcodeItem>,
        page: u32,
        pages: u32,
    },
}

The tagged enum DecodeReply lets the frontend distinguish "show a message" from "here are results" by reading reply.kind.

startup_status reports a license problem once, before the first decode:

// src-tauri/src/commands.rs
#[tauri::command]
pub fn startup_status(state: State<AppState>) -> Option<String> {
    state.reader.lock().unwrap().as_ref().err()
        .map(|err| format!("{err}. {LICENSE_HINT}"))
}

open_image is async because a modal file dialog must not block the thread that pumps window messages. It uses the dialog plugin's callback API plus a one-shot channel:

// src-tauri/src/commands.rs
#[tauri::command]
pub async fn open_image(app: AppHandle) -> Option<String> {
    let mut dialog = app.dialog().file()
        .set_title("Open image or PDF")
        .add_filter("Images & PDF",
            &["jpg", "jpeg", "png", "bmp", "tif", "tiff", "gif", "webp", "pdf"]);
    if let Some(dir) = samples_dir() {
        dialog = dialog.set_directory(dir);
    }

    let (tx, mut rx) = tauri::async_runtime::channel(1);
    dialog.pick_file(move |file| { let _ = tx.try_send(file); });

    rx.recv().await.flatten()
        .and_then(|path| path.into_path().ok())
        .map(|path| path.to_string_lossy().into_owned())
}

The other commands stay synchronous. Tauri runs sync commands on the main thread, which keeps the native Capture Vision handle on a single thread — the same thread-affinity contract the Slint UI relies on. The camera worker (Step 9) owns a second reader instance for its own thread, so the two never share a handle.

decode_path is the heart of the app. It stops the camera, validates the path, asks the bridge for one entry per page, and stores each page's pixels together with its barcodes:

// src-tauri/src/commands.rs
#[tauri::command]
pub fn decode_path(state: State<AppState>, path: String) -> DecodeReply {
    stop_camera_inner(&state);

    let path = path.trim().to_string();
    if path.is_empty() {
        return DecodeReply::Message { status: "Enter an image path or click \"Open Image...\".".into() };
    }
    if !std::path::Path::new(&path).exists() {
        return DecodeReply::Message { status: format!("File not found: {path}") };
    }

    let guard = state.reader.lock().unwrap();
    let reader = match guard.as_ref() {
        Ok(reader) => &reader.0,
        Err(err) => return DecodeReply::Message { status: format!("{err}. {LICENSE_HINT}") },
    };

    // One PageImage per rasterized page; the preview uses the same bitmap that
    // was decoded, so barcode coordinates need no conversion.
    let mut pages: Vec<PageImage> = reader
        .decode_pages(&path)
        .unwrap_or_default()
        .into_iter()
        .filter(|page| !page.rgb.is_empty() && page.width > 0 && page.height > 0)
        .map(|page| PageImage {
            rgb: page.rgb,
            width: page.width as u32,
            height: page.height as u32,
            items: page.barcodes.into_iter().map(to_item).collect(),
            jpeg: None,
        })
        .collect();

    // The SDK cannot rasterize every format the dialog accepts (WebP, for one).
    // Fall back to the image crate for those so the preview still appears.
    if pages.is_empty() {
        if let Some(page) = decode_with_image_crate(&path, reader) {
            pages.push(page);
        }
    }

    let mut store = state.media.lock().unwrap();
    store.pages = pages;
    store.current = 0;
    store.preview_seq += 1;

    let page_count = store.pages.len() as u32;
    let total: usize = store.pages.iter().map(|page| page.items.len()).sum();
    let preview = store.pages.first().map(|page| Preview {
        seq: store.preview_seq,
        width: page.width,
        height: page.height,
    });
    let items = store.pages.first().map(|page| page.items.clone()).unwrap_or_default();
    drop(store);

    let status = if total == 0 {
        "No barcode found.".to_string()
    } else if page_count > 1 {
        format!("Decoded {total} barcode(s) across {page_count} pages.")
    } else {
        format!("Decoded {total} barcode(s).")
    };

    DecodeReply::Decoded { status, preview, items, page: 0, pages: page_count }
}

set_page switches the preview to another page without decoding the file again — every page is already in MediaStore:

// src-tauri/src/commands.rs
#[tauri::command]
pub fn set_page(state: State<AppState>, page: u32) -> DecodeReply {
    let mut store = state.media.lock().unwrap();
    if store.pages.is_empty() {
        return DecodeReply::Message { status: "No document loaded.".into() };
    }

    let index = (page as usize).min(store.pages.len() - 1);
    store.current = index;
    store.preview_seq += 1;

    let pages = store.pages.len() as u32;
    let current = &store.pages[index];
    let preview = Preview { seq: store.preview_seq, width: current.width, height: current.height };
    let items = current.items.clone();

    DecodeReply::Decoded {
        status: format!("Page {} of {pages}.", index + 1),
        preview: Some(preview),
        items,
        page: index as u32,
        pages,
    }
}

The coordinate-space decision is deliberate. The SDK rasterizes a page and the bridge decodes the same bitmap it returns for the preview, so overlay points and the displayed image always share one coordinate space — whether the source is an EXIF-rotated phone photo or page 3 of a PDF. Preview bytes are encoded lazily in the next step, so decoding a 4-page 2481×3509 document stays fast.

Step 6: Serve Pixels over a Custom media: Protocol

Sending a 1280×720 frame as base64 through the IPC channel on every camera tick would waste megabytes a second. Instead, Rust keeps the loaded pages and the latest camera JPEG in a MediaStore and serves them over a registered URI scheme. Pages are stored as raw RGB and JPEG-encoded on first view, then cached:

// src-tauri/src/media.rs
pub struct PageImage {
    pub rgb: Vec<u8>,          // raw RGB888 until the page is first viewed
    pub width: u32,
    pub height: u32,
    pub items: Vec<BarcodeItem>,
    pub jpeg: Option<Vec<u8>>, // encoded once, then cached
}

#[derive(Default)]
pub struct MediaStore {
    /// `/preview.jpg` serves `pages[current]`; a single image is just one page.
    pub pages: Vec<PageImage>,
    pub current: usize,
    pub preview_seq: u64,
    pub frame_jpeg: Vec<u8>,
    pub frame_seq: u64,
}

pub fn handle(ctx: UriSchemeContext<'_, Wry>, request: Request<Vec<u8>>) -> Response<Vec<u8>> {
    let state = ctx.app_handle().state::<AppState>();
    let mut store = state.media.lock().unwrap();
    let current = store.current;

    // The frontend appends ?seq=N so each new frame bypasses the image cache.
    let (body, content_type) = match request.uri().path() {
        "/preview.jpg" => match store.pages.get_mut(current) {
            Some(page) => {
                if page.jpeg.is_none() {
                    page.jpeg = encode_jpeg(&page.rgb, page.width, page.height);
                    // The cached JPEG replaces the raw buffer; switching back to
                    // this page later serves it without re-encoding.
                    page.rgb = Vec::new();
                }
                (page.jpeg.clone().unwrap_or_default(), "image/jpeg")
            }
            None => (Vec::new(), "image/jpeg"),
        },
        "/camera.jpg" => (store.frame_jpeg.clone(), "image/jpeg"),
        _ => return Response::builder()
                .status(StatusCode::NOT_FOUND).body(Vec::new()).unwrap(),
    };

    Response::builder()
        .status(StatusCode::OK)
        .header(header::CONTENT_TYPE, content_type)
        .header(header::CACHE_CONTROL, "no-store")
        .body(body)
        .unwrap()
}

Lazy encoding matters for multi-page documents. A 2481×3509 PDF page is about 26 MB of raw RGB, and eagerly PNG-encoding four of them in a debug build blocked the UI for seconds. JPEG-encoding one page on demand takes a fraction of that time, and dropping the raw buffer afterward keeps memory bounded. When the pager moves to a new page, the <img> requests the same path with a new seq, so the handler encodes that page once and caches it. The camera path stays separate and keeps pushing one JPEG per frame.

The handler is registered in main.rs with .register_uri_scheme_protocol("media", media::handle). The frontend builds a platform-correct URL with convertFileSrc:

// ui/app.js
const { invoke, convertFileSrc } = window.__TAURI__.core;

function mediaUrl(name, seq) {
  return `${convertFileSrc(name, "media")}?seq=${seq}`;
}

convertFileSrc("camera.jpg", "media") produces http://media.localhost/camera.jpg on Windows and media://localhost/camera.jpg elsewhere. The seq counter is a cache-buster: each new page or frame increments it, so the <img> always fetches fresh bytes. The payload travels as a normal HTTP response with Cache-Control: no-store, not as JSON — which is exactly why this channel exists separately from commands and events.

The frontend is three static files. index.html is the toolbar, preview pane, results list, and status bar:

  <div class="status" id="status">Open an image to start.</div>

<script type="module" src="app.js"></script>

The script is type="module" because app.js uses top-level await for listen and startup_status. app.js grabs the Tauri API from the injected global and wires the buttons to commands:

// ui/app.js
const { invoke, convertFileSrc } = window.__TAURI__.core;
const { listen } = window.__TAURI__.event;

// Shared by a fresh decode and by page switches: both replies carry the preview
// and the results of whichever page is current.
function applyDecoded(reply) {
  setStatus(reply.status);
  view.page = reply.page ?? 0;
  view.pages = reply.pages ?? 0;
  if (reply.preview) {
    // waitForLoad: show the new page first, draw its overlay afterwards.
    showPreview(mediaUrl("preview.jpg", reply.preview.seq),
                reply.preview.width, reply.preview.height, true);
  } else {
    clearPreview();
  }
  renderResults(reply.items);
  updatePager();
}

async function decode(path) {
  setCameraOn(false); // the backend stops the camera before decoding a file
  const reply = await invoke("decode_path", { path });
  if (reply.kind === "message") {
    setStatus(reply.status);
    return;
  }
  applyDecoded(reply);
}

async function gotoPage(delta) {
  if (view.pages <= 1) return;
  const target = view.page + delta;
  if (target < 0 || target >= view.pages) return;
  const reply = await invoke("set_page", { page: target });
  if (reply.kind === "message") {
    setStatus(reply.status);
    return;
  }
  applyDecoded(reply);
}

el.decode.addEventListener("click", () => decode(el.path.value));
el.path.addEventListener("keydown", (event) => {
  if (event.key === "Enter") decode(el.path.value);
});

el.prev.addEventListener("click", () => gotoPage(-1));
el.next.addEventListener("click", () => gotoPage(1));
document.addEventListener("keydown", (event) => {
  if (view.pages <= 1 || event.target === el.path) return;
  if (event.key === "ArrowLeft") {
    gotoPage(-1);
    event.preventDefault();
  } else if (event.key === "ArrowRight") {
    gotoPage(1);
    event.preventDefault();
  }
});

The pager stays out of the way for single-page images and the camera, and only appears when the reply reports more than one page:

// ui/app.js
function updatePager() {
  const show = view.hasPreview && view.pages > 1;
  el.pager.hidden = !show;
  if (!show) return;
  el.pageLabel.textContent = `Page ${view.page + 1} / ${view.pages}`;
  el.prev.disabled = view.page <= 0;
  el.next.disabled = view.page >= view.pages - 1;
}

Because set_page only swaps the current index in MediaStore, switching pages is instant after the first view of that page. The arrow keys call the same gotoPage path; the handler ignores them while the path input has focus so the caret still moves normally.

The results list is built with textContent, never innerHTML, because barcode text is untrusted input that could contain markup:

// ui/app.js
function renderResults(items) {
  view.items = items;
  el.count.textContent = items.length;
  el.results.replaceChildren();

  items.forEach((item, index) => {
    const row = document.createElement("div");
    row.className = index % 2 ? "row alt" : "row";
    for (const [className, text] of [
      ["row-format", `${index + 1}. ${item.format}`],
      ["row-text", item.text],
      ["row-location", item.location],
    ]) {
      const line = document.createElement("div");
      line.className = className;
      line.textContent = text; // safe: no HTML parsing
      row.append(line);
    }
    el.results.append(row);
  });

  layout();
}

One CSS detail matters for the preview. The placeholder uses display: flex, which would override the browser's default [hidden] { display: none } rule, so the stylesheet forces it:

/* ui/style.css */
/* .placeholder sets display:flex, which would override the UA [hidden] rule. */
[hidden] {
  display: none !important;
}

Without this, hiding the placeholder or the stage with the hidden attribute would not actually hide it.

Step 8: Draw Pixel-Aligned Barcode Overlays

The overlay is a <canvas> stacked on the <img>. The trick that keeps coordinates simple: give the canvas the image's own pixel size, then stretch both to the same letterboxed rectangle. The canvas coordinate space then equals the image coordinate space, so barcode points are drawn without conversion.

// ui/app.js
// Letterbox the image inside the preview pane, then give the overlay canvas the
// image's own pixel size so barcode coordinates need no conversion.
function layout() {
  if (!view.hasPreview || !view.width || !view.height) return;
  const box = el.preview.getBoundingClientRect();
  const scale = Math.min(box.width / view.width, box.height / view.height);
  const width = view.width * scale;
  const height = view.height * scale;
  el.stage.style.width = `${width}px`;
  el.stage.style.height = `${height}px`;
  el.stage.style.left = `${(box.width - width) / 2}px`;
  el.stage.style.top = `${(box.height - height) / 2}px`;

  if (el.overlay.width !== view.width) el.overlay.width = view.width;
  if (el.overlay.height !== view.height) el.overlay.height = view.height;
  drawOverlay(scale);
}

function drawOverlay(scale) {
  const ctx = el.overlay.getContext("2d");
  ctx.clearRect(0, 0, el.overlay.width, el.overlay.height);
  // Wait until the new page/frame is actually visible; drawing boxes over the
  // previous image while the next one decodes looks broken.
  if (!view.imageReady || !view.items.length) return;
  ctx.lineWidth = Math.max(1, 2 / scale);
  ctx.strokeStyle = "#00b0ff";
  // Stroke only: a translucent fill tints the barcode and makes a small QR look
  // colour-shifted once the preview is scaled down.
  for (const item of view.items) {
    ctx.beginPath();
    item.points.forEach(([x, y], i) => (i ? ctx.lineTo(x, y) : ctx.moveTo(x, y)));
    ctx.closePath();
    ctx.stroke();
  }
}

// The <img> tells us when the new pixels are actually on screen.
el.image.addEventListener("load", () => {
  view.imageReady = true;
  layout();
});

showPreview sets view.imageReady = false before it swaps the <img> source (file pages pass waitForLoad = true). layout() still sizes the stage and clears the canvas immediately, but drawOverlay returns until the load event fires. At that point the new page is visible and the boxes are drawn. Camera frames skip the wait, because the previous frame is already on screen and the stream replaces it every ~33 ms.

layout() computes a contain-fit rectangle (the smaller of the width/height ratios) and centers it. The canvas backing store is set to view.width × view.height — the image's intrinsic pixels — while CSS stretches it to the letterboxed size. The only scale-dependent value is lineWidth = 2 / scale, which keeps the outline about two screen pixels regardless of zoom, matching the Slint version. A ResizeObserver re-runs layout() whenever the pane resizes:

// ui/app.js
new ResizeObserver(layout).observe(el.preview);

The CSS that stacks the image and canvas in the same box:

/* ui/style.css */
.stage { position: absolute; }
.stage img,
.stage canvas {
  position: absolute;
  inset: 0;
  width: 100%;
  height: 100%;
}

Because the decoder ran on the same per-page bitmap that became the preview (Step 3 and Step 5), the points line up with the displayed pixels even for EXIF-rotated photos — no rotation or offset math is needed here. The overlay draws only the outline; a translucent fill over a dense QR code reads as a colour shift when the preview is scaled down.

Step 9: Stream the Native Camera

The camera is native, not the webview's getUserMedia. On Windows the bundled litecam library captures from Media Foundation and delivers RGB frames through a C ABI. The Rust wrapper copies each frame out and releases the native buffer:

// src/camera.rs (shared with the Slint GUI)
extern "C" {
    fn litecam_create() -> *mut c_void;
    fn litecam_open(handle: *mut c_void, index: c_int) -> c_int;
    fn litecam_grab(handle: *mut c_void, width: *mut c_int,
                    height: *mut c_int, size: *mut c_int) -> *mut u8;
    fn litecam_release(handle: *mut c_void);
    fn litecam_destroy(handle: *mut c_void);
}

impl Camera {
    /// Grab one frame, copying the RGB bytes out and releasing the native buffer.
    pub fn grab(&mut self) -> Option<Frame> {
        let mut width = 0;
        let mut height = 0;
        let mut size = 0;
        let ptr = unsafe { litecam_grab(self.handle, &mut width, &mut height, &mut size) };
        if ptr.is_null() || width <= 0 || height <= 0 || size <= 0 {
            unsafe { litecam_release(self.handle) };
            return None;
        }
        let rgb = unsafe { std::slice::from_raw_parts(ptr, size as usize) }.to_vec();
        unsafe { litecam_release(self.handle) };
        Some(Frame { rgb, width, height })
    }
}

start_camera spawns a worker thread that owns its own reader instance, so the native handle stays on that thread. The loop grabs a frame, caps itself near 30 fps, decodes, encodes JPEG, stores it, and emits an event:

// src-tauri/src/commands.rs
#[cfg(windows)]
fn spawn_camera(app: AppHandle, stop: Arc<AtomicBool>) {
    thread::spawn(move || {
        let mut camera = match crate::litecam::Camera::open(0) {
            Ok(camera) => camera,
            Err(err) => return camera_failed(&app, err),
        };
        // The camera owns its reader: the native handle stays on this thread.
        let reader = match scanner::BarcodeReader::new(scanner::DEFAULT_LICENSE) {
            Ok(reader) => reader,
            Err(err) => return camera_failed(&app, err),
        };

        let mut last_frame = Instant::now();
        let mut first_frame = true;
        while !stop.load(Ordering::Relaxed) {
            let Some(frame) = camera.grab() else {
                // The device can open while another app keeps it busy; ReadSample
                // then fails forever. Fail loudly instead of hanging the UI.
                if first_frame && last_frame.elapsed() > Duration::from_secs(3) {
                    return camera_failed(&app,
                        "Camera opened but delivered no frames. Close other apps using the \
                         camera (browser tabs, video calls) and try again.".into());
                }
                thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(10));
                continue;
            };
            first_frame = false;

            // Cap near 30 fps so decoding and JPEG encoding do not flood the
            // event channel with frames the webview never shows.
            let pause = Duration::from_millis(33).saturating_sub(last_frame.elapsed());
            if !pause.is_zero() { thread::sleep(pause); }
            if stop.load(Ordering::Relaxed) { break; }

            let items = reader.decode_buffer(&frame.rgb, frame.width, frame.height)
                .unwrap_or_default().into_iter().map(to_item).collect();
            let Some(jpeg) = encode_jpeg(&frame.rgb, frame.width as u32, frame.height as u32) else {
                continue;
            };

            let seq = {
                let state = app.state::<AppState>();
                let mut store = state.media.lock().unwrap();
                store.frame_jpeg = jpeg;
                store.frame_seq += 1;
                store.frame_seq
            };
            let _ = app.emit("camera-frame", CameraFrame {
                seq, width: frame.width as u32, height: frame.height as u32, items,
            });
            last_frame = Instant::now();
        }
    });
}

The frontend listens for the event and repaints the same preview/overlay/results path used for still images:

// ui/app.js
await listen("camera-frame", (event) => {
  const frame = event.payload;
  view.page = 0;
  view.pages = 0;
  showPreview(mediaUrl("camera.jpg", frame.seq), frame.width, frame.height);
  renderResults(frame.items);
  updatePager();
  setStatus(`Camera: ${frame.items.length} barcode(s)`);
});

await listen("camera-error", (event) => {
  setCameraOn(false);
  setStatus(event.payload);
});

Camera frames hide the pager (view.pages = 0) because the live stream is a single surface. If no frame arrives within three seconds, the worker emits camera-error instead of leaving the status on "Starting camera..." — almost always because another app (a browser tab using getUserMedia, a video call, or a second scanner instance) holds the device.

This is the event channel doing what events are for: pushing data the webview did not explicitly request. The seq in each payload tells the <img> which JPEG to fetch from the media: protocol. On non-Windows platforms start_camera returns a clear error ("Camera capture is only wired for Windows in this example."), while image and PDF decoding still work everywhere.

Step 10: Lock Down Security with Capabilities and CSP

Tauri blocks every potentially dangerous command by default; you grant access explicitly in a capability file. This app grants the main window only core:default (invoke + events):

// src-tauri/capabilities/default.json
{
  "$schema": "../gen/schemas/desktop-schema.json",
  "identifier": "default",
  "description": "The main window may call the app commands and listen to events. The file dialog is opened from Rust, so no dialog permission is needed here.",
  "windows": ["main"],
  "permissions": ["core:default"]
}

Notice what is not granted: no dialog permission. The file picker is opened from Rust (open_image calls app.dialog()), so the webview never needs the ability to open dialogs itself. This is the principle of least privilege applied to the IPC surface — the webview can call your five commands and listen to events, and nothing else.

The CSP in tauri.conf.json (Step 1) restricts where images and connections may come from, and the results list uses textContent (Step 7) so untrusted barcode text cannot inject markup. Together these keep the webview side safe even though it renders data decoded from arbitrary files.

Step 11: Build and Run

With the SDK and litecam vendored in the repo, building is a single Cargo command — no Node.js, no bundler, no npm install:

cd examples/rust/tauri/src-tauri
cargo run --release

On Windows you can double-click tauri/run.bat. The first build compiles the Dynamsoft bridge and links the SDK, so it takes longer than later builds.

If you want the Tauri CLI for dev-server orchestration and installers, it is optional:

cd examples/rust/tauri
npm install
npm run dev      # tauri dev
npm run build    # tauri build → src-tauri/target/release/bundle/

Because there is no devUrl, Tauri embeds the frontend assets into the binary in both debug and release. If you edit ui/*.js or ui/*.css, rebuild (or restart cargo run) to see the change — a webview reload alone will not pick up disk edits.

Source Code

Get the complete sample project source code on GitHub.

title: Compact and Decodable Electrocardiogram Text for Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.22827v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When a twelve-lead electrocardiogram is written as text for a large language model, the number of tokens has to be balanced against the information lost through compression. This paper presents a deterministic encoding that writes eight independent leads as amplitude letters and exact time gaps and recovers the remaining four limb leads algebraically. The key points are selected with a cardiac-cycle-dependent tolerance, the amplitudes are parameterized by a 26-letter logarithmic codebook learned from a training set, and a 10-step tolerance schedule keeps all records within a fixed token budget. The encoding was applied to 21,388 records from the public PTB-XL database and evaluated using an exact decode-and-re-encode round trip, waveform reconstruction error, and a paired comparison of convolutional classifiers trained with 5 different seeds on signals from the original and decoded databases. All records were contained in 4,080 tokens (average: 2,866 tokens, 64.3% fewer than a per-sample transcription), and all stored lead strings were exactly reproduced. The average correlation between the decoded and reference signals was 0.982. The macro-averaged area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.9167 for the reference signals and 0.9157 for the decoded signals (paired difference -0.0010; 95% patient-level bootstrap interval, -0.0028 to 0.0007), within the pre-specified non-inferiority margin of -0.010; this is not a confirmatory result, because the test fold had been used during encoder development. The diagnostic content of a compact text can therefore be preserved, while the language model's ability to read the text is yet another matter.

title: ExiST: Existence-Aware Self-Training for Semi-Supervised Multi-Organ Segmentation
description:
arXiv:2611.23581v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Semi-supervised multi-organ segmentation should learn more than a dozen organs from a handful of labeled scans, and the smallest organs occupy less than one percent of the foreground. We identify a failure mode of self-training that is specific to this regime. When a teacher misses a small organ in a scan, every voxel of that organ receives the confident pseudo-label background, and the student is trained toward the organ absence. Repeated over many scans, this loop extinguishes tail organs. In a pilot study, removing the gallbladder from the pseudo-labels reduced its Dice on AMOS from 36.5 to 1.0. We argue that a missing organ should be treated as unresolved rather than absent and propose Existence-aware Self-Training (ExiST). It builds pseudo-labels by leave-one-out consensus of independently trained networks, screens them with a quality gate on validation scans, and infers, per scan and per organ, whether the organ was found. For every unresolved organ, the background voxels of that scan receive the set-valued target, trained with a marginal cross-entropy that accepts either answer and a Dice term that skips uncertain voxels. We show that this loss never pushes a candidate organ toward absence and never favors one member of the set, which leaves the decision to labeled evidence. ExiST outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods and reaches 77.1 mean Dice on Synapse with 20% labeled scans and 75.9 on AMOS with 5% labeled scans.

title: What a Hex Code Taught Me: A Freelancer's Notes on Using Invert Image Tools for Dark Palettes
description:
Last spring a client asked me for a dark theme on a site that had only ever been light. They gave me four brand colors, a deadline, and one request: "make it feel the same, just dark." I did what many freelancers do in a hurry. I opened a tool, typed in the hex codes, and started to invert image swatches to see what came out. This post is about what that shortcut gave me, and where it let me down.

The shortcut

The idea is simple. Inversion subtracts each channel from 255. A light cream becomes a deep brown, a bright blue becomes a soft orange. The result is not a design, but it is a fast way to see what an "opposite" palette looks like.

For hex codes I used the hex inverter on the invert image page. You type a hex value, read the inverse and copy it. No account, no watermark, and as far as the page says, nothing leaves the browser for local files. For a quick sanity check on a client's palette, that is about as light as tools get.

What worked

It showed me contrast relationships. When a cream background became a dark brown, I could see immediately which text colors would likely stay readable. It gave me a first draft for surfaces in minutes.

It started a conversation. I showed the client two swatch sheets: the original and the flipped version. They pointed at the flipped orange and said, "that is actually closer to our old logo." I would never have tried that color myself.

It was a good test of my assumptions. I thought the dark theme would need only a couple of changes. The flipped swatches made me look at every color in the palette, and I found two accents that were too close together in the dark version.

What did not work

A pure inversion is not a dark theme. A bright blue button turns orange, which can break the meaning your client has attached to the color. A green "success" tone turns magenta. Grey text stays grey, but at the wrong contrast. If you ship the raw numbers, the interface will feel wrong even if each color is technically the opposite.

So I treated the flipped colors as raw material. I moved them toward the brand hues by hand, then checked contrast ratios with a proper accessibility checker. The inverter gave me a starting point, not an answer.

Using the same idea on images

The same tool also handles images, so I tried it on the client's hero illustration and some flat screenshots in their docs. The tool accepts JPG, PNG, WebP, HEIC and TIFF up to 20 MB, and exports PNG, JPEG or WebP at the original pixel size. For the screenshots, PNG kept the transparency and edges clean. For the hero illustration, a partial flip using the strength slider felt closer to the brand than a full one. When I had a stack of small assets, the batch page took up to 30 images and gave me a ZIP, so I did not spend my evening clicking.

Three rules I follow now

  1. Treat inversion as a sketch. Use it to explore, never to ship.
  2. Keep meaning-carrying colors by hand. Success, error and warning colors should be chosen on purpose.
  3. Show the client both versions. A flipped palette is a cheap way to ask a better question.

A short note on professionalism

Clients do not pay me to press a button; they pay me to know when a button is not enough. If you use a shortcut, say so, and say what you did afterward. My client appreciated seeing the rough flipped swatches next to the final palette, because it explained the thinking.

If you work with palettes, I would like to hear what quick checks you rely on. When it comes to the humble invert image trick, I find it most useful as a conversation starter, and the final colors always need a human to decide.
