title: Make the agent use the existing Link component, not a raw <a>, for internal routes
description:
The agent adds a “Back to settings” control as <a href="/settings">. The app already has a Link (or RouterLink, or Next.js Link) that prefetches, keeps the client transition, and applies the active class from the design system. The raw anchor does a full reload, loses draft state on the page, and looks unstyled for a frame.

I’ve started treating a raw <a> to an internal path as a merge question, not as a finished navigation change. External URLs, mailto:, and file downloads can stay anchors. In-app paths should go through the shared component.

Why the raw anchor sneaks in

The model has seen millions of HTML examples. href="/settings" looks correct, and it will work in the preview. What it will not do is honor the app’s scroll restoration, locale prefix, base path, or analytics hook that lives on Link. A new tab target also disappears: the shared component may already set it, or may explicitly forbid it for internal routes.

A full reload on an internal click is easy to miss in a happy-path click-through and expensive in a form or a wizard.

A simple navigation policy

  • Internal paths use the shared Link
  • External URLs use <a> (or the shared ExternalLink if you have one), with rel set the way the app already sets it
  • Do not invent a second wrapper to “add prefetch”
  • Hash links and in-page anchors follow the existing pattern, not a new one-off onClick

If the repo has a lint rule for this (@next/next/no-html-link-for-pages, a custom ESLint check), paste the rule into the prompt. If it does not, a one-line review grep for <a href="/ is enough.

What to put in the prompt 

Internal routes must use the existing Link component (see src/components/Link or next/link).
Do not add a raw <a> for an in-app path.
External URLs, mailto, and file downloads may use <a>, with the existing rel/target helpers.
Do not invent a new NavLink or PrefetchLink.

In review, search the diff for <a. Each hit should be external, a download, or justified. If the href is a path the router owns, send it back.

Reject / send back

Reject

  • <a href="/dashboard"> in a page that already imports Link
  • A new SmartLink helper when Link already exists
  • An in-app anchor that forces target="_blank"
  • A click handler that window.location.href = to an internal path

Accept

  • Link (or the repo’s named wrapper) for in-app paths
  • A raw anchor for an external docs URL, with the existing rel
  • A genuine download link that the shared Link does not support

title: Multipart Upload Selection for Large Private Documents from 100 MB to 1 GB Explained
description:
Short answer: choose multipart upload for large private customer-support documents, especially 100 MB to 1 GB PDF and ZIP files on unreliable connections; keep a single PUT for ordinary small PDFs and office files because it has fewer states to coordinate.

The deciding constraint isn't raw capacity. It's the failure unit. A failed single PUT restarts the whole object, while multipart lets the client retry one part. For a support portal, every upload also needs a tenant-owned object key, an expiring download link, and an application record that says who may retrieve it. Infrai is a reasonable option for teams that expect storage to sit beside other backend capabilities and want one consistent REST contract instead of adding another SDK and credential set. Its public discovery surface describes 295 routes across 20 modules and includes runnable Go examples; that makes the time to a first verified request unusually concrete. I recommend trying it for the private upload boundary when reducing integration surface matters, while keeping authorization and upload state in your own application.

How do large PDF and ZIP retries expose the right multipart upload boundary?

Start with a policy, not a magic industry threshold. The 100 MB boundary below is an application decision for this example: files below it take the short single-request path, while files from 100 MB through the portal's 1 GB limit take the multipart path. Your mileage may vary if clients have stable office networks, or if mobile uploads dominate. Measure completion and retry behavior before moving the line. Multipart wins when restarting a full upload is expensive or likely. Each part is its own retry unit, so a brief connection loss doesn't throw away all prior progress. The catch is state: the service must remember the upload ID, accepted part numbers, checksums or provider-returned part identifiers, tenant ID, object key, and terminal status. Completion must consume one authoritative parts list. A retry must never create two logical attachments. Single PUT is still the right default for normal documents because it has one request, one success condition, and much less stale state. Don't make a 2 MB invoice follow a multipart state machine merely because the 700 MB diagnostic bundle needs one. Tenant isolation comes first: build object keys from an internal tenant identifier rather than a user-supplied folder, keep objects private or signed-only, and issue short-lived presigned download URLs only after an application authorization check. Never treat possession of an object key as permission. This storage boundary has no public/public-read ACL, which suits this workflow but rules out permanent public links and static website hosting.

Retry one part.

Treat credentials and upload state as one failure domain

The important comparison is where operational ownership lands. Direct providers expose their own account, credential, SDK, and feature surface. An aggregation layer narrows that surface, but its common contract may omit specialist controls. Here is the practical split for this workload:

Option Setup and credential shape Best fit Boundary to verify
AWS S3 Direct provider integration Teams that need provider-specific storage controls Your application still owns tenant authorization and upload state
Cloudflare R2 Direct provider integration Teams standardizing directly on R2 Validate the exact multipart and lifecycle behavior you plan to operate
Alibaba Cloud OSS Direct provider integration Teams already operating in the OSS ecosystem Account and SDK conventions remain provider-specific
Tencent Cloud COS Direct provider integration Teams already operating in the COS ecosystem Account and SDK conventions remain provider-specific
Google Cloud Storage or Backblaze B2 Direct specialist integration Workloads committed to GCS or B2 Infrai doesn't cover these vendors
Infrai Plain HTTP under one key and one billing relationship Teams adding storage alongside other backend modules No object versioning, object lock, cross-region replication, or migration tool

Infrai's primary advantage here is breadth behind a consistent interface: adding another backend capability is another discovered REST operation, not a fresh SDK integration. The supporting benefit is inspectability. Discovery is public, needs no key, and returns request and response schemas plus runnable examples, so a team can confirm the contract before distributing a production credential.

That convenience isn't universal. Stick with AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, Alibaba OSS, or Tencent COS directly when a provider-specific control is part of your design. Choose Google Cloud Storage or Backblaze B2 directly when either is a hard platform requirement. For regulated retention, use an external solution that provides object lock or WORM behavior; this storage surface has neither versioning nor object lock. FedRAMP requirements also need a separate compliance assessment rather than an inference from an API shape.

Make the policy and integration probe explicit in Go

The smallest safe example is the decision layer that runs before any provider call. It validates the tenant, normalizes the file name for display only, derives the storage key from trusted identifiers, and returns one of two modes. The threshold is configuration, so changing it doesn't rewrite upload code.

package main

import (
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "path/filepath"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

type UploadMode string

const (
    SinglePut UploadMode = "single-put"
    Multipart UploadMode = "multipart"
)

type Policy struct {
    MultipartAt int64
    MaximumSize int64
}

type UploadPlan struct {
    Mode        UploadMode
    ObjectKey   string
    DisplayName string
}

func getBucket(client *http.Client, apiKey, bucket string) ([]byte, error) {
    endpoint := strings.ReplaceAll(
        "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/bucket/get/{bucket}",
        "{bucket}",
        url.PathEscape(bucket),
    )
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
        req.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Second << attempt
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds > 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("bucket lookup returned %s: %s", resp.Status, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, errors.New("bucket lookup remained rate limited after retries")
}

func planUpload(policy Policy, tenantID, attachmentID, fileName string, size int64) (UploadPlan, error) {
    if tenantID == "" || attachmentID == "" {
        return UploadPlan{}, errors.New("tenant and attachment IDs are required")
    }
    if size <= 0 || size > policy.MaximumSize {
        return UploadPlan{}, fmt.Errorf("file size %d is outside policy", size)
    }

    displayName := filepath.Base(strings.ReplaceAll(fileName, "\\", "/"))
    digest := sha256.Sum256([]byte(tenantID + ":" + attachmentID))
    objectKey := fmt.Sprintf("tenants/%s/attachments/%s", tenantID, hex.EncodeToString(digest[:]))

    mode := SinglePut
    if size >= policy.MultipartAt {
        mode = Multipart
    }
    return UploadPlan{Mode: mode, ObjectKey: objectKey, DisplayName: displayName}, nil
}

func main() {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    bucket := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BUCKET")
    if apiKey == "" || bucket == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_BUCKET are required")
    }
    body, err := getBucket(&http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}, apiKey, bucket)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("bucket=%s\n", body)

    policy := Policy{MultipartAt: 100 * 1024 * 1024, MaximumSize: 1024 * 1024 * 1024}
    plan, err := planUpload(policy, "tenant_42", "attachment_9f2", "logs.zip", 734003200)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("mode=%s key=%s name=%s\n", plan.Mode, plan.ObjectKey, plan.DisplayName)
}

This program verifies the configured private bucket through a real Infrai call, then runs the provider-independent upload policy. Request bodies and completion fields should come from the selected provider's current schema, not from a copied blog snippet. Query the public capability discovery document and use its Go example. API calls use Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY; uploads remain private, and that authorization header must not be forwarded to a returned presigned URL.

For multipart, persist the state transition before acknowledging it to the browser. Use a stable application attachment ID as the idempotency anchor, retry HTTP 429 responses with exponential backoff while honoring Retry-After, and explicitly abort a failed multipart session. There is no automatic cleanup rule for abandoned fragments. This is where missed cleanup becomes a bill and a runbook entry — quiet failure, but still failure.

Overwrite protection needs the same discipline. Strict If-Match conditional writes aren't available, so serialize changes with a queue or guard them with a database transaction and generation field. A key should identify one immutable attachment attempt; publishing a replacement should point the support record at a new key rather than overwrite the old bytes.

Prove isolation before defining rollback

Verification should prove invariants, not just report a green response. In staging, upload one small PDF through single PUT and one large ZIP through multipart. Interrupt a part, resume it, and confirm that only that part is retried. Then attempt a download as the owning tenant, another tenant, and an unauthenticated client. The first gets an expiring link; the others don't.

Check four records after completion: the application attachment is terminal, the object key starts with the trusted tenant prefix, the reported size matches the accepted upload, and no active multipart state remains. Also exercise a client-visible 429 retry. A tight loop is an incident generator.

Rollback is boring by design. Disable new multipart starts with a feature flag, allow already-created sessions to complete for a bounded drain window, and abort the rest explicitly. Route files below the single-request limit back to PUT. Files above that limit should receive a retryable maintenance response from your application rather than silently switching to a full-object upload that clients may not be able to finish.

Don't delete completed objects during control-plane rollback. Detach the application record only after authorization and retention checks, and keep deletion as a separate, auditable operation. Lifecycle expiration can't provide minute-level rollback cleanup because its minimum is one day.

Draw the specialist boundary after the rollback drill

Use multipart for the 100 MB to 1 GB class when individual-part retries materially improve completion; use single PUT for the everyday support attachment. Keep tenant authorization, overwrite coordination, and cleanup in the application no matter which storage vendor receives the bytes.

For teams that value a small integration surface across several backend services, Infrai is worth evaluating for this private storage boundary. For teams that need public hosting, browser-direct CORS self-service, strict conditional writes, versioning, object lock, cross-region replication, or GCS/B2 coverage, a specialist or direct provider is the better fit. If this boundary matches your system, start with the large-document upload guide.

References

  • Cloudflare R2 documentation
  • FedRAMP
  • Infrai storage lifecycle discovery

title: Password Reset Email Backend: Why I Audit Abuse Prevention and Expiry
description:
Short answer: build a password reset email backend around application-owned abuse controls, an identical public response for every address, and an audit trail that preserves token expiry alongside the send result. For a media reader trying to regain access, delivery reliability means receiving a usable link before its short deadline. An accepted send alone cannot establish that result.

My design choice is to make the remaining validity window the decision criterion. This is a proposed experiment, with synthetic timestamps below, rather than a report of measured provider performance. The evaluation constraint is strict: a message status must never be treated as proof that a reader received a usable reset link.

The tempting implementation accepts an address, sends an email, and returns success. That is easy to sketch in a notebook. It leaves three different questions tangled together: was this request allowed, was the send accepted, and could the reader still use the token? Separating those questions gives an Express backend a clearer contract, while a small Python harness makes the policy easy to inspect before taking it from notebook-to-prod.

How should a password reset email backend audit expiry before a send?

For this workflow, start the audit record at request time. Record token expiry and the send result as distinct values. Then decide which later message or event evidence your monitoring process needs. Pull-based checks can supply operational evidence, but the time your worker observes an event must remain distinguishable from any timestamp the event actually supplies. Otherwise, a slow polling interval can look like slow delivery, and the provider comparison becomes misleading.

Acceptance is intermediate.

Consider an illustrative policy with a 300-second validity window and a 60-second minimum remaining budget before dispatch. Those numbers are design inputs, not a security standard or provider guarantee. If local processing has already consumed most of that window, sending the same nearly expired link gives the reader little chance to finish. A freshness check makes that condition visible. The application still needs an explicit recovery policy; this check does not renew or invalidate tokens by itself.

This matters for a media product because regaining access is the job the reader sees. A support dashboard showing a successful API call answers a narrower question. I would retain both observations, then evaluate the gap instead of hiding it inside one success counter.

Keep abuse decisions ahead of the send

Apply per-IP and per-account rate limits in the application. They protect different boundaries: a single source can target many accounts, and multiple sources can target one account. Set the thresholds through your own abuse evaluation; no defensible universal number follows from choosing an email API. A rejected request should not become an email send merely because a different delivery provider is available.

Return the same public response for existing and nonexistent accounts, such as: "If this address is eligible, you will receive reset instructions." Keep detailed send outcomes in the internal audit trail. The public wording should not expose account existence or reveal whether suppression prevented dispatch. Equal wording is one control, so the evaluation should also look for account-dependent differences in response behavior.

The useful trade-off is deliberate: more internal evidence, less public detail.

Use a fixed reset template for this path. I'd keep generative text outside the delivery decision: an eval-driven recovery flow needs reproducible messages, and prompt-cost awareness starts with asking whether a model call helps at all. It adds no necessary decision here. This leaves the Python harness focused on expiry, throttling decisions, and audit completeness rather than prompt variation.

Compare providers against the same deadline

There is no measured winner in this comparison. Resend, Postmark, and Amazon SES are three real candidates to evaluate through their official documentation and a common acceptance plan. Their placement below describes the integration decision to investigate; it does not assert an inbox-delivery ranking.

Candidate Decision to investigate Boundary for this reset flow
Resend Start with its documented email integration and test a focused send workflow. Do not infer account abuse protection or usable-link delivery from a successful send response.
Postmark Assess its email workflow against the same transactional reset requirements. Verify how its documented message evidence maps to your expiry audit before selecting it.
Amazon SES Assess the email integration within the AWS operational setup your team would maintain. Include configuration and monitoring work in the trial, rather than comparing only the send call.

These are different adoption questions. A team evaluating a focused email integration has a different starting point from a team evaluating how email fits its AWS operations. Neither starting point settles the delivery question. Run the same scenarios, retain equivalent evidence, and make the selection conditional on the results. The linked documentation is a starting point for that verification, not evidence of comparative performance.

Infrai is another option when the application benefits from 295 routes across 20 modules under one REST API and one key, allowing another backend capability to follow the same integration contract; its public, self-describing discovery surface can also help inspect schemas before wiring an adapter. For this workflow, plan pull-based message and event checks, application-owned reset tokens and email-code fallback, and direct API sending. Those boundaries mean assessing polling cadence and token management as part of the choice. If the requirements include SMTP relay, pushed delivery events, or voice, WhatsApp, or RCS recovery, select an integration whose documented contract meets those requirements.

The breadth advantage is conditional. It matters when the media application actually needs adjacent backend capabilities; a service choosing email alone should weigh the email workflow on its own evidence. No route count establishes reliability.

A focused expiry audit in Python

The send adapter below accepts an application-prepared request body. Set INFRAI_BASE_URL to the platform's versioned API base, INFRAI_API_KEY to the secret key, and RESET_EMAIL_PAYLOAD to a JSON object matching the current email-send schema. Prepare that payload from the documented schema rather than treating application audit fields as provider parameters. Set RESET_OPERATION_ID to a durable identity for this one approved send, reused across retries, and RESET_TOKEN_EXPIRES_AT to its timezone-aware ISO timestamp. Only run the adapter after abuse admission and token issuance; this script performs a real send.

from datetime import datetime, timezone
from email.utils import parsedate_to_datetime
import json
import os
import time
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


base_url = os.environ["INFRAI_BASE_URL"].rstrip("/")
if not base_url.startswith("https://"):
    raise ValueError("Use an HTTPS API base")
expires_at = datetime.fromisoformat(os.environ["RESET_TOKEN_EXPIRES_AT"])
if expires_at.tzinfo is None:
    raise ValueError("Token expiry must include a timezone")
payload = json.loads(os.environ["RESET_EMAIL_PAYLOAD"])
if not isinstance(payload, dict):
    raise ValueError("The send payload must be a JSON object")
request = Request(
    base_url + "/email/send",
    data=json.dumps(payload).encode("utf-8"),
    headers={
        "Authorization": "Bearer " + os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"],
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Accept": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": os.environ["RESET_OPERATION_ID"],
    },
    method="POST",
)
for attempt in range(4):
    if (expires_at - datetime.now(timezone.utc)).total_seconds() < 60:
        raise RuntimeError("Insufficient remaining token validity")
    try:
        with urlopen(request, timeout=15) as response:
            print(json.dumps(json.load(response), indent=2))
        break
    except HTTPError as error:
        reason = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
        if error.code != 429 or attempt == 3:
            raise RuntimeError(f"HTTP {error.code}: {reason}") from error
        delay = 2 ** attempt
        retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
        if retry_after:
            try:
                delay = max(delay, float(retry_after))
            except ValueError:
                retry_at = parsedate_to_datetime(retry_after)
                delay = max(
                    delay,
                    (retry_at - datetime.now(timezone.utc)).total_seconds(),
                )
        time.sleep(delay)

The network example prints the provider's JSON response without assuming any response fields. Persist its send result with the request time and token expiry in the application's audit trail. It retries only explicit rate-limit responses; other HTTP errors surface their response bodies. Evaluate the documented idempotency contract before deployment, and keep that operation identity bound to the same payload. The next example checks the deadline policy with synthetic inputs.

This standard-library example exercises one decision before a send adapter runs. It uses synthetic data, makes no network requests, and writes an audit-shaped result to standard output. Its field names belong to the application, not a provider response schema. In production, the record would join the application's durable audit trail.

from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
import json


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ResetAttempt:
    request_id: str
    requested_at: datetime
    token_expires_at: datetime
    send_result: str


def assess_dispatch(attempt, checked_at, minimum_remaining_seconds):
    if minimum_remaining_seconds < 0:
        raise ValueError("minimum_remaining_seconds must be nonnegative")
    if checked_at < attempt.requested_at:
        raise ValueError("check precedes request")
    remaining = (attempt.token_expires_at - checked_at).total_seconds()
    fresh = remaining > 0 and remaining >= minimum_remaining_seconds
    record = asdict(attempt)
    record.update(
        checked_at=checked_at,
        remaining_seconds=remaining,
        freshness_decision="eligible" if fresh else "withhold",
    )
    return record


issued_at = datetime(2026, 11, 18, 12, 0, tzinfo=timezone.utc)
for elapsed_seconds in (15, 250, 300):
    attempt = ResetAttempt(
        request_id=f"media-reader-demo-{elapsed_seconds}",
        requested_at=issued_at,
        token_expires_at=issued_at + timedelta(seconds=300),
        send_result="not_attempted",
    )
    record = assess_dispatch(
        attempt,
        checked_at=issued_at + timedelta(seconds=elapsed_seconds),
        minimum_remaining_seconds=60,
    )
    print(json.dumps(record, default=lambda value: value.isoformat()))

At 15 seconds, the record is eligible on freshness alone. At 250 seconds, only 50 seconds remain, so dispatch is withheld under this illustrative policy. At expiry, dispatch is withheld too. None of those outcomes says an email was delivered. The send result deliberately remains separate.

That distinction is the example's point. It is not a complete reset service: abuse admission, secure token issuance and validation, account lookup, persistence, and the actual send adapter remain application responsibilities. An eligible freshness decision must still pass those controls before dispatch.

For the adapter, handle rate limiting with bounded backoff and honor Retry-After when present. Before retrying a write, verify its documented idempotency behavior and keep the same operation identity. Also recheck the expiry budget. A retry that starts with a fresh token can finish with a stale one.

Measure before copying the choice

Take the notebook policy into an evaluation that includes an eligible request, an unknown account, per-IP and per-account throttling, delayed processing, an expired token, and a retry near expiry. Verify that the public response stays consistent while the internal audit records the appropriate decision. Test the transitions, not just the happy send.

Then measure request-to-dispatch time, message-status observation delay, and remaining validity at the delivery evidence your chosen integration actually exposes. Label the limits of that evidence. Provider acceptance, later delivery evidence, and successful token redemption are separate observations; collecting them separately lets an investigation identify which stage consumed the deadline. Track duplicate dispatches and missing audit fields alongside those timings.

Choose the backend only after that exercise. For this media reset flow, I would prioritize a usable validity window and explainable send outcomes over a shorter integration demo. The application controls abuse and token lifetime; the provider choice must fit the monitoring process that makes delivery assessable.

References

The sources below support provider evaluation and reset-flow review. They do not supply a comparative delivery benchmark or establish the illustrative expiry thresholds used here.

Further reading

  • Resend official documentation
  • Postmark developer documentation
  • Amazon SES developer guide
  • OWASP Forgot Password Cheat Sheet

title: Transactional Outbox in Go: Reliable Event Publishing Without Distributed Transactions
description:
Your API creates an order and commits it to PostgreSQL.

The next step is publishing an OrderCreated event to Kafka so that inventory, notifications, and analytics services can react.

You write something like this:

func (s *OrderService) CreateOrder(
    ctx context.Context,
    order Order,
) error {
    if err := s.repo.Create(ctx, order); err != nil {
        return err
    }

    return s.publisher.Publish(ctx, OrderCreated{
        OrderID: order.ID,
    })
}

It looks straightforward.

But there is a failure window.

What happens if PostgreSQL commits the order successfully and Kafka is unavailable?

The order exists, but no event is published.

What if Kafka accepts the event, but your application crashes before recording that it was published?

Your application might publish the same event again after restarting.

These are not unusual edge cases. They are consequences of coordinating independent systems without a shared transaction.

The transactional outbox pattern addresses this problem by storing the business change and the event to be published in the same database transaction.

Instead of trying to atomically commit to PostgreSQL and Kafka, we make the database transaction the source of truth and publish events asynchronously.

In this article, we'll build a PostgreSQL-backed transactional outbox in Go, implement concurrent workers, handle retries and leases, and explore the delivery guarantees that matter in production.

1. The Dual-Write Problem

A dual write happens when an application needs to update two independent systems as part of one logical operation.

For example:

HTTP Request
     |
     v
Create Order in PostgreSQL
     |
     v
Publish OrderCreated to Kafka

There are two possible execution orders.

Database first 

1. PostgreSQL commit succeeds
2. Kafka publish fails
3. Application returns an error

The order exists, but downstream services never receive the event.

Retrying the entire HTTP request might create another order unless the endpoint is idempotent.

Message broker first 

1. Kafka publish succeeds
2. PostgreSQL commit fails
3. Application returns an error

Now downstream services have received an event for an order that does not exist.

Neither order solves the problem.

A database transaction cannot automatically include a Kafka publish. They are independent systems with independent failure and commit semantics.

Distributed transactions and two-phase commit are possible in some environments, but they introduce operational and architectural complexity.

The transactional outbox pattern takes a different approach.

2. How the Transactional Outbox Works

The central idea is simple:

Store the business change and the event in the same database transaction.

Instead of publishing directly to the broker, insert an event into an outbox_events table.

                 HTTP Request
                      |
                      v
               PostgreSQL TX
                      |
              +-------+-------+
              |               |
              v               v
          Create Order    Insert Event
              |               |
              +-------+-------+
                      |
                    COMMIT
                      |
                      v
                 Outbox Worker
                      |
                      v
                 Message Broker
                      |
                      v
              Downstream Consumers

If the transaction commits, both the order and the outbox event exist.

If the transaction rolls back, neither exists.

This eliminates the inconsistency between the business write and the durable record of the event that must be published.

It does not make publishing exactly once. We'll discuss that distinction later.

3. Designing the Outbox Table

Let's start with a PostgreSQL schema.

CREATE TABLE outbox_events (
    id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,

    event_id UUID NOT NULL UNIQUE,

    aggregate_type TEXT NOT NULL,
    aggregate_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    event_type TEXT NOT NULL,

    payload JSONB NOT NULL,

    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),

    published_at TIMESTAMPTZ,

    attempts INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    next_attempt_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),

    claim_token UUID,
    lease_until TIMESTAMPTZ,

    last_error TEXT
);

CREATE INDEX idx_outbox_pending
    ON outbox_events (next_attempt_at, id)
    WHERE published_at IS NULL;

Let's look at the important fields.

Field Purpose
event_id Stable identifier used for deduplication
aggregate_type Business entity type
aggregate_id Entity identifier
event_type Event name
payload Serialized event data
published_at Publication completion timestamp
attempts Number of publication attempts
next_attempt_at Earliest time the event can be retried
claim_token Identifies the worker currently holding the lease
lease_until When another worker can reclaim the event
last_error Most recent publication error

Why do we need both claim_token and lease_until?

A worker can crash after claiming an event. Without a lease, the event might remain stuck forever.

A lease makes the event available again after a bounded period.

The claim token prevents an old worker from updating a row after another worker has reclaimed it.

This is a form of ownership fencing for database updates. It does not prevent an expired worker from publishing to the broker, so consumers still need deduplication.

4. Writing the Business Change and Event Atomically

The outbox only works if the business write and event insertion share the same transaction.

Let's define an event:

package outbox

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "time"

    "github.com/google/uuid"
)

type Event struct {
    ID            uuid.UUID
    AggregateType string
    AggregateID   string
    Type          string
    Payload       json.RawMessage
    CreatedAt     time.Time
}

A repository method can insert the event using the same sql.Tx as the business operation.

func Insert(
    ctx context.Context,
    tx *sql.Tx,
    event Event,
) error {
    const query = `
        INSERT INTO outbox_events (
            event_id,
            aggregate_type,
            aggregate_id,
            event_type,
            payload,
            created_at
        )
        VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, $5, $6)
    `

    _, err := tx.ExecContext(
        ctx,
        query,
        event.ID,
        event.AggregateType,
        event.AggregateID,
        event.Type,
        event.Payload,
        event.CreatedAt,
    )

    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("insert outbox event: %w", err)
    }

    return nil
}

Now let's use it in an order service.

func (s *OrderService) Create(
    ctx context.Context,
    req CreateOrderRequest,
) error {
    tx, err := s.db.BeginTx(ctx, nil)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("begin transaction: %w", err)
    }

    defer tx.Rollback()

    order := Order{
        ID:        uuid.NewString(),
        Customer:  req.CustomerID,
        Amount:    req.Amount,
        CreatedAt: time.Now().UTC(),
    }

    if err := s.orders.Insert(ctx, tx, order); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("insert order: %w", err)
    }

    payload, err := json.Marshal(OrderCreated{
        OrderID:   order.ID,
        Customer:  order.Customer,
        Amount:    order.Amount,
        CreatedAt: order.CreatedAt,
    })
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("marshal event: %w", err)
    }

    event := outbox.Event{
        ID:            uuid.New(),
        AggregateType: "order",
        AggregateID:   order.ID,
        Type:          "order.created",
        Payload:       payload,
        CreatedAt:     time.Now().UTC(),
    }

    if err := outbox.Insert(ctx, tx, event); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("insert event: %w", err)
    }

    if err := tx.Commit(); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("commit order transaction: %w", err)
    }

    return nil
}

There is no Kafka call inside this transaction.

That is intentional.

The transaction only guarantees that the order and its event record are persisted together.

The actual event publication happens asynchronously.

What if the commit response is lost?

Suppose PostgreSQL commits successfully, but the connection drops before the application receives the commit response.

The application might not know whether the transaction succeeded.

This is another reason the HTTP operation should be idempotent.

A retry should not blindly create another order and another event. Use the idempotency mechanism from the previous article, or a durable business uniqueness constraint, to recognize the logical operation.

The outbox guarantees atomic persistence of the event record with the business write. It does not replace request-level idempotency.

5. Claiming Events With Multiple Workers

A single worker can process pending events, but production systems often need multiple workers.

Imagine three worker instances:

Worker A
Worker B
Worker C

If all three execute the same query:

SELECT *
FROM outbox_events
WHERE published_at IS NULL;

they can select the same events.

That creates duplicate work immediately.

PostgreSQL provides a useful mechanism for this problem:

FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED.

It allows workers to claim different rows without waiting for rows already locked by other workers.

However, we should not hold a database transaction open while publishing to Kafka.

Instead, we use a short transaction to claim a batch, commit it, and publish outside the transaction.

Claiming a batch 

WITH candidates AS (
    SELECT id
    FROM outbox_events
    WHERE
        published_at IS NULL
        AND next_attempt_at <= NOW()
        AND (
            lease_until IS NULL
            OR lease_until < NOW()
        )
    ORDER BY id
    FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
    LIMIT $1
)
UPDATE outbox_events AS events
SET
    claim_token = $2,
    lease_until = NOW() + ($3 * INTERVAL '1 second'),
    attempts = attempts + 1
FROM candidates
WHERE events.id = candidates.id
RETURNING
    events.id,
    events.event_id,
    events.aggregate_type,
    events.aggregate_id,
    events.event_type,
    events.payload,
    events.attempts;

Parameters:

  • $1: batch size.
  • $2: unique claim token for this batch.
  • $3: lease duration in seconds.

The FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED clause prevents workers from claiming the same locked rows.

The UPDATE records ownership and establishes a lease.

Once the transaction commits, the worker can publish the returned events.

A simplified Go representation:

type ClaimedEvent struct {
    ID            int64
    EventID       uuid.UUID
    AggregateType string
    AggregateID   string
    Type          string
    Payload       []byte
    Attempts      int
}

type Claim struct {
    Token  uuid.UUID
    Events []ClaimedEvent
}

The repository method should execute the claim query in a short transaction and return the rows after committing.

The key design rule:

Never keep database row locks open while waiting for a message broker.

A slow broker should not hold database transactions and locks indefinitely.

6. Publishing Events Outside the Transaction

Define a small publisher interface:

type Publisher interface {
    Publish(
        ctx context.Context,
        event ClaimedEvent,
    ) error
}

The implementation can use Kafka, RabbitMQ, NATS, or another messaging system.

The outbox worker should not depend on the broker's concrete client.

Now let's define the worker:

type Worker struct {
    repo      Repository
    publisher Publisher

    batchSize int
    lease     time.Duration
}

A useful repository interface:

type Repository interface {
    Claim(
        ctx context.Context,
        limit int,
        lease time.Duration,
    ) (Claim, error)

    MarkPublished(
        ctx context.Context,
        id int64,
        token uuid.UUID,
    ) error

    ScheduleRetry(
        ctx context.Context,
        id int64,
        token uuid.UUID,
        delay time.Duration,
        cause error,
    ) error
}

The worker processes one claimed batch:

func (w *Worker) ProcessBatch(
    ctx context.Context,
) error {
    claim, err := w.repo.Claim(
        ctx,
        w.batchSize,
        w.lease,
    )
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("claim outbox events: %w", err)
    }

    for _, event := range claim.Events {
        if err := ctx.Err(); err != nil {
            return err
        }

        publishCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(
            ctx,
            10*time.Second,
        )

        err := w.publisher.Publish(publishCtx, event)
        cancel()

        if err != nil {
            delay := retryDelay(event.Attempts)

            scheduleErr := w.repo.ScheduleRetry(
                ctx,
                event.ID,
                claim.Token,
                delay,
                err,
            )

            if scheduleErr != nil {
                return fmt.Errorf(
                    "schedule retry for event %s: %w",
                    event.EventID,
                    scheduleErr,
                )
            }

            continue
        }

        if err := w.repo.MarkPublished(
            ctx,
            event.ID,
            claim.Token,
        ); err != nil {
            return fmt.Errorf(
                "mark event %s as published: %w",
                event.EventID,
                err,
            )
        }
    }

    return nil
}

This is a sequential batch processor. You can add bounded parallelism later, but the ownership and completion rules should remain the same.

Notice that the worker does not delete an event immediately after publishing it.

It marks the event as published.

This makes it possible to inspect publication history, measure delivery delays, and troubleshoot failures.

For large systems, published rows should eventually be archived or removed according to a retention policy.

7. Marking Events as Published Safely

The claim token must be checked when updating an event.

UPDATE outbox_events
SET
    published_at = NOW(),
    claim_token = NULL,
    lease_until = NULL,
    last_error = NULL
WHERE
    id = $1
    AND claim_token = $2
    AND published_at IS NULL;

Why is this important?

Consider this sequence:

  1. Worker A claims an event.
  2. Worker A pauses for a long time.
  3. Its lease expires.
  4. Worker B reclaims the event.
  5. Worker A resumes.

Without an ownership check, Worker A could update the event even though Worker B now owns it.

The claim token prevents that stale update.

Your repository should also check RowsAffected().

If no row was updated, the claim is no longer owned by that worker, or the event has already been completed.

However, there is an important limitation.

The claim token protects database state. It cannot stop Worker A from publishing to Kafka after its lease expires.

A lease is not a distributed lock over the external broker.

That is why consumer-side deduplication remains necessary.

8. Retry Strategy and Backoff

Message brokers can be temporarily unavailable.

A worker should not retry a failed event continuously.

That creates unnecessary load and can make an existing outage worse.

Use exponential backoff with jitter.

func retryDelay(attempt int) time.Duration {
    const (
        base = time.Second
        max  = 5 * time.Minute
    )

    if attempt < 1 {
        attempt = 1
    }

    exponent := min(attempt-1, 8)

    delay := base * time.Duration(1<<exponent)

    if delay > max {
        delay = max
    }

    jitter := time.Duration(
        rand.Int64N(int64(delay/2) + 1),
    )

    return delay/2 + jitter
}

This implementation assumes a Go version with math/rand/v2.

The delay grows with each failed attempt but is capped to prevent excessively long retry intervals.

The retry update can look like this:

UPDATE outbox_events
SET
    next_attempt_at = NOW() + ($1 * INTERVAL '1 second'),
    claim_token = NULL,
    lease_until = NULL,
    last_error = $2
WHERE
    id = $3
    AND claim_token = $4
    AND published_at IS NULL;

The repository should pass a bounded, sanitized error message rather than storing arbitrary error output indefinitely.

What about permanently failing events?

Some events will never succeed without intervention.

Examples:

  • Invalid payload.
  • Unsupported schema version.
  • Message exceeds broker limits.
  • A downstream system permanently rejects the event.

A production design needs a poison-event policy.

Possible approaches:

  • Maximum attempt count.
  • Dead-letter table or queue.
  • Manual replay.
  • Alerting and operational investigation.
  • Event quarantine without losing the original payload.

Do not silently delete failed events.

A dead-letter policy should preserve enough information to investigate and replay the operation safely.

Also remember that a maximum retry count is a business and operational decision. Some important events may require indefinite retry with alerting rather than permanent abandonment.

9. The Most Important Failure Window: Publish Succeeds, Database Update Fails

Let's examine the most important scenario.

1. Worker claims event
2. Worker publishes event to Kafka
3. Kafka acknowledges the message
4. Worker crashes
5. published_at is never updated
6. Lease expires
7. Another worker claims and publishes the event again

The event is delivered twice.

This is expected behavior.

The outbox pattern provides durable, at-least-once publication when configured with retries and recovery. It does not provide exactly-once delivery across PostgreSQL and an external broker.

The consumer must be idempotent.

This is not an optional optimization. It is part of the design.

10. Consumer-Side Deduplication

Every event should have a stable identifier.

For example:

{
  "event_id": "b89b5f43-0d7c-45d7-8a9b-9dbcf9fcb1f8",
  "event_type": "order.created",
  "aggregate_id": "order-123",
  "payload": {
    "order_id": "order-123"
  }
}

The consumer stores processed event IDs.

CREATE TABLE processed_events (
    consumer_name TEXT NOT NULL,
    event_id UUID NOT NULL,
    processed_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),

    PRIMARY KEY (consumer_name, event_id)
);

The consumer should insert the deduplication record and apply its business change in the same transaction.

func (c *Consumer) Handle(
    ctx context.Context,
    event Event,
) error {
    tx, err := c.db.BeginTx(ctx, nil)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("begin transaction: %w", err)
    }

    defer tx.Rollback()

    result, err := tx.ExecContext(
        ctx,
        `
        INSERT INTO processed_events (
            consumer_name,
            event_id
        )
        VALUES ($1, $2)
        ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
        `,
        "inventory-service",
        event.ID,
    )
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("insert processed event: %w", err)
    }

    affected, err := result.RowsAffected()
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("read affected rows: %w", err)
    }

    if affected == 0 {
        // Already processed.
        return tx.Commit()
    }

    if err := c.inventory.ApplyEvent(ctx, tx, event); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("apply inventory event: %w", err)
    }

    if err := tx.Commit(); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("commit consumer transaction: %w", err)
    }

    return nil
}

The broker message should only be acknowledged after the database transaction commits.

If the consumer crashes before committing, the transaction rolls back and the message can be delivered again.

If the transaction commits but the broker acknowledgement is lost, the message may be delivered again. The processed_events constraint makes the second delivery harmless.

There is still an important boundary:

If the consumer's business operation calls an external API, that external side effect needs its own idempotency or outbox strategy.

Deduplication only protects effects committed inside the same transaction.

11. Event Ordering Is a Separate Problem

The outbox query uses:

ORDER BY id

Does this guarantee that every event reaches consumers in business order?

Not necessarily.

Multiple workers can claim different events and publish them at different speeds.

Consider:

Order 123:

1. order.created
2. order.paid
3. order.shipped

Worker A claims order.created and becomes slow.

Worker B claims order.paid and publishes it first.

The broker might receive the events in the wrong order.

If ordering matters, define the ordering boundary explicitly.

Possible strategies include:

  • Partition events by aggregate ID.
  • Use a stable aggregate key in Kafka.
  • Maintain an aggregate version or sequence number.
  • Ensure only one active publisher processes a given aggregate.
  • Use a per-aggregate dispatch mechanism.

For example, add:

ALTER TABLE outbox_events
ADD COLUMN aggregate_version BIGINT;

Then enforce uniqueness where appropriate:

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_outbox_aggregate_version
ON outbox_events (
    aggregate_type,
    aggregate_id,
    aggregate_version
);

A stable Kafka partition key helps preserve order within a partition, but it does not fix out-of-order publication before messages reach Kafka.

If strict per-aggregate ordering is required, the dispatcher must also enforce it.

This is an important trade-off: stronger ordering constraints can reduce parallelism.

12. Running the Worker Continuously

The worker needs a lifecycle.

A simple polling loop:

func (w *Worker) Run(ctx context.Context) error {
    ticker := time.NewTicker(500 * time.Millisecond)
    defer ticker.Stop()

    for {
        if err := w.ProcessBatch(ctx); err != nil {
            if ctx.Err() != nil {
                return ctx.Err()
            }

            w.logger.Error(
                "outbox batch failed",
                "error",
                err,
            )
        }

        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return ctx.Err()

        case <-ticker.C:
        }
    }
}

This is intentionally simple.

A production worker should also consider:

  • Immediate processing when work is found.
  • Adaptive polling when the queue is empty.
  • Bounded parallel publishing.
  • Graceful shutdown.
  • Lease renewal for long-running publication.
  • Per-event timeouts.
  • Database and broker connection health.
  • Backpressure when the broker slows down.

One detail is worth emphasizing:

The lease duration must be longer than the expected processing time, or the worker must renew its lease while processing.

Otherwise, another worker may reclaim an event while the original worker is still publishing it.

Even with lease renewal, consumer deduplication remains the final protection against duplicate delivery.

13. Testing the Outbox

A few unit tests are useful, but the most important guarantees involve database transactions and concurrent workers.

Use PostgreSQL integration tests for the following scenarios.

Test 1: Business transaction rollback

  • Insert an order.
  • Insert an outbox event.
  • Force the transaction to fail.
  • Verify that neither record exists.

Test 2: Concurrent workers

  • Insert multiple pending events.
  • Start several workers concurrently.
  • Verify that no two active claims own the same row at the same time.
  • Verify that all events eventually become eligible for publication.

Test 3: Publish succeeds, mark-published fails

  • Make the publisher succeed.
  • Simulate a database failure during MarkPublished.
  • Let the lease expire.
  • Verify that the event can be published again.
  • Verify that the consumer processes the event only once.

Test 4: Worker crash and lease recovery

  • Claim an event.
  • Simulate a worker crash.
  • Wait until the lease expires.
  • Verify that another worker can claim it.

Test 5: Stale worker

  • Worker A claims an event.
  • Its lease expires.
  • Worker B reclaims it.
  • Worker A attempts to update the row.
  • Verify that the old claim token cannot update the event.

Test 6: Poison event

  • Configure the publisher to fail permanently.
  • Verify retry scheduling.
  • Verify that the event reaches the configured dead-letter or alerting policy.

Test 7: Ordering

If your application requires per-aggregate ordering:

  • Insert multiple events for the same aggregate.
  • Process them with multiple workers.
  • Verify that consumers observe the expected sequence.

Avoid testing only the happy path. Most outbox bugs appear between two successful operations.

14. Observability: Know When Events Are Falling Behind

A transactional outbox can be functioning correctly while downstream systems are still experiencing serious delays.

You need visibility into the queue.

Useful metrics include:

outbox_pending_events
outbox_oldest_pending_age_seconds
outbox_publish_attempts_total
outbox_publish_failures_total
outbox_publish_duration_seconds
outbox_events_published_total
outbox_lease_expirations_total
outbox_dead_letter_events_total

Some useful operational signals:

Signal What it might indicate
Pending event count increasing Publisher throughput is below event creation rate
Oldest event age increasing Events are not being delivered quickly enough
Retry count increasing Broker or network instability
Lease expirations increasing Workers are crashing or taking too long
Dead-letter count increasing Events require investigation

Avoid using event IDs, aggregate IDs, or customer IDs as metric labels. They create high-cardinality metrics.

For logs and traces, event IDs and aggregate IDs are useful correlation fields.

A particularly valuable metric is:

NOW() - MIN(created_at)

for unpublished events.

The oldest pending event age often tells you more about the health of the pipeline than the total pending count.

A queue containing 10,000 events might be healthy if they were created seconds ago. A queue containing 20 events might be unhealthy if the oldest has been waiting for an hour.

15. Scaling and Operational Trade-offs

The transactional outbox is straightforward to introduce, but the operational model deserves attention.

Polling vs. CDC

The implementation in this article uses polling.

A worker periodically queries PostgreSQL for pending events.

Advantages:

  • Simple architecture.
  • No additional CDC infrastructure.
  • Easy to inspect and operate.
  • Works with standard PostgreSQL deployments.

Disadvantages:

  • Polling creates database queries even when the queue is empty.
  • High event volume can increase database load.
  • Batch sizing and polling intervals need tuning.

An alternative is Change Data Capture (CDC).

Tools such as Debezium can capture database changes from the PostgreSQL write-ahead log and publish them to a broker.

Advantages:

  • Avoids repeated polling queries.
  • Can scale well for high-volume event streams.
  • Integrates naturally with Kafka-based architectures.

Disadvantages:

  • Additional infrastructure and operational complexity.
  • Schema and connector management.
  • More complex replay and recovery behavior.
  • Still requires idempotent consumers.

The right choice depends on throughput, latency requirements, operational capacity, and existing infrastructure.

Retention and cleanup

Published events should not accumulate forever.

A cleanup job can delete old published events in batches:

WITH old_events AS (
    SELECT id
    FROM outbox_events
    WHERE published_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '7 days'
    ORDER BY id
    LIMIT 1000
)
DELETE FROM outbox_events
WHERE id IN (
    SELECT id FROM old_events
);

The retention period should reflect debugging, replay, compliance, and recovery requirements.

For larger systems, consider partitioning by creation time or moving published events to an archive.

Never remove unpublished events just because they are old.

Backpressure

If event creation is faster than publication, the outbox grows.

A worker cannot solve an indefinitely increasing backlog by polling more frequently.

Monitor the publication rate and pending age.

Consider bounded publishing concurrency, broker capacity, database capacity, and alert thresholds.

The outbox is durable storage, not infinite capacity.

16. Production Checklist

Before deploying a transactional outbox, verify the following:

  • [ ] Business changes and outbox inserts share one database transaction.
  • [ ] Every event has a stable unique ID.
  • [ ] Event payloads have an explicit schema and versioning strategy.
  • [ ] Workers claim rows using FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED.
  • [ ] Database transactions are short and never span broker publication.
  • [ ] Claims have bounded leases.
  • [ ] Stale workers cannot update records owned by newer claims.
  • [ ] Retry scheduling uses exponential backoff and jitter.
  • [ ] Poison events have an explicit handling policy.
  • [ ] Consumers deduplicate events using durable event IDs.
  • [ ] Consumer deduplication and business writes share a transaction.
  • [ ] Ordering requirements are explicitly defined.
  • [ ] Graceful shutdown and lease recovery are tested.
  • [ ] Pending event age and retry rates are monitored.
  • [ ] Published event retention and cleanup are configured.
  • [ ] HTTP operations that create events are idempotent.

Conclusion

Reliable event publishing is not just about calling Kafka after a database insert.

It is about handling the failure windows between independent systems.

The transactional outbox pattern gives your application a durable boundary: when a business transaction commits, the event that represents that change is committed with it.

A separate worker handles publication, retries failures, and recovers abandoned work.

But the pattern does not guarantee exactly-once delivery.

A publisher can crash after the broker accepts an event. A lease can expire while a worker is still running. A message can be delivered more than once.

That's why the complete design needs stable event IDs, consumer-side deduplication, explicit ordering rules, and operational visibility.

Don't try to make two independent systems commit together. Make the intent durable in one transaction, then deliver it reliably.

That's the foundation of a dependable event-driven architecture in Go.

Further Reading

  • Microservices.io — Transactional Outbox
  • Debezium — Outbox Event Router
  • PostgreSQL — SELECT and FOR UPDATE
  • PostgreSQL — INSERT and ON CONFLICT
  • Go — database/sql
  • Apache Kafka — Message Delivery Semantics

title: Google indexed 30 of my 547 pages. Here's what was wrong with my React SPA.
description:
I run GAGPedia, a free fan-made calculator and guide site for the Roblox game Grow a Garden: trade (Win/Fair/Loss) checks, plant values with mutation multipliers, pet XP tools, a codes page and some strategy guides. It's a Vite + React + TypeScript single-page app on Vercel, with game data in Supabase.

After eight months live, Search Console looked like this:

  • 547 URLs in the sitemap, 30 indexed
  • 508 "Discovered – currently not indexed"
  • 39 clicks from Google in total

Meanwhile Bing (plus Yahoo and DuckDuckGo, which use its index) was sending roughly ten times more search visits than Google. So the pages weren't broken. Google just didn't think most of them were worth indexing. Here's what I found and fixed, in order of impact.

1. 487 pages that were 80% the same

The site generated a page for every pet (372) and every plant (115). Each one came out of the same template: about 325 words, of which one or two sentences were actually unique (an XP rate, a rank, a tier). I diffed two pet pages and they were 80% identical word for word.

That's textbook thin programmatic content, and on a young site with few backlinks it doesn't just fail to rank — it drags down how Google sees everything else.

Deleting the pages wasn't an option, since Bing ranks them and players use them. So the fix is a Googlebot-only noindex, which other crawlers ignore:

<meta name="googlebot" content="noindex, follow" />

follow keeps link equity flowing from those pages to the calculators and hub pages. I also dropped them from sitemap.xml, which went from 547 URLs to 60: the pages I actually want in Google. The rule lives in one constant, so a page can come back once it has real unique content.

2. My best articles were 120 words long (to a crawler)

The "Crawled – currently not indexed" list was mostly my Academy guides: 1,000–3,000-word articles. The prerendered HTML told a different story. The build step wrote a short summary into each page's static HTML, and the real article only appeared after JavaScript ran. To a crawler's first fetch, my longest guide was ~125 words.

The fix was to server-render the actual React components at build time, inside the existing Vite plugin's closeBundle hook:

const server = await createServer({
  configFile: false,
  root: process.cwd(),
  resolve: { alias: { "@": path.resolve("src") } },
  esbuild: { jsx: "automatic" },
  appType: "custom",
  server: { middlewareMode: true, hmr: false },
  ssr: { resolve: { externalConditions: ["module-sync"] } },
});
const mod = await server.ssrLoadModule("/src/ssr/articles.tsx");
// mod.renderArticleMain(route) -> renderToString(<MemoryRouter>…) -> <main>…</main>

Two gotchas cost me most of the time:

  • react-router v7 under Node resolved to its CommonJS build, so Vite's SSR loader couldn't see named exports like MemoryRouter. Its package exports only point at the ESM build under the module-sync condition, hence externalConditions: ["module-sync"].
  • jsxDEV is not a function. Loading the app's own Vite config in serve mode compiled JSX for React's dev runtime, while the build process runs with NODE_ENV=production. A standalone config with esbuild's automatic JSX runtime fixed it.

Any render error falls back to the old summary, so a broken article can never fail a deploy. The guides now ship 800–2,400 words of real HTML each.

3. The flash I introduced (and then fixed)

The static HTML lives inside #root, and main.tsx clears it before React mounts. But the browser paints that static HTML first, so on every reload visitors saw a plain, differently styled page for a moment. Light-theme users got a dark page.

Two lines in the <head> hide it for JavaScript-capable browsers, with a timeout in case the app never loads:

<style>html.js-app #seo-prerender { visibility: hidden; }</style>
<script>
  document.documentElement.classList.add('js-app');
  setTimeout(function () {
    if (document.getElementById('seo-prerender'))
      document.documentElement.classList.remove('js-app');
  }, 4000);
</script>

Crawlers and no-JS visitors still get the full content. It's the same content React renders.

4. Every visitor downloaded an auth SDK

A source-map breakdown of the main bundle showed the full Supabase client (auth, storage, realtime, postgrest) at the top. Public pages only use it to refresh game data, and they already render from bundled seed data through React Query's initialData. So the public hooks now import the client on demand:

export function getSupabase() {
  clientPromise ??= import("@/integrations/supabase/client").then((m) => m.supabase);
  return clientPromise;
}

Main bundle: 210 KB → 152 KB gzipped. The client is now its own chunk that loads after the page is on screen.

5. Telling Bing the moment a deploy goes live

Since Bing was already my biggest search source, I added IndexNow: a public key file, plus a GitHub Action that runs on Vercel's deployment_status event for successful Production deploys. It reads the live sitemap and POSTs every URL to api.indexnow.org. The first run got back 202 Accepted for all 60 URLs.

6. The audit script that couldn't see 115 broken links

The project has a small Python audit for titles, canonicals, JSON-LD and internal links. On Windows it reported thousands of errors, which made it useless, so nobody noticed it was wrong. It built routes with str(path), which gave backslashes on Windows, so every internal link looked broken. Switching to .as_posix() (and reading files as UTF-8) brought it down to one real problem: every plant page linked to /mutations/none, a page that doesn't exist. Fixed that, and the audit now passes with 0 errors across 549 pages.

What I'd tell my past self

  • Read Search Console's "why not indexed" reasons before writing anything new. "Discovered" and "Crawled – currently not indexed" are Google telling you about quality, not about crawling.
  • Look at your raw HTML, not your rendered page. curl and a word count would have caught the 120-word articles months earlier.
  • Programmatic pages need programmatic uniqueness. If the template is 80% of the page, the page probably shouldn't be in Google yet.

It's too early for results, since Google takes weeks to re-crawl. I'll post an update with the indexing numbers once they move.

Disclosure: I worked through these fixes with an AI coding assistant (Claude), which also helped draft this post. I've checked every number here against Search Console, Analytics and the live site; code snippets are trimmed versions of what's in the repo.

title: One /* in .taurignore and tauri dev watched nothing
description:
tauri dev is one of those things you stop thinking about. You save a Rust file, it rebuilds, the app comes back. So when it quietly stops rebuilding, it takes a while to even notice.

That's what issue #9163 was about. It had been open since March 2024. The reporter wanted tauri dev to watch only a few things, so they wrote their .taurignore as an allow list. Trimmed a little (their file also kept icons/), it looked like this:

/*
!/*.toml
!/*.rs
!/src

Ignore everything at the top, then bring back the .toml files, the .rs files and src/. Same file as a .gitignore? Works fine. As a .taurignore? tauri dev stopped watching the app completely. Edit src/main.rs, nothing happens.

I picked it up, and the fix got merged in tauri-apps/tauri#16398. The fix that got merged is not the one I sent first, though, and that part is honestly the most useful bit of this story.

Reproducing it

Tauri's repo has a tiny app in bench/tests/helloworld. I dropped the .taurignore into its src-tauri folder and ran tauri dev. The CLI prints every folder it's watching, and the app folder just wasn't in the list.

Why it happened

The dev watcher lives in crates/tauri-cli/src/interface/rust.rs. Before my change it did roughly this:

for path in watch_folders {
  if !ignore_matcher.is_ignore(&path, true) {
    // watch every entry of `path`
  }
}

So before watching a folder, it asked the ignore matcher: is this folder itself ignored? For the app folder, that's the same folder the .taurignore sits in.

The matcher comes from the ignore crate (the one ripgrep uses). Patterns in an ignore file are relative to the file's own folder, so the crate strips that folder off the path before matching. Ask it about the folder itself and you're left with an empty path. And /* matches the empty path too.

So the app folder counted as ignored and got skipped. The !/src lines never had a chance, because they bring back things inside the folder, and the watcher never looked inside.

Git doesn't have this problem because it never applies a .gitignore to the folder the file lives in. Only to what's below it. That one difference was the whole bug.

My first fix

Since git was the behaviour everyone expected, I copied it. In IgnoreMatcher::is_ignore, skip an ignore file when the path you're asking about is that file's own folder. Everything inside the app matched exactly like before, and a .taurignore in a parent folder could still ignore a child folder.

I wrote the test first, using the .taurignore above, and watched it fail on the old code. Then the fix, and the test passed. tauri dev on the bench app showed the app folder in the "Watching … for changes" log again. Then I opened the PR.

The review

Legend-Master from the Tauri team requested changes. His point was that negative patterns are tricky to support, and treating /* at the root as a special case didn't really make sense. Then he asked whether we should just always watch the folders and filter the change events instead.

He was right, and when I thought about it, it was a better way to see the problem. My fix answered "is this folder ignored?" more carefully. His idea was to stop asking that question about the watch folders at all. A watch folder is something you told Tauri to watch. The ignore rules are about what's in it.

The fix that got merged

I reworked the PR around that. A new helper, watch_targets, lists what to watch: every entry of every watch folder that isn't ignored.

fn watch_targets(watch_folders: &[PathBuf]) -> Vec<(PathBuf, RecursiveMode)> {
  let mut targets = Vec::new();
  for path in watch_folders {
    lookup(path, |file_type, p| {
      if p != *path {
        let mode = if file_type.is_dir() {
          RecursiveMode::Recursive
        } else {
          RecursiveMode::NonRecursive
        };
        targets.push((p, mode));
      }
    });
  }
  targets
}

lookup already existed. It walks one level of the folder with the ignore crate's WalkBuilder, set up to read .taurignore (plus the watcher rules Tauri ships with), so ignored entries never come back from it. The walk also hands back the folder itself, which is what the p != *path check skips.

The watch loop then stops asking about the folder:

// logging lines left out
for (path, mode) in watch_targets(&watch_folders) {
  let _ = watcher.watch(&path, mode);
}

Change events are still filtered by IgnoreMatcher::is_ignore, same as before, so touching an ignored file doesn't trigger a rebuild.

Two tests cover it, both with the .taurignore from the issue. The first, watch_targets_watch_a_folder_whose_taurignore_matches_it, checks that the watched entries are exactly Cargo.toml and src. The second, ignore_matcher_filters_events_under_a_root_wide_pattern, checks that the matcher the event loop uses keeps src/, src/main.rs and Cargo.toml, and ignores README.md and assets/.

And the real check: with that file, editing README.md triggers no rebuild, and editing src/main.rs triggers one.

Legend-Master approved it. He mentioned that from his experience with parcel's watcher (the one VS Code uses), it seemed to watch the whole folder and match ignore patterns before events reach the app, and this change basically matches that. FabianLars approved too. It was merged on 12 November 2026 and shipped in tauri-cli and @tauri-apps/cli 2.12.5.

What I'm keeping from this one

The reporter's file was the best test fixture I could have asked for. I barely changed it.

When something works as a .gitignore and not as your file, ask what git does differently. That question is what pointed me at the root folder.

And the big one for me: my first fix passed its tests, but it added a special case. The maintainer's version deleted the question that caused the bug, and the code got simpler. I'll take that trade every time.

Thanks Legend-Master and FabianLars for the reviews. If you've hit this before, or you do file watching differently in your project, I'd really like to hear how. Drop a comment.
