title: The Transaction Only Covers Your Database. The Provider Key Is What Saves You
description:
Two readers asked me the same question from opposite sides last week, and I have been running it ever since. itsvicmoreno asked it on my piece about claiming a delivery once: the processed-keys table stops the second copy, but what if the receiver crashes between writing the key and charging the card? sunnatulla_dev asked the matching half on the other piece: he had already tried it in his own head, one crash, two attempts, zero charges: the key written, the retry refused as a duplicate, and nothing ever charged.

Both of them were right to worry. A key and a charge are two separate writes, and a crash can land between them. Which order breaks first, and what actually saves you? I crashed the receiver on purpose, in both orders, against four different shapes, with the same $29 payment for the same order, and counted the charges from the receiver's own tables. The results are clear, and one of them made me change my mind about a fix I used to recommend without thinking.

Problem 1: key first, and the payment quietly never happens

The first crash is the one sunnatulla_dev described. The receiver writes the key, then dies before the charge. The sender sees the connection drop and tries again. The retry finds the key already in the table and gets a polite 200 duplicate. Nothing charges. Ever.

My run: 2 attempts, 0 charges. Exactly his shape, down to the numbers. The customer is never charged, the order sits unpaid, and nobody gets an error. The system looks healthy from every angle except the one that matters: no money moved. A duplicate refusal is only correct if the first attempt actually did the work, and here it did not. The key is a promise that the charge happened, and the crash broke the promise.

This is the quiet failure, and I think it is the one people underestimate. A double charge shows up in a bank statement and somebody shouts. A lost charge shows up weeks later, in a report, as revenue that never arrived, and by then nobody remembers the crash.

Problem 2: charge first, and the customer pays twice

Now flip the order. The receiver charges first, then dies before writing the key. The retry finds no key, so it charges again. Same $29, same order, second charge.

My run: 2 attempts, 2 charges. $58 for a $29 order. This is the order that breaks first, and itsvicmoreno's question bet exactly that: the charge lands and the key never does. The retry has nothing to check, because the only record of the first charge lives at the provider, and this receiver never asks the provider anything.

So both orders are broken, in opposite directions. Key first loses the payment. Charge first doubles it. If you have to pick a failure, pick the lost one — at least nobody's card was charged twice. But picking a failure is not a design. The fix has to cover both orders, not one.

Problem 3: the transaction saves your database, not your money

The first fix people reach for is the obvious one: put the key and the charge in one transaction, so they commit together or roll back together. I ran it. Crash before the commit, the whole thing rolls back, the retry charges exactly once. 2 attempts, 1 charge. It works.

But it works only inside your own database. The transaction covers the key and your local record of the charge. The charge itself happens at the provider, outside your database, outside your transaction, outside everything you can roll back. If the crash lands between the provider's charge and your mark-done, the transaction has nothing to say about it. The provider took the money. Your database says processing. The retry has to decide, and the transaction cannot decide for it.

I used to describe the single transaction as the answer to this problem. It is not the answer. It is a good answer to a smaller problem: keeping your own records consistent. The money lives somewhere else, and the fix has to reach there.

Problem 4: the lease has to be measured, and 30 seconds was a guess

The second fix is a status column with a lease. The key goes in as processing, with a time limit. A retry while the lease is alive gets a 409 and waits. After the lease expires, the row can be reclaimed and the charge retried. A crashed holder stops holding the row, eventually.

sunnatulla_dev ran this shape in his own test with a 30 second lease: the copy in flight got a 409, the crashed one got a 409, then it was reclaimed at 60 seconds, one charge each. My job was to check that number, and to set the lease from something real instead of 30 seconds picked out of the air.

So I measured first. One hundred real charge calls through the receiver, and I took the p99, the time almost every healthy call finishes inside. Run 1: p99 1.89 seconds, so the lease was 2.39 seconds. Run 2: p99 0.96 seconds, lease 1.46 seconds. The p99 moved between runs because handler time on this small machine includes scheduling stalls; run 1 even caught a 5.48 second stall. That is the point of measuring: the lease has to beat the longest a healthy handler can actually run on the machine it runs on, stalls included, plus slack. A lease picked from a round number cannot know that.

Then I crashed the lease arm and retried every half second. Run 1: three 409s, reclaimed 3.21 seconds after the crash, 1 charge. Run 2: two 409s, reclaimed 2.12 seconds after the crash, 1 charge. Not 60 seconds. The reclaim lands one retry after the lease expires, so the honest number is the lease plus your retry gap. His 60 seconds came from his 30 second lease plus his retry rhythm, not from the mechanism. With a lease set from p99, the crashed row is reclaimable roughly one lease after the crash, about two to three seconds here.

One more detail that matters: while the charge runs, the handler renews the lease, every third of a lease. Without that, a slow-but-alive charge gets reclaimed mid-flight and charges twice, which is the exact failure the lease was supposed to prevent. A lease without renewal is a timer that punishes the slow and rewards the dead.

Problem 5: the provider key is the only shape that survives both orders

The third fix is the one itsvicmoreno pointed at. Insert the key as processing, pass that same key to the provider as its idempotency key, then mark it done. A retry that finds processing does not charge again. It asks the provider: did this key already charge? If yes, mark it done and stop.

I crashed this shape after the provider charge, before the mark-done. 2 attempts, 1 provider charge, 1 local charge. The retry asked, the provider said already charged, nothing charged twice. Then I ran it in the charge-first order too: provider charge first, local key still pending, crash, retry, and the retry asked the provider first, before touching the local key table. Same result: 1 provider charge. It is the only shape in the test that stays at exactly one charge in both orders, including the window the transaction cannot see.

That is my claim, and I expect people to argue with it: the single transaction is the wrong place to put your trust, because the money does not live in your database. The status column with a measured lease is good and honest, and I would keep it as the backstop. But the thing that actually saves you from a crash between the key and the charge is the provider's own idempotency key, the same key on both sides, with the retry asking instead of charging. Everything else is bookkeeping about a charge that already happened somewhere else.

Have you ever been charged twice for one order, or had a payment quietly never go through after a crash? Which side did it break on, and what did the retry do: ask first, or charge first? I would like to hear what it was, because the retry is where the money is decided, and most of us never look at it until it has already decided wrong.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

title: Polarity Composition Hypothesis: Causal Evidence from Negation in NLI
description:
arXiv:2611.23185v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We investigate how language models process negation in natural language inference (NLI). We propose the \textit{Polarity Composition Hypothesis}, a high-level causal model of this computation. Behavioral evaluations show that language-model predictions largely conform to the proposed hypothesis. Using Distributed Alignment Search, we identify causally effective subspaces aligned with the variables in the polarity-composition hypothesis. These representations transfer across negation forms and partially to a subset of MNLI. We release the dataset and code.

title: Building a Locale-Aware Slug Generator That Handles Spanish Accents
description:
URL slugs for Spanish-language content break if you just call .toLowerCase().replace(/\s+/g, '-'). The accented characters á é í ó ú ñ ü are valid UTF-8 but most slug generators strip them, producing unreadable URLs or, worse, collisions (año and ano are different words).

Normalise, then map

The standard approach uses Unicode NFD decomposition to separate base letters from combining marks, then drops the marks:

function slugify(text) {
  return text
    .normalize('NFD')
    .replace(/[\u0300-\u036f]/g, '')  // strip combining marks
    .replace(/ñ/gi, 'n')               // ñ decomposes differently
    .toLowerCase()
    .replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, '-')
    .replace(/^-|-$/g, '');
}

The ñ special-case matters: NFD splits ñ into n + combining tilde, but some fonts and copy-paste paths deliver a precomposed ñ (U+00F1) that survives the regex. Handling both is safer.

Collision detection

Two distinct Spanish phrases can produce the same slug after stripping. A content platform like bonus at Casinito that serves a Latin American audience needs a uniqueness check at insert time, appending a numeric suffix when a collision is found:

async function uniqueSlug(base, existing) {
  let candidate = base;
  let i = 1;
  while (existing.has(candidate)) candidate = `${base}-${++i}`;
  return candidate;
}

SEO note

Google handles UTF-8 slugs fine, but many analytics tools and affiliate trackers silently truncate or encode them. If your stack includes third-party tracking, ASCII-safe slugs avoid a whole class of broken attribution.

title: One WebRTC stack, sixteen languages: deleting the mirrors
description:
grpc-over-datachannels started the way most multi-language
projects do: one WebRTC stack (ICE, DTLS, SCTP) written in
Rust, then mirrored by hand into Go and JavaScript so each
native stack could run standalone. Three implementations
of the same protocols, kept in sync by discipline and a
conformance suite.

That discipline already failed once. In v0.32 a fragment
reassembly bug — fragments merged across a message
boundary — wedged ordered delivery in one stack while the
others were fine. The fix taught us the actual lesson: the
state machines that must not drift should not exist three
times. So 0.44.0 deletes two of them.

Sans-io cores, two consumption shapes

The Rust stack was already mostly pump-driven: feed a
datagram in, get packets and events out, no sockets or
threads inside. We finished that extraction for all three
protocols:

  • SCTP: dc-sctp-ffi (C ABI) + dc-sctp-wasm
  • DTLS: the handshake lifted into a resumable flight machine (DtlsHandshake), dc-dtls-ffi + dc-dtls-wasm
  • ICE: the agent turned out to be sans-io already; gathering/TURN/mDNS were always host-side. dc-ice-ffi
    • dc-ice-wasm

Go consumes the cores through cgo behind small seams
(sctpAssoc, DtlsConn, the IceAgent API). JavaScript
consumes the same cores compiled to Wasm. The browser
bridge and every generated facade language ride the same
Rust runtime. There is now exactly one SCTP, one DTLS,
and one ICE implementation in the project.

The honest cost: about 311 ns per delivered message
across the FFI versus 173 ns for the old mirrored Go
stack. We measured it, and we'd pay it again: it's the
price of one conformance-tested implementation instead of
three that can drift. Throughput on the echo path is
~8,300 messages/second at 0.36 ms mean RTT (mux_bench).

Flipping the defaults found the bugs

The mirrors stayed as the default until every consumer
was wired. Flipping Go and JS to the Rust cores — then
deleting the mirrors — is where the interesting failures
lived:

  • The DTLS pump that died on undefined. In the Wasm adapter, one non-application DTLS record (a session ticket) mapped Rust's None to JavaScript undefined, the receive check tested only for null, and every endpoint pump threw. Sequential tests passed; eight concurrent rendezvous dials killed all eight pumps.
  • The 64-packet queue. Bursty MiB messages overflowed the peer's small DTLS demux queue; the drops became SCTP retransmit storms and truncated chunk echoes — but only on the (slightly slower) FFI path. The queue is 4096 deep now, and there's a permanent queued tail-drop blast regression test in the Rust suite.
  • A registry test that raced itself. Two client endpoints shared one in-memory transport and raced for frames; it hung for 9m56s in GitHub CI before timing out (that failure is what the current public CI red was sitting on). One transport pair per client; fixed.
  • Public CI archaeology. The generated repos' Go, browser, and interop jobs each needed the cores built before use — three generator fixes, shipped as export fixups.

Oracles without mirrors

Deleting a second implementation deletes your differential
oracle, so the conformance net is now mirror-free by
design: OpenSSL differentials for DTLS (dtls_openssl,
crypto_openssl), the shared SCTP vectors through every
surface, the ICE consent/trickle suites against the core,
and full Go + JS suites that only have the Rust path to
run on. make ci-status sweeps the generated repos'
CI in one command; it's all green on v0.44.0.

The mirrors totaled roughly 4,400 lines of Go and
JavaScript. What's left is one stack, maintained once,
spoken everywhere.

title: Implementing a Fair Shuffle Algorithm for a Card Game UI
description:
The Fisher-Yates shuffle is the standard fair shuffle. The mistake most developers make is not in the algorithm — it is in the random number generator they feed it.

Fisher-Yates, correctly 

function shuffle(arr) {
  const a = [...arr];
  for (let i = a.length - 1; i > 0; i--) {
    const j = Math.floor(Math.random() * (i + 1));
    [a[i], a[j]] = [a[j], a[i]];
  }
  return a;
}

The common bug: using Math.floor(Math.random() * a.length) instead of Math.floor(Math.random() * (i + 1)). The first produces a biased distribution — some permutations are more likely than others.

Why Math.random() is insufficient

Math.random() uses a PRNG (xorshift128+ in V8) with a 128-bit state. For a 52-card deck, there are 52! ≈ 2^226 possible permutations. A 128-bit PRNG can only produce 2^128 distinct sequences — a vanishingly small fraction. For a display-only shuffle (like a card game tutorial), this is fine. For anything involving real outcomes, use crypto.getRandomValues:

function cryptoRandom(max) {
  const arr = new Uint32Array(1);
  crypto.getRandomValues(arr);
  return arr[0] % max; // slight bias for large max, acceptable for max < 2^20
}

Visual fairness

Even a mathematically fair shuffle can look unfair. If the same card appears in the first position three times in a row, users suspect cheating. A game interface like play at Spinhub that displays dealt hands needs to balance actual fairness with perceived fairness — sometimes that means showing the shuffle animation longer, not changing the algorithm.

Testing fairness

Run the shuffle 1M times, count how often each element lands in each position. The chi-squared test should show no significant deviation from uniform:

from scipy.stats import chisquare
observed = [count_in_position[i][j] for j in range(n)]
stat, p = chisquare(observed)
assert p > 0.01

Takeaway

The algorithm is trivial. The randomness source and the user perception of randomness are where the real engineering lives.

title: How We Built a 165 µs Reversible PII Anonymizer for LLMs & MCP in Rust (212x Faster Than Presidio)
description:
Every time an AI agent, RAG pipeline, or MCP tool sends a prompt to an external LLM API, there is a high chance it carries sensitive data: customer emails, credit card numbers, IBANs, national tax IDs, PostgreSQL connection strings, or leaked API keys.

Most teams try to solve this in one of two ways:

  1. Python NLP pipelines (like Microsoft Presidio + spaCy): ~35 ms per prompt, ~450 MB RAM footprint, and no native support for restoring streamed SSE tokens.
  2. Cloud DLP APIs (like AWS Comprehend PII): 80–250 ms of network latency, \$100+ per million requests, and you still have to send raw PII over the wire to a third-party cloud.

At GLASTOR®, we needed sub-millisecond, zero-egress, reversible PII protection that works inline with OpenAI/Anthropic SSE streams and Model Context Protocol (MCP) agents.

So we built pii-veil in Rust — and you can test it right now in your browser (100% client-side WebAssembly, zero data leaves your device):

👉 Live WASM Playground: https://pii-veil.pages.dev

👉 Open-Source Repository: https://github.com/glastor-core/pii-veil

The Hard Problem: Reversible Streaming Restoration

Redacting an outgoing prompt is only half the problem. If you replace maria@startup.io with [EMAIL_1] and 4532-0151-1283-0366 with [CREDIT_CARD_1], the LLM responds using those semantic placeholders:

"Invoice sent to [EMAIL_1] for card [CREDIT_CARD_1]."

In production, LLMs stream responses token-by-token over Server-Sent Events (SSE). A placeholder like [EMAIL_1] frequently arrives split across chunk boundaries:

Chunk 1: "Invoice sent to [EMA"
Chunk 2: "IL_1] for card [CREDIT_"
Chunk 3: "CARD_1]."

Naive regex replacement breaks immediately on split chunks. pii-veil solves this with StreamingRestorer, a state-machine buffer that detects partial placeholder prefixes at chunk boundaries and restores them in 69.65 µs per SSE chunk without buffering the entire response.

Benchmarks: pii-veil vs. Presidio vs. AWS Comprehend

Measured on standard x86_64 hardware using Rust's criterion statistical harness (reproducible via cargo bench -p pii-veil-core --bench bench_throughput):

Metric / Capability 🛡️ GLASTOR® pii-veil 🐍 Microsoft Presidio ☁️ AWS Comprehend
Typical Prompt Latency (1 KB, 7 entities) 165.68 µs (0.165 ms) ~35 ms ~140 ms
Single-Entity Scan Latency 4.01 µs ~12 ms ~90 ms
1 MB Throughput Buffer 20.58 ms (~46.3 MiB/s) ~4,200 ms (4.2 s) Not supported
Speedup Baseline (1x) ~212x faster ~848x faster
SSE Streaming Restoration 69.65 µs / chunk ❌ Not supported ❌ Not supported
Memory Footprint < 15 MB (Distroless) ~450 MB (spaCy) Cloud Service
Cost per 1M Requests \$0.00 (Self-Hosted) Compute cost \$100.00+ USD

Why is it ~212x faster? 

Presidio: Prompt -> Python -> spaCy NLP -> Tokenizer -> Non-SIMD Regex -> Copies [25–60 ms]
pii-veil: &str -> Rust Zero-Copy Slices -> Aho-Corasick SIMD Pre-Filter -> Checksum Validators -> In-Place Vault [0.16 ms]

Instead of loading a 450 MB ML model to detect structured PII and secrets, pii-veil combines SIMD-accelerated aho-corasick pre-filtering with 18 detectors backed by mathematical checksums (Luhn for credit cards, ISO 13616 Mod-97 for IBANs, Mod-23 for Spain DNI/NIE, Mod-11 for Argentina CUIT/CUIL and Chile RUT) to eliminate false positives.

Drop-In Usage: CLI, Proxy, MCP & GitHub Actions

1. Redact & Restore with an Authenticated Encrypted Vault 

veil redact \
  --text "Charge maria@startup.io (CUIT 20-12345678-6) on card 4532-0151-1283-0366" \
  --vault-out vault.enc \
  --vault-pass "my-secret-passphrase"

veil restore \
  --text "Invoice sent to [EMAIL_1] (tax ID [NATIONAL_ID_1]) for card [CREDIT_CARD_1]." \
  --vault vault.enc \
  --vault-pass "my-secret-passphrase"

2. Built-in HTTP/SSE Proxy & MCP Server

  • veil proxy --listen 127.0.0.1:8080 --echo: Transparently redacts outgoing LLM JSON payloads and restores incoming text/event-stream SSE responses.
  • veil mcp: Zero-dependency JSON-RPC 2.0 MCP server over stdio exposing veil_redact, veil_restore, veil_redact_json, and veil_scan directly to Claude Desktop, Cursor, and Windsurf.

3. CI/CD DLP Gatekeeper (glastor-core/pii-veil@v1) 

- name: 🛡️ PII & Secret DLP Audit
  uses: glastor-core/pii-veil@v1
  with:
    path: "."
    exclude: "examples,tests"
    fail-on-detect: "true"

Try It in 3 Seconds

  • Live WASM Demo (zero backend): https://pii-veil.pages.dev
  • GitHub Repo & Multi-Language SDKs (Rust, Python, Node.js, Go): https://github.com/glastor-core/pii-veil
  • Follow the open-source ecosystem: @glastor-core on GitHub

Engineered by *GLASTOR®** — High-Performance Rust Systems, AI Infrastructure & DevSecOps Engineering. Need on-premise air-gapped deployments, SOC 2 / HIPAA / GDPR compliance logs, or custom DLP rules? Reach out at founder@glastor.es.*

title: When WireMock Becomes Shared Infrastructure: Why I Build StubDeck
description:
WireMock is easy to like when it is local.

You create a few stub mappings, start the server, point your application at it, and get predictable responses. For a single developer, JSON files and the Admin API are often enough.

The interesting problems start when the same WireMock instance becomes shared infrastructure.

Now several developers are changing mappings. The number of stubs grows. Multiple mappings can target the same endpoint. Someone changes a priority. Someone else changes the same mapping. A runtime change works, but nobody is sure whether it has been persisted.

At that point, the problem is no longer just creating mocks. It is managing shared state.

That is the problem I wanted to explore with StubDeck.

StubDeck is an independent open-source project. It does not replace WireMock and is not affiliated with the WireMock project. It acts as a management layer around an existing WireMock environment.

The point where JSON stops being enough
A normal WireMock mapping is simple:

{
  "request": {
    "method": "GET",
    "urlPath": "/api/customer/123"   
  },
  "response": {
    "status": 200,
    "jsonBody": {
        "name": "John"
    }
  }
}

With a small local setup, I would not add another tool. Editing the file directly is faster.

A shared environment creates a different set of questions:

  • How many mappings are registered right now?
  • Which endpoints already have stubs?
  • Why did this request hit that mapping?
  • Are several mappings competing for the same request?
  • Which priorities are configured?
  • Who changed this mapping?
  • Does it have a pending runtime change?
  • Has the current runtime state been persisted?

Those questions are not about JSON syntax. They are about visibility, coordination, and state management.

Making overlapping mappings visible
One of the first areas I focused on was overlapping mappings.

POST /api/payments
POST /api/payments
POST /api/payments

The same method and URL do not automatically mean the mappings are equivalent. Headers, body matchers, query parameters, and other request criteria can make them intentionally different.

But this is still a useful place to look for ambiguity.

WireMock has a priority mechanism for this. A lower numeric value means a higher priority. If multiple matching stubs have the same priority, the most recently added matching stub takes precedence.

StubDeck groups mappings by method and URL on a Conflicts page so these areas can be inspected directly instead of discovered by searching through files.

POST /api/payments  

Priority 1    Payment declined by risk
Priority 5    Payment approved
Priority 10   Default payment response

When a mapping is saved, StubDeck can apply a conflict strategy: BLOCK, WARN, or ALLOW.

A form when it helps, raw JSON when it does not
For common changes, a form is convenient:

Method:     POST
URL:        /api/payments
Status:     200
Priority:   5

But a WireMock mapping can be much richer than a fixed form. I did not want the UI to hide WireMock itself.

The editor therefore supports both a form for common request/response fields and a Raw JSON view. JSON can be validated before it is saved, and templates provide starting points for common REST and error scenarios.

Pending changes become ownership
The next problem appears only when several people use the same server.

StubDeck tracks runtime changes that have not yet been persisted or discarded. A pending change has an owner. While that pending change exists, another user cannot silently overwrite or delete the same mapping.

Pending change by: Ivan Petrov

This is deliberately simpler than a distributed collaborative editing model. It solves a practical problem: make ownership of an unfinished runtime change visible and prevent accidental overwrites.

Runtime state is not persisted state
This matters especially in containerized shared environments.

WireMock exposes an Admin API for changing mappings at runtime and an operation for persisting mappings. Treating runtime state and persisted state as the same thing can produce a surprise after a restart.

StubDeck makes the distinction explicit and exposes two high-level actions:

Save to disk
Discard changes

The goal is not to invent a new persistence model. It is to make the existing lifecycle visible.

Who changed this mapping?
Once a mock server becomes shared, this question appears sooner or later.

StubDeck keeps a changelog for CREATE, UPDATE, and DELETE operations, including the user, mapping, and timestamp.

2026-11-07 15:42
UPDATE
ivan.petrov
POST /api/payments

That does not turn StubDeck into a version control system, but it is enough to answer a common debugging question quickly.

Two ways to connect
StubDeck supports two mapping sources:

  • File system for direct work with mapping JSON files.
  • Admin API for an already running WireMock instance.

StubDeck does not proxy mocked application traffic. It sits next to WireMock as a management layer.

Why not just keep editing JSON?
You should, when that is the simplest solution.

If one developer owns a small local WireMock setup, adding a management UI can be unnecessary overhead.

The tool starts to make sense when several conditions appear together:

  • many mappings
  • shared WireMock
  • multiple developers
  • overlapping endpoints
  • runtime changes

That is the distinction I care about. StubDeck is not an attempt to make JSON prettier. It is an attempt to manage a shared WireMock environment.

Current state and limitations
The current project uses Java 25 and Spring Boot 4.0.5. The local development environment uses WireMock 3.13.2 through Docker Compose, together with a test LDAP server.

There are also intentional limitations in the first public version:

  • one WireMock instance is managed at a time;
  • StubDeck itself must run as a single application replica;
  • a production Docker image for StubDeck is not provided yet;
  • multi-instance and multi-replica support are roadmap items.

The single-replica restriction is not a throughput limitation. Pending-change ownership and the changelog currently depend on local application state. Multiple replicas would need shared state and coordination to preserve consistent behavior.

What I want to build next
The first major direction is multi-instance support.

The second direction is change management. Instead of recording only individual actions, I want to treat a group of changes as a unit:

Change set #42
+ CREATE  POST /payments
~ UPDATE  GET  /accounts/*
- DELETE  GET  /legacy/user

[View diff]  [Apply]  [Discard]

That naturally leads to diffs, rollback, review, and eventually promotion of a change set between environments.

Why I am publishing it
I am publishing StubDeck because I want to understand how common this problem is outside the environments I have worked with.
I am especially interested in teams that:

  • have hundreds or thousands of mappings;
  • share one WireMock instance across developers or teams;
  • run separate DEV, QA, or integration environments;
  • need an audit trail for mapping changes;
  • regularly deal with overlapping stubs and priority questions.

GitHub: https://github.com/SlavaDenisenko/stubdeck

If that sounds familiar, I would like to hear how you manage it today and which part is the most painful.

Technical references

  • WireMock stubbing and priority: https://wiremock.org/docs/stubbing/
  • WireMock Administration API: https://wiremock.org/docs/standalone/administration/
  • WireMock Admin API reference: https://wiremock.org/docs/standalone/admin-api-reference/

title: VRLLM: Turning LLMs into Powerful Tabular Classifiers
description:
arXiv:2611.22308v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on text, but whether pretrained LLMs are effective for large-scale tabular classification remains unclear, as many previous works demonstrate that LLMs' tabular data classification performance falls behind tree-based models or neural architectures designed for tabular data. At Visa Research, we managed to fine-tune a pretrained Llama 3.2 1B LLM on billions of rows of labeled tabular data and make it outperform a wide array of tabular classifiers and even our competitive production deep learning model. For ease of reference, we refer to the model as the Visa Research LLM (VRLLM). In this paper, we share how we achieved this exciting result, covering data preparation, training recipe, ablation studies of design choices and deployment validation. We also benchmark frontier LLMs on the same task and analyze their prediction behavior across model families and generations. Our interpretability experiments suggest that VRLLM learns feature-specific predictive associations, while component ablations indicate that the earliest two FFN layers contribute to the emergence of linearly decodable task information. Our paper provides an engineering recipe and a focused empirical case study on adapting compact LLMs to industrial tabular prediction tasks.

title: Our desktop app's whole interface is 485 words, our website is 35,841, and the 23 words only the app knows are all about things going wrong
description:
Notifio is two codebases that have to agree with each other: an Electron app that does the work on your machine, and a Next.js site that explains and sells it. I have measured plenty of ways they disagree on numbers, like 33 of our 38 pages saying we check every 30 seconds and 25 of them promising no limit on something the app caps at 15.

This time I wanted the words rather than the numbers. Does the product speak the language its own marketing taught the reader?

The two corpora

The app side is every string a user can read in the renderer: JSX text nodes and quoted copy across the 13 .tsx files that make up the window.

renderer .tsx files                        13
distinct user-visible strings             113
mean string length                       24.2 characters
longest string                             77 characters
word tokens                               485
distinct words                            195
distinct content words (stop words out)   153

The site side is the visible text of all 38 URLs in the sitemap, with script and style content stripped:

word tokens      35,841
distinct words    2,877

Seventy-four times as many words to sell the thing as there are inside the thing. I knew the app was terse, because its status lines are one word each by design and six of its numbers are deliberately not a settings screen. I did not know it was 485 words terse. The entire interface of a paid product fits in a third of this blog post.

The overlap is good 

app content words that also appear somewhere on the site   130   (85%)
app content words that appear on none of the 38 pages       23

Eighty-five per cent is better than I expected from two codebases with no shared string table and no copy review between them. The shared half is the vocabulary you would hope for: search, site, listing, reply, session, token, monitor, email.

The direction of the imbalance is the interesting part though. Here is how often each side uses the nouns they share:

word         app UI    site
alerts            1     431
rental            0     156
monitor           2     155
portal            0      63
search           14     248
sites             2     235
listing(s)        5     204
finds             2       5

The site's single most used noun is "alerts", 431 times, and the app's interface says it once. "Rental" is on the site 156 times and is not in the app at all, which is defensible: by the time you are in the window you know what you are looking for. "Portal" appears 63 times on the site and never in the product, and that one is a marketing word that leaked into our own documentation.

The reverse case is "finds", our word for what the app has caught. The window has a Latest Finds panel. The site says "finds" five times and "listings" 204 times. The thing a reader has been trained for 204 repetitions to call a listing is labelled something else the moment they pay.

The 23 words the site has never heard of 

baseline, cleared, confirmation, context, emailed, escape, failed,
invalid, latest, loading, meanwhile, opened, pause, press, redo,
reset, resetting, retry, sections, switched, unknown, untested, verifying

Read that list as a group and it is not a random sample of the app's vocabulary. It is failure, waiting and undo: failed, invalid, unknown, retry, verifying, loading, resetting, cleared, redo, pause. Those are the words a product uses when it is not succeeding, and a marketing site is written entirely in the voice of things succeeding. Thirty-eight pages, 35,841 words, and not one of them is "failed".

That is a tone problem on the site and a support problem in practice. I checked whether the exact strings the app shows when something is wrong appear anywhere we publish:

string the app can show        pages of 38 containing it
"License invalid"                                      0
"Not activated"                                        0
"Activation failed. Please try again."                 0
"Could not start checkout"                             0
"Not set up"                                           0
"Site changed"                                         0
"Find history cleared"                                 0
the bare words invalid / failed / retry                0
"activation token"                                     5

A user whose app says License invalid and who does the obvious thing, searching our site or the web for that phrase, finds nothing of ours. Our help page answers six questions, one of which is about a lost activation token, and that is the only place where the unhappy path is written down at all. Our 125 FAQ questions across 30 pages are all about what happens when things work.

What I am doing with this

Three changes, in the order I believe in them:

  1. Put the app's error strings on the help page verbatim, each with the two or three things that cause it. This is cheap, it is honest, and it is the only version of this that helps somebody at 11pm with a window that says License invalid. Verbatim matters: the string has to be greppable, so it should be the same characters the app renders, not a paraphrase.
  2. Settle on "listings" everywhere, including in the window. We have one word on the site used 204 times and a different word in the product used twice, and the product should lose that argument.
  3. Leave the 485 words alone. The temptation when you measure a UI this small is to pad it, and the app's terseness is the reason a window can say what it is doing in one line.

The measurement itself is about fifty lines of regex over the renderer plus a text extraction of the live pages, which means it can be a test rather than an essay: fail the build if a user-visible string in the app contains a word that appears nowhere on the site. I am not going to write that test yet, because today the answer it would give is twenty-three words long and every one of them is correct.

If you want to see both halves, the words that sell it are on notifio.app and in the guides, and the words inside it are in a window you get from the download page. There are far fewer of the second kind than you would guess.

title: Understanding Cross-Modal Inconsistency through Representation Subspaces in Omni Models
description:
arXiv:2611.22619v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Omni Models process audio, vision, and text within a unified language backbone, yet often produce different answers for semantically equivalent inputs across modalities. Existing representation-level analyses do not distinguish between information that predicts whether disagreement will occur and the representation whose perturbation affects the model's answer. In this paper, we estimate a low-dimensional Answer Subspace from answer-position representations and use it to separate answer-related components from the remaining representation. Across three Omni Models and two multimodal reasoning tasks, information predictive of cross-modal inconsistency lies mainly outside the Answer Subspace, concentrating in a reproducible two-dimensional representation that is not explained by a fixed modality offset. Matched interventions reveal distinct behavioral roles: perturbing the Answer Subspace substantially changes the model's predictions, whereas perturbing the disagreement representation, like a random subspace of the same dimensionality, leaves them almost unchanged. Our key finding is that cross-modal disagreement can be induced by misaligning modality-specific answer representations: perturbing the Answer Subspace for only one modality induces disagreement, whereas applying the same perturbation to both largely preserves agreement. Thus, the representation that predicts disagreement is distinct from the answer-level representation through which disagreement can be induced, showing that linear decodability does not imply behavioral efficacy.

title: PeriaTrace: Tooth-Level Grounding Diagnosis and Patient-Facing Explanations from Periapical Radiographs
description:
arXiv:2611.23012v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Periapical radiographs (PRs) are central to endodontic diagnosis, but interpreting them and preparing reports are time-consuming. Technical language can limit patients' understanding, while existing automated methods often lack tooth-level links between findings and image evidence. We present PeriaTrace, a three-stage framework integrating tooth-level diagnosis, visually grounded report generation, and patient-friendly explanations and care recommendations. PeriaTrace was developed and evaluated using 12,877 PRs from an internal dataset and two external clinical cohorts. In internal evaluation, it achieved a macro Dice coefficient of 85.35%, BLEU-4 of 0.6504, an F1 score of 94.37% for joint tooth localization and F\'ed\'eration Dentaire Internationale (FDI) identification, and a grounding-tag F1 score of 77.93%. In the two external cohorts, senior endodontists considered 91.16% and 84.52% of reports suitable for retention or revision without complete rewriting. Generation averaged 4.41 seconds per PR, several tens of times faster than manual drafting. Among 196 survey participants without medical backgrounds, 96.4% preferred reports with plain-language explanations and care recommendations, and 84.7% found visual localization cues helpful. PeriaTrace may enable faster, evidence-traceable reporting while supporting clinical review and patient communication. (Abridged version)

title: CAFE-AQI: Coverage-Aware Day-Ahead AQI Forecasting with Early Warning and Conformal Uncertainty in Bangladesh
description:
arXiv:2611.23815v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Next-day air quality forecasting often assumes city records are equally complete and independent. However, an audit of a large Bangladesh dataset revealed a sharp coverage expansion after August 2022 and showed that 103 city labels correspond to only 61 unique AQI trajectories. To address these issues, this paper presents CAFE-AQI, a coverage-aware framework for forecasting next-day maximum AQI. It also estimates the probability of Unhealthy-or-worse conditions (AQI >= 151). Data were divided chronologically into training (2022-2023), calibration (2024), and testing (2025). To prevent duplicate records from dominating training and evaluation, identical trajectories were weighted. The framework combines temporal and pollutant features with a five-neighbor spatial context. It also includes a class-balanced warning head and risk-conditional conformal calibration aimed at providing early warnings and prediction intervals. Evaluation on the duplicate-balanced 2025 data gave an MAE of 9.76, an RMSE of 15.04, and an R-squared value of 0.910 for CAFE-AQI. Its MAE was 3.63 AQI lower than persistence (95% CI: 3.49-3.76), with lower errors in each of the 61 trajectory groups. For unhealthy-air warnings, the F1-score was 0.908 and the AUROC was 0.982. The nominal 90% intervals covered 92.09% of observations. When an entire spatial block was excluded from training, the MAE remained 10.66, showing that the lightweight model transferred reasonably well to unseen locations.

title: Atlas for Government: The Only FedRAMP® Class D Certified Cross-Cloud Operational Database
description:
Federal, state, and local agencies are under mounting pressure to modernize legacy systems, adopt AI, and protect sensitive data, all at the same time. Many of the databases that can currently handle an agency's most sensitive, high-impact workloads are native to a single cloud and run nowhere else, leaving agencies with a limited set of authorized options and little room to change course when missions, mandates, or threats shift.

MongoDB is the intelligent data platform for the AI era, and today we're extending it to the workloads where the stakes are highest: MongoDB Atlas for Government has achieved FedRAMP® Class D Certification. Formerly known as FedRAMP High, Class D is the highest level of assessment under the Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP). Atlas for Government has also added support for Azure Government, expanding its existing support for AWS GovCloud and Commercial Regions and Google Cloud Assured Workloads.

Together, these milestones make MongoDB Atlas for Government the only FedRAMP Class D (High) Certified cross-cloud operational database in the world. Public sector organizations and the independent software vendors (ISVs) that serve them can now run their most sensitive mission-critical workloads—including production AI applications built on real-time operational data—on a single platform and on the cloud provider of their choice, across AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud. To learn more, visit the MongoDB Atlas for Government product page or the FedRAMP Marketplace page.

What is MongoDB Atlas for Government?

MongoDB Atlas for Government is an independent, dedicated environment of the MongoDB Atlas intelligent data platform built specifically for the U.S. public sector and the ISVs that build government solutions. It brings the core capabilities of MongoDB’s intelligent data platform to government, giving agencies a fully managed way to deploy, run, and scale mission-critical applications in the cloud, including transactional workloads, search, vector search for AI applications, and time series data, all within a single, unified data platform.

Atlas for Government is operated by MongoDB employees who are United States persons on U.S. soil, and all encryption within MongoDB-managed infrastructure is FIPS 140-3 validated. The platform maintains a 99.995% uptime SLA and has been generally available since 2021.

MongoDB Atlas for Government is already trusted across the federal government. MongoDB works with 13 U.S. Federal Cabinet-level agencies. With FedRAMP Class D (High) certification, agencies like these can bring even more sensitive, high-impact workloads to Atlas for Government. For example, a health agency could modernize benefits and eligibility systems that handle protected health information and personally identifiable information. A financial agency could run real-time fraud detection across high-volume transaction streams. And a civilian agency could build an AI application that lets analysts search policy and case records in natural language, without that data leaving a FedRAMP Class D (High) environment.

What is FedRAMP Class D (High)?

FedRAMP provides the standardized authorization framework that cloud service providers (CSPs) must successfully navigate to demonstrate compliance with federal security requirements before hosting federal agency workloads. In 2026, FedRAMP moved away from labeling these standards Low, Moderate, and High, replacing them with a four-tier Certification Class system, A through D. FedRAMP Class D (High) is the direct successor to what was previously known as FedRAMP High, and it remains the most rigorous tier a CSP can achieve within the FedRAMP program.

FedRAMP Class D (High) certification is designed for cloud services that support an agency's high-impact systems, where a security failure could have severe or catastrophic consequences for operations, assets, or people. This includes systems tied to national security, law enforcement, and emergency response, as well as high-impact modernization initiatives across civilian agencies. Achieving this certification requires meeting hundreds of stringent security controls covering everything from access management to incident response.

MongoDB Atlas for Government achieved FedRAMP Moderate authorization in 2023 and has been a trusted, fully managed data platform for federal agencies and ISVs since then. With FedRAMP Class D (High) certification, that foundation is now extended to high-impact workloads, including production AI applications. Agencies can bring those workloads to the cloud on a platform that meets the security and compliance requirements for high-impact systems, and build secure, production-grade AI applications on top of them.

Freedom to run anywhere: Now spanning AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud

With the addition of support for Azure Government, MongoDB Atlas for Government now runs across all three major cloud providers: AWS (both GovCloud and AWS commercial regions), Google Cloud (via Assured Workloads), and Azure Government. This makes MongoDB Atlas for Government the only FedRAMP Class D (High) certified, cross-cloud database in the world.

For public sector organizations, this cross-cloud support is about more than convenience. A database tied to a single cloud provider limits an agency's options if costs rise, a mission requirement changes, or a new mandate calls for a different cloud environment. MongoDB Atlas for Government gives agencies and ISVs the freedom to run their workloads on the cloud that best fits their needs today, and to change that decision later without rewriting their applications. Within FedRAMP-certified cloud environments (AWS GovCloud, Google Cloud Assured Workloads, and Azure Government), data can be distributed across providers to optimize for performance, cost, or resilience, and to strengthen disaster recovery with automatic failover across providers.

Getting started on Azure Government works the same way as it does on AWS GovCloud or Google Cloud Assured Workloads. Agencies and ISVs can create a project in Atlas for Government, designate it as a FedRAMP Class D (High) Gov Regions Only project, and select Azure as the cloud provider when creating a cluster.

Protecting data and powering AI at the highest level

FedRAMP Class D (High) sets a high bar for how a provider documents, assesses, and maintains its security program, but that is only one part of the picture. Agencies handling the country's most sensitive data also need assurance that the data itself stays protected, even if a system is compromised.

MongoDB Atlas for Government provides robust protection for sensitive data, supporting workloads that include Personally Identifiable Information (PII), Protected Health Information (PHI), and Criminal Justice Information Services (CJIS) data. Data at rest is protected using database encryption with Customer Managed Keys, and data in transit is protected via TLS.

For organizations that require protection beyond the authorization boundary, MongoDB Queryable Encryption performs encryption and decryption client-side, so designated fields remain encrypted throughout their lifecycle, in transit, at rest, and in use. MongoDB, cloud operators, and even the organization's own database administrators never have access to keys or unencrypted data.

This same secure foundation enables agencies to deploy production AI applications in their high-impact environments. MongoDB Atlas for Government includes MongoDB Vector Search, allowing teams to build retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and other AI-powered applications directly on top of their operational data. Instead of standing up a separate vector database and building a pipeline to keep it in sync, agencies can run transactional workloads, search, and vector search in a single, FedRAMP Class D-certified environment, reducing both complexity and risk.

How to get started with MongoDB Atlas for Government

With FedRAMP Class D (High) certification and support for Azure Government, MongoDB’s intelligent data platform for the AI era now reaches the public sector’s highest-stakes missions. MongoDB Atlas for Government gives public sector organizations and ISVs a secure, fully managed, and truly multi-cloud way to run their most sensitive workloads and build production AI applications.

To get started, visit the MongoDB Atlas for Government product page, view the FedRAMP Marketplace listing, or refer to the Atlas for Government documentation for setup details.

FAQ

What is MongoDB Atlas for Government?

MongoDB Atlas for Government is an independent, dedicated environment of MongoDB Atlas built for the U.S. public sector and the ISVs that build government solutions. It is a fully managed, FedRAMP Class D (High) certified operational database.

What is FedRAMP Class D (High)?

FedRAMP Class D (High) is the highest tier in FedRAMP’s four-tier Certification Class system and the direct successor to what was previously known as FedRAMP High. It is designed for cloud services that support high-impact government systems.

Which cloud providers does Atlas for Government support?

Atlas for Government runs on AWS (GovCloud and Commercial Regions), Google Cloud (via Assured Workloads), and Azure Government. Within FedRAMP-certified cloud environments, data can be distributed across providers with automatic failover.

Can agencies build AI applications on Atlas for Government?

Yes. MongoDB Vector Search enables teams to build retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and other AI applications directly on operational data, in a single FedRAMP Class D (High) certified environment, without a separate vector database or sync pipeline.

title: Cutting LLM Fine-Tuning Memory in Pure Kotlin: Fused Linear Cross-Entropy and the JVM Vector API
description:
When fine-tuning language models like Qwen2-0.5B or Llama-3 on a constrained heap, the biggest memory and compute bottleneck often isn't self-attention. On models with a small hidden dimension and a large vocabulary, the bottleneck is the output projection head (lmHead) and cross-entropy loss.
I ran into this while working on v1.1.0 of Kotensor (io.github.tspstudio:kotensor), an open-source, pure-Kotlin Transformer and reverse-mode autograd engine for JVM 17+ and Android with no native C++ or JNI dependencies. Inference was already reasonably fast and ran within tight mobile memory limits, but running a LoRA fine-tuning step on the full 24-layer Qwen2-0.5B architecture inside a 6 GB JVM heap consistently failed with OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space.
At first I looked for a reference leak in the autograd graph, assuming intermediate activations weren't being freed between steps. Once I actually calculated the tensor sizes at the output layer, though, it became obvious that the problem was just raw array allocation in the output head.

This post goes over the math behind that bottleneck and the changes I made in pure Kotlin to get the full 24-layer model training inside 2.84 GB of heap: prompt loss masking before projection, chunked fused linear cross-entropy, in-place transposed matrix multiplication, and SIMD acceleration via the JVM Vector API (jdk.incubator.vector).

1. Looking at the Numbers on a 151,936-Token Vocabulary

Qwen2-0.5B has a hidden size of D = 896 and a vocabulary size of V = 151,936. That means the final linear projection matrix W_head ([896 x 151,936]) holds 136.1 million parameters, which is roughly 544 MB in FP32.
In a standard autograd training step with a batch of N = 64 tokens, three things happen at once:

  1. Logit and Probability Materialization: Multiplying the [64 x 896] hidden states by W_head produces a [64 x 151,936] logit tensor (9.72 million floats, or ~38.9 MB). Standard cross-entropy then allocates an equally large array for softmax probabilities and another for the logit gradients during the backward pass (~116 MB total just for the output activations).
  2. Transposed Weight Copy in Backward: In Kotensor v1.0.0, the general matrix multiplication backward pass (dH = dLogits * W^T) transposed the right-hand matrix into a temporary array before multiplying. For W_head, that meant allocating a fresh 544 MB FloatArray on every step while all 24 layers of forward activations were still live in memory.
  3. Unmasked Prompt Tokens: In instruction fine-tuning, roughly 70% of a batch consists of system prompt and user query tokens that shouldn't contribute to the loss. Projecting all 64 tokens across 151,936 columns costs 52 billion FLOPs per step, even though most of those rows get masked out right after. Combined with the activations of 24 Transformer blocks, that 544 MB temporary transpose and 116 MB of vocabulary buffers were enough to push the JVM past a 6 GB heap limit. --- ## 2. Filtering Prompt Tokens Before Projection Usually, crossEntropyLoss(logits, targets, ignoreIndex = -100) takes the full [batch, seqLen, vocabSize] logit tensor and skips the masked indices during the softmax loop. That works fine when memory isn't tight, but it means you already paid the cost of multiplying the masked rows through W_head. To avoid doing that work in the first place, I moved the IGNORE_INDEX = -100 check ahead of the linear projection so only the active target positions are gathered: 
const val IGNORE_INDEX = -100
private fun activeRows(targets: IntArray, ignoreIndex: Int, vocabularySize: Int): IntArray {
    var active = 0
    for (target in targets) {
        if (target == ignoreIndex) continue
        require(target in 0 until vocabularySize) {
            "target $target out of bounds $vocabularySize"
        }
        active++
    }
    val rows = IntArray(active)
    var next = 0
    for (i in targets.indices) {
        if (targets[i] != ignoreIndex) rows[next++] = i
    }
    return rows
}

In our benchmark batch of 64 tokens where only 18 tokens belong to the assistant's response, filtering the indices first drops the number of projected rows from 64 to 18. That cuts the output-layer FLOPs by about 72% before changing anything else.

3. Chunked Fused Linear + Cross-Entropy

Filtering out the prompt tokens helps, but on longer responses we still don't want to allocate an [activeTokens x 151,936] tensor or hold onto a full probability matrix until backward() runs.
To fix this, I added fusedCrossEntropyLoss in Loss.kt. Instead of calling lmHead.forward(hidden) and passing the result to the loss function, fusedCrossEntropyLoss takes hidden and head directly and processes the active tokens in fixed chunks of at most FUSED_CHUNK_ELEMENTS = 1 shl 22 floats (4,194,304 elements, or 16 MB).
For each chunk of active rows:

  1. It copies only chunkRows hidden states into a small inputs buffer and projects them into a reusable logits buffer.
  2. It computes the row-wise maxLogit and sumExp for the log-sum-exp loss: 
   loss_i = maxLogit_i + ln(sum_v(exp(z_{i,v} - maxLogit_i))) - z_{i, target_i}
  1. While the chunk's logits are still in cache, it overwrites the logits buffer in-place with the analytical softmax gradient (prob - indicator) / activeTokens, and immediately multiplies that gradient back into hiddenGrad using MatMul.multiplyTransposedB (which reads W_head transposed in-place rather than copying the 544 MB array): 
private const val FUSED_CHUNK_ELEMENTS = 1 shl 22
@JvmOverloads
fun fusedCrossEntropyLoss(
    hidden: Tensor,
    head: Projection,
    targets: IntArray,
    ignoreIndex: Int = IGNORE_INDEX
): Tensor {
    val dimension = head.inSize
    val vocabularySize = head.outSize
    val weight = (head as? Linear)?.weight
    val quantized = (head as? QuantizedLinear)?.weight
    val bias = head.bias
    val rows = activeRows(targets, ignoreIndex, vocabularySize)
    val active = rows.size
    if (active == 0) return emptyLoss()
    val chunkRows = (FUSED_CHUNK_ELEMENTS / vocabularySize).coerceIn(1, active)
    val inputs = FloatArray(chunkRows * dimension)
    val logits = FloatArray(chunkRows * vocabularySize)
    val rowMax = FloatArray(active)
    val rowSum = FloatArray(active)
    val scale = 1.0f / active.toFloat()
    val hiddenGrad = if (hidden.requiresGrad) FloatArray(active * dimension) else null
    val chunkGrad = if (hiddenGrad != null) FloatArray(chunkRows * dimension) else null
    var totalLoss = 0.0f
    var start = 0
    while (start < active) {
        val count = minOf(chunkRows, active - start)
        projectRows(hidden.data, rows, start, count, dimension, vocabularySize, weight, quantized, bias, inputs, logits)
        for (r in 0 until count) {
            val offset = r * vocabularySize
            var maxLogit = -1e9f
            for (v in 0 until vocabularySize) {
                val logit = logits[offset + v]
                if (logit > maxLogit) maxLogit = logit
            }
            var sumExp = 0.0f
            for (v in 0 until vocabularySize) {
                sumExp += kotlin.math.exp(logits[offset + v] - maxLogit)
            }
            rowMax[start + r] = maxLogit
            rowSum[start + r] = sumExp
            totalLoss += maxLogit + kotlin.math.ln(sumExp) - logits[offset + targets[rows[start + r]]]
        }
        if (hiddenGrad != null && chunkGrad != null) {
            logitGradients(logits, count, vocabularySize, targets, rows, start, rowMax, rowSum, scale)
            if (weight != null) {
                MatMul.multiplyTransposedB(logits, weight.data, chunkGrad, count, vocabularySize, dimension, accumulate = false)
            } else if (quantized != null) {
                MatMul.multiplyByQuantizedTransposed(logits, quantized, chunkGrad, count, accumulate = false)
            }
            System.arraycopy(chunkGrad, 0, hiddenGrad, start * dimension, count * dimension)
        }
        start += count
    }
    val meanLoss = totalLoss / active.toFloat()
    lateinit var out: Tensor
    out = Tensor(floatArrayOf(meanLoss), intArrayOf(1, 1), listOfNotNull(hidden, weight, bias)) {
        val upstreamGrad = out.grad[0]
        if (hiddenGrad != null && hidden.requiresGrad) {
            val target = hidden.grad
            for (r in 0 until active) {
                val destination = rows[r] * dimension
                val source = r * dimension
                for (d in 0 until dimension) {
                    target[destination + d] += upstreamGrad * hiddenGrad[source + d]
                }
            }
        }
    }
    return out
}

One side benefit here is how clean the backward closure becomes during LoRA or QLoRA training. Since lmHead is frozen (weight.requiresGrad == false), we don't need to keep the vocabulary logits around at all. When loss.backward() runs, it just scales the [active x 896] hiddenGrad buffer and adds it into hidden.grad.

(Note: if weight.requiresGrad is true for full fine-tuning, the actual implementation in Loss.kt recomputes the chunked logits during the backward closure to accumulate weight.grad via MatMul.multiplyTransposedA, trading a second forward projection for the same 16 MB memory cap).

4. Using the JVM Vector API (jdk.incubator.vector)

For the scalar matrix multiplication kernels in MatMul.kt, I originally structured the inner loops as y[j] += a * x[j] (axpy) over 32 x 256 cache tiles. HotSpot's C2 JIT compiler auto-vectorizes that pattern well as long as both arrays are indexed by a plain loop variable j with no offset arithmetic inside the brackets.
The problem is that multiplyTransposedB naturally wants to compute dot products across rows (sum += a[j] * b[j]), and C2 refuses to auto-vectorize floating-point dot-product reductions because floating-point addition isn't associative.
To get around C2's auto-vectorization limits on desktop and server JVMs, I added an optional SimdKernels implementation using Java's Incubator Vector API (jdk.incubator.vector). It uses FloatVector.SPECIES_PREFERRED and fused multiply-add (fma) across four rows at a time (axpy4 and dot4):

import jdk.incubator.vector.FloatVector
import jdk.incubator.vector.VectorSpecies
@JvmField
internal val FLOAT_SPECIES: VectorSpecies<Float> = FloatVector.SPECIES_PREFERRED
fun axpy4(
    y0: FloatArray, y1: FloatArray, y2: FloatArray, y3: FloatArray, x: FloatArray,
    a0: Float, a1: Float, a2: Float, a3: Float, len: Int
) {
    val species = FLOAT_SPECIES
    val step = species.length()
    val bound = species.loopBound(len)
    val va0 = FloatVector.broadcast(species, a0)
    val va1 = FloatVector.broadcast(species, a1)
    val va2 = FloatVector.broadcast(species, a2)
    val va3 = FloatVector.broadcast(species, a3)
    var j = 0
    while (j < bound) {
        val xv = FloatVector.fromArray(species, x, j)
        xv.fma(va0, FloatVector.fromArray(species, y0, j)).intoArray(y0, j)
        xv.fma(va1, FloatVector.fromArray(species, y1, j)).intoArray(y1, j)
        xv.fma(va2, FloatVector.fromArray(species, y2, j)).intoArray(y2, j)
        xv.fma(va3, FloatVector.fromArray(species, y3, j)).intoArray(y3, j)
        j += step
    }
    while (j < len) {
        val xv = x[j]
        y0[j] += a0 * xv
        y1[j] += a1 * xv
        y2[j] += a2 * xv
        y3[j] += a3 * xv
        j++
    }
}

When the JVM starts with --add-modules jdk.incubator.vector, MatMul picks up SimdKernels automatically. On Android ART, where the Vector API module doesn't exist, it falls back to the tiled scalar kernels.

5. Benchmarks on Qwen2-0.5B

I measured a rank-8 LoRA training step on the Qwen2-0.5B shape (24 layers, hidden dimension 896, vocabulary 151,936, LoRA attached to wQ and wV, 64-token batch with 18 active response tokens) on a 2-core Intel Xeon container with AVX-512, running JDK 21 with a 6 GB heap limit. Numbers below are the mean of three steps after one warm-up step:

Metric v1.0.0 (Naive Head + Unmasked) v1.1.0 (Fused Head + Masked, Scalar) v1.1.0 (+ JVM Vector API)
Active Tokens Projected 64 / 64 18 / 64 18 / 64
Output-Head FLOPs / Step 52.0 Billion 9.8 Billion 9.8 Billion
Output-Head Latency 2.70 s 0.70 s 0.33 s
4-Layer Step Latency 3.87 s 1.46 s 0.81 s
Full 24-Layer Step Latency OutOfMemoryError (> 6 GB) 4.62 s 3.04 s
Heap Used After Step (24 Layers) > 6.00 GB (Failed) 2.84 GB 2.84 GB

Output-layer time dropped from 2.70 seconds to 0.33 seconds, and peak memory stayed under 2.85 GB for the full 24-layer step.
With the output head fixed, most of the remaining 3.04 seconds per step is spent propagating input gradients backward through the 24 frozen Transformer blocks (~0.11s per block) so they reach the adapters in the early layers. Because v1.1.0 also added early backward termination via requiresGrad, restricting LoRA to the upper blocks (LoRAAdapter(model, blockIndices = 20 until 24)) lets the autograd engine stop backpropagation at layer 20 and skip layers 0 through 19 entirely.
If you want to inspect the full implementation or test the engine yourself, the code is on GitHub at https://github.com/TSPstudio/kotensor and published on Maven Central as io.github.tspstudio:kotensor:1.2.0.

title: PACD: Provenance-Aware Consensus Decoding for Mitigating Cross-Modal Hallucinations in Omnimodal Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.22456v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Omnimodal large language models (Omni-LLMs) integrate audio, video, and text for multimodal reasoning, yet remain vulnerable to cross-modal hallucinations, where one modality improperly influences predictions about another. Existing training-free decoding methods mitigate these errors through modality perturbation or relevance-based weighting. However, due to interference from irrelevant modality cues during fusion and difficulty detecting shared errors, these methods may suppress correct unimodal predictions and allow erroneous consensus to persist. To address these limitations, we propose Provenance-Aware Consensus Decoding (PACD), a training-free framework for mitigating cross-modal hallucinations. PACD comprises two complementary paths based on whether the branches reach consensus. For non-consensus cases, Relevance-Guided Candidate Arbitration identifies task-relevant unimodal evidence and selectively arbitrates between predictions using alternative candidates. For consensus cases, Provenance-Based Consensus Recovery leverages the outranking principle to evaluate the consistency and strength of layer-wise modality evidence for alternative answers, selectively resolving erroneous consensus under confidence constraints. Extensive experiments on four Omni-LLMs and five benchmarks across two tasks demonstrate the superiority of PACD. Compared to existing methods, PACD achieves up to 27.6% relative improvement over standard decoding across CMM, AVHBench, and SVHalluc for cross-modal hallucination mitigation, and an average relative improvement of 7.7% over best baseline across OmniVideoBench and FutureOmni for general audio-visual reasoning.

title: How 5 Companies Use AI Coding Agents and Assistants Across the SDLC
description:
An agent-generated pull request has a green build and a full set of tests. A reviewer compares it with the ticket and discovers that the agent guessed how duplicate requests should behave. Every generated test uses the same guess.

The team can still fix the change during review. An earlier opportunity was to catch the missing rule when the agent proposed its implementation plan.

Start with an invoice request that can be retried

Consider a hypothetical invoice API. The ticket says the endpoint should handle duplicate submissions. That leaves several decisions open. Should a retry return the existing invoice? What happens if the caller reuses the same idempotency key with a different amount? What happens when two requests arrive together?

The approved plan could spell out three outcomes. A request with the same key and payload returns the existing invoice ID. A request with the same key and a different payload gets a conflict response. Two simultaneous requests with the same key and payload create one invoice record.

Those decisions give the agent something concrete to implement and the reviewer a way to judge the result.

Stage What the agent can prepare What the engineer can verify
Requirements A draft specification and a list of open questions The duplicate-request rules and acceptance criteria
Implementation An API change, a database migration, and a branch The database constraint, transaction boundaries, and existing behaviour
Testing API, integration, and concurrency tests Whether tests cover changed payloads and simultaneous requests
Merge A pull request with a summary of check results Which checks passed, how the change can be deployed, and who will own it

Two sequential requests can pass even when simultaneous requests create two records. A concurrency test gives the reviewer evidence about that third acceptance criterion. The reviewer can also check whether the test exercises the same database constraint the application uses in production.

Treat a failed test as a decision point

Suppose a generated integration test fails because it expects a conflict when the same key is reused with a different amount. The implementation currently returns the original invoice regardless of the payload.

The failure could indicate a bad implementation, a faulty test fixture, or a requirement that changed after the test was written. An engineer can trace it back to the approved rule and decide what needs to change. Here, the policy already says that a different payload should produce a conflict, so the implementation needs correction.

That review matters when the same agent wrote the code and the tests. A reviewer can add an independent scenario from the approved ticket and confirm that it fails against the incorrect implementation before the fix goes in.

Five company approaches developers can compare

GeekyAnts describes agents drafting requirements and plans, implementing changes, and running tests. Engineers approve the plan before coding, decide how to handle failures, and review and merge changes from a separate branch. The engineer who merges the change owns it in production. Requirements-to-release video

Thoughtworks documents how AI/works turns requirements and existing system context into a specification, then generates implementation stories, code, and tests from it. The specification gives reviewers a place to check that a change preserves existing invoice rules.

Globant describes a Test AI Agent that drafts and executes test plans. Teams evaluating AI-assisted QA can ask how generated plans cover concurrency, unexpected input, and behaviour across service boundaries.

EPAM describes using CodeMie in its own delivery process to keep requirements and architecture connected to implementation, QA, and release. The workflow illustrates how an approved rule can stay visible as work moves from a ticket to a pull request.

Accenture collaborated with GitHub on a randomized Copilot trial with enterprise developers and also studied adoption. The research gives teams a reference for evaluating how a coding assistant fits into an existing engineering workflow.

Put the evidence in the pull request

A pull request template can make this workflow easier to repeat. Three fields are enough for the invoice example. Link to the approved acceptance criterion, show the evidence for the riskiest behaviour, and name the person who owns the change after merge.

For the concurrency rule, that could mean linking to the ticket and attaching an integration test result showing that simultaneous retries produced one invoice. A reviewer can then start with the behaviour that matters and inspect the code that protects it.

Where does an AI coding agent need to pause in your team’s workflow?

title: How I Built a 100% Client-Side PDF Powerhouse with WebAssembly and React (Zero Cloud Uploads)
description:
Why Does Every Online PDF Tool Want Your Credit Card and Your Tax Returns?

Earlier this month, I had to upload a signed certificate to a government application portal. The portal had one strict requirement:

"Uploaded PDF must be strictly below 100 KB."

I did what everyone does: searched "compress PDF under 100kb" on Google.

Every single top result was a multi-million-dollar SaaS product that:

Forced me to upload a sensitive personal document to an undisclosed remote server.
Compressed it to 125 KB (still rejected by the portal!).
Locked the "Extreme Compression" slider behind a $12/month subscription.
Or hit me with: "You have reached your free daily quota of 2 files. Enter your credit card."

I got frustrated enough that I decided to see how far we could push modern web browser primitives—WebAssembly, HTML5 Canvas, Web Workers, and pdf-lib—to build a completely private, zero-server alternative.

That experiment became PDFCraft
(Source on GitHub
).

Here is the technical breakdown of how we achieved 100% client-side PDF manipulation with zero cloud leaks.

  1. The Core Architecture: Zero-Cloud Processing

Traditional PDF websites use server-side Python/C++ pipelines (e.g., Poppler, Ghostscript, or LibreOffice in Docker containers). That architecture has major drawbacks:

Massive Server Costs: Running headless PDF engines across millions of files costs thousands in server bills.
Privacy Risks: Uploading legal contracts, tax documents, and medical scans creates massive GDPR and compliance liabilities.

Instead, PDFCraft operates entirely on the client device:

User Device (Local Memory)
├── File Input (Drag & Drop)
│ └── ArrayBuffer / Blob in Local Memory
├── Local Processing Engines
│ ├── pdf-lib (Vector streams, page tree manipulation, e-signatures)
│ ├── HTML5 Canvas (Quantization, resolution scaling, image crunching)
│ └── Web Workers (Off-main-thread compute without freezing the UI)
└── Instant Download
└── Direct Blob URL (0 bytes transmitted to any backend)

  1. The Target Size Squeezer: Hitting Exact 100KB/200KB Ceilings

Standard compressors just say "Low, Medium, High". But portal upload bots don't care about "High"—they care about ≤ 95 KB or ≤ 195 KB.

To guarantee that a PDF always comes in under the portal limit:

Binary Stream Extraction: We extract embedded page streams and rasterize page canvases at high DPI.
Dynamic Binary Search Quantization: Instead of guessing a single JPEG quality factor, our algorithm runs an in-memory binary search across resolution scale and quantization factors:
It tests quality brackets (e.g. 0.85 -> 0.65 -> 0.45) in milliseconds.
If the generated PDF stream exceeds the target ceiling (say, 95 KB), it immediately downscales background image coordinates while preserving vector text edge sharpness.
Iterative Verification: The final byte buffer is measured before download. If it's 94.2 KB, it is delivered immediately.

  1. Zero-Account E-Signing (ESIGN Compliant)

Instead of forcing users to sign up for DocuSign or Adobe Sign just to put an initials stamp on a 2-page lease, we implemented an in-browser vector signature pad:

Signatures are captured via HTML5 Canvas with cubic Bézier curve smoothing for natural pen strokes.
The vector paths are converted directly into clean PNG byte streams and embedded into the PDF page tree using pdf-lib's drawImage and drawText.
The entire signing session happens offline—even with airplane mode turned on!

  1. 60-Second ATS Resume Studio

Most online resume builders let you design your resume for 30 minutes, only to hit you with a paywall modal at the download step.

PDFCraft includes a built-in ATS Resume Studio that:

Formats single-page vector PDF resumes compatible with applicant tracking systems (Workday, Greenhouse, Lever).
Includes a local keyword scanner that compares your resume against any job description in real-time.
Exports directly as clean, uncompressed vector text that machine parsers can read with 100% accuracy.

  1. What We Learned

Modern browser engines (V8, WebAssembly, Web Workers) are powerful enough to replace 90% of cloud utilities. You don't need a heavy backend server to compress a PDF, sign an agreement, or extract spreadsheet tables.

🌐 Live Web App: https://pdf-craft-vert.vercel.app/
📦 Open Source Repository: https://github.com/Vishnu-cod/pdf-craft

I'd love to hear feedback from the developer community! What utilities would you like to see built into the client-side suite next?

title: JEPA as a Transferable Optimizer: Learning and Understanding Black-Box Optimization from Reward-Agnostic Pretraining
description:
arXiv:2611.23608v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Black-box optimization evaluates candidates through simulations, rollouts, or experiments, often without gradients. Learned optimizers are usually judged by whether they outperform existing methods. We ask a complementary question: what information does a learned optimizer use from its search history? We introduce JEPA-PS (JEPA Policy Search), based on a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture. It is pretrained on random rollouts using parameter vectors and scalar returns. Its latent-prediction objective predicts the next point in an optimization trajectory rather than its reward or gradient, allowing us to examine what was tried and how well it performed. At test time, JEPA-PS reads a short evaluation history and proposes a candidate in one forward pass, without task descriptions, reward shaping, or test-time gradients. We evaluate it on 15 control environments against 12 optimizers, including evolutionary methods, Bayesian optimization, CMA-ES, and an LLM optimizer. JEPA-PS is competitive with tuned classical baselines and outperforms the LLM optimizer by more than 2x on Swimmer at 71x lower per-step cost. It also transfers zero-shot to environments excluded from pretraining. Null-model comparisons and decoder-training ablations indicate that its latent representation carries information beyond simple history statistics; every trained decoder variant performs worse than the default frozen representation. Our main finding is that the history JEPA-PS uses depends on the task. On smooth landscapes it uses the full trajectory, whereas on rugged landscapes the best-seen point carries nearly all the signal. This memory requirement has a weak positive correlation with fitness-distance correlation (FDC; r=0.112, n=7), while an independent reward-ordering sensitivity probe does not corroborate the relationship (r=-0.024, n=7). Code: https://github.com/mdebnath22/jepa-props.
