title: loadbalancer: an HTTP reverse-proxy load balancer in Go, built to learn
description:
A load balancer is easy to describe: requests come in, and you send each one to one of several backends. The interesting questions start right after that sentence. Which backend? How do you know one of them is dead? What do you do with a request that was already sent to a dead one? And how do you change the list of backends without dropping the traffic that is flowing right now?

loadbalancer is my learning project for those questions. It is an HTTP reverse-proxy load balancer in Go, using only the standard library and fsnotify. It has three balancing strategies, active health checks, a passive circuit breaker per backend, retries for idempotent requests, config hot reload and Prometheus metrics.

What it does

The request path is short enough to show in full:

request ─► pick(): candidates = healthy ∧ breaker ready ∧ not tried yet
              strategy.Pick(candidates) → breaker.Acquire()
         ─► forward(): ReverseProxy to the backend
              transport error → breaker.Failure(), retry if idempotent
              5xx             → breaker.Failure(), response is passed through
              otherwise       → breaker.Success()

A backend is a candidate only if the health checker says it is healthy, its circuit breaker is ready, and this request has not tried it yet. The strategy picks one of the candidates, and the request is forwarded through httputil.ReverseProxy.

Next to the proxy port there is an admin port with /metrics in the Prometheus text format and /status, a JSON view of the pool.

What I built from scratch, and what it teaches

Retries around httputil.ReverseProxy. By default, when the proxy cannot reach a backend, it writes a 502 to the client, and then it is too late to try another one. Here the error handler records the failure instead of writing a 502, so the request can still go to another backend. Retries are deliberately narrow: only GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE, PUT and DELETE requests without a body, and only when the backend could not be reached, so nothing has been written to the client yet. A 5xx response is never retried; it is passed through.

Balancing algorithms. There are three strategies: round robin, weighted, and least connections with rotating tie-breaks. The weighted one is nginx's smooth weighted round robin. With weights 5, 1, 1, a naive implementation gives a a a a a b c: five requests in a row to the same backend. The smooth version gives a a b a c a a, which keeps the same proportions and spreads them out.

Two ways to detect a dead backend. Active checks probe a path such as /healthz on a timer. One goroutine probes every backend concurrently each interval, and thresholds stop one lost probe from making the pool flap. Passive checks watch real traffic, and they work even when the backend has no health endpoint. That is the circuit breaker.

The circuit breaker state machine. After failure_threshold consecutive failures, the breaker goes from closed to open and the backend stops receiving traffic. Once cooldown has passed, exactly one trial request is let through: the half-open state. A success closes the breaker, and a failure opens it again. Two methods keep this correct under concurrency: Ready() has no side effects and is used to filter candidates, and Acquire() reserves the single half-open slot. When the health checker sees a backend recover, its breaker is reset too.

Reloading without dropping traffic. Apply validates the new config first, so an invalid file is rejected and the old config stays. It then reuses the *Backend values whose URL is unchanged, keeping their in-flight count, health and breaker state, and restarts the health checker. Both SIGHUP and file changes trigger it, and file changes are debounced. One detail I did not expect: the watcher looks at the directory, not the file, because editors replace files by renaming.

How to use it

Install the binary with Go:

go install github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/loadbalancer/cmd/loadbalancer@latest

Or run it from a clone of the repository:

cp lb.example.json lb.json      # edit the backend URLs
go run ./cmd/loadbalancer -config lb.json
curl localhost:8080/            # proxied
curl localhost:9090/metrics     # Prometheus metrics
curl localhost:9090/status      # JSON view of the pool
kill -HUP <pid>                 # reload (saving the file also reloads)

The config is one JSON file:

{
  "listen": ":8080",
  "admin": ":9090",
  "strategy": "weighted",              // round_robin | weighted | least_conn
  "retries": 2,                        // extra attempts for idempotent requests
  "backends": [{"url": "http://127.0.0.1:9001", "weight": 3}],
  "health_check": {"path": "/healthz", "interval": "5s", "timeout": "1s",
                   "healthy_threshold": 2, "unhealthy_threshold": 2},
  "circuit_breaker": {"failure_threshold": 5, "cooldown": "10s"}
}

Leave health_check.path empty to turn off active checks, and set failure_threshold to 0 to turn off the breaker.

The tests need nothing external:

go test -race ./...

They all run against httptest backends. They cover strategy order and distribution, least connections with a blocked backend, breaker state transitions on a fake clock, a retry around a dead backend, health checks taking a backend out and putting it back, a reload that keeps state, the fsnotify watcher and the metrics output.

Things to know

This is a learning project. The README lists what a production load balancer has and this one does not:

  • It serves HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 to the client through net/http only. There is no TLS termination config: put it behind something, or add ListenAndServeTLS. There is no WebSocket-specific handling beyond what ReverseProxy already does, and no TCP (L4) mode.
  • No sticky sessions, no consistent hashing, no slow start for recovered backends, and no outlier detection beyond consecutive failures.
  • Changing listen or admin needs a restart. The reload logs a warning.
  • Metrics are written by hand in the Prometheus text format, and there are no latency histograms.
  • The breaker counts any 5xx from the backend as a failure. That includes a 500 caused by one bad request.

What I learned

The first lesson is that a retry is a promise about the request, not about the proxy. You can only retry when you know nothing reached the client and the request is safe to send twice. That is why the list of methods is short and why bodies are excluded. Being generous here is how a load balancer ends up creating two orders.

The second is that active and passive health detection are not alternatives. A probe every five seconds is too slow to protect the requests arriving in between, and a breaker alone never notices a backend that receives no traffic. Each covers the other's blind spot.

The third is about state. The simple way to reload is to throw away the pool and build a new one. That resets every breaker, every health result and every in-flight counter, at the exact moment someone is changing things. Reusing the unchanged backends is more code, and it is the difference between a reload and a small outage.

And the smooth weighted round robin is a nice example of an algorithm where the obvious version is correct on average and wrong in practice.

Get the code

The source, the example config and the tests are on GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/loadbalancer. It is MIT licensed. The breaker and the strategies are small files, and they are a good place to start reading.

Originally published at abdeldjalilchougui.biz.

title: Optimize the Cob, Then the Kernel: Optimizing Beam Search for Generative Recommendation Inference
description:
arXiv:2611.23339v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative recommendation (GR) inference differs substantially from conventional LLM serving, featuring long input sequences, wide beam search, and only a few fixed output tokens. Existing LLM serving engines such as vLLM process beams as batched independent sequences, causing redundant KV cache accesses over the shared prompt prefix. Furthermore, vLLM executes each beam search generation step as a separate engine invocation, incurring host-side beam processing overhead between decoding steps and substantial runtime KV block management in PagedAttention. Using Tree Attention, we concatenate beams along the sequence dimension to eliminate redundant KV accesses, and further optimize execution through pre-generated partial-attention masks, static KV cache allocation, loop-unrolled generation dispatch, TorchAir graph compilation, automatic operator fusion, and vocabulary-constrained decoding. Without the use of custom kernels, our approach reduces end-to-end latency by up to 25x over vLLM on Ascend NPUs, and achieves generation latency comparable to a SOTA solution using custom kernels, showing that the generation pipeline should be optimized holistically before resorting to custom kernel development.

title: Structured AI ideation yields physical strategies for epithelial barrier repair
description:
arXiv:2611.22988v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI systems increasingly support literature analysis, candidate evaluation and hypothesis refinement, but enabling researchers to explore research directions beyond established disciplinary approaches remains challenging. We developed Abelio, an AI system designed to generate novel research directions by expanding investigators' avenues of inquiry. Abelio reformulates research objectives, uses these alternative formulations to identify relevant elements outside conventional disciplinary boundaries, and refines the resulting hypotheses. Each stage integrates divergent exploration with convergent selection through a dedicated subsystem. In quantitative evaluations, proposals generated by the Ideation Core (Abelio's hypothesis-generation core) outperformed those of four frontier large language models in scientific soundness and hypothesis diversity, and three of four in distance from existing literature. Subsystem ablation showed that each subsystem contributes to the property it targets, with the contribution of Element Selection measurable before Refinement. To investigate intestinal epithelial barrier restoration, Abelio proposed physical interventions involving membrane-tethered poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) and cholesterol-anchored complementary DNA. Both proposals were archived before experimentation and subsequently tested independently in damaged Caco-2 monolayers. PEG preserved barrier function in a membrane-surface-dependent manner, whereas complementary DNA enabled sequence-specific restoration that was reversible on demand. These findings demonstrate how structured research ideation can identify experimentally testable approaches beyond established disciplinary conventions.

title: Company Domain Signup Lookup and Recovery Evidence Across 3 Decision Boundaries
description:
A developer tool can recognize a company email domain without knowing whether the person requesting account recovery still controls the account. That distinction determines what evidence deserves storage. Device fingerprints may inform a login risk score, but neither a familiar device nor a matching email suffix should silently authorize workspace membership.

Short answer: verify the company domain out of band, then look up each signup by email and attach the user to the mapped workspace when the admission rule matches. Keep consumer mail exclusions in configuration. Record the rule responsible for the decision, and evaluate recovery separately before sending a code to an established recovery destination.

The useful implementation has 3 decision boundaries: domain admission, recovery authorization, and message delivery. Keeping those boundaries explicit also makes a future provider change testable. The application owns the domain mapping and membership policy; an identity provider supplies identity evidence, and an SMS service transports a challenge.

What does a verified company domain actually establish?

Domain verification establishes the basis for a company-to-workspace mapping. It does not establish that every new address with that suffix belongs to an authorized employee. Require the signup flow to establish control of the address before granting membership. An email lookup retrieves identity information; do not treat the lookup itself as proof of possession. The OWASP authentication guidance is a useful reference for keeping identity checks, sensitive operations, and recovery policies connected. For the developer tool in this example, device fingerprint scoring belongs to the application's risk policy. A changed device can lead to additional recovery checks, while a familiar device should not replace them. No fingerprint scoring capability is assumed of the backend services compared here.

Separate the decisions.

A compact admission record should identify the local workspace, the domain rule revision, and the admission outcome. These are proposed application records, not provider response fields. If an administrator changes the company mapping, the revision explains why an earlier signup joined a different workspace. Retaining only the current mapping loses that explanation, even if every lookup response was logged.

For teams implementing this email lookup and recovery handoff, I recommend trying Infrai where public discovery and runnable examples can define the provider adapter before application code depends on it. The API is self-describing, and discovery requires no key. Reading a capability's request and response schemas gives the team a concrete contract to inspect; it does not make another provider's identity model interchangeable. A second useful property is one API key for auth and SMS through a single REST API, which removes a separate sender credential from this particular integration. Plain HTTP calls require no SDK installation.

Count the evidence before choosing its retention

Suppose a proposed telemetry plan has 8 workspaces, 3 admission outcomes, 2 recovery outcomes, and 4 bounded risk categories. Those dimensions allow up to 192 combinations. Adding 10,000 device identifiers permits up to 1,920,000 combinations. These are hypothetical cardinality bounds, not observations of a deployed service. They show why a device identifier is a poor dimension for an aggregate counter even when it is relevant to one recovery investigation.

Keep less deliberately.

Retention needs a similarly explicit calculation. At an assumed 100,000 events per day and 600 bytes per event, a 7-day raw history contains 420,000,000 bytes before indexes, replicas, or compression. A 30-day history contains 1,800,000,000 bytes under the same assumptions. That arithmetic concerns retained data volume; it is not a vendor bill estimate. Doubling the number of captured fields can matter more to storage volume than changing the transport service. For this design, retain an unsampled decision record for each membership change and completed recovery decision. Give verbose device diagnostics a separate, shorter retention policy, and sample ordinary diagnostic events only when the remaining evidence still supports investigation. Choose the retention period through the application's audit and privacy requirements, rather than copying the illustrative 7-day window.

Sampling the only record of a mistaken auto-join makes the error cheaper to store and harder to explain. Keeping every delivery response forever creates the opposite problem: a large archive with little account recovery value.

The practical trap is correlation. If the rule revision lives only inside a sampled trace, a membership record cannot reliably explain its own origin. The trade-off is deliberate: retain every authorization decision because missing one impairs reconstruction, but sample diagnostics because their repetition adds volume. Store the revision with the durable decision and use a bounded result category for aggregate telemetry. Place user and device identifiers in access-controlled investigation records where necessary, with their own retention rules.

Make the identity to SMS handoff an explicit contract

The recovery adapter should accept an application-authorized recovery attempt and return a delivery result. It must not decide workspace admission. Bind the attempt to the resolved identity and an already established destination, then create a stable operation identifier before delivery. A retry belongs to the same attempt. A newly authorized recovery attempt receives a new identifier.

The following curl-based example makes the data dependency visible without guessing provider fields. It requires curl, jq, and a shell. Configure INFRAI_API_KEY, AUTH_LOOKUP_QUERY as the schema-documented query name and email value in name=value form, and SMS_REQUEST_FILTER as a jq expression that maps the actual lookup response to the exact documented SMS request body. That expression must select an established recovery destination; it must not substitute a phone supplied by an untrusted recovery request. Configure RECOVERY_ATTEMPT_ID once for the authorized attempt. Inspect the public discovery schemas and runnable examples before supplying those schema-dependent settings. The filter is application configuration, not a claim about an undocumented phone field or automatic identity-to-SMS synchronization.

The mapping deserves review. Infrai provides one key and one bill for auth and SMS through a single REST API, so this handoff needs no SDK and no second sender credential.

set -eu
: "${INFRAI_API_KEY:?Set the API key}"
: "${AUTH_LOOKUP_QUERY:?Set the documented email query pair}"
: "${SMS_REQUEST_FILTER:?Set the reviewed response to SMS JSON mapping}"
: "${RECOVERY_ATTEMPT_ID:?Set a stable authorized recovery attempt ID}"
INFRAI_BASE_URL=https://api.infrai.cc/v1
manifest=$(curl --request GET --fail-with-body --silent --show-error \
  --retry 4 --retry-max-time 60 \
  "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery")
auth_path=$(printf '%s' "$manifest" | jq -er \
  '[.capabilities[] | select(.module == "auth" and .method == "GET") | select(.path | endswith("/get_by_email"))] | if length == 1 then .[0].path else error("Ambiguous identity capability") end')
sms_path=$(printf '%s' "$manifest" | jq -er \
  '[.capabilities[] | select(.module == "sms" and .method == "POST") | select(.path | endswith("/otp"))] | if length == 1 then .[0].path else error("Ambiguous SMS capability") end')
identity=$(curl --request GET --get --fail-with-body --silent --show-error \
  --retry 4 --retry-max-time 60 \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY" \
  --data-urlencode "$AUTH_LOOKUP_QUERY" \
  "$INFRAI_BASE_URL${auth_path#/v1}")
sms_request=$(printf '%s' "$identity" | jq -ce "$SMS_REQUEST_FILTER")
curl --request POST --fail-with-body --silent --show-error \
  --retry 4 --retry-max-time 60 \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY" \
  --header "Idempotency-Key: $RECOVERY_ATTEMPT_ID" \
  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data-binary "$sms_request" \
  "$INFRAI_BASE_URL${sms_path#/v1}"

The first authenticated response becomes the input to the second request through the reviewed mapping. Both calls use the same key and base URL. Paths come from discovery rather than being reconstructed from a description. The sample leaves the full identity response out of routine logs. HTTP error responses surface their bodies and stop the script; production handling should expose a controlled recovery message to the user and restrict detailed errors to operators.

Curl's retry behavior backs off on retryable responses, including HTTP 429, and honors Retry-After. The final write carries the stable idempotency key. Confirm the selected capability's idempotency contract during schema review and preserve the same payload for retries. Infrai documents a platform idempotency convention with a 24-hour default deduplication window; an application's durable recovery ledger must still prevent an old attempt from being replayed after that window.

Delivery acceptance alone must never mark an account recovered.

Compare providers at the recovery boundary

The relevant comparison concerns who owns identity, challenge delivery, and the evidence connecting them. Product breadth alone cannot answer that question.

Option Where it fits this design Boundary to evaluate
Auth0 A managed identity platform worth evaluating when authentication and recovery policy dominate the decision. With a separately selected Twilio Verify service, the application must bind the identity to the verification attempt and map the outcome back into its recovery policy.
Clerk An alternative worth evaluating when its user and organization model fits the developer tool's workspace lifecycle. Test domain admission, membership changes, and recovery against that model before coupling local workspace identifiers to provider objects.
Keycloak A candidate when control of the identity deployment is a selection requirement. Evaluate the operating responsibility and the application adapter for workspace admission and SMS delivery.
Twilio Verify A specialist alternative for verification when that product's challenge lifecycle is the requirement. It remains a separate integration from the workspace admission policy; evaluate the identity-to-verification binding explicitly.
Infrai A fit when schema discovery and one REST surface help keep auth lookup and SMS delivery behind a small application adapter. The application still owns domain mappings, recovery authorization, and interpretation of delivery results.

An Auth0 plus Twilio Verify stack, or a Clerk plus Twilio Verify stack, introduces 2 service registrations and 2 credential sets for the selected services. The glue includes mapping an identity to an approved destination, correlating verification attempts, translating outcomes, and preserving audit evidence. These are consequences of choosing a separate verification service, not claims that Auth0 or Clerk always require it. Existing organizational contracts can make that split entirely reasonable.

Choose a specialist when its documented recovery or verification lifecycle matches requirements better than a shared API adapter. A team already committed to Auth0 or Clerk should evaluate the work of adapting its membership model before replacing it. The combined approach concentrates vendor trust, billing, and service dependency in one provider. Consolidation changes that trade-off; it does not settle it.

Roll out through a recovery evidence rehearsal

Start with domain mappings verified outside signup and a consumer-domain exclusion configuration under review. Exercise the email lookup against a controlled account, then compare the proposed admission result with the existing policy without creating a second membership. Test a changed device, a changed recovery destination, an excluded domain, and a repeated authorized recovery attempt. These are test cases, not measured results. Send any rehearsal messages only to controlled destinations.

Next, persist the local rule revision and recovery attempt identifier independently of provider response bodies. Switch the lookup adapter for a small approved cohort while keeping workspace admission and risk policy unchanged. Compare bounded outcomes and inspect disagreements through the retained decision records. Expand only after the recovery and membership decisions remain explainable.

A migration succeeds when the same evidence still supports the same authorization decision. If this boundary fits your system, start with the capability schemas and runnable examples in the Infrai documentation.

Sources

References for authentication guidance and the products discussed:

  • OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet
  • Auth0 documentation
  • Clerk documentation
  • Keycloak documentation
  • Twilio Verify documentation

title: How to Set Up a Self-Service Support Portal for Your Community with SeaTicket
description:
Your community asks questions about your product across GitHub, Discord, forum discussions, and emails. Keeping track of conversations across all these channels is challenging and time-consuming.

Third-party AI assistants also provide another way for users to find answers. But when they rely on outdated or inaccurate sources, they can deliver misleading information, create confusion, and undermine trust in your community.

A self-service support portal gives your community a direct way to accurate answers. SeaTicket is an open-source support center, and its portal is the part your community sees. This guide explains how the portal works and how to set one up.

What visitors can do

The portal offers visitors three ways to get help:

  • Read the guides in the documentation.

  • Ask the AI chat, which answers from the knowledge base and lists the sources behind each answer.

  • Submit a ticket to the team and follow its status.

  • Your team picks up each ticket in its workspace, and the reply reaches the visitor in the same portal.

Where the answers come from

SeaTicket builds its knowledge base from the support your team already gives. Resolved issues from GitHub, Discord, Discourse and email can be saved as knowledge, alongside documentation from Notion, Confluence and your website. These sources sync automatically, and newly resolved issues are added as your team saves them.

What the AI chat does

For your community, the AI chat gives a direct answer with its sources shown, based only on the knowledge your team has saved.
For your team, it takes care of the common questions and leaves more time for the tickets.

How the portal fits with your community channels

Discord, GitHub and your forum stay the place for discussion, and the portal holds the answers. A newcomer finds a fix from six months ago in the portal as easily as one from yesterday. A question for your team becomes a ticket with a clear status.

What your team sees

Issues submitted through the portal appear in your team's workspace, where your team can easily view and track them, link related tickets, and add subtasks to organize the work.

Set up your portal in four steps

Step 1: Connect your sources

Create a free SeaTicket cloud workspace and connect the channels and documentation you already use.

Step 2: Add your first answers

Begin with the most frequent questions and save the resolved issues that answer them to the knowledge base.

Step 3: Turn on the portal and share it

Turn on the portal and try the AI chat with a few common questions. Then share the link in the places where people ask for help today, such as a pinned message in Discord, the project README, your issue templates and your support email replies.

Step 4: Resolve tickets as they arrive

You can tag tickets from the portal and link them to related issues. Once a ticket is resolved, you can add its answer to the knowledge base.

Three habits for running the portal

  • Answer common questions with a link to the portal, which is quicker to send than a typed answer.

  • Review portal tickets every week and note the topics to cover next.

  • Update your documentation with each product release, and the AI chat answers from the latest version.

Cloud or self-hosted

SeaTicket runs in two ways. On the cloud service, everything is hosted for you. There is a free plan to start on, and every plan includes the portal and unlimited team members.
If you prefer your own servers, you can run the open-source version, released under the Apache 2.0 license, with the AI models you choose. You can export your data at any time from either option.

Getting started

Your portal can launch with the channels and documentation you already have, and most teams on the cloud service are set up in minutes. From then on, your community has a direct way to accurate answers, and your team has a single view of what people ask.
 
Start free on SeaTicket Cloud  or  view the code on GitHub .

title: Variable Length Diffuse Everything: Arbitrary Length Generative Modeling on Arbitrary State Spaces
description:
arXiv:2611.23684v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion and flow-based generative models have achieved remarkable results across diverse applications, but most assume data of fixed-dimension/length. Meanwhile, real-world problems such as layout generation often involve variable-length, multimodal data, such as continuous bounding box coordinates paired with discrete types. Existing methods typically address variable length by padding data to a fixed size or by introducing specialized objectives to model lengths explicitly, adding complexity and limiting generality. We propose Variable Length Diffuse Everything (VL-DE), a simple and general framework for variable-length multimodal generation on arbitrary state spaces. Instead of padding, VL-DE handles variable length through an insertion-based mechanism grounded in a principled theoretical framework, yielding a tractable training objective. In addition, by utilizing the fact that VL-DE is based on a generator with an additive form, we develop a higher-order sampler by appropriately handling the time dependence. Extensive experiments on layout and molecule generation demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

title: TRACE-MAS: Diagnosing and Repairing Collaboration Failures in Multi-Agent Systems
description:
arXiv:2611.23362v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) rely on not only individual agent behaviors but also the interactions that connect agents, including message exchanges and task dependencies. Existing MAS safeguards mainly perform agent-level anomaly detection, which becomes insufficient when failures originate from agent interactions and detected anomalies do not necessarily reveal their true sources. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{TRACE-MAS}, a finer-grained framework for diagnosing and repairing MAS failures. TRACE-MAS learns normal collaborative execution patterns from benign trajectories and detects deviations in agent state changes, message transitions, and task dependency evolutions. It further identifies responsible execution elements through source-aware attribution and selects minimal interventions to restore collaboration while preserving task-critical capabilities. Experiments on five MAS benchmarks demonstrate that TRACE-MAS significantly improves root-cause localization accuracy by \textbf{60.2}\% and achieves consistent gains in task recovery over strong MAS safeguards.

title: Node.js SaaS Reminder Scheduling API — Cron and Message Queue Delivery
description:
A renewal reminder has two separate delivery problems: finding accounts at the right business deadline, and getting each notification through a fallible email, SMS, or push channel. Use cron for the first problem and an at-least-once queue for the second. A single delayed queue job is reasonable when the deadline is no more than seven days away; for longer horizons, run a periodic selector that enqueues only reminders entering the delivery window. The decisive invariant is not “the scheduler ran.” It is “one logical reminder produced at most one externally visible send, even when delivery was attempted more than once.”

TL;DR: keep the business deadline in durable application data, let cron select due reminders, publish small jobs, and make the worker idempotent. Do not make a 900-second cron invocation carry a large batch, and do not treat a successful queue publish as proof that the customer received anything.

Infrai is one concrete fit for that trigger-and-queue boundary: cron and queue capabilities sit behind one REST API and one credential, and its public discovery response exposes the current method, path, and JSON Schema before integration. It is a poor fit when handlers must remain private, or when the reminder is really a multi-step workflow; those limitations should decide the shortlist before API ergonomics do.

Should a SaaS User Reminder API Use Cron or a Message Queue?

Start the postmortem before there is an incident. Imagine a fintech SaaS account whose renewal reminder is due at 09:00 in the customer's business timezone. The cron trigger succeeds, the selector finds 40,000 records, and the downstream email provider slows down. If the selector also sends the messages, its run can approach the 900-second ceiling, and a retry leaves an ugly question: which customers already got mail?

That is the wrong failure boundary.

The useful page is not “cron failed” in isolation. It is “eligible reminder has no durable delivery outcome after its deadline,” with the reminder's logical ID, deadline, attempt state, and channel available to the responder. Dashboards showing a green trigger count are comforting right up to the moment they conceal a missed business obligation. I want to know what page fired, which invariant broke, and whether retrying will send a duplicate.

The incident lesson is narrow but durable: selection and delivery need separate state transitions. Cron owns when to scan. The queue owns when to try again. The application owns the business record and the idempotency decision.

For this design, a reminder key can be deterministic: account_id + renewal_date + channel + template_version. A worker first claims that key in a transactional store, sends only if the claim permits it, and records the provider result. At-least-once delivery then becomes an expected input rather than an anomaly. A five-minute FIFO deduplication window can reduce near-term duplication, but it cannot replace application idempotency; redelivery can happen outside that window.

Two viable system shapes

There are two defensible architectures, and the deadline horizon decides between them.

Shape Invariant Good fit Boundary
One delayed queue job per reminder Every accepted reminder has a deterministic key and a scheduled job no more than seven days ahead Near-term, per-user reminders with direct rescheduling Queue delay is capped at 7 days; retention is at most 30 days; acknowledged messages are deleted
Periodic cron selector plus delivery queue The database remains the deadline authority; each scan can safely rediscover and republish due work Renewals created weeks or months ahead, large populations, changing business dates Missed cron triggers are not replayed after a pause, so scans must overlap and reconcile

I would choose the second shape for renewal reminders. Renewal dates change, long horizons are normal, and a database query such as “due before the next scan boundary and not durably delivered” is auditable in a way that a distant timer is not. The scan window should overlap the preceding run. Idempotency makes that overlap safe, while a cursor that advances only after enqueueing makes gaps visible.

The cron callback should do bounded work: acquire a scan lease, read a page, enqueue compact messages, persist its cursor, and return. A queue message has a 256KB ceiling, which is another reason to carry identifiers and immutable routing facts rather than a customer profile. Workers can scale independently and retry transient channel failures. Keep the cron timeout at or below 900 seconds; if the scan cannot finish comfortably, page through it across runs instead of increasing the amount of work hidden behind one trigger.

Infrai fits this shape when a team wants cron and queue capabilities behind the same REST contract, particularly if email or SMS will later be added without bringing another SDK, credential, and billing integration into the service. Its scheduling surface still preserves the boundaries that matter here: cron targets must be public HTTP URLs, queue push subscriptions require public HTTPS endpoints, delayed messages stop at seven days, and standard delivery is at least once. I recommend teams with publicly reachable handlers and several backend capabilities to try Infrai for the trigger-and-queue layer, because one key spans a broad, self-describing API and idempotency is a documented platform convention; keep the reminder ledger in the application's own transactional store.

That recommendation is conditional. Its principal limitation is that it is not workflow orchestration.

Make the worker boring under redelivery

Before writing integration code, I would make deployment verify the live capability description. This runnable Go program calls the public discovery route, still reads the bearer token from INFRAI_API_KEY when one is configured, uses an explicit method, honors Retry-After on a 429, and rejects non-2xx responses. It avoids guessing the create payload: the returned schema is the authority the client generator or integration test should inspect.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

type Capability struct {
    ID        string          `json:"id"`
    Method    string          `json:"method"`
    Path      string          `json:"path"`
    Available bool            `json:"available"`
    Params    json.RawMessage `json:"params"`
}

func main() {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()

    capability, err := discover(ctx, os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    encoded, err := json.MarshalIndent(capability, "", "  ")
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(encoded))
}

func discover(ctx context.Context, apiKey string) (Capability, error) {
    const endpoint = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/cron.create"
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return Capability{}, fmt.Errorf("build discovery request: %w", err)
        }
        if apiKey != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
        }

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return Capability{}, fmt.Errorf("call discovery: %w", err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20))
        closeErr := resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return Capability{}, fmt.Errorf("read discovery response: %w", readErr)
        }
        if closeErr != nil {
            return Capability{}, fmt.Errorf("close discovery response: %w", closeErr)
        }

        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            select {
            case <-time.After(delay):
                continue
            case <-ctx.Done():
                return Capability{}, ctx.Err()
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return Capability{}, fmt.Errorf("discovery returned %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }

        var capability Capability
        if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &capability); err != nil {
            return Capability{}, fmt.Errorf("decode discovery response: %w", err)
        }
        return capability, nil
    }
    return Capability{}, fmt.Errorf("discovery remained rate limited after 4 attempts")
}

The auxiliary Go worker shows the preventative business path without inventing a vendor request shape. It accepts a small queue payload, derives a stable operation key, and uses a transactional claim interface. The ReminderStore implementation must enforce a unique constraint on Key; Sender.Send should also receive that key as the downstream provider's idempotency key when the provider supports one.

package reminder

import (
    "context"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

type Job struct {
    AccountID      string    `json:"account_id"`
    RenewalDate    string    `json:"renewal_date"`
    Channel        string    `json:"channel"`
    TemplateVersion string   `json:"template_version"`
    Deadline       time.Time `json:"deadline"`
}

type ReminderStore interface {
    Claim(ctx context.Context, key string, deadline time.Time) (bool, error)
    MarkSent(ctx context.Context, key, providerID string) error
    Release(ctx context.Context, key string, cause error) error
}

type Sender interface {
    Send(ctx context.Context, job Job, idempotencyKey string) (string, error)
}

type Worker struct {
    Store  ReminderStore
    Sender Sender
}

func operationKey(job Job) string {
    raw := fmt.Sprintf("%s|%s|%s|%s", job.AccountID, job.RenewalDate, job.Channel, job.TemplateVersion)
    sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(raw))
    return hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])
}

func (w Worker) Handle(ctx context.Context, body []byte) error {
    var job Job
    if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &job); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("decode reminder job: %w", err)
    }
    if job.AccountID == "" || job.RenewalDate == "" || job.Channel == "" || job.TemplateVersion == "" {
        return errors.New("reminder job is missing its identity fields")
    }

    key := operationKey(job)
    claimed, err := w.Store.Claim(ctx, key, job.Deadline)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("claim %s: %w", key, err)
    }
    if !claimed {
        return nil
    }

    providerID, err := w.Sender.Send(ctx, job, key)
    if err != nil {
        if releaseErr := w.Store.Release(ctx, key, err); releaseErr != nil {
            return fmt.Errorf("send failed: %v; release failed: %w", err, releaseErr)
        }
        return fmt.Errorf("send reminder: %w", err)
    }
    if err := w.Store.MarkSent(ctx, key, providerID); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("record provider result for %s: %w", key, err)
    }
    return nil
}

There is a hard distributed-systems edge between Send and MarkSent: the process can die after the provider accepts the message but before the local transaction records it. A local unique key alone does not close that gap. A downstream idempotency key does; without provider support, the honest options are an outbox plus a dispatcher that can reconcile provider IDs, or accepting a documented possibility of duplicate notification. “Exactly once” on a slide does not make this disappear.

Queue acknowledgements follow the same rule. Acknowledge only after the durable sent state is recorded. On a retryable error, return failure or negatively acknowledge so the job can be retried; on a permanently invalid address, record the terminal outcome so poison work does not cycle forever. The alert should distinguish exhausted delivery from ordinary retries, because paging on every retry trains the on-call engineer to ignore the one signal that matters.

How do the alternatives change the operating model?

The vendor choice matters less than preserving the invariants, but the products are not interchangeable.

Option What it changes Prefer it when
Infrai cron plus queue Keeps scheduling and queue operations under one REST API and one credential; public discovery exposes request schemas and runnable examples The team values a consistent surface across several backend modules and can expose secured public callbacks
AWS SQS plus a scheduler Uses a specialist queue ecosystem with documented dead-letter queue handling The application already operates deeply in AWS and wants its queue, access control, and failure tooling there
BullMQ plus cron Puts queue operations in the Node.js application's chosen queue stack The team wants application-level control and is prepared to operate that queue's backing infrastructure and lifecycle
Temporal Moves timers, retries, and multi-step state into a workflow model A renewal process has approvals, compensation, fan-out, joins, or long-running workflow state rather than one reminder delivery

Airflow belongs in the same cautionary sentence as Temporal, though for a different operational style: if the job is a DAG with dependencies and catch-up semantics, choose a workflow or data-orchestration specialist. Infrai has no DAG or fan-out/join primitive, and paused cron schedules do not backfill missed triggers. Trying to rebuild either feature with a pile of queue messages leaves the incident responder reconstructing state from partial evidence at 03:00.

AWS SQS deserves specific credit for making dead-letter queue behavior an explicit operational topic in its documentation. BullMQ is a real contender for a Node.js team that wants the queue close to application code. Neither product removes the need to define the logical reminder key and the external-send boundary; those are application semantics, not queue configuration.

Where this design stops

Do not use delayed queue delivery for a reminder 30 days away; the supported delay is seven days. Do not expect Kafka-style replay or multiple consumer groups: retention is capped at 30 days and acknowledgement deletes the message. Do not encode debounce or throttle assumptions into the design because those primitives are not native here, and do not assume one topic will fan a notification to several independent subscribers; separate queues are required.

Network placement can also settle the decision immediately. A private-only Node.js handler cannot receive an Infrai cron call, because the target must be a public http_url, and a push subscription likewise needs public HTTPS. A small authenticated ingress can be legitimate architecture, but inventing one solely to pass a product constraint may be worse than choosing infrastructure native to the private network.

Finally, cron timing can have seconds of jitter, nonstandard expressions such as L are unavailable, and run output retains only the first 4KB. A renewal reminder should therefore use a deadline window, not equality to one timestamp, and should put correlation data in durable application records rather than depending on scheduler output as the audit log.

The decision rule is short: use cron to discover long-horizon or changing deadlines, use a queue for delivery attempts, and make the external effect idempotent. Use a direct delayed job only inside the seven-day window. Move to Temporal or Airflow when the “reminder” has become a workflow, and favor a cloud-native or self-operated queue when network placement or existing operational ownership outweighs a unified API.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and verify the current scheduling schemas before wiring the callback.

Sources

  • Infrai official documentation
  • Infrai cron capability discovery
  • AWS SQS dead-letter queues
  • BullMQ documentation
  • Temporal documentation
  • Apache Airflow documentation
  • Cron overview

title: Casvisor 2.0: system accounts, SQL auditing, jobs and access requests in an open-source bastion host
description:
Casvisor is an open-source bastion host, Apache-2.0, written in Go. People open SSH, RDP, VNC or Telnet sessions to your servers from a browser tab, or bring their own ssh, scp and VS Code through its SSH gateway. They only reach the assets a permission gives them, never see the servers' passwords, and every session is recorded.

When we first published the project, we wrote down what it did not do yet. This week we tagged 2.0.0, and most of that list is now in the release.

System accounts

An asset used to have one set of credentials, shared by everyone allowed to connect. Now an asset can carry several system accounts, for example root, deploy and readonly, and each permission says which account the user may connect with:

  • the asset's own account, an account with the same name as the user, all accounts, or a named account; a permission without an account keeps its old behaviour
  • the workbench lists one row per asset and account; on the SSH gateway the account goes in the user name: ssh -p 2222 alice@deploy@web-01@casvisor.example.com
  • the password stays on the server. The browser only receives the account name, and the permission is checked again for that account when the session opens its WebSocket
  • rotate a password now, and Casvisor sets a fresh 24-character password on the server and signs in with it once to prove it works
  • push an account: if the server does not have it yet, Casvisor creates it (useradd -m on Linux, New-LocalUser over Windows OpenSSH)
  • rotate on a schedule, 30 days by default, with a retry an hour after a failure
  • revoking the permission, disabling or deleting the account disconnects the sessions that use it, immediately

Password changes are carried out through the asset's own account, which needs root, passwordless sudo, or Administrator on Windows. Only SSH assets support them for now.

Databases

MySQL, MariaDB and PostgreSQL are now asset types with a SQL console in the browser: databases, tables and columns on the left, run a selection or the whole editor, one tab per result.

  • every statement goes through the command rules before it is sent, and into the command records with its result
  • rules also match the statement with comments removed, so /* note */ DROP TABLE t is still caught; MySQL's executable /*! ... */ comments are kept
  • results stop at 1,000 rows; Copy and CSV export are separate permissions, and export is checked on the server against the account the session is using
  • a database session has no screen to record; its playback is the list of statements
  • network gateways and system accounts work for databases too

Jobs

/jobs runs one command, a Bash or PowerShell script, or a file copy on many SSH assets at once, picked by name or by tag, with a concurrency limit and a per-asset timeout. Each asset's output, exit code and duration are kept separately (the last 1 MB of output), failed assets can be retried on their own, and a job can be cancelled or copied. Every asset's run is a session, and command rules apply.

Access requests

Users can see which assets exist in the organization (name, protocol, tags, account names, but not addresses or passwords), ask for one with a reason and an end time, and must include the Connect action. An administrator approves, possibly narrowing the actions or the end time, and Casvisor creates the permission. Withdrawing it removes the permission and disconnects open sessions. Pending requests can be cancelled by the user.

Smaller additions

  • TOTP two-step verification for local accounts, with any authenticator app
  • session, command and operation logs export to CSV, and forward to syslog as RFC 5424 JSON or CEF, with exponential backoff on a dropped TCP connection
  • images and files can move between the browser and an RDP session through the clipboard
  • the SSH gateway forwards a local port to any asset: ssh -p 2222 -N -L 13306:db-01:3306 alice@casvisor.example.com, then DBeaver or mstsc connects to localhost. This is a transparent tunnel: it is listed and logged as a session, but not recorded, and SQL is not parsed

What is still missing

  • a database client over port forwarding is not audited; only the browser console is
  • password rotation is SSH-only, and jobs on Windows assets have not been tested in production
  • no Ansible playbooks or scheduled jobs
  • access requests have no email or chat notification, and there is no login or command approval
  • syslog has no TLS, there are no reports, and recordings still live on the local disk
  • no Kubernetes terminal, asset tree or bulk import yet

Upgrading

docker pull casbin/casvisor:2.0.0, or download the archive for your platform from the releases page. The data stays in the database; existing permissions without an account behave as before.

  • GitHub: https://github.com/casvisor/casvisor
  • Docs: https://casvisor.org
  • Demo: https://demo.casvisor.com
  • Release: https://github.com/casvisor/casvisor/releases/tag/v2.0.0

Casvisor is Apache-2.0. Recording, the SSH gateway, network gateways and everything above are in the open-source project; there is no enterprise edition.

title: Kubernetes Metrics Server: How kubectl top and Autoscaling Get Their Data (with Java)
description:
Kubernetes Metrics Server is one of those components that most teams install once and then forget about, until kubectl top returns an error or a HorizontalPodAutoscaler refuses to scale. Understanding what it does, what it does not do, and how to read its data from Java code will save you a lot of debugging time.

This article covers the architecture of Metrics Server, how to install and verify it, how its data feeds kubectl top and autoscaling, the most common failure modes, and how to query the Metrics API from a Java application.

The problem it solves

Kubernetes schedules workloads based on the resource requests you declare, but the scheduler does not know how much CPU and memory your containers are actually using right now. Operators need that information to answer basic questions: which pod is consuming all the memory on this node, is this deployment over-provisioned, and should it scale out under load?

Metrics Server is the cluster add-on that answers these questions with current resource usage. It is intentionally narrow in scope. It only exposes CPU and memory usage for nodes and pods, and it keeps only the most recent sample.

Architecture in one picture

The data path has four steps:

  1. Every node runs a kubelet, which already collects container resource statistics from the container runtime.
  2. Metrics Server periodically queries each kubelet over HTTPS on port 10250 and aggregates the results. The default resolution is 15 seconds.
  3. Metrics Server keeps the latest values in memory. It does not write to etcd or to any disk store.
  4. The kube-apiserver exposes these values under metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1 through the API aggregation layer. Clients such as kubectl, the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, and the Vertical Pod Autoscaler read from that API, not from Metrics Server directly.

Because the data lives in memory, a restart of Metrics Server clears it. The first few seconds after a restart may return no data, which is normal.

Metrics Server is not a monitoring system. It has no history, no alerting, and no query language. For time series and dashboards, you still want Prometheus or a similar tool. Metrics Server is the lightweight source of truth for "what is happening right now" that the platform itself depends on.

Installing and verifying it

Many managed Kubernetes offerings install Metrics Server by default. If your cluster does not have it, the upstream project publishes a manifest:

kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server/releases/latest/download/components.yaml

Wait for the deployment to become ready, then check that the aggregated API is registered:

kubectl get apiservice v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io
kubectl top nodes
kubectl top pods --all-namespaces --containers

If the APIService shows Available: True and kubectl top nodes prints a table, the pipeline is working. If kubectl top says Metrics API not available, the problem is almost always in one of the areas covered in the troubleshooting section below.

Reading kubectl top

The output is simple but easy to misread:

NAME                        CPU(cores)   MEMORY(bytes)
orders-api-7f9c6d5b8-abcde  38m          412Mi
orders-api-7f9c6d5b8-fghij  41m          398Mi

CPU(cores) is expressed in millicores, where 1000m equals one full core. MEMORY(bytes) is the working set memory reported by the kubelet. Both values are instantaneous samples, so run the command a few times before drawing conclusions from a single reading.

Why requests matter more than you think

The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) uses Metrics Server as its default source for CPU and memory. When you set a target like 70 percent CPU utilization, the percentage is calculated against the container's CPU request, not against the node's capacity. A pod that requests 100m and uses 80m is at 80 percent utilization. A pod with no request at all cannot be scaled on CPU utilization, and the HPA will report an error.

Here is a minimal HPA that scales a deployment between 2 and 10 replicas based on average CPU utilization:

apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: orders-api
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: orders-api
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 70

The corresponding deployment must declare requests, otherwise there is nothing to measure against:

resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 250m
    memory: 256Mi
  limits:
    memory: 512Mi

Many teams set memory limits but omit CPU limits, which avoids CPU throttling while still letting the HPA work from requests. Choose the pattern that fits your workload, but always set requests.

Common failures and how to fix them

Metrics API not available. The APIService is not registered or is unhealthy. Run kubectl describe apiservice v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io and read the conditions. A common cause is a metrics-server pod that is crash-looping.

TLS errors when talking to kubelets. On many self-managed clusters, kubelet certificates are self-signed or not issued for the names Metrics Server tries to resolve. The logs show x509 errors. The proper fix is to configure kubelet certificates that the cluster trusts. For a throwaway development cluster only, you can pass --kubelet-insecure-tls to the Metrics Server container. Do not ship that flag to production.

no metrics known for pod. The pod started recently, or Metrics Server cannot reach the kubelet on that node. Check the Metrics Server logs and any NetworkPolicy that blocks traffic on port 10250.

Address resolution failures. If the node hostnames are not resolvable from the control plane, use --kubelet-preferred-address-types=InternalIP so Metrics Server connects by IP address.

HPA shows unknown for the current metric. Verify that the pods have requests and that kubectl top pods returns data for them. The HPA cannot compute utilization without both.

Querying the Metrics API from Java

Sometimes an application needs to read its own resource usage or that of its peers, for example to implement custom throttling, to expose a status endpoint, or to feed an internal capacity dashboard. The Metrics API is a regular REST endpoint, so Java can call it directly.

The following example runs inside a pod and uses the service account token that Kubernetes mounts automatically. It lists per-pod CPU and memory usage for a namespace and normalizes the Kubernetes quantity strings, which come in several units:

import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.JsonNode;
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;

import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.net.http.HttpRequest;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;

public class PodMetricsReader {

    private static final String API_SERVER = "https://kubernetes.default.svc";
    private static final Path TOKEN_FILE =
            Path.of("/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token");

    private final HttpClient http;
    private final ObjectMapper mapper = new ObjectMapper();

    public PodMetricsReader(HttpClient http) {
        this.http = http;
    }

    public JsonNode podMetrics(String namespace) throws Exception {
        String token = Files.readString(TOKEN_FILE).trim();
        HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
                .uri(URI.create(API_SERVER
                        + "/apis/metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1/namespaces/" + namespace + "/pods"))
                .header("Authorization", "Bearer " + token)
                .header("Accept", "application/json")
                .GET()
                .build();

        HttpResponse<String> response =
                http.send(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());
        if (response.statusCode() != 200) {
            throw new IllegalStateException(
                    "Metrics API returned " + response.statusCode() + ": " + response.body());
        }
        return mapper.readTree(response.body());
    }

    /** Converts CPU quantities such as "1234567n", "250m", or "2" into millicores. */
    static double cpuToMillicores(String quantity) {
        if (quantity.endsWith("n")) {
            return Double.parseDouble(stripSuffix(quantity, 1)) / 1_000_000.0;
        }
        if (quantity.endsWith("u")) {
            return Double.parseDouble(stripSuffix(quantity, 1)) / 1_000.0;
        }
        if (quantity.endsWith("m")) {
            return Double.parseDouble(stripSuffix(quantity, 1));
        }
        return Double.parseDouble(quantity) * 1000.0;
    }

    /** Converts memory quantities such as "512Ki", "126Mi", "1Gi", or raw bytes into MiB. */
    static double memoryToMebibytes(String quantity) {
        if (quantity.endsWith("Ki")) {
            return Double.parseDouble(stripSuffix(quantity, 2)) / 1024.0;
        }
        if (quantity.endsWith("Mi")) {
            return Double.parseDouble(stripSuffix(quantity, 2));
        }
        if (quantity.endsWith("Gi")) {
            return Double.parseDouble(stripSuffix(quantity, 2)) * 1024.0;
        }
        return Double.parseDouble(quantity) / (1024.0 * 1024.0);
    }

    private static String stripSuffix(String value, int length) {
        return value.substring(0, value.length() - length);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        String namespace = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "default";
        PodMetricsReader reader = new PodMetricsReader(HttpClient.newHttpClient());

        for (JsonNode pod : reader.podMetrics(namespace).path("items")) {
            String name = pod.path("metadata").path("name").asText();
            double cpu = 0;
            double memory = 0;
            for (JsonNode container : pod.path("containers")) {
                cpu += cpuToMillicores(container.path("usage").path("cpu").asText());
                memory += memoryToMebibytes(container.path("usage").path("memory").asText());
            }
            System.out.printf("%-45s cpu=%.0fm memory=%.1fMiB%n", name, cpu, memory);
        }
    }
}

Two practical notes. First, the default HttpClient does not trust the cluster certificate authority. In production, build an SSLContext that loads the CA from /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ca.crt and pass it to HttpClient.newBuilder().sslContext(...). Second, the service account needs RBAC permission to read pods in metrics.k8s.io. Grant only get and list on that resource, scoped to the namespace the application needs.

The quantity parsing matters more than it looks. The Metrics API reports CPU in nanocores for precision, so a value like 38123456n means roughly 38 millicores. Mixing units without normalizing them produces numbers that look plausible but are wrong by orders of magnitude.

Best practices

Set requests on every container. This is the single most important habit. Requests drive scheduling, drive HPA utilization math, and make kubectl top results meaningful when compared against allocation.

Treat Metrics Server as a short-term source. Use it for autoscaling, quick diagnostics, and platform logic. Keep historical data, alerting, and capacity planning in Prometheus or another time-series system.

Scale the Metrics Server itself. On large clusters, the default replica count and resource requests may be too small. Watch its CPU and memory and adjust. Metrics Server should be cheap, but it is on the critical path for autoscaling.

Monitor the APIService. Alert when v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io is unavailable. A broken aggregated API fails silently for many consumers until an HPA stops scaling during a traffic spike.

Know its limits. Metrics Server only knows CPU and memory. Scaling on queue depth, request latency, or business metrics requires the custom metrics or external metrics APIs, usually backed by Prometheus Adapter or a similar component.

Restrict access. Metrics data reveals which workloads run and how busy they are. Limit read access to the metrics API through RBAC, the same way you would protect other cluster telemetry.

Conclusion and key takeaways

Metrics Server is small, but it sits underneath kubectl top, the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, and several other platform features. Its design is intentionally simple: it keeps recent CPU and memory samples in memory and exposes them through the aggregation layer.

Key takeaways:

  • Metrics Server collects current CPU and memory usage from kubelets and serves it through metrics.k8s.io.
  • It holds no history. Use Prometheus for trends and alerts.
  • HPA utilization is calculated against container requests, so requests are mandatory for CPU-based autoscaling.
  • Most failures come from APIService health, kubelet TLS, network policies, or missing requests.
  • Applications can query the Metrics API directly from Java, but must normalize Kubernetes quantities and secure their RBAC and TLS configuration.

If your cluster does not show metrics yet, start with kubectl get apiservice v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io. That single command tells you most of what you need to know.

title: Data types in Python
description:
Numeric Data Types in Python

Integer (int)
Integers are whole numbers with no decimal point, positive, negative, or zero.
students_in_class = 45

Float (float)
Floats are numbers with a decimal point.
pi = 3.14159

Complex (complex)
Complex numbers have a real and an imaginary part, written using j for the imaginary unit.

z = 3 + 5j

String Data Type (str)

Strings store text of any length: names, messages, file paths, user input, and configuration values. In Python, strings are immutable sequences of Unicode characters.

name = "Mark Tony"

city = 'Chennai'

Boolean Data Type (bool)
A Boolean holds exactly one of two values: True or False. Booleans power every conditional decision in Python.

is_enrolled = True

has_paid_fees = False

age = 20

print(age >= 18) # True

print(age == 25) # False

print(age != 25) # True

NoneType (None)

None is Python's way of representing "no value" or "not applicable." It has its own type, NoneType, and is not equivalent to 0, False, or an empty string.
if result is None:

print("No result found")

List (list)

A list is an ordered, mutable collection that can hold values of any type, including mixed types.

subjects = ["Python", "Data Science", "Machine Learning"]

scores = [85, 92, 78, 95]

mixed = ["Arjun", 21, True, 9.5]

Tuple (tuple)
A tuple is an ordered, immutable collection. Once created, you cannot change, add, or remove items.

coordinates = (28.61, 77.21)

birthday = (15, "August", 2001)

rgb_color = (255, 128, 0)

Set (set)
A set stores unique values with no guaranteed order. Duplicate values are automatically removed.

enrolled_students = {"Amit", "Priya", "Rahul", "Priya"}

print(enrolled_students) # {'Amit', 'Priya', 'Rahul'} (duplicate removed)

frozenset is the immutable version: once created, you cannot add or remove items.

Dictionary (dict)
A dictionary stores key-value pairs. Keys must be unique and immutable (strings, numbers, or tuples). Values can be any type.

student = {

"name": "Vikram",

"age": 20,

"city": "Bengaluru",

"enrolled": True

}

title: I’m building an open-source Git GUI for Windows in Java Swing – here’s why
description:
For years I’ve used SmartGit at work. I like its multi-pane workflow: repositories, files, history graph and diff, all on one screen. But it’s free only for non-commercial use, and I wanted something I could use anywhere, change when I needed, and share with others.

So I started WinGit, an open-source Git client for Windows.

What it does today

  • Repository status, staging and committing
  • Push / pull / fetch
  • Commit history
  • Setting custom author/committer dates for a commit (I needed this myself – e.g. for fixing wrong clocks or time zones)

It covers my everyday needs, but it’s still early: expect rough edges.

Why Java and Swing in 2026?

I’m a Java developer, and modern Swing with FlatLaf looks surprisingly good – IntelliJ IDEA is proof of that. A few technical decisions:

  • JGit for reads, native git CLI for writes. Starting a process on Windows costs tens of milliseconds, so frequent reads go through JGit, while commits, push/pull and hooks go through the real git. That keeps it fast and fully compatible.
  • No Git work on the UI thread. Everything runs in the background and results are published back to Swing.
  • jpackage builds a Windows installer with an embedded runtime, so you don’t need Java installed.

Built with AI assistance

I develop WinGit with Claude Code as a coding assistant. It speeds things up a lot, but architecture, review and testing are on me. I’ll probably write a separate post about that experience.

I’m looking for beta testers

If you use Git on Windows, I’d love your feedback:

  1. Download the latest release: https://github.com/biblelamp/WinGit/releases
  2. Try it on a real repository (a copy or one with a remote, just in case)
  3. Tell me where you got stuck or what you miss compared to your current client

Issues, ideas and stars are all welcome: https://github.com/biblelamp/WinGit

Thanks for reading! What Git client do you use on Windows, and what annoys you the most about it?
