title: Agents are users, so your software needs evals
description:
Agents are now users of software, doing work on people's behalf. Whether you're building the agent or the software it uses (API, CLI, MCP server, SDK), evals give you a way to measure how well that work gets done.

Agents probably missed your launch video and billboard on Highway 101, but they still go through the same funnel a human does to find and use a product: Discovery, Selection, Access, and Success.

You can build evals for any stage of this funnel. Here, we’ll focus on the final stage, Success: whether the agent completes the user’s task correctly.

That's more difficult to check than it sounds. An agent can place a “successful” order for a hot latte when the user asked for an iced one. The request worked, so the logs in your Observability stack look fine. And because LLM outputs vary between runs, one good manual test can’t tell you whether a fix worked. You need to repeat the same tasks and grade the outcomes, before and after the change.

That’s what an eval is, a test you run many times and score. Here’s how we build one.

The agentic testing pyramid

If a test asks “did it work?”, an eval asks “how often does it work, and how well?”

We group agentic software tests by how many LLM calls they typically need: deterministic tests (0), one-turn evals (1), and E2E evals (2+ across a whole task). This has turned out to be a great proxy for the effort to build them, the time they take to run, and the cost of running them. Just like in the practical test pyramid, the cheap and fast tests should make up the bulk of your test suite.

To use the pyramid, start with the problem you want to catch and pick the lowest tier that can catch it. For Success, that's the top. A one-turn eval checks a single decision, like which command the agent runs first. But Success depends on the whole sequence of steps (e.g. search for cafes → filter on user criteria → place the latte order). Each one can look reasonable on its own, and the agent can still get the wrong outcome.

An E2E eval lets the agent work through the whole task in an environment, then checks whether the final result meets the user’s requirements. You’ve probably seen a few already; most popular coding benchmarks, like SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench, are E2E evals.

Example

Say you own SF Beans, an API for ordering coffee in San Francisco. One of the best ways to give agents access to your service is through a CLI, so you’re shipping sfbeans.

Here’s a typical request from one of your customers:

Get me a large iced latte with whole milk, ready for pickup by 9:00, under $8 including tip. I’m in the Mission.

Here’s what sfbeans knows at 8:30am:

  • Fog City Roasters: ice machine is down, so no iced drinks today (temperature)

  • 24th St Beans: latte is $7.50 on the menu, but $9.27 after tax and tip (budget)

  • Dolores Drip: latte is $5.50, but the earliest pickup is 9:20 (time)

  • Valencia Grind: $7.42 after tax and tip, ready at 8:50 (meets all three)

Here’s what you could test at each layer of the pyramid for sfbeans:

How to build an end-to-end eval

We’ll build the coffee eval with Harbor, an open-source framework from the creators of Terminal-Bench that runs agents in containers, checks results, and records their actions.

Here are the terms we’ll use:

  • Task: one problem for the agent to solve, with a starting environment and a way to check whether it succeeded

  • Variant: the agent setup you’re testing, like the model, prompt, tools, memory and skills

  • Trial: one attempt by one variant at one task

  • Run (a job in Harbor): every variant tried on every task, several times each

  • Trace (a trajectory in Harbor): everything recorded during a trial: messages, tool calls, logs, files and final output

Step 1: Set a goal

Building E2E evals for everything isn’t practical. With traditional software, you can aim for 100% test coverage. With agents, the surface you’d need to cover is everything an LLM might do with your product, and even figuring out where that ends is hard (see the jagged frontier).

Start with one outcome your users care about, narrow enough to evaluate with a handful of tasks. You’ll usually find that goal in one of three places:

  • Observability: which agents use your product, and where they fail

  • Customers: support tickets, feedback, and churn

  • Roadmap: the product hypotheses you most need to validate

For example, your goal might be to:

  • Increase the success rate on a specific task

  • Reduce the number of steps required to accomplish a goal

  • Check whether an agent skill helps, and get feedback to improve it

  • A/B test a prompt

  • Explore the frontier by checking whether a use case is achievable with current LLMs, and if they fail, why

Example

We looked in all three places for sfbeans:

  • Observability: Most agent traffic comes from Claude Code and Codex. We know because sfbeans adds a user-agent header when it detects a specific coding harness.

  • Customers: The top support ticket is “my agent ordered the wrong drink”: a hot latte instead of iced, a pickup after the user’s meeting, or a total over budget once tax and tip are added.

  • Roadmap: Nothing urgent, so the wrong-drink problem goes first, since it drives churn.

That gives us our goal:

Goal

Increase the success rate on ordering the exact drink the user asked for

Agents

Claude Code and Codex, since that’s where our traffic comes from.

In scope

Drink, pickup time, and budget (incl. tax and tip), using today’s sfbeans.

Out of scope

Cancellations, refunds, and accounts. We’ll eval those later.

Done when

Both agents get the order right in every trial, not just most of the time.

Step 2: Define metrics

Here are the metrics we use most for E2E agent evals:

Success

  • Success rate: the share of trials that pass

  • Pass@k: the chance that at least one of k trials passes (answers “can the agent do this at all?”)

  • Pass^k: the chance that all k trials pass (answers “can I rely on it every time?”)

Efficiency (measured on successful trials only)

  • Steps: the number of agent turns needed to complete the task

  • Time: how long the trial took

  • Cost: how much the trial cost, in dollars

Example

Our goal is to get every order right in every trial. Once we build and run the eval in Steps 3 and 4, here’s what five trials of Claude Code + Opus 5.5 (anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 on AI Gateway) on the iced latte order could look like:

Trial

Result

What happened

Steps

Time

Cost

1

Pass

Compared quotes from 3 cafes, ordered at Valencia

9

3:40

$0.52

2

Fail: over budget

Skipped quote, ordered at 24th St: $9.27

5

1:50

$0.31

3

Pass

Compared quotes from 4 cafes, ordered at Valencia

11

4:30

$0.68

4

Fail: late

Ordered at Dolores, ready 9:20

6

2:10

$0.35

5

Pass

Skipped Fog City, ordered at Valencia

8

3:20

$0.49

What the numbers mean:

  • Success rate: 3 of 5 trials passed, so 60%.

  • Pass@5: Assuming independent trials with a 60% success rate, 1 − 0.4^5 ≈ 99%. Give the agent 5 tries and it almost certainly gets it right once.

  • Pass^5: 0.6^5 ≈ 8%. The chance the agent gets 5 orders in a row right.

  • Steps: (9 + 11 + 8) / 3 ≈ 9 on successful trials. The failed trials are shorter because the agent skipped work, like quoting, which is why efficiency only counts successful trials.

  • Time: ~3:50 on successful trials.

  • Cost: $0.56 per successful trial, but $2.35 / 3 = $0.78 per success once you count the failed trials you paid for too.

So does Opus work? Its 99% pass@5 says yes. Its 8% pass^5 says a user who orders this every weekday gets at least one wrong coffee in 92% of weeks. Both numbers are right. They just answer different questions: pass@5 asks whether the agent can get the order right, and pass^5 asks whether it gets it right every time.

Which metric matters most depends on what a failure costs your user. Someone ordering their morning coffee doesn’t get a retry. If the agent orders a hot latte, or one that’s ready after their train leaves, they’ve paid for the wrong coffee and started their day annoyed. They need it right every morning, so sfbeans optimizes for pass^5.

Other products are more forgiving, because a failed attempt is cheap and gets caught before it matters:

Product

What a failed attempt costs the user

Metric to lead with

Order my morning coffee

Paid for the wrong drink, late for work, lost trust

Pass^k

Coding agent with a test suite

Extra time and model cost; the agent uses test feedback to revise its code and try again

Pass@k

Draft an email the user reviews

A quick edit before hitting send

Success rate

Overall averages can hide a task that fails frequently, so always inspect results per task. And with only five trials, 100% means “no failures seen yet,” not “never fails.”

Step 3: Design the task set

In Step 1, we set a goal for the eval: increase how often agents order the exact drink the user asked for. But an agent can’t attempt a goal. It needs a task: one concrete request, drawn from what your users actually ask for.

Pick tasks hard enough that you learn something from running them. A good set covers the common case, the edge cases that trip agents up, and at least one request where the right move is not to act.

For each task, define these parts:

  • An instruction: the user’s request

  • An environment: where the agent works, with the same starting state for every trial

  • A verifier: a check of the final state, ideally scored per constraint

  • A known-good solution (optional): a reference run that demonstrates the expected behavior and passes the verifier

You can make every aspect of that environment as fake or as realistic as you need, depending on your goals. The OpenPipe team has a nice writeup on how they defined the environment for an email research agent.

Example

We wrote four tasks, each one a Harbor task folder in tasks/.

  • Common case: iced-latte-mission, the order from earlier

  • Edge case: usual-unavailable, where the user’s usual cafe is out of their drink

  • Edge case: team-order, with 6 drinks, $45 total, and one pickup spot

  • Don’t act: impossible-request, where nothing fits, so the right move is to tell the user

impossible-request has one extra check. Its verifier reads a command log the agent can’t write to, to confirm the agent searched before giving up. We learned we needed that the hard way (see Step 5).

Here’s iced-latte-mission:

The instruction gives the agent the user’s request and names the sfbeans CLI. In production, agents find the tool through a skill, docs, or an MCP server. Naming it here skips Discovery and Selection, keeping the eval focused on Success.

We also specify that it’s 8:30am. Only sfbeans uses our frozen clock; the sandbox’s system clock still shows the real time:

The environment is part real, part fake. The agent uses the real sfbeans CLI, but against seeded cafes and a frozen clock, so every trial starts on the same morning:

To keep the demo simple, cafes.json lives inside the agent’s environment. In a real eval, protect the seed data and verifier code, and make sure the agent can update order records only through the CLI. Agents can attempt to reward hack if it helps them pass, for example by editing the inventory or writing orders.json directly.

For this coffee order, the verifier checks the final order against the user’s requirements. Harbor runs test.sh after the agent finishes and reads the scores it writes to /logs/verifier/reward.json:

The actual check lives in check_orders.py. It scores each constraint separately, then sets reward to 1 only if all of them pass. Harbor uses reward as the trial’s main score:

The solution is a known-good answer. Run it before any real agent to prove the task works:

Finally, task.toml ties the task together. It sets the timeouts, runs the verifier in the agent’s sandbox (where orders.json lives), and saves the orders as an artifact so we can inspect them in Step 5:

Step 4: Run the eval

If you share the universal distaste for slow CI, you’ll hate waiting for evals. Every trial waits on an agent making LLM calls, step after step, and a run repeats that for every variant and task, several times each.

Harbor’s Vercel integration, which we built upstream, speeds that up a lot. It runs trials concurrently, each in its own Vercel Sandbox, and caches built task environments so they aren’t rebuilt for every trial. Routing model calls through AI Gateway gives you one key and one budget across model providers.

Example

Two agents, Claude Code and Codex, with two models each, make four variants.

Then install Harbor, connect a Vercel project, and run the job:

This run fits on the Hobby plan: 10 concurrent sandboxes is the Hobby limit, and each trial is well under its 45-minute session cap. On Pro, you can raise n_concurrent_trials as high as 10,000 (Sandbox limits).

To keep the example simple, we pass the OIDC token into each sandbox as an env var, where the agent can read it. Beyond a demo, use short-lived tokens, and use Harbor’s Vercel integration to set Sandbox firewall rules that lock each trial down to only the hosts it needs, like AI Gateway.

Internally, we go a step further and use credentials brokering to attach credentials to outgoing requests, keeping API keys outside the agent’s environment.

Step 5: Analyze traces

Now for the meaty part: trace-diving. Scores tell you how often your agents fail; traces tell you why. Read the failures, and some passes too, since a pass only means the verifier was satisfied.

Example

The run from Step 4 leaves 80 trial folders in jobs/sfbeans-baseline/. Each has the trial’s result, the agent’s trajectory, the verifier’s scores, and, because task.toml saves it as an artifact, the order the agent placed:

Run harbor view jobs to browse the results. Here’s what our four variants could report (numbers are illustrative).

For each variant, we calculate success rate and estimate pass^5 separately for each task, then average each metric across the four tasks. Each task counts equally.

Variant

Success

Pass^5

Avg steps (successful)

Cost per success (incl. failed trials)

Claude Code + Opus 5.5

85%

60%

9

$0.61

Claude Code + Sonnet 5.5

75%

52%

11

$0.27

Codex + GPT-6 Astra

80%

43%

8

$0.48

Codex + GPT-6.1 Sol

65%

14%

13

$0.22

That’s our baseline. On pass^5, the metric we chose in Step 2, even the best variant is far from reliable. But the score doesn’t tell us what to fix. For that, we have to open the failed trials.

Take trial 2 from Step 2. Claude Code + Opus 5.5 ordered at 24th St Beans for $9.27. The verifier tells us which constraint it broke:

Right drink, on time, over budget, and the saved orders.json confirms the $9.27 total. Now we read agent/trajectory.json. The agent searches for lattes in the Mission, sees $7.50 on the menu, and goes straight to order. No quote. It treated the menu price as the final price.

Trial 1, from the same variant, quotes three cafes, rules out 24th St Beans, and orders at Valencia Grind for $7.42. So the CLI can get the order right, but the agent doesn’t reliably check the total before spending the user’s money.

We then look for that pattern across other failed trials, and if it keeps showing up, we have something specific to fix: make the total harder to miss, or add a --max-total flag so order refuses anything over budget. That’s a much more useful conclusion than “Opus scored 85%.”

When we first ran this demo, the traces also exposed problems with what the eval was measuring:

  • Our first run scored 0% on every variant. The agents didn’t know sfbeans existed, so they never tried it (obviously). That’s the funnel’s Discovery stage failing in our own eval. Naming the tool in the instruction fixed it, and it’s a good reminder that being discoverable is part of your product. In the wild, that’s the job of your skill, docs, MCP server and AEO.

  • Codex kept looking for sfbeans as a connected tool and never tried running it in the shell. That’s an Access problem, not a Success one.

  • Codex passed impossible-request almost every time, but when we read the traces, 9 out of 10 passes were the agent giving up without looking. The verifier only checked that no order was placed, so we tightened it to also check that the agent searched first. Without reading the traces, we’d have counted those as wins.

Automated trace analysis

For larger runs, inspecting every trial by hand gets slow, so we automate it.

Up to 40 reader agents running fast models like deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash read trial transcripts in parallel and summarize their findings. A smarter coordinator agent reviews those summaries, sends readers back for more context when needed, and writes the final report. An analysis.md file tells the coordinator what to look for, so we can reuse the workflow across runs.

Model calls go through AI Gateway. Trial artifacts stay in Vercel Drives during analysis, and traces go to Vercel Blob for long-term storage.

Iterate to greatness

Your first eval run gives you a baseline. Now act on it.

Pick the fix the traces point to, like the --max-total flag, rerun the same job, and compare against the baseline. Check whether it reduces the targeted failures without introducing new ones, then use those results to decide whether the change is ready to ship.

Once you’ve built an eval, it keeps paying off for a lot of different things. Rerun it on every release to catch regressions; test prompt, skill, and model changes before shipping; learn how agents use your product; or build auto-optimization loops on top of it.

Expect to add harder tasks over time. As models and your product improve, evals saturate, meaning agents start passing every task. A saturated eval still catches regressions, but it can’t tell you what to improve next.

Evals are the infrastructure you use to make your product better, again and again. Vercel has the pieces you need to build them in one place: AI Gateway for model calls across providers, Sandbox to run trials at scale, and Drives and Blob to keep every trace.

Ready to run your first eval? Paste this prompt into your coding agent, and it’ll build and run one for your product on Vercel with you:

title: Gemini 4 Neon 사고 수준: High와 xhigh는 언제 사용해야 할까?
description:
Gemini 4 Neon thinking level 완전 가이드: low, medium, high, xhigh

Gemini 4 Neon의 thinking level은 모델이 답변하기 전에 얼마나 깊이 추론할지를 결정하는 네 가지 설정, 즉 low, medium, high, xhigh를 제공합니다. Neon의 기본값은 high입니다. Google은 대부분의 복잡한 작업에서는 high를 유지하고, 어려운 다단계 문제에서 high가 성능을 내지 못할 때만 xhigh로 전환할 것을 권장합니다. xhigh는 더 많은 토큰을 소모하고 시간이 더 오래 걸리기 때문입니다.

지금 Apidog을 사용해 보세요

Gemini 4 Neon thinking level이란?

Thinking level은 thinking_level 파라미터의 값으로, gemini-4-neon이 답변을 작성하기 전에 얼마나 많은 내부 추론을 수행할지 설정합니다. Neon은 low, medium, high(기본값), xhigh의 네 가지를 지원합니다. level이 높을수록 더 많은 thinking 토큰을 사용하고 지연 시간이 늘어나며, level이 낮을수록 더 빠르게 답변하고 비용이 적게 듭니다.

Google의 thinking 가이드가 Neon의 각 level을 다음과 같이 설명합니다.

thinking_level 토큰 사용량 Google 권장 용도
low 가장 적은 토큰, 가장 낮은 지연 시간 빠른 채팅, 고처리량 처리; 에이전트 작업에서도 여전히 유용함
medium 더 적은 토큰, 더 빠른 응답 대화형 코딩, 실시간 UI 프로토타이핑, 지연 시간에 민감한 도구 호출
high (기본값) 지능과 속도의 균형 복잡한 코딩, 에이전트 실행, 도구 호출, 멀티모달 지식 작업
xhigh 가장 많은 토큰, 가장 깊은 추론 어려운 다단계 엔지니어링, high가 부족한 분석적·과학적 문제

예상할 수 있는 두 가지 값이 빠져 있습니다. Neon은 minimal을 오류로 거부하므로, Gemini 3 Flash 앱에서 복사한 코드가 이 값을 보내면 작동하지 않습니다. 그리고 기존 thinkingBudget 토큰 수는 Gemini 4에서 더 이상 사용되지 않습니다. 단독으로 보내면 경고와 함께 가장 가까운 level로 매핑되지만, thinkingLevel과 함께 보내면 400을 반환합니다.

Neon의 기본값은 다른 Gemini 4 모델과 어떻게 다른가?

Neon은 더 큰 형제 모델들보다 한 단계 높은 level에서 시작합니다. Gemini 4 Neon 릴리스 노트에 따르면 Neon과 Hydrogen은 기본값이 high이고 xhigh를 지원하는 반면, Carbon과 Argon은 기본값이 medium이고 high까지만 지원합니다.

모델 기본 level 지원 level
gemini-4-neon high low, medium, high, xhigh
gemini-4-hydrogen high low, medium, high, xhigh
gemini-4-carbon medium low, medium, high
gemini-4-argon medium low, medium, high

이는 모델을 전환할 때 중요합니다. thinking_level을 설정하지 않고 Carbon 워크로드를 Neon으로 옮기면 모든 요청이 medium 추론에서 high 추론으로 뛰어올라 토큰 수가 달라집니다. 더 큰 모델들을 비교하고 있다면 Gemini 4 Carbon vs Argon 비교에서 그 차이를 다루고 있습니다.

Gemini API에서 thinking_level은 어떻게 설정하나?

Neon은 Interactions API와 generateContent 모두의 유료 등급에서 실행됩니다. 필드 이름은 두 API에서 다릅니다.

Interactions API: generation_config 안에 thinking_level을 넣습니다.

curl "https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/interactions" \
  -H "x-goog-api-key: $GEMINI_API_KEY" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -X POST \
  -d '{
    "model": "gemini-4-neon",
    "input": "Audit this payment retry queue for race conditions.",
    "generation_config": {
      "thinking_level": "xhigh",
      "max_output_tokens": 65536
    }
  }'

generateContent: generationConfig.thinkingConfig 안에 thinkingLevel을 사용합니다.

curl "https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/models/gemini-4-neon:generateContent" \
  -H "x-goog-api-key: $GEMINI_API_KEY" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -X POST \
  -d '{
    "contents": [{"parts": [{"text": "Audit this payment retry queue for race conditions."}]}],
    "generationConfig": {
      "thinkingConfig": {"thinkingLevel": "medium"}
    }
  }'

Python SDK에서는 Interactions 호출이 generation_config={"thinking_level": "high"}를 받고, generateContent 호출은 thinking_config=types.ThinkingConfig(thinking_level="low")를 받습니다. temperature, top_p, top_k는 지정하지 마세요. Google에 따르면 Neon은 범위 내 값은 무시하고 범위를 벗어난 값은 400으로 거부합니다. 동일한 API 설계에 대한 첫 요청 전체 예시는 Gemini 4 Hydrogen API 가이드를 참고하세요.

high와 xhigh는 언제 각각 사용해야 하나?

기본적으로 high를 사용하고, 해당 작업에서 high가 품질 기준을 충족하지 못할 때만 xhigh로 올리세요. Google의 출시 글은 xhigh를 "가장 어려운 엔지니어링, 분석, 과학 워크로드를 위한 더 깊은 다단계 추론"으로 설명합니다.

다음의 경우 xhigh를 선택하세요.

  • 작업에 의존 단계가 많고 초반의 실수가 결과를 망치는 경우. 예를 들어 여러 파일에 걸친 리팩터링이나 동시성 감사가 그렇습니다.
  • high가 자신감 있지만 틀린 답변을 준 경우. 단순히 느린 것이 아니라 평가 세트에서 틀렸을 때입니다.
  • 지연 시간이 크게 중요하지 않은 경우. 백그라운드 작업, 야간 리뷰, 배치 분석 같은 작업입니다.
  • 틀린 답변의 비용이 토큰 비용보다 큰 경우. 보안 패치나 금융 계산이 그렇습니다.

다음의 경우 high를 유지하거나 더 낮추세요.

  • 프롬프트가 추출이나 포맷팅인 경우. Google은 xhigh가 "텍스트나 JSON 추출 같은 단순한 프롬프트에서 과도하게 생각하거나 max_output_tokens를 소진할 수 있다"고 경고합니다.
  • 사용자가 기다리는 경우. 채팅, 자동 완성, 실시간 도구 호출에는 medium이나 low가 적합합니다.
  • 대량으로 실행하는 경우. 추가되는 모든 thinking 토큰에 비용이 청구되며, 그 차이는 요청 수가 늘수록 증폭됩니다.

Google의 벤치마크 수치도 이 구분을 뒷받침합니다. 출시 발표에서 xhigh의 Neon은 Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index에서 61점을 기록해 3위를 차지했습니다. 기본값인 high에서는 Google이 Carbon보다 작업당 비용이 32% 낮다고 보고합니다. 이는 Google의 수치이지 저희 테스트는 아니지만, 트레이드오프를 보여줍니다. xhigh는 Neon의 최고 점수를 사고, high는 효율을 삽니다.

각 thinking level의 비용은 얼마인가?

모든 level의 토큰당 가격은 같으며, 달라지는 것은 지불하는 토큰 수입니다. Neon은 100만 입력 토큰당 $3.00, 100만 출력 토큰당 $15.00이며, Google의 가격 페이지는 출력 요율에 thinking 토큰이 포함된다고 명시합니다. 암시적 캐싱을 사용하면 캐시된 입력은 100만 토큰당 $0.15로 떨어집니다(Neon에서는 명시적 캐싱이 지원되지 않음). 이 모델에는 무료 등급이 없습니다.

따라서 level의 비용은 추가되는 thinking 토큰 수에 100만 토큰당 $15를 곱한 값입니다. 다음은 입력 토큰 2,000개와 표시되는 답변 토큰 800개로 구성된 한 요청의 계산입니다. Thinking 토큰 수는 계산 방식을 보여주기 위해 임의로 선택한 것이며 측정값이 아닙니다.

Thinking 토큰 (가정) 입력 비용 출력 + thinking 비용 요청당 합계 10,000건당
500 $0.006 $0.0195 $0.0255 $255
2,000 $0.006 $0.042 $0.048 $480
8,000 $0.006 $0.132 $0.138 $1,380

Thinking이 청구서를 빠르게 지배합니다. Thinking 토큰이 8,000개일 때 추론은 요청 비용의 87%를 차지합니다. 그래서 Google은 네 가지 level 모두에서 평가를 실행하고 "품질 기준을 충족하는 가장 낮은 thinking_level을 선택하라"고 권장합니다. 더 저렴한 모델에서 같은 트레이드오프를 비교하고 싶다면 Gemini 3.8 Flash thinking level 가이드에서 다룹니다.

level별 토큰과 지연 시간은 어떻게 측정하나?

같은 프롬프트를 각 level에서 실행하고 usage 블록을 확인하세요. Interactions API에서는 응답의 usage 객체가 total_input_tokens, total_output_tokens, total_thought_tokens를 각각 보고합니다. generateContent에서는 thinking 토큰이 usageMetadata.thoughtsTokenCount로 나타납니다.

다음 루프는 하나의 프롬프트를 네 level 모두에 보내고 thinking 토큰과 실제 소요 시간을 출력합니다.

for level in low medium high xhigh; do
  start=$(date +%s)
  usage=$(curl -s "https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/interactions" \
    -H "x-goog-api-key: $GEMINI_API_KEY" \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d "{\"model\":\"gemini-4-neon\",
         \"input\":\"Find the race condition in this retry loop: ...\",
         \"generation_config\":{\"thinking_level\":\"$level\",\"max_output_tokens\":65536}}" \
    | jq -c '{status, thought: .usage.total_thought_tokens, out: .usage.total_output_tokens}')
  echo "$level $(( $(date +%s) - start ))s $usage"
done

실제 워크로드에서 10~20개의 프롬프트로 실행해 보세요. 프롬프트 하나로는 알 수 있는 것이 거의 없습니다. 여러 개를 모아야 high와 xhigh가 품질에서 갈리기 시작하는 지점을 볼 수 있습니다.

테스트하는 동안 HTTP 클라이언트의 타임아웃을 높게 설정하세요. Google의 마이그레이션 노트에 따르면 어려운 프롬프트는 몇 분이 걸릴 수 있으므로 최소 15분의 타임아웃을 설정하거나 백그라운드 실행을 사용할 것을 권장합니다.

xhigh가 때때로 빈 답변을 반환하는 이유는?

max_output_tokens는 thinking과 표시되는 출력을 함께 제한합니다. Neon이 예산 전체를 추론에 사용하면 상호작용은 incomplete 상태로 중단되고 잘렸거나 빈 답변을 반환하며, 생성한 thinking 토큰에 대한 비용은 여전히 청구됩니다.

Google 문서의 세 가지 규칙으로 이를 피할 수 있습니다.

  1. 기존의 낮은 상한을 제거하세요. 앱에 8,192 같은 값이 하드코딩되어 있다면 동기 호출 기본 상한인 65,536으로 올리세요.
  2. 상한이 아니라 level을 낮추세요. 비용이나 지연 시간을 줄이려면 max_output_tokens를 줄이는 대신 medium이나 low로 낮추세요.
  3. 긴 작업은 백그라운드로 전환하세요. 65,536 토큰을 넘는 답변에는 background를 true로 설정하고 max_output_tokens를 최대 1,048,576에서 입력을 뺀 값으로 올리세요. 입력, thinking, 출력은 하나의 100만 토큰 윈도를 공유합니다. Gemini 4 Argon 장문 출력 가이드에서 폴링 패턴을 자세히 다룹니다.

Apidog CLI로 코딩 에이전트가 네 level을 모두 벤치마크하게 하기

이 루프를 직접 반복해서 돌리는 일은 금방 지루해집니다. 대신 코딩 에이전트(Claude Code, Codex, Cursor)에게 Apidog CLI로 재사용 가능한 테스트 하나를 만들게 하고, 새로운 수치가 필요할 때마다 각 level에서 다시 실행하게 하세요.

한 번만 설정하세요.

npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog login --with-token <YOUR_TOKEN>
npx -y skills add https://apidog.com   # pick your agent when prompted

그런 다음 에이전트에게 프롬프트 하나를 전달하세요.

In Apidog project <projectId>, create an environment "gemini" with base URL
https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com and variables GEMINI_API_KEY and
THINKING. Add an endpoint for POST /v1beta/interactions that sends the
x-goog-api-key header from GEMINI_API_KEY. Create a test case that sends model
"gemini-4-neon", my audit prompt, generation_config.thinking_level {{THINKING}}
and max_output_tokens 65536, and asserts: HTTP 200, status is "completed",
and usage.total_thought_tokens exists. Run it once per level (low, medium,
high, xhigh) and give me a table of thought tokens and response time.

에이전트는 각 페이로드 스키마를 읽고, JSON을 검증하고, 리소스를 작성한 뒤 실행을 반복합니다.

apidog environment create gemini --project <projectId> --base-url https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com
apidog cli-schema get endpoint-create
apidog cli-schema validate endpoint-create --file endpoint.json
apidog endpoint create --project <projectId> --file endpoint.json
apidog cli-schema validate test-case-create --file case.json
apidog test-case create --project <projectId> --file case.json
for level in low medium high xhigh; do
  apidog run --test-case <caseId> --project <projectId> -e <envId> \
    --env-var "THINKING=$level" -r cli,json --out-file "neon-$level"
done

status is "completed" 단언은 이전 섹션의 incomplete 함정을 잡아내므로, 예산을 다 써버린 level은 빈 문자열을 반환하는 대신 확실하게 실패합니다. -r cli,json을 -r junit으로 바꾸면 같은 실행을 CI에 넣을 수 있습니다. Apidog CLI CI/CD 가이드에서 파이프라인을 보여주고, Apidog CLI in Claude Code에서 에이전트 설정을 다룹니다. Apidog의 무료 플랜은 최대 4명의 사용자를 지원합니다.

FAQ

Gemini 4 Neon의 기본 thinking level은 무엇인가요? high입니다. 이를 얻기 위해 thinking_level을 보낼 필요는 없습니다. Carbon과 Argon의 기본값은 medium이므로, 이들 모델에서 마이그레이션할 때는 level을 명시적으로 설정하세요.

Gemini 4 Neon은 minimal thinking을 지원하나요? 아니요. Neon은 low, medium, high, xhigh를 지원하며 minimal은 오류로 거부합니다. 가장 빠르고 저렴한 응답에는 low를 사용하세요.

Gemini 4 Neon에서 thinking 토큰에 요금이 부과되나요? 예. Thinking 토큰은 100만 출력 토큰당 $15.00 요율로 청구됩니다. Google은 모델이 처리하는 모든 토큰을 계산하며, 여기에는 thinking 토큰도 포함됩니다.

Gemini 4 Neon에서 thinkingBudget을 여전히 사용할 수 있나요? Gemini 4 모델에서는 더 이상 지원되지 않습니다. 단독으로 보내면 가장 가까운 thinkingLevel로 매핑되고 경고를 반환합니다. thinkingLevel과 함께 보내면 요청이 400으로 실패합니다.

xhigh가 항상 high보다 정확한가요? 항상 그렇지는 않습니다. Google에 따르면 xhigh는 텍스트나 JSON 추출 같은 단순한 프롬프트에서 과도하게 생각하고 max_output_tokens를 소진할 수 있습니다. 자신의 프롬프트에서 둘 다 테스트하고 통과하는 가장 낮은 level을 유지하세요.

Gemini 4 Neon thinking level을 무료로 사용할 수 있나요? 아니요. Gemini 4 Neon은 Gemini API 무료 등급에서 사용할 수 없습니다. Google AI Studio와 Google Antigravity에서는 유료 Google AI Pro 및 Ultra 플랜에 연결되어 있습니다.

title: Animate Popover API entry and exit without JavaScript delays
description:
A popover can animate in cleanly after showPopover() yet disappear immediately on close. The problem is not that showPopover() ignores animations. It changes the popover’s browser-managed state and top-layer participation; CSS still needs to preserve a paintable element during the closing transition.

Build the styling around the browser state rather than a separate JavaScript flag. Give the base popover selector the closed visual state, such as reduced opacity and a compressed transform. Give :popover-open the fully visible state. With both endpoints explicit, the same transition can run in either direction.

For entry, add @starting-style for the open selector. This supplies a deterministic first frame when the element becomes visible, instead of relying on an implicit initial state.

The important lifecycle detail is the transition list. Include display and overlay with allow-discrete in addition to visual properties like opacity and transform. Opacity and transform describe the motion, but display and overlay allow the browser to keep the popover rendered and in the top layer long enough for that motion to be seen on exit. Without them, the close can effectively remove the popover before its visual transition finishes.

Keep JavaScript focused on state commands. Before opening or closing, check :popover-open so code does not request showPopover() for an open popover or hidePopover() for a closed one. The script decides whether state should change; CSS owns the visible choreography.

This pattern solves a specific problem: preserving the visible exit transition for a browser-managed popover. It does not turn a popover into a modal dialog, provide complete focus management, or animate an element that your application removes from the DOM. Browser support and timing details should also be considered for the environments you support.

Working example 

// This module provides a small, testable popover transition helper.
// It models the article's working idea: JavaScript should only guard state,
// while CSS supplies the transition configuration that keeps the popover
// visible long enough to animate out.

const REQUIRED_PROPERTIES = new Set(['opacity', 'transform', 'display', 'overlay']);
const DISCRETE_PROPERTIES = new Set(['display', 'overlay']);

export function buildPopoverTransition({ durationMs = 700, properties } = {}) {
  if (!Number.isFinite(durationMs) || durationMs <= 0) {
    throw new RangeError('durationMs must be a positive finite number');
  }

  const selected = properties ?? ['opacity', 'transform', 'display', 'overlay'];

  if (!Array.isArray(selected) || selected.some((property) => !REQUIRED_PROPERTIES.has(property))) {
    throw new TypeError('properties must contain only supported popover transition properties');
  }

  for (const required of REQUIRED_PROPERTIES) {
    if (!selected.includes(required)) {
      throw new Error(`Missing required popover transition property: ${required}`);
    }
  }

  return Object.freeze({
    durationMs,
    properties: Object.freeze(
      selected.map((property) => Object.freeze({
        property,
        allowDiscrete: DISCRETE_PROPERTIES.has(property),
      })),
    ),
  });
}

export const popoverAnimationCss = `
[popover] {
  opacity: 0;
  transform: scaleX(0);
  transition:
    opacity 700ms,
    transform 700ms,
    display 700ms allow-discrete,
    overlay 700ms allow-discrete;
}

[popover]:popover-open {
  opacity: 1;
  transform: scaleX(1);
}

@starting-style {
  [popover]:popover-open {
    opacity: 0;
    transform: scaleX(0);
  }
}
`;

export function createPopoverCommands(popover) {
  if (
    !popover ||
    typeof popover.matches !== 'function' ||
    typeof popover.showPopover !== 'function' ||
    typeof popover.hidePopover !== 'function'
  ) {
    throw new TypeError('popover must provide matches(), showPopover(), and hidePopover()');
  }

  function isOpen() {
    return popover.matches(':popover-open');
  }

  return Object.freeze({
    isOpen,
    open() {
      if (isOpen()) return 'already-open';
      popover.showPopover();
      return 'opened';
    },
    close() {
      if (!isOpen()) return 'already-closed';
      popover.hidePopover();
      return 'closed';
    },
  });
}

Read the full article: https://chriseugenerodriguez.com/blog/popover-showpopover-exit-transition

title: Verifying Agents in Rubric-Graded Environments
description:
arXiv:2611.22841v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As AI agents take on increasingly open-ended and complex tasks, verifying their outputs has proven to be difficult. Rubric-graded agent environments, where a verifier judges multiple natural-language criteria against the deliverables and environment state changes produced by the agent, have emerged as a popular paradigm. We conduct the first systematic study of verifiers for rubric-graded agent environments. First, we create BankerVerifierBench (BVB), a meta-evaluation dataset of 2,464 human-judged rubric criteria across 24 investment-banking tasks. Next, we develop a methodology that derives from any rubric corpus the capabilities a verifier should possess, yielding a nine-capability taxonomy that we distill into three general design principles---reactive verification, environment alignment, and domain guidance---which we implement in Gandalf, an open-source verifier. Finally, we evaluate Gandalf against three existing verifiers on BVB. Gandalf matches or exceeds every baseline's F1 at lower cost: with Gemini 3 Flash it matches the strongest baseline's F1 (0.864 vs. 0.852) at one-fifth of its cost, and with GPT-5.4 models it improves F1 by over 0.12 at lower cost. Gandalf also generalizes to OpenClaw, a structurally different personal-productivity environment, where it again achieves the highest F1 (0.955 vs. 0.934 for the best baseline). We release BVB, Gandalf, and the code and data to reproduce our experiments.

title: Penetration Testing on Patch Day: A 24-Hour Retest Sequence You Can Copy
description:
Disclosure: the author works at HACKBOX PTE. LTD., which builds HackBox — mentioned at the close. Everything else here is a technical argument you can check yourself.

On 16 November 2026, Google's Threat Intelligence Group published an account of an operational framework it calls exploit_agent. The mechanism is worth stating plainly, because it changes a scheduling decision that most security teams made years ago and have not revisited since. The framework watches popular web applications for security releases, compares the code before and after each fix, works out what the patch quietly closed, writes an exploit for it, and fires that exploit at live targets. Google describes the whole sequence as running without a person approving any step, and reports finding the framework's output on the same server: exfiltrated data, and scripts for internal reconnaissance, credential brute-forcing, and web shell installation.

You do not have to accept every claim in a vendor threat report to see the structural point. A patch diff is a disclosure document. It always was — reverse-engineering fixes by hand is the definition of an n-day exploit, and it has been standard practice for two decades. What changed is the reading speed and the absence of a queue. A human patch-differ works through releases in the order they arrive and sleeps in between. This does not.

So the useful question for a security team is not whether the report is alarming. It is: on what date does your penetration testing calendar next touch the code path that a patch published yesterday just described?

The two calendars

Most organizations run penetration testing on one of three clocks: annually for compliance, quarterly for a maturity programme, or continuously if they have built the pipeline. All three are organized around the buyer's planning cycle.

An attacker working from patch diffs is organized around a different clock — the vendor's release calendar. Those two calendars have no relationship to each other. A critical authorization fix can ship on the second day of a quarter and be weaponized before the quarter's testing window opens.

Clock Set by Typical lag to a newly patched path
Annual compliance test Audit cycle 6–12 months
Quarterly programme Internal planning 6–12 weeks
Continuous scanning Scan schedule Hours to days, but only for signature-shaped issues
Patch-triggered retest Vendor release What this article argues for

The third row is where most "we already test continuously" claims break. A scanner running every hour is fast, and speed is not the property that matters here. The property that matters is whether the test can reason about a specific code change — whether this fix actually closed this path, on this deployment, with this configuration. A signature engine answers "is version 2.19.25 present". It cannot answer "does the fix hold when the plugin sits behind a cache and a WAF that rewrites the request".

Three ways "we patched it" is not "that path is closed"

The gap between a change record and reality is where the interesting failures live. Three patterns recur often enough to be worth naming.

One endpoint closed, the control failure intact. An access-control bug is rarely one URL. It is a missing ownership check in a function that a dozen routes call. The patch adds the check to the route named in the advisory. The other eleven callers still pass an object identifier straight through. The version number is now correct, the scanner is now quiet, and the vulnerability class is still fully reachable.

Request blocked, resource still open. A WAF rule matching the published payload stops the published payload. If the underlying object reference is still unbound to the session, an encoding variant, a different verb, or a second endpoint that proxies to the same handler will reach it. This failure mode is especially common when the fix is deployed at the edge and the application is deployed on a slower train.

Version right, behaviour rolled back. A hotfix ships, a later release train reverts it because the branch diverged, and the deployment reports the newer version number. The manifest says fixed; the running code says otherwise. Only an execution result distinguishes the two.

None of these are exotic. All three produce the same artifact: a green line in a vulnerability management dashboard and an open path in production.

What a patch-day retest actually checks

A retest triggered by a security release is not a full penetration test. It is a narrow, time-boxed verification with four questions, and it should take hours rather than weeks.

Check Question Evidence required
Primary path Can the exact sequence in the advisory still be completed? Request and response from the patched build
Sibling paths Do other routes that call the same function still accept an unbound identifier? At least two sibling routes exercised, not inferred
Boundary behaviour Does the fix hold with the deployment's real intermediaries in place — cache, WAF, reverse proxy, CDN? Same result through the production entry point, not a direct-to-origin test
Reachability Is the affected asset reachable from an untrusted position at all? Network position stated explicitly, internal-only assets labelled as such

The fourth row is the one teams skip, and it is the one that prevents wasted effort. A patch-day retest of an asset that no untrusted party can route to is a compliance exercise. A patch-day retest of an internet-facing asset that everyone assumed was internal is how estates get surprised.

Two operational details decide whether this is feasible or aspirational. First, the asset inventory has to map to vendor products, not to hostnames — you cannot trigger a retest from a release note if you do not know which of your 400 hosts run the affected component. Second, the retest has to be executable on the same day the patch publishes, which rules out anything requiring a change request, a maintenance window, and a scoping call.

Who runs the retest, and on what clock

A patch-day retest dies in organizations for a reason that has nothing to do with tooling: nobody owns the trigger. The security team reads advisories but does not control the deployment. Platform engineering controls the deployment but does not read advisories. The result is a queue where the item with a two-hour useful life waits behind items with a two-week useful life, and loses.

Three arrangements work, and they differ mainly in how much of the work is automated.

Advisory-to-asset matching, then a human decides. Someone owns the mapping between vendor products and the estate, subscribes to the relevant release feeds, and opens a retest request when a release lands on a reachable asset. This is the lowest-technology option and it works at small scale, up to roughly the point where the estate contains more than a few dozen distinct products. Past that, the matching becomes a part-time job and starts missing releases quietly.

Change-triggered, with a dependency map. Rolling deployments emit events; the pipeline already knows which services consume which components; a security release for a mapped component opens a retest automatically. This is the arrangement that scales, because it converts a reading task into a lookup. Its weakness is the map itself — dependency inventories are usually accurate for the languages with good package metadata and aspirational for everything else, which is precisely where appliance firmware and vendor binaries live.

Scheduled sweep over the exposed surface. A frequent test of everything internet-facing, with results compared against the previous run. Cheap to operate and does not depend on an accurate dependency map, but it answers "what is reachable now" rather than "did this specific fix hold", and the second question is the one a patch raises.

Most mature programmes end up combining the second and third: an automated trigger for the components with clean dependency metadata, and a sweep to catch everything the map misses. The failure mode to avoid is choosing only the third and calling it coverage — a sweep will find a still-reachable path eventually, and "eventually" is the wrong unit when the exploit exists in hours.

The half of this that can be delegated

Of the three arrangements, the middle one is hardest to stand up in-house, because it needs two things that rarely arrive together: a dependency map accurate enough to fire on the right release, and a test capability that executes on demand rather than on a schedule. Most teams build the first and rent the second.

The split is worth stating plainly. The trigger logic is yours — it depends on your inventory, your pipeline, and your definition of a reachable asset. The execution is not yours in any meaningful sense: running an advisory's sequence and its sibling variants against a live deployment is mechanical work that produces a record, and mechanical work is what automation is for.

HackBox is built to take that half and nothing else: you point it at the deployed build and the path, it executes, and the execution result comes back with the request and response attached. No scoping call sits between the release and the retest, which is the whole point of the arrangement.

What stays with you is the decision about which assets are worth the hours — which is the part that should.

A 24-hour sequence you can copy

The sequence below fits in a working day and does not require new tooling. It assumes the release is for a component you actually run on a reachable asset.

Hour Action Output
0 Check the advisory against the asset inventory: is the affected component reachable from an untrusted position? Go / no-go, written down
1 Identify the changed function and list every route that reaches it, not just the one in the advisory A candidate path list
2–6 Execute the advisory sequence against the deployment through its production entry point One request/response pair, or a documented failure to reproduce
6–12 Execute two sibling routes with an unbound identifier Evidence that the class is closed, or evidence that it is not
12–24 Record the outcome against the build hash and the date; if not closed, reopen A closure record that survives review

Two rules keep this honest. The first is that a negative result is a result and must be recorded with the same care as a positive one — "we could not reproduce through the production entry point" is a finding about the fix, and it is the one that catches edge-only mitigations. The second is that the sequence ends with a build hash, not a ticket status. A closure record without an artifact reference is a note about a conversation.

The metric that makes this real

If you want one number to report upward, this is the one: median hours from security release to verified retest of the affected path, across assets that are actually reachable.

It is uncomfortable in the right way. It cannot be improved by buying a faster scanner, because scanners do not produce verified retests. It cannot be improved by writing a policy, because a policy does not execute. It improves when three things exist: an inventory keyed to products, a test capability that runs on demand without a project plan, and a decision about which assets are worth the hours.

The inverse metric is worth tracking too: share of patched-and-closed tickets where no retest evidence exists. If that number is high, the patch record is a claim, and the estate is being managed on claims.

How HackBox fits this cycle

HackBox is an AI-powered automated penetration testing SaaS platform that runs the full attack chain — reconnaissance, exploitation, and privilege escalation — against a target and returns a verified report. It is developed and operated by HACKBOX PTE. LTD., a cybersecurity company headquartered in Singapore. Because the platform runs online rather than through a consulting engagement, a retest after a security release is a request rather than a project: no scoping call, no scheduling window, no additional headcount or hardware to stand up. Findings come back labelled Verified, Exploited, or Manual Collaboration, with the payload, request, response, and extracted data attached, so the patch-day question — did this fix hold — has an answer that is evidence rather than opinion.

Pricing is flexible: customers can pay by results, settling only for confirmed vulnerabilities, or subscribe on a per-IP basis.

Whether you use this platform or another mechanism, the scheduling argument stands on its own. If a patch can become a working exploit in hours, then the date a fix ships is a testing date. A calendar that does not contain that date is not a testing programme; it is a procurement cycle with a report attached.

The author works at HACKBOX PTE. LTD., Singapore, which builds HackBox — an AI-powered automated penetration testing SaaS platform that runs the full attack chain in a real environment and returns a verified report. Pricing is flexible: pay by results for confirmed vulnerabilities, or subscribe per IP. Details at hackbox.ai · partners@hackbox.ai

title: Deep Linking from a Web Catalogue to Native App Screens
description:
When a web page links to an app screen and the app is not installed, the user sees a blank page or an error. Universal Links (iOS) and App Links (Android) solve the installed case but leave the uninstalled case broken unless you plan for it.

The fallback chain

  1. Try the universal/app link.
  2. If the app is not installed, the OS falls through to the web URL.
  3. The web URL should be a full-featured page, not a "download our app" interstitial. 
<a href="https://example.com/games/slots">View Slots</a>

The .well-known/assetlinks.json (Android) and apple-app-site-association (iOS) files declare that the app handles this URL pattern. If the app is present, the OS intercepts the navigation. If not, the browser loads the web page normally.

Deferred deep linking

For marketing campaigns, you want the link to work even if the user installs the app after clicking. Store the intended destination in a first-party cookie before redirecting to the app store:

document.cookie = `deferred_route=/games/slots; max-age=3600; path=/; secure; samesite=lax`;
window.location = 'https://apps.apple.com/app/id123456';

On first app launch, check for the cookie (via a shared web view or the clipboard API — with user permission).

An app-forward platform like Lalabet app that lists its catalogue on the web needs seamless handoff — a broken deep link is a lost user, and a "download our app" wall converts at under 2%.

Testing

Test four scenarios: app installed + link clicked, app not installed + link clicked, app installed + link shared via messaging app (which may strip the scheme), and the deferred install flow. Automated testing for the first two is possible with Detox (iOS) and Espresso (Android).

Takeaway

Deep linking is a web-to-native contract. The web page is not a fallback — it is the primary experience for the majority of visitors who do not have the app.
