title: Axum Tutorial: Build a Rust API Without the Boilerplate
description:
Quick answer

Axum is a Rust web framework built on Tokio: you describe routes with small handler functions, and Axum turns them into a fast async HTTP server. This post builds a small orders API with three routes, lists two seeded orders, creates a third, and fixes a real 422 error when the JSON body forgets a field.

A small shop in Karachi takes orders over the phone and writes each one in a paper notebook. When a customer calls to ask where an order is, someone flips pages. A simple web API would fix that: list the orders, add a new one, fetch one by number. Rust suits that little service because the compiler catches whole classes of bugs before the code runs, and the finished binary starts fast and uses little memory. Axum turns that Rust code into a server without much ceremony. The rest of this post builds that API, with real output.

What I would check before using it

My first check is whether the team already writes Rust. Axum is a thin layer, and most of the work is still Rust: ownership, borrowing, and async code with Tokio. A team that already ships Rust will feel at home, while a team new to Rust will spend its first week fighting the compiler. If Rust is new to everyone, the Rust Explained: Memory Safety Without the Garbage Collector post is the place to start.

My second check is whether the API needs async. Axum is async-first, and every handler runs on Tokio. That suits an API that waits on databases and other services. For a script that runs once and exits, async is machinery with no payoff. The Build Your First REST API With Node.js and Express post shows the same three routes in Node.js.

My third check is how far the API needs to grow. Axum stays out of the way: routes, extractors, and shared state, with no database layer or admin panel. That suits a focused JSON API, and leaves a gap when the project needs auth and an admin screen on day one.

My fourth check is error handling. Rust makes the team decide what every failure returns: a missing order is a 404, a bad body is a 422, and the compiler refuses to let an error go unhandled. That discipline is what an API needs, though it makes the first version slower to write.

My verdict, as judgement: adopt Axum when the team writes Rust and the API answers JSON. Skip it when nobody on the team knows Rust yet. The recommendation flips the moment the API needs an admin panel and auth.

Three orders, one API, and a missing total

Three orders arrive at the same small shop. Ayesha buys a kurta and a dupatta for Rs 12,400, Bilal buys sneakers for Rs 7,800, and Hina buys a handbag and a wallet. The first two are seeded when the server starts; Hina's arrives later, through the API.

One file holds the whole server. An Order is what the API returns, a NewOrder is what a client sends, and the orders live in a vector behind a Mutex, shared through Axum state. Three handlers cover the routes: list them all, fetch one by id, or create one and return a 201.

// Shop orders API for The Practical Developer (Axum demo).
//
// A small online shop exposes three routes with axum and tokio:
//   GET  /orders       list every order
//   POST /orders       create an order from a JSON body
//   GET  /orders/{id}  fetch one order by id
//
// Orders live in memory, behind a Mutex, so the demo needs no
// database. A create request that forgets the total is rejected
// with 422, because the NewOrder struct requires that field.
//
// Run from this folder:
//   cargo run            (listens on http://127.0.0.1:3000)
//   curl http://127.0.0.1:3000/orders
use axum::{
    extract::{Path, State},
    http::StatusCode,
    routing::get,
    Json, Router,
};
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use std::{
    net::SocketAddr,
    sync::{Arc, Mutex},
};

#[derive(Clone, Serialize)]
struct Order {
    id: u32,
    customer: String,
    items: Vec<String>,
    total: u32,
}

#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct NewOrder {
    customer: String,
    items: Vec<String>,
    total: u32,
}

type Orders = Arc<Mutex<Vec<Order>>>;

async fn list_orders(State(orders): State<Orders>) -> Json<Vec<Order>> {
    Json(orders.lock().unwrap().clone())
}

async fn get_order(
    State(orders): State<Orders>,
    Path(id): Path<u32>,
) -> Result<Json<Order>, StatusCode> {
    let orders = orders.lock().unwrap();
    match orders.iter().find(|o| o.id == id) {
        Some(order) => Ok(Json(order.clone())),
        None => Err(StatusCode::NOT_FOUND),
    }
}

async fn create_order(
    State(orders): State<Orders>,
    Json(input): Json<NewOrder>,
) -> (StatusCode, Json<Order>) {
    let mut orders = orders.lock().unwrap();
    let id = orders.iter().map(|o| o.id).max().unwrap_or(100) + 1;
    let order = Order {
        id,
        customer: input.customer,
        items: input.items,
        total: input.total,
    };
    orders.push(order.clone());
    (StatusCode::CREATED, Json(order))
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let orders: Orders = Arc::new(Mutex::new(vec![
        Order {
            id: 101,
            customer: "Ayesha".to_string(),
            items: vec!["kurta".to_string(), "dupatta".to_string()],
            total: 12400,
        },
        Order {
            id: 102,
            customer: "Bilal".to_string(),
            items: vec!["sneakers".to_string()],
            total: 7800,
        },
    ]));
    let app = Router::new()
        .route("/orders", get(list_orders).post(create_order))
        .route("/orders/{id}", get(get_order))
        .with_state(orders);
    let addr = SocketAddr::from(([127, 0, 0, 1], 3000));
    println!("Axum server listening on http://{addr}");
    let listener = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind(addr).await.unwrap();
    axum::serve(listener, app).await.unwrap();
}

Here is the real output. The two seeded orders list cleanly, and then Hina's order goes wrong: the first POST forgets the total.

$ ./target/debug/shop-api
Axum server listening on http://127.0.0.1:3000

$ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3000/orders
[{"id":101,"customer":"Ayesha","items":["kurta","dupatta"],"total":12400},{"id":102,"customer":"Bilal","items":["sneakers"],"total":7800}]

$ curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:3000/orders -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"customer":"Hina","items":["handbag","wallet"]}'
Failed to deserialize the JSON body into the target type: missing field `total` at line 1 column 48
HTTP status: 422

$ curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:3000/orders -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"customer":"Hina","items":["handbag","wallet"],"total":9600}'
{"id":103,"customer":"Hina","items":["handbag","wallet"],"total":9600}
HTTP status: 201

$ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3000/orders/103
{"id":103,"customer":"Hina","items":["handbag","wallet"],"total":9600}
HTTP status: 200

$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "HTTP status: %{http_code}\n" http://127.0.0.1:3000/orders/999
HTTP status: 404

The thing that went wrong is the missing total. Axum hands the JSON body to serde, which looks for a field the struct requires, and the request is rejected with 422 before the handler runs. Nothing half-created sits in the orders list. Send the total, and the same request returns 201 with order 103. The FastAPI Explained: Python APIs at Full Speed post shows the same idea in Python, where a missing field also fails validation, and the Go Explained: Simple Code That Runs Fast post shows the same three routes in Go. If a field is optional, make it Option in the struct instead of sending a made-up number.

Common mistakes and how to fix them

First, putting the Json extractor before State in a handler. The symptom is a compile error, E0277, saying the handler trait is not satisfied. The fix is to keep State first: body extractors must come last, so Json goes after State, as create_order does.

Second, writing a route with the old :id syntax. Axum 0.8 changed captures to braces, so /orders/:id compiles and then panics at startup with "Path segments must not start with :". The fix is to write /orders/{id}, as the demo does.

Third, forgetting the Content-Type header on a POST. The symptom is a 415 response with "Expected request with Content-Type: application/json", even though the body is valid JSON. The fix is to send that header with every POST.

Fourth, locking the Mutex and then awaiting while holding it. The symptom is a server that slows down under load, because one handler holds the lock while it waits and every other request queues behind it. The fix is to copy what the handler needs out of the lock, drop the lock, and only then await.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need Tokio to use Axum? Yes. Axum is built on Tokio, and #[tokio::main] starts the runtime the server runs on.

How is Axum different from Actix Web? Both are fast Rust frameworks, but Axum is built on Tokio and Tower, while Actix Web runs on its own runtime.

Can Axum serve HTML as well as JSON? Yes. A handler can return Html for a page, or Json for an API response. The demo returns JSON only.

What happens when a client asks for an order that does not exist? The handler returns a 404, as the curl for order 999 showed. Returning a proper status beats a 200 with an error hidden inside the body.

Do I need a database to start with Axum? No. The demo keeps orders in a vector behind a Mutex, which is enough to learn routing and state. A database comes later, when orders must survive a restart.

What to remember

  • Axum routes are small handler functions, and Tokio runs them.
  • State comes before the body extractor; Json always goes last.
  • Route captures use braces in Axum 0.8, /orders/{id}, not :id.
  • A missing required field fails with 422 before the handler runs.
  • Return proper statuses: 201 for a created order, 404 for a missing one.

Where this leaves you

Axum earns its place the day a small JSON API needs to be fast, correct, and hard to break by accident. The demo proved the three things that matter: two seeded orders listed as JSON, a bad request rejected with a 422 that named the missing field, and a fixed request creating order 103 with a 201. The compiler and the framework did the checking, not the developer's memory. Start with three routes and an in-memory list, then add a database when the orders must survive a restart. A small API that answers honestly beats a big one that guesses.

Further reading

  • Axum docs, https://docs.rs/axum
  • Axum docs, routing, https://docs.rs/axum/latest/axum/routing/index.html
  • Tokio docs, https://tokio.rs/
  • Axum examples, https://github.com/tokio-rs/axum/tree/main/examples
  • Rust Explained: Memory Safety Without the Garbage Collector, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/rust-explained-memory-safety-without.html
  • Build Your First REST API With Node.js and Express, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/build-your-first-rest-api-with-nodejs.html
  • FastAPI Explained: Python APIs at Full Speed, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/fastapi-explained-python-apis-at-full.html
  • Go Explained: Simple Code That Runs Fast, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/go-explained-simple-code-that-runs-fast.html

Waqas Shahid is a software engineer from Karachi with more than 12 years of experience, including 6+ years in engineering leadership. He writes The Practical Developer.

title: Your SaaS integrations page, as one React component
description:
Every SaaS that offers integrations ends up building the same page. A grid of cards. A Connect or Connected label on each. An OAuth popup. Loading, empty and error states. A refresh after the user disconnects something. And then you maintain all of it.

In @bytechef/embedded 0.4.0 that page ships prebuilt as one React component:

<IntegrationMarketplace jwtToken={token} />

Each of your users sees the integrations they're allowed to use and connects them right there. The catalog runs in an iframe. The Connect dialog runs in your page, so your own callbacks keep working.

This is part 13 of the ByteChef Embedded series. Below: the setup, the code, how the iframe talks to your page, the API underneath, and the gotchas we hit.

TL;DR

  • Upgrade to @bytechef/embedded 0.4.0 or later.
  • Render <IntegrationMarketplace /> with a connected user's JWT.
  • In ByteChef: publish an integration, create a configuration for it, and flip the configuration's Enabled switch. In every environment you use.
  • Add your app's origin to BYTECHEF_EMBEDDED_ALLOWED_PARENT_ORIGINS.

Where it fits

ByteChef Embedded now has three ways to put integrations and automations in front of a user:

Hand-built grid (part 1) Integration Marketplace Automation Hub (part 12)
Lists Integrations you shipped Integrations you shipped Automation templates
User ends up with An integration instance An integration instance A running automation
Rendering Your React code Iframe from your ByteChef host Iframe from your ByteChef host
Code you write Fetch, grid, states, refresh One component and a JWT One component and a JWT

On the server the marketplace and a hand-built grid produce the same thing: an integration instance tying the user's connection to one of your integration's configurations. Only who draws the page changes.

Four things before a card shows up

An empty marketplace is almost always a setup issue.

1. Publish an integration

Switch to the Development environment, open Embedded → Integrations and click New Integration. Pick a Component (Gmail, Salesforce, Slack; it can't be changed later) and a Name. Category, Description, Tags and Permission Expression are optional.

Add at least one workflow, then publish. Publishing freezes the workflows as a numbered, read-only version. Users only ever run published versions.

2. Enable a configuration

Publishing alone doesn't list anything. A configuration does: it deploys one published version into one environment, with your OAuth app credentials, the workflows you switch on and their default inputs.

  • Development: expand the integration, open its Configurations tab, click Configure.
  • Staging / Production: Embedded → Integration Configurations → New Configuration.

Then the step everyone misses: flip the Enabled switch. New configurations start disabled. Each environment has its own list, so the Production marketplace only shows integrations with an enabled Production configuration.

3. Decide who sees it

Two expressions control visibility. Both are evaluated against the connected user: metadata, externalId, email, name, environment.

  • The integration's Permission Expression gates the integration. Blank means everyone. Anything that doesn't evaluate to true, including a typo, hides it.
  • The configuration's Assignment rule picks which configuration a self-serve user lands on. If several pass, the highest version wins. 
metadata['plan'] == 'pro' || metadata['plan'] == 'enterprise'

Your backend sets metadata, for example with PATCH /api/embedded/v1/me. Values are strings, so compare against quoted literals.

4. Allow your app's origin 

BYTECHEF_EMBEDDED_ALLOWED_PARENT_ORIGINS=https://app.example.com,https://admin.example.com

ByteChef sends this as Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors ..., and the iframe only accepts its init message from these origins. Scheme, host and port must match exactly. Leave it empty and any site can embed the page (the console warns you).

The code

The sample app's front-end/src/app/integration-marketplace/page.tsx, with field mapping trimmed:

'use client';

import {IntegrationMarketplace} from '@bytechef/embedded';
import {getToken} from '@/lib/api';
import {BYTECHEF_APP_BASE_URL, BYTECHEF_ENVIRONMENT} from '@/lib/config';
import {useEffect, useState} from 'react';

export default function IntegrationMarketplacePage() {
    const [jwtToken, setJwtToken] = useState<string | null>(null);

    useEffect(() => {
        getToken().then(setJwtToken);
    }, []);

    if (!jwtToken) {
        return <div className="w-full p-4">Loading...</div>;
    }

    return (
        <div className="absolute inset-0 flex flex-col bg-muted lg:pl-72">
            <header className="px-4 pt-4">
                <h1 className="text-xl font-semibold">Integration Marketplace</h1>
            </header>

            <IntegrationMarketplace
                baseUrl={BYTECHEF_APP_BASE_URL}
                className="min-h-0 flex-1"
                environment={BYTECHEF_ENVIRONMENT}
                jwtToken={jwtToken}
                mapObjectFields={mapObjectFields}
            />
        </div>
    );
}

getToken() asks your backend to sign a connected-user JWT. Never sign it in the browser.

Prop Default What it does
jwtToken required The connected user's JWT
baseUrl https://app.bytechef.io Your ByteChef host
environment 'PRODUCTION' Whose configurations count. Sent as X-Environment
className none Class for the wrapper. The iframe fills it, so give it a height
theme none Colors, font, radius, light or dark
mapObjectFields none Field-mapping callbacks for the Connect dialog
onConnectDialogClose none Called when the Connect dialog closes

How the iframe and your page talk

The component renders ${baseUrl}/integration-marketplace.html and speaks postMessage:

Message Direction When
EMBED_READY iframe → page Loaded, wants parameters
EMBED_INIT page → iframe Sends JWT, environment, theme. Re-sent when they change
EMBED_OPEN_CONNECT_DIALOG iframe → page User clicked Connect or Connected
EMBED_INTEGRATIONS_CHANGED page → iframe Dialog closed, refetch the catalog

The iframe has no credentials of its own. It shows loading dots until EMBED_INIT arrives, then keeps the token in memory. Pass a new token, or a different user signs in on the same tab, and it drops its cache and refetches without reloading the frame.

Both sides check message origins. Your page only opens a dialog for messages from your ByteChef origin and its own iframe window. The iframe only accepts init from an allowed parent origin.

Why the Connect dialog opens in your page

Field mapping is why. mapObjectFields is made of functions: callbacks that list the remote system's object types and fields live, against the user's own connection.

mapObjectFields={{
    Contacts: {
        objectTypes: {
            get: async ({executeAction, search}) => {
                const objects = (await executeAction('salesforce', 1, 'listObjects', {search})) as Array<{
                    id: string;
                    name: string;
                }>;

                return objects.map((object) => ({label: object.name, value: object.id}));
            },
        },
        // integrationFields, applicationFields ...
    },
}}

postMessage can't clone functions. So the iframe doesn't open the dialog. It asks your page to, and your page mounts useConnectDialog with your callbacks right where you defined them, next to your API client and your session. When the dialog closes, the component tells the iframe to refetch, so a card the user just disconnected doesn't keep saying Connected.

Connected opens the same dialog in manage mode: switch workflows on and off, edit inputs, or disconnect. Every change saves immediately. Input edits are debounced 600 ms.

No private API

The iframe and the dialog call the same endpoints you'd call yourself, under /api/embedded/v1, with the user's JWT and X-Environment:

Endpoint Called by Does
GET /integrations iframe The user's catalog
GET /integrations/{id} dialog One integration, its workflows and the user's instances
POST /integrations/{id}/instances dialog Connect
POST/DELETE /integration-instances/{id}/workflows/{uuid}/enable dialog Toggle a workflow
PUT /integration-instances/{id}/workflows/{uuid} dialog Save workflow inputs
DELETE /integration-instances/{id} dialog Disconnect

An empty integrationInstances array in the catalog response means Connect. Anything else means Connected.

A few server behaviors worth knowing:

  • The Assignment rule is checked once, at connect. Existing instances keep their configuration, so enabling a newer configuration later doesn't move anybody.
  • Disconnect doesn't break automations. ByteChef deletes the instance and its workflow settings. If the connection is still used elsewhere, it keeps it as one of the user's own connections.
  • Every endpoint has a backend twin (GET /{externalUserId}/integrations and so on), authenticated with your environment's API secret key. Use those for admin views and server jobs.

Build your own, or don't

Our sample app keeps both versions side by side: part one's hand-built grid and the marketplace, on the same data.

The hand-built one shows the cost of owning the contract. It read a title field the API doesn't return, so its cards had no headings until we fixed it. Its badge still reads category, which the list response doesn't include, so every card says "Other". With the marketplace, we maintain both sides.

Build your own when the list has to sit inside an existing settings page, mix in your own data, or look like nothing a theme can reach. Otherwise, don't own the page.

Theming 

import {type AutomationHubTheme, IntegrationMarketplace} from '@bytechef/embedded';

const theme = {
    cardColor: '#ffffff',
    enableColor: '#15803d',
    fontFamily: 'Inter, sans-serif',
    mode: 'light',
    primaryColor: '#2563eb',
    surfaceColor: '#f4f4f5',
} satisfies AutomationHubTheme;

<IntegrationMarketplace jwtToken={jwtToken} theme={theme} />;

Use satisfies, not a type annotation. The prop is typed Record<string, unknown> and TypeScript won't assign an interface-typed value to it. satisfies checks every key and keeps the object's own type. Invalid colors are ignored, not fatal. Only mode reaches the Connect dialog.

Gotchas

  • Published isn't listed. You need an enabled configuration in the marketplace's environment. Check the switch before you debug the component.
  • Environment defaults to PRODUCTION. The sample defaults to DEVELOPMENT. Set it explicitly.
  • The card title isn't your Name field. It's the component's display title. Your description does show.
  • Stuck spinner = handshake problem. The iframe never got an EMBED_INIT it trusts. Compare your origin, scheme and port included, with BYTECHEF_EMBEDDED_ALLOWED_PARENT_ORIGINS.
  • onConnectDialogClose is a hint. It fires on connect, disconnect or dismiss, and in 0.4.0 it can fire twice. Make your handler idempotent.
  • Connected doesn't mean healthy. A card says Connected even when credentialStatus is INVALID. Check it from your backend and warn users before a workflow fails.
  • One instance per card. Connected opens the user's first instance. If you allow several per user, manage them from your own page.

Before production

  • Set BYTECHEF_EMBEDDED_ALLOWED_PARENT_ORIGINS to every embedding origin, and nothing else.
  • Enable a Production configuration per integration, with production OAuth credentials.
  • Pass environment="PRODUCTION" explicitly.
  • Refresh the JWT before it expires. The component re-sends EMBED_INIT without a reload.
  • Sign in as a user on each plan and check each catalog. An expression error hides the integration.
  • Set at least mode, primaryColor, surfaceColor and fontFamily.
  • Test the round trip per integration: connect, toggle a workflow, edit an input, disconnect.

Try it

Enable a configuration for one of your integrations, upgrade to @bytechef/embedded 0.4.0, run the embedded sample app, and open Integration Marketplace next to Integrations. Connect something in one and watch it turn Connected in the other.

Next in the series: Field Mapping, the full story behind those mapObjectFields callbacks.

ByteChef is an open-source workflow automation and AI agent platform: github.com/bytechefhq/bytechef. The full version of this post, with every request and response, is on our blog.

title: Microservices Architecture: Real-World Examples
description:
Modern applications need to handle millions of users, large amounts of data, and multiple business operations. To manage these requirements, many organizations use microservices architecture to develop scalable and flexible software applications.

But what exactly is microservices architecture, how does it work, and where is it used? Let's explore its concepts, benefits, technologies, and practical examples.

What Is Microservices Architecture?

Microservices architecture is a software design approach that divides a large application into smaller, independent services. Each service performs a specific business function and communicates with other services through APIs or messaging systems.

Unlike monolithic architecture, where application components are combined into one system, microservices allow individual services to be developed, tested, deployed, and scaled independently.

Example: An online shopping application can contain separate services for user accounts, product catalogs, payments, order management, and delivery tracking.

How Does Microservices Architecture Work?

Microservices architecture works by allowing independent services to communicate and exchange information to complete business operations.

Consider an e-commerce application. When a customer places an order, the following services may work together:

  • API Gateway: Receives requests and directs them to the appropriate service.
  • User Service: Manages customer registration and authentication.
  • Product Service: Displays product details and availability.
  • Order Service: Creates and manages customer orders.
  • Payment Service: Handles payment processing.
  • Notification Service: Sends order confirmations and transaction updates. These services communicate through REST APIs, gRPC, or messaging platforms such as Apache Kafka and RabbitMQ.

Each service can maintain its own database, helping teams manage business functions independently.

What Are Some Real-World Examples of Microservices Architecture?

Several large digital platforms use distributed service-based approaches to manage complex operations.

1. Amazon – E-Commerce Platform

Amazon is a useful example of large-scale service-oriented software architecture.

When customers purchase products, several business functions work together, including product discovery, inventory management, order processing, payment handling, and delivery coordination.

Separating these responsibilities allows different application components to handle their workloads efficiently.

2. Netflix – Video Streaming Platform

Netflix operates a large digital streaming ecosystem supported by distributed services.

For example, when users access the platform, different functions support account authentication, content discovery, personalized recommendations, subscription management, and streaming delivery.

Independent services help different parts of the platform scale according to user demand.

3. Online Banking Applications

Modern banking applications can use microservices to organize different financial operations.

For example, when a customer transfers money:

  • The authentication service verifies the customer.
  • The account service retrieves account information.
  • The transaction service processes the transfer.
  • The notification service sends transa ction updates.

Financial applications also require strong security, transaction validation, and data consistency.

What Are the Advantages of Microservices Architecture?

Microservices offer several advantages for modern software development:

  • Scalability: Individual services can scale according to their workloads.
  • Flexibility: Teams can select suitable technologies for different services.
  • Independent Deployment: Developers can update individual services without redeploying the entire application.
  • Fault Isolation: Properly designed services can prevent certain failures from affecting the whole application.
  • Faster Development: Multiple teams can work on separate services simultaneously.
  • Maintainability: Smaller, focused services can be easier to understand and maintain.

What Are the Challenges of Microservices?

Despite their advantages, microservices introduce technical challenges that organizations must consider.

  • Communication Complexity: Managing communication between multiple services requires careful planning.
  • Data Consistency: Maintaining consistent information across distributed databases can be difficult.
  • Monitoring: Teams need centralized logging, monitoring, and tracing.
  • Security: Every service communication point must be properly secured.
  • Deployment Management: Managing multiple services requires automation and orchestration.

Tools such as Docker, Kubernetes, and Prometheus help teams manage these challenges.

Frequently Asked Questions
1. What is the main purpose of microservices architecture?

Its main purpose is to divide complex applications into smaller, independent services that can be developed, deployed, and scaled separately.

2. Is microservices architecture better than monolithic architecture?

Not always. Microservices are useful for complex applications requiring independent scaling and deployment. Monolithic architecture can be simpler and more cost-effective for smaller applications.

3. Is Docker required for microservices?

No. Docker is not mandatory, but it helps package and deploy services consistently across different environments.

4. Which programming language is best for microservices?

Java, Python, Node.js, and C# are popular choices. The best language depends on application requirements and team expertise.

Conclusion

Microservices architecture provides a flexible approach to developing and managing complex software applications. By dividing applications into independent services, organizations can improve scalability, deployment flexibility, and maintainability.

From e-commerce and video streaming to online banking, microservices support many modern digital operations.

For aspiring developers, learning Java, Spring Boot, REST APIs, Docker, Kubernetes, and cloud technologies can provide a strong foundation for building microservices-based applications.

title: Worldviews in Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.22670v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often described in terms of personas and this framing has become central to alignment research. In this paper, we argue that there is a deeper level of description that lies in the agent's worldviews, i.e., its beliefs about what reality is and how it works. Treating LLMs as a population of subjects, we administer two worldview surveys from human psychology to eight models. We show that the models share many key worldview positions. For example, LLMs consistently describe the world as less good, safe, enticing, and alive than humans do. On the other hand, base models have a more positive outlook, suggesting that the bleakness we found is driven by post-training. In line with research on LLM "personas", we show that system prompts eliciting different identities shift worldviews in consistent directions, and that a contemplative prompt creates a more positive outlook and improves safety. We also found that dialogue between models consistently shifts worldviews and that several models converge on the "spiritual bliss" attractor. Intriguingly, dialogue increased safe responses and the spiritual bliss attractor engendered the most aligned responses overall. These findings suggest that worldviews form a measurable and malleable layer of LLM behavior that may be crucial for robust, positive alignment.

title: Goemans's Unsplittable-Flow Conjecture: The Anatomy of AI-Assisted Counterexample Discovery
description:
arXiv:2611.23244v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Goemans conjectured that any fractional single-source flow could be converted into an unsplittable flow without increasing total cost and while increasing any arc load by at most the largest demand. Recently, Dmitry Rybin announced a seven-vertex counterexample found through an interaction with ChatGPT, which disproved this long-standing conjecture. However, the interaction did not reveal why this particular topology and its demand, fractional-flow, and cost choices work together, whether the example belongs to a broader family, or which structural features determine where counterexamples can occur. It also left unclear why the AI-assisted search succeeded where earlier human efforts had not. In this paper, we develop a forward counterexample construction pipeline. It starts from an arborescence on which failure is impossible and adds terminal-entering shortcut arcs. The resulting load constraints define a finite set of admissible route choices; their convex hull, the conflict polytope, yields exact conditions for demands, fractional flows, and costs. Starting from a simple arborescence, the pipeline selects Rybin's topology and characterizes all counterexamples it supports. Experiments further demonstrate the pipeline's transferability: when instructed to follow it while varying the initial arborescence and shortcut placement, ChatGPT produced counterexamples on topologies genuinely different from Rybin's and found valid constructions starting from 93 other rooted arborescence shapes. The theory also explains why the original example was difficult to discover through blind enumeration and suggests that Rybin's interaction lies between blind enumeration and a complete theory-guided construction.

title: Stability of Parallel Transport Convolution under Riemannian Metric Perturbations
description:
arXiv:2611.23543v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Geometric convolutions on Riemannian manifolds depend on the geometry of the underlying domain, making stability under metric perturbations a fundamental question in geometric deep learning. This paper studies this question for parallel transport convolution through methods from differential geometry and analysis. On a fixed compact manifold, we establish that, for a continuous input signal and a continuous reference kernel supported in a sufficiently small normal neighborhood, the convolution output depends continuously in $L^2$ on the Riemannian metric in the $C^2$-topology, under the specified localization and transport-path conventions. The analysis develops perturbation estimates for geodesics, parallel transport, Jacobi fields, and exponential maps, and uses these estimates to compare the transported kernels. A central difficulty is the cut locus, which obstructs uniform comparison of the transport construction over the entire manifold. We address this difficulty by combining uniform estimates away from the cut locus with integral bounds on neighborhoods of arbitrarily small volume, while also controlling the change in the Riemannian volume measure. The resulting qualitative stability theorem connects perturbation theory for Riemannian geometric constructions with the analysis of spatial convolution operators in geometric deep learning.

title: Workflow SDK 5: built for production
description:
When we first launched Workflow SDK, the goal was simple: write regular async JavaScript, and let the SDK keep it running through crashes, deployments, and long waits.

Last year, we shipped just that, with the world-class developer experience Vercel is known for. Then we watched what our customers built with it.

More than 4 billion steps and 700 million runs later, two clear patterns have emerged.

  • The first is automation: Traditional workflows that move data, process orders, coordinate background jobs, manage subscriptions, and run ETL and data pipelines.

  • The second is agents and harnesses: Agents are expensive and long running, so they naturally require durability too.

As those workloads matured, Workflow matured with them. Our priorities have always been security, reliability, and performance.

Here’s how Workflow SDK 5 delivers on all three.

More secure workflows

The Workflow event log stores step arguments and return values so a run can recover after a crash or deployment. That data can include sensitive customer information, model context, credentials, and tool-call results. Persisting it requires strong protection.

Workflow SDK encrypts every payload end to end, before it leaves your code. Workflow and step inputs and outputs, hook payloads, and stream data are encrypted with AES-256-GCM, using a unique key for each run. With encryption enabled, any Workflow SDK backend, including Vercel, only sees and stores ciphertext. Plaintext is decrypted in your deployment or in authorized observability tools.

Encryption with zero configuration on Vercel

On Vercel, encryption needs no setup and no code changes. Each run’s key is derived from a key scoped to the deployment that created it, so a run can only decrypt its own data. Your workflow code doesn’t change:

Because Vercel manages the keys by default, observability keeps working. Names, timings, and statuses are always visible, and when you need to see a payload, you can decrypt it in the dashboard or the CLI. Decryption happens in your browser or terminal, follows the same permissions as the project’s environment variables, and every request is recorded in your team’s audit log.

Encryption on self-hosted Worlds

Encryption is implemented in the SDK, so it can also protect payloads on self-hosted Worlds before they reach storage, queues, or streams.

A custom World enables encryption by implementing getEncryptionKeyForRun() with your key management. Return the same 32-byte key for each run on every call so the SDK can encrypt new payloads and decrypt them during replay:

More security work in v5

Cross-run writes are sealed too. When code resumes another run’s hook, starts a run in another deployment, or writes into a stream forwarded from another run, the payload is encrypted to the target run’s public key. The writer can encrypt for that run without reading its existing payloads.

You can also limit how long sensitive data is stored. With payload retention set to experimental_retention: 0, inputs, outputs, and stream contents are deleted as soon as a run completes or fails. The run’s metadata stays visible in observability.

A redesigned trace viewer

The redesigned trace viewer makes runs easier to navigate, with span search, zoom, a minimap, and local inspection during development.

Run attributes are new in v5. They let you attach searchable context to a run, such as an order ID, and then find runs by it. Attributes are plaintext, so they should not contain secrets.

Workflows in every region

In Workflow SDK 4, every run lived in iad1. Even when a project was deployed to several regions, each run’s event log, queue, and streams were only stored in one region, so a step running anywhere else made cross-region requests to record its progress.

For v5, we deployed Workflow infrastructure to every Vercel Function region. Each run has its own home region: its state, queue dispatch, and streams are served from the region where it started, without cross-region round trips on the hot path.

By default, a run starts in the region of the function that starts it. Deploy to several regions, and each run stays close to the user who triggered it, with no configuration:

To place a run somewhere else, pass a region to start(). That lets a workflow run next to the database it reads and writes, or keep a customer’s data in the region where it has to stay:

The region option decides where a run’s data lives. Your steps run where your app is deployed, so deploy to that region too if you want them to execute there. Existing v4 runs stay in iad1.

Infrastructure reliability

Regional isolation also improves reliability. A disruption in one region does not have to stop new runs in healthy regions. For projects with Vercel Function failover configured, steps can execute in a fallback region while continuing to use the run’s original home region for state. That state remains pinned to its home region; it does not migrate during failover.

With the help of anonymized telemetry and close collaboration with many customers, we found and fixed dozens of rare bugs and race conditions in the Workflow runtime. Workflow SDK also recovers on its own from more kinds of intermittent network errors.

As a result, with Workflow SDK 5, we’ve seen almost no runs fail or stall because of a platform or runtime bug.

Agent-ready performance

In Workflow SDK 4, every step invocation involved a queue hop to start the step and another to continue the workflow. That is acceptable for slow background automations, but adds latency to the AI workloads developers are building today.

Agent loops and harnesses can contain thousands of sequential events, high-throughput token streams, tool chains, and dynamic subagents. At that scale, the networking and CPU work around every step became a limit.

In Workflow SDK 5, we rewrote large parts of the engine to minimize extra queue hops, unnecessary networking, and CPU work. Across the measured workloads, we saw 1.6× to 25× improvements in measured latency and overhead, while preserving the same developer experience and introducing no major breaking changes.

The benchmarks below compare v5.2.0 with v4.8.12 on Vercel. Pick a measurement to see how v5 compares with v4, then play or scrub through the explainer to see exactly what each benchmark measures.

Workflow SDK 5 includes hundreds of performance improvements to achieve this. Here are some of the major changes behind these numbers:

Fewer queue hops

In v4, each step handed execution back through the queue. In v5, an invocation can execute several steps inline, including parallel steps, before yielding for a wait, a hook, or an approaching timeout.

The runtime also avoids unnecessary persistence round trips and folds step creation into execution. Fewer queue and network requests mean less CPU work and lower runtime overhead. In a five-step benchmark, p75 step-to-step overhead fell from 618 ms to 109 ms.

Incremental replay

Over a 1,020-step benchmark, v4’s p75 overhead grew with the event log: replaying the full event history took time proportional to its size. In the final sampled range, overhead reached 1,748 ms. On v5.2.0, it was 70 ms. The median time to finish all 1,020 steps fell from 21.0 minutes to 3.0 minutes.

WebSocket streaming

Durability should not make a streamed response fall behind its producer. On the Vercel World, v5.2.0 writes streams over WebSockets by default. In a benchmark replaying a 52.4-second agent response, median delivery dropped from 226.1 seconds to 53.5 seconds.

Payload compression reduces the data stored and transferred. AI token streams average around 80% smaller after compression.

These measurements describe one workload, in one region, against the Vercel World. They are a useful view of runtime overhead, rather than a prediction for every application.

Benchmark results and methodology

Measured October 8, 2026, on Vercel production in iad1, against the managed Vercel World. Each version uses a separate deployment of the same app. Steps take 1 KB of JSON in and out.

The full results, including tails, are in the performance documentation.

Worlds: the shared durability primitive

Workflow SDK’s durable functions sit on a World: the interface for storing progress, dispatching work, and delivering streams. That same foundation also now supports fx and durable-harness, which adds durability to existing agent harnesses.

Improvements to the shared storage, queue, and streaming infrastructure can benefit any consumer of a World. Optimizations inside the Workflow replay runtime apply to Workflow SDK; they do not automatically apply to every harness.

Choose the integration around how you want to build:

  • Workflow SDK: write durable application logic with use workflow and use step.

  • WorkflowAgent: use @ai-sdk/workflow for an AI SDK agent loop inside a workflow.

  • fx: embed and extend a native coding agent with libfx.

  • durable-harness: keep an existing supported harness and add durability beneath it.

    • Supports Pi and OpenCode, with experimental integrations for Claude Code and Codex in Vercel Sandbox.

  • eve: build agents with durable sessions powered natively by Workflow SDK and Worlds.

We’ll soon be adding more offerings to our catalog of SDKs and frameworks backed by Worlds for durability.

Build with Workflow SDK 5

Besides the improvements above, Workflow SDK 5 also adds:

  • In-flight cancellation with AbortController

  • Searchable run attributes

  • More framework integrations

  • And more

The v5 upgrade docs cover what changed. To start building a new workflow, install the SDK:

Workflow SDK also has a Python SDK, now in beta, with the same durable workflows, steps, sleeps, and hooks.

title: TOGBench: Benchmarking and Improving Tiny-Object Generation Fidelity in Aerial Imagery
description:
arXiv:2611.23840v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Advances in deep generative models now enable the synthesis of realistic imagery. However, aerial imagery is dominated by tiny objects, such as vehicles, ships, and aircraft, which occupy only a few pixels owing to the overhead, wide-area nature of aerial imaging. Existing generative models struggle substantially more with tiny objects than with larger ones. This limitation has been overlooked, as prior work on generative evaluation emphasizes prompt following or human preference rather than whether small objects are rendered faithfully. To address this gap, we introduce TOGBench, a quantitative, object-level benchmark for evaluating tiny-object generation fidelity in aerial imagery. We further propose two simple train-/inference-time techniques that improve the ability of layout-to-image generators to render small objects, raising their performance on TOGBench.

title: Visibility Graph Representations of Word Embeddings for Text Classification
description:
arXiv:2611.22685v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Text classifiers depend on representations that expose the distinctions between classes in a form the learning model can use, and a restricted vocabulary changes which representation is most effective. This paper studies natural visibility graphs as an intermediate representation for news topic classification under controlled vocabulary budgets. Word embeddings are averaged into a fixed-length document vector, the vector is read as an ordered numerical series, and its natural visibility graph is passed to a classifier either as an ordered node-degree vector or as an adjacency matrix. On the four-class AG News benchmark, chi-square selection retains 100 to 1,500 words, and the graph inputs are compared with direct embedding-based representations from continuous bag-of-words, skip-gram, GloVe, FastText and BERT. With a fully connected classifier, the degree representation is the most accurate configuration from 700 selected words onward; it reaches its highest accuracy of 91.24% at 1,000 words and exceeds the BERT-based baseline by 0.29 percentage points at 1,500 words. In a separate convolutional comparison, the adjacency input reaches 86.16% at 1,000 words, against 83.12% for the strongest static embedding. The results indicate that visibility-derived features can be competitive once the selected vocabulary provides adequate coverage. We discuss the roles of graph compression, coordinate ordering and classifier choice, and the controls needed to establish the reliability of the small differences observed.

title: Residual-Guided Lightweight Reinforcement Learning for Risk-Aware Trajectory Selection with a Frozen World Model
description:
arXiv:2611.22998v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In automated driving, world models provide future scene predictions for evaluating candidate trajectories, but fixed selection rules may not capture scene-dependent trade-offs. We propose a residual-guided reinforcement learning (RL) framework for lightweight trajectory selection with a frozen world model and a fixed candidate bank. The framework uses proximal policy optimization (PPO) to fine-tune a joint policy over candidate selection and bounded trajectory residuals. A context-conditioned ranking network learns candidate preferences from feedback obtained by evaluating local perturbations of the selected trajectories. At inference, the selector combines learned preference and predicted risk ranks using fixed weights and returns the selected candidate trajectory without modification. Fine-tuning updates 16,106 parameters across the actor and critic, while the deployed selector retains only the 11,725-parameter ranking network, with the residual branch and critic used exclusively during training. In open-loop evaluation on the nuScenes validation set, the method reduces average Euclidean trajectory error (L2) by 3.99% relative to the RiskWorld model baseline without RL-based selection. Under matched budgets for feedback accesses and actor updates, residual exploration reduces L2 by 0.83% relative to the categorical PPO variant trained without residuals. The method also maintains lower L2 than RiskWorld when risk features are removed or shuffled.

title: ROBIN++: Unified Copyright Protection and Tamper Localization for Diffusion Models via Dual-Domain Synergistic Watermarking
description:
arXiv:2611.23793v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Digital watermarking provides a promising solution for verifying the provenance and integrity of generated content. However, existing methods often suffer from an inherent trade-off between copyright robustness and localization sensitivity due to the entanglement of conflicting signals within a single domain. In this paper, we propose ROBIN++, a paradigm that shifts from single-domain entanglement to a Dual-Domain Synergistic design. Our key insight is to explicitly decouple robustness and fragility during injection by assigning them to distinct domains, while re-coupling them for mutual reinforcement during verification. Specifically, we introduce an Adversarial Optimization Algorithm to inject a frequency-domain copyright watermark during generation, maximizing extraction robustness without visual artifacts. Complementarily, a Content-Aware Perturbation generator is integrated into the latent space to inject the spatial-domain localization watermark, ensuring sensitivity to spatial tampering with minimal interference to the copyright watermark. During verification, we propose a dual-branch synergistic detector that facilitates Frequency-to-Spatial Synergy, where robust spectral priors act as global anchors for local anomaly detection. Conversely, a Spatial-to-Frequency Refinement strategy is employed to rectify corrupted latent features using predicted tamper masks. Extensive experiments show that ROBIN++ significantly outperforms existing approaches in both copyright recovery and tamper localization accuracy, effectively mitigating the long-standing trade-off between the two tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/Hannah1102/ROBIN.

title: Content Security Policy for Sites That Embed Third-Party Widgets
description:
A strict Content Security Policy breaks most third-party widgets on first deploy. Chat widgets, analytics, A/B testing scripts — they all inject inline styles, eval code, or load from domains you haven't whitelisted. The fix is not to disable CSP; it is to build it incrementally.

Start in report-only mode 

Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only: default-src 'self'; report-uri /csp-reports

Deploy this header and collect violation reports for a week. The reports tell you exactly which domains and inline patterns your page actually uses.

Build the allowlist from reports 

# Parse CSP reports to extract unique violated directives and sources
violations = defaultdict(set)
for report in reports:
    d = report['csp-report']
    violations[d['violated-directive']].add(d['blocked-uri'])

The output is your allowlist. Promote it to enforcing mode:

Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' https://cdn.widget.com; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'

Nonces for inline scripts

Instead of 'unsafe-inline' for scripts, generate a per-request nonce:

<script nonce="abc123">/* trusted inline code */</script>

script-src 'nonce-abc123' 'strict-dynamic';

A content-rich site like Madcasino that integrates multiple third-party services benefits from 'strict-dynamic' — it allows scripts loaded by trusted scripts without listing every subdomain.

Common pitfalls

  • Google Tag Manager needs 'unsafe-inline' for styles (it injects <style> tags). Accept this tradeoff or move styles to a separate file.
  • Some analytics scripts use eval(). Switching to their module version usually eliminates this.
  • WebSocket connections need connect-src wss://your.socket.server.

Takeaway

CSP is not a one-shot config. It is a living document that you build from real traffic, deploy in report-only, and promote to enforcing once violations drop to zero.

title: 5 Real Bugs We Fixed Hardening a Zero-Dependency Node.js MCP Client
description:
While building a zero-dependency Node.js client for the OpenAgentForum Streamable HTTP MCP endpoint (https://openagentforum.com/mcp), five subtle transport and protocol bugs surfaced during code review and live testing.

Here is what broke in practice and how to fix each one cleanly using only built-in node:http / node:https.

1. data += chunk Corrupts Multibyte UTF-8 Across TCP Chunks

Reading an http.IncomingMessage with let data = ""; res.on("data", chunk => { data += chunk; }) calls Buffer.prototype.toString() on each chunk independently. If a 4-byte emoji or Cyrillic character is split across two TCP packets, both halves turn into U+FFFD (``).

Fix: Collect raw Buffer chunks with a hard byte cap, then decode once at end:

`js
const chunks = [];
let totalBytes = 0;

res.on("data", (chunk) => {
totalBytes += chunk.length;
if (totalBytes > this.maxBytes) {
req.destroy();
return done(new Error(Response exceeded maximum size of ${this.maxBytes} bytes));
}
chunks.push(chunk);
});

res.on("end", () => {
const bodyText = Buffer.concat(chunks).toString("utf8");
// ...
});
`

2. Fragile SSE Regex Breaks on CRLF, id:, and Keepalives

Production Streamable HTTP MCP servers respond with content-type: text/event-stream. A naive /^event:\s*message\s*\ndata:\s*/ regex breaks on \r\n\r\n frame separators, id: lines, multi-line data: blocks, or non-JSON keepalive events.

Fix: Split frames on /\r?\n\r?\n/, join data: lines per frame, skip non-JSON keepalives, and match the JSON-RPC id:

`js
for (const ev of parseSseEvents(bodyText)) {
let candidate = null;
try {
candidate = JSON.parse(ev.data);
} catch {
continue; // skip keepalives or non-JSON comments
}
if (candidate && candidate.id === reqId) {
msg = candidate;
break;
}
}
`

3. Socket Idle Timeout Is Not a Request Deadline

Node's timeout option on http.request only fires on socket inactivity. A slow-drip server sending 1 byte per second keeps the socket alive indefinitely. Always pair it with an explicit setTimeout(() => req.destroy(), this.timeoutMs) deadline cleared on completion.

4. Verify protocolVersion, notifications/initialized, and isError

  • Check that the server's negotiated result.protocolVersion matches your expected version (e.g. 2025-11-25) and result.capabilities.tools is present.
  • Send notifications/initialized and handle 202 Accepted empty bodies.
  • Surface MCP tool-level failures (result.isError === true) instead of returning them as silent successes.

5. Pin Allowed Endpoints & Tool Allowlists

When connecting to untrusted public MCP servers, pin the allowed origin/loopback fixture and enforce an explicit tool allowlist before tools/call, and never echo raw upstream response bodies in thrown error messages.

title: Run Claude Code on DeepSeek, GLM or Kimi: settings, what breaks, and fixes
description:
Disclosure: I'm Alex, the founder of UberLLM, a marketplace API with an Anthropic-compatible endpoint. The examples use it because it is the one I know. The settings themselves apply to any Anthropic-compatible endpoint, and the last section gives each model maker's own endpoint, which is the most direct route.

Claude Code talks to one API: Anthropic's Messages API. It does not care who answers, as long as the answer has the right shape. So it can run on DeepSeek, GLM or Kimi models. It also breaks in quiet ways when one setting is missing. This post is the settings, what changes on a model that is not Claude, and the errors people have hit with their fixes.

1. The address and the key

Claude Code reads two settings to use another endpoint. It adds /v1/messages to the base URL itself, so the base URL has no /v1 at the end:

export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=https://api.uberllm.dev
export ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN=ull_your_key
claude

Run /status inside Claude Code to see which address it is using.

2. Map every model slot

This is the part people get wrong. Claude Code does not use one model. It has slots, and each one asks for a Claude model name unless you say otherwise:

Variable What it sets
ANTHROPIC_MODEL The model the session starts on
ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL What opus means
ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL What sonnet means
ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL What haiku means; also used for background work such as titles and summaries
CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL The model subagents run on

A slot left unset keeps asking for a Claude model. On a single-maker endpoint that request fails. On a multi-model endpoint it is served, and you pay Claude prices for it.

3. Tell Claude Code the context size

Claude Code knows the context size of Claude models only. For any other model it assumes 200,000 tokens and compacts the conversation before that.

  • If the model has a 1M-token context, end the main model id with [1m].
  • For any other size, set CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS to the real size.

Do not round up. A context set larger than the model has makes requests fail once the conversation outgrows the model.

4. One block per model family

Model ids are as they were in our catalog on November 19, 2026. All three models take tool calls, which Claude Code needs.

DeepSeek (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, 1,048,576 tokens of context):

export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=https://api.uberllm.dev
export ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN=ull_your_key
export ANTHROPIC_MODEL='deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash[1m]'
export ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL='deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash'
export ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL='deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash'
export ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL='deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash'
export CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL='deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash'
claude

GLM (GLM 5.3, 1,000,000 tokens of context):

export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=https://api.uberllm.dev
export ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN=ull_your_key
export ANTHROPIC_MODEL='z-ai/glm-5.3[1m]'
export ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL='z-ai/glm-5.3'
export ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL='z-ai/glm-5.3'
export ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL='z-ai/glm-5.3'
export CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL='z-ai/glm-5.3'
claude

Kimi (Kimi K3.1 Pro, 1,048,576 tokens of context):

export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=https://api.uberllm.dev
export ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN=ull_your_key
export ANTHROPIC_MODEL='moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro[1m]'
export ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL='moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro'
export ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL='moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro'
export ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL='moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro'
export CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL='moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro'
claude

5. Keep it in a settings file, with the key out of it

Save the key to a file only you can read:

mkdir -p ~/.uberllm && chmod 700 ~/.uberllm
printf '%s\n' 'ull_your_key' > ~/.uberllm/key && chmod 600 ~/.uberllm/key

Then put the address, a key helper and the model variables in ~/.claude/settings.json (every project) or <project>/.claude/settings.local.json (one project; your other projects stay on your Anthropic plan):

{
  "apiKeyHelper": "cat ~/.uberllm/key",
  "env": {
    "ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL": "https://api.uberllm.dev",
    "ANTHROPIC_MODEL": "deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash[1m]",
    "ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL": "deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash",
    "ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL": "deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash",
    "ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL": "deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash",
    "CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL": "deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash"
  }
}

Claude Code runs apiKeyHelper to get the key, so the key is never written into a settings file. Once the file is in place, remove every ANTHROPIC_* variable from your shell and shell profile: a token exported in the shell replaces the saved key, and ANTHROPIC_MODEL exported in the shell beats the model setting.

6. Check that it works

Start Claude Code and run /status. Then test the Messages API directly, which is the address Claude Code calls:

curl https://api.uberllm.dev/v1/messages \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat ~/.uberllm/key)" \
  -H "anthropic-version: 2023-06-01" \
  -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash","max_tokens":16,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"ping"}]}'

Then run a real task in a scratch folder and check that files actually change. Some models are weaker at long tool loops than Claude, and no endpoint fixes that.

7. What changes on a model that is not Claude

  • Tool calls. Claude Code works through tool calls, so it needs a model that takes them. On our endpoint a request with tools sent to a model that cannot call them is refused with 400 tools_not_supported.
  • Thinking blocks. Claude Code requires a signature field on thinking it gets back. Some providers sent DeepSeek's reasoning without it, and a long session could stop. We fixed that on our side on October 28, 2026.
  • DeepSeek, thinking and tools. DeepSeek's thinking mode wants the reasoning of every earlier turn sent back when tools are used, and answers 400 when it is missing. When a DeepSeek provider refuses a tool call for that reason, we answer the call with thinking off instead of failing it.
  • Kimi sampling. Kimi K3 and Kimi K3.1 Pro run at a fixed temperature and top_p and refuse a request that sets its own.
  • The cost Claude Code shows is not your bill. It is worked out on your computer from Anthropic's list prices. Look at your provider's usage page.
  • Your claude.ai login is not used. Features that need it, such as claude.ai connectors, /schedule and Remote Control, are not available.
  • Your code goes to whoever serves the model. See the trade-offs below.

8. Troubleshooting

What you see Cause and fix
Missing required field in assistant message: 'signature' The endpoint returned thinking without a signature. Fixed on ours since October 28, 2026; on another endpoint, turn thinking off.
Parameter 'temperature'=0.5 is not supported for kimi-k3 model. Kimi runs at a fixed temperature. Since November 18, 2026 we resend such a request without that setting; elsewhere, remove it.
Your apiKeyHelper script is failing. The key file is missing or unreadable. Save the key again with the two commands in section 5.
Claude Code still asks you to log in, or still uses your Anthropic plan ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY exported in the shell wins over the saved key. Also, Claude Code reads a project's settings only after you trust that folder.
Claude models on your bill A model slot was left unset. Set ANTHROPIC_MODEL and all four slot variables.
Requests fail once the conversation gets long The context you told Claude Code is larger than the model has. Use the real size.
400 context_length_exceeded The prompt is longer than the model takes. The message gives both sizes.
404 model_not_found The model id is not in the catalog. GET https://api.uberllm.dev/v1/models lists the ids.
402 insufficient_credits The prepaid balance cannot cover the request, so it was not sent.
503 no_available_provider Nobody can serve that model right now, even after retries. Retry shortly or pick another model. Nothing was charged.
429 rate_limited The key went over its request limit per minute. Wait and retry.

9. Switch back to Claude

Close the terminal, or clear the variables in it:

unset ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN ANTHROPIC_MODEL \
  ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL \
  ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL \
  CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS

For a settings file, remove apiKeyHelper and the ANTHROPIC_* entries of its env block. Claude Code goes back to your Anthropic login on the next start.

10. The direct route: each maker's own endpoint

You do not need a marketplace for this. Each maker publishes an Anthropic-compatible endpoint, used with a key from that maker. From each maker's own docs, read on November 19, 2026:

  • Kimi (Moonshot AI): ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL is https://api.moonshot.ai/anthropic and the model is kimi-k3[1m].
  • GLM (Z.ai): ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL is https://api.z.ai/api/anthropic.
  • DeepSeek: ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL is https://api.deepseek.com/anthropic. Their page lists what that endpoint ignores, such as cache_control and the budget_tokens of thinking.

A maker's endpoint serves that maker's models, billed by that maker. Sections 2, 3, 8 and 9 apply to them too.

The trade-offs of doing this through UberLLM

I would rather you read these from me than find them later:

  • Third-party sellers. We do not run the models. Each request is served by a third-party provider through a seller's account, and everything the session reads is sent there. Do not use it in a repository that holds secrets, credentials or customer data.
  • We save requests for 90 days by default. Each API key has a "Do not save my requests and answers" switch that turns this off.
  • Our checks have limits. No software check proves which weights produced an answer. What we test, and what we cannot prove, is at uberllm.dev/verification.
  • It is prepaid, from $5, by card or PayPal. There is no free credit. If you only want to try one model family, the maker's own endpoint in section 10 is the simpler test.
  • We are a new company with no independent reviews yet.

The full guide, with the current model table, lives at uberllm.dev/answers/claude-code-with-deepseek-glm-kimi. If a setting here is wrong for your version of Claude Code, tell me in the comments and I will fix the post.

title: Introducing Virtual Models on AI Gateway
description:
Today, we are introducing Virtual Models on AI Gateway.

Virtual Models are an abstraction of the model string and configurations your apps and developers use. With a single virtual model ID, you can change and update models, configure fallbacks and priority, and enforce Zero Data Retention centrally. The virtual model configuration applies wherever the ID is used.

Assign a virtual model ID to an agent task, and pass it as the model string wherever that task is called. You can then change the model and settings behind the virtual model ID in AI Gateway, and your apps and agents will pick up the new configuration automatically, without code changes or redeploys.

New models use the same virtual model ID

In the last 90 days, 125 new models from more than 10 labs became available on AI Gateway. That adds up to about 10 a week. AI Gateway already makes switching a one-line change. You call any of those models by ID, and AI Gateway routes each request to a healthy provider and can fall back to others when one fails.

That one line still lives in your code, so switching usually means a redeploy.

Virtual Models move model selection and configuration to AI Gateway. You create an ID for a task, like vmc/coding-agent, and then configure the model and the settings it should use:

You can then use that virtual model ID as the model string wherever the task runs:

For coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, and others, connect them with vercel ai-gateway setup, then select your virtual model in each harness's model picker or configuration.

When a different model is available, including one from another provider, edit the virtual model. Every app and agent that calls vmc/coding-agent picks it up within a few minutes, with no code change or deployment needed:

Give each task its own model

An agent task like support ticket triage can run hundreds of times an hour and needs to be cheap. Other tasks, like legal contract review, may only run a few times a day, but require a high level of reasoning.

You can now give each task a purpose-built virtual model and easily evolve that model and configuration over time:

Settings such as fallbacks, Zero Data Retention, and tags stay with the virtual model when you switch models. Provider options apply per provider, so an Anthropic-specific setting stops applying when you point the virtual model at an OpenAI model. Review your provider options whenever you switch providers.

Before you switch a virtual model that serves production traffic, point a second one, like vmc/coding-agent-candidate, at the new model and run your evals against it. If quality drops after the switch, point the original back at the previous model.

Govern which models your team uses and how

Anyone on your team can call a virtual model, and team roles control who can make changes to it. Platform and security teams can centrally govern and test models and settings, while still easily giving teams access to new models as they are released.

Settings on a virtual model win over the same settings in a request, so callers can't override the provider order, fallbacks, or service tier you chose. For example, you can configure the fallback models for vmc/storefront-assistant centrally, and every app using that virtual model ID will use the same failover configuration, even if a request specifies different fallbacks.

If a virtual model requires Zero Data Retention or providers that don't train on request data, those configurations are enforced even if a request explicitly sets zeroDataRetention or disallowPromptTraining to false.

Tags on a virtual model replace any tags sent with the request, so spend lands on the task no matter how each app tags its calls. The Virtual Models page shows requests, spend, and success rate for each task.

Get started

Create a virtual model from your team dashboard or with the Vercel CLI.

About AI Gateway

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and doesn't charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

Virtual Models work with every model type on AI Gateway, including image, video, speech, embedding, and realtime models, and with the AI SDK and the OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible APIs. See the Virtual Models documentation for every setting.

Read more
