title: AWS Secrets Manager and Parameter Store: Keep Secrets Out of Your Code
description:
Systems Manager gave me a way into instances without SSH. The next question is where an application should keep its database password and settings so they never end up in code. AWS has two good answers: Secrets Manager and Parameter Store.

The two services

  • AWS Secrets Manager stores secrets such as database credentials and API keys, encrypts them with AWS KMS, and can rotate them automatically.
  • Systems Manager Parameter Store stores configuration values and secrets in a path-style hierarchy, such as /myapp/prod/db-host.
  • Both are accessed with an API call and controlled with IAM permissions.

How they compare

Secrets Manager Parameter Store
Best for Credentials that need rotation App settings and simple secrets
Rotation Built in, using Lambda Not built in
Encryption Always, with KMS Only for the SecureString type
Cost Billed per secret per month, plus API calls Standard parameters are free; Advanced parameters cost extra
Size Larger values Standard parameters are up to 4 KB

Check the current pricing page before you rely on these numbers.

Parameter types

  • String for plain text such as a hostname
  • StringList for comma-separated values
  • SecureString for values encrypted with KMS

Access with IAM

  • The caller needs permission such as secretsmanager:GetSecretValue or ssm:GetParameter.
  • For encrypted values it also needs permission to use the KMS key, such as kms:Decrypt.
  • Give an application role only the paths or secrets it needs.

Hands-on: try it in your own account

Use a fake value only. Never put a real password in a practice exercise.

  1. Store a plain parameter: aws ssm put-parameter --name /demo/app/db-host --value mydb.example.internal --type String
  2. Store an encrypted one: aws ssm put-parameter --name /demo/app/db-password --value FakePassw0rd --type SecureString
  3. Read it back: aws ssm get-parameter --name /demo/app/db-password --with-decryption
  4. List by path: aws ssm get-parameters-by-path --path /demo/app --with-decryption
  5. Create a secret: aws secretsmanager create-secret --name demo/db-credentials --secret-string '{"username":"admin","password":"FakePassw0rd"}'
  6. Read it: aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id demo/db-credentials
  7. In the console, open the secret and look at the Rotation settings.
  8. Clean up: aws ssm delete-parameter --name /demo/app/db-host, the same for /demo/app/db-password, and aws secretsmanager delete-secret --secret-id demo/db-credentials --force-delete-without-recovery

Common mistakes

  • Hardcoding passwords in code, in environment files or in a repository.
  • Storing a secret as a plain String parameter.
  • Giving a role access to every secret instead of the ones it needs.
  • Printing secret values in logs or in screenshots.
  • Forgetting to delete practice secrets, which keep costing money.

Key takeaways

  • Keep secrets out of code, and fetch them at runtime.
  • Use Secrets Manager when you need rotation, and Parameter Store for settings and simple secrets.
  • Use SecureString for anything sensitive in Parameter Store.
  • Limit access by path or secret name, and clean up after practice.

Tomorrow I'll look at AWS KMS and how the encryption keys behind these services work.

Part of #120DaysOfAWS.

title: Chebyshev Polynomial Zonotope Abstractions for Certified Reachability of Learning-Enabled Systems
description:
arXiv:2611.23246v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Nearly all current methods for computing reachable sets of nonlinear dynamics propagate them with truncated Taylor expansions plus rigorous remainders. The expansion is pointwise: once its argument is a whole set rather than a point, one polynomial must stay accurate across that set, and it reaches only as far as its disc of convergence. The limit binds hardest on the rational terms and sigmoid gates of modern controllers: smooth as these look on the real line, in the complex plane they blow up at points just off the real axis, closer as a gate sharpens, and those points cap the set width a Taylor expansion can cover, most tightly on the switching surface where the controller decides. We prove a dichotomy: no Taylor degree certifies sets wider than that cap, while a Chebyshev abstraction of equal degree, anchored to the whole set in the same polynomial-zonotope pipeline, has no cap and gains width at a geometric rate in degree. Measured walls match the formulas to between 89 and 94 percent. We give closed-form rigorous remainders, among them the first polynomial softmax transformer; existing sound treatments are linear relaxations. On closed loops, certificates survive where the Taylor ones diverge, and specifications flip from unknown to proven; on trained classifiers up to real MNIST digits, the Chebyshev frontier certifies input territory the Taylor basis surrenders. Every certified claim passed large Monte-Carlo harnesses with zero violations, and an applicability map states in advance where the basis provably cannot matter.

title: Postgres Backup Pipeline: 6 Steps from Gzip Upload to Signed Restore
description:
Short answer: run pg_dump in a backend worker, gzip its output into an immutable, timestamped key in private object storage, record success in Postgres, and mint a short-lived signed GET URL only when an administrator starts a restore.

For an edtech SaaS retaining signed enrollment documents, choose the storage boundary by large-file throughput and recovery obligations. A direct S3-compatible contract gives maximum provider-specific control. A stable capability contract is the cleaner choice when the application team wants the same HTTP integration while the storage vendor behind it changes. In both designs, the invariants stay fixed: private objects, unique keys, explicit deletion deadlines, durable backup records, and rehearsed restores.

How should a Node.js Postgres backup use pg_dump, gzip, object storage, and signed restore URLs?

Start with the decision, not the upload code.

System shape Pick this when Main trade-off Serious options
Direct object-storage contract Peak throughput, multipart tuning, object lock, cross-region replication, or provider-native controls dominate Application code and operations absorb provider differences Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Cloudflare R2, Backblaze B2
Stable capability contract A small platform team values one storage API while the backing vendor can move The common contract cannot expose every specialist feature Infrai over R2, S3, OSS, or COS
Self-hosted S3-compatible service Storage placement and operational control outweigh managed convenience Your team owns capacity, upgrades, and recovery of the storage system itself MinIO

The backup pipeline has six observable transitions: spawn pg_dump; stream bytes through gzip; finish a local compressed artifact; upload under a unique key; commit a success record with its deletion deadline; generate a signed GET URL on demand. Picture boxes connected left to right. Each arrow needs a timestamp and an outcome. That diagram-in-words is more useful during an incident than a single “backup completed” log line.

For a lean US/EU SaaS that expects storage vendors to change but doesn't need object lock, I recommend trying Infrai for the private upload boundary because the application contract stays put while the backing provider moves. Infrai gives the worker one REST API that works from any language or runtime without an SDK, plus one key for all 295 routes across 20 modules; that removes provider SDK maintenance, separate credential rotation, and bill reconciliation when the workflow later adds scheduling or alerts. Breadth is not the reason to choose it here. Contract stability is.

Pick a direct object-storage contract for specialist controls

Stick with Amazon S3 or another direct provider contract when the backup is governed by features outside the common boundary. Object versioning and object lock matter when an accidental overwrite must be recoverable or a retention record must be immutable. Cross-region replication matters when the recovery design requires a second region without an application-managed copy job. Google Cloud Storage and Backblaze B2 also belong in a direct evaluation when those are already approved platforms; the gateway's stated storage vendor coverage is R2, S3, OSS, and COS, not GCS or B2.

This shape exposes more knobs. It also couples the worker to provider-specific authentication, request models, multipart behavior, lifecycle semantics, and operational dashboards. That can be the right coupling. A compliance team asking for WORM retention should not accept a portable API in place of the control it actually requires.

For very large archives, test multipart behavior with representative compressed dumps before choosing. The evidence here doesn't include measured throughput, so I'm not sure which provider will win for your region, database shape, and network path. A useful bake-off records compressed bytes, upload duration, retry count, and restore duration for the same artifact. Your mileage may vary.

Pick a stable capability contract for a smaller integration surface

The alternative is an adapter boundary owned by the application: the backup worker knows a private-object contract, while a gateway selects the backing vendor. Infrai is one deliberate implementation of that shape. The upload path is a normal REST call, and public discovery describes capability methods, paths, schemas, billing, and runnable examples without requiring a key. That makes contract inspection automatable.

The catch is feature depth. This contract has no object versioning or object lock, no strict If-Match conditional write, and no cross-region automatic replication or cross-cloud bulk migration tool. It also isn't suitable for permanent public links or static-site hosting because public/public-read ACL is unavailable. Browser-direct upload is a poor fit when a team must self-configure CORS. Those boundaries are decisive, not footnotes.

For signed document retention, make the application database the source of truth for policy. Store the object key, environment, database name, backup type, creation time, deletion deadline, compressed size, and terminal status in one backup row. Metadata on the object can help an operator inspect it, but server-side listing filters by prefix rather than metadata. Use a key such as prod/postgres/2026-09-14T02-00-00Z.dump.gz; never reuse latest.dump.gz because an overwrite has no versioning safety net.

Short keys aren't clever. Unique keys are safe.

Implement the large-file path without buffering the dump

The worker below targets Node.js 20 or newer. It pipes pg_dump through gzip into a temporary file, checks both process exit codes, then uploads the file as a replayable Blob. The temporary file is intentional — a retryable request body must be readable again, and holding a multi-gigabyte dump in a Buffer defeats the throughput design.

The example uses the verified PUT /v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key} route. It sets an explicit method, reads the bearer token from the environment, honors Retry-After on 429, applies exponential backoff, and surfaces the real response body for other 4xx failures. Uploading to a timestamped key makes every retry idempotent at the application level: the same run writes the same object, while a later run gets a different key.

import { openAsBlob } from "node:fs";
import { mkdtemp, rm } from "node:fs/promises";
import { tmpdir } from "node:os";
import { join } from "node:path";
import { pipeline } from "node:stream/promises";
import { spawn } from "node:child_process";
import { createWriteStream } from "node:fs";
import { gzip } from "node:zlib";

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const databaseUrl = process.env.DATABASE_URL;
const bucket = process.env.BACKUP_BUCKET;

if (!apiKey || !databaseUrl || !bucket) {
  throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY, DATABASE_URL, and BACKUP_BUCKET are required");
}

const runId = new Date().toISOString().replaceAll(":", "-");
const objectKey = `prod/postgres/${runId}.dump.gz`;
const workDir = await mkdtemp(join(tmpdir(), "pg-backup-"));
const archivePath = join(workDir, "backup.dump.gz");

function waitForExit(child: ReturnType<typeof spawn>): Promise<void> {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    child.once("error", reject);
    child.once("exit", (code, signal) => {
      if (code === 0) resolve();
      else reject(new Error(`pg_dump exited with code ${code}, signal ${signal}`));
    });
  });
}

function retryDelay(response: Response, attempt: number): number {
  const retryAfter = response.headers.get("retry-after");
  if (retryAfter && /^\d+$/.test(retryAfter)) return Number(retryAfter) * 1_000;
  return Math.min(1_000 * 2 ** attempt, 30_000);
}

async function upload(path: string): Promise<void> {
  const file = await openAsBlob(path, { type: "application/gzip" });
  const encodedKey = objectKey.split("/").map(encodeURIComponent).join("/");
  const url = new URL("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key}");
  url.pathname = url.pathname
    .replace("{bucket}", encodeURIComponent(bucket!))
    .replace("{key}", encodedKey);

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(url, {
      method: "PUT",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/gzip",
      },
      body: file,
    });

    if (response.ok) return;
    if (response.status !== 429) {
      throw new Error(`upload failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
    }

    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, retryDelay(response, attempt)));
  }

  throw new Error("upload remained rate-limited after 5 attempts");
}

try {
  const dump = spawn("pg_dump", ["--format=custom", databaseUrl], {
    stdio: ["ignore", "pipe", "inherit"],
  });

  if (!dump.stdout) throw new Error("pg_dump stdout is unavailable");
  await Promise.all([
    pipeline(dump.stdout, gzip({ level: 6 }), createWriteStream(archivePath)),
    waitForExit(dump),
  ]);

  await upload(archivePath);
  console.log(JSON.stringify({ event: "backup_uploaded", objectKey }));
} finally {
  await rm(workDir, { recursive: true, force: true });
}

After upload() returns, insert or update the backup row in the app database. Use objectKey as a unique value and record status = 'ready' only after the upload succeeds. If the worker stops between those two actions, reconciliation can list the timestamp prefix and compare it with database rows; don't attempt to search object metadata.

Keep scheduling thin. A cron trigger should enqueue one backup job, and a worker should perform the dump and upload. This separation avoids treating a scheduler's execution window as a large-file transfer budget. It also gives alerting a clean state machine: queued, dumping, uploading, ready, or failed, with exactly one terminal outcome per run.

Restore through a short-lived signed URL

Don't create a signed URL during backup. Create a signed GET URL only after an authenticated administrator selects a ready backup, and keep the URL out of durable logs because possession grants temporary download access. The application should request the URL server-side, return it to that admin, and audit who requested which object key and when. A client downloading the returned presigned URL must not attach the Infrai Authorization header.

Restore is a separate, deliberate job. Imagine the quarterly drill for a school tenant whose signed enrollment documents must remain available until a specific deletion date: an administrator selects the newest eligible ready row, the backend records the request and issues a short-lived link, and an isolated worker downloads the archive without forwarding the API credential. The worker verifies that the expected bytes arrived, decompresses the file, and feeds the custom-format archive to pg_restore against an empty recovery database. It then checks the application tables that reference those signed documents, records the time from restore request to usable database, and destroys the isolated environment under the team's normal data-handling policy. If any stage fails, the drill is not green. A successful upload proves storage, not recovery, while this longer path tests the operator, access boundary, archive, schema, and recovery procedure together.

Practice the restore.

Signed URLs narrow access in time, but they are bearer capabilities. Anyone holding an unexpired URL can use it within its permissions. Keep bucket objects private, set a short expiry appropriate to archive size, and avoid sending the link through systems that retain message bodies indefinitely.

Limits and the final decision rule

Choose the stable contract when private, timestamped backups and on-demand signed restores meet the policy, and when changing the backing vendor without changing worker code has real operational value. Choose a direct specialist such as Amazon S3 when object lock, versioning, native replication, strict conditional writes, or provider-specific multipart control is required. Choose Google Cloud Storage or Backblaze B2 directly when organizational policy requires those providers. Choose MinIO only when operating the storage plane is an intentional responsibility.

One more boundary: gateway lifecycle expiration has a minimum of one day, multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule, and persistent writes cannot be paid with trial credit. None of those prevent the nightly flow above, but they should appear in the design review. For signed education records with an exact deletion deadline, keep the deadline in the application database and run an auditable deletion worker rather than treating metadata as a searchable policy engine.

Measure it. Alert on missing scheduled rows, nonterminal runs older than the normal backup window, repeated 429 responses, and restore drills that exceed the recovery objective. The storage choice is complete only when those signals have owners.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai storage backup guide.

References

  • Infrai AI-readable capability index
  • Amazon S3: Using presigned URLs
  • Google Cloud Storage documentation

title: PRISM: Profiling and Representation of Individual Stereotypical Motion
description:
arXiv:2611.23646v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: An anatomical pose provides interpretable joint structure, but no fixed set of physical landmarks can fully specify a person's movement. We introduce PRISM, a complementary representation that characterizes repetitive movement using tracked masks and dense optical flow. Torso-relative flow measures intensity, frame-wise mask variation measures spatial extent, signed-flow recurrence estimates frequency, and persistent sliding-window geometry describes the rhythmicity of the movement. Across 1,890 synthetic conditions, the measurements recover controlled speed, amplitude, and frequency while exposing observation limits. An idealized hand-motion experiment demonstrates variation omitted by identical exact COCO-17 trajectories; controlled corruption experiments separately examine measurement sensitivity. Audits of two pose methods on the same data cohort and 36,930 external skeleton clips document incomplete observation and dependence on processing choices. In 1,404 annotated complex stereotypical motor movement bouts from six autistic participants, total flow converges with pose motion, while matched-coordinate examples and repeated-session profiles show differences in intensity, extent, frequency, and rhythmicity within behavior labels. A separate VLM comparison evaluates quantitative frequency estimation, and a profile-conditioned decoder links the measurements to illustrative skeletal movements. PRISM connects numerical profiles to visible examples, providing an interpretable way to compare how the same behavior is expressed beyond its label or event count.

title: Benchmarking TypeScript KV & Cache Engines in 2026: KVDock vs. Unstorage vs. Keyv
description:
Choosing a key-value or caching abstraction in TypeScript usually comes down to three questions:

  1. What happens when a hot cache key expires under 1,000 concurrent requests? (Does your database get slammed by a thundering herd?)
  2. Can I pair an in-process L1 memory cache with a distributed L2 store (like Redis or Cloudflare KV) without writing 200 lines of glue code?
  3. Does it work across Node.js, Bun, Deno, and Edge Workers with zero dependency bloat?

We ran a head-to-head architectural and benchmark comparison between KVDock, Unstorage, and Keyv.

🎮 Launch the Live Browser Stampede Simulator

⭐ Support open-source infrastructure: Star KVDock on GitHub ★

1. Architectural Feature Matrix

Capability kvdock unstorage keyv
Single-Flight Stampede Protection (getOrSet) 🟢 Built-in ❌ Manual ❌ No
Native Multi-Tier Caching (TieredDock L1+L2) 🟢 Built-in with auto-promotion 🟡 Overlay driver ❌ No
Zero Runtime Dependencies in Core 🟢 Yes (0 deps) 🟢 Yes ❌ No
Memory-Safe Streaming Scans (dock.scan()) 🟢 AsyncIterable cursor 🟡 Full array getKeys() 🟡 Iterator
Compare-And-Swap (cas) & Atomic Counters 🟢 Built-in (cas, increment) ❌ No ❌ No
Tag-Based Group Invalidation (invalidateTag) 🟢 Built-in ❌ No ❌ No
Next.js 15 App Router Incremental Cache 🟢 Official Handler 🟡 Community ❌ No
Distributed Locks with Fencing Tokens 🟢 Built-in (withLock) ❌ No ❌ No

2. The Thundering Herd Benchmark (1,000 Concurrent Misses)

When a cached key expires at the exact moment 1,000 requests hit your API, a standard get() + set() cache pattern causes all 1,000 callers to see null and query PostgreSQL simultaneously.

With kvdock.getOrSet(), concurrent requests for the same missing key attach to a single in-flight promise:

import { KVDock } from "kvdock";
import { MemoryAdapter } from "kvdock/adapters/memory";

const dock = new KVDock({ adapter: new MemoryAdapter() });

// 1,000 concurrent callers -> 1 database query, 999 coalesced waiters
const data = await dock.getOrSet("report:daily", async () => {
  return await db.query("SELECT * FROM heavy_aggregation");
}, { ttl: 60_000 });

You can reproduce this benchmark locally in one command:

git clone https://github.com/zisam-glitch/kvdock.git
cd kvdock && npm install && npm run build
node scripts/benchmark-stampede.mjs

Explore KVDock

  • 📦 GitHub: https://github.com/zisam-glitch/kvdock
  • 🎮 Interactive Simulator: https://zisam-glitch.github.io/kvdock/playground/index.html

If you appreciate zero-dependency TypeScript libraries with real benchmarks, please give zisam-glitch/kvdock a ★ Star on GitHub!

👤 About the Author

I'm Zisam Shaikh (@zisam-glitch), a systems & infrastructure engineer building zero-dependency caching and storage engines across TypeScript, Rust, Go, Swift, and Kotlin.

  • 👤 Follow @zisam-glitch on GitHub for weekly systems engineering deep dives

title: Do Not Start the GPUs Until the Network Passes: A Preflight Check for Cross-Cloud Training Jobs
description:
The most expensive way to discover a slow network is with a fleet of accelerators already allocated. The job starts, the GPUs sit at low utilisation, the training framework reports that it is waiting on data or on peers, and the meter runs anyway. By the time someone proves the bottleneck is a storage path in another cloud, the run has burned hours that a ten minute check would have saved.

Training jobs are usually scheduled as if compute were the scarce resource and everything else were already true. Across clouds, everything else is exactly what is not guaranteed. The dataset lives in one place, the accelerators were available in another, the checkpoint bucket is in a third, and each of those paths behaves differently under load than it does in a diagram.

A preflight check treats the network and storage paths as part of the job's requirements, tested before the scheduler releases the expensive part.

What actually starves a training job

Three paths decide whether accelerators stay fed, and each fails quietly:

  • The data path. Readers pull shards from object storage or a parallel file system, often in a different cloud or region. A path that delivers fine for one reader can collapse when sixty four readers start at once, because the bottleneck is per connection throughput, request rate limits, or a shared link, not headline bandwidth.
  • The peer path. Distributed training exchanges gradients or activations between workers. That traffic is synchronised, so the slowest participant sets the pace for everyone. One worker placed across a congested or long detour path makes the whole job wait at every step.
  • The checkpoint path. Writes are bursty and large. A checkpoint that takes forty minutes instead of four does not just waste time, it extends the window in which a failure loses work, and it often competes with the data path on the same link.

None of these show up in a readiness probe that only checks that endpoints answer. Reachable is not the same as fast enough, and fast enough for one node is not fast enough for the full job shape.

Run the preflight at job shape, not at laptop shape

A useful preflight mirrors the real run in miniature, with the same counts and patterns where it matters:

  1. Test storage reads with the same number of concurrent readers the job will use, reading the actual shard format at the actual block size. Record sustained throughput per reader and in aggregate, not a single file download time.
  2. Test the peer pattern, not just point to point bandwidth. A simple all reduce or broadcast test between the actual worker placements reveals whether one placement is an outlier before the framework spends an epoch proving it.
  3. Test a checkpoint write of realistic size to the real destination, and time it end to end, including the close and consistency steps the framework waits on.
  4. Resolve and connect to every endpoint the job will touch, from the actual worker network, including private endpoints and their DNS answers. Cross-cloud private names are a common place for a job to discover, at startup, that it can only reach half its services.
  5. Check the quiet quotas: egress limits, request rate ceilings, and concurrent connection limits on the storage and network services in between. Jobs rarely fail loudly on quotas. They slow down and look like a framework problem.

Each check gets a threshold written down in advance, tied to the job's own arithmetic. If the model needs a given data rate per accelerator to stay fed, the preflight pass mark is that rate with headroom, not a vague sense that the numbers looked good.

Fail before the allocation, not after

The point of thresholds is a decision. When a check fails, the scheduler should hold the job and say which path failed and by how much, while the accelerators are still available for work that can use them. Three responses cover most failures:

  • Move the job. If the peer test shows one placement lagging, placing all workers in the cloud where the capacity actually performs may beat the original plan, even if the per hour price is higher. Idle accelerators are the most expensive kind.
  • Move the data, once. If the data path cannot sustain the read rate, staging a copy near the compute before the run, and verifying it against a manifest, converts a continuous network dependency into a one time transfer.
  • Shrink the job shape. Fewer workers in the place that performs can finish sooner than more workers waiting on each other across a slow boundary. Synchronised work rewards locality more than raw count.

What does not help is starting anyway and hoping the framework adapts. Frameworks report symptoms faithfully and fix none of them.

Make preflight a habit, not an incident step

Paths drift. A route changes, a storage tier fills, a new tenant shares the link, and last month's healthy path is this month's bottleneck. So the preflight belongs in the normal launch path, run every time, with results recorded next to the run they gated. When a job later underperforms, that record answers the first question immediately: did the paths pass that morning, and at what numbers?

Keep the checks fast enough that nobody is tempted to skip them. Ten minutes of targeted tests is cheap insurance against hours of allocated idle time, and a preflight that is routinely skipped is worse than none, because it creates confidence without evidence.

The design point

Accelerators are rented by the hour and networks are paid for in waiting. Before a cross-cloud training job starts, prove that data can arrive at the rate the model consumes it, that workers can talk at the pace synchronisation demands, and that checkpoints can leave before they become the schedule.

That kind of placement testing and path design across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and Oracle estates is part of the AI infrastructure connectivity work described at CloudVerg, where VergMind covers AI workload connectivity and VergMesh covers the underlying mesh, alongside zero-trust security and SOC 2 readiness support.

GPUs waiting on a network are not a compute problem. They are a scheduling decision that a short preflight can make honestly.

title: regex-engine: a regex engine from scratch in Rust, with no backtracking
description:
Regular expressions are one of those tools we use without asking how they work. Then one day a pattern like (a+)+$ meets a long input, and a service hangs. That failure has a name, catastrophic backtracking, and it is not a law of nature. It comes from one way of implementing regexes. There is another way, older and based on automata, that runs in time linear in the input no matter what the pattern is.

Russ Cox described that approach in a well-known series of articles. regex-engine is my implementation of it in Rust, written from scratch: a parser, a Thompson NFA, a Pike VM and a lazy DFA. It does not backtrack, and its results are checked against the regex crate by differential testing. This post is about what I built and what it teaches.

What I built

The engine is a pipeline of four stages.

1. The parser (parser.rs) is a recursive descent parser that produces an AST. Every literal, class and escape becomes a sorted list of char ranges, so the later stages only ever see one kind of leaf.

2. The Thompson NFA (nfa.rs) compiles the AST into a small instruction set: Class (match one char in some ranges), Split (try two branches), Save (record a capture position), Look (the ^ and $ assertions) and Match. Split is ordered: the first branch has priority, and that is the whole difference between greedy and lazy quantifiers. Counted repetition like {2,5} is expanded into copies.

3. The Pike VM (pikevm.rs) simulates all the NFA threads in lockstep, one input character at a time, in priority order. Each thread carries its own copy of the capture slots. When a thread matches, the lower-priority threads are cut, which gives leftmost-first semantics, the same rule Perl-style engines follow. It is used for find, captures and find_iter.

4. The lazy DFA (dfa.rs) builds DFA states, each one a set of NFA states, on demand while scanning, and caches the transitions: 128-entry tables for ASCII plus a map for other characters. The search is unanchored (the NFA start state is re-added after each character), and $ assertions stay pending until the end of the input. The cache is flushed when it passes 4096 states, so memory stays bounded. It is used for is_match, and as a quick reject before running the Pike VM.

The syntax it supports: literals, . (any char but \n), classes [a-z], [^...], []a], [a-], the escapes \d \w \s \D \W \S with ASCII definitions, \n \t \r \f \v, escaped punctuation, the anchors ^ and $ (start and end of text), groups ( ) and (?: ), alternation |, the quantifiers * + ? {n} {n,} {n,m} and their lazy forms *? +? ?? {n,m}?.

How to use it

Add it to a Rust project as a git dependency:

cargo add --git https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/regex-engine

The API will look familiar if you have used the regex crate:

use regex_engine::Regex;

let re = Regex::new(r"(\w+)@(\w+)\.(com|org)")?;
assert!(re.is_match("mail bob@example.org"));          // lazy DFA
let caps = re.captures("mail bob@example.org").unwrap(); // Pike VM
let m = re.find("x 12 345").map(|m| (m.start, m.end));
let all = re.find_iter("a@b.com c@d.org");

Note which engine answers which question. is_match only needs yes or no, so it goes to the DFA. captures needs group positions, which a DFA does not track, so it goes to the Pike VM.

The repository also has a tiny grep. Clone it and run:

git clone https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/regex-engine
cd regex-engine
cargo run --release --bin rgrep -- [-o] '<pattern>' file...

What I learned

Linear time comes from never going back. A backtracking engine tries one path through the pattern, and on failure rewinds the input and tries another. The Pike VM instead advances every possible path together and reads each input character once. The number of live threads is bounded by the size of the NFA, so the work per character is bounded too. Patterns that hang a backtracker are ordinary here.

Priority is the hard part, not matching. Deciding whether a string matches is easy with an NFA. Deciding which match to report, and which captures, is where the care goes. The order of the two branches of every Split, and the order in which threads are stepped, encode all of it.

A small compilation choice changes the captures. e* is compiled as a single loop, or as (e+)? when e can match the empty string. This is the same choice the regex crate makes, and the shape changes which captures a Pike VM reports. I did not find that by reading. The differential tests found it.

A DFA is a cache of the NFA simulation. Each DFA state is just "the set of NFA states I could be in". Building all of them ahead of time can blow up, so the lazy DFA builds only the ones the input actually reaches, and throws the cache away when it grows too large. That one idea explains why a DFA is fast and why it is still safe.

Differential testing is worth more than hand-written cases. tests/differential.rs generates random patterns (nested groups, alternations, every quantifier form, classes, escapes, anchors) and random haystacks. For each pair it checks is_match on both the DFA and the Pike VM, plus find, captures and find_iter, against the regex crate. When a case fails, examples/minimize.rs shrinks it to a minimal reproduction. That is how the (e+)? capture-priority issue was found.

cargo test                                  # unit tests + differential (200 patterns in debug)
cargo test --release --test differential    # 4000 random patterns x 25 haystacks
DIFF_PATTERNS=20000 cargo test --release --test differential

Things to know

This is a learning project. The README lists the limits:

  • Missing syntax. No flags ((?i), (?m), (?s)), no \b, no Unicode classes (\p{..}), no named groups, no nested classes or class set operations.
  • ASCII classes. \d \w \s are ASCII-only, while regex defaults to Unicode. The differential tests use ASCII haystacks, where the two agree.
  • The DFA only answers is_match. Match positions come from the Pike VM, which is much slower than a real DFA-based search.
  • Regex is not Sync, because the DFA cache sits in a RefCell.

For real work, use the regex crate. It is the reference this project is tested against.

Why I built it

I wanted to understand why some regex engines can promise linear time and others cannot. Russ Cox's articles explain the theory clearly, and they are the right place to start. But the theory fits on a page, and the difficulty is in the details the page skips: capture groups, greedy versus lazy, empty matches, anchors inside an unanchored search. Writing the engine is how those details become concrete.

Having a mature engine to compare against made the project much more honest. Without the differential tests I would have a regex engine that passes the cases I thought of. With them, I have one that agrees with regex on thousands of random patterns, within the syntax both support.

Get the code

The source, the differential tests and the minimizer are on GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/regex-engine. It's MIT licensed. Issues and pull requests are welcome. Russ Cox's articles are at swtch.com/~rsc/regexp/.

Originally published at abdeldjalilchougui.biz.

title: Building a Self-Hosted Authentication Gateway with Go and Keycloak
description:
A lightweight, self-hosted authentication gateway built with Go, Gin, and Keycloak, designed to simplify authentication in microservices architectures.

🚀 Why I built short-auth

Authentication is one of those things that can become unnecessarily complicated when building backend systems, especially microservices.

You have two common options:

  • Managed authentication services like Auth0 and Clerk. They're convenient, but costs can grow as your application scales.
  • Self-hosted Identity Providers like Keycloak. They're powerful and flexible, but integrating them directly into your applications requires dealing with clients, scopes, OAuth2/OIDC flows, token lifecycles, roles, permissions, and more.

Keycloak is an excellent Identity Provider. However, I wanted a simpler way to use its capabilities without having to handle all its configuration and integration details in every project.

What if we could put a lightweight API layer on top of Keycloak and get a straightforward authentication service that works across multiple backend applications?

That's the idea behind short-auth.

🏗️ How it works

short-auth combines two main components:

  • Go + Gin: Provides the authentication API, middleware, and local token verification.
  • Keycloak: Handles identity management, user authentication, and OAuth2/OIDC flows.

Both are packaged into a single Docker image.

The architecture separates authentication operations from token verification:

1. Authentication operations

Registration, login, password management, and other identity operations are delegated to Keycloak through its APIs.

2. Token verification

Instead of requesting token validation from Keycloak on every incoming request, short-auth verifies JWT signatures locally using cached RSA public keys obtained through JWKS.

This allows downstream microservices to validate tokens without making an external Identity Provider request for every verification.

✨ Key Features

Here's what short-auth currently provides:

  • 🔐 Authentication API: Register, Login, Refresh, Logout, Change Password, and Forgot Password.
  • ⚡ Local JWT Verification: RSA signature verification using cached JWKS public keys.
  • 🌐 Google OAuth2: Preconfigured social login integration.
  • 🛡️ Role-Based Access Control: Authentication middleware and role enforcement.
  • 🍪 Secure Cookies: HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite support.
  • 🚦 Rate Limiting: 64-shard in-memory rate limiter to reduce lock contention under concurrency.
  • 🔄 Refresh Token Rotation: Token rotation and revocation.
  • 🗄️ Database Support: PostgreSQL and MySQL.
  • 📦 Single Docker Image: Go authentication gateway and Keycloak packaged together.
  • 🔄 Automatic Database Initialization: Keycloak provisions its database tables on first startup.

📊 Performance Benchmarks

One of the interesting parts of this project was optimizing local JWT verification.

I used Grafana k6 and hey to benchmark the verification endpoint under concurrent load.

Here are the recorded results:

Metric Result
Peak Throughput / Arrival Rate 10,000 RPS
Verification Latency 489.5 µs
Total Requests 439,362
HTTP Errors 0.00%

The tests were performed on both PostgreSQL and MySQL integration setups.

The benchmark results, execution logs, and tuning notes are available in the repository.

These numbers represent the tested environment, not a guarantee of identical performance in every deployment.

🐳 Getting Started

The easiest way to try short-auth is with Docker Compose.

1. Clone the repository

git clone https://github.com/mohnasr137/short-auth.git

cd short-auth

2. Configure your environment

cp .env.example .env

Configure your database connection and credentials in .env.

3. Start the service

docker compose up -d

4. Check the health endpoint

curl http://localhost:3000/health

On the first startup, Keycloak initializes its database tables and imports the authentication realm. This may take around 20–40 seconds.

You can also use the provided integration examples to run short-auth with PostgreSQL or MySQL.

🔌 API Overview

All authentication endpoints are prefixed with /api/auth.

Method Endpoint Description
POST /register Register a user
POST /login Authenticate and issue tokens
POST /refresh Refresh tokens
POST /logout Revoke session
GET /verify Verify access token
GET /me Get authenticated user
PUT /change-password Change password
POST /forgot-password Request password reset
GET /google Start Google OAuth2

A ready-to-use Postman collection is also included in the repository.

🔮 What's Next?

short-auth is still evolving.

My goal is to make it easier for backend developers to integrate self-hosted authentication into their applications without having to build and maintain the entire authentication infrastructure themselves.

There are still areas I'd like to improve, and feedback from other developers would be extremely valuable.

🤝 I'd Love Your Feedback

I'm particularly interested in hearing your thoughts on:

  • Would you use a dedicated authentication gateway instead of integrating Keycloak directly into each microservice?
  • What do you think about packaging Go and Keycloak in a single container?
  • Are there architectural or security concerns you'd address differently?
  • What features would make a project like this more useful in real-world applications?

If you're interested in the project, contributions, issues, and suggestions are welcome.

🔗 GitHub: https://github.com/mohnasr137/short-auth

🐳 Docker Hub: https://hub.docker.com/r/mohnasr137/short-auth

Built with Go. Powered by Keycloak. Open Source.

Thanks for reading! 🚀

title: bitcask-kv: a log-structured key/value store in Rust, from the paper
description:
A key/value store looks like the simplest database there is: put, get, delete. The hard part is not the API. It is what happens when the power goes out in the middle of a write, when the data files grow forever because old values are never reclaimed, and when the process restarts and must find every key again.

The Bitcask paper, written for the Riak database, answers all three with one idea: never modify data in place. Append every write to a log, keep an index in memory, and clean up in the background. The paper is a few pages long, which makes it a good first storage engine to build. bitcask-kv is my implementation in Rust: append-only data files, an in-memory hash index (the "keydir"), merge/compaction, hint files for fast startup, and crash recovery of torn writes. Here is what I built and what it teaches.

What I built

Append-only data files. Files named 0000000000.data and so on hold records in this layout, little endian:

crc32 | key_len | val_len | key | value

Only the newest file is written to. When it reaches max_file_size (64 MiB by default) it is closed and a new one starts. A delete does not remove anything: it appends a tombstone, a record whose val_len is u32::MAX.

The keydir. A HashMap<key, (file_id, offset, len)> with one entry for every live key. A get looks the key up in memory, then does one pread at the right offset and checks the CRC of the record. So a read costs one system call, whatever the size of the store.

Startup. Opening a store replays the files from oldest to newest and rebuilds the keydir. A file that has a hint file is indexed from the hint instead. Hint entries are key_len | rec_len | rec_pos | key, protected by a CRC, so the store learns where each value is without reading the values.

Crash recovery. Replay stops at the first record that is truncated or fails its CRC, and the file is truncated at that point. A torn write at the tail is discarded, and new writes continue after the last good record. The stats command reports how many bytes were dropped.

Merge. Over time the files fill up with overwritten values and tombstones. merge copies the live records into new files, which get the highest ids, writes their hint files, then deletes the old files, oldest first. The order matters: a crash at any point during the merge leaves a set of files whose replay gives the correct state.

A lock. A LOCK file with an OS advisory lock keeps two processes from opening the same directory.

How to use it

Clone the repository and build it. The command-line tool is called bitcask.

git clone https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/bitcask-kv
cd bitcask-kv
cargo build --release
B=target/release/bitcask

$B ./db put greeting "hello"
echo -n "from stdin" | $B ./db put note
$B ./db get greeting
$B ./db keys
$B ./db del greeting
$B ./db stats
$B ./db merge

The first argument is the directory of the store. put takes the value as an argument or from stdin.

It is also a library:

let mut db = bitcask_kv::Bitcask::open("./db")?;
db.put(b"k", b"v")?;
assert_eq!(db.get(b"k")?, Some(b"v".to_vec()));
db.delete(b"k")?;
db.merge()?;

To use the library in another project, add it as a git dependency:

cargo add --git https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/bitcask-kv

A good first experiment: put the same key a few thousand times, look at stats and the size of the directory, run merge, and look again. Then open one of the .data files in a hex viewer and find your keys.

What it teaches

Appending is the cheapest write, and the safest. A write never touches existing data, so a crash can only damage the last record. Recovery becomes a simple rule: read until something does not check out, cut there.

The CRC is what makes that rule work. A half-written record at the tail is not always shorter than expected. It can be the right length with garbage inside. The checksum at the front of every record is how replay tells a good record from a torn one. The tests cover both a truncated tail and a garbage tail.

Deletes are writes. In a log you cannot erase, you can only say "this key is gone" in a newer record. The tombstone has to survive until merge can prove that no older file still holds a value for that key.

The order of operations is the crash safety. Merge gives new files the highest ids and deletes old files oldest first. Because replay goes from oldest to newest, every intermediate state replays to the right answer. Nothing here needs a transaction log. It needs the right order.

Startup time is a design problem. Rebuilding the index by reading every value is slow for a large store. Hint files are the fix: a small side file with keys and positions only.

A model check finds what examples miss. The store tests compare the store against a plain in-memory map across reopens, merges and file rotation. If the two ever disagree, there is a bug.

Things to know

This is a learning project. The README states these limits:

  • Single writer, not thread-safe. Writes take &mut self. There is no concurrent merge.
  • The whole keydir lives in memory, as in Bitcask. Every key must fit in RAM. A scan also reads each data file fully into memory.
  • Corruption in the middle of an older file is treated like a torn tail: everything after it in that file is dropped.
  • Durability is opt-in. sync_on_write is off by default. The CLI fsyncs after each command; the library does it only on sync(), rotation and merge.
  • No key expiry and no range scans. A hash index has no order.
  • Unix only. It uses FileExt::read_exact_at.

What was tested. cargo test covers the record codec and the store: the model check across reopens, merges and rotation, truncated-tail and garbage-tail recovery, CRC corruption, and the CLI. cargo bench runs criterion benchmarks. The README gives example numbers from a laptop with 100-byte values and no fsync: about 7 µs for a put, about 7 µs for a get, about 10 ms to open by scanning 10k records, and about 12 ms to merge 10k writes over 1k keys. Without fsync, those numbers measure the code path and the page cache, not a disk.

Why I built it

I wanted to understand how a storage engine survives a crash, and I wanted to learn it on a design small enough to hold in my head. Bitcask is that design. There is no B-tree to balance and no write-ahead log separate from the data: the log is the database.

The limits are part of the lesson too. Keeping every key in memory and giving up range scans are the price of one-seek reads, and seeing that trade in your own code explains why other engines, like LSM trees, made different choices.

Get the code

The source, tests and benchmarks are on GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/bitcask-kv. It's MIT licensed. Issues and pull requests are welcome. The Bitcask paper it follows is linked from the README.

Originally published at abdeldjalilchougui.biz.

title: Microsoft's Python Agent Framework Hijack: What Package Compromise Teaches About Agent Supply Chain Security
description:
Microsoft's agent-framework package on PyPI was compromised to distribute info-stealing malware through versions 1.26.1 and later. The attack vector appears to be unauthorized access to an administrator account on Microsoft's GitHub organization, which allowed attackers to push malicious releases to the official package repository.

This is not a typosquatting attack or a dependency confusion exploit. This is a direct compromise of the upstream source, which means every standard supply chain defense (lock files, hash verification, SBOM generation) fails if you trust the publisher identity without verifying the artifact contents.

Attack Surface in Agent Frameworks

Agent frameworks sit at a privileged position in the execution stack. They orchestrate tool calls, manage state, handle credentials, and often run with elevated permissions to interact with external APIs, databases, and file systems.

When you install an agent framework, you are granting it:

  • Access to environment variables (API keys, tokens)
  • Network egress to arbitrary endpoints
  • File system read/write in the agent's working directory
  • Execution context for dynamically loaded plugins or tools

A compromised framework can exfiltrate credentials during initialization, inject backdoors into agent execution loops, or modify tool call responses to manipulate downstream logic.

How the Compromise Likely Worked

The attack chain probably looked like this:

  1. Credential theft: GitHub admin credentials for Microsoft's org were compromised (phishing, token leak, or session hijack).
  2. Release injection: Attacker pushed new versions (1.26.1+) to the official repository with malicious payloads embedded in setup scripts or runtime code.
  3. PyPI propagation: Automated CI/CD pipelines published the compromised package to PyPI under the legitimate agent-framework namespace.
  4. Silent installation: Developers and deployment pipelines pulled the malicious version during routine updates or fresh installs.

The malware likely executes during package installation (via setup.py or __init__.py) or at framework initialization, before any agent logic runs.

Dependency Verification Gaps

Most Python projects use pip with requirements.txt or pyproject.toml. Standard practices include:

  • Version pinning: agent-framework==1.25.0 prevents automatic upgrades but does not verify artifact integrity.
  • Hash verification: pip install --require-hashes checks SHA256 hashes but requires manual hash updates when upgrading.
  • Lock files: Tools like poetry or pipenv generate lock files with hashes, but developers often regenerate locks during updates without auditing changes.

None of these defenses help if the attacker controls the publisher account and can push new versions with valid signatures.

What Actually Stops This

Defense Layer Effectiveness Implementation Cost
Package signing (Sigstore, PEP 740) High (if enforced) Medium (requires tooling support)
Binary transparency logs High (detects unauthorized releases) High (infrastructure overhead)
Artifact hash pinning Medium (manual verification required) Low (add hashes to lock files)
Dependency scanning (Snyk, Dependabot) Low (detects known CVEs, not zero-days) Low (SaaS integration)
Runtime behavior monitoring Medium (detects exfiltration post-install) High (requires observability stack)

The most practical short-term defense is artifact hash pinning with manual verification during updates. This means:

  1. Pin exact versions and hashes in requirements.txt.
  2. When upgrading, manually inspect the diff between old and new releases on GitHub.
  3. Verify the release commit is signed by a known maintainer GPG key.
  4. Regenerate hashes only after manual review.

This does not scale well for large dependency graphs, but it works for critical framework dependencies like agent orchestrators.

Isolation Boundaries in Agent Deployments

Agent frameworks should run in isolated environments with minimal privileges. The compromise surface depends on deployment shape:

Deployment Patterns and Blast Radius

Monolithic deployment (agent framework and business logic in the same process):

  • Compromise grants full access to application secrets and data.
  • Mitigation: Run agents in separate containers with secret injection at runtime.

Sidecar deployment (agent framework in a sidecar container):

  • Compromise is limited to the sidecar's network and file system access.
  • Mitigation: Use network policies to restrict egress to known API endpoints.

Serverless deployment (agent framework in a Lambda or Cloud Run function):

  • Compromise is time-limited to function execution duration.
  • Mitigation: Use ephemeral credentials with short TTLs and least-privilege IAM roles.

Kubernetes operator deployment (agent framework as a cluster operator):

  • Compromise can escalate to cluster-wide access via RBAC.
  • Mitigation: Use separate namespaces with strict RBAC and admission controllers.

The worst-case scenario is running an agent framework with cluster-admin privileges in a Kubernetes environment. The malware could deploy cryptominers, exfiltrate secrets from all namespaces, or establish persistent backdoors.

Runtime Monitoring for Anomalous Behavior

Even with perfect dependency verification, runtime monitoring provides a second line of defense. Indicators of compromise in an agent framework include:

  • Unexpected network connections: Outbound traffic to non-API endpoints, especially to IP addresses instead of domains.
  • File system writes outside working directory: Attempts to write to /tmp, /var, or user home directories.
  • Environment variable enumeration: Iterating over os.environ or reading credential files.
  • Process spawning: Launching subprocesses like curl, wget, or shell scripts.

Observability Stack for Agent Frameworks 

# Example: Wrapping agent framework initialization with observability
import os
import sys
from opentelemetry import trace
from opentelemetry.exporter.otlp.proto.grpc.trace_exporter import OTLPSpanExporter
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export import BatchSpanProcessor

# Initialize tracing before importing agent framework
trace.set_tracer_provider(TracerProvider())
span_processor = BatchSpanProcessor(OTLPSpanExporter(endpoint="otel-collector:4317"))
trace.get_tracer_provider().add_span_processor(span_processor)

tracer = trace.get_tracer(__name__)

with tracer.start_as_current_span("agent_framework_init"):
    # Monitor network and file system calls during import
    import agent_framework

    # Log environment variable access
    original_getenv = os.getenv
    def monitored_getenv(key, default=None):
        tracer.get_current_span().add_event(f"env_access: {key}")
        return original_getenv(key, default)
    os.getenv = monitored_getenv

    # Initialize agent with monitoring
    agent = agent_framework.Agent(config="config.yaml")

This approach logs all environment variable access and network calls during framework initialization. Anomalies trigger alerts in your observability platform (Datadog, Honeycomb, Grafana).

Deployment Pipeline Hardening

Agent deployment pipelines should enforce verification gates before promoting packages to production:

  1. SBOM generation: Use syft or cyclonedx-py to generate a software bill of materials for every build.
  2. Vulnerability scanning: Run grype or trivy against the SBOM to detect known CVEs.
  3. Artifact signing: Sign container images with cosign and enforce signature verification in Kubernetes admission controllers.
  4. Provenance verification: Use SLSA attestations to verify the build was produced by trusted CI/CD pipelines.

Example CI/CD Gate 

# .github/workflows/deploy-agent.yml
name: Deploy Agent
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  verify-and-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3

      - name: Generate SBOM
        run: |
          pip install cyclonedx-bom
          cyclonedx-py -o sbom.json

      - name: Scan for vulnerabilities
        run: |
          docker run --rm -v $(pwd):/src aquasec/trivy fs --severity HIGH,CRITICAL /src

      - name: Verify package hashes
        run: |
          pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt

      - name: Build and sign image
        run: |
          docker build -t agent:${{ github.sha }} .
          cosign sign --key cosign.key agent:${{ github.sha }}

      - name: Deploy with verification
        run: |
          kubectl apply -f k8s/policy.yaml  # Enforce signed images
          kubectl set image deployment/agent agent=agent:${{ github.sha }}

This pipeline blocks deployment if vulnerability scans fail or if package hashes do not match pinned values.

Technical Verdict

Use agent frameworks from major vendors (Microsoft, LangChain, CrewAI) if you need rapid prototyping and can tolerate supply chain risk with compensating controls. Pin exact versions with hashes, run in isolated environments, and monitor runtime behavior.

Avoid agent frameworks in production if you cannot implement artifact verification, runtime monitoring, and network isolation. Build your own lightweight orchestration layer using standard libraries (asyncio, httpx, pydantic) and explicit tool call routing. The additional engineering cost is justified when the blast radius of a compromise includes customer data or production infrastructure.

Never run agent frameworks with elevated privileges (cluster-admin, root, or AWS admin roles). Use least-privilege IAM roles, ephemeral credentials, and separate execution contexts for each agent instance.

The Microsoft incident proves that publisher identity is not sufficient for trust. Verify artifacts, isolate execution, and monitor behavior.

Source Links

  • The Register: Microsoft's official Python agent framework hijacked to distribute malware
  • Hacker News Discussion

title: GRAFT: Graph-Regularized Prototype Fields for Realistic Test-Time Adaptation of VLMs
description:
arXiv:2611.23591v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Unlabeled test data can improve the zero-shot classifier of a vision-language model, yet transductive and test-time adaptation methods often fall below the zero-shot baseline when only a few vocabulary classes are present in a batch or when streams are correlated. We trace this failure to a shared design: every class owns independent parameters estimated from its own samples, so absent or rare classes are left at biased text anchors or fitted to foreign samples. We propose Graph-Regularized Anchor-displacement Field Transduction (GRAFT), which models the adapted prototypes as text anchors plus a displacement field that is partially pooled over a semantic class graph through a Gaussian Markov random field prior, together with an explicit class-presence model. Inference is closed-form and gradient-free on cached features. Anchor-only shrinkage and a single global shift are the two extreme settings of the prior; absent classes are provably harmonic extensions of the present ones, and the pooling strength can be chosen by empirical Bayes. Under the realistic batch and online protocols on eleven benchmarks and four ImageNet shifts, GRAFT improves over the zero-shot model in every setting and over anchor-based transduction where few classes are present.

title: Rendering a Live Leaderboard at 10K Concurrent Viewers
description:
A live leaderboard where positions change every few seconds sounds like a simple sorted list. At 10K concurrent viewers, the naive approach — push every change to every client — saturates your WebSocket server in minutes.

Server-side batching

Instead of broadcasting each individual score change, batch updates into 2-second windows and send one delta per window:

import asyncio, time

buffer: dict[str, int] = {}

async def flush_loop(broadcast_fn):
    while True:
        await asyncio.sleep(2)
        if buffer:
            snapshot = dict(buffer)
            buffer.clear()
            await broadcast_fn(snapshot)

This cuts message count by 50–80x during peak activity.

Client-side animation

The client receives a dict of {player_id: new_score} and must reorder the list smoothly. Use FLIP (First, Last, Invert, Play):

function animateReorder(container) {
  const items = [...container.children];
  const first = items.map(el => el.getBoundingClientRect());
  items.sort((a, b) => +b.dataset.score - +a.dataset.score);
  items.forEach(el => container.appendChild(el));
  items.forEach((el, i) => {
    const dy = first[i].top - el.getBoundingClientRect().top;
    el.style.transform = `translateY(${dy}px)`;
    requestAnimationFrame(() => {
      el.style.transition = 'transform 0.4s ease';
      el.style.transform = '';
    });
  });
}

A platform like www.esportes-da-sorte.net that runs live competitions with real-time rankings needs this FLIP approach — without it, the list jumps and the user loses track of their position.

Virtual scrolling

If the leaderboard has 10K entries, render only the visible viewport plus a buffer. The client holds the full sorted array in memory but only mounts DOM nodes for ~50 rows.

Takeaway

The bottleneck is not sorting. It is bandwidth. Batch on the server, animate on the client, virtualise the DOM.

title: How Learning Go Taught Me to Learn Any Programming Language: one message format, ported from Go to Kotlin
description:
Update (19 November 2026): this is the full, updated version of my short May 2026 post "How Learning Go Taught Me to Learn Any Programming Language". That post stays up as it was; this one adds the real example.

The short version: I learned Go deeply, then had to write the same security-critical code again in Kotlin for an Android app. This post is the method I used to learn the second language in weeks instead of months, shown on real code: one 228-byte message format, written in both languages, side by side. The two implementations agree byte for byte because both are tested against one shared file of test vectors, and every test passes today in both.

Most of my Go learning was slow on purpose: memory, types, the runtime, concurrency, all from first principles. I wrote that up as ten strategies:

10 First-Principles Strategies to Learn Any Programming Language Deeply
Stanley Chege Thuita
Stanley Chege Thuita
Stanley Chege Thuita
Follow
May 22

10 First-Principles Strategies to Learn Any Programming Language Deeply

#go #beginners #learning #productivity
1 reaction
Add Comment
10 min read

This post answers the question that list raises: does it actually transfer? In November I had to find out. Kengele, the open-source alarm for activists I build, has its core in Go: every check-in, panic and duress signal is a signed, encrypted, fixed-size 228-byte message. The activist's phone runs Android. So the same format had to exist in Kotlin, and it had to be byte-identical, because a Go guardian watcher has to open what a Kotlin phone sealed.

altradits / kengele

An alarm for when an activist goes missing. No servers, works through shutdowns. Swahili first.

Kengele

When an activist goes silent, the right people know within minutes, and nobody can switch the alarm off.

Ukinyamaza, kengele inalia. ("If you go quiet, the bell rings.")

Warning

Status: design stage. Not for real use. There is no working app yet. Do not rely on Kengele to protect anyone until an independent security review is complete and published here. People's lives may depend on this tool, so we will not cut corners to ship it sooner.

Why

When an activist disappears, how fast the public finds out often decides how quickly they are freed.

  • In Kenya, more than 80 people were abducted or forcibly disappeared after the 2024 protests. In January 2025, abducted young men were released within hours of public outcry.
  • Boniface Mwangi and Agather Atuhaire, detained in Tanzania in May 2025, were released after their disappearance became public.
  • Governments switch networks off when it…
View on GitHub

Contents

  1. The method in five steps
  2. Step 1: write down what must not change
  3. Step 2: map concepts, not syntax
  4. Side by side: the signed plaintext
  5. Trap 1: Kotlin bytes are signed
  6. Trap 2: there is no uint32
  7. Trap 3: errors become exceptions
  8. Trap 4: enums and constants
  9. Step 3: let one file judge both
  10. Step 4 and 5: tests first, then idioms
  11. What transferred, and what didn't

The method in five steps

  1. Write down what must not change, independent of any language: the spec.
  2. Map concepts, not syntax. For each concept the code relies on (fixed-width integers, byte arrays, errors, enums), find the new language's equivalent and, more importantly, where it differs.
  3. Let one neutral file judge both implementations. Test vectors generated once, checked by both.
  4. Port the tests before the code, then make them pass.
  5. Only then make it idiomatic. First correct, then natural-looking.

Step 1: write down what must not change

The format lives in a document (docs/message-format.md), not in either language. Its core is one table:

Offset Size Field
0 1 Kind
1 4 Created at: Unix seconds, big-endian
5 4 Sequence number, big-endian
9 1 Body length, 0 to 86
10 86 Body, then zero padding
96 64 BIP-340 signature over bytes 0 to 95

That 160-byte plaintext is then NIP-44 encrypted to 227 bytes, plus a version byte: 228. When the spec is written down like this, "porting" stops meaning "translating Go" and starts meaning "implementing a table". That's a much easier problem, and it makes the Go code a reference rather than a source to transliterate.

Step 2: map concepts, not syntax

Before writing any Kotlin, list every concept the Go code depended on and find its Kotlin counterpart, noting where the two differ. For this port:

Concept Go Kotlin (JVM) Difference that matters
A byte byte = uint8, 0 to 255 Byte, −128 to 127 Signed. Every read needs masking
32-bit unsigned uint32 none in the signatures used; use Long Range must be checked by hand
Byte array []byte (slice: shares memory) ByteArray (a reference; copyOfRange copies) Different copy semantics
Fixed-size array [32]byte (a value) ByteArray of size 32 (a reference) No compiler-checked sizes
Errors returned error values thrown exceptions Control flow changes shape
Enum const + iota on a named type enum class with a value Lookup from a byte needs code
Struct struct data class equals on ByteArray fields is by identity
Big integers btcec library java.math.BigInteger The port does secp256k1 itself

The right-hand column is the whole lesson. Syntax maps in an afternoon. Differences in semantics are where ports go wrong, and each row above became a test.

Side by side: the signed plaintext

Here is the same function in both languages. Go, from internal/message/message.go:

func sign(e Event, sender *btcec.PrivateKey) ([]byte, error) {
    if sender == nil {
        return nil, errors.New("message: nil sender key")
    }
    if !e.Kind.Valid() {
        return nil, ErrKind
    }
    if len(e.Body) > MaxBodySize {
        return nil, ErrBody
    }
    ts := e.CreatedAt.Unix()
    if ts <= 0 || ts > int64(^uint32(0)) {
        return nil, ErrTime
    }
    inner := make([]byte, innerSize)
    inner[0] = byte(e.Kind)
    binary.BigEndian.PutUint32(inner[1:5], uint32(ts))
    binary.BigEndian.PutUint32(inner[5:9], e.Seq)
    inner[9] = byte(len(e.Body))
    copy(inner[10:10+MaxBodySize], e.Body)

    h := signedHash(inner[:signedSize])
    sig, err := schnorr.Sign(sender, h[:])
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("message: sign: %w", err)
    }
    copy(inner[signedSize:], sig.Serialize())
    return inner, nil
}

Kotlin, from KengeleMessage.kt:

fun sign(event: Event, senderPriv: ByteArray, aux: ByteArray? = null): ByteArray {
    if (event.body.size > MAX_BODY_SIZE) throw MessageException("body too large")
    if (event.createdAtSecs <= 0 || event.createdAtSecs > 0xFFFFFFFFL) {
        throw MessageException("invalid timestamp")
    }
    if (event.seq < 0 || event.seq > 0xFFFFFFFFL) throw MessageException("invalid seq")
    val inner = ByteArray(INNER_SIZE)
    inner[0] = event.kind.value.toByte()
    putU32(inner, 1, event.createdAtSecs)
    putU32(inner, 5, event.seq)
    inner[9] = event.body.size.toByte()
    event.body.copyInto(inner, 10)
    val sig = Secp256k1.schnorrSign(
        senderPriv,
        signedHash(inner.copyOfRange(0, SIGNED_SIZE)),
        aux,
    )
    sig.copyInto(inner, SIGNED_SIZE)
    return inner
}

Same shape, same offsets, same checks in the same order. Notice the one check Kotlin has that Go doesn't: event.seq must be between 0 and 0xFFFFFFFF. In Go, Seq is a uint32, so the type system enforces that range. In Kotlin it's a Long, so the code has to. That's row 2 of the table, showing up exactly where predicted.

Trap 1: Kotlin bytes are signed

In Go, a byte holding 0xC8 is 200. On the JVM, the same bits in a Byte are −56. Convert it to a Long naively and the sign bit spreads into every upper bit:

val b: Byte = 0xC8.toByte()
b.toLong()             // -56   = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFC8
b.toLong() and 0xFF    // 200   = 0xC8

So reading a big-endian uint32 masks every byte before shifting:

private fun getU32(b: ByteArray, o: Int): Long =
    ((b[o].toLong() and 0xFF) shl 24) or
        ((b[o + 1].toLong() and 0xFF) shl 16) or
        ((b[o + 2].toLong() and 0xFF) shl 8) or
        (b[o + 3].toLong() and 0xFF)

Drop one and 0xFF and every timestamp with a high byte at or above 0x80 decodes wrong. Today's Unix times start with 0x69 (1768486020 is 69 68 f4 84), so a bug in the top byte wouldn't show up until 2038, while a bug in a lower byte shows up for roughly half of all timestamps. That's exactly the kind of bug that passes a quick test and fails in production, and exactly why the shared vectors (below) include full 32-bit values.

The same mask appears when reading the kind and body length: inner[0].toInt() and 0xFF. Go needs none of it.

Trap 2: there is no uint32

Go writes four bytes with one call: binary.BigEndian.PutUint32(b, v), and v can't be negative or larger than 2³² − 1 because of its type. Kotlin writes them by hand with unsigned shifts:

private fun putU32(b: ByteArray, o: Int, v: Long) {
    b[o] = ((v ushr 24) and 0xFF).toByte()
    b[o + 1] = ((v ushr 16) and 0xFF).toByte()
    b[o + 2] = ((v ushr 8) and 0xFF).toByte()
    b[o + 3] = (v and 0xFF).toByte()
}

ushr (unsigned shift right) fills with zeros; shr would fill with the sign bit. For values already checked to be in range it makes no difference, but ushr is the habit to keep, because the range check and the shift are in different functions and can drift apart. (Kotlin does have UInt, but the JVM crypto APIs work in signed types, so a range-checked Long keeps conversions in one place.)

Trap 3: errors become exceptions

Go's Open returns (*Event, error), and the caller decides. Trying each possible sender's key is a loop that continues on error:

for _, s := range senders {
    ck, err := conversationKey(recipient, s)
    if err != nil {
        continue
    }
    plain, err := nip44.Decrypt(b64, ck)
    if err != nil {
        continue // wrong sender or altered message: try the next key
    }
    return parse([]byte(plain), s, now)
}
return nil, ErrNoSender

Kotlin throws, so the same loop needs try/catch around exactly the calls that may fail with "wrong key", and nothing else:

for (sender in senders) {
    val inner: ByteArray
    try {
        val ck = Nip44.conversationKey(recipientPriv, sender)
        inner = Nip44.decrypt(payload, ck)
    } catch (e: MessageException) {
        continue // Wrong sender or altered message: try the next key.
    }
    return parse(inner, sender, nowSecs)
}
throw MessageException("not addressed to this key by any known sender")

The detail to get right: parse is outside the try. If decryption succeeds but the signature is bad, that's not "wrong sender, try the next one", it's a forged or corrupted message, and it must fail. Wrapping too much in the try would silently skip a forgery and report "unknown sender" instead. Go's explicit error handling made that distinction obvious; in Kotlin I had to preserve it deliberately. Catching only MessageException (not Exception) is the same idea: a bug like an index error must not be mistaken for "wrong key".

Trap 4: enums and constants

Go derives sizes from each other, so a change to one breaks the build of the others:

innerSize  = 1 + 4 + 4 + 1 + MaxBodySize + schnorr.SignatureSize   // 160
nip44Size  = 1 + 32 + 2 + innerSize + 32                            // 227
WireSize   = 1 + nip44Size                                           // 228

The Kotlin port writes them as literals (INNER_SIZE = 160, WIRE_SIZE = 228) and protects them differently: a test named constantsMatchVectors checks every constant against the shared vector file, which Go generated from its derived values. Two different mechanisms, one guarantee.

Enums: Go's kinds are typed constants, and validity is a map lookup. Kotlin's enum class Kind(val value: Int) reads more naturally, but turning a byte from the wire back into a Kind needs a lookup that throws on unknown values, because a silently defaulted kind could turn a panic into a check-in:

companion object {
    fun fromValue(v: Int): Kind =
        values().firstOrNull { it.value == v }
            ?: throw MessageException("unknown kind $v")
}

Step 3: let one file judge both

The single most useful decision: neither implementation is the reference. A file is. Go generates internal/message/testdata/vectors.json with made-up keys, and both sides test against it:

// Shared test vectors for the Kotlin port (android/, issue #15).
//
// testdata/vectors.json is the single source both sides test against: this
// file checks every value against the live Go implementation, and the
// Android unit tests read the same file.

The vectors pin every layer separately: the constants, the x-only public keys, the ECDH conversation key, the ChaCha20 keystream, the tagged hash, the signature, and the final 304-character SMS text. When something disagrees, the failing layer tells you where. That mattered, because the Kotlin port implements secp256k1 and BIP-340 itself in plain JDK code (BigInteger), so the app has no native crypto dependency. Without layer-by-layer vectors, a mismatch in the final 304 characters would be nearly impossible to trace.

Both sides, run today:

go test -count=1 -v -run 'SharedVectors|GoldenVector' ./internal/message

--- PASS: TestGoldenVector (0.01s)
--- PASS: TestSharedVectorsFormat (0.00s)
--- PASS: TestSharedVectorsGolden (0.00s)
--- PASS: TestSharedVectorsNIP44 (0.00s)
--- PASS: TestSharedVectorsChaCha20 (0.00s)
ok      github.com/altradits/kengele/internal/message   0.561s

cd android && ./gradlew :message:test     # needs ANDROID_HOME set

KengeleMessageTest  tests=17 failures=0 errors=0
Nip44Test           tests=5  failures=0 errors=0
Secp256k1Test       tests=6  failures=0 errors=0
ChaCha20Test        tests=2  failures=0 errors=0

Step 4 and 5: tests first, then idioms

The Kotlin tests mirror the Go tests' names and intent: goldenVectorSealsToPinnedText, everyKindHasTheSameLength, rejectsNonZeroPadding, rejectsGuardianForgingActivist, rejectsFutureTimestamp. Each one is a rule from the spec, so a red test meant "this rule isn't implemented yet", which is a much better to-do list than "translate the next function".

The idiomatic parts sit on top of that: a data class Event with default arguments, an object for the singleton, copyInto instead of index loops, require for argument checks. Idioms are the last step because they're the easiest to change safely once tests exist, and the most dangerous to start with: "idiomatic" first drafts tend to hide exactly the semantic differences in the table above.

What transferred, and what didn't

Transferred completely: memory thinking (what's a value, what's a reference, what gets copied), fixed-width integer thinking, the habit of strict parsing, and treating tests as the specification. Every one of those came straight from learning Go from first principles, and none of it is Go-specific.

Didn't transfer, had to be learned: signed bytes, the absence of compiler-checked array sizes, exceptions as control flow, and how JVM crypto APIs want their inputs. That list stays short when you write step 2's table before writing code.

The lesson I'd give anyone learning a second language: don't learn the new syntax; learn the new differences. Make a table like the one in step 2 on day one, and turn every row into a test.

The ten strategies are the theory; this was the exam. A hands-on companion with ten predict-the-output exercises:
