title: GTA: Generative Tower of Agents for Scalable Holonic Scene Generation
description:
arXiv:2611.23727v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Scalable world modeling requires coordinating scene-wide goals with fine-grained objects and dynamic characters under limited time and context budgets. We introduce GTA (Generative Tower of Agents), which represents every unit at every level of an adaptive scene hierarchy as a holon, both a self-contained construction task and a composable scene unit. Parallel agents recursively plan the hierarchy top-down, generate assets, and assemble and refine them bottom-up. Uniform interfaces carry scene-wide requirements down the hierarchy, guiding local construction so that each holon fits into the larger one. GTA accelerates scalable world modeling through high-throughput parallel execution while preserving well-structured layouts and fine-grained asset details. GTA then populates the assembled environments with dynamic human characters whose appearance and motion are guided by the scene, yielding realized 4D worlds. Project page: https://zt-zeng-tao.github.io/GTA/

title: Oracle publica 655 patches e corrige falha Java4Shell
description:
Escopo da atualização de novembro

A Oracle publicou 655 patches de segurança na Atualização Crítica de Segurança (CSPU) de novembro de 2026. Desse total, 640 aparecem nas matrizes de risco dos produtos. Os demais incluem vulnerabilidades adicionais corrigidas pelos patches e CVEs de terceiros que a empresa considera não exploráveis em seus produtos.

Pouco mais de 300 patches corrigem falhas que podem ser exploradas remotamente sem autenticação. O pacote também resolve 62 vulnerabilidades críticas, incluindo seis classificadas com severidade máxima, o que torna a atualização relevante para organizações que utilizam os produtos afetados.

Produtos com mais correções

O Hyperion recebeu o maior conjunto, com 267 patches, dos quais 107 corrigem falhas remotas exploráveis sem autenticação. A atualização de Supply Chain inclui 74 correções, sendo 36 para vulnerabilidades com essa mesma condição de exploração.

Fusion Middleware e E-Business Suite receberam 71 patches cada. No Fusion Middleware, 53 tratam de falhas remotas sem autenticação; no E-Business Suite, são 19. Communications recebeu 31 correções, incluindo 21 desse tipo, enquanto Analytics teve 29, com nove vulnerabilidades remotas sem autenticação.

Java4Shell e outros produtos afetados

A atualização do Java SE corrige 11 falhas, todas exploráveis remotamente, entre elas Java4Shell, identificada como CVE-2026-114938. O problema envolve corrupção de memória e pode levar a vazamentos de memória e à execução remota de código.

Siebel CRM recebeu 19 patches, nove para falhas remotas sem autenticação; PeopleSoft teve 13, incluindo seis desse grupo. Financial Services Applications e Virtualization receberam 11 correções cada, com uma e três falhas remotas sem autenticação, respectivamente. Para MySQL, foram publicados dez patches, três voltados a falhas desse tipo.

As correções de severidade máxima incluem cinco falhas no Fusion Middleware e uma em Analytics. Também receberam patches Database Server, APEX, Autonomous Health Framework, REST Data Services, Application Testing Suite, Commerce, Construction and Engineering, Enterprise Manager e JD Edwards.

Aplicação das correções

A Oracle não mencionou exploração de nenhuma dessas vulnerabilidades em ambientes reais, mas recomenda-se que as organizações apliquem os patches o quanto antes. Falhas em produtos da empresa são alvos atrativos para atacantes.

As equipes de TI podem consultar as matrizes de risco da atualização para identificar as correções correspondentes aos produtos usados em seus ambientes. A lista abrange aplicações empresariais, middleware, bancos de dados e Java SE, por isso a revisão deve considerar os sistemas efetivamente utilizados por cada organização.

Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/oracle-libera-655-patches-de-seguranca-e-corrige-falha-java4shell/

title: mmTherm: Absolute 3D Human Pose Estimation from Low-Resolution Thermal Images and mmWave Radar
description:
arXiv:2611.23477v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Absolute 3D human pose estimation (HPE) aims to recover both a person's body pose and their global position in 3D space. Privacy-preserving millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar provides distance and direction measurement capabilities, but its sparse point clouds make HPE under-constrained. Low-resolution thermal imaging can provide complementary observations of body direction and structure. However, our evaluation shows that a strong feature-level fusion baseline loses much of its localization and HPE advantage when generalizing to unseen subjects, with radial localization becoming less accurate than a radar-only baseline. Motivated by this finding, we introduce mmTherm, a lightweight framework that explicitly incorporates the complementary geometric properties of thermal imaging and mmWave radar. It combines body structure and joint directions estimated from thermal images with range information from radar to localize the body and reconstruct its 3D pose. Experiments on OctoNet show that mmTherm reduces cross-user absolute joint error by 33% and root localization error by 38% relative to the strongest corresponding baselines, while requiring substantially fewer parameters and less computation at inference.

title: Most Powerful and Low-RAM Coder: Why We’re Slashing Memory with LuxurAI Cowork V2.0.0 (Tauri + Rust)
description:
We launched LuxurAI Cowork V1.1 on November 17 with autonomous desktop execution. Now, we are preparing V2.0.0 — re-engineered from the ground up in Tauri + Rust for ultra-low RAM consumption, sub-second native OS control, and zero compromise on perception power.

🚀 What We Built

When we shipped LuxurAI Cowork V1.1, our goal was simple: give developers an autonomous desktop coworker that sees their screen via our cloud-hosted Neo Model and executes real-world developer tasks — debugging terminal stack traces, verifying local environments, and navigating developer tools — in under 10 seconds from a single prompt.

The feedback was electric. But as builders writing code on everyday developer laptops, we noticed an undeniable problem across the AI industry:

Every modern AI companion eats RAM like a second Chrome browser.

Traditional AI desktop clients and code editors often bundle an entire Chromium instance and heavy Node.js runtimes. Even while idling in the system tray, they consume 350MB to 800MB+ of RAM.

When your machine is already balancing Docker containers, VS Code, local PostgreSQL, and dozens of browser tabs, an AI coworker should not be hogging another gigabyte of memory.

That is why we are launching LuxurAI Cowork V2.0.0 Soon: a complete architectural migration to Tauri and compiled Rust, dropping the client RAM footprint to ~35MB–50MB while retaining 100% of the perception and execution power of V1.1.

⚡ The Engineering Problem: Why AI Desktops Feel Heavy

Building desktop agents with standard Electron/Node wrappers allows fast early prototyping, but introduces three major bottlenecks in production:

  1. Chromium Process Sprawl: Bundling Chromium means multi-process overhead, GPU helper processes, and memory bloat just to render a lightweight companion HUD.
  2. Garbage Collection Micro-Stutters: Periodic JavaScript garbage collection cycles create micro-latencies during high-DPI desktop perception loops.
  3. Pure-Vision Latency: Relying only on raw visual screen-scraping and coordinate guessing can take 10–20 seconds and introduces coordinate misses.

We wanted an AI coworker that feels as lightweight and instantaneous as a native Win32 utility — booting in milliseconds and respecting system resources.

🛠️ The V2.0.0 Solution: Dual-Engine Architecture in Pure Rust

In V2.0.0, we decoupled the client architecture into two synchronized layers:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ LuxurAI Cowork V2.0 Architecture │
├──────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┤
│ Native Frontend (Tauri / OS) │ Compiled Rust Engine Core │
│ • Native Windows WebView2 │ • Windows UI Automation │
│ • Instant Floating HUD │ • Direct Accessibility Tree │
│ • Memory: ~35 MB - 50 MB │ • Zero-Allocation Loop │
└─────────────────▲────────────────┴─────────────────▲────────────────┘
│ │
└─────────────────┬────────────────┘
│ Low-Latency Stream
▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ LuxurAI Cloud GPU Cluster (Neo Model) │
│ • Real-time Multimodal Screen Perception │
│ • Spatial Reasoning & Task Planning │
│ • Within 10s Task Execution │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

1. Structural Accessibility Tree over Guesswork

Instead of blindly screenshotting the screen and guessing where buttons live, V2.0.0 uses native Windows UI Automation (UIA) hooks directly in Rust:

  • Sub-Second Element Matching (0.2s): Inspects foreground application windows, control hierarchies, terminal outputs, and input fields with zero marshalling overhead.
  • Non-Intrusive Execution: Interacts with UI controls structurally without violently hijacking or locking the user's physical mouse pointer.
  • Visual Fallback: When working with canvas-rendered apps, custom games, or non-standard interfaces, it falls back seamlessly to Neo Model vision perception.

2. Client Memory: Slashed by ~85%

By moving from Electron to Tauri (leveraging the OS's native WebView2 and compiled Rust binaries):

  • Idle Memory: Slashed from 350MB–800MB down to ~35MB–50MB.
  • Cold Startup Time: Reduced from 3–4 seconds to sub-200 milliseconds.
  • Binary Footprint: Lean, native distribution without packing redundant browser engines.

3. Preserving 100% of V1.1 Perception Power

A common question developers ask: "If you cut the client RAM so drastically, does the AI lose its capabilities?"

Not at all. The heavy cognitive reasoning and multi-modal screen perception do not run on your laptop battery. They live on our dedicated cloud GPU cluster powered by Neo Model.

The local Rust client acts purely as a high-speed, zero-latency sensory and execution bridge. You get the full intelligence of our cloud vision model with none of the local hardware drag.

📊 Side-by-Side Comparison

Feature Standard Electron AI Desktops LuxurAI Cowork V1.1 LuxurAI Cowork V2.0.0 (Upcoming)
Client Core Chromium + Node.js Native Hybrid Bridge Compiled Rust + Tauri
Idle RAM Usage 350 MB – 800 MB+ ~77 MB package ~35 MB – 50 MB RAM
Element Perception Screen-scraping / Vision only Hybrid UIA + Vision Native UI Tree (0.2s) + Neo Model
Startup Time 3.5s – 5.0s ~1.5s < 200 ms
Task Execution Variable / IDE-limited < 10s full execution < 10s full execution
Human-in-the-Loop Often opaque Fail-closed safety dial Fail-closed safety dial

🇮🇳 Transparent Economics: Built from First Principles

We are two young founders building independently from India — Achyut Srivastava (14) and Shubham Dangi (15) under NexInova.

We refuse to charge developers expensive $200/month foreign SaaS subscriptions or demand monthly retainers for software that sits idle in your system tray. LuxurAI runs on a transparent pay-as-you-go credit architecture:

  • ₹0.25 (25 paise) per credit
  • Zero monthly lock-in or recurring fees
  • World-class desktop agent capabilities accessible to students, independent builders, and production teams alike.

💬 Community Roadmap & Discussion

LuxurAI Cowork V1.1 is live, and the V2.0.0 Rust release is currently undergoing final stability testing:

  1. What is your biggest frustration with existing desktop AI agents — RAM consumption, latency, or lack of terminal autonomy?
  2. When an AI agent executes terminal commands on your system, do you prefer a floating approval pill or a keyboard hotkey confirmation?

Drop your thoughts in the comments below — we read and respond to every developer feedback!

  • 🌐 Platform & Beta Access: luxurai.in
  • 📖 Technical Architecture: luxurai.in/llms.txt
  • 📦 Python SDK on PyPI: pypi.org/project/luxur-ai/

title: Isthmus: Bridging Supervision Islands Restores Uncertainty and Stability in One-Step Flows
description:
arXiv:2611.23616v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: One-step flow maps are increasingly used as posterior samplers, where the point of sampling is the uncertainty that the samples carry. We find that the one-step sampler loses this uncertainty and becomes less stable. Compared with multi-step samples of the same network, its samples lose variance and decorrelate. Supervising the one-step jump directly makes this worse; the samples collapse further toward the conditional mean and break down when training is extended. We trace both failures to the locations where training places its pairs of start and end times. Only pairs on the diagonal of the time triangle receive targets from data, and the pair used for one-step sampling is either left unsupervised or supervised on an island, a set of pairs that the self-consistency identity does not connect to the diagonal, where the objective neither determines the one-step map nor anchors its training. We bridge the island with an isthmus, which places 5% of the training pairs along the whole edge of the triangle that joins the one-step pair to the diagonal. The error of the one-step map is then bounded by the self-consistency residual along this edge. With the network, the loss and the inference code unchanged and at no added cost, the isthmus improves one-step sampling across several flow-map objectives, in MRI reconstruction, face inpainting, and unconditional generation on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet 32x32. On brain MRI, it restores one-step calibration to 0.96 and the correlation with multi-step samples to 0.93; both vary far less across seeds, and the agreement holds when training is extended to three times its length.

title: Which Tokens, in What Order, and How Fast? A Theoretical Analysis of On-Policy Distillation Objectives
description:
arXiv:2611.23397v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model to match a teacher model based on its own generations. When using OPD, one must choose whether to apply it at the sequence or token level and which divergence to minimize. However, despite the wide adoption of OPD in practice, the formal understanding of which OPD objective is appropriate for a given setting is limited. Toward addressing this gap, we theoretically analyze how the choice of OPD objective governs which tokens are prioritized, in what order, and how efficiently. Our analysis reveals that sequence-level OPD exhibits a future agreement bias, which myopic token-level objectives avoid. This bias induces a reverse learning order, in which sequence-level OPD first matches the teacher at later token positions, while at earlier positions it can favor tokens that are improbable under the teacher, and thus often undesirable. As for the choice of divergence, we prove that it strongly influences the amenability of OPD to gradient-based optimization. In particular, while the forward KL divergence enjoys a well-behaved objective landscape, other $f$-divergences, such as reverse KL, can suffer from vanishing gradients even when the student and teacher are far apart. Across language model post-training settings, we demonstrate the implications of these theoretical findings for which OPD objective is preferable, highlighting the importance of accounting for the interplay between the student, teacher, and task at hand.

title: ACUS: An Angular Calibrated Uncertainty Score for Incomplete-View CT
description:
arXiv:2611.23752v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sparse-view and limited-arc computed tomography (CT) are commonly treated as projection completion: a network fills an unmeasured view, and the result is ranked by similarity to one ground-truth image. That score can be high even when the query angle is far from every acquired measurement, because a learned prior may invent anatomy the scan never constrained. Existing protocols therefore leave a basic question unanswered: how does predictive reliability change with distance from the acquired views? We propose the Angular Calibrated Uncertainty Score (ACUS) to answer that question. ACUS is the Winkler interval score of a nominal 90% predictive interval on held-out projections, binned by distance to the nearest acquired view. It charges interval width and adds a large miss penalty when a held-out pixel falls outside the interval, so a narrow band helps only when coverage holds. We use collapse on acquired angles as a necessary consistency check on the predictor. On chest and dental cone-beam orbits, interval width grows with the angular gap. Empirical coverage ranges from 77% to 92%, and the peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of the point estimate falls as the width rises. Nearest-neighbor, interpolation, and point completion, each given one residual scale, have zero reported far coverage and incur outside-distance penalties. ACUS exposes gap-dependent overconfidence that a point-estimate PSNR alone does not measure.

title: Stability Does Not Mirror Plasticity: A Module-Level View of Declarative and Procedural Learning in Transformers
description:
arXiv:2611.23427v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Plasticity and stability in continual learning are typically studied at the entire-model level and in a task-agnostic manner, yet prior work has reported divergent conclusions across settings. Inspired by cognitive distinctions between declarative and procedural memory, we instead study how plasticity and stability vary across transformer modules and task types. In a controlled synthetic environment with clean measurement, we show a double dissociation: query-key (QK) and value-output (VO) projections are the most plastic on procedural tasks, whereas MLPs are the most plastic on declarative memorization. Stability, however, does not simply mirror plasticity: when learning a new procedure, updating QK retains over half of the stored declarative memory, while updating MLPs retains far less and updating VO loses roughly four-fifths. Targeted module reset-and-recovery experiments explain this asymmetry: plasticity tracks which module is best suited to a task's primary computation or storage, whereas stability depends on all ways the existing capability relies on that module, including access to information stored in other modules. Experiments on a realistic model and tasks broadly echo these asymmetric dynamics. Overall, our work shows that plasticity and stability depend on different aspects of a module's functional role, offering a task-dependent, module-level perspective on continual learning.

title: MoE--LoRA Methods for Multilingual Adaptation: A Systematic Empirical Study
description:
arXiv:2611.23158v2 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Routed low-rank adapters offer a parameter-efficient means to improve the performance of large language models (LLMs) across tasks. Hence, it is assumed that they can also be used to improve the support of low-resource languages in LLMs, which currently serve English far better than the thousands of other languages spoken worldwide. However, this assumption has never been verified empirically under a shared multilingual evaluation protocol. We address exactly this gap by comparing eight low-rank adaptation (LoRA) methods on a frozen base model, using 146 training runs across 200 unique languages and more than 10,000 evaluations. Our results suggest that a reduced-scale search can identify viable configurations of LoRA methods but does not reliably predict their relative performance, as the top-ranking configuration is never best at scale. LoRA reliably improves language-model fit on translation data, consistently degrades reading comprehension, and benefits low-resource languages most. These findings suggest that LoRA methods should be regarded as targeted tools rather than general-purpose means for improving the multilingual capabilities of LLMs.

title: A physics layer that draws nothing: reading interface forces back as CSS variables
description:
Most interface physics runs one way. Something moves, and the page watches.

I build Fundamental, a relational field runtime for interfaces. Elements bend a shared field, and the field bends them back. The second half is the part I care about. The field reports what it feels as live CSS variables, so the page can style itself from the result.

Bodies

A body is any element with a data-body attribute. Its value is one or more force tokens.

<field-root render="dots"></field-root>
<h1 data-body="attract" data-strength="1.2" data-feedback>Mass</h1>
<button data-body="repel" data-range="240">Keep clear</button>

<field-root> goes on the page once. It finds every [data-body] element and wires it into the field. With data-feedback, an element gets the write-back. Its --d and --field-density variables change as the field moves around it. Those are ordinary CSS variables. Any rule can read them.

Nothing on screen by default

A field created without a render mode draws nothing. It still runs the simulation and reports through --field-* variables, events, queries and snapshots. The particle canvas is opt-in with render: 'dots', as above. The demo looks like particles, so this surprises people. The particles are one render surface, not the system.

Trying it needs no build step.

import { createField } from 'https://esm.sh/@fundamental-engine/vanilla';
createField(document.querySelector('canvas'), { render: 'dots' });

Turn the motion off

Nothing-on-screen-by-default has a twin on the time axis. The field is a measurement, not an animation. --field-* is a value; motion is one way to show the page moving toward it.

So prefers-reduced-motion isn't a fallback I hand-wrote. The integrator stops at dt = 0, the simulation holds one frame, and the variables keep the exact value they already had. In CSS you drop your transition and keep reading the number.

.headline { transform: translateY(calc(var(--field-density, 0) * -2px)); transition: transform 140ms; }
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { .headline { transition: none; transform: none; } }

Motion is spent; meaning is not. It only holds, though, where the ranking also lives somewhere static — an authored weight, DOM order — so I check that per surface rather than claim it everywhere.

Where it stands

It is a 0.x preview at 0.12.0, MIT licensed, with seven packages on npm. It ships in production apps and has no third-party adopters yet.

The core API is frozen and grows additively. The query, snapshot, diff and replay APIs are experimental. Swift and Kotlin ports exist at preview status, built from source only.

I haven't shown that this model fits every interface. It fits the ones where an element should behave according to what is near it.

Elements bend the field. The test is what a page does when the field bends back.

Related: https://fundamentalengine.com/

title: Simpler Tiny Recursive Models
description:
arXiv:2611.23677v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Small models that execute deep looped computational graphs have shown great experimental results on puzzle-like problems like Sudoku, finding shortest paths through mazes, etc. The most well-known one is TRM (tiny recursive model), a simplification of HRM (hierarchical reasoning model). However, the underlying recursion is complicated and involves a high-level and a low-level state, a nested loop recursion, and the network calls with different input and output signatures depending on where we are in the loops. These mechanisms are needed to avoid memorization and overfitting. We propose STRM, a simplified design with a single state and a uniform update. STRM does not sacrifice generalization, improves training speed and final performance. Our key architectural choices that allow our simpler recursion to work are exponential moving updates on the states with varying rates that are jittered during training and readout of the solution on slow-updating channels only. We test STRM on Sudoku-Extreme, PPBench and Maze-Hard with the same data, parameters and compute as TRM: we improve over TRM by $3.8$ points on Sudoku-Extreme and $8.4$ points on PPBench and match it on Maze-Hard. On ARC-AGI-1 and ARC-AGI-2, STRM improves over the published TRM results by $5.4$ and $0.5$ points. We will release our code upon acceptance of the paper.

title: Storing the Gemma 4 K=V Cache Once: Exact Global-KV Memory Savings in a Paged Serving Engine with Unchanged Attention Kernels
description:
arXiv:2611.23035v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: In the global attention layers of Gemma 4 31B, the value is the normalized key projection, and the key is the value scaled by a fixed weight, with rotary position encoding on one quarter of its dimensions. The Gemma 4 report states that this design reduces the global KV cache by up to 37.5%, but the open serving engines that we checked still store a full key and a full value: 1,024 values per KV head and token. We store one 640-value row instead, exact in real arithmetic, and an unchanged paged attention kernel reads it through two overlapping strided views as its key cache and its value cache. In a vLLM prototype with the 16-bit 31B model, the outputs are bit-identical to an emulation of the same arithmetic on the stock cache, 2 of 432 final answers differ from the stock engine (within its run-to-run noise), and the steady decode KV memory per request falls by a factor of 1.34 to 1.40 at 32K to 64K tokens. On a prefill/decode pair of two A100 GPUs with NIXL transfer and CPU offload, a decode engine with a full 15 GiB pool ran 1.38 times the stock decode tokens per step for 16K-token prompts (repeated to 0.06%) and 1.24 times for 8K-token prompts; a model of the vLLM block pool predicted both ratios to within 1% (the engine was 0.7% to 0.9% higher) and matched the change between them. The eager decode throughput rose by 1.30 and 1.11 times, and on this path the compact engine gave the same output tokens as the emulation for 8 prompts at batch 1. The run-time prototype makes an eager step 4% to 9% slower at equal batch, and the method does not yet stack with an 8-bit KV cache at the default scale.

title: Right Diagnosis, Unsafe Route: Auditing Clinical AI Decision Trajectories and Corrective Oversight for Validity and Potential Harm
description:
arXiv:2611.22612v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A clinical AI system can reach a correct final diagnosis through intermediate decisions that could have harmed the patient, and can repair an error while introducing new risks. Most evaluations score final diagnoses; even stepwise benchmarks, which release a case's evidence over time, score whether systems reach the right diagnosis or gather the right information, not whether the decisions a patient passes through are safe. We make patient safety the target of stepwise evaluation. A trajectory audit replays real admissions checkpoint by checkpoint, lets each system decide with only the evidence released so far, and rates every test, treatment and disposition for its potential harm to the patient and, separately, for clinical validity, against the documented final diagnosis and physician-written disease rubrics yet on the evidence available when the decision was made. An LLM judge scores every decision, and a physician reference standard (triple annotation and senior adjudication of a stratified sample) calibrates the rates. An oversight audit branches each trajectory at its first actionable error and measures, on the same branches, whether corrective feedback repairs the error and whether it introduces new harm. Across 300 cases from a hospital cardiology cohort, MIMIC-IV and the public ASCENT benchmark, with up to seven AI systems per source, 55.2% of hospital trajectories reaching an acceptable final diagnosis passed through a decision with moderate or severe potential harm and 24.8% through a clinically unacceptable one; the harm rates were 76.2% on MIMIC-IV and 39.6% on ASCENT. Structured corrections resolved 73.6% of first errors versus 24.8% after bare rejection, yet new potentially unsafe decisions followed 30.2% of corrections versus 19.7% of rejections. A correct final diagnosis does not certify a safe trajectory, and a successful correction does not certify a safe recovery.

title: Amazon Route 53 now supports health checks for private endpoints
description:
Amazon Route 53 now offers Private Endpoint Health Checks, enabling business-critical workloads that never touch the public internet, such as internal APIs, databases, and self-hosted nodes behind internal load balancers or in private subnets, to use native health monitoring and automatic DNS failover. Customers can health-check any reachable private target by IP address, domain, or port over HTTP, HTTPS, or TCP. Customers can associate these health checks with Route 53 DNS records across routing policies in private hosted zones, so Route 53 routes traffic only to healthy endpoints and manages failover automatically. 

Previously, teams built custom control loops using Amazon CloudWatch alarms, AWS Lambda functions, and the Route 53 API to achieve DNS failover for private resources. With this approach, failover took several minutes and added operational burden. Detection and DNS failover with Private Endpoint Health Checks are designed to complete in seconds rather than minutes, the service is fully managed, and nothing is exposed to the public internet. 

The feature supports on-premises and hybrid endpoints reachable from the VPC over AWS Direct Connect or AWS Site-to-Site VPN, enabling resilience patterns such as active-passive disaster recovery and cross-Region DR over AWS Transit Gateway or AWS Cloud WAN. Amazon Route 53 Private Endpoint Health Checks is available today in all AWS commercial regions. To learn more, visit the Amazon Route 53 Developer Guide and the Route 53 pricing page.

title: Best MCP Servers on GitHub for Daily Work: Files, Git, Browser, Databases
description:
The most useful MCP servers for everyday work are the reference servers from the Model Context Protocol project (files, Git, web fetch), GitHub's own server for repositories and issues, Microsoft's Playwright server for browser tasks, and Google's MCP Toolbox for databases. All four are open source on GitHub, and each installs with a single command or a short JSON block. This guide lists what each one does, how to install it, its license, and how to connect it to Claude Code without handing over more access than you need.

Who this is for and what you will have at the end

This is for developers, IT admins and technical founders who already use an AI assistant such as Claude Code and want it to touch real tools: a project folder, a Git history, a browser or a database. By the end you will have a short list of vetted repos, working install commands, a project-level .mcp.json you can share with a team, and a checklist for deciding whether to trust any other MCP server you come across.

If you want to build your own server instead of installing one, see Build Your First MCP Server in Python. If you are looking for Claude Skills rather than MCP servers, see Best Claude Skills GitHub Repos.

How MCP servers connect to your AI app

MCP is a protocol that lets an AI app call tools exposed by a separate program. There are two common ways a server is reached:

Transport How it runs Typical use
stdio The AI app starts the server as a local process and talks to it over standard input and output Local tools: files, Git, a local browser
HTTP (remote) The AI app connects to a URL Hosted servers, such as GitHub's

The Model Context Protocol README notes that servers default to stdio, so running one directly in a terminal looks like it hangs: it is waiting for a client to talk to it. That is normal.

Prerequisites

  • Claude Code installed. The commands below use its claude mcp command; the JSON blocks also work in most other MCP clients.
  • Node.js, for servers started with npx.
  • uv, for servers started with uvx (the Git and Fetch reference servers use it).
  • Docker, only if you choose the Docker route for the GitHub server.

How to add a server in Claude Code

Claude Code's MCP documentation gives two forms. Remote HTTP servers:

claude mcp add --transport http <name> <url>

Local stdio servers:

claude mcp add [options] <name> -- <command> [args...]

The -- matters for stdio servers. Per the documentation, it separates Claude's own options (--transport, --env, --scope) from the command that runs the server, and everything after it is passed to the server untouched.

Servers are stored by scope:

Scope Loads in Shared with team Stored in
Local (default) Current project only No ~/.claude.json
Project Current project only Yes, via version control .mcp.json in the project root
User All your projects No ~/.claude.json

Choose with --scope local, --scope project or --scope user. To see what is configured, run claude mcp list. Inside Claude Code, /mcp shows server status and handles sign-in for remote servers that use OAuth.

1. modelcontextprotocol/servers: the reference servers

What it does. This is the project's collection of reference servers. According to its README (checked 2026-11-19), the maintained ones are Everything (a test server), Fetch (web content fetching and conversion), Filesystem (file operations with configurable access controls), Git (read, search and manipulate repositories), Memory (a knowledge-graph memory), Sequential Thinking and Time.

Who it is for. Anyone starting with MCP. These are the most common first servers and the ones other guides assume you have seen.

Install commands from the README:

# Filesystem: only the folder you list is accessible
npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem /path/to/allowed/files

# Git
uvx mcp-server-git

# Fetch
uvx mcp-server-fetch

# Memory
npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-memory

Connecting the Filesystem server to Claude Code, limited to one folder:

claude mcp add --transport stdio files -- npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem /home/you/projects/contoso-site

The folder argument is the access control. Give it the one project folder, not your home directory.

Windows note. The README says to wrap npx commands with cmd /c in client configs.

License. The README states Apache License 2.0 for new contributions, with existing code remaining under MIT. GitHub's license field for the repository reads NOASSERTION, because of that mix.

Repo facts (GitHub API, 2026-11-19): about 92,091 stars, last push 2026-11-18, not archived.

What moved out of this repo

Many servers people remember from older tutorials are no longer here. The README lists these as archived and moved to the servers-archived repository: AWS KB Retrieval, Brave Search, EverArt, GitHub, GitLab, Google Drive, Google Maps, PostgreSQL, Puppeteer, Redis, Sentry, Slack and SQLite. If a tutorial tells you to run @modelcontextprotocol/server-github or the PostgreSQL server, use the maintained replacements below instead. The README says Brave Search is replaced by the official @brave/brave-search-mcp-server and that Slack is now maintained by Zencoder.

2. github/github-mcp-server: repositories, issues and pull requests

What it does. GitHub's official MCP server lets an assistant work with repositories, issues and pull requests. Its default toolsets, per the README, are context, repos, issues, pull_requests and users.

Who it is for. Developers who want to ask an assistant to summarize an issue, review a pull request or search a repo without leaving the terminal.

Install options from the README:

  • Remote server hosted by GitHub, URL https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/, with "type": "http" in your host config. Authentication can be OAuth or a personal access token.
  • Docker, local: 
docker run -i --rm \
  -e GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN=<your-token> \
  ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server
  • A local binary built with go build -o github-mcp-server ./cmd/github-mcp-server, run as github-mcp-server stdio with the token set in the environment.

For Claude Code, the remote route follows the HTTP pattern above:

claude mcp add --transport http github https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/

Then run /mcp inside Claude Code to complete authentication. This command combines GitHub's URL with Claude Code's documented HTTP syntax; the exact authentication prompts depend on your account and Claude Code version, so check /mcp for status.

Limit what it can do. The README describes two controls. --toolsets repos,issues,pull_requests (or the GITHUB_TOOLSETS environment variable, which takes precedence) exposes only the toolsets you name. --read-only skips all write tools, and the README says it takes priority even over tools requested explicitly with --tools. For a first trial, enable read-only.

Token advice from the README. Minimum suggested scopes are repo, read:packages (for Docker image access) and read:org (for team access). It also recommends separate tokens per project, periodic rotation, and keeping tokens out of version control.

License. MIT. Repo facts (2026-11-19): about 34,576 stars, last push 2026-11-18, not archived.

3. microsoft/playwright-mcp: a real browser for the assistant

What it does. Playwright MCP lets an assistant drive a browser: open pages, read what is on them and interact. It is useful for checking a staging site, reproducing a front-end bug or filling a form during testing.

Who it is for. Developers and QA engineers testing web apps.

Install, from the README:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "playwright": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": [
        "@playwright/mcp@latest"
      ]
    }
  }
}

For Claude Code the README gives:

claude mcp add playwright npx @playwright/mcp@latest

Security. The README says plainly that "Playwright MCP is not a security boundary." A browser that can open arbitrary pages can read content from those pages, and Claude Code's documentation warns that servers that fetch external content can expose you to prompt injection. Point it at sites you control, avoid logged-in sessions for sensitive systems, and do not combine it with a server that can write to production.

License. Apache-2.0. Repo facts (2026-11-19): about 39,868 stars, last push 2026-11-18, not archived.

4. googleapis/mcp-toolbox: databases

What it does. MCP Toolbox for Databases is an open source MCP server for databases. Per its README it offers prebuilt generic tools such as list_tables and execute_sql, and a framework for custom tools defined in a tools.yaml file. Listed supported databases include Google Cloud options (AlloyDB, BigQuery, Cloud SQL, Spanner, Firestore) and others such as PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle, MongoDB, Redis, Elasticsearch, CockroachDB, ClickHouse, Couchbase, Neo4j, Snowflake and Trino.

Who it is for. Analysts and developers who want an assistant to explore a schema and draft queries.

Install, from the README:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "toolbox-postgres": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": [
        "-y",
        "@toolbox-sdk/server",
        "--prebuilt=postgres",
        "--stdio"
      ]
    }
  }
}

Set the database connection environment variables described in the project's Prebuilt Tools Reference. For custom tools, the README shows npx @toolbox-sdk/server --config tools.yaml.

Rename. The repository was formerly googleapis/genai-toolbox (originally "Gen AI Toolbox for Databases") and is now googleapis/mcp-toolbox. Older tutorials and bookmarks may use the previous name. Update a local clone with git remote set-url origin https://github.com/googleapis/mcp-toolbox.git.

Safety. execute_sql can run whatever SQL the database user is allowed to run. Connect with a read-only database account, ideally against a replica or a copy, never a production primary with a write-capable user.

License. Apache-2.0. Repo facts (2026-11-19): about 16,905 stars, last push 2026-11-19, not archived.

Share a setup with your team

To give a whole project the same servers, add them with project scope so they are written to .mcp.json:

claude mcp add --transport http github --scope project https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/

The resulting file uses the format from Claude Code's documentation:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "shared-server": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://example.com/mcp"
    }
  }
}

.mcp.json supports ${VAR} and ${VAR:-default} expansion in command, args, env, url and headers, so tokens can stay out of the committed file. Claude Code prompts for approval in interactive sessions before using project-scoped servers from .mcp.json.

Verify the setup

Run:

claude mcp list

Claude Code's documentation says the list shows health statuses such as Connected, Needs authentication and Failed to connect. Inside a session, /mcp shows the same status and handles OAuth sign-in. Then ask the assistant for something harmless and observable, such as listing the files in the allowed folder or listing open issues in a public repo.

Troubleshooting

Symptom Likely cause Fix
Server runs in a terminal but nothing happens stdio servers wait for a client Run it through your MCP client instead
Status shows Needs authentication Remote server needs OAuth Run /mcp and sign in
Status shows Failed to connect Missing Node.js or uv, or a typo in the command Run the command by hand to see the error
npx fails on Windows Client cannot launch npx directly Wrap with cmd /c, as the README advises
CLI treats your server name as an environment variable --env swallowed the name Put another option, such as --transport stdio, between --env and the name
Old tutorial's server package not found Server was archived Use the maintained replacements above

Before you trust any other MCP server

  • Open its repository and check the license, the last commit date and whether it is archived.
  • Read what tools it exposes. A server that can write, delete or send is a larger risk than one that reads.
  • Prefer the vendor's own server (GitHub, Microsoft, Google) over a lookalike with a similar name.
  • Start with the narrowest scope and read-only credentials.
  • Remember that content fetched by a server can contain instructions aimed at the model.

Summary checklist

  • Start with Filesystem limited to one folder, plus Git.
  • Add GitHub's server in read-only mode before enabling writes.
  • Use Playwright MCP on sites you control only.
  • Use MCP Toolbox with a read-only database account.
  • Verify with claude mcp list and /mcp after each addition.

What we checked

  • Opened the README of modelcontextprotocol/servers on github.com on 2026-11-19 and copied the maintained-server list, the install commands and the archived-server list from it.
  • Queried the GitHub API for modelcontextprotocol/servers, github/github-mcp-server, microsoft/playwright-mcp and googleapis/mcp-toolbox on 2026-11-19: stars, last push date, license field and archived flag are as stated above. Star counts change daily.
  • Cross-checked license wording: the GitHub API reports NOASSERTION for modelcontextprotocol/servers, while its README states Apache-2.0 for new contributions and MIT for existing code.
  • Confirmed the repository rename from genai-toolbox to mcp-toolbox: the GitHub API returned the full name googleapis/mcp-toolbox when queried by the old name, and the README carries a rename notice.
  • Read Claude Code's MCP documentation (code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp) on 2026-11-19 for the claude mcp add syntax, scopes, .mcp.json format and the security warning. The page redirected from docs.claude.com.
  • Not tested hands-on: we did not run any of these servers or connect them to a live Claude Code session; the one command that combines GitHub's URL with Claude Code's HTTP syntax is assembled from the two documents, not run. The first 100,000 characters of the long Claude Code and GitHub README pages were read; the remainder was not.

Last tested: 2026-11-19

References

  • https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers
  • https://github.com/github/github-mcp-server
  • https://github.com/microsoft/playwright-mcp
  • https://github.com/googleapis/mcp-toolbox
  • https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp

This guide was researched and drafted with AI assistance and checked against the vendor documentation listed in its References. Read the maintained version and related guides on EpiFive.

title: Building a PDF Editor in the Browser with pdf.js and pdf-lib: 7 Lessons
description:
I recently built a PDF editor that runs entirely in the browser: you open a PDF, add text, shapes, highlights and images, and download the result. No server touches the file. Along the way I hit a handful of problems that cost me time, so here they are with the fixes.

Disclosure: I run Signplify, and the editor is one of its free tools. The code snippets below are simplified from what I actually shipped.

The architecture in one paragraph

  • pdf.js renders each page to a canvas for display.
  • A transparent overlay on top of the canvas holds the annotations (text, shapes, images). Their coordinates are stored in PDF points, not screen pixels.
  • pdf-lib loads the original bytes, draws the annotations onto the real pages and saves a new file.

Keeping the overlay in points means zooming never changes the data, only how it is drawn.

Lesson 1: PDF coordinates start at the bottom-left, and the page box may not start at zero

Browsers measure from the top-left. PDFs measure from the bottom-left. If you forget the flip, everything lands upside down. A second trap is that a page’s visible area is its crop box, which can have a non-zero origin.

const cb = page.getCropBox();          // pdf-lib
const X = x => cb.x + x;
const Y = y => cb.y + cb.height - y;   // flip the y axis

// a rectangle that the user drew with its top-left at (a.x, a.y)
page.drawRectangle({
  x: X(a.x),
  y: Y(a.y + a.h),                     // pdf-lib draws from the bottom-left corner
  width: a.w,
  height: a.h,
});

I store everything with a top-left origin in the overlay and convert only when exporting.

Lesson 2: render sharp on retina screens without breaking your coordinates

If you render the canvas at CSS size it looks blurry on high-DPI screens. Render at zoom * devicePixelRatio, then size it back with CSS. For the overlay, use an SVG whose viewBox is the page size in points.

const v1 = page.getViewport({ scale: 1 });
const dpr = window.devicePixelRatio || 1;
const v = page.getViewport({ scale: zoom * dpr });

canvas.width = Math.floor(v.width);
canvas.height = Math.floor(v.height);
canvas.style.width = v1.width * zoom + 'px';

svg.setAttribute('viewBox', `0 0 ${v1.width} ${v1.height}`);

The SVG scales automatically, so a shape at (100, 100) in points stays at (100, 100) whatever the zoom.

Lesson 3: text baselines are not where you think

In the browser, a text box is positioned by its top edge. In a PDF, drawText positions the baseline. If you place the PDF text at the same y as the box, it ends up too high or too low.

With CSS line-height: 1.2 and an Arial-like font (ascent about 0.905, descent about 0.212), the first baseline sits at roughly 0.9465 times the font size below the top of the box:

const baseline = a.y + a.size * 0.9465 + lineIndex * a.size * 1.2;
page.drawText(line, { x: X(a.x), y: Y(baseline), size: a.size, font });

I checked this by exporting the PDF and rendering it with pdftoppm, then comparing it with what the editor showed.

Lesson 4: a full re-render can destroy the element the user is typing in

My first version rebuilt the overlay DOM every time something changed. Clicking with the Text tool created a text box and focused it, but then the same click event bubbled to a page-level “click on empty space deselects” handler. That handler called the render function, which replaced the focused element, so the box lost focus and the empty annotation was deleted.

The fix was small once I saw it: ignore events whose target is the capture layer.

page.addEventListener('pointerdown', e => {
  if (tool === 'select' && e.target.id !== 'cap' && !e.target.closest('.ann, .txt')) {
    select(null);
  }
});

The general lesson is that re-rendering and focus do not mix. Either update elements in place while editing, or make sure nothing triggers a re-render between creating an editable element and focusing it.

Lesson 5: undo and redo with plain JSON snapshots

For a small editor, you do not need a command pattern. Keep the annotations in one array, and push a JSON snapshot before every change.

function snap() {
  undoStack.push(JSON.stringify(anns));
  redoStack = [];
}
function undo() {
  if (!undoStack.length) return;
  redoStack.push(JSON.stringify(anns));
  anns = JSON.parse(undoStack.pop());
}

One caveat: store images in a separate map and reference them by key, otherwise every snapshot contains the full image data.

Lesson 6: standard fonts only cover WinAnsi

StandardFonts.Helvetica in pdf-lib cannot encode characters outside WinAnsi. Passing something like an Arabic letter or an emoji to drawText throws an error. I sanitize the text before exporting: map curly quotes and dashes to plain equivalents, replace anything else unsupported with a question mark, and tell the user how many characters were replaced. To support other scripts you need to embed a font that contains those glyphs.

Lesson 7: rotated pages need their own handling

pdf.js applies a page’s /Rotate value when it renders, but your pdf-lib coordinates assume an unrotated page. Edits then land in the wrong place. I detect page.rotate and show a warning, and I suggest rotating the file to zero first. Doing the full transform is possible, but I decided it was not worth the complexity for a first version.

Testing without clicking around

Two things made testing painless. First, a headless Chromium script (Puppeteer) that opens the editor, uploads a sample PDF, draws shapes with simulated mouse events, exports, and checks the annotation data. Second, rendering the exported PDF with pdftoppm and looking at it, which caught the baseline and coordinate bugs immediately.

Checking that nothing is uploaded

Because the whole point was privacy, you can verify it yourself. Open DevTools, go to the Network tab, and edit a PDF. If no request carries the file, it stayed on the device.

What it cannot do

  • It adds content on top of a PDF. It does not rewrite the original text, which would require parsing and re-laying out the content streams.
  • A white box hides text visually but does not remove it. For sensitive data you need real redaction.
  • Added text uses a standard font, so it will not always match the original typography.

If you want to try it, the editor is at signplify.com/tools/pdf-editor, and there are related tools for annotating, filling and signing and redacting PDFs. I would be glad to hear which edge cases break it for you, especially odd PDFs.

title: COTTI: Contrastive Training and Time-Aware Inference for Robust Industrial Recommendation under Promotional Drift
description:
arXiv:2611.22597v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Promotional events shift traffic composition, purchase behavior, and the scale of conversion probabilities on different time horizons. We present \textbf{COTTI} (\textbf{CO}ntrastive \textbf{T}raining and \textbf{T}ime-aware \textbf{I}nference), an industrial recommendation framework that separates historical representation learning from event-time score adjustment. Cross-Period Contrastive Alignment (CPC) regularizes paired histories of the same user with adaptive consistency weights. Active Re-weighting (RW) controls the influence of promotional examples through historical-interest distance. Adaptive Boundary Alignment (ABA) combines stochastic prediction variability with a temporal event kernel to adjust logits while keeping predictor parameters fixed. We analyze the weighted objective and bound ABA-induced probability and ranking changes. On Fliggy data, COTTI attains an offline AUC of 0.8127, compared with 0.8101 for TEN and 0.8123 for TEN with ABA. Cross-category analysis reveals improved discrimination alongside declines in paid-item recall for novel categories. End-to-end measurements give a p99 latency of 38.9\,ms and throughput of 14,700 requests/s; enabling ABA adds 2.2\,ms to p99. A ten-day online experiment against the serving HDR model yields relative gains of 3.14\% in conversion rate and 2.68\% in revenue per mille. Together, these results characterize the trade-off between aggregate prediction, novel-category discovery, and serving cost in promotional recommendation.

title: Voice Typing on Windows
description:
Voice typing is when you speak and the text appears on screen by itself. On Windows you can write emails, notes and messages this way without pressing keys. Below is how to turn on voice typing on Windows — and what to do if you want something simpler.

Built-in Windows voice typing (Win + H)

Windows 10 and 11 have built-in voice typing. Put the cursor in any text field and press Win + H — a small microphone panel appears. Speak, and the words type themselves.

  • Open a document, an email or any input field.

  • Press Win + H.

  • Wait for “Listening” and start speaking.

  • To stop, click the microphone or say “Stop dictating”.

It is free. The downsides: it needs the internet, you sometimes have to dictate punctuation as words (“comma”, “period”), and the panel does not save the text — you copy it by hand.

If the built-in tool is not enough

Sometimes you just want a window with a Record button so you can speak your text and save it to a file right away. For that there is a separate program, VoiceNote: press “Record” and speak — the app types your speech as text for you. You can copy or save the finished text, and everything runs on your own computer.

More about the VoiceNote program

How to speak so you fix less

  • Speak calmly and clearly, without rushing.

  • Use short phrases and make pauses.

  • Remove background noise — close the window, turn off music.

  • Check that the right microphone is selected in the system.

FAQ

Why does Win + H not work?**Check that the microphone is on and selected in sound settings, and that the system is up to date. On older Windows builds the feature may have a different name.

Can I dictate without the internet?****The built-in tool usually needs the internet. If you want something that runs on the computer itself, a separate program is a better fit.

Which language does it work in?**
Russian and other languages — the language is chosen in the settings.

In short

  • The quick, free way is the built-in Windows voice typing (Win + H).

  • In it, punctuation is often dictated as words.

  • If you want a window with a Record button and saving — VoiceNote.

title: Beyond Attention Matrices: Exploring ASK LATTICE
description:
By the webXOS Team | github.com/webxos |
November 20, 2026

"An alternative to attention matrices."

For the past decade, the AI landscape has been entirely dominated by the Transformer architecture and its reliance on massive attention matrices. But as we push into late 2026, a new paradigm is emerging from the independent developer scene. Enter ASK LATTICE · QFM (Quantum Frequency Modulation)—a single-file cognitive lattice that promises to rethink how we process, recall, and generate information.

In this post, we’re diving deep into the newly released Build 2.4.0 of ASK LATTICE, exploring its unique pipeline, its OSINT capabilities, and why it might just be the cognitive tool we’ve been waiting for.

Try it for free at https://agentowl.netlify.app/asklattice or Download the Raw at: https://huggingface.co/webxos/ask-lattice-v1

What is ASK LATTICE · QFM?

At its core, ASK LATTICE is a single-file cognitive lattice. Unlike traditional LLM interfaces that simply pass text through a massive neural net, QFM treats information processing as a dynamic, multi-stage field.

The architecture is defined by a fascinating, sequential pipeline:
dict → osint fan → engrams → llm stages → live fieldNETIDBAUDIO

Instead of brute-forcing context windows, QFM modulates "frequencies" of thought. It starts with dictionary enrichment, fans out to gather real-world OSINT (Open Source Intelligence) data, crystallizes the concepts into "engrams," and finally feeds them through staged LLM processing to generate a live, multi-modal field output.

The Interface: A Cognitive Control Deck

Firing up the ASK LATTICE HTML model feels less like using a chatbot and more like booting up a cyberpunk telemetry deck. The interface is divided into highly functional, real-time monitoring sections:

1. The Command Controls

The top-level controls give the user granular power over the cognitive load:

  • RUN / CANCEL: Execute or halt the lattice sequence.
  • DEEP: Activates the deep-processing mode for comprehensive essay generation.
  • AUDIO / SIM / OFFLINE: Toggle live field audio synthesis, simulation modes, or force a completely offline, local-only run.

2. Real-Time Telemetry (The Meters)

One of the most striking features of QFM is its transparency. The METERS dashboard tracks the "pulse" of the lattice in real-time:

  • HZ & IDLE: Monitoring the frequency modulation and system readiness.
  • NODES & EDGES: Visualizing the cognitive graph as it builds (starting at 0 and expanding as the prompt is processed).
  • DICT / FAN / LLM: Progress bars for the dictionary resolution, OSINT fan-out, and final LLM staging.

3. Concurrent OSINT Fan

QFM doesn't just hallucinate; it verifies. The SOURCE STATUS panel tracks a Concurrent Fan (6), meaning the lattice simultaneously queries six different OSINT nodes. It tracks the STATE, MS (latency), and HITS for each source, ensuring the final output is grounded in ranked, real-world evidence.

The Pipeline: From Prompt to "Engram"

When you enter a prompt and hit RUN, the lattice goes through a beautiful, orchestrated sequence. The OUTPUT section streams the "composed run report," which breaks down the AI's "thought process" into distinct phases:

  1. Word Enrichment: Before the LLM even sees the prompt, the dict stage resolves and enriches the vocabulary. The WORD ENRICHMENT meter tracks exactly how many semantic nodes are unlocked.
  2. Engram Recall: The system pulls relevant "engrams" (cognitive memory units) based on the enriched dictionary and live OSINT hits.
  3. LLM Pre-Plan & Streamed Draft: The staged LLM reviews the engrams and OSINT evidence, creating a structural pre-plan before streaming the final draft.
  4. Live FieldNETIDBAUDIO: The final output is rendered not just as text, but as a multi-modal "field" state, ready for audio synthesis or further network routing.

The Power of "DEEP" Mode

If you toggle the DEEP switch, the lattice shifts from rapid-response to deep synthesis. In this mode, the system compiles all the engram recall, ranked OSINT evidence, and LLM pre-planning into a highly cohesive, 200–400 word essay. It’s perfect for researchers and analysts who need dense, verified, and deeply reasoned outputs rather than quick chat replies.

Why an "Alternative to Attention Matrices"?

The tagline of ASK LATTICE is bold: "an alternative to attention matrices."

Traditional attention mechanisms calculate the relationship of every token to every other token, resulting in massive computational overhead (the $O(N^2)$ complexity problem). By utilizing Quantum Frequency Modulation and a Lattice structure, QFM implies a shift toward sparse, resonance-based graph computing.

Instead of paying attention to everything, the lattice "tunes" into the specific frequencies of the prompt, pulling only the relevant nodes and edges into the active graph. This allows for:

  • Single-file deployment: The entire cognitive engine runs locally in a single HTML file.
  • Keyless, Session-Only LLM Endpoints: No API keys required. The LLM endpoint is optional and ephemeral, prioritizing user privacy and local-first computation.
  • Drastically reduced latency: By relying on OSINT fans and dictionary enrichment before the LLM stage, the actual generation phase is highly focused and incredibly fast.

Getting Started with QFM Build 2.4.0

The current iteration, QFM build 2.4.0, is available now. Because it is a single-file HTML model, there is no complex installation, no Docker containers, and no server setup required. You simply open the file, enter your prompt, and watch the lattice build its cognitive graph in real-time.

  • Live Demo / App: webxos.netlify.app
  • Source Code & Documentation: github.com/webxos
  • Models & Weights: huggingface.co/webxos

title: ROSMonitoring in Action: Runtime Monitoring and Enforcement for ROS 2 Actions
description:
arXiv:2611.22407v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Robotic applications often rely on long-running operations, such as navigation, manipulation, and inspection, which in ROS~2 are commonly implemented as actions. Unlike topics and services, actions involve a structured lifecycle comprising goal submission and acceptance, feedback, status updates, result retrieval, and cancellation. Existing versions of ROSMonitoring support topics and services, but do not reconstruct this lifecycle or expose action-level events to a runtime-verification oracle. In this paper, we extend ROSMonitoring with runtime monitoring and enforcement for ROS~2 actions. Actions are declared directly in the monitoring configuration and automatically instrumented through the underlying ROS~2 communication endpoints. The generated monitor reconstructs action-level events, correlates them through goal identifiers, maintains the state of active goals, and translates violations into protocol-aware enforcement operations. These include goal rejection, cancellation, message suppression, and protocol-compliant responses generated directly by the monitor when the original communication cannot be forwarded. We evaluate the implementation through controlled stress tests that vary the number of action invocations, workload size, and clientâ€“server topology. The results show approximately linear growth in monitoring cost with repeated action invocations under a fixed workload, while larger action workloads and a greater number of configured clientâ€“server pairs introduce additional overhead. These results characterise the scaling behaviour of the current implementation under the tested sequential workloads while highlighting the main performance limitations of the current synchronous implementation.

title: Can Decision Models Replace LLMs in Real-World Contact Center Classification and Judging Tasks?
description:
arXiv:2611.22949v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Contact center systems often need to make bounded decisions, such as identifying a caller's intent, retrieving the knowledge-base article that answers a query, assessing agent compliance, or judging the output of AI models used in production. Decision models return a typed answer and its probability directly, making them a promising cost-effective alternative to generative Large Language Models (LLMs) in such bounded conversational tasks. However, their effectiveness in real-world contact center applications remains unclear. In this paper, we compare nine decision models against thirteen generative LLMs in zero-shot settings across eight contact center use cases: six classification tasks and two judging tasks. Our experiments demonstrate that many decision models can match the performance of frontier LLMs on contact center classification, and API-based closed decision models achieve this at the lowest per-request cost among the API models we evaluate. We further observe that their confident predictions are more accurate, enabling selective routing in real-world production scenarios. Across classification tasks, the main weakness of most decision models is abstention: they rarely choose the no-answer option, which accounts for most of their gap to the strongest LLMs (although Gemini-Decision-1 is the notable exception in this regard). We also find that the judging quality of decision models drops sharply for smaller models, and they are also more prone to position bias. In short, our findings provide practical guidance for selecting decision models based on abstention behavior, confidence, and deployment cost, rather than overall accuracy alone.

title: How to Compress an Image to Exactly 50 KB in the Browser (No Upload, Plain JavaScript)
description:
Job portals, university admissions and government forms love strict upload limits: "Photo must be under 50 KB", "Signature must be under 20 KB". Most online compressors give you a quality slider and leave you to guess. I wanted a tool where you type 50 KB and get the best-looking JPG that fits, without uploading the photo to a server.

It turns out you can do this in about 60 lines of plain JavaScript. Here's the approach I used.

1. Draw the image onto a canvas

The browser already has a JPEG encoder: canvas.toBlob(). We just need the image on a canvas first.

function draw(img, w, h) {
  const c = document.createElement('canvas');
  c.width = w;
  c.height = h;
  const ctx = c.getContext('2d');
  ctx.fillStyle = '#fff';           // JPEG has no transparency, so fill PNG gaps with white
  ctx.fillRect(0, 0, w, h);
  ctx.imageSmoothingQuality = 'high';
  ctx.drawImage(img, 0, 0, w, h);
  return c;
}

const toBlob = (canvas, q) =>
  new Promise(resolve => canvas.toBlob(resolve, 'image/jpeg', q));

The white fill matters: without it, transparent PNG areas turn black in the JPG.

2. Binary-search the JPEG quality

File size grows with quality, so finding the highest quality that still fits is a classic binary search. Seven rounds gets you within about 1% of the best value.

async function bestQuality(canvas, limitBytes) {
  let lo = 0.05, hi = 0.95, best = null;

  const top = await toBlob(canvas, hi);
  if (top.size <= limitBytes) return { blob: top, q: hi };   // already fits

  for (let i = 0; i < 7; i++) {
    const mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
    const blob = await toBlob(canvas, mid);
    if (blob.size <= limitBytes) { best = { blob, q: mid }; lo = mid; }
    else hi = mid;
  }
  return best; // null if even low quality is too big at this size
}

3. Prefer a smaller sharp image over a big blurry one

This is the part most tools skip. If a 4000 × 3000 phone photo has to fit in 20 KB, quality 5% looks terrible. Shrinking the image a bit and keeping quality at 70% looks far better, and forms rarely need 12 megapixels anyway.

So the search runs in tiers. First it tries to keep quality at 70% or more, shrinking the image by 15% at a time. Only if that fails does it accept 50%, then 30%, and finally anything.

async function compressToSize(img, targetKb) {
  const limit = targetKb * 1024;
  const startW = img.naturalWidth, startH = img.naturalHeight;

  for (const minQ of [0.7, 0.5, 0.3, 0.05]) {
    let w = startW, h = startH;
    for (let step = 0; step < 30; step++) {
      const r = await bestQuality(draw(img, w, h), limit);
      if (r && r.q >= minQ) return { ...r, w, h };
      if (Math.max(w, h) <= (minQ > 0.05 ? 400 : 16)) break; // don't go too small at this tier
      w = Math.max(16, Math.round(w * 0.85));
      h = Math.max(16, Math.round(h * 0.85));
    }
  }
  return null; // genuinely impossible, so ask for a bigger target
}

The 400 px floor stops the good-quality tiers from turning a passport photo into a thumbnail. Only the last tier is allowed to go really small.

4. Hook it up 

input.addEventListener('change', async () => {
  const file = input.files[0];
  const img = new Image();
  img.src = URL.createObjectURL(file);
  await img.decode();

  const result = await compressToSize(img, 50);
  if (!result) return alert('Could not reach 50 KB. Try a larger target.');

  link.href = URL.createObjectURL(result.blob);
  link.download = file.name.replace(/\.[^.]+$/, '') + '-50kb.jpg';
  console.log(`${result.w}×${result.h} at ${Math.round(result.q * 100)}% → ${(result.blob.size / 1024).toFixed(1)} KB`);
});

Everything stays on the user's device, so there's no server cost and no privacy worry about ID photos.

Things I learned

  • toBlob is async and fairly fast. A full search is usually 10–40 encodes, which takes well under a second for normal photos.
  • Cancel stale runs. If the user changes the target while a search is running, keep a job counter and drop results from older runs.
  • HEIC won't decode in most browsers outside Safari, so tell iPhone users to export as JPG first.
  • Big targets don't need tiers. For 200 KB and up, the first pass almost always fits at full size.

Try it

If you want to see it working, I built this into a free tool: Compress Image to KB. Pick 20, 50, 100 or 200 KB, or type any size. It's part of DailyNexaTools, a set of free browser-based tools I'm building (PDF, image, developer tools and calculators), with no sign-up and no uploads.

Questions or improvements welcome in the comments. I'd especially like to hear if anyone has tried WebP or AVIF output for size targets.

title: geo-algos: classic geospatial algorithms from scratch in Rust
description:
Most map features rest on a handful of old algorithms. Is this point inside that zone? How far apart are these two cities? Can this GPS track be drawn with fewer points? Which ten places are nearest to me? Libraries answer all of these in one call, and that is the right way to do it in real work. It also means you can use them for years without knowing how they decide.

geo-algos is my learning project for looking inside. It implements classic geospatial algorithms from scratch in Rust, with no runtime dependencies. Each one is checked against a brute-force or independent reference with property tests. The README says it plainly, and so will I: for real work, use the geo and rstar crates. This one is for learning.

What it does

There are four modules:

Module What it does
pip Point in polygon with holes: ray casting (even-odd) and winding number (non-zero), with an explicit Boundary result
distance Haversine (sphere) and Vincenty inverse (WGS84 ellipsoid) with bearings and a convergence error
simplify Douglas-Peucker polyline simplification, iterative, with no recursion depth limit
rtree R-tree: Guttman insert with linear or quadratic split, STR bulk load, range query, best-first kNN

What I built from scratch, and what it teaches

Point in polygon: two rules, and the edge cases. Ray casting counts how many edges a horizontal ray from the point crosses: odd means inside. The trap is a ray that passes exactly through a vertex. The fix is a half-open rule, so that vertex is counted once. The winding number (Sunday's version) uses only orientation tests. The two methods agree on simple rings and differ on self-intersecting ones: the centre of a pentagram is outside under even-odd and inside under non-zero, and there is a test for it. Polygon::locate checks the rings first, so a point exactly on an edge comes back as Boundary instead of an arbitrary answer.

Distances: sphere or ellipsoid. Haversine treats the Earth as a sphere of mean radius 6,371,008.8 m. It is simple, and it is off by up to about 0.5% compared with the ellipsoid. Vincenty's inverse formula works on the WGS84 ellipsoid and iterates on the longitude difference. It gives sub-millimetre accuracy and is checked against Vincenty's own Flinders Peak to Buninyong line (54,972.271 m). It has a known weakness: nearly antipodal points can fail to converge. Here that case is returned as VincentyError::NoConvergence instead of a wrong number.

Douglas-Peucker: a guarantee you can test. The algorithm keeps the endpoints, finds the point farthest from the chord between them, and recurses while that point is beyond epsilon. The textbook version is recursive; this one uses an explicit stack, so a very long line cannot overflow the call stack. The property test checks the guarantee itself: every dropped point is within epsilon of the segment that replaced it.

The R-tree: a spatial index. Nodes are stored in an arena (a Vec) and referenced by index, which avoids fighting the borrow checker over parent and child pointers. insert follows Guttman's paper: ChooseLeaf by least enlargement, then a split on overflow (quadratic PickSeeds/PickNext, or linear seeds), then adjusting bounding boxes up to the root. bulk_load is Sort-Tile-Recursive (STR), which packs nodes full when you have all the data up front. nearest is a best-first search with a min-heap keyed by MINDIST, so entries come out in exact distance order. And validate() checks the invariants: equal leaf depth, fan-out bounds and tight bounding boxes.

How to use it

Add it to a Rust project from GitHub:

cargo add --git https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/geo-algos

Or clone the repository and run what is there:

cargo test                      # unit tests + proptest checks
cargo run --example demo        # small tour of every module
cargo bench                     # criterion benchmarks

A short example from the README shows three of the modules:

use geo_algos::{haversine, LonLat, Point, Polygon, RTree, Entry, Rect};

let d = haversine(LonLat::new(3.0588, 36.7538), LonLat::new(-0.6417, 35.6971)); // ~352 km

let sq = |a: f64, b: f64| vec![Point::new(a, a), Point::new(b, a), Point::new(b, b), Point::new(a, b)];
let donut = Polygon::new(sq(0.0, 10.0), vec![sq(4.0, 6.0)]);
assert!(donut.contains(Point::new(1.0, 1.0)));
assert!(!donut.contains(Point::new(5.0, 5.0))); // in the hole

let tree = RTree::bulk_load(vec![Entry::point(Point::new(1.0, 2.0), "a")], 16);
let near = tree.nearest(Point::new(0.0, 0.0), 1);

The first line measures a distance between two longitude and latitude pairs, about 352 km. The polygon is a square with a square hole, so a point in the hole is not contained. The last two lines build an R-tree with a node capacity of 16 and ask for the nearest entry to the origin.

How it is tested

The tests are where the "checked against a reference" promise is kept. There are 39 unit tests next to the code: edge cases, boundaries, holes, a pentagram, degenerate inputs and known distances.

Then there are 8 proptest properties in tests/properties.rs. Property tests generate random inputs and check that a rule always holds:

  • point in polygon against an analytic star-polygon reference, plus ray casting against winding number;
  • holes against a closed-form predicate;
  • the metric axioms for Haversine;
  • Vincenty within 0.6% of Haversine;
  • the Douglas-Peucker tolerance guarantee;
  • R-tree range and kNN results against brute force, for insert-built trees (both splits) and STR trees.

The last one is the pattern I like most. A linear scan over all the points is slow and obviously correct, so it is the perfect judge for an index that is fast and easy to get subtly wrong.

The README also has a benchmark table, with an honest warning: it was measured with cargo bench -- --quick on a laptop that was busy with other builds, so the numbers are orders of magnitude only. With that warning: Haversine is around 0.23 µs and Vincenty around 2 µs per call, an STR bulk load of 50k points takes about 52 ms, and inserting the same 50k points one by one takes about 0.3 to 0.5 s.

Things to know

The README lists the limits, and they matter if you are tempted to use this beyond learning:

  • This is a learning project. For real work use the geo and rstar crates.
  • Everything is plain f64 with no robust predicates. Boundary detection is exact only when the arithmetic is: vertices and axis-aligned edges work, but a point interpolated along a slanted edge may land a hair inside or outside.
  • The planar algorithms treat lon/lat degrees as flat x/y. Nothing handles the antimeridian, and the Douglas-Peucker epsilon is in input units.
  • The R-tree has no deletion and no R*-tree reinsertion. kNN distance is measured to each entry's bounding rectangle.
  • Hole validity (holes inside the exterior, not overlapping) is assumed and not checked.

What I learned

The first lesson is that geometry code is mostly about the cases a drawing does not show: the ray through a vertex, the point on an edge, the two points on opposite sides of the planet. The main idea of each algorithm fits in a paragraph. The rest of the code is there for those cases.

The second is that a slow reference is a great tool. Almost every module here is tested by comparing it with something simpler: brute force for the R-tree, a closed-form predicate for holes, Haversine as a sanity bound for Vincenty. When the two disagree on a random input, proptest shrinks it to a small example, and the bug is usually visible at once.

The third is specific to Rust. A tree with parent and child links is awkward with references and comfortable in an arena with indices.

And returning Boundary or NoConvergence as explicit results taught me something general: when an algorithm has an input it cannot answer well, say so in the type instead of returning a guess.

Get the code

The source, the demo example, the tests and the benchmarks are on GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/geo-algos. It is MIT licensed, and no external data is used.
