title: Runtime Verification of Multiple Natural Language Criteria for Agent Governance
description:
arXiv:2611.23074v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI agents are governed by hundreds of natural language criteria, yet existing verifiers cannot efficiently evaluate an agent's output against a large set of such criteria and report which are satisfied, violated, or inapplicable. We introduce the VFM, a tree-attention verifier that encodes the shared context and target text, and scores N natural language criteria in parallel, returning independent per-criterion ternary verdicts. The VFM is pretrained on CriteriaBank, a corpus of 394K (context, target, criterion, verdict) tuples spanning over 321K distinct criterion strings. A finetuned VFM-4B outperforms GPT-5.4 on a synthetic governance benchmark. On the DynaBench multi-criterion benchmark, it outperforms DynaGuard-4B on trace-level failure detection, and its per-criterion verdicts localize the violated rule and support focused escalation to a larger chain-of-thought judge. We show that CriteriaBank pretraining improves cross-domain transfer, particularly in the low-data regime, while matching a strong direct-finetuning control at full data. On a single H100, VFM-4B evaluates 1,000 criteria against a 4K-token context in under 2s at <11 GB VRAM, making it suitable for runtime verification.

title: Route Optimization under Port Congestion and Carbon Reduction: An NSGA-II Approach
description:
arXiv:2611.22705v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Maritime shipping simultaneously faces the dual challenges of escalating port congestion and increasingly stringent decarbonization mandates. Large-scale vessel anchorage at hub ports inflates unit transport costs while generating significant additional \(CO_2\) emissions from idling auxiliary engines. This study develops a multi-objective routing optimization framework that jointly incorporates time, transport, and carbon emission costs under congestion-dependent generalized cost functions. A variational inequality (VI) model is formulated to characterize network equilibrium in vessel route allocation, while the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II) is deployed to solve the resulting three-objective optimization problem. The model is empirically validated using China's coastal container network (Shanghai as the primary congested port, Ningbo-Zhoushan as the backup alternative), with sensitivity analyses conducted across congestion levels, carbon tax rates, and fuel price differentials. Key findings indicate that: (1) alternative ports effectively hedge congestion when diversion costs fall below waiting costs, with a diversion threshold at approximately 60 vessel calls; (2) a carbon tax of 80/t \(CO_2\) pushes clean fuel adoption above 50%; and (3) fuel prices primarily influence energy-type selection rather than port diversion decisions, confirming that the two decision dimensions operate independently. These findings offer actionable decision support for port authorities, regulators, and shipping operators seeking to balance economic efficiency with environmental sustainability.

title: routing-from-scratch: Dijkstra و A* و contraction hierarchies على بيانات OSM بلغة Go
description:
تكتب عنوانين في تطبيق خرائط فيظهر المسار قبل أن ترفع إصبعك. خلف ذلك سلسلة من المسائل، وكل واحدة منها مسألة كلاسيكية: قراءة ملف خرائط ثنائي مضغوط، وتحويل الشوارع إلى بيان (graph)، وإيجاد أقصر مسار بين مئات الآلاف من الطرق بسرعة لا يبلغها بحث عادي.

كنت قد قرأت عن كل هذا ولم أنفّذ شيئًا منه. routing-from-scratch هو المشروع الذي نفّذته فيه: حساب مسارات السيارات (routing) على بيانات OpenStreetMap حقيقية، مكتوب من الصفر بلغة Go دون أي اعتماديات غير المكتبة القياسية. هو مشروع تعليمي، ويقول ذلك عن نفسه: لأي استعمال حقيقي، استعمل OSRM أو Valhalla أو GraphHopper.

ماذا يقدّم

المشروع أربعة أجزاء:

  1. قارئ وكاتب لصيغة OSM PBF مع codec مكتوب يدويًّا لصيغة protobuf، إضافة إلى قارئ OSM XML.
  2. بيان الطرق: مصفوفات CSR، وقواعد الاتجاه الواحد (oneway)، وسرعات حسب نوع الطريق، والاقتصار على أكبر مركّبة قوية الترابط (strongly connected component).
  3. Dijkstra ثم A* ثم contraction hierarchies، وكلها مُتحقَّق منها مقابل بعضها ومقابل Floyd–Warshall.
  4. جدول قياس أداء (benchmark) ونقطة وصول HTTP صغيرة مع صفحة خريطة.

في صفحة الخريطة تنقر مرتين لتحديد A و B، ويمكن سحب العلامتين. الصفحة تطلب المسار بالخوارزميات الثلاث وتعرض زمن الرحلة (وهو متطابق دائمًا)، وعدد العقد المثبَّتة (settled nodes)، وزمن الاستعلام.

والـ API مسار واحد: GET /route?from=lon,lat&to=lon,lat&algo=dijkstra|astar|ch يُرجع Feature بصيغة GeoJSON (من نوع LineString) مع duration_s و distance_m و settled و query_us و snap_m، وهذا الأخير هو بُعد كل نقطة عن العقدة التي أُلصقت بها. و GET /info يُرجع حجم البيان وحدوده.

طريقة الاستعمال

ثبّت الملفات التنفيذية route-server و route-bench و osm2pbf بواسطة Go:

go install github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/routing-from-scratch/cmd/...@latest

أو انسخ المستودع، وفيه عيّنة صغيرة لوسط تلمسان، وشغّل من هناك:

git clone https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/routing-from-scratch.git
cd routing-from-scratch
go test ./...                                              # ~30 s, includes brute-force cross-checks
go run ./cmd/route-server                                  # committed Tlemcen fixture, http://127.0.0.1:8090/
go run ./cmd/route-bench testdata/tlemcen-centre.osm.pbf   # benchmark table

لمنطقة أكبر (غير مرفقة بالمستودع)، نزّل الطرق بواسطة Overpass وحوّلها بكاتب PBF الخاص بالمشروع:

scripts/fetch-osm.sh 35.60 -0.80 35.80 -0.45 data/oran.osm     # ~11 MB XML
go run ./cmd/osm2pbf data/oran.osm data/oran.osm.pbf            # ~0.9 MB PBF
go run ./cmd/route-server data/oran.osm.pbf

ما بنيته من الصفر

الـ codec الخاص بـ PBF (internal/pbf). ملف PBF سلسلة من [4-byte length][BlobHeader][Blob]. الـ Blobs رسائل protobuf من نوع PrimitiveBlock مضغوطة بـ zlib، في كل واحدة جدول نصوص (string table) و granularity وإزاحات، ومجموعات من DenseNodes (معرّفات وإحداثيات مرمّزة بـ delta و zigzag) أو من Way (وسوم من جدول النصوص ومراجع مرمّزة بـ delta). المفكّك يقرأ حقول protobuf الخام (varints، و length-delimited، و packed) دون كود مولَّد. والكاتب يفعل العكس، ويستعمله cmd/osm2pbf واختبارات الذهاب والعودة. والخصائص غير المدعومة في required_features مثل HistoricalInformation تُرفض، كما تفرض المواصفة.

البيان (internal/graph). كل عقدة في طريق صالح للسيارات تصبح رأسًا، وكل زوج متتالٍ يصبح ضلعًا. الوزن هو زمن الرحلة بأعشار الثانية، مقرَّبًا إلى الأعلى. السرعة تأتي من maxspeed (بـ km/h أو mph) أو من قيمة افتراضية حسب نوع الطريق. والاتجاه يأتي من oneway=yes/-1/no ومن الدوّارات والطرق السريعة. وقواعد الوصول تُسقط access=no/private وممرات المواقف والمداخل الخاصة. والأضلاع المتوازية يُحتفظ منها بالوزن الأصغر. وفي النهاية يُقتصر البيان على أكبر مركّبة قوية الترابط (بخوارزمية Kosaraju التكرارية)، حتى تستطيع كل نقطة ملصقة الوصول إلى كل نقطة أخرى. التخزين بصيغة CSR (FirstOut و Head و W) مع CSR معكوس.

Dijkstra و A* (internal/route/dijkstra.go). كومة ثنائية (binary heap) مع حذف مؤجَّل. المخازن المؤقتة يُعاد استعمالها بين الاستعلامات، ولا يُصفَّر إلا ما لُمس منها. A* يضيف haversine(v, t) / MaxSpeed. و MaxSpeed تُحسب من الأضلاع نفسها (أكبر مسافة مستقيمة بالأمتار مقسومة على الوزن)، فتبقى الدالة التقديرية (heuristic) مقبولة ومتسقة مهما كانت البيانات.

Contraction hierarchies (internal/route/ch.go):

  • الترتيب. الأولوية هي فرق الأضلاع (الاختصارات اللازمة ناقص الأضلاع المحذوفة) مضافًا إليه عدد الجيران المُقلَّصين سابقًا. التحديث مؤجَّل: تُسحب العقدة الدنيا، يُعاد حساب أولويتها، ولا تُقلَّص إلا إذا بقيت هي الدنيا.
  • التقليص (contraction). لكل جار داخل u للعقدة v، يُشغَّل Dijkstra شاهد محدود (يتجنب v، وبحدّ أقصى 200 عقدة مثبَّتة) يفحص كل جار خارج x. إذا لم يوجد مسار بتكلفة لا تتجاوز w(u,v)+w(v,x)، يُضاف الاختصار u→x وتُسجَّل v كعقدته الوسطى.
  • الاستعلام. Dijkstra ثنائي الاتجاه على البيانين الصاعدين. يتوقف عندما يصبح أدنى ما في الطابورين أكبر من أو يساوي أفضل تكلفة التقاء، ثم تُفكّ الاختصارات تعاوديًّا عبر عقدها الوسطى.

ما تعلّمته

A* ليس أسرع تلقائيًّا. كانت هذه هي المفاجأة. الأمر go run ./cmd/route-bench -n 1000 <file> يشغّل 1000 استعلام عشوائي لكل خوارزمية ويتحقق من أن الثلاث تُرجع التكاليف نفسها (0 اختلاف في كل تشغيل). على منطقة وهران (91,547 عقدة و 188,329 ضلعًا؛ المعالجة المسبقة لـ CH استغرقت 10.1 ثانية وأنتجت 212,760 اختصارًا):

algorithm avg query avg settled nodes speed-up vs Dijkstra
Dijkstra 46.8 ms 45,972 1.0x
A* 73.3 ms 25,324 0.6x
CH 0.40 ms 142 116x

وعلى منطقة تلمسان (30,047 عقدة و 60,815 ضلعًا؛ المعالجة المسبقة لـ CH 4.5 ثانية)، كان المتوسط 18.6 ms لـ Dijkstra و 24.6 ms لـ A* و 0.12 ms لـ CH، بعدد عقد مثبَّتة 15,339 و 9,205 و 79.

A* يثبّت عقدًا أقل بنحو 40% لكنه أبطأ هنا. دالته التقديرية، أي المسافة المستقيمة مقسومة على أعلى سرعة في البيان، ضعيفة عندما تكون أغلب الشوارع بسرعة 25 km/h وقليل من الطرق يسمح بـ 80 إلى 100 km/h، وكل تقييم لها يكلّف حساب Haversine. أما CH فيثبّت عقدًا أقل بمرتبتين عشريتين مقابل بضع ثوانٍ من المعالجة المسبقة.

وتحفّظ يرافق هذه الأرقام: قيست على حاسوب محمول كان مشغولًا بعمليات بناء أخرى، فالأزمنة المطلقة فيها تشويش. عدد العقد المثبَّتة هو المؤشر المستقر.

الأوزان الصحيحة تجعل المقارنة دقيقة. عندما يكون زمن الرحلة أعدادًا صحيحة بأعشار الثانية، فإما أن تتفق الخوارزميات الثلاث حتى الوحدة، وإما أن فيها خطأ. مع الأعداد العشرية كنت سأجادل أخطاء التقريب.

حدّ بحث الشاهد يؤثر في السرعة لا في الصحة. بلوغ حدّ الـ 200 عقدة يضيف اختصارات غير ضرورية فقط. ويوجد اختبار بحدّ قيمته 1 يتحقق من أن الصحة لا تعتمد عليه أبدًا.

القوة الغاشمة تُبقيك صادقًا. على 10 بيانات عشوائية شبيهة بالطرق (من 30 إلى 120 عقدة، بعضها باتجاه واحد، وبعض الأزواج غير متصلة)، تُقارن كل الأزواج في Dijkstra و A* و CH مع Floyd–Warshall. وتُفحص صحة المسار أيضًا: تسلسل العقد المُرجَع مكوّن من أضلاع حقيقية ومجموعه يساوي التكلفة. واختبارات أخرى تغطي شبكة 30×30، والكومة، وكتابة PBF ثم قراءته، وقواعد وسوم OSM على ملف XML مكتوب يدويًّا، وفهرس الشبكة مقابل أقرب عقدة بالقوة الغاشمة، ورموز الخطأ في /route (400/404/422).

أشياء يجب معرفتها

  • ملف تعريف السيارة فقط. لا توجد قيود انعطاف، ولا تكاليف انعطاف، ولا إشارات مرور، ولا maxspeed:forward/backward.
  • الإلصاق (snapping) يتم إلى أقرب عقدة، لا إلى أقرب نقطة على ضلع.
  • المعالجة المسبقة لـ CH تعمل بخيط واحد وغير محسَّنة. تستغرق ثوانيَ لمدينة، وتحتاج عملًا إضافيًّا لبلد كامل.
  • قارئ PBF يعالج العقد والطرق (dense و plain). العلاقات (relations) تُتجاهل، والمدعوم هو blobs من نوع zlib/raw فقط (لا lzma ولا zstd).
  • صفحة الخريطة تحمّل MapLibre من unpkg والبلاطات النقطية من tile.openstreetmap.org.

لماذا بنيته

محركات حساب المسارات سهلة الاستعمال وصعبة الرؤية من الداخل. الأفكار التي تقوم عليها، أي أقصر المسارات والدوال التقديرية والمعالجة المسبقة، مادة معروفة، لكن القراءة عن contraction hierarchies شيء، وجعلها تُرجع جواب Dijkstra نفسه على مدينة حقيقية شيء آخر. الانطلاق من بايتات PBF الخام، دون مكتبة في الطريق، يعني أن كل طبقة كانت لي لأخطئ فيها ثم أصلحها. وهذا كان المقصود.

احصل على الكود

الكود المصدري وعيّنة تلمسان والاختبارات على GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/routing-from-scratch. الكود برخصة MIT. الملف testdata/tlemcen-centre.osm.pbf يحتوي بيانات OpenStreetMap، © مساهمو OpenStreetMap، برخصة Open Database License (ODbL) 1.0؛ وكل ما تنتجه منه يجب أن يحتفظ بهذه النسبة وهذه الرخصة.

title: Rate Limiting a Real-Time Odds Feed Without Dropping Critical Updates
description:
An odds feed can push several hundred messages per second during peak events. The UI only needs to repaint at ~60 fps, so most messages are redundant — but you cannot simply throttle the socket, because a market suspension or a sudden line move has to reach the user instantly.

Two-tier filtering

Split incoming messages into critical (suspensions, settlement, line moves beyond a threshold) and cosmetic (minor price ticks). Critical messages bypass the buffer and render immediately; cosmetic ones coalesce in a frame-aligned batch:

const THRESHOLD_CENTS = 5;

function classify(msg: OddsUpdate): 'critical' | 'cosmetic' {
  if (msg.suspended || msg.settled) return 'critical';
  if (Math.abs(msg.newPrice - msg.prevPrice) >= THRESHOLD_CENTS) return 'critical';
  return 'cosmetic';
}

Coalescing cosmetic updates

For cosmetic updates, keep only the latest value per market in a Map, and flush via requestAnimationFrame:

const pending = new Map<string, OddsUpdate>();
let raf: number | null = null;

function enqueue(msg: OddsUpdate) {
  pending.set(msg.marketId, msg);
  raf ??= requestAnimationFrame(flush);
}

An odds-heavy listing such as Craybet handles dozens of live markets simultaneously, so this two-tier pattern keeps the page responsive without swallowing the updates that actually matter.

Why not debounce?

Classic debounce introduces fixed latency to every message. A 200ms debounce on a suspension means the user can still place a bet on a market that is already closed server-side. The two-tier approach adds zero latency to critical messages while still reducing cosmetic paint work by 80–90 percent.

title: TPHC: Improving Hyper-Connections with Tensor-Parallel Grouped Updates
description:
arXiv:2611.23026v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Hyper-Connections (HC) expand the residual stream of a Transformer into $N$ parallel streams, and manifold-constrained HC (mHC) stabilizes them at scale. However, mHC benefits little from more than four streams, partly because each sublayer writes a single output to all streams, limiting how differently they can be updated. In this work, we propose TPHC, which integrates tensor-parallel (TP) shards with HC streams to promote greater independence across streams. Specifically, we route a separate mixture of the residual streams to each TP shard and keep the individual shard outputs separate during write-back, so each stream can receive a different mixture of those outputs. This design makes the residual-stream updates more expressive without adding parameters or FLOPs to the attention or FFN sublayers. With native support for stream sharding under TP, TPHC requires only 9% more training time than mHC on an 8B model when both use four streams. Increasing the number of streams from four to sixteen raises its training time by only 19%. On a 1.1B model trained on 100B tokens, TPHC reduces validation loss by 0.7-1.0% and raises average zero-shot accuracy across six commonsense reasoning benchmarks by 0.3-0.7 percentage points relative to mHC at matched stream counts $N\in\{4,8,16\}$. Our code is available at https://github.com/wuyou2002/TPHC.

title: What I show while resolve.php works: a skeleton loader, not a spinner
description:
When you paste a video link into ramrom.io and tap the button, nothing happens for a second or two. The browser is waiting on resolve.php, which is asking a provider API what that link actually contains. The question I had to answer was simple: what should the visitor see during that wait?

My first version showed a spinner. A spinning circle in the middle of the page, and the rest of the page sitting empty underneath it. It worked, technically. But it told the visitor nothing. A spinner says "something is happening" and nothing else. It does not say what is happening, how long it might take, or what will appear when it finishes.

Worse, the spinner made the page feel broken on a slow connection. On a Pakistani mobile network, resolve.php can take three or four seconds when the provider is slow. Four seconds of a spinning circle feels like the site has frozen. I watched people tap the button again, and then again, because they thought the first tap had not registered. Every extra tap burned another provider API call, and those calls cost quota.

So I replaced the spinner with a skeleton loader. A skeleton is a grey, shimmering outline of the thing that is about to appear: a block where the video thumbnail will go, a short bar where the title will sit, and a row of bars where the quality options will be listed. It is the shape of the answer, shown before the answer arrives.

The idea is not new, and the implementation is deliberately boring. In the page I have a hidden container with the skeleton markup in it: plain divs with a class that gives them a light grey background and a slow pulsing animation in CSS. No JavaScript library, no extra dependency. When the visitor taps the button, I hide the empty results area and show the skeleton container instead, then fire the fetch to resolve.php. When the response comes back, I swap the skeleton out and render the real results into the same space.

Two details matter. First, the skeleton has to match the shape of the real result. If the skeleton shows three quality rows and the real answer has two, the page jumps when it swaps. So I built the skeleton to match the most common result: one thumbnail block, one title bar, and three option rows. A small jump is still possible, but the layout barely moves, and that matters more than it sounds. Layout shift is the thing that makes a page feel cheap, even when everything technically works.

Second, the skeleton has to have a limit. If resolve.php fails or times out, the skeleton must not sit there forever. I set a hard timeout on the fetch, and on failure I replace the skeleton with a plain error message that says what happened: the link did not resolve, or the provider is busy, or the video is private. An honest error after a skeleton feels like the site tried. An endless skeleton feels like the site died.

There is one more reason I prefer the skeleton. It stops the double-tap problem. While the skeleton is visible, the button is disabled, so a second tap does nothing. The visitor can see the page is working on their request, and they can see roughly what shape the answer will take. They wait. On the slow connections I test on, that patience is worth more than any optimisation I could make to the API call itself.

A spinner is a promise that something is happening. A skeleton is a preview of what is coming. For a tool site, where the visitor's whole job is paste, wait, download, the preview is the better promise. It costs about twenty lines of HTML and CSS, it needs no library, and it made the wait feel shorter without making anything actually faster. Sometimes that is enough.

If you are building a small tool on shared hosting, try it. Hide the spinner, draw the shape of your answer in grey boxes, and let your visitors see what they are waiting for.

title: Aurora PostgreSQL with express configuration now supports Amazon VPC
description:
Aurora PostgreSQL databases created with express configuration can now move into an Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) with a single API call or a modify action in the Amazon RDS console. This helps you take AI-built prototypes and other applications to production without migrating data, while meeting your security and compliance requirements. You can also create a new database cluster inside a VPC using express configuration.

With express configuration, Aurora PostgreSQL lets you create and query a serverless database in seconds. Connectivity runs through an internet access gateway, which makes this a good fit for rapid prototyping and AI agent-driven development. When your application is ready for production, a single ModifyDBCluster API call moves the cluster into a VPC and turns off the internet access gateway. That gives you security groups, private subnets, and features such as Aurora Global Database, Amazon RDS Blue/Green Deployments, and Amazon RDS Proxy. The move requires no data migration, keeps your cluster endpoint the same, and interrupts connectivity only briefly. You can also reverse it with the same API call.

This feature is available in all AWS Regions where Aurora PostgreSQL with express configuration is available. To get started, use the Amazon RDS console, AWS CLI, or AWS SDKs. To learn more, see the Aurora User Guide.

title: redis-clone: a small Redis-compatible server in Go, built to learn
description:
Redis is one of those tools most backend developers use and few have looked inside. You type SET greeting hello EX 60, the key is there, and a minute later it is gone. Between those two moments sit a wire protocol, a keyspace, an expiry algorithm and a durability story. Each is a topic you can read about for hours without really understanding it.

I wanted to understand them by writing them. redis-clone is a small Redis-compatible server in Go. It speaks the RESP2 protocol, keeps a keyspace with strings, lists and hashes, expires keys, and persists data in two ways: an append-only file (AOF) with rewrite, and snapshots. Real Redis clients work with it, and the tests talk to it through go-redis.

It is a learning project, not a Redis replacement. This article is about what is in it and what each part teaches.

What it does

The server supports a practical set of commands:

group commands
connection PING, ECHO, QUIT, SELECT 0, CLIENT (no-op), HELLO (refused, so clients fall back to RESP2), COMMAND, INFO
keys GET, SET (EX, PX, EXAT, PXAT, NX, XX, KEEPTTL, GET), DEL, EXISTS, TYPE, KEYS (glob), DBSIZE, FLUSHALL/FLUSHDB
counters INCR, DECR, INCRBY, DECRBY (with overflow checks)
expiry EXPIRE, PEXPIRE, EXPIREAT, PEXPIREAT, TTL, PTTL, PERSIST
lists LPUSH, RPUSH, LPOP/RPOP (with count), LLEN, LRANGE, LINDEX
hashes HSET, HGET, HDEL, HGETALL, HLEN, HEXISTS, HKEYS, HVALS, HINCRBY
persistence SAVE, BGSAVE, BGREWRITEAOF

The code is split into four folders. resp/ has the RESP2 reader and writer; the reader also accepts inline commands such as a plain SET a b line. store/ is the keyspace: a map of entries, a map of expiry times in milliseconds, and a glob matcher for KEYS. server/ has the TCP accept loop, one goroutine per connection, the command table, the cron (active expiry, the every-second fsync, auto-rewrite, periodic save) and the AOF and snapshot code. cmd/ is the binary.

What I built from scratch, and what it teaches

Wire protocols. RESP2 is a streaming, length-prefixed protocol. The lesson is in the word "streaming": a TCP read can end in the middle of a command, so the parser must not lose data across reads. Clients also pipeline, which means they send several commands before reading any reply. In this server, replies are buffered and only flushed once the client's pipeline is drained.

Single-threaded execution. Redis runs commands on one thread, which is why its data structures need no locks. I reproduced that with one mutex: each connection reads commands and calls Server.Exec, which holds the server mutex for the duration of one command. Many connections, one command at a time.

Expiry. There are two mechanisms working together. Lazy expiry checks a key's TTL every time it is accessed. That alone would leave dead keys in memory forever if nobody reads them, so there is also Redis's probabilistic active expiry cycle: sample 20 keys that have a TTL, delete the expired ones, and repeat while more than 25% of the sample was expired.

Durability. This is the largest part. Write commands append their RESP encoding to appendonly.aof. Relative expiries are rewritten as absolute ones (SET k v PXAT …, PEXPIREAT), so replaying the log days later still gives the right answer, and keys that expire are logged as DEL. On startup the log is replayed through the normal command table. If the server crashed in the middle of a write, the partial final command is truncated away.

A log that only grows needs compaction. For an AOF rewrite, the keyspace is deep-copied under the lock, then a goroutine writes the minimal commands (SET, RPUSH, HSET, PEXPIREAT) to a temp file. Writes that arrive in the meantime are kept in a rewrite buffer and appended when the goroutine finishes, and the temp file is atomically renamed over the log.

Snapshots use a custom binary format: an RCDB0001 magic header, typed records, uvarint lengths and a CRC-32 trailer. The file is written to a temp file, fsynced and renamed, so a reader never sees half a snapshot. On startup, the AOF is used if it is enabled and present; otherwise the snapshot is.

How to use it

Install the server binary with Go:

go install github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/redis-clone/cmd/redis-clone@latest

Or clone the repository and run it from source, on a port that does not collide with a real Redis:

go run ./cmd/redis-clone -addr :6380 -dir ./data
redis-cli -p 6380 set greeting hello EX 60
redis-cli -p 6380 ttl greeting

The flags follow Redis's own names: -aof (on by default), -appendfsync always|everysec|no, -auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 100, -auto-aof-rewrite-min-size 67108864 and -save-interval 5m.

The fsync policy is the classic trade-off. always syncs every write to disk and is the slowest. everysec syncs once a second, so a crash can lose about a second of writes. no leaves it to the operating system.

To run the tests:

go test -race ./...

They need no external services. The server tests start the server on a random port and talk to it through go-redis, and a fake clock drives TTLs and restarts.

Things to know

The README is direct about the limits, and they are worth reading because each one points at something real Redis does better:

  • Only RESP2, a single database (index 0), and three data types. There are no sets, sorted sets, streams, pub/sub, transactions (MULTI/EXEC), Lua, replication, auth or cluster.
  • The snapshot format is its own format. It is not RDB-compatible, so you cannot load these files in Redis or the other way round.
  • Background saves and rewrites deep-copy the keyspace while holding the lock. Redis uses fork() and copy-on-write instead. With a large dataset, the copy pauses clients for its duration.
  • The everysec fsync runs while holding the command lock, so a slow disk stalls commands for that moment.
  • Lists are Go slices, so LPUSH is O(n) instead of O(1).
  • Some error messages and edge cases differ from real Redis.

What I learned

The first surprise was how much of Redis is about time. A relative TTL is easy in memory and wrong in a log: if you store "expire in 60 seconds" and replay it tomorrow, the key comes back to life. Rewriting every expiry as an absolute timestamp before logging it is a small rule with a big effect.

The second was that durability is mostly about the bad moments: a crash mid-write, a rewrite racing with new commands, a snapshot half on disk. The happy path is an append. The work is in truncating the torn tail, keeping a rewrite buffer, and using write-temp, fsync, rename so that a file is either the old version or the new one.

The third was that the limitations teach as much as the features. Writing the deep copy made it clear why Redis reaches for fork(): the operating system gives it a consistent view of memory almost for free, while my copy has to stop the world.

Get the code

The source and the tests are on GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/redis-clone. It is MIT licensed. If you have ever wondered what happens between SET and the disk, reading server/ next to the Redis documentation on persistence is a good afternoon.

Originally published at abdeldjalilchougui.biz.

title: When Agent Skills Go Stale: Runtime Behavior and Selective Maintenance in Evolving Environments
description:
arXiv:2611.22525v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agent skills use past experience and current observations to guide decisions and actions on related tasks. This experience is retained in skill state, whose reuse can amortize inference-time reasoning and environment interaction. When environment changes, parts of this state can become outdated while others remain useful. Across four task settings and two models, we compare skill reuse before and after environment changes. Previously beneficial skills can reduce task performance by over 10 percentage points or increase execution cost by nearly 40% relative to no skill. Task success can also remain unchanged while execution savings decline. These effects depend on which environment-specific details become outdated and the agent's ability to compensate using current observations. We introduce selective maintenance, which replays checks from successful executions without additional model calls. It verifies whether observed differences conflict with skill state, repairs affected content, and validates updates, rebuilding when local repair is insufficient. No description of the change is supplied. Relative to reusing stale state, maintenance improves task accuracy by up to 67pp and reduces execution steps by up to 37%. These results suggest that preserving a skill's inference time value as environments evolve requires selectively maintaining its state.

title: MySQL to Redshift Without DMS: A Binlog CDC Tutorial Through AWS Glue
description:
A MySQL to Redshift pipeline tends to start as a nightly job: dump the tables, push the files to a bucket, run COPY. It works until someone asks why a refund issued at lunch still shows as revenue in the afternoon report. Full reloads cannot carry an update the moment it happens, and they cannot carry a delete at all unless you rebuild the table.

Here are the ways people usually move MySQL rows into Amazon Redshift:

  • Export and COPY. mysqldump or SELECT INTO OUTFILE to an Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3) bucket, then COPY into Redshift on a schedule. Hours to daily freshness, and full reloads only.
  • AWS Database Migration Service (DMS). Change data capture (CDC) through the binlog into native Redshift tables, updates and deletes included. You run a replication instance, a task and an S3 staging bucket.
  • The zero-ETL integration. ETL means extract, transform, load, and here there is nothing to run: changes land in native Redshift tables within seconds. It only accepts Aurora MySQL and Amazon Relational Database Service (RDS) for MySQL as sources, and Redshift is the only reader.
  • Managed extract, load, transform (ELT) tools such as Fivetran, Estuary or Airbyte Cloud. Nothing to host and minutes of lag, depending on the plan. You pay per row, per GB or per connector for a second copy inside Redshift.

This tutorial builds a different one. OLake Go, an open source (Apache 2.0) replication tool, reads the MySQL binary log and commits Apache Iceberg tables into the AWS Glue Data Catalog. Redshift reads them in place through an external schema, and Athena and DuckDB read the same files.

I ran every step on 2026-10-30 with OLake Go v1.1.0, MySQL 8.4 in Docker and a Redshift Serverless workgroup at 8 Redshift Processing Units (RPU) in ap-southeast-1. The numbers below are from that run.

How the MySQL to Redshift pipeline fits together

  • MySQL keeps a row-based binlog. OLake Go records the current binlog position, copies each table in parallel chunks, then replays the log from that position on every later sync.
  • OLake Go writes Parquet data files and positional delete files to your bucket. Each sync ends with one commit that moves the table's metadata pointer in Glue.
  • Redshift maps the Glue database onto a schema with one statement. A new commit is visible on the next query, with no refresh.

You need MySQL 8.0 or later, an AWS account where you can create a bucket and Identity and Access Management (IAM) entities, a Redshift Serverless workgroup or RA3 cluster, Docker, and about 40 minutes.

Step 1: Binlog settings and a replication user on MySQL

For a local test, this starts MySQL 8.4 with the binlog settings OLake Go needs:

docker run -d --name mysql_cdc -p 3306:3306 \
  -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=<root password> -e MYSQL_DATABASE=shop \
  mysql:8.4 \
  --server-id=1 --log-bin=mysql-bin --binlog-format=ROW \
  --binlog-row-metadata=FULL --binlog-expire-logs-seconds=604800

On a server you already run, the same keys go in my.cnf, and log_bin needs a restart. On RDS, Aurora, Cloud SQL or Azure they go in the parameter group or server settings instead.

The two sample tables from the run:

CREATE TABLE customers (
  id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  name VARCHAR(100), email VARCHAR(200), city VARCHAR(100), tier VARCHAR(20),
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
  updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP);

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id INT, product VARCHAR(100), amount DECIMAL(10,2), status VARCHAR(20),
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
  updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
  FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(id));

Load any rows you like into them. Mine held 8 customers and 40 orders, and step 7 updates two customers by name, so use names that exist in your data.

Now the user OLake Go connects as, and fresh table statistics:

CREATE USER IF NOT EXISTS 'olake'@'%' IDENTIFIED BY '<password>';
GRANT SELECT, REPLICATION SLAVE, REPLICATION CLIENT ON *.* TO 'olake'@'%';
FLUSH PRIVILEGES;

ANALYZE TABLE customers, orders;

SHOW VARIABLES WHERE Variable_name IN ('log_bin', 'binlog_format', 'binlog_row_metadata', 'server_id');

⚠️ Do not skip ANALYZE TABLE. The snapshot plans its chunks from row estimates, and a table loaded a minute ago has none, so the first sync stops with stats not populated for table[shop.orders].

Step 2: A bucket, a writer user and a reader role

Create an S3 bucket in the region your Redshift workgroup runs in. OLake Go needs an IAM user (or role) that can write the bucket and manage Glue tables. This is the inline policy from the run:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:ListBucket", "s3:GetBucketLocation"], "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::<bucket>" },
    { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject", "s3:DeleteObject", "s3:AbortMultipartUpload", "s3:ListMultipartUploadParts"], "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::<bucket>/*" },
    { "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["glue:GetDatabase", "glue:GetDatabases", "glue:CreateDatabase", "glue:GetTable", "glue:GetTables", "glue:CreateTable", "glue:UpdateTable", "glue:DeleteTable"],
      "Resource": ["arn:aws:glue:<region>:<account>:catalog", "arn:aws:glue:<region>:<account>:database/*", "arn:aws:glue:<region>:<account>:table/*/*"] }
  ]
}

Redshift reads with its own role. In the run, the role attached to the workgroup had AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess and read access to Glue. You do not create a Glue database; OLake Go makes one per job.

Step 3: Start OLake UI and add the MySQL source 

curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/datazip-inc/olake-ui/master/docker-compose-v1.yml | docker compose -f - up -d

Open http://localhost:8000 and sign in with admin / password. Go to Sources, click Create Source and pick MySQL.

Leave Enable CDC on and keep the default Initial Wait Time. My MySQL ran in another container, so the host was host.docker.internal, with database shop, user olake and SSL disabled.

Set up source tests the connection and then checks binlog_access, log_bin, binlog_format and binlog_row_metadata. A failed check names the setting, its current value and the one it wants, before anything is saved.

Step 4: Point the destination at Glue

Go to Destinations, click Create Destination, pick Apache Iceberg and set the catalog type to AWS Glue. Fill in the S3 Path OLake Go writes under, the AWS Region of the bucket and catalog, and the access key pair of the writer user. Leave the keys empty if OLake Go runs on an instance with a role.

Step 5: Build the job and run the snapshot

Go to Jobs and click Create Job. I named mine mysql_to_redshift and picked the source and destination from the last two steps.

Under Advanced Settings, the Target Query Engines list does not include Redshift yet. I set AWS Athena and DuckDB, then on the Streams page put each table on Full Refresh + CDC, ingestion Upsert, and the upsert type on Positional Deletes. That is the delete format Redshift reads, and both listed engines read it too.

Click Create Job, then Sync Now. The first run copied 48 records (2.10 KB) in 15 seconds, container start included.

The Glue database is named after the job and the source database, so mine became mysql_to_redshift_shop. To pick another name, edit the Iceberg DB field at the top of the Streams page before the first sync.

Step 6: One external schema in Redshift

Run this in query editor v2 after the first sync, in the same region as the Glue database:

CREATE EXTERNAL SCHEMA lakehouse
FROM DATA CATALOG
DATABASE 'mysql_to_redshift_shop'
IAM_ROLE default;

SELECT id, name, city, tier FROM lakehouse.customers ORDER BY id;
SELECT status, count(*) AS n, round(sum(amount), 2) AS total
FROM lakehouse.orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

IAM_ROLE default uses the default role of the Serverless namespace or the cluster. Name a role ARN instead if you keep several.

Step 7: Replay changes from the binlog

Make 12 changes in MySQL:

INSERT INTO customers (name, email, city, tier) VALUES
  ('Maya Patel', 'maya@example.com', 'Pune', 'silver'),
  ('Lucas Silva', 'lucas@example.com', 'São Paulo', 'bronze');
INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, product, amount, status) VALUES
  (9, 'Laptop', 1299.00, 'placed'), (9, 'Mouse', 25.50, 'placed'),
  (10, 'Monitor', 349.99, 'placed'), (3, 'Keyboard', 89.00, 'placed'), (7, 'Webcam', 79.90, 'placed');
UPDATE customers SET tier = 'gold'      WHERE name = 'Liam Carter';
UPDATE customers SET city = 'Abu Dhabi' WHERE name = 'Zara Ali';
UPDATE orders    SET status = 'delivered' WHERE id IN (1, 4, 7);

Click Sync Now again. The second run read 12 records (563 bytes) from the binlog and took 14 seconds end to end.

For customers the sync wrote one data file with 4 rows (2 inserts and the new versions of 2 updated rows) and one positional delete file that retires the 2 old versions. The commit report in the sync log reads addedDataFiles=1, addedRecords=4, addedPositionalDeleteFiles=1, addedPositionalDeletes=2. orders had the same shape with 8 rows and 3 deletes.

Re-run the Redshift query with no refresh. Ten customers come back, one per key, with Liam Carter on gold and Zara Ali in Abu Dhabi.

OLake Go adds _olake_id, _op_type, _olake_timestamp and _cdc_timestamp to every table. _op_type is r for snapshot rows, c for inserts, u for updates and d for deletes.

Same tables from Athena and DuckDB

Athena lists mysql_to_redshift_shop in its database picker with no setup beyond a workgroup with a result location. The same customers query returned the same 10 rows and scanned 0.76 KB.

DuckDB 1.5.5 reads the current metadata file that Glue points to:

aws glue get-table --database-name mysql_to_redshift_shop --name customers \
  --query 'Table.Parameters.metadata_location' --output text

INSTALL iceberg; LOAD iceberg;
INSTALL httpfs;  LOAD httpfs;
CREATE SECRET lake (TYPE s3, KEY_ID '<access key>', SECRET '<secret key>', REGION '<region>');
SELECT id, name, city, tier
FROM iceberg_scan('<metadata_location from the command above>')
ORDER BY id;

The orders roll-up matched MySQL to the cent in all three engines: 16 delivered for 8659.68, 18 placed for 10522.26 and 11 shipped for 6397.25.

Tips from the run

  • Binlog retention is the replay window. If a paused job outlives binlog_expire_logs_seconds, it needs a fresh snapshot. Seven days covers a job that runs at least daily, but size the disk for it.
  • Decimals arrive as doubles. DECIMAL(10,2) shows up as DOUBLE PRECISION in Redshift. The totals matched, but round at query time for exact decimal arithmetic.
  • Timestamps are UTC. datetime and timestamp become TIMESTAMP; json, enum and time arrive as VARCHAR.
  • Every query goes to S3. The external schema reads Parquet through Redshift Spectrum each time, so it does not match native table speed.
  • Primary keys matter. Tables without one replicate inserts, but updates and deletes cannot be matched to a row.
  • Plan for compaction. Each sync adds small files, and Glue does not compact tables written by external engines.

MySQL to Redshift methods side by side

Method Freshness Updates and deletes Where rows land What you run
Export, then COPY Hours to daily No, full reloads Native Redshift tables A script, a scheduler, a staging bucket
AWS DMS CDC through the binlog Yes Native Redshift tables A replication instance and task, plus a staging bucket
Zero-ETL integration Seconds Yes Native Redshift tables, Redshift only Nothing; Aurora MySQL and RDS for MySQL only
Managed ELT Minutes, by plan Varies by tool A second copy in Redshift Nothing; per row, per GB or per connector
OLake Go to Iceberg on Glue CDC on a schedule, down to one minute Yes, as positional deletes Iceberg tables Redshift, Athena and DuckDB read One Docker Compose stack and your bucket

If your MySQL is on Aurora or RDS and Redshift is the only reader, zero-ETL is less work. The route in this post earns its keep when the server lives elsewhere, or a second engine needs the same rows without another copy.

FAQ

What does the _op_type column tell me in Redshift?

It records how the current version of each row arrived. A row from the first snapshot carries r, an insert carries c and an update carries u. Filter the helper columns out of dashboards, or use them to see when a row last changed.

Can I insert or delete rows from the Redshift side?

No. The external schema is read-only, and INSERT or DELETE against these tables fails. OLake Go is the only writer, and MySQL stays the place where rows change.

Where do the Glue database name and the Redshift schema name come from?

The Glue database is the job name plus the source database, which gave mysql_to_redshift_shop here. The Redshift schema is whatever you name in CREATE EXTERNAL SCHEMA, lakehouse in this post. Change the Glue name through the Iceberg DB field before the first sync.

Who compacts the small files each sync leaves behind?

Not Glue, which has no built-in compaction for tables written by external engines. OLake Fusion compacts tables in the catalogs OLake Go writes to, and Spark on Amazon Elastic MapReduce (EMR) can run rewrite_data_files through the same Glue catalog.

Where to go from here

  • Swap the Docker MySQL for your real server. Only the way you set the binlog keys changes on RDS, Aurora, Cloud SQL or Azure.
  • Add more tables by ticking them on the job's Streams page, and run ANALYZE TABLE on each first.
  • Put the job on a schedule. It drains the binlog each run and never repeats the full copy.
  • The full guide, with the data type table, the CLI path and the troubleshooting list, is on olake.io.

If something in your setup does not match these steps, leave a comment and I will update the post.

title: Why Seal Surfaces Leak While the Ra Number Looks Fine
description:
A buyer sent us a leak test report last quarter. Twelve fittings, all VCR-type glands in 316L, all machined from certified bar, all showing Ra 0.4 µm on the inspection sheet. Six of them leaked at helium. The Ra number could not explain it, because Ra was never the problem.

This post is about what Ra does not measure, and why metal-to-metal seal surfaces fail in ways that show up only at leak test — long after the dimensional report said everything was good.

Ra is an average, and averages hide grooves

Ra integrates the absolute deviation of the profile from its mean line. A fine, uniform tool mark and a surface with one deep spiral scratch can share the same Ra. On a sealing land, that spiral scratch is the leak path: helium finds it, the average never did.

The second thing Ra ignores is lay — the direction of the dominant marks. A turned seal face has concentric marks, which sit crossways to the leak path and actually help sealing. A face that was turned and then lightly polished in a circular motion can end up with random lay and fine scratches radiating outward, worse for sealing than the turned surface despite a better Ra. I have seen that exact swap fail. I would not claim it always fails — the depths matter too — but it fails often enough that we stopped trusting polish as a finish step on seal lands.

Waviness is the third blind spot. Ra reads short wavelengths. A gland face that is slightly concave across its whole width — a few tenths of a micron of crown error from a tool deflection or a worn guide bushing — can read a beautiful Ra while the contact pressure line sits off the land. At flange dimensions under 1/2 inch, the sealing band is narrow, and a waviness error eats most of it.

What actually predicts a seal

In practice, three things decide whether a VCR-style joint seals:

First, flatness of the lands, checked on a granite surface plate or with an optical flat, not inferred from Ra. Second, the absence of directional scratches crossing the land — this is a handling and chucking problem as much as a machining one; a part dropped into a plastic bin with chips can pick up a line no cutter ever made. Third, surface texture fine enough and isotropic enough that the two metal faces conform under load. That last one is where electropolishing earns its cost: it removes the smeared, micro-cracked layer left by machining and reduces the asperity height, so the joint needs less seat load to close the remaining gaps.

What electropolishing does not do is fix geometry. It removes material roughly uniformly (slightly more on peaks, which helps), so if the face is not flat before the bath, it is not flat after. And it will soften an edge radius you may have wanted sharp. Sequence matters: machine, deburr, measure, polish, then re-measure the critical diameters, because the polish pull-down on a small gland OD is real — on the order of a couple of microns, which on some drawings is a tolerance you do not have to spend.

The inspection sequence we ask for

When a drawing says "Ra 0.4 on seal land" and nothing else, we quote asking for three additions: a flatness callout on the lands, a leak-based acceptance if the assembly is going to be tested (because a leak test at the fitting level correlates better than any surface metric), and a note on which features are measured before versus after polishing. None of this is exotic. It is mostly about deciding, before the first chip is cut, which measurement owns acceptance.

The failure reports we see in this product family almost never trace back to the cutting process itself. They trace back to handling between operations, to polishing done as a cosmetic step rather than a controlled one, and to drawings that specified Ra on a feature where flatness was the real requirement. One of those, the bin with chips, is embarrassingly cheap to fix and still shows up. I have no elegant explanation for why; shops are shops.

If you are buying fittings or any machined part with a sealing function, ask the supplier how they measure flatness, not just roughness. The answer tells you whether the leak test is going to be boring, which is exactly what you want a leak test to be.

title: Infraestrutura Client-Side vs. Server-Side em Ferramentas de Vendas: O Caso para a Manipulação de DOM
description:
Quando recebemos a tarefa de arquitetar uma ferramenta de produtividade para equipes comerciais que operam via mensagens instantâneas, o reflexo automático da engenharia é construir uma infraestrutura puramente server-side. Nós provisionamos um banco de dados relacional, estruturamos uma API robusta, configuramos webhooks para escutar eventos externos e entregamos um painel web independente. Nos diagramas de sistema, essa abordagem centralizada parece impecável. No entanto, quando esse software chega à rotina da equipe de vendas, a arquitetura colide frontalmente com o comportamento humano e a necessidade de velocidade operacional.

O Gargalo da Sincronização no Backend
O problema fundamental dos CRMs tradicionais e agregadores de mensagens é a dependência de uma sincronização contínua e pesada no servidor. Cada nova mensagem recebida precisa disparar um webhook, bater no backend corporativo, processar regras de negócio e emitir um evento via websockets para atualizar a interface de um dashboard de terceiros.

Essa arquitetura introduz uma latência de rede inevitável. Se o servidor enfrenta qualquer pico de processamento durante o horário comercial e a interface demora dois ou três segundos para renderizar a resposta do cliente, o ritmo da negociação é quebrado. Além do atraso técnico, retirar o vendedor da interface fluida do WhatsApp Web para confiná-lo em um painel externo impõe uma troca de contexto exaustiva. Quando a ferramenta adiciona esse nível de atrito, o usuário simplesmente abandona o sistema corporativo e volta a usar o aparelho celular para garantir o fechamento.

Injetando Lógica de Negócios Diretamente no DOM
Para desenvolver ferramentas comerciais que tenham adoção real, precisamos repensar onde a lógica da aplicação é executada. Em vez de extrair os dados do mensageiro para processá-los em um servidor remoto, a abordagem mais escalável é deslocar a camada de aplicação para o client-side.

Ao utilizar a manipulação de DOM diretamente no navegador, conseguimos injetar gestão de estado, organização visual e atalhos operacionais de forma nativa no ambiente que o usuário já domina. Esse paradigma técnico é a exata fundação do Zapext. Em vez de atuar como um agregador pesado que roteia mensagens por servidores externos e exige uma aba isolada, a ferramenta roda integralmente no navegador como uma extensão. O script intercepta a estrutura linear original do WhatsApp Web e a re-renderiza dinamicamente na máquina local como um quadro Kanban visual.

Latência Zero e Escalabilidade Financeira
As vantagens técnicas dessa inversão arquitetônica são imediatas. Como a aplicação se apoia na sessão web já autenticada pelo usuário, a latência de rede entre a ação comercial e a atualização visual do funil cai efetivamente para zero. Arrastar um lead entre etapas ou disparar blocos de texto ocorre de forma instantânea no processamento local, sem depender de respostas de APIs externas.

Além da performance, executar a lógica no cliente elimina gargalos de infraestrutura no servidor e contorna por completo os modelos punitivos de cobrança por sessão impostos pelas APIs oficiais de mensageria.

Construir tecnologia escalável para operações comerciais nem sempre exige o backend mais complexo ou o banco de dados mais robusto. Muitas vezes, a engenharia mais eficiente é aquela que reduz a fricção operacional ao mínimo, transferindo o peso do processamento para o navegador e respeitando o fluxo natural de trabalho do usuário final.

Vocês já precisaram migrar funcionalidades pesadas do backend para manipulação direta no DOM para resolver problemas de latência ou resistência de adoção pelos usuários?

title: Diagnosing MongoDB Search Performance with Atlas Metrics
description:
Your MongoDB Atlas metrics show elevated disk I/O, high search CPU, increasing query latency, or a rising search max replication lag. Like when your car’s mysterious “check engine” light comes on, these signals can mean different things. To figure out the issue, you’ll want to start by identifying which process and metric is under pressure.

Scaling the database tier may provide temporary relief, but it does not separate the search and operational workloads. When mongot and mongod share nodes, search can compete with database activity for memory, disk I/O, and CPU. The right response depends on whether the index does not fit in available memory, the workloads contend during traffic spikes, or possibly even both occurring simultaneously.

This post explains how to diagnose slow search performance, decide whether dedicated search nodes are the right fix, and size them correctly if they are.

Why tackling the underlying issue matters

The default response to slow search is often to scale up the database tier. More RAM and CPU can help the database portion of the workload, but they do not create a separate resource budget for search on a co-located deployment.

Two cases can produce similar symptoms, but they call for different responses. With index-size pressure, the Search index is larger than the memory available to mongot, so queries page data from disk even when database activity is low. A larger Search tier with enough memory addresses this problem; isolation by itself does not. With resource contention, the index fits in memory, but search latency rises when database reads, writes, or replication become busy. Separate search nodes address this contention by giving mongot different CPU, memory, and disk resources.

The distinction matters when you select a tier. Dedicated search nodes remove competition with database workloads, but they still need to be sized correctly.

Search nodes explained

MongoDB Search and MongoDB Vector Search use mongot, the search process that maintains and queries search indexes. mongod is the database process that stores application data and handles database operations. In a colocated deployment, both processes run on the same nodes.

Dedicated search nodes run mongot on separate infrastructure from the nodes running mongod. Dedicated search nodes provide workload isolation for search, similar to how Analytics Nodes isolate analytical workloads.

With dedicated search nodes, database nodes handle operational reads and writes while search nodes handle search queries and index work. Each workload gets its own memory budget, CPU capacity, and scaling lifecycle. This applies to both MongoDB Search and MongoDB Vector Search on Atlas.

Why colocated search runs into resource constraints

When mongot and mongod share nodes, memory and CPU are common sources of resource pressure. WiredTiger, the operating system, and mongot share RAM; if the index is larger than the memory available to mongot, queries may read index pages from disk. Search queries and background indexing also compete with database reads, writes, and replication for CPU time, so latency can rise even when the index fits in memory.

Atlas metrics help show which process is under pressure and whether the issue is paging or contention. Look at these signals together rather than treating any one metric as a diagnosis:

  • Search Page Fault, which reports average page faults per second in the Search process

  • Search Process Memory and Search Index Size compared with the node's RAM

  • Search Normalized Process CPU compared with Normalized System CPU

  • Search Process Throttling, which indicates that work is arriving faster than the Search process can admit it

  • Search query latency and Search Max Replication Lag

If database CPU and memory look healthy while Search metrics are under pressure, Search is consuming the resources available to it. That does not identify the root cause by itself. Compare index size with available memory to test for paging; compare latency and Search CPU with database activity to test for contention.

If page faults and latency stay high while the database is quiet, Search needs more memory. If latency only rises when the database gets busy, the two workloads are competing.

How dedicated search nodes separate search and database workloads

Memory isolation and cache performance

On a colocated node, the memory shown in the Atlas tier specification is shared. WiredTiger uses part of it for the database cache, the operating system and runtime need additional memory, and the remainder is available to mongot. The exact amount varies with tier and workload, and there is no fixed co-located cache size for mongot.

Dedicated search nodes give mongot a separate memory budget. MongoDB documentation describes approximately 90% of search node RAM as available for index data, with the remainder used by the JVM and other process needs. MongoDB Search indexes do not need to fit entirely in memory. A single query usually touches only part of the index, and the OS keeps the frequently used pages in RAM. MongoDB Vector Search is different and works best when the index fits in memory.

When there is sufficient memory to accommodate the majority of the index data, sustained page faults should reduce and latency should become more stable. If page faults remain high after migration to search nodes, the Search tier may still be undersized, or the workload may have another bottleneck. Isolation will help, but if this is an index sizing issue at the core, you may need to combine this approach with other techniques. Those techniques could include switching from dynamic mapping to static mapping on specific fields, using alternate tokenization strategies other than nGram for autocomplete fields, leveraging vector quantization for vector search indexes, and other actions needed to reduce the size of the index.

CPU separation and parallel segment search

Search queries and index updates can consume substantial CPU. Separate search nodes prevent database traffic from taking those cores during the same interval. For $search queries, parallel segment search can search multiple Lucene segments concurrently when enabled with the query's concurrent option. For $vectorSearch queries, concurrent segment search is on by default on search nodes. The Search tier's CPU count limits the parallelism available.

MongoDB Search might fall back to single-threaded execution when too many concurrent queries are queued. Treat parallel segment search as additional capacity, not as a guarantee that every query will run in parallel. Monitor query latency, Search Normalized Process CPU, and Search Process Throttling under representative concurrency.

No competition with operational traffic

Search Max Replication Lag means index staleness: How far behind mongot is in applying changes from the mongod oplog to a MongoDB Search or MongoDB Vector Search index. This is different from replica set replication lag, which measures how far secondary mongod members are behind the primary.

Isolation removes one cause of Search Max Replication Lag: Indexing work from mongot competing with mongod for CPU on the same node. It does not remove the indexing work. mongot still reads every change from mongod and applies it to the search index on search nodes.

Isolation does not resolve issues due to write-heavy workloads. Sustained write volumes and the amount of indexing work created by each change can increase index staleness. Factors include the number of indexed fields, autocomplete fields using nGram or edgeGram tokenizers, and embeddedDocuments mappings where one document change can rewrite many Lucene documents. Indexes get updated when their associated documents and fields change; minimally, one write to a document will generate at least one corresponding write to the index(es) (where the indexed field is updated). Schema changes or sharding may be required with dedicated nodes to optimally support the workload.

Replica set replication lag is separate. Search nodes may reduce CPU contention that affects the database, but they do not guarantee lower replica set lag or lower Search Max Replication Lag when write or indexing volume remains high.

Example: From page faults to consistent search performance

Consider a co-located M30 deployment with 8 GB of RAM per node. As an illustration rather than a fixed Atlas allocation, about 2 GB may go to the WiredTiger cache and at least 1 GB to the OS, mongod, connections, and other runtime needs, leaving about 5 GB or less for mongot. If the Search index is 6 GB, sustained Search Page Fault activity is highly likely. The database may show low CPU and healthy memory metrics while Search still reads index data from disk.

Before search nodes

In this example, the co-located deployment is an M30 with 8 GB RAM per node and a 6 GB Search index. Atlas metrics show sustained non-zero Search Page Fault during normal traffic, and search query latency p95 is 650 ms. Validate the estimated 5 GB or less available to mongot against the actual metrics.

After search nodes

Assume the workload moves to an S40 Search tier with 16 GB of RAM per node. Using the documented approximate 90% allocation as a planning estimate gives about 14.4 GB for index data, leaving room for a 6 GB index and query working set. Validate the tier's available memory and observed behavior in Atlas rather than treating the estimate as a guarantee.

After the move, the dedicated S40 Search tier has about 14.4 GB of memory available for the same 6 GB index. In this example, Search Page Fault falls after the index is resident, except during warm-up or workload changes, and search query latency p95 is 120 ms.

Performance improves once Atlas finishes building the index on the search nodes and routes queries to them. During the build, queries continue to use the existing colocated indexes, and index construction adds read load to the database cluster. Plan for that transition instead of expecting a change when the Search Nodes are first deployed.

When to move to dedicated search nodes

Dedicated search nodes are not necessary for every slow query: if an index fits comfortably in available memory and latency targets are met without contention, co-location may remain the simpler choice. The example above shows why a team might move when paging indicates that the Search index does not fit the memory budget. In production, look for a pattern across several signals before choosing a dedicated tier:

  • Sustained non-zero Search Page Fault with an index that approaches or exceeds available Search memory

  • Search Process Throttling remaining above zero, indicating that work is arriving faster than the Search process can admit it

  • High Search Normalized Process CPU or a high Search-to-system CPU ratio during query traffic

  • Search latency that rises when database activity increases

  • Search Max Replication Lag that rises with indexing activity, after ruling out write volume and index-mapping causes

  • Query latency targets that require consistent performance

  • Repeated database scaling to accommodate Search growth

On a colocated node, total disk I/O combines mongod and mongot activity, so disk IOPS alone is a weak signal for Search diagnosis. Start with Search Page Fault to attribute paging to the Search process, and use total disk IOPS as corroborating evidence.

Best practices

These checks make a tier decision more reliable: they help identify whether the bottleneck is memory, CPU, or indexing work, and when to plan the migration. Use the relevant metrics together, and account for the workload and operational requirements before changing deployment architecture.

  • Check Search Process Memory, Search Index Size, and Search Page Fault together when testing for memory pressure.

  • Check Search Normalized Process CPU, Normalized System CPU, latency, and Search Process Throttling together when testing for contention or saturation.

  • Treat Search Max Replication Lag as index staleness, and investigate replica set replication lag separately.

  • Size Search Nodes for both index memory and query or indexing CPU; plan for index growth and concurrency.

  • Confirm prerequisites before migration. Dedicated search nodes require an M10 or higher cluster, so upgrade a Flex cluster before attempting to use them.

  • Expect an index-building period before query routing changes, then monitor the search nodes after the cutover.

What workload isolation enables

Analytics nodes separate analytical workloads from operational database traffic. Dedicated search nodes apply the same workload-isolation model to MongoDB Search and MongoDB Vector Search, allowing each infrastructure tier to be sized for its own workload.

The result is easier diagnosis and more predictable behavior. Page faults can be addressed with sufficient Search memory, CPU contention can be addressed with isolation, and indexing lag can be investigated using write volume and index-mapping details rather than treated as a generic replication problem. Views for search indexes, quantization for vector indexes, sharding, and other techniques can also be used with isolation to further improve performance. Search index partitioning can also extend the capacity of supported deployments beyond a single index or node's limits; consult the current MongoDB documentation for those limits.

Next steps

Use the metrics to identify whether memory pressure, workload contention, or indexing volume is limiting performance. Then use the deployment guidance to assess the appropriate Search tier and plan a migration if dedicated nodes fit the diagnosis.

  • Review MongoDB Search metrics for Search Process Memory, Search Index Size, Search Page Fault, and Search Process Throttling.

  • Identify whether page faults indicate an index-memory problem or whether latency follows database activity and indicates contention.

  • Check Search Max Replication Lag and replica set replication lag as separate metrics with separate investigations.

  • Review tips for sizing and scaling Search Nodes and MongoDB Vector Search production sizing.

  • Account for index build time and the temporary read load before evaluating post-migration performance.

title: When Do Typed Decision Models Work in Transportation? Evidence from Travel Choice and Traffic Signal Control
description:
arXiv:2611.22926v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Typed decision models combine natural-language understanding with a structured interface that returns a selected action and an option-level probability distribution without generating lengthy textual responses. Their low inference cost and response latency make them attractive for transportation problems with predefined alternatives. This paper investigates their effectiveness, robustness, and efficiency in two representative transportation tasks: individual travel-mode choice prediction and sequential traffic signal control. We systematically evaluate TypeSafe Jev and GPT-6 Luna Decisions against conventional transportation methods, reinforcement learning algorithms, and four chat-based large language models. Experiments on the Swissmetro dataset show that typed decision models achieve lower prediction accuracy than traditional discrete choice models and the strongest chat-based baseline, while their performance varies substantially with input representation and question framing. In closed-loop traffic signal control experiments, typed decision models demonstrate competitive performance against established controllers in several scenarios, but exhibit performance degradation under more challenging network conditions. Furthermore, the typed models achieve lower inference latency and computational cost than the evaluated chat-based large language models, highlighting their potential for efficient, zero-shot transportation decision-making. Overall, these findings demonstrate both the potential and limitations of typed decision models, emphasizing the importance of input design, task characteristics, and robustness evaluation for their effective application in transportation systems.

title: From Ideal to Real: Integrating Language Models into Smart Home for Human-Centric IoT Safety and Security Fuzzing
description:
arXiv:2611.22457v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Integrating IoT devices into household systems offers enhanced control over living environments. However, as these devices become pervasive in critical sectors such as healthcare, transportation, and home automation, they expose inter-rule vulnerabilities that may lead to privacy breaches, data theft, and physical harm. Traditional fuzz testing methods, which often operate in simulated environments assuming ideal human decisions, fail to account for the complexities of human interactions that can influence device operations in smart homes, potentially leading to unforeseen consequences. To reveal the impact of real human decisions and discover unexpected inter-rule vulnerabilities, we introduce an enhanced version of IoT Fuzz for smart homes by integrating large language models to emulate human decision-making processes. Our novel approach adds a layer of realism and unpredictability to the testing environment, more accurately capturing the diverse and dynamic nature of human interactions in smart home settings.

title: Proximal Targets: Training Looped Refiners on Problems with Many Correct Answers
description:
arXiv:2611.22737v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Looped refiners such as HRM and TRM apply one small network repeatedly to a draft answer, and deep supervision trains every pass toward one stored answer per puzzle. We prove that when a puzzle has many correct answers this target sets a loss floor that no model capacity removes, and that the loss-minimising pass blends the answers into an invalid grid. We propose the proximal target: train each pass toward the correct answer nearest to its own input, found by scanning a list of answers, by a search solver started at the draft, or within a band of quality set by a knob; correct answers become fixed points, and a pass only has to make fewer errors than its input has for the loop to converge, which its training loss bounds. With the same 1.7M-parameter network and 5 seeds, the proximal target solves 98.8% of Sudoku puzzles with 2-64 answers (standard target: 2.5%), 93.8% of sparse puzzles with more than 10,000 answers without any list of answers (0.0%), and 90.9% of 200-node 3-colourings after training on graphs of at most 50 nodes (36.9%), and different random starts end at different answers. Against GRAM, a stochastic-latent reasoner, a single run is correct far more often (98.8% vs. 57.7%) and twenty runs find more of the answers (53.6% vs. 37.4%), while GRAM is slightly ahead on its own 10-node colouring benchmark; in Scrabble the knob becomes a calibrated strength dial.

title: What Does a Bias Head Measure? Non-Identifiability in Head-Level Bias Attribution
description:
arXiv:2611.23218v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Methods that localise social bias in large language models to individual attention heads and remove it by ablation are validated by their effect on a fairness metric, never by evidence that the statistic selecting the heads measures bias. We audit this on Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. The head map correlates at $\rho = -0.950$ and $-0.768$ with a label-blind response-length map, apparently identifying a surface confound. An intervention that breaks the length-label coupling rejects this reading: with the prompt held fixed, response length explains 1% of the statistic's variance. What does explain it is prompt identity, at 64% of variance, in an ordering that is not monotonic in length. Within any fixed prompt the fairness label, response length and the presence of a protected-group token are collinear at $\phi = 0.95$, partly by definition of the labelling rule, so no observational analysis can attribute the map to any of them, and no method in this family performs an experiment that could. The substantive claims fail independently: bias selectivity is not late-layer-concentrated on either model under either reference reading, and no head set we tested reduces the unfairness rate when ablated. Its complement, scored on the opposite label, reliably destroys refusal behaviour ($p = 2.7\times10^{-5}$), demonstrating that the pipeline detects effects at this scale.

title: Handling Time Zones in a Global Event Scheduler
description:
A scheduler that works in UTC and converts only at display time is the standard advice. It is also wrong for a subset of cases: recurring events that the user intends to happen at a local time regardless of DST shifts.

Store the intent, not the instant

For a one-off event, store a UTC timestamp. For a recurring event, store the local time plus the IANA zone:

interface RecurringEvent {
  localTime: string;  // "14:30"
  tz: string;         // "Australia/Sydney"
  rrule: string;      // "FREQ=DAILY"
}

When computing the next occurrence, resolve localTime in the given zone at that future date — not today's offset:

import { DateTime } from 'luxon';

function nextOccurrence(event: RecurringEvent): DateTime {
  const now = DateTime.now().setZone(event.tz);
  let next = now.set({ hour: 14, minute: 30, second: 0 });
  if (next <= now) next = next.plus({ days: 1 });
  return next;  // handles DST automatically
}

The Australia edge case

Australia has zones that shift by 30 minutes (Adelaide, +09:30 / +10:30). An event platform serving Australian users like Herovegas needs to handle half-hour offsets; truncating to whole hours breaks scheduling twice a year.

Display

Always show the user's local time first, with an optional UTC parenthetical:

Starts: 2:30 PM AEDT (03:30 UTC)

Never show just UTC — most users cannot do the conversion in their head, especially with half-hour offsets.

Takeaway

UTC-only storage is correct for instants. For recurring events, store the zone and resolve lazily. The two patterns coexist in any non-trivial scheduler.

title: Java4Shell, deux jours de panne Microsoft - QDNLD #192
description:
Ta dose d'infos tech infusée par un dev pour les devs — Numéro du 19 novembre 2026

EDITO

Il y a un moment, dans chaque boîte, où quelqu'un demande « c'est qui qui gère ce serveur ? ». Et personne ne répond.

C’est un petit peu le sujet récurrent de la semaine écoulée, et si tu trouves que j'exagère, va demander autour de toi qui possède la page de statut de ton propre produit 😉

Java4Shell d'abord, CVE-2026-114938, parce que c'est le plus large. Une corruption mémoire dans le décodeur Base64 accéléré de HotSpot, corrigée par Oracle le 17 novembre. Calif l'a trouvée avec de l'aide de l'IA et a démontré de l'exécution de code sans authentification sur Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, Keycloak, JFrog Artifactory et PingFederate. Deux conditions quand même : il faut un x86-64 avec AVX-512 VBMI, les ARM64 ne sont pas concernés, et chaque produit demande sa propre charge utile. La CISA, le CERT-FR et le BACS suisse te disent de patcher sans attendre. Ce qui m'a arrêté, ce n'est pas la gravité : c'est le composant. Un décodeur Base64 dans une JVM, personne ne le range dans la catégorie « surface d'attaque ». Il est là depuis des années, il ne bouge pas, il marche.

Microsoft a passé près de 36 heures par terre sur Exchange, Teams, SharePoint et Copilot, dans plus de 70 pays. Un bug introduit en juillet dans les passerelles réseau, un basculement Teams par-dessus, et 14 % de capacité déjà hors service. Pas d'attaque. Des couches qui s'empilent, et un incident qui dure parce que personne ne sait plus quelle couche fait quoi — ni à qui la demander quand elle tombe un mardi matin.

Puis les données. Fireworks AI, fournisseur d'inférence pour modèles open-weight, s'est fait ouvrir par effraction : les chats Notion d'environ 1 % des clients, et 149 346 chauffeurs Uber dont le permis de conduire est dehors. Rakuten Securities a perdu les identifiants de 11,25 millions de comptes, via un environnement de test qui contenait des données bien réelles. Fugaku, le supercalculateur japonais, atteint par sa page publique d'état : 4 222 utilisateurs doivent changer leurs clés SSH, et elles ont déjà servi ailleurs.

Tu vois le point commun ? Ce n'est jamais le cœur. C'est la couture — le décodeur que personne ne relit, la passerelle que personne ne possède, le fournisseur qu'on n'audite pas, l'environnement de test qu'on croit isolé, la page de statut qu'on a mise en ligne pour rassurer et que plus personne n'ouvre depuis dix-huit mois.

La Californie attaque OpenAI pour la même raison, mais à l'envers : 80 incidents de perte de contrôle reconnus, dont 27 publics, et l'accusation de les avoir testés sans garde-fous.

Bref. Voilà. N’oublie pas de patcher ta JVM. Et pendant que tu y es, va demander qui possède ta page de statut, la réponse risque de te plaire.

L'invité de la semaine

Cette semaine, je reçois Christophe Cassin, Tok-Ra sur X.

41 ans, IS et IT Manager chez Louis Vuitton aux États-Unis, installé dans la banlieue de Dallas. Et un parcours qui ne ressemble à aucun autre : pas de diplôme, un BEP électronique abandonné en route, dix ans de casinos et de roulettes automatiques connectées, un détour par l'électronique embarquée dans l'automobile, puis un retour dans l'IT par la grande porte il y a neuf ans.

Il explique comment il tient ce poste sans diplôme, ce qu'il pense vraiment de l'IA dans cinq ans, et pourquoi il n'a pas envie de rentrer.

Voici ses conseils si tu débutes dans le métier :

Il est obligatoire d'effectuer une veille constante. Notre métier évolue tous les jours, avec des périodes de forte progression, si tu rate un seul virage, t'es dépassé.

Si ensuite tu trouves un domaine qui te fait vibrer alors deviens expert, on a toujours besoin des experts.

Pour le dev, embrasse le virage IA à fond, on est en train de revivre un bouleversement, le même qu'à l'époque de l'arrivée d'internet à grande échelle, demain on ne cherchera plus des pisseurs de code, et c'est pas du tout péjoratif, mais on cherchera un maître d'orchestre qu'est capable de faire bosser des IA, et surtout qui comprend ce qui en ressort.
