title: CoScan: Multi-Scale Content-Adaptive Space-Filling Scans for Causal State-Space Image Restoration
description:
arXiv:2611.23717v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Selective state-space models (SSMs) have recently shown strong potential for efficient image restoration. A central difficulty, however, is that a 2D feature map typically needs to be linearized into a 1D token sequence for causal state-space updates, making restoration performance highly sensitive to the imposed scan order. Existing deterministic scans follow space-filling principles but remain fixed and content-agnostic, and can yield fragmented or semantically inconsistent contexts under degradations. We propose \textbf{CoScan}, a \textbf{co}ntent-adaptive \textbf{scan}-order design for causal vision SSMs. CoScan learns image-dependent space-filling traversals via differentiable proxy supervision driven by \textbf{scan-quality objectives} that \textit{encourage short-range coherence and causal predictability, while preserving spatial adjacency}. To support hierarchical restoration backbones, we introduce an \textbf{efficient multi-scale scan construction by coarsening a fine-level minimum spanning tree}, producing coherent scans across feature resolutions. In addition, a \textbf{frequency-guided start selection strategy} is designed to \textit{place informative structures early in the sequence prefix to strengthen causal context formation}. Plugged into existing Mamba-based backbones, CoScan yields consistent improvements across several restoration benchmarks with minimal overhead and shows promising results on high-level vision tasks. Code will be released at https://github.com/dongw22/CoScan

title: What's in a Tree ? Hierarchical $n$-gram models as controlled approximators of language
description:
arXiv:2611.23093v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Hierarchical models have been proposed as synthetic settings for studying language. However, their relevance to realistic language corpora remains underexplored. In this work, we introduce tree-grams, autoregressive generative $n$-gram models that build the conditional probability tensor $p(x_n \mid x_{1:n-1})$ through a hierarchical composition of order-2 and order-3 tensors. $n$ controls the maximal context window, whereas a rank hyperparameter $d$ controls model capacity, yielding an interpretable and systematically scalable family of approximators of language. We show how tree-grams outperform existing $n$-gram baselines, while remaining competitive with deep transformer-based language models. We demonstrate the utility of such controlled approximations by using tree-grams as generative models. In particular, we show that hyperparameter transfer under $\mu$P can be made more robust when narrower models are tuned on simpler data, generated by tree-grams with moderate $n$ and $d$. In addition, we show that entropy and effective range of correlations control performance gap after fine-tuning. This is because tree-grams allow us to explicitly control horizon and capacity. When allowed to route across candidate topologies, we observe emergent sparsity in tree-grams. Such concentrated routing permits pruning upto 95\% of topologies without significant change in performance.

title: How I built a browser-local batch image workflow with Canvas and ZIP
description:
Preparing product images is rarely one operation. You may need to fit every image into the same canvas, choose a background color, convert formats, rename the files, and download the set. Repeating those steps for each file is tedious.

I built a batch product image workflow for PNGDock to put those operations in one browser session. This post covers the implementation choices and the limits I had to make explicit. The workflow is free to try without an account. Its image processing and ZIP creation happen in the browser; the selected images are not uploaded for this workflow.

Start with limits, not the processing loop

The tool accepts PNG, JPEG, and WebP files. At present, it caps a batch at 20 files, 12 MB per file, 80 MB of source files in total, and 32 megapixels per image. It also caps the combined output size for a ZIP at 150 MB.

Those limits are part of the design. A compressed source file can decode into a much larger bitmap, and a browser may hold the decoded image, canvas, encoded output, and ZIP data at different points in the workflow. A file-size check alone cannot protect memory usage.

Each candidate file is checked before entering the queue. The tool verifies its extension and reported MIME type, tries to decode it, reads its dimensions, and rejects images above the pixel limit. Browser-side validation is still not a security boundary for a server, but here it keeps the local workflow from accepting inputs it is unlikely to handle well.

Decode and process one image at a time

The processing loop is sequential. For each file, it creates an ImageBitmap when the browser supports it, with an image-element fallback. It draws the decoded image into a target-size canvas, encodes the result, then releases the bitmap and clears the canvas dimensions.

The core fit calculation is small:

const scale = fit === "cover"
  ? Math.max(targetWidth / image.width, targetHeight / image.height)
  : Math.min(targetWidth / image.width, targetHeight / image.height);

const drawWidth = image.width * scale;
const drawHeight = image.height * scale;

context.drawImage(
  image,
  (targetWidth - drawWidth) / 2,
  (targetHeight - drawHeight) / 2,
  drawWidth,
  drawHeight
);

cover fills the canvas and crops the overflow. contain keeps the whole image visible and may leave empty space around it. The user can keep that space transparent or fill it with white or a chosen color. For JPEG output, a transparent choice becomes white because JPEG has no alpha channel.

One important distinction: a canvas background is not background removal. If the source photo contains a wall or a tabletop, choosing white does not cut the subject out. The page says this plainly, because the two operations are easy to confuse.

Encode according to the selected format

The browser's canvas.toBlob() handles the initial PNG, JPEG, or WebP encoding. A quality control applies to JPEG and WebP. PNG output gets an additional pass through an OxiPNG WebAssembly module, and the tool keeps the optimized file only if it is smaller than the initial PNG.

This still does not guarantee that every output will be smaller than its input. Dimensions, image content, format, and the source file's existing compression all matter. The interface shows source and result sizes so the user can compare them.

I also invalidate previous results when an export setting changes. Otherwise, a queue could silently contain files rendered with different dimensions or formats while presenting them as one batch.

Build the ZIP locally

Each successful result can be downloaded separately. For the whole set, the tool builds a ZIP in the browser. It writes ZIP local file headers, CRC-32 checksums, a central directory, and an end-of-central-directory record, then creates a Blob for download.

The ZIP entries use the already encoded image bytes. ZIP does not need to compress those bytes again, which is useful because PNG, JPEG, and WebP are already compressed formats.

Generated names are sanitized, length-limited, and made unique even when two source files would produce the same output name. A failed image stays visible in the queue and can be retried without discarding successful results. The user can also stop after the image currently being processed.

What browser-local actually means

The image bytes stay in the browser for this particular workflow. That does not mean the site makes zero network requests: it still loads the application code, and ordinary site analytics may send non-image events. It means this workflow does not send the selected image content to an image-processing server.

There are trade-offs. A large batch can still consume substantial memory, processing speed depends on the user's device, and a browser tab can be closed before export. The current limits and sequential loop are deliberate ways to keep those risks manageable, not claims that the browser can process arbitrarily large collections.

If you build similar tools, I would test the failure paths early: a corrupt file in the middle of a batch, two names that collide after sanitization, a PNG whose optimized version is larger, and a ZIP that crosses the output cap. The happy path is only half of the experience.

The live workflow and source repository are available if you want to inspect or try the implementation. I would be interested in hearing which browser-side failure cases or memory constraints you have run into with batch image tools.

Disclosure: This article was drafted with AI assistance and checked against the PNGDock project source. Please review the implementation details and wording before publishing.

title: Tic-Tac-Toe Minimax Algorithm in Java
description:
In Part 1, I built a tic-tac-toe bot with a layered brain: 7 small strategies, asked one by one. It worked. I couldn't beat it anymore. But it was hard to scale. A bigger board needs more conditions, and every new condition is one more place for things to break.

It also couldn't really look ahead. Only two of the strategies, Fork and BlockFork, thought about the next move. The rest just read the board as it is right now.

So this time I threw all 7 rules away to make a single rule.

The idea: play every game

Instead of teaching the bot tic-tac-toe, we let it imagine every possible game from here, and pick the move that leads to the best ending.

Every finished game gets a score:

  • Bot wins → positive
  • Human wins → negative
  • Draw → 0

Then both players take turns inside the bot's head. On the bot's turn, it picks the highest score (maximize). On the human's turn, it assumes the human picks the lowest (minimize). That's where the name comes from: minimax.

One thing to be clear about: the bot doesn't play for the "highest chance" of winning. It assumes the human plays perfectly, and picks the best result it can guarantee.

I didn't come up with this. It's a classic algorithm, I just happened to read about it and implement it. It also has a few variations that make it even better, more on those at the end.

How the minimax algorithm works

makeMove: try every cell

makeMove is the bot's turn. We go over the board, and for every empty cell we place the bot there, ask minimax how good that is, and take the move back. The cell with the best score is our move.

for (int i = 0; i < board.getSize(); i++) {
    for (int j = 0; j < board.getSize(); j++) {
        if (!board.getCell(i, j).isEmpty()) continue;

        // bot just moved here, so it's the human's turn next
        Cell cell = board.getCell(i, j);
        cell.setPlayer(bot);
        int current = minimax(board, 0, false, bot, winCheck);
        cell.clearCell();

        if (score < current) {
            score = current;
            bestMove = cell;
        }
    }
}

Notice the false. The bot has just moved, so minimax starts from the human's reply.

minimax: base conditions first

minimax uses recursion, and the first thing a recursive approach needs is a base condition. I repeat: don't forget to add an exit condition to a recursive function.

Before anything else, minimax checks if the game is already over: bot win, human win, or a draw. If it is, it returns the score.

If not, we keep playing. On the bot's turn we try every empty cell with the bot and keep the highest score. On the human's turn we do the same with the human and keep the lowest.

if (winCheck.isWinner(bot))   return 10 - depth;
if (winCheck.isWinner(human)) return depth - 10;
if (winCheck.isDraw())        return 0;

if (isBotTurn) {
    int maxValue = Integer.MIN_VALUE;
    // for every empty cell:
    cell.setPlayer(bot);
    maxValue = Math.max(maxValue, minimax(board, depth + 1, false, bot, winCheck));
    cell.clearCell();
    return maxValue;
} else {
    // same thing with the human, using Math.min
}

(Ignore the depth for now, we'll get to it.)

Place, try, take it back

This is the part that makes it "imagining". The bot plays moves on the real board, and takes each one back right after: setPlayer → minimax → clearCell.

If you forget the clearCell, every imagined move stays on the board, and by the end of the search the board is full of pieces nobody really played.

You could make a copy of the board and use that too, so that your real games don't get affected.

The bugs I hit

My first version had the right idea, but it was full of small mistakes:

  • The win check didn't say who won. It returned 1 for any winner, so to the bot, the human winning looked just as good as the bot winning.
  • No undo. I set cells but never cleared them, so tried moves piled up on the board.
  • The min branch never returned. It computed minValue, then fell through to return 0. Every human turn looked like a draw, so the bot never saw a threat coming.
  • true instead of false. In makeMove I passed isBotTurn = true right after the bot's move, so the bot played twice in a row in its own head.

Why makeMove has its own loop

This was my first question. minimax already loops over the cells on the bot's turn. Why not just call it once from makeMove?

Because minimax only returns a score. It can tell you "the best the bot can get is a draw", but not which cell gets there. By the time it returns, every cell has been cleared again.

And what if we keep the loop, but don't set the cell? Then every call sees the exact same board, every cell gets the same score, and the bot always picks the first empty cell. Setting the cell is what makes the score belong to that cell.

(You can make minimax return the cell too, but the cell only matters at the top level. Deeper down, the number is all you need.)

Problem 1: the bot can look silly → depth scoring

With plain 1 / -1, a win right now and a win three moves from now look exactly the same to the bot. So sometimes it skips the obvious win and takes the long route. It still wins, but to a human it looks like a mistake.

The fix: count how deep we are in the search, and use it in the score.

if (winCheck.isWinner(bot))   return 10 - depth;   // sooner win = higher score
if (winCheck.isWinner(human)) return depth - 10;   // later loss = less bad

Now the bot prefers the fastest win. And if it's ever losing, it picks the slowest loss and makes the human work for it.

Problem 2: it's slow on bigger boards → depth limit and alpha-beta pruning

Minimax tries every possible game. On 3×3 that's fine, the first move on an empty board takes well under a second. On 4×4 the number of games explodes.

Here's how fast it grows. The first move has every cell to pick from, the next one has one less, and so on. So the number of ways to play out a full board is cells × (cells - 1) × … × 1, or cells!

Grid Empty cells Ways to play out the board Compared to 3×3
3×3 9 362,880 1×
4×4 16 ~20.9 trillion ~58 million×
5×5 25 ~1.55 × 10²⁵ ~43 billion billion×

This is an upper bound. Real games end early when someone wins, so the bot searches fewer. But the growth is the point: one extra row and column, and 3×3's "well under a second" turns into millions of times more work.

The usual fix is a depth limit: stop searching after a few moves and estimate how good the board looks. That needs a way to score unfinished boards, which my code doesn't have yet. Another fix is alpha-beta pruning, which skips branches that can't change the result.

On 3×3 the bot doesn't need either, so I've left both out.

Seeing it think

I also added one small print to the bot, so every move says which strategy picked it:

BOT is playing 0 0 (by MiniMaxStrategy)

Is it really unbeatable?

Instead of trusting my own games against it, I made two bots play each other: 100 games per match, swapping who moves first every game.

  • Against my Part 1 rule-based bot (win → block → fork → block fork → center → corner): 100 draws. Both sides play almost perfectly, so nobody wins.
  • Against a bot that just makes random moves: 88 wins, 12 draws, 0 losses. Minimax wins when the opponent makes mistakes. 
Results after 100 games:        Results after 100 games:
ALICE (rules) wins: 0           RANDY (random) wins: 0
BOB (minimax) wins: 0           CAROL (minimax) wins: 88
Draws: 100                      Draws: 12

200 games, zero losses. The best anyone can do against it is a draw.

Rules vs minimax

My rules (Part 1) Minimax
How it works Hand-written tic-tac-toe knowledge Tries every possible game
Speed Instant Slower (it searches everything)
Looks ahead Only Fork and BlockFork Every move, to the end of the game
Works on 3×3 only, really Any board (with a depth limit)

Wrapping up

Same unbeatable bot. Zero tic-tac-toe knowledge. Seven rules replaced by one recursive function.

If you want to take it further, alpha-beta pruning and a depth limit are where to start.

The full code is on GitHub: system-design/lld/tic-tac-toe

title: Weight Space Programming for Vision Language Model Repair
description:
arXiv:2611.23615v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In weight-space programming, a language model edits a network's weights directly, without gradients. We ask what a successful repair of this kind relies on. We plant faults in the weights of two vision-language models, SmolVLM-256M and LFM2-VL-450M, and check each edit made by a coding agent against the original weights. Without being told where to look, the agent finds rescaled rows in the projector and noise in the vision encoder of both models, infers the unknown scale factors, restores most or all of the rescaled weights to their exact original values, and returns accuracy to near its original level; programs that it writes from such weights repair unseen checkpoints of the same model without feedback. These repairs depend on a trace of how the faults were computed. The original weights have 16-bit precision, and faults computed in 32-bit arithmetic leave low bits that only the damaged weights carry. Rounding those bits away leaves each model's answers to our test questions unchanged, and the agent, unaided, then restores no weight exactly: on SmolVLM it no longer finds the damage, and in a single session on LFM2-VL its only gain comes from rescaling answer-token embeddings, which changes how often the model answers yes. Marking the damaged weights again in their low bits brings the edits back to them. Rounded weights still hold statistical evidence of the rescaling, in the distribution of stored values and in row norms, and one sentence in the prompt that names such a statistic directs the agent's edits to the damaged rows on both models. Swapped rows or columns, which leave the set of stored values unchanged, are not found unaided on either model within our session budgets. We recommend that studies of weight repair report the number format of the weights and include a rounded control.

title: Figma Code Layer Animation: Make Captured Hovers, Transitions and Keyframes Play
description:
Originally published on Crafttor.

TL;DR: A Figma frame can look exactly like a web page, but it cannot run the page's CSS. Hover states, transitions and keyframe animations need a browser engine. A Figma code layer animation runs that CSS for real. Capture the page with WebCapture to Figma, keep the frame for editing, and put the same page in a code layer when the motion has to play.

You import a polished landing page into Figma. The layout, gradients and buttons are right. Then you press present and hover a button. Nothing happens.

That is not a bug in your capture. It is the difference between a drawing of a page and a page that runs.

Why a Figma frame cannot play CSS animation

A Figma prototype has its own interaction model. You draw variants, connect them with triggers such as "while hovering" or "on click", and pick a Smart Animate or dissolve transition. It is a good system for designing new interactions.

CSS works differently. A hover in CSS is a rule like this:

.card {
  transition: transform 200ms ease-out, box-shadow 200ms ease-out;
}
.card:hover {
  transform: translateY(-4px);
  box-shadow: 0 12px 24px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.12);
}

A keyframe animation is a named timeline the browser runs on its own:

@keyframes float {
  0%, 100% { transform: translateY(0); }
  50% { transform: translateY(-8px); }
}
.badge { animation: float 3s ease-in-out infinite; }

Figma's prototype engine does not read selectors, pseudo classes or @keyframes. So a Figma prototype cannot replay CSS animations, however faithful the frame looks. To rebuild them as prototype interactions, you would draw a variant for every state and wire each trigger by hand.

Where WebCapture puts the motion

When you import a page with WebCapture to Figma, it detects hover states, transitions, CSS keyframe animations, scroll reveal effects and sticky or fixed positioning. It saves them with each layer as plugin data.

So on the frame, the motion is recorded, not lost. The data travels with the layer. But a frame is still a frame. It shows the resting state, and the motion waits for something that can run it.

That something is a code layer. As the plugin puts it: a frame looks like the page, a code layer runs it.

Behaviour On the imported frame In a code layer
Layout, colours, type, icons Editable layers Rendered by real HTML and CSS
Hover states Recorded as plugin data Play when you hover
Transitions Recorded as plugin data Play with their real timing
Keyframe animations Recorded as plugin data Loop as on the live site
Links Prototype connections Work as links

If you want the full background on capturing the motion itself, read how to capture hover states and CSS animations from any website. This post is about the next step: making that motion play inside Figma.

Two routes to a Figma code layer animation

After an import, the plugin offers two ways to carry the page into a runnable form. Both keep your editable frame untouched.

Route 1: Download HTML

Download HTML saves the page as a ready to run HTML, CSS and JS project. Its images and Google fonts are inside the project. Hover states, CSS animations and links work in it. If you recorded a flow with the Chrome extension, it replays too.

Open it in a browser and you have a local, working copy of the motion to study and tweak.

Route 2: Copy prompt for Claude

Copy prompt gives Claude, with the Figma MCP connected, everything it needs to add that project as a code layer beside your frame.

There is a reason Claude does the last step. Figma plugins cannot create code layers themselves, because the Plugin API has no way to make one. So the plugin prepares everything, and Claude finishes the job through the MCP.

Here is the flow:

  1. Import the page with WebCapture to Figma at the width you need.
  2. Run Copy prompt from the plugin after the import.
  3. Paste the prompt into Claude with the Figma MCP connected.
  4. Let Claude add the code layer next to your frame.
  5. Set the code layer to the size the prompt names. Code layers cannot be resized from the API, so you do this by hand.
  6. Press play and hover the elements that should move.

For a longer walkthrough of this route, see turning a website into a runnable Figma code layer.

Check the motion once it plays

Once the code layer is running, test it like you would test a staging build. A short checklist helps:

  • Hover every interactive element. Buttons, cards, nav links and icons. Each one should change the way it does on the live site.
  • Watch the timing. A 200ms ease out should feel quick and settled. If it feels sluggish, compare with the live page in a browser tab.
  • Let loops run. Keyframe animations with infinite should keep cycling without a visible jump at the loop point.
  • Scroll the layer. Scroll reveal effects and sticky headers depend on scrolling inside the layer, so scroll the whole page.
  • Click links. They should still go where they went on the live page.
  • Compare against the frame. The resting state in the code layer should match the frame beside it.

If something does not play, open the downloaded project in a desktop browser first. If it plays there, the issue is the layer size or setup. If it does not play there either, inspect the CSS. Our guide to inspecting CSS animations in Chrome DevTools shows how to slow an animation down and read its curve.

Editing the animation, not just viewing it

A running code layer is not the end of the road. Because it is real code, you can change the motion directly.

Common edits designers make:

  • Shorten a slow transition. Change transition: transform 400ms to 200ms for a snappier hover.
  • Swap the easing. Try cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.8, 0.2, 1) for a softer settle than plain ease.
  • Respect reduced motion. Wrap the decorative loops in a media query so users who ask for less motion get it: 
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .badge { animation: none; }
}
  • Tone down the lift. A translateY(-4px) might become -2px for a calmer product UI.

Keep your edits small and check each one by hovering in the layer. That way you always know which change caused what.

Frame and code layer: use both

You do not have to choose. Use the frame to edit copy, swap images, adjust spacing and hand off values. Use the code layer to show how the page feels and to test CSS motion edits without leaving Figma.

One practical habit: name them clearly, for example "Pricing page / frame" and "Pricing page / code layer". Then nobody edits the frame expecting the motion to update.

Capture or rebuild only designs you own or have permission to use.

Privacy and cost, briefly

The URL you enter is rendered on Apify with your own API token, and a free Apify account is enough to start. Nothing from your Figma file is uploaded. For pages behind a login, use the Chrome extension, which needs no token. The plugin never sends anything to an AI, and it is free.

Try it on a page with real motion

Pick a page you own with a few hover effects and one looping animation. Import it, run Copy prompt, and put the code layer beside the frame. Then hover. The difference between "recorded" and "playing" is obvious within a few seconds.

Get WebCapture to Figma on the Figma Community and make your captured motion play.

FAQ

Why do my imported hover states not work in Figma's prototype mode?

A Figma prototype cannot replay CSS animations. WebCapture records hovers, transitions and keyframes as plugin data on each layer, but they only play in a code layer or in the downloaded HTML project.

Can the WebCapture plugin create the code layer by itself?

No. The Figma Plugin API has no way to create a code layer. The plugin prepares a prompt, and Claude with the Figma MCP connected adds the code layer for you.

Why is my code layer the wrong size?

Code layers cannot be resized from the API. Set the layer to the size named in the prompt, then press play.

Do scroll reveals and sticky headers work too?

WebCapture detects scroll reveal effects and sticky or fixed positioning and saves them with each layer. In a running code layer, scroll inside the layer to see them.

Is my Figma file sent anywhere?

No. Nothing from your Figma file is uploaded. Only the URL you enter is sent to Apify to be rendered.

title: Diagnose Vercel CLI setup problems with vercel doctor
description:
Vercel CLI now includes vercel doctor, which checks your setup and shows the command that fixes each problem it finds.

It checks the CLI version and install, your login and current team, the project link, and your project configuration in vercel.json. It also reports active incidents from the Vercel status page.

Each check reports OK, Warning, Failed, or Skipped. When vercel upgrade can't update the installed CLI, the install check shows where the CLI runs from and how to reinstall it.

Doctor runs without a login or a linked project, and it never prompts, logs in, or links a project, so coding agents can run it before guessing at a fix. Add --json to get each check's status and suggested commands as structured output.

Update to the latest CLI version and run vercel doctor to check your setup, or read the doctor command reference.

title: مستويات التفكير في Gemini 4 Neon: متى تستخدم High مقابل xhigh
description:
تتيح لك مستويات التفكير في Gemini 4 Neon أربعة إعدادات تحدد مدى عمق استدلال النموذج قبل أن يجيب: low وmedium وhigh وxhigh. القيمة الافتراضية في Neon هي high. وتوصي Google بالاحتفاظ بـhigh في معظم الأعمال المعقدة، والانتقال إلى xhigh فقط عندما يخفق high في المسائل الصعبة متعددة الخطوات، لأن xhigh يستهلك عددًا أكبر من الرموز ويستغرق وقتًا أطول.

{% cta https://apidog.com/?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation %}
جرّب Apidog اليوم
{% endcta %}

ما هي مستويات التفكير في Gemini 4 Neon؟

مستويات التفكير هي قيم المعامل thinking_level التي تحدد مقدار الاستدلال الداخلي الذي يقوم به gemini-4-neon قبل كتابة الرد. يدعم Neon أربعة مستويات: low وmedium وhigh (الافتراضي) وxhigh. تستهلك المستويات الأعلى رموز تفكير أكثر وتضيف زمن استجابة، بينما تجيب المستويات الأدنى بسرعة أكبر وبتكلفة أقل.

إليك كيف يصف دليل التفكير من Google كل مستوى بالنسبة إلى Neon:

thinking_level استهلاك الرموز الاستخدام المقترح من Google
low أقل عدد من الرموز، وأقل زمن استجابة الدردشة السريعة، والمعالجة عالية الإنتاجية؛ ولا يزال قادرًا على المهام الوكيلية
medium استهلاك أقل للرموز، واستجابات أسرع البرمجة التفاعلية، والنماذج الأولية للواجهات المباشرة، واستدعاءات الأدوات الحساسة لزمن الاستجابة
high (الافتراضي) توازن بين الذكاء والسرعة البرمجة المعقدة، والتنفيذ الوكيلي، واستدعاء الأدوات، والعمل المعرفي متعدد الوسائط
xhigh أكبر عدد من الرموز، وأعمق استدلال الهندسة الصعبة متعددة الخطوات، والمشكلات التحليلية والعلمية التي يخفق فيها high

هناك قيمتان قد تتوقعهما لكنهما غائبتان. يرفض Neon القيمة minimal ويعيد خطأً، لذا فإن أي كود منسوخ من تطبيق Gemini 3 Flash سيتعطل إذا أرسل هذه القيمة. كذلك أصبح عدد الرموز القديم thinkingBudget مهجورًا في Gemini 4: فعند إرساله منفردًا، يُترجم إلى أقرب مستوى مع تحذير؛ وعند إرساله مع thinkingLevel، يعيد الخطأ 400.

كيف يقارن المستوى الافتراضي في Neon بغيره من نماذج Gemini 4؟

يبدأ Neon بدرجة أعلى من أشقائه الأكبر. ووفقًا لـملاحظات إصدار Gemini 4 Neon، فإن Neon وHydrogen يستخدمان high افتراضيًا ويدعمان xhigh، في حين يستخدم Carbon وArgon القيمة medium افتراضيًا ويقتصران على high كحد أقصى.

النموذج المستوى الافتراضي المستويات المدعومة
gemini-4-neon high low، medium، high، xhigh
gemini-4-hydrogen high low، medium، high، xhigh
gemini-4-carbon medium low، medium، high
gemini-4-argon medium low، medium، high

وهذا مهم عند تبديل النماذج. فإذا نقلت عبئًا من Carbon إلى Neon دون تعيين thinking_level، فسيرتفع كل طلب من الاستدلال بمستوى medium إلى high، ما يغيّر عدد رموزك. وإذا كنت توازن بين النماذج الأكبر، فإن مقارنتنا بين Gemini 4 Carbon وArgon تغطي هذا الفارق.

كيف تعيّن thinking_level في Gemini API؟

يعمل Neon على الطبقة المدفوعة من كلٍّ من Interactions API وgenerateContent. ويختلف اسم الحقل بينهما.

Interactions API: ضع thinking_level داخل generation_config.

curl "https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/interactions" \
  -H "x-goog-api-key: $GEMINI_API_KEY" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -X POST \
  -d '{
    "model": "gemini-4-neon",
    "input": "Audit this payment retry queue for race conditions.",
    "generation_config": {
      "thinking_level": "xhigh",
      "max_output_tokens": 65536
    }
  }'

generateContent: استخدم thinkingLevel داخل generationConfig.thinkingConfig.

curl "https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/models/gemini-4-neon:generateContent" \
  -H "x-goog-api-key: $GEMINI_API_KEY" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -X POST \
  -d '{
    "contents": [{"parts": [{"text": "Audit this payment retry queue for race conditions."}]}],
    "generationConfig": {
      "thinkingConfig": {"thinkingLevel": "medium"}
    }
  }'

في حزمة Python SDK، يأخذ استدعاء Interactions الوسيط generation_config={"thinking_level": "high"}، ويأخذ استدعاء generateContent الوسيط thinking_config=types.ThinkingConfig(thinking_level="low"). اترك temperature وtop_p وtop_k خارج الطلب: إذ تقول Google إن Neon يتجاهل القيم ضمن النطاق ويرفض القيم الخارجة عنه بالخطأ 400. للحصول على دليل كامل للطلب الأول على نفس تصميم الـAPI، راجع دليل Gemini 4 Hydrogen API.

متى تستخدم high مقابل xhigh؟

استخدم high افتراضيًا، ولا ترقّ مهمة إلى xhigh إلا بعد أن يخفق high في معيار الجودة لديك. ويصف منشور الإطلاق من Google xhigh بأنه «استدلال أعمق متعدد الخطوات لأصعب أعباء الهندسة والتحليل والعلوم».

اختر xhigh عندما:

  • تتضمن المهمة خطوات مترابطة كثيرة ويُفسد خطأ مبكر النتيجة، مثل إعادة هيكلة متعددة الملفات أو تدقيق التزامن.
  • يعطي high إجابة واثقة لكنها خاطئة على مجموعة التقييم لديك، لا مجرد إجابة أبطأ.
  • لا يمثل زمن الاستجابة أهمية كبيرة، كما في المهام الخلفية أو المراجعات الليلية أو التحليل الدفعي.
  • تكلفة الإجابة الخاطئة أكبر من تكلفة الرموز، كما في تصحيحات الأمان أو الحسابات المالية.

وابقَ على high (أو انزل إلى مستوى أدنى) عندما:

  • يكون الطلب للاستخراج أو التنسيق. تحذّر Google من أن xhigh «قد يسبب تفكيرًا مفرطًا أو يستنفد max_output_tokens في الطلبات الأبسط مثل استخراج النصوص أو JSON».
  • يكون المستخدم في انتظار الرد. فالدردشة والإكمال التلقائي واستدعاءات الأدوات المباشرة تناسب medium أو low.
  • تعمل بحجم كبير. فكل رمز تفكير إضافي يُحتسب عليك، والفارق يتضاعف عبر الطلبات.

وأرقام Google القياسية تدعم هذا التقسيم. ففي إعلان الإطلاق، يحصل Neon عند xhigh على 61 في مؤشر الذكاء من Artificial Analysis، محتلًا المرتبة الثالثة. وعند المستوى الافتراضي high، تذكر Google تكلفة أقل بنسبة 32% لكل مهمة مقارنة بـCarbon. هذه أرقام Google وليست اختباراتنا، لكنها تُظهر المقايضة: يشتري xhigh أعلى نتيجة لـNeon، بينما يشتري high الكفاءة.

كم تبلغ تكلفة كل مستوى تفكير؟

لكل مستوى السعر نفسه لكل رمز؛ ما يتغير هو عدد الرموز التي تدفع مقابلها. تكلفة Neon 3.00 دولارات لكل مليون رمز إدخال و15.00 دولارًا لكل مليون رمز إخراج، وتذكر صفحة الأسعار من Google أن سعر الإخراج يشمل رموز التفكير. وينخفض الإدخال المخزَّن مؤقتًا إلى 0.15 دولار لكل مليون عبر التخزين المؤقت الضمني (التخزين المؤقت الصريح غير مدعوم في Neon). ولا توجد طبقة مجانية لهذا النموذج.

إذن تكلفة أي مستوى هي رموز التفكير التي يضيفها، مضروبة في 15 دولارًا لكل مليون. إليك الحساب لطلب واحد يتضمن 2,000 رمز إدخال وإجابة ظاهرة من 800 رمز. أعداد رموز التفكير افتراضية، اختيرت لإظهار الحساب وليست مقيسة:

رموز التفكير (افتراضية) تكلفة الإدخال تكلفة الإخراج + التفكير الإجمالي لكل طلب لكل 10,000 طلب
500 0.006 دولار 0.0195 دولار 0.0255 دولار 255 دولارًا
2,000 0.006 دولار 0.042 دولار 0.048 دولار 480 دولارًا
8,000 0.006 دولار 0.132 دولار 0.138 دولار 1,380 دولارًا

يهيمن التفكير على الفاتورة بسرعة. فعند 8,000 رمز تفكير، يشكّل الاستدلال 87% من تكلفة الطلب. لهذا تنصح Google نفسها بتشغيل التقييم لديك على المستويات الأربعة و«اختيار أدنى thinking_level يلبي معيار الجودة لديك». ويغطي دليل مستويات التفكير في Gemini 3.8 Flash المقايضة نفسها على نموذج أرخص إذا أردت المقارنة.

كيف تقيس الرموز وزمن الاستجابة لكل مستوى؟

شغّل الطلب نفسه عند كل مستوى واقرأ كتلة الاستخدام. في Interactions API، يذكر كائن usage في الاستجابة total_input_tokens وtotal_output_tokens وtotal_thought_tokens كلًّا على حدة. وفي generateContent، تظهر رموز التفكير باسم usageMetadata.thoughtsTokenCount.

ترسل هذه الحلقة طلبًا واحدًا عند المستويات الأربعة جميعًا وتطبع رموز التفكير إضافةً إلى الزمن الفعلي:

for level in low medium high xhigh; do
  start=$(date +%s)
  usage=$(curl -s "https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/interactions" \
    -H "x-goog-api-key: $GEMINI_API_KEY" \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d "{\"model\":\"gemini-4-neon\",
         \"input\":\"Find the race condition in this retry loop: ...\",
         \"generation_config\":{\"thinking_level\":\"$level\",\"max_output_tokens\":65536}}" \
    | jq -c '{status, thought: .usage.total_thought_tokens, out: .usage.total_output_tokens}')
  echo "$level $(( $(date +%s) - start ))s $usage"
done

شغّلها على 10 إلى 20 طلبًا من عبئك الحقيقي. فالطلب الواحد لا يخبرك بالكثير؛ أما مجموعة الطلبات فتُظهر أين يبدأ high وxhigh بالاختلاف في الجودة.

اضبط مهلة عميل HTTP على قيمة عالية أثناء الاختبار. فملاحظات الترحيل من Google تقول إن الطلبات الصعبة قد تستغرق دقائق عدة، وتقترح مهلة لا تقل عن 15 دقيقة، أو التنفيذ في الخلفية.

لماذا يعيد xhigh أحيانًا إجابة فارغة؟

يحدّ max_output_tokens من التفكير والإخراج الظاهر معًا. فإذا أنفق Neon الميزانية كلها في الاستدلال، يتوقف التفاعل بحالة incomplete ويعيد إجابة مقتطعة أو فارغة، وستدفع مع ذلك مقابل رموز التفكير التي أنتجها.

هناك ثلاث قواعد من وثائق Google تجنّبك ذلك:

  1. أزل الحدود المنخفضة القديمة. إذا كان تطبيقك يثبّت قيمة مثل 8,192، فارفعها إلى 65,536، وهو الحد الافتراضي للطلبات المتزامنة.
  2. اخفض المستوى، لا الحد. لتقليل التكلفة أو زمن الاستجابة، انزل إلى medium أو low بدلًا من تقليص max_output_tokens.
  3. استخدم التنفيذ الخلفي للأعمال الطويلة. للإجابات التي تتجاوز 65,536 رمزًا، اضبط background على true وmax_output_tokens حتى 1,048,576 ناقص الإدخال. فالإدخال والتفكير والإخراج تتقاسم نافذة واحدة من مليون رمز. ويشرح دليل الإخراج الطويل في Gemini 4 Argon نمط الاستقصاء الدوري.

دع وكيل البرمجة لديك يقيس المستويات الأربعة باستخدام Apidog CLI

إعادة تشغيل تلك الحلقة يدويًا تصبح مملة. بدلًا من ذلك، دع وكيل البرمجة لديك (Claude Code أو Codex أو Cursor) يبني اختبارًا واحدًا قابلًا لإعادة الاستخدام باستخدام Apidog CLI ويعيد تشغيله عند كل مستوى متى أردت أرقامًا جديدة.

أعدّه مرة واحدة:

npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog login --with-token <YOUR_TOKEN>
npx -y skills add https://apidog.com   # pick your agent when prompted

ثم أعطِ وكيلك طلبًا واحدًا:

In Apidog project <projectId>, create an environment "gemini" with base URL
https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com and variables GEMINI_API_KEY and
THINKING. Add an endpoint for POST /v1beta/interactions that sends the
x-goog-api-key header from GEMINI_API_KEY. Create a test case that sends model
"gemini-4-neon", my audit prompt, generation_config.thinking_level {{THINKING}}
and max_output_tokens 65536, and asserts: HTTP 200, status is "completed",
and usage.total_thought_tokens exists. Run it once per level (low, medium,
high, xhigh) and give me a table of thought tokens and response time.

يقرأ الوكيل مخطط كل حِمل ويتحقق من صحة JSON الخاص به، ثم يكتب الموارد ويكرر التشغيل:

apidog environment create gemini --project <projectId> --base-url https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com
apidog cli-schema get endpoint-create
apidog cli-schema validate endpoint-create --file endpoint.json
apidog endpoint create --project <projectId> --file endpoint.json
apidog cli-schema validate test-case-create --file case.json
apidog test-case create --project <projectId> --file case.json
for level in low medium high xhigh; do
  apidog run --test-case <caseId> --project <projectId> -e <envId> \
    --env-var "THINKING=$level" -r cli,json --out-file "neon-$level"
done

يلتقط التحقق من أن status is "completed" فخ incomplete من القسم السابق، بحيث يفشل أي مستوى يستنفد ميزانيته بصوت عالٍ بدلًا من إرجاع سلسلة فارغة. واستبدل -r cli,json بـ-r junit لينتقل التشغيل نفسه إلى CI؛ ويعرض دليل Apidog CLI لخطوط CI/CD خط الأنابيب، ويغطي Apidog CLI في Claude Code إعداد الوكيل. وتغطي خطة Apidog المجانية ما يصل إلى 4 مستخدمين.

الأسئلة الشائعة

ما مستوى التفكير الافتراضي في Gemini 4 Neon؟ high. لا تحتاج إلى إرسال thinking_level للحصول عليه. ويستخدم Carbon وArgon القيمة medium افتراضيًا، لذا عيّن المستوى صراحةً عند الترحيل منهما.

هل يدعم Gemini 4 Neon التفكير الأدنى (minimal)؟ لا. يدعم Neon المستويات low وmedium وhigh وxhigh، ويرفض minimal بخطأ. استخدم low لأسرع وأرخص الاستجابات.

هل تُحتسب رموز التفكير في فاتورة Gemini 4 Neon؟ نعم. تُحتسب رموز التفكير بسعر الإخراج البالغ 15.00 دولارًا لكل مليون رمز. وتحتسب Google كل رمز يعالجه النموذج، بما في ذلك رموز التفكير.

هل يمكنني الاستمرار في استخدام thinkingBudget مع Gemini 4 Neon؟ إنه مهجور في نماذج Gemini 4. فعند إرساله منفردًا، يُترجم إلى أقرب thinkingLevel ويعيد تحذيرًا. وعند إرساله إلى جانب thinkingLevel، يفشل الطلب بالخطأ 400.

هل xhigh أدق دائمًا من high؟ ليس دائمًا. تقول Google إن xhigh قد يفرط في التفكير في الطلبات البسيطة مثل استخراج النصوص أو JSON وقد يستنفد max_output_tokens. اختبرهما على طلباتك الخاصة واحتفظ بأدنى مستوى يجتاز الاختبار.

هل يمكنني استخدام مستويات التفكير في Gemini 4 Neon مجانًا؟ لا. Gemini 4 Neon غير متاح في الطبقة المجانية من Gemini API. وفي Google AI Studio وGoogle Antigravity، يرتبط بخطط Google AI Pro وUltra المدفوعة.

title: HealthCLBench:Evaluating Context Learning in Health Conversations through Controlled Case Clusters
description:
arXiv:2611.22362v2 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Complex health conversations require answers grounded in individual information and currently valid evidence. We evaluate health context learning: acquiring, integrating, and applying relevant context during inference with fixed model parameters to answer health questions and respond appropriately to changes in facts, evidence, or task goals. To our knowledge, Chinese-language medical benchmarks have yet to systematically combine explicit contextual difficulties, controlled case variations, and member-specific medical criteria for open-ended answers. We introduce HealthCLBench, comprising 328 controlled clusters, 1,103 cases, and 4,931 rubric criteria across medical consultation and everyday health management. Members share backgrounds while evidence, patient states, or task goals change; each has its own medical scoring requirements. A 70-person medical team annotates and reviews the simulated cases and their rubrics. Human review of 700 full-context responses from the original evaluation yields 90.5% pooled agreement with the original automated judgments at the rubric-item level. We report full-context and query-only results for seven general-purpose models and Ant Afu. Across the eight systems, scores with full context are 11.83 to 31.76 case points and 10.87 to 38.97 geometric cluster points higher than those with the current question alone. GPT-6 Astra leads both full-context metrics at 75.03 and 60.42, followed by Claude Opus 5.5 and Ant Afu. Cross-condition differences describe score changes under the reported evaluation settings. Response comparisons reveal failures in checking historical information, expressing uncertainty when warranted, and ensuring recommendations respect required conditions. The resource supports model comparison and targeted follow-up evaluation.

title: Has Your Company Been Audited for Oracle Java? Here's What You Need to Know
description:
Over the past 18 months, thousands of companies have received audit notices from Oracle about unlicensed Java installations. If you manage IT infrastructure at a company with 20+ staff, this matters to you.

The Problem

On September 20, 2026, Oracle JDK 21 moved from free (NFTC) to paid (OTN) licensing. If your company auto-updates Java on employee machines, any Oracle JDK 21 installed after the September update may trigger audit notices—even if nobody is actively using it.

Which Versions Are Free?

Free (no audit risk):

  • OpenJDK (GPL + Classpath Exception)
  • Eclipse Temurin (Eclipse Foundation)
  • Amazon Corretto (AWS-supported, free LTS)
  • Azul Zulu Community Edition
  • Oracle JDK 8 up to build 8u202 (January 2022)

Paid (audit risk):

  • Oracle JDK 8 after build 8u202
  • Oracle JDK 11, 17 (OTN-only after Sept 2026)
  • Oracle JDK 21 (free until Sept 2026, then OTN-paid)
  • Oracle JDK 22+ (OTN-paid immediately)

5-Step Audit You Can Run Right Now

  1. Find all Java installations on your fleet
  2. Extract vendor, version, and build number
  3. Cross-check the license against the roadmap
  4. Triage machines with paid versions
  5. Plan your replacement strategy

You're not doing anything wrong by having Java installed. The problem is that Oracle changed the licensing mid-year. Thousands of companies are in the same situation. Use this moment to clean up your Java footprint and move to free, well-maintained alternatives.

If you receive an audit notice from Oracle, consult your legal team. But first, knowing which machines have which Java versions is the first step to being in control.

title: Most Forms Don't Need an Inbox: Why Every Formpit Form Now Picks a Mode
description:
When I started building form pages for Formpit, I copied the thing Formpit already did well: every response lands in an inbox and stays "New" until you reply. Then I looked at what people actually make with forms, and most of them never need a reply. This is the story of that mistake, the simple rule I ended up with, and how it changed the product.

Where the inbox came from

Formpit started as a form backend for contact forms. For a freelancer or a small business, a contact form isn't done when the email arrives. It's done when you've replied. So every submission is marked New, Replied or Closed, you can reply from Formpit itself, and it reminds you about anything that has been waiting for two days.

When I added form pages, forms you build in Formpit and share as a link or a QR code with no website needed, I reused that flow without thinking twice. A response is a message, a message needs an answer. Simple.

Nobody replies to 60 RSVPs

The first starting points I built were RSVP, registration, feedback, order and file upload forms. While testing the RSVP one, I filled it in as a host would, and realised I would never reply to a single guest. I'd want three things: how many people said yes, how many guests they're bringing in total, and whether anyone has dietary needs.

In the inbox flow, those 60 RSVPs would sit there as "New". Reminders would nag about them. The unanswered count would never reach zero. The product would keep telling the host they were behind on work that doesn't exist.

Search data told the same story. When I looked at what people search for in Ahrefs, "rsvp form", "sign up sheet", "survey" and "registration form" came up again and again. Contact forms, the one kind that really needs a reply, were just one entry in a long list.

The rule: is someone waiting on an answer?

I posted about this on X and Threads, and other builders put it better than I had. One said: default RSVPs and surveys to a live count, and only open an inbox when a person is waiting on an answer. Another said a count tells you something happened, and one line of free text tells you why.

That gives one question to ask about any form:

Form Is someone waiting on an answer? What it needs
Contact form Yes An inbox
Quote request Yes An inbox
RSVP No A headcount
Registration or sign-up No A list and a total
Feedback or survey No Averages, plus the comments
File collection No The files, in one place
Order Not usually A table, with a confirmation email

What the two modes do

So every Formpit form now has a mode.

Collect

  • Summary: how many people chose each option, averages and totals for ratings and numbers, and the latest written answers.
  • Table: every response, sortable and filterable, with a CSV download.
  • Email: one for every response, one summary a day, or none.
  • Closing: stop after a number of responses or on a date, with your own message.

  • No guilt: nothing is marked unanswered and nothing sends reminders.

    Conversation

  • Each response lands in an inbox as New, Replied or Closed.

  • You reply from Formpit, and the reply goes to the person's email.

  • Anything waiting two days gets a reminder.
    Both modes use the same builder and give you the same link, QR code and embed code. Only what happens after someone presses Send is different.

Defaults, not a quiz

I didn't want people to learn the word "mode" before making their first form. You start by picking what the form is for, and each starting point comes with the right mode: Contact and Quote request start as conversations, and RSVP, registration, feedback, order and file forms start in Collect.

If the guess is wrong, you switch in the side panel at any time. Switching to Collect moves anything still marked New out of the unanswered count. Switching to Conversation turns on an email for every response, because someone is now waiting on you.

How it works under the hood

The change was smaller than I expected, which usually means the model was right:

  • One column. Each form has a mode of collect or conversation.
  • One status. Responses to a Collect form are saved with the status received instead of new. Unanswered counts and reminders only look at new, so they ignore these without any special cases.
  • One summary function. The summary is worked out from the form's own question types: choices become counts, ratings and numbers become averages and totals, and text questions show the latest answers. The same function writes the daily summary email. 
// After the submission is saved
if (form.mode === 'collect') {
  setStatus(submissionId, 'received'); // nothing to answer
}

Because the summary comes from the question types, a new kind of question gets a summary for free, and nobody has to set up a chart.

What I'd tell another builder

  • Use your product as the person on the other end. I only saw the problem when I filled in the form as a host. Reading the code would never have shown it.
  • When two groups need opposite things, choose a default for each. A setting hidden in the options would have left most people with the wrong one.
  • Say the lesson out loud. Posting about it got me clearer explanations than my own, and some of them are now in this article. If you're making an RSVP, a sign-up sheet or a survey, you can try Collect mode yourself at formpit.com/create. Form pages are free up to 500 responses a month, and nobody needs an account to answer.

Which kind of form do you make most often: one you count, or one you reply to?

title: Introducing BudgetApp: Building an Open Source Desktop Application with Python and PySide6 🐍
description:
Exploring desktop development, local-first storage, PDF generation, and software architecture through a practical Python project.

Hey DEV Community! 👋

Are you passionate about Python? Have you ever wanted to move beyond scripts and build a complete desktop application?

Today, I'd like to introduce BudgetApp, one of the open-source projects I'm developing as part of ConnectApp, my independent initiative focused on building reusable software, sharing knowledge, and exploring responsible software engineering.

BudgetApp is a desktop application developed with Python and PySide6 (Qt) to help users create, organize, and manage business quotations.

But beyond its practical purpose, the project is also an opportunity to explore something I find particularly interesting:

How can we build desktop applications that are useful, maintainable, and respectful of users' data?

💻 Why Python and PySide6?

Python is widely used for automation, backend development, data processing, and artificial intelligence.

However, it's also an excellent language for building desktop applications.

Combined with PySide6, the official Python bindings for Qt, it provides a powerful foundation for creating graphical user interfaces.

With BudgetApp, I'm exploring several important areas of desktop development:

  • Python for application logic.
  • PySide6 for the graphical interface.
  • SQLite for local data persistence.
  • MySQL as an optional remote database alternative.
  • PDF generation for business quotations.
  • Data validation and consistent calculations.
  • Software architecture and separation of responsibilities.

These technologies offer practical opportunities to learn how a real application works beyond a simple programming exercise.

📋 What does BudgetApp do?

BudgetApp is designed to make the preparation and management of business quotations more straightforward.

Its documented workflow includes:

✅ Managing company and customer information.

✅ Creating and editing quotations.

✅ Adding items, quantities, prices, discounts, and VAT.

✅ Calculating and reviewing totals.

✅ Searching previously saved quotations.

✅ Tracking quotation statuses, such as draft, sent, and accepted.

✅ Exporting quotations as PDF documents.

✅ Working with Spanish and English document output.

The goal is to organize the entire quotation workflow in one desktop environment.

Instead of managing separate spreadsheets, documents, and calculations, users can work with a more structured process.

🗄️ Local-first or remote storage? You choose.

One of BudgetApp's interesting features is its approach to data persistence.

The application supports two storage options:

SQLite — Local storage

A suitable choice for users who prefer keeping their business information on their own computer.

It avoids the need to maintain a separate database server for a simple desktop workflow.

MySQL — Optional remote storage

For scenarios where an external database is required, BudgetApp also supports a configurable MySQL connection.

This introduces different infrastructure, configuration, and security responsibilities.

The application uses the operating system's secure credential storage for remote database passwords.

An important distinction: remote MySQL support does not automatically mean that the application provides multi-user collaboration or conflict-free synchronization.

📄 Generating PDF quotations

PDF generation is another interesting engineering challenge in BudgetApp.

A quotation involves more than placing text on a page.

The application needs to organize customer details, quotation items, quantities, prices, discounts, taxes, and final totals.

It also needs to produce a document that remains understandable outside the application.

This makes PDF generation a useful area for exploring data formatting, calculations, document structure, and validation.

It also raises a privacy consideration:

Once a PDF is exported and shared, the application no longer controls where that document goes.

That's why users should review the information included before distributing it.

🏗️ Learning software architecture through a real project

One of the principles I try to follow throughout ConnectApp is that open-source projects should remain understandable and maintainable.

BudgetApp explores architectural ideas inspired by Clean Architecture, particularly the separation of business models, persistence, and user-interface responsibilities.

However, the project is still evolving.

Some responsibilities and dependencies need further refinement, which makes the codebase an opportunity to discuss architectural decisions and improvements rather than presenting it as a perfect reference implementation.

For developers and students, there are interesting questions to explore:

  • How should a PySide6 interface interact with business logic?
  • How can persistence be separated from quotation calculations?
  • How should different database implementations be organized?
  • How can financial calculations be tested reliably?
  • How should errors, backups, and restoration be handled?

These are the types of questions that turn a programming project into a software engineering learning experience.

🎓 A project for Python students and developers

I believe one of the best ways to improve as a developer is to work with applications that solve real problems.

BudgetApp can be especially interesting if you're:

  • Learning Python and looking for a more complete project.
  • Exploring PySide6 or Qt desktop interfaces.
  • Interested in SQLite and MySQL.
  • Learning software architecture and modular design.
  • Practicing PDF generation and data validation.
  • Looking to contribute to an evolving open-source application.

You don't need to be an expert in every technology.

Studying the architecture, reviewing calculations, improving documentation, or proposing tests can be valuable ways to participate.

🔐 Open Source, privacy, and software quality

At ConnectApp, I believe that Open Source doesn't mean second-class software.

Making an application's source code available should encourage transparency, maintainability, responsible engineering, and collaboration.

Privacy is also an important part of that philosophy.

BudgetApp gives users a choice between local SQLite storage and optional remote MySQL storage, but each configuration comes with its own responsibilities.

Local storage doesn't automatically guarantee security, and external storage requires careful configuration.

The project remains under development, so anyone adapting it for business use should review its current documentation, test workflows with sample data, and evaluate whether it meets their requirements.

🤝 Let's learn and build together!

I'd love to connect with Python developers, students, educators, and anyone interested in desktop software engineering.

BudgetApp is another opportunity to demonstrate how open-source projects can become practical learning resources.

Whether you want to review the code, share ideas, discuss architecture, or propose improvements, your feedback is welcome.

Here's a question for the DEV Community:

When building a desktop application in Python, what do you find most challenging: designing the UI, structuring the architecture, handling local databases, or packaging the application?

I'd love to hear about your experiences!

🌍 Explore BudgetApp and ConnectApp

📋 BudgetApp project page: https://www.connectapp.es/es/aplicaciones/budget-app/

🌐 ConnectApp: https://www.connectapp.es

💻 GitHub: https://github.com/ManuelAf-ConnectApp

ConnectApp — Open Source Software. Real Privacy. Freedom to Create.

Because learning Python isn't just about writing code. It's about discovering how to build software that people can actually use. 🚀

title: Label-Free Role-Aware Segmentation of Classroom Recordings: Recovering the Teacher from Transferable Structure
description:
arXiv:2611.23609v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: How much the teacher talks and when are among the most informative and costly-to-measure signals of teaching. Yet, classroom audio is among the most sensitive data an AI system can process: recordings capture minors and fall under GDPR, preventing raw audio from leaving the recording device. We present a teacher-student segmentation pipeline designed to meet exactly this constraint: label-free at inference, running on a recording device, and requiring no per-session calibration. The pipeline chains a lightweight voice activity detector, compactly pretrained speaker embeddings, agglomerative clustering, and a small logistic regression that assigns the teacher role based on session-relative structure rather than voice identity. We show that our structural cue transfers across classrooms, languages, and acoustic conditions.
  In leave-one-teacher-out cross-validation on 292 recordings from 63 teachers across English and German corpora, our pipeline achieves teacher F1 of 0.81 and 0.87, respectively, outperforming both enrollment-based baselines and a 30-second supervised enrollment ceiling. On a commodity smartphone, its performance matches pyannote, a strong neural diarization tool, while running 4.8x faster at comparable peak memory at a real-time factor of ~0.18. We also find that transcribing filtered audio only marginally increases teacher's word error rate from $0.26$ to 0.28. Residual failures concentrate where teacher and student voices are not acoustically separable. However, we show how to flag these sessions label-free at inference so that they can be routed to human review, enabling selective, privacy-preserving deployment.

title: routing-from-scratch: Dijkstra, A* and contraction hierarchies on real OSM data in Go
description:
You type two addresses into a map app and a route appears before you lift your finger. Behind that is a chain of problems, each one a classic: read a compressed binary map file, turn streets into a graph, and find the shortest path among hundreds of thousands of roads faster than a plain search could.

I had read about all of these and implemented none. routing-from-scratch is where I did: car routing on real OpenStreetMap data, written from scratch in Go with no dependencies beyond the standard library. It is a learning project, and it says so about itself: for anything real, use OSRM, Valhalla or GraphHopper.

What it does

The project has four parts:

  1. An OSM PBF reader and writer with a hand-written protobuf wire codec, plus an OSM XML reader.
  2. A road graph: CSR arrays, oneway rules, speeds per highway type, and reduction to the largest strongly connected component.
  3. Dijkstra, then A*, then contraction hierarchies, all checked against each other and against Floyd–Warshall.
  4. A benchmark table and a small HTTP endpoint with a map page.

On the map page, you click twice to set A and B, and the markers can be dragged. The page asks for the route with all three algorithms and shows their travel time (always identical), settled nodes and query time.

The API is one route: GET /route?from=lon,lat&to=lon,lat&algo=dijkstra|astar|ch returns a GeoJSON Feature (a LineString) with duration_s, distance_m, settled, query_us and snap_m, which is how far each point was from its snapped node. GET /info returns the graph size and bbox.

How to use it

Install the route-server, route-bench and osm2pbf binaries with Go:

go install github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/routing-from-scratch/cmd/...@latest

Or clone the repository, which includes a small fixture of central Tlemcen, and run from there:

git clone https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/routing-from-scratch.git
cd routing-from-scratch
go test ./...                                              # ~30 s, includes brute-force cross-checks
go run ./cmd/route-server                                  # committed Tlemcen fixture, http://127.0.0.1:8090/
go run ./cmd/route-bench testdata/tlemcen-centre.osm.pbf   # benchmark table

For a bigger extract (not committed), download roads with Overpass and convert them with the project's own PBF writer:

scripts/fetch-osm.sh 35.60 -0.80 35.80 -0.45 data/oran.osm     # ~11 MB XML
go run ./cmd/osm2pbf data/oran.osm data/oran.osm.pbf            # ~0.9 MB PBF
go run ./cmd/route-server data/oran.osm.pbf

What I built from scratch

The PBF codec (internal/pbf). A PBF file is a sequence of [4-byte length][BlobHeader][Blob]. Blobs are zlib-compressed protobuf PrimitiveBlocks, each with a string table, granularity and offsets, and groups of DenseNodes (delta and zigzag encoded ids and coordinates) or Ways (string-table tags, delta-encoded refs). The decoder reads raw protobuf fields (varints, length-delimited, packed) without generated code. The writer does the reverse and is used by cmd/osm2pbf and the round-trip tests. Unsupported required_features such as HistoricalInformation are rejected, as the spec requires.

The graph (internal/graph). Every node of a drivable way becomes a vertex and every consecutive pair becomes an edge. The weight is travel time in tenths of a second, rounded up. Speed comes from maxspeed (km/h or mph) or a per-type default. Direction comes from oneway=yes/-1/no, roundabouts and motorways. Access rules drop access=no/private, parking aisles and driveways. Parallel edges keep the minimum weight. Finally the graph is cut down to its largest strongly connected component (iterative Kosaraju), so every snapped point can reach every other one. Storage is CSR (FirstOut, Head, W) plus a reverse CSR.

Dijkstra and A* (internal/route/dijkstra.go). A binary heap with lazy deletion. Buffers are reused between queries, and only the touched entries are reset. A* adds haversine(v, t) / MaxSpeed. MaxSpeed is computed from the edges themselves (max straight-line metres divided by weight), so the heuristic is admissible and consistent whatever the data.

Contraction hierarchies (internal/route/ch.go):

  • Ordering. Priority is the edge difference (shortcuts needed minus edges removed) plus the number of already contracted neighbours. Updates are lazy: pop the minimum, recompute it, and only contract it if it is still the minimum.
  • Contraction. For each in-neighbour u of v, a bounded witness Dijkstra (avoiding v, at most 200 settled nodes) checks every out-neighbour x. If no path of cost at most w(u,v)+w(v,x) exists, it adds the shortcut u→x and records v as its middle node.
  • Query. Bidirectional Dijkstra on the upward graphs. It stops when both queue minima are at least the best meeting cost, then shortcuts are unpacked recursively through their middle nodes.

What I learned

A* is not automatically faster. This was the surprise. go run ./cmd/route-bench -n 1000 <file> runs 1000 random queries per algorithm and checks that all three return the same costs (0 mismatches on every run). On the Oran extract (91,547 nodes, 188,329 edges; CH preprocessing 10.1 s, 212,760 shortcuts):

algorithm avg query avg settled nodes speed-up vs Dijkstra
Dijkstra 46.8 ms 45,972 1.0x
A* 73.3 ms 25,324 0.6x
CH 0.40 ms 142 116x

On the Tlemcen extract (30,047 nodes, 60,815 edges; CH preprocessing 4.5 s), Dijkstra averaged 18.6 ms, A* 24.6 ms and CH 0.12 ms, with 15,339, 9,205 and 79 settled nodes.

A* settles about 40% fewer nodes but is slower here. Its heuristic, straight-line distance divided by the fastest speed in the graph, is weak when most streets are 25 km/h and a few roads allow 80 to 100 km/h, and each heuristic evaluation costs a Haversine. CH settles two orders of magnitude fewer nodes in exchange for a few seconds of preprocessing.

A caveat that comes with these numbers: they were measured on a laptop that was busy with other builds, so the absolute times are noisy. The settled-node counts are the stable signal.

Integer weights make comparisons exact. With travel time in tenths of a second as integers, three algorithms either agree to the unit or they have a bug. With floats, I would have been arguing with rounding.

A witness-search limit affects speed, not correctness. Hitting the 200-node limit only adds unnecessary shortcuts. A test with a limit of 1 checks that correctness never depends on it.

Brute force keeps you honest. On 10 random road-like graphs (30 to 120 nodes, partly one-way, some unreachable pairs), all pairs for Dijkstra, A* and CH are compared with Floyd–Warshall. Path validity is checked too: the returned node sequence is made of real edges and sums to the cost. Other tests cover a 30×30 grid, the heap, the PBF write-then-read round trip, OSM tagging rules on a hand-written XML, the grid index against brute-force nearest, and the /route error codes (400/404/422).

Things to know

  • Car profile only. There are no turn restrictions, turn costs or traffic signals, and no maxspeed:forward/backward.
  • Snapping goes to the nearest node, not the nearest point on an edge.
  • CH preprocessing is single-threaded and unoptimised. It takes seconds for a city and would need work for a country.
  • The PBF reader handles nodes and ways (dense and plain). Relations are skipped, and only zlib/raw blobs are supported (no lzma/zstd).
  • The map page loads MapLibre from unpkg and raster tiles from tile.openstreetmap.org.

Why I built it

Routing engines are easy to use and hard to see into. The ideas behind them, shortest paths, heuristics, preprocessing, are standard material, but reading about contraction hierarchies and making one return the same answer as Dijkstra on a real city are different things. Starting from the raw PBF bytes, with no library in the way, meant every layer was mine to get wrong and then fix. That was the point.

Get the code

The source, the Tlemcen fixture and the tests are on GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/routing-from-scratch. The code is MIT licensed. The fixture testdata/tlemcen-centre.osm.pbf contains OpenStreetMap data, © OpenStreetMap contributors, under the Open Database License (ODbL) 1.0; anything you produce from it must keep that attribution and licence.

Originally published at abdeldjalilchougui.biz.
