title: Leaving Oracle: the licence is the easy part
description:
First published on the Tech Style blog.

Philip Marks wrote recently about the UK public sector and Oracle. A first look at procurement records, he said, found more than £7 million of Oracle Database related contract awards in 2026 alone, and that is only the contracts he could identify. His question was a fair one: how long can tight budgets keep paying for renewals when PostgreSQL has no licence fee at all?

We agree with the direction. But in our experience the licence is the easy part of leaving. Here is where the lock-in really sits, and why we started building Paritas.

Where the lock-in sits

The contract. Licences are usually priced by processor, with options and packs on top, and support renews every year as a share of what you paid. Move to new hardware or to a cloud and the licensing rules come with you. Every renewal is a negotiation you cannot walk away from, because the alternative is not ready.

The code. This is the big one. A long-lived Oracle estate holds years of PL/SQL: packages, triggers, collections, exception handlers, calls into DBMS_ and UTL_ packages that applications lean on without anyone remembering why. Nobody wants to rewrite it, and nobody can afford to stop the business while they do.

The behaviour. Even code that converts cleanly can answer differently. On Oracle, SELECT 1 UNION SELECT 2 INTERSECT SELECT 2 returns 2. On PostgreSQL it returns 1 and 2, because INTERSECT binds tighter there. A FOR i IN REVERSE 1 .. 3 loop runs three times on Oracle and not at all on PostgreSQL. An empty string is NULL on Oracle and a value on PostgreSQL. None of these raises an error. They turn up later as wrong numbers.

The people. As Philip says, finding people who can migrate, architect and support a PostgreSQL estate is as hard as the technology. A team that has spent fifteen years in PL/SQL is an asset, and a migration that throws their knowledge away is a risk.

Put together, this is why so many estates stay put. Not loyalty, and not the licence. The cost of being sure the new system gives the same answers.

What we are building

Paritas is an Oracle-compatible database built on PostgreSQL. It runs in Oracle mode only, so your applications talk to it as they would to Oracle and real PL/SQL compiles and runs. Underneath, it is PostgreSQL, with PostgreSQL's tools, drivers and extensions, and no proprietary format to be locked into next.

We do not claim it is a perfect copy of Oracle. Nobody honestly can. Our promise is narrower and, we think, more useful: we can tell you exactly where compatibility ends for your own code, with measured evidence. Every answer Paritas gives is checked against a real Oracle Database 21c. Where it differs, it goes on our list of limitations, which runs to more than 900 entries, each saying what happens and most saying what to do instead.

Around Paritas we are building the tools a migration needs. pgrecon, our free assessment tool, is out today: it reads an Oracle schema and tells you what it contains before a migration is priced. Development tools and connectivity drivers are coming, and none of them is available yet. The enterprise layers we are working on power the PostgreSQL underneath Paritas, and they are being built so they can power plain PostgreSQL as well.

Leaving on your own terms

The way out of lock-in is not a leap. It is knowing, before you commit, which of your code will behave the same, which will not, and what each difference costs to fix. That turns a renewal from a hostage negotiation into a choice.

Paritas is in development and not for sale yet. We are aiming to release it next quarter. If you are weighing a move off Oracle, read more at tech-style.co/product-paritas, try pgrecon at tech-style.co/product-pgrecon, or write to us at tech-style.co/contact?topic=Paritas.

title: AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store raises API throughput limits
description:
AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store has increased the default throughput limits for five API operations. For accounts that have turned on the higher throughput setting, the quotas have changed as follows, in transactions per second (TPS):

  • GetParametersByPath (from 100 to 500 TPS)
  • PutParameter (10 to 50)
  • DeleteParameter (5 to 50)
  • DescribeParameters (10 to 100)
  • GetParameterHistory (10 to 100)

Parameter Store provides powerful, hierarchical storage for configuration data. The higher quotas give more headroom to workloads that call these operations in bursts. Examples include applications that load configuration by path when many AWS Lambda functions start at once, infrastructure as code deployments that create or update many parameters, and cleanup jobs that bulk-delete stale parameters.

title: GPT-6.2 in a React chat: get the timestamp out of your system prompt
description:
By the Cuelark Team. Every model detail below comes from OpenAI's own announcement and API docs, and the SDK details come from the Vercel AI SDK's release notes and published package, all checked on 19 November 2026. The code ran on our machine against a local mock of the documented Responses stream. We had no OpenAI API key for this test, so read it as a wiring test, not a quality review.

OpenAI released gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol on November 17. The headline numbers are about price and benchmarks. For anyone running a chat UI, though, the more important line is in the migration guide: starting with GPT-6.2, the Responses API drops reasoning items when you edit anything that came before them. A very common chat pattern, putting today's date and the current page into the system prompt, counts as that kind of edit. Nothing errors. The model just loses its earlier reasoning on every turn.

Here's what changed, what we saw in a two-turn test with the AI SDK, and the small fix.

What the docs say

From the announcement and the model pages for Astra and Sol:

  • Price per 1M tokens: Astra costs $8 input, $0.40 cached input and $40 output. Sol costs $2, $0.10 and $10, the same rates as GPT-6.1 Sol. Requests over 272K input tokens cost more.
  • Context: a 1,050,000-token window, up to 922,000 input tokens, and 128,000 max output tokens. Input is text and images, output is text.
  • Endpoints: both models work with Responses and Chat Completions, but tool calling needs the Responses API.
  • Removed settings: a reasoning effort of none is rejected, and temperature and top_p should be dropped. Flex processing isn't supported. Instead, background mode now has discounted two-hour and eight-hour completion windows (public beta).

The Using GPT-6.2 guide lists two behaviour changes that matter for chat apps:

  1. Prefix edits drop reasoning. If you edit earlier history, the API drops the reasoning items that came after the edit. It does the same when you switch to certain other models or when the end user changes. The guide warns that "answer quality can decline and the model may use more tokens to repeat earlier work."
  2. Top-level instructions moved. GPT-6.2 appends instructions after input. Reusable instructions should go in a developer message at the start of input. Top-level instructions are now meant for guidance that applies to the current request only.

The reasoning guide also lists end_user_mismatch. If the safety_identifier changes between requests, or is sent on only one of them, earlier reasoning is removed too.

What happened with the AI SDK

We used ai@7.0.177 and @ai-sdk/openai@4.0.121. 4.0.120 added the GPT-6.2 model IDs. 4.0.121 started returning input_transformations in provider metadata, which is how you can see dropped reasoning at all.

Our mock uses fetch, streams the documented SSE events, and applies the documented checks: prefix_mismatch and end_user_mismatch. It's built from the docs. It isn't a captured OpenAI response.

The "before" route is one you've probably written:

system: `You are Acme's support assistant. Today is ${new Date().toISOString()}. The user is on the ${user.page} page.`,

The AI SDK sends system as the first developer item in input. That's the right place for stable text, but this text isn't stable. On turn two, input[0] had a new timestamp and page, so it no longer matched what came before the turn-one reasoning item. The response reported:

[{ "id": "rs_1", "type": "reasoning", "action": "removed", "reason": "prefix_mismatch" }]

The prompt caching guide gives the same advice for cache hits: move timestamps and user-specific content to the end, not the beginning.

The fix: a static system prompt, per-turn context in instructions 

// app/api/chat/route.js
import { streamText, convertToModelMessages } from 'ai';
import { openai } from '@ai-sdk/openai';
import { createHash } from 'node:crypto';

const SYSTEM = "You are Acme's support assistant. Answer from the order data you are given.";

export async function POST(req) {
  const { messages, user } = await req.json();

  const result = streamText({
    model: openai('gpt-6.2-sol'),
    system: SYSTEM, // never changes, so it stays a stable, cacheable prefix
    messages: await convertToModelMessages(messages),
    providerOptions: {
      openai: {
        reasoningSummary: 'auto',
        // GPT-6.2 appends this after input, so it can change every turn
        instructions: `Today is ${new Date().toISOString()}. The user is on the ${user.page} page.`,
        // send it on every request, with the same value for the whole conversation
        safetyIdentifier: createHash('sha256').update(user.id ?? user.sessionId).digest('hex').slice(0, 32),
      },
    },
  });

  return result.toUIMessageStreamResponse({
    sendReasoning: true,
    messageMetadata: ({ part }) =>
      part.type === 'finish-step'
        ? { dropped: part.providerMetadata?.openai?.inputTransformations ?? [] }
        : undefined,
  });
}

We drove both routes the way useChat does: post the UI messages, rebuild the assistant message with readUIMessageStream, append it, and ask a follow-up. With the fixed route, input[0] was byte-identical on both turns, the new page name arrived in top-level instructions, and dropped was empty. The turn-one reasoning went back as an item_reference and was kept.

One detail we got wrong at first: inputTransformations is on the finish-step part's provider metadata, not on finish. Read it there, or you'll see nothing.

On the client, your shadcn chat stays the same. Show reasoning parts in a collapsible block and text parts as the answer. In development, it helps to log message.metadata.dropped.

Honest limits

  • We didn't call the real API. The checks in our mock follow the docs. Before you ship, run one real two-turn request and look at input_transformations.
  • Signing in mid-chat still drops reasoning. If the identifier goes from a session hash to a user hash, that's an end_user_mismatch, and our fixed route hit it too. Decide whether a conversation keeps the identifier it started with.
  • instructions aren't cached. OpenAI bills those tokens at the uncached input rate on every request, so keep them short.
  • History trimming counts as an edit. Rewriting or shortening old tool outputs, or summarising old turns at the front, changes the prefix. The keep-the-prefix guide suggests compaction, or placing summaries at the end. Deleting whole items without editing the rest doesn't trigger prefix_mismatch on its own.
  • Changing settings mid-chat. Changing reasoning.effort, tools or text.format between requests can also change the prefix. The docs suggest appending configuration_update or additional_tools items instead. We didn't test those here.

Sources

  • Introducing GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, OpenAI
  • OpenAI API changelog
  • Using GPT-6.2
  • GPT-6.2 Astra model page and GPT-6.2 Sol model page
  • Keep the prefix unchanged
  • Reasoning models: reasoning item removal
  • Prompt caching
  • @ai-sdk/openai 4.0.120 and 4.0.121

If you'd rather not hand-build the reasoning block and message list, Cuelark UI has shadcn-style components for AI chat that work with this setup.

title: Run Mobilerun with local and cheap models Ollama, DeepSeek, Qwen, OpenRouter
description:
Every step a phone agent takes is a model call. Read the screen, pick one action, tap, repeat. A simple task can be 10 of those. A test suite can be thousands.

So the first question people ask after getting Mobilerun working is always the same: can I run this on something cheaper? Or on my own machine, with no API key at all?

Yes. The open-source Mobilerun framework doesn't care where the model lives. This post shows what runs where, the exact local setup with Ollama and Qwen, the hosted setup for DeepSeek and OpenRouter, and what actually changes your results.

The problem with "which model is best?"

You'll find plenty of opinions about which model is best for phone agents. You won't find a published Mobilerun benchmark broken out by Ollama, DeepSeek, Qwen and OpenRouter. We haven't published one yet either.

That matters, because the answer depends on things only you know: your tasks, your device, your hardware, and whether you run with vision. So instead of a ranking, we'll give you the setup for each option and a simple way to measure them on your own work.

What runs where

The Mobilerun framework runs on your machine. It controls an Android device through Portal and ADB. The LLM provider is a separate choice you make in config or on the command line.

Here's how the options split:

  • Ollama runs inference locally. No model API key.
  • DeepSeek is a hosted API. It uses DEEPSEEK_API_KEY.
  • OpenRouter is a hosted API that routes to many models. It uses OPENROUTER_API_KEY.
  • Qwen is a model family, not a provider. You can run Qwen locally through Ollama, and Qwen models are also available through hosted providers like OpenRouter.

Install and run it locally with Ollama and Qwen

You need Python 3.11 to 3.13. Python 3.14 isn't supported yet, and the docs warn that installing on 3.14 silently falls back to an old version. You also need ADB and an Android device with USB debugging on.

Install the framework:

Install Ollama, connect your Android device, then set up Portal and check the connection.

mobilerun setupmobilerun pingCopy

If ping prints "Portal is installed and accessible. You're good to go!", you're ready. Pull the model and run a task:

ollama pull qwen3:8bmobilerun run "Turn on dark mode" --provider Ollama --model qwen3:8b --base_url http://localhost:11434Copy

That's the whole loop running on your hardware. The framework talks to Ollama at localhost:11434, and no request leaves your machine for inference.

Pass --provider and --model together. The CLI guide is clear that passing only one makes the run fail before the agent starts.

To make Ollama the default instead of typing flags every time, add a profile to your config file. Mobilerun creates it at ~/.config/droidrun/config.yaml on Linux, ~/Library/Application Support/droidrun/config.yaml on macOS, and %LOCALAPPDATA%\droidrun\droidrun\config.yaml on Windows. Yes, the folder still says droidrun. You can also point MOBILERUN_CONFIG or --config at your own file.

One Ollama detail worth knowing: Mobilerun sets the context size itself. The default context_window is 32,768, which keeps most models on the GPU. Setting it to -1 asks for the model's full context, which preallocates the whole KV cache and can spill onto your CPU.

DeepSeek and OpenRouter: hosted, pay per call

For the hosted options, set the key and pick the provider and model with CLI flags.

DeepSeek:

export DEEPSEEK_API_KEY=your-keymobilerun run "Turn on dark mode" --provider DeepSeek --model deepseek-flashCopy

OpenRouter, here with a hosted Qwen model:

export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=your-keymobilerun run "Turn on dark mode" --provider OpenRouter --model qwen/qwen3.8-flashCopy

Or save them as profiles so every run uses them:

llm_profiles:  fast_agent:    provider: DeepSeek    model: deepseek-flashllm_profiles:  fast_agent:    provider: OpenRouter    model: qwen/qwen3.8-flashCopy

A note on mobilerun configure. The wizard's provider list today is gemini, openai, anthropic, xai, ollama, openai_like, minimax and zai. DeepSeek and OpenRouter aren't in it as named options, so use the CLI flags or the YAML profile for those. Model IDs change often on both services, so check DeepSeek's and OpenRouter's model lists before you copy ours.

What affects your results

Swapping the model is one line. Whether the task finishes is a different story. These are the four things that change the outcome.

Accessibility tree by default. Out of the box, the agent reads Android's accessibility tree, a structured list of what's on screen with text and bounds. No screenshots. That works with text-only models, including qwen3:8b.

--vision adds screenshots. With vision on, the agent gets a screenshot alongside the tree on every step. That needs a vision-capable model. If you test vision on a local model, pull one that accepts images. For local vision models that downsize images in a way Mobilerun can't detect, the docs suggest capping the screenshot so tap coordinates stay accurate:

agent:  model_screenshot_max_side: 1280Copy

There's also --vision-only, which drops the tree and drives the device from screenshots alone.

Native tool calling vs the fallback protocol. Mobilerun uses native tool calling where the model supports it. For other models, it falls back to a text protocol where the model writes tool calls as XML and the framework parses them. In v0.7.4 the native path covers providers like DeepSeek, OpenAI and xAI. Ollama and OpenRouter go through the fallback. If a model writes broken tool-call markup three times in a row, the run stops, and smaller models hit this more often.

Your hardware. With Ollama, speed is your GPU, your RAM and the model size. The same model can feel quick on one laptop and painful on another.

Success and speed will vary with the model, the task, the device and the hardware. That's why the next section exists.

Some tips to keep the numbers honest:

  • Run mobilerun --version and record it. Results change between releases.
  • Keep --steps the same across runs. The default is 15, and complex tasks may need more.
  • Turn on --tracing to see tokens per step, or use --debug and --save-trajectory action to see where a run went wrong.
  • Count completed tasks, not tokens. A cheap model that fails half the time isn't cheap.

On cost: Ollama removes per-call model API fees, but local hardware still has a cost. The GPU, the power and the machine that's busy while it runs all count. Hosted APIs flip that. No hardware to own, but you pay for every call.

Honest limits

  • There are no published per-provider Mobilerun benchmarks yet. Anyone giving you a confident ranking is guessing.
  • Small local models are more likely to drift from the tool-call format, especially on busy screens.
  • qwen3:8b is a text model. Keep --vision off with it, or switch to a vision-capable model.
  • The framework is the open-source, bring-your-own-device path. You manage the phone, ADB, Portal and the model.

Don't want to manage a device?

If you'd rather skip the phone and the ADB setup, Mobilerun Cloud gives you hosted devices and a managed agent behind an API. You send a task, it runs on a phone in the cloud. If you want to keep your own model and your own device, the open-source framework will always let you.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I run Mobilerun with no API key at all? Is Qwen a provider?

Which model is the cheapest per task? Can I use DeepSeek or OpenRouter from mobilerun configure? 

The takeaway

The model is your choice, and the right one is the one that finishes your tasks on your hardware. Measure it, don't guess it. If you'd rather not manage a device at all, start at cloud.mobilerun.ai.

Docs: Quickstart · CLI and providers · Ollama profiles · Vision mode

Also Read:

  • Running an AI Agent on Your Android Device
  • How to Turn Old Android Phones into AI Agents (Complete Guide)
  • How to connect your mobile device to Mobilerun cloud

title: How Java HashMap Works Internally: Hashing, Buckets, Collisions, Resizing and Performance
description:
Understanding the internal implementation of HashMap is essential for every Java developer, especially when building high-performance backend applications and microservices.

We use HashMap almost everywhere in Java applications.

Whether we are caching API responses, storing configuration properties, processing transactions, maintaining session data, or building in-memory lookup structures, HashMap is one of the most frequently used data structures.

But have you ever wondered:

  • How does HashMap store key-value pairs internally?
  • How does it identify the bucket for a particular key?
  • What happens when two keys generate the same hash?
  • How does HashMap handle collisions?
  • Why does HashMap resize automatically?
  • Why does Java 8 introduce Red-Black Trees inside HashMap?
  • What makes HashMap operations approximately O(1)?

Let's understand the internal implementation step by step, using Java 21 examples.

1. What Is HashMap?

HashMap is a part of the Java Collections Framework and implements the Map interface.

It stores data in key-value pairs.

Map<Integer, String> employees = new HashMap<>();

employees.put(101, "John");
employees.put(102, "David");
employees.put(103, "Michael");

System.out.println(employees.get(102));

Output:

David

Unlike a List, HashMap does not maintain insertion order.

Important characteristics:

  • Stores key-value pairs.
  • Allows one null key.
  • Allows multiple null values.
  • Does not guarantee iteration order.
  • Is not thread-safe.
  • Provides approximately O(1) average-time performance for basic operations.

But internally, how does it achieve this performance?

Let's explore.

2. Internal Data Structure of HashMap

Internally, HashMap uses an array of nodes.

Each node stores:

  • Hash
  • Key
  • Value
  • Reference to the next node

The simplified internal structure looks like this:

static class Node<K,V> implements Map.Entry<K,V> {

    final int hash;
    final K key;
    V value;
    Node<K,V> next;

}

The important field here is:

Node<K,V>[] table;

This is the internal bucket array.

Each array position represents a bucket, and each bucket can contain one or more entries.

3. How HashMap Calculates the Hash

When we insert an entry using put(), HashMap first calculates the hash of the key.

Simplified Java 8+ implementation:

static final int hash(Object key) {

    int h;

    return (key == null)
            ? 0
            : (h = key.hashCode()) ^ (h >>> 16);
}

Let's understand this expression:

h ^ (h >>> 16)

Here:

  • h represents the original hashCode.
  • >>> performs an unsigned right shift.
  • ^ represents the bitwise XOR operation.

Why does HashMap perform this additional calculation?

Because Java hashCode is a 32-bit integer, but HashMap uses a power-of-two-sized array to determine the bucket index.

The index calculation uses the lower bits of the hash.

By XORing the upper 16 bits with the lower 16 bits, HashMap helps distribute information from the higher bits into the lower bits.

This improves hash distribution in many cases.

Important: Hash spreading does not eliminate collisions. It helps reduce poor distribution.

4. How HashMap Calculates the Bucket Index

After calculating the hash, HashMap determines where the entry should be stored.

The bucket index is calculated using:

index = (n - 1) & hash;

Where:

  • n is the capacity of the internal array.
  • hash is the spread hash value.
  • & is the bitwise AND operator.

Why not use the modulo operator?

index = hash % n;

HashMap uses bitwise AND because its capacity is always a power of two.

For example:

Capacity = 16

n - 1 = 15

15 in binary = 00001111

The operation:

index = (n - 1) & hash;

is efficient and selects the bucket using the lower bits.

Example:

Capacity = 16
Hash = 35

Index = (16 - 1) & 35

Index = 15 & 35

Index = 3

Therefore, the entry is stored in bucket index 3.

5. What Happens When Two Keys Have the Same Hash?

This is called a hash collision.

Consider:

Map<String, Integer> map = new HashMap<>();

map.put("Aa", 100);
map.put("BB", 200);

Interestingly:

System.out.println("Aa".hashCode());
System.out.println("BB".hashCode());

Both produce the same hashCode:

2112
2112

Both entries are directed to the same bucket.

Does HashMap overwrite the existing value?

No.

HashMap handles collisions by storing multiple entries in the same bucket.

In Java 8 and later, the bucket initially uses a linked list.

Bucket 3

  Node("Aa", 100)
          |
          v
  Node("BB", 200)
          |
          v
        null

When retrieving a value, HashMap:

  1. Calculates the hash of the key.
  2. Identifies the bucket.
  3. Compares the hash.
  4. Checks key equality using reference equality or equals().
  5. Returns the matching value.

This is why implementing equals() and hashCode() correctly is extremely important.

6. How HashMap Handles Collisions: Linked List to Red-Black Tree

This is one of the most important improvements introduced in Java 8.

Before Java 8, HashMap used linked lists to handle collisions.

In a heavily populated bucket, searching could degrade to O(n).

Java 8 introduced a mechanism called Treeification.

When a bucket contains too many entries, HashMap can convert its linked list into a Red-Black Tree.

Important implementation constants:

static final int TREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 8;

static final int UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 6;

static final int MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY = 64;

Let's understand them.

TREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 8

When a bucket reaches the treeification threshold, HashMap may convert the linked list into a Red-Black Tree.

MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY = 64

If the overall HashMap capacity is below 64, HashMap prefers resizing the table instead of treeifying the bucket.

UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 6

During resizing, a tree bin can convert back into a linked list when its population becomes sufficiently small.

Why use a Red-Black Tree?

Because searching a balanced tree takes approximately O(log n), compared with O(n) for a linked list.

The actual implementation has additional details, including collision distribution and tree balancing.

7. How HashMap Resizing Works

HashMap does not allocate an unlimited array.

It grows automatically when the number of entries crosses a threshold.

Two important concepts:

Initial Capacity

Default initial capacity:

16

Load Factor

Default load factor:

0.75

The resize threshold is calculated as:

threshold = capacity * loadFactor;

For example:

Initial Capacity = 16

Load Factor = 0.75

Threshold = 16 * 0.75

Threshold = 12

When the number of mappings exceeds the threshold, HashMap resizes its internal array.

The new capacity is generally doubled:

16 → 32 → 64 → 128 → 256

Why does HashMap resize?

As the number of entries increases, collisions may become more frequent.

Increasing capacity helps distribute entries across more buckets.

What happens during resizing?

During resizing:

  1. A new, larger bucket array is allocated.
  2. Existing entries are redistributed into the new array.
  3. Entries are placed into their appropriate new buckets.
  4. The new array becomes the internal table.

Java 8 introduced an optimization for redistribution.

Because capacity doubles, entries from an existing bucket either:

  • Remain at the same index.
  • Move to the index obtained by adding the old capacity.

This avoids recalculating the complete hash for every entry.

8. How put() Works Internally

Let's understand the simplified flow of the put() operation.

Map<Integer, String> employees = new HashMap<>();

employees.put(101, "John");

Internally, the process is approximately:

put(key, value)
       |
       v
Calculate hash
       |
       v
Calculate bucket index
       |
       v
Is bucket empty?
   /       \
 Yes        No
  |          |
Insert     Check existing nodes
  |          |
  |       Same key?
  |        /    \
  |      Yes     No
  |       |       |
  |   Replace    Continue
  |   value      searching
  |               |
  |          Add new node
  |               |
  +---------------+
          |
          v
   Check resize threshold
          |
          v
       Return

This is a simplified conceptual flow. The actual implementation also handles tree bins, null keys, and other special cases.

9. How get() Works Internally

Retrieving a value follows a similar process.

String employee = employees.get(101);

HashMap:

  1. Calculates the key's hash.
  2. Determines the bucket index.
  3. Checks the first node.
  4. Compares hash and key equality.
  5. Traverses the linked list or searches the tree if necessary.
  6. Returns the matching value.

If the key does not exist, it returns null.

This explains why HashMap provides approximately O(1) average-time lookup.

10. Why Are equals() and hashCode() Important?

One of the most common mistakes developers make is overriding equals() without overriding hashCode().

Consider:

class Employee {

    private int id;

    Employee(int id) {
        this.id = id;
    }

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object obj) {

        if (this == obj) {
            return true;
        }

        if (!(obj instanceof Employee)) {
            return false;
        }

        Employee other = (Employee) obj;

        return this.id == other.id;
    }
}

Now consider:

Map<Employee, String> employees = new HashMap<>();

employees.put(new Employee(101), "John");

System.out.println(
    employees.get(new Employee(101))
);

Without a matching hashCode() implementation, the lookup may fail.

Why?

Because two logically equal objects may produce different identity-based hash codes.

The contract is:

  • If two objects are equal according to equals(), they must have the same hashCode.
  • Objects with the same hashCode are not necessarily equal.

Correct implementation:

@Override
public int hashCode() {
    return Integer.hashCode(id);
}

Real-world lesson: Always implement equals() and hashCode() together when defining custom key objects.

Also, avoid modifying fields that participate in equals() and hashCode() while an object is being used as a HashMap key. Doing so can make the entry difficult to retrieve.

11. Time Complexity of HashMap

Let's look at the typical performance characteristics.

Operation Average Case Worst Case
put() O(1) O(n)
get() O(1) O(n)
remove() O(1) O(n)
containsKey() O(1) O(n)

With tree bins, heavily collided buckets can provide O(log n) lookup behavior under normal balanced-tree conditions.

However, resizing can require O(n) work.

These complexities describe the general implementation behavior, not a guarantee that every individual operation always takes constant time.

12. HashMap vs ConcurrentHashMap

A common question in backend development is:

Should we use HashMap or ConcurrentHashMap?

Feature HashMap ConcurrentHashMap
Thread-safe No Yes
Null key One allowed Not allowed
Null values Allowed Not allowed
Concurrent access Requires external synchronization Supports concurrent operations
Performance Good for single-threaded access Designed for concurrent access

Example:

Map<String, Integer> map = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

In a multithreaded application, using HashMap without proper synchronization can lead to incorrect behavior when multiple threads modify it concurrently.

ConcurrentHashMap provides thread-safe operations and is generally a better choice for shared mutable maps.

Remember: Thread-safe individual operations do not automatically make multi-step business workflows atomic.

13. Real-World Usage in Enterprise Applications

HashMap is not just an interview topic. It plays an important role in enterprise backend development.

Consider a banking application.

We may use HashMap for:

1. Transaction Processing

Map<String, Transaction> transactionCache =
        new HashMap<>();

Useful for temporary in-memory lookups within a controlled execution context.

2. Configuration Management

Map<String, String> applicationConfig =
        new HashMap<>();

3. Grouping Transactions

Map<String, List<Transaction>> transactionsByAccount =
        new HashMap<>();

4. API Response Transformation

Map<String, Object> response = new HashMap<>();

response.put("status", "SUCCESS");
response.put("transactionId", "TXN1001");
response.put("amount", 5000);

In production applications, choose the appropriate concurrency model and cache technology based on data size, lifecycle, consistency, and deployment architecture.

For distributed caching across multiple microservice instances, an in-memory HashMap is not a replacement for Redis or another distributed cache.

14. Best Practices for Using HashMap

A few practical recommendations:

  1. Initialize HashMap with a suitable capacity when the approximate number of entries is known.
  2. Use immutable objects as keys wherever possible.
  3. Always implement equals() and hashCode() consistently for custom keys.
  4. Avoid using HashMap for shared mutable state without synchronization.
  5. Use ConcurrentHashMap for appropriate concurrent access scenarios.
  6. Do not depend on HashMap iteration order.
  7. Use LinkedHashMap when insertion order matters.
  8. Use TreeMap when sorted key ordering is required.
  9. Avoid unnecessarily large initial capacities because they increase memory consumption.
  10. Consider distributed caching solutions for cross-instance application caching.

15. Key Takeaways

Let's summarize what happens internally:

  • HashMap stores entries in an internal array of buckets.
  • It uses hashCode() and hash spreading to calculate the hash.
  • Bucket indexes are calculated using (n - 1) & hash.
  • Collisions are handled using linked lists.
  • Java 8 introduced Red-Black Tree bins for heavily populated buckets.
  • Default initial capacity is 16.
  • Default load factor is 0.75.
  • Resizing generally doubles the capacity.
  • Correct equals() and hashCode() implementations are essential.
  • HashMap is not thread-safe.

Understanding these internals helps us write better Java applications, troubleshoot performance issues, and make informed architectural decisions.

A good Java developer knows how to use HashMap. An experienced Java engineer understands what happens behind the scenes.

Interview Questions to Test Your Understanding

  1. Why is HashMap capacity always a power of two?
  2. Why does HashMap use h ^ (h >>> 16)?
  3. What happens when two different keys have the same hashCode?
  4. What is the difference between collision handling in Java 7 and Java 8?
  5. Why does HashMap convert a linked list into a Red-Black Tree?
  6. What are TREEIFY_THRESHOLD and MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY?
  7. What happens when the load factor threshold is exceeded?
  8. Can two different objects have the same hashCode?
  9. Why is HashMap not thread-safe?
  10. What happens if we modify a key after inserting it into a HashMap?

If you can explain these questions with internal implementation details and practical examples, you have a strong understanding of HashMap.

What's Next?

In the next article, we'll explore another important Java Collections topic:

HashMap vs LinkedHashMap vs TreeMap: Internal Differences, Performance and Real-World Use Cases.

Follow me for more practical Java, Spring Boot, Microservices, Kafka, System Design and Enterprise Architecture insights.

title: How to Build a Side Hustle Around GTA 6 Using AI
description:
GTA 6 is generating huge excitement across the gaming community. But beyond playing the game, it may create opportunities for content creators, bloggers, streamers, and digital entrepreneurs.

If you're interested in gaming and AI, here's how you can combine both to build a potential side hustle.

1. Start a Gaming YouTube Channel

Create gameplay videos, tutorials, tips, challenges, and interesting moments.

AI tools can help you brainstorm video ideas, write scripts, and organize your content.

2. Try Game Streaming

Platforms like YouTube and Twitch give creators opportunities to build communities through live gameplay.

Consistency and audience engagement matter more than simply streaming for hours.

3. Launch a Gaming Blog

Write guides, walkthroughs, news, reviews, and tips.

A focused gaming blog can attract search traffic over time, although ranking takes patience and quality content.

4. Explore Affiliate Marketing

You can create useful content around gaming accessories, PCs, controllers, and other products.

If readers purchase through your affiliate links, you may earn a commission, depending on the program.

5. Use AI to Create Content Faster

AI can help with outlines, brainstorming, editing, and turning ideas into structured articles.

However, AI-generated content still needs human review. Accuracy, originality, and your own experience make a difference.

6. Create Digital Products

Consider gaming guides, checklists, templates, or beginner resources. Focus on solving a real problem rather than publishing generic content.

7. Offer Freelance Services

Gaming websites and creators may need writers, video editors, thumbnail designers, or social media managers.

You can develop these skills and offer them as freelance services.

A Small AI Workflow That Can Help

You don't need dozens of tools to get started.

For example:

  • Brainstorm content ideas with an AI assistant.
  • Write a clear outline.
  • Draft your article or video script.
  • Review and edit the text to make it sound natural.
  • Estimate the token count before sending long prompts to an LLM.

For the last two steps, you can try PromptBurn, which offers two free tools:

  • Free AI Text Humanizer: Rewrites text using Natural, Casual, Professional, and Simple styles.
  • LLM Token Calculator: Estimates how many tokens your text contains.

Both tools are free to use, with no API key required.

Final Thoughts

GTA 6 may offer exciting opportunities for people who enjoy gaming and creating content. But building an audience or earning money takes time, consistency, and useful content.

Start with one idea, learn what your audience wants, and improve as you go.

What are you planning to create around GTA 6: YouTube videos, live streams, or gaming articles?

title: Workflow SDK adds idempotent starts
description:
The Workflow SDK's start() function can now admit a run and claim a hook in one atomic step. Duplicate workflow starts fail safely. The atomic start replaces the previous getHookByToken()-then-start() pattern, whose gap between the lookup and the start left a documented duplicate-start race.

Subscribe to messages inside the run

The claimed Hook exists from the moment the run is admitted, so resumeHook works even before the run begins executing, and early payloads are buffered and delivered in order. Inside the workflow, createHook({ token }) with the same token binds to the already-claimed hook: guaranteed, registering nothing new, adding no step, and resolving getConflict() to null.

Idempotency with no extra code

The token is the idempotency key, and it comes from your own domain: an order ID, an invoice ID, an import ID, or a request ID. The token alone guarantees idempotency. Exactly one run owns it, and a duplicate start() throws HookConflictError carrying the owner's conflictingRunId and never becomes a run. The workflow doesn't have to open the hook at all, and if it never does, the token was only an idempotency key and the run completes normally.

Setting experimental_minRetention keeps the token unavailable after the run ends, counted from start(), so late duplicates are still refused.

Upgrade to workflow 5.4.0 and read the idempotency documentation to get started.

title: Entropy-Regularized Integrated Gradients for Stable Feature Attribution
description:
arXiv:2611.23600v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Path-based attribution methods like Integrated Gradients (IG) are widely used to interpret neural networks, yet imperceptible input perturbations can drastically alter their attribution maps while leaving model predictions unchanged. We introduce Entropy-Regularized Integrated Gradients (ERIG), a path-based attribution method that intrinsically attenuates gradient irregularities along the integration path using maximum-entropy softmax weighting with temperature parameter $\tau$. We quantify the effect of the entropy-regularized weighting on attribution stability by using the Lipschitz properties of the model and its gradients. We decompose the attribution change under an input perturbation into a model-response term, whose bound is $\tau$-independent, and a weight-variation term, whose bound decreases at rate $\mathcal{O}(1/(2\tau))$. Their ratio $R(\tau)$ characterizes the trade-off between gradient information and attribution stability. We further add a new dimension to attribution evaluation by adapting classical noise estimators into two metrics, LINV-C and LINV-P, that quantify attribution noise. Across eleven CNN and Transformer backbones on ImageNet and Oxford-IIIT Pet datasets, our experiments show that, relative to the next-best method, ERIG remains comparable on ranking-based fidelity metrics while improving localization by approximately 24% and attribution stability by approximately 47-fold on average, reaching up to four orders of magnitude improvement over IG, all at negligible additional computational cost.

title: AWS Elemental MediaTailor adds Dynamic Avail Sizing for live HLS
description:
AWS Elemental MediaTailor now supports Dynamic Avail Sizing, which reduces the slate viewers see when ad breaks, also called avails, in live HLS streams go unfilled. MediaTailor is a server-side ad insertion and channel assembly service that personalizes ads in live and on-demand video streams.

When the ad decision server returns fewer ads than a break allows, dynamic avail sizing omits the unfilled time and resumes programming early instead of showing slate. To keep playback continuous, MediaTailor holds back a configurable reserve of content behind the live edge and draws on it when a break ends early. When the reserve runs low, MediaTailor requests extra ad time in later breaks to refill it. Free ad-supported streaming TV (FAST) channel operators can use dynamic avail sizing to keep viewers watching programming instead of filler content.

Customers turn on dynamic avail sizing for each playback session by adding query parameters to the session initialization URL, with no change to their playback configuration. To learn more, see Dynamic avail sizing in the AWS Elemental MediaTailor User Guide.

title: Beyond Cross-Modal Reconstruction: Participant-Level Evaluation of sEMG-Kinematic Coupling in Post-Stroke Gait
description:
arXiv:2611.23856v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Accurate cross-modal reconstruction is often treated as evidence of physiological coupling, although it may simply reflect temporal patterns shared across participants. We tested whether frozen bidirectional models captured subject-specific neuromuscular coupling between electromyographic activity and gait kinematics in 82 held-out able-bodied and 43 post-stroke participants. Complete source-modality removal and cross-participant source substitution, along with a cycle-position-age-sex template baseline, were applied. Learned bilateral asymmetry was also compared with transparent waveform and derivative asymmetry for predicting Performance-Oriented Mobility Assessment (POMA) scores in the case of repeated nested cross-validation. Complete source removal increased reconstruction RMSE by 6.90% for electromyography-to-kinematics and 11.38% in the reverse direction. In contrast, cross-participant substitution increased RMSE by only 1.68% and 1.67%, respectively, while the template reduced RMSE by 2.89% and 0.55%. For POMA prediction, walking speed, age, and sex achieved an MAE of 3.693, compared with 4.229 and 4.427 after adding absolute and signed learned asymmetry, respectively. In all of the 20 repeated evaluations, all asymmetry representations performed worse than the covariate baseline. No localized learned feature remained significant after covariate adjustment and false-discovery-rate correction. The model mainly relied on shared gait-phase patterns, with no clear subject-specific coupling or added clinical value. Participant-level controls are therefore needed before reconstruction accuracy is treated as evidence of individualized physiology.

title: Faster Cricket Dashboards: Caching, Time-Series Storage, and Better Queries
description:
At Stumped Analytics in Nagpur, our league dashboards refresh too slowly. My takeaway from reading Stack Exchange: adding Redis or switching databases isn’t a diagnosis. First, understand repeated work, access patterns and acceptable staleness.

1. Cache the dependencies—not just the delivery

Managing Cache Invalidation highlights derived-data dependencies, while Stack Overflow’s layered-cache example explains coordinating local copies.

In cricket, correcting one delivery can change innings totals, bowling figures and leaderboards. I’d test match/innings-scoped cache versions, invalidation after committed writes, and bounded TTLs. Pub/sub can help refresh local caches, but it isn’t a durable consistency guarantee.

2. Choose storage around the reads

The discussions on time-series schemas and relational versus non-relational storage reinforce the importance of workload-specific design.

For cricket, I’d preserve durable delivery-level facts with stable event identities, explicit ordering and correction history. Over-, innings- and season-level summaries should be rebuildable accelerators—not replacements for the original deliveries. Ball order matters; timestamps alone don’t define the cricket sequence.

A time-series extension is worth evaluating if the measured workload justifies it—not simply because the data has timestamps.

3. Reduce query work before hiding it

Threads on dashboard performance and latest-value queries suggest inspecting execution plans, matching composite indexes to real filters, and avoiding unnecessary historical scans.

My experiment plan: compare cold and warm p95 response times, rows scanned, and ingestion-to-dashboard lag. Then test late-arriving deliveries and score corrections.

These are design hypotheses, not a claimed speed-up. The goal is a dashboard that is both faster and trustworthy.

title: Contract-Explicit Evaluation: From Auditing Learned Readers to Scoped Certificates
description:
arXiv:2611.22665v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Evaluation readings of document-level relation extraction (DocRE) systems depend jointly on the model and the evaluation contract: gold version, scoring function, threshold. Rankings reverse across contracts, yet no existing method determines which comparisons survive the reversal. We address this gap with contract-explicit evaluation: a preregistered five-step protocol (Declare, Measure, Scope, Certify, Hedge), operationalizing the classical concordance decomposition of Kendall's rank correlation, that scopes certifiable regions and delivers distribution-free census certificates across two ecosystems. In the DocRE audit (44 training runs of one in-house architecture family), the scoring dimension scopes to a census certificate (three flagged instances, Clopper--Pearson upper bound 0.146); the confirmatory record includes registered negatives, and the audit prices its own simplification finding---the calibration dial's entire margin is one withdrawn commit. In an LLM-judge census (17 judges, 49,938 battles), 12.25% of leaderboard comparisons require hedging at the pre-declared split criterion (bound 0.124; panel-robust 0.143), with an exploratory two-tier reading certifying 69% at a bound \le 0.072 and a validity decomposition against released human labels (65% of contested battles are judge error, not ambiguity). The cross-model certificate is withdrawn on real confidence scores; the failure spectrum maps the boundary. The protocol, map, ledger, and per-instance artifacts are released.

title: Desacoplamento de Sistemas Comerciais: Por Que Sua Base de Dados Primária Nunca Deveria Receber Webhooks Diretamente
description:
A maioria dos pipelines de dados comerciais nasce de um atalho pragmático. Você precisa capturar leads de uma nova campanha de aquisição, configura um webhook na plataforma de anúncios e aponta essa requisição diretamente para um endpoint da sua API que grava o registro no PostgreSQL, ou envia o payload direto para a API do CRM corporativo. Em ambiente de homologação, a arquitetura responde em poucos milissegundos e tudo parece pronto para escalar.

O problema de engenharia aparece no exato segundo em que a campanha entra no ar e traz volume real.

O Gargalo das Conexões Simultâneas
O tráfego gerado por mídia paga nunca cresce em uma curva suave e previsível. Ele chega em rajadas agressivas e caóticas. Expor sua base de dados primária diretamente a essa volatilidade da internet aberta é um antipadrão arquitetônico severo.

Bancos relacionais como o PostgreSQL são extremamente robustos, mas foram projetados para executar transações estruturadas e consultas previsíveis, não para servir de linha de frente absorvendo centenas de conexões HTTP simultâneas disparadas por plataformas externas. Quando uma campanha viraliza ou dispara lotes de webhooks ao mesmo tempo, o pool de conexões do banco se esgota rapidamente e os bloqueios de escrita começam a se enfileirar. Se o webhook aponta diretamente para um CRM SaaS, você estoura o limite de requisições por minuto da API em questão de segundos.

A Perda Invisível de Dados Comerciais
O impacto mais destrutivo dessa arquitetura acoplada acontece longe dos olhos da operação. Enquanto o seu banco luta para liberar conexões ou o CRM bloqueia o excesso de chamadas, as requisições de entrada ficam penduradas aguardando resposta. A plataforma de origem espera apenas alguns segundos antes de encerrar a conexão por timeout.

Quando a conexão cai, o payload desaparece em trânsito. Não há registro no banco, não há erro visível para o time comercial e a empresa literalmente queima orçamento de marketing capturando clientes qualificados que evaporam antes mesmo de entrar no funil.

A Camada de Absorção como Escudo
Para blindar a integridade dos dados comerciais, é mandatório desacoplar completamente o momento da ingestão do momento da persistência. A base de dados primária precisa ser tratada como um ativo isolado, protegido contra a imprevisibilidade do tráfego externo.

A solução estrutural consiste em posicionar uma camada intermediária de retenção na frente dos seus sistemas centrais. A responsabilidade exclusiva desse middleware é interceptar o webhook instantaneamente, devolver um 200 OK para encerrar a requisição de origem com segurança e armazenar o evento em uma fila controlada. A partir daí, os dados são despachados para o destino final em um ritmo constante e cadenciado.

É exatamente para preencher essa lacuna de infraestrutura sem exigir que a equipe mantenha servidores de mensageria complexos do zero que roteadores comerciais dedicados como o Zapflux entram na arquitetura. Operando como uma camada de absorção de alta disponibilidade, a ferramenta segura o impacto das rajadas de tráfego, retém os payloads com segurança e orquestra a entrega limpa para o seu banco PostgreSQL ou CRM apenas na velocidade que o servidor de destino suporta processar.

Projetar sistemas comerciais resilientes exige assumir que o tráfego externo sempre será hostil à estabilidade da sua infraestrutura interna. Ao eliminar integrações diretas de ponta a ponta e introduzir um middleware de desacoplamento, você protege a saúde do seu banco de dados e garante que picos de acesso nunca resultem na perda silenciosa de receitas.

Como vocês costumam estruturar o controle de concorrência e o isolamento do banco de dados quando precisam ingerir webhooks de alto volume em produção?

title: npm ERESOLVE unable to resolve dependency tree: 4 fixes
description:
npm install stops before writing anything, and instead of a package list you get a tree dump:

npm error code ERESOLVE
npm error ERESOLVE unable to resolve dependency tree

npm error While resolving: my-app@1.0.0
npm error Found: react@18.3.1
npm error Could not resolve dependency:
npm error peer react@^19.0.0 from chart-lib@2.4.0

The line that matters is always peer … from …: the project already decided one version, a dependency's peerDependencies excludes it, and npm refuses to guess.

Why it happens at all

Since npm 7, peer dependencies are installed automatically and a conflicting peer range is a hard error. npm 6 installed peers only with a warning, so this class of failure did not exist before. npm builds one tree per project, and each package name resolves to exactly one directory — node_modules/react cannot be two versions.

A four-line reproduction in an empty directory:

mkdir eresolve-demo && cd eresolve-demo
npm init -y
npm pkg set dependencies.react="^18.3.1"
npm pkg set dependencies.chart-lib="^2.4.0"   # this version peers on react@^19 
npm install
# npm error code ERESOLVE

Read the tree before you pick a flag

Line npm prints What it tells you
While resolving: the package whose dependencies are being resolved
Found: the version already chosen for that name, and who asked for it
Could not resolve dependency: the package whose peer range excludes that version 
npm ls react                              # which versions exist, and who requires them
npm explain chart-lib                     # why the package is in the tree at all
npm view chart-lib peerDependencies --json
npm view chart-lib versions --json | tail -20

That last pair is the cheapest fix path: if a newer patch widened the peer range, upgrading beats every override you could write.

Four strategies, in the order worth trying

Strategy What it changes Lockfile Take it when
Upgrade the dependent its peerDependencies range clean a release accepts your version — always first
overrides resolution for the whole tree clean and reproducible a transitive package lags behind
--legacy-peer-deps skips peer installation (npm 6 behaviour) records the skipped peers plugin ecosystem, migration in progress
--force installs anyway, may duplicate can hold duplicates and broken peers never in CI; a local unblock only

npm install --strict-peer-deps is the inverse: it refuses to auto-pick when ranges conflict, which is what you want in CI when failing is better than drifting.

overrides that actually apply 

{
  "dependencies": { "react": "^19.1.0", "chart-lib": "^2.4.0" },
  "overrides": { "chart-lib": { "react": "$react" } }
}
  • $react means "the version the root manifest resolves", so the pin follows your own dependency instead of being copied in and going stale.
  • The field applies to the entire tree, including packages you never import directly.
  • In a workspace, overrides inside a package's own package.json is ignored. Only the root counts: 
npm pkg set 'overrides.react=$react' -w .    # writes the root manifest
npm install --workspaces

If two workspaces genuinely need different React majors, they need separate lockfiles and separate installs. No override makes one node_modules hold two Reacts safely.

When the tree is already installed

npm reuses an existing node_modules, so an overrides edit can silently fail to reach a nested copy:

rm -rf node_modules package-lock.json && npm install

A merge that combined two lockfiles can raise ERESOLVE on a manifest that is perfectly fine. Inspect before deleting anything:

npm ls --all 2>&1 | grep -i "invalid\|peer\|ERR"
npm install --package-lock-only    # does the manifest resolve at all?

--package-lock-only is the safe first move after a merge: it answers the question without destroying a working node_modules you may still need. npm ci is the only command that promises "exactly this lockfile or nothing".

The traps in the containment strategies

  • --legacy-peer-deps typed once in one terminal is recorded nowhere. The next person's npm ci fails the same way — put it in .npmrc or remove the need for it.
  • --force silences the error by installing conflicting copies. The failure then reappears at runtime as two React instances, a dead context, or an invalid hook call.
  • peerDependenciesMeta: { optional: true } means npm 7+ does not fail when the peer is absent, so an ERESOLVE naming an optional peer usually points at a second, real conflict above it in the tree.
  • A yarn.lock beside a package-lock.json produces two disagreeing resolutions. Commit one, delete the other.
  • Node 20 ships npm 10 and Node 18 ships npm 9; the error text and resolution details differ. Pin the Node version in CI and in .nvmrc.
  • A global install has no overrides field to edit. Use npx some-cli@latest or npm exec --package=some-cli@latest -- some-cli --help for one-off tools instead.

Version cheat sheet

npm Peer dependencies Conflict result
6 warnings only, not installed npm WARN, working tree
7 installed automatically ERESOLVE (introduced here)
8 installed automatically, overrides supported ERESOLVE, fixed by overrides
8.3+ $package references inside overrides pin to the root's own version
9 / 10 / 11 same rules, npm error prefixes richer Could not resolve text

A package-lock.json generated by npm 6 will not reproduce on npm 10, because npm 6 never recorded the peers it skipped.

The longer version, with the workspace and lockfile cases in full, is on my site: npm ERESOLVE unable to resolve dependency tree: 4 fixes.

title: Java4Shell pode permitir execução remota em Jira e Confluence
description:
Falha alcança o runtime Java empacotado

A Calif, empresa que identificou a CVE-2026-114938, conseguiu execução remota de código sem autenticação em configurações padrão do Jira e do Confluence. Em 19 de novembro de 2026, a Atlassian ainda não havia publicado um alerta específico sobre a falha.

O Java4Shell pode atingir o runtime Java que acompanha os produtos. Por isso, uma atualização comum do sistema operacional, feita por apt ou dnf, não necessariamente corrige Jira e Confluence: cada instalação pode continuar usando a versão de Java empacotada com o produto.

Confira runtimes e versões corrigidas

Nos testes descritos, imagens de Jira, Jira Service Management, Confluence e Bitbucket, além do JRE do instalador Linux do Jira, usavam builds vulneráveis. As verificações incluíram Jira 11.3.13 e 10.7.4, Confluence 11.0.1, 10.2.20 e 9.5.4, e as imagens atuais de Bitbucket.

As versões corrigidas do Temurin são 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1 e 25.0.5.1, ou posteriores. Confira o runtime efetivamente usado com java -version; as páginas da Atlassian sobre Java empacotado por versão podem ajudar, mas também podem estar desatualizadas.

A condição vulnerável exige um host x86-64 com os quatro recursos de CPU avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi e bmi2. A verificação abaixo lista os recursos encontrados; mesmo que falte algum, a atualização continua recomendada porque uma migração de máquina virtual ou troca de nó pode mudar o processador disponível.

grep -oE '(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)' /proc/cpuinfo | sort -u

Desative temporariamente o decoder vulnerável

Enquanto o runtime corrigido não estiver disponível, a medida temporária é desativar o decoder com -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics. A flag reduz o desempenho de operações Base64 e pode ser passada às imagens Docker da Atlassian pela variável JVM_SUPPORT_RECOMMENDED_ARGS.

sudo docker run -d --name jira -p 8080:8080 -e JVM_SUPPORT_RECOMMENDED_ARGS='-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics' atlassian/jira-software:latest

Se a variável já tiver opções para trust store ou memória, acrescente a flag à mesma string, separada por espaço, em vez de defini-la duas vezes. Para verificar a opção na JVM do contêiner Jira, o artigo usa o comando abaixo; Confluence aceita a mesma variável.

sudo docker exec -u jira jira sh -c 'jcmd $(pgrep -f catalina | head -1) VM.version; jcmd $(pgrep -f catalina | head -1) VM.flags -all | grep UseBASE64Intrinsics'

Em implantações Kubernetes, os charts Helm Data Center recebem opções adicionais em additionalJvmArgs, no arquivo values.yaml. Após a implantação, confirme a flag com jcmd dentro de um pod; a configuração, por si só, não comprova que a JVM a recebeu.

Configure instalações Linux e Windows

Uma instalação Linux do Jira usa /opt/atlassian/jira/bin/setenv.sh para os argumentos da JVM. O comando abaixo altera a linha vazia padrão; se ela já contiver opções, preserve-as e acrescente a flag dentro das aspas existentes.

sudo sed -i 's/^JVM_SUPPORT_RECOMMENDED_ARGS=""/JVM_SUPPORT_RECOMMENDED_ARGS="-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics"/' /opt/atlassian/jira/bin/setenv.sh

Depois, reinicie o serviço e confira catalina.out para confirmar que o argumento chegou à JVM. No Confluence instalado, a opção segue a configuração de CATALINA_OPTS; em um serviço Windows, ela é adicionada na aba Java da configuração do Tomcat.

Substitua o runtime para corrigir a falha

A correção permanente é instalar um runtime Temurin corrigido, inclusive substituindo o JRE empacotado em instalações compatíveis. No procedimento para Linux, o runtime antigo é mantido como backup, o novo é instalado no diretório jre/ com as permissões preservadas e o Jira é reiniciado.

Após a troca, confirme a versão do processo em execução e, se necessário, reinicie JVMs que tenham sido iniciadas antes da substituição do runtime. A versão encontrada no disco não atualiza automaticamente o código já carregado por um processo ativo.

Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/java4shell-execucao-remota-jira-confluence/
