title: Done, But Still Working: Anytime Evaluation of When Coding Agents Should Stop
description:
arXiv:2611.22901v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Coding agents often continue working after their own tests pass. Does this additional work improve the patch, and how much could be saved by stopping earlier? We study these questions through anytime evaluation: replaying recorded runs, scoring intermediate patches with hidden tests, and measuring the cost incurred at each step. For policies that only stop a run or select an earlier patch, this allows paired comparisons without generating new trajectories, provided replay preserves the relevant states. Across about 6,000 runs of eight open models in two scaffolds on SWE-bench Verified, we find substantial differences in the value of continued work. The hindsight saving available at passing self-tests ranges from under 1% to 57%, depending on the model and scaffold. A rule that stops after the same patch passes twice saves 23% in a preregistered replication, but the preregistered quality test does not establish non-inferiority. We explain these differences by measuring how often a rule fires, how often the patch changes afterwards, and whether those changes repair or break it. Fine-tuning agents to imitate the rule saves 30% over six seeds, while quality preservation remains uncertain. Our results help identify both the opportunities and the risks of early stopping.

title: A JSONB Side Table Only Wins on Rows You Rewrite Twice
description:
I have a table that holds issue reports. Each row has a few fields that change all day (a status, a counter, a timestamp) and one big JSONB column holding the whole issue body. The status flips every time someone triages an issue, the body almost never changes, and the write-ahead log on that database had started to feel like the most expensive part of the whole setup. A reader, johnnylemonny, left a comment on my last piece about JSONB under write load, and his point was blunt: do not split the hot fields into a side table. The big payload already lives outside the row in TOAST, he said, so an update that only touches the hot fields rewrites a narrow tuple with an 18-byte pointer where the payload used to be. The side table would save almost nothing and charge you a second insert, a second primary key index, and a join on every read.

I believed him. Almost. The reasoning is clean, and clean reasoning about databases has a way of being right right up until you measure it. So I measured it: same workload, two shapes, two payload sizes, everything twice. One thousand rows, hot fields updated in scattered rounds the way a real triage queue updates them, and the log measured before and after each batch so every number below is bytes that actually got written.

My claim before the numbers: the side table is not a saving. It is a bet on how often you rewrite the row. And like most bets, it pays on some rows and loses on others, and the payload size decides which.

Problem 1: HOT fires everywhere, and that changes the whole argument

The first surprise is how completely HOT wins. Across the eight cells, 7,996 of 8,000 hot-field updates were HOT updates, every cell at 99.9 percent or better. No index maintenance, no new index entries, just a new tuple version on the same page. That needs two things to be true: the columns you change are not indexed, and the page has free space. I gave the tables room with a fillfactor of 80, and I updated rows scattered across the table instead of sweeping the whole thing in one go.

That second detail matters more than it looks. My first attempt swept all 1,000 rows in a single update, and HOT fired only about a quarter of the time, because rewriting every row on a page burns through its free space in one pass. Scattered writes are what a live queue actually does, and under scattered writes HOT is not a sometimes thing. It is the whole story. If your hot fields are indexed, or your pages are packed full, none of what follows applies, and that is the first thing to check before you believe any number in this piece, including mine.

Problem 2: with a small payload, the split wins by a lot

When the payload is small, about 170 bytes, it stays inside the row. Then the in-table shape pays for it on every update: 368 bytes of log per hot-field update, because each new tuple version carries the payload along. Move the payload to a side table and the same update costs 150 bytes. That is a 218-byte saving per update, about 59 percent, and it is the only cell where the split looks like an obvious win.

But the split charges rent. Inserting a row now costs 513 bytes of log instead of 334, the extra insert plus its primary key index. Divide one by the other and the break-even is under one update per row: 179 bytes extra on the insert, 218 saved on each update. Any row that gets rewritten even once has paid for the split. Most rows in a triage queue get rewritten more than once, so for small inline payloads the side table is a fair trade, and the argument against it mostly fails.

Problem 3: with a big payload, TOAST does most of the work, not all of it

This is the cell johnnylemonny was actually arguing about, and he was mostly right. When the payload is about 8,180 bytes of real text, it spills out of the row into TOAST (five thousand toast chunks across my thousand rows), and the in-table hot update drops from 368 bytes to 231. The pointer really is cheap. The whole point of his comment survives the measurement: the scary version of this story, where every status flip rewrites eight kilobytes of issue body, does not happen. HOT plus TOAST already killed it.

Where his comment goes too far is the word "matching." The in-table update costs 231 bytes and the side-table update costs 151. The side table still wins, by 80 bytes per update, about 35 percent. The tuple version in the main table is still wider than the slim side row, pointer or not. Eighty bytes is not much, and on the insert side the split still charges its 182 bytes, so the break-even moves to about two and a quarter rewrites per row. But it is not zero, and "the split saves nothing" is the kind of clean claim that only survives until someone measures it. He reasoned from the mechanics. The mechanics said the pointer is 18 bytes. The measurement says the row around the pointer still costs you.

Problem 4: the insert is the payload, wherever you put it

The least surprising number is also the one that kills the most arguments. Inserting a row with an eight-kilobyte payload costs about 9,054 bytes of log in the table and 9,236 in the split shape. The payload has to be written once, wherever it lives, and TOAST writes it either way. The split adds 182 bytes to a nine-thousand-byte operation. If you were hoping the side table would make inserts cheaper, it will not, in either size: for the small payload the split makes inserts more expensive, and for the large one it makes them trivially more expensive. The split is a tax on writes that create rows and a discount on writes that change them. Whether that trade is good depends on your ratio of creates to rewrites, and nothing else.

Reads, for completeness: a thousand point lookups took between 0.12 and 0.29 seconds in both shapes, and the spread between my two repetitions was bigger than any gap between the shapes. At this size there is no join tax worth quoting. On a bigger table, with colder caches, there might be. This run cannot tell you that, and I am not going to pretend it can.

Problem 5: the run I threw away

I should say plainly that my first version of this run measured the wrong thing. The "large" payload I built was eight thousand copies of the same letter, and Postgres compressed it down to 173 bytes inside the row, so nothing ever spilled to TOAST and both sizes measured the same small thing. Real issue bodies do not compress fifty to one. I rebuilt the payload out of hundreds of different hashes so it would not compress, confirmed five thousand toast rows, and ran everything again. The numbers above are the second run. The lesson is boring and worth writing down: a test payload has to behave like the real data, and repeating characters do not.

The other honest limit: these are a thousand rows on one machine, hot fields unindexed, pages given room. Change any of that — an indexed status column, the default fillfactor, a vacuum that cannot keep up — and HOT stops firing, and the in-table shape gets expensive in exactly the way this piece says it does not. The numbers are real. Their range is narrow.

So the rule I am keeping is simple enough to fit on a sticky note. If the payload stays inline, split when rows get rewritten at all. If the payload spills to TOAST, split only when a row gets rewritten more than twice. And if a row is written once and never touched again, do not split it: you are paying an insert, an index, and a join for a discount you will never collect.

johnnylemonny's comment was the reason this piece exists, and he was right about the mechanism and wrong about the size of the saving, which is the best kind of comment to get. Where do you draw the line in your own tables — do you split hot fields out, or do you trust HOT and leave the row alone? And if you have measured it rather than reasoned it, what did the log actually say?

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

title: Contract Review Retrieval Explained: Node.js Fallbacks for Cited Change Alerts
description:
A legal contract review workspace should fail toward a smaller, cited answer, not a confident guess: keep a lexical search path, a vector path, and a human-review state, then expose which path produced each citation. The deciding constraint is grounding. A fast answer that cannot point to the exact clause is a failed answer.

Short answer: use a two-stage retrieval architecture with explicit fallbacks, preserve page and clause coordinates in every chunk, and abstain when evidence does not meet a citation threshold.

Grounding wins.

The concrete job here is watching a web page for changes and alerting a reviewer about a contract clause or policy page. That sounds like a diff problem until the first layout redesign turns every line into noise. Retrieval must identify the same legal provision across HTML versions, then let a reviewer inspect the source span that triggered the alert.

What should a fallback prove before an alert is trusted?

Start with an evidence contract. Every candidate passage carries a document ID, source URL, retrieval timestamp, page number when available, clause heading, character offsets, and a content hash. The generator receives those fields alongside text. The UI can then render a citation that survives re-ranking and makes an audit trail possible.

A useful decision rule is deliberately boring:

  1. Run lexical retrieval against normalized clause text and headings.
  2. Run vector retrieval only when the query has enough semantic content and the index is fresh.
  3. Merge and re-rank candidates, deduplicating by clause ID rather than by similar wording.
  4. Require two independent signals, or a high lexical score plus a direct quote, before creating an alert.
  5. If the threshold is missed, return needs_review with the best candidates and no generated legal conclusion.

The RAG paper describes retrieval as a way to connect generation to an external memory. In a contract workspace, that memory is not an abstract embedding store; it is versioned source material. The fallback is successful only if it keeps provenance intact.

How can Node.js keep lexical, vector, and human fallbacks consistent?

Use one result shape at the boundary. The underlying engines can differ, but the rest of the application should not branch on vendor-specific response fields. This TypeScript sketch keeps the policy visible and makes an abstention a first-class outcome.

type Evidence = {
  clauseId: string;
  text: string;
  sourceUrl: string;
  hash: string;
  page?: number;
  heading?: string;
};

type Hit = Evidence & {
  lexical: number;
  semantic: number;
  source: "lexical" | "vector";
};

type Retrieval =
  | { status: "grounded"; hits: Hit[] }
  | { status: "needs_review"; hits: Hit[]; reason: string };

interface Searcher {
  search(query: string, limit: number): Promise<Hit[]>;
}

export async function retrieve(
  query: string,
  lexical: Searcher,
  vector: Searcher | null,
): Promise<Retrieval> {
  const lexicalHits = await lexical.search(query, 8);
  const semanticHits = vector ? await vector.search(query, 8) : [];
  const merged = [...lexicalHits, ...semanticHits]
    .sort((a, b) => (b.lexical + b.semantic) - (a.lexical + a.semantic))
    .filter((hit, index, all) =>
      all.findIndex((other) => other.clauseId === hit.clauseId) === index,
    )
    .slice(0, 5);

  const top = merged[0];
  const hasQuote = Boolean(top?.text && top.text.length >= 40);
  const hasTwoSignals = Boolean(top && top.lexical > 0 && top.semantic > 0);
  if (!top || (!hasQuote && !hasTwoSignals)) {
    return {
      status: "needs_review",
      hits: merged,
      reason: "Evidence did not meet the citation policy",
    };
  }
  return { status: "grounded", hits: merged };
}

The exact score cutoffs belong in evaluation configuration, not in a blog post or a prompt. Tune them against a labeled set of clause changes. Your mileage may vary: a short indemnity clause and a long privacy policy need different minimum quote lengths, even when they share a vocabulary.

Where do retrieval fallbacks fail in contract change detection?

The common failure is not a missing model. It is a broken identity map. If a parser keys chunks by character offset, a one-line insertion shifts every later chunk and produces a false alert. Imagine a page whose termination clause starts at offset 18,400 on Monday; a cookie-banner sentence inserted near the top moves it to 18,447 on Tuesday, so an offset-based diff reports a change even when the clause text is byte-for-byte identical. Stable clause IDs should come from heading paths and normalized anchors; when those are unavailable, map old and new passages with a similarity step and mark the mapping as uncertain. Keep both the proposed mapping and its confidence so a reviewer can see why an alert was grouped.

Another trap is embedding drift. Re-indexing with a new model can change nearest neighbors without any source edit. Store the embedding model ID, index build timestamp, and chunking configuration with each retrieval run. During a rebuild, compare alerts from the old and new index before switching traffic. A lexical path remains valuable because exact terms such as “governing law” and “termination for convenience” are often the strongest signal.

Parsing errors deserve their own state. An empty extraction, a truncated PDF, or a page that requires authentication should produce source_unavailable, not a zero-result answer that looks like “no change.” The alert should include the last successful hash and ask for review. Three words: preserve the last truth.

For a web page watcher, normalize boilerplate, navigation, and timestamps before diffing. Keep the raw response for audit, but retrieve from the cleaned representation. Record HTTP validators such as ETag and Last-Modified when available; they reduce needless parsing, while the content hash remains the final identity check.

Which implementation trade-offs matter more than the model name?

A small team can combine PostgreSQL full-text search with a vector extension, Elasticsearch with a dense-vector field, or a hosted vector database. These are evidence about implementation styles, not rankings. PostgreSQL keeps transactional metadata beside clauses; Elasticsearch offers mature text analysis and distributed indexing; a hosted vector database can reduce operational work but adds a network and policy boundary. None removes the need for clause IDs, freshness checks, or abstention.

The catch is operational. A vector-only design is not suitable when exact legal terms, citations, or newly added clauses dominate the query. A lexical-only design is a poor fit for paraphrased obligations across templates. Stick with a single lexical index when the corpus is small, terms are stable, and a reviewer can inspect every hit; add semantic retrieval when labeled evaluation shows it recovers misses without increasing unsupported alerts.

Measure before copying the architecture: citation precision, citation recall, unsupported-answer rate, stale-index rate, p95 retrieval latency, and cost per reviewed document. Split the test set by document type and by edit pattern, including heading changes, inserted paragraphs, and reordered lists. A single aggregate score hides the failure that legal teams notice first: a plausible alert attached to the wrong clause.

How should the workspace expose uncertainty to reviewers?

Make the fallback visible in the event record. Store retrieval_path, candidate scores, source hashes, and the policy decision next to the generated summary. Show the changed quote, its before-and-after context, and a link that resolves to the exact source version. A reviewer should be able to reject an alert without deleting the evidence that caused it.

Retries need boundaries. Retry transient fetches with capped exponential backoff, but do not retry a deterministic parse failure forever. Queue re-indexing separately from alert generation so a delayed index cannot silently suppress a change. Emit metrics for each transition: fetched, normalized, indexed, retrieved, grounded, and needs review.

I would ship the lexical path first, then add vectors behind the same interface and compare decisions in shadow mode for one release cycle. That keeps the blast radius small and gives the team a real error budget. The fastest route to trust is a clear abstention, backed by a citation, when the system is unsure.

References

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/ETag
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Last-Modified
  • https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/textsearch.html
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/dense-vector.html

title: How to add a contact form to a static site without Formspree or Netlify Forms
description:
A static site is easy until someone needs to write to you.

mailto: leaks your address to scrapers. A Google Form looks like a Google Form. And the usual next step — Formspree, Basin, Netlify Forms, a serverless function plus a database — is either a monthly bill or a small project of its own.

You can host a tiny form backend yourself. This post walks through a working setup: a plain HTML form, a Node.js endpoint with no npm dependencies, a honeypot, and an inbox that is just a file on disk.

The finished starter is called Formbox Lite. It is free and MIT licensed. You can follow along and write it yourself, or clone the repo at the end and run node server.js.

1. The form on your site

No JavaScript required:

<form action="https://forms.yourdomain.com/f/contact" method="POST">
  <label>Name <input type="text" name="name" required></label>
  <label>Email <input type="email" name="email" required></label>
  <label>Message <textarea name="message" required></textarea></label>

  <input type="text" name="_gotcha" tabindex="-1" autocomplete="off"
         style="position:absolute;left:-8000px" aria-hidden="true">

  <input type="hidden" name="_next" value="/thanks.html">
  <button type="submit">Send</button>
</form>

The _gotcha field is a honeypot. People never see it. A lot of bots still fill every input they find. If that field is not empty, the server should pretend the submit worked and then throw the message away.

_next is where the browser goes after a successful HTML submit. The server must only redirect to a path on your own origin, or you have built an open redirect.

2. A server that only does one thing

You do not need Express for this. Node's built-in http module is enough:

  • POST /f/contact accepts application/x-www-form-urlencoded or application/json
  • Reject an empty body
  • Reject the honeypot (with a fake success)
  • Rate-limit by a hash of the client address — do not store raw IPs
  • Append a JSON object to data/submissions.jsonl
  • Redirect to /thanks.html, or return { ok: true, id } if the client asked for JSON

JSON Lines is an underrated database for a contact form. You can read it with any editor, back it up by copying one file, and grep it when you need to. You only outgrow it when you have many forms, search, or notifications — not on day one.

3. An inbox you can actually open

A raw .jsonl file works, but a /inbox page is nicer when you are testing. On localhost it can be open. In production, put a password in front of it and serve it over HTTPS.

That is the whole product for a personal site: form, endpoint, file, inbox.

4. What this does not do (yet)

A one-form starter will not:

  • email you when a message arrives
  • post to Slack or a CRM
  • run captcha or a serious spam model
  • manage ten forms for ten sites

If you need those, you are in "real form backend" territory. I also make a fuller kit for that. For a single contact page, the lite server is enough.

5. Run it 

# download the zip from the link above and unzip it
cd formbox-lite
node server.js

Open http://127.0.0.1:3000, send a message, then open /inbox. There is a short go-live checklist in the README (HOST, PUBLIC_URL, ALLOWED_ORIGIN, INBOX_PASSWORD, a persistent disk).

Download (free, pay-what-you-want): https://richestcountry.gumroad.com/l/formbox-lite

If you want the multi-form dashboard, spam filtering, SMTP and signed webhooks: Formbox Kit ($19).

Questions and patches are welcome. Tell me what broke when you put it in front of a real site.

title: Why have a Security Operations Centre (SOC)?
description:
As businesses continue to digitise, they will begin to heavily utilise cloud services, web-based applications, remote working capabilities and complex networks.Whilst these can increase efficiency within an organisation, they can also introduce new vulnerabilities to exploit.

In order to detect and act upon advanced cyber threats in a timely manner, businesses should ensure that they are constantly monitored, threats are detected quickly, and incidents are managed effectively. This is where a Security Operations Centre can be beneficial.

What Is a Security Operations Centre?

A Security Operations Centre (SOC) is a group of people, processes and technologies that work together to monitor, detect, investigate and manage cyber security threats. The SOC ensures that the digital infrastructure of businesses is secure.

Within the Security Operations Centre, activity on networks, devices, servers, cloud services and applications within an organisation are constantly monitored. If suspicious activity is detected, the security analysts will investigate and respond appropriately to reduce further damage.

Depending upon an organisations needs, a SOC can be provided by internal staff, by an external Cyber security provider, or a mixture of both.

Why do Businesses Need a SOC?

Cyber attacks can occur at any time. If monitoring is not implemented within the organisation, suspicious activity may not be identified in a timely manner, causing significant damage.

Benefits of having a SOC include the following.

  • Continuous Monitoring

Security analysts within the SOC continuously monitor an organisations IT infrastructure. Information from various systems is gathered and investigated to detect unusual activity, unauthorised access and possible vulnerabilities.

By performing continuous monitoring, suspicious activity can be detected quickly in order to reduce the risk of large scale issues.

  • Threats Detected Quickly

By detecting threats early in their lifecycle, the impact they could cause to your organisation can be minimised. Within a SOC, security monitoring tools, threat intelligence and behaviour analysis can be used to detect signs of compromise.

Detection of threats early means that phishing attacks, malware, ransomware and unauthorised access to accounts can be identified and responded to quickly, preventing attackers from affecting many systems.

  • Quick Incident Response

If cyber threats are identified in good time, businesses should respond to them quickly.

Analysts within the SOC will investigate alerts, and determine how severe an incident is. Based on this, predefined responses to incidents will be performed. This may include isolating infected devices, disabling suspicious accounts, blocking malicious connections and resetting credentials.

By having defined incident responses in place, disruption within businesses can be minimised and threats prevented from spreading throughout businesses systems.

  • Reduce Risk and Disruption

Cyber incidents can lead to financial loss, disruption to operations, damage to reputation and exposure of confidential information.

Having a SOC in place can reduce this risk. By identifying vulnerabilities, monitoring suspicious activity and improving incident responses, the risk of incidents occurring can be reduced. Performing regular security assessments and continuous monitoring within the organisation can improve overall security.

  • Improved Compliance

Many industries have specific security and data protection requirements. Having a SOC in place can improve compliance within businesses. By recording security data, logging incidents, monitoring access and creating reports, compliance can be improved.

This can allow businesses to be better prepared for security assessments, and prove that they have good security management in place.

  • Key Tools within a SOC

There are several key tools that can be utilised within a Security Operations Centre to improve threat visibility and response.

  • Security Information and Event Management (SIEM)
    – SIEM tools allow security log data to be collected from various systems. This enables security teams to determine suspicious patterns of activity, and investigate possible incidents.

  • Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR)
    – EDR tools monitor devices such as laptops, desktops and servers. They can detect malicious activity and assist with investigation and containment.

  • Security Orchestration Automation and Response (SOAR)
    – SOAR tools automate repetitive security tasks and streamline incident response processes within businesses. Security analysts can then focus on more complex security investigations.

  • Threat Intelligence
    – Threat intelligence tools give insight into new cyber threats, malicious IP addresses, types of attacks and vulnerabilities.

Using these tools enables SOC teams to better understand threats, prioritise alerts and respond to incidents efficiently.

NOC vs SOC

Although both Security Operations Centres and Network Operations Centres monitor IT infrastructures within businesses, they have different roles.

While a SOC aims to protect systems from cyber threats, a NOC focuses on ensuring networks operate with optimum availability, performance and stability.

Within a SOC, suspicious logins and potential malware will be investigated. Within a NOC, network outages, connection issues and performance issues with servers will be investigated.

Both NOCs and SOCS support business continuity, however they focus on different priorities.

Should SMES have a SOC?

Small and medium sized enterprises hold valuable customer data, finances, applications and confidential company data. However, creating an internal SOC may be expensive as it requires substantial investment in infrastructure, tools and skilled staff.

To help alleviate this issue, businesses can use Managed Security Services or SOC as a service.

This means that businesses can benefit from expert cyber security support, security monitoring, threat detection and incident management without having to employ large numbers of staff in security.

Depending on the infrastructure, requirements and budget of the business, businesses can choose which method of security monitoring they would like to use.

Best Practices

To improve the effectiveness of an SOC, the following Best Practices should be taken into consideration.

  • Ensure continuous monitoring of critical systems.
  • Implement appropriate SIEM and endpoint security tools.
  • Create procedures for managing incidents.
  • Regularly review security alerts, and investigate any unusual activity.
  • Train staff to be aware of phishing/social engineering attacks.
  • Perform vulnerability testing and audits.
  • Measure performance using metrics, such as Mean Time to detect and Mean Time to respond.
  • Regularly update security procedures and policies.

By doing this, businesses can have a more proactive approach to security.

Conclusion

A Security Operations Centre is an important feature within modern cyber security strategies. They allow businesses to monitor their digital environment, detect threats, manage incidents and reduce the risk of cyber attacks.

As businesses become increasingly digital, it is no longer optional to implement proactive security monitoring. Whether internally or with a managed security provider, having an efficient Security Operations Centre in place can help organisations protect valuable assets, and ensure business continuity.

To learn more about the key roles, tools within SOC operations and business benefits, take a look at this guide: Security Operations Centre in modern Cybersecurity

title: Tests that prove something: break a copy and see the test fail
description:
A green suite only counts if it can go red. So when a test is written for a fix, the practice in Yonto Player's repo is to revert the fix and watch that test fail, and to break the exact line the test claims to hold. This post is how that loop works, how to run it safely, and what to do with fakes so the loop is cheap.

Two questions, both answered by failing

There are two claims a change can make, and each has its own proof.

The first is "this fixes a behaviour". The proof is a test that fails without the fix. The repo's fix workflow ranks the ways to hold a fix in order: a compile error, then a test that fails when the fix is reverted, then a measurement in the PR body for something the harness cannot assert. Where the shape allows it, the test is written first and watched failing for the right reason, then the fix turns it green.

The second is "this rule holds". The proof is a mutation: change the code in the one way that breaks the rule, and a test has to go red. If nothing does, that is information too, and there are a few readings of it, covered below.

Mutate one decision at a time

The repo's testing notes are specific about how to mutate, because a careless mutation proves less than it looks like.

  • Revert one site and one decision at a time. A combined revert going red proves something is pinned, but never that everything is. If a change has three decisions, each gets its own revert and its own named test.
  • Revert the connection as well as the logic. The CompositionLocalProvider, the callback a screen is handed, the argument at the one call site: these look like plumbing, and they are the lines most easily left unpinned. Where the connection is a parameter, drop its default. A compile error saying no value was passed for the parameter is proof that cannot rot.
  • For a guard over a sequence, break the member that makes the proof hardest. Break the last item of a loop, not the first. If the run stops at the first item, "nothing before it was affected" is a fact about ordering, not about your code. Then break two and check that the failure reports both.
  • When a mutation survives, read it four ways. The line may be untested (add a test). It may change nothing the function returns for any input (delete it). It may change the result in a way today's only caller cannot see (test the function directly). Or the fixture may not be able to tell the difference (change the fixture).

An example you can check

Here is a real shape from the codebase, as a simplified sketch. A small cache keeps an answer for a time-to-live, and takes its clock as a constructor parameter, defaulting to the system clock.

// Simplified sketch, not the real file.
class ExpiringCache<K, V>(
    private val ttlMillis: Long,
    private val clock: () -> Long = ::nowMillis,
) {
    // ...
    // inside get(): a cached entry is fresh while
    //   clock() - entry.loadedAt < ttlMillis
}

And the shape of the tests, with the clock as a plain variable the test owns:

// Simplified sketch of the tests.
private var now = 1_000_000L
private val cache = ExpiringCache<String, Int>(ttlMillis = 5_000, clock = { now })

@Test fun `a fresh entry is answered without loading again`() = runTest {
    load(1)
    now += 4_999
    load(2)
    assertEquals(1, loads)
}

@Test fun `an entry older than the ttl is reloaded`() = runTest {
    load(1)
    now += 5_000
    load(2)
    assertEquals(2, loads)
}

The pair sits on both sides of the boundary, 4,999 and 5,000. That is the point of the mutation: change < to <= in the freshness check and the entry counts as fresh at exactly 5,000, so the second test sees one load instead of two and goes red. A suite with only the first test would stay green through that mutation.

An injected clock is what makes this possible at all. Time is a parameter, so the test moves it by hand: no sleeping and no waiting for a real five seconds, so the clock cannot make the test flaky.

Do it on a copy

A mutation is a deliberately broken version of your code, so it never belongs in the tree you are working in. The safe loop is:

# Simplified sketch of the loop. All paths and names are generic placeholders.
COPY=$SCRATCH/mutation-copy
rm -rf "$COPY" && cp -R "$REPO" "$COPY"      # the real tree is never touched
cd "$COPY"

rm -f build/test-results/test/*.xml           # no old result can answer for this run

perl -pi -e 's/< ttlMillis/<= ttlMillis/' src/Cache.kt
git diff --quiet -- src/Cache.kt && { echo "mutation did not apply"; exit 1; }

./gradlew test --tests '*CacheTest' || true   # a red run is the point

ls build/test-results/test/*.xml >/dev/null || { echo "no tests ran"; exit 1; }
grep -l '<failure' build/test-results/test/*.xml   # lists result files holding a failure; open one to see which test

Three details matter more than the rest.

Work on a copy. The real tree stays exactly as you left it, and throwing the copy away is the whole cleanup. There is no step that restores anything, so there is nothing to forget.

Check that the mutation applied. A scripted replace that matches nothing is a silent no-op, and the run that follows is then an unmutated run. Assert that the diff is not empty before you read anything into the result.

Check that tests ran before counting failures. Zero failures from zero tests also reads as green. So the repo's notes say to delete the test's result files before the run and check that they exist afterwards, The same habit covers a rebase or a conflict in a test file: compare the test names against where you came from, because counting @Test annotations misses a removal netted against an addition.

What fakes are for

A fake is the other half of this practice. A real source or a real clock makes a mutation round slow and noisy, and a fake makes it fast and exact.

The repo has a fake content source with call counters, so a test can assert that a second screen load did not ask the source again. It also has gates: a category or a detail call can be held until the test completes a deferred, which lets a test assert what is on screen while a call is still in flight. That matters because a state flow conflates values, so "it never went blank" cannot be asserted by collecting; you hold the call and look while it is held.

One caution from the same notes: a gated fake reads its answer after its gate opens, so set an older answer back before opening the gate.

What a red test does not tell you

A green mutation round is evidence that a test is not vacuous. It is not evidence that the thing works. Mutation shows a test notices a change in the code; it cannot notice what the harness makes impossible. A bug that depends on the order of UI frames cannot show up under a test dispatcher that runs launched work eagerly, so breaking the line still turns the test red while saying nothing about a television. Claims about frame ordering, timing and what is on screen when are settled on a device, and a scripted smoke test covers the basics of starting, reaching Home, finding a title and playing it.

Try it

Pick the last test you wrote. Make a copy of the project, break the one line it claims to hold, confirm the mutation applied, run it with the old results deleted, and check which test went red. If none did, you have found out something the green suite could not tell you.

Read more

  • Test and debug a plugin: linting, running and recording a plugin on your computer, and writing tests for it.
  • Write a plugin: the plugin developer docs.
  • The plugin SDK and CLI: open source, including the CLI's tests.

title: Java4Shell no OpenJDK pode permitir execução remota via Base64
description:
Falha Java4Shell no OpenJDK

Pesquisadores da Calif divulgaram a Java4Shell, vulnerabilidade CVE-2026-114938 de corrupção de memória no decodificador Base64 AVX-512 do OpenJDK. A falha recebeu classificação de gravidade 9,2 e pode permitir que invasores provoquem uma gravação fora dos limites da heap.

O problema pode ser acionado com uma string malformada terminada em um sinal de igual isolado. De acordo com o relato, essa entrada pode levar ao vazamento de memória sensível ou, em determinadas condições, à execução remota de código antes da autenticação.

Possíveis efeitos da exploração

A gravação fora dos limites da heap é o mecanismo descrito pelos pesquisadores para explicar os riscos da vulnerabilidade. Entre os resultados possíveis estão a exposição de dados sensíveis armazenados na memória e a execução de código remotamente sem autenticação prévia.

Jira, Jenkins e Keycloak estão entre as plataformas citadas como exemplos de sistemas que podem ser afetados. O alerta não confirma ataques bem-sucedidos nesses produtos; descreve os possíveis impactos da falha em plataformas importantes.

Atualização de segurança

Embora a Calif considere a vulnerabilidade difícil de explorar, a Oracle publicou uma atualização crítica de segurança na terça-feira. A Agência de Segurança Cibernética e de Infraestrutura dos Estados Unidos (CISA) também pediu que as organizações atualizem seus sistemas imediatamente.

Equipes responsáveis por ambientes OpenJDK devem priorizar a aplicação da atualização de segurança e verificar os sistemas que dependem do decodificador afetado. O risco descrito inclui tanto a exposição de memória sensível quanto a possibilidade de execução remota antes da autenticação.

Risco de exposição prolongada

Os pesquisadores da Calif alertaram que sistemas vulneráveis podem permanecer expostos por cinco a dez anos, diante da lentidão com que algumas organizações corrigem sua infraestrutura. O intervalo é um alerta sobre o tempo que falhas sem correção podem continuar presentes.

A recomendação da CISA para atualizar imediatamente reforça a importância de tratar a Java4Shell como prioridade de segurança. Organizações que mantêm sistemas vulneráveis devem aplicar a atualização crítica da Oracle para reduzir o período em que a falha pode ser explorada.

Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/falha-java4shell-openjdk-execucao-remota-codigo-base64/

title: Checking Broken URLs After a Site Migration — a small on-demand tool
description:
Checking Broken URLs After a Site Migration — a Small On-Demand Tool

Migrations move URLs. A redirect map that looks complete in a spreadsheet can still produce 404s, redirect loops, or unresolved hosts once the new site is live. The annoying part is that you often find out from Search Console days later.

I built a small Actor to check exactly the references you hand it — no site crawling, no background monitoring, no alerts. This post shows the input, a real output, and where the tool deliberately stops.

The input

  • urls: public http/https URLs you supply.
  • sitemapUrls: up to 10 public sitemap.xml files; <loc> entries are expanded.
  • maxUrls: 1–200 per run (default 200). concurrency: 1–10. timeoutMs: 1,000–30,000.

Exact duplicates are removed. Larger catalogues are checked in separate runs.

A real result

The following is the Actor's own local reproduction output (2026-11-18), used here because it shows the exact field shape. It is not a paid customer run.

{"status":"ok","statusCode":200,"inputUrl":"https://example.com/",
 "finalUrl":"https://example.com/","redirectChain":[],"redirectCount":0,
 "contentType":"text/html; charset=utf-8","elapsedMs":105}

{"status":"broken","statusCode":404,
 "inputUrl":"https://example.com/definitely-not-a-real-page-r011",
 "finalUrl":"https://example.com/definitely-not-a-real-page-r011",
 "redirectChain":[],"redirectCount":0,
 "contentType":"text/html; charset=utf-8","elapsedMs":61}

{"status":"network_error","statusCode":null,"inputUrl":"https://invalid.invalid/",
 "finalUrl":"https://invalid.invalid/","error":"fetch failed",
 "redirectChain":[],"redirectCount":0,"contentType":"","elapsedMs":12}

Three cases in one run: a healthy page, a confirmed dead page, and a host that could not be reached. The distinction matters — network_error is not proof that a page is broken, so a QA pass should investigate it rather than file it as a 404.

Each record also carries redirectChain as ordered from → status → to hops, which is useful when a migration produced chains instead of single 301s.

What this is good for

  • Pre-launch QA of a redirect map on staging.
  • A bounded post-launch check of the URLs that carry traffic or backlinks.
  • Verifying a sitemap subset after a domain or platform move.

What it does not do

  • Maximum 200 URLs per run. It is not a full-site crawler.
  • On demand only — no scheduling, continuous monitoring, alerts or webhooks.
  • No authentication, private pages, personal data, or resale of third-party data.
  • Results reflect the moment of the check.

Price

Pay per event: US$ 1.20 per 1,000 URLs checked (US$ 0.0012 per URL) on the primary event. A full 200-URL run is about US$ 0.24. No subscription is required.

Try it: https://apify.com/deyvison-md91/sitemap-integrity-auditor

I am the author of the Actor; this post discloses that interest. The example output comes from my own local reproduction, not from a customer.

title: Clustering in pure-attention hardmax transformers and its role in sentiment analysis
description:
arXiv:2407.01602v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Transformers are extremely successful machine learning models whose mathematical properties remain poorly understood. Here, we rigorously characterize the behavior of transformers with hardmax self-attention and normalization sublayers as the number of layers tends to infinity. By viewing such transformers as discrete-time dynamical systems describing the evolution of points in a Euclidean space, and thanks to a geometric interpretation of the self-attention mechanism based on hyperplane separation, we show that the transformer inputs asymptotically converge to a clustered equilibrium determined by special points called \textit{leaders}. We then leverage this theoretical understanding to solve sentiment analysis problems from language processing using a fully interpretable transformer model, which effectively captures `context' by clustering meaningless words around leader words carrying the most meaning. Finally, we outline remaining challenges to bridge the gap between the mathematical analysis of transformers and their real-life implementation.

title: Send the Firefighters to the Fires
description:
Send the firefighters to the fires

Enterprise software keeps forgetting a century of good advice about what deserves our attention.

If a user’s job is to fix what’s broken, the screen should show what’s broken first. Sounds pretty obvious. It’s also not new. Frederick Taylor argued for it in 1903. Xerox PARC designed for it in the ’90s. Industrial control rooms wrote it into a standard. Yet enterprise software keeps forgetting this.

Imagine a fire department that dispatches trucks in the order houses were built. Or by date last renovated. Every house gets a visit eventually, and some of them happen to be on fire. That’s pretty absurd, right? Yet I’ve seen the equivalent more times than I care to remember.

A lot of enterprise work boils down to one job: here’s a collection of things, some of them have problems, go fix the problems. Devices out of compliance. Certificates about to expire. Invoices that failed to reconcile. Tickets breaching SLA. The KPI is simply “issues resolved.”

The UI has one job: get the user to the fires and hand them the hose.

So how did we forget? Not because the ideas are hard. Enterprise software just has a habit of designing for everyone except the person actually using it. It’s designing for the buyer in the demo, for the team racing to ship, for the data model that sorts things for free. None of them pay for it. But the user does, every shift, one scroll at a time.

Start with the job

Clayton Christensen had a simple idea: people don’t buy products for their features. They hire them to get a job done. It’s now known as Jobs to Be Done, or JTBD (Christensen et al., 2016; open-access overview). In enterprise triage, the job is about as plain as it gets: fix what’s broken. Finding it should be the product’s job.

So why do so many screens ignore this? Here’s the pattern I see over and over again. A screen lists 400 objects, and twelve need attention. They’re scattered somewhere between page 3 and page 17. It’s Where’s Waldo, except Waldo is a production outage.

Sometimes there’s a status column. Maybe a small red pill, sitting politely in column six of a list sorted by anything but what matters. A human can work out which items are broken. But the interface is acting obtuse and unhelpful.

Consider the following twenty services. I’ll keep coming back to them.

Before: 20 rows, sorted by last updated, every column visible

After: focus on the fires

In the first table, the two critical services sit in rows sixteen and nineteen, and nothing calls them critical. You have to cross-reference Health and Tier yourself: search-index is only Degraded, but it’s Tier 1; mail-relay is Failing, but it’s Tier 3. Meanwhile, Uptime reads 99.92% for payments-gw, which is failing right now. The fires-first view does that math for you. Same data, different job.

Now imagine hearing that table instead. If the headers are marked up properly, a screen reader announces which column you’re in as you move through it (W3C, F91). So a screen reader user can walk down the Health column one cell at a time. That’s still twenty announcements to find six problems, plus a hop to the Tier column for each one. And that’s the best case: many enterprise data grids are built from divs, virtualized, or paginated, and those shortcuts break. Many enterprises don’t hire people who can build accessible tables (Brad Frost calls them front-of-the-front-end developers), but that’s another story. For every column of noise we leave in, someone has to sit through it.

None of this is malicious. Nobody in the review said “hey, let’s bury the critical issues!” The order happened by default, because nobody dug into the JTBD.

The table as a design cop-out

Bad sort order is an outcome of enterprise’s unfortunate love affair with the table as a magic bullet.

The reasoning goes: we don’t know exactly what users want, so let’s give them all the data and let them search, filter, and sort. It sounds like giving users control. In reality, it’s an abdication.

Those are tools for exploring and hunting: browsing to see what’s there, or tracking down something you know exists. But when they become the main interface for task work, the product team has handed its job to the user. Every session, someone sorts by health, scrolls past the Passing rows, cross-checks the tier, and finds payments-gw. Again. Multiply that by every user, every day. That’s triage the product could have done once.

At some point, some smarty-pants will suggest saved filters: let users build and save their own “To-dos” view (health is failing, sorted by tier). Problem solved, right? Not quite! That’s a workaround stacked on the cop-out. Users end up designing the default screen for you because you shipped the wrong one.

Why smart teams keep doing this

To be fair, the people shipping these screens aren’t careless. The forces pushing them toward the table are real, and a lot of them trace back to one thing: in sales-led enterprise software, the buyer isn’t the user.

Jason Lemkin said it bluntly back in 2012: “you, the end user, aren’t the customer for most true enterprise software” (Lemkin, SaaStr). A year later, Martin Eriksson made the same distinction for product managers: “the user and the purchaser are different people with different needs” (Eriksson, Mind the Product).

The buyer’s worst case is a boring demo. The user’s worst case is an outage with their name on it. Guess who the screen gets designed for. Not every lazy sort comes from sales, but a sales-led motion makes lazy sorts easier to ship and harder to undo.

Defaults feel safe. Every record has a created_at and an updated_at, so sorting by them is free. “Severity” doesn’t exist until someone designs it. Meanwhile, stakeholders worry that if healthy items aren’t visible, users will assume they’re missing, and on an RFP checklist, a hidden column might as well not exist. So everything stays on screen.

Nobody talks to each other. Taiichi Ohno’s 5 Whys only works if you can reach the person with the answer. In enterprise, there are too many layers between the people willing to ask and the people able to answer. The only two people reliably talking are the salesperson and the buyer. The salesperson is paid for the close, and asking why five times only gets in the way. Conway’s law predicts the result: systems mirror how their makers communicate. A neutral sort is what that silence looks like on screen.

“Ask ‘why’ five times about every matter.”
 — Taiichi Ohno, Toyota

Dashboards are built for the demo. People love dashboards that look like command centers in movies. Walls of screens! Scrolling numbers! Blinking maps! Stephen Few was criticizing exactly this two decades ago, arguing that dashboards should support real-time situation awareness for decision making, not impress the room (Few, 2007; Information Dashboard Design, 2006). Density still wins sales calls, which is the sales motion showing up in the UI. Developers and PMs love it too: every widget and column is a feature someone built.

Tables are cheap and familiar. Every component library ships one, and every IC has built a dozen, so it’s what everyone reaches for first. Inline editing is one prop away, so someone will eventually float turning every cell into a form field. Cheap to build, expensive to use.

Notice what these have in common? Each one optimizes for the team’s comfort or the buyer’s first impression, not the user’s job. The table can never be wrong, because it never commits to anything.

Tables aren’t the enemy

To be clear, I’m not anti-table. Reporting, analysis, and bulk admin are table work. User questions can change week to week, and pinning them down takes the kind of conversations we’ve already seen are rare. Designing for that is tough, so a flexible table is an honest answer.

The line I draw is this: open-ended questions need flexible tables. Known jobs need opinionated ones.

Yet sometimes the best table is the one you don’t build! Think about what people actually do with a big table, and where that work belongs:

  • Slice and pivot? Let them export to (or integrate with) the BI tools they already know.
  • Report up to leadership? Send a scheduled summary, not a screenshot of 400 rows.
  • Reconcile against another system? That’s an integration or an API. Please don’t subject a human being to comparing two systems row by row.
  • Hand evidence to auditors? Send an export instead of buying them a seat, which only gets them a login they’ll barely use, to a worse BI tool.

Excel, Tableau, and Power BI are established, they’re good at analysis, and your users already know them. Your product doesn’t need to compete. Just keep the fires list live and in-app.

So the question isn’t table or no table. It’s what goes in it, and in what order. If you can write the user’s job in one sentence, and “resolve the issues” is that sentence, you know enough to decide: fires first, ranked by severity, healthy rows summarized. A table sorted by last updated with every row at equal weight is just an inventory. It tells users what exists, not what needs their attention.

Management by exception, a century later

One of my core design principles fits in four words: no news is good news. I didn’t invent it. In 1903, Frederick Taylor called it the exception principle: a manager shouldn’t be swamped with every report, only with what deviates from the standard (Taylor, Shop Management).

“The manager should receive only condensed, summarized, and invariably comparative reports.”
 — Frederick Winslow Taylor, Shop Management (1903)

Swap “manager” for “user” and it’s a design brief. There’s no reason to emphasize what’s working. Working is the expected state; it’s what the customer pays for. But there’s every reason to emphasize what isn’t, because that’s the only part that needs a human.

Every pixel that gives a healthy object the same weight as a broken one is friction against the KPI. If the metric is issues resolved, a screen that hides issues isn’t neutral. It’s working against the business. And noise isn’t just visual. For a screen reader user, it’s time.

So design as if the user’s job performance depends on your decisions. Because it does! When issues slip through the cracks, nobody blames the designer who picked the default sort. They blame the user who didn’t spot payments-gw in time. They inherit our defaults, our clutter, and our shallow thinking, and they’re the ones who get penalized for it.

That’s the bar. It’s not “does it follow the design system” or “did stakeholders sign off.” It’s “does this make the person using it better at their job?”

What control rooms already know

Ironically, real control rooms don’t look like the movies. In refineries and power plants, operator screens are guided by the ISA-101 standard for industrial interfaces (ISA, 2015), which builds on the high-performance HMI work of Bill Hollifield and colleagues (The High Performance HMI Handbook). Normal operation stays gray and calm. Color is saved for when something’s wrong.

https://medium.com/media/3a2b27bedfc398539b462d0027464e6c/href

The unsexy truth is that sometimes, that’s all a dashboard needs to be: a prioritized list of what’s on fire and the means to put it out, not a bunch of widgets fighting for the user’s attention. Many may not like it, but that’s what peak performance looks like. Operators knew it long before enterprise SaaS did.

Silence has to be earned

Here’s a fair objection: users need reassurance. If I only show problems, how does anybody know the rest is fine?

Sure, Jakob Nielsen’s first usability heuristic covers it. Systems should keep users informed about what is going on, through appropriate feedback within reasonable time (Harley, NN/g). No news is only good news if the silence is trustworthy. An empty screen could mean everything is healthy, or that the sync broke an hour ago. If users can’t tell the difference, they’ll go back to scanning the full table.

So design the quiet state as deliberately as the loud one. Don’t list the healthy items. Summarize them with confidence.

Just a count, a timestamp, and a way to dig deeper. You’re still reporting the good news. You’re just not giving it top billing.

Mark Weiser and John Seely Brown described this balance in 1995 as calm technology: information that sits in the periphery of our attention and moves to the center only when it matters (Weiser and Brown, 1995). In their words, the periphery is “informing without overburdening.” That’s the quiet state. It gives users permission to stop looking. Giving users their time back might be the most underrated thing an enterprise tool can offer.

What fires-first actually looks like

A fires-first approach isn’t just the same table with a different sort. Here’s what separates it, with credit where it’s due.

  • Severity, not just status. A small fire next to a gas station beats a big one in an empty lot. An expired certificate on payments-gw outranks one on a test server, even if both say “Failing.” Health tells you what broke. Tier tells you how much it matters. Severity needs both. Remember that severity doesn’t exist until someone designs it? This is what designing it looks like.
  • Urgency and importance are separate axes. The idea is usually traced to a 1954 Eisenhower speech, and Stephen Covey, A. Roger Merrill, and Rebecca Merrill turned it into four quadrants in First Things First (Hoang, Rework). Plot issues on that matrix, and users can make meaningful choices about what to fix now, schedule, delegate, or snooze.
  • Lead straight into investigation. Fires seldom have a one-click fix. The real job is usually figuring out what went wrong, so each item should invite investigation.
  • Notify, so nobody has to watch. People have better things to do than babysit your app. When payments-gw catches fire, tell the person who can fix it, wherever they already work: email, Slack, Teams. The fires list is where they go to act, not where they sit and wait.
  • Restraint on alerts. Healthcare has studied the opposite failure for years. When clinicians are flooded with warnings, they become desensitized and start overriding the critical ones along with the trivial ones (AHRQ PSNet, “Alert Fatigue”). If 300 of 400 items say “Warning,” your users will do the same. A severity model that can’t say “this doesn’t matter now” isn’t a severity model.
  • Let users snooze. Some fires can’t be fought today: a vendor hasn’t replied, or the fix needs a maintenance window. Snoozing dials down the noise without pretending the issue is solved, and it comes back on schedule.
  • Resolution is visible. When a fire goes out, it leaves the list and the count drops. That feedback loop makes the KPI real to the person doing the work.
  • Everything is still one click away. The full table, healthy rows included, for the audit, the export, and the curious.
“I have two kinds of problems, the urgent and the important.”
— Dwight D. Eisenhower, quoting J. Roscoe Miller, 1954

The top-right quadrant leads the fires list. Everything else still has a home.

Not sure where to start? Watch how users triage today: what they sort by, what they scroll past, what they export. Your users have already mentally drafted the spec.

Dispatch, not census

A census counts everyone equally. That’s its job. A dispatch center decides who needs help first and sends people there.

Most enterprise dashboards are built like a census: complete, neutral, accurate. And no help to someone whose job is putting out the fires.

Taylor got there in 1903. Weiser and Brown in 1995. Few in 2006. The ISA-101 committee in 2015. Same direction, a century apart. The knowledge isn’t missing. What’s missing is defining what “on fire” means, ranking it, designing the quiet state, and wiring up the notifications.

Do the extra work so your users don’t have to. That’s the job.

Further reading

In order of appearance:

  • Clayton M. Christensen, Taddy Hall, Karen Dillon, and David S. Duncan, “Know Your Customers’ ‘Jobs to Be Done,’” Harvard Business Review, September 2016. Open-access overview: Kelsey Miller, “The Jobs to Be Done Framework Explained & Real-World Examples,” Harvard Business School Online, 2020 (updated 2026)
  • W3C, “F91: Failure of Success Criterion 1.3.1 for not correctly marking up table headers,” WCAG 2.2 Techniques
  • Brad Frost, “Front-of-the-front-end and back-of-the-front-end web development,” bradfrost.com, 2021
  • Jason Lemkin, “Real Ent Software Don’t Need No Stinkin’ UI/UX,” SaaStr, 2012
  • Martin Eriksson, “Consumer vs Enterprise Product Management,” Mind the Product, 2013

title: Introducing Vercel CI
description:
Coding agents are opening more pull requests than ever, and each one waits on CI before anyone can review or merge it. Most CI systems run the entire workflow on every push, even a one-line change. The more your agents push, the more time you spend waiting on CI.

Today, we're announcing Vercel CI in Beta. It runs only the tasks affected by your code change, and spins up only the compute those checks need, the same way Fluid compute scales with your traffic.

At Vercel, our CI now keeps up with our coding agents. Time from git push to "CI passed" is 2-6x faster than it was before.

How it works

Vercel CI uses Turborepo to understand your tasks and which ones depend on each other. It reads turbo.json, so if you're already using Turborepo, there's no separate CI config to write.

If you're not on Turborepo yet, add turbo.json and the turbo package. It works in single-package repos too.

Then tag the tasks you want Vercel CI to run.

"tags": ["ci"] is all you need to get started. No workflow YAML to maintain, no drift between your CI config and turbo.json, and Remote Cache is on by default.

When you or your agent push code, Vercel CI determines which tasks need to run based on the change. Tasks whose inputs haven't changed come from cache. The remaining tasks each run on their own machine, powered by Hive, Vercel's compute layer, and start as soon as their dependencies finish.

Vercel CI gives each task the compute it needs and nothing more.

Running your CI on Vercel

To get started, follow the documentation or prompt your agent from your repo:

Once set up, you or your agent can watch and inspect CI through the Vercel dashboard, Vercel CLI, or Vercel MCP. When something fails, go straight to the failing task, see what's blocked behind it, and open its logs, or search across recent runs to see whether a test has been flaky all week.

Vercel CI posts a check to your pull request on GitHub, so your existing branch protection rules can block merges on failure, the same way they do today.

Closing the loop

Vercel CI has already completed nearly 8 million tasks across our own repositories and the private beta, and we're just getting started. We're working to keep shrinking the time between writing code and running it in production.

As we work toward general availability, we plan to add:

  • Advanced observability

  • A vc ci CLI command for distributed execution before pushing code

  • More granular test selection

Vercel CI is available in Beta today on all plans. Read the docs and try it on your repository.
