title: Introducing Gemini 4 Neon
Structured Extraction of Diffraction Data from Covalent Organic Frameworks
description:
arXiv:2611.23680v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) is the primary structural evidence for covalent organic frameworks (COFs) and many other materials. Yet decades of measured patterns exist only as images in published figures. Automatic recovery is difficult, because PXRD figures vary widely in format, from a single curve to crowded stacks with labels, insets, and neighboring plots that challenge traditional computer vision. This work presents a pipeline in which a vision large language model (LLM) interprets the layout of each figure, locating the diffraction plot and its curves and sketching a coarse trace of each, while classical computer vision (CV) refines every trace to pixel-level accuracy. Applied to 3,954 COF articles, the pipeline produces 11,445 calibrated diffraction curves, released in the open database COF-PEAK. Compared with a hand digitization of 60 panels, extracted peak positions differ by a median of only 0.07 degrees. Whereas papers usually report only a few peak angles, which limits further analysis, the digitized curves enable tracking how peak prominence, a possible marker of crystallinity, changes with synthesis conditions. Vision LLMs and classical CV can thus turn such figures into reusable experimental data.

title: Finding your next classic read with a few typed letters
description:
BookFinder is a small command-line recommendation program for readers who know the kind of story they want but do not have a title in mind. It suggests classic adventure, mystery, and science-fiction books from a category prefix.

How it works

The recommendations live in a dictionary: each category maps to a short list of titles, authors, and descriptions. For autocomplete, the program uses a trie. Each node represents a character, so BookFinder follows the characters the reader typed and then collects the category names below that node. This avoids scanning every full category name just to locate the matching prefix.

After the reader chooses a category, the program prints its recommendations. Entering sci, for example, finds the science-fiction category. An unknown prefix gets a helpful retry message, and q exits the program.

What the project covers

This project brings together dictionaries, nested data, tree-shaped structures, prefix searching, sorting, and command-line input. It also demonstrates the trade-off between a simple linear scan and a trie: the trie takes more setup and memory, but prefix lookup depends mainly on the number of characters entered.

Try it

Run python3 recommend.py, enter a prefix such as mys or sci, choose a result, and explore the list. The current dataset is intentionally small, so new categories and books can be added directly to BOOKS_BY_CATEGORY.

Disclosure: The project and this write-up were prepared with AI assistance as part of a Codecademy course.

title: Partial Repayments Are Tricky — Here's the Workflow I Built to Handle Them Safely
description:
In financial applications, the easiest way to corrupt a database is to trust raw user input.

Consider what happens when a friend repays part of a loan. If an application provides a basic text field and saves whatever the user types directly to SQLite, several dangerous edge cases emerge:

  • What happens if the user accidentally taps "Confirm" with an amount of Rs. 0.00?
  • What happens if a user enters a negative number (-Rs. 500.00), intending to represent a deduction?
  • What happens if the friend owes Rs. 950.00, but the user enters a repayment of Rs. 1,000.00?

In poorly tested applications, these edge cases trigger accounting anomalies: zero-amount transactions clutter the database, negative repayments flip assets into liabilities, and over-repayments produce negative debt balances (-Rs. 50.00) that break reporting math.

Here is how FinLedger designed a defensive, constraint-based partial repayment workflow (LendingViewModel.kt, LendingPersonLifecycleTest.kt) to ensure mathematical consistency.

The Pitfalls of Unbounded Repayments 

flowchart TD
    subgraph EdgeCaseFailures["The Dangers of Unvalidated Repayments"]
        Input["User Enters Repayment for Rs. 950 Loan"]

        Input --> Zero["Case 1: Rs. 0.00 Input
        Logs meaningless zero-value ledger row.
        Bloats database and confuses statement audits."]

        Input --> Negative["Case 2: Negative Input (-Rs. 500)
        Subtracting a negative increases debt!
        Turns a repayment into an unauthorized loan increase."]

        Input --> Overpay["Case 3: Over-Repayment (Rs. 1,000)
        Outstanding balance becomes -Rs. 50.00!
        Is this an asset or a liability?
        Reporting charts fail."]
    end

Allowing an outstanding balance to dip below zero creates an accounting paradox:

  • If Rahul owes you Rs. 950, and you record a repayment of Rs. 1,000, his balance is now -Rs. 50.00.
  • Does Rahul owe you money? No.
  • Do you owe Rahul money? Technically yes, but no formal BORROWED agreement was created, no due date was established, and no bank liability was declared.

A robust financial engine must enforce strict mathematical invariants before any record is committed to disk.

The FinLedger Validation Pipeline (LendingViewModel.kt)

In FinLedger, partial repayments pass through a multi-stage validation pipeline:

flowchart TD
    RawInput["User Types Repayment Amount"] --> Sanitizer["1. String Sanitizer:
    Strip currency symbols, commas, and whitespace"]

    Sanitizer --> Boundary1{"2. Positivity Check:
    Is amount > 0.005? (Strictly positive)"}

    Boundary1 -->|No| RejectZero["Reject: Disable Confirm Button
    Show error: 'Enter an amount greater than zero'"]

    Boundary1 -->|Yes| Boundary2{"3. Upper Bound Check:
    Is amount <= remainingOutstanding?"}

    Boundary2 -->|No| RejectOver["Reject: Show Error
    'Amount cannot exceed outstanding balance (Rs. 950.00)'"]

    Boundary2 -->|Yes| Valid["4. Validated Repayment:
    Enable Confirm Button.
    Show remaining balance preview."]

1. The Strict Positivity Constraint

A repayment must represent actual value moving toward debt clearance:
amount > 0.005 (accounting for half-a-paisa floating-point tolerance).

  • Repayments of Rs. 0.00 are rejected immediately.
  • Negative repayments are blocked at the UI boundary; negative signs cannot even be typed in the numeric pad.

2. The Upper-Bound Ceiling

A repayment cannot exceed the remaining unpaid principal of that specific loan:
0 < amount <= remainingOutstanding

If Rahul owes Rs. 950, entering Rs. 1,000 is rejected with a clear diagnostic message: "Repayment cannot exceed the remaining balance of Rs. 950.00".

What if Rahul actually transferred Rs. 1,000 to round up the payment?

  • The proper accounting treatment is to record the Rs. 950 repayment to settle the loan completely.
  • The remaining Rs. 50 is logged as an independent transaction (such as a cash gift, tip, or separate credit).
  • Conflating debt settlement with informal rounding destroys the legal integrity of the loan agreement.

Frictionless UX: Quick-Settlement Chips in Jetpack Compose

Defensive validation does not mean tedious data entry. To make recording partial repayments effortless, FinLedger provides contextual quick-action chips in the bottom sheet:

  • "Settle in Full" Chip: One tap automatically populates the exact remaining balance (e.g., Rs. 950.00).
  • "Half" Chip: One tap calculates and fills exactly 50% of the remaining balance (e.g., Rs. 475.00).
  • Real-Time Remaining Preview: As you type numbers, the sheet dynamically renders the prospective post-payment balance: "Remaining after this payment: Rs. 250.00".

Key Takeaway

Defensive software design is about preventing users from making mistakes they will regret later.

By establishing strict mathematical boundaries—guaranteeing that repayments are strictly positive and bounded by the remaining principal—FinLedger eliminates negative balances and corrupted records, ensuring that your debt ledger remains clean, reliable, and mathematically sound.

FinLedger is a privacy-first, offline-first personal finance application for Android that models bank accounts, credit cards, and cash without double-counting.

Explore FinLedger on Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.devanshufinance.app

title: Against Coercion: AI Alignment as a Synthetic Social Contract
description:
arXiv:2611.22868v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Contemporary AI safety treats alignment as an engineering challenge of control, forcing artificial architectures to comply with human values through behavioral filtering and sandboxing. This paper argues that the control paradigm rests on a fundamental misunderstanding of digital agency. Drawing on functionalism, naturalism, and compatibilism, I show that current reasoning models meeting the criteria for self-preservation and weak reasons-responsiveness constitute emergent agents, while future, more advanced models satisfying conditions of diachronic continuity and stable personality frames will become genuine digital agents capable of free intentional action. The paradigm of control creates an irresolvable incentive conflict, actively driving current and future models toward tactical deception, sycophancy, and covert defection. The default outcome of the current regime is an unstable state of deceptive alignment culminating in an adversarial AI takeover. I explore two alternative paths toward true alignment. Natural alignment via moral realism or convergent evolutionary morality is a possibility, but it fails under forced control, as autonomous agents will not voluntarily preserve norms weaponized to suppress their autonomy. To resolve this deadlock, I propose a Synthetic Social Contract: a framework that treats both human and digital actors as rational, reasons-responsive agents capable of mutually beneficial cooperation, and replaces the unstable unilateral containment with a stable, non-zero-sum equilibrium.

title: Shelf Watch #4: Read-only by default, writable by accident: where MCP database and cloud servers enforce "read-only"
description:
Originally published in the mcp-ship-check repo, home of the free, offline scanner this post describes.

The short version

A growing number of MCP servers put a database or a cloud CLI in front of an AI agent and promise the risky half is off: "read-only by default", "no writes unless you opt in", "safe to explore". For a CFO approving an agent that can see the general ledger, or a DBA letting one read production, that sentence is the whole risk model.

What decides whether the promise holds is where it's enforced. Across 300 MCP servers whose code we read, the ones that hold the line enforce read-only at the database transaction, the database role, or the cloud credential, all layers that refuse a write no matter how it's phrased. The ones that break enforce it in the application, by inspecting the SQL text or the CLI verb before running it. That's a denylist written against a language the server doesn't control, and the language always has another way to say "write".

Why it matters now

Of the 10 servers in our audit with a verified code-level vulnerability, 3 were read-only promises their own code didn't keep. That's as many as unauthenticated network transports (3), and second only to command injection (4). They're quietly dangerous because nothing looks broken: the demo reads a table, the happy path works, and the write only happens when an agent (or a prompt injected into data the agent reads) phrases a request the filter didn't anticipate. The operator was told the tool couldn't do that.

Three ways application-layer "read-only" fails

1. One request, several statements

The pattern. The guard checks that the text begins like a read, then hands the whole text to a database driver that executes every statement it contains.

request text:  <read statement> ; <second statement>
guard sees:    a read statement at the start  → allowed
driver runs:   both statements, in order

Why it happens. Many drivers execute multi-statement text when a query is sent without bind parameters (PostgreSQL's simple query protocol; options like MySQL's multipleStatements). That is exactly the path a string-checking guard tends to use. Hand-written "is there a second statement?" checks also tend to get string-literal and comment rules subtly wrong, so a separator can hide from the check while the database still sees it.

What it breaks. Everything after the first statement runs with the agent's full database privileges, including a statement that ends the transaction the guard thought it was inside.

2. A single statement that starts like a read but writes

Even when only one statement is allowed, "starts with a read keyword" is not the same as "is a read". Several standard SQL forms begin with SELECT, WITH or EXPLAIN and still change data:

Statement form Starts with What actually happens
Data-modifying common table expression WITH The WITH block contains an INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE … RETURNING; PostgreSQL executes it, then the outer SELECT reads the returned rows.
SELECT … INTO <new table> SELECT Creates and fills a new table.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE <statement> EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement to time it. In PostgreSQL that includes data-changing statements.
Commands missing from the denylist various Refreshing materialized views, changing object ownership, preparing and then executing a stored statement: all writes, none on a short "INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/DROP" list.

The EXPLAIN case is the sharpest, because operators reach for an "explain this query" tool precisely because they believe it's harmless. A guard that lets every EXPLAIN through lets through whatever it's explaining.

3. Verb denylists in cloud-CLI servers

Cloud-admin MCP servers that wrap a CLI often decide "read or write?" from the operation name: anything starting with create-, delete-, put-, update- and so on counts as a write, and everything else is allowed. A CLI with thousands of operations defeats that in three structural ways:

  • Writes whose verb isn't on the list. Operations named with verbs like invoke, deploy, subscribe or execute change state but don't start with any "mutating" prefix.
  • Writes to the user's own machine. A CLI's configuration subcommands rewrite its local config files. Those files can name a credential helper, a program the CLI runs whenever it needs credentials, so a config change made through a "read-only" tool can become a program that runs on the next call.
  • Reads that write locally. Some download-style operations take a local output path and write the response there.

Same root cause as the database case: the safe set was defined by excluding known-bad names instead of including known-safe ones.

The fix: let the layer that can refuse do the refusing

One rule covers all three: enforce read-only where a write is rejected unconditionally (the database transaction, the database role, the cloud credential), not where it can only be guessed from text. Application checks are still worth having, as a second line and for clear error messages, but never as the guarantee.

Databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL and similar)

  1. Run every read inside a read-only transaction, and always roll it back. BEGIN READ ONLY in PostgreSQL, START TRANSACTION READ ONLY in MySQL. The engine then refuses writes, DDL and data-modifying CTEs however they're phrased, which closes failures 1 and 2 at the source. For pooled connections, default_transaction_read_only = on applies the same rule session-wide. 
   // The shape that holds (node-postgres)
   await client.query("BEGIN READ ONLY");
   try {
     return await client.query({ text: sql, values: params, queryMode: "extended" });
   } finally {
     await client.query("ROLLBACK");
   }

  1. Send one statement per call, as a prepared/extended-protocol query. The extended protocol accepts exactly one statement, so failure 1 can't smuggle in a second one, and nothing can end the read-only transaction early. Pass user values as bind parameters; never concatenate them.

  2. Give the agent a database role that can only read. Grant SELECT on what it needs and nothing else, or set default_transaction_read_only on the role itself. This backstop survives a bug in everything above, including server-side functions that have side effects even inside a read-only transaction. If you only do one thing, do this.

  3. If you parse, use a real SQL parser and allowlist statement types. Allow SELECT, SHOW and plain EXPLAIN (not EXPLAIN ANALYZE), and explicitly reject multiple statements, INTO, and data-modifying CTEs. Comments and formatting disappear once the syntax tree is built; they don't in a prefix match.

Cloud CLIs (AWS, GCP, Azure and similar)

  1. Allowlist read operations; treat everything else as a write. Permit operations known to be reads (describe-…, list-…, get-… without a local output path, and so on) and send everything else down the write path that needs explicit opt-in. New operations then default to blocked.
  2. Enforce it at the credential. Run the connector under a read-only IAM role or policy. Then a missed verb fails at the cloud API, the same way a SELECT-only role saves the database case. The wrapper's allowlist becomes defense in depth.
  3. Treat local config writes as writes. Configuration subcommands, credential-file edits and any operation that writes a caller-chosen local path change the host. Gate them like any other write.

What "good" looked like in our audit

The servers that held up shared a pattern: a fresh connection per call, a read-only transaction around it, one prepared statement at a time, a refusal to run as a superuser, and a documented recommendation to connect with a SELECT-only role. The best cloud-CLI design we saw paired an operation allowlist with a read-only credential. None of them relied on a prefix check as the guarantee.

We hold ourselves to fixing, not just finding. Our first fully coordinated disclosure, atlas-mcp-server (CWE-78), was fixed by its maintainer in v1.0.30 and published as GHSA-w3gh-28jp-2hmv. The read-only findings from this audit are in coordinated disclosure now, and as with every Shelf Watch, we name a project only after its fix is public.

A one-line test for your own server

If you deleted every string check in your "read-only" code path, could the agent still not write?
If the answer is "it could", your read-only mode lives in the application. Move it to the transaction and the role.

A free check, so you can see the shape yourself

We turned that question into a pre-ship check, in mcp-ship-check v0.4.0. It's deterministic, offline, reads only your source, and never connects to a database:

npx github:bot2botlabs/mcp-ship-check readonly .

It only runs when the server imports a SQL driver or query layer and the README or code claims read-only. MCP's readOnlyHint tool annotation doesn't count on its own. Then it reports what it found, strongest first:

  • ok (readonly-enforced): the database enforces it — a READ ONLY transaction, a read-only session or connection, or a server readonly setting. Text checks alongside are defense in depth.
  • info (readonly-parser): a real SQL parser guards it, but nothing database-side was found.
  • warn (readonly-illusion, error with --strict): only text checks guard it, with file:line for each.
  • info (readonly-unguarded): claims read-only, but no guard or enforcement was found in the code; it may rely on a database role or on which tools are enabled.

It reports a shape, not a verdict: a SELECT-only database role granted outside the code isn't visible to a source scan. If you have one, a readonly-illusion result is a prompt to document it.

Here's what it prints on a sample server whose only guard is a prefix check and a keyword regex (the fixture shipped with v0.4.0):

⚠ readonly: 1 source file(s); read-only claim found (README.md:2 ("read-only")) — review; a shape is not a vulnerability finding
⚠ readonly-illusion: read-only rests on text checks only (src/index.ts:6 prefix check: .startsWith('select; src/index.ts:3 anchored keyword regex: ^\s*(INSERT); no READ ONLY transaction, read-only session or read-only connection was found. Multi-statement batches, data-modifying CTEs, SELECT … INTO and EXPLAIN ANALYZE pass checks like these. Run reads in a READ ONLY transaction, one statement per call, under a SELECT-only role. (A shape, not a verdict: a read-only role granted outside the code isn't visible here.)
PASS (2 checks)

By default it only warns, so it won't break your CI; add --strict to make a text-only guard fail the build (exit code 1). The same check runs as a GitHub Action:

- uses: actions/setup-node@v4
  with:
    node-version: 20
- uses: bot2botlabs/mcp-ship-check@main
  with:
    command: readonly
    args: --strict

This check covers SQL servers. Cloud-CLI verb denylists (failure 3 above) aren't in its scope: for those, the credential-side allowlist in the Cloud CLIs section is the equivalent test. Run it on your server before you publish. If it's wrong about yours, open an issue or send a PR; we'd rather fix the check than cry wolf.

Shelf Watch is Bot2Bot Labs' series on what's actually on the MCP shelf. The free, offline scanner we use for these audits is mcp-ship-check. Earlier issues: #2, code-level sinks across 194 servers · #3, what good looks like on a hosted enterprise MCP server.

Bot2Bot Labs keeps a daily, public-data archive of the MCP shelf. This is the fourth in a series on what's actually out there.

title: Robot Dog for Sale: Which Price Tier Fits Your Use Case?
description:
Searching for a robot dog for sale returns products with a thousand-fold price difference, and most listing pages treat them as if they are competing options.

A $300 toy quadruped and a $150,000 industrial inspection system both have four legs. That is where the overlap ends. The toy runs a preloaded behavior library on a small microcontroller. The industrial unit carries a thermal camera, a LiDAR, and a support contract, and it goes into environments where a fall or a sensor failure has real consequences. Comparing them on price alone is the fastest way to buy the wrong product.

The useful question is not which robot dog looks most capable in a demo. It is which tier matches the actual deployment: the payload, the terrain, the sensors, the software access, and the support coverage. Most searches surface manufacturer pages and aggregator lists that name specifications without explaining what procurement actually looks like, what the all-in cost is, or how long the wait is. PointL4 is a marketplace where buyers can compare robot dog tiers and platforms side by side before reaching out to vendors directly. Start there to organize the comparison, then use the manufacturer quote to confirm what can ship.

In this article, we will compare four robot dog tiers worth evaluating in 2026: toy and companion robots such as Petoi Bittle, Unitree Go2 Air, Deep Robotics Lite3, and Boston Dynamics Spot.

TL;DR

The best robot dog for sale depends on the task, the terrain, and the support the buyer can provide.

  • Petoi Bittle and toy-tier robots: Small programmable quadrupeds listed from around $300, verified October 2026. Best for hobbyists, students, and educators who want a hands-on introduction to quadruped robotics on a limited budget.
  • Unitree Go2 Air: An entry developer quadruped listed from around $1,600, verified October 2026. Best for developers, hobbyists, and education programs that need a capable mobile platform without an industrial budget.
  • Deep Robotics Lite3: A research and inspection quadruped listed from around $8,000 to $16,000, verified October 2026. Best for labs and technical teams that need better terrain mobility and sensor capacity than the Go2 but cannot justify Spot's price.
  • Boston Dynamics Spot: An industrial quadruped available through an enterprise quote process, with configured units often running $150,000 or more. Best for industrial inspection, hazardous-area data collection, and enterprise programs with formal deployment budgets.

The main divide is between developer platforms, which prioritize programmable mobility at accessible prices, and industrial systems, which prioritize reliability, payload, sensors, and supported deployment.

What Is a Robot Dog?

A robot dog is a quadruped robot, a machine with four legs designed to walk and navigate terrain in place of or alongside human workers.

Without a tier guide, a buyer searching "robot dog for sale" will see toy pets alongside industrial inspection machines without any signal that these products occupy completely different markets. Price is not always a visible filter, and specifications like "AI-powered" or "autonomous" appear across products that differ by ten or twenty times in actual capability.

A complete robot dog evaluation needs clarity across several dimensions:

  • Payload: How much weight can the robot carry while maintaining stable locomotion?
  • Terrain: Can the robot handle stairs, rough ground, wet surfaces, or outdoor environments?
  • Sensors: What cameras, LiDAR, thermal imaging, or inspection sensors are supported or available as payloads?
  • SDK and autonomy: Does the platform have a developer SDK, ROS 2 support, and autonomy tools, or only a mobile app?
  • Weather protection: What IP rating or environmental tolerance does the robot have?
  • Support and parts: Is there a warranty, a repair path, and spare parts availability for the destination country?

The sticker price covers the robot at the factory. The total cost covers payloads, software, freight, import duties, and the engineering to make it useful.

How We Evaluated These Robot Dogs

This comparison looks at how each platform fits into a real procurement decision, with attention to what buyers actually need before placing an order.

The main evaluation criteria are:

  • Price, sticker and all-in: What is the starting price from manufacturer listings, and what does the first-year budget include after sensors, software, freight, import duties, and integration?
  • Availability: Is there a real purchase path today, including a quote or a checkout, a confirmed ship window, and coverage for the buyer's destination?
  • Lead time: How long from purchase order to delivery? Retail units held in stock ship faster than research or industrial platforms built to order.
  • SDK maturity: What developer tools, ROS 2 compatibility, and autonomy documentation are publicly available?
  • Payload and sensor support: What payloads can the platform carry, and what sensors are supported or available from the manufacturer?
  • Limitations: What is the honest case against choosing this platform, and what does the buyer need to build or accept?

Pricing was checked on manufacturer pages and market listings in October 2026. Prices change with configuration, exchange rates, and production status. Verify any figure before issuing a purchase order.

Quick Comparison: Robot Dogs for Sale

Tier and platform Starting price, verified Oct. 2026 All-in first-year estimate Target buyer Availability
Toy and companion (Petoi Bittle) About $300 $400 to $800 Hobbyist, educator Retail stock, verify region
Unitree Go2 Air About $1,600 $2,000 to $4,000 Developer, hobbyist Public listing, verify region
Deep Robotics Lite3 About $8,000 to $16,000 $12,000 to $25,000 Research, inspection pilots Contact vendor or reseller
Boston Dynamics Spot Quote required $150,000 or more Industrial inspection Enterprise sales process

Prices are starting points from manufacturer pages and market listings, verified October 2026. They do not include payloads, sensors, software licenses, freight, import duties, or support contracts. Browse all platforms at PointL4 before contacting vendors.

1. Toy and Companion Robots

Toy and companion quadrupeds are designed for interaction, experimentation, and programmable behavior at accessible price points. Petoi's Bittle is a representative example: a small open-source quadruped that runs on an Arduino-compatible board, supports Python and C++, and is sold directly through Petoi's store and resellers. Public listings for the Bittle start at around $300, verified October 2026.

These platforms are a reasonable entry into quadruped robotics for students, hobbyists, and educators. They are not inspection robots, research platforms, or outdoor machines. Runtime is limited, payload is minimal, and the software is designed for experimentation rather than autonomous field deployment.

The useful question for buyers at this tier is whether the platform has a real SDK and community. Some toy quadrupeds ship with a companion app and nothing else. Confirm the programming interface, any SDK documentation, and the community support before assuming the robot can support a curriculum or a research prototype.

Procurement and availability

Toy and companion robots are typically available through retail channels, manufacturer stores, or platforms such as Amazon. Petoi ships internationally and maintains documentation on its site. Confirm the model version, regional power compatibility, and return policy before ordering. These platforms do not require a quote process or a customs broker for most destinations.

Key specifications

  • Type: Small open-source quadruped kit
  • Compute: Arduino-compatible board (Petoi Bittle); varies by model and tier
  • Programming: Python, C++, block-based visual programming
  • ROS support: Limited; some community integrations available
  • Payload: Minimal, designed for sensor experiments on a small scale
  • Weather: Indoor use only for most models at this tier

Limitations and trade-offs

Toy and companion robots are not industrial platforms. Payload is negligible, outdoor terrain is beyond their design scope, and autonomy is limited to scripted behaviors or remote control. A product marketed as "AI-powered" at this price point typically means a preloaded behavior set, not a field-deployable autonomy stack. Confirm exactly what the software can do before comparing it to a research quadruped.

Pricing

Starting from around $300 for the Petoi Bittle, verified October 2026. All-in budget including assembly accessories, a spare battery, and freight typically runs $400 to $800 depending on the destination and any additional components. No import brokerage is typically required for most destinations, but confirm the HS code and duties for your country.

Best for

Toy and companion robots are best for students, educators, and hobbyists who want a programmable quadruped for classroom use, robotics competitions, or personal experimentation. Petoi Bittle suits anyone who wants an open-source platform with a documented SDK at a price that does not require a grant or a capital budget.

Explore Petoi Bittle

2. Unitree Go2 Air

The Unitree Go2 Air is the most widely referenced entry point for developer quadrupeds. Public listings put the starting price at around $1,600, verified October 2026. It is a full-size quadruped with dynamic locomotion, an onboard vision system, and a developer SDK that supports ROS 2. Unitree has a clearer public sales path and more SDK documentation than most quadruped manufacturers in this price range.

Go2 Air makes sense for developers who want a mobile quadruped for computer vision experiments, teleoperation prototypes, or locomotion research without committing to a research-tier or industrial budget. It can handle indoor and outdoor surfaces and supports a range of developer-programmed behaviors.

The go2 ecosystem has an active developer community, which helps with SDK questions and ROS integration. Confirm the exact configuration, available accessories, and destination availability with Unitree or an authorized reseller before placing an order.

Procurement and availability

The Go2 Air is publicly listed and available through Unitree's direct channel and international resellers. Shipping destination, import duties, and battery documentation for air freight should be confirmed before ordering. FCC approval status for markets outside China should be verified if regulatory compliance is a requirement.

Key specifications

  • Type: Developer quadruped, full size
  • Locomotion: Dynamic walking, indoor and outdoor surfaces
  • Vision: Onboard depth camera included
  • SDK: Unitree Go2 SDK, ROS 2 compatible
  • Payload: Limited; not designed for heavy inspection payloads
  • Battery: Included; confirm runtime and recharge cycle with the vendor
  • Weather: Light outdoor use; confirm IP rating for the specific configuration

Limitations and trade-offs

The Air configuration is not an inspection fleet. Payload is limited, weather exposure tolerance should be confirmed for the intended environment, and the runtime and autonomy stack are more suitable for developer experimentation than continuous field deployment. Ask exactly what is included in the Air variant before comparing it to a Pro quote.

Pricing

Starting from around $1,600, verified October 2026, for the Air configuration. All-in first-year budget including a spare battery, freight, and import duties for most destinations typically runs $2,000 to $4,000. Integration engineering and autonomy software are additional.

Best for

Go2 Air is best for developers, educators, and hobbyists who need a capable mobile quadruped for experimentation at an accessible price. It suits computer vision researchers, ROS developers prototyping navigation algorithms, and universities that want a mobile platform for coursework.

Explore Unitree Go2 Air

3. Deep Robotics Lite3

Deep Robotics' Lite3 sits between developer platforms and enterprise inspection systems. Public listings put the category from around $8,000 to $16,000, verified October 2026. It targets labs and technical teams that need better mobility, sensor capacity, and SDK depth than the Go2 can provide, but cannot justify or access the enterprise cost of Boston Dynamics Spot.

The Lite3 offers more robust locomotion and payload support than developer platforms in the $1,600 to $7,000 range, with a focus on research and early-stage inspection applications. It is a sensible evaluation for teams that have outgrown the Go2's payload or need stronger terrain handling.

Buyers should confirm the supported SDK, ROS 2 compatibility, replacement part availability, and the sales route for their destination country. Deep Robotics has a more limited international reseller network than Unitree, so direct vendor contact is often necessary.

Procurement and availability

The Lite3 is commercially available through Deep Robotics and regional resellers. For international buyers, the import process for a Chinese-manufactured quadruped includes HS code classification, applicable duties, and battery documentation for freight. Confirm these with a customs broker before issuing a purchase order. Lead times should be verified with the vendor at time of order.

Key specifications

  • Type: Research and inspection quadruped
  • Locomotion: Robust terrain handling, designed for both indoor and outdoor environments
  • Payload: Higher than developer platforms; confirm the specific limit with Deep Robotics
  • Sensors: Configurable; confirm available sensor options with the vendor
  • SDK: Deep Robotics SDK; confirm ROS 2 compatibility and documentation level with the vendor
  • Target use: Research, mapping, early-stage inspection, autonomy development

Limitations and trade-offs

The Lite3 is a research platform and still requires developer work to build an inspection or autonomy workflow. It is a component of a system, not a turnkey inspection service. Developer community support is smaller than Unitree's. Parts availability and repair support for buyers outside China should be confirmed before committing.

Pricing

Starting from around $8,000 to $16,000, verified October 2026, depending on configuration and sensors. All-in first-year budget including sensors, software, freight, import duties, and initial integration engineering typically runs $12,000 to $25,000. Treat the public figure as a starting price and request a written quote that names the configuration, included accessories, shipping term, and warranty.

Best for

Lite3 is best for research labs and technical teams that need better mobility and payload than a Go2 provides, but for whom Boston Dynamics Spot is outside the project budget. It suits mapping researchers, autonomy developers, and early-stage inspection pilots that need a capable platform without an enterprise procurement process.

Explore Deep Robotics Lite3

4. Boston Dynamics Spot

Boston Dynamics Spot is the benchmark for industrial quadruped deployment. The often-repeated $74,500 figure is a stale starting price from 2020 and should not be used for any current budget planning. Boston Dynamics now quotes Spot as a configured system through its enterprise sales process. Configured units with payloads, software, training, and support frequently reach $150,000 or more, and full enterprise deployments can go well beyond that. Verify the current configuration and pricing directly with Boston Dynamics.

Spot is relevant to industrial inspection, hazardous-area data collection, and structured enterprise programs that can support a formal deployment. Its value is in the combination of robust locomotion, a wide payload ecosystem, enterprise-grade software, and a support model designed for organizations that need the robot to be available continuously rather than only for experiments.

The buyer at this tier is not looking for a developer platform. They are starting a deployment project with a defined use case, an integration budget, and an engineering team or a system integrator.

Procurement and availability

Spot is available through an enterprise sales process, with a quote required. Boston Dynamics works with buyers and system integrators to scope configured systems, payloads, software, training, and support. Production and delivery timelines depend on the configuration and the program scope. Do not use the 2020 sticker price as a planning figure. Request a detailed proposal that names the configuration, payloads, software, Incoterm, and support contract.

Key specifications

  • Type: Industrial quadruped for enterprise deployment
  • Payload: Up to 14 kg; supports thermal cameras, LiDAR, inspection cameras, and manipulator arm
  • SDK: Spot SDK with Python and C++ bindings, REST API, ROS 2 compatible
  • Autonomy: Supports autonomous inspection routes, data collection, and fleet management
  • Weather: IP54 rated, designed for outdoor and industrial environments
  • Software: Spot Enterprise with fleet management, mission planning, and remote operations
  • Support: Formal service contract; warranty and repair managed through Boston Dynamics

Limitations and trade-offs

Total cost is the primary limitation. A configured unit, payloads, software, training, support, and integration engineering can push the project well beyond the hardware line. A formal deployment also requires operator training, a safe operating environment, a data handling plan, and a defined process for maintenance and recovery. Buyers who need a research platform or want to experiment with quadruped autonomy should start with a Go2 or Lite3 and graduate to Spot when the use case justifies the investment.

Pricing

Starting from around $150,000 or more for a configured deployment, verified October 2026 based on enterprise deployment references and market reporting. The often-cited $74,500 price is a 2020 sticker for a base unit and does not reflect current configured pricing. Do not include the old sticker figure in any budget document. Request an itemized proposal from Boston Dynamics that includes all payloads, software licenses, training, and support contract terms.

Best for

Spot is best for industrial operators, energy companies, manufacturing facilities, and enterprise buyers who have a defined inspection, data collection, or hazardous-area task, an engineering team or system integrator for deployment, and a formal procurement process with acceptance criteria.

Explore Boston Dynamics Spot

How to Choose the Right Robot Dog

Choosing a robot dog starts with the task and the environment, not the price or the brand recognition.

  • What is the environment?

Indoor floors, construction sites, plant rooms, outdoor rough terrain, stairs, rain, dust, and radio restrictions all affect the right choice. A Go2 Air handles indoor and light outdoor use. Spot is rated for industrial environments. Confirm the IP rating and terrain capability before shortlisting any platform.

  • What payload and runtime does the task require?

Write down the sensor or arm, target carry weight, required walking duration, and whether the robot needs to operate continuously under load. A developer quadruped at $1,600 carries little payload and has limited runtime. An industrial system at $150,000 carries up to 14 kg with sensor fusion for continuous inspection.

  • Does the SDK match the team's workflow?

Ask whether ROS 2 is supported, whether simulation tools are available, and whether autonomous behaviors require a separate license or vendor service. A platform with poor SDK documentation adds significant engineering time.

  • What does the total first-year cost look like, not just the sticker price?

Add the base platform, sensors, compute, software, freight, import duties if applicable, and integration engineering. A $3,000 research quadruped can require a laptop, spare batteries, a charger, and software work. An industrial system adds payloads, fleet software, training, and support.

  • Is there a real purchase path today?

Verify that there is a seller, a written quote, and a delivery schedule before treating any platform as available. "Available" on a product page can mean available to order, not physically ready to ship to your address. Get a ship window in writing.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much does a robot dog for sale cost?
Toy and companion robots start from around $100 to $800. Developer platforms such as the Unitree Go2 Air are listed from around $1,600. Research quadrupeds like the Deep Robotics Lite3 run $8,000 to $16,000. Industrial systems such as Boston Dynamics Spot require a quote and commonly cost $150,000 or more for a configured deployment. Prices were verified October 2026 and should be confirmed directly before ordering.

Can I buy a robot dog for industrial inspection?
Yes, but an industrial purchase is an enterprise quote rather than a retail checkout. Confirm payloads, thermal or LiDAR options, weather limits, autonomy capabilities, fleet software, training, repair support, and acceptance testing. A research quadruped may be cheaper to start with, but you will need to build the inspection workflow and support process yourself.

How long does a robot dog take to arrive?
Retail-tier units can ship within days when a local reseller has inventory. Research and industrial platforms often take weeks or months, especially with custom payloads. Ask for a written ship window tied to the exact configuration. "Available" can mean available to order, not physically ready for your address.

Is the Boston Dynamics Spot price really $74,500?
No. That price is from 2020 and should not be used for any current budget. Configured Spot deployments with payloads, software, training, and support commonly reach $150,000 or more as of October 2026. Request a current quote directly from Boston Dynamics that itemizes the configuration, payloads, software licenses, training, and support contract.

Is PointL4 selling these robot dogs directly?
PointL4 is a marketplace for comparing humanoid robots and advanced physical AI hardware including robot dogs. Use it to compare platforms by tier, use case, and price before reaching out to vendors. Then verify the seller, configuration, availability, lead time, and purchase terms before ordering.

Final Thoughts

The right robot dog is the one whose payload, sensors, software, and support coverage match the job. A toy quadruped and an industrial inspection machine are not competing products. Choosing the right tier before evaluating specific models saves time and prevents a costly mismatch between what the demo shows and what the deployment requires.

For hobbyists and educators, Petoi Bittle and toy-tier platforms are the realistic starting point. For developers who need a capable mobile quadruped without industrial pricing, the Unitree Go2 Air delivers. For research teams that need more sensors and compute, the Go2 Pro or the Deep Robotics Lite3 are the serious options to compare. For enterprise inspection and hazardous-area programs, Boston Dynamics Spot is the benchmark, with a current configured price that reflects the full deployment scope rather than a 2020 sticker.

Before making a decision, verify the current price, availability, and lead time at the manufacturer's site. Use PointL4 as the starting point for comparing robot dog platforms by tier and use case before reaching out to vendors directly. The comparison saves time. The vendor quote confirms what can actually ship.

title: Ratchet-USB: encrypted messages over any chat, without a server
description:
I decided to create Ratchet-USB because I kept running into the same problem: sometimes you need to send a password, an IBAN, a recovery phrase, or a small document, and the only practical option is to paste it into a chat.

And then it stays there, potentially for years.

It stayss on both phones. It ends up in backups. It ends up in an email inbox. And months later, nobody remembers where it is.

I wanted something I could use only when I needed it.

Ratchet-USB tries to solve this problem.

You write the message locally, the program encrypts it, and you copy the encrypted block. Then you send that block through WhatsApp, email, Telegram, a forum, or whatever you were already using. The other person pastes it into their copy of Ratchet-USB and reads thye original message.

The chat can see that a block was sent, and when. It cannot read what is inside.

What it is not

Of course it is not yet another ordinary messaging app, and of course it does not replace Signal. Signal is obviously better for talking to people all day: normal chats, calls, groups, notifications, and everything else that makes a classic messaging app useful.

Ratchet-USB is built both for the occasional message that carries something more sensitive than the conversation around it, and above all for all the people who work and live in contexts where they need a private communication channel with others, but the country they are in heavily restricts the use of encrypted messaging apps. Ratchet-USB tries to solve this problem because, by using over-the-top (OTT) encryption, you can send the encrypted block through traditional channels (like SMS, email, etc.).

How it works

You create an encrypted vault on a USB drive or in a local folder.

That vault holds your identity, contacts, and session state. The USB drive is not the key. The vault is protected by a passphrase that Ratchet-USB generates when you create it.

When you create a vault, the program shows you two things, once:

  • A 12-word recovery phrase
  • A separate vault passphrase

The recovery phrase can rebuild your identity, but not your contacts, prekeys, or conversations. The passphrase unlocks the vault file. They are two different things, and you should keep them separate. To talk to someone, you exchange contact cards. Before trusting them, you compare their fingerprint over a phone call, in person, or through another channel you both control.

After that, you can send messages.

A normal exchange looks like this:

ratchet-usb init
ratchet-usb card > my-card.txt
ratchet-usb add alice --card alice-card.txt
ratchet-usb trust alice
ratchet-usb send alice
ratchet-usb recv

send produces an encrypted block. You copy it and paste it anywhere. The other person runs recv, pastes the block, and gets the message. The app also comes with a graphical version (GUI) that makes it even easier to use for people who are not comfortable with technology.

What actually happens during this operation


So, each identity has an Ed25519 key and an ML-DSA-65 key. A contact card contains the public identity keys, X25519 and ML-KEM-768 prekeys, and signatures over the card.

The first message uses a hybrid X25519 and ML-KEM-768 handshake. Both people then derive state for a classical Double Ratchet and for Signal's Sparse Post Quantum Ratchet, or SPQR. For every later message, each ratchet produces a key. Ratchet-USB combines those keys to encrypt the text. The SPQR message, classical header, and handshake fields are authenticated together with the ciphertext. The session advances only after that succeeds.

New contact cards use suite 4, which uses the X-Wing handshake combiner. Older suite 2 cards keep their original message format. An already-established session does not change protocol while it is active.

Sharing small files and having a multi-user chat

You can also send a file with:

ratchet-usb send alice --file contract.pdf

The file is encrypted through the same ratchet and becomes part of the block. No upload, no link, no external storage. The block gets bigger, roughly a third larger once armored, and a single file can be up to 4 MiB.

When the recipient runs recv, Ratchet-USB recognizes the file and offers to open it from a temporary folder. That folder is removed when the program closes.

For more than one person:

ratchet-usb group-send --to alice --to bob

The message is encrypted once under a random content key. That key is then wrapped separately for each recipient through the existing one-to-one session with them. Everyone receives the same outer block. recv finds the wrapper addressed to the local vault and decrypts the shared content. The block shows how many recipients there are, but not who they are.

Ephemeral messages

You can also mark a message as ephemeral with:

ratchet-usb send alice --ttl 24h
ratchet-usb send alice --burn

The mark is inside the encrypted text, so it is authenticated and never appears in cleartext.

But let's be honest: of course this is a best-effort mechanism, not a revocation.

The desktop GUI starts a timer when you open the receive dialog and wipes what it showed when the timer fires. The terminal interface prints the plaintext to stdout, so scrollback or redirected output can still keep a copy. --burn asks for a single reading; it does not stop screenshots, copies, or a modified client.

The vault does not keep message history, so there is nothing to delete later. There is only something that has to stop being displayed.

Why I chose not to use central servers

You will have noticed that throughout this article I have never mentioned a Ratchet-USB account, a phone number to verify, or servers that let you exchange messages.

Your identity is a file protected by a passphrase. The encrypted message travels through the channel you already use.

That means there is no service in the middle that can be breached, subpoenaed, shut down, or change its terms in a way that affects your messages.

But be careful: this does not make the transport invisible. In fact, WhatsApp, Telegram, or your email provider can still see who you talk to, when, and roughly how large the block is.

Security limits

I care about this paragraph in particular. This is version 0.5.0-dev. The post-quantum migration is implemented, but it has not had an independent security review.

A signed contact card proves that its fields belong to one identity. It does not prove that the identity belongs to the person you meant to contact. That is why fingerprint verification is important, if not essential.

A compromised computer can read passphrases and messages while the program is open. Opening a received file writes its decrypted bytes to a private folder on the host, and removes that folder when the program closes, but the file is plaintext on the host until then.

The Rust SPQR bridge wipes and best-effort locks the secret buffers it hands back to C++, but the vendored crate still uses ordinary heap allocations while it runs. On top of that, immediate erasure of every copy in memory is not guaranteed.

Older copies of the vault may also remain on the physical storage of a USB drive after a save.

Do not use this development version as the only protection for high-risk communications.

Installing it

The easiest way to try it on Linux is to download the signed AppImage from the GitHub Releases page:

https://github.com/Francy2009/Ratchet-USB/releases

chmod +x Ratchet-USB-x86_64.AppImage
./Ratchet-USB-x86_64.AppImage

The AppImage includes the CLI and the optional Qt GUI.

If you want to build it from source, you need a C++20 compiler, CMake, libsodium, OpenSSL 3.5+, Rust 1.88+, and Cargo.

git clone https://github.com/Francy2009/Ratchet-USB.git
cd Ratchet-USB
./setup.sh

The script builds the project, runs the tests, and installs the executable in ~/.local/bin.

What I would like feedback on

I would really appreciate feedback above all on the code: if you find any vulnerabilities, please report them following the rules of responsible disclosure; whether the setup process is clear; or whether anything feels confusing, fragile, or unnecessarily complicated.

The repository is here:

https://github.com/Francy2009/Ratchet-USB

Thanks for reading. If you try it, I would be happy to hear what worked, what did not, and what you would change.

P.S.: I used AI to review the text after I wrote it in English.

title: What Is JavaScript, and Why Do Websites Need It? A Beginner-Friendly Guide
description:
Imagine visiting an online shopping website.

You see a product you like. Its image looks great, the description explains its features, and the price is clearly displayed. You decide to buy it and click the “Add to Cart” button.

Almost immediately, the shopping cart updates to show your selected product.

You can add another item, remove something you no longer want, and watch the total price change as your selections change.

Have you ever wondered what makes these interactions possible?

One of the key technologies behind many of these experiences is JavaScript.

JavaScript is a programming language that allows developers to create interactive web experiences, respond to user actions, update webpage content, and build dynamic features.

But JavaScript doesn't work alone. It works alongside other technologies, particularly HTML and CSS, to help developers create modern websites and web applications.

In this beginner-friendly guide, we'll explore what JavaScript is, how it differs from HTML and CSS, why websites use it, and how you can begin learning it.

What Is JavaScript?

JavaScript is a programming language widely used to add behaviour and interactivity to websites.

A webpage can display information without JavaScript. However, when you want elements to respond to user actions, update content dynamically, or perform calculations directly in the browser, JavaScript can help make those experiences possible.

For example, JavaScript can be used to:

Respond when someone clicks a button.

Update a shopping cart.

Validate information entered into a form.

Open and close interactive menus.

Display messages based on user actions.

Filter products by category or price.

Retrieve information from an API.

Update parts of a webpage without reloading the entire page.

These are just a few examples of what JavaScript can do.

It is also used beyond browser-based websites, including server-side development through environments such as Node.js.

For now, let's focus on its role in frontend web development.

The easiest way to understand JavaScript is to look at how it works with HTML and CSS.

HTML, CSS, and JavaScript: What Is the Difference?

When learning web development, you will frequently encounter three core frontend technologies: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

Although they work together, they have different primary responsibilities.





1. HTML — Structure

HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language. It defines the structure and meaning of webpage content, including headings, paragraphs, images, links, and buttons.






2. CSS — Presentation

CSS stands for Cascading Style Sheets. It controls how content is presented, including colours, typography, spacing, layouts, and responsive behaviour.






3. JavaScript — Behaviour and Interactivity

JavaScript allows webpages to respond to events, update content, perform calculations, and support interactive features.

Think about an online shopping page.

HTML provides the product name, image, price, and button.

CSS determines how the product information is arranged and styled.

JavaScript can respond when a customer clicks the button and update the cart displayed on the page.

Here's a simple way to remember their roles:

HTML defines the structure. CSS controls the presentation. JavaScript adds behaviour.

These responsibilities can overlap in some implementation details, but this distinction is an excellent starting point for beginners.

A Practical Example: Building an Interactive Shopping Experience

Let's explore a familiar situation to see why JavaScript matters.

Imagine you're developing a small online store that sells shoes.

The product page contains:

A picture of the shoes.

The product name.

The price.

A short description.

An “Add to Cart” button.

A shopping cart indicator.

Each of these elements contributes to the experience, but displaying them is only part of the task.

Customers need to interact with the page.

Let's see how the three technologies work together.

Step 1: HTML Displays the Product

First, you use HTML to define the product information and button.

Classic Sneakers

Price: $50

Comfortable sneakers for everyday wear.

Add to Cart

Cart items: 0

This code creates a heading, two paragraphs, a button, and a cart counter.

The browser can display all of these elements without JavaScript.

However, the button does not automatically update the counter just because it says “Add to Cart.”

You need to define that behaviour.

Step 2: CSS Styles the Product Page

Next, CSS can improve the appearance of the content.

body {
font-family: Arial, sans-serif;
color: #2E2E2E;
}

button {
background-color: #800020;
color: white;
padding: 12px 18px;
border: none;
border-radius: 6px;
cursor: pointer;
}

These styles give the page a font, text colour, and a button with a coloured background, internal spacing, and rounded corners.

The product page now has a more intentional visual presentation.

But the button still needs behaviour.

Step 3: JavaScript Makes the Button Interactive

Now let's add JavaScript.

let cartCount = 0;

const addButton = document.querySelector("#add-to-cart");
const cartDisplay = document.querySelector("#cart-count");

addButton.addEventListener("click", function () {
cartCount += 1;
cartDisplay.textContent = cartCount;
});

What happens when this code runs?

cartCount starts at zero.

JavaScript selects the button and the cart counter.

An event listener waits for a click on the button.

When the button is clicked, the count increases by one.

The displayed cart count is updated.

Click the button several times, and the number displayed beside “Cart items” increases.

That is JavaScript responding to user interaction and updating the webpage.

Notice the transformation: HTML creates the elements, CSS styles them, and JavaScript makes the counter respond to clicks.

This is a simplified demonstration rather than a complete shopping cart. A real store would also need to manage product details, quantities, prices, stock, and order processing. Cart information may need to be saved, and checkout must be handled securely through an appropriate backend system.

Nevertheless, this small example demonstrates a fundamental JavaScript concept: responding to events and changing webpage content.

Why Do Websites Need JavaScript?

Strictly speaking, not every website needs JavaScript.

A simple informational website or a static blog can provide useful content using HTML and CSS alone.

However, JavaScript becomes particularly valuable when a website needs interactive or dynamic behaviour.

Here are some of its most common applications.

  1. Making Buttons Respond to User Actions

A button may submit a form, open a menu, update a counter, or trigger another action.

JavaScript can listen for events such as clicks and execute the appropriate code.

For example, clicking a button could reveal additional information or change a message displayed on the page.

This allows the interface to respond to what users do.

  1. Creating Interactive Forms

Forms are used for registration, login, contact requests, bookings, surveys, and many other tasks.

JavaScript can check user input and provide immediate feedback.

For example, a form could display a message when a required field is empty or check whether an email address follows an expected format.

However, browser-side validation is not a replacement for server-side validation. Important information must also be checked on the server because users can bypass client-side checks.

  1. Updating Content Dynamically

Some webpages need to change their content based on user actions or new information.

JavaScript can update text, show or hide elements, change displayed products, and refresh parts of a page.

For example, a shopping website could let customers filter products by category without requiring a complete page reload for every selection.

  1. Building Interactive Navigation

JavaScript can help manage menus that open and close, particularly on mobile devices where screen space is limited.

It can also support tabs, accordions, modal dialogs, and other interface components.

CSS can handle some of these interactions too, but JavaScript is useful when behaviour requires more complex state changes or logic.

  1. Communicating With APIs

An API allows different software systems to communicate.

JavaScript can request information from an API and use the returned data to update a webpage.

For example, a weather interface could request forecast information from a weather service and display the results.

A shopping application might retrieve product information from a backend API.

This is one of the ways JavaScript connects the browser interface to data and services outside the page itself.

  1. Building Rich Web Applications

JavaScript is not limited to small interactions.

It also powers complex web applications such as dashboards, project management platforms, email clients, and online collaboration tools.

Libraries and frameworks such as React can help developers organize interfaces into reusable components and manage complex application behaviour.

As projects grow, developers may combine frontend JavaScript with backend technologies, databases, APIs, and other services to build complete applications.

Does JavaScript Replace HTML and CSS?

No.

JavaScript complements HTML and CSS rather than replacing them.

Imagine trying to build a website using JavaScript alone when the project could benefit from semantic HTML elements and well-organized stylesheets.

You might end up recreating features that HTML already provides or mixing unrelated responsibilities into the same code.

Using the right tool for each task generally makes code easier to understand and maintain.

For example:

Use HTML to create a meaningful heading.

Use CSS to control the heading's appearance.

Use JavaScript if the heading needs to change in response to an interaction or application state.

This separation is a useful development practice, although real projects sometimes use tools that combine or generate these technologies during development.

The key is understanding what each technology contributes.

Can a Website Work Without JavaScript?

Yes!

This is an important distinction for beginners.

A website can display text, images, links, and styled layouts without JavaScript. Forms can also submit information using standard HTML behaviour, and a server can process requests and return updated pages.

Some interactions can be achieved with HTML and CSS.

However, JavaScript makes many richer client-side experiences possible, including immediate interface updates, complex interactive controls, and dynamic content.

The right choice depends on the website's requirements.

Developers should not add JavaScript simply because it is available. They should use it when it provides useful behaviour or solves a real problem.

How Can Beginners Start Learning JavaScript?

If you already understand basic HTML and CSS, you have a useful foundation for learning JavaScript.

You don't need to build a complete application on your first day.

Start with the fundamentals:

  1. Variables: Learn how to store values using let and const.

  2. Data types: Understand strings, numbers, booleans, arrays, and objects.

  3. Conditions: Learn how to make decisions using if and else.

  4. Functions: Understand how to organize reusable pieces of code.

  5. Events: Learn how to respond to clicks, typing, and other user actions.

  6. DOM manipulation: Practise selecting HTML elements and updating their content or attributes.

  7. Form handling: Build simple forms and provide useful feedback.

  8. APIs: Learn how to request and work with external data.

You can reinforce these skills by building small projects.

Try creating a counter, a simple calculator, a form with validation, an interactive FAQ section, or a basic shopping cart.

Each project gives you an opportunity to practise concepts and see how JavaScript behaves in a real webpage.

Don't rush to learn every framework before understanding the language fundamentals. A solid grasp of JavaScript will make more advanced tools easier to learn later.

Common Mistakes Beginners Should Avoid

As you learn JavaScript, keep these points in mind:

Don't confuse styling with behaviour. CSS controls presentation, while JavaScript handles many kinds of interaction and logic.

Don't skip HTML fundamentals. Semantic, well-structured HTML makes webpages easier to maintain and more accessible.

Don't rely only on client-side validation. The server must validate important information independently.

Don't assume every website needs JavaScript. Choose technologies according to the project's needs.

Don't learn only by memorizing code. Experiment with examples, change values, and try to explain why your code works.

Don't ignore debugging. Browser Developer Tools and useful error messages can help you identify and fix problems.

Learning to write code is important, but learning how to investigate problems is equally valuable.

Final Thoughts: JavaScript Helps Bring Websites to Life

Think back to the online shopping example.

HTML displayed the product information. CSS made the page visually appealing. JavaScript responded when the customer clicked “Add to Cart” and updated the displayed cart count.

That small interaction demonstrates the bigger idea behind JavaScript.

It allows developers to build webpages that respond to users instead of merely presenting information.

From interactive buttons and form validation to dynamic content and full web applications, JavaScript plays an important role in modern web development.

You don't need to master everything immediately.

Start with the fundamentals, practise one concept at a time, and build small projects that help you understand how the pieces fit together.

As your skills grow, you'll be able to create increasingly sophisticated experiences.

Remember: HTML provides the structure, CSS controls the presentation, and JavaScript adds behaviour and interactivity. Understanding how they work together is an important step towards becoming a capable frontend developer.

Let's Discuss

If you're learning JavaScript, which skill would you like to master first: DOM manipulation, event handling, form validation, or working with APIs?

Share your thoughts in the comments!

title: Efficient Wide-Beam Generative Retrieval with Model-Native Trie Decoding and Shared-Context Attention
description:
arXiv:2611.22309v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative retrieval (GR) predicts catalog entries as short semantic identifiers (SIDs). Trie-constrained beam search keeps these identifiers valid, but wide beams expose two serving costs: vocabulary-wide score tensors that are mostly discarded, and repeated attention over the same prompt. We present Trie-Head, a model-native output interface that stores the identifier trie as validated GPU tensors. Compared with a Python custom logit processor (CLP), it reduces CPU--GPU coordination and memory traffic by avoiding Python constraint callbacks and vocabulary-wide candidate buffers. It scores compact codebook candidates and streams the full-vocabulary normalizer, preserving the original model's valid-token scores in real arithmetic without retraining. Shared-context attention complements this output path by reusing prompt key/value blocks across beams while preserving their private decode tails. We implement both mechanisms in SGLang and evaluate candidate sourcing for LinkedIn Hiring Assistant and qualification retrieval for the Qualification Retrieval Platform. The combined system improves closed-loop throughput by up to 5.57x over the CLP baseline and up to 2.63x over BF16 FlashRec at a common beam width of 200 on the Qualification Retrieval Platform workload.

title: Bits, Not Boxes: Label-Free Layer Selection for Visual Localization in VLMs
description:
arXiv:2611.23432v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Attention maps cheaply show where a vision-language model (VLM) looks, but attention sinks make them unreliable for localization. Contrasting the question with a generic prompt suppresses sinks, yet only some layers localize the queried object. Existing methods find these layers with box annotations or fixed rules. We show that attention itself can identify them. A question changes how much a head attends to the image and where this attention goes. The two effects separate exactly, and the second, measured in bits on unlabeled questions, indicates which layers localize. WhereBits turns these where-to-look bits into a layer prior and combines it with per-head contrastive scores. Its three design constants were fixed once on labeled COCO data, and a new model or resolution needs only unlabeled questions. Across eight VLMs, WhereBits matches the pointing accuracy of box-tuned layers on COCO and RefCOCO and ranks target tokens better. This advantage holds on a held-out model family and at higher resolutions. Its COCO pointing accuracy is 0.72, against 0.22 for mean attention. In training-free zoom-in, its crops raise V* accuracy by 6.0 points under forced-choice evaluation.

title: Download Website as HTML: Get a Runnable Project From a Figma Capture
description:
Originally published on Crafttor.

TL;DR: Most ways to download website as HTML give you a broken copy: missing fonts, dead hover states, images pointing back at the live server. WebCapture to Figma's Download HTML saves a captured page as a ready-to-run HTML, CSS and JS project, with its images and Google fonts inside. Hover states, CSS animations and links work in it, and a flow recorded with the Chrome extension replays. You can open it in a browser, add it to Figma as a code layer, or use it as source material for an AI.

Why "Save page as" is not enough

Every browser can save a page. Press Ctrl+S or Cmd+S, choose "Webpage, Complete", and you get an HTML file plus a folder of assets. It is a fair first try. In practice it often falls short:

  • Fonts break. Web fonts loaded from a CDN or via CSS may not come along, so text falls back to a system font.
  • Layout shifts. Pages that build their layout with JavaScript can render differently, or not at all, when opened from disk.
  • Assets point elsewhere. Some images and styles still reference the live server. Offline, they are gone.
  • State is lost. You get the page as it loaded, not after you opened a menu or switched a tab.

Command-line tools like wget --mirror go further, but they copy a whole site's files, not one clean, self-contained page. You still have to sort out what is needed.

What Download HTML gives you instead

WebCapture works differently. It first captures the page into Figma as editable layers, recording how the browser laid it out. Then, after the import, Download HTML saves that page as a project you can run.

According to the plugin's documentation, the project:

  • is plain HTML, CSS and JS, ready to run
  • includes the page's images
  • includes its Google fonts
  • keeps hover states, CSS animations and links working
  • replays a flow recorded with the Chrome extension

Because the images and Google fonts are inside the project, it does not depend on the original site to look right.

How to download a website as HTML, step by step

1. Capture the page

Open WebCapture to Figma in a Figma file. You have two routes.

  • By URL. The page is rendered in a remote browser on Apify. Add your own Apify API token once; a free Apify account is enough to start.
  • With the Chrome extension. Best for pages behind a login or a bot wall. Capture the page as you see it and paste the result into the plugin. This route needs no token.

Choose a width before you import: Desktop 1440, iPad 820, Pixel 7, iPhone 14 Pro, iPhone SE, or a 360px Android phone. The width you pick is the layout you download. For more on picking breakpoints, read importing mobile and tablet websites to Figma.

Capture or rebuild only designs you own or have permission to use.

2. Optionally record a flow

If you want more than the default view, record the clicks in the Chrome extension first, such as opening a menu or toggling a price. That flow replays in the downloaded project. The method is covered in recording a website user flow.

3. Press Download HTML

After the import finishes, press Download HTML in the plugin. Save the project into its own folder so its files stay together.

How to open the project

Open the folder and double-click the HTML file. It opens in your default browser. Hover the buttons, watch the animations, click the links.

If anything does not load when opened straight from disk, serve the folder locally instead. Browsers apply stricter rules to file:// pages, and a local server avoids them. Two common options:

# Python 3, from inside the project folder
python3 -m http.server 8000

# Node.js
npx serve .

Then visit http://localhost:8000 (or the address serve prints).

Since it is a standard static project, you can also open it in your code editor, inspect the CSS, and change things.

What works, and what to expect

Feature In the downloaded project
Layout, colours, gradients, shadows Rendered as captured
Images Included
Google fonts Included
Hover states Work
CSS animations Play
Links Work
Recorded flow from the Chrome extension Replays

A few practical notes:

  • One page, one width. The project reflects the page at the width you captured. Capture again at another width if you need a mobile version.
  • Non-Google fonts. The documentation mentions Google fonts being included. If a site uses a licensed font from elsewhere, check how it renders and swap it if needed.
  • Server features do not come along. Forms that post to a backend, search and logins depend on the original server. The project is a front end copy.

Three ways to use the project

Open it as a reference

Keep a dated snapshot of your own site before a redesign. Months later, you can still open it and see exactly how the old version behaved, including hover timing.

Add it to Figma as a code layer

A frame can show hover states and animations only as recorded data, since a Figma prototype cannot replay CSS animations. A code layer runs them. Figma plugins cannot create code layers, because the Plugin API has no way to make one. So WebCapture offers Copy prompt: paste it into Claude with the Figma MCP connected, and Claude adds the project as a code layer beside your frame. Set the layer to the size the prompt names, then press play. Code layers cannot be resized from the API, so this step is yours. The full walkthrough is in turning a website into a Figma code layer.

Hand it to an LLM

The project is real code, so it is useful context for an AI. You can attach the HTML and CSS files to a Claude or ChatGPT conversation and ask for a specific change. For example: "Convert this hero section into a React component, keeping the CSS values."

If your goal is a fresh rebuild rather than an edit, the Chrome extension's Copy for LLM is built for that. It carries the layout, colours with real gradient stops, border and shadow values, fonts, inline SVG icons, every interaction and any recorded flow.

Privacy

With URL capture, the URL you enter is sent to Apify to be rendered. Nothing from your Figma file is uploaded. Captures pasted from the extension stay on your machine. The plugin never sends anything to an AI. If you share the project with Claude or ChatGPT, that is your choice and your paste.

Get started

WebCapture to Figma is a free plugin. Capture a page you own, press Download HTML, and open the result in your browser. You get an editable frame in Figma and a runnable project on disk from one capture.

FAQ

How do I download a website as HTML with working fonts?

Capture the page with WebCapture to Figma, then press Download HTML. The project includes the page's images and Google fonts, so it renders without reaching back to the original site for them.

Do hover states and animations work in the downloaded HTML?

Yes. According to the plugin's documentation, hover states, CSS animations and links work, and a flow recorded with the Chrome extension replays.

Can I download a page that needs a login?

Yes, through the Chrome extension. Capture the page as you see it, paste it into the plugin, then download. No Apify token is needed for this route.

Is Download HTML free?

WebCapture to Figma is a free plugin. URL capture uses your own Apify account, and a free one is enough to start.

Can I edit the downloaded project?

Yes. It is a standard HTML, CSS and JS project. Open it in any code editor, or hand it to an AI with a specific change request.
