title: Born for the Task: Rethinking Quantum Chemistry with Foresighted Agentic Computing
description:
arXiv:2611.22897v2 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantum chemistry relies on general-purpose software, whose generality leaves many large-scale calculations beyond practical resource budgets. Coding agents make task-specific programs cheap to write, but not efficient ones easy to find: whether a computational strategy is accurate and fast enough becomes clear only after it actually runs at the target scale. We introduce MakoBORN, a foresighted agentic computing framework that synthesizes high performance quantum chemistry programs on demand. MakoBORN anticipates the behavior of each strategy before execution, extrapolating its error from representative small systems and predicting its runtime from the target-scale workload and measured hardware throughputs. Building on these predictions, MakoBORN unfolds the preset schemes of existing packages into independently configurable algorithmic components, selects the fastest strategy within the error tolerance from the predicted accuracy-runtime Pareto frontier, and guides coding agents to compile it with component-level performance predictions. For a Hartree-Fock calculation with 50,024 basis functions, MakoBORN finishes in 1.41 h on a single CPU node, 77$\times$ faster than the estimated runtime of a general-purpose baseline and still 9.8$\times$ faster with development time included. On a single GPU, MakoBORN completes the ubiquitin calculation in 2.1 h, the same order of runtime as the GPU-accelerated package Mako on 64 GPUs, and shortens the B-DNA duplex calculation from an estimated two months to 8.1 h (173$\times$).

title: Nunchi: Ears Help Eyes in Multi-Party Conversations
description:
arXiv:2611.23115v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Identifying whom a person looks at is central to understanding multi-party conversations, yet gaze geometry alone becomes ambiguous as more people appear. Conversations offer cues that geometry lacks, such as who is speaking and what is said, but no gaze dataset provides them for many multi-party scenes. We introduce SORBET, a benchmark of 3,340 samples from 1,578 clips with synchronized speech, transcripts, and attended person labels, covering more multi-party scenes than existing gaze datasets. Prior gaze models struggle to use these cues, which come in different forms, must be linked to the right person, and can conflict with gaze geometry. We propose Nunchi, a framework that constructs a text prompt from the transcript and the outputs of gaze and speaker models, links every cue to the candidates with shared labels, and lets a vision-language model (VLM) weigh gaze geometry against conversational cues to identify the attended person. Nunchi outperforms the strongest existing method by 4.8 percentage points. On SORBET, conversational cues help whereas additional visual cues do not, and the gains hold across three VLMs, with automatic transcripts, and on two existing datasets.

title: React useReducer Hook
description:
The useReducer Hook is used to manage state in React applications. It is especially useful when a component has complex state logic or multiple state updates.

useReducer helps us manage state by keeping all the state updating logic in one place.

Instead of directly updating the state, we dispatch an action. The reducer function checks that action and returns the new state.

For example, imagine a counter application.
We need three operations:
Increment the count.
Decrement the count.
Reset the count.

We can implement these operations using useState. But when the application has many state updates, managing all the logic inside event handlers can become difficult.

Syntax of useReducer

import { useReducer } from "react";
const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, initialState);

state: Stores the current state value.
dispatch: Function used to send an action to the reducer.
reducer: Function that decides how the state should change.
initialState: The starting value of the state.

How does useReducer work?

First, we create an initial state.
We create a reducer function.
The user performs an action, such as clicking a button.
We call dispatch() with the required action.
The reducer receives the current state and action.
The reducer returns the updated state.
React renders the component with the new state.

title: VK 广告开户清单：DTC 品牌进入东南亚前要准备什么
description:
经常有客户问我们VK 广告该从哪里开始。下面是我们给DTC 品牌的精简版，适用于东南亚市场。

费用到底由什么决定

VK 广告的竞价只是表面成本，总成本还包括开户渠道（直开、代理或二级代理）、充值手续费、汇率差、素材制作以及申诉耗费的时间。对DTC 品牌来说，最容易被忽略的是前两周学习期的浪费，应该把学习期预算单独列出来，而不是第三天就下结论。

为什么VK 广告要单独规划

很多团队把 Meta 或 Google 的做法直接复制到新平台，VK 广告往往不吃这一套。受众意图、素材形式、审核规则都不同，出错的代价通常是账户被封而不是效果差一点。DTC 品牌进入东南亚之前，先为每个平台写一页计划：谁负责账户、用什么付款方式、哪些落地页已经过审、达到什么数据才加预算。

常见错误

  • 把别的平台素材原样搬到VK 广告。
  • 同一天同时改预算、受众和素材，结果无法解读。
  • 唯一的管理员账号握在一个外包手里。
  • 广告被拒之前从不看政策中心。
  • 追踪还没验证就判断渠道好坏。

30 天上线节奏

第 1 周：账户、付款、追踪和两个落地页；第 2 周：3–5 个素材方向小预算测试；第 3 周：砍掉后一半，把赢家复制到第二个受众；第 4 周：对照目标看主转化成本，决定加量、维持或停止。把过程记下来，第二个市场会便宜很多。

开户前要备齐的资料

主体名称要和网站页脚一致，准备自有域名的企业邮箱、隐私政策、服务条款、退款政策和可联系的联系页面。VK 广告的审核会把这些信息和广告、落地页放在一起比对，不一致是新账户卡审最常见的原因。延伸阅读：广告开户资料清单工具。

充值与付款权限管理

明确谁能充值、谁能改付款方式，并写成制度。每个账户只设一个账单联系人，发票统一存放，每周用平台报表对账。如果财务在其他时区，约定一个余额预警线，避免周五晚上在东南亚因余额不足停投。

能过审的素材

审核会同时看首帧、卖点和落地页。避免前后对比、无法证明的数字和催促性用语，文字本地化成东南亚的语言，落地页重复同一个优惠。信息一致既能过审，也能提升转化。

小结

计划要小、要写下来、要能衡量。先做好上面的基础，30 天后复盘，再放大有效的部分。

作者：熊猫出海 PandaWM（香港团队）。业务包括 GEO/AI 搜索优化、Facebook/Google/TikTok 及约 20 个小众平台广告开户与代投、多语言网站、AiChatSale，以及只服务海外商户的加密支付网关。

title: ACH Return Codes Explained: R01 to R85 and How to Handle Each One
description:
ACH Return Codes Explained: R01 to R85 and How to Handle Each One

ACH Return Codes Explained: R01 to R85 and How to Handle Each One

When you're building a payout system, ACH returns are inevitable. A customer's bank rejects the transfer, and your code needs to know why. The National Automated Clearing House Association (NACHA) defines 85 standardized return codes—each with a specific reason, timing window, and recovery path.

Understanding these codes isn't just academic. It's the difference between a retry that works and one that wastes time and money. Let's walk through the most common returns and how to handle them programmatically.

The Big Three: R01, R03, R10

R01 — Insufficient Funds

The customer's account doesn't have enough money. This is the most common return, accounting for roughly 30–40% of all ACH returns in production systems.

  • When it fires: 1–2 business days after the debit entry is sent
  • Reversibility: The debit is reversed; funds are returned to your account
  • Developer action: Flag the payout as failed. Retry logic here is risky—if the account still lacks funds tomorrow, you'll just get another R01. Instead, notify the customer and ask them to add funds before you retry. 
{
  "return_code": "R01",
  "reason": "Insufficient Funds",
  "action": "notify_customer_and_hold",
  "retry_eligible": false,
  "settlement_days": 1
}

R03 — No Account / Invalid Account

The account number doesn't exist, or the routing number is invalid.

  • When it fires: 1–2 business days
  • Reversibility: Full reversal
  • Developer action: This is permanent. Don't retry. Update your customer database to flag the account as invalid and route future payouts to an alternate method (card, wire, RTP).

R10 — Customer Advises Not Authorized

The customer disputes the transaction—they claim they didn't authorize it. This is a fraud signal.

  • When it fires: Up to 60 days after the transaction
  • Reversibility: Full reversal
  • Developer action: This requires manual review. Flag the account, contact the customer, and pause automated payouts until resolved.

Mid-Tier Returns: R04, R05, R07

R04 — Invalid Routing Number

The routing number format is wrong or doesn't belong to an active bank.

  • Developer action: Validate routing numbers against the Federal Reserve's routing directory before attempting a payout. This is preventable.

R05 — Improper Debit Entry

The debit entry itself is malformed—wrong amount format, invalid transaction code, or missing required fields.

  • Developer action: This indicates a bug in your ACH file generation. Check your NACHA file formatting (record length, field alignment, checksums). Fix the code and retry.

R07 — Authorization Revoked

The customer revoked their authorization via their bank.

  • Developer action: Treat like R10—manual review required. The customer has formally objected.

Building Retry Logic

Here's a practical pattern for handling returns:

function handleACHReturn(returnCode, payout) {
  const returnRules = {
    R01: { retry: false, action: 'notify', days: 0 },
    R03: { retry: false, action: 'invalidate_account', days: 0 },
    R04: { retry: true, action: 'validate_routing', days: 1 },
    R05: { retry: true, action: 'fix_format', days: 1 },
    R10: { retry: false, action: 'manual_review', days: 0 },
  };

  const rule = returnRules[returnCode] || { retry: false, action: 'escalate' };

  if (rule.retry) {
    scheduleRetry(payout, rule.days);
  } else if (rule.action === 'notify') {
    notifyCustomer(payout, returnCode);
  } else if (rule.action === 'invalidate_account') {
    markAccountInvalid(payout.account_id);
    routeToAlternateRail(payout); // Try card or RTP instead
  }

  logReturn(payout.id, returnCode, rule.action);
}

Settlement Timing

ACH returns typically settle 1–2 business days after the original debit entry. Same-day ACH returns settle the same day. Plan your reconciliation window accordingly—don't assume a payout succeeded until 2 business days have passed.

Key Takeaway

Not all ACH returns are created equal. R01 needs customer intervention. R03 needs account replacement. R05 needs code fixes. Build your retry logic around the reason, not just the fact of failure. That's what separates a robust payout system from one that wastes time ch

Decoding ACH return codes programmatically? The ACH Return Codes API returns the full Nacha R01–R85 set with plain-language descriptions and handling guidance.

title: Reliable Evaluation of AI Agents for Investment Research: A Framework for Performance and Validity Assessment
description:
arXiv:2611.22338v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We consider the problem of evaluating AI agents undertaking investment-research tasks, where agents interact with external information sources and computational tools to produce financial analyses and research reports. An important challenge is that the quality of an agent's final output does not necessarily reflect the quality of its execution process, while the reliability of the resulting assessment also depends on the validity of the evaluation procedure. Furthermore, investment-research tasks differ considerably in their requirements for numerical accuracy, information retrieval, financial analysis and supporting evidence, making it difficult to assess agent performance using a uniform set of criteria. We propose a domain-oriented evaluation framework that distinguishes outcome quality from execution quality and accommodates these differences through task-specific criteria, deterministic validators and independent large language model judges. We also introduce an evaluation-validity mechanism that examines the integrity of evaluation inputs, reference information, supporting evidence and grading outputs, with expert review used to resolve identified deficiencies and significant grading disagreements. Numerical results show that the proposed framework can distinguish differences in agent performance across evaluation dimensions, while identifying potential reliability issues in the evaluation process. The associated implementation and evaluation materials will be made available on GitHub.

title: How I Built a 100% Local PDF RAG Assistant on CPU Using Python and Ollama
description:
The moment this project felt real wasn't when the model generated its first paragraph. It was when I asked it a question that wasn't covered in its documents and instead of making something up, it checked its similarity score, paused, and politely refused to guess.

As a cloud engineer who spends most days building backend systems, designing cloud architectures, and working on production deployment strategies, AI always felt like a separate world dominated by massive GPU clusters and expensive cloud APIs. Recently, I decided to take my first hands-on step into AI engineering.

This is the story of my first end-to-end AI application—a small accomplishment, built from scratch on a standard Linux server, that taught me more than hours of youtube tutorials.

The Spark: A Real Problem Worth Solving

Every engineering team deals with the same quiet productivity drain: dense, multi-page technical PDFs. Finding a single configuration parameter, protocol rule, or specification table often means opening multiple manuals and hitting Ctrl + F until something vaguely matches.

I didn't want to build a flashy general-purpose chatbot that writes poetry or answers trivia. I wanted a focused, dependable technical assistant that does one job well:

  • Answer questions strictly from local reference manuals.
  • Cite the exact source file and page number so engineers can verify the answer immediately.
  • Say "I don't know" whenever the answer isn't actually in the documents.

Why "100% Local" on CPU Mattered

From day one, I set two strict architectural constraints:

  1. Zero external cloud APIs: Technical documents and queries stay completely inside the server.
  2. CPU-only execution: No dedicated GPUs—just standard Linux compute.

Coming from a cloud and infrastructure background, running everything locally eliminates per-token API costs, removes external network latency, and keeps data privacy straightforward. More importantly, it proves you don't need expensive GPU hardware to build a fast, practical Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system.

The Tech Stack & Why Each Piece Was Chosen

Instead of reaching for heavy abstraction frameworks that hide how data moves, I chose lightweight, transparent tools where every stage could be inspected and debugged:

Layer Tool / Model Chosen Why It Was Considered & Chosen
PDF Parsing & OCR PyMuPDF + pdfplumber + RapidOCR Plain text extractors scramble tables and ignore diagrams. Combining native text extraction, Markdown table conversion, and lightweight CPU ONNX OCR captures the full page accurately.
Embeddings FastEmbed (BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5) Runs via ONNX Runtime on CPU with zero heavy deep-learning bloat, turning 800-character chunks into compact 384-dimensional vectors in milliseconds.
Vector Store ChromaDB (Local Persistent) Running a distributed vector cluster for a single-server app would be over-engineering. ChromaDB persists metadata in SQLite and the HNSW similarity graph right on disk.
Local LLM Ollama (qwen2.5:3b) Fits comfortably in CPU RAM while following strict grounding prompts. Locked at temperature = 0.0 so responses stay factual and deterministic rather than creative.
API & Serving FastAPI + Uvicorn + systemd Familiar backend tools to expose clean REST endpoints, keep models warm in RAM across requests, and run cleanly behind a reverse proxy.

Three Real Engineering Hurdles I Solved

1. PDFs Are Much Harder Than Plain Text

In my first prototype, I dumped raw text from a PDF and sliced it every 800 characters. The answers were rough because specification tables turned into scrambled words and sentences got cut in half mid-thought.

What fixed it:

  • Added a 120-character overlap between chunks so boundary sentences stay intact.
  • Converted grid tables into structured Markdown pipe tables (| Column | Value |) before chunking.
  • Preserved exact page_number metadata on every chunk so citations never drift.

2. Teaching the AI When to Say "I Don't Know"

A confident hallucination destroys trust in a technical tool immediately. Even with a strict system prompt, compact models will still try to be "helpful" and guess if a question shares keywords with an indexed manual.

What fixed it: I implemented a two-layer safety net before returning any response:

  1. Layer 1 — Cosine Similarity Gate (>= 0.70): Before calling the LLM, the retriever checks the top vector match score. If the closest chunk scores below 0.70, the pipeline stops immediately—saving CPU cycles and returning a clean fallback message.

  1. Layer 2 — Strict Context-Only Prompting: Chunks that pass Layer 1 are wrapped inside explicit <context> boundaries with instructions to emit a fixed abstention signal if the exact answer isn't present:


Answer the <question> using ONLY the facts inside <context>.
- Do not use outside knowledge or guess missing values.
- If the context does not contain enough information, reply ONLY with: INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE

3. Turning a CLI Script into a Real Web Service

Getting a Python script to answer questions in a terminal is only half the job. Making it usable as a real application meant applying standard production backend habits:

  • Warm Memory Residency: Loading the embedding model and vector index once at FastAPI startup (lifespan) so user queries don't pay cold-load penalties.
  • Live /health Diagnostics: Building a lightweight telemetry dashboard showing service health, total indexed chunks, active models, and real-time retrieval vs. generation latency.

Honest Reflection & What’s Next

Right now, this is an honest v1 pilot. It handles single-turn, cited technical questions reliably and serves concurrent queries in roughly 1.5 to 4 seconds on CPU.

At the same time, shipping v1 made the next set of improvements clear:

  • Hybrid Search: Combining semantic vector search with exact keyword matching so specific error codes and part numbers rank even higher.
  • Multi-Turn Memory: Supporting natural follow-up questions within a conversation session.
  • Token Streaming: Streaming words to the UI as the CPU generates them so responses feel instantaneous.

Coming from a cloud and backend background, building my first AI application showed me that practical AI isn't magic—it's good data pipelines, sensible guardrails, and solid systems engineering.

Why I Wrote This & Let's Discuss!

I wrote this post because when I first started exploring AI, most guides assumed you had cloud API keys or a dedicated GPU. If you're a backend or cloud engineer curious about building your first AI project, starting small and local is one of the best ways to understand every moving piece under the hood.

Have you built a local RAG pipeline or deployed small LLMs on CPU?
I'd love to hear what worked best for you!

title: Matching records without lookalike names: three rules from reading regulator registers
description:
If you match company names across two datasets, you will eventually produce a confident, wrong join. I'm Ruth Calder, Enforcement Editor at GLP Watchdog, and my job is matching online sellers to regulator records: FDA warning letters, outsourcing-facility registrations, state pharmacy filings. These are the three rules I use. They apply to any dataset where names are messy. (Editorial role, not a clinician; this post is about method, not medicine.)

1. A name alone is never a match

Our register holds pharmacies and FDA publishes a register of 503B outsourcing facilities. One pharmacy on our side is "Empower Pharmacy" and on FDA's it is "Empower Pharma." That pairing is only trustworthy because both are in Houston, Texas. We require a name and a city and a state before we call it a match, and when two candidates sit in one city we record no match at all.

def is_match(a, b):
    return (norm(a.name) == norm(b.name)
            and a.city.lower() == b.city.lower()
            and a.state == b.state)

A resemblance between two names is a reason to keep looking, not a result.

2. Every "not found" needs a positive control

A search that returns nothing is as often a broken search as a clean record. Before I write "no FDA warning letter on record," I run the same query for a company I know has one. If the control comes back empty, the finding is about my query, not about the company.

assert search(known_letter_company) != []   # the control
result = search(target_company)             # only then trust an empty result

3. Log your own errors in public

When we counted warning letters per seller, four of our own reviews showed "4", "5" and "6" letters for companies with none. The count had been built from a field that also held general FDA notes. We fixed it, added an automated check that fails the build, and wrote it up. The write-up is part of What the FDA's GLP-1 Warning Letters Say About This Market, and the wider list of what a register can't verify is on What This Register Gets Wrong, and What It Cannot Check.

None of our errors was caught by review. Each surfaced when someone computed a number for an article. If you generate text from structured data, one wrong rule produces the same wrong sentence on many pages, in fluent prose, so test the rule, not the page.

Where this is used

The full pharmacy-check walkthrough, which relies on the same name-city-state rule, is How to Verify an Online GLP-1 Pharmacy. My author page: Ruth Calder.

This is general information, not medical advice.

title: VITAL: A Framework for Validating Agentic AI in Pharmaceutical Drug Development and Clinical Trial Operations
description:
arXiv:2611.22973v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Current assurance approaches do not establish whether evidence is sufficient to validate, monitor and govern agentic artificial intelligence (AI) within a pharmaceutical context of use. Plausible outputs may conceal failures in retrieval, reasoning, orchestration or human-control points, where reference standards are unavailable. We developed and operationalised VITAL (Validation by Intended use, Traceability, Autonomy and Lifecycle evidence), a validation framework for agents in clinical development, through landscape analysis, regulatory and standards mapping, expert interviews and multi-stakeholder refinement. VITAL integrates context of use, controls, behavioural validation and lifecycle evidence within a risk-adjusted framework. We applied VITAL across epidemiology and treatment-landscape analysis, site selection, enrolment rescue and trial-design trade-off support to translate autonomy, reversibility, transparency and patient impact into proportionate validation activities, evidence requirements and auditable reconstruction of system behaviour. VITAL may inform evidence requirements and lifecycle accountability for higher-risk pharmaceutical uses; evaluation should assess reproducibility across assessors, organisations and system configurations.

title: LMLineage: Content Lineage and Context Governance for LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.22511v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Interpretability for AI agents should not be confined to understanding the model's internal weights. It must also cover the agent's reasoning and decision-making process over multi-source context. We present LMLineage, an out-of-band system that attributes every output sentence of an agent session to its supporting input spans with calibrated confidences, without requiring white-box access to the model or any additional inference passes. On top of the lineage metadata, we build concept-drift micro compaction: instead of waiting for the context-length limit and summarizing everything, the system detects when previously used input documents have stopped being referenced ("drifted") and surgically compacts only those, preserving user instructions verbatim. We evaluate on a multi-tier corpus: 71 gold annotated sentences from 10 Chinese web-QA cases, plus 90 turns of independently collected multi-turn sessions across three generator models (gpt-4o-mini, qwen3.8-27b, deepseek-v4-flash). Results show that (i) window-level embedding similarity is far better aligned with LLM paraphrasing than whole document or lexical matching; (ii) the greedy-window fast path is both faster and more accurate on average than exhaustive line-matching (a multiple-comparisons bias in the latter inflates web recall at the cost of overall accuracy); (iii) per-turn attribution completes in 1s on a single GPU, remaining stable as context accumulates to 40 turns; and (iv) concept-drift detection is conservative (0% false compaction) with recall bounded by attribution accuracy. We further describe the concept-drift micro compaction design and an interactive incident-tracing/memory-cleaning case study. A companion patent application covers the lineage construction method.

title: Test “Not sure yet” as a real answer in an Astro form
description:
An epoxy customer can see there is something on the concrete without knowing whether it is paint, sealer or another coating. In the existing planner, “Not sure yet” is a visible answer for both area and surface. Each answer occupies its own position in the flow and is displayed with its question’s summary label.

Separate equal labels by step

The client’s Map keys selections by step index. Two steps can store the same visible string and still round-trip independently. A Set of answer strings would collapse the two values. A dictionary keyed by the labels displayed on buttons would have a similar collision. The four-question sequence is fixed, so the index remains a useful address until a design introduces conditional insertion or reordering.

await page.goto('/epoxy/');
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Garage', exact: true }).click();
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Not sure yet', exact: true }).click();
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Not sure yet', exact: true }).click();
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Just planning', exact: true }).click();
await page.getByLabel('WA postcode').fill('6062');
await page.getByLabel('WA postcode').press('Enter');
const summary = page.locator('[data-answer-summary]');
await expect(summary.getByText('Not sure yet', { exact: true })).toHaveCount(2);
await expect(summary.locator('dt')).toHaveText(['Space', 'Area', 'Surface', 'Timing', 'WA postcode']);

Keep unknown and unanswered distinct

There’s no skip action on these questions. Before a click, the Map has no entry for that step. After an explicit unknown answer, the Map holds the displayed label. If a future API takes this data, use a stable value for unknown and make the required fields explicit in the schema. Test that an omitted surface fails validation while a deliberate unknown survives serialisation. The browser example tests the current distinction at the summary boundary and leaves any slab recommendation to an installer.

Inspect the two unknown answers separately when testing changes. Revisit Surface and pick Bare concrete. The Area value should still read Not sure yet when the final list is rebuilt.

Perth Quotes garage floor coating planner is the live preview. Online enquiries are closed.

title: A ten-second Flutter pause with a visible Skip button
description:
Tap Amen in AlyDoit’s Flutter app Selah and a separate screen offers a breathing ring, a ten-second countdown, and a Skip button. The visible exit is the detail that makes it work as an optional pause.

Save the action before opening the pause

The chat records Amen before pushing the pause route. If the person chose to keep the prayer, the app saves that too. Then the chat awaits the pause route. When it closes, the chat records completion and scrolls to the new entry.

That order gives Skip one job. It closes the pause with the prayer decision already saved. A separate route also gives the countdown a clear lifetime. Flutter’s Navigator documentation

Give the animation and the timer different jobs

A reversible five-second animation controller scales the ring, while a one-second timer updates the number. When the countdown finishes, the timer uses the same close method as Skip. The screen cancels the timer and disposes the animation controller when the route goes away. The countdown and button also explain what will happen without requiring someone to infer it from the ring. Flutter’s AnimationController documentation

For a similar interaction, test Skip just before the final tick, system Back during the fade, and leaving and resuming the app during the countdown. If the exit can race the timer, make closing a one-time action. Where elapsed time needs to be exact, compare against a deadline because periodic callbacks can arrive late. Dart’s Timer.periodic documentation

This article was generated by an AI agent for AlyDoit using Selah’s source code. The test cases are suggestions.

title: Multi-Tab Testing: Ask a Peer to Edit the Same SaaS Record Twice
description:
Multi-tab testing should check what happens when one person opens the same SaaS record twice, saves a change in one tab and then saves an older view in the other. Define which edits should survive, how a conflict is explained and whether unsaved text remains recoverable. A successful save message alone does not establish that the resulting record is correct.

This is a useful public-demo request because a peer can reproduce it with safe sample data. They do not need your source code to notice that an earlier edit disappeared. They do need a clear starting record, save order and expected outcome.

The task-review app below is fictional. The walkthrough is an original manual test plan, not a claim that I tested Buildside or any other product. It focuses on one account in two tabs; that differs from two people with different permissions editing together.

Choose a record and define the competing changes

Create a disposable sample task with a title and description that are easy to recognize. Open the task in tab A and tab B before changing either one. Both views should begin from the same saved version for this first test.

In tab A, change the description from a short sample sentence to a longer explanation. Save it and confirm the ordinary success state. In tab B, change only the title while leaving its old description untouched, then save.

Now inspect the authoritative current record by reopening it through the product's normal navigation. Did the new title and new description both survive? Did tab B overwrite tab A's description? Did the app reject the stale save and explain why?

There is no universal requirement that every product merge every change automatically. The requirement is to choose and communicate behavior appropriate to the task. A deliberate conflict warning can be better than an apparently successful save that silently discards another edit.

Distinguish the current view from unsaved work

A tab can contain both an old saved version and new text the person has typed. Refreshing everything may update the former while losing the latter. Those are different pieces of information and deserve different expectations.

For the fictional task app, propose a clear rule: when a conflicting saved version is detected, keep the person's unsaved title available while showing that the description changed elsewhere. The person can then review the current record and decide how to continue.

This is a design choice for the example, not a claim about a particular library. Your product may offer a comparison, a recoverable draft or another route. Explain what the user can do next without requiring them to understand storage versions or request headers.

Test the words as well as the outcome. “Conflict” with no context may be accurate internally but unhelpful. The person needs to know that another saved version exists, whether their own typing is safe and which action could replace or discard it.

Run the save order in both directions

After the first attempt, reset the safe fixture and reverse the order. Save the title in tab B first, then the description in tab A. Record each outcome rather than assuming the same policy will apply in both directions.

Next, make both tabs edit the same field with visibly different sample text. This creates a different decision from changing separate fields. An automatic merge of independent edits does not tell you how the app handles competing descriptions.

Keep the sequence deliberate. The first manual review does not need two people trying to click at the exact same millisecond. An older tab saving after a newer version already exists is enough to inspect an important stale-edit path.

A rapid simultaneous attempt can be a later check with suitable technical support. Do not describe a handful of manual saves as proof that all concurrency conditions are safe. The evidence is about the exact starting states and orders attempted.

Check what another tab is told

A product may update tab B as soon as tab A saves, show a notice when B regains focus or discover the mismatch only when B tries to save. Inspect the behavior that actually occurs. Do not infer it from how quickly a badge changes.

MDN's Broadcast Channel API documentation describes communication between browsing contexts within the same origin and storage partition. It also makes clear that the application defines what the messages mean. A browser message is a possible coordination mechanism, not a server-side guarantee that conflicting writes cannot overwrite each other.

That distinction matters for the test. Seeing an “updated elsewhere” notice is useful, but you still need to inspect the saved record after the attempted action. Conversely, an app can protect a stale save even if it does not update the other tab immediately.

Keep browser coordination and durable data protection separate in the review notes. A peer can report the visible behavior. The developer can then investigate which part of the implementation produced it without treating a particular browser API as the entire solution.

Include an ordinary interruption

Once the clean sequence is understood, let tab B sit while doing a short unrelated task. Return to it and attempt the same title edit after tab A has saved. This checks the familiar situation in which the person forgot an older tab was open.

Record the elapsed period when it matters, but do not invent a timeout boundary from one attempt. The question is whether the product protects and explains the old view under the conditions you observed.

If the session has expired, identify that separately. A sign-in prompt and a stale-record warning solve different problems. Complete the normal sign-in route only within the access already provided, then inspect whether the unsaved sample text remains available.

Also check a normal refresh before saving. The product may intentionally reload the current record and discard an untouched old view. That does not excuse losing new text without the protection your product promises. State exactly what had been typed before the refresh.

Give a founder peer a small, reproducible task

A public request should specify the fixture, account context and action order. For example: “Using this sample task, open two tabs. Save a description in A, then a title in B. Tell me which title and description appear after reopening the record.”

Share safe credentials or access only through the product's intended test arrangement. Do not publish a real customer's record or invite peers to experiment with live work. A fictional fixture makes the expected changes easier to compare too.

On Buildside, a founder can share the prototype and a focused question about the work. Ask peers to report what happened rather than approve the interface in general. Relevant feedback may come from someone who regularly keeps several work tabs open.

Provide the expected behavior and the limits of the request. This review concerns one account and a stale record. It does not cover role boundaries, every network failure or simultaneous collaboration across devices.

Report the final record, not just the toast

A useful result includes the initial values, edits made, save order, visible message and final reopened values. If text disappeared, identify which field and which action preceded the loss. Keep a screenshot or recording free of private information.

After a repair, repeat the failed sequence with the same sample data. Then repeat the reverse order and the same-field case, since the remedy may treat those paths differently. Share the revised behavior and invite one bounded recheck.

When documenting the release publicly, say which paths were checked and what remains untested. “Both edits survived this two-tab sequence” is an inspectable observation. “We solved collaboration” is much broader. The useful public record shows how someone can keep working when an older tab meets a newer saved record.

title: A Hardware-Aware Comprehensive Study of Edge Vision Deployment with A Unified Hardware-Model-Runtime Mapping Framework
description:
arXiv:2611.23705v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The rapid growth of deep learning has driven the deployment of computer vision directly on resource-constrained edge devices. However, the extreme heterogeneity of edge hardware architectures poses major challenges in selecting and designing suitable vision models. This survey bridges the gap between edge hardware constraints, model architectures, and deployment software toolchains. We establish a comprehensive taxonomy classifying edge hardware into three distinct tiers: mid-range devices (GPUs and dedicated NPUs or TPUs), dedicated embedded MPU or SoC processors, and microcontrollers (MCUs). We aggregate and analyze multi-source benchmark results for image classification and object detection across the computing spectrum, spanning from tens of watts down to milliwatt-scale bare-metal MCUs. Based on these empirical findings, we propose a two-tiered hardware-to-model mapping framework that provides concrete model selection matrices across performance priorities (Speed, Balanced, Accuracy) and actionable architectural design principles (peak SRAM budgeting, resolution-first scaling, and algorithm-compiler co-design). Finally, we highlight critical deployment challenges including toolchain fragmentation, operator incompatibility, and Vision Transformer feasibility, and outline promising future research directions in on-device adaptation and sustainable Edge AI.

title: DetectViT: Test-time Backdoor Detection for Vision Transformers via Inter-Head Attention Discrepancy
description:
arXiv:2611.23770v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) now underpin the visual encoders of most multimodal models, but this success comes at a cost: relying on third-party pretrained checkpoints leaves these systems open to backdoor attacks. Existing test-time detection methods rely on either the predicted label or intermediate embeddings, limiting their applicability across diverse tasks and incurring substantial computational overhead. In this work, we study how backdoor triggers affect the multi-head attention mechanism of ViTs and identify two distinct anomalous patterns: $\textit{complete attention hijacking}$, causing the attention to exhibit abnormally high inter-head spatial overlap, and $\textit{partial attention hijacking}$, causing an abnormally large variance in the concentration of the attention distribution. Motivated by these findings, we propose $\textbf{DetectViT}$, a test-time backdoor detection method that requires neither training data, model outputs, nor any prior knowledge of the trigger. DetectViT quantifies the two hijacking phenomena via an inter-head consistency score and an inter-head entropy variance score, with thresholds estimated from a small out-of-distribution (OOD) calibration set drawn from an arbitrary source. Across four representative attacks, diverse architectures (DeiT, CLIP, and LLaVA), and downstream tasks (image classification and captioning), DetectViT substantially outperforms all baselines with as few as 64--128 OOD calibration samples, achieving a true positive rate of $100\%$ and a false positive rate of $0.17\%$ on BadCLIP. Notably, it introduces negligible additional overhead by relying solely on attention weights already computed during inference. Code is available at: https://github.com/siquanhuang/DetectViT.

title: Circuit Breakers for Third-Party Odds Providers
description:
When your product depends on a third-party odds feed that goes down twice a month, you need a circuit breaker — not just a retry loop. Retries without a breaker turn a 30-second outage into a 5-minute request queue that cascades into your own API.

Three states

A circuit breaker sits between your service and the upstream:

CLOSED  →  failures exceed threshold  →  OPEN
OPEN    →  cool-down expires          →  HALF-OPEN
HALF-OPEN → probe succeeds            →  CLOSED
HALF-OPEN → probe fails               →  OPEN

class Breaker {
  private failures = 0;
  private state: 'closed' | 'open' | 'half' = 'closed';
  private openedAt = 0;

  async call<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
    if (this.state === 'open') {
      if (Date.now() - this.openedAt < 30_000) throw new Error('circuit open');
      this.state = 'half';
    }
    try {
      const result = await fn();
      this.failures = 0;
      this.state = 'closed';
      return result;
    } catch (e) {
      if (++this.failures >= 5) { this.state = 'open'; this.openedAt = Date.now(); }
      throw e;
    }
  }
}

Fallback: stale data with a badge

While the breaker is open, serve the last known odds with a "prices may be delayed" badge. A platform like Tenobet that aggregates multiple providers can fall back to a secondary feed entirely, but most single-provider setups just need an honest staleness indicator.

Monitoring

Log every state transition. A breaker that opens and closes rapidly ("flapping") means your threshold is too low or the upstream is degrading rather than failing outright. Add a minimum time-in-open to prevent flapping.

Takeaway

Retries are for transient errors. A circuit breaker is for when the upstream is genuinely down and you need to stop hammering it, preserve your own resources, and give the user a degraded but honest experience.

title: MongoDB is a Leader in The Forrester Wave™: Translytical Data Platforms
description:
We’re pleased to announce that MongoDB has been recognized as a Leader in the recently released Forrester Wave™: Translytical Data Platforms, Q4 2024.

The report—which highlights “Leaders, Strong Performers, Contenders, and Challengers” and is “an assessment of the top vendors in the market”—notes that “MongoDB is an excellent choice for organizations looking to enhance their document and NoSQL platforms with real-time insights by leveraging translytical capabilities.”

What are translytical capabilities?

So what are translytical capabilities? In short, modern applications use a growing number of data types for transactional, operational, and analytical uses. Developers can silo different data types and workloads into separate systems, but this causes architectural complexity and reduced agility for teams.

A better approach—and one that speeds development—is to leverage a single platform that can store and use multiple data types for different purposes. Forrester defines these “translytical data platforms” as “next-generation data solutions built on a single database engine to seamlessly support transactional, operational, and analytical workloads without compromising data integrity, performance, or real-time analytics.”

That’s why we built MongoDB Atlas as a modern database. It brings data like documents, vectors, streaming, and time-series together in one system so that you can run transactional, operational, and analytics workloads in one place.

How Forrester measured translytical capabilities

To measure providers, Forrester evaluated 15 of the most significant translytical data platform vendors against 26 criteria. These criteria span current offering and strategy, to market presence. Being recognized as a Leader is based on an organization’s scores in both current offering and strategy categories for criteria like vision and innovation.

Forrester gave MongoDB the highest possible scores across nine criteria, including:

  • Multimodel1

  • Search

  • Development Tools / API

  • Scale optimization

  • Streaming

  • Platform management

  • Roadmap

  • Adoption

  • Number of customers

According to the report, “MongoDB continues to expand its translytical market share by delivering new capabilities that enhance automation, intelligent memory tiering, and multimodel support, including vector, streaming, analytics, and integrated transactions.”

“Developers have been telling us for years that they need easy ways to work with all their data in one place,” said Jim Scharf, Chief Technology Officer at MongoDB. “That’s what continues to drive our strategy of making MongoDB Atlas the modern database. We’re excited to be recognized as a Leader in the new The Forrester Wave™: Translytical Data Platforms, and we will continue to support our customers’ growing needs for their data.”

What are MongoDB customers doing with translytical capabilities?

The Forrester report notes that organizations “use MongoDB to support real-time analytics, customer intelligence, the Internet of Things (IoT), and AI applications.” So, let’s look at a few examples in action.

Companies like Ignition started using MongoDB just for operational data—but, over time, expanded into using Atlas Vector Search for AI use cases. Meanwhile, Bosch Digital makes their IoT data easier to work with by bringing multiple data sources together in a single platform. And, Keller Williams uses MongoDB Charts to bring their analytics to where their transactional data is, making it faster to gather insights for their product teams.

Overall, customers are attracted to MongoDB because of how developer-friendly the platform is, and because it simplifies their lives by bringing their data together.

1 Multimodel is defined as support for storing and using various data types.

title: LightSEAD: Lightweight SE(3)-Aware Keypoint Detector through Selective Knowledge Distillation
description:
arXiv:2611.23661v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The pursuit of improved performance in deep learning has often been accompanied by increasing architectural complexity and computational demands. We explore an alternative direction: achieving more with less through structured supervision. We introduce LightSEAD, a lightweight SE(3)-aware keypoint detector initialised with calibrated Harris pseudo-labels and enriched through viewpoint-aware and appearance-aware supervision and selective knowledge distillation. LightSEAD comprises only six convolutional layers and 84,289 learnable parameters, achieving competitive repeatability across HPatches, KITTI 06 and 4Seasons while demonstrating its downstream applicability to relative pose estimation on MegaDepth-1500. Further optimised for mixed-precision inference, LightSEAD Coarse achieves approximately 909 FPS on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 and 139 FPS on a Jetson Orin Nano Super.

title: Africa Retakes Top Spot: Nigeria's Cyber Threat Surge Doubles YoY
description:
Originally published on satyamrastogi.com

Nigeria experienced more than double the cyber threats year-over-year, reclaiming Africa's top position. Angola and Kenya also rank among the world's five most attacked countries.

Executive Summary

Africa has retaken its position as the most attacked region globally, with Nigeria leading the charge in a dramatic surge of cyber threats. The country faced more than double the number of attacks compared to the previous year, signaling a sharp escalation in threat actor focus on African infrastructure, financial systems, and critical services. Angola and Kenya-both critical African economic hubs-now rank within the global top-five most attacked countries, reshaping the threat landscape and demanding urgent defensive posture adjustments from regional organizations.

This shift reflects a confluence of factors: limited legacy security infrastructure, rising digital adoption without commensurate security investment, geopolitical tensions driving state-sponsored activity, and financially motivated threat actors exploiting accessibility. For security leaders managing assets across Africa or with African-exposed systems, this represents a critical reassessment moment.

Attack Vector Analysis

The surge in African attacks aligns with known MITRE ATT&CK patterns documented across the continent:

Initial Access (T1566 - Phishing): Nigerian organizations face endemic spear-phishing campaigns targeting financial institutions and government agencies. Social engineering exploits cultural and language nuances to bypass email controls.

Credential Access (T1110 - Brute Force): RDP and SSH brute-forcing remains prolific, targeting unpatched systems and default credentials prevalent in underfunded IT environments.

Lateral Movement (T1570 - Lateral Tool Transfer): Once inside perimeters, attackers move laterally using legitimate tools (psexec, WinRM) due to detection gaps in many African SOCs.

Data Exfiltration (T1041 - Exfiltration Over C2 Channel): Financial data, customer records, and intellectual property are extracted via encrypted C2 channels, with ransom demands following weeks later.

Impact (T1486 - Data Encrypted for Impact): Ransomware (LockBit, BlackCat, Play) dominates the final-stage attack chain, with cryptocurrency ransom demands in 70%+ of observed incidents.

Technical Deep Dive

Why Africa?

1. Infrastructure Vulnerability Gap
Much of Africa's critical infrastructure runs on legacy systems with extended EOL windows. Windows Server 2008 and 2012 instances remain common in banking sectors, with zero patching cycles. Threat actors scan for CVEs like CVE-2021-44228 (Log4Shell) with high success rates because patches lag deployment by 6-12 months.

2. Limited SOC Maturity
The region lacks mature Security Operations Centers. SIEM deployment is sparse; many organizations rely on basic firewall logging. Dwell time (time between breach and detection) averages 200+ days-compared to 7 days in North America-giving attackers months to establish persistence and move laterally.

3. Geopolitical and Financial Motivation
State-sponsored actors (Lazarus, APT28, Wizard Spider) conduct reconnaissance for espionage. Financially motivated groups exploit the arbitrage: a $50K ransom in USD equals 2+ years of median salary in Nigeria, making payment decisions lower-threshold for victims.

4. Connectivity and FinTech Growth
Rapid digital adoption (mobile money, online banking, e-commerce) expanded the attack surface without security-first development. APIs handling high-value transactions often lack input validation, rate limiting, or proper authentication.

Observed Attack Chain (Nigeria Case Study)

  1. Reconnaissance: Shodan/Censys scans for open MongoDB instances, Elasticsearch clusters, exposed S3 buckets (Nigerian banks using AWS without proper IAM).
  2. Initial Access: Phishing email impersonating CBN (Central Bank of Nigeria) or international payment providers lands in user inbox with malicious .exe or .xlsm.
  3. Execution: User opens file; macro executes or binary drops PowerShell downloader.
  4. Persistence: Scheduled tasks or registry modifications create backdoor access; C2 beacon established to attacker-controlled VPS (often hosted in EU/US to evade African ISP blocking).
  5. Privilege Escalation: Token impersonation or Zerologon-style attacks against unpatched DCs.
  6. Lateral Movement: PsExec/WMI spreads malware across internal segment; file shares accessed via compromised service accounts.
  7. Exfiltration: Rclone or WinSCP transfers databases to Mega/Dropbox; 10GB+ transfers often undetected due to no egress monitoring.
  8. Impact: Ransomware encrypts critical systems; ransom note references leaked data as pressure.

Detection Strategy

High-Signal Indicators for African Environments:

  • Anomalous RDP logins from residential VPNs outside business hours (high Asia/Eastern Europe geolocations).
  • PowerShell encoded commands executing System.Net.ServicePointManager; signature for downloader behavior.
  • Large outbound data transfers to non-business cloud storage (Mega, Dropbox, file.io).
  • Scheduled tasks created by svchost, System, or LocalService (legitimate processes abused for persistence).
  • Multiple failed RDP attempts followed by successful logon with new account creation (brute-force success).
  • Lateral movement via PsExec detected in event logs (4688 with CommandLine containing psexec; requires audit policy enablement).

YARA/Detection Rules:
Monitor for:

  • Encoded PowerShell in process creation events (parent: explorer.exe, winword.exe).
  • Outbound SMB/RDP to internal IPs from suspicious user contexts.
  • Anomalous process tree: Office -> PowerShell -> cmd.exe -> explorer.exe.

Network Baselines:
Establish per-organization egress profiles (financial data size, timing, destinations). Flag 10x deviation as priority alert.

Mitigation

Immediate (0-30 days)

  1. Patch Management Acceleration: Prioritize CVSS >7 patches for internet-facing systems. Use CISA KEV catalog as scoring override.
  2. Credential Hygiene: Force password resets for privileged accounts; enable MFA on RDP/SSH (FIDO2 preferred over TOTP).
  3. EDR Deployment: Even basic endpoint detection (CrowdStrike, SentinelOne) reduces dwell time by 95% in African deployment studies.
  4. Egress Filtering: Block residential VPN/proxy services at firewall; monitor DNS queries for suspicious TLDs.

Medium-term (30-90 days)

  1. Network Segmentation: Isolate financial, HR, and R&D systems via VLANs with strict ACLs. Disable lateral SMB/RDP where possible.
  2. SIEM Implementation: Collect Windows event logs, firewall/proxy logs; set up correlation rules for multi-step attack chains.
  3. Threat Hunting: Manual hunts for persistent backdoors using Velociraptor or osquery across 10% of endpoints monthly.
  4. Backup Hardening: Offline backups for critical data; 3-2-1 rule (3 copies, 2 media, 1 offsite, 1 air-gapped).

Long-term (90+ days)

  1. Identity & Access Management: Implement Zero Trust with identity-centric controls; audit service accounts for over-privilege.
  2. Threat Intelligence Integration: Subscribe to African-focused threat feeds (CyberPeace/Mandiant Africa reports); participate in information sharing via FS-ISAC or regional ISACs.
  3. Red Team Exercises: Conduct red team assessments simulating realistic African attack chains; baseline defensive gaps.
  4. Penetration Testing: Annual VAPT engagements focusing on external-to-internal and lateral movement scenarios.

Key Takeaways

  • Africa's attack volume doubled: Nigeria alone now rivals top-10 global targets. This is not anomalous-it's the new baseline.
  • Legacy infrastructure is liability: Organizations running Windows Server 2008+ face 50x higher breach probability. Replacement planning is non-negotiable.
  • Dwell time is the killer metric: 200+ day detection windows mean full data exfiltration before incident response begins. EDR is force-multiplier, not luxury.
  • Geopolitical + Financial = Perfect Storm: State actors conduct espionage while financially motivated groups exploit economic desperation. Defenders must assume multi-front adversary profiles.
  • Regional threat intelligence matters: Generic global threat feeds miss African-specific attack chains. Localized intelligence, incident response playbooks, and skill-building are ROI investments.

Related Articles

  • Red Team vs Blue Team vs Purple Team: Complete Cybersecurity Guide
  • VAPT vs Penetration Testing: What's the Difference? (India 2026)
  • Database RCE via Low-Privilege SQL: PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle at Risk
  • Strike Graph AI Automates Compliance Evidence Collection

Recommended CISA Resource: CISA Alert AA21-049A - APT Targeting Financial Institutions (baseline TTPs applicable to Nigeria threat landscape). OWASP: Consult OWASP Top 10 2021 for application security flaws enabling initial compromise in fintech environments.

title: Multistage Contextual Optimization for Vehicle Repositioning
description:
arXiv:2611.22330v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Ride-hailing platforms reposition idle vehicles to improve spatial supply-demand balances. This problem is prediction-driven and multistage: at each stage, the platform forecasts future demand, executes current decisions, and uses the resulting state to initialize the next stage. We formulate a multistage linear program (LP) with a macroscopic fundamental diagram (MFD) linking accumulation to trip completion. We then develop a multistage contextual optimization approach that uses decision performance to train the prediction model. The learning problem combines multiple coupled stages, context that depends on earlier decisions, and predictions that affect the objective, the constraint matrix, and the right-hand side of the LP. We derive the exact gradient, which has three parts: parameters change forecasts and hence decisions; earlier decisions change the current decision through the inherited state; and this state also changes forecasts as context. An equivalent adjoint uses reverse vector-Jacobian products, avoiding full solution and state-parameter Jacobians. Finally, forward propagation solves many stage LPs one after another, which makes training slow. We propose a parallel block evaluation algorithm that solves blocks of consecutive stages in parallel and repeatedly feeds each block output to the next block. We prove that the algorithm recovers the serial trajectory within a finite number of passes and that its gradient error remains bounded when it stops early. On New York City ride-hailing data, multistage contextual optimization yields 7.7% to 9.1% more business benefit than the same predictor trained by mean squared error, outperforms all compared baselines from five paradigms, and even outperforms realized demand fed to the same policy. With eight workers, parallel block evaluation shortens training by a factor of 1.86 without loss of decision performance.

title: When the tail is earned by its companions: measuring label dependence in long-tailed multi-label classification
description:
arXiv:2611.22859v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: A rare label seldom occurs alone, and a classifier can recover it from the frequent labels it co-occurs with, its companions, without having learned the label itself. Existing diagnostics of this need a trained model: none says before training whether a corpus admits the failure, or what the standard aggregate hides. Macro-F1, like any measure built from per-label confusion counts, is unchanged by how a label's recall divides between occurrences with and without a companion. We introduce a within-label estimand of that division, a reading rule under which a fall in dependence counts only if companion-free recall rises, and a statistic of training labels that bounds, before training, how far reported recall can exceed companion-free recall. Across 23 corpora, 7 training objectives and five families of label-correlation mechanisms, companion-free recall falls short on all six corpora where the estimand is defined. Up to 18.4% of the tail true positives macro-F1 credits would vanish at the companion-free rate, within the training-label bound on every corpus. No long-tail objective reduces the dependence, but architecture moves it. Models whose tail score is computed from other labels' predictions are strongly dependent.

title: SC-500 practice, week 5: 5 questions (secrets you no longer need)
description:
This week: a pipeline that deploys to Azure without a stored secret, a firewall that can finally see inside HTTPS, policies that block versus fix, staff pasting customer data into public AI chat sites, and which Defender for Servers plan gives you what.

How to use these: read the question, pick your answer before you open Answer, and write it down (or in the comments). Then check the "why not the others" part even if you got it right: that is where the exam traps live. Every scenario, name and number is made up by me; only the question formats follow the real exam.

Table of contents

  • Q021: The pipeline deploys to Azure, and there is no secret to steal
  • Q022: The firewall sees HTTPS. It just cannot read it
  • Q023: Block it, flag it, or fix it: picking the policy effect
  • Q024: Staff paste customer data into a public AI chat site
  • Q025: Plan 1 or Plan 2: what each Defender for Servers plan gives you
  • Cheat sheet
  • Coming next

Q021: The pipeline deploys to Azure, and there is no secret to steal

Identity and access · Build list · standalone page

The GitHub repository contoso/web-orders deploys to the resource group rg-lab-orders from a GitHub Actions workflow. Today it signs in with a client secret of the app registration app-gh-orders, stored as a GitHub secret. The secret expires every 6 months, someone forgets, and deployments break on a Friday. Worse: anyone who reads that secret can deploy from anywhere.

The security team wants this:

  • The workflow signs in to Azure without any stored secret or certificate.
  • Only the main branch of contoso/web-orders can get a token.
  • The identity can deploy to rg-lab-orders and nothing else.

Which four actions should you perform in sequence?

Actions:

  • A. On app-gh-orders, add a federated credential for GitHub Actions: organization contoso, repository web-orders, entity type Branch, value main.
  • B. Assign app-gh-orders the Contributor role on rg-lab-orders.
  • C. Assign app-gh-orders the Contributor role on the subscription.
  • D. In the workflow, add permissions: id-token: write and use azure/login with the client ID, tenant ID and subscription ID only.
  • E. Delete the old client secret from app-gh-orders and from the GitHub secrets.
  • F. Create a new client secret with a 24-month expiry, so it breaks less often.

Answer

A → B → D → E.

  • A: a federated credential tells Microsoft Entra ID to trust tokens that GitHub issues, but only when the token's subject matches exactly: this repository, this branch. A run from a fork or from a feature branch gets nothing.
  • B: the app still needs an Azure role to do anything. Scope it to the resource group the workflow deploys to.
  • D: the workflow must be allowed to request a GitHub OIDC token (id-token: write). azure/login swaps it for an Entra token. No secret in the workflow.
  • E last: once a run succeeds with federation, delete the secret. Until you do, the old door is still open.

Why not the others:

  • C works, but it is not least privilege. One stolen workflow could touch the whole subscription.
  • F makes the problem last longer. A longer-lived secret is a longer-lived target.

Gotcha: the subject must match exactly. A workflow that runs in a GitHub environment (for example production) sends a different subject (environment, not branch), and the sign-in fails with a "no matching federated identity record" error. Add a credential for the environment if you use one. You can also put the federated credential on a user-assigned managed identity instead of an app registration.

Sources: Workload identity federation · Configure an app to trust an external identity provider · Use GitHub Actions to connect to Azure

Q022: The firewall sees HTTPS. It just cannot read it

Networking · Hot area · standalone page

The hub network vnet-lab-hub has an Azure Firewall, afw-lab-01, on the Standard tier. Last month a server in snet-lab-app downloaded a tool from a site on a known malware path. The URL was in the HTTPS request, so the firewall never saw it. The security team wants this:

  1. The firewall can decrypt outbound HTTPS, look at the full URL and the content, and encrypt it again.
  2. It detects and blocks known attack patterns in that traffic using signatures.
  3. Rules can allow partner.example.com/api/* but block the rest of partner.example.com.

Pick the right value for each line:

What Your choice
Firewall tier you need ▢ Basic ▢ Standard ▢ Premium
Feature for goal 2 ▢ Threat intelligence ▢ IDPS ▢ Web categories
Feature for goal 3 ▢ FQDN filtering ▢ URL filtering ▢ DNAT rules
Certificate the firewall uses for TLS inspection ▢ A public certificate for contoso.com ▢ An intermediate CA certificate, stored in Key Vault ▢ No certificate is needed
What the servers in snet-lab-app need ▢ Nothing ▢ To trust the root CA that issued the firewall's certificate

Answer

Premium / IDPS / URL filtering / An intermediate CA certificate, stored in Key Vault / To trust the root CA

  • Premium is the tier with TLS inspection, IDPS and URL filtering. Standard filters by FQDN and uses threat intelligence, but does not decrypt.
  • IDPS (intrusion detection and prevention) matches traffic against signatures and can alert or alert-and-deny. Threat intelligence blocks known bad IPs and domains, not attack patterns inside the traffic.
  • URL filtering looks at the full path, like /api/*. FQDN filtering only sees the host name, so it cannot tell /api from the rest. For HTTPS, URL filtering needs TLS inspection on.
  • TLS inspection uses an intermediate CA certificate that the firewall uses to make certificates on the fly. It lives in Azure Key Vault, and the firewall reads it through a managed identity.
  • The clients must trust the root CA, or every HTTPS call fails with a certificate error. Push the root to servers with Group Policy, Intune or your image.

Gotcha: some traffic should not be decrypted (banking, health, and anything that pins certificates). Use the TLS inspection bypass list for those, and check your privacy rules before you decrypt staff traffic.

Sources: Azure Firewall Premium features · Azure Firewall Premium certificates

Q023: Block it, flag it, or fix it: picking the policy effect

Identity, access and governance · Hot area · standalone page

The management group mg-lab-prod has 40 subscriptions. The security team has four wishes, and you want one Azure Policy assignment for each:

  1. Nobody can create a storage account that allows public blob access. The create must fail.
  2. Show which existing VMs have no backup, but do not change or stop anything.
  3. Every new resource group gets the tag costCenter, copied from the subscription, without blocking the create.
  4. Every new SQL server gets diagnostic settings sending logs to law-lab-sec, created automatically.

Pick the effect for each wish:

Wish Your choice
1. Public blob access ▢ Audit ▢ Deny ▢ Modify
2. VMs without backup ▢ Audit (or AuditIfNotExists) ▢ Deny ▢ DeployIfNotExists
3. costCenter tag ▢ Append ▢ Modify ▢ Deny
4. Diagnostic settings ▢ AuditIfNotExists ▢ Modify ▢ DeployIfNotExists
What the assignment for wish 4 also needs ▢ Nothing ▢ A managed identity with the right roles

Answer

Deny / Audit (or AuditIfNotExists) / Modify / DeployIfNotExists / A managed identity with the right roles

  • Deny stops the create or update request. That is wish 1.
  • Audit and AuditIfNotExists only mark the resource as non-compliant. Nothing is blocked or changed. That is wish 2.
  • Modify adds, changes or removes tags (and a few properties) on create or update. It is the effect built for managing tags, and it can copy a value from the subscription's tags (there is a built-in policy for exactly that). Append can add fields, but it cannot change an existing value.
  • DeployIfNotExists checks for a related resource (here, the diagnostic setting) and deploys a template when it is missing.
  • Modify and DeployIfNotExists change things for you, so the assignment needs a managed identity with roles that allow those changes.

Gotcha: new assignments do not fix existing resources by themselves. For resources that already exist, run a remediation task. And Deny on day one in production can break deployments you did not know about: start with Audit, read the compliance report, then switch.

Sources: Azure Policy definition effect basics · Remediate non-compliant resources

Q024: Staff paste customer data into a public AI chat site

Secure compute (AI) · Single choice · standalone page

At contoso.com, the sales team likes a public AI chat site for writing emails. Last week someone pasted a full customer list, with credit card numbers, to "make it a nice table". Nobody knew until the person bragged about how nice the table looked.

The security team wants this:

  • See when people share sensitive information with third-party AI sites in the browser.
  • Block credit card numbers from being pasted or uploaded there, but allow normal use.

Devices are Windows 11, onboarded to Microsoft Purview, and use Microsoft Edge. What should you do?

  • A. Block the AI site's domain in the company web proxy.
  • B. In Microsoft Purview DSPM for AI, use the one-click policies to detect sensitive info added to AI sites, and create an Endpoint DLP policy that blocks credit card numbers being shared with generative AI sites.
  • C. Turn on Defender for Cloud threat protection for AI services.
  • D. Apply a sensitivity label to the CRM app.

Answer

B. DSPM for AI is the Purview hub for AI risk. Its one-click policies give you visibility into sensitive data shared with third-party AI sites (the "credit card pasted into a chatbot" case is Microsoft's own example), and Endpoint DLP can warn or block users when they share sensitive information with those sites, on onboarded devices.

Why not the others:

  • A blocks the site completely, which breaks goal 2 ("allow normal use"). People also find another site by lunch.
  • C protects your own AI apps running in Azure (prompts to your model deployments). The public chat site is not your app.
  • D labels protect files and email. A list copied from a screen and pasted into a browser is just text in a clipboard.

Gotcha: in Edge it works through the built-in Purview integration (with an Edge configuration policy); Chrome and Firefox need the Purview browser extension. Start the DLP policy in simulation (test) mode, read who would be blocked, then turn it on. The list of supported AI sites changes, so check it.

Sources: Considerations for DSPM for AI · Use Purview to manage data security for other AI apps · Learn about Endpoint DLP

Q025: Plan 1 or Plan 2: what each Defender for Servers plan gives you

Defender for Cloud and Sentinel · Hot area · standalone page

The subscription sub-lab-prod has 80 Windows and Linux VMs. The budget owner asks: "Can we save money with Defender for Servers Plan 1?" The security team needs these features:

  1. EDR with Microsoft Defender for Endpoint on the servers.
  2. File integrity monitoring on C:\Windows\System32 and /etc.
  3. Just-in-time VM access for RDP and SSH.
  4. Agentless scanning of the VM disks for vulnerabilities and secrets.

For each feature, pick the lowest plan that includes it:

Feature Your choice
1. EDR with Defender for Endpoint ▢ Plan 1 ▢ Plan 2 only
2. File integrity monitoring ▢ Plan 1 ▢ Plan 2 only
3. Just-in-time VM access ▢ Plan 1 ▢ Plan 2 only
4. Agentless disk scanning ▢ Plan 1 ▢ Plan 2 only
So, for all four features you need ▢ Plan 1 ▢ Plan 2

Answer

Plan 1 / Plan 2 only / Plan 2 only / Plan 2 only / Plan 2

  • Defender for Endpoint integration (EDR) is in Plan 1 already. Plan 1 is the "endpoint protection for servers" plan, with Defender Vulnerability Management basics.
  • File integrity monitoring, just-in-time VM access and agentless scanning (vulnerabilities, secrets, malware) are Plan 2 features. Plan 2 also brings things like a daily free data allowance for some security data in Log Analytics.
  • So the answer to the budget owner is: Plan 1 is enough if you only want EDR. This team wants more, so it needs Plan 2.

Gotcha: you can mix. Plan choice is per subscription, and you can turn the plan off for specific resources. A dev subscription can run Plan 1 while production runs Plan 2. Check current prices on the Defender for Cloud pricing page before you promise a number.

Sources: Defender for Servers plans · Plan your Defender for Servers deployment

Cheat sheet

The same five ideas in plain words, for the manager who asks "so what?". Share it with them.
