title: IP44 Socket vs IP67: Which Rating Fits Your Site?
description:
Quick Answer

An IP44 socket is a socket rated to keep out solid objects larger than 1.0 mm and water splashed against it from any direction. An IP67 socket adds 30 minutes of temporary immersion at 1 m depth. Each rating is tested in one defined condition, so IP44 will not survive a hose jet and IP67 will not survive a pressure washer.

This guide compares what each digit actually proves, how the mated pair changes the answer, and where each rating belongs on a working site.

What Do the Two Digits in IP44 and IP67 Measure?

An IP code is a two-digit ingress protection rating published in IEC 60529, the international standard for enclosure sealing. The first digit covers solid objects, from a fingertip to fine dust. The second digit covers water, from vertical drips to high-pressure jets. Each digit is tested separately, on a defined sample, in a defined state.

On an industrial socket the code describes the product, not the installation. It says nothing about the cable, the gland, the panel cutout or the way the socket was mounted. Those parts decide whether the rating is still true after the first winter outdoors.

What the First Digit Covers for a Socket

Level 4 is the usual baseline for indoor industrial sockets. A 1.0 mm diameter probe pushed with 1 N of force must not reach live parts, and the enclosure must stop solid objects of 1.0 mm and above. Level 5 adds dust protection with limited ingress, and level 6 is dust tight. Most splash-proof sockets stop at 4, while watertight versions usually reach 6.

What the Second Digit Covers for Water

The water digits step up through different test rigs. Splash, jet and immersion are not variations of one test; they load the seal from different directions, at different pressures and for different times. A socket that passes a splash test can still take water the moment someone rests a hose against the lid.

Water digit Test condition Where it usually belongs
IPX4 Splashing water from any direction, 10 min at roughly 10 L/min Covered workshop, plant room, under a canopy
IPX5 6.3 mm nozzle, 12.5 L/min at 30 kPa, 3 min from about 3 m Open loading bay, edge of a wash area
IPX6 12.5 mm nozzle, 100 L/min at 100 kPa, 3 min from about 3 m Deck wash, jet cleaning a few metres away
IPX7 Temporary immersion, 30 min with the lowest point 1 m under water Open yard socket, pit, slab that can flood
IPX9K 80 °C water at 80 to 100 bar, 14 to 16 L/min, four angles Food and beverage washdown zones

Where Does IP44 Stop Working?

An IP44 socket handles rain, a mop splash and condensation running down a wall. It stops working when water arrives with speed. A garden hose at close range already delivers something closer to the IPX5 jet than to the IPX4 splash, and a washdown lance is two digits further away again.

Driving rain on an exposed wall is the other weak case. The test sprays from any direction for 10 minutes, but it does not reproduce wind pushing water into a lid lip for a full season. Sites that leave sockets facing the weather usually move those positions to IP67 even when the covered positions stay at IP44.

What Does an IP67 Socket Actually Survive?

IP67 makes two claims at once: dust tight at digit 6, and 30 minutes of immersion at digit 7. The immersion test puts the lowest point of the sample 1 m below the surface for 30 minutes, with no spraying and no pressure applied. Water may enter, provided it does not reach a harmful quantity or affect operation.

What the Immersion Test Does Not Cover

It does not cover 3 m, 8 hours, or water arriving at 80 bar. Continuous immersion is IP68, where depth and duration are agreed between buyer and maker rather than fixed by the standard. High-pressure cleaning is IP69K. An IP67 socket standing in a flooded pit for a week has left its test envelope, even though the label still reads IP67.

Does the Rating Apply to the Socket, the Plug or the Pair?

This is the most common source of field failures. A manufacturer tests and publishes a rating for one defined condition, and for a panel socket that condition is often the closed lid. For a plug and socket together it is the mated pair, and usually the pair from the same series.

IEC 60309-1 splits industrial plugs and sockets into splash-proof types, rated IP44, and watertight types, rated IP67. A watertight socket with a splash-proof plug in it is a compromise, not a rated assembly. Match both halves, and read the datasheet for the exact state that was tested.

The unmated state is the weak point. An IP67 socket with the lid hanging open is a funnel, and a spring that has lost tension defeats the seal without leaving a mark. This is why tethered lids and spare gaskets belong on the maintenance list, not in a drawer.

Which Rating Fits Which Location?

Most sites do not need one rating everywhere. The differences are modest per unit and significant per installation, so the practical method is to grade the location and match the socket to it. The table below is a starting point, not a substitute for the project specification.

Location Minimum rating Reason
Indoor workshop, dry floor IP44 Splash only; quick service access matters
Covered yard, canopy edge IP44 to IP65 Wind-driven rain reaches the lid
Open yard, no shelter IP67 Standing water and pooled rain
Washdown bay, food line IP67, with IP69K where jets are aimed Pressure and temperature, not volume
Construction site distribution IP44 minimum, IP67 at ground level IEC 60364-7-704 treats these as a special case

Construction and demolition sites deserve a separate note. IEC 60364-7-704 handles socket outlets on such sites as a special case and commonly sets IP44 as the floor for the assembly. Units that sit on the ground or in a puddle are still better served by a watertight version, because the rating was never meant to survive standing water.

Why Do Sealed Sockets Still Fill With Water?

Water inside a sealed enclosure rarely comes past the gasket. It usually travels down the cable, through a gland that does not match the jacket, or condenses out of the air pocket when the temperature drops overnight.

What Cable Entry Does to the Rating

A socket is rated with its own entry, and once a gland is fitted the assembly inherits the gland's seal and the installer's torque. A jacket diameter outside the clamping range leaves a path along the sheath, and water follows it by capillary action into the terminal chamber. Measure the jacket rather than the conductor, and check the gland range before ordering.

Why Condensation Forms Inside a Sealed Socket

A sealed enclosure that warms by day and cools at night pulls moisture out of the cable and the trapped air. No IP rating addresses that. A drain point, a breather membrane or a desiccant does, and the same failure path is covered in our review of the common causes of industrial connector failure in harsh environments.

What Do You Lose by Specifying IP67 Everywhere?

Watertight construction is not free. Gaskets, tighter tolerances, heavier lids and higher insertion force all add cost and time, and every service visit ends with a lid that has to be re-seated correctly. A torn gasket turns an IP67 socket into an unrated one with no visible warning.

There are practical losses too:

  • Sealed sockets hold moisture in as effectively as they keep it out, so a wet assembly stays wet.
  • Usable cable range narrows as the entry gets tighter.
  • Inspection takes longer, because the state of the seal is hidden under the lid.
  • Every service visit ends with a lid that must be re-seated, and a torn gasket is invisible.

Where a location is genuinely dry, an IP44 socket is easier to live with, and the budget is better spent on the positions that face water. The same logic applies to the plug on the cable: a watertight plug on a splash-proof cordset does not raise the rating of either part.

How Should the IP Requirement Be Written on a Drawing?

Two digits on a drawing are ambiguous. They say nothing about the state tested, the standard applied, or the cable entry the socket must accept. A supplier can meet that line item exactly and still deliver something that fails in service, so the requirement needs the surrounding conditions attached.

The IP Rating Requirement Checklist

  • Rating and standard: state IP44 or IP67 to IEC 60529, not the digits alone.
  • Tested state: closed lid, mated pair, or unmated with the cap fitted.
  • Cable entry: gland type and thread, plus the jacket diameter range the socket must accept.
  • Environment beyond water: UV exposure, salt spray, wash chemicals and ambient temperature.
  • Evidence: the test report, or at minimum the state and duration that were tested.
  • Service items: tethered lid, spare gaskets and expected mating cycles per shift.

Housing material belongs on the same list. A polyamide that absorbs water or ages under UV will loosen its grip on the gasket long before the contacts wear, which is why material choice decides long-term reliability as much as the rating does.

Which Evidence Should a Supplier Provide?

Ask for the test state before the test number. A report that shows IP67 on a closed lid tells you the gasket works; it does not tell you the socket stays sealed with a plug inserted in the rain. Ask which sample was tested, whether it was mated, and how long the sample had been in service before the test.

For the wider picture, our guide to how IP67, IP68 and IP69K affect application selection covers the upper end of the scale, and the comparison of IP65 to IP69K housings shows what changes inside a product when the second digit rises.

WEIPU has manufactured circular and industrial connectors since 1996, and the TYP range carries the same IEC 60309 pin configurations in splash-proof and watertight builds. Treat the catalogue as an evaluation starting point: verify the part number, the tested state behind the rating, and the gland range against the current datasheet before the socket goes on a drawing.

Conclusion

IP44 and IP67 answer different questions. IP44 says the socket tolerates splashing from any direction; IP67 says it tolerates 30 minutes under 1 m of still water. Neither says anything about jets, cable entries, condensation or the state of the lid. Grade the site, write the tested condition on the drawing, match plug to socket, and measure the cable before choosing the gland. Then check the report rather than the two digits.

Related Products for Outdoor and Washdown Sockets

The TYP range splits the same IEC 60309 pin configurations into splash-proof IP44 and watertight IP67 builds, so a site can be graded without changing the plug convention between areas. The four parts below cover the two most common split points: plugs on the cable side, and panel sockets where the water actually arrives.

  • The 16 A 3-pin IP44 cable plug by TYP231 is the splash-proof half for covered bays and indoor distribution.
  • The 16 A 3-pin IP67 cable plug by TYPR171 adds a sealed shell and cap for open yards and wet slabs.
  • The 32 A 3-pin IP44 angled panel socket by TYP3801 suits panel edges that see splashes but never jets.
  • The 63 A 5-pin IP67 angled panel socket by TYP3924 covers three-phase positions exposed to standing water.

Each part exists in several current ratings and pin counts, so confirm the contact layout and the tested state of the rating against the datasheet before ordering. The full range of IP44 and IP67 plugs and sockets, with the tested state written on each datasheet, is listed on the TYP IEC 60309 connector page.

Discuss Your IP44 Socket Requirements

Send the working conditions and we will reply with specific part numbers plus the evidence behind each rating, rather than a generic catalogue page. The more of the following you can supply, the shorter the review loop:

  • Installation: indoor, covered or exposed; panel position and mounting height.
  • Cable: jacket outer diameter, conductor cross-section, and whether a gland is already specified.
  • Electrical: current, voltage, pin count, and any three-phase or neutral requirement.
  • Environment: target IP rating, cleaning method and pressure, UV, salt and ambient temperature.

For drawings, samples or a rating review, contact the WEIPU engineering team and describe the socket position you are working on.

title: Confidence-Based Materials Data Quality Assessment via Domain Knowledge and Graph-Structured Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.23342v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The rapid development of materials machine learning relies on large-scale, heterogeneous datasets, yet model reliability is often compromised by imperfect data from diverse experiments, simulations, and database integration. Real-world materials databases may contain measurement errors, failed calculations, missing or duplicate records, and hidden violations of physicochemical constraints. Such problems are difficult to identify because corrupted samples may remain statistically plausible rather than appearing as explicit outliers. In this paper, we propose a confidence-based materials data quality assessment framework that integrates domain knowledge with graph-structured learning. Data quality is formulated as a continuous confidence estimation problem rather than a binary anomaly identification task, enabling sample-level assessment and historical-reference-based batch comparison. A nine-dimensional feature-quality prior and duplicate-aware sample initialization are calibrated using materials domain rules and statistical evidence. Confidence is further refined through sample-feature bipartite graph propagation and weakly supervised graph attention, while a Memory-GAT module provides historical reference scoring. Experiments on 23 ODDS benchmark datasets show that the generic module achieves an average AUC-ROC of 0.866. In five repeated mixed-contamination experiments on mp\_20, rule calibration improves HistGradientBoostingRegressor test $R^2$ from $0.538\pm0.008$ to $0.616\pm0.014$. Graph refinement increases average precision from $0.943\pm0.004$ to 0.953\pm0.004$, while the rule-calibrated configuration has the highest mean test $R^2$ among the evaluated screening configurations. Five repeated MACE subset experiments further show an increase in $R^2$ from $0.590\pm0.053$ to $0.880\pm0.027$ after rule-based screening.

title: Celery visibility_timeout: 214 LLM Jobs Ran Twice on Redis
description:
The bug showed up as a spreadsheet problem. My nightly pipeline summarizes long PDFs with Claude and writes one row per document. One morning, document 4471 had two summaries. Slightly different wording, start times 61 minutes apart, same Celery task ID.

Same task ID is the part that made my stomach drop. That isn't a retry. That's the broker handing the exact same message to a second worker while the first one was still chewing on it. The cause was Celery visibility_timeout on the Redis broker, and over 14 nights it quietly ran 214 of my 1,380 jobs at least twice.

TL;DR

  • On the Redis (and SQS) broker, Celery's visibility_timeout defaults to 3600 seconds. Any message a worker has taken but not acknowledged within that hour gets pushed back onto the queue and delivered again.
  • With acks_late=True, a task isn't acknowledged until it finishes. Any task that runs longer than an hour gets redelivered while it's still running.
  • Prefetch makes it worse: messages sitting in a worker's prefetch buffer are also unacknowledged. Short tasks queued behind long ones can hit the hour without ever starting.
  • Fix: raise visibility_timeout above your longest task plus queue wait, set worker_prefetch_multiplier = 1, and add an idempotency guard per job.
  • Trade-off: a higher timeout means a task lost in a real worker crash waits that long before it's retried.

What does Celery visibility_timeout actually do?

Celery visibility_timeout is how long the Redis transport waits for an acknowledgement before assuming the worker died and putting the message back on the queue. Redis has no native concept of "this consumer has this message," so Kombu fakes it.

When a worker reserves a message, Kombu copies it into an unacked hash with a timestamp. When the task is acknowledged, the entry is removed. Kombu periodically scans that hash, and anything older than visibility_timeout gets restored to the queue as if it had never been delivered.

That's a reasonable design for crash recovery. It just has no idea the difference between "the worker died" and "the worker is on minute 73 of a big PDF."

My setup

Nothing exotic:

  • 2 worker boxes, --concurrency=4 each, prefork pool
  • Redis as broker, Postgres for results and job state
  • Each job: split a PDF into chunks, summarize each chunk with Claude, then merge into a final summary
  • Runtime: most jobs 4 to 15 minutes, a long tail of 60 to 110 minutes for big documents
  • acks_late=True on the task, because I wanted a crashed job to come back

That last line is the one I'd written with pride. "If a worker dies mid-job, the job gets retried. Very robust." It was robust in exactly the way that bills you twice.

How I found 214 duplicate runs

Every job writes a job_runs row when it starts, keyed by Celery's task_id. A real retry gets a new row with the same task ID too, so I couldn't just count rows. I needed runs that overlapped in time:

SELECT a.task_id, count(*) AS runs
FROM job_runs a
JOIN job_runs b
  ON a.task_id = b.task_id
 AND a.id <> b.id
 AND a.started_at < coalesce(b.finished_at, now())
 AND b.started_at < coalesce(a.finished_at, now())
WHERE a.started_at > now() - interval '14 days'
GROUP BY a.task_id;

Results for the 14 nights:

Metric Count
Jobs dispatched 1,380
Jobs that ran at least twice 214
Of those, ran three times 9
Duplicates from long runtime (acks_late) 171
Duplicates from waiting in prefetch 43

The second run almost always started 60 to 62 minutes after the first. That gap is the fingerprint. If you see duplicates clustered at exactly your timeout plus a little scan lag, stop looking for a bug in your code.

Why did tasks longer than one hour run twice?

Tasks longer than one hour ran twice because acks_late=True delays the acknowledgement until the task returns, so the message stays in Redis's unacked hash for the whole runtime. At the 3600-second mark, Kombu restores it and another worker picks it up.

Here's the part that scared me more than the duplicates. When the first run finally finishes and acks, it doesn't cancel the restored copy. That copy is a fresh delivery with its own timer. If the second run also takes more than an hour, it gets restored again. In principle a 70-minute job loops forever.

Mine didn't, and not because of anything clever. My pipeline caches chunk summaries in Postgres. The second run found the chunks the first run had already finished and skipped them, so it was usually faster. The 9 triple runs were the biggest documents, where even the cached rerun crossed the hour.

So the only thing standing between me and an infinite loop of paid API calls was a cache I'd added for a completely unrelated reason.

Why did short tasks get duplicated too?

Short tasks got duplicated because prefetched messages count as unacknowledged, even when they haven't started. With the default worker_prefetch_multiplier = 4 and concurrency 4, each worker box reserves up to 16 messages at once.

Picture a box where all 4 processes grab big documents that take 90 minutes. The 12 messages sitting behind them in the prefetch buffer are reserved, not started, and their timer is running. At 60 minutes they get restored, the other box runs them, and 30 minutes later the original box runs them too.

These 43 were the expensive ones. A long job's duplicate partly hit the chunk cache. A prefetched short job's duplicate ran from scratch in parallel on another machine, full price, no cache hits.

What did the duplicates cost?

Across the 14 nights, the duplicate runs consumed about 23 million input tokens on the Claude API. That was roughly 11% of the pipeline's total input tokens for the period. Not a catastrophe, but it was 11% of the bill buying literally nothing, plus two summaries per document that my downstream code had to dedupe.

The less visible cost: every duplicate occupied a worker slot, which pushed more jobs into the prefetch buffer, which created more prefetch duplicates. The bug fed itself on busy nights. My worst night had 31 duplicates; my quietest had 4.

How do you fix Celery visibility_timeout on Redis?

You fix it by setting visibility_timeout longer than your longest possible task plus its worst queue wait, cutting prefetch to 1 for long tasks, and making the task itself idempotent. Here's the config before and after:

# before
app.conf.task_acks_late = True
# visibility_timeout: default 3600
# worker_prefetch_multiplier: default 4

# after
app.conf.task_acks_late = True
app.conf.worker_prefetch_multiplier = 1
app.conf.broker_transport_options = {
    "visibility_timeout": 12 * 3600,  # 12h, longest job is ~2h
}

Put this in the shared config module that every process imports: workers, beat, and the web app that calls .delay(). The restore scan can run from any client connected to the transport, and you don't want one process quietly using the 1-hour default.

Then the seatbelt, because config drifts and someday someone will add a 14-hour job:

@app.task(bind=True, acks_late=True)
def summarize_doc(self, doc_id: int):
    if db.job_is_done(doc_id):
        return  # a duplicate delivery after success

    key = f"summarize:{doc_id}:lock"
    if not redis_client.set(key, self.request.id, nx=True, ex=6 * 3600):
        log.warning("duplicate delivery doc=%s task=%s", doc_id, self.request.id)
        return

    try:
        run_pipeline(doc_id)
        db.mark_done(doc_id)
    finally:
        redis_client.delete(key)

The done check catches redeliveries after a successful run. The SET NX lock catches concurrent ones. The lock TTL is your crash escape hatch: if a worker dies holding it, the job is blocked for at most 6 hours.

Did the fix work?

Yes. Over the next 14 nights, 1,302 jobs ran with 0 overlapping duplicates, and the idempotency guard logged 0 skips. Zero skips is what I want to see: the guard isn't doing the work, the config is. The guard is there for the day I'm wrong about the longest job.

I also tested the failure path on staging with visibility_timeout temporarily set to 5 minutes and a kill -9 on a worker mid-job. The job came back after about 5 minutes and ran once. In production that same scenario now means a 12-hour wait, which I'm fine with for a nightly batch. For a user-facing queue, I'd split long jobs into a separate queue with its own timeout instead.

What I'd tell myself before turning on acks_late

  1. acks_late and visibility_timeout are one setting. Never touch one without the other.
  2. Your timeout budget is runtime plus queue wait, not just runtime. Prefetch is queue wait you can't see in Flower.
  3. Same task ID, overlapping runs, ~60 minutes apart is a diagnosis, not a mystery.
  4. LLM tasks are the worst case. They're long, they're variable, and every duplicate is real money.
  5. Idempotency isn't optional on any queue that promises at-least-once delivery. Redis-backed Celery promises exactly that.

So why did my Celery jobs run twice on Redis?

My Celery jobs ran twice because the Redis broker's visibility_timeout defaults to one hour, and any message not acknowledged within that hour is put back on the queue for another worker. With acks_late=True, every job longer than 60 minutes crossed that line while still running, and with the default prefetch of 4, short jobs waiting behind long ones crossed it without ever starting. That added up to 214 duplicate runs out of 1,380 and about 11% wasted input tokens. Raising visibility_timeout to 12 hours, setting worker_prefetch_multiplier = 1, and adding a per-job idempotency lock brought duplicates to zero over the next 1,302 jobs.

title: Building a Zero-Signup Rule 46 GST Tax Invoice Generator in React with A4 Vector PDFs
description:
Every small business owner, freelancer, and consultant in India eventually confronts the same administrative roadblock: generating a compliant GST Tax Invoice without paying for bloated desktop accounting software.

Under Section 31 of the CGST Act, 2017 and Rule 46 of the CGST Rules, 2017, an Indian tax invoice must satisfy strict statutory requirements:

  1. Distinct serial numbers (consecutive and unique for the financial year).
  2. Supplier and recipient GSTIN, PAN, and full address.
  3. Official Place of Supply (POS) with state name and 2-digit statutory state code.
  4. Correct tax segregation: Intra-State (50% CGST + 50% SGST) vs. Inter-State (100% IGST).
  5. 6-digit or 8-digit HSN/SAC codes with aggregated tax rate summaries.
  6. Statutory total amount expressed in Indian numbering words (Lakhs and Crores, not Millions).

We recently open-sourced and shipped a 100% free, zero-signup web utility at QRBX GST Invoice Maker. Here is how we engineered the core statutory logic and vector print architecture.

1. Place of Supply (POS) & Tax Segregation Algorithm

Under Indian GST laws, whether you levy CGST+SGST or IGST depends solely on whether the Place of Supply (POS) matches the supplier's registered state:

export interface TaxSplit {
  isInterstate: boolean;
  cgstRate: number;
  cgstAmount: number;
  sgstRate: number;
  sgstAmount: number;
  igstRate: number;
  igstAmount: number;
}

export function calculateStatutoryTax(
  sellerStateCode: string,
  placeOfSupplyCode: string,
  taxableValue: number,
  gstRate: number
): TaxSplit {
  // Intra-State supply: Supplier and Place of Supply are in the same state
  const isInterstate = sellerStateCode !== placeOfSupplyCode;

  if (isInterstate) {
    return {
      isInterstate: true,
      cgstRate: 0,
      cgstAmount: 0,
      sgstRate: 0,
      sgstAmount: 0,
      igstRate: gstRate,
      igstAmount: (taxableValue * gstRate) / 100,
    };
  }

  // Intra-State supply: Tax is equally divided into Central (CGST) and State (SGST)
  const halfRate = gstRate / 2;
  const halfTax = (taxableValue * halfRate) / 100;

  return {
    isInterstate: false,
    cgstRate: halfRate,
    cgstAmount: halfTax,
    sgstRate: halfRate,
    sgstAmount: halfTax,
    igstRate: 0,
    igstAmount: 0,
  };
}

2. Converting Amounts into Indian Numbering Words (Lakhs & Crores)

Standard Western algorithms partition numbers in groups of thousands (1,000,000 = One Million). Indian statutory invoices require the Vedic numbering format (1,00,000 = One Lakh; 1,00,00,000 = One Crore).

export function numberToIndianWords(num: number): string {
  if (num === 0) return "Zero Rupees Only";

  const ones = ["", "One", "Two", "Three", "Four", "Five", "Six", "Seven", "Eight", "Nine",
    "Ten", "Eleven", "Twelve", "Thirteen", "Fourteen", "Fifteen", "Sixteen", "Seventeen", "Eighteen", "Nineteen"];
  const tens = ["", "", "Twenty", "Thirty", "Forty", "Fifty", "Sixty", "Seventy", "Eighty", "Ninety"];

  function convertTwoDigits(n: number): string {
    if (n < 20) return ones[n];
    return `${tens[Math.floor(n / 10)]} ${ones[n % 10]}`.trim();
  }

  function convertThreeDigits(n: number): string {
    const hundred = Math.floor(n / 100);
    const rest = n % 100;
    const parts: string[] = [];
    if (hundred > 0) parts.push(`${ones[hundred]} Hundred`);
    if (rest > 0) parts.push(convertTwoDigits(rest));
    return parts.join(" ");
  }

  const integerPart = Math.floor(Math.abs(num));
  const paise = Math.round((Math.abs(num) - integerPart) * 100);

  const crore = Math.floor(integerPart / 10000000);
  const lakh = Math.floor((integerPart % 10000000) / 100000);
  const thousand = Math.floor((integerPart % 100000) / 1000);
  const remainder = integerPart % 1000;

  const result: string[] = [];
  if (crore > 0) result.push(`${convertThreeDigits(crore)} Crore`);
  if (lakh > 0) result.push(`${convertThreeDigits(lakh)} Lakh`);
  if (thousand > 0) result.push(`${convertThreeDigits(thousand)} Thousand`);
  if (remainder > 0) result.push(convertThreeDigits(remainder));

  let text = `INR ${result.join(" ")} Rupees`;
  if (paise > 0) {
    text += ` and ${convertTwoDigits(paise)} Paise`;
  }
  return `${text} Only`;
}

3. Pixel-Perfect A4 Vector PDF Generation Without Bloat

Rather than bundling bulky client-side canvas renderers that produce blurry rasterized PDFs, we isolate the printable DOM into a dedicated print stylesheet:

@page {
  size: A4 portrait;
  margin: 8mm 10mm;
}

@media print {
  html, body {
    background: #ffffff !important;
    color: #000000 !important;
    width: 100% !important;
    -webkit-print-color-adjust: exact !important;
    print-color-adjust: exact !important;
  }
  .no-print {
    display: none !important;
  }
  .invoice-sheet {
    box-shadow: none !important;
    border: none !important;
    max-width: 100% !important;
    margin: 0 auto !important;
  }
}

When triggered, Chrome, Safari, and Edge instantly render sharp, selectable-text vector PDFs in under 100 milliseconds.

Live Tools & Resources

  • Live Invoice Maker: https://qrbx.tech/gst-invoice-maker
  • Indian HSN & SAC Code Directory: https://qrbx.tech/hsn-sac-codes
  • Open-Source GitHub Repository: github.com/amtechsci/qrbx-gst-invoice-maker

title: Paper trading a crypto bot: how to test with virtual money
description:
Crypto is risky and you can lose money. Paper trading cannot lose real money, but it does not predict real results.

Paper trading means running a strategy with simulated money before you risk real money. For a crypto trading bot it is the cheapest way to learn what the bot does, and what you do when it does it.

Paper trading, backtesting and play money

Method Data What it tells you What it cannot tell you
Backtest Past prices How a rule would have behaved historically Future results; easy to overfit
Paper trading Live prices, simulated orders How the rule behaves going forward Real fills, fees and your nerves
Play money (Waveleta) Live prices, EUR 1,000 virtual Same, on the rule the live account uses Real fills, fees and your nerves

A 7-day plan

  1. Write the rule down. Waveleta's is one daily trend rule: after each UTC daily close, a coin is "in" while its close is more than 4% above its 100-day average, "out" once it is more than 4% below.
  2. Start with a fixed virtual balance and do not top it up.
  3. Log every decision in one sentence.
  4. Include the boring days: staying out is a decision too.
  5. Check what the stop-loss does on a down day.
  6. Compare with a real account's public record, losses included: https://waveleta.com/track-record/live
  7. Price it: real orders pay exchange fees.

What paper trading hides

Slippage (a real order can fill worse), fees (they compound against frequent trades) and emotion (nothing is at stake).

Try it

Waveleta gives you EUR 1,000 of play money: no real orders, no exchange key, 14 days free with no card, then the founding price EUR 9/month until 31 December 2026. Full guide: https://waveleta.com/guides/paper-trading-crypto-bot?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=guide-paper

title: 228 bytes that can't be read, faked or told apart: Kengele's wire format and Nostr gift wraps in Go
description:
The short version, for everyone: When an activist presses "I'm safe" or "help" in Kengele, a small message goes to their trusted contacts. That message can travel over the internet, by SMS, or hop phone to phone. Whoever carries it (a relay server, a phone company, a stranger's phone) must not be able to read it, fake it, or even tell a cry for help from a routine check-in. This post shows exactly how that works, byte by byte, with code you can run.

Kengele is an open-source alarm for activists in East Africa. If an activist goes quiet during a watch window, each of their guardians' devices raises the alarm on its own. There is no Kengele server: messages travel over public Nostr relays, an encrypted SMS fallback, and (in v0.2) a Bluetooth mesh.

altradits / kengele

An alarm for when an activist goes missing. No servers, works through shutdowns. Swahili first.

Kengele

When an activist goes silent, the right people know within minutes, and nobody can switch the alarm off.

Ukinyamaza, kengele inalia. ("If you go quiet, the bell rings.")

Warning

Status: design stage. Not for real use. There is no working app yet. Do not rely on Kengele to protect anyone until an independent security review is complete and published here. People's lives may depend on this tool, so we will not cut corners to ship it sooner.

Why

When an activist disappears, how fast the public finds out often decides how quickly they are freed.

  • In Kenya, more than 80 people were abducted or forcibly disappeared after the 2024 protests. In January 2025, abducted young men were released within hours of public outcry.
  • Boniface Mwangi and Agather Atuhaire, detained in Tanzania in May 2025, were released after their disappearance became public.

This one is about the message itself: the 228 bytes every check-in, duress check-in and panic is made of, and the three layers of Nostr wrapping around them.

Kengele is still in design and not for real use until an independent security review is published. All code is at commit e10d277.

Who is the adversary on the wire?

The threat model names several, and the wire format has to hold against all of them at once:

Adversary What they want What they can do
A relay operator Read check-ins, map who protects whom Store and inspect every event they carry
A telecom operator or state Spot panics, block alarms, trace activists See every SMS: numbers, timing, content
A stranger's phone in a mesh Read or alter what it carries Hold and forward messages for hours
Captors with the activist's phone Send a convincing "I'm safe" Use the activist's real keys under coercion
A compromised guardian Forge the activist's events Hold one guardian's key

Two things follow. First, every carrier is untrusted: the message must be secure end to end, independent of the path. Second, the path changes: the same bytes must work over a websocket to a relay, inside two SMS segments, and through a Bluetooth hop. So the format is defined once, in internal/message, and the transports only carry it.

Five goals for one message

From docs/message-format.md:

  1. Nobody can fake it. Each event is signed by its sender with a BIP-340 Schnorr key, the same kind of key Nostr uses.
  2. Carriers can't read it. Each event is encrypted separately to each guardian with NIP-44 v2.
  3. Carriers can't tell kinds apart. Every message is exactly the same size. A duress check-in or a panic looks like an ordinary check-in to everyone except the guardian who decrypts it.
  4. It fits in two SMS. The text form is 304 characters from the GSM-7 basic set: two concatenated SMS hold 306.
  5. The original time survives. The sender's timestamp is inside the signature, so a message delivered days later still proves when it was made.

Goal 3 is the one people underestimate. If a panic message were even one byte longer than a check-in (because it carried a location, say), a telecom could flag every panic in real time without decrypting anything. Size is metadata.

The layout, byte by byte

There are seven event kinds. Their numbers are part of the format and never change:

const (
    KindCheckIn         Kind = 1 // activist: "I am safe"
    KindDuressCheckIn   Kind = 2 // activist, forced: looks like a check-in to everyone but guardians
    KindPanic           Kind = 3 // activist: panic trigger
    KindMissed          Kind = 4 // guardian: a check-in deadline passed
    KindGuardianConfirm Kind = 5 // guardian: confirms the alarm (towards 2 of 3)
    KindAllClear        Kind = 6 // activist or guardian: found safe, stand down
    KindGoingDark       Kind = 7 // activist: pre-arming before a shutdown
)

The kind travels only inside the encryption. From the outside, every message is this:

Wire message: 228 bytes

Offset Size Field
0 1 Format version, 0x01
1 227 NIP-44 v2 payload

NIP-44 v2 payload: 227 bytes

Offset Size Field
0 1 NIP-44 version, 0x02
1 32 Random nonce
33 162 ChaCha20 ciphertext of a 2-byte length (always 160) and the 160-byte signed plaintext
195 32 HMAC-SHA256

Signed plaintext: 160 bytes, inside the encryption

Offset Size Field
0 1 Kind
1 4 Created at: Unix seconds, big-endian
5 4 Sequence number, big-endian
9 1 Body length, 0 to 86
10 86 Body, then zero padding to 86 bytes
96 64 BIP-340 signature

The sizes are constants in code, derived from each other so that changing one breaks the build of the others:

const (
    Version     byte = 1
    MaxBodySize      = 86

    innerSize  = 1 + 4 + 4 + 1 + MaxBodySize + schnorr.SignatureSize // 160
    signedSize = innerSize - schnorr.SignatureSize                    // 96

    // version + nonce + (2-byte length + padded plaintext) + mac
    nip44Size = 1 + 32 + 2 + innerSize + 32 // 227

    WireSize = 1 + nip44Size          // 228
    TextSize = (WireSize*8 + 5) / 6   // 304 base64url characters

    MaxSMSChars  = 306 // two concatenated GSM-7 segments
    MaxClockSkew = 10 * time.Minute
)

Why 86 bytes of body? Because 160 is a NIP-44 padding boundary. NIP-44 pads plaintexts to hide their length; by choosing a plaintext that is already exactly on a boundary, padding adds nothing, and the whole thing still fits in 304 characters. 86 bytes is enough for a typed place name ("Milimani law courts"), a 32-byte key plus a sequence number for guardian messages, or a 70-byte guardian confirmation carrying a Shamir share.

Signing: BIP-340 with a domain tag

sign builds the 160-byte plaintext and signs its first 96 bytes:

func sign(e Event, sender *btcec.PrivateKey) ([]byte, error) {
    ...
    inner := make([]byte, innerSize)
    inner[0] = byte(e.Kind)
    binary.BigEndian.PutUint32(inner[1:5], uint32(ts))
    binary.BigEndian.PutUint32(inner[5:9], e.Seq)
    inner[9] = byte(len(e.Body))
    copy(inner[10:10+MaxBodySize], e.Body)

    h := signedHash(inner[:signedSize])
    sig, err := schnorr.Sign(sender, h[:])
    ...
    copy(inner[signedSize:], sig.Serialize())
    return inner, nil
}

The hash is a BIP-340 tagged hash:

// signTag separates Kengele signatures from Nostr event signatures and any
// other protocol that uses the same keys (BIP-340 tagged hash).
const signTag = "kengele/event/v1"

func signedHash(data []byte) [32]byte {
    tag := sha256.Sum256([]byte(signTag))
    h := sha256.New()
    h.Write(tag[:])
    h.Write(tag[:])
    h.Write(data)
    ...
}

This matters because Kengele keys are secp256k1 keys, the same curve and signature scheme as Nostr and Bitcoin Taproot. Without domain separation, a Kengele signature over some 96 bytes could, in principle, be presented as a valid signature in another protocol that hashes differently, or the other way round. With the tag kengele/event/v1, a Kengele signature is only ever valid as a Kengele signature.

Two deliberate choices:

  • The signature does not cover the recipient. The same signed event goes to every guardian, and can later be handed to a lawyer, a court or OpenTimestamps as proof of what the activist sent and when. If the signature were bound to one guardian, that proof would be per-guardian and harder to present.
  • The time is signed. CreatedAt is inside the signed bytes, so a message carried through a three-day shutdown still proves it was made at 14:07 on day one.

Encrypting: NIP-44 v2 per guardian

NIP-44 v2 is Nostr's audited encryption scheme: ECDH on secp256k1 gives a shared secret, HKDF turns it into a conversation key, each message gets a random 32-byte nonce, ChaCha20 encrypts and HMAC-SHA256 authenticates.

SealAll signs once and encrypts once per guardian:

func SealAll(e Event, sender *btcec.PrivateKey, recipients [][32]byte) ([][]byte, error) {
    inner, err := sign(e, sender)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    out := make([][]byte, 0, len(recipients))
    for _, r := range recipients {
        w, err := encrypt(inner, sender, r, nil)
        ...
        out = append(out, w)
    }
    return out, nil
}

Per-guardian encryption costs a few hundred bytes more per event than encrypting once to a group key, but it means there is no group key to leak, add guardians to or revoke. Removing a guardian is just not encrypting to them any more.

encrypt also checks that the NIP-44 output is exactly the size the format promises, and refuses to send anything else:

if len(payload) != nip44Size {
    return nil, ErrSize
}

That is a cheap, permanent guard against a library upgrade silently changing padding and breaking goal 3.

No sender key on the wire

Look at the wire layout again: there is no sender public key. A carrier sees 228 random-looking bytes and nothing else. So how does a guardian know who sent it?

They try. A guardian watches over a handful of people, and Open tries each one's conversation key until one authenticates:

func Open(wire []byte, recipient *btcec.PrivateKey, senders [][32]byte, now time.Time) (*Event, error) {
    if len(wire) != WireSize {
        return nil, ErrSize
    }
    if wire[0] != Version {
        return nil, ErrVersion
    }
    b64 := base64.StdEncoding.EncodeToString(wire[1:])

    for _, s := range senders {
        ck, err := conversationKey(recipient, s)
        if err != nil {
            continue
        }
        plain, err := nip44.Decrypt(b64, ck)
        if err != nil {
            continue // wrong sender or altered message: try the next key
        }
        return parse([]byte(plain), s, now)
    }
    return nil, ErrNoSender
}

NIP-44's MAC check makes this safe: a wrong key fails authentication, so there is no risk of "decrypting" garbage with the wrong sender. And because the signature inside is then verified against the same key that decrypted it, a compromised guardian cannot forge an activist's event: they could encrypt to another guardian, but they cannot produce the activist's Schnorr signature.

The cost is linear in the number of senders. For a family guardian with three people, that is nothing. For an organisation running a watcher for hundreds of activists, it might need a short rotating recipient hint, which would leak a little metadata. That trade-off is listed as an open question in the docs rather than decided silently.

Why 228 bytes and 304 characters

The SMS fallback is not an afterthought; in Tanzania in 2025 SMS kept working while data was off. The text form is unpadded base64url:

// EncodeText turns a wire message into the SMS-safe text form: unpadded
// base64url, whose alphabet is entirely in the GSM-7 basic character set.
func EncodeText(wire []byte) string {
    return base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(wire)
}

Why base64url and not standard base64? Standard base64 uses + and /, which are in GSM-7, but its = padding and some phones' habit of joining segments with whitespace cause trouble. More importantly, every base64url character (A–Z a–z 0–9 - _) is in the GSM-7 basic set, so none costs two septets. 228 bytes become exactly 304 characters, and two concatenated SMS hold 2 × 153 = 306.

A single SMS is impossible, and the docs say why: the 64-byte signature plus NIP-44's 32-byte nonce and 32-byte MAC already take 171 characters before any content. Two SMS is the floor for a message that is both authenticated and confidential.

There is deliberately no "KENGELE:" prefix on the SMS. A fixed marker would let a filter at the telecom find and drop every Kengele message.

Strict decoding

Everything that comes off the wire is treated as hostile. parse checks, in order: the length, the signature, the kind, the timestamp, the body length, and that every padding byte after the body is zero.

k := Kind(inner[0])
if !k.Valid() {
    return nil, ErrKind
}
ts := binary.BigEndian.Uint32(inner[1:5])
created := time.Unix(int64(ts), 0).UTC()
if ts == 0 || created.After(now.Add(MaxClockSkew)) {
    return nil, ErrTime
}
n := int(inner[9])
if n > MaxBodySize {
    return nil, ErrBody
}
for _, b := range inner[10+n : 10+MaxBodySize] {
    if b != 0 {
        return nil, ErrBody
    }
}

Why insist on zero padding when the signature already covers it? Because strict parsing removes whole classes of "two encodings, one meaning" bugs. If non-zero padding were allowed, the same logical event would have many valid byte forms, and every system that hashes events (deduplication, OpenTimestamps) would have to agree on which one counts.

Old timestamps are accepted on purpose: store-and-forward means a real panic can arrive days late. Future timestamps more than 10 minutes ahead are rejected, so a captor cannot pre-sign a week of "I'm safe" check-ins with future dates. Replays of old ones are stopped above this layer, by the watcher's per-sender sequence numbers.

DecodeText is just as strict on the SMS side: the wrong length, any = or any whitespace is rejected, and the SMS transport is responsible for stripping what phones add when they join segments.

The Nostr layer: rumor, seal, gift wrap

The Kengele message is already signed and encrypted. Why wrap it again for Nostr?

Because a plain Nostr event leaks a lot. Every Nostr event has a pubkey (who sent it), a created_at (when), tags (to whom) and a signature. If an activist published their encrypted check-in as a normal event, every relay would see "this key sent something to that key at 14:07, then again at 15:37, then at 17:07". That rhythm alone reveals a watch window, and the sender key links the activist to their guardians.

NIP-59 gift wraps and NIP-17 private messages fix most of this with three layers. internal/transport/nostr/wrap.go builds them:

Layer Kind Signed by Encrypted to created_at
Rumor 14 nobody (unsigned) — real time
Seal 13 the sender's key recipient (NIP-44) real time minus random 0–48 h
Gift wrap 1059 a fresh one-time key recipient (NIP-44) real time minus random 0–48 h 
rumor := gn.Event{
    Kind:      gn.KindDirectMessage, // 14
    PubKey:    senderPubHex,
    CreatedAt: gn.Timestamp(now.Unix()),
    Tags:      gn.Tags{{"p", recipientHex}},
    Content:   message.EncodeText(wire), // the 304-character Kengele message
}
rumor.ID = rumor.GetID()

The rumor is unsigned on purpose. If it leaked, it would not be a signed statement anyone could prove the sender made. (The Kengele message inside it is signed, but only a guardian can decrypt that.)

The seal encrypts the rumor to the guardian and is signed with the sender's real key, so the guardian knows who it is from. Its timestamp is moved back by a random amount:

sealAt, err := jitter(now, rnd)
seal := gn.Event{Kind: gn.KindSeal, CreatedAt: sealAt, Tags: gn.Tags{}, Content: sealContent}
if err := seal.Sign(senderSec); err != nil { ... }

The gift wrap encrypts the seal again, this time with a brand-new key generated for this one message, and is signed by that throwaway key:

oneTime := gn.GeneratePrivateKey()
ck2, err := nip44.GenerateConversationKey(recipientHex, oneTime)
wrapContent, err := nip44.Encrypt(seal.String(), ck2)
gw := gn.Event{
    Kind:      gn.KindGiftWrap, // 1059
    CreatedAt: wrapAt,          // jittered again, independently
    Tags:      gn.Tags{{"p", recipientHex}},
    Content:   wrapContent,
}
if err := gw.Sign(oneTime); err != nil { ... }

A relay sees only the outer layer: a kind 1059 event from a key it has never seen and will never see again, addressed to the guardian, with a timestamp somewhere in the last two days.

The jitter uses crypto/rand, not math/rand, because a predictable jitter is no jitter at all:

func jitter(now time.Time, rnd io.Reader) (gn.Timestamp, error) {
    n, err := rand.Int(rnd, big.NewInt(int64(MaxJitter/time.Second)))
    if err != nil {
        return 0, fmt.Errorf("nostr: jitter: %w", err)
    }
    return gn.Timestamp(now.Unix() - n.Int64()), nil
}

Wrap also refuses to wrap anything that is not a well-formed Kengele message, so this transport can never be turned into a general channel for leaking other data:

if len(wire) != message.WireSize || wire[0] != message.Version {
    return gn.Event{}, fmt.Errorf("nostr: wrap: %w", message.ErrSize)
}

Unwrapping, and the impersonation rule

Unwrap reverses the layers and checks every signature. The most important check is NIP-17's rule that the rumor's author must be the seal's signer:

// NIP-17: the rumor's author must be the seal's signer, or anyone could
// seal a rumor that claims to come from someone else.
if rumor.Kind != gn.KindDirectMessage || rumor.PubKey != seal.PubKey || rumor.Sig != "" {
    return nil, sealer, ErrMalformed
}

Without it, Mallory could take any rumor claiming to be from Amina, seal it with Mallory's own key, and the guardian would see "from Amina" in the rumor. With it, the claimed author must match the key that actually signed the seal.

So a guardian checks two signatures on every message: the Nostr seal, and the Kengele event inside, which message.Open verifies. The transport's Receive then drops anything whose sealer is not one of the people this guardian watches over.

Run it yourself: what a relay sees

This example seals a check-in and a panic with made-up keys, gift-wraps both, and prints what a relay would see next to what the guardian sees. Save it as internal/transport/nostr/blog_example_test.go in a clone:

blog_example_test.go (click to expand) 
package nostr

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/hex"
    "fmt"
    "time"

    "github.com/altradits/kengele/internal/message"
    "github.com/btcsuite/btcd/btcec/v2"
)

func Example_whatARelaySees() {
    activist, _ := btcec.PrivKeyFromBytes(bytes.Repeat([]byte{0xa1}, 32)) // made-up test keys
    guardian, _ := btcec.PrivKeyFromBytes(bytes.Repeat([]byte{0xb2}, 32))
    gPub := message.PublicKey(guardian)
    aPub := message.PublicKey(activist)
    now := time.Date(2026, 1, 15, 14, 7, 0, 0, time.UTC)

    for i, k := range []message.Kind{message.KindCheckIn, message.KindPanic} {
        ev := message.Event{Kind: k, CreatedAt: now, Seq: uint32(i + 1), Body: []byte("Kisumu")}
        wire, _ := message.Seal(ev, activist, gPub)
        gw, _ := Wrap(wire, activist, gPub, now, nil)

        fmt.Printf("%s: wire %d bytes, sms text %d chars\n", k, len(wire), len(message.EncodeText(wire)))
        fmt.Printf("  outer kind %d, signed by activist? %v, backdated? %v, content %d chars\n",
            gw.Kind, gw.PubKey == hex.EncodeToString(aPub[:]), gw.CreatedAt.Time().Before(now) || gw.CreatedAt.Time().Equal(now), len(gw.Content))

        got, sealer, _ := Unwrap(&gw, guardian)
        opened, _ := message.Open(got, guardian, [][32]byte{sealer}, now)
        fmt.Printf("  guardian opens: %s from activist? %v, body %q\n", opened.Kind, opened.Signer == aPub, opened.Body)
    }
    // Output:
    // check-in: wire 228 bytes, sms text 304 chars
    //   outer kind 1059, signed by activist? false, backdated? true, content 2140 chars
    //   guardian opens: check-in from activist? true, body "Kisumu"
    // panic: wire 228 bytes, sms text 304 chars
    //   outer kind 1059, signed by activist? false, backdated? true, content 2140 chars
    //   guardian opens: panic from activist? true, body "Kisumu"
}


git clone https://github.com/altradits/kengele
cd kengele
# save the file above as internal/transport/nostr/blog_example_test.go
go test -run Example_whatARelaySees -v ./internal/transport/nostr

Our output (Go 1.26.5):

check-in: wire 228 bytes, sms text 304 chars
  outer kind 1059, signed by activist? false, backdated? true, content 2140 chars
  guardian opens: check-in from activist? true, body "Kisumu"
panic: wire 228 bytes, sms text 304 chars
  outer kind 1059, signed by activist? false, backdated? true, content 2140 chars
  guardian opens: panic from activist? true, body "Kisumu"

The two lines in the middle are the whole point. To the relay, the check-in and the panic are the same kind, the same size (2,140 characters of ciphertext), signed by unrelated throwaway keys, at unrelated times. Only the guardian's key turns one of them into "panic".

Test vectors, so other implementations agree

An Android app (Kotlin) and a Go watcher must produce and accept exactly the same bytes. So the format ships a golden vector with made-up keys: activist key 0xa1 × 32, guardian key 0xb2 × 32, nonce 0x01 × 32, a check-in at 2026-01-15 14:07 UTC, seq 1, body Kisumu. TestGoldenVector checks the exact 304-character output, and TestNIP44OfficialVector checks the NIP-44 library against the first vector in the specification itself, so a regression in the dependency would be caught here too.

go test -count=1 -v ./internal/message

--- PASS: TestRoundTripEveryKind (0.04s)
--- PASS: TestSealAllOpensForEachGuardian (0.00s)
--- PASS: TestSMSTextFitsTwoSegments (0.00s)
--- PASS: TestEveryKindHasTheSameLength (0.01s)
--- PASS: TestRejects (0.01s)

TestEveryKindHasTheSameLength is goal 3 as a test.

Sending through outages

The transport in transport.go adds the reliability layer:

  • Publish everywhere. Send publishes the same gift wrap to every configured relay in parallel, plus the guardian's inbox relays (a signed kind 10050 list) if known.
  • Only an explicit OK true counts. A timeout or a dropped connection is not acceptance.
  • Outbox on failure. If fewer than MinAccepted relays accept (default 1), the wrap goes to an outbox and Send reports Queued. Run retries with backoff from 5 seconds to 5 minutes, republishing the same gift wrap only to relays that have not accepted it yet.
  • Look back 48 hours. Because wraps are backdated by up to two days, every subscription asks for events that far back from the last time it was connected. Otherwise a message sent during an outage, then backdated, would fall outside the window and be missed.
  • Deliver once. Receive remembers recent gift-wrap IDs and message hashes (10,000 by default), so a message carried by five relays, or re-wrapped by the sender, reaches the watcher once.
  • Report connectivity. After every publish round, and whenever a receive connection opens or drops, the transport reports Status{Reachable, Total, At}. That is the signal the deadline engine uses to tell "the activist went quiet" from "we cannot reach any relay".

One implementation note: the relay client is a small NIP-01 client written on github.com/coder/websocket, not go-nostr's Relay. In go-nostr v0.52.3, Relay.Close raced with its own goroutines under go test -race, and Publish could report success if the connection dropped before the relay answered. For a tool where "sent" must mean sent, both were disqualifying. go-nostr is still used for events, signatures, NIP-44 and envelopes.

go test -race -count=1 -v ./internal/transport/nostr

--- PASS: TestWrapUnwrapRoundTrip (0.01s)
--- PASS: TestOuterEventHidesSenderTimeAndContent (0.05s)
--- PASS: TestUnwrapRejects (0.00s)
--- PASS: TestActivistToGuardiansOverRelays (0.62s)
--- PASS: TestDuplicateSuppression (0.42s)
--- PASS: TestPartialAcceptance (0.01s)
--- PASS: TestOutageQueuesThenRetryAfterReconnect (0.17s)
--- PASS: TestReceiveReconnects (0.10s)
--- PASS: TestUnknownSenderDropped (0.42s)
--- PASS: TestInboxRelayList (0.00s)
--- PASS: TestSeenSetEvicts (0.00s)
ok      github.com/altradits/kengele/internal/transport/nostr   2.427s

Kengele ships no default relays. The activist and guardians choose at least three, run by different operators in different countries, ideally outside the country whose government is the threat. Nobody, including us, needs to run a relay for Kengele to work.

What a carrier can still see

Encryption hides content and kind. It does not hide everything, and the docs list what leaks:

  • That a message was sent, when it reached the relay, and its size (always the same, so the size itself reveals nothing).
  • The recipient's key in the gift wrap's p tag, needed for delivery. Guardians should use a key made only for Kengele, never their everyday Nostr identity, so it does not link to a public profile.
  • IP addresses of whoever publishes or subscribes, unless they use Tor or a VPN.
  • Rhythm. The created_at is randomised, but the relay's own receive time is not. During a watch window, a relay could see a regular pattern of wraps to one key every 90 minutes.
  • Over SMS, phone numbers and timing. That is why SMS is opt-in per activist.

Open questions we would love help with

  1. Constant-time MAC check. The NIP-44 library in go-nostr v0.52.3 compares the MAC with bytes.Equal, not a constant-time compare. Over SMS this is hard to exploit, but it should be fixed upstream, not worked around here.
  2. Trying every sender. Fine for a family; an organisation watching hundreds may need a recipient hint, which leaks a little.
  3. Cover traffic. Should check-ins be sent with a random delay, or with dummy traffic, to hide the watch-window rhythm?
  4. A persistent, encrypted outbox. Today it lives in memory, so a phone restart loses queued messages. How to store it without leaving something to find on a seized phone is a threat-model question.
  5. NIP-42 relay auth. Some inbox relays only serve kind 1059 to the authenticated recipient. Not supported yet.

How to help

Kengele is free, MIT-licensed and not for real use yet. We are open to collaboration, guidance and any form of participation:

  • Nostr developers: review wrap.go and client.go against NIP-01, NIP-17, NIP-44 and NIP-59. Tell us what we got wrong.
  • Cryptographers: the message format is small enough to review in an afternoon. Break it.
  • Kotlin developers: implement the format against the shared test vectors so the Android app and the Go watcher can never disagree.
  • Anyone who works with activists: tell us what the threat model is missing.

Start with CONTRIBUTING.md. Report security issues privately as described in SECURITY.md.

Not sponsored. Every life is worth watching over. Look out for each other.

title: Go Checkout Rollback — Idempotency Bounds Feature Flag Retries and Duplicate Writes
description:
For checkout feature flag retries, use idempotency to make duplicate writes preserve the desired kill-switch state. Treat a lost response as an unknown outcome until reconciliation establishes the state; otherwise a second toggle can undo the rollback that the first request already completed.

TL;DR: Feature flag retries need idempotent backend logic, a stable operation identity, and verification of the observed state. For an e-commerce AI agent loop, keep rollback control separate from the latency and cost measurements that decide whether the loop should continue. A successful write response alone is insufficient evidence that every checkout worker has adopted the new state.

How can feature flag retries turn duplicate writes into a rollback reversal?

A toggle describes a transition relative to whatever state exists when the backend executes it. Suppose a checkout agent is enabled, the rollback request flips it off, and the response disappears. Retrying the toggle flips it on again. Two accepted writes can therefore leave the operator looking at the original state, even though the backend executed both requests correctly; an integration error seen by the caller does not establish that a write failed.

Preserve the intent.

The operational distinction is between “invert the flag” and “make agent execution disabled.” Repeating the second instruction preserves the target value, provided the backend implements deterministic set semantics. Read the current state first to establish a baseline, then use an explicit set or rollout value, but do not mistake that preliminary read for concurrency control: another operator can change the flag between the read and the write. Serialize changes through a controller or require a backend concurrency mechanism whose actual contract has been verified.

For checkout, a dedicated kill switch should stop admission of new agent work at the boundary chosen by the application. Decide separately what happens to work already running and to purchase mutations already committed. A flag cannot retract an order.

Bound the control loop before sizing telemetry

Measure agent-loop latency and accumulated call cost under a shared operation identity, and record retry attempts separately from logical operations so that repeated delivery does not inflate the apparent number of shopper actions. The decision record should preserve the desired flag value, the controller generation, the time of observation, and the observed value. These are application-owned record fields, not a proposed vendor request schema. Keep shopper content out of that record unless it is necessary.

Use explicit SLOs for both checkout behavior and control propagation. As an illustrative planning exercise, a team might choose a 2-second observation interval and a 30-second rollback verification deadline; those are proposed operating parameters, not measured service performance or a vendor guarantee. With 600 workers polling independently every 2 seconds, budget for 300 reads per second before retries, dashboard queries, or ordinary traffic. A shared controller can reduce upstream reads, but it also adds a distribution path whose failure and propagation delay belong in the rollback SLO.

Budget retries too.

The latency of a retried agent step includes time waiting between attempts, while the cost accounting must include every billable attempt associated with the logical action. Do not add a cumulative total to the same ledger twice. Keep raw attempt records and derive the operation total from distinct attempts; retain the operation's end-to-end elapsed time separately from individual call duration. Otherwise a rollout can appear faster merely because the slow attempts disappeared from the aggregate.

Infrai fits teams that want one REST API and a single API key across 295 routes in 20 modules, with unified billing on one bill; the application-facing contract stays stable when the vendor behind a capability changes. Its specified per-call cost, latency, vendor, and request metadata supports attribution inside the agent loop. Sharing a credential across backend capabilities reduces credential configuration for a controller that observes flags alongside agent activity. The trade-off is a broader credential boundary, so scope access to the controller's operational role. That contract is useful only if the application still owns the rollback policy and verifies the semantics of the particular write capability, rather than assuming that a platform idempotency convention makes every operation safe.

Implement one intent and replay its result

Start with a read-only observation of the actual flag. This standalone Go program reads the versioned API base URL from INFRAI_API_BASE_URL, the credential from INFRAI_API_KEY, and the flag key from FLAG_KEY. Configure the base URL for the intended deployment, including its version prefix. The program prints the response without guessing its schema; production reconciliation must validate the documented response and compare its state with the durable intent. A read cannot authorize a write.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func observe() error {
    base := strings.TrimRight(os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_BASE_URL"), "/")
    key, flag := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"), os.Getenv("FLAG_KEY")
    parsed, err := url.Parse(base)
    if err != nil || parsed.Scheme != "https" || parsed.Host == "" || key == "" || flag == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("configure an HTTPS versioned base URL, credential, and flag key")
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 10 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(*http.Request, []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet,
            base+"/flags/get/"+url.PathEscape(flag), nil)
        if err != nil { return err }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        res, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return err }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(res.Body, 1<<20))
        res.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil { return readErr }
        if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retry := res.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retry); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if seconds > 30 { return fmt.Errorf("rate-limit delay exceeds observation budget") }
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            } else if when, err := http.ParseTime(retry); err == nil {
                delay = time.Until(when)
                if delay < 0 { delay = 0 }
            }
            timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
                continue
            }
        }
        if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("flag read status %d: %s", res.StatusCode, body)
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("observation attempt budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := observe(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The following Go program is a local, deterministic demonstration of a write that commits before its response is lost. It uses no network and exercises no vendor API. Save it as main.go and run it with the Go toolchain. The operation identity stays fixed across the retry, and the ledger refuses reuse of that identity with a different target.

package main

import (
    "errors"
    "fmt"
)

var errLostResponse = errors.New("response lost after commit")

type controller struct {
    enabled bool
    intents map[string]bool
}

func (c *controller) set(id string, desired, loseResponse bool) error {
    if previous, exists := c.intents[id]; exists {
        if previous != desired {
            return errors.New("operation identity reused with different intent")
        }
        return nil
    }
    c.enabled = desired
    c.intents[id] = desired
    if loseResponse {
        return errLostResponse
    }
    return nil
}

func main() {
    c := controller{enabled: true, intents: make(map[string]bool)}
    const operation = "checkout-agent-disable-42"
    err := c.set(operation, false, true)
    if errors.Is(err, errLostResponse) {
        err = c.set(operation, false, false)
    }
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if c.enabled {
        panic("rollback target not observed")
    }
    fmt.Println("rollback target observed: agent disabled")
}

This intentionally small example has one process and one writer. In production, persist the operation record and state update atomically, serialize competing generations, and define record retention to cover the full retry horizon; an in-memory map cannot provide those properties across a restart. If an old disable operation is replayed after a newer enable operation, return its historical result without silently executing it again, then reconcile against the latest authorized generation. Historical success and current state are different observations.

Transport retries also need a deadline, bounded backoff, and handling for rate limits that honors Retry-After when present. An exhausted retry budget leaves an unresolved operation for reconciliation. It must not trigger a toggle as a recovery shortcut.

Buy or build the controller boundary?

A feature management product and an analytical store answer different questions. Buying a flag service can move control-plane work out of the platform backlog; building the controller gives the team direct ownership of intent ordering, at the expense of storage, concurrency, recovery, and on-call responsibility. Compare the following candidates using the same lost-response and stale-generation tests before making a procurement decision. The acceptance requirements below are evaluation criteria, not claims that every product implements them.

Option Proposed role in this checkout design Acceptance boundary and trade-off
LaunchDarkly Candidate external flag control plane Verify explicit desired-state updates, adoption visibility, and recovery evidence; an external control plane adds a dependency to the rollback path.
Unleash Candidate flag control plane evaluated against the platform's operating model Verify the chosen deployment's polling behavior and ownership of recovery; include operational work in the buy-versus-build review.
Flagsmith Candidate flag control plane evaluated against the same rollback contract Verify concurrent edits, stale callers, and repeated desired-state writes; a familiar flag UI does not establish retry semantics.
Application-owned controller Implement operation ordering and a durable intent ledger Offers direct control over reconciliation policy; the team must implement and operate persistence and recovery.
ClickHouse Analytical storage candidate for attempt and decision records Useful to evaluate separately from flag control; choosing an analytical store leaves the write controller and its SLO as distinct responsibilities.
Sentry Candidate for the error-review side of the workflow Evaluate how an ambiguous write appears to the responder; error review alone cannot establish the desired flag state.
Datadog Candidate for the latency and operational-review side Evaluate correlation of agent attempts with controller decisions; require a separate acceptance test for rollback control.
Grafana Candidate for the SLO-review side Evaluate whether the selected data sources expose attempt totals and adoption delay; a dashboard cannot replace a durable intent ledger.

There is no winner from a feature checklist alone. Keep the external candidates in the comparison until a representative integration demonstrates the required behavior, and require a build proposal to survive the same exercise instead of giving internal code a free pass. An analytics choice should not decide who is allowed to re-enable the checkout agent.

Verify adoption, then release the rollback

Before rollout, exercise three synthetic cases: a committed write with a lost response, a repeated request carrying the same operation identity, and an old generation delivered after a newer one. Include a controller restart in the durable implementation. Verify both the stored intent and the state observed by the checkout admission path; a ledger that says “disabled” is not sufficient if workers are still admitting new agent work.

Keep the kill switch asserted while investigating latency or cost regressions. Re-enable through a new, authorized desired-state operation after the verification criteria pass, then reconcile any explicit rollout value against the intended cohort. A timeout is a reason to investigate propagation and observation, not permission to alternate the flag until a response looks reassuring.

The telemetry boundary needs an equally explicit acceptance review. Use application-owned change records rather than assuming flag history is available, and measure adoption directly rather than assuming evaluation statistics exist. Plan for polling clients. Arrange threshold notifications and missed-job detection in the operating design, and do not infer a distributed span tree from trace identifiers carried by log records. Where the workflow requires replay, symbolication, per-user erasure, export, or configurable retention, verify that requirement separately before sending production data. These are selection gates, not promises supplied by a generic observability label.

The release condition is concrete: the latest authorized target is observed at the admission boundary, unresolved writes have an owner, and the agent-loop measurements account for retries. Until then, leave the rollback intent intact.

References

  • LaunchDarkly documentation
  • Unleash documentation
  • Flagsmith documentation
  • ClickHouse documentation
  • Sentry documentation
  • Datadog documentation
  • Grafana documentation

title: Vercel Security Review now in public beta
description:
Vercel Security Review is now in public beta for Pro and Enterprise teams. Once enabled, every push to a connected GitHub repository is automatically reviewed for vulnerabilities, and findings are reported in the Vulnerabilities dashboard.

What triggers a review

Security Review runs automatically when code is pushed to a connected GitHub repository. Because reviews start from push events rather than pull requests, direct and force pushes to your production branch are reviewed as well. Every project affected by a single push is reviewed together.

What a finding includes

Each finding records the project, environment, branch, and commit, with a summary, a suggested fix, and an AI-generated severity rating.

Security Review adds its own GitHub check to each commit it reviews. When there's a pull request, it also posts findings as review comments that link back to each finding. On public repositories, finding details stay in the dashboard.

Fixes and resolution

Clicking Fix with Vercel Agent on a vulnerability report hands the finding to Vercel Agent, which proposes a fix and opens a pull request for you to review. Nothing merges until you approve it.

To fix findings with your coding agent instead, use vercel security vulnerabilities in the Vercel CLI, or copy any finding as Markdown or JSON.

Security policies

Teams can write security policies in plain language, for all projects or specific ones, to give Security Review more context about how they build. Set a team policy in Agent settings and a project policy in the project's Security settings.

Limitations

Security Review analyzes source code. It isn't a security audit, and it doesn't perform runtime or penetration testing. It helps you find vulnerabilities but doesn't guarantee your application is free of them.

Pricing

Security Review is billed at the Vercel Agent rate: provider inference at the underlying token rate with no markup, plus the Vercel Token Rate of $0.25 per million tokens (input, cached, output). Reviews run on each push to GitHub, so cost scales with how often you push and how much code changes.

Security reviews are free until November 10, 2026, and fixes made with Vercel Agent are billed at the Vercel Agent rate.

Enable Security Review in your team’s Agent settings, or read the documentation and the announcement to learn more. The CLI command needs Vercel CLI 65.10.0 or later.
