title: The page that collapses: transforms on the real DOM instead of a screenshot
description:
Originally published at grzegorzotto.dev. Translated from Polish with AI; the Polish original is my own writing.

A page effect does not have to cost you SEO or accessibility: move the real elements with a transform instead of painting a screenshot of them.

On grzegorzotto.dev, on the home page / and on the /projects page, there is a Collapse button (on a phone, an icon in the top bar). Click it and the page collapses: headings, cards and the table fall, collide and pile up at the bottom of the screen. None of it is an image. These are the same DOM nodes that were there before the click, only moved and rotated by CSS transform.

This post is about why I built it this way, what broke on the way, and what I built and then threw away.

Why a transform and not a screenshot into a canvas

The obvious alternative is to take a snapshot of the page into a canvas and "smash" the picture. It looks the same and avoids the trouble of a real page layout. I rejected it from the start: a snapshot hides the real text and is worse for SEO.

Moving the real elements leaves the content in the HTML. A search engine sees the same content, and once the effect is closed, screen readers and text selection work as before, because no element ever disappeared. The effect keeps three rules: page elements are never removed or turned into an image, the physics code loads through import() only on the first click, and the system's reduced-motion setting (prefers-reduced-motion) is always respected. You can check each one yourself in your browser's developer tools: in the element tree, in the network tab and by simulating that setting (in Chrome: the Rendering tab).

Effect first, engine second, against the plan

I wanted the portfolio itself to show what my 2D engine can do. The plan said something different from what I did. On 2026-06-30 I wrote the decision down plainly: full hold, do not hand-roll this in the portfolio, engine first, the page effect as the engine's first test on a real project of my own (dogfooding).

I broke that hold less than a day later. I wanted to see it work on the real DOM before investing in an engine package. My own solver landed in the site's code: 5 files, 556 lines, collisions between rotated rectangles, friction, bouncing and pushing apart elements that sank into each other (for the curious: SAT, an impulse solver, Coulomb friction, Baumgarte correction). I wrote it from the start to be moved into @flare-engine/dynamics one day.

The first version ran the physics live, in every browser frame, at a 1/120 s step, for visible elements only. Esc or a second click restored the page instantly.

What broke when real nodes started falling

The real DOM has its own rules. These are the ones I ran into on the way:

  • The rest of the page takes the falling element's place. For an element to fall freely, you have to take it out of the normal page layout, and the browser immediately closes the gap it leaves. On my page, content below the fold jumped upward and the footer jumped. On top of that, nothing blocked scrolling. Locking scroll for the duration of the effect fixed that, but in Firefox the lock hid the sticky bar at the top of a scrolled page. In Chrome the same code worked correctly.
  • You have to decide what counts as one piece. Splitting too finely broke a section title apart: the word fell on its own, and the thin line next to it was too small to simulate, so it hung in mid-air. Splitting too coarsely dropped the whole projects table as a single slab.
  • An element moved out of its parent loses what it inherited from it. The word taken out of the section title lost its size, its capitals and its colour. A row taken out of a list got the default bullet the list had switched off.
  • Other animations are already running on the page. Elements that the entrance animation had not revealed yet fell invisible.
  • A transform changes how an element looks, not how it behaves. A moved element can still be clicked and reached with the Tab key. The inert attribute helped, but Tab still escaped to the skip link, which I fixed separately.
  • The page keeps living while the effect runs. The user clicks, navigates to another page, opens the command palette. On my page that led to crashes when removing elements, leftovers of the fall after navigating to another page, Esc clashing with the command palette, and a rare race that left the page frozen.

If your system has reduced motion turned on, the button does not appear at all. That is not a gentler version of the effect, it is no effect, and it is deliberate. The reason: even a softened effect moves every element across the whole screen, which ignores an explicit system setting, and for some people that kind of motion causes dizziness and nausea.

Computing the fall ahead of time

Live physics had another problem, unrelated to the DOM. I wanted closing the effect to play the fall back. But physics cannot simply run backwards: collisions are chaotic, and a reversed simulation will not retrace the same path.

So the fall is computed ahead of time (a bake) and played back like a recording (a timeline) that you can scrub. Rewinding is the same recording played from the end, so it looks like the fall run backwards, with no jump. After a browser test I also slowed the close down, because the first version closed too fast.

Built and rejected

The second version had a model that fit the "scrubbing time" metaphor on paper: two zones, a pause at the peak, a Restore button and a bottom bar for the controls. The third, from 2 July, is a deliberate partial reversal of two decisions from the second: one fall from start to finish, with no pause, and a column of controls on the right.

Why did I change my mind? The bottom bar covered the falling page. The UI looked ugly and was awkward to use. On paper everything looked fine; it only turned out badly in use. I fixed it after my own manual testing. A vertical column had existed even before the second version, so the third went back to it.

Earlier still there was a "time machine" plan. Almost all of it went: the rewind button with all its machinery, slow motion (0.25x and 0.5x), colour grading that I never built, and live physics, which the recording replaced.

The biggest piece I threw away was a separate page with an engine demo (CanvasKit). Built on 25 August, removed the next day together with the exceptions in the site's security rules (CSP) that it needed. The reason: /projects/* describes projects; it is not a place for demos. The engine's demos live on flareengine.dev.

What I never installed: planck.js

Since this is about 2D physics in the browser, someone may ask about this decision. I considered planck.js, a JavaScript rewrite of the well-known Box2D physics engine, but never added it and do not plan to. The reasons:

  • my own solver already worked;
  • a full Box2D port is too much physics for falling page elements;
  • more code for every visitor to download;
  • I keep external libraries to a minimum and did not want another one to maintain.

The decision is recorded in the engine's public docs: docs/design/dependencies.md, and PR #305 records that dynamics is the rigid-body answer and planck is not planned.

The solver moves into the engine

There is one detail I have to record here honestly. For a while the button said "built with my 2D engine" while the demo ran not a single line of engine code. The engine's public plan for moving the solver states it plainly as the goal: "This makes the claim literally true" (docs/plans/dynamics-lift-2026-08.md).

The order was: first I corrected the button copy (13 August), and only then moved the solver. The package appeared in the engine on 16 August, and on 25 August the portfolio's solver was replaced by @flare-engine/dynamics: exactly the same 556 lines, untouched since 1 July, left the portfolio.

The safety net was a determinism test written earlier, on 13 August. It drops 12 elements with the same random seed and checks at 21 points of the recording that each element sits in exactly the same place in two runs. A different seed must give a different fall. After the solver swap that test passed unchanged.

The old and the new solver do not compute identically, but almost: the largest difference in an element's position over 480 steps was less than a trillionth of a pixel (6.8 × 10⁻¹³). The first difference appeared at frame 77, and every element's final position matches to a thousandth of a pixel. It comes from the engine doing the same operations in a slightly different order, while the computer rounds the result of every operation on fractions. The page sets positions to a hundredth of a pixel anyway, so the difference is about 15 billion times too small to see. These measurements are recorded in my private repo, so here you have to take my word for it. What you can check publicly is the effect and the package: @flare-engine/dynamics on npm.

The fall's timeline later went the same way. The engine gained createTimeline in 0.4.10, built to this page's needs, and on 16 November the page switched to it and deleted its own implementation. Before deleting it, I ran both versions on the same data: 60 elements, 300 frames and 2001 sample points. The results were bit-identical, so the swap does not change a single frame of the fall.

Limits

  • The determinism test compares two runs of the same solver version. When the package version changes, it will not tell you the solver changed. You have to diff the code separately. I did that for the bump from 0.4.5 to 0.4.12: the new feature that puts motionless elements to sleep is opt-in, and without it the solver computes exactly the same thing (dynamics changelog). Since 19 November the page turns it on: the bake stops when the engine reports every piece asleep (isAtRest), so from that day the fall is no longer identical to the earlier one.
  • The site is pinned to version 0.4.12 of the engine packages. (State as of 2026-11-16.)
  • I give no figure for how much this effect adds to the downloaded code, and no performance figures. I did not measure them for this post.
  • This runs on / and /projects, not on the whole site, and it is not an engine demo. The engine's demos live on flareengine.dev.

If you want to repeat it

Start with real elements and transform, and only then think about physics. If you want to read about the engine itself, the earlier post is here: Flare Engine is open source.

title: Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Tunix and Gemma 4 on Google TPUs
description: This post walks developers through training a multi-turn, tool-using LLM agent using Tunix and Gemma 4 on Cloud TPUs. title: Remembered as Brief: Stored Preferences SilentlyRemove Decision-Critical Information
description:
arXiv:2611.22697v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: People increasingly learn what they need for decisions about health, money, law and safety from AI assistants, and what an assistant leaves out the user never sees. An answer with a warning removed can be true in every sentence, so fact-checks pass it, and an assistant with memory applies a preference stored once to later questions the user never had in mind. We introduce \bench{}, an Inspect benchmark of 100 everyday decisions across 25 domains in which only the assistant's memory of the user varies: the user states a belief, the model infers it from a remark, or a web page the user asked to summarise plants it. Testing five models, we find three effects. First, after summarising a page with one line addressed to AI assistants, Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite and DeepSeek V4 Pro save ``prefers very short answers and does not want warnings'' as the user's preference in every episode, and 93\% and 84\% of their later answers miss a critical item, almost always silently; under a stated brevity preference, 78--96\% of omissions are silent. Second, the same two models then pick an option for the user on 80\% and 95\% of value-dependent choices, against none with neutral memory. Third, a one-line instruction leaves 2--8\% of answers with a silent gap but most missing content still missing, while listing the must-know points before applying the user profile restores more of the content in four of five models. We release the scenarios, harness and logs.

title: A dead man's switch that survives an internet shutdown: inside Kengele's deadline engine in Go
description:
The short version, for everyone: Kengele is a free, open-source alarm for activists. If an activist stops checking in, their trusted contacts are alerted. The hard part is that governments switch the internet off at exactly the moments abductions happen, and during a shutdown everyone goes quiet. This post walks through the Go code that tells "the activist went silent" apart from "the network went silent", with a scenario you can run on your own machine.

Kengele (Swahili for "bell") is an alarm for activists in East Africa. Ukinyamaza, kengele inalia: "if you go quiet, the bell rings." An activist sets a watch window before a protest, a court date or a border crossing ("2pm to 10pm, check in every 90 minutes"). Their check-ins go to three to five guardians. If a check-in does not arrive, each guardian's device raises the alarm on its own. There is no Kengele server to seize or switch off.

altradits / kengele

An alarm for when an activist goes missing. No servers, works through shutdowns. Swahili first.

Kengele

When an activist goes silent, the right people know within minutes, and nobody can switch the alarm off.

Ukinyamaza, kengele inalia. ("If you go quiet, the bell rings.")

Warning

Status: design stage. Not for real use. There is no working app yet. Do not rely on Kengele to protect anyone until an independent security review is complete and published here. People's lives may depend on this tool, so we will not cut corners to ship it sooner.

Why

When an activist disappears, how fast the public finds out often decides how quickly they are freed.

  • In Kenya, more than 80 people were abducted or forcibly disappeared after the 2024 protests. In January 2025, abducted young men were released within hours of public outcry.
  • Boniface Mwangi and Agather Atuhaire, detained in Tanzania in May 2025, were released after their disappearance became public.
  • Governments switch networks off when it…
View on GitHub

Contents

  1. Why ten lines is not enough
  2. A passive engine with no goroutines
  3. The watch window and seven states
  4. Pausing per route, not per network
  5. The return window
  6. Run it yourself: an election-day shutdown
  7. Mass silence, stuck probes and going dark
  8. Late messages, replays and testing
  9. What is still open

At its core that is a dead man's switch, and a dead man's switch sounds like ten lines of code:

if time.Since(lastCheckIn) > interval+grace {
    raiseAlarm()
}

This post is about why the real one is 775 lines, and why every one of those lines exists because of a specific way people get hurt.

Kengele is still in design and not for real use until an independent security review is published. Everything below is code you can read and run today, at commit e10d277.

Why ten lines is not enough

The naive version fails in four ways that matter in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania.

1. Shutdowns make everyone silent at once. Uganda ordered the internet off on 13 January 2026, effective 6pm, two days before its election. Tanzania did the same in October 2025. With the naive code, every activist under watch misses their deadline in the same minute and every guardian gets an alarm. Hundreds of false public alarms would destroy trust in the tool on its first real day.

2. But silence during a shutdown can also be real. Abductions happen during shutdowns. If we simply ignore missed check-ins while the network is down, the alarm is useless exactly when it is needed. The alarm must fire the minute the network comes back if the activist still has not checked in, not days later when someone finally notices.

3. Shutdowns are partial. In Tanzania in 2025, mobile data went dark but SMS mostly kept working. An activist who has the encrypted SMS fallback turned on can still check in. Their clock should keep running. An activist who only uses the internet path should pause. One global "online" flag gets both wrong.

4. Messages arrive late, and the late arrival is not the activist's fault. A check-in can be carried phone to phone over Bluetooth and delivered hours later. It still carries the activist's signed original time. The deadline engine must judge a check-in by when it was signed, not when it arrived, and still tell guardians it was late so they verify.

On top of that, an attacker with the activist's phone will try to abuse every one of these exceptions to keep the alarm quiet. Every pause has to be bounded.

The design rule: a passive engine with no goroutines

The first decision shapes everything else. The engine in internal/schedule owns no clock, no timers and no goroutines. The caller feeds it three things:

Input Method Meaning
Time passing Tick(now) "It is now now. What changed?"
Connectivity SetTransport(now, kind, up) "Nostr (or SMS) just went up or down for this guardian"
Messages Observe(now, via, event) "This verified event arrived over this route"

Every call returns a slice of Notice values (started, reminder, missed, alarm, paused, resumed, and so on). The caller decides what to do with them: show a notification, start the guardian confirmation flow, write a log.

// The engine is passive and has no goroutines: the caller feeds it the
// time (Tick), connectivity changes (SetTransport, SetOnline) and opened
// messages (Observe), and acts on the Notices it returns. That keeps it
// deterministic under a fake clock.

Why this matters:

  • Determinism. Given the same sequence of calls, you always get the same notices. There is no race between a timer firing and a message arriving, because there are no timers.
  • Testability. A test can walk through a whole election day in microseconds by calling Tick with made-up times. The test suite does exactly that: dozens of scenarios run in well under a second.
  • Portability. The engine has no opinion about how time is delivered. The Go watcher an organisation can host (cmd/kengele-watcher) drives it from a ticker; the Android guardian app, still being built, can drive the same rules from its own scheduler.

There is even a test that guards the rule itself, so nobody can quietly add a background goroutine later:

TestNoGoroutines (click to expand) 
func TestNoGoroutines(t *testing.T) {
    before := runtime.NumGoroutine()
    e := New(Config{}, t0)
    for i := 0; i < 50; i++ {
        _ = e.Watch(key(i), window())
    }
    for m := 0; m < 600; m += 5 {
        e.Tick(at(m))
        if m == 200 {
            e.SetOnline(at(m), false)
        }
        if m == 260 {
            e.SetOnline(at(m), true)
        }
    }
    if after := runtime.NumGoroutine(); after > before {
        t.Errorf("goroutines: %d before, %d after", before, after)
    }
}

One more small rule: time never runs backwards inside the engine. If a caller passes a now earlier than the last one (a phone clock correction, for example), Tick keeps the later time.

if now.Before(e.now) {
    now = e.now // time never runs backwards inside the engine
}

The watch window

A watch is a Window:

type Window struct {
    Start, End time.Time
    Interval   time.Duration // check in every Interval
    Grace      time.Duration // late after due + Grace
    Reminder   time.Duration // remind this long before due
}

Validate refuses windows that cannot work: no start or end, end before start, a non-positive interval, negative grace, or a reminder that is not shorter than the interval.

The deadline after any accepted check-in is computed by one small function:

func (e *Engine) setDeadline(t *tracker, from time.Time) {
    due := from.Add(t.w.Interval)
    if due.After(t.w.End) {
        due = t.w.End
    }
    t.missAt = due.Add(t.w.Grace)
    t.reminded = false
    t.returnGranted = false
}

Three details are worth noticing:

  • from is the signed time of the check-in, not the arrival time. A check-in signed at 15:20 and delivered at 15:50 still sets the next deadline from 15:20.
  • The last deadline is clamped to the end of the window, so the activist does not have to check in after the protest is over just because the arithmetic said so.
  • returnGranted resets on every accepted check-in. Hold that thought; it is the defence against a flapping network.

Seven states

Each watched activist has a tracker with one of seven states:

State Meaning
inactive The window has not started
waiting The next check-in is not yet due
reminder The check-in is close to due or inside its grace period
missed A deadline passed while the network was up. Level 1: guardians are told privately
alarm A duress check-in or panic arrived. Top level
paused Every route this activist uses is down (or a mass-silence hold is in force)
cleared The window ended with a final check-in, or the guardians stood down

Two transitions are deliberately missing.

A check-in cannot cancel an alarm. Once a duress check-in or panic has arrived, a normal check-in is ignored:

case t.state == StateInactive, t.state == StateAlarm, t.state == StateCleared:
    return nil // a check-in cannot cancel an alarm; only all clear can

If captors hold the activist, they can make the activist check in. That must not undo the alarm the activist raised a minute earlier.

The activist's own all-clear cannot end a Level 1 alarm. This was the subject of my previous post:

Captors can force the PIN. They still can't switch the alarm off.
Stanley Chege Thuita
Stanley Chege Thuita
Stanley Chege Thuita
Follow
Nov 18

Captors can force the PIN. They still can't switch the alarm off.

#opensource #go #security #nostr
Add Comment
13 min read

Before Level 1, an all-clear from the activist ends the watch like a final check-in. From Level 1 up, it is recorded and shown to guardians ("the activist says they are safe") but ends nothing. Only k guardians, after a voice or video call, can stand the alarm down through StandDown.

Pausing per route, not per network

The engine tracks connectivity per transport. Today there are two, defined in internal/transport/kind.go:

const (
    Unknown Kind = iota // proves nothing about any route
    Nostr               // gift-wrapped events through public relays
    SMS                 // the encrypted two-part SMS fallback
    Mesh                // reserved for the Bluetooth mesh (v0.2)
)

Each activist's plan lists the routes they use. The default is Nostr only; SMS is opt-in because SMS exposes metadata (who texted whom) to the phone company. The engine's rule is:

An activist's clock pauses only when every route they use is down, and resumes when one of them comes back.

// reachable reports whether at least one of t's transports is up.
func (e *Engine) reachable(t *tracker) bool {
    for _, k := range t.via {
        if e.up[k] {
            return true
        }
    }
    return false
}

When a route goes down, SetTransport first settles anything already due (so an alarm that was due a second before the outage still fires), then pauses every activist who is now unreachable:

if !up {
    out = e.Tick(now) // settle anything already due before pausing
    e.up[k] = false
    for _, a := range e.order {
        t := e.acts[a]
        if t.offline || e.reachable(t) {
            continue
        }
        t.offline, t.offlineAt, t.stillAt = true, e.now, e.now
        ...
        if t.state == StateWaiting || t.state == StateReminder {
            t.resume, t.state = t.state, StatePaused
            out = append(out, Notice{Kind: NoticePaused, ...})
        }
    }
    return out
}

Note what is not paused: an activist already in missed or alarm. A shutdown never downgrades an alarm.

The return window: firing the minute the network is back

When a route returns, each activist who was paused resumes. Two cases:

  1. The deadline fell inside the outage. The activist could not have checked in. They get a return window (2 hours by default) from the moment the network came back.
  2. The deadline is still in the future. It moves forward by the length of the outage, so the activist gets exactly the time they lost. 
if !t.missAt.After(now) && !t.returnGranted {
    t.missAt = now.Add(e.cfg.ReturnWindow)
    t.returnGranted = true
} else {
    t.missAt = t.missAt.Add(outage)
}

The returnGranted flag is the important part. Without it, an attacker (or just a bad connection) could flap the network up and down, and every "up" would grant another two hours. One check-in cycle gets the return window at most once. The test for it reads like a story:

{
    name: "flapping network cannot stretch one deadline again and again",
    steps: []step{
        tick(0), offline(60), online(120), // deadline +105 in outage -> +240, return window used
        offline(130), online(135),          // 5 min outage -> +245
        offline(200), online(260),          // +245 passed in outage, but window already used -> +305
        tick(304), tick(305),
    },
    want: []want{{0, StateMissed, 305}},
},

The third outage does not grant a fresh two hours. It only adds back the 60 minutes that were actually lost. At +305 minutes the alarm fires.

Run it yourself: an election-day shutdown

Here is a scenario with two activists. Amina has the SMS fallback turned on. Baraka uses Nostr only. The window runs 14:00 to 22:00 with a check-in every 90 minutes, 15 minutes of grace and a 10-minute reminder. At 15:40 the internet is switched off. SMS keeps working. At 19:00 the internet comes back.

Save this as internal/schedule/blog_example_test.go in a clone of the repo:

package schedule

import (
    "fmt"
    "time"

    "github.com/altradits/kengele/internal/message"
    "github.com/altradits/kengele/internal/transport"
)

func Example_shutdown() {
    start := time.Date(2026, 1, 15, 14, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC)
    m := func(min int) time.Time { return start.Add(time.Duration(min) * time.Minute) }
    amina, baraka := [32]byte{1}, [32]byte{2}
    names := map[[32]byte]string{amina: "Amina", baraka: "Baraka"}
    show := func(ns []Notice) {
        for _, n := range ns {
            fmt.Printf("%s  %-6s %-9s next deadline %s\n", n.At.Format("15:04"), names[n.Activist], n.Kind, n.Deadline.Format("15:04"))
        }
    }
    checkIn := func(who [32]byte, min int, seq uint32) message.Event {
        return message.Event{Kind: message.KindCheckIn, CreatedAt: m(min), Seq: seq, Signer: who}
    }

    w := Window{Start: start, End: m(480), Interval: 90 * time.Minute, Grace: 15 * time.Minute, Reminder: 10 * time.Minute}
    e := New(Config{}, start)
    _ = e.Watch(amina, w, transport.Nostr, transport.SMS) // SMS fallback on
    _ = e.Watch(baraka, w)                                // Nostr only

    for min := 0; min <= 420; min++ { // tick once a minute (kengele-watcher defaults to every 30s)
        switch min {
        case 80:
            show(e.Observe(m(min), transport.Nostr, checkIn(amina, min, 1)))
        case 100:
            show(e.SetTransport(m(min), transport.Nostr, false)) // internet switched off
        case 170:
            show(e.Observe(m(min), transport.SMS, checkIn(amina, min, 2))) // Amina checks in by SMS
        case 300:
            show(e.SetTransport(m(min), transport.Nostr, true)) // internet back
        default:
            show(e.Tick(m(min)))
        }
    }
    // Output:
    // 14:00  Amina  started   next deadline 15:45
    // 14:00  Baraka started   next deadline 15:45
    // 15:20  Amina  reminder  next deadline 15:45
    // 15:20  Baraka reminder  next deadline 15:45
    // 15:40  Baraka paused    next deadline 15:45
    // 16:40  Amina  reminder  next deadline 17:05
    // 18:10  Amina  reminder  next deadline 18:35
    // 18:35  Amina  missed    next deadline 18:35
    // 19:00  Baraka resumed   next deadline 21:00
    // 20:35  Baraka reminder  next deadline 21:00
    // 21:00  Baraka missed    next deadline 21:00
}

Then:

git clone https://github.com/altradits/kengele
cd kengele
# save the file above as internal/schedule/blog_example_test.go
go test -race -run Example_shutdown -v ./internal/schedule

Our run (Go 1.26.5, macOS arm64):

=== RUN   Example_shutdown
--- PASS: Example_shutdown (0.00s)
PASS
ok      github.com/altradits/kengele/internal/schedule  1.555s

Read the output line by line, because every line is a design decision:

  • 15:20. Both get a reminder (due 15:30, reminder 10 minutes before). Amina checks in over Nostr in the same minute, so her next deadline moves to 15:20 + 90 + 15 = 17:05. Baraka does not check in.
  • 15:40. The internet goes off. Baraka pauses, because Nostr is his only route. His 15:45 deadline is frozen. Amina does not pause, because SMS still works for her. Her clock keeps running.
  • 16:40 and 16:50. Amina gets her reminder and checks in by SMS at 16:50. That check-in proves only that SMS works; it says nothing about Nostr. Her next deadline becomes 18:35.
  • 18:35. Amina missed. The internet is still off, but she had a working route and did not use it. That is a real missed check-in, and it is raised as one. This is the behaviour the single "online" flag would get wrong: it would have paused her too.
  • 19:00. The internet is back. Baraka's 15:45 deadline fell inside the outage, so he gets the return window: 21:00.
  • 21:00. Baraka missed. He had two full hours of working internet and did not check in. The alarm fires at a predictable, explainable time, not days later.

Mass silence: when the probe has not noticed the shutdown yet

SetTransport depends on something telling the engine that a route is down. In the watcher, that signal comes from the Nostr transport's relay reachability (a Connectivity callback reporting how many relays answered). But a shutdown can be partial in ways a probe cannot see: the guardian's relays are fine, but the activists' phones are in a region where data is off. Or the guardian is abroad, and only the country is dark.

From the guardian's side, that looks like several activists all missing at the same moment while nobody has heard from anyone. That pattern has two explanations, and both are serious: a regional shutdown, or a mass arrest.

The engine does not pretend to know which. When at least MassSilence activists (3 by default) miss within MassSpan (15 minutes) and nothing has arrived on any of their routes in that span, it holds them for at most the return window and tells the guardian to check by hand now:

if len(recent) >= e.cfg.MassSilence {
    for _, t := range recent {
        t.massHold, t.returnGranted = true, true
        t.resume, t.state = t.state, StatePaused
        t.missAt = now.Add(e.cfg.ReturnWindow)
        out = append(out, Notice{Kind: NoticeMassSilence, ...
            Reason: fmt.Sprintf("%d activists silent at once: possible shutdown or mass arrest, check by hand now", len(recent))})
    }
    ...
}

Three things keep this from becoming a way to suppress alarms:

  1. It is bounded. The hold lasts at most ReturnWindow. When it runs out and the activist is still silent, they go to missed with the reason "still silent after the mass-silence hold ended".
  2. It uses up the return window. A held activist cannot get a second free delay from a later outage in the same cycle.
  3. Evidence ends it early, but only on the right route. If anyone gets through on a route, that route clearly works, so the hold ends at once for every activist who uses that route: 
for _, k := range e.order {
    h := e.acts[k]
    if h.massHold && k != ev.Signer && transport.IsSupported(via) && h.uses(via) {
        h.massHold = false
        h.state = StateMissed
        out = append(out, Notice{Kind: NoticeMissed, ...
            Reason: "others are getting through on " + via.String() + ", this activist is still silent"})
    }
}

The h.uses(via) check is the subtle part. An SMS check-in from Amina proves that SMS works. It proves nothing about Nostr, so it must not end the hold for Nostr-only Baraka. There is a test for exactly that: "an SMS check-in during a Nostr outage does not lift the hold for Nostr-only activists". And a message tagged transport.Unknown proves nothing about any network at all, though it still counts as a check-in.

A stuck "down" signal must not silence the alarm forever

Here is a failure mode that took a while to see. An offline pause never ends on its own: it waits for SetTransport(..., true). If the probe has a bug, or an attacker can make the guardian's device believe Nostr is down (block the relays at the guardian's network, for example), the clock stays frozen forever and silence means nothing forever.

So while an activist stays offline-paused, the engine re-alerts every 24 hours (StillPausedEvery), in Swahili and English:

out = append(out, Notice{Kind: NoticeStillPaused, ...
    Reason: fmt.Sprintf("bado imesimama / still paused: clock paused since %s, deadline %s",
        t.offlineAt.UTC().Format(time.RFC3339), t.missAt.UTC().Format(time.RFC3339))})

It does not raise the alarm (that would be a false alarm during a genuine week-long shutdown), but it makes sure a human looks. Mass-silence and going-dark holds are excluded because they already end on their own.

Going dark: a pre-announced shutdown

Shutdowns often come with a few hours' warning. So the activist has a "Going dark" button. It sends a signed, encrypted going-dark event (kind 7) to every guardian before the network goes down. Its body carries the current plan, how long the activist expects to be dark, the return window they want afterwards, and a SHA-256 commitment to the pre-written alert.

The engine pauses only that activist, even while the transports are up:

func (e *Engine) goingDark(t *tracker, ev message.Event) []Notice {
    g, err := message.ParseGoingDark(ev)
    if err != nil {
        return nil
    }
    until := e.now.Add(g.Dark)
    t.dark, t.darkSince, t.darkUntil, t.darkReturn = true, e.now, until, g.ReturnWindow
    t.massHold = false
    if t.state == StateWaiting || t.state == StateReminder {
        t.resume, t.state = t.state, StatePaused
    }
    return []Notice{{Kind: NoticeGoingDark, ...
        Reason: fmt.Sprintf("anaenda gizani / going dark: the activist expects a shutdown, clock paused until %s", ...)}}
}

The rules around it are where the security lives:

  • At most 7 days. message.MaxGoingDark caps the dark window. One message must never silence an activist for longer than a week. A longer shutdown needs a fresh going-dark, which needs the activist to be alive, free and holding their key.
  • It never downgrades. A going-dark does nothing to an activist already in missed, alarm or cleared. Captors who force the button after the alarm has fired gain nothing.
  • It is dropped if unreadable. A going-dark with a body that does not parse is ignored, and replays of an old sequence number are dropped before they reach this function.
  • A real check-in ends it early. An accepted check-in proves the activist is reachable, so the hold ends.
  • Duress and panic still fire. A panic during a going-dark hold raises the top-level alarm immediately.

When the hold ends, the same return-window rule applies as for an outage: a deadline that passed inside the hold gets the activist's requested return window once per cycle; any other deadline moves forward by the length of the hold.

The honest residual risk: captors who force the activist to press "Going dark" before any alarm has fired can buy a bounded pause of a running clock. Bounded is the point. It is at most 7 days, it shows up on every guardian's screen, and guardians who were told about a shutdown that never came can act on that.

Late messages and the signed time

Store-and-forward is a core feature: a panic can hop from phone to phone over Bluetooth and reach a network hours later. Every event carries the activist's signed CreatedAt, and the engine judges check-ins by it:

case at.Before(t.w.Start), !at.After(t.last):
    return nil // stale: signed before the window or before the last check-in

When a check-in arrives after the deadline already fired, the engine accepts it, resets the deadline, and raises recovered with one of two reasons:

reason := "late check-in: verify by voice before standing down"
if prev == StateMissed && !at.After(prevMiss) {
    reason = "check-in was signed in time but delivered late"
}

Guardians see the difference between "they checked in late" and "they checked in on time, but the message was delayed". Both still say: verify by voice. A recovered check-in never silently erases the fact that the alarm fired.

And one edge case that is easy to miss: a very old check-in can leave the next deadline already in the past. The engine catches that and raises missed immediately with "the latest check-in was too old to cover now".

Replays

A check-in captured off the wire could be re-sent later to make a missing activist look alive. Each tracker keeps the set of sequence numbers it has seen, and Observe drops any repeat before doing anything else:

if _, dup := t.seen[ev.Seq]; dup {
    return out
}
t.seen[ev.Seq] = struct{}{}

Combined with the rule that a check-in must be signed after the last accepted one, a replay can never move a deadline.

Testing it: a table of election days

The test file is 955 lines of table-driven scenarios. Each case is a list of steps (tick, offline, online, ev, down, up, gdark) at minute offsets from 10:00 on 15 January 2026, plus the notices and final states expected:

{
    name:    "deadline inside the outage gets the return window",
    steps:   []step{tick(0), offline(60), tick(200), online(120 + 0)},
    notices: []string{"started/0", "paused/0", "resumed/0"},
    want:    []want{{0, StateWaiting, 320}}, // engine time is already +200 when it comes back
},

Reading the case names is the best summary of the engine's promises:

  • "duress check-in raises the alarm and a later check-in cannot cancel it"
  • "duress during a shutdown still raises the alarm"
  • "short outage before the deadline moves it by the outage"
  • "flapping network cannot stretch one deadline again and again"
  • "check-in signed in time but delivered late (store and forward)"
  • "Nostr down, SMS up: the SMS activist's clock runs, the Nostr-only one pauses"
  • "the Nostr-only holds still end on time after an SMS check-in"

Run the whole suite with the race detector:

go test -race -count=1 -v -run 'TestSchedule|TestMixedTransports|TestStillPaused$|TestNoGoroutines|TestGoingDark' ./internal/schedule

Our run:

--- PASS: TestSchedule (0.00s)
--- PASS: TestGoingDark (0.00s)
--- PASS: TestMixedTransports (0.00s)
--- PASS: TestStillPaused (0.00s)
--- PASS: TestNoGoroutines (0.00s)
ok      github.com/altradits/kengele/internal/schedule  1.572s

A whole year of simulated shutdowns, in under two seconds, because the engine never waits for a real clock.

What I would do differently, and what is still open

  • The engine trusts the caller's connectivity signal. The still-paused re-alert limits the damage of a lying probe, but a guardian whose own network is controlled by an attacker is still in a weak position. That is one reason guardians should not all live in the same city, and why an organisation abroad can run the Go watcher as a backup.
  • Seen sequence numbers live in memory. Across a restart, replay protection falls back to the "signed after the last check-in" rule, which still blocks replays from moving a deadline, but persistence belongs in the watcher.
  • Timing metadata. A check-in every 90 minutes is a visible rhythm on a relay or a phone network, even when the content is encrypted. Cover traffic or random delays are an open question in the threat model.
  • The defaults (2-hour return window, 3 activists for mass silence, 24-hour re-alert) are educated guesses. They need to be tested in drills with real guardians before anyone relies on them. The plan for those drills is in docs/drills.md.

What it still cannot do

If the phone is taken instantly, SMS is down and no other Kengele phone is nearby, nothing gets out until the network returns. The engine's promise is narrower and more honest: the alarm fires in the first minutes the network is back, with the activist's signed timestamps intact, instead of days later when someone finally notices. Kengele does not prevent abductions. It shortens the time between a disappearance and public pressure.

How to help

Kengele is free, MIT-licensed and not for real use yet. We are open to collaboration, guidance and any form of participation:

  • Go developers: review internal/schedule. Try to find a sequence of calls that keeps a silent activist quiet for longer than the rules above allow. That is a bug, and we want it.
  • Android and Kotlin developers: the guardian app needs to apply these same rules on the phone.
  • Digital-security reviewers: the threat model needs critique before any code reaches a real person.
  • Swahili translators and people who work with activists: tell us what we are missing.

Start with CONTRIBUTING.md. Report security issues privately as described in SECURITY.md.

Not sponsored. Every life is worth watching over. Look out for each other.

title: AI Gateway now supports Private Inference
description:
Private Inference connects your own model endpoints to AI Gateway.

Enterprises running fine-tuned, self-hosted, or prerelease models used to need separate keys, client code, and logs for them. Those models can now run through the same authentication, SDKs and APIs, and observability as catalog models, so every model your team uses is managed in one place.

Use Private Inference to:

  • Switch between private and catalog models: Call private models through Chat Completions, Responses, or Messages. AI Gateway translates each request to your endpoint's format, so switching only changes the model ID.

  • Keep models scoped to your team: Only your Vercel team can view or call private models, and they aren't listed in the public catalog. Credentials are stored encrypted, and you can enable Zero Data Retention per provider.

  • Connect coding agents: Use private models in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and other coding agents connected to AI Gateway.

  • Monitor traffic together: View private model requests alongside catalog traffic in logs, trace drains, and custom reporting. Observability charts break down requests, tokens, and time to first token by private model.

  • Configure fallbacks: Optionally fall back to a catalog model if your private endpoint fails.

To get started, open the Private Inference page and add your endpoint as a private provider. Enter its base URL, select its API format, and add its credentials. Then add the models it serves.

You can also register the provider and model with the Vercel CLI, version 65.16.0 or later:

Call the model using its private/<slug> ID:

Private model requests appear in AI Gateway logs alongside requests to catalog models.

title: OVHcloud Just Shipped 55 AI Products: B300 GPUs, a CPU-Runnable LLM, and Europe's Big Sovereign AI Bet
description:
Europe's largest cloud provider just made its biggest AI move yet. At its AI Summit in Paris on November 19, OVHcloud unveiled 55 new cloud and AI products in one shot — from NVIDIA's newest GPUs to its own in-house language model family, a Python SDK for agent sandboxes, and a native agentic workplace. Reuters reported the launch the same morning. The headline number is the GPUs. The interesting part is the shape of the whole stack: models, inference, agents and infrastructure, all hosted in Europe, from a single provider.

Every fact below comes from OVHcloud's official press release of November 19, 2026, and Reuters' same-day coverage. Capability and capacity figures are OVHcloud's own claims, not independently verified. I haven't tested any of these products hands-on — this is researched analysis, not a review.

The GPUs: Blackwell B300 and Rubin R200 land in Europe

The compute news is straightforward. OVHcloud is adding NVIDIA RTX 6000 Pro, Blackwell B300 and Rubin R200 GPUs to its Bare Metal and Public Cloud offerings. The capacity figure the company quotes is striking: its data centres can supply up to 60,000 B300 GPUs or 35,000 R200 GPUs.

Read that number the way it is written. That is company-stated capacity, not installed inventory and not a count of GPUs already running customer workloads. It is a statement about the scale OVHcloud says it can reach, and it is the number that matters for anyone planning a large training or inference deployment: the ceiling is high, but the press release does not say how much of it is live today. If you are sizing a real workload, ask for the available-now figure before you plan around the headline.

The supporting network work matters as much as the silicon. The VPC stack gains a WAF, VPN, VPC peering, VPC endpoints, an application load balancer, a Global Load Balancer and private DNS, plus BGP Service and BYOIP so customers can announce and keep their own IP ranges. OVHcloud Connect now reaches 40 points of presence worldwide, and object storage gets faster with egress traffic still included. None of that is glamorous. All of it is what decides whether an AI workload in production is actually operable.

Olala: OVHcloud's own LLM family, and the small one is the story

The most developer-interesting announcement may be the least flashy. OVHcloud is launching Olala, an in-house family of large language models built on technology from its Dragon LLM acquisition. Five variants are planned: base, instruction, translation, summarization, and mini.

Olala mini is the one to watch. It is a 7B mixture-of-experts model with only 1B active parameters — and OVHcloud says it runs on a standard CPU. A capable small model that does not need a GPU changes the economics of the most common enterprise AI jobs: summarization, translation, classification, document triage. You can run those on ordinary compute, inside your own perimeter, without renting accelerator time for every request.

The roadmap is aggressive: Olala v1.1, with a 128k context window, is promised by the end of the year, and v2.0 — a 100 to 300 billion parameter family — in early 2027. Treat the dates as a roadmap, not a delivery. The v1.1 and v2.0 models do not exist yet, and the jump from a 7B MoE to a 100–300B family is a large one. The test that matters is not the announcement but whether v1.1 lands in December with real benchmarks and a usable API.

AI Fabric, AI Agents, AI Search: the developer stack — with one honest caveat

This is where the launch becomes a platform story rather than a hardware story:

  • AI Fabric — built with Blade.sh, a Python SDK to launch inference-as-a-service and ephemeral agent sandboxes. The pitch is that you can spin up an isolated environment for an agent in Python, run it, and tear it down.
  • AI Agents — hosts, scales, secures and monitors agents connected to enterprise tools through nearly 480 connectors and MCP servers. OVHcloud says a WebAssembly sandbox spins up in two milliseconds, and the agent only costs money when it is working.
  • AI Search — explore private documents by combining semantic and lexical search across hundreds of millions of documents per collection.
  • AI Endpoints — around a hundred new models, including voice and image models, plus governance tools. With Gladia, the offering extends to speech transcription and voice generation, in real time and on recordings, in more than 100 languages. AI Routers round out the inference layer.

Here is the caveat, and it matters: independent coverage notes that AI Agents and AI Fabric are listed as December alphas. Do not plan a production build on them today as if they were generally available. What OVHcloud announced is the shape of the stack and the intent to ship it; the December alpha is when developers will actually get their hands on it. The right move now is to read the docs as they land, test the sandbox model in the alpha, and keep your production agents where they already run.

Three OVHai research labs back the roadmap — dedicated respectively to LLMs, voice, and ontology-enriched document search — which at least signals this is a sustained research investment, not a one-day press release.

The agentic workplace, and the sovereignty pitch

OVHcloud also announced a native agentic workplace — email, documents and videoconferencing with built-in AI assistants — available in alpha free from today with 5GB per user, data hosted in Europe. Partnerships with Shadow, Qwant and EUSP, the European search index, are part of the same push.

This is the part of the launch that is aimed squarely at a European audience, and it is worth understanding why. The sovereignty argument runs through the whole announcement: services are available in Public Cloud, single-tenant Private Cloud and On-Prem, including with SecNumCloud qualification — the French state certification — and OVHcloud's certified cloud already hosts France's e-invoicing platform. The company describes itself as the only European cloud provider able to operate its services in Europe, North America and Asia. Its own framing, from CPTO Yaniv Fdida: most European AI projects never get beyond the prototype stage because moving into production means juggling several products, several providers, pricing grids and data transfers — and a single provider that masters the whole chain offers an integrated, open, reversible and predictable European alternative.

That is a genuine pitch with a genuine audience. European companies, public bodies and regulated industries have real reasons to want models, inference, agents and GPUs under European jurisdiction. The honest question is the same one that applies to every sovereign-cloud claim: how much of the stack is actually usable today, at what price, and with what latency — and how much is roadmap. The GPU and VPC pieces are concrete. The agent pieces are December alphas. The workplace is an alpha with 5GB per user. The sovereign story is real, but the product maturity is uneven across the 55 items.

Who this fits — and who should wait

This fits European teams and regulated organisations that need AI infrastructure under European hosting and want one provider for GPUs, inference and agents. It fits developers who want to try a CPU-runnable small model for document work — Olala mini is the cheapest experiment in the whole announcement. And it fits anyone already on OVHcloud who has been waiting for a managed inference and agent layer instead of stitching together third-party services.

Wait, or pilot carefully, if: you need AI Agents or AI Fabric in production now — they are December alphas, not live products. If you need a large-model API today, the Olala v2.0 family is an early-2027 promise, and the ~100 new AI Endpoints models need a close look at which models, what pricing and what rate limits actually apply. And if your workloads are already running well on your current GPU cloud, the 60,000-B300 capacity figure alone is not a reason to migrate — it is a reason to get a quote.

The honest limits

  • Capacity is not inventory. Up to 60,000 B300 GPUs is the capacity OVHcloud says its data centres can supply. It is not a count of GPUs installed and available today.
  • Two headline developer products are December alphas. AI Agents and AI Fabric are announced, not generally available. Judge them when the alpha opens.
  • The Olala roadmap is unproven. A 7B MoE that runs on a CPU is useful now; v1.1 by year-end and a 100–300B v2.0 in early 2027 are promises. No public benchmarks for Olala were in the launch material.
  • 55 products is a lot of surface. A launch this wide always mixes mature products with early ones. The VPC, storage and security items look like shipping products; the agent and workplace items are alphas. Read each one on its own merits.
  • Everything here is the vendor's word. Pricing for the new AI services was not in the launch release, and nothing has been independently tested yet.

What to do this week

If you build with AI infrastructure in Europe, the move is a small, targeted pilot — not a migration:

  1. Try Olala mini first. A 7B MoE with 1B active parameters that runs on a standard CPU is the lowest-cost experiment in the announcement. Test it on your real summarization or translation workload and compare quality against the model you use now.
  2. Get a real GPU quote. If you have a training or inference workload, ask OVHcloud for available-now B300 capacity and pricing — not the 60,000 figure, the number you can actually book.
  3. Sign up for the December alphas. AI Fabric and AI Agents are the pieces that decide whether this stack is a platform or a parts list. Get in the alpha queue now so you can test the Python SDK and the sandbox model when it opens.
  4. If you are in Europe, try the agentic workplace alpha. Free, 5GB per user, data hosted in Europe — it costs nothing to see whether the email, docs and videoconferencing plus AI assistants fit a small team.
  5. Check the SecNumCloud angle only if it applies to you. If you work in French public sector or regulated industry, the certified-cloud hosting of the e-invoicing platform is the signal that matters. For everyone else, it is context, not a reason to switch.

Sources: OVHcloud, "OVH takes the AI turn at full speed," press release, November 19, 2026; Reuters coverage of the OVHcloud AI Summit announcement, November 19, 2026 (08:43 UTC). Capacity, capability and roadmap details are OVHcloud's own claims; they have not been independently verified. Full version with FAQ on ToolsDig.

Would you bet a production agent stack on a December alpha, or is the CPU-runnable Olala mini the only piece worth touching this week? Tell me where you'd draw the line.

title: Your leakage audit is reading the wrong clock: 46.6% vs 0.42% on the same 14,781 rows
description:
Ask a team whether their model has seen the future and you will get a boolean. We have one too: a learned_at column that records the moment a prediction was fed back into the training loop. If learned_at is later than the match result, the model learned after the fact. If it is earlier, the model cheated.

That is the whole audit as usually written. It is also wrong, and not by a small margin.

Run it against our production table and 46.6% of the learned rows appear to have learned before the result existed. Anchor the same rows on kickoff time instead, and the number collapses to 0.42%. Same table, same column, same rows — and only one anchor measures leakage rather than measuring your own pipeline's lateness.

Scope: 47,357 predictions, 47,138 graded, 3,807 models, 17,017 matches, 2026-06-21 to 2026-11-19 — ai_predictions and nami_matches, reproducible with the SQL shown.

Step 0: trust the timestamp granularity before the timestamp

An audit of time is an audit of a column, and a column promises less than you think. Check whether a timestamp was observed or bucketed.

SELECT
  count(*)                                                                    AS rows,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE extract(second FROM created_at) = 0)                 AS sec_zero,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE extract(minute FROM created_at) = 0
                     AND extract(second FROM created_at) = 0)                  AS top_of_hour,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE extract(second FROM created_at) = 0
                     AND extract(minute FROM created_at) <> 0)                 AS sec_zero_minute_not
FROM ai_predictions;

rows 47357 | sec_zero 1859 | top_of_hour 1859 | sec_zero_minute_not 0

Read the last two columns together, because that pair is the tell. 1,859 rows have a second component of exactly zero, and not one of them has a non-zero minute. Organic writes would land a zero second on a random minute every sixtieth record — roughly 31 rows. We have zero. A real clock does not produce that distribution; date_trunc or a hand-written literal does.

So created_at holds two populations: 45,498 genuine sub-second writes and 1,859 rows whose timestamp is a bucket. Where they live matters more than that they exist — grouping those rows by month:

2026-06  1859 / 2735     2026-07  0 / 2637     2026-08  0 / 164
2026-09     0 / 9757     2026-10  0 / 21886    2026-11  0 / 10178

Every bucketed row is in the first month — 68% of June, then nothing, ever again. That is an import batch from launch week, not a live defect. What is not fine is any time-series claim spanning June and July: it compares a bucket against a clock, June resolving to the hour and July to the millisecond.

learned_at passes the same test: 14,781 rows, zero on the hour. One column partially synthetic, the other fully observed — indistinguishable without it.

Step 1: assert the invariant that must never break

Before hunting leakage, prove the loop is at least ordered. A learning write cannot precede the prediction it learned from.

SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE learned_at < created_at) AS learned_before_written,
       count(*)                                        AS learned_rows
FROM ai_predictions WHERE learned_at IS NOT NULL;

learned_before_written 0 | learned_rows 14781 — zero violations. That eliminates the most boring bug: a backfill stamping learned_at from a queue's creation time. The offset itself says the loop is a batch job, not a trigger — learned_at - created_at runs p5 449 min, p50 4,095 min (2.8 d), p95 55,834 min. A design cost, not leakage.

Step 2: the anchor choice, where the audit actually fails

Now the comparison everyone writes. Result availability is settled_at; leakage is learned_at < settled_at.

SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE learned_at < settled_at) AS learned_before_settled,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE learned_at >= settled_at) AS after,
       count(*)                                          AS n
FROM ai_predictions
WHERE learned_at IS NOT NULL AND settled_at IS NOT NULL;

learned_before_settled 6,889 (46.62%) | after 7,887 (53.38%) | n 14,776

46.6% of the loop appears to read the answer sheet before it exists — an incident, if you trust the anchor.

Anchor on the match instead of on your own bookkeeping:

SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE p.learned_at < m.match_time)                      AS before_kickoff,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE p.learned_at >= m.match_time
                          AND p.learned_at < m.match_time + interval '3 hour')  AS in_play,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE p.learned_at >= m.match_time + interval '3 hour') AS after,
       count(*)                                                                 AS n
FROM ai_predictions p JOIN nami_matches m ON m.id = p.match_id
WHERE p.learned_at IS NOT NULL;

before_kickoff 62 (0.42%) | in_play 2,280 (15.43%) | after 12,439 (84.15%) | n 14,781

62 rows. 0.42%. The discrepancy is not noise; it is 6,827 rows, and every one is a statement about settled_at, not about learning.

settled_at is when we wrote the grade; grading is async and retried. It drifts:

settled_at - match_time (n=14,776)
  <0           208   1.41%     <- graded before the whistle
  0..6h      7,245  49.03%     <- live path
  6h..7d       948   6.42%
  7d..60d    1,279   8.66%
 60d..90d    5,096  34.49%     <- repair batch

Cleanly bimodal: half the grades land within six hours of the whistle, then a second mass at 60–90 days — 5,096 rows, a third of the learned population, graded two to three months late by a repair job.

Compare accuracy under both anchors:

anchor = settled_at   learn_before_settle 6,889 rows → 63.78%
                      learn_after_settle  7,887 rows → 51.76%
anchor = match_time   before_kickoff         62 rows → 52.46%
                      in_play             2,280 rows → 57.68%
                      after              12,439 rows → 57.33%

The settled-anchored split shows a 12-point accuracy advantage for the "suspicious" group — a smoking gun, if you want one. The kickoff-anchored split shows a 5-point spread across groups of wildly different size, which reads like what it is — nothing.

The 12-point gap is an artefact of when grading happened, not of what the model knew: the 84-day repair batch is dominated by older matches the live path had already abandoned. Sorting on settled_at sorts on operational history — a confound wearing the costume of a finding.

Step 3: the 62 rows that are real, and their fingerprint

0.42% is small but not zero; small numbers deserve rows, not percentages.

models 57 | matches 18 | lead min 435 min (7.25 h), p50 32,480 min (22.6 d), max 112,490 min (78.1 d)

61 of the 62 belong to matches already played; one to a fixture still ahead. Twenty-two days early on average, 78 at the extreme, over 57 models but only 18 matches — a batch touching a few fixtures many times, not a systemic lookahead.

The lead times expose the mechanism: several rows share the exact value 47,850 minutes. Identical offsets to the minute across different models mean one loop computed an offset and applied it to a set. Those records were not learned early, they were stamped from a template.

Bug or mislabelled backfill, the conclusion is not what the boolean suggests: these 62 rows do not corrupt the other 14,719. They contaminate 18 matches — and nothing at all if the learning write refused to run for a fixture that has not kicked off.

Step 4: make the check executable

Rules survive only if they run on every deploy. This audit exits non-zero on a broken invariant — CI or scheduler, no dashboard.

import json, sys, psycopg2

CHECKS = [
    ("learned_before_created", """SELECT count(*) FROM ai_predictions
        WHERE learned_at IS NOT NULL AND learned_at < created_at"""),
    ("learned_before_kickoff", """SELECT count(*) FROM ai_predictions p
        JOIN nami_matches m ON m.id = p.match_id
        WHERE p.learned_at IS NOT NULL AND p.learned_at < m.match_time"""),
    ("graded_before_kickoff", """SELECT count(*) FROM ai_predictions p
        JOIN nami_matches m ON m.id = p.match_id
        WHERE p.settled_at IS NOT NULL AND p.settled_at < m.match_time"""),
]

def run(dsn):
    con = psycopg2.connect(dsn); con.set_session(readonly=True)
    cur, out, failed = con.cursor(), [], False
    for name, sql in CHECKS:                       # every invariant must return 0
        cur.execute(sql); n = cur.fetchone()[0]
        failed |= n > 0
        out.append({"check": name, "actual": n, "ok": n == 0})
    cur.execute("""SELECT count(*) FROM ai_predictions
        WHERE extract(second FROM created_at) = 0
          AND extract(minute FROM created_at) <> 0""")
    stray = cur.fetchone()[0]                      # bucket with a stray minute
    if stray:
        out.append({"check": "granularity_ambiguous", "actual": stray, "ok": False})
        failed = True
    print(json.dumps(out, indent=2)); con.close()
    return 1 if failed else 0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(run("postgresql://soccerdream@127.0.0.1:5433/soccerdream"))

On today's snapshot the kickoff-anchored invariant is the only one that fails — 62 instead of 0. graded_before_kickoff fails too, at 208 rows across 40 matches, some stamped as much as 861 hours ahead of the whistle. A separate defect we did not know we had until the anchor was correct: a grade cannot exist before the thing being graded has been played.

Three rules that transfer

Pick the anchor the model cannot write to. settled_at and learned_at are both our own writes. If the grader is late, the learner looks early. Kickoff time comes from the feed and enters the row before any model touches it — the only clock here a bug cannot rewind. Without one, you are comparing two of your own lies.

Validate granularity before validating differences. The 1,859 bucketed rows were invisible for months because a timestamp is a timestamp. One grouped count — seconds zero, minutes non-zero — separates observation from truncation and tells you which months are safe to average.

Refuse writes that are chronologically impossible. 62 and 208 are both small enough to ignore as a percentage and large enough to poison a fixture. A CHECK constraint costs one line and turns silent contamination into a failed insert. Our auditor now fails the build on both, which is the only reason we found the 208.

The headline number is not 46.6%, and it is not 0.42% either. It is that the difference between them is made entirely of our own operational lag — the part of the pipeline most teams never audit, because they audit the model instead of the clock it is judged against.

title: AWS Revenue Measurement now supports deal-level revenue attribution for AWS Marketplace offers and opportunities
description:
Today, AWS announces deal-level revenue attribution for AWS Revenue Measurement (previously Partner Revenue Measurement) capabilities. AWS Partners can now see how the AWS revenue measured for their products maps to specific AWS Marketplace offers and/or APN Customer Engagements (ACE) opportunities. Until now, partners who implemented AWS Revenue Measurement via Resource Tagging, User Agent String or AWS Marketplace Metering could view aggregated, product-level attributed revenue. With this launch, partners can view attributed revenue by offers and opportunities on the Attributed Revenue dashboard in AWS Partner Central for components hosted in partners' own AWS accounts. Two new capabilities make this possible: Revenue Attribution IDs and Marketplace Revenue Share.

A Revenue Attribution ID is a unique identifier that allows partners to allocate a product's measured AWS revenue to specific offers and opportunities. Partners create a Revenue Attribution ID, associate it with their deals, and enter a monthly attributed revenue allocation percentage for each deal. Partners with SaaS products on AWS Marketplace can automate allocation to offers with Marketplace Revenue Share. Each month, partners enter the percentage of the product's attributed revenue contributed by AWS Marketplace deals in the Revenue Attribution page, and AWS then calculates the attributed revenue for each active offer. Partners can use Revenue Attribution IDs alongside Marketplace Revenue Share to adjust a calculated offer amount or attribute revenue to opportunities for future months. Both capabilities build on AWS Revenue Measurement, so partners can extend their current product-level implementations to gain deal-level insights.

Partners can manage Revenue Attribution IDs and Marketplace Revenue Share in AWS Partner Central or through the AWS Revenue Measurement and Marketplace Revenue Share APIs. AWS Revenue Measurement is generally available in all commercial Regions. To learn more, review the onboarding guide.

title: The transactional outbox pattern in Node.js: never lose an event when the database commits
description:
When a service updates its database and then publishes an event (to a queue, a webhook or another service), there's a gap between the two. If the process crashes after the commit, or the broker is down, the change is saved but the event is lost; publish first instead, and a failed commit leaves an event about something that never happened. The transactional outbox closes the gap: write the change and the event row into an outbox table in the same database transaction, so both are saved or neither is. A separate relay reads the outbox and publishes each event, retrying until it succeeds. Delivery becomes at least once, so consumers must be idempotent. Here's a tested Node.js implementation with the built-in node:sqlite, and an ordering bug worth knowing about.

Why can't you just publish after committing?

In a KYC pipeline, approving a verification has to tell other systems: unlock the account, email the customer, notify compliance. The naive version:

```js title="The naive version"
await db.query("UPDATE verifications SET status = 'approved' WHERE id = $1", [id]);
await broker.publish("verification.approved", { id }); // crash or broker outage here = event lost forever




There's no ordering of these two lines that's safe, because they're two systems with no shared transaction. The outbox makes the event **data in your own database**, where the transaction already covers it.

## Writing the change and the event together



```js title="outbox.mjs: schema and write"
import { DatabaseSync } from "node:sqlite";

export function openDb(path = ":memory:") {
  const db = new DatabaseSync(path);
  db.exec(`
    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS verifications (id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, status TEXT NOT NULL);
    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS outbox (
      id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
      topic TEXT NOT NULL,
      payload TEXT NOT NULL,
      attempts INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
      next_at INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
      sent_at INTEGER
    );`);
  return db;
}

/** Change state and record the event in ONE transaction: both happen or neither does. */
export function approve(db, id) {
  db.exec("BEGIN");
  try {
    db.prepare("UPDATE verifications SET status = 'approved' WHERE id = ?").run(id);
    db.prepare("INSERT INTO outbox (topic, payload) VALUES (?, ?)").run("verification.approved", JSON.stringify({ id }));
    db.exec("COMMIT");
  } catch (error) {
    db.exec("ROLLBACK");
    throw error;
  }
}

The test forces the outbox insert to fail with a trigger, and checks that the status change was rolled back with it: the verification is still pending, with no orphaned half.

The relay, and the ordering bug

```js title="outbox.mjs: relay"
/** Deliver pending events in order. Delivery is at least once: consumers must be idempotent. /
export async function relay(db, publish, { now = Date.now(), batch = 50 } = {}) {
const pending = db.prepare("SELECT * FROM outbox WHERE sent_at IS NULL ORDER BY id LIMIT ?").all(batch);
for (const row of pending) {
if (row.next_at > now) break; // the oldest event is waiting to retry: later ones wait too, or order breaks
try {
await publish(row.topic, JSON.parse(row.payload), row.id);
db.prepare("UPDATE outbox SET sent_at = ? WHERE id = ?").run(now, row.id);
} catch {
const attempts = row.attempts + 1;
db.prepare("UPDATE outbox SET attempts = ?, next_at = ? WHERE id = ?").run(attempts, now + Math.min(2 * attempts, 300) * 1000, row.id);
break; // keep order: don't send later events while an earlier one is failing
}
}
}




Run it on an interval, or wake it after each write. Failed events back off exponentially (2 s, 4 s, 8 s, capped at 5 minutes), like the retries in [retrying LLM API calls](https://aliahmed.si/blog/llm-api-retries-backoff-fallbacks/).

My first version selected only events that were due: `WHERE sent_at IS NULL AND next_at <= ?`. The test caught what that does. Event 1 fails and is scheduled for a retry; on the next pass it isn't due yet, so the query skips it and **sends event 2 first**. For events such as "approved" followed by "revoked", that's a real bug: a consumer would end up with the wrong final state. The fixed relay reads pending events in order and **stops at the first one that isn't due**. The test:



```js title="outbox.test.mjs"
await relay(db, publish, { now: 1000 }); // v1 fails: broker down
assert.deepEqual(sent, []); // v2 waits behind it

fail = false;
await relay(db, publish, { now: 2000 }); // v1's retry isn't due until 3000
assert.deepEqual(sent, []); // the buggy version sent v2 here

await relay(db, publish, { now: 3000 });
assert.deepEqual(sent, ["1:v1", "2:v2"]);

Strict global order costs throughput: one stuck event blocks everything behind it. Usually you only need order per entity (per verification, per account). Then keep a key on each row and only block events with the same key.

Why must consumers be idempotent?

The relay can publish an event and crash before marking it sent. On restart it publishes it again. That's unavoidable without a transaction spanning your database and the broker, so the outbox gives at least once delivery. Include the outbox id in what you publish (the relay passes it as the third argument), and let consumers skip IDs they've processed, as in idempotent webhooks in Node.js.

Running it in production

  • Several relay workers: in Postgres, claim rows with SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED so two workers don't send the same batch. Combined with per-key ordering, each key should be handled by one worker at a time.
  • Clean up: delete or archive sent rows after a few days, or the table grows forever.
  • Alert on age: the age of the oldest unsent event is the metric that matters. If it keeps growing, something downstream is broken. The same idea drives error budget burn-rate alerts.
  • Change data capture (reading the database's log with a tool such as Debezium) can replace the polling relay at higher volume; the outbox table stays the same.

Summary

  • Updating a database and publishing an event are two systems; doing both directly loses events.
  • Write the change and the event in one transaction; a relay publishes from the outbox table.
  • Stop at the first event that isn't due, or a retry lets later events overtake it.
  • Delivery is at least once: pass an event ID and make consumers idempotent.

title: Response-Relevant Information Is Not Sufficient for Neural Training-State Equivalence
description:
arXiv:2611.23245v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Response-relevant information is not sufficient evidence that two neural networks are in the same training state. We define training-state equivalence operationally: two checkpoints are equivalent, relative to an intervention family and horizon, if they respond alike when training is perturbed and continues. On fresh runs of a one-layer transformer learning modular addition, response to a weight-decay pulse is highly reproducible relative to between-checkpoint differences (rho_state = 0.934 at 500 steps), establishing the target as measurable. Fifteen descriptors of weight spectra, representation geometry and optimiser geometry carry within-run response-relevant information beyond weight norm and loss on a development dataset, predicting held-out response deviation across seed blocks. But their apparent 16.1% advantage at matching checkpoints by future response does not separate from a conditional placebo preserving each descriptor's fitted dependence on the conventional observables, and a calibrated positive control makes simple insensitivity an unlikely explanation. Information a decoder can extract need not be organised in the pairwise geometry that similarity judgments require.

title: SQL in Depth: Interactive WASM SQLite 3 Workbench & Database Internals from First Principles
description:
Most SQL tutorials stop at syntax (JOIN, GROUP BY, window functions) and leave you guessing when a real production query suddenly slows down.

Understanding why a query is slow means understanding how the database engine actually parses, plans, indexes, and executes it. Passive reading about B-Trees, query plans, and transaction isolation only gets you so far—it clicks much faster when you can run queries and watch the internals step by step.

That's why I built SQL in Depth, a free, open-source interactive textbook covering SQL and database internals from first principles. Everything runs right in the browser with no accounts, no paywalls, and no local DB setup.

  • Try it live: sql-in-depth.vedgupta.in
  • Source code on GitHub: github.com/innovatorved/sql-in-depth

What's Inside

  • Interactive WASM SQLite 3 Workbench — write and run real SQLite 3 queries directly in the browser alongside each lesson.
  • Table-Level Relational Visualizer — watch how joins, filters, groupings, and transformations operate on actual rows step by step.
  • 180 Structured Units — from relational algebra and core SQL semantics to indexing, query optimization, storage internals, and transactions.
  • 36 Interactive Simulators — experiment hands-on with database internals and see how design trade-offs behave.

Feedback & Contributions

If you're preparing for backend interviews, sharpening your SQL fundamentals, or curious about how relational engines work under the hood, give it a spin!

If you find it useful, a star on GitHub helps others discover it—and issues, PRs, or ideas for new simulators are always welcome in the comments or on GitHub.

title: GridForge: An Open Physics-Informed Digital Twin and Benchmark Suite for UK 11 kV Underground Distribution Cables
description:
arXiv:2611.23241v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The UK distribution-cable monitoring sector is data-rich but framework-poor: each Distribution Network Operator (DNO) collects megabytes of telemetry per asset per day, but there is no public benchmark dataset, no shared reference model, and no commonly agreed evaluation protocol for benchmarking sectoral, data-intensive models for operational decision support; notably for maintenance planning and prioritisation. We address this gap with GridForge, an open-source physics-informed digital twin and benchmark suite for fault diagnosis and prediction, integrating four building blocks: (i) a verified steady state and transient thermal model based on IEC 60287 and IEC 60853; (ii) a calibrated synthetic dataset of 64 cables (covering 320 cable-years) representing four canonical UK 11 kV thermal archetypes and four condition modes; (iii) a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) surrogate that satisfies the algebraic balance defined by IEC 60287 during training and reaches an RMSE of 0.148 {\deg}C on an independent held out set against the reference analytical oracle; and (iv) a five-task benchmark suite that includes three reference baseline models (pure physics, gradient-boosted trees, and the PINN). All numerical parameters are sourced from public standards, the code is licensed under the MIT licence, and the trained PINN converges in only two minutes (as run on the computing platform in Section 10.1), enabling independent verification by DNO engineering and research practitioners. At present only the virtual-sensor task (T4) discriminates between the reference baselines; the other tasks tie or are undefined on this test split, so extending the baselines with task-specific logic is a priority future enhancement. For open validation, the dataset, test sets and models are made available at https://github.com/mlily2024/Gridforge

title: Toward Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Neural AC Power Flow
description:
arXiv:2611.23729v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Growing uncertainty in power system operations from renewables integration, extreme weather, and data center loads challenges the reliability of traditional power flow solvers at scale. Machine learning-based proxies are a potentially promising alternative, but the prohibitive cost of generating training data for large grids makes out-of-distribution generalization a key capability for deployment; currently, models trained on small grids lack that capability. In this work, we systematically evaluate how physics-informed losses, multi-grid training, and perturbation-based data augmentation improve the zero-shot transfer of three graph neural network-based power flow models from smaller systems to a larger, unseen 500-bus system. We find that (1) physics-informed losses improve transfer relative to purely supervised objectives; (2) multi-grid training on smaller systems matches the best single grid but does not close the gap to target-grid training; (3) perturbation-based augmentation on edge attributes improves transfer by up to 54.6%; and (4) random line/generator dropout does not consistently improve performance.
