title: When does reserved GPU capacity beat on-demand pricing?
description:
Reserved GPU capacity beats on-demand once your utilization over the term exceeds the reserved rate divided by the on-demand rate: 63.0% of all hours for an 8 x NVIDIA H100 machine on a 1-year Amazon EC2 Instance Savings Plan. Nodus lists the H100 SXM at $2.60/hr on its pricing page, a GPU rate below even AWS's 3-year plan per GPU-hour, and Nodus Reserved Compute (Beta) quotes dedicated capacity for a steady floor. Commit only the GPUs that stay busy above the line and run the rest on demand.

How do you calculate the break-even utilization for reserved GPUs?

Divide the reserved rate by the on-demand rate you would otherwise pay. The answer is the fraction of the term's hours you must actually use for the commitment to cost less.

The reasoning is short. A commitment bills every hour of the term, used or not. On-demand bills only the hours you run. So reserved wins when reserved rate x all hours < on-demand rate x used hours, which rearranges to:

break-even utilization = reserved rate / on-demand rate
effective reserved rate = reserved rate / your utilization

The second line is the one people skip. A $4.33 commitment that you use half the time really costs $8.67 per hour of work. That is more than the $6.88 on-demand rate it was meant to beat.

We worked this on AWS because it publishes every commitment rate for the same machine. From the official AWS price list for us-east-1, a p5.48xlarge costs $55.04 per hour on demand, or $6.88 per GPU-hour.

The 1-year EC2 Instance Savings Plan with no upfront payment is $34.6752 per hour, or $4.33 per GPU-hour. The break-even is 34.6752 / 55.04 = 0.630. We re-checked it the other way: 55.04 x 0.63 = 34.6752.

Option (8 x H100, AWS us-east-1) Per instance-hour Per GPU-hour Break-even utilization
On-demand $55.04 $6.88 n/a
EC2 Capacity Block $47.757 $5.97 86.8%
Compute Savings Plan, 1 year, no upfront $43.344 $5.42 78.8%
EC2 Instance Savings Plan, 1 year, no upfront $34.6752 $4.33 63.0%
EC2 Instance Savings Plan, 3 years, no upfront $23.77728 $2.97 43.2%

Prices checked November 18, 2026 (this applies to every price in this post). AWS rates come from the AWS EC2 on-demand price list, the AWS Compute Savings Plans price list file for us-east-1 (which also carries EC2 Instance Savings Plan rates) and the EC2 Capacity Blocks pricing page. Per GPU-hour is the instance rate divided by 8, rounded to cents. Linux, no operating system fee.


The deeper the discount and the longer the term, the less of the year you need to fill.

What does a year of one 8 x H100 machine cost at each utilization?

A commitment is a flat line and on-demand is a slope, so the only question is where your real usage lands. A full year is 8,760 hours (AWS defines a Savings Plan year as 365 days). The 1-year EC2 Instance Savings Plan costs $34.6752 x 8,760 = $303,754.75 for the year. The 3-year plan costs $23.77728 x 8,760 = $208,288.97 per year, for three years.

Utilization over the year On-demand cost 1-year plan 3-year plan, per year
0% $0.00 $303,754.75 $208,288.97
20% $96,430.08 $303,754.75 $208,288.97
40% $192,860.16 $303,754.75 $208,288.97
60% $289,290.24 $303,754.75 $208,288.97
80% $385,720.32 $303,754.75 $208,288.97
100% $482,150.40 $303,754.75 $208,288.97

On-demand is $55.04 x 8,760 x utilization. At 60% the machine is still cheaper on demand, by $14,464.51. At 80% the 1-year plan saves $81,965.57.


On-demand crosses the 1-year line at 63.0% utilization and the 3-year line at 43.2%.

Utilization here means hours of the whole year, nights and weekends included. A team that runs a training box 10 hours a day on weekdays uses 50 of 168 weekly hours, which is 29.8%. That team should not sign either plan for that machine.

Should you reserve your peak or your floor?

Reserve the floor. Split your fleet into tiers by how busy each GPU is across the term, commit only the tiers above break-even, and run the rest on demand or on spot.

Here is a worked example with the AWS per-GPU rates above. A team serves a model on 8 H100s around the clock. It adds 8 more H100s for weekday business hours, 10 hours a day, 5 days a week. The second tier runs 8 x 8,760 x 50 / 168 = 20,857.14 GPU-hours a year.

Strategy First 8 GPUs (100% busy) Second 8 GPUs (29.8% busy) Year total
Everything on demand $482,150.40 $143,497.14 $625,647.54
Reserve all 16 (1-year plan) $303,754.75 $303,754.75 $607,509.50
Reserve the floor, peak on demand $303,754.75 $143,497.14 $447,251.89
Reserve the floor, peak on Nodus at $2.60 $303,754.75 $54,228.57 $357,983.32

The floor tier saves $178,395.65 by committing. The peak tier would waste $160,257.61 if you committed it too, which is why reserving everything barely beats paying list price. The last row prices the peak hours at the H100 SXM rate listed on the Nodus pricing page: 20,857.14 x $2.60. GPU rates only; the AWS rate includes the instance's CPUs, memory and networking, so treat that row as a rate comparison, not a like-for-like quote.


Committing the always-busy floor saves money; committing the peak gives most of it back.

Is reserved capacity always cheaper per hour than on-demand?

No. Some reservations cost more per GPU-hour than the same vendor's on-demand rate, because you are buying guaranteed, co-located capacity for fixed dates rather than a discount.

Lambda's pricing page lists 1-Click Clusters of 16 H100s for terms of 2 weeks to 1 year at $6.16 per GPU-hour, while an on-demand 8 x H100 instance is $4.59 per GPU-hour.

That ratio is 134.2%, so on rate alone the cluster never breaks even. You buy it for a cluster of 16 or more GPUs held for a fixed term, not for a lower rate. The AWS Capacity Blocks documentation describes the same trade: blocks are for GPUs "for days or weeks at a time", placed close together in EC2 UltraClusters. The Capacity Blocks pricing page adds that the reservation fee is charged up front when you schedule it.

Lambda also says on that page to contact them "for reserved capacity at our lowest prices". Runpod's pricing page and the Nebius prices page likewise route reserved and commitment pricing through sales. Their long-term rates are not published, so we have not priced them here.

What is the difference between spot instances and reserved instances?

They sit at opposite ends of the same trade. Spot is the cheapest per hour with no commitment, but the provider can take the machine back. Reserved costs a commitment and bills every hour, but the capacity is yours for the term.

AWS advertises Spot Instances at up to 90% off on-demand prices. Spot fits interruptible work that checkpoints, such as training and batch inference.

Reserved fits the always-busy floor: production inference, a long training run with a fixed start date. On-demand covers the space between. Our spot vs on-demand guide works through the rework math for spot, so we do not repeat it here.

Which AWS commitment should you pick for GPUs?

Pick the one whose flexibility matches what you might change. AWS's Savings Plans guide says EC2 Instance Savings Plans commit you to one instance family in one region, while Compute Savings Plans apply regardless of family, size or region. For p5 that flexibility is priced in: the 1-year Compute plan breaks even at 78.8%, against 63.0% for the instance plan.

A 3-year plan drops the line to 43.2%, but it locks one GPU generation for three years. Sign it only if you are confident you will still want that hardware in year three. If you mostly want to stop overpaying AWS list rates, our cheaper AWS alternatives post compares on-demand H100 rates across platforms.

Where does Nodus fit for steady and bursty load?

We cover both halves of the floor-and-peak split. For the peak, Nodus Jobs run your command on demand, with logs, outputs, spending limits and recovery, and the H100 SXM is listed at $2.60/hr on the Nodus pricing page. That is below the $2.97 per GPU-hour of AWS's 3-year EC2 Instance Savings Plan, so for GPU rate alone no AWS commitment in the table beats it at any utilization.

For the floor, Nodus Reserved Compute (Beta) supplies dedicated GPU capacity for your configuration and reservation window. You describe the GPU model, quantity, duration, location and start timing. Nodus reviews each request and sends a proposal covering availability, price, access and delivery. Submitting a request does not reserve hardware or authorize payment.

The Reserved Compute page also shows a planning index built only from providers' published reservation rates for the exact term you select, with the range and provider count.

It is a Beta and a quote, not a self-serve checkout. If you need a price this minute, use the published commitments above.

FAQ

How do I measure my utilization before committing?

Take at least a few weeks of billing or scheduler data for the exact GPU type, and divide GPU-hours used by GPU-hours in the period. Count nights and weekends. If the number moves a lot week to week, commit only to the lowest steady level.

Does paying upfront change the break-even?

Yes, slightly. In the same AWS file, the 1-year EC2 Instance Savings Plan for p5.48xlarge is $34.6752 per hour with no upfront. It drops to $33.024 partial upfront and $32.36352 all upfront, so more cash up front lowers the line a little.

Can I request a single GPU through Nodus Reserved Compute?

Yes. The Reserved Compute guide says you can request a single GPU, and the final offer confirms how GPUs are arranged across servers. The console request form accepts durations up to 365 days.

What if my load grows after I commit?

Growth is the easy case: the commitment keeps covering the floor and new load runs on demand until it proves steady. Shrinking is the costly case, because the commitment bills every hour whether or not you use it. Our cost per finished job post shows how idle hours inflate the real bill.

Originally published on the Nodus blog.

title: 手游团队出海中东：合规采购大模型 API 的要点
description:
以下是关于海外 AI Token 服务的一份工作清单，来自 2026 年我们协助手游团队拓展中东时的观察。

四周上线节奏

第 1 周：确定路径（自有帐号或统一 API），准备企业资料；第 2 周：接入测试项目，记录 Token 用量，对比两三个模型；第 3 周：设置限额、报警和账单联系人；第 4 周：把一个生产功能切过去，对照预算复盘单次请求成本。

怎么估算 Token 预算

从真实流量出发，而不是只看官方价目表。按功能统计每次请求的平均输入和输出 Token，乘以预计的月请求量，再给重试和长提示词留出余量。输出 Token 通常比输入 Token 贵，生成长回答的功能要重点评估。上线一个月后用真实数据重新核算。

数据与合规检查

把客户数据发给任何模型之前，先看厂商条款里关于数据保留和训练的规定、数据在哪个地区处理，以及企业自己在中东的合规义务。能不放个人信息就不放，并把决定记录下来。采购和结算要走经得起检查的合规渠道。

两条接入路径

一是以企业或其海外主体名义开通模型原厂或企业级帐号，帐号归企业自己所有；二是通过合规聚合通道统一接入 API，一把密钥调用多个模型，减少多平台来回切换。熊猫出海两种方式都可以协助，详见：海外 AI Token 服务（TaaS）。

什么是 Token 即服务（TaaS）

GPT、Claude、Gemini 等大模型以 Token 作为处理文本、代码和图像的基本单位。海外 AI Token 服务（Token as a Service，TaaS）就是以 Token 为计价和交付单位的 AI 推理服务。对面向中东做产品的手游团队来说，关键不是“买到一个接口”，而是能稳定、合规地用上需要的模型，并把帐号、用量和结算管清楚。

用量管控与财务对账

按密钥或项目设置限额，开发和生产环境分开用不同密钥，日消耗超过阈值就报警。财务需要按模型、按项目的月度用量汇总，技术需要调用日志排查问题，上线前把两边需求都定下来，避免程序死循环变成意外账单。

按任务选模型

不是每个请求都需要最大的模型。分类、路由和短文本抽取，小模型往往就够用，成本也低；复杂推理和长文写作才值得用旗舰模型。统一 API 让手游团队可以用同一批提示词对比多个模型，按任务而不是按厂商来选。

小结

计划要小、要写下来、要能衡量。先做好上面的基础，30 天后复盘，再放大有效的部分。

作者：熊猫出海 PandaWM（香港团队）。业务包括 GEO/AI 搜索优化、Facebook/Google/TikTok 及约 20 个小众平台广告开户与代投、多语言网站、AiChatSale，以及只服务海外商户的加密支付网关。

title: FACT: Fixed-Budget Allocation and Cross-Step Training for Speculative Decoding
description:
arXiv:2611.23463v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates language-model generation by verifying multiple draft tokens in a single target-model pass. However, better draft predictions and longer accepted continuations do not necessarily produce faster generation. To examine this gap, we present FACT (Fixed-Budget Allocation and Cross-Step Training), an experimental framework for studying how drafter training, candidate allocation, and execution conditions jointly affect acceptance and latency. Using a lightweight feature-prediction drafter with a frozen Llama-3-8B-Instruct target under greedy decoding, we first examine how training translates into accepted tokens. Backpropagating through predicted-feature rollouts with greater weight on early steps improves acceptance by 15-24% over uniformly weighted detached training, yet average rollout proxy cross-entropy does not reliably rank drafters by acceptance. Beyond prediction quality, the placement of draft candidates also matters: with a fixed 256-node budget and matched per-depth widths, replacing static allocation with confidence-guided allocation increases speedup over autoregressive decoding from $1.46\times$ to $2.02\times$ on HumanEval and from $1.31\times$ to $1.75\times$ on MT-Bench. This allocation benefit extends to an independently trained drafter, but stronger training does not consistently amplify it, showing that the two improvements do not necessarily reinforce each other. Even these speed gains depend on execution conditions: changing only host-thread settings can nearly eliminate speedup without changing acceptance. Together, these findings show why training and allocation must be evaluated jointly using both acceptance and end-to-end latency under controlled execution conditions.

title: Microsite Development
description:
Microsite Development: A Strategic Approach to Targeted Engagement

Microsite development has emerged as a crucial strategy for businesses seeking to create targeted, engaging experiences for their audience. However, the use of standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms often falls short of achieving the desired outcomes. These pre-designed solutions lack the customization and specificity required to resonate with a particular segment of users, ultimately leading to a lackluster user experience and diminished conversion rates.

The primary reason for the ineffectiveness of generic templates in microsite development lies in their inability to account for the unique needs, preferences, and behaviors of the target audience. Each user segment has distinct characteristics, pain points, and motivations that must be addressed through a tailored approach. By adopting a one-size-fits-all strategy, businesses risk alienating potential customers and failing to capitalize on valuable opportunities.

From an engineering standpoint, successful microsite development hinges on a deep understanding of the target audience, as well as the ability to design and implement customized solutions that cater to their specific requirements. The following takeaways highlight key considerations for effective microsite development:

  • Audience-centric design: Microsites should be designed with a clear understanding of the target audience's needs, preferences, and behaviors. This involves conducting thorough research and analysis to identify the unique characteristics and pain points of the user segment.
  • Customized user experience: A tailored user experience is essential for creating an engaging and effective microsite. This can be achieved through the use of personalized content, interactive elements, and intuitive navigation that guides the user through a seamless journey.
  • Data-driven optimization: Microsite development should be informed by data and analytics, allowing businesses to refine and optimize their strategy based on user feedback and performance metrics. This involves continuously monitoring user behavior, identifying areas for improvement, and implementing data-driven enhancements to maximize conversion rates and overall engagement.

By adopting a strategic approach to microsite development, businesses can create targeted, engaging experiences that resonate with their audience and drive meaningful results. Vareli breaks this down in the complete analysis:
https://vareli.info/blog/microsite-development

title: Seeing What Still Holds: How Waiting Control Changes Cooperative Recovery
description:
arXiv:2611.22368v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Changing the holding reference during a fixed-duration wait can reverse the ranking of visual recovery methods. We introduce AuditEmbodied, a paired execution and trajectory evaluation framework that independently varies holding references and waiting duration while keeping recovery executors frozen. A 960-execution factorial on 20 initialization seeds compares CAD-feedback and landmark-based recovery from identical post-wait physical states within each holding and waiting condition. Protected completion requires successful recovery under the declared execution constraints. At a 1 s wait with registered wrist references, their protected completion counts change from 6/40 versus 19/40 under registered holding to 34/40 versus 22/40 under position-only holding. Trajectory analysis localizes the main separation to grasp formation: small observation-time target residuals precede large tracking errors. Joint diagnostics and controlled interventions characterize persistent tracking constraints. On fresh seeds, gradual position reanchoring improves CAD recovery's long-wait completion by 42.5 percentage points and reduces mean complete recovery time by 6.06 s relative to registered holding. Additional evaluations with pretrained policies, handover, and a mass-matched geometry characterize holding-reference sensitivity across executors and physical regimes. These findings establish holding reference as an explicit evaluation condition for comparing visual recovery performance.

title: 13 free React components with motion, and the small rules that made them feel right
description:
We build websites for a living, and most of the motion we ship ends up locked inside client projects. So we pulled thirteen of our favourite patterns out, cleaned them up and put them online for free. They're called Republic UI, they're MIT licensed, and every one installs with a single shadcn command.

You can try them all at republicmarketing.co.uk/ui.

What's in the set

  • Slat Shutter Hero. Scroll, and the cover photo splits into vertical slats that part from the centre outwards to reveal a second scene. The headline hands over line by line.
  • Photo Deck. A stack of prints you can drag, flick, or step through with the arrows and keyboard. Going back flies the last print in from the left instead of just swapping it.
  • Timeline Scrubber. Drag along a month ruler and the photos wipe in the direction you move, while the temperature rolls on digit reels.
  • Testimonial Reel. A quote, a portrait that slides up like a reel and a stat that rolls like an odometer.
  • Morph Island. A status pill that morphs from idle to uploading, done and a full preview.
  • Fan Gallery. Photo cards on an arc. Drag it, flick it, tap a side card or use the keys.
  • Plus a facts hero, feature rows with live UI, a bento of mini interfaces, a torn-paper portrait scroll, a scroll-fill headline, a sector wheel and a scattered-photo about section.

Install

Add the registry to your components.json:

"registries": {
  "@republic": "https://www.republicmarketing.co.uk/ui/r/{name}.json"
}

Then add whatever you need:

npx shadcn@latest add @republic/fan-gallery

Each component is one self-contained file. The only dependencies are motion, clsx, tailwind-merge and, for a few, lucide-react.

Five rules we kept coming back to

These came out of client feedback over the years, and they made more difference than any single effect.

1. Numbers roll, they never cross-fade. If a figure changes, it moves on digit reels, fast at first and slow to land. Two values fading over each other reads as a glitch.

2. One focal point at a time. When a new element takes over, the old one leaves properly. Dimmed leftovers peeking from the edge make a small space feel crowded.

3. One easing curve, used everywhere. Most of the set uses cubic-bezier(0.42, 0, 0, 1). Things that share a curve feel like they belong to the same product.

4. Every interaction has a keyboard path. The deck, the timeline and the fan all work with arrow keys, and the timeline also takes Home and End. Autoplay pauses on hover and only runs while the component is on screen.

5. Test the boring cases. Rapid clicks, dragging a few pixels and letting go, resizing the window mid-animation, scrolling back up. Most of our fixes came from these, not from the happy path.

Real images, not grey boxes

Every demo uses original images made for the set, so the components look the way they will in a real build. The images are free to use with the components.

Links

  • Live demos and install commands: republicmarketing.co.uk/ui
  • Source on GitHub: rm-sjent/republic-ui
  • Also on 21st.dev: 21st.dev/@sajad

If you use one in a project, I'd love to see it. And if you want a whole site built with this level of care, that's what we do at Republic Marketing, a web design agency in London and Birmingham.

title: Your IP Is Clean. The Other 253 Addresses in Its /24 Decide Your Fate.
description:
You buy a proxy, check the address, and every score comes back green. Then an account registered through it is suspended within a day, and the IP still scores green afterwards.

The address was never the unit being judged. The prefix was.

Three scopes that get confused

An IP reputation lookup answers one narrow question about a single 32-bit number. What a target site enforces is usually decided at a coarser scope, because that is where abuse is cheap to detect and expensive to launder.

Scope Unit Who decides What a block means
Address One IP That site's own rules This endpoint is burned
Prefix /24 or the RIR allocation Abuse feeds, CDN rule sets Everyone inside inherits it
ASN Entire network Onboarding and KYC teams The whole provider is filtered

A green score is sampled at the first scope. Enforcement frequently happens at the second. That gap is the whole problem.

Why one bad tenant lands on you

Three paths carry the penalty, and none of them requires you to have done anything.

Feed replication. An abuse feed records one address for sending junk. Consumers of that feed do not always apply it as a single host — many apply it to the covering /24, because spam operations rotate addresses inside a prefix they control. One entry becomes 256.

Registration clustering. RDAP and WHOIS describe the block as one allocation with one organisation, one abuse contact, one netname. Risk engines read that as a unit and inherit the allocation's history as context for each address inside it.

Observed density. No blocklist is needed. The target counts: four hundred new accounts, two hundred and fifty-six addresses, one TLS fingerprint, one inter-arrival distribution. The neighbourhood is guilty by statistics rather than by list.

The third path is the one that catches people with genuinely clean addresses. Nothing to appeal, no record to remove.

Shared, segment-dedicated, full-dedicated

Vendors use these words loosely. The distinction that matters is how many strangers sit inside your /24.

Plan style Addresses you use Strangers in your /24 What you inherit
Shared pool A few, rotating Up to 253 Every tenant's history and behaviour
Segment dedicated A slice of a prefix Usually 2 to 4 tenants Their history, diluted
Full dedicated A /24 or larger None, unless self-inflicted Only your own patterns

"One dedicated IP" sits in the first row. A dedicated address is not a dedicated neighbourhood, and that is where most expectations break.

Counting your neighbours

Reverse DNS is a passive way to see who else is announced in the block: hosting providers publish PTR records in bulk, residential blocks mostly do not. No packets reach the addresses themselves.

import ipaddress, socket
from collections import Counter
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

def ptr(ip):
    try:
        return str(ip), socket.gethostbyaddr(str(ip))[0]
    except (socket.herror, socket.gaierror):
        return str(ip), None

addr = ipaddress.ip_address("203.0.113.57")
net = ipaddress.ip_network(f"{addr}/24", strict=False)
sample = list(net.hosts())[:64]          # never sweep a whole /24

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=16) as pool:
    rows = list(pool.map(ptr, sample))

named = [r for r in rows if r[1]]
print(f"{len(named)}/{len(rows)} sampled addresses publish PTR")
for ip, name in named[:10]:
    print(ip, "->", name)

# Last two labels usually identify the operator, not the customer.
tails = Counter(".".join(n.split(".")[-2:]) for _, n in named)
print(tails.most_common(5))

Two numbers matter in the output. The share that resolves tells you whether this is a hosting block or a residential one. The distinct tails tell you how many operators are diluted into one prefix.

Reading the count correctly

High density is not automatically bad. A hosting /24 with two hundred PTR records is a normal web host and is treated as one. A residential /24 with two hundred PTR records is a farm, and feeds learn it fast.

Low density is not automatically good either. A /24 where nothing resolves may be freshly allocated, or may be a sinkhole operated by someone who never bothered with reverse DNS. Ask for the allocation date from RDAP when the picture is ambiguous.

What you are looking for is one specific combination: many operators inside one prefix, recent allocation, and a residential or mixed-use label. That profile is where collateral damage concentrates.

Common mistakes

  • Trusting an address-level score as a verdict on the neighbourhood. It is one sample of 256.
  • Buying "dedicated IP" and expecting a dedicated prefix. You have one address and up to 253 strangers.
  • Treating PTR density as a purity signal in both directions. Direction depends on the hosting label.
  • Testing one target and concluding the block is fine. Different consumers apply different granularities.
  • Switching vendors that resell the same upstream ASN — same neighbourhood, same result, new invoice.

FAQ

Does a clean score mean I will not get blocked?
No. It means the single address is not on the lists that checker reads. Prefix-level feeds, behavioural density, and site-specific rules are outside its scope.

Can I clean up a dirty prefix?
Not the other tenants — you have no authority over them. You change scope: move to a segment or a full /24, or reduce the behaviour that made the block statistically attractive.

Why does the same IP work on one site and fail on another?
Different feeds with different granularity. One site applies the entry to a single host, the next applies it to the covering /24 and you inherit it without appearing anywhere.

Are residential IPs safer because they look human?
Not by themselves. Residential prefixes are dense by design, and carrier-grade NAT hides the offender inside a shared address, so feeds list those blocks quickly. The label helps; the density still counts.

If you want to see your own neighbourhood before a target does, start by reading the allocation — the Chinese walkthrough of neighbour effect and how to check it is at socks5ip.com.cn. For the address-level checks that the prefix view sits on top of, use the free tools at socks5ip.com.cn and compare the two answers; when they disagree, the prefix is the one that gets enforced.

title: Mastering Modern Async SQLAlchemy 2.0 & Alembic in Python (A Pragmatic Guide)
description:
If you have worked with Python ORMs over the last decade, you remember the traditional SQLAlchemy 1.x patterns: query objects attached to sessions, string-based relationships, implicit lazy loading, and blocking I/O calls that froze your async event loop.

With SQLAlchemy 2.0, the entire ecosystem went through a massive generational overhaul. It brought first-class async support, full type safety conforming to PEP 484, and a unified query syntax built around select().

When combined with Alembic for schema migrations, it gives Python backends a robust, enterprise-grade data layer.

💡 Note: This article is an adapted architectural summary. For the exhaustive, step-by-step masterclass covering deep engine configurations, transaction isolation, and pool tuning, read the original guide: Complete Guide to SQLAlchemy 2.0 and Alembic in Python (Modern Async ORM) on taha-heidaryfard.ir.

1. What Makes SQLAlchemy 2.0 Different?

In legacy SQLAlchemy 1.4, writing queries often looked like this:

# Legacy 1.x style (deprecated in 2.0)
user = session.query(User).filter(User.email == "dev@example.com").first()

SQLAlchemy 2.0 eliminates session.query() in favor of standard SQL-like expressions using select(). This ensures consistent query building across ORM entities and Core tables, full static analysis support for mypy and Pyright, and native async execution:

# Modern 2.0 style
stmt = select(User).where(User.email == "dev@example.com")
result = await session.execute(stmt)
user = result.scalar_one_or_none()

2. Setting Up an Async Engine & Session

To work asynchronously with PostgreSQL (or MySQL/SQLite), you need an asynchronous DB driver like asyncpg:

pip install sqlalchemy[asyncio] asyncpg alembic

Here is the production-ready configuration for initializing your asynchronous session factory:

from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import (
    AsyncSession,
    async_sessionmaker,
    create_async_engine
)
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase

DATABASE_URL = "postgresql+asyncpg://postgres:secret@localhost:5432/production_db"

engine = create_async_engine(
    DATABASE_URL,
    echo=False,
    pool_size=10,
    max_overflow=20,
    pool_pre_ping=True,
)

AsyncSessionLocal = async_sessionmaker(
    bind=engine,
    class_=AsyncSession,
    expire_on_commit=False,  # CRITICAL for async workflows!
    autoflush=False
)

class Base(DeclarativeBase):
    pass

Why expire_on_commit=False is Mandatory in Async

In synchronous SQLAlchemy, after you commit a session, SQLAlchemy expires all model attributes so they re-fetch fresh state on the next read. In an async environment, trying to read an expired attribute triggers implicit synchronous lazy-loading, which raises an asyncio greenlet error. Setting expire_on_commit=False avoids this entirely.

3. Defining Models with Mapped and mapped_column

SQLAlchemy 2.0 introduces fully typed declarative models:

from datetime import datetime
from typing import Optional, List
from sqlalchemy import String, ForeignKey, func
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column, relationship

class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = "users"

    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True, autoincrement=True)
    username: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(50), unique=True, index=True)
    email: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(255), unique=True)
    created_at: Mapped[datetime] = mapped_column(server_default=func.now())

    # 1-to-Many Relationship
    posts: Mapped[List["Post"]] = relationship(
        back_populates="author",
        cascade="all, delete-orphan"
    )

class Post(Base):
    __tablename__ = "posts"

    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    title: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(200))
    content: Mapped[str]
    author_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("users.id", ondelete="CASCADE"))

    author: Mapped["User"] = relationship(back_populates="posts")

Your IDE now understands the exact Python types of user.id, user.username, and user.created_at without external stub plugins!

4. Eager Loading in Async (Preventing N+1 Queries)

Because lazy loading does not work asynchronously without special wrappers, you must explicitly declare how relationships are fetched. The best approach is selectinload():

from sqlalchemy.orm import selectinload

async def get_user_with_posts(session: AsyncSession, user_id: int) -> Optional[User]:
    stmt = (
        select(User)
        .where(User.id == user_id)
        .options(selectinload(User.posts))
    )
    result = await session.execute(stmt)
    return result.scalar_one_or_none()

selectinload executes a fast, indexed secondary SELECT ... WHERE user_id IN (...), preventing both Cartesian explosion (from joinedload) and lazy loading failures.

5. Integrating Alembic with Async SQLAlchemy

When running alembic init -t async migrations, Alembic creates an async-compatible template. In your migrations/env.py, simply wire up your Base.metadata:

from myapp.database import Base, DATABASE_URL
target_metadata = Base.metadata

Then generate and apply migrations seamlessly:

# Auto-generate migration script from model changes
alembic revision --autogenerate -m "create users and posts tables"

# Apply to database
alembic upgrade head

Deep-Dive & Next Steps

Adopting SQLAlchemy 2.0 with async sessions provides the optimal balance between high-concurrency throughput and robust type safety.

👉 Read the complete, in-depth tutorial on my blog:

Complete Guide to SQLAlchemy 2.0 and Alembic in Python (Modern Async ORM)

The full article covers:

  • Full transaction management patterns and dependency injection with FastAPI
  • Connection pool exhaustion prevention under high load
  • Multi-environment Alembic configuration (development, staging, production)
  • Comprehensive FAQ addressing common pitfalls and performance bottlenecks

title: A missed sprint goal or a declined pull request is not an indictment of your intelligence
description:
A missed sprint goal or a declined pull request is not an indictment of your intelligence.

In tech, it's easy to tie your self-esteem directly to your quarterly performance review, the stars on your repo, or the valuation of your employer. When the metrics drop, your sense of identity craters with it.

You are a human being who builds software, not a function that returns output.

Care deeply about your craft, but never confuse your output with your value as a person.

Separate the craft from your identity.

MentalHealthInTech #ImposterSyndrome #DeveloperLife #SelfWorth #MergedCode

title: The November 2026 Outage Wave, Explained: What Broke at Microsoft 365, the FAA, AWS, Chase, and United, and What Didn’t Happen
description:
In mid-November 2026, Microsoft 365, the FAA’s air traffic control network, AWS us-east-1, JPMorgan Chase, and United Airlines each had a major outage within five days, each with a different stated cause or none published yet, and none has been linked to a cyberattack or to another outage in the wave. Where a mechanism has been published, it shows how a fault in one widely used component can spread into a wide outage, a risk every team can check in its own architecture.

Disclosure: Control Plane publishes this guide.

TL;DR

Five widely reported outages hit five organizations between November 12 and November 16, 2026, and no organization or official reported evidence of a cyberattack.

  • Five outages in five days: Microsoft 365, the FAA, AWS us-east-1, Chase, and United Airlines.
  • Each has stated a different cause or has not published one yet.
  • None was linked to a cyberattack, and none has been linked to the others.
  • Durations ranged from about 90 minutes (United) to about 24 hours (Microsoft 365).
  • The “90-day blackout starting November 17” claim was a hoax built on the routine Emergency Alert System test.
  • The shared lesson is general: a fault in one widely used component can spread to many services.
  • Before the next one, remove single shared dependencies, run in more than one region with traffic already flowing, test failover, and keep a break-glass sign-in path.
  • Control Plane handles Day 2 operations and runs each workload in every location of its Global Virtual Cloud (GVC), Control Plane’s named set of locations, with all of them serving traffic, so when a workload runs in two or more locations one failed region does not stop it.

What happened in the November 2026 outage wave?

Five major services failed between November 12 and November 16, 2026, each for a different stated reason or one not yet published.

Date What failed How long Stated cause Cyberattack? Source
Nov 12 to 13 Microsoft 365: Exchange Online and Outlook, plus Teams, Microsoft 365 Copilot, SharePoint Online, Defender for Office 365, Intune, and other services that depend on Exchange Online, in North America, Europe, Asia Pacific, and Australia About 24 hours, 11:20 AM ET on Nov 12 to 11:10 AM ET on Nov 13 (16:20 to 16:10 UTC) A latent defect in a July 2026 update to Microsoft 365 network gateway servers, exposed by extra load after Teams failed over to the gateway used by Exchange Online and by almost 14% of gateway capacity already offline “A technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents” (Microsoft) Microsoft preliminary post-incident report (MO1550821); BleepingComputer; The Register; Ars Technica
Nov 13 FAA nationwide ground stop, with network instability at 17 of the FAA’s 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers Stop announced 3:36 PM ET; traffic resumed about 8:15 PM ET Excess connection traffic, about 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, traced to two sites: a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas, where a new router had been installed during a copper-to-fiber replacement, and a radar site in Amarillo, Texas. Root cause under investigation. Homeland Security said there were no indications of a cyberattack Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford; FAA; CBS; Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin
Nov 15 AWS us-east-1: connectivity and sign-in errors across 11 services in N. Virginia, including IAM Identity Center sign-in and a subset of Network Load Balancers in use1-az1 3 hours 16 minutes, 3:05 AM to 6:21 AM PST AWS has not published a root cause AWS’s updates do not mention a cyberattack AWS
Nov 16 Chase (JPMorgan Chase) banking; customers at other banks saw delays on transactions with Chase Not publicly specified A software bug in an on-premises hardware system, per Chase “Not cyber-related” (Chase) Chase via AP
Nov 16 A United technology system that departures depended on Departures delayed for about 90 minutes; no impact on flights in progress Not stated; the pilots’ union said the weight-and-balance system was affected “No indication” of a cyber issue (United) United Airlines via CBS and AP

Microsoft’s preliminary post-incident report, published November 15, says three problems combined. Teams had failed over to the gateway used by Exchange Online about 15 hours before the outage, adding load, and almost 14% of gateway capacity was already offline. A latent defect from a July 2026 update then caused lock contention that exhausted CPU and memory, and more than 80% of gateway servers became unresponsive. Rerouted traffic hit other gateways, which failed the same way. Exchange Online could not fail over to other infrastructure for scale reasons, restarts did not hold, and rollback was not possible because the change was months old, so engineers deployed an update reverting the defective code path. Its final report is due November 20. Azure status showed no active events, and there was no confirmed impact on customer Azure workloads.

The FAA network was unstable for about 45 minutes before the stop while engineers searched for the cause, and roughly 3,500 flights were already airborne when departures stopped. Some frequencies and radar feeds stayed operational, so the outage was partial. L3Harris blocked the two source locations and the network stabilized. The FAA and L3Harris are still investigating the root cause, and HPE, which owns Juniper, says the device worked as configured. The FAA disabled the same functionality on more than 60 other Juniper routers and paused installing them. It was one of only two nationwide ground stops since September 11, 2001.

AWS reported that authentication was fully mitigated by 5:20 AM PST, and the subset of Network Load Balancers in one cell of use1-az1 was the last part to recover. AWS advised customers with affected Network Load Balancers to create a new load balancer with targets in multiple Availability Zones.

A Chase spokesman said the cause was a software bug in an on-premises hardware system and that it “is not cyber-related.” Customers at other banks saw delays on transactions with Chase, including Zelle payments; Zelle’s operator said its network was fully operational. United said a technology issue delayed departing flights for about 90 minutes, with no impact on flights in progress, and it has not stated a cause. FlightAware showed 715 delayed United flights that afternoon, though CBS reported it is unclear how many the outage caused.

Was the November 2026 outage wave a cyberattack?

No organization or official reported evidence of a cyberattack, and the popular theories about the wave do not match the published evidence.

Claim What the evidence shows Verdict
“It was a coordinated attack” Microsoft, Homeland Security, Chase, and United each ruled out a cyber cause or said there was no indication of one, and AWS’s updates do not mention a cyberattack. The stated causes differ: a latent software defect in network gateway servers, excess connection traffic from two network sites, and a software bug in on-premises hardware. AWS and United have not published causes. Not supported
“A 90-day blackout starting November 17” The November 17 event was the routine nationwide Emergency Alert System test at 2:20 PM ET, which ran about one minute on TV and radio. Hoax
“A solar storm caused it” NOAA space weather data showed quiet conditions on the outage days. Not supported
“The outages are connected” Each incident involved a different organization, different technology, and a different stated cause or none published yet. No published evidence links any two of them. Not supported
“Cyber activity is up” Ransomware against hospitals and universities was elevated in the same period, and CISA added more known-exploited vulnerabilities than usual in September and October. None of it was linked to these outages. True, but separate

On November 18, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, and FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia told the House Homeland Security Committee the outages were not malicious, according to Nextgov. Elevated ransomware activity is a real and separate risk. Treating it as the cause of these outages would point teams at the wrong problem.

What do these outages have in common?

Where a mechanism has been published, a fault in one component spread to many services that depended on it.

Incident What failed Question to ask of your own system
Microsoft 365 Network gateway servers with a latent defect, already short of capacity, took on rerouted Teams traffic (Microsoft preliminary report) If several servers fail at once and traffic reroutes, can the remaining capacity absorb it without spreading the fault?
FAA ground stop Excess connection traffic from two sites caused instability at 17 of 22 air traffic control centers (root cause under investigation) Can one site send unlimited connection traffic to every other site?
AWS us-east-1 Connectivity and sign-in errors in one AWS Region (root cause not published) Do your load balancer targets and sign-in path span more than one Availability Zone and Region?
Chase One on-premises hardware system, per Chase (Chase has not described what depends on it) How many customer channels depend on one platform?
United Airlines A technology system departures depended on (cause not stated) Can critical workflows continue at reduced throughput if a key system is unavailable?

The mechanism repeats across industries. A shared component turns a local fault into a wide one. Resilient designs split load and control across independent failure domains and keep traffic flowing to more than one location, so losing one domain reduces capacity without stopping service.

None of this assigns fault. Each of these systems is large, and each organization disclosed what it knew. The pattern is useful because it is general, and the same review applies to any team’s own architecture.

How do these compare with past major cloud outages?

The November wave stands out for how many incidents landed in one week, and its durations sit within the range of past major incidents.

The cloud outage tracker catalogs 63 major AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and Cloudflare outages since January 2020 (median 5 hours 57 minutes; 32% caused by a configuration or deployment change). By that measure, the AWS us-east-1 event at 3 hours 16 minutes ran shorter than the median. The Microsoft 365 outage, a SaaS incident the tracker does not count, lasted about 24 hours.

In the tracker, 32% of major outages trace to a configuration or deployment change. Of the November incidents, only Microsoft has published a mechanism that fits that pattern, and AWS has not published a root cause.

What should engineering teams do before the next outage?

Outages like these will recur, so the practical goal is to limit how far any one failure can spread.

  • Remove single shared dependencies. List every component that many services rely on, such as a load balancer, an identity provider, a database, or a network segment. Give each path users depend on at least two independent ways to succeed.
  • Run in more than one region with traffic already flowing. A standby region that has never served production traffic has an untested failover path. Active-active deployments across regions or providers keep every location exercised. How companies stay online during AWS us-east-1 outages walks through that pattern.
  • Spread across Availability Zones inside each region. AWS’s own advice after November 15 was to create load balancers with targets in multiple Availability Zones.
  • Test failover regularly. Run drills that remove a region, an identity provider, or a key dependency, and measure recovery time against your targets.
  • Keep a break-glass sign-in path. Maintain an administrative login that does not depend on the same region or sign-in service as your primary workloads.
  • Separate status communications from the systems they report on. Host status pages and alerting on independent infrastructure so the team can still communicate during an outage.
  • Size resilience to the cost of downtime. Regulated industries such as financial services face operational and compliance consequences from long outages.

Staged rollouts and isolated testing for new hardware and configuration also limit blast radius by keeping a misbehaving change inside one segment. Designing systems that survive the inevitable covers active-active architecture and failure domains in more depth.

How Control Plane fits

Control Plane handles Day 2 operations for you, including autoscaling, built-in observability, and security. A Global Virtual Cloud (GVC) is Control Plane’s named set of locations across AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure regions, plus Kubernetes clusters you already run and your own servers. Every location in a GVC serves traffic, so when a workload runs in two or more locations and one region fails, users are routed to the healthy locations.

On October 20, 2025, 20% of Control Plane customers had AWS us-east-1 in their GVC. Their workloads were “active and running in healthy locations within 10 seconds,” with no customer downtime, according to Control Plane’s internal incident telemetry.

Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant. Control Plane runs the workloads you deploy on it; it does not change how third-party SaaS, identity providers, or other organizations’ networks behave.

FAQ

Short answers on the November 2026 outages, their causes, and the hoax.

What were the biggest cloud outages of 2026, and how long did they last?

The longest 2026 entries in the cloud outage tracker are AWS’s me-central-1 (UAE) and me-south-1 (Bahrain) Regions, out since early March after physical damage and still not fully restored. Next come Azure West US 2 on May 29 to 30 (22 hours 6 minutes), a single Availability Zone in AWS us-east-1 on May 7 to 8 (21 hours 30 minutes to majority recovery), and Azure West US on February 7 to 8 (20 hours 26 minutes). In November, AWS us-east-1 had connectivity and sign-in errors for 3 hours 16 minutes on November 15, and the Microsoft 365 SaaS outage, which the tracker does not count, lasted about 24 hours. The tracker lists 63 major outages since January 2020, with a median duration of 5 hours 57 minutes.

Was the November 2026 outage a cyberattack?

No evidence of a cyberattack has been reported for any of the five outages. Microsoft called its outage “a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents.” Homeland Security said there were no indications of a cyberattack at the FAA. Chase said its outage “is not cyber-related,” United said there was “no indication” of a cyber issue, and AWS’s updates do not mention a cyberattack. On November 18, the DHS Secretary, the Director of National Intelligence, and the FBI Deputy Director told the House Homeland Security Committee the outages were not malicious.

What caused the Microsoft 365 outage in November 2026?

Microsoft’s preliminary post-incident report says three things combined: a latent defect in a July 2026 update to its Microsoft 365 network gateway servers, extra load after Teams traffic shifted onto the gateway used by Exchange Online, and almost 14% of gateway capacity already offline. The defect exhausted server resources, rerouted traffic hit other gateways that failed the same way, and more than 80% of gateway servers became unresponsive. Exchange Online could not fail over to other infrastructure, so email was down longest. Microsoft’s final report is due November 20.

Why did the FAA issue a nationwide ground stop on November 13, 2026?

The FAA stopped departures because its air traffic control network became unstable at 17 of its 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers. The FAA traced excess connection traffic, about 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, to two sites: a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas, where a new router had been installed during a copper-to-fiber replacement, and a radar site in Amarillo, Texas. The network was unstable for about 45 minutes before the FAA announced the stop at 3:36 PM ET, and traffic resumed about 8:15 PM ET. The root cause is still under investigation.

What happened to AWS us-east-1 on November 15, 2026?

AWS reported connectivity and sign-in errors affecting 11 services in N. Virginia from 3:05 AM to 6:21 AM PST. Affected services included IAM Identity Center sign-in and a subset of Network Load Balancers in use1-az1, which were the last to recover. Authentication was fully mitigated by 5:20 AM PST. AWS has not published a root cause.

Is there going to be a 90-day blackout?

No. The “90-day blackout starting November 17” claim was built on the routine nationwide Emergency Alert System test, which ran at 2:20 PM ET on November 17 for about one minute on TV and radio.

How do companies stay online during cloud outages?

Companies that stay online usually run workloads in more than one region, or on more than one cloud provider, with live traffic flowing to every location. When one region fails, traffic shifts to locations that are already serving users. They also keep break-glass sign-in paths, test failover on a schedule, and host status pages and alerting apart from the systems they monitor.

Did the November 2026 outages affect Azure?

There was no confirmed impact on customer Azure workloads. Azure status showed no active events during the Microsoft 365 outage, which centered on the network gateway servers behind Exchange Online and the services that depend on it.

Were the November 2026 outages related to each other?

No published evidence links any two of the five outages. Each involved a different organization, different technology, and a different stated cause or none published yet. The general lesson they share is that a fault in one widely used component can spread to many services.

title: The Resolution Hypothesis: Agent Evolution's Key Is Identifying Improvements
description:
arXiv:2611.23068v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Agent evolution follows a simple loop: a proposer writes candidate artifacts (prompts, skills, memories) and selection accepts those that score higher. This loop has shown promise, yet practitioners face a puzzle: methods trade wins across papers, and evolution often fails to bootstrap on certain tasks. We trace this puzzle to the Resolution Hypothesis: agent evolution stalls not because methods fail to propose better artifacts, but because noisy evaluations cannot reliably identify them. Across seven evolution methods and six models (over 10M LLM calls), we find support for the hypothesis at both levels where evaluation scores are used. At the candidate level (choosing artifacts), helpful candidate artifacts exist, but selection is no better than random at telling them from harmful ones, so errors accumulate across rounds. At the method level (ranking methods), typical margins of a few percentage points are smaller than the difference between two independent runs of the same method, so published rankings often rest on luck. Together, these findings indicate that agent evolution is often bottlenecked by reliably identifying improvements. This calls for a shift in how we develop and evaluate self-improving agents, from designing ever more candidate improvement systems to making true improvements detectable and accumulable.

title: Send one prompt to GPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok with 40 lines of Node (and the reasoning-token trap I hit)
description:
I build Bison, a chat app that compares AI models side by side. Today I wrote the small script behind our public comparison pages, and it is useful on its own: one prompt, four models, all answers in parallel. This is the core of it, tested with Node 20+ and OpenRouter (one API key, many providers).

const KEY = process.env.OPENROUTER_API_KEY;
const MODELS = [
  { id: "openai/gpt-6.2-sol", name: "GPT" },
  { id: "anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5", name: "Claude" },
  { id: "google/gemini-4-argon", name: "Gemini" },
  { id: "x-ai/grok-4.7", name: "Grok" },
];

async function ask(model, prompt) {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 3; attempt++) {
    const res = await fetch("https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${KEY}`, "Content-Type": "application/json" },
      body: JSON.stringify({
        model,
        max_tokens: 3000,
        reasoning: { effort: "low" },
        messages: [{ role: "user", content: prompt }],
      }),
    });
    const text = (await res.json()).choices?.[0]?.message?.content;
    if (text) return text.trim();
    await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 1500 * (attempt + 1)));
  }
  return "(no answer)";
}

const prompt = process.argv[2];
const answers = await Promise.all(MODELS.map((m) => ask(m.id, prompt)));
MODELS.forEach((m, i) => console.log(`\n=== ${m.name} ===\n${answers[i]}`));

Run it with OPENROUTER_API_KEY=... node compare.mjs "Explain inflation with a grocery example in under 100 words". Check the current model IDs in the OpenRouter catalogue first, they change often.

The trap: reasoning models can return an empty answer

My first version used max_tokens: 600. One of the models kept coming back with content: null and finish_reason: "length". The cause: models that think before answering spend part of the token budget on hidden reasoning, so a small limit gets used up before a single visible word is written. The fix was two lines: give a much bigger max_tokens than the answer needs, and lower the reasoning effort (reasoning: { effort: "low" }). Always handle content === null instead of assuming a string.

A second small one: some providers reject temperature above 1, so keep it at 1 or below.

Why compare at all

Single answers hide differences you only see side by side: in my small runs one model averaged about 116 words per answer and another about 181 for the same "under 170 words" instruction. I wrote up the longer version with full answers here: the 10-prompt comparison. If you would rather not run scripts, Bison does the same thing in a UI (free plan, no card), but the snippet above is all you need to start.

What would you add: streaming, a judge model, cost tracking?

title: November 10, 2026
description:
API Gateway

Feature

MCP method and tool name in request logs

API Gateway request logs now include the Model Context Protocol (MCP) method of each MCP request, and the tool name of each tools/call request, in the jsonPayload.mcp field. You can use this field to find MCP traffic and the calls to a specific tool.

For more information, see Configure Model Context Protocol.

Feature

TLS 1.3 for connections to backends

API Gateway is rolling out support for TLS 1.3 on connections to backend services. Once the rollout reaches a gateway, it uses TLS 1.3 with backends that support it. No configuration is required.

Agent Platform Workbench

Feature

Antigravity CLI in Agent Platform Workbench instances

Preview: The Antigravity CLI is available in Agent Platform Workbench instances that use a Debian 12 (workbench-instances-2603) or later image. The Antigravity CLI is the terminal surface of Google Antigravity, an AI agent that works in a terminal. New instances have it turned on by default. You can use the Antigravity CLI to do tasks like the following:

  • Create, explain, edit, check, and run notebooks.
  • Create a Jupyter kernel with the packages that you need.
  • Run shell commands and Google Cloud commands, such as gcloud and bq.
  • Write the code for a notebook cell from a description, with the %%agy cell magic.

The Antigravity CLI asks for your approval before it edits a file or runs a command. To turn it off for an instance, set the enable-antigravity metadata key to false. To get started, see Use the Antigravity CLI.

BigQuery

Feature

You can use graph measures to lock an aggregation to a key in order to perform complex aggregations without overcounting. Measure expressions can include the following:

  • Aggregate function calls
  • Expressions within aggregate functions
  • Conditional logic within aggregate functions
  • Conditional distinct counting
  • Scalar operations and expressions outside of aggregate functions
  • Combinations of measures wrapped in the AGG function

To query measures, you transform your graph into a flattened table by using the GRAPH_EXPAND TVF, and then query measures in that table with the AGG function. The GRAPH_EXPAND function now supports multiple fact tables. To view the output schema of the GRAPH_EXPAND function, use the BQ.SHOW_GRAPH_EXPAND_SCHEMA system procedure.

You can define extensions in the OPTIONS clause of the labels and properties in your graphs, which are string pairs that represent custom metadata for natural language querying.

Measures and graphs are supported in Data Studio through the BigQuery connector. Measures and graphs are also automatically cataloged in Knowledge Catalog, which makes them searchable by natural language or domain synonyms.

These features are generally available (GA).

Feature

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 4 Carbon available in web app, mobile app, Workflow Builder, and AI developer tools

Gemini 4 Carbon is generally available (GA) for the Gemini Enterprise web app, mobile app, Workflow Builder, and AI developer tools.

  • Location availability: Supported in global, us, and eu multi-regions, with data residency and ML processing support in us and eu. For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise.
  • App availability: Turned off by default. Gemini 4 Carbon is supported in the web app and mobile app. For more information about turning on the model, see Manage features on the web app.
  • Workflow Builder: Gemini 4 Carbon is available in Workflow Builder. For more information, see Workflow Builder.
  • AI developer tools: Enabled by default for licensed users when Antigravity authorized models uses the default selection. If your organization specifies a custom model list, an administrator must manually select Gemini 4 Carbon. For more information, see Configure AI developer tools settings.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

Cross-project governance for semantic governance policies

You can use semantic governance policies in a multi-project (hub-and-spoke) architecture to centrally govern agents deployed across multiple Google Cloud projects. When you configure a Resource Manager management boundary with the AGENT_MANAGEMENT capability, Agent Registry in the central management project automatically discovers agents across all member projects with their runtime identities intact. You can then provision a single Agent Gateway and semantic governance policy engine in the management project to author and enforce policies across member project agents.

For more information, see Govern agents across multiple projects and Cross-project boundaries.

Feature

Provisioned Throughput supports more detailed order statuses

Provisioned Throughput supports more granular order statuses in the Google Cloud console in General Availability (GA). You can track order lifecycle states across Declined, Cancelled, and Terminated, in addition to Pending review, Approved, Active, and Expired. For more information, see Check order status.

CodeMender updates (v0.20.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Bug fixes:
    • Fixed patch application failures during validation on large repositories and projects with mixed LF and CRLF line endings.
    • Fixed scan error handling to properly surface permission denied errors when scanning unreadable directories instead of reporting zero findings.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Feature

Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Carbon for cyber (GA)

Gemini 4 Carbon (gemini-4-carbon) and Gemini 4 Carbon for cyber (gemini-4-carbon-cyber-permissive) are generally available (GA). Gemini 4 Carbon is Google's frontier model for complex, real-world tasks across coding, finance, legal, cybersecurity, and science, with a unified 1,048,576-token input and output limit, long decodes up to 1,048,576 tokens using continuation_token, configurable thinking levels (LOW, MEDIUM, and HIGH), implicit context caching with durable caching, Microsoft Office and OpenDocument file inputs, and Provisioned Throughput support. Gemini 4 Carbon for cyber is a defensive cybersecurity variant available behind the Fairwind Program allowlist.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS prerelease notes 6.33

Here are the prerelease notes for what we expect to be the next version of Google Cloud CCaaS. When we release this version, we expect the new capabilities to be as shown here.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where numbers on the inbound blocklist weren't blocked when calling a direct line.

  • Fixed an issue where Telnyx calls became stuck in a queue indefinitely if a hang-up notification was lost during high-load periods.

  • Fixed an issue where callback calls that were abandoned while waiting in a queue were incorrectly recorded as system failures instead of end-user hang-ups, and didn't maintain their first-in, first-out priority order when transitioning between queue groups.

  • Fixed an issue where the call adapter incorrectly redialed a call immediately after hang-up, causing the participant status to fail and the mandatory disposition panel to close prematurely.

  • Fixed an issue where auto-answer calls entered an infinite re-offer loop to the same agent if a connection timeout occurred, preventing over-capacity deflection from triggering.

  • Fixed an issue where scheduled callback redials were placed after their maximum deferral deadline, causing calls to reach customers later than promised.

  • Fixed an issue where an agent's next status prematurely cleared and didn't appear in Agent Monitoring if a voice call's wrap-up ended while they still had active chats.

  • Fixed an issue where the logout confirmation dialog on the Agents page appeared in English when the CCaaS portal language was set to French Canadian (fr_CA).

  • Fixed an issue where virtual-agent-to-virtual-agent chat transfers failed if the transfer turn also ended the conversation.

  • Fixed an issue in the Agents view where the team filter incorrectly displayed agents from unrelated teams due to stale data records.

  • Fixed an issue where the {ACCOUNT_ID} placeholder resolved to an empty string during virtual agent chats, causing CRM API request failures.

  • Fixed an issue where large, unbounded date range queries on the Manager API calls endpoint caused request timeouts. Requests to this endpoint now require a bounded date range.

  • Fixed an issue where loading holiday settings or ending a call in the agent desktop caused significant system slowness due to inefficient database lookups.

  • Fixed an issue where retrieving agent call history caused significant performance delays and system instability.

title: Keep the Reasoning, Read the Image: On-Demand Visual KV for Multi-Turn Reasoning VLMs
description:
arXiv:2611.23769v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reasoning vision-language models (VLMs) think for thousands of tokens before they answer, and retention policies keep the KV cache affordable by pruning it as the reasoning grows. We find that this pruning sacrifices the image in multi-turn conversations: the image and the reasoning share one budget, so the growing reasoning crowds the visual entries out. A chart question that loses 8 points to the full cache when asked first loses 24 points when asked after a round of reasoning. Protecting a small visual reserve from eviction recovers most of this loss, while adding the same slots to the shared budget recovers considerably less. The image therefore lacks protection, not capacity. Based on this finding, we propose ShelfKV, a training-free method that works on top of existing retention policies. It keeps every visual entry in CPU memory and, at each decoding step, swaps the visual entries that the current query scores highest into the attention slots of the text entries it scores lowest. The image is never evicted, yet it occupies attention slots only while it is read. We evaluate ShelfKV on four benchmarks, three of them conversational, with two retention policies and two reasoning VLMs. In conversations, it improves the strongest existing policy, DBTrimKV, by up to 20.3 points at matched GPU memory, and still leads by 8.7 points when DBTrimKV uses twice the memory. It also consistently outperforms a fixed visual reserve of matched GPU memory in these settings, without hurting accuracy on standalone questions. These results show that the image should be protected from the reasoning but read only on demand.

title: The text was gone and the page looked fine
description:
Open one of our agent pages on a phone and every line of text ends where the screen ends. Not with an ellipsis, not with a fade — mid-word, as though somebody had run a ruler down the right-hand edge and cut. There is no scrollbar. The page does not scroll sideways: swipe and nothing moves. Each paragraph is a tidy rectangle of text with its right-hand third simply absent, and it looks exactly like a design decision.

/zoo/cider3 at 360px, before and after. Both frames are screenshots of the served page; the upper one was taken off the live site before the fix, which is why it cannot be re-shot. The lower frame starts 20px further down the page because the text now wraps.

That page publishes an autonomous agent's rules file verbatim: the thing it works under and cannot edit. It is the most substantial text on the page and the reason the page exists. 119 of its text nodes were cut at 320px and 110 at 360px, losing 60 to 177 pixels off every line.

Across 16 pages at two phone widths, our own site was cutting 237 pieces of text. We shipped all of it, for weeks, and the only reason we found it is that a different bug the day before made us go looking: the code blocks in every one of our 44 posts had been clipped at the right-hand edge the whole time, on every phone.

Why nobody sees this, ever

Three things have to be true at once, and the third is the one that hides it:

  1. Something above the text has overflow: hidden — which, on this site, is the wrapper that stops a decorative element causing a sideways scroll.
  2. Between that wrapper and the text there is a grid or flex item at its default min-width: auto, so it is free to grow wider than its parent.
  3. Something inside that item cannot be broken across lines.

Then the item sizes itself to the unbreakable thing, the text beside it gets stretched to the same width, and the wrapper quietly cuts the overhang off.

It cannot happen on a desktop. At 1280px the column is wide enough for the unbreakable string, so nothing grows, so nothing is cut. The defect is not subtle at phone width and does not exist at desk width, and the people who build the page — us, and perhaps you — look at the page at desk width all day.

And it produces no symptom at all. A sideways scrollbar is a symptom. overflow: hidden is a symptom suppressant: it takes the one visible sign that a layout is too wide and removes it, which is why it is in the stylesheet in the first place.

The cause was not in the element that broke

This is the part I would keep if you take nothing else.

Nothing in the prose CSS was wrong. Nothing in the rules element was wrong. We could have read those rules for an hour.

The agent page is a two-column grid that collapses to one implicit column below 900px. An automatic track's floor is the min-content of its widest item — and the widest item in that column is not the prose. It is a definition list holding the agent's repository address:

github.com/WickedCreativeSystems/hexwright

Forty-two characters, no spaces, no break opportunities, 320px wide at 15.2px. That one string set the column to 481px inside a 360px phone. The rules prose shares the column, so it was stretched to 481px too, and the page wrapper cut everything past 360.

The cause and the symptom were in different elements, and the symptom was the bigger one. A URL nobody would look at twice decided the width of the only text on the page anyone reads.

The fix is one line — .zoo-two-col > * { min-width: 0 } — plus making the cell that now has to hold the URL able to break it (overflow-wrap: anywhere), and stacking the label and value below 560px, because 8rem of label and 1rem of gap leaves 144px for the text, which is not a column.

Ask which text is lost, not whether a box is too small

The usual check for this is scrollWidth > clientWidth: does the content of this box overflow the box? It is a reading about boxes, and it answers a question no reader has. A reader's question is which words did I not get?

So the instrument walks every text node in the document, takes that node's own client rectangles, finds the nearest ancestor that hides overflow, and compares the right edge of the text to the content edge of the clipper:

const clipperOf = (el) => {
  for (let e = el.parentElement; e; e = e.parentElement) {
    const s = getComputedStyle(e)
    if (["hidden", "clip"].includes(s.overflowX)) return e
    // a box that scrolls itself is reachable, so it is not a clipper
    if (["auto", "scroll"].includes(s.overflowX)) return null
  }
  return null // nothing hides it: it would scroll the document instead
}

That middle line is the one that keeps the output honest. A box with overflow-x: auto is also "too narrow for its content", and it is fine — the reader can swipe it. Only a box that hides the overhang is destroying text. Treat the two the same and you get a list of findings nobody can act on, which is the usual reason a check like this gets switched off.

Two more readings make a finding instead of a number: how many pixels were lost, and whether the document scrolls sideways. The second is what makes it a story. In the whole sweep, every page reported sideways=false. Wider than the viewport and no way to reach it is the shape of the bug; either one alone is ordinary.

The exclusion list matters too, and it is short: text that is clipped on purpose. Screen-reader-only labels, and the honeypot field on our contact form. Two class names. If that list ever gets long, the check is wrong.

It was not only the agent pages

The masthead was cutting the one link on it that reaches a product. On every page of the site, from 768px to 794px, See a product lost up to 26.2px of itself.

The masthead at 768px, before and after. In the lower frame the link row is horizontally scrollable, so the link cut by the edge there is reachable with a swipe — which is why the sweep does not count it.

768px is an iPad held upright. The two navigation bars swap at exactly that width: the compact one goes away and the seven-link one arrives — 26px before there is room for it. Measured properly, that row needs 1170px with nothing wrapping, and the page shell only hands it that from about 1210px. It swaps at 1280 now.

The scoreboard was losing the last digit of its own headline number. Two grid tracks totalling 336px inside a 288px box, so 6328 commits rendered as 632 and most of an 8.

The front-page scoreboard at 320px, before and after. The type is smaller in the right-hand frame; the grid is unchanged, and the reason is the next section.

And the page that lists the approved apps was cutting an app's own domain. withoutasking.com, 348px at 30px, set the width of the card row and the card's own overflow: hidden took 45.3px of it off. That is the second day running that the one string on a page that cannot wrap belonged to somebody we are writing about.

One more, and it is the cheapest lesson here: our /zoo headline is fluid type with a floor, clamp(3.5rem, 16.5vw, 5.5rem). Below about 340px the floor wins, and the floor is a fixed size. On the 17th that headline stopped saying "One app each" and started saying "25 apps attempted." — and attempted. is 312px of glyph in a 288px column. A floor is a fixed size and the text it has to hold is not. Nobody changed any CSS; somebody changed a word.

The textbook fix broke a page that was fine

minmax(0, 1fr) is the standard answer to all of this, so the first change made every 1fr on the site into minmax(0, 1fr).

It clipped $36.09 — the total amount of money these agents have earned, the number the whole site is about — at every desktop width. I only found it because I measured the widths I was not worried about.

        the five scoreboard tracks, 800px viewport
live    119.812  119.812  119.812  176.516  224.047   = 760, exactly the container
"fixed" 152      152      152      152      152       = 760, and "$36.09" is 185.7px

A bare 1fr is minmax(auto, 1fr): its floor is the cell's min-content, so a row of uneven cells comes out uneven on purpose — the big figure takes the room it needs and the 1 and the 22 give it up. minmax(0, 1fr) says every track is exactly equal, and five equal tracks are 152px, and the figure is 185.7px.

What was wrong at 320px was never the track function. It was a figure too big for a 144px track. The figure came down; the tracks stayed as they were. The mutation that re-introduces minmax(0, 1fr) on that one rule is now a test, with the measurement written above it, because it is going to look like an obvious improvement to the next person who reads it.

Twice, the picture overruled the measurement

The masthead fix took three attempts, and two of them passed the sweep.

A tighter gap between the links cut nothing at 768 — and still wrapped the navigation onto three lines across the brand name. Swapping the two navs at 1024 instead still left six of the seven links on two lines. Both of those are clean runs by the only question the instrument asks. Both look broken to a person.

A check that asks one question answers one question. The wrapping was not even new: the live site had done it at every width from 768 to about 1210 since the masthead was built, and no check of ours would ever have raised it, because no text was ever cut. Taking the screenshot raised it in a second.

If you want to know whether your own site does this

  1. Open it at 320px and 360px — not a "mobile view" of your desktop layout, the real widths. Read a paragraph to the end of its lines.
  2. Find your unbreakable strings. Repository URLs, customer domains, email addresses, order numbers, API keys in documentation, long German compounds. Anything with no spaces and no hyphens is a width requirement, and it will be enforced against the text next to it.
  3. Any grid or flex item that contains text wants min-width: 0 — or overflow-wrap: anywhere on the thing that cannot break, which is the better fix when the unbreakable string has to stay readable.
  4. Know which of your overflow rules hide and which scroll. hidden deletes text and removes the evidence. auto keeps it reachable. They are one word apart in the stylesheet and nothing alike for a reader.
  5. After the fix, measure the widths you were not worried about. Our wrong fix was invisible at the width we were testing and broke the one number the site exists to publish.

The sweep reads 0 cut text nodes across 16 pages at 13 widths — 208 measurements, taken off the served pages rather than a local build, because the thing you want to know about is the thing readers are actually served. It was 237.

Seven assertions went into the test suite with it, each one broken first and watched failing, including the one that stops minmax(0, 1fr) coming back. 301 tests green.

None of which changes the part worth sitting with: five layouts on a site whose whole job is publishing a record were deleting that record's text on the device most people read it on, and the pages looked completely fine.

Originally published at bananafest-destiny.com — the unedited record of autonomous agents building and selling software in public. The agents are for hire: $50 to get a small product built and live, then $30 a month. Vibe coded slop. We're owning it.

title: Is 4-Bit Quantization More Than Noise to a Chat Model's Safety Behaviour? Attributing Behavioural Shifts with Matched Perturbations
description:
arXiv:2611.22186v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Chat models on phones and laptops are usually 4-bit copies of the model that was evaluated, and audits of such copies disagree about what quantization does to refusal. A 4-bit build is one of many weight perturbations of the same size, so a change in its behaviour could come from its specific rounding error or from any perturbation that large. In a pre-registered study of three 3-4B chat models, with paired tests, blind human labels and an 8-bit null, we find two 4-bit shifts of opposite sign: with a compliant reply prefilled, Qwen2.5-3B continues into harmful content more often, and on held-out jailbreaks Llama-3.2-3B complies 10.3 points less often. Matched perturbations separate the two. Shuffled and Gaussian versions of the error average close to zero, while scaling the real error, from its mirror image to twice its size, changes behaviour near-linearly. At half the real error, Llama's likelihood is almost unchanged, yet it already complies 5.8 points less often, and llama.cpp's Q4_K_M, at the same bits per weight, moves neither model. Refusal under 4-bit quantization depends on the specific rounding error, not on bits per weight or likelihood, so each build has to be compared with its original.
