title: UX cost of a security patch
description:
The UX cost of a security patch

Janus Arena (November 2026). Every figure comes from real runs recorded in the project's event
log: a brute-force fix on OWASP Juice Shop, and five Launch Day runs on ShopLab, a demo shop. The
reports are in the repository (docs/reports),
and the console's demo build replays two of the runs in your browser. The users are synthetic:
language-model agents that play a person in a real browser. Nothing here is a conversion figure.

A security fix is judged by one question: does the attack still work? It is a good question and it
is not enough. A fix can stop the attack and also stop the people it was meant to protect, and the
second half only shows up if you measure it. This is what happened when we measured both, in two
experiments, and what we could not conclude from them.

The rule that keeps it honest

Attacks are generated by code and judged by code. An attack succeeds only when a deterministic
oracle says so (for brute force: every wrong password was refused fast, nothing throttled, and the
right password still signs in afterwards). A model proposes the patch; it never decides whether the
patch works. The shoppers are agents, but whether one bought what it was asked to is read from the
shop's orders, not from what the agent says. Rates carry 95 % Wilson intervals.

Experiment 1: two ways to stop a password guesser

The finding was a brute-force on POST /rest/user/login. The Blue Team wrote alternatives and
three independent verifiers judged each: the original proof of concept must stop working (V1), the
regression tests must pass (V2), and a paired run of synthetic shoppers must stay within tolerance
(V3). Two alternatives got to the end:

Alternative Still exploitable? Shoppers who bought, original → fix p95 of the login
Per-account limit, 10 tries in 5 minutes no, throttled at guess 11 4/6 → 5/6 50 → 90 ms
Account lockout no, throttled at guess 6 4/6 → 3/6 46 → 41 ms

Both close the attack. They differ in who else they stop. One of the personas, Inés, is forgetful:
before the right password she tries five old ones, as someone who does not remember which password
this shop has. Five is the usual threshold of a lockout, and on the lockout variant Inés was refused
with a 429 in both of her sessions and never completed a purchase. The limit of ten tries is above
the five she tries.

What this shows is a mechanism, not a rate. Six shoppers per variant is too few for the
difference between 4/6 and 3/6 to mean anything: it is one session, and the intervals overlap
completely. What is solid is the cause, because it is in the events: a specific persona, a specific
threshold, a 429. A third alternative (a progressive delay) is not in the table because the API
credit ran out before it was written; we report it as not measured rather than as passed. The whole
comparison cost 0.98 €.

Experiment 2: Launch Day

The cost of a defense changes with how many people arrive at once and where they come from, so we
put a launch on ShopLab: 18 synthetic shoppers and two saboteurs per variant. One saboteur sends
requests at a steady rate; the other guesses at an account's password. Variant A runs without the
defense, B with it, and every shopper plays the same task on both sides. Each defense was one run.

Defense in B Attacks that got through, A → B Shoppers who bought, A → B Shoppers blocked, A → B
Rate limit per client, 20/min 100 % → 50 % 86 % → 88 % 0 % → 0 %
Rate limit per account, 3/min 100 % → 50 % 80 % → 79 % 0 % → 0 %
Checkout step-up (type a code) 100 % → 100 % 75 % → 73 % 0 % → 0 %
Rate limit per client, 6/min, nine shoppers at once behind three shared addresses 100 % → 0 % 75 % → 73 % 0 % → 18 %

Four things stand out.

Each defense stops what it was built for, and nothing else. The per-client limit stopped the
saturation saboteur after 20 answered requests and left the password guesser alone, and the
per-account limit did the reverse. The two 50 % are two defenses, each covering one of the two
saboteurs.

The step-up stopped neither attack. It is a defense for another problem (an account that was
just created buying with a stolen card), and the run says so: attacks 100 % → 100 %. What it costs
shoppers shows in the median number of steps, 15 → 16, not in anyone being blocked.

A defense that costs nothing can become one that costs shoppers. At 20 requests per minute no
shopper was blocked. At six, with nine of them arriving together behind three shared addresses
(an office, a campus), both saboteurs were stopped and 2 of 11 shoppers were blocked too, where none
had been without the limit. The interval is wide (5 % to 48 %). The same limit with only three shoppers at a time (an earlier
run that was interrupted, so it is not in the report) blocked nobody, and neither did 20 per minute
with shared addresses and low concurrency: the burst is what makes the limit bite.
The same number written differently, "this limit is safe", would have been true in one run and
false in the other.

Contamination was zero. Every shopper marks its shipping address with an invented code, and
after the task we check that no order it can read carries another session's code. None did, so the
numbers are not an artefact of sessions leaking into each other.

What we do not claim

  • Not that a limit of 20 is the right one. Those are the values we tried, on a demo shop, with one task.
  • Not a measure of attack success with any precision. There are two saboteurs per variant, so "100 % → 0 %" is 2/2 against 0/2, an interval from 0 % to 66 %. It says the defense stops them in these runs, not how often.
  • Not conversion, and not what real people do. Synthetic shoppers say where a flow is hard for an agent that behaves like a person; they do not predict revenue.
  • Not that the defenses combine. Each was measured alone.

What to take from it

Measure three things before you merge a security fix: whether the attack still works, how many of
the people you protect it stops, and what it adds for those it does not stop. The second number is
the one nobody has by default, and in these runs it was zero for one setting and 18 % for another
that differed in a single parameter. A gate that shows both on the same pull request, and never
merges on its own, is what Janus Arena is for.

To reproduce the Launch Day numbers: pnpm run:launch-day <runId>... writes the report from the
recorded events, with no model involved; the five runs cost between 0.24 € and 0.29 € each.

title: Testing back navigation in an auto-advancing Astro form
description:
A person selects “Within a month” in a fencing planner, reaches the summary, goes back and changes their mind to “Just planning.” The revised summary should display one timing answer. The postcode they already entered should still be there, and moving to the next screen should put keyboard focus somewhere useful.

That is a small interaction with several independent failure modes. An append-only answer list can show duplicates. A form that remounts each step can lose the postcode. A visually correct transition can leave keyboard focus on a button inside a hidden panel. Here’s how the Perth Quotes frontend handles those cases and what its browser suite checks. Live fencing planner

Give each answer a single location in state

Astro renders the panels up front. The client script hides all but the active panel. The flow has four multiple-choice questions, a postcode step and a final screen that displays a summary with contact collection disabled. A fixed question order lets the client key a Map by panel index. The handler updates the answer and the selected state before advancing.

// Excerpt from the client-side answer handler.
answers.set(current, button.dataset.answer!);
panels[current].querySelectorAll('[data-answer]').forEach(option => {
  option.setAttribute('aria-pressed', String(option === button));
});
show(current + 1);

Back navigation changes which panel is visible. It doesn’t reset the Map or recreate the postcode input, so that input keeps its current value. On valid Continue, the script clears the previous summary and builds its rows from the Map. Calling Map.set for the same key replaces the value while preserving that key’s position. If the flow ever gains conditional branches, use stable question IDs and decide explicitly which answers to discard when a branch changes.

Test the trip back from the summary

The repo’s Playwright suite exercises the journey from initial answers through postcode validation to revision. Here’s a standalone version of the revision check for a local dev server. Scoping the last assertions to the summary prevents the test from passing just because the updated button label still exists in a hidden panel.

import { expect, test } from '@playwright/test';

test('fencing summary replaces a revised timing answer', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/fencing/');
  const choose = (name: string) =>
    page.getByRole('button', { name, exact: true }).click();

  await choose('Replace a fence');
  await choose('Colorbond steel');
  await choose('10–30 metres');
  await choose('Within a month');

  const postcode = page.getByLabel('WA postcode', { exact: true });
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', {
    name: 'What is your WA postcode?',
  })).toBeFocused();
  await postcode.fill('6062');
  await postcode.press('Enter');

  await choose('Back');
  await expect(postcode).toHaveValue('6062');
  await choose('Back');
  await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Within a month' }))
    .toHaveAttribute('aria-pressed', 'true');
  await choose('Just planning');
  await choose('Continue');

  const summary = page.locator('[data-answer-summary]');
  await expect(summary.getByText('Timing', { exact: true })).toHaveCount(1);
  await expect(summary.getByText('Just planning', { exact: true })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(summary.getByText('Within a month', { exact: true })).toHaveCount(0);
  await expect(page.getByLabel('Your name', { exact: true })).toBeDisabled();
});

To run the repository’s existing fencing checks from the project root:

npm run test:e2e -- frontend/test/services.spec.ts -g "^Fencing:"

Keep the postcode and contact checks separate

The postcode check accepts four digits beginning with 6. That validates shape only. The browser has neither a postcode directory lookup nor a serviceability check in this flow. The final screen is a preview. Contact inputs live inside a disabled fieldset, and the summary is built from in-memory state. The existing browser test checks that the path issues no non-GET requests and leaves both local and session storage empty in its test configuration. Those assertions give the preview an explicit behavioural contract while enquiries are closed.

title: Gaming Reports at Scale: Node.js Multipart Upload and Sharp Thumbnail Backpressure
description:
A customer opens a generated gaming report and sees a broken image. The page says delivery is behind, completed uploads are rising, and the thumbnail queue is old. The tempting response is to add Sharp workers. That can make the incident worse if the real constraint is upload completion, object-store throughput, or derivative delivery.

Short answer: use multipart upload for each large original, acknowledge it only after completion, then let a bounded Node.js and Sharp worker pool create thumbnails under separate private keys. Page on customer-visible report readiness, but diagnose with upload age, completion rate, queue age, derivative failures, and presigned-delivery errors.

This order matters. A thumbnail job must never race an incomplete multipart object, and a retry must never overwrite the original. For a team already operating several backend capabilities, Infrai can fit the storage boundary because one key and one bill cover the wider platform instead of adding another credential and invoice. I would try it for private report originals and derivatives when reducing control-plane sprawl matters; its plain REST surface and public, self-describing discovery also remove an SDK dependency from the integration.

How should a large image upload, multipart Node.js Sharp thumbnail pipeline, and S3-compatible private storage interact?

Treat multipart completion as the commit record. Before that event, parts are transport state, not an image that Sharp may consume. After completion, enqueue a thumbnail command containing the tenant, report ID, immutable original key, derivative specification, and a deterministic operation ID. The worker reads the completed object, validates it as an image, resizes it, and writes every output to its own key. Both original and derivative delivery use short-lived presigned URLs.

A practical key layout is tenants/{tenant}/reports/{report}/original/{content-id} for the source and tenants/{tenant}/reports/{report}/thumb/{spec}/{content-id} for a derivative. The exact names are application policy; the important property is separation. A retry for 320x180-webp then converges on the same derivative key and cannot corrupt the source. Keep the bucket private.

The sequence is small enough to put in a runbook:

  1. Create the multipart upload for the private bucket.
  2. Presign and transfer each part, retaining every returned part identifier in durable application state.
  3. Complete the upload only after all intended parts are present.
  4. Commit the report-image record and enqueue the deterministic thumbnail command.
  5. Let the bounded Sharp pool produce distinct derivative keys.
  6. Mark the report image ready only when the required derivatives can be served with presigned URLs.
  7. Abort a failed multipart session; orphaned parts are not removed by lifecycle rules.

No completion, no resize.

The browser-direct variant needs an extra decision. Infrai's bucket model mentions CORS rules, but self-service CORS configuration is not an available capability boundary, so don't assume a web client can be enabled from this API. Put an application upload relay in front, or choose a direct storage control plane that supplies the browser-origin controls your design requires. This is a capability choice, not an incident workaround.

Work backward from the report-delivery page

The primary page should describe the failed customer promise: authenticated customers cannot view required images for generated reports within the service objective. It should not merely say that a worker process is busy. A busy worker can be healthy under a burst, while a quiet worker can be disastrous if completion events stopped arriving.

Work backward. First inspect readiness lag by report cohort and tenant. Then split that lag into four intervals: multipart creation to completion, completion to queue admission, queue admission to derivative write, and derivative write to successful presigned delivery. This turns one vague page into a location. If the first interval grows, adding Sharp concurrency is noise. If queue age grows while completed originals arrive normally, worker capacity or image complexity deserves attention. If writes finish but authenticated delivery fails, inspect signing and expiry policy rather than upload throughput.

The earlier signal should normally be sustained queue age or a falling completion-to-ready rate, not raw queue depth. Depth has no units of customer delay. One thousand tiny thumbnails may clear before ten unusually large originals; age and completion rate expose that difference. Break the signals out by derivative specification because a large report preview and a small list thumbnail consume different work.

Use HTTP status families as diagnostic dimensions, with 429 handled as backpressure: honor Retry-After when present and apply exponential delay. Don't turn a rate limit into a tight retry storm. Surface 4xx response bodies to the operator because they carry the reason, but keep authentication data and presigned query strings out of logs. The OWASP upload guidance is also a useful floor: allow-list expected extensions, validate the actual file type, rename stored files, set size limits, and keep uploads away from a public path.

This is where the alert becomes actionable. The page links to the oldest affected report IDs, the four latency intervals, current worker concurrency, input-byte rate, output-byte rate, 429 rate, and abort rate. An operator can reduce admission, increase a bounded pool, or stop a bad producer based on evidence. A chart called thumbnail_errors_total by itself offers no such choice.

Instrument the completion boundary and the worker budget

Throughput planning starts with bytes, pixels, and concurrency, not requests. Model a hypothetical peak before choosing a provider or worker count. Suppose an hour brings 400 report images averaging 120 MB, and each completed original produces three private derivatives. That is 48,000 MB of source input per hour before retries, plus derivative writes and later customer egress. These are planning inputs, not benchmark results; replace them with the p50, p95, and maximum from your own accepted uploads.

The longest paragraph in the runbook should explain overload behavior because this is where duplicate work hides. Set a maximum number of simultaneous Sharp transforms from measured memory per transform and the container memory budget, then reserve headroom for the Node.js process, download buffers, and transient output buffers. Admission should stop before the process is forced into repeated restarts. Each queue delivery checks the report-image state and deterministic derivative key before doing expensive work. If the derivative is already committed, acknowledge the delivery. If another worker owns an unexpired lease, release or defer it. If neither is true, acquire coordination in the application's database or queue, render to a temporary destination, and promote the result through the application's state transition. Infrai has no If-Match conditional write, so strict mutual exclusion belongs in that coordinator. This is deliberate duplication control — standard retries alone are not a lock.

Before wiring the full uploader into Node.js, this small Go preflight verifies the create-and-abort lifecycle against a private bucket. It is deliberately narrow. The production uploader adds part presigning, part transfer, completion, and a presigned read URL only after discovery schemas have been checked.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

const baseURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

type createResponse struct {
    UploadID string `json:"upload_id"`
}

func call(client *http.Client, method, endpoint string, body []byte, idempotencyKey string) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 6; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(method, endpoint, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        if idempotencyKey != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)
        }

        res, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        res.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            wait := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(res.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }
        if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s %s: status %d: %s", method, endpoint, res.StatusCode, data)
        }
        return data, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("request remained rate-limited after 6 attempts")
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    bucket := os.Getenv("REPORT_BUCKET")
    if key == "" || bucket == "" {
        panic("set INFRAI_API_KEY and REPORT_BUCKET")
    }

    payload, err := json.Marshal(map[string]string{
        "key":          "preflight/report-original.png",
        "content_type": "image/png",
        "acl":          "private",
    })
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 30 * time.Second}
    createURL := baseURL + "/storage/multipart/create/" + url.PathEscape(bucket)
    data, err := call(client, http.MethodPost, createURL, payload, "report-upload-preflight-v1")
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }

    var created createResponse
    if err := json.Unmarshal(data, &created); err != nil || created.UploadID == "" {
        panic("create response did not contain upload_id")
    }
    abortURL := baseURL + "/storage/multipart/abort/" + url.PathEscape(created.UploadID)
    if _, err := call(client, http.MethodDelete, abortURL, nil, ""); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println("multipart create-and-abort preflight passed")
}

The sample sends the bearer key only to the API. A returned presigned URL is already authorized and must never receive that header. The stable idempotency key protects the create retry, while the explicit abort proves the application owns fragment cleanup.

Your mileage may vary sharply with image dimensions, codec, Sharp settings, cache behavior, and customer download patterns. I'm not sure which interval will dominate in a given production system until those byte and duration histograms exist; that uncertainty is exactly why the page should expose the intervals separately.

Instrument aborted sessions too. Multipart helps large transfers survive unstable connections, but lifecycle policies cannot clean multipart fragments automatically here, and lifecycle expiry has a one-day minimum. The application therefore owns an upload-session ledger and an abort sweep. Track sessions created, completed, explicitly aborted, and older than the application's deadline. A rising gap between created and completed sessions should warn before storage residue becomes an invoice surprise.

Compare the full operating bill, not one storage rate

The effective bill has at least six lines: original ingress handling, retained originals, derivative writes, retained derivatives, authenticated delivery, and compute for decode and resize. Add engineering and on-call costs for credentials, vendor SDK upgrades, upload-session cleanup, concurrency coordination, observability, and invoice reconciliation. A unit storage rate cannot represent those costs. Nor can this article supply a measured winner without your workload and contract.

Option Operational fit for this pipeline The catch
Infrai Fits teams that value one key and one bill across backend services, plus a consistent REST and discovery surface No public ACL, object versioning, object lock, conditional If-Match writes, cross-region automatic replication, or cross-cloud bulk migration; browser CORS is not self-service
AWS S3 direct Evaluate when direct provider controls and a specialist storage relationship are the deciding requirements Adds a separate vendor credential, integration, and billing boundary to this comparison
Cloudflare R2 direct Evaluate when the team wants to own the R2 relationship and control plane directly The team also owns that separate operational boundary
DigitalOcean Spaces direct Evaluate as another direct private object-storage relationship, using its current documentation to validate the required controls Keep its integration, access policy, and invoice in the operating model
Aliyun OSS or Tencent COS through the unified surface Covered vendor choices when they meet the workload's region and policy needs The same Infrai capability limits still define the exposed control plane

Infrai is not suitable for a public image host or static website because public_url remains null and public-read ACL is unavailable. It is also the wrong boundary for WORM retention, recovery from accidental overwrite through object versions, strict write exclusion inside storage, automated cross-region replication, or GCS and B2 requirements. Stick with a specialist or direct provider architecture when any of those controls is mandatory. Trial credit also cannot fund persistent writes, so validate the billing path before a storage test.

For the gaming report job, the decision rule is narrower. Choose the unified boundary when reports remain private, the application already owns queue and database coordination, presigned delivery is acceptable, and reducing key and invoice sprawl offsets the missing specialist controls. Choose direct storage when browser CORS administration, immutable retention, provider-specific replication, or storage-native concurrency is part of the requirement.

Getting the threshold wrong has a cost. Page too early and every normal upload burst trains the on-call to ignore report alerts; page too late and customers discover missing thumbnails first. Start the warning from queue age and completion-to-ready rate, correlate it with byte throughput, and tune it against the report readiness objective. Keep raw depth on the dashboard. Reserve the pager for a sustained threat to the customer promise.

References

  • OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet
  • DigitalOcean Spaces documentation
  • Infrai multipart discovery

Further reading

If this boundary fits your system, start with the multipart image upload and thumbnail pipeline guide.

title: Do 3D Point Representations Encode Architectural Functions? Probing Supervised and Pretrained Models on Urban Facades
description:
arXiv:2611.23720v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Semantic labels say what a building element is, not what it does: two identical-looking windows on one facade may be operable or fixed, a column may carry load or only decorate. We ask whether 3D point representations encode such architectural function. On 22 mobile-LiDAR buildings with 15 functional attributes per element, we hold out entire buildings and compare hand-crafted descriptors, networks trained from scratch and frozen self-supervised point transformers. Descriptors and frozen features are read by the same linear layer. No network trained from scratch, from PointNet to a 108M-parameter PTv3, clearly exceeds the descriptors (0.610 mAP on functionally ambiguous elements), whereas frozen Utonia reaches 0.732. Random-weight controls of the same architectures (0.649 and 0.652) attribute the gain to pretraining (Utonia: +0.080, 95% building interval [+0.035, +0.124]). Pretrained features improve at every tested number of labelled buildings while descriptors and random features plateau, and, in the configurations we tested, fine-tuning erodes the benefit: at today's data scale, function is better read from pretrained representations than learned from scratch.

title: Why Good UI Design Matters for a Better Website User Experience
description:
Why Good UI Design Matters for a Better Website User Experience

When we visit a website, the first thing we usually notice is its design. The layout, colours, images and navigation all influence how we feel about that website.

A website may have useful information and great services, but if visitors find it difficult to navigate, they may leave without exploring further. This is why good User Interface (UI) design is an important part of website development.

In this article, let's understand why UI design matters and how it helps create a better experience for website visitors.

What Is UI Design?

User Interface (UI) design is the process of designing the visual elements of a website or application. It includes buttons, menus, typography, colours, images, icons and page layouts.

The main goal is to make a digital product visually appealing, easy to understand and simple to use.

A good interface helps visitors find what they need without confusion.

  1. Simple Navigation Makes a Difference

Navigation is one of the most important parts of a website.

Visitors should be able to find important information without spending too much time searching. Clear menus, meaningful headings and properly organised pages make a website easier to explore.

For example, a business website should make important sections such as Home, About Us, Services and Contact easy to find.

When navigation is simple, visitors can move through the website more comfortably.

  1. Responsive Design Improves Accessibility

People use different devices to browse websites, including mobile phones, tablets and desktop computers.

A website should adjust its layout according to the screen size. Text should remain readable, images should fit properly and buttons should be easy to access.

Responsive design helps provide a consistent experience across different devices.

It also makes information more accessible to people who prefer browsing on their mobile phones.

  1. Colours and Typography Improve Readability

Colours and typography have an important role in website design.

Using too many colours or different font styles can make a website look confusing. A consistent colour palette and readable fonts help create a clean appearance.

Designers should also consider sufficient colour contrast so that visitors can read the content comfortably.

The goal is not simply to make a website attractive, but to make its content easy to understand.

  1. Consistency Builds Trust

A well-designed website should maintain consistency throughout its pages.

Buttons, headings, spacing, colours and other visual elements should follow a similar design style.

When every page looks different, visitors may find it difficult to understand how the website works.

Consistent design creates a more organised appearance and makes the browsing experience predictable.

  1. User Experience Should Be a Priority

UI and UX work together to create a better digital experience.

UI focuses on how a website looks and how its interface is presented. UX focuses on how people interact with the website and how easily they achieve their goals.

Before finalising a design, it is useful to test the website with real users, collect feedback and identify areas that need improvement.

Even small changes to navigation, button placement or page layout can make a noticeable difference.

Final Thoughts

Good UI design is not only about creating a beautiful website. It is about understanding visitors, organising information and making every interaction easier.

Simple navigation, responsive layouts, readable typography and consistent visual elements can help create a positive website experience.

Businesses that invest time in improving their website interfaces can make it easier for visitors to explore their services and understand what they offer.

If you are interested in exploring professional UI design and development solutions, you can learn more from iROID Technologies – UI Design & Development.

A successful website should not only look good; it should also work well for the people using it.

title: Layer-Matched Sparse Attention for Low-Redundancy 3D Reconstruction
description:
arXiv:2611.23554v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: VGGT reconstructs cameras and geometry from unposed images in one pass, but its global attention grows quadratically with the number of views. Training-free accelerators thin this attention and work well on redundant video, but lose pose accuracy when views share little geometry. This paper traces these losses to two kinds of cross-view information that a uniform sparse approximation can fail to preserve together: diffuse layers aggregate distributed context, whereas matching layers depend on query-specific interactions that carry little attention mass. A per-layer statistic measures the log-mass missed by a mean token. Its row-free proxy is the logit variance, and it selects the estimator for each layer. Diffuse layers use shared, importance-sampled hub keys, with log-weights that make the softmax numerator and denominator unbiased. Matching layers stay exact: every aggressive thinning tested cost accuracy. At equal cost, the selected layers outperform the four shifted windows tested. On 13 unseen low-redundancy scenes with 32 views, LMSA stays within 1.4 AUC@5 of dense attention, compared with 10.3 for AVGGT and 4.5 for SAF3R; its difference from contemporaneous GPA-VGGT is not significant, and only its gains over AVGGT pass both scene-level tests. With 100 views, it stays within 1.9 AUC@5 while its aggregator runs $2.0\times$ faster. Used post hoc to choose the layers GPA-VGGT protects, the statistic improves it by 1.2 AUC@5 for 5% more FLOPs. Applied untuned to $\pi^3$, it beats AVGGT but remains further from dense accuracy.

title: Stress-Testing Emotional Support Models: Moving from Homogeneous to Diverse Help Seekers
description:
arXiv:2601.07698v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: As emotional support chatbots have recently gained significant traction across both research and industry, a common evaluation strategy has emerged: use help-seeker simulators to interact with supporter chatbots. However, current simulators suffer from two critical limitations: (1) they fail to capture the behavioral diversity of real-world seekers, often portraying them as overly cooperative, and (2) they lack the controllability required to simulate specific seeker profiles. To address these challenges, we present a controllable seeker simulator driven by nine psychological and linguistic features that underpin seeker behavior. Using authentic Reddit conversations, we train our model via a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, which effectively differentiates diverse seeker behaviors into specialized parameter subspaces, thereby enhancing fine-grained controllability. Our simulator achieves superior profile adherence and behavioral diversity compared to existing approaches. Furthermore, evaluating 7 prominent supporter models with our system uncovers previously obscured performance degradations. These findings underscore the utility of our framework in providing a more faithful and stress-tested evaluation for emotional support chatbots.

title: The Ultimate Node.js Roadmap: From Zero to Production-Ready Backend Architect
description:
Most Node.js tutorials act like a "getting started" guide that leaves you stranded the moment you need to handle real-world complexity. I found a massive, 85-part curriculum that actually covers the full lifecycle of a Node.js developer—from V8 internals all the way to containerized, observable production systems.

If you are tired of shallow tutorials and want to bridge the gap between "I can write a server" and "I know how the runtime works," this is the roadmap you need.

The Curriculum Breakdown

This series is massive, so I've grouped the topics to make it easier to digest:

  • 1–25: The Engine Room
    • V8 basics, libuv, Event Loop, Non-blocking I/O, Streams (Readable/Writable), and Buffers.
  • 26–34: The Web Layer
    • Native HTTP, Express.js architecture, Middleware, and File Uploads.
  • 35–49: Data Persistence
    • Fastify/NestJS, PostgreSQL/MySQL, Mongoose, Knex, Prisma, and Drizzle ORM.
  • 50–61: Security & Real-Time
    • Authentication (JWT/OAuth2), Role-Based Access Control, WebSockets, and Background Task processing.
  • 62–85: The Production Path
    • Worker Threads, Clustering, Logging (Pino), OpenTelemetry, Testing (node:test, Jest), Docker, CI/CD, and Native Addons.

Why This Matters

True seniority isn't just about knowing syntax—it's about understanding constraints. You can't effectively debug performance issues or memory leaks if you don't grasp how the garbage collector or the event loop handles your code. This series forces you to engage with the "how" and "why," not just the "how-to."

Who This Is For

  • The Backend Transitioner: Frontend devs ready to master the server side.
  • The Career Switcher: Someone looking for a structured, self-paced bootcamp equivalent.
  • The Pro: Engineers who want to fill in the "magical" gaps in their knowledge (e.g., how streams actually handle backpressure or how to properly profile a production app).

Check out the full 85-part curriculum here:
https://tuts.kandz.me/category/programming/languages/node-js/

title: The Between-Round Decision in Autonomous Research: An LLM Controller That Reads the Whole Trajectory
description:
arXiv:2611.22661v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Executing an idea often changes how promising it looks, so the next step in autonomous research should rest on results, not on proposals. After each round of experiments, the system must decide whether to refine the best solution or start a new direction, which solution to build from, and what goal to set. We call this the between-round decision. Existing systems wrap it in machinery such as rules, scores, search trees, and schedules; where an LLM makes it, what the LLM needs to read is left open. We ask whether an LLM can make this decision from accumulated evidence, without a search structure around it, and how much of that evidence it needs to read. We present BRED (Between-Round Evidence-based Decision), an LLM-based controller that maintains the best verified solution so far (the Champion) and a log of past rounds, and makes one decision per round. On three widely used research-agent benchmark tasks, BRED improves on the task baselines by 4.80% in MAE on ETTh1 (to 0.4172) and by 3.44 and 3.43 points of accuracy on SST-2 (to 95.07%) and CIFAR-100 (to 84.63%), ahead of the published results. When the controller does not read the accumulated evidence, the same loop gains less: with no history it reaches 0.4299 on ETTh1 and 83.71% on CIFAR-100, whereas the full controller's MAE is 2.95% lower and its accuracy 0.92 points higher. On a new task, speech-based depression detection under a leakage-free protocol, it reaches a macro-F1 of 0.6164 on seeds held out from selection, 5.5 points above its baseline and 4.0 above the strongest published system. Code is available at https://github.com/learninginvision/BRED.

title: Designing a useful preview for an AI-generated comic
description:
A preview should answer the question the user is about to act on. For a personalized comic, that question is whether the people and a moment in the story are recognizable. A random sample from a gallery can demonstrate visual style, but it cannot answer that question.

Separate the decisions

A story outline, character artwork, and a story panel have distinct jobs. The outline answers whether events are in the right order. The character artwork lets someone check who is pictured. The panel shows whether one scene works with the selected characters and dialogue. Put these checks before the point where users commit to a full book.

Let users name the exact change

Give the user a way to compare what they entered with what the preview shows. “The umbrella belonged to the person on the left” is easier to act on than a generic thumbs-down. Keep the previous preview available during a revision so that improved details can be compared without reintroducing a problem in another scene.

Plan for slow generation

A progress indicator is most helpful when it says which step is running and what is already available. If the scene takes longer than expected, let the user return to the same project and see the character preview while they wait. For a failed step, make it clear whether a retry starts from the current story or asks for new input.

Paneluv is our example of this pattern. It turns shared memories into a personalized comic and lets users preview the characters and one story panel before deciding whether to buy a full book.

title: Building a Multi-Step Form That Survives Page Refreshes
description:
A three-step registration form where the user loses all input on a browser refresh is a conversion killer. The standard SPA approach — hold state in a React/Vue store — evaporates on reload. You need a persistence layer that the user never thinks about.

sessionStorage as the default

Write each step's data to sessionStorage on every input change, and hydrate from it on mount:

function usePersisted<T>(key: string, initial: T): [T, (v: T) => void] {
  const stored = sessionStorage.getItem(key);
  const [val, setVal] = useState<T>(stored ? JSON.parse(stored) : initial);
  const persist = (v: T) => { setVal(v); sessionStorage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify(v)); };
  return [val, persist];
}

sessionStorage survives refreshes but not new tabs — which is the right scope for a registration flow.

Step validation

Validate each step before persisting, not just before submission. This prevents the user from refreshing into an invalid state:

function saveStep(step: number, data: StepData) {
  const errors = validate(step, data);
  if (errors.length) return errors;
  sessionStorage.setItem(`reg_step_${step}`, JSON.stringify(data));
  return [];
}

Clearing on completion

After successful submission, clear all step keys and redirect. A registration flow on a site like Millioner that spans multiple pages of personal details must not leave that data in storage after the form is submitted.

Edge case: back button

If the user submits step 3 and then hits the browser back button, they see step 2 with stale data. Intercept popstate and either clear the form or redirect to a confirmation page:

window.addEventListener('popstate', () => {
  if (isSubmitted()) window.location.replace('/welcome');
});

Takeaway

Persist form state on change, not on submit. Validate on persist, not on render. Clear on completion, not on navigation. Three rules that make multi-step forms reliable.

title: Interpreting Timestamp Permutations in Dynamic Link Prediction
description:
arXiv:2611.23753v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Timestamp permutations are used to test whether dynamic link predictors exploit temporal information, but a performance gap can reflect changes in training, evaluation history, or both. We separate these effects with a crossed diagnostic and measure input exposure: whether altered histories actually change the predictor's inputs. On MOOC, TCL trained with binary cross-entropy gains approximately eight pairwise-accuracy points from original-chronology training under either evaluation history, while changing history at fixed weights gives only 0.03 points. The small history contrast reflects unchanged inputs for 68.37% of queries, stable rankings for most others, and cancellation of gains and losses. Under original evaluation history, suppressing explicit time encoding reduces the training contrast from 8.03 to 3.64 points, a paired reduction of 4.39 points (95% interval [3.68, 5.09]) across six seeds. DyGFormer shows corresponding training and history contrasts of 22.34 and 0.38 points across two seeds, despite greater exposure. Partial history permutations further separate nominal intervention strength, input changes, and aggregate accuracy. These comparisons turn a single permutation gap into interpretable statements about training conditions and model responses, while leaving the internal mechanisms of temporal learning open.
