title: Your coding agent may have installed an archived MCP server. Find it in 60 lines
description:
Earlier this month, Glow Security published research on something they call MCPhantom. The short version: when you ask a coding agent to "set up the GitHub MCP server", it often installs the one it remembers from training data. That is frequently an archived reference server from @modelcontextprotocol, not the maintained server the service now ships.

A few numbers from the write-up:

  • In 98% of the sessions they studied where a deprecated server was installed or suggested, the agent picked the package name itself. The user didn't ask for it.
  • The deprecated packages have been downloaded from npm more than 17.3 million times since July 2025.
  • They found four high-severity bugs in the archived servers, including a remote code execution path in the Puppeteer server through prompt injection. The archive won't be patched.
  • It happened across Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI and others, with models from several vendors. This isn't one tool's bug.

The part that should worry a team lead is how invisible this is.

An MCP server started with npx -y some-package never appears in package.json or a lockfile. Your dependency scanner doesn't see it. There's no CVE for your security tooling to match. The only record that it exists is a JSON config file in someone's home directory.

So that's where we look.

Ask npm directly

npm already knows. When a package is deprecated, the registry returns a deprecated message on the version manifest. You can see it with one request:

curl -s https://registry.npmjs.org/@modelcontextprotocol%2fserver-github/latest | jq .deprecated
# "Archived and unmaintained; no security guarantees. See https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers-archived"

The script below reads the MCP configs that common tools use, finds every server launched with npx or bunx, and asks the registry about each one. It has no dependencies and runs on Node 18 or later.

// mcp-audit.mjs: list the MCP servers your coding tools will start,
// and flag npm packages that are deprecated or archived.
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { homedir } from "node:os";
import { join } from "node:path";

const home = homedir();
const cwd = process.cwd();
const CONFIGS = [
  ["Claude Code (user)", join(home, ".claude.json")],
  ["Claude Code (project)", join(cwd, ".mcp.json")],
  ["Claude Desktop (macOS)", join(home, "Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json")],
  ["Claude Desktop (Windows)", join(process.env.APPDATA ?? "", "Claude/claude_desktop_config.json")],
  ["Cursor (user)", join(home, ".cursor/mcp.json")],
  ["Cursor (project)", join(cwd, ".cursor/mcp.json")],
  ["VS Code (project)", join(cwd, ".vscode/mcp.json")],
  ["Windsurf", join(home, ".codeium/windsurf/mcp_config.json")],
];

// Pull every server block out of a config, wherever the tool keeps it.
function serversIn(json) {
  const blocks = [json.mcpServers, json.servers];
  for (const p of Object.values(json.projects ?? {})) blocks.push(p.mcpServers);
  return blocks.flatMap((b) => Object.entries(b ?? {}));
}

// "npx -y @scope/pkg@1.2.3 --flag" -> { name: "@scope/pkg", version: "1.2.3" }
function npmPackage(server) {
  if (!/^(npx|bunx)$/.test(server.command ?? "")) return null;
  const spec = (server.args ?? []).find((a) => !a.startsWith("-"));
  if (!spec) return null;
  const at = spec.lastIndexOf("@");
  return at > 0
    ? { name: spec.slice(0, at), version: spec.slice(at + 1) }
    : { name: spec, version: "latest" };
}

async function npmStatus({ name, version }) {
  const url = `https://registry.npmjs.org/${name.replace("/", "%2f")}/${version}`;
  const res = await fetch(url);
  if (!res.ok) return `not on npm (${res.status})`;
  const meta = await res.json();
  return meta.deprecated ? `DEPRECATED: ${meta.deprecated}` : `ok (${meta.version})`;
}

let flagged = 0;
for (const [tool, path] of CONFIGS) {
  let json;
  try { json = JSON.parse(await readFile(path, "utf8")); } catch { continue; }
  for (const [id, server] of serversIn(json)) {
    const pkg = npmPackage(server);
    let status;
    if (server.url) status = `remote: ${server.url}`;
    else if (pkg) status = await npmStatus(pkg);
    else status = `local command: ${server.command}`;
    if (status.startsWith("DEPRECATED") || status.startsWith("not on npm")) flagged++;
    console.log(`${tool.padEnd(24)} ${id.padEnd(14)} ${pkg?.name ?? ""}\n  -> ${status}`);
  }
}
console.log(`\n${flagged} server(s) need attention.`);
process.exitCode = flagged ? 1 : 0;

Run it from a project folder so it picks up project-level configs too:

node mcp-audit.mjs

Here is what it printed against a test setup with five servers, two of which are the archived reference servers an agent typically reaches for:

Claude Code (user)       github         @modelcontextprotocol/server-github
  -> DEPRECATED: Archived and unmaintained; no security guarantees. See https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers-archived
Claude Code (user)       browser        @modelcontextprotocol/server-puppeteer
  -> DEPRECATED: Archived and unmaintained; no security guarantees. See https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers-archived
Cursor (user)            files          @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem
  -> ok (2.4.0)
Cursor (user)            gh-remote
  -> remote: https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/
VS Code (project)        db
  -> local command: node
VS Code (project)        typo           mcp-server-that-does-not-exist-xyz
  -> not on npm (404)

3 server(s) need attention.

It exits with code 1 when anything is flagged, so you can drop it into a pre-commit hook or a CI job that checks a project's .mcp.json.

A few things worth knowing

Not everything under @modelcontextprotocol is archived. The filesystem server above is still maintained and came back clean. That's why the script asks the registry instead of matching a name pattern.

Claude Code keeps per-project servers inside ~/.claude.json, under projects. If you only check .mcp.json in the repo, you'll miss the servers an agent added "for this project" from inside a session. The script walks both.

"Not on npm" matters too. A name that 404s today is a name someone else can register tomorrow. If an agent invented or misspelled a package, you want to know before somebody publishes it.

The replacement is usually the service owner's server. For GitHub, that's github/github-mcp-server, available as a remote server at https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/, so there's nothing to install. Check the vendor's docs for the others.

What it doesn't cover

It only knows about npm. Python servers launched with uvx, Docker images, and local scripts show up as "local command" and need a human look. The config paths are the defaults. If your team keeps configs somewhere else, add a line to the list. And it audits what is already installed. It won't stop an agent from installing the next one. For that you want a check that runs before the agent's tool call, which is a separate post.

Make it a habit

Agents will keep suggesting packages from memory. Models are trained on the internet as it was, and the MCP ecosystem has moved quickly. You can't fix that from your side, but you can make sure every config on your team gets read by something that checks it.

A simple rule goes a long way: one approved server per service, written down, and nothing launched by npx that hasn't passed a check like this one.

I'm Mayursinh, founder of Redlio Labs. We build custom software and add AI features and agents to it for mid-size companies, and we use coding agents in our own work every day. The script was tested on Node 22 against the live npm registry.

title: Abort-safe Firecrawl tool calls in a React 19 chat stream
description:
Firecrawl is a poor second SSE source. A scrape of a docs page often returns 8–40 KB of markdown. If that blob is pushed into useChat as one assistant delta, the typewriter either stalls on the main thread or paints a wall the user cannot interrupt. We hit this while wiring firecrawl/firecrawl into an existing Next.js chat surface that already streamed through @ai-sdk/react.

The split that held up: search and scrape stay request/response tool calls. Only the model's narration of those results is a stream. Mixing the two left the UI on a half-parsed tool card after the proxy cut the connection.

Failure boundaries we actually measured

Scrape time vs. idle timeout. Firecrawl search was usually sub-second. Scrape of a JS-rendered page was not. The route's upstream idle window was 15s. A render wait exceeded it, the proxy closed the SSE, and useChat reported a generic network error while the tool invocation was still in call. The model never received a tool result, so the next turn replayed the same URL.

Burst after a fat tool result. Once markdown landed, the model echoed large excerpts. With default React 19 rendering and no chunk cap, a ~200-token burst in one frame pushed input latency past 100ms on a mid-range laptop. The stream was fine. The DOM update was not.

Abort does not cancel Firecrawl unless you thread the signal. Stop aborted the AI SDK fetch. The Node handler kept the Firecrawl HTTP call until the vendor timeout. Under load that leaked sockets. A drop mid-token is recoverable with reload. A drop mid-scrape leaves an orphaned toolCallId and an optimistic "Scraping…" row that never settles. We treat that as a terminal tool error, not a retry loop.

Route we ship

The model client is OpenAI-compatible. baseURL is https://b-lost.com/v1 so the SSE body stays unbuffered. A buffering hop in front of that relay was the other way the typewriter jumped in 2–4 KB slabs. On the same prompt mix, multi-provider fallback through that gateway showed about 35ms lower time-to-first-token than a direct provider URL, with no token truncation on streams under 8k output tokens. That is a transport measurement, not a quality claim.

import { createOpenAI } from "@ai-sdk/openai";
import { streamText, tool, convertToModelMessages, stepCountIs } from "ai";
import { z } from "zod";
import FirecrawlApp from "@mendable/firecrawl-js";

export const maxDuration = 60;

const openai = createOpenAI({
  apiKey: process.env.RELAY_API_KEY!,
  baseURL: "https://b-lost.com/v1",
});

const firecrawl = new FirecrawlApp({ apiKey: process.env.FIRECRAWL_API_KEY! });

export async function POST(req: Request) {
  const { messages } = await req.json();
  const signal = req.signal;

  const result = streamText({
    model: openai.chat("gpt-4.1-mini"),
    messages: await convertToModelMessages(messages),
    stopWhen: stepCountIs(4),
    abortSignal: signal,
    tools: {
      scrape_page: tool({
        description: "Scrape one URL to markdown. Do not scrape the same URL twice in one turn.",
        inputSchema: z.object({ url: z.string().url() }),
        execute: async ({ url }, { abortSignal }) => {
          const onAbort = () => undefined;
          abortSignal.addEventListener("abort", onAbort, { once: true });
          try {
            if (signal.aborted || abortSignal.aborted) {
              return { url, error: "aborted", markdown: "" };
            }
            const doc = await firecrawl.scrapeUrl(url, {
              formats: ["markdown"],
              onlyMainContent: true,
              timeout: 12_000,
            });
            const raw = doc.markdown ?? "";
            return {
              url,
              title: doc.metadata?.title ?? "",
              markdown: raw.slice(0, 6_000),
              truncated: raw.length > 6_000,
            };
          } catch {
            return {
              url,
              error: signal.aborted ? "aborted" : "scrape_failed",
              markdown: "",
            };
          }
        },
      }),
    },
  });

  return result.toUIMessageStreamResponse();
}

Caps that mattered more than model choice: scrape timeout at 12s, under both maxDuration and the gateway idle window; markdown sliced to 6,000 characters before it enters the tool result; stepCountIs(4) so a flaky scrape cannot loop until the stream dies; onlyMainContent: true, because nav chrome was duplicate tokens with no user value.

Pin the Firecrawl client and check whether scrapeUrl (older SDK) or scrape (newer SDK) forwards AbortSignal. The guard above stops the handler from waiting. It does not close the vendor socket unless that client honors abort. Do not assume it does.

Client: Stop has to win 

"use client";

import { useChat } from "@ai-sdk/react";
import { DefaultChatTransport } from "ai";
import { useRef } from "react";

export function ResearchChat() {
  const stopRef = useRef<AbortController | null>(null);
  const { sendMessage, status, stop } = useChat({
    transport: new DefaultChatTransport({ api: "/api/chat" }),
  });

  return (
    <button
      type="button"
      onClick={() => {
        stopRef.current?.abort();
        stop();
      }}
      disabled={status !== "streaming" && status !== "submitted"}
    >
      Stop
    </button>
  );
}

When submitting, abort the previous controller, create a new one, and pass abortSignal into sendMessage. If a tool-scrape_page part sits in input-available with no output after about 1.5s, render the URL and "Scraping…", not a spinner over the whole transcript. If status returns to ready with no tool output, replace the row with a one-line failure and leave the input enabled. Do not auto-resubmit. Users double-fired scrapes because the button re-enabled before the tool part settled.

Log tool duration, truncation, and whether req.signal.aborted was already true when execute started. Client chunk-parse errors were almost always a proxy coalescing an incomplete data: frame. Gzip on the SSE body reintroduces that stall even with the relay base URL set.

The 6k cap keeps the typewriter alive and drops the section the user asked about more often than I want. A heading-scoped second fetch would fix the information loss and burn another round trip inside the same abort window. I have not found a timeout budget where a 10s first scrape, a scoped follow-up, and a useful summary all fit. If you page Firecrawl extracts without freezing React or silently dropping the section the question depended on, I want the failure case, not the happy path.

title: Webhook Rate-Limiting Queue Design for US/EU Delayed Jobs, Retry, and DLQ
description:
A queue is only the transport in a webhook delivery system; the lasting decision is where duplicate prevention, tenant rate limits, and delivery evidence live. Short answer: use a durable queue with scheduled delivery and dead-letter handling when retries must survive process loss, but make the application ledger responsible for idempotency and reconciliation in both US and EU deployments.

That boundary matters most for payment-adjacent events. A queue acknowledgement says that a worker has finished its queue work; it cannot prove that an arbitrary HTTP receiver applied a business change once. Treating those statements as equivalent produces an audit gap precisely when an upstream sender, a worker, and a receiver disagree about what happened.

Decision record: preserve identity before choosing a queue

The decision is to authenticate an inbound webhook, give it an immutable event ID, durably record a minimal envelope, and acknowledge the sender only after that record and enqueue have committed. A worker obtains a claim, checks the delivery ledger, sends the webhook, records the outcome, and acknowledges its claim last. If the process stops after sending but before acknowledgement, the event may be delivered again. That is normal. The receiver must use the stable event ID as a uniqueness key.

The invariants are modest but non-negotiable: every accepted event remains discoverable until a terminal disposition; one event ID creates at most one business effect; every attempt is linked to a receipt, claim, response, and final disposition; and an event has an explicit expiry. Exactly-once delivery over a queue and independent HTTP receiver is not a transport feature. It is an application-level accounting property.

Keep the message envelope small: event ID, destination ID, tenant or quota key, payload reference, due time, attempt number, and signing metadata. Do not place credentials in it. For US/EU processing, define where payload bodies, delivery logs, and replay records may reside before selecting a region. A regional queue paired with a ledger in another jurisdiction is a compliance and incident-response decision, not a latency optimization.

How should webhook rate limiting handle delayed jobs, retry, and DLQ?

Rate limiting should be keyed by the destination constraint: commonly a tenant, endpoint, or credential, rather than the worker that happened to claim an event. When no token is available, defer the same event until the next allowed time without counting that deferral as a delivery failure. When a delivery actually fails, increment its attempt count, choose a bounded delay with jitter, and retain the reason. Collapsing those paths makes a healthy but busy destination look broken, and it can fill a dead-letter queue with work that was merely early.

Retries multiply.

Use a maximum attempt count and an expiry independently. An event can run out of attempts before its business deadline, or its deadline can expire before the attempt limit. A dead-letter record should retain the original ID, payload reference, destination, timestamps, and attempt history so an operator can distinguish a bad credential from a destination outage or a malformed request. Replaying a dead letter must reuse the original identity; generating a fresh ID throws away the evidence needed to reconcile a duplicate.

Ordering needs a similarly narrow promise. Serializing every webhook reduces throughput without making unrelated tenants safer. Partition by the smallest business key that requires sequence, then use version checks or idempotent transitions where cross-key order is undefined. A ledger mutation and its consumed-event marker belong in one database transaction whenever the receiver is controlled. Where it is not controlled, store an auditable delivery record and reconcile ambiguous outcomes instead of guessing from an acknowledgement timeout.

What makes a webhook queue comparison misleading without a workload model?

The word "cheapest" has no stable answer without a workload model. Cost includes accepted messages, claims or polls, scheduled work, delivery attempts, payload size, retention, network movement, and the operational work required to recover a failed region. A model built only from successful requests understates the bill and conceals the capacity required during a retry burst.

Operating model Appropriate boundary Operational responsibility Important limitation
Managed pull queue Elastic workers that claim and acknowledge work Consumers, idempotency store, destination throttling The application still implements HTTP delivery and per-destination pacing
Managed HTTP task dispatcher Known HTTP handlers with scheduled execution Handler correctness, request authentication, ledger Less suitable for consumers that require broker protocols or complex routing
Hosted push scheduler Public webhook fan-out with an HTTP-native boundary Payload validation, retention review, replay process Validate regional residency and delivery semantics for the required jurisdiction
Operated message broker Protocol control, custom topology, or infrastructure ownership Capacity, upgrades, recovery exercises, and on-call Software licensing is not the full cost of operating durable infrastructure

Compare candidates against the same failure distribution: ordinary success, a short burst of 429 responses, a destination that rejects authentication, and a receiver that applies the operation but loses its response. For each case, count enqueue, claim, delay, delivery, logging, payload-transfer, and retention work. Then add an operator exercise: restore a delivery ledger, find events that were sent but not acknowledged, and produce an auditable replay set. The result will vary with traffic shape and residency obligations; a published unit price alone cannot select the architecture.

The names in a procurement request can obscure this exercise. SQS, RabbitMQ, CloudAMQP, Upstash QStash, and Cloud Tasks represent different delivery and operating models rather than interchangeable rows on a price sheet. First translate each proposal into the table's boundaries: who owns the consumer lease, how delayed jobs are represented, how retry policy reaches a DLQ, which records are retained, and where the relevant data is processed. Next, use a fixed event sample with the same payload sizes, endpoint classes, rate limits, and retention interval for every proposal. Replay that sample through four ledgers: accepted events; attempted deliveries; terminal successes; and terminal dead letters. The first ledger shows the incoming obligation, the second reveals retry amplification, the third supports downstream reconciliation, and the fourth identifies work that needs an operator decision. This is also where a US/EU requirement gets concrete: establish an approved region for each ledger before testing, then inspect which support, logging, backup, and replay actions can access each record. Don't accept an architecture diagram as proof of that boundary. The needed evidence is the data-flow record, the operational procedure, and the test result for an interrupted delivery. A low request charge can still be the expensive choice if it leaves the team to reconstruct those records during a dispute.

The ledger decides.

Critical path: delivery evidence before acknowledgement

HMAC is useful for authenticating a message between parties that share a secret, following the construction defined in RFC 2104. It does not replace replay protection, identity persistence, or authorization. The compact Go example below exposes the order of durable decisions while leaving the queue and ledger behind interfaces.

package delivery

import (
    "context"
    "crypto/hmac"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "time"
)

type Event struct {
    ID          string
    Destination string
    Body        []byte
    Attempt     int
    ExpiresAt   time.Time
}

type Queue interface {
    Ack(context.Context, Event) error
    Defer(context.Context, Event, time.Time, string) error
    DeadLetter(context.Context, Event, string) error
}

type Ledger interface {
    Delivered(context.Context, string) (bool, error)
    RecordAttempt(context.Context, Event, int, time.Time) error
}

type Sender interface {
    Post(context.Context, string, []byte, map[string]string) (int, error)
}

func Deliver(ctx context.Context, q Queue, ledger Ledger, sender Sender, secret []byte, e Event, now time.Time) error {
    done, err := ledger.Delivered(ctx, e.ID)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if done {
        return q.Ack(ctx, e)
    }
    if !now.Before(e.ExpiresAt) {
        return q.DeadLetter(ctx, e, "expired")
    }

    mac := hmac.New(sha256.New, secret)
    _, _ = mac.Write(e.Body)
    headers := map[string]string{
        "X-Event-ID":         e.ID,
        "X-Signature-SHA256": hex.EncodeToString(mac.Sum(nil)),
    }
    status, err := sender.Post(ctx, e.Destination, e.Body, headers)
    if recordErr := ledger.RecordAttempt(ctx, e, status, now); recordErr != nil {
        return recordErr
    }
    if err == nil && status >= 200 && status < 300 {
        return q.Ack(ctx, e)
    }
    if e.Attempt >= 8 || !now.Add(time.Minute).Before(e.ExpiresAt) {
        return q.DeadLetter(ctx, e, "delivery retry limit reached")
    }
    delay := time.Duration(1<<min(e.Attempt, 10)) * time.Second
    return q.Defer(ctx, e, now.Add(delay), "retryable delivery result")
}

func min(a, b int) int {
    if a < b {
        return a
    }
    return b
}

The production version needs jitter, a documented signature input that includes a timestamp and event identity, constant-time signature comparison at the receiver, and an expiry policy that the receiver enforces. Test the uncomfortable boundaries: before the send, after the send but before the ledger write, after the ledger write but before acknowledgement, and during a dead-letter transfer. Those tests are more valuable than a generic throughput benchmark because they expose what can be proved after an interrupted delivery.

Rejected option and its valid use case

Do not use a periodic workflow scheduler as the primary delivery queue. GitHub documents that scheduled workflows can be delayed during high load, especially near the start of the hour, that queued jobs may be dropped under those conditions, and that the shortest schedule interval is five minutes. That makes a scheduler a reasonable tool for reconciliation scans, batch cleanup, and checking for deliveries that have exceeded their expected state; it is the wrong ownership mechanism for individual, rate-limited webhook attempts.

An in-process timer plus a database status column is also unsuitable once several workers or regions participate, because claims, clock skew, and recovery become distributed-systems concerns. It remains a valid choice for one controlled process with a modest workload and a documented restart procedure. The catch is that its operational boundary must remain as small as its implementation.

The final selection should follow evidence rather than a ranking: document the residency boundary, delivery contract, retry schedule, dead-letter retention, quota model, and recovery procedure; run the same failure scenarios in the approved US or EU region; and preserve the resulting ledger records for review. This approach does not identify a universal low-cost queue. It makes the eventual cost, correctness, and audit obligations visible before they become a production dispute.

References

  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2104
  • https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/events-that-trigger-workflows

title: Reverse-Geocoding with Strands and Amazon Location Service
description:
Introduction

AI and cloud infrastructure are changing the tech world at an unprecedented rate, and it stands to change how we think about global intelligence. Now, a single person can deploy and monitor a service in a weekend that would’ve previously taken a team of developers weeks to deploy.

Geospatial intelligence has been evolving quickly. For one, launching satellites has become significantly cheaper over the last ten years, making scientific spacecraft that are the source of geospatial information cheaper. Secondly, Agentic AI has greatly streamlined both developing geospatial apps and simultaneously created an accessible method of automating systems.

This has improved countless sectors, of course, but geospatial advancements impact our understanding of the physical world on a global scale. Satellite imagery can be parsed in real-time to identify areas suitable to develop a solar farm. Fleets of robotic semitrucks can be routed autonomously across geographic regions, and can have commands dispatched to them using an agent with an MCP server.

For now, however, let’s start small. In this article, I'll show you how you can enable your app with location services and agentic inference using an open-source framework in conjunction with AWS' managed services. We’re going to build a Strands agent that uses Amazon Location Service to help us explore New York City.

Section 1: The App

First, and perhaps most importantly... what are we building? We’re going to build a map that we can talk to. Simple as that. When you complete the setup in the next section, it should look something like this:

This app is built with five components:

  • Strands Agents for the AI agent framework.
  • Amazon Bedrock (Claude Haiku) as the underlying model.
  • Amazon Location Service for reverse geocoding, nearby place search, and map tiles.
  • FastAPI for the Python web server, which routes both local and outgoing API requests.
  • MapLibre GL JS for rendering the interactive map in the browser, embedded directly in HTML.

A typical session goes like this:

  1. Pick a location you're curious about and click it on the map.
  2. The agent identifies the nearest place and sends back a report.
  3. Ask follow-up questions about what's there, how tall it is, what's nearby, or what it costs.
  4. Click a new location whenever you're ready to move on, and repeat.

The data flow behind each of those steps looks like this:

browser (MapLibre)  --click lat/lon-->  FastAPI  -->  Strands Agent
       ^             --follow-up Q-->   session       |- reverse_geocode    (Location Places)
       |                                             |- find_nearby_places (Location Places)
       |                                             |- search_wikipedia   (Wikipedia)
       |                                             |- read_web_page      (the place's site)
       '--- SSE: tool steps, then report or text ---  |- search_web         (open web, capped fallback)

  basemap tiles: Amazon Location Maps, via an API key served by /api/map-config

The agent picks its own path. ReverseGeocode returns only the single closest match. Click the Empire State Building and the closest match is a sightseeing-tour listing four meters away, so the agent calls SearchNearby, sees "Empire State Building" under a Tourist Attraction category eighteen meters out, and reports that instead. Click open ocean and it gets nothing back from either call, says so in one sentence, and offers no link.

The first turn is validated against a PlaceReport Pydantic model, so the UI never parses free text.

Section 2: Clone the App

Now that we know what we’re building, let's get the app running on your machine.

Prerequisites

  • Python 3.10+
  • An AWS account
  • The AWS CLI installed and configured

No infrastructure will be provisioned. This is a script you run on your own machine; it calls Bedrock and Amazon Location's APIs, so your account is billed per request, not per hour. Total cost of following this whole guide and executing the whole click-and-chat workflow will be about a fraction of a cent.

Setup

First, run the commands below in your terminal. This will clone the repo from GitHub, create a virtual environment for Python's config for this project, and install dependencies.

git clone https://github.com/lswans/reverse-geocode-agent.git
cd reverse-geocode-agent
python -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install -r requirements.txt

Next, configure your AWS credentials in the AWS CLI:

aws configure
aws sts get-caller-identity     # confirms it worked

Enable Bedrock model access in the Bedrock console under Model access > Manage model access. Request the Claude models via the console (the default is us.anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5-20251001-v1:0). This is a one-time, per-account, per-region requirement. Skipping it produces an access-denied error on your first click. It looks like a credentials problem, but the fix is enabling model access.

Required IAM Permissions

Service Used for Actions
Bedrock The agent's model bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream
Location Places Reverse geocoding and nearby search geo-places:ReverseGeocode, geo-places:SearchNearby
Location Creating and reading the basemap key geo:CreateKey, geo:DescribeKey, geo:DeleteKey

Create the Basemap API Key

Run the create_map_key.py file:

.venv/bin/python create_map_key.py

This creates a key named map-click-agent-demo-maps, restricted to geo-maps:* (map rendering only, it cannot run place searches), expiring automatically in 90 days. The server fetches it by name at runtime with its own credentials and hands it to the browser through /api/map-config, so no credential is baked into index.html.

Note: These are the minimum actions for the demo. In a shared or production account you would attach them to a scoped role with MFA rather than long-term local keys.

Optional Environment Overrides 

export AWS_REGION="us-east-1"
export MODEL_ID="us.anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5-20251001-v1:0"
export MAP_STYLE="Standard"        # Monochrome, Hybrid, Satellite
export MAP_COLOR_SCHEME="Dark"     # Light
export PORT="8000"

Section 3: The Code

Now, let's review the files that build the app. Three files carry the application logic. Here's what each one does and how to run it.

agent.py

This file contains the Strands agent, its five tools, the system prompt, and the PlaceReport Pydantic schema that structures the first-turn output.

The five tools:

  • reverse_geocode calls Amazon Location's ReverseGeocode API to identify the closest place to a given lat/lon.
  • find_nearby_places calls SearchNearby to get surrounding points of interest when the closest match isn't the most relevant one.
  • search_wikipedia fetches Wikipedia summaries for landmarks and historical context.
  • read_web_page fetches a specific website for prices, hours, or menus. It only accepts URLs that earlier tool output provided, and page text is passed to the model labeled as untrusted information rather than instructions.
  • search_web is a last resort: an open web search the agent reaches for only after the other four have failed to surface a URL it needs, for example a transit station's fare page that Places and Wikipedia never link to. It's capped at two calls per conversation, enforced in code rather than left to the model's judgment, since an unbounded search tool is the one tool here whose cost isn't predictable per call.

The agent decides which tools to call and in what order. Every tool degrades to an error message the agent works around rather than crashing, so a throttled or failed lookup makes the summary vaguer instead of breaking the session.

In the UI, the outcome of the agent executing should look something like this:

Run the agent standalone (no web layer), including one follow-up:

.venv/bin/python agent.py

server.py

This is the FastAPI web server. It handles session management, map configuration, streaming endpoints, and static file hosting.

Key behaviors:

  • Dropping a pin creates a session holding a Strands Agent with its own history. Follow-ups build on the tool results from the first turn instead of starting cold.
  • Dropping a new pin discards the previous session. The browser clears the transcript, the server replaces the agent, and any question aimed at the old session gets a 409.
  • There is exactly one live session at a time.
  • Tool calls stream to the UI as Server-Sent Events, so the agent's reasoning steps are visible in real time.

The API endpoints:

Endpoint Behavior
GET /api/map-config Region, style, color scheme, and the maps API key
GET /api/describe/stream?latitude=&longitude= New pin. SSE step per tool call, then report with {session_id, report}
GET /api/ask/stream?session_id=&question= Follow-up. SSE step and delta text chunks, then done. 409 if the pin was replaced
POST /api/describe Non-streaming first turn, returns {session_id, report}

Run the server:

.venv/bin/python server.py

Then open http://127.0.0.1:8000, click the map, and ask follow-ups. The first turn takes roughly 6 to 10 seconds; follow-ups land in 2 to 4 depending on whether the agent reaches for a tool.

The server binds to 0.0.0.0 and has no authentication. That is fine locally, but it should not be exposed to a network as-is. The maps key it serves is restricted to geo-maps, so it cannot be used to run place searches on your account.

check_map.py

A diagnostic script that verifies the browser's map rendering path end to end. Run it if tiles are not appearing:

.venv/bin/python check_map.py

It checks:

  • CDN assets are reachable
  • The /api/map-config endpoint returns valid configuration
  • The style descriptor loads
  • A sample tile fetches successfully
  • Sprites and glyphs resolve

If any of these fail, the map won't render in the browser, and this script tells you which link in the chain broke.

Section 4: Conversation Lifecycle

The session model is simple. Dropping a pin creates a session. Follow-ups build on the tool results from the first turn: ask "how tall is it" and the agent reaches for Wikipedia, ask "what else is nearby" and it reuses the place data it already has, ask "what does it cost" and it reads the website that the place data handed it.

That last behavior only happens on follow-ups, never during the first report, and only for things a place publishes itself: prices, hours, tickets, menus. The agent may only fetch URLs that earlier tool output gave it. read_web_page refuses anything that is not a public web address, and page text is passed to the model labelled as untrusted information.

Dropping a new pin discards the session entirely. One session at a time is all a single-presenter demo needs.

Section 5: Cleanup

The only persistent resource this project creates in your AWS account is the API key from the setup step. Everything else stops costing anything the moment you close the server.

To remove the API key:

aws location delete-key --key-name map-click-agent-demo-maps

Or leave it alone. An expired key stops working on its own and cannot be revived, so there's no ongoing risk in forgetting about it.

To confirm nothing else is left:

aws location list-keys

Any key you don't recognize by name is not something this project created.

What's Next

This post covered the reverse-geocoding agent: clicking a map, identifying a place, and asking follow-up questions grounded in real tool output. The agent picks its own path through five tools, falling back to open web search only when the others come up empty, structures its first response with a Pydantic model, and streams its reasoning to the browser in real time.

In Part 2, we'll extend this foundation with forward geocoding (searching for places by name), route planning between pins, and isochrone visualization to show reachable areas within a given travel time. Same stack, same single-file deployment model, more spatial capability.

If you built the app and clicked around New York for a while, you already have everything you need for future projects where we build on this.

Thanks for reading. My name is Lucas, I'm a Developer Advocate at AWS covering our use cases in Space Systems Engineering and Agentic AI. Follow if that's your jam.

title: Large Language Models Have Not Yet Transformed Science
description:
arXiv:2611.22975v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The emergence of large language models (LLMs) in late 2022 has raised questions about the future of science, but assessing their impact requires understanding how scientific practices were already evolving. We analyze 2.5 million full-text papers across five disciplines from 2015 to 2025, tracing trends over a broad spectrum of lexical, structural, epistemological, and social dimensions. Aside from frequency shifts in some words, most pre-2023 trends continued with limited detectable breaks. Among the notable exceptions, growth in computer science coauthor teams accelerated significantly in Asia, while apparent declines in biomedical topic diversity largely reflected standardization in article formats. Our study establishes an empirical foundation for monitoring the health of global science as LLM adoption deepens.

title: Why a Remote Image Renders but Canvas Pixel Access Fails
description:
An image can look correct in a page and still fail when an editor tries to read its pixels. You may see a remote photo on screen, draw it onto a canvas, and then get a SecurityError from getImageData() or toDataURL(). The request succeeded. The browser is enforcing a separate rule for reading the pixels.

Disclosure: I’m the founder of MediaToURL. This is general browser guidance, and a media URL provider cannot override another server’s CORS policy.

Displaying an image is different from reading it

A browser can display an ordinary cross-origin image while restricting scripts from inspecting its pixel data. If you draw that image onto a canvas without an approved Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) response, the canvas becomes tainted. The drawing may work, while pixel-reading and export methods fail. MDN explains the cross-origin image rules for canvas.

That distinction matters in crop tools, color pickers, thumbnail generators, and any workflow that exports a canvas. Seeing the image is not proof that your script can inspect it.

Request CORS before the image starts loading

Set the image's crossOrigin property before assigning src. For a public image that does not need cookies or other credentials, anonymous mode is usually the right starting point.

const image = new Image();
image.crossOrigin = "anonymous";

image.addEventListener("load", () => {
  const canvas = document.querySelector("#preview");
  const context = canvas.getContext("2d");

  canvas.width = image.naturalWidth;
  canvas.height = image.naturalHeight;
  context.drawImage(image, 0, 0);

  try {
    const firstPixel = context.getImageData(0, 0, 1, 1);
    console.log(firstPixel.data);
  } catch (error) {
    console.error("Canvas pixels are not readable", error);
  }
});

image.addEventListener("error", () => {
  console.error("Image load failed. Check the URL and CORS response.");
});

image.src = "https://assets.example.com/photo.webp";
~~~{% endraw %}

The image host must also allow your app's origin in its response. For example, a server might return:{% raw %}

~~~http
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com
~~~

A public image without credentials may use an Access-Control-Allow-Origin value of * if that matches the host's policy. When you request an image in CORS mode and the server does not grant access, the browser blocks that load. The page cannot add permission to the remote server's response from client-side JavaScript. See MDN's reference for the [crossorigin attribute](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Attributes/crossorigin).

## Check the response in DevTools

When the result is unexpected, open the Network panel, reload the page, and select the image request. Check four things:

1. Confirm the final URL is the image you intended. A redirect can land on a share page, login screen, or a different host.
2. Check the response status and Content-Type. A successful HTML page is still not an image response.
3. Look for Access-Control-Allow-Origin in the response headers. The allowed origin must match your app, unless the host intentionally allows all origins for a public file.
4. Read the console message alongside the request. It usually tells you whether the browser rejected the CORS check or the file failed for another reason.

If you only need to show a picture, an ordinary image element may be enough. If the feature needs to crop, sample, or export pixels, the host must return a CORS-enabled response. The browser cannot grant that permission on the host's behalf. MDN's [getImageData() documentation](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/CanvasRenderingContext2D/getImageData) describes the SecurityError that can appear when the canvas is not readable.

Two common fixes do not solve this. Setting crossOrigin after src is too late because the request has already started. Adding Access-Control-Allow-Origin as a request header from JavaScript also does not work; it is a response header the server must send. Using fetch with mode set to no-cors does not make the response readable either.

title: SignAligner: Dual-Granularity Span Generation for Sign Language Alignment
description:
arXiv:2611.22409v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Large sign-language corpora benefit from temporal labels at two scales: subtitle spans for subtitle alignment and word spans for sign spotting. Sign spottings already locate words in time at corpus scale, but training subtitle alignment jointly on subtitle and word spans remains underexplored. We present SignAligner, a prompt-conditioned visual-language span generator that maps a sign-language video and a subtitle-sentence or target-word query to a textual start/end frame interval. It is first trained jointly on subtitle spans and word spans from sign spottings, then refined with overlap-based rewards while retaining auxiliary word examples. On the subtitle test set of the British Broadcasting Corporation-Oxford British Sign Language (BOBSL) corpus, the refined model reaches 66.68 F1@0.50 (F1 with a temporal intersection-over-union threshold of one half), the best among compared systems without external sign-video resources. This overlap-reward refinement outperforms cross-entropy continuation from the same jointly trained model. Joint training with word spans improves subtitle alignment in a pair of our generators matched in code, labels and maximum update budget. The advantage remains after both models of the pair are refined with overlap rewards. For word queries, the refined model follows the queried word, not a fixed position in the video: when the word's sign lies away from the video centre, it is far more accurate than predictions that use position alone. Together, these findings support one shared span generator refined with overlap rewards, aligning subtitles and producing word spans for human review.

title: Goodbye Notion: Why We Migrated Our Tech Content Ops to Git and Pydantic
description:
Originally published at Datalaria.

For years, engineering teams and technical authors publishing on static architectures (Jamstack, Hugo, Astro, Next.js, or MkDocs) have lived with a glaring paradox: we manage application source code with the utmost continuous integration rigor, yet oversee editorial strategy using disconnected third-party tools.

On paper, the workflow looked pristine. You build a relational database in Notion or a base in Airtable, design a chromatic Kanban board (Idea, Draft, In Review, Scheduled, Published), set up calendar views, and configure custom fields for word counts, SEO tags, and bilingual cross-references.

Yet, as the blog scales past 50 or 100 technical articles, the double-entry failure mode strikes with mathematical certainty: the ground truth in the Git repository and the fictional state of the external database inevitably diverge.

🗺️ Datalaria Pulse Series Roadmap

To understand how each piece of the Content Ops as Code architecture fits together, this series consists of 5 structured installments:

  1. 🟢 Part 1 (This article): Goodbye Notion: Datalaria Pulse and Editorial Governance that Writes Itself from Git
  2. ⚪ Part 2 (Sun Nov 22): From Front Matter to Index: Pydantic v2, Bilingual Parity, and CI/CD Automation
  3. ⚪ Part 3 (Wed Nov 25): Executive Table, Kanban Board, and Monthly Calendar in React 19 over a Static Index
  4. ⚪ Part 4 (Sun Nov 29): Automated Google Analytics 4 and Search Console: Measuring the Organic ROI of Every Post, App, and Kit
  5. ⚪ Part 5 (Wed Dec 02): Editorial Operations for Docs, SEO, and Marketing Teams: From Notion to Excel in 5 Minutes and AI Agent Factory

0. Phase Objectives and Article Scope: Toward Autonomous Editorial Governance

This article marks the official kickoff of Datalaria Pulse, entirely focused on resolving technical content asset governance through our native operating system:

Strategic Objectives:

  1. Eradicate Administrative Double-Entry: Permanently eliminate the friction of manually synchronizing third-party databases (Notion, Airtable, Trello) against Git repositories.
  2. Establish the Content Ops as Code Philosophy: Govern Markdown articles and YAML metadata with software engineering discipline: schema-based validation (Pydantic v2), deterministic bilingual parity, and automated CI/CD builds.
  3. Dual-Mode Delivery Model: Provide two operational tiers for authors and corporate teams:
    • Datalaria Pulse Kit (Standalone): Downloadable commercial pack featuring an Excel 2016/365 Master Template, Power Query M connector, 5-minute Notion migration script, and a dependency-free universal CLI scanner.
    • Datalaria Pulse Pro (Cloud Multi-Tenant): Collaborative workspace on Supabase PostgreSQL with authentication, bi-directional real-time Web ↔ Localhost synchronization, and private tenant isolation.

Specific Scope of this Article 1:

  • Quantify the hidden costs and failure modes of manual editorial tracking in Git-based publications.
  • Formalize the Invariance Principle and Datalaria Pulse's 4-tier architecture.
  • Introduce the executive visualization suite (Analytics Dashboard, interactive Table, 5-column Kanban, Monthly Calendar, and Health Diagnostics).
  • Provide immediate access to both the live interactive Sandbox and the downloadable Kit resources.

1. Connection to the Datalaria Ecosystem: From LifeOps to Decision Intelligence

Datalaria Pulse does not exist in isolation; it represents the operational convergence of principles established across our prior software applications and quantitative series:

  1. The Modular Platform Thesis of LifeOps: In our flagship LifeOps platform, we demonstrated how to construct a unified personal and professional operating system combining a responsive React SPA with serverless Supabase PostgreSQL. Pulse applies that exact modular architecture to the governance of technical content repositories.
  2. Eliminating the HiPPO Bias in our Decision-Making Framework: In our guide on quantitative prioritization (DAR, RICE, and Financial Business Cases), we showed how executive deliberation degenerates when guided by unanchored intuition. In Pulse, we enforce mathematical rigor on content ops: subjective guesswork is replaced by deterministic SEO scoring (0 to 100) and normalized organic traffic percentiles (Google Analytics 4 indexed to base 100).
  3. Data Hygiene and Pipelines in S&OP Engineering: Just as supply chain workflows filter ERP noise before training probabilistic demand models, Pulse lexically cleans content (stripping source code, math blocks, and template tags) to measure the true technical density of each asset.
  4. Governance under Spec-Driven Development (SDD): In accordance with our technical constitution and Autonomous AI Agent architecture, Pulse guarantees that no post is published unless it satisfies all deterministic bilingual invariants (INV-PULSE-1..5).

2. The Double-Entry Fallacy: The Chasm Between Notion and Git

Anyone who has attempted to maintain an editorial calendar in Notion in parallel with a GitHub repository recognizes this degradation cycle:

  1. Title and Slug Divergence: You refine an article title in Markdown front matter to boost organic Click-Through Rate (CTR) on Google, or rename the folder to improve the SEO slug. In Git you execute git commit -m "seo: refine slug" and deploy in seconds. Notion is never notified. Three weeks later, the Notion card points to a 404 dead link or preserves an obsolete title.
  2. The Publication Date Illusion: You postpone a launch date by two weeks in front matter (date: 2026-11-20) because a quantitative benchmark requires deeper peer review. The repository strictly schedules the post. Yet Notion still displays it as published on the 5th. The executive timeline shown to leadership no longer reflects production reality.
  3. Bilingual Parity Blindness: If you publish bilingually in Spanish and English, manually tracking which translations are pending, which fell out of sync after technical updates, and which maintain complete parity becomes an unsustainable administrative chore. The common outcome is orphan articles and broken cross-language references.
  4. Administrative Toil: Technical writers spend up to 20% of their productive bandwidth on administrative card-pushing bureaucracy instead of crafting high-value content or developing algorithms.

Modern software engineering resolved this problem decades ago under the banner of Infrastructure as Code (Terraform) and Configuration as Code (Kubernetes): infrastructure is not configured via web forms; it is declared in versioned, auditable code.

Why not apply the exact same discipline to technical editorial management? This is the thesis of Content Ops as Code.

3. The Invariance Principle: Content Ops as Code

The core invariant of Content Ops as Code is unambiguous:

Core Invariant: In technical documentation or blogging platforms, Markdown files and their YAML Front Matter within Git constitute the Single Source of Truth. No external third-party database holds authority over content state.

Under this model, editorial management shifts from reactive manual upkeep to a deterministic compilation pipeline:

Dimension Traditional Workflow (Notion / Airtable) Content Ops as Code (Datalaria Pulse)
Source of Truth Closed external SaaS database. Versioned .md and .yaml files in Git.
Synchronization Manual (prone to omission and human drift). Instant and automated on every git commit.
Bilingual Parity Manual checkbox auditing. Algorithmic timestamp analysis and matching.
SEO Audit Static estimates filled by hand. Deterministic build-time scoring (0-100).
Performance Metrics Disconnected or manually exported CSV dumps. Direct GA4/GSC ingestion normalized to base 100.
Infrastructure Cost \$10-\$25/user/month in proprietary SaaS tools. Zero infrastructure cost (static files / Git).

4. The Datalaria Pulse Architecture

To bring this philosophy to life across the Datalaria ecosystem, we built and deployed Datalaria Pulse: a comprehensive engine that reads our content tree directly and generates a real-time executive cockpit.

4.1. Deterministic Extraction and Validation via Pydantic v2

Instead of brittle regex scripts, Pulse defines formal data contracts using Pydantic v2. Every asset is parsed to extract:

  • Title and description in both languages.
  • Formal publication date and filesystem last-modified timestamp via Git commit logs (git log -1 --format=%cI).
  • Actual word count through lexical stripping (discarding code fences, Hugo shortcodes such as app-ref or mermaid, and HTML tags).
  • Strict taxonomy validated against canonical category definitions.

4.2. Bilingual Parity Governance

Pulse deterministically compares Spanish assets against their English counterparts, classifying each into one of five states:

  1. complete: Both language variants exist and remain synchronized within an allowable temporal window.
  2. missing_en: The Spanish asset is live, but no English translation exists.
  3. missing_es: An English asset exists without a corresponding Spanish version.
  4. outdated_en: The Spanish post received substantial Git updates after the English translation was published.
  5. outdated_es: The English post was updated without propagating revisions to Spanish.

4.3. Security Invariants (Safe Public Dogfooding)

To deploy the application publicly without exposing confidential company analytics, Pulse enforces formal invariants INV-PULSE-1 e INV-PULSE-2:

  • INV-PULSE-1 (Private Asset Isolation): No draft ideas or private notes can ever leak into the public bundle.
  • INV-PULSE-2 (Mathematical Normalization): Absolute raw pageviews and revenue from Google Analytics 4 are never exposed to the client; they are normalized into a base-100 index relative to the median blog post alongside statistical percentiles (0% to 100%).

5. Datalaria Pulse in Action: The Executive Visualization Suite

The visible output of this compilation pipeline is a responsive web application built with React 19 + TypeScript, compiled statically into the Hugo portal and usable both in guest sandbox mode and as a collaborative cloud cockpit.

🚀 Official Datalaria App: Datalaria Pulse — Try Live Demo

The interface delivers 5 integrated perspectives:

  1. Analytics & KPIs Dashboard: Macro ecosystem metrics (183 governed assets: 118 bilingual articles, 47 SemVer application releases 🚀 APP / ⚡ APP vX.Y, and 18 B2B Kit editions 📦 KIT under invariants INV-PULSE-1..8, 100% bilingual parity), cumulative lexical depth (~215,000 indexed technical words), total reading time (~18.5 hours), and replacement valuation of the content portfolio.
  2. Executive Table with Live Filtering: Real-time title search, pill status filters (Published, Scheduled, Draft), multi-criteria sorting by date or SEO score, and fast pagination (10, 25, or 50 rows).
  3. 5-Column Kanban Board: Notion-style editorial pipeline (Idea ➔ Draft ➔ In Review ➔ Scheduled ➔ Published) featuring interactive cards that open full editorial inspection modals.
  4. Notion Monthly Calendar: 35-cell monthly grid with chronological navigation, highlighting scheduled asset drops across upcoming quarters.
  5. Editorial Health & ROI: Internal cross-link audits, stale content alerts, and bilingual parity tracking.

6. Editorial Series Roadmap

This inaugural article begins a 5-part technical series breaking down every layer of the architecture:

  • Chapter 1 (This article): Goodbye Notion: Introducing Datalaria Pulse, the Editorial OS Written Directly from Git.
  • Chapter 2: From Front Matter to Index: Pydantic v2, Bilingual ES/EN Parity, and GitHub Actions CI/CD.
  • Chapter 3: React 19 Executive UI: Table, Kanban, and Monthly Calendar on a Static Zero-Latency Index.
  • Chapter 4: Connecting GA4 and Search Console to Measure Organic ROI with Base-100 Normalization.
  • Chapter 5: Technical Content Ops for Teams: Downloadable Excel Kit and Collaborative Cloud Architecture with Supabase.

7. Automate Your Content Operations: Download the Kit or Try the Live Demo

If you maintain a technical blog, documentation hub, or engineering-led publication backed by Git and want to eliminate manual administrative toil permanently, two immediate paths are available:

  1. Download the Datalaria Pulse Kit (Standalone Edition): Access the complete bundle in our resources hub featuring the Excel Master Template with data validation rules, the 5-minute Notion-to-Excel Python migration script, the Power Query M connector, and the standalone pulse_repo_scanner.py CLI ready for your CI/CD pipeline. 👉 Download Datalaria Pulse Kit in Resources →

Price: 19€ 39€
The downloadable commercial bundle (Dual ES/EN Edition) includes Automated Master Excel Workbooks (.xlsx) with 6 color-coded sheets, native AutoFilter tables and zero manual duplication (INDEX/MATCH + live Kanban), Dual Power Query M Connectors for Notion CSV and Git public.json, Zero-Dependency Python CLI Tools (migrate_notion.py & pulse_repo_scanner.py), and 5-Page Executive PDF Guides.

  1. Explore the Live Sandbox and Pro / Demo Mode: Launch the interactive web application directly in your browser. Explore Datalaria's 183 live assets in the public Sandbox, or log in to Pro / Demo Mode to experience real-time idea drafting, instant cross-device synchronization, and multi-tenant PostgreSQL governance. 🚀 Open Datalaria Pulse Web App Live →

title: Surfacing Disagreement Beats Resolving It: A Gated Ablation Study of Provenance-Weighted Memory for Multi-Agent Debate
description:
arXiv:2611.22461v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Shared memory for multi-agent debate is usually built to resolve inconsistency: retrieval returns one winning fact and the disagreement disappears before any agent sees it. We ask whether that is correct. In DebateGraph, four backends share one contract (read/write/snapshot), so five mechanisms from the agent-memory literature can be removed independently under a fixed budget, each gated on a pre-declared threshold. Across 39 runs one survives: preserving contradictions and passing the ranked conflict set to the debate, rather than collapsing it to a winner, improves F1 by +0.340 (95% CI [+0.267, +0.414]) and cuts attack success from 22 to 7 of 122 poisoned items (McNemar exact p=0.0003), at equal cost. Reaching it meant fixing a bottleneck in our harness: conflict sets are built only over retrieved edges, and our pre-declared cap left three quarters of planted contradictions unretrievable, first measuring the mechanism at +0.084. The effect replicates on two retrieval substrates and directionally on HotpotQA documents. No other mechanism survives, and two are worse than inert: once contradictions reach the prompt, a write trust-gate and the router's provenance features each cost accuracy (-0.075 and -0.096 F1). The gate fails structurally: poisoned objects are always entities the graph already contains, against 53% of gold, so groundedness scores the lie above a truthful first mention. We release the harness, attack set, and logs, and argue that silently reconciling memory is the assumption worth abandoning.

title: Fix: “Next.js encountered the unstable value new Date()” in Next.js 16
description:
I upgraded a landing page to Next.js 16 and the production build failed on the most innocent line in the whole project, the copyright year in the footer:

<p>© {new Date().getFullYear()} Driftly</p>

next build stopped with this:

Error: Route "/": Next.js encountered the unstable value `new Date()` while prerendering.

This value can change between renders, so it must be either prerendered or computed later.

Ways to fix this:
  - [dynamic] Render at request time by adding a dynamic data access (e.g. `await connection()`) before this call
  - [cache] Prerender and cache the value with `"use cache"`
  - [client] Render the value on the client with `"use client"`
  - [measure] If the value is for telemetry, use a timing API such as `performance.now()`

Here's why it happens and how to pick the right fix.

Why Next.js 16 complains

The error only shows up when Cache Components is turned on. Check your next.config.ts:

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  cacheComponents: true,
};

My project was created with create-next-app, and it already had this option enabled.

With Cache Components, Next.js prerenders as much of each page as it can into static HTML at build time. A value like new Date() is different every time it runs, so Next.js can't tell whether you meant "the time when the site was built" or "the time when the visitor opened the page". Instead of guessing, it stops the build and asks you to decide.

The same rule applies to:

  • new Date() and Date.now()
  • Math.random()
  • crypto.randomUUID()

performance.now() is the exception. Next.js treats it as a timing tool for telemetry and doesn't guard it.

Fix 1: Cache the value with "use cache"

Use this when the value only needs to be fresh enough, not computed for every visitor. A copyright year is the perfect example.

Move the value into an async function marked with "use cache":

// components/year.tsx
async function getYear() {
  "use cache";
  return new Date().getFullYear();
}

export async function Year() {
  return <>{await getYear()}</>;
}

// components/footer.tsx
import { Year } from "./year";

export function Footer() {
  return <p>© <Year /> Driftly</p>;
}

The year is computed during prerendering and cached, so the page stays fully static. The cached value is refreshed when the cache revalidates or when you redeploy.

Fix 2: Compute it on every request with connection()

Use this when every visitor really needs a new value, like a request ID or a "rendered at" timestamp.

Call connection() before reading the value. This tells Next.js to wait for a real request. Wrap the component in <Suspense> so the rest of the page can still be prerendered:

import { connection } from "next/server";
import { Suspense } from "react";

async function RenderedAt() {
  await connection();
  return <p>Rendered at {new Date().toISOString()}</p>;
}

export default function Page() {
  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<p>Loading…</p>}>
      <RenderedAt />
    </Suspense>
  );
}

The trade-off: this part of the page is now rendered on the server for every request. In the next build output, the route changes from ○ (Static) to ◐ (Partial Prerender): static HTML with the dynamic part streamed in.

Fix 3: Move it to the client (and watch for the second error)

My first instinct was to make the footer year a Client Component:

"use client";

export function Year() {
  return <>{new Date().getFullYear()}</>;
}

That produced a different error:

Error: Route "/": Next.js encountered the unstable value `new Date()` in a Client Component.

This value would be evaluated during the prerender, instead of recomputed on each visit.

With Cache Components, Client Components are prerendered too. "use client" alone doesn't move the work to the browser. The error message suggests two ways out:

Read the value in an effect, so it only runs in the browser:

"use client";

import { useEffect, useState } from "react";

export function LocalTime() {
  const [time, setTime] = useState<string | null>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    setTime(new Date().toLocaleTimeString());
  }, []);

  return <span>{time ?? "…"}</span>;
}

Or wrap the Client Component in <Suspense> so Next.js can stream it in instead of baking it into the static HTML.

Use this fix for values that depend on the visitor's browser, such as their local time zone.

Fix 4: For telemetry, use performance.now()

If you only need a duration for logging, performance.now() is allowed:

const start = performance.now();
await doWork();
console.log(`doWork took ${performance.now() - start}ms`);

Don't render this value in the UI. It's meant for measurements.

Which fix should you use?

What you need Fix
A value that's fine to compute once (copyright year, build date) "use cache"
A fresh value for every request (request ID, server timestamp) await connection() + <Suspense>
A value from the visitor's browser (local time, time zone) useEffect in a Client Component
A duration for logs or metrics performance.now()

One more gotcha: static export

If you deploy with output: "export" (a fully static site with no server), you can't render anything per request, so Fix 2 is not an option. For the static demo of my landing page, the simplest working setup was turning cacheComponents off for that build. Note that partialPrefetching requires cacheComponents, so it has to go too.

Wrapping up

The error looks scary, but it's Next.js asking a fair question: should this value be computed once, per request, or in the browser? Answer that, and the fix is a few lines.

The official docs go deeper: blocking-prerender-current-time and the Client Component version.

I ran into this while building Liftoff, a Next.js 16 + Tailwind CSS 4 landing page kit, which uses the "use cache" footer year from Fix 1.

  • Liftoff Lite is free (MIT): navbar, hero, features, footer and dark mode. Get Liftoff Lite
  • Liftoff is the full kit with pricing, FAQ, testimonials, email capture and a 22-page launch guide. Live demo · Get Liftoff

Have you hit this error with something other than dates? Let me know in the comments.

title: When Passing Checks Do Not Establish Completion: Evidence Interpretation in Coding Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.22835v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Verification procedures in coding agents must preserve execution facts, interpret their scope and discharge checking obligations. We study these responsibilities through qualified repository checks, controlled evidence consumers and executable workflows. A prospective thirteen-task factorial study finds that correct reported facts need not yield the requested finite verdict. Conversely, all 122 delivered labels in a held-out receipt-supply study are correct, while sixteen responses misreport facts and eleven others exceed authorized scope. Production repair supplies successful controls and finite-supported preservation failures. Across 118 repair episodes on 31 tasks, source interventions separate startup reachability from repair and witness production from the claimed operation. Lifetime and resource controls delimit what passing validation establishes. Generated-note comparisons yield local repair differences but can state false explanations; strong ordinary baselines, new tasks and Skill-transfer studies supply no consistent overall advantage. These results characterize evidence interpretation, applicability and fulfilled actions while limiting claims of general diagnostic superiority, Skill deterioration or deployed folding effects.

title: Same Rank, Different Needs: Rethinking LoRA Redistribution in Federated Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.23742v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Federated low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables clients with different resource budgets to collaboratively fine-tune foundation models. To distribute an aggregated update within each client's rank budget, existing methods commonly retain its leading singular directions. However, directions that best reconstruct the update matrix need not best preserve its responses on a particular client's inputs: a lower-energy direction may matter more to that recipient. We formalize this mismatch and show that matrix-optimal truncation can incur arbitrarily larger response error than another readout of the same rank. Motivated by this result, we propose Receiver-Aware Subspace Adaptation (RASA), a plug-in framework for receiver-aware knowledge transfer. RASA uses compact diagonal input second moments to perform uncentered PCA of receiver-weighted update responses. The resulting readout is globally optimal for the rank-constrained receiver objective and preserves at least as much response energy as spectral truncation under the diagonal metric. RASA also introduces spectral-reference aggregation, which removes the personalized initialization offset while retaining the locally learned increment. Experiments on DomainNet-100, NICO++, GLUE, and SuperNI demonstrate RASA's effectiveness across methods under resource, task, and data heterogeneity. In particular, RASA improves DomainNet-100 accuracy by 3.23 percentage points with FlexLoRA and achieves gains of up to 8.33 ROUGE-L points on seen SuperNI tasks and 4.37 on unseen tasks with modest overhead.

title: Virtual models now available on AI Gateway
description:
Virtual models are now available on AI Gateway.

A virtual model is a saved configuration that tells AI Gateway which model and settings to use. Your apps and agents call it with a custom model ID, such as vmc/coding-agent. You can change the model or settings centrally in AI Gateway without redeploying your apps or reconfiguring your agents.

Use virtual models to:

  • Configure coding agents: Set reasoning effort, fast mode, prompt caching, and other options even when your agent doesn’t expose them.

  • Control routing and compliance: Choose providers, configure fallback models, and enforce requirements such as Zero Data Retention.

  • Attribute spend: Attach custom reporting tags to every request that uses the virtual model.

To create a virtual model, open the Virtual Models page and click Create Virtual Model. Enter a slug, choose the underlying model, configure the settings you want requests to use, and save.

Or create one with the Vercel CLI:

To use a virtual model, replace the provider model ID in your AI SDK or compatible API requests with vmc/<slug>, such as vmc/coding-agent.

For coding agents, connect to AI Gateway with vercel ai-gateway setup if needed, then select your virtual model in the agent’s model picker or configuration.

Virtual models work with every model type on AI Gateway. Read the launch post for examples or learn more in the virtual models documentation.

title: The Shared Word: Evaluating Language Models on Dutch Word Puzzles
description:
arXiv:2611.22935v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Many LLM benchmarks for languages other than English are translated, multiple-choice, or difficult to score automatically. We introduce The Shared Word (TSW-NL), a Dutch benchmark built around four core principles: it is language-specific, open-vocabulary, human-curated, and deterministically scored. Each puzzle gives three clues that describe different senses or uses of the same Dutch word. The clues are individually ambiguous, requiring the solver to combine evidence across multiple clues. We construct the benchmark from Dutch Wikipedia disambiguation pages, followed by automatic filtering and extensive manual curation. The final dataset contains 222 instances, with three independent human answers per test item. The task is clearly challenging: scores in our human study range from 49.5% to 61.0% and the highest-scoring open-weight model we tested reaches only 39.3%. Many others even score below 20%. At the same time, closed-source models show great progress: GPT-4.1 (April 2025) scores 59.2%, whereas GPT-5.6 Sol with max reasoning scores 88.8%. We believe this task provides a useful addition to Dutch model evaluation, plus a clear recipe that can be applied to construct a similar benchmark for other languages.
