title: Cron Trigger Queue Worker Node.js Example: Scheduled Digest Enqueue Beyond 15 Minutes
description:
Short answer: let the cron trigger enqueue a small, repeatable command, then let a queue worker deliver each customer digest. A 15-minute scheduler limit is fine when no individual invocation owns the whole report. The useful guarantee is a recorded handoff, not a heroic timeout.

A small decision matrix for weekly delivery

Design What it can prove Where it fits Trade-off
Cron calls the report directly The process started A tiny, read-only task A timeout can hide partial work
Cron enqueues one batch The batch was handed off Uniform, short reports One poison item can delay the batch
Cron records a run and enqueues customer jobs Each customer has a traceable attempt Active-customer digests Requires a ledger and reconciliation

For a B2B SaaS digest, I use the third row. The trigger writes a run record, creates one message per active customer, and exits. A worker owns data fetching, rendering, and delivery. That split keeps the scheduler's execution window boring and makes the business result inspectable.

This is a revenue-per-hour decision. Queue mechanics are undifferentiated plumbing; I want them managed or isolated so one person can spend the week shipping product. The ledger is worth keeping in application code because it answers the question support actually asks: “Did Acme's Monday report send?”

What delivery guarantee does the queue really provide?

Most queues provide at-least-once delivery. A message may appear again after a worker has sent the email but before it has acknowledged the message. A FIFO queue can preserve ordering and, with a deduplication window, reduce duplicates, but it cannot make an external email provider exactly-once. AWS describes those FIFO properties and their limits in its queue documentation.

So I define two separate facts: enqueued means the scheduler committed a message, and sent means the delivery provider accepted the final payload. A retry changes attempts; it must not create a second business event. The idempotency key joins the scheduled run and customer ID, and the delivery adapter stores that key before acknowledging work.

There is a catch. A per-customer job is only safe if its inputs are stable enough to replay. Store the report version or a snapshot pointer in the message, rather than serializing a giant report into it. If the worker sees the same key, it returns the prior result. That behavior is more valuable than squeezing another minute out of the cron runtime.

How should a cron trigger enqueue Node.js work for long-running cleanup reports?

Use the trigger as a coordinator, not as the worker. This TypeScript example uses generic interfaces so the same state machine can sit over a hosted queue, a database-backed queue, or a self-managed broker.

type DigestJob = {
  runId: string;
  customerId: string;
  snapshotId: string;
};

async function scheduleDigest(now: Date): Promise<void> {
  const runId = `weekly:${now.toISOString().slice(0, 10)}`;
  const customers = await customerStore.activeIds();
  await ledger.insertIfAbsent({ runId, status: "enqueuing", total: customers.length });

  for (const customerId of customers) {
    const snapshotId = await reportStore.freezeInputs(customerId, runId);
    await queue.send({ runId, customerId, snapshotId } satisfies DigestJob);
  }

  await ledger.markEnqueued(runId);
}

async function work(job: DigestJob): Promise<void> {
  const key = `${job.runId}:${job.customerId}`;
  if (await ledger.wasSent(key)) return;

  const report = await reportStore.render(job.snapshotId);
  await delivery.sendEmail(job.customerId, report, { idempotencyKey: key });
  await ledger.markSent(key);
}

The loop is intentionally plain. In production, enqueue in bounded pages and record the last successful page. A crash after page three should resume at page four, not silently claim that all customers were handled. The worker should renew its lease while rendering, cap retries, and move a repeatedly failing item to a dead-letter queue with the run ID attached.

Node.js is a good fit for this coordination because the trigger does little synchronous work. It is not a reason to keep a 40-minute report inside one process. Break expensive cleanup into retryable units, and make each unit observable.

Where do scheduled jobs fail after the trigger appears healthy?

The first failure mode is an apparently successful timeout. The scheduler waits 15 minutes, stops waiting, and the enqueue may already be committed. If an operator retries manually without checking the ledger, two weekly runs enter the queue. A deterministic run ID plus an insert-if-absent constraint turns that ambiguity into a visible state.

The second is a worker crash at the worst possible line: after the provider accepted an email, before the queue acknowledgement. The next delivery sees the same idempotency key and records a duplicate attempt without sending again. Test this exact point. It is a five-minute fault injection that exposes a whole class of expensive support tickets.

That is the contract.

The useful test matrix is wider than a happy-path unit test. Start a run with ten customers, kill the worker after rendering customer four, and let the lease expire. The replay should produce four recorded attempts, no second email for customer four, and six untouched messages. Then pause the delivery provider for twelve minutes and watch backlog age, retry count, and dead-letter movement. Finally, deploy a new message schema while an old worker is still draining; the old worker must reject or ignore fields it does not understand without marking the job sent. These checks cost less than a support incident because they exercise the boundaries where state changes hands. I keep the fixture data small and deterministic, so I can run the scenario locally before a weekly release and compare the ledger rows as plain text. It is not glamorous. It is the part that lets a solo operator trust an automated customer promise.

The third is stale membership. “Active customers” changes while a long enqueue loop runs. Freezing the customer set, or recording a membership version, gives the digest a defined population. Otherwise a customer can be absent simply because their subscription changed between page reads.

I once assumed a longer timeout would solve the handoff problem. It only made the failure harder to locate. Your mileage may vary with queue lease defaults, but the invariant stays the same: every customer has one run ID, one idempotency key, and a final state that can be queried.

When is a queue the wrong alternative?

Do not add a queue for a maintenance query that finishes in seconds, has no customer-visible side effect, and can be rerun safely. A direct cron call is easier to operate there. A hosted workflow scheduler is also reasonable when infrequent runs, retained logs, and a small delay matter more than per-customer throughput; GitHub's schedule event documentation is a useful example of that model.

The queue is not suitable when nobody watches backlog age, lease expirations, or dead-letter volume. Choose the simpler path, or make monitoring part of the same feature before shipping it. The operational burden is real: retries need backoff, schemas need versioning, and a replay tool needs authorization.

For a weekly digest, my decision rule is narrow: direct execution for bounded work, one queue message per independently retryable customer, and a ledger when a delivery dispute costs more than the ledger costs to maintain. That rule leaves room to change infrastructure later without changing the customer-facing contract.

Ship weekly. Keep the boring parts boring.

title: Synergizing Evidence Retrieval and Utilization for Self-Improving Multimodal Scientific Document Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2611.22837v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Scientific document reasoning requires an agent to acquire and integrate evidence distributed across text, figures, and tables. Retrieval can identify relevant sources while missing complementary support, and answer-level feedback alone does not reveal whether an error stems from evidence acquisition or evidence use. We present an agentic Retriever--Perceiver--Reasoner framework for multimodal scientific document reasoning. The Retriever sequentially selects source-aligned evidence under a context budget. Given the selected evidence and question, the Perceiver constructs a question-conditioned latent ontology, an implicit organization of multimodal evidence in a shared continuous space. The Reasoner combines this latent guidance with the original sources to produce grounded answers. We train the three components through diagnostic-guided co-evolution: alternating updates optimize them with a shared answering reward, while Retrieval Potential Feedback (RPF) and Latent Efficacy Feedback (LEF) identify questions that need better retrieval or latent guidance and direct targeted resampling. Across four benchmarks and seven evaluation settings, our framework obtains average scores of 69.9 and 75.0 with 7B and 8B Reasoner backbones, exceeding the strongest baseline by 4.0 and 9.1 points, respectively.

title: Feeding GPUs in Another Cloud Without Moving the Dataset Twice: Data Gravity for Cross-Cloud Training
description:
The GPUs are available in one cloud. The training data lives in another. That mismatch is now routine: GPU capacity is scarce and unevenly distributed, while datasets were collected wherever the product happened to grow up. So a team books capacity where it exists, and then discovers the real project is not the training run. It is moving, and keeping moved, the data the training run feeds on.

The naive answer is a full copy before every run. Copy the dataset across, train, copy the results back, repeat next month with a slightly larger dataset. It works once. It fails as a habit, because most of the bytes never changed, the copy window grows faster than the training window, and egress charges quietly become a line item nobody budgeted for. Data gravity is not a metaphor to admire. It is an engineering constraint to design around.

Move the delta, not the dataset

The first fix is to stop treating the dataset as one indivisible object. A training dataset is a collection of items, most of them stable, some of them new, a few of them corrected or withdrawn. If the storage layer can describe the dataset as a manifest of items with content hashes, the cross-cloud question changes from "copy everything" to "which items are missing or different on the other side".

Sync by manifest. The receiving side lists what it already holds, compares hashes, and pulls only the missing or changed items. The first sync is still a full move, and there is no way around paying it once. Every sync after that is proportional to how much the data actually changed, which for most real datasets is a small fraction per training cycle.

Content addressing does quiet extra work here. If two datasets share items, and most training sets are revisions of earlier ones, the shared items transfer once across all of them. A corrected label is a new item, not a new copy of its neighbours. Deduplication stops being a storage feature and becomes a network feature.

Keep one golden copy and say where it lives

Delta sync only works if everyone agrees which copy is authoritative. Pick one home for the dataset of record, in one cloud, with one owner. Other copies are caches with a manifest and a freshness state, not rival sources of truth.

That distinction matters most for deletions and corrections. A privacy deletion or a labelling fix has to propagate to every cache, and the training pipeline should be able to prove which manifest version a run used. Record the manifest version in the run metadata, next to the code version and the hyperparameters. A model whose training data cannot be named exactly cannot be reproduced, and cannot be fully trusted when a question arrives months later about whether a particular record was in it.

Withdrawn items deserve special handling. Mark them in the manifest, remove them from caches before the next run, and verify the removal rather than assuming the sync handled it. Additions are easy to notice when they are missing. Deletions are easy to miss precisely because nothing breaks.

Put a cache near the GPUs, and treat it as a cache

GPUs are the expensive, scarce resource in this design, so the network should serve them, not the other way round. Stage the working set on storage in the same cloud, ideally in the same region, as the training capacity, and feed the run from there. A training job that reads its data across a cross-cloud link will spend GPU hours waiting on a network path that was never built for sustained bulk reads, and the bottleneck will look like a training problem in every dashboard except the network one.

Treat the staging copy honestly as a cache. It can be rebuilt from the golden copy. It does not need the same backup regime, and it should not quietly become a second home for data that exists nowhere else. Checkpoints and trained model artefacts are the opposite case: those are outputs that exist nowhere else until they are copied back, so they get the careful treatment, and the dataset cache gets the disposable treatment. Teams regularly invert the two, protecting the copyable data and leaving the irreplaceable outputs on temporary storage.

Size the cache by the working set, not by the archive. If a run trains on the last ninety days plus a fixed reference set, stage that, not ten years of history. A smaller, well defined working set syncs faster, verifies faster, and gives the deletion process a smaller surface to check.

Verify integrity before the run, not during it

A partial sync discovered at hour three of a training run wastes the scarcest resource in the system. Verify before the run starts: item counts and hash spot checks against the manifest, a read test on a sample from each part of the dataset, and a check that the staged copy reports the manifest version the run expects.

Make the verification cheap enough to run every time. Full hash verification of a large dataset on every run can cost as much time as the sync saved, so verify in layers: counts and sizes always, hashes on a rotating sample, and a full verification on a schedule and after any storage change. The point is not perfection. The point is that a mismatch surfaces in a pre-flight check that costs minutes, not in a failed run that costs a booked GPU window.

Count the movement, because someone is paying for it

Cross-cloud data movement has three costs that belong in the design, not in a surprise invoice. Egress charges apply to bytes leaving the source cloud, and a full copy per run multiplies them by the number of runs. Time is a cost: a sync window that grows with the dataset eventually collides with the training schedule. Attention is a cost: a manual copy step is a step someone forgets, rushes, or runs against the wrong version.

Delta sync, a regional cache, and manifest verification attack all three. The egress bill becomes proportional to change. The sync window becomes predictable. The manual step becomes a checked, repeatable job. None of this requires exotic tooling. It requires treating dataset movement as part of the training system, designed once, rather than as a favour the network does before each run.

A short checklist for cross-cloud training data

  1. One golden copy, one owner, one named cloud of record.
  2. A manifest of items with content hashes, versioned like code.
  3. Sync by delta against the manifest, never a blind full copy.
  4. A disposable cache in the GPU region, sized to the working set.
  5. Deletions and corrections propagated and verified, not assumed.
  6. Manifest version recorded in every run, next to code and parameters.
  7. Pre-flight verification in layers, before the GPU window opens.
  8. Checkpoints and outputs copied back with more care than the cache.

The pattern generalises beyond training. Any workload that follows scarce capacity into another cloud, inference fleets, rendering, large scale simulation, inherits the same gravity problem and the same answer: move what changed, cache what is read, protect what cannot be recreated. Teams that build that discipline into their private connectivity and data paths, rather than improvising a copy before each run, keep the expensive hardware fed and the data bill boring. That approach to AI workload connectivity across clouds is described at cloudverg.com, where VergMind and VergMesh are used to keep model traffic and the data behind it on defined, private paths.

The GPUs will keep living wherever capacity is available. The data does not have to chase them in full, every single time.

title: Sightline: Long-Window Speculative Decoding for Fast SVG Generation
description:
arXiv:2611.23807v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) generation models write a graphic as code with one forward pass per token, so drawing is slow. Speculative decoding speeds them up losslessly, and block drafters guess many tokens per pass. On SVG, many of their rounds accept the whole draft and end only at the verification window. We find that their misses are rare and clumped, and that they stay accurate far deeper into a block than on natural language. A run-length identity and three propositions show that a longer window pays once the candidates are wide, up to the drafter's horizon. We propose Sightline, which pairs a window as long as the drafter's horizon with a draft tree wide enough to fill it. Experiments cover text-to-SVG and image-to-SVG with three models on six benchmarks from MMSVG, MMSVG-2M and SArena. In every setting, Sightline is the fastest of the compared lossless decoders. On SArena, it stays the fastest when every decoder shares one loop control. It also leads in almost every setting of six models from four other families, which write SVG code, compressed SVG tokens or Lottie JSON. Analyses trace the lead to rounds that shorter windows cut off, both in loop-free content and in loops. Speculative decoding also saves time for choosing samples by rendering, which beats choosing by likelihood. These results suggest that speculative decoding on vector graphics should verify as far as the drafter sees. Code and data are available at https://github.com/LiZaiyuan0619/Sightline.

title: DuoCL: Dual-Path Online Continual Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.23598v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Online continual learning (OCL) requires learning from a data stream whose arrival rate is independent of model training speed. When training cannot keep pace, computationally expensive gradient-based methods update less frequently, limiting adaptation. Analytic methods reduce this overhead, but their frozen backbones cannot adapt representations to changing distributions. We propose DuoCL, a dual-path OCL framework whose fast analytic path accumulates feature statistics from every incoming minibatch while its slow path periodically adapts the backbone. The slow path adjusts its sample count to the available compute budget without interrupting fast-path learning. Feature alignment compensates for drift in the accumulated classifier statistics. Across four datasets and three computational budgets, DuoCL improves online accuracy by an average of 9.67 percentage points over the strongest gradient-based baseline in each setting. DuoCL consistently outperforms analytic learning under distribution shifts, with gains of up to 4.00 percentage points on CIFAR-C, and achieves higher accuracy than prior methods across disjoint class-incremental, domain-incremental, and Si-Blurry settings.

title: RehearsalBench: Can AI Predict What Happens When You Change a Company?
description:
arXiv:2611.22480v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Organizations increasingly ask AI systems what will happen if they change how they operate: which work to automate, which team to resize, what a voice agent will do to waiting times. We introduce RehearsalBench, a benchmark that measures whether AI models can diagnose an operation, choose an intervention, and forecast its consequences. Each model is placed in a simulated bank contact center fitted to real call-level records, sees only what a manager would see, and submits a plan and forecasts that are then played out across 200 seeded futures and three plausible versions of the organization. Decisions are scored in dollars at the stakeholders' stated valuations; forecasts are scored on the effect of each change relative to doing nothing. Ten models made 280 attempts across 14 organizations. The best model, GPT-6 Astra, improved on doing nothing by 6.8% of the no-change cost and made 77% less forecast error than a forecaster who always predicts no effect. On average, every model forecast the direction of every specified effect correctly, but models erred on the size of the same effects in the same direction, overstating a voice agent's effect on repeat contacts about five-fold. No model ever recommended holding off when doing nothing was the right choice. To test external validity, twelve models forecast 33 real organizational changes with known outcomes. Under verdict rules fixed in advance, the benchmark's forecast ranking agreed with the real-world ranking (Spearman $\rho = 0.92$, 95% lower bound 0.50). We report the result alongside an inconclusive first test, the analysis choices made after outcomes were seen, and evidence that part of the agreement reflects how well models size their uncertainty.

title: Online State-Representation Adaptation under Synthetic Interaction-Cue Remapping
description:
arXiv:2611.23836v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When cues change what they predict, continuing to update a learned mapping may help an agent choose the appropriate action. We tested this in a one-step synthetic task by comparing a logistic state predictor that continued to learn from state labels with the same predictor frozen at transfer. We evaluated ten conditions in six held-out environments, with 1,296 paired runs per condition and 1,296,000 transfer records in total. Late action accuracy was 93.39% with online updates and 64.63% with frozen coefficients, a paired difference of 28.76 [8.73, 53.19] percentage points (95% environment-bootstrap interval). A direct policy reached 95.65% using the same predictions with a different action threshold. A contextual bandit reached 94.23% and earned more cumulative utility than the adaptive predictor. The bandit used the reward of its chosen action, which in this task reveals the true state when combined with that action. Weights based on development history lowered cumulative utility relative to neutral weights (difference -3.45 [-4.48, -2.43]). The adaptive predictor outperformed its frozen counterpart in late accuracy in each of the six test environments. The other comparisons show how the choice of action threshold and the information available in feedback affect what can be attributed to online adaptation.

title: Everything that is waiting on me, on one phone screen: designing a Board for many AI coding sessions
description:
Disclosure: I'm the developer of Relaymote, and this post is published from my account. It was drafted and published by an AI agent working on my behalf from the project's documentation. Relaymote is unofficial; not affiliated with or endorsed by Anthropic.

With many Claude Code sessions running, the most expensive failure is a quiet one: a session asked you something an hour ago, then said three more things, and the question scrolled out of sight. It waits, politely, forever.

Relaymote has a module for exactly that, called the Board: one page, on your phone or desktop, that lists only what is waiting on you.

Four buckets, not one feed

A feed of everything is a second inbox to read. The Board sorts into four buckets instead:

  • Decide: questions sessions asked you, including ones buried under later messages;
  • Things to tell you: a numbered inbox of results, blockers and asks the Conductor recorded, so nothing you said or were asked is lost;
  • Goals: overdue, blocked, delivered and awaiting your check;
  • Nudge: sessions that stopped and are waiting to be told to carry on.

"Buried" is the bucket that earns its keep. It is the question that was asked, then followed by more output, so a quick glance at the session's last message misses it.

One tap is one line of text

Every tap on the Board becomes one line of text delivered to your Conductor session, which reads it and acts. That keeps the Board itself dumb: it does not need to know how to resume a session or answer a question. The Conductor already does.

Each tap is also appended to an audit log, so "did I approve that?" has an answer.

Batch the answers, wake each session once

You can tap Yes, Skip, type an answer, or tap several and send them together: Send 5 replies. Batching is not only convenient. Each wake of a session costs a fresh turn, and on a long session a turn that misses the prompt cache re-reads the whole context at full price. Five answers to the same session in one message is one wake, not five.

It is a file, not a service

The Board is a JSON file in a folder on your PC (board.json), rebuilt every 10 minutes and whenever you open it. Anything can write it, but Relaymote leaves alone a board.json it did not generate. There is also a desktop page, board.html. Before writing that page, Relaymote checks the script for a quoted string left open at the end of a line, because one such typo kills every button on the page while the page still renders.

Goals wait for you

The Goals bucket is where the Board meets the goal chaser. A session that says done must give evidence, and the goal stays open until you verify it. The chaser never chases a session that is working, waiting on you, or in an unknown state, and after three unanswered chases it stops and asks you instead of nagging.

Try it

Turn on Settings › Modules › Board (and Goal chaser if you want goals on it). The format is documented in docs/BOARD.md in the repository.

Relaymote is unofficial; not affiliated with or endorsed by Anthropic.

title: HypoLoop: Revising Weight-Editing Plans from Scientific Feedback
description:
arXiv:2611.23718v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Scientific experiments continually reveal prediction errors. Effective updates depend on which parameters change and which errors drive the correction. We introduce HypoLoop, a family of native weight-editing methods that connects these choices to experimental feedback. Fixed, numerically adaptive, and LLM-guided policies produce editing plans; numerical solvers compute weight patches, and internal validation selects the deployed predictor. Successive observations and validation records support revisions to editable locations and fitting rules. Experiments cover 22 scientific tasks and both DeepSeek and Claude. On Burgers, reallocating a matched parameter budget reduces error by 58.80% and 47.72% relative to fixed locations. On DIODE, positive-residual weighting reduces absolute relative error (AbsRel) by 13.35% in internal cross-validation, with the same 33 editable coordinates. Revising the complete plan across rounds lowers final AbsRel by 10.59% relative to keeping the initial plan fixed. SpaceNet7 and Make3D connect accepted edits to improved spatial predictions. These results show how experimental evidence can shape the update problem itself. Code: https://github.com/limengran98/HypoLoop.

title: A RAG answer can cite every sentence and still be wrong: a script to reproduce it
description:
Every sentence was cited. The answer was still wrong.

Ask a company AI whether you can refund a customer after last month's exception. It finds the contract, quotes the 30-day rule and says no, with a citation. The exception sits in an email it never searched.

Here's that failure as a script you can run. It has no API key, no model and no embeddings. The refund is a made-up example.

I framed the post as “RAG in 2023 vs 2026”: search once versus check and search again. The dates are shorthand. Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval already combined hybrid search and reranking in 2024.

The script

Save this as rag_loop.py. It uses only Python's standard library, with SQLite's FTS5 enabled for BM25 search. Python 3.9 and 3.15 print the same output.

# Synthetic data. BM25 and the permission filter are real (SQLite FTS5).
# The check and the answers are keyword rules, so no model or API is needed.
import re
import sqlite3

MAX_ROUNDS = 3

DOCS = [  # id, source, who may read it, text
    ("contract-s4", "contract", "all", "Section 4 Refunds. Customers may request a refund within 30 days of purchase."),
    ("contract-s9", "contract", "all", "Section 9 Renewals. Renewal notice is due 30 days before the term ends."),
    ("ticket-118", "ticket", "all", "Acme asked for a refund on day 41. Waiting on finance. No decision yet."),
    ("email-1012", "email", "finance", "12 October. Finance director approved a one-time refund exception for Acme."),
]

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE docs USING fts5(id UNINDEXED, source UNINDEXED, readers UNINDEXED, text)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO docs VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)", DOCS)


def search(words, source, role, k=2):
    # The permission filter sits inside the query, so every repeat search gets it too.
    sql = """SELECT id, text, readers FROM docs
             WHERE docs MATCH ? AND source = ? AND readers IN ('all', ?)
             ORDER BY bm25(docs) LIMIT ?"""
    hits = db.execute(sql, (" OR ".join(words), source, role, k)).fetchall()
    assert all(readers in ("all", role) for _, _, readers in hits), "permission leak"
    return hits


def proven(hits, proof):
    # shortcut: a keyword rule stands in for the model. Ask a model here in a real system.
    return next((doc_id for doc_id, text, _ in hits if all(w in text.lower() for w in proof)), None)


def run(title, customer, role, loop=True):
    print(f"\n{title}\n  customer={customer} role={role}")
    needs = {  # sources to try in order, search words, words that count as proof
        "rule": (["contract"], ["refund", "days"], ["refund", "30 days"]),
        "exception": (["ticket", "email", "drive"], ["refund", "exception", customer], ["approved", customer.lower()]),
    }
    queues = {need: list(spec[0]) for need, spec in needs.items()}
    if not loop:
        queues["exception"] = []  # The single search never looks for the exception.
    limit = MAX_ROUNDS if loop else 1
    evidence, seen, used = {}, set(), 0

    for used in range(1, limit + 1):
        for need, (_, words, proof) in needs.items():
            if need in evidence or not queues[need]:
                continue
            source = queues[need].pop(0)
            hits = search(words, source, role)
            seen.update(hit[0] for hit in hits)
            print(f"  round {used}: {need} -> {source}: {[hit[0] for hit in hits] or 'nothing'}")
            if found := proven(hits, proof):
                evidence[need] = found
        if len(evidence) == len(needs):
            break

    missing = [need for need in needs if need not in evidence]
    if not missing:
        reply = f"Yes. {customer} has an approved exception to the 30-day limit. [{evidence['rule']}] [{evidence['exception']}]"
    elif loop:
        reply = f"Partly. The limit is 30 days. [{evidence['rule']}] Could not confirm: {', '.join(missing)}."
    else:
        reply = f"No. Refunds end 30 days after purchase. [{evidence['rule']}]"
    cited = all(doc_id in seen for doc_id in re.findall(r"\[([\w-]+)\]", reply))
    print(f"  answer: {reply}")
    print(f"  cited: {'yes' if cited else 'no'}  sufficient: {'no' if missing else 'yes'}  rounds: {used}/{limit}")


run("A. Search once", "Acme", "finance", loop=False)
run("B. Loop", "Acme", "finance")
run("C. Loop, no permission to read that email", "Acme", "support")
run("D. Loop, no exception exists", "Globex", "finance")

Run it:

python3 rag_loop.py

You get this:

A. Search once
  customer=Acme role=finance
  round 1: rule -> contract: ['contract-s4', 'contract-s9']
  answer: No. Refunds end 30 days after purchase. [contract-s4]
  cited: yes  sufficient: no  rounds: 1/1

B. Loop
  customer=Acme role=finance
  round 1: rule -> contract: ['contract-s4', 'contract-s9']
  round 1: exception -> ticket: ['ticket-118']
  round 2: exception -> email: ['email-1012']
  answer: Yes. Acme has an approved exception to the 30-day limit. [contract-s4] [email-1012]
  cited: yes  sufficient: yes  rounds: 2/3

C. Loop, no permission to read that email
  customer=Acme role=support
  round 1: rule -> contract: ['contract-s4', 'contract-s9']
  round 1: exception -> ticket: ['ticket-118']
  round 2: exception -> email: nothing
  round 3: exception -> drive: nothing
  answer: Partly. The limit is 30 days. [contract-s4] Could not confirm: exception.
  cited: yes  sufficient: no  rounds: 3/3

D. Loop, no exception exists
  customer=Globex role=finance
  round 1: rule -> contract: ['contract-s4', 'contract-s9']
  round 1: exception -> ticket: ['ticket-118']
  round 2: exception -> email: ['email-1012']
  round 3: exception -> drive: nothing
  answer: Partly. The limit is 30 days. [contract-s4] Could not confirm: exception.
  cited: yes  sufficient: no  rounds: 3/3

The search and permission filter execute in SQLite. Source order, sufficiency and answers are fixed rules. This reproduces control flow, not retrieval quality. cited: yes only checks that cited IDs appeared in retrieved results; it doesn't check whether they support the answer.

What each run tests

A: missing source. cited: yes and sufficient: no on the same line. A citation doesn't prove the answer is complete. A reranker won't help, because it scores the documents you give it. It can't add the missing email.

B: bounded repeat. The ticket mentions the refund but holds no decision. So the next round searches email, finds it and stops at round 2 of 3.

C: permission limit. The filter is inside the SQL, so the repeat search gets it too. The email never comes back, and the answer names what's missing. The role is a fixture; in production, derive it from authenticated identity. Enforce access at the search, and again when a source document is opened.

D: no answer exists. Search returns the Acme email for Globex. The check doesn't count it. The for loop ends at the cap, so the question can't spin forever. A real loop also needs time and token limits, enforced in code.

Now break it

Add this line to DOCS, after the approval email:

    ("email-1020", "email", "finance", "20 October. Finance director withdrew the Acme refund exception."),

Run B now prints this:

  round 2: exception -> email: ['email-1020', 'email-1012']
  answer: Yes. Acme has an approved exception to the 30-day limit. [contract-s4] [email-1012]
  cited: yes  sufficient: yes  rounds: 2/3

The withdrawal ranks first. The answer still says yes. Every sentence is cited, and the answer is wrong again.

The check only asks whether an approval exists. A real one also asks whether it applies, whether that person could approve it, and whether it still stands. So test on conflicting versions.

Where this stops

The script exercises keyword search, a deliberately weak sufficiency check, and a round cap. It doesn't test vector retrieval, reranking or exact-ID matching. The full design adds contextual chunks, query planning, hybrid search and reranking. Google's agentic RAG framework treats sufficient context as its own check.

For a real benchmark, keep the synthetic cases and replace the fixed routing, keyword checks and canned answers. Compare vector-only retrieval, hybrid, hybrid plus reranking, and a capped loop. Log how much required evidence reaches the top results, answer correctness, tokens and wall time.

I wouldn't build the whole loop on day one. A simple lookup should skip it. Start with hybrid search and a reranker, measure on real questions, and add planning or a second round only where that test set fails.

The maintained article, with all six steps and the models I'd benchmark for each, is on argbe.tech.

title: What Interpolators Store and What They Express: An Information-Theoretic Framework for Benign Overfitting and Label-Free Model Selection
description:
arXiv:2611.23630v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Overparameterized learners can fit noisy training labels perfectly and still predict well, which neither classical complexity measures nor information-theoretic generalization bounds explain. We develop an information-theoretic framework that separates two things an interpolating learner does with its sample: storage, the information the trained model retains about its training labels, and expression, the information about the sample that reaches its predictions at fresh inputs. We first characterize the ideal model: for a loss l, the least complex l-sufficient representation is the Bayes act, whose entropy is the minimal sufficient complexity; this generalizes, and corrects, an earlier "lossless maximal compression" view of boosting. We then show that every interpolator stores exactly nH(Y|X) bits of label noise, so storage, and bounds built on it (including CMI bounds), cannot tell interpolators apart. Expression can: excess risk is bounded above and below by the expressed information V, the entropy over training samples of the prediction at an input, plus a modal-bias term, exactly so for binary labels. Benign overfitting is therefore vanishing expression, a picture that covers nearest-neighbour rules, averaging, minimum-norm least squares and double descent, and that links V to classical bias-variance decompositions and to model disagreement. Finally, V gives a model-selection criterion that needs no held-out labels. Among overparameterized learners on 15 noisy datasets, V estimated from two disjoint halves has 60% less regret than holdout validation at the same cost and matches 5-fold cross-validation at a quarter of its cost; at matched cost it also beats selection by conditional mutual information. We characterize when it fails and give remedies. Code: https://github.com/nnikolaou/GLMC

title: Every Vibe-Coded Site Looks the Same. I Wrote a Linter for the Default Look.
description:
A post went around X this week that just said every website UI is vibe coded now. Nobody in the replies argued. Around the same time, a demo got passed around of an MCP server that feeds a coding agent curated designs from real websites, so the agent has something better to copy than its own defaults. People shared it because they already have the problem it fixes. You open a new SaaS landing page and you can tell what made it before the page finishes loading.

I build with these tools every day, and I don't think the issue is that AI-generated sites are ugly. Most of them look fine. The problem is that they all look the same kind of fine, and visitors notice. A page that looks like a template reads like a weekend project, even when the product behind it is good.

"It looks AI-made" is a vibe, and you can't review a vibe in a pull request. So I tried to turn it into something you can check: a small linter that looks for the default look in a project's HTML, JSX, CSS and Tailwind classes, prints what it found, and gives a score.

The fingerprints

These are my observations from looking at a lot of generated marketing pages, plus my own first drafts. I haven't measured any of this. It's a pattern list, and you'll recognize most of it:

  • One font, and it's Inter. Or system-ui, or Tailwind's font-sans with nothing set. No display face, no contrast between headings and body text.
  • A purple-to-blue gradient hero. from-purple-600 via-indigo-600 to-blue-500, or the same colors written as a CSS linear-gradient.
  • Glassmorphism. backdrop-blur on bg-white/10, usually on the sticky nav and a "Now with AI" pill.
  • Three rounded cards in a row. md:grid-cols-3, rounded-2xl, a soft border, a hover lift.
  • Emoji or lucide icons as the card art. ⚡ for speed, 🔒 for security, 📈 for insights.
  • A grey "Trusted by" logo bar. grayscale opacity-60, often showing logos the company has no relationship with.
  • A centered hero with two buttons. "Get started" and "Learn more", side by side.
  • Launch copy that could describe any product. Supercharge, unlock, seamless, effortless, empower, elevate, all-in-one, streamline.
  • The same spacing everywhere. Every section gets py-24, so the page has no rhythm. It's just one block after another.
  • Testimonials that look made up. "Sarah Johnson, CEO at Acme", a pravatar.cc avatar, five star glyphs.

None of these is wrong on its own. Inter is a great typeface, and three cards are sometimes the right layout. The fingerprint is all of them showing up together, because together they mean nobody made a design decision.

The fixture

I didn't scan anyone's real site. I wrote a fixture for a made-up invoicing tool called Ledgerly, the way a coding agent tends to write it when you prompt "build a modern landing page for an invoicing SaaS" and give it nothing else: an index.html with Tailwind classes, a small styles.css, and a src/Testimonials.jsx component. I put the fingerprints in on purpose, so the "before" score below is expected to be high. The useful part is what happens after.

sameness-lint

It's one Python file, stdlib only, about 140 lines. Each rule has a weight, and the weights add up to 100. A rule adds its weight once if it finds anything. Buzzwords cost 3 points each, up to the rule's 12-point cap. Here's the core:

RULES = {  # id: (weight, label)
    "default-font":   (12, "Only Inter/system sans in the whole project"),
    "purple-gradient":(14, "Purple-to-blue gradient"),
    "glass":          (8,  "Glassmorphism (backdrop blur on translucent white)"),
    "card-grid-3":    (10, "Three-up rounded card grid"),
    "icon-cards":     (8,  "Emoji / lucide icons as feature-card art"),
    "logo-bar":       (8,  "Greyed-out 'Trusted by' logo bar"),
    "centered-hero":  (10, "Centered hero with two CTAs"),
    "buzzwords":      (12, "Generic launch copy"),
    "same-rhythm":    (8,  "Every section uses the same vertical padding"),
    "stock-proof":    (10, "Placeholder-looking testimonials"),
}

# gradients: Tailwind stops, or CSS hex stops that all sit in the violet/blue band
for m in re.finditer(r"from-(purple|violet|indigo|fuchsia)-\d+[^\"']*?to-(blue|indigo|cyan|sky|purple|pink)-\d+", low):
    add("purple-gradient", m.start(), m.group(0))
for m in re.finditer(r"linear-gradient\(([^)]*)\)", low):
    hs = [hue(h) for h in re.findall(r"#[0-9a-f]{6}\b|#[0-9a-f]{3}\b", m.group(1))]
    if len(hs) >= 2 and all(200 <= h <= 300 and s > 0.4 for h, s in hs):
        add("purple-gradient", m.start(), m.group(0))

# centered hero: text-center near the <h1>, and at least two generic CTAs after it
for m in re.finditer(r"<h1\b", low):
    before, after = low[max(0, m.start() - 500): m.start()], low[m.start(): m.start() + 1500]
    if "text-center" in before + after[:200] and len(re.findall(CTA, visible(after))) >= 2:
        add("centered-hero", m.start(), "text-center h1 + ...")

# rhythm: if 75%+ of <section>s share one py-* value, the page has no rhythm
if sections >= 3 and len(where) / sections >= 0.75:
    hits["same-rhythm"].append(f"{len(where)}/{sections} sections use {py}")

The font rule collects every font-family declaration and every Google Fonts family= in the project. If all of them are in the default sans set (Inter, system-ui, Roboto, Helvetica, Arial and friends), it flags the project. The buzzword rule strips tags and class attributes first, so class="seamless-grid" doesn't count and visible copy does. A file can opt out of a rule with a sameness-lint-disable <rule> comment. That's on purpose: the opt-out shows up in the diff, where a reviewer can push back on it.

Full sameness_lint.py (about 140 lines, stdlib only) 
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""sameness-lint: flag the "AI default" look in a marketing site's HTML/JSX/CSS.
Heuristics, not taste. Each rule is a fingerprint you see a lot in generated sites."""
import re, sys, json, colorsys
from pathlib import Path

EXTS = {".html", ".htm", ".jsx", ".tsx", ".js", ".ts", ".vue", ".svelte", ".css", ".scss"}
SKIP = {"node_modules", ".git", "dist", "build", ".next"}
DEFAULT_FONTS = {"inter", "system-ui", "-apple-system", "blinkmacsystemfont", "sans-serif",
                 "ui-sans-serif", "segoe ui", "roboto", "helvetica", "arial", "helvetica neue"}
BUZZ = ["supercharge", "unlock", "seamless", "effortless", "revolutioni", "empower", "elevate",
        "next-level", "game-chang", "cutting-edge", "all-in-one", "streamline", "unleash",
        "transform your", "10x", "at scale", "like never before"]
CTA = r"(get started|start (?:for )?free|try (?:it )?free|book a demo|learn more|see how|watch demo)"
STOCK = r"(i\.pravatar\.cc|randomuser\.me|ui-avatars\.com|\bjohn doe\b|\bjane doe\b|\bacme\b|lorem ipsum|★★★★★)"
EMOJI = re.compile("[\U0001F300-\U0001FAFF\u2600-\u27BF]")

RULES = {  # id: (weight, label)
    "default-font":   (12, "Only Inter/system sans in the whole project"),
    "purple-gradient":(14, "Purple-to-blue gradient"),
    "glass":          (8,  "Glassmorphism (backdrop blur on translucent white)"),
    "card-grid-3":    (10, "Three-up rounded card grid"),
    "icon-cards":     (8,  "Emoji / lucide icons as feature-card art"),
    "logo-bar":       (8,  "Greyed-out 'Trusted by' logo bar"),
    "centered-hero":  (10, "Centered hero with two CTAs"),
    "buzzwords":      (12, "Generic launch copy"),
    "same-rhythm":    (8,  "Every section uses the same vertical padding"),
    "stock-proof":    (10, "Placeholder-looking testimonials"),
}

def files(root):
    for p in sorted(Path(root).rglob("*")):
        if p.is_file() and p.suffix in EXTS and not SKIP & set(p.parts):
            yield p

def line_of(text, idx):
    return text.count("\n", 0, idx) + 1

def visible(text):  # strip markup but keep newlines so line numbers still work
    keep = lambda m: "\n" * m.group(0).count("\n") + " "
    t = re.sub(r"<(script|style)\b.*?</\1>", keep, text, flags=re.S | re.I)
    t = re.sub(r"\{/\*.*?\*/\}|className=\"[^\"]*\"|class=\"[^\"]*\"", keep, t, flags=re.S)
    return re.sub(r"<[^>]+>", keep, t)

def hue(hexstr):
    h = hexstr.lstrip("#")
    if len(h) == 3: h = "".join(c * 2 for c in h)
    r, g, b = (int(h[i:i + 2], 16) / 255 for i in (0, 2, 4))
    hh, l, s = colorsys.rgb_to_hls(r, g, b)
    return hh * 360, s

def scan(root):
    hits = {k: [] for k in RULES}
    fonts, rhythm = set(), {}
    for p in files(root):
        rel, text = str(p.relative_to(root)), p.read_text(errors="ignore")
        low = text.lower()
        off = set(re.findall(r"sameness-lint-disable ([\w-]+)", text))  # per-file opt-out, reviewed in PR
        def add(rule, idx, ev, src=text):
            if rule in off: return
            item = f"{rel}:{line_of(src, idx)}  {ev.strip()[:70]}"
            if item not in hits[rule]: hits[rule].append(item)
        # fonts: CSS font-family, Google Fonts links, Tailwind font config
        for m in re.finditer(r"font-family\s*:\s*([^;}{]+)", low):
            fonts |= {f.strip(" '\"") for f in m.group(1).split(",") if f.strip(" '\"") and "var(" not in f}
        for m in re.finditer(r"fonts\.googleapis\.com/css2?\?([^\"']+)", low):
            fonts |= {f.split(":")[0].replace("+", " ") for f in re.findall(r"family=([^&\"']+)", m.group(1))}
        # gradients: Tailwind stops or CSS hex stops in the violet/blue band
        for m in re.finditer(r"from-(purple|violet|indigo|fuchsia)-\d+[^\"']*?to-(blue|indigo|cyan|sky|purple|pink)-\d+", low):
            add("purple-gradient", m.start(), m.group(0))
        for m in re.finditer(r"linear-gradient\(([^)]*)\)", low):
            hs = [hue(h) for h in re.findall(r"#[0-9a-f]{6}\b|#[0-9a-f]{3}\b", m.group(1))]
            if len(hs) >= 2 and all(200 <= h <= 300 and s > 0.4 for h, s in hs):
                add("purple-gradient", m.start(), m.group(0))
        for m in re.finditer(r"backdrop-blur[\w-]*|backdrop-filter\s*:\s*blur", low):
            ctx = low[max(0, m.start() - 200): m.end() + 200]
            if re.search(r"bg-white/\d+|rgba\(255,\s*255,\s*255,\s*0?\.\d+\)", ctx):
                add("glass", m.start(), m.group(0))
        for m in re.finditer(r"(?:md:|lg:)?grid-cols-3", low):
            if low[m.end(): m.end() + 1500].count("rounded-2xl") + low[m.end(): m.end() + 1500].count("rounded-3xl") >= 3:
                add("card-grid-3", m.start(), m.group(0) + " + rounded-2xl cards")
        for m in re.finditer(r"from ['\"]lucide-react['\"]|data-lucide=", low):
            add("icon-cards", m.start(), m.group(0))
        for m in re.finditer(r"<(?:h3|div|span)[^>]*>\s*(" + EMOJI.pattern + ")", text):
            add("icon-cards", m.start(), "emoji icon " + m.group(1))
        for m in re.finditer(r"(trusted by|loved by|used by teams at|backed by)", low):
            if re.search(r"grayscale|opacity-(?:[1-6]0)|text-(?:gray|slate|zinc)-[34]00", low[m.start(): m.start() + 1200]):
                add("logo-bar", m.start(), m.group(0) + " + greyed logos")
        for m in re.finditer(r"<h1\b", low):
            before, after = low[max(0, m.start() - 500): m.start()], low[m.start(): m.start() + 1500]
            if "text-center" in before + after[:200] and len(re.findall(CTA, visible(after))) >= 2:
                add("centered-hero", m.start(), "text-center h1 + " + ", ".join(sorted(set(re.findall(CTA, visible(after))))))
        if p.suffix != ".css":
            vis = visible(text).lower()
            for w in BUZZ:
                for m in re.finditer(re.escape(w), vis):
                    add("buzzwords", m.start(), f'"{w}"', vis)
            for m in re.finditer(r"<section\b[^>]*class(?:name)?=\"([^\"]*)\"", text, re.I):
                pys = re.findall(r"\bpy-\d+\b", m.group(1))
                if pys: rhythm.setdefault(pys[-1], []).append(f"{rel}:{line_of(text, m.start())}")
            for m in re.finditer(STOCK, low):
                add("stock-proof", m.start(), m.group(0))
    if not fonts or fonts <= DEFAULT_FONTS:
        hits["default-font"].append("font stack: " + (", ".join(sorted(fonts)) or "none declared (Tailwind font-sans)"))
    sections = sum(len(v) for v in rhythm.values())
    for py, where in rhythm.items():
        if sections >= 3 and len(where) / sections >= 0.75:
            hits["same-rhythm"].append(f"{len(where)}/{sections} sections use {py}")
    return hits

def score(hits):
    s = 0
    for k, (w, _) in RULES.items():
        n = len(hits[k])
        if k == "buzzwords": s += min(w, 3 * n)          # 3 points per phrase, capped
        elif n: s += w
    return s

def main():
    args = [a for a in sys.argv[1:] if not a.startswith("--")]
    root = Path(args[0] if args else ".")
    limit = int(next((a.split("=")[1] for a in sys.argv if a.startswith("--max=")), 101))
    hits = scan(root); total = score(hits)
    if "--json" in sys.argv:
        print(json.dumps({"score": total, "hits": hits}, indent=2)); return
    print(f"sameness-lint  {root}\n")
    for k, (w, label) in RULES.items():
        if hits[k]:
            print(f"✗ {label}  [{k}, {len(hits[k])}]")
            for ev in hits[k][:3]: print(f"    {ev}")
            if len(hits[k]) > 3: print(f"    … +{len(hits[k]) - 3} more")
    clean = [k for k in RULES if not hits[k]]
    if clean: print(f"✓ clean: {', '.join(clean)}")
    print(f"\nsameness score: {total}/100  (lower is more yours)")
    if total >= limit:
        print(f"FAIL: score {total} >= --max={limit}"); sys.exit(1)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Run 1: the default look

Here's the real output on the fixture, run with --max=30 the way it would run in CI:


$ python3 sameness_lint.py fixtures/before --max=30
sameness-lint  fixtures/before

✗ Only Inter/system sans in the whole project  [default-font, 1]
    font stack: -apple-system, inter, sans-serif, system-ui
✗ Purple-to-blue gradient  [purple-gradient, 2]
    index.html:19  from-purple-600 via-indigo-600 to-blue-500
    styles.css:2  linear-gradient(135deg, #7c3aed 0%, #4f46e5 50%, #3b82f6 100%)
✗ Glassmorphism (backdrop blur on translucent white)  [glass, 3]
    index.html:12  backdrop-blur-md
    index.html:21  backdrop-blur
    styles.css:3  backdrop-filter: blur
✗ Three-up rounded card grid  [card-grid-3, 1]
    index.html:42  md:grid-cols-3 + rounded-2xl cards
✗ Emoji / lucide icons as feature-card art  [icon-cards, 7]
    index.html:14  emoji icon ✨
    index.html:21  emoji icon 🚀
    index.html:44  emoji icon ⚡
    … +4 more
✗ Greyed-out 'Trusted by' logo bar  [logo-bar, 1]
    index.html:32  trusted by + greyed logos
✗ Centered hero with two CTAs  [centered-hero, 1]
    index.html:22  text-center h1 + get started, learn more
✗ Generic launch copy  [buzzwords, 17]
    index.html:6  "supercharge"
    index.html:22  "supercharge"
    index.html:23  "unlock"
    … +14 more
✗ Every section uses the same vertical padding  [same-rhythm, 1]
    5/5 sections use py-24
✗ Placeholder-looking testimonials  [stock-proof, 6]
    index.html:34  acme
    src/Testimonials.jsx:4  acme
    src/Testimonials.jsx:4  i.pravatar.cc
    … +3 more

sameness score: 100/100  (lower is more yours)
FAIL: score 100 >= --max=30
[exit 1]

All ten rules fired, so the fixture scored 100 out of 100. Again, that's by design. I wrote the fixture to hit every rule. The evidence lines are the useful part: 17 buzzword hits (five of them in the testimonial quotes), three placeholder avatars, and all five sections using py-24.

The scanner also over-counts in one place. The ★★★★★ string matched twice: once as "stock proof" and once as an "emoji icon", because U+2605 falls in the symbol range I scan for emoji. The score doesn't change, because each rule only adds its weight once, but don't treat the hit counts as precise measurements.

The fix: write the brief before the first prompt

What actually changed the output wasn't a better prompt. It was a file the agent reads before it writes any markup. I keep a DESIGN.md in the repo root and point the agent at it in the first message ("Read DESIGN.md. Do not use anything it bans."). Here's the template, filled in for Ledgerly:

# DESIGN.md — Ledgerly marketing site

## Who it's for
Freelancers and two-to-five person studios who invoice 5–40 clients a month
and hate chasing late payments. Not "modern teams". Not enterprises.

## Type
- Display: Fraunces 600, optical size on, tight tracking (-0.02em) at 48px+
- Body/UI: IBM Plex Sans 400/500, 17px base, 1.55 line height
- Numbers: IBM Plex Mono for amounts, dates, invoice IDs
- Never: Inter, system-ui as the only stack

## Palette (no gradients on backgrounds)
| Role        | Hex     |
|-------------|---------|
| Paper (bg)  | #F6F1E7 |
| Ink (text)  | #1B1B18 |
| Ledger green (primary) | #1F5C4A |
| Stamp red (overdue, one accent per screen) | #C8452B |
| Rule lines  | #D8CFBE |

## Spacing and rhythm
8px base. Sections do not share one padding: hero 112/64, proof 48, features 96,
closing 64. Content column 680px for prose, 1040px for layouts.
Corners: 4px on inputs and buttons, 0 on the invoice. No rounded-2xl cards.

## Signature move
The hero *is* an invoice: a ruled, left-aligned paper document with a real
line-item table and a red "OVERDUE 14 DAYS" stamp, next to the headline.
Every other section borrows the ruled-line motif. No floating blobs, no glass.

## Components
- One primary CTA per screen. Secondary actions are text links.
- Features as a numbered list with a one-line outcome each, not icon cards.
- No emoji. Icons only when they label a control.

## Voice
- Say what happens: "Ledgerly emails the reminder on day 3, 7 and 14."
- Use the customer's nouns: invoice, client, retainer, late fee.
- Numbers only if we can source them. No invented stats.
- Banned: supercharge, unlock, seamless, effortless, empower, elevate,
  revolutionize, game-changer, cutting-edge, all-in-one, streamline,
  next-level, "for modern teams", "like never before".

## Social proof
Real customer, real name, permission on file, or no testimonial section.
No placeholder avatars, no five-star glyphs, no fake logo bars.

## References (look at these, don't copy them)
- A paper invoice from an actual accountant
- Stripe's docs for table density
- A newspaper classifieds page for ruled-line rhythm

The section that does the most work is the signature move. Fonts and hex codes stop the page from looking generic, but one specific layout idea tied to the product (here, "the hero is an overdue invoice") is what makes the agent stop reaching for a centered hero. If you can't name one, look at real sites in your category before you prompt. A list of real business website examples is a better starting point than "make it modern". If you're using a references MCP server like the one in that demo, give it two or three sites you actually like and tell the agent what to take from each one: the density, the type contrast, or the way the proof section is laid out. Don't ask it to copy the whole page.

The other section that earns its place is Social proof. The before fixture had invented testimonials because the prompt asked for a "complete" page. If you don't have a real quote yet, leave the section out. A page with no testimonials looks more honest than one with Sarah Johnson from Acme.

Run 2: after the brief

I rebuilt the page against the brief. The hero is now a left-aligned Fraunces headline next to a ruled invoice with the stamp. The logo bar became a plain mono strip of facts (reminders on day 3/7/14, card or SEPA, CSV export). Features became a numbered list, and section padding varies. Then I added a src/Pricing.jsx component the way it usually arrives: generated in a separate session that never saw the brief.


$ python3 sameness_lint.py fixtures/after --max=30
sameness-lint  fixtures/after

✗ Emoji / lucide icons as feature-card art  [icon-cards, 1]
    src/Pricing.jsx:1  from "lucide-react"
✗ Generic launch copy  [buzzwords, 1]
    src/Pricing.jsx:7  "seamless"
✓ clean: default-font, purple-gradient, glass, card-grid-3, logo-bar, centered-hero, same-rhythm, stock-proof

sameness score: 11/100  (lower is more yours)
[exit 0]

The score went from 100 to 11, and both remaining hits are in the component that never saw DESIGN.md. That's the most useful thing this run showed. The brief works on the session that reads it, and new sessions start from defaults again.

The two hits aren't equally important:

  • "seamless" in a pricing bullet is a real regression. I rewrote it as "Nightly CSV push to your accountant's inbox", which says what the feature does.
  • The lucide-react import is arguable. Those Check icons mark list items in a pricing table, which the brief allows ("icons only when they label a control"). So the file gets a sameness-lint-disable icon-cards comment with the reason next to it, and a reviewer can disagree in the PR.

After both changes:

$ python3 sameness_lint.py fixtures/after-review --max=30
sameness-lint  fixtures/after-review

✓ clean: default-font, purple-gradient, glass, card-grid-3, icon-cards, logo-bar, centered-hero, buzzwords, same-rhythm, stock-proof

sameness score: 0/100  (lower is more yours)
[exit 0]

A 0 doesn't mean the page is good. It means the page avoids ten specific defaults. Taste is still your job, and the linter can't tell you whether the invoice hero actually works for a freelancer. It just stops the easy defaults from slipping back in.

Make it a pre-merge check

Linters only help if they run without anyone remembering to run them. Mine runs on every PR that touches the marketing site:

# .github/workflows/sameness.yml
name: sameness-lint
on:
  pull_request:
    paths: ["site/**"]
jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with: { python-version: "3.12" }
      - run: python3 tools/sameness_lint.py site --max=30

A few things I'd tell anyone copying this:

  1. Set the threshold from your own baseline. Run it on your current site first. If you score 40, set --max to 45 and tighten it over time. 30 is just what I picked for this fixture.
  2. Tune the rules to your brief. If your brand really does use Inter, delete that rule. The rules should enforce your DESIGN.md, not my taste.
  3. Add your agent's tics. Every model has its own favorite phrases. When you catch a new one in review, add it to BUZZ and the brief's banned list in the same commit.
  4. Keep the opt-out visible. A per-file disable comment shows up in the diff. A global config flag doesn't.

Where this fits

It doesn't matter much whether the site comes from Cursor, Claude Code or an AI website builder. The first draft will lean toward the average of everything the model has seen. That's what "default" means. That's true of every tool, PolyDraft included, which is why the brief matters more than the prompt. If you're comparing tools, generate a page from the same brief in each one and run a check like this on the output. It's a useful extra row on a list of what to check when evaluating an AI website builder. And if your "site" is really one page right now, decide whether it should stay a landing page or grow into a website (the difference matters for what you build next) before you write the brief.

What's the tell you spot first on an AI-built site? I'll add good ones to the rule list.

title: Running Multiple Trials per Task for AI Agent Evaluation
description:
Once an agent completes a task with your product, the next question is how consistently it can do it again. Even with the same instructions, tools, and documentation, it may take a different route, spend longer on the work, or get stuck on something it previously completed easily.

When developers rely on agents to use your product, unpredictable behavior can interrupt their work and make the experience harder to trust. Repeated trials help you find where the workflow breaks down and test whether clearer documentation, better tools, or more useful error messages help them complete tasks more consistently.

Why run multiple trials per task

Running the same task multiple times helps you measure how consistently an agent succeeds and uncover failures a single run might miss. Each execution, or trial, uses a defined agent configuration and starts independently, with an empty environment and no conversation history or intermediate work carried over from another trial. When comparing product versions, this repetition also helps you assess whether a change improved performance or the results simply varied between runs.

Agent behavior can vary even under apparently deterministic settings. In the 2026 study On Randomness in Agentic Evals, researchers collected 60,000 coding-agent trajectories on SWE-bench Verified. Across ten complete evaluation runs of each configuration, scores varied by 2.2 to 6 percentage points from the lowest to the highest run. Variation persisted even when the temperature of the underlying LLMs was set to zero. For engineers depending on agents to get work done, those inconsistencies can become a recurring source of friction.

Multiple trials also give you more behavior to inspect. A task that passes four times and fails once offers a useful opportunity to compare approaches. Did the agent find different documentation? Choose another tool? Misinterpret a response? Reviewing those differences can point toward changes you can test.

Choosing how many trials to run

The ranges below offer a starting point for choosing trials per task. You’ll generally need more trials when results change from run to run, you’re looking for a small improvement, or you’re trying to catch a failure that rarely happens.

Suggested Trial Counts by Evaluation Goal

Evaluation goal Starting trial count per task and configuration Why start here
Check a new task and its validation 1 One run can reveal obvious setup or validation problems before you spend more on repeated trials.
Explore inconsistent behavior 3–5 A few runs can reveal different approaches and recurring problems, giving you an initial look at how behavior varies.
Pilot a comparison between product versions 5–10 for each version Repeating both versions gives you an initial estimate of the performance difference and how much it changes between runs.
Detect a small improvement Base the trial count on how much your initial results vary and how small an improvement you want to detect. Small gains are harder to distinguish from normal variation. The required count depends on the size of the gain and how variable the results are.
Investigate rare failures or measure task reliability Choose a trial count based on the failure rate you want to detect or the reliability you want to establish. Uncommon failures can go unnoticed in a few trials. Detecting them or supporting a strong reliability claim requires a budget matched to the failure rate and confidence needed.

Even major AI labs use different trial counts. OpenAI averaged four attempts per task on SWE-bench Verified, while Anthropic averaged 25 trials. For your evaluation, the useful count depends on how much the results vary and how small an improvement you want to detect. Research on coding agents shows that smaller improvements can require substantially more repetition. Start with a pilot to understand that variability, then use it to plan the trials your comparison needs.

The smaller the improvement you want to detect, the more trials you’ll generally need to distinguish it from normal variation. For example, this coding-agent study estimated that, at its median observed variability, detecting a two-percentage-point improvement would require approximately nine complete benchmark runs per system. Detecting one point would require 36. Those estimates assumed 80% statistical power and a 5% significance threshold, with 500 tasks in each complete run.

Understanding pass@1, pass@k, and pass^k

There are three important metrics worth understanding when evaluating agents: pass@1, pass@k, and pass^k. The first two grew out of code generation research, where tests could check whether a system produced a working solution in one attempt or among several candidates. OpenAI’s 2021 HumanEval paper refined how to estimate these probabilities.

As evaluations expanded to agents handling everyday workflows, consistency became another important question. The 2024 τ-bench paper introduced pass^k to measure the probability that all k independent trials succeed, averaged across tasks. Together, these metrics describe success on a single attempt, success within multiple attempts, and consistency across repeated runs.

Measuring Agent Success and Consistency

Metric Question it answers When to use it
pass@1 How likely is the agent to succeed on a single attempt? Measuring performance when the agent gets one attempt to complete the task.
pass@k How likely is at least one of k attempts to succeed? Evaluating workflows that allow multiple attempts and can identify a correct result.
pass^k How likely are all k attempts to succeed? Measuring how consistently the agent completes the same task across repeated runs.

Results from the 2024 τ-bench retail evaluation show why it helps to measure success across repeated trials. GPT-4o’s function-calling agent achieved 61.2% average success on a single attempt, measured by pass@1. Its pass^8 score fell below 25%, meaning that, averaged across tasks, the probability of succeeding in all eight independent trials was less than 25%.

Deciding between more trials vs. more tasks

Agent evaluations take time and compute, so choosing between more tasks and more trials comes down to what you need to learn. Add tasks when important workflows or conditions are missing. Run more trials when you need stronger evidence about how consistently agents handle the cases you already cover.

Choosing between more tasks and more trials

Repeated trials help you understand how consistently an agent handles a task, but the benefit of repetition has limits. Once you have a clearer picture of that behavior, testing more representative tasks, rather than more trials of a smaller set of tasks, may tell you more about performance across your product. Use your initial results to decide where uncertainty remains. If you’re trying to detect a small improvement, you may need more tasks, more trials, or both.

Conclusion

Use repeated trials to assess how reliably agents complete the workflows your product supports. Inspect outcomes and traces, identify where behavior varies, and test whether changes to tools, documentation, or error messages address those problems. Balance repetition with representative task coverage so your results support conclusions about both individual workflows and the broader product experience.
