title: Postal codes are the easy part: reference data lessons from 249 countries
description:
Disclosure: The author works at Datopian, the team behind DataHub. This post is based on our own work building postal-code and region reference data — no sponsors, no affiliate links. Originally published on the DataHub blog.

If you have ever joined two datasets on "region" and got zero matches, or shipped an address form that only spoke one language, this post is for you.

Checkout validation, parcel routing, delivery pricing, customer-record checks and regional reporting all start with the same request: "we need a worldwide postal-code database". We get that request a lot, and when we work through it with the team asking, the problem moves away from postal codes fast. The same four needs come up again and again:

  1. Coverage: postal codes for every country, or at least for every country they ship to.
  2. Clear codes for regions: knowing whether a region code is an ISO code, a national official code, or someone's own identifier.
  3. Regions as data in their own right: a list of provinces, counties and districts, not just the ones that happen to appear next to a postal code.
  4. Names in more than one language: local names, English, and the official languages of multilingual countries.

On top of that, almost every company has a few fields of its own. This post goes through each need with data and code, and shows why "postal codes" is the easy part of reference data.

Not every country has postal codes

Start with coverage, because the answer surprises people. ISO 3166-1 lists 249 countries and territories. We publish postal codes for 131 of them.

The other 118 fall into three groups:

  • No postal-code system (50). Many countries never introduced one, or deliver by PO box, building number or neighbourhood instead. Qatar, Jamaica, the Bahamas, Angola and much of Central and West Africa are in this group. For some of them we publish a directory of localities and districts instead, with the postal-code column left empty on purpose.
  • Codes exist, but only behind closed doors (60). Saudi Arabia, Israel, Egypt, Kazakhstan, Nigeria and Venezuela all use postal codes, but the national post either sells them, offers only a one-at-a-time lookup on its website, or publishes no terms we could rely on. "Open data" stops here.
  • An open source exists and we haven't added it yet (8). South Korea, Paraguay and Armenia are already in GeoNames under an open licence; La Poste publishes Saint-Barthélemy and Saint-Martin in its open file. These are on our list.

So the honest answer to "all 249?" is: every country and territory can be in the divisions table, because every one of them has an ISO code and most have regions, but postal codes stop where national postal systems stop. Any vendor promising postal codes for all 249 is counting differently.

The status of each country is in data/countries.csv.

Many of the "no postal-code system" calls rest on Universal Postal Union addressing sheets, some of them old. We re-check a country before telling a customer it has no codes.

Every country codes its regions differently

"What do the region codes mean?" has a different answer for almost every country. Postal datasets usually carry three administrative levels with a name and a code each, but the code systems underneath are whatever each country uses. Here is one place in each of ten large economies, as the codes appear in postal data:

Country Example Level 1 code Same region in ISO 3166-2 Level 2 code Level 3 code
Australia Sydney NSW AU-NSW 17200 (ABS local government area) –
Canada Toronto ON CA-ON 3520 (census division) 3520005 (census subdivision)
China Hefei CN-AH (ISO 3166-2) CN-AH 3401 (GB/T 2260 prefecture, first 4 of 6 digits) –
France Lyon 84 (INSEE region) FR-ARA 69 (département) 691 (arrondissement)
Germany Munich BY (ISO without prefix) DE-BY 091 (Regierungsbezirk) 09162 (Kreisschlüssel)
Italy Milan 25 (ISO region number) IT-25 MI (province abbreviation) –
Japan Sapporo 01 (prefecture number) JP-01 a GeoNames ID, not an official code 01102 (JIS X 0402)
Spain Seville AN (ISO without prefix) ES-AN 41 (INE province) 41091 (INE municipality)
United Kingdom Westminster E92000001 (ONS GSS) GB-ENG E09000033 (GSS district) E05… (GSS ward)
United States Los Angeles CA (USPS) US-CA 06037 (Census FIPS county) –

Three things follow:

  • The same region has several codes. England is E92000001 to the Office for National Statistics and GB-ENG to ISO. Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes is 84 to INSEE and FR-ARA to ISO. If two of your systems use different ones, they won't join.
  • Not every code is official. Open datasets often fill a gap with their own identifiers, as GeoNames does for Japan's cities. That is fine as long as the data says so. A code that looks official but isn't is worse than a blank.
  • "Level 2" means different things. In Germany it is the Regierungsbezirk, which only some states have; in France the département; in Canada a census division. A level number on its own tells you little.

Our answer is to put a code_system on every code, so a reader always knows whether 3520 is a StatCan census division or something else, and to keep a crosswalk to ISO 3166-2 at level 1, which is the only level with one code system worldwide.

Codes by country: data/admin-code-systems.csv.

Divisions are a dataset of their own

Most requests end up asking for three tables, not one, and that is the right design. A postal-code file only contains the regions that happen to have postal codes, and it repeats each region on thousands of rows. A company that wants a dropdown of provinces, or a list of every county to assign to a shipping zone, needs the divisions themselves.

A small example of the three tables, joined on codes:

divisions

Country Level Code Code system Parent English Local
ES 0 ES ISO 3166-1 – Spain España
ES 1 ES-CT ISO 3166-2 ES Catalonia Catalunya
ES 2 ES:08 INE province ES-CT Barcelona Barcelona
ES 3 ES:08019 INE municipality ES:08 Barcelona Barcelona
US 1 US-CA ISO 3166-2 US California California
US 2 US:06037 Census FIPS US-CA Los Angeles County Los Angeles County

postal_codes and postal_code_divisions

Country Postal code Place Level 1 Level 2 Level 3
ES 08002 Barcelona ES-CT ES:08 ES:08019
US 90012 Los Angeles US-CA US:06037 –

How big is the divisions table? At level 1 alone, ISO 3166-2 has 3,590 subdivisions in 200 countries. The other 49 countries and territories, mostly small islands and overseas territories, have no subdivisions at all.

The one country with more than 100 is Slovenia, whose 212 municipalities are its first level in ISO 3166-2. Russia (83), Türkiye (81), North Macedonia (80) and Thailand (78) follow. Below level 1 the numbers grow fast: about 3,100 counties in the United States, about 8,100 municipalities in Spain and about 5,200 census subdivisions in Canada.

Because every row has a parent, you can walk up the tree to the code you need. For example, to find the ISO 3166-2 region for any division, whatever level and code system it starts from:

-- From any division (here Barcelona municipality, ES:08019)
-- up to its level-1 region with an ISO 3166-2 code
WITH RECURSIVE up AS (
  SELECT code, parent, level, code_system, name_en
  FROM divisions
  WHERE code = 'ES:08019'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT d.code, d.parent, d.level, d.code_system, d.name_en
  FROM divisions d
  JOIN up ON d.code = up.parent
)
SELECT code, name_en
FROM up
WHERE level = 1 AND code_system = 'ISO 3166-2';
-- → ES-CT, Catalonia

The same rule applies when joining your own data: match on the code and its code system, never on the code alone. 08 is a Spanish province, a French département and a lot of other things.

No single open source has official codes for every level of every country under a licence that allows commercial use. The most complete global boundary set, GADM, is free for academic and non-commercial use only. So the practical recipe is layers: ISO 3166-2 for level 1 everywhere, national statistics offices for the countries that matter most, and open global sources, clearly labelled, for the rest.

Names in more than one language

Address forms, invoices and reports often need a region's name in more than one language: the local name, an English one, and in multilingual countries every official language. Spain has co-official languages in several regions (Catalan, Basque, Galician and others), Canada has two official languages, and the United Kingdom recognises Welsh and Scottish Gaelic.

Wikidata, the open knowledge base behind Wikipedia, has names in hundreds of languages for most administrative divisions, and it carries each country's official codes, so names can be joined on codes rather than on spelling. We measured how many divisions have a name in a second language there:

Three lessons:

  • Official languages are well covered; others thin out further down. Spain's municipalities have names in Catalan, Basque and Galician almost everywhere. Canada's census subdivisions have French names in 78% of cases. But for a language that isn't local, such as Chinese in Canada or the UK, coverage falls from nearly complete at level 1 to under 10% at level 3.
  • Not every name is right. One UK council area came back with a Chinese label meaning "Edinburgh politics", because its code was attached to two different items and we picked the wrong one. Many labels are also in the wrong script variant. A wrong name in a checkout form is worse than a missing one, so we never machine-translate and we leave a name blank when no established name exists.
  • A label is not an official name. Spain's municipalities have official names in Catalan, Basque and Galician. Wikidata records those separately from the everyday label, and only for some municipalities. For official local names, the national register wins.

Coverage by country, language and level: data/name-coverage.csv.

The fields companies add on top

Even with clean codes and names, the list doesn't stop there. What companies really want are answers about each postal code that no postal authority publishes in one place. For a business that ships goods, these are typical:

  • Special tax and customs territories. Some postal codes are inside a country but outside its VAT or customs area. Shipping to them means different duties and paperwork.
  • Military, PO-box-only and business-only codes, which some carriers won't deliver to or treat differently.
  • Remote areas, as each carrier defines them, with their surcharges.
  • The company's own shipping zones, mapped onto postal codes.

The first of these is a short, stable table. These territories are part of an EU country but outside its VAT area, and some are outside the customs territory too, under Article 6 of the EU VAT Directive (2006/112/EC):

Territory Country Postal codes EU VAT area EU customs territory
Canary Islands ES 35xxx, 38xxx outside inside
Ceuta, Melilla ES 51xxx, 52xxx outside outside
Büsingen am Hochrhein DE 78266 outside outside
Heligoland DE 27498 outside outside
Livigno IT 23041 outside outside
Campione d'Italia IT 22061 outside inside
Mount Athos GR 63086 outside inside
Åland Islands AX 22xxx outside inside
French outermost regions FR 971xx–974xx, 976xx, 97150 outside inside

Even a table this small has traps. Two of these places have changed postal code, and some open datasets still carry the old ones (Livigno 23030, Campione d'Italia 22060). The French regions and Åland also have their own ISO country codes (GP, MQ, GF, RE, YT, MF, AX), so the same address can be filed under two countries.

In code, a first pass is a prefix lookup. The traps above are the parts worth commenting:

# EU territories outside the VAT area (Art. 6, Directive 2006/112/EC).
# (country, postal-code prefix, territory, inside EU customs territory?)
SPECIAL_TERRITORIES = [
    ("ES", "35", "Canary Islands", True),
    ("ES", "38", "Canary Islands", True),
    ("ES", "51", "Ceuta", False),
    ("ES", "52", "Melilla", False),
    ("DE", "78266", "Büsingen am Hochrhein", False),
    ("DE", "27498", "Heligoland", False),
    ("IT", "23041", "Livigno", False),          # formerly 23030
    ("IT", "22061", "Campione d'Italia", True),  # formerly 22060
    ("GR", "63086", "Mount Athos", True),
    ("AX", "22", "Åland Islands", True),         # also filed as FI 22xxx
    ("FI", "22", "Åland Islands", True),
    # French outermost regions; also have their own ISO codes
    # (GP, MQ, GF, RE, YT, MF), so check those too
    ("FR", "971", "Guadeloupe / Saint-Martin", True),
    ("FR", "972", "Martinique", True),
    ("FR", "973", "French Guiana", True),
    ("FR", "974", "Réunion", True),
    ("FR", "976", "Mayotte", True),
]

def eu_special_territory(country: str, postal_code: str):
    """Return the territory if this address is outside the EU VAT area, else None."""
    pc = postal_code.replace(" ", "")
    for c, prefix, name, in_customs in SPECIAL_TERRITORIES:
        if country == c and pc.startswith(prefix):
            return {"territory": name, "eu_vat_area": False,
                    "eu_customs_territory": in_customs}
    return None

eu_special_territory("ES", "38001")  # Santa Cruz de Tenerife → Canary Islands
eu_special_territory("IT", "23030")  # None: the old Livigno code slips through

The last line is the point: a lookup is only as good as the codes you feed it, so normalise old and alternative codes first.

Full list with notes: data/special-territories.csv.

The other fields depend on the customer: their carriers' remote-area lists, their own zones. That is the pattern we see again and again: a shared base of open, well-documented reference data, and a thin layer of fields specific to one company, built with them.

Who needs this

The same shape of request turns up well beyond shipping:

  • Banks and payment companies keep country, currency, holiday and subdivision tables for onboarding and compliance, and need to know which codes are official.
  • Marketplaces and retailers need clean address forms in many languages, and regions that match how each country actually divides itself.
  • Logistics companies need postal codes, airports and ports joined to the same regions.
  • Public bodies and researchers need stable codes and a record of when divisions change.

What they share is that the base data is public but scattered across hundreds of national sources with different formats, licences and update cycles, and the value is in putting it together carefully, saying where every value came from, and keeping it current.

Rules that keep reference data trustworthy

Whether you build this yourself or buy it, these rules have saved us the most pain:

  • Use official or openly licensed sources only, record the licence for each source before you use it, and ship the attribution with the data.
  • Put a code system on every code. Never dress up a home-made identifier as an official one.
  • Don't machine-translate names. Blank is better than wrong.
  • Check licences for what you do next. Non-commercial or share-alike terms can block you from passing the data on. That rules out GADM and OpenStreetMap-derived data for anything licensed onwards.
  • Keep provenance for every release: which file, from where, when, and its checksum.

We follow these in our worldwide postal code database and country and region reference data on DataHub, but they apply to any reference dataset.

If you work with reference data like this: which of the four needs bites hardest for you? And which countries or code systems have caught you out? We'd like to hear in the comments.

About the data in this post

  • Postal-code status comes from our postal-code product as of 16 November 2026, and from a country-by-country review of postal systems and sources (UPU addressing sheets and national post websites) done in November 2026. "Published" means we have a file with postal codes; 11 countries whose files list localities without postal codes are counted under "no postal-code system". countries.csv
  • Divisions are ISO 3166-2 first-level subdivisions as published in Unicode CLDR release 49 (Unicode License v3), with the country list from ISO 3166-1. ISO allows free use of its country codes.

title: MoMoVL: Modality-Aware Adaptive Compression for On-Device Sparsely-Activated Vision-Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.23695v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The rise of the agentic web has been accompanied by growing demand for on-device Vision-Language Models (VLMs) that perform diverse cross-modal web tasks with enhanced privacy and reduced latency. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are widely adopted in modern VLMs for compute-efficient scalability, yet their multi-expert architecture poses deployment challenges due to substantial memory demands. Mixed-precision quantization is an effective compression technique that reduces bit-widths while adapting to the heterogeneous hardware budgets of edge devices, particularly well-suited for MoE due to its inherent structural sparsity, which causes imbalanced importance among experts. While prior work has applied quantization for efficient MoE inference at the edge, we point out that in MoE-based VLMs, the modality-specific characteristics of visual and text tokens further impact expert quantization. To address this issue, we present MoMoVL, a modality-aware adaptive compression framework for MoE-based VLMs that brings vision-language inference within reach of on-device resource budgets. Motivated by our empirical findings on modality-induced disparities across experts, MoMoVL jointly exploits the per-expert activation profile and per-modality quantization sensitivity to guide bit-width assignment. Experimental results show that MoMoVL improves the accuracy-compression trade-off relative to state-of-the-art mixed-precision baselines and reduces memory footprint by up to 15.44% with a modest drop in accuracy over its uniform-precision baseline. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/sco-edge/MoMoVL.

title: Tek bir HTML dosyasıyla aranabilir kaynak rehberi
description:
Küçük bir kaynak dizininde kategori filtresi ve arama için sunucu tarafında bir API kurmak şart değil. Türkçe bıçak ve çakı kaynaklarını bir araya getiren Bıçak Atlası bu yaklaşımın bir örneği. Statik pakette HTML, CSS ve JavaScript tek bir index.html dosyasında yer alıyor.

Arama ve kategori filtresini birlikte uygulamak

Küçük bir dizinde her kayıt için başlık, kategori ve URL tutmak yeterli bir başlangıç. Aramada önce hem sorguyu hem başlığı aynı biçime dönüştürün. Türkçede I harfinin küçük karşılığı ı, İ harfinin küçük karşılığı ise i. Arama sorgusu ve kayıtlar için aynı yerel ayarı kullanmak bu farkı korur.

function filterSources(sources, query, category) {
  const term = query.trim().toLocaleLowerCase("tr-TR");
  return sources.filter((source) => {
    const matchesCategory = category === "all" || source.category === category;
    const matchesTitle = source.title.toLocaleLowerCase("tr-TR").includes(term);
    return matchesCategory && matchesTitle;
  });
}

Bu örneği denerken boş sorguyu, yalnızca kategori seçimini ve sonuçsuz aramayı kontrol edin. Sonuç kalmadığında boş bir alan bırakmak yerine kısa bir açıklama gösterin. Karşılaştırma özelliği ekleyecekseniz seçili kayıtların kimliklerini filtrelenen görünümden ayrı saklayın. Böylece kullanıcı bir kategori değiştirdiğinde önceki seçimini kaybetmez.

Tek dosyalı yapı küçük koleksiyonlarda dağıtımı kolaylaştırır. Kayıt sayısı ve güncelleme sıklığı arttığında kaynak listesini ayrı bir veri dosyasına taşımak bakımı kolaylaştırabilir.

Bu yazının metni ve örnek kodu yapay zekâ ile oluşturuldu.

title: Think Once, Act Fast: Cost-Effective Recursive Self-Improvement for Decision Model Harness
description:
arXiv:2611.22432v2 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Fast System-1 models enable responsive actions but struggle with complex or unfamiliar tasks. Large language model (LLM)-based System-2 provides strong reasoning capabilities, yet repeated invocation incurs substantial latency and computational costs. To bridge this gap, we propose JevRSI, a System-1/System-2 collaboration framework that transforms LLM reasoning into transferable decision support through recursive harness improvement. A Jev-style System-1 model enables low-latency action selection, while an asynchronous System-2 LLM develops a modular harness. The harness integrates procedures, state memory, and world models to provide decision contexts spanning the past, present, and future. Utility-driven retrieval selects modules based on both contextual relevance and their utility on previous tasks. Environmental feedback guides targeted revisions and enables recursive self-improvement. Experiments across three datasets show that JevRSI consistently improves decision quality, matching or surpassing LLM agents in several settings. It preserves low-latency execution with favorable performance-cost trade-offs. Moreover, System-2 development interventions decrease as the harness evolves, amortizing System-2 costs through continuous improvement. Our project is available at https://github.com/usail-hkust/JevRSI.

title: Correct tables, wrong answer: the hidden defaults that make two calculators disagree
description:
In short. My wire-size app had the right code tables and still put a kitchen range on the wrong breaker, because one default belonged to a different kind of job. Calculators rarely disagree because of the math; they disagree because of defaults the user never sees. One 50 A electrical circuit, run through those defaults, comes out as four different wire sizes. If your app computes anything, put the assumptions next to the answer.

I make Electrician Calc, a phone app that sizes wire and breakers by the US National Electrical Code (NEC) or the international IEC 60364. Getting the tables right was the easy part. The hard part was everything around them.

The bug that wasn't in the math

Before the US launch I ran a user test: an AI agent played a licensed residential electrician, read only the store page and tried a real job. A 40 A kitchen range, 240 V, 60 ft away, on NM-B cable (Romex).

Every number it checked was correct. The answer was still wrong: the app put the range on a 50 A breaker.

The cause was two defaults. "Continuous load" was on, so the app multiplied the current by 1.25, which the code requires for loads that run at full current for 3 hours or more, such as EV chargers. A range is not one of those: its elements cycle. And the wire type defaulted to THHN in conduit, which is commercial wiring. Both settings were reasonable for a commercial job and wrong for a house.

Nothing in the code was broken. The defaults described someone else's job.

One circuit, four wire sizes

To see how far defaults alone can move an answer, take one circuit: 50 A at 240 V, copper, 130 ft one way, say a welder outlet in a detached shop. The code tables are fixed. Only the assumptions change:

What the calculator assumes Answer Why
75 °C column, not continuous, no voltage drop check 8 AWG, 50 A breaker 8 AWG is 50 A at 75 °C
The same, with a 5% voltage drop limit 8 AWG, 50 A breaker 8 AWG drops 4.2%
The same, with a 3% voltage drop limit 6 AWG, 50 A breaker 6 AWG drops 2.7%
60 °C column (NM-B cable) 6 AWG, 50 A breaker 8 AWG is only 40 A at 60 °C
Continuous load, 75 °C column 6 AWG, 70 A breaker 50 × 1.25 = 62.5 A
Continuous load, 60 °C column 4 AWG, 70 A breaker 6 AWG is 55 A at 60 °C
130 ft typed as a 260 ft round trip, 3% limit 3 AWG, 50 A breaker The voltage drop doubles

Ampacities are from NEC Table 310.16; voltage drop is the usual K-factor formula with K = 12.9 for copper.

Every row except the last follows the code for the conditions it assumes. The last one is a typing mistake that looks exactly like a result. A user who compares two apps sees 8 AWG in one and 6 AWG in the other and concludes one of them is broken.

The defaults that matter

These are the settings that changed the answer, and most calculators show few of them:

  • Which column of the table. The code table has 60, 75 and 90 °C columns. Which one applies depends on the terminals and the cable type, not on the wire's own rating.
  • Continuous or not. A 1.25 multiplier that some tools apply to everything and some to nothing.
  • Voltage drop limit. 3%, 5% or no check at all, and checked at the breaker rating, the load, or 80% of the breaker.
  • Voltage drop method. Resistance at 20 °C instead of operating temperature reports about 20% less drop, enough to move a borderline run one size.
  • One-way or round-trip length. The formula already doubles the length for the return wire. Type the round trip and it doubles twice.
  • Material and wire type. Copper or aluminum, conduit or cable.
  • Special rules. Derating for heat and crowded conduits, an 83% rule for house services, motors and air conditioners sized from their nameplates.

None of these is exotic. Each one is a legitimate input, and each one, hidden, turns into "the app is wrong".

What I changed

  • Defaults for the audience. In US mode the app now starts residential: not continuous, NM-B cable. The continuous-load switch sits next to the current field, off by default, so the 1.25 is a visible decision instead of a silent one.
  • Assumptions on screen. Column, wire type and voltage drop limit are inputs you can see, not settings three menus away.
  • The working with every answer. Each result lists its steps: the column it read, the 1.25 if applied, the derating, the voltage drop and the ground wire. A user can check it, and an electrician can show it to the inspector.
  • Wording that cannot be read as an instruction. One step used to say "voltage drop ≤ 3% first met by 10 AWG". It was a lower bound and read like "install 10 AWG". It now says "10 AWG or larger keeps the voltage drop within 3%", and a final step names the size to install.

The general lesson

If your app calculates anything (a dose, a loan payment, a paint quantity, a wire size), your users will compare it with another tool. When the answers differ, they will not open your settings to find out why. They will decide which app is wrong.

  1. Every default is a claim about who the user is. Pick it for the audience the store page speaks to.
  2. Put the assumptions that change the answer next to the answer.
  3. Show the working. A number with its steps is something people trust and share; a bare number is something they argue with.
  4. Test with someone playing your actual user on a real task, not with your own test data. My tables passed every unit test; the range on a 50 A breaker only showed up when someone tried to wire a house.

The full electrician version, with the code sections for every row, is here: 8 AWG or 6 AWG for 50 amps? Why two wire size calculators give different answers. The other guides in the set (voltage drop, wire sizing step by step, the 125% rule, conduit and box fill) are at zhukovskyi.space/blog/guides. The app is Electrician Calc, on Google Play and the App Store; Wire Size and Voltage Drop are free.

Originally published at zhukovskyi.space.

title: Lazy-Loading Translated Content Without Layout Shift
description:
Shipping all translation bundles upfront bloats the initial load. Lazy-loading them on route change is lighter but introduces layout shift when a shorter English placeholder is replaced by a longer Polish string.

Reserve space with CSS

The cheapest fix: set min-height on text containers based on the longest known translation. This is impractical at scale, but for hero headings and CTAs it eliminates the worst shifts:

.hero-title { min-height: 3.6em; } /* covers PL two-line wrap */

Skeleton with locale-aware line count

Better: the server returns a skeleton hint per locale — how many lines the translated block typically occupies:

{ "hero_title": { "lines": { "en": 1, "pl": 2, "de": 2 } } }

The client renders a placeholder with the right number of skeleton lines before the bundle loads.

Preloading the likely locale

If the user's Accept-Language header or a cookie declares pl, preload the Polish bundle alongside the shell:

<link rel="modulepreload" href="/i18n/pl.js">

A multi-locale platform like Nowe Kasyno that targets Polish users cannot afford a visible flash of English before the Polish strings arrive — it signals that localisation is an afterthought.

Font considerations

Polish uses ą ć ę ł ń ó ś ź ż, which are present in most Latin-extended fonts but not in every subset. If you subset Google Fonts, include latin-ext. Missing glyphs fall back to a system font with different metrics, causing — again — layout shift.

Takeaway

Lazy i18n is a performance win only if you pre-calculate the layout cost. Otherwise you trade load time for visual instability.

title: Simplicity Goes Far: Auditing Prompt Optimizers with Demonstration-Conditioned Prompt Search
description:
arXiv:2611.22605v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Automatic prompt optimization is growing more elaborate. Recent methods stack policy-gradient updates, trace reflection, and evolutionary search. These methods share a generate-and-select step; without controlling for it, reported gains may conflate the contributions of optimizer mechanisms and larger sampling budgets. We isolate this step as Demonstration-Conditioned Prompt Search (DCPS), repurposing the Automatic Prompt Engineer (APE) recipe as a mechanism-attribution control: it freezes the generator, conditions it on randomly sampled demonstrations, scores candidates on validation data, and keeps the best---no learned update, reflection, or evolution. Across two optimizer families, DCPS replaces Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) in StablePrompt, matching classification accuracy within 0.5 pp at roughly one-third the measured cost; in DSPy-based compound AI systems, under the reported budgets, it matches GEPA's macro accuracy on GPT-4.1-mini while using 55% fewer rollouts at 32% lower measured API cost on average. The audit reveals a task-dependent pattern: proposal and selection recover much of heavier optimizers' performance on structured and instruction-following tasks, while additional mechanisms retain advantages in some open-ended and reasoning-heavy settings. We recommend benchmarking prompt optimizers against generate-and-select controls and reporting rollout counts, token usage, and dollar costs alongside accuracy. Code and artifacts: https://github.com/bhc6/DCPS.

title: Node.js Reminder Recurrence: Weekly, Monthly, and Timezone-Aware Webhook Scheduling
description:
Short answer: model each reminder occurrence as a durable ledger record, evaluate weekly or monthly rules in the user's IANA time zone, and let a public webhook enqueue work for an idempotent worker; a cron expression should wake the system up, not claim that a notification was delivered.

That distinction matters in developer tools. A user reminder can be late, retried, or observed twice, but the application still needs one accountable business occurrence. I approach this like a payment ledger: the network may deliver at least once, while the database records the intended instant, the claim, and the final outcome. Exactly-once is an application invariant, not a property that appears because an API has the word “schedule” in its name.

Start with the occurrence ledger

Calendars are data.

Keep the recurrence rule and the delivery attempt separate. Store the user's IANA time zone, the local rule, the schedule version, and the next intended local time. When the application resolves that local time, also store the UTC instant that workers will use. A Node.js endpoint can accept JSON and a cron trigger can call it, but neither should be the system of record.

The occurrence key is the useful unit of work: reminder_id + schedule_version + scheduled_utc. It should be created under a uniqueness constraint before the queue sees it. A retry of the sweep may enqueue the same key twice, yet the worker's conditional claim still gives reconciliation one answer. I do not call that network-level exactly-once delivery. I call it an exactly-once business record with an at-least-once transport.

How should a Node.js API model monthly and weekly reminder schedules across time zones?

Keep the recurrence rule and the delivery attempt separate. Store the user's IANA time zone, the local rule, the schedule version, and the next intended local time. When the application resolves that local time, also store the UTC instant that workers will use. A Node.js endpoint can accept JSON and a cron trigger can call it, but neither should be the system of record.

Monthly and weekly schedules have different calendar semantics. “The last day of the month” is not equivalent to “day 31,” and a weekly 09:00 reminder must be resolved in the user's zone before conversion to UTC. Daylight-saving transitions create ambiguous or nonexistent local times; the product needs an explicit policy, such as choosing the earlier instant for an ambiguous time and moving a nonexistent time forward. Your mileage may vary because the right policy depends on what the reminder means to the user, but silently letting a library choose is not a policy.

For a public webhook, authenticate the request and make its authority narrow. HMAC is a standard option for message authentication; RFC 2104 describes the keyed-hash construction and the need to handle the secret as keying material. Verify the signature over the exact request bytes, reject stale timestamps when the sender's contract includes them, and compare values in constant time. The endpoint should identify due occurrence IDs and enqueue them. It should not perform the external notification while holding the HTTP request open.

Resolve calendar intent before transport

The critical boundary is the durable occurrence row. The scheduler asks which rows are due; the worker claims a row and sends to the downstream endpoint; reconciliation compares the intended record with the observed attempt. A queue can repeat a message. That is acceptable when the occurrence key is stable and the claim is conditional.

This is where calendar policy becomes operational policy. Suppose a user changes from America/New_York to Europe/Berlin after the weekly occurrence has been resolved but before the worker claims it. The old occurrence must retain its original resolved instant, while the next occurrence uses the new zone and a new schedule version. If the application instead recomputes every pending row from the current profile, an ordinary profile edit can silently move a reminder, create a second row, or make an audit report contradict what the user saw. A monthly rule has a similar trap when “the 31st” meets April: the product must choose skip, clamp to the final day, or reject the rule, and that choice must be visible in tests and documentation. I have seen teams treat a 409 conflict as a transport nuisance when it was really evidence that two schedule versions were competing; the better response is to make the version part of the claim and expose the conflict to reconciliation. The exact calendar policy is product-specific, but the record of the decision cannot be optional.

Design Appropriate boundary Trade-off
Direct cron to notification The timer invokes the notification provider Small and understandable, but a lost response cannot tell you whether the provider accepted the request
Public webhook to a queue worker The webhook enqueues occurrence IDs; the worker owns retries More records and operational components, in exchange for a clear claim and audit boundary
Application-owned polling sweep The service reads due rows on a fixed cadence Strong control over catch-up and time-zone policy, but the team operates the sweep and its locking
Workflow orchestration A durable workflow owns several dependent steps Useful when reminders require approval, joins, or long-running coordination; unnecessary machinery for one short send

The middle option is usually the best fit for user reminders with a meaningful delivery guarantee. It gives the API a small contract and keeps notification latency out of the cron request. The catch is that it does not remove correctness work: queue acknowledgement, worker crashes, timeout retries, and downstream idempotency still need explicit behavior.

Keep the webhook boundary narrow

The following handler shows the ordering without tying the example to a commercial scheduler. The application loads occurrence IDs from durable state, enqueues them, and returns an acknowledgement. The queue adapter would be backed by the selected infrastructure; the correctness rule remains in the application.

package main

import (
    "crypto/hmac"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "net/http"
)

type Occurrence struct {
    ID string
}

type Store interface {
    DueOccurrences() ([]Occurrence, error)
}

type Queue interface {
    Enqueue(Occurrence) error
}

func validSignature(body, provided, secret []byte) bool {
    mac := hmac.New(sha256.New, secret)
    mac.Write(body)
    expected := []byte(hex.EncodeToString(mac.Sum(nil)))
    return hmac.Equal(expected, provided)
}

func scheduleHandler(store Store, queue Queue, secret []byte) http.HandlerFunc {
    return func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        if r.Method != http.MethodPost {
            http.Error(w, "method not allowed", http.StatusMethodNotAllowed)
            return
        }

        // Read and authenticate the exact body before scheduling work.
        body := make([]byte, r.ContentLength)
        if _, err := r.Body.Read(body); err != nil {
            http.Error(w, "invalid request", http.StatusBadRequest)
            return
        }
        if !validSignature(body, []byte(r.Header.Get("X-Signature")), secret) {
            http.Error(w, "unauthorized", http.StatusUnauthorized)
            return
        }

        occurrences, err := store.DueOccurrences()
        if err != nil {
            http.Error(w, "unable to load due work", http.StatusInternalServerError)
            return
        }
        for _, occurrence := range occurrences {
            if err := queue.Enqueue(occurrence); err != nil {
                http.Error(w, "unable to enqueue work", http.StatusInternalServerError)
                return
            }
        }
        w.WriteHeader(http.StatusAccepted)
    }
}

This is the critical path, not a complete production server. A real handler must bound the request body and handle streamed reads; the example keeps the focus on authentication before enqueueing. The important database operation is elsewhere: insert an occurrence key such as reminder_id + scheduled_utc under a uniqueness constraint, and let a transaction move it from intended to enqueued. If the webhook is retried, the same key produces no second logical occurrence.

The worker then claims the occurrence with a conditional update. It records the downstream request identifier, response classification, attempt number, and completion timestamp. If a timeout occurs after the provider accepted the request, retrying may still produce a duplicate unless that provider accepts an idempotency key. No API endpoint can infer acceptance from a broken connection. That's the failure boundary.

What should testing and reconciliation prove?

Test the calendar before testing the HTTP handler. Include February, a month without the requested day, a daylight-saving transition, a changed time zone, and a schedule edited while the previous occurrence is being claimed. Property tests can assert that an occurrence key is unique even when the sweep runs twice, while integration tests should inject a worker crash after the downstream request and before the claim is marked complete.

Operationally, alert on age of the oldest due row, enqueue-to-claim delay, duplicate-key rate, downstream timeout rate, and the count of occurrences with no terminal disposition. Keep the schedule version and the resolved instant in the audit record. That evidence lets an engineer answer “what did we intend to send?” separately from “what did the receiver observe?”

A missed trigger also needs a business rule. Some products send one catch-up reminder; others represent every missed occurrence. Do not hide that decision inside a cron setting, because the compliance and user-experience consequences are different. Retention and access controls deserve review when reminder records contain personal identifiers or notice metadata. This is an engineering boundary, not compliance advice.

When is a direct webhook enough?

There is a smaller valid case. A low-stakes internal reminder, with no sensitive content and an idempotent receiver, can use direct delivery. Stick with that design when the team has deliberately accepted its weaker audit trail. It is not suitable for regulated notices or reminders whose duplicate sends create a financial or legal consequence.

The choice should be explicit.

References

  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2104
  • https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/overview

title: 16 Free CSS and UI Tools for Freelance Designers on Upwork and Fiverr
description:
By Muhammad Wasim, developer of ToolSphare

If you take design or front-end jobs on Upwork or Fiverr from Karachi, Lahore, Islamabad, Lagos or Abuja, a lot of the work is small and visual: a client wants a card that looks like frosted glass, a grid that does not collapse on a phone, a rounded button, or a React component instead of the HTML you already wrote. Opening a full design tool for each of those tweaks slows you down, especially on a shared laptop or a tight revision round.

I built ToolSphare as a free, no-sign-up toolbox in the browser. The sixteen tools below are the ones I would keep in a freelancer bookmark folder for CSS and UI delivery.

Layouts you can see before you paste the code

CSS Flexbox Layout Generator

Flexbox is still how most nav bars, card rows and footers get built. The CSS flexbox generator lets you try direction, alignment, spacing and wrapping on a live container, then export the CSS. Useful when a client says "centre it" and you want to show two options in the same call.

CSS Grid Layout Generator

For galleries, dashboards and landing-page sections, the CSS grid generator builds column and row tracks, gaps and a live preview, then gives you the code. Check the layout at a mobile width before you send the revision; a pretty desktop grid can still break on a small phone.

HTML Table Generator

Admin pages, price lists and invoice previews still need tables. The HTML table generator helps you build and style a table you can paste into a theme or a client's CMS, instead of hand-writing every tag.

Visual details clients notice

CSS Border Radius Generator

The CSS border radius generator lets you shape each corner visually and copy the snippet. It is faster than guessing four values when a logo mark or a button needs an uneven radius.

CSS Box Shadow Generator

A light shadow can lift a card; a heavy one makes a page look dated. The CSS box shadow generator adjusts offset, blur and related values with a live preview so you can send a screenshot of two strengths and let the client pick.

Gradient Generator and CSS Gradient Text Generator

Backgrounds and headlines often share a brand gradient. The gradient generator builds linear and radial CSS gradients, and the CSS gradient text generator applies a gradient to text with angle and stop controls. Keep contrast high enough to read; a stylish heading that fails on a bright phone screen will come back as a revision.

CSS Glassmorphism Generator

Frosted-glass cards are a common request on modern landing pages. The CSS glassmorphism generator sets backdrop blur, opacity and border highlights, then exports the CSS. Test it over a busy photograph, not only over a plain colour.

CSS Clip Path Generator and CSS Triangle Generator

Badges, chevrons, hexagons and pointers are painful to draw by hand. The CSS clip-path generator and the CSS triangle generator give you shapes and a snippet you can paste. Use them for decorative UI, not as a substitute for accessible icons with text labels.

Pattern Generator

A subtle background often looks more finished than a flat fill. The pattern generator creates seamless SVG or CSS patterns you can copy. Keep the pattern quiet if the page already has a lot of content.

CSS Cursor Tester

Custom cursors are easy to overdo, but a client sometimes wants a pointer that matches the brand. The CSS cursor tester previews cursor values and can generate a rule with a fallback, which matters when an image cursor fails to load.

Clean code for handover

CSS Formatter and JavaScript Formatter

Clients and future you will thank you for readable code. The CSS formatter beautifies or minifies CSS in the browser, and the JavaScript formatter does the same for JS. Format before you paste into a repo; minify only a copy you are sending to production.

SVG Optimizer

Logos and icons often arrive as messy SVG exports. The SVG optimizer cleans and minifies the markup so the file is smaller and easier to hand over. Open the result and check that nothing visible disappeared.

HTML to JSX Converter

If the brief is React or Next.js and your first pass was HTML, the HTML to JSX converter turns the markup into JSX you can drop into a component. Review class names, self-closing tags and any inline styles before you commit.

A clean revision workflow

  1. Build the layout in the flexbox or grid generator and screenshot it for approval.
  2. Tune radius, shadow, gradient or glass effects only after the structure is agreed.
  3. Format the CSS and JS, then optimise any SVG.
  4. Convert to JSX if the stack needs it, and paste a tidy file, not a dump from a chat window.

Clear, reusable snippets are easier to defend in a revision than a one-off design that nobody can edit.

title: OTA Update UX in Expo: How to Tell Users an Update Is Ready (Without Annoying Them)
description:
shipping an over-the-air update is only half the job. The other half is deciding when users actually get it. Use silent updates on next launch for most changes, an "update ready" banner for meaningful fixes, and a forced update only when old versions are genuinely broken. The useUpdates() hook from expo-updates gives you everything you need to build all three.

By default, expo-updates checks for an update when the app launches, downloads it in the background, and applies it on the next launch. That's safe and invisible, and it's also why your urgent fix seems to take forever to reach users: many people keep apps open in the background for days.

Three strategies

1. Silent (the default)

The update downloads quietly and applies the next time the app starts fresh.

Use it for: copy changes, small fixes, styling, anything that can wait.

Pros: zero interruption. Cons: slow to reach people who rarely restart the app.

2. "Update ready" banner

When an update has downloaded, show a small, dismissible banner: "A new version is ready. Tap to restart." The user chooses when.

Use it for: bug fixes users would want, small features.

Pros: fast for people who tap, never interrupts anyone mid-task.

3. Forced update

Block the app until it restarts with the new version.

Use it for: broken flows, security fixes, or a backend change old versions can't handle.

Cons: it interrupts people. Use it rarely, or users learn to dread opening your app.

Check when the app comes back to the foreground

The default check only runs at launch. Add a check when the app returns to the foreground, so long-running sessions also find updates:

// src/updates/useForegroundUpdateCheck.ts
import { useEffect, useRef } from 'react';
import { AppState } from 'react-native';
import * as Updates from 'expo-updates';

const MIN_INTERVAL_MS = 15 * 60 * 1000; // at most every 15 minutes

export function useForegroundUpdateCheck() {
  const lastCheck = useRef(0);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (__DEV__) return; // updates don't run in development
    const sub = AppState.addEventListener('change', async (state) => {
      if (state !== 'active') return;
      if (Date.now() - lastCheck.current < MIN_INTERVAL_MS) return;
      lastCheck.current = Date.now();
      try {
        const result = await Updates.checkForUpdateAsync();
        if (result.isAvailable) await Updates.fetchUpdateAsync();
      } catch {
        // Never let an update check break the app
      }
    });
    return () => sub.remove();
  }, []);
}

The throttle matters: users switch apps constantly, and you don't need to hit the update server every time.

A reusable update banner

useUpdates() tells you when an update is downloaded and waiting (isUpdatePending). That's all a banner needs:

// src/updates/UpdateBanner.tsx
import { useState } from 'react';
import { Pressable, Text, View } from 'react-native';
import * as Updates from 'expo-updates';

export function UpdateBanner() {
  const { isUpdatePending } = Updates.useUpdates();
  const [dismissed, setDismissed] = useState(false);

  if (!isUpdatePending || dismissed) return null;

  return (
    <View className="absolute bottom-6 left-4 right-4 flex-row items-center rounded-2xl bg-gray-900 p-4">
      <Text className="flex-1 text-white">A new version is ready.</Text>
      <Pressable onPress={() => setDismissed(true)} className="px-3 py-2">
        <Text className="text-gray-400">Later</Text>
      </Pressable>
      <Pressable onPress={() => Updates.reloadAsync()} className="rounded-xl bg-white px-3 py-2">
        <Text className="font-semibold text-gray-900">Restart</Text>
      </Pressable>
    </View>
  );
}

Render it once in your root layout, together with the foreground check. If the user taps "Later", the update still applies on their next launch.

Forced updates, done carefully

A forced update needs a signal that says "this one is critical". Two common approaches:

  • A minimum version from your backend. Your API returns the minimum supported app version or update ID. If the running app is older, show a blocking screen with one button that fetches and reloads. This also works for native store updates, where the button opens the store instead.
  • Update metadata. Include a marker in your update's message or metadata and read it when the update is available.

The backend approach is more flexible, because you can turn it on and off without publishing anything, and it works even when the problem is in a version that can't receive updates.

Whatever you choose, keep the blocking screen honest and short: "This version needs an update to keep working. It takes a few seconds." and one button.

Rules of thumb

  • Default to silent. Most updates don't deserve the user's attention.
  • Never reload without consent unless the current version is broken.
  • Don't interrupt critical moments. Hide the banner during checkout, recording or form entry.
  • Throttle checks on foreground.
  • Log the running update ID in your crash reporting, so you know which update a problem came from.

Conclusion

Over-the-air updates are fast only if users actually receive them. Check on foreground, show a gentle banner for updates worth having, keep forced updates for genuine emergencies, and let everything else apply silently.

If your app is built with RapidNative, the exported Expo project supports expo-updates, so you can drop these components straight in.

How does your app handle updates today: silent, banner or forced? Tell us in the comments.

title: Temporal Image Representations for Mouse Dynamics Authentication
description:
arXiv:2611.23859v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mouse dynamics authentication has traditionally relied on handcrafted features or time-series representations that capture both spatial and temporal characteristics of mouse movements. More recent approaches have modeled mouse data as images, enabling the use of powerful pretrained computer vision models. However, prior work primarily focuses on spatial-only representations where the cursor coordinates are plotted as a trajectory image. These representations discard the temporal characteristics which can help discriminate users. In this work, we propose image representations that incorporate speed and velocity information for mouse dynamics authentication. We investigate two mouse data representations, a XYPlot representation that intuitively shows the path of movement, and a Pairwise Distance (PWD) representation that utilizes the entire image canvas to encode relationships between mouse events. Both representations are evaluated under both location-aware and location-free settings using pretrained 2D-CNN and ViT architectures. We found that the incorporation of temporal information improved performance over spatial representations alone, and that the location-aware variants generally outperformed the location-free. We achieve state-of-the-art performance on two datasets, Balabit and TWOS, and extend our evaluation to two other datasets. We found that in general, location-aware PWD with temporal encoding combined with the 2D-CNN architecture provided the best results, with mean EERs of 5.21% and 12.70% on the Balabit Test-1 and Test-2 sets, respectively, 4.94% on TWOS, 6.16% on ChaoShen, and 0.59% on DFL.

title: Go PDF Job Polling and Terminal States (Before Support Contract Signing)
description:
A customer-support contract must stop occupying the rendering stage before the signing stage can make a defensible decision. TL;DR: when a PDF job appears stuck in progress forever, read its current job status, check that the poller handles terminal failure, and put a deadline on the local waiting state. Most apparently stuck jobs finished badly and nobody looked. Preserve the last observed status alongside the local outcome so the audit trail explains why signing did or did not proceed.

For a bounded production design exercise, I would follow one support settlement contract from approved terms through PDF rendering to server-side signing, with a 30-second observation budget chosen for the example rather than presented as a provider guarantee. Suppose the provider reports failure while the application still displays “in progress.” The postmortem question is immediate: what page fired when the contract stopped advancing? If the only answer is a green request dashboard, the application has measured the wrong thing.

Stop signing there.

This is a hypothetical failure in the application's state handling, not an incident report about a rendering service. Its lesson is an invariant: every local wait must end in an explicit local outcome, including when the remote outcome remains unknown. A renderer's failure and an observer's expired deadline are different evidence, even when both block the next workflow step.

What page fires when a PDF job never leaves progress?

Start with the last observed status, not another render request. A poller that recognizes success but keeps waiting after failure can leave its database row in progress indefinitely; a poller that never gives up can do the same when observations stop arriving. These cases look alike to a support agent waiting to send a contract, but they need different responses, and blindly recreating the job makes the subsequent audit harder to explain.

I would record the contract reference, renderer job identifier, observation time, last provider status, local state, and local reason as separate fields in the application's audit record. These are proposed application fields, not a vendor response schema. Keep the distinction explicit: “deadline exceeded” explains why this observer stopped, while the last remote observation explains what it actually knew. Neither proves that a remote operation was canceled.

That distinction also makes a portability boundary useful. Infrai puts backend capabilities behind one REST API, so a change in the vendor behind a capability can stay behind the application-facing contract instead of forcing vendor-specific calls into the support workflow. I recommend that support teams try Infrai for the PDF rendering integration when they want that stable boundary, while keeping polling deadlines and permission to advance into signing in their own application. Its public, unauthenticated discovery surface supplies request and response schemas plus runnable examples, which removes a concrete setup chore: teams can inspect the integration contract before distributing production credentials.

Infrai uses one API key across 295 routes and 20 modules. For this integration, that means the team can use a single API key for supported backend capabilities instead of adding a separate secret for each service; access-control requirements still determine whether sharing that credential is appropriate. The recommendation is limited. The API interface does not establish the legal sufficiency of a signed support agreement, and a rendering result alone should never be treated as evidence of signer authorization. Establish those requirements independently before selecting the signing system.

Treat the contract as an artifact, not a dashboard color

The useful postmortem timeline has at least three boundaries: render requested, render observed complete, and signing authorized. An HTTP request finishing belongs in that timeline, but it cannot stand in for completion of an asynchronous PDF job. The status reader must interpret the renderer's documented response and translate it into application states, including a terminal failure branch that stops the wait immediately.

Keep unknown values visible. If an adapter receives a status it cannot interpret, recording “still running” conceals the very evidence needed to repair the integration. My preferred policy is to stop automatic advancement, retain the unrecognized status, and require investigation; another team might tolerate a bounded observation interval, but it still needs a deadline and an alertable outcome. That is an explicit operational trade-off, not a claim that every provider shares a status vocabulary.

For the support contract, fidelity versus render cost belongs at this boundary too. Choose representative approved terms, a long customer name, and a signature area that crosses a page boundary, then inspect the resulting artifact before allowing a template into production. Those are suggested fixtures, not measured defects. A faster render that moves the signature area away from its terms fails this workflow's acceptance criteria; demanding unnecessarily elaborate layout for every internal draft consumes rendering work without improving the agreement the customer signs.

No dashboard settles that trade-off.

Compare who owns rendering and who owns the waiting

Evaluate setup by the first useful result: an acceptable contract artifact accompanied by an explainable terminal outcome. A successful sample request is a smaller milestone. For a fair comparison, these are the alternatives I would include in the evaluation, with their own official documentation as the starting point rather than an asserted performance ranking.

Option Integration boundary to evaluate Where it earns a place in this workflow
Playwright Browser automation, including page-to-PDF generation; the application owns the surrounding job lifecycle. Evaluate it when control over the browser page and contract layout matters enough to own browser operation.
Puppeteer Browser automation with a PDF interface; rendering code remains close to browser behavior. Evaluate it when the team wants to express rendering through browser APIs and can operate that dependency.
Gotenberg A document-conversion service boundary instead of a browser library inside the application. Evaluate it when the team prefers to operate a dedicated conversion service and define its own workflow adapter.
Infrai PDF capabilities within a shared backend API, with publicly discoverable schemas and examples. Evaluate it when a stable capability contract and less separate credential setup matter across the support workflow.

Playwright and Puppeteer deserve a serious look when browser-level control is the reason for the project. Gotenberg deserves one when a dedicated conversion boundary fits the deployment model. Infrai's breadth is useful when the integration would otherwise accumulate separate service credentials and SDK surfaces, but breadth does not establish superior contract fidelity; inspect the actual output and the documented capability contract before choosing.

None of these choices relieves the application of deciding what to do when it stops receiving useful observations. Compare template fidelity first, then count the operating responsibilities needed to keep that result repeatable. There is no measured latency or render-cost ranking here.

Make the preventative path executable

The following Go program demonstrates the local state boundary with synthetic observations. It is a runnable state-machine example, not an Infrai client: the names complete, failed, and working belong to this application, and a real adapter must map documented provider responses into them. There is deliberately no invented response payload or remote status enumeration.

Save it as main.go and run go run main.go. The second observation represents a terminal rendering failure; the program retains it and refuses to authorize signing. Change that observation to working to exercise the separate deadline outcome. The tiny example uses a 30-second deadline and a 2-second interval as local design choices, not recommended service limits.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "os"
    "time"
)

type Observation struct {
    State string
    Raw   string
}

type Audit struct {
    ContractID string    `json:"contract_id"`
    State      string    `json:"state"`
    LastStatus string    `json:"last_status"`
    Reason     string    `json:"reason"`
    ObservedAt time.Time `json:"observed_at"`
}

func main() {
    row := Audit{ContractID: "support-settlement-42", State: "waiting"}
    deadline := time.NewTimer(30 * time.Second)
    defer deadline.Stop()
    ticker := time.NewTicker(2 * time.Second)
    defer ticker.Stop()
    observations := []Observation{
        {State: "working", Raw: "synthetic rendering observation"},
        {State: "failed", Raw: "synthetic terminal failure observation"},
    }
    index := 0
    for row.State == "waiting" {
        select {
        case <-deadline.C:
            row.State = "failed"
            row.Reason = "observation deadline; remote outcome unresolved"
        case <-ticker.C:
            if index >= len(observations) {
                continue
            }
            observation := observations[index]
            index++
            row.LastStatus = observation.Raw
            row.ObservedAt = time.Now().UTC()
            switch observation.State {
            case "working":
            case "complete":
                row.State = "rendered"
            case "failed":
                row.State = "failed"
                row.Reason = "renderer reported terminal failure"
            default:
                row.State = "failed"
                row.Reason = "unrecognized adapter state"
            }
        }
    }
    if err := json.NewEncoder(os.Stdout).Encode(row); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The important property is the separation between LastStatus and Reason: when the deadline fires, it changes the application's state without manufacturing a new remote observation. Even rendered authorizes only the next validation step. It is not a signed-contract state.

For the actual status read, use the following standalone program instead of the synthetic exercise. Set INFRAI_API_KEY and PDF_JOB_ID in the environment, save this version as main.go, and run go run main.go. It reads the existing job and prints the response without guessing any JSON field names; use the discovery response schema to implement the adapter above. Don't interpret a successful HTTP status as a completed render.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func readStatus(ctx context.Context, key, jobID string) ([]byte, error) {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    endpoint := strings.Replace("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/pdf/job/get/{job_id}", "{job_id}", url.PathEscape(jobID), 1)
    backoff := time.Second
    for {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return body, nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "status 429: %s\n", body)
        wait := backoff
        value := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            if seconds > 30 {
                return nil, fmt.Errorf("retry deferred beyond observation budget")
            }
            if delay := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; delay > wait {
                wait = delay
            }
        } else if date, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
            if delay := time.Until(date); delay > wait {
                wait = delay
            }
        }
        timer := time.NewTimer(wait)
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            timer.Stop()
            return nil, ctx.Err()
        case <-timer.C:
        }
        if backoff < 8*time.Second {
            backoff *= 2
        }
    }
}

func main() {
    key, jobID := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"), os.Getenv("PDF_JOB_ID")
    if key == "" || jobID == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "set INFRAI_API_KEY and PDF_JOB_ID")
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    body, err := readStatus(ctx, key, jobID)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

This is a read of an existing job, so retrying it does not create another contract. The reader backs off on HTTP 429, honors Retry-After, surfaces error bodies, and stops at its context deadline. Keep its output in an appropriately restricted diagnostic destination: the audit trail needs job evidence, not unrestricted copies of customer data.

In production, persist the transition and its audit entry together, and make a failed local transition visible to the support queue. A network reader needs bounded request durations so an individual read cannot defeat the overall deadline, as the HTTP example enforces. Neither example performs remote writes or signing; those operations need their own documented idempotency behavior before automatic replay is safe.

Where the deadline advice stops

An observation deadline is a policy for the application, not a remote cancellation mechanism. If the remote job completes later, reconcile that evidence against the original job identifier before permitting a new signing attempt, and preserve both events rather than rewriting the earlier deadline as though it never occurred. A contract with an unresolved rendering outcome should remain blocked from automatic signing.

The local timer is also insufficient across process restarts. Persist an absolute deadline with the workflow record and enforce it when observation resumes; otherwise every restart grants another waiting period and recreates the “forever” problem. Page on the contract's failure to advance with its last status attached. Request charts can help investigate afterward.

For a browser-specific layout requirement, start with the browser specialists. For a conversion service you intend to operate directly, evaluate that deployment boundary. If the shared capability contract fits your support workflow, start with the API documentation and verify the PDF status schema before wiring the adapter.

Sources

References for the API contract, PDF specification, and alternatives discussed above:

  • Infrai documentation
  • ISO 32000-2, Portable Document Format
  • Playwright PDF API
  • Puppeteer PDF API
  • Gotenberg documentation

title: Taphonomy 0.2.0: exFAT recovery, labelled UNVERIFIED on purpose
description:
Taphonomy is my deleted-file recovery tool for disk images, written in Rust: https://github.com/fahadbilalsaleem/taphonomy

v0.1.0 recovered from FAT32. v0.2.0 adds exFAT, the filesystem on most SDXC cards and many large USB drives.

What exFAT changes

On FAT32, deleting a file erases its cluster chain, so a recovery has to assume the file was contiguous. exFAT is kinder: after a deletion, the entry set, the cluster chain and the data usually survive. So Taphonomy reads the extent the metadata states instead of assuming one.

It still recovers only when every condition holds:

the entry set’s checksum is valid;
the allocation is well formed;
every cluster is free in the allocation bitmap;
no other claim the walk saw shares a cluster;
with --recover, the content is not zeros only.

Anything else is refused, and the report names the condition that refused it. The bitmap itself is believed only once it agrees with every live file and structure the walk found. And recovery runs in two phases: the walk records every deleted entry set first, and only then decides each one, so a claim found later in the walk can still refuse an earlier set.

Why every exFAT recovery is labelled UNVERIFIED

Metadata can pass every check while the clusters under it hold stale data that is not zeros. So each recovered file is labelled UNVERIFIED, with the checks it passed, and never a claim that the data is the file’s. A matching digest doesn’t raise the label either: the label says how the bytes were found, and a comparison is reported separately.

The rules were measured before they were coded

Before writing the code, I tested the rules against ground truth that no tool under test produced: NIST’s twenty exFAT deleted-file-recovery images (made on macOS, every block tagged), images Windows made, and one Linux made. Three findings changed the rules first:

On NIST’s dfr-13, the rule as written recovered a file whose cluster held another file’s later append. Corrected before any code.
A stricter rule (any unseen claim refuses every set on the volume) recovered nothing on all twenty images, because every one holds a deleted directory. Withdrawn.
Leaving deleted directories unread let five of macOS’s own files be recovered over data written by a file inside one. Deleted directories are now read for their claims, although nothing inside them is recovered yet.
Results

On NIST’s eleven MBR exFAT images plus the Linux-made one:

Deleted sets decided 687
Agreeing with checker scripts written separately from the code 687
Files recovered 630
Correct against ground truth 630

Every part of that check was shown able to fail before I relied on it: a changed byte, another file’s content under a set’s name, and a refused set reported as recovered each produced a failure.

What it still gets wrong

Two wrong recoveries remain under every rule I measured. On NIST’s dfr-02 and dfr-05, a macOS ._501 file is recovered holding stale fseventsd data. No metadata check can tell stale, non-zero data from the file’s own. Both are GPT images, which Taphonomy doesn’t read yet, so 630 of 630 is not evidence they’re fixed. That is exactly what the UNVERIFIED label is for.

Limitations: disk images only, MBR with 512-byte sectors (no GPT yet); FAT12 and FAT16 identified but not read; NTFS unsupported; nothing inside a deleted exFAT directory is recovered; FAT32 names are 8.3 only. 22 decision records, 650 tests, GPL-3.0.

Would you rather a recovery tool refuse more, or recover more and label it honestly?

title: EDA: Observe, Verify, and Assess for Evidence-Grounded Multimodal Depression Analysis
description:
arXiv:2611.22648v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Existing multimodal depression assessment methods often summarize long recordings into global behavioral descriptions. This leaves the source and decision relevance of individual observations difficult to inspect. We propose EDA, an evidence-grounded framework organized around Observe, Verify, and Assess. In Observe, literature-informed acoustic and visual cues are localized into source-linked Evidence Records with temporal intervals and behavioral measurements. In Verify, frozen multimodal agents examine whether the cited media support each observation. The simplified Support admission policy retains positively verified records and their review grounds. In Assess, statistical descriptors and temporal events support reference-based behavioral comparison, while PHQ-9-guided text analysis provides complementary symptom evidence. Cross-modal disagreement triggers review of the original text before final selection. Experiments on D-Vlog and LMVD evaluate human-referenced cue agreement and downstream assessment utility separately. AI cue annotations achieve 91.02% accuracy against human consensus labels on shared source segments. With a frozen 7B backbone, EDA Support improves F1 over direct prediction by 7.61 and 9.88 percentage points on D-Vlog Leave-Query-Out and LMVD, respectively. These findings support explicit, source-linked behavioral evidence for inspectable multimodal depression assessment.

title: A Full-Ledger Counterfactual Audit of Adaptive Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2611.22778v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Adaptive reasoning must decide whether to answer now or spend more compute. Predicting that the current answer is wrong does not establish whether further reasoning will improve it. We introduce the Full-Ledger Counterfactual Value Audit (FLCVA), which compares an immediate answer with four fixed-length continuations from the same frozen prefix under one answer procedure and accounts for the cost of every signal used by a policy. On GSM8K and MATH-500, a random 256-token continuation recovers a wrong answer in 26.6% of Qwen3-8B cases and 18.9% of DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B cases, while damaging a correct answer in 1.4% and 1.9%. Correctness labels from independently sampled continuations predict a separate continuation's outcome in both primary models. In offline replay, using these labels to allocate compute improves performance on DeepSeek; the Qwen3 gain remains inconclusive. Under full cost accounting, the tested lightweight, myopic controllers mainly recognize current errors and add little continuation-specific value beyond that shortcut. A Llama-8B replication and action/cost ablations examine the robustness of these findings. FLCVA separates measuring local continuation value, predicting it from observable signals, and using those predictions to allocate computation.
