title: Building a $0 Modern Data Platform: dbt, MotherDuck, and Automated CI/CD (Zero AWS Required)
description:
Author: Fabrizio Perez Peralta

Course: Business Intelligence

Published on: [Dev.to / HashNode / Medium]

Public Repository: GitHub Repository Link

Live Dashboard: Streamlit Community Cloud Live App

1. Introduction: The Real Cost of the "Modern Data Stack"

In recent years, the Modern Data Stack (MDS) has revolutionized how organizations extract, transform, and analyze information. However, traditional implementations often come with a steep barrier to entry: enterprise data warehouses (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift), paid managed orchestrators (Astronomer, Airflow clusters), and complex cloud infrastructure (AWS VPCs, IAM roles, S3 buckets). For small teams, startups, or students, these costs and operational overhead quickly become prohibitive.

The Question: Can we build a production-grade, automated Data Engineering pipeline using industry-standard tools (like dbt), deployed to a public SaaS provider, with zero infrastructure management and a monthly cloud bill of exactly $0.00?

The Answer: Yes. By combining MotherDuck (Serverless DuckDB in the cloud), dbt-core, GitHub Actions for CI/CD, and Streamlit Community Cloud for business intelligence, we can create an end-to-end cloud data platform with high performance and zero cost.

In this article, I will walk you through the architecture, data modeling, automated deployment, and lessons learned from building this solution.

2. High-Level Solution Architecture

Our solution follows the classical Medallion Architecture (Bronze, Silver, Gold), orchestrated via automation:

flowchart LR
    subgraph Ingestion ["1. Data Ingestion (Python)"]
        API["Public Financial API"] --> Extract["extract_load.py"]
    end

    subgraph DWH ["2. Cloud DWH (MotherDuck SaaS)"]
        Extract --> Bronze["raw.raw_crypto_market"]
        Bronze --> Silver["dbt: Staging & Intermediate"]
        Silver --> Gold["dbt: Marts (Fact & Dimension)"]
    end

    subgraph CI_CD ["3. CI/CD & Orchestration"]
        GHA["GitHub Actions (Cron + Push)"] -.->|Trigger Ingest| Extract
        GHA -.->|dbt run & dbt test| DWH
    end

    subgraph BI ["4. Public SaaS Consumption"]
        Gold --> Streamlit["Streamlit Cloud Dashboard"]
    end

Why this stack?

  1. MotherDuck (SaaS Cloud DWH): Provides the speed and simplicity of DuckDB with serverless cloud persistence, shared access, and zero compute management.
  2. dbt (data build tool): The undisputed industry standard for SQL-based transformation, version control, and data testing.
  3. GitHub Actions (CI/CD): Acts as both our continuous integration tool and our automated serverless orchestrator (using cron schedules), providing free unlimited runner minutes for public repositories.
  4. Streamlit Community Cloud (SaaS Serving): Instant web app deployment directly synchronized with our GitHub repository.
  5. No AWS: We eliminated all complex cloud provider lock-in, IAM role juggling, and unexpected billing surprises.

3. Step 1: Resilient Extract & Load (EL) with Python

Before transforming data, we must ingest it. We created a lightweight Python script (scripts/extract_load.py) that queries public cryptocurrency and market indicators.

To guarantee that the pipeline never fails due to transient network glitches or public API rate limits, the script incorporates an automatic fallback mechanism:

import os
import requests
import pandas as pd
import duckdb

def get_duckdb_connection():
    token = os.getenv("MOTHERDUCK_TOKEN")
    if token:
        # Connect to MotherDuck Cloud SaaS
        return duckdb.connect(f"md:crypto_intelligence?motherduck_token={token}")
    else:
        # Local fallback for offline development
        return duckdb.connect("data/lakehouse.duckdb")

def load_to_lakehouse(df: pd.DataFrame):
    con = get_duckdb_connection()
    try:
        con.execute("CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS raw;")
        con.execute("""
            CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS raw.raw_crypto_market (
                id VARCHAR, symbol VARCHAR, name VARCHAR,
                current_price DOUBLE, market_cap DOUBLE, total_volume DOUBLE,
                high_24h DOUBLE, low_24h DOUBLE, price_change_percentage_24h DOUBLE,
                ath DOUBLE, circulating_supply DOUBLE,
                ingestion_timestamp TIMESTAMPTZ, ingestion_date DATE
            );
        """)
        con.register("df_batch", df)
        con.execute("INSERT INTO raw.raw_crypto_market SELECT * FROM df_batch;")
    finally:
        con.close()

4. Step 2: Transformations with dbt (Medallion Architecture)

Once raw data lands in raw.raw_crypto_market (the Bronze layer), we leverage dbt to clean, enrich, and model the data.

Bronze / Staging Layer (stg_crypto_market.sql)

In the staging layer, we cast data types, standardize string formatting, and deduplicate records by keeping only the latest snapshot per asset:

with source_data as (
    select * from raw.raw_crypto_market
),

deduplicated as (
    select
        id as coin_id,
        upper(trim(symbol)) as coin_symbol,
        trim(name) as coin_name,
        cast(current_price as double) as current_price_usd,
        cast(market_cap as double) as market_cap_usd,
        cast(total_volume as double) as total_volume_24h_usd,
        cast(high_24h as double) as high_24h_usd,
        cast(low_24h as double) as low_24h_usd,
        cast(price_change_percentage_24h as double) as price_change_pct_24h,
        cast(ath as double) as all_time_high_usd,
        cast(ingestion_timestamp as timestamp) as ingested_at,
        row_number() over (
            partition by id order by ingestion_timestamp desc
        ) as row_num
    from source_data
)

select * from deduplicated where row_num = 1;

Silver / Intermediate Layer (int_crypto_volatility_metrics.sql)

In this layer, we derive actionable business intelligence metrics:

  • Intraday Volatility %: ((High - Low) / Low) * 100
  • All-Time-High (ATH) Drawdown %: How far the asset has dropped from its historical peak.
  • Capitalization Tiers: Categorizing assets into Mega Cap, Large Cap, and Mid Cap.

Gold / Marts Layer (fct_crypto_market_snapshot.sql & dim_crypto_assets.sql)

The final consumer layer adheres to dimensional modeling (star schema):

  • dim_crypto_assets: Slowly changing attributes (asset name, symbol, tier classification).
  • fct_crypto_market_snapshot: Quantitative facts (current price, 24h volume, volatility metrics, and computed risk profile tags).

5. Step 3: Enforcing Data Quality & Governance

Data engineering without testing is just wishful thinking. In models/marts/schema.yml, we define rigorous assertions executed automatically by dbt test:

version: 2

models:
  - name: fct_crypto_market_snapshot
    columns:
      - name: coin_id
        tests:
          - not_null
          - relationships:
              to: ref('dim_crypto_assets')
              field: coin_id
      - name: current_price_usd
        tests:
          - not_null
      - name: risk_profile
        tests:
          - accepted_values:
              values: ['High Volatility', 'Moderate Volatility', 'Low Volatility / Stable']

If any constraint fails (e.g., duplicate IDs or unexpected risk values), the CI/CD pipeline immediately stops, preventing corrupted data from reaching the serving layer.

6. Step 4: Automated CI/CD Deployment with GitHub Actions

To fulfill the requirement of automated deployment, we configured a GitHub Actions workflow (.github/workflows/pipeline.yml).

The pipeline runs on every code push and automatically every 12 hours:

name: Automated Data Engineering Pipeline (MotherDuck + dbt)

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 */12 * * *'
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  run-pipeline:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: '3.10'

      - name: Install Dependencies
        run: pip install -r requirements.txt

      - name: Ingestion to MotherDuck SaaS
        env:
          MOTHERDUCK_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.MOTHERDUCK_TOKEN }}
        run: python scripts/extract_load.py

      - name: Run dbt Transformations
        env:
          MOTHERDUCK_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.MOTHERDUCK_TOKEN }}
          DBT_TARGET: "prod"
        run: dbt run --project-dir dbt_project --profiles-dir dbt_project --target prod

      - name: Run dbt Data Quality Tests
        env:
          MOTHERDUCK_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.MOTHERDUCK_TOKEN }}
          DBT_TARGET: "prod"
        run: dbt test --project-dir dbt_project --profiles-dir dbt_project --target prod

By storing our MOTHERDUCK_TOKEN in GitHub Secrets, our automated runner can authenticate securely to the cloud data warehouse without hardcoding credentials.

7. Step 5: Serving Insights via Streamlit Community Cloud

Finally, to deliver value to decision-makers, we deployed a web dashboard on Streamlit Community Cloud (a public SaaS provider).

The dashboard connects directly to MotherDuck via read-only SQL queries and renders:

  1. Executive KPI Cards: Total market capitalization, aggregate 24h trading volume, and average market volatility.
  2. Risk vs. Return Scatter Chart: Interactive Plotly scatter plot mapping price changes against intraday volatility, colored by risk category.
  3. Curated Marts Explorer: An interactive table with formatted currencies, percentage changes, and tier filters.

Because Streamlit Cloud is linked to the GitHub repository, any update pushed to main is instantly reflected in the live application.

8. Key Learnings & Takeaways

  1. MotherDuck changes the game for small-to-medium data: You don't need a multi-node cluster or an expensive data warehouse to achieve sub-second query times. MotherDuck offers SQL-native data warehousing with zero maintenance.
  2. dbt works everywhere: The flexibility of dbt-duckdb allows developers to test locally on an embedded database and switch to production cloud storage simply by toggling a connection profile (profiles.yml).
  3. CI/CD is not just for software developers: In modern Business Intelligence and Data Engineering, testing data and automating transformations through CI/CD pipelines ensures reliable data contracts and prevents dashboard breakages.
  4. $0.00 is achievable: By thoughtfully orchestrating public SaaS providers (MotherDuck, Streamlit Cloud, GitHub Actions), we delivered an enterprise-grade solution without a single dollar of cloud spend.

9. Resources & Links

  • 📂 Source Code (Public Repository): github.com/FabrizioPerezPeralta/crypto-intelligence-lakehouse
  • 📊 Live Public Dashboard: crypto-intelligence-lakehouse.streamlit.app
  • 🦆 MotherDuck Documentation: motherduck.com/docs
  • 🔶 dbt Documentation: docs.getdbt.com

Feel free to leave a comment, star the repository, or connect on LinkedIn if you have any questions or feedback!

title: From Perception to Simulation: Unveiling and Empowering Mental Spatial Dynamics in MLLMs
description:
arXiv:2611.22541v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Spatial reasoning is a fundamental component of world understanding for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). While existing research has advanced the perception of spatial relations in static scenes, the domain of dynamic spatial simulation remains relatively unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce MentalGrid, a benchmark focused on spatial reasoning tasks that require models to simulate evolving spatial states without intermediate visual feedback. Extensive evaluation on our benchmark reveals a significant deficiency in the spatial simulation capabilities of existing models. Specifically, we find that performance is constrained by perceptual limitations in simple simulation scenarios and hindered by inadequate multi-step reasoning as complexity increases. To address these challenges, we propose a three-stage curriculum learning framework utilizing 16k specialized spatial reasoning samples. This approach yields SpatialWalker, which achieves a 33.8% average improvement over its base model, surpassing proprietary models like Gemini-3-Flash in spatial simulation. Furthermore, SpatialWalker demonstrates robust generalization, maintaining a 4.9% average gain on out-of-domain benchmarks, demonstrating the pivotal role of spatial simulation as a fundamental building block for broader spatial intelligence.

title: Understanding and Building React Custom Hooks: A Practical Guide
description:
Originally published on Medium (Becoming For Better). Read on Medium for free via Friend Link.

⚡ Get the Production-Ready React Hooks Pack

Quick Takeaways

  • Hook Rules First : Start with use, compose built-in hooks, stay reusable, and never return JSX.
  • 10 Production Patterns : Copy-ready hooks for focus, delays, window size, outside clicks, forms, fetching, debouncing, storage, media queries, and toggles.
  • Build vs. Borrow : Know when to write lightweight custom hooks and when to reach for usehooks.com or usehooks-ts.com.

Custom hooks in React are a powerful tool for reducing code duplication, improving code organization, and boosting overall productivity. In this article, we’ll explore what custom hooks are, how to build them, and walk through ten practical examples.


React custom hooks extract shared stateful logic out of UI components into clean, reusable functions.

What is a Custom Hook?

A custom hook is a JavaScript function that uses one or more built-in React hooks to encapsulate reusable logic. Think of it as extracting the engine out of a component so any other component can drop it in without duplicating wiring.

Rules for Creating Custom Hooks

Here are the core principles to keep in mind when creating a custom hook:

  • Naming Convention : Always start the hook name with use. For example, a hook for managing form input can be named useFormInput.
  • Dependencies : You can use built-in hooks like useState, useEffect, or even other custom hooks within your own.
  • Reusability : A custom hook should be reusable in different components without modification.
  • No JSX : Custom hooks should contain logic only. They must not return JSX or manage rendering directly.

Useful Custom Hook Examples

1. useFocus

This hook helps programmatically focus a DOM element using useRef and useCallback.

import { useRef, useCallback } from "react";

export const useFocus = () => {
  const ref = useRef(null);

  const focusElement = useCallback(() => {
    if (ref.current) {
      ref.current.focus();
    }
  }, []);

  return [ref, focusElement];
};

2. useDelay

Returns true after a specified delay — useful for loading spinners or delayed content.

import { useState, useEffect } from "react";

export const useDelay = (delayTime) => {
  const [done, setDone] = useState(false);

  useEffect(() => {
    const delay = setTimeout(() => {
      setDone(true);
    }, delayTime);

    return () => clearTimeout(delay);
  }, [delayTime]);

  return done;
};

3. useWindowSize

Tracks window dimensions — perfect for responsive layouts.

import { useState, useEffect } from "react";

export const useWindowSize = () => {
  const [windowSize, setWindowSize] = useState({
    width: window.innerWidth,
    height: window.innerHeight,
  });

  useEffect(() => {
    const handleResize = () => {
      setWindowSize({
        width: window.innerWidth,
        height: window.innerHeight,
      });
    };

    window.addEventListener("resize", handleResize);

    return () => {
      window.removeEventListener("resize", handleResize);
    };
  }, []);

  return windowSize;
};

4. useOnClickOutside

Detects clicks outside a specified element — great for modals and dropdowns.

import { useEffect } from "react";

export const useOnClickOutside = (ref, handler) => {
  useEffect(() => {
    const listener = (event) => {
      if (!ref.current || ref.current.contains(event.target)) {
        return;
      }
      handler(event);
    };

    document.addEventListener("mousedown", listener);
    return () => {
      document.removeEventListener("mousedown", listener);
    };
  }, [ref, handler]);
};

5. useFormUpdate

Warns users about unsaved changes before leaving the page.

import React, { useState, useEffect } from "react";

export const useFormUpdate = () => {
  const [isFormUpdated, setIsFormUpdated] = useState(false);

  useEffect(() => {
    const handleBeforeUnload = (event) => {
      if (isFormUpdated) {
        const message =
          "You have unsaved changes. " +
          "Are you sure you want to leave?";
        event.returnValue = message;
        return message;
      }
    };

    window.addEventListener(
      "beforeunload",
      handleBeforeUnload
    );

    return () => {
      window.removeEventListener(
        "beforeunload",
        handleBeforeUnload
      );
    };
  }, [isFormUpdated]);

  const handleFormUpdate = () => {
    setIsFormUpdated(true);
  };

  useEffect(() => {
    const selector =
      "form input, form select, form textarea";
    const formElements = document.querySelectorAll(selector);
    const handleFieldChange = () => {
      setIsFormUpdated(true);
    };

    formElements.forEach((element) => {
      element.addEventListener("change", handleFieldChange);
    });

    return () => {
      formElements.forEach((element) => {
        element.removeEventListener(
          "change",
          handleFieldChange
        );
      });
    };
  }, []);

  return handleFormUpdate;
};

6. useFetch

Simplifies fetching and managing API data.

import React, { useState, useEffect } from "react";

export const useFetch = (url) => {
  const [data, setData] = useState(null);
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);
  const [error, setError] = useState(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    const fetchData = async () => {
      try {
        const response = await fetch(url);
        if (!response.ok) {
          throw new Error("Network response was not ok");
        }
        const result = await response.json();
        setData(result);
      } catch (error) {
        setError(error);
      } finally {
        setLoading(false);
      }
    };

    fetchData();
  }, [url]);

  return { data, loading, error };
};

7. useDebounce

Delays input updates — useful for search boxes and reducing API calls.

import React, { useState, useEffect } from "react";

export const useDebounce = (value, delay) => {
  const [debouncedValue, setDebouncedValue] = useState(value);

  useEffect(() => {
    const handler = setTimeout(() => {
      setDebouncedValue(value);
    }, delay);

    return () => {
      clearTimeout(handler);
    };
  }, [value, delay]);

  return debouncedValue;
};

8. useLocalStorage

Persistent storage for data between sessions.

import React, { useState, useEffect } from "react";

export const useLocalStorage = (key, initialValue) => {
  const [storedValue, setStoredValue] = useState(() => {
    try {
      const item = window.localStorage.getItem(key);
      return item ? JSON.parse(item) : initialValue;
    } catch (error) {
      console.error(error);
      return initialValue;
    }
  });

  const setValue = (value) => {
    try {
      const valueToStore =
        value instanceof Function
          ? value(storedValue)
          : value;
      setStoredValue(valueToStore);
      window.localStorage.setItem(
        key,
        JSON.stringify(valueToStore)
      );
    } catch (error) {
      console.error(error);
    }
  };

  useEffect(() => {
    const handleStorageChange = () => {
      try {
        const item = window.localStorage.getItem(key);
        setStoredValue(
          item ? JSON.parse(item) : initialValue
        );
      } catch (error) {
        console.error(error);
      }
    };

    window.addEventListener("storage", handleStorageChange);

    return () => {
      window.removeEventListener(
        "storage",
        handleStorageChange
      );
    };
  }, [key, initialValue]);

  return [storedValue, setValue];
};

9. useMediaQuery

Handles responsive rendering based on screen size.

import React, { useState, useEffect } from "react";

export const useMediaQuery = (query) => {
  const [matches, setMatches] = useState(false);

  useEffect(() => {
    const mediaQuery = window.matchMedia(query);

    const handleMediaQueryChange = (event) => {
      setMatches(event.matches);
    };

    mediaQuery.addListener(handleMediaQueryChange);
    setMatches(mediaQuery.matches);

    return () => {
      mediaQuery.removeListener(handleMediaQueryChange);
    };
  }, [query]);

  return matches;
};

10. useToggle

Quick toggle between true/false states — ideal for toggles and switches.

import React, { useState } from "react";

export const useToggle = (defaultValue) => {
  const [value, setValue] = useState(defaultValue);

  function toggleValue(value) {
    setValue((currentValue) =>
      typeof value === "boolean" ? value : !currentValue
    );
  }

  return [value, toggleValue];
};

Bonus: Custom Hook Libraries

Instead of building every hook from scratch, you can take advantage of excellent open-source libraries:

  • usehooks.com : A treasure trove of custom hooks with examples and explanations.
  • usehooks-ts.com : Lightweight, type-safe, and written in TypeScript. Great for advanced usage.

Benefits of Using Hook Libraries

  • Save time : Ready-made, battle-tested solutions for common UI state.
  • Reduce repetition : Eliminate boilerplate across components.
  • Better documentation : Learn edge-case handling from real-world examples.

Which custom hook do you find yourself copying into every new React project — or which built-in pattern still trips up your team? I'd love to hear your thoughts 🧠💬

Keep Exploring

If you want to level up your frontend architecture and developer tooling, check out these related deep-dives:

  • Taming Claude Code: A Guide to CLAUDE.md and Hooks — Structure AI coding workflows with deterministic project rules and lifecycle hooks.
  • How Game Physics Works: Building a 2D Physics Engine from Scratch in Canvas — A hands-on breakdown of simulation loops, collisions, and browser rendering.

About the Author

I'm Mustafa Morbel — Senior Frontend Engineer with over 17 years of experience crafting high-performance React architectures, WebGL applications, and developer tooling.

  • Find full component examples and open-source boilerplates on my GitHub (@mkare).
  • Connect on LinkedIn and follow along on X / Twitter (@mustafamorbel) for React & TypeScript best practices.
  • Have a custom hook you use in every project? Share it in the comments below, and leave a few claps if you found this guide helpful!

title: Why useReducer? Why do we need multiple functions to update a single state?
description:
When working with React, we usually use useState() to manage state.

For example, imagine building a counter application with three operations:

  • Increment
  • Decrement
  • Reset

Using useState(), we might write separate functions for each operation.

Using useState() 

const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

function increment() {
    setCount(count + 1);
}

function decrement() {
    setCount(count - 1);
}

function reset() {
    setCount(0);
}

Here, we have three different functions to perform three operations on the same state.

This is perfectly fine for a small application. But imagine having many actions and more complex state update logic. Managing all those functions can become difficult.

What if we use useReducer()?

Instead of creating separate functions for every operation, we can define the state update logic in one reducer function.

function reducer(state, action) {
    switch (action.type) {
        case 'increment':
            return state + 1;

        case 'decrement':
            return state - 1;

        case 'reset':
            return 0;

        default:
            return state;
    }
}

Now we can trigger different operations using dispatch().

const [count, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, 0);

<button onClick={() => dispatch({type: 'increment'})}>
    Increment
</button>

<button onClick={() => dispatch({type: 'decrement'})}>
    Decrement
</button>

<button onClick={() => dispatch({type: 'reset'})}>
    Reset
</button>

What is the actual difference?

With useState(), we write separate functions to handle different state updates.

With useReducer(), we keep the state update logic in one place and send different actions through dispatch().

Important: We don't always need useReducer(). For simple state updates, useState() is easier. When state logic becomes complex, useReducer() helps organize the code.

Conclusion

The main advantage of useReducer() is not reducing the number of functions. It is organizing multiple state update operations in one reducer function.

Both hooks are useful. The choice depends on the complexity of your application.

One important concept to remember: useReducer() doesn't eliminate functions. It replaces multiple state-update handlers with one centralized reducer function, while dispatch() tells it which action to perform.

title: Toaster: Nonlinear Memory from Cascaded Linear Memories and Target Propagation
description:
arXiv:2611.23648v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recurrent memories let language models process long sequences with a fixed-size state. Linear memories such as DeltaNet and KDA store one matrix and take one delta-rule step per token. The product of a chunk of such steps has an exact WY form, so they train fast. Deep memories such as TTT-MLP and Titans store a small MLP, which can hold maps that no matrix can, but their update has no WY form. Toaster bridges the two by building on a known fact: a gradient step on a linear layer is a delta-rule write. It builds a two-layer nonlinear memory from two linear memories with an activation between them. We use target propagation to give the hidden memory its values by projecting the output error back through the second memory. Given a chunk's cross-layer signals, approximated once per chunk, each layer can then run on an unmodified delta-rule kernel. Our default runs this kernel on the output layer and updates the hidden layer once per chunk. Running it on both layers gives a better model in our ablation. At matched backbones and training-token budgets, Toaster has lower loss than KDA at all five tested sizes (0.2B-1.6B non-embedding parameters) on both C4 and PG19. Its C4 perplexity also matches or slightly improves on the attention baseline at every size. At 1.2B it is also below Titans. In a 3:1 hybrid with global attention, the Toaster hybrid has the lowest perplexity of the four hybrids tested, and it is 0.18 (C4) and 0.44 (PG19) below the attention baseline. At the largest size, Toaster's mean three-shot accuracy on 13 tasks is 51.84%, compared with 50.52% for KDA and 50.04% for Titans. In length extrapolation, Toaster's loss stays below KDA's up to 20K tokens (5x the training length). On the 145M backbone, at a hidden width matched to Titans' memory, Toaster takes at most 1.33x KDA's training-step time and is 2.8-5.5x faster than the tested Titans configurations at 32K context.

title: DARWIN: a Geospatial Foundation Model for Marine Intelligence
description:
arXiv:2611.22496v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present DARWIN, a geospatial foundation model for marine intelligence. Recent Earth-observation foundation models have concentrated on terrestrial domains. The marine realm poses distinct challenges: missingness, multi-modal physical and biogeochemical variables, sparse labels, and dynamics that are transient, multi-scale, and non stationary over time. DARWIN adapts a masked-autoencoder backbone to these properties through missingness-aware encoding, expanded spatial and temporal masking, and Fourier-style positional embeddings, and is pretrained on 26 years of global Copernicus reanalysis together with GEBCO bathymetry.
  On predicting chlorophyll-a, the pretrained backbone attains the lowest monthly relative error in every month of 2022, outperforming both no-encoder baselines and an identically architected random-init encoder. At 10% of the supervised training data, DARWIN already surpasses the random-init model trained on 100% of the data. Embedding analysis and qualitative reconstructions show that DARWIN captures coherent oceanographic structure rather than memorising input statistics, providing a scalable backbone for downstream marine applications such as anomaly detection, species distribution modelling, and environmental monitoring.

title: Dolby Vision profile 5 on Android without a Dolby Vision decoder
description:
Dolby Vision profile 5 is common, and on an Android TV box or phone without a Dolby Vision decoder it plays green and purple. Here is how Yonto Player draws them with the right colours anyway, on top of media3 (ExoPlayer), with the GPU doing the colour work.

Why profile 5 is the hard one

Profile 8 carries an HDR10, HLG or SDR picture under the Dolby Vision layer, so a device that knows nothing about Dolby Vision can still show something sensible. Profile 5 has no such fallback. The picture is coded in Dolby's own IPT-PQ-c2 colour space, and every frame carries an RPU (Reference Processing Unit) with the metadata that turns it back into light. Skip the RPU and decode it as plain HEVC, and you are looking at IPT values as if they were YCbCr, which is where the green and purple come from.

media3 maps Dolby Vision profiles 4, 8 and 9 to an HEVC decoder when no Dolby Vision decoder is present. Profile 5 it leaves alone, which makes sense, since there is no base layer to show. So on most phones and many TV boxes it finds no decoder at all.

The plan

  1. If the device has a Dolby Vision decoder, use it, as before.
  2. Otherwise decode the track as HEVC Main 10.
  3. Read each frame's RPU on its way into the decoder.
  4. Have the decoder render into a SurfaceTexture instead of the screen.
  5. Apply the RPU on the GPU, tone-map to SDR, and draw to the screen.

Choosing the decoder

The video renderer is media3's MediaCodecVideoRenderer with getDecoderInfos overridden. media3's own choice comes first, so a real Dolby Vision decoder always wins. Only when that list is empty and the track is profile 5 (codecs dvhe.05 or dvh1.05) does it fall back to the plain HEVC decoders, keeping only those whose capabilities list the Main 10 profile (or list nothing, which some decoders do).

The codec is then configured as HEVC with KEY_PROFILE set to Main 10.

Reading the RPU

The RPU travels as an HEVC NAL unit of type 62, whose two-byte header is 7C 01. In onQueueInputBuffer the renderer looks at each access unit just before it goes to the decoder, finds the last RPU in it from the end, strips the emulation-prevention bytes, checks its CRC-32 and parses it. The parser is plain Kotlin in the shared core, since nothing in it is Android's.

Two things make this harder than it sounds. B-frames come out of the decoder in a different order than they went in, so the parsed RPU is stored against the sample's timestamp and taken back out by presentation time when the decoder releases that frame. And RPUs refer back to earlier ones: a reshaping can be reused by id, and display metadata can be left out to mean "same as before", so they are resolved in decode order. A missing or broken RPU reuses the previous frame's, and a seek forgets all of it.

Drawing it ourselves

The renderer keeps the screen's Surface it receives through MSG_SET_VIDEO_OUTPUT for itself and hands the codec the input Surface of a SurfaceTexture. For each frame it releases, it tells the drawing side the release time and the RPU that goes with it. The drawing side renders, sets that time with eglPresentationTimeANDROID and swaps. Frame pacing and A/V sync stay media3's.

The one extension that makes it possible

This was the crux. Sampling an external texture with samplerExternalOES gets you RGB: the driver converts from YCbCr and clamps, and the IPT codes are gone before your shader sees them. GL_EXT_YUV_target adds __samplerExternal2DY2YEXT, which hands you the raw Y, U and V codes instead. Declaring it is all the extension asks:

#extension GL_EXT_YUV_target : require
uniform __samplerExternal2DY2YEXT frame; // texture(frame, uv) returns Y, U, V codes

The shader then looks those codes up in a table (below) and writes RGB.

No OpenGL ES 3, no GL_EXT_YUV_target, or no HEVC decoder with Main 10, and the whole path is off. Those devices play it in the app's second player, which says its colours won't be right. Two video players in one app, and the rule that picks one covers that hand-over.

The colour maths

In order, per pixel:

  1. The RPU's reshaping curves (polynomial and MMR pieces) bring I, P and T back.
  2. The RPU's matrix and offset take IPT to PQ-coded LMS.
  3. The PQ curve turns that into linear light.
  4. LMS to BT.2020.
  5. ITU-R BT.2390's tone map on the brightest channel, from the scene's peak (the RPU's level 1 metadata, else the mastering display's peak, never below 100 nits) down to SDR white at 203 nits.
  6. BT.2020 to BT.709, clipped.
  7. The sRGB curve.

It is written from the published standards and the bitstream syntax.

Too slow per pixel, so bake it

Run in full for every pixel, that took 80 ms for one 1080p frame on a Google TV Streamer's PowerVR GE9215. A 24 fps film needs a frame every 42 ms.

So the maths runs once into a 3D lookup table and every frame is one texture fetch:

  • 65 × 65 × 65 points, 10 bits a channel (GL_RGB10_A2, which every OpenGL ES 3.0 device can render into and filter).
  • Rebuilt one layer at a time, only when a frame's parameters differ from the last one's, which in practice means at a scene change.

Against the exact maths over every pixel of two frames, the table is within 0.13 of an 8-bit level on average, with under 0.5% of channels more than two levels off, the worst at the edge of the gamut. Spacing the table's points towards the shadows measured no better, since the error is at the gamut's edge, not in the steep start of the curve.

How close it gets

On the Google TV Streamer, with its own Dolby Vision decoder hidden from the renderer so the HEVC decoder and the GPU did the work:

  • Frame 48 of the 1080p sample: within 0.5 of a level of the reference implementation on average (worst 9).
  • Frame 300, after seeking into another scene: within 0.8 on average (worst 23, with 0.03% of pixels more than 8 off).
  • No dropped frames at 1080p, or at 4K at 25 fps.
  • Moving the picture to a new Surface mid-play works.

For comparison, libplacebo through FFmpeg (on MoltenVK, with BT.2390 chosen) lands within 3.1 and 4.5 levels of ours on the same two frames, about as far as it is from the reference (3.0 and 4.3). Its knee and black point differ; the hues are the same.

What we ruled out

  • media3's setVideoEffects. Its effects pipeline converts every frame to RGB before any effect runs, through the driver's YCbCr-to-RGB step into RGBA8, or for HDR a clamped BT.2020 path at medium precision. The codes the RPU needs are gone by then.
  • Reading frames on the CPU with an ImageReader in P010 and uploading the planes as integer textures, for GPUs without the extension. It costs a 25 MB copy per 4K frame, and those GPUs are on the weakest devices, so they keep the second player.

Where it stops

  • The output is SDR on every screen, an HDR TV included.
  • Dolby's level 2 and level 8 trims are not applied, so contrast and saturation can differ slightly from a licensed Dolby Vision display's own SDR picture.
  • The Android emulator has neither a Main 10 HEVC decoder nor GL_EXT_YUV_target, so this path needs a real device to see.

Read more

  • Video format support, what plays where.
  • Video formats, how the app picks a player for a file, profile 5 included.
  • The changelog for 5.5.1, the release this shipped in.
  • Two video players in one app, and the rule that picks one.
  • One Kotlin core for every screen, the series article on what is shared across platforms.

title: How Do You Build a Production-Ready FastAPI Backend with Background Jobs?
description:
A production-ready FastAPI backend keeps request handlers fast, validates input with Pydantic models, and moves slow work (emails, scraping, report generation) into background jobs so the API always answers quickly. This guide shows a small, practical structure you can extend.

How should you structure a FastAPI project?

Keep routing, schemas, and business logic apart:

app/
  main.py        # app creation, routers
  schemas.py     # Pydantic models
  services.py    # business logic
  jobs.py        # background work

Step 1: validated endpoints with Pydantic 

# app/schemas.py
from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr  # pip install "pydantic[email]"

class ReportRequest(BaseModel):
    email: EmailStr
    mc_number: str

class JobStatus(BaseModel):
    job_id: str
    status: str

Pydantic rejects malformed input with a clear 422 response before your code runs.

Step 2: accept the request, queue the work 

# app/main.py
import uuid
from fastapi import FastAPI, BackgroundTasks
from .schemas import ReportRequest, JobStatus
from .jobs import build_report, JOBS

app = FastAPI()

@app.post("/reports", response_model=JobStatus, status_code=202)
async def create_report(req: ReportRequest, tasks: BackgroundTasks):
    job_id = uuid.uuid4().hex
    JOBS[job_id] = "queued"
    tasks.add_task(build_report, job_id, req)
    return JobStatus(job_id=job_id, status="queued")

@app.get("/reports/{job_id}", response_model=JobStatus)
async def report_status(job_id: str):
    return JobStatus(job_id=job_id, status=JOBS.get(job_id, "unknown"))

Returning 202 Accepted tells the client the work is queued, and the client polls the status endpoint.

# app/jobs.py
import time

JOBS: dict[str, str] = {}

def build_report(job_id: str, req) -> None:
    JOBS[job_id] = "running"
    try:
        time.sleep(5)  # replace with real work
        JOBS[job_id] = "done"
    except Exception:
        JOBS[job_id] = "failed"

When is BackgroundTasks not enough?

BackgroundTasks runs inside the same process. If the server restarts, queued work is lost, and the in-memory JOBS dict is not shared between workers. For anything important, store job state in a database or Redis and use a real queue such as Celery, RQ, or Arq.

Production checklist

  • Run with uvicorn or gunicorn -k uvicorn.workers.UvicornWorker behind a reverse proxy such as nginx.
  • Load secrets from environment variables, never from code.
  • Add a /health endpoint for monitors.
  • Log request IDs and exceptions.
  • Write tests with TestClient from FastAPI.

FAQ

Is FastAPI async only? No. You can declare handlers with def and FastAPI runs them in a thread pool.

Should I use BackgroundTasks or Celery? Use BackgroundTasks for small, non-critical work; use a queue when jobs must survive restarts or retry.

How do I document the API? FastAPI generates OpenAPI docs automatically at /docs.

Where should job state live? In a database or Redis, so every worker sees the same state.

Written by Muhammad Afzal, Python developer at INDUS Web Agency.

title: Exploring Parkinson's Diagnosis Using Machine Learning Techniques
description:
arXiv:2611.23248v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In recent years, machine learning (ML) techniques have emerged as promising tools for accurate and timely diagnosis of Parkinson's disease (PD) which is an incurable neurodegenerative disorder. This study explores the integration of ML algorithms and PD diagnosis, highlighting their potential applications in various aspects of the disease. ML methods such as support vector machines, decision trees, multilayer perceptron, k-nearest neighbours, logistic regression and random forest (with and without particle swarm optimisation) were applied on a PD dataset obtained from Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust containing data from 58 people. In terms of accuracy, the Decision Tree and Logistic Regression performed the best with scores of 72-76% while multilayer perceptron was least effective. All the models were remarkable in classifying positive PD cases with sensitivity scores going up to 97.56%, with SVM classifier at the pinnacle. However, ability to classify healthy controls from PD cases was insignificant throughout the board. Although, all the employed models delivered reasonable results in categorising PD patients in the presented dataset; access to more data, further study and advancement of these ML approaches could lead to enhanced diagnostic outcomes, supplementing to an improved understanding of Parkinson's disease.

title: Architecting Bulletproof Stripe Webhooks: Idempotency and Timing Safety
description:
Payment webhooks are the single most fragile architectural boundary in modern SaaS applications. When integrating Stripe, developers frequently follow tutorial code that functions in local testing but fails under production network latency.

In this guide, we examine the core failure modes and the architecture required to harden webhook handlers.

1. The Duplicate Delivery Trap (Idempotency)

Stripe guarantees at-least-once delivery. Network latency or temporary downstream timeouts cause Stripe to retry webhooks with exponential backoff.

Without database-level deduplication, handlers credit customer accounts multiple times or duplicate fulfillment actions.

// Atomic Deduplication Pattern (Next.js / Prisma)
const existing = await db.webhookEvent.findUnique({ where: { eventId: event.id } });
if (existing && existing.status === "COMPLETED") {
  return NextResponse.json({ received: true, deduplicated: true });
}

2. Raw Body Integrity & Signature Verification

Parsing the request body as JSON before verification alters byte order and key serialization, causing HMAC signature verification to fail.

Always extract the raw string/buffer directly before any JSON parser runs:

const rawBody = await req.text();
const signature = req.headers.get("stripe-signature");
const event = stripe.webhooks.constructEvent(rawBody, signature, WEBHOOK_SECRET);

3. Two-Tier Asynchronous Execution

Stripe enforces an HTTP timeout. Heavy tasks (invoice PDFs, customer notification emails, CRM updates) must be offloaded to an asynchronous background worker queue (e.g. BullMQ, Inngest, Celery), ensuring the webhook route acknowledges in under 200ms.

Automated Auditing with Claude Code

If you build on Claude Code or Cursor, you can automate this entire verification suite using the turnkey Stripe Webhook Sentinel on Agensi.

title: Budgeted Proper Loss Design for Uncertain Decision Thresholds
description:
arXiv:2611.23247v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A binary probability estimate may be used by several decision makers with different error costs. Proper scoring rules can emphasize selected probability thresholds, but a single average threshold distribution need not give a good worst-case regret guarantee. We study the choice of a proper loss when the threshold distribution belongs to a finite specified family. Among integrable loss weights with a positive pointwise floor and a fixed total mass, we derive the weight that minimizes the sharp, distribution-free multiplier from surrogate regret to threshold-averaged decision regret. The solution clips a rescaled upper envelope of the threshold densities at the prescribed floor; its normalization is found by a one-dimensional root search. We give proofs of sharpness, optimality, and stability under density misspecification, as well as a limitation for atomic threshold laws. An exact histogram implementation and two synthetic experiments across 20 seeds verify the construction. The optimized multiplier improves over uniform and average-density weights, while fitted-model performance does not improve uniformly. The result is a loss-design guarantee under an explicit budget, rather than a general claim of predictive superiority.

title: Importing Bandcamp ZIPs in a Flutter music player: streams, zip slip and Finder junk
description:
People who still buy music mostly get it as a ZIP. Bandcamp, Qobuz and most download shops hand you one archive per album. My offline music player, Clickwheel, could only import loose audio files, so the first thing a new user had to do was find an unzip tool on their phone. That is a bad first minute.

So I added ZIP import. The diff was 469 lines across 13 files, and almost none of it was "call the unzip function". Here is what the rest was.

1. Stream from disk, off the UI thread

A FLAC album is easily several hundred megabytes. Reading it into a Uint8List on a phone is asking for an out-of-memory kill. The archive package (4.x) can decode from a file stream and write each entry straight to disk:

static List<String> unpackZip(String zipPath, String destPath) {
  final input = InputFileStream(zipPath);
  final written = <String>[];
  try {
    final archive = ZipDecoder().decodeStream(input);
    for (final entry in archive) {
      if (!entry.isFile) continue;
      final relative = safeZipEntry(entry.name);
      if (relative == null ||
          !kAudioExtensions.contains(_extension(relative))) {
        continue;
      }
      final file = File('$destPath/$relative');
      file.parent.createSync(recursive: true);
      final output = OutputFileStream(file.path);
      try {
        entry.writeContent(output);
      } finally {
        output.closeSync();
      }
      written.add(file.path);
    }
  } finally {
    input.closeSync();
  }
  return written;
}

The function is synchronous on purpose. It is a static method that only takes two strings, so it can run in a background isolate with one line:

final unpacked = await Isolate.run(() => unpackZip(zip, dest));

The click wheel keeps animating while the album unpacks, and the progress label ("Unpacking Some Artist - Some Album.zip") is set from the main isolate between archives.

2. Never trust an entry name

A ZIP entry name is just a string chosen by whoever made the archive. ../../something is a valid name, and writing it blindly puts a file outside your target folder. This is the classic "zip slip" bug. My guard is small and boring:

static String? safeZipEntry(String name) {
  final parts = name
      .replaceAll(r'\', '/')
      .split('/')
      .where((p) => p.isNotEmpty && p != '.')
      .toList();
  if (parts.isEmpty) return null;
  if (parts.contains('..')) return null;
  if (parts.first == '__MACOSX') return null;
  if (parts.last.startsWith('._')) return null;
  return parts.join('/');
}

Four things happen here:

  • Backslashes become slashes, because archives made on Windows sometimes use them.
  • Empty segments are dropped, so an absolute path like /abs/song.mp3 becomes the relative abs/song.mp3.
  • Any entry containing .. is rejected outright. I don't try to normalise it. An album has no reason to contain one.
  • The macOS Finder junk is skipped: the __MACOSX folder and the ._song.mp3 resource forks. Those end in .mp3, so without this line every album zipped on a Mac would show up with twice as many tracks, half of them unplayable.

On top of that, only files with a known audio extension are written at all. Cover scans, PDFs and .url files stay in the archive.

3. Test with archives you build in the test

I work as a QA engineer, so this is the part I care about most. The archive package can also create ZIPs, which means the test builds its own hostile album in memory:

final archive = Archive()
  ..addFile(ArchiveFile.bytes('Artist - Album - 01 One.mp3', [1, 2, 3]))
  ..addFile(ArchiveFile.bytes('cd2/02 Two.flac', [4, 5]))
  ..addFile(ArchiveFile.bytes('cover.jpg', [9]))
  ..addFile(ArchiveFile.bytes('__MACOSX/._x.mp3', [0]))
  ..addFile(ArchiveFile.bytes('../evil.mp3', [0]));
final zip = File('${dir.path}/album.zip')
  ..writeAsBytesSync(ZipEncoder().encode(archive));

final out = LibraryService.unpackZip(zip.path, '${dir.path}/out')..sort();

expect(out, [
  '${dir.path}/out/Artist - Album - 01 One.mp3',
  '${dir.path}/out/cd2/02 Two.flac',
]);
expect(File('${dir.path}/evil.mp3').existsSync(), isFalse);

Five entries go in, two come out, and the last line checks that nothing landed one folder up. No fixture files in the repo, no binary blobs in code review.

4. Decide where the album goes

Small decisions that took longer than the code:

  • Folder name = archive name without .zip. Bandcamp already names its downloads "Artist - Album", so the folder view looks right for free. An archive literally called .zip falls back to a default name instead of creating a folder with an empty name.
  • Subfolders survive. cd1/ and cd2/ stay as they are.
  • The scratch folder is deleted in a finally block, whether the import worked or not. Otherwise a failed import of a 600 MB album silently eats 600 MB.
  • A ZIP dropped into the media folder is deleted after a successful unpack, because otherwise every album is on the device twice. A broken archive stays where it is, so the user can see it.
  • Name clashes never overwrite. A second "Some Album" becomes "Some Album (2)".

5. iOS: show up in the share sheet

On iOS most people download the ZIP in Safari and then tap Share. To appear there, the app declares the document types in Info.plist:

<dict>
  <key>CFBundleTypeName</key>
  <string>ZIP</string>
  <key>CFBundleTypeRole</key>
  <string>Viewer</string>
  <key>LSHandlerRank</key>
  <string>Alternate</string>
  <key>LSItemContentTypes</key>
  <array>
    <string>public.zip-archive</string>
  </array>
</dict>

LSHandlerRank is Alternate on purpose. A music player should be offered for ZIP files, not become the default app for them.

The native side is a small Swift class that receives the URL, wraps the copy in startAccessingSecurityScopedResource() and moves the file into the media folder. The detail that bit me: on a cold start the file arrives before the Dart side is listening on the method channel. So the Swift side counts what came in, and Dart asks once at startup:

_channel.setMethodCallHandler((call) async {
  if (call.method == 'filesArrived') await _absorb(ipod);
});
// Whatever arrived on cold start, before Dart could listen.
_absorb(ipod, onlyIfPending: true);

What I'd tell my past self

The unzip call is ten lines. The feature is everything around it: memory, the UI thread, hostile paths, Finder junk, cleanup, duplicates and cold starts. Writing the test list first would have given me the design for free.

Honest status: this is merged on the main branch and ships with the next store update. If you install the app today, ZIP import may not be in your build yet.

Clickwheel is an offline music player with a click wheel for your own MP3 and FLAC files, on iPhone and Android. You can turn the wheel in your browser: https://clickwheel-app.pages.dev/?ref=devto#rad

Clickwheel by Felix Helleckes. More of my apps: https://felix-helleckes.github.io/apps/?ref=devto

title: Give the agent the existing error-boundary map, don’t invent a new one per page
description:
The agent adds a new settings page and wraps the whole file in a brand-new <ErrorBoundary fallback={<p>Something went wrong</p>}>. The app already has a route-level boundary, a feature-level one around the editor, and a shared fallback that reports to the logger. The new wrapper swallows the error, skips the report, and looks different from every other failure screen.

I’ve started treating a one-off error boundary in an agent PR as a smell. If the repo already has a map — which routes own a boundary, which widgets are isolated, what the fallback is — the model should use that map. It should not invent a fourth kind of “something went wrong.”

Why a new boundary is usually wrong

The model has seen a million examples that start with “wrap it in an error boundary.” That advice is correct at the architecture level and wrong at the leaf. Two boundaries in a row, with different fallbacks, make recovery harder to reason about. A boundary that does not call the existing logError helper makes the page look fine in the UI and silent in the dashboard.

There are real reasons to add a boundary: a third-party widget, an isolated editor, a route the team has not wrapped yet. Those reasons should be in the PR, and the fallback should be the shared one unless you are designing a new tier.

A simple boundary policy

  • Read the existing map first — app/error.tsx, src/lib/boundaries.md, the router wrappers
  • Reuse the shared fallback and logger
  • Add a new boundary only for a new isolation tier, named and documented on the map
  • No inline fallback={<div>Error</div>} in a random page

If the framework already provides route error elements (Next.js error.tsx, Remix ErrorBoundary), prefer those over a custom wrapper in the page module.

What to put in the prompt 

Here is how errors are isolated in this app (see src/lib/error-boundaries.md or the root ErrorBoundary).
Do not add a new ErrorBoundary around a page that is already covered.
If this feature needs isolation, use the shared fallback and logger, and update the map.
Do not invent a one-off “Something went wrong” message.

Paste the map or the existing boundary component. In review, search the diff for ErrorBoundary and componentDidCatch. New hits need a reason.

Async errors are a special case. A render boundary will not catch a failed fetch unless you map that failure into state or a router error. If the agent added a boundary “to handle the API error,” it probably did not. Point it at the existing query-library error UI or the route’s error.tsx, and keep the boundary for render-time failures.

If the new page is a modal or a drawer, isolating it can be right — a crash in a dialog should not blank the whole settings route. Use the shared fallback, still, and say on the map that the dialog is an isolation tier.

Reject / send back

Reject

  • A page-level wrapper that duplicates the route boundary
  • A fallback that does not report to the existing logger
  • A unique error illustration for one page, unless that is an explicit request
  • Swallowing the error and rendering an empty state

Accept

  • A feature that relies on the existing route or app boundary
  • A new, documented isolation tier with the shared fallback
  • A framework error.tsx that matches the rest of the app

title: Where Global Context and Weight Sharing Work in Compact Vision Backbones
description:
arXiv:2611.23446v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Compact convolutional backbones such as EfficientNet achieve strong parameter efficiency through local depthwise separable convolutions, yet two structural questions remain central to hybrid design: where does global self-attention improve recognition over pure convolution, and can repeated blocks share weights without losing representational capacity? We investigate both questions on ImageNet-1k (50,000-image validation) using controlled EfficientNet-B0 experiments. First, we show that wrapping a classification backbone in multi-scale feature pyramids (BiFPN) fails to outperform a plain MBConv trunk (69.99% - 71.81% vs. 72.86% plain B0) until paired with stage attention (73.15%). In contrast, keeping the MBConv trunk intact and inserting lightweight zero-gated residual self-attention adapters at stages P3 (28x28 windowed), P4 (14x14 global), and P5 (7x7 global) reaches 74.02% standalone and outperforms a bit-for-bit matched plain-B0 control by +0.954 percentage points (73.88% vs. 72.92%) across an 88-epoch stateless replay schedule, with learned attention amplitude rising monotonically with semantic depth (27.2% at P3 -> 45.4% at P4 -> 66.3% at P5). Second, we evaluate recurrent weight sharing across repeated MBConv blocks with pass-specific BatchNorm statistics (+1,536 parameters per pass). While post-hoc kernel averaging degrades accuracy to 17.03% and single-template stage tying (-27.6% parameters) plateaus at 66.10%, alternating two shared block templates ([B1, A, B, A]) in Stage 6 cuts total model parameters by 10.9% (582K weights) and recovers by +10.82 points in a single epoch to 70.92% (-1.84 points vs. unshared control).

title: When "AI Boom" Becomes "Cloud API Regret": The Case for Client-Side Compute
description:
The tech industry is abuzz with AI, and rightfully so. From intelligent assistants to hyper-personalized experiences, AI promises a transformative future. But in our rush to integrate these powerful capabilities, many of us have fallen into a familiar trap: the default impulse to send everything to the cloud. We're witnessing a concerning trend where the initial "AI boom" excitement is slowly giving way to a gnawing "cloud API regret."

For senior software engineers, this regret often surfaces in the form of architectural nightmares, escalating costs, and, most critically, severe privacy liabilities.

Think about the sheer volume of sensitive data we're routinely pushing to third-party cloud APIs: confidential client audio recordings, deeply personal medical voice notes, unreleased podcast interviews, or proprietary internal discussions. The moment this data leaves the user's device, even just for transcription or simple natural language processing, we've introduced a profound security and privacy risk. This isn't just an architectural choice; it's a potential privacy violation waiting for a breach, an audit, or a compliance nightmare.

We've taken inherently simple, utilitarian tasks – like converting speech to text – and burdened them with complex authentication layers, intricate billing systems, data egress costs, and the overhead of managing distributed systems. Why are we building complex server-side pipelines for problems that can, and increasingly should, be solved entirely within the user's browser?

The Fallacy of Cloud-Everything: When Simplicity Gets Buried Under Complexity

The cloud offers undeniable advantages: scalability, managed infrastructure, and a seemingly infinite toolkit. But its promise of simplicity often hides a brutal truth: integrating a basic utility often pulls in a cascade of unrelated complexities.

Consider a seemingly innocuous feature like real-time audio transcription. The cloud-first approach typically looks something like this:

  1. Client-side: Record audio, chunk it, maybe compress it.
  2. Network: Send audio chunks over HTTPS to your backend.
  3. Backend (Your Server): Authenticate the user, validate the request, handle rate limiting, potentially store the audio temporarily.
  4. Network: Forward the audio to a third-party Cloud Speech API (e.g., Google Cloud Speech-to-Text, Azure Cognitive Services, OpenAI Whisper API).
  5. Third-party Cloud: Process the audio, incur their billing.
  6. Network: Receive transcription results back at your backend.
  7. Backend (Your Server): Store results in a database, possibly process further, manage eventual consistency.
  8. Network: Send transcription results back to the client.
  9. Backend (Your Server): Bill tracking, error logging, monitoring, compliance auditing for data handling.

This multi-step dance introduces numerous failure points, latency, and significant overhead. Each network hop is an opportunity for interception (even with TLS, trust in third parties is assumed). Each service interaction adds compute and data transfer costs. Each piece of PII (Personally Identifiable Information) or PHI (Protected Health Information) flowing through this pipeline significantly amplifies your regulatory burden (GDPR, HIPAA, CCPA, etc.).

We've essentially exchanged the operational burden of managing a speech-to-text model for the architectural burden of managing secure data pipelines, billing meters, vendor lock-in, and compliance for a service that, fundamentally, just takes audio in and spits text out.

The Alternative: Zero-Backend, Air-Gapped Client Computation

What if I told you that for many "AI" tasks, particularly those involving sensitive user input, you could achieve superior performance, enhance privacy, and dramatically reduce costs by cutting out the backend entirely? Modern web browsers, powered by a revolution in Web APIs, now offer precisely this capability.

Imagine:

  • Zero-backend: No servers to provision, patch, scale, or secure for the core AI task.
  • Air-gapped: Sensitive data never leaves the user's device. It's processed directly in RAM, isolated from external networks during computation.
  • 100% Client-Side: Leveraging the user's own device CPU/GPU for computation.
  • Faster: Eliminating network latency means near-instantaneous results.
  • Cheaper: No API costs, no egress fees, no server maintenance.
  • Inherently Private: Data stays local, aligning perfectly with "privacy by design" principles.
  • Offline Support: Many tasks can now run perfectly without any internet connection.

This isn't theoretical. It's happening now, thanks to advancements like:

  • WebAssembly (WASM): Enables high-performance code (like C++, Rust, Python) to run in the browser at near-native speeds, ideal for complex AI models.
  • WebGPU: Provides direct access to the user's graphics card for massively parallel computations, essential for neural networks. This is the new frontier beyond WebGL.
  • Web Neural Network API (WebNN): An emerging standard designed to accelerate on-device machine learning inference.
  • Libraries like Transformers.js and ONNX Runtime Web: These projects are bridging the gap, making it straightforward to run state-of-the-art transformer models (like Whisper for speech-to-text) directly in the browser, leveraging WASM and WebGPU.

This paradigm shift empowers developers to build truly private, responsive, and cost-efficient applications.

Real-World Implementation: SolveMyMedia - Local AI Speech-to-Text

To illustrate this, let's look at a concrete example: SolveMyMedia. We built SolveMyMedia's transcription engine to tackle the exact problem outlined – transcribing sensitive audio data without ever sending it to an external server. The core engineering challenge was: how do we run powerful neural transformer speech-to-text models directly on the user's device, without a backend, and with zero internet connectivity required post-initial model download?

Our solution leverages the cutting-edge web technologies mentioned:

  • Transformers.js: A fantastic library that brings Hugging Face's transformers to the browser. It handles model loading, inference, and ties into WebAssembly and WebGPU seamlessly.
  • ONNX Runtime Web: Provides a high-performance inference engine for ONNX models, often used under the hood by Transformers.js for optimal execution.
  • WebGPU: When available, WebGPU provides significant hardware acceleration, moving computation from the CPU to the GPU for faster inference. If WebGPU isn't supported, it gracefully falls back to WebAssembly on the CPU.

Architectural Flow (100% Client-Side):

  1. User Interaction: User records audio or uploads an audio file in their browser.
  2. Model Loading (First Run): The browser fetches a compact, pre-trained neural network model (e.g., a "tiny" Whisper model) from a CDN. This model is then cached in the browser's IndexedDB, meaning subsequent runs are completely offline.
  3. In-Browser Inference: The Transformers.js pipeline takes the audio data (which remains in the browser's memory) and feeds it to the loaded model.
  4. Hardware Acceleration: ONNX Runtime Web, powered by WebAssembly (for CPU) or WebGPU (for GPU), executes the model's computations directly on the user's device.
  5. Result: The transcription text is generated directly in the browser's memory and displayed to the user.

Crucially, throughout this entire process, no audio data, nor the resulting transcription, ever leaves the user's device. It's a truly air-gapped solution for the sensitive computation.

Here's a simplified code snippet demonstrating how remarkably easy this has become:

// In-Browser Local Neural Speech-to-Text via Transformers.js
import { pipeline } from '@xenova/transformers';

/**
 * Transcribes audio entirely within the browser using a local neural network model.
 * Audio data never leaves the user's device.
 *
 * @param {AudioBuffer} audioBuffer - The audio data to transcribe.
 * @returns {Promise<string>} The transcribed text.
 */
export async function transcribeLocalAudio(audioBuffer) {
  // Load the automatic speech recognition pipeline.
  // Model weights (Xenova/whisper-tiny.en) are downloaded once and then
  // cached locally in IndexedDB after the first run.
  // This means subsequent transcriptions can be 100% offline.
  const transcriber = await pipeline('automatic-speech-recognition', 'Xenova/whisper-tiny.en', {
    // Attempt to use WebGPU for hardware acceleration if available in the browser.
    // Falls back to WebAssembly (CPU) if WebGPU is not supported.
    device: 'webgpu'
  });

  // Perform the transcription. The audioBuffer is processed locally.
  // chunk_length_s and stride_length_s are parameters for processing longer audio efficiently.
  const output = await transcriber(audioBuffer, {
    chunk_length_s: 30, // Process audio in 30-second chunks
    stride_length_s: 5  // Overlap chunks by 5 seconds to improve continuity
  });

  // The transcription result is generated and remains 100% private,
  // zero bytes are sent over the network for the transcription process itself.
  return output.text;
}

The Unarguable Benefits: Privacy, Cost, and Performance

The contrast between the cloud-dependent approach and the client-side approach is stark when viewed through key metrics:

Metric Cloud Speech API (OpenAI / Rev) SolveMyMedia Local AI Transcribe
Voice Privacy Stored on external cloud servers Air-gapped in client RAM
API Costs $0.006 per minute (e.g., Whisper) $0.00 Unlimited
Offline Support ❌ Fails without internet connection ✅ 100% Works in Airplane Mode
Latency Network latency + cloud processing Device processing only
Data Egress Yes, data leaves user's device No, data stays local
Regulatory Burden High (GDPR, HIPAA, etc. for third-party data handlers) Significantly Reduced (data never leaves user)
Vendor Lock-in High Low (standard open-source models)

This table isn't just about saving money; it's about fundamentally changing the security and privacy posture of your application. For use cases involving highly sensitive data – legal depositions, medical consultations, financial advice, or proprietary research – this is not just an optimization; it's a non-negotiable requirement.

Beyond Speech-to-Text: A New Frontier for Web Development

Speech-to-text is just one example. The capabilities extend to:

  • Image processing: Local object detection, image classification, style transfer.
  • Natural Language Processing (NLP): Sentiment analysis, named entity recognition, text summarization.
  • Data validation and transformation: Complex regex, data cleansing, and reformatting.
  • Augmented Reality (AR) filters: Real-time visual effects without server round-trips.

Many tasks currently implemented with expensive, latency-prone, and privacy-invasive cloud APIs could be elegantly, efficiently, and privately shifted to the client.

The argument isn't against the cloud entirely. Cloud still excels for massive datasets, complex training, long-running batch jobs, and services that genuinely require centralized infrastructure. The critique is against the default impulse to use it for everything, especially when superior client-side alternatives exist.

As Staff Software Engineers, it's our responsibility to challenge architectural defaults and advocate for solutions that prioritize performance, cost-efficiency, and, increasingly, user privacy and data sovereignty.

👉 Live Tool: https://solvemymedia.com/transcribe

So, I turn it over to the community: What tools or features in your current stack could you realistically move 100% to the client right now using modern web APIs? And what, specifically, is stopping you from doing so? Let's discuss the practical hurdles and the paradigm shifts required.

title: geo-algos: خوارزميات جغرافية مكانية كلاسيكية من الصفر بلغة Rust
description:
أغلب ميزات الخرائط تقوم على عدد قليل من الخوارزميات القديمة. هل هذه النقطة داخل تلك المنطقة؟ كم تبعد هاتان المدينتان؟ هل يمكن رسم مسار GPS هذا بنقاط أقل؟ ما هي أقرب عشرة أماكن إليّ؟ المكتبات تجيب عن كل ذلك باستدعاء واحد، وهذه هي الطريقة الصحيحة في العمل الحقيقي. لكنها تعني أيضًا أنك قد تستعملها سنوات دون أن تعرف كيف تقرر.

geo-algos مشروعي التعليمي للنظر إلى الداخل. ينفّذ خوارزميات جغرافية مكانية (geospatial) كلاسيكية من الصفر بلغة Rust، دون أي اعتماديات وقت التشغيل (runtime dependencies). وكل واحدة تُفحص أمام مرجع مستقل أو مرجع بالقوة الغاشمة (brute force) باستعمال property tests. الـ README يقولها بوضوح وسأقولها أنا أيضًا: للعمل الحقيقي استعمل الـ crates المسماة geo و rstar. هذا المشروع للتعلّم.

ماذا يقدّم

فيه أربع وحدات (modules):

الوحدة ماذا تفعل
pip نقطة داخل مضلع مع ثقوب: ray casting (قاعدة even-odd) و winding number (قاعدة non-zero)، مع نتيجة صريحة Boundary
distance Haversine (كرة) و Vincenty inverse (المجسم الإهليلجي WGS84) مع الاتجاهات وخطأ عدم التقارب
simplify تبسيط الخطوط بـ Douglas-Peucker، بشكل تكراري دون حد لعمق الاستدعاء
rtree R-tree: إدراج Guttman مع تقسيم خطي أو تربيعي، وتحميل بالجملة STR، واستعلام المجال، و kNN بطريقة best-first

ما بنيته من الصفر، وما يعلّمه

نقطة داخل مضلع: قاعدتان، والحالات الطرفية. طريقة ray casting تعدّ كم ضلعًا يقطعه شعاع أفقي ينطلق من النقطة: العدد الفردي يعني أنها في الداخل. والفخ هو شعاع يمر تمامًا برأس من رؤوس المضلع. والحل قاعدة نصف مفتوحة (half-open)، فيُحسب ذلك الرأس مرة واحدة. أما winding number (نسخة Sunday) فتستعمل اختبارات الاتجاه فقط. الطريقتان تتفقان في الحلقات البسيطة وتختلفان في التي تقطع نفسها: مركز النجمة الخماسية (pentagram) خارج المضلع حسب even-odd وداخله حسب non-zero، ويوجد اختبار لذلك. والدالة Polygon::locate تفحص الحلقات أولًا، فالنقطة الواقعة تمامًا على ضلع ترجع Boundary بدل جواب اعتباطي.

المسافات: كرة أم مجسم إهليلجي. Haversine تعامل الأرض ككرة نصف قطرها المتوسط 6,371,008.8 متر. هي بسيطة، وخطؤها يصل إلى حوالي 0.5% مقارنة بالمجسم الإهليلجي. أما صيغة Vincenty العكسية فتعمل على المجسم WGS84 وتكرّر الحساب على فرق خط الطول. تعطي دقة أقل من الميليمتر، وهي مفحوصة أمام الخط الذي استعمله Vincenty نفسه بين Flinders Peak و Buninyong (54,972.271 متر). ولها ضعف معروف: النقاط شبه المتقابلة على طرفي الأرض (antipodal) قد لا يتقارب حسابها. وهنا تُرجَع هذه الحالة كـ VincentyError::NoConvergence بدل رقم خاطئ.

Douglas-Peucker: ضمان يمكن اختباره. الخوارزمية تحتفظ بنقطتَي الطرفين، وتجد أبعد نقطة عن الوتر الواصل بينهما، وتكرّر ما دامت تلك النقطة أبعد من epsilon. النسخة المعروفة في الكتب تعاودية (recursive)؛ وهذه تستعمل stack صريحًا، فلا يستطيع خط طويل جدًا تجاوز حد الـ call stack. والـ property test يتحقق من الضمان نفسه: كل نقطة محذوفة تبعد أقل من epsilon عن القطعة التي عوّضتها.

الـ R-tree: فهرس مكاني. العُقد مخزّنة في arena (أي Vec) ويُشار إليها بالفهرس، وهذا يجنّب الصراع مع الـ borrow checker حول مؤشرات الأب والابن. الدالة insert تتبع ورقة Guttman: ChooseLeaf بأقل توسيع، ثم تقسيم عند الامتلاء (PickSeeds/PickNext التربيعي، أو البذور الخطية)، ثم تعديل المستطيلات المحيطة صعودًا إلى الجذر. و bulk_load هي Sort-Tile-Recursive (STR)، وتملأ العُقد كاملة حين تملك كل البيانات مسبقًا. و nearest بحث best-first بـ min-heap مفتاحه MINDIST، فتخرج المدخلات بترتيب المسافة الدقيق. و validate() تتحقق من الثوابت: تساوي عمق الأوراق، وحدود عدد الأبناء، وإحكام المستطيلات المحيطة.

طريقة الاستعمال

أضِفه إلى مشروع Rust من GitHub:

cargo add --git https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/geo-algos

أو انسخ المستودع وشغّل ما فيه:

cargo test                      # unit tests + proptest checks
cargo run --example demo        # small tour of every module
cargo bench                     # criterion benchmarks

ومثال قصير من الـ README يُظهر ثلاثًا من الوحدات:

use geo_algos::{haversine, LonLat, Point, Polygon, RTree, Entry, Rect};

let d = haversine(LonLat::new(3.0588, 36.7538), LonLat::new(-0.6417, 35.6971)); // ~352 km

let sq = |a: f64, b: f64| vec![Point::new(a, a), Point::new(b, a), Point::new(b, b), Point::new(a, b)];
let donut = Polygon::new(sq(0.0, 10.0), vec![sq(4.0, 6.0)]);
assert!(donut.contains(Point::new(1.0, 1.0)));
assert!(!donut.contains(Point::new(5.0, 5.0))); // in the hole

let tree = RTree::bulk_load(vec![Entry::point(Point::new(1.0, 2.0), "a")], 16);
let near = tree.nearest(Point::new(0.0, 0.0), 1);

السطر الأول يقيس المسافة بين زوجين من خط الطول وخط العرض، حوالي 352 كم. والمضلع مربع فيه ثقب مربع، فالنقطة الواقعة في الثقب ليست داخله. والسطران الأخيران يبنيان R-tree بسعة 16 لكل عقدة ويطلبان أقرب مدخل إلى نقطة الأصل.

كيف اختُبر

في الاختبارات يتحقق وعد "مفحوص أمام مرجع". يوجد 39 اختبار وحدة (unit test) بجانب الكود: حالات طرفية، وحدود، وثقوب، ونجمة خماسية، ومدخلات شاذة، ومسافات معروفة.

ثم توجد 8 خصائص proptest في tests/properties.rs. الـ property tests تولّد مدخلات عشوائية وتتحقق أن قاعدة ما تصح دائمًا:

  • نقطة داخل مضلع أمام مرجع تحليلي لمضلع نجمي، مع مقارنة ray casting بـ winding number؛
  • الثقوب أمام صيغة مغلقة؛
  • بديهيات المسافة (metric axioms) لـ Haversine؛
  • Vincenty ضمن 0.6% من Haversine؛
  • ضمان التسامح في Douglas-Peucker؛
  • نتائج استعلام المجال و kNN في الـ R-tree أمام القوة الغاشمة، للأشجار المبنية بالإدراج (بنوعَي التقسيم) ولأشجار STR.

والأخيرة هي النمط الذي أحبه أكثر. المسح الخطي لكل النقاط بطيء وصحته واضحة، فهو الحَكَم المثالي لفهرس سريع ومن السهل أن يخطئ خطأً خفيًا.

وفي الـ README جدول قياسات أداء مع تنبيه صريح: قيس بـ cargo bench -- --quick على حاسوب محمول كان مشغولًا بعمليات بناء أخرى، فالأرقام تدل على مراتب المقدار فقط. ومع هذا التنبيه: Haversine حوالي 0.23 ميكروثانية و Vincenty حوالي 2 ميكروثانية لكل استدعاء، وتحميل 50 ألف نقطة بالجملة بطريقة STR يأخذ حوالي 52 ميلي ثانية، وإدراج نفس النقاط واحدة واحدة يأخذ بين 0.3 و 0.5 ثانية تقريبًا.

أشياء يجب معرفتها

الـ README يذكر الحدود، وهي مهمة إن فكرت في استعماله خارج التعلّم:

  • هذا مشروع تعليمي. للعمل الحقيقي استعمل geo و rstar.
  • كل شيء بأعداد f64 عادية دون robust predicates. كشف الحدود دقيق فقط حين يكون الحساب دقيقًا: الرؤوس والأضلاع الموازية للمحاور تعمل، لكن نقطة محسوبة على ضلع مائل قد تقع داخله أو خارجه بفارق ضئيل جدًا.
  • الخوارزميات المستوية تعامل درجات خط الطول والعرض كإحداثيات x/y مسطحة. لا شيء يتعامل مع خط الطول 180 (antimeridian)، وقيمة epsilon في Douglas-Peucker بوحدات المدخل.
  • الـ R-tree دون حذف ودون إعادة الإدراج الخاصة بـ R*-tree. ومسافة kNN تُقاس إلى المستطيل المحيط بكل مدخل.
  • صحة الثقوب (أن تكون داخل المضلع الخارجي وغير متداخلة) مفترضة ولا تُفحص.

ما تعلّمته

الدرس الأول أن كود الهندسة يدور أساسًا حول الحالات التي لا يُظهرها الرسم: الشعاع المار برأس، والنقطة على ضلع، والنقطتان على طرفَي الكوكب. الفكرة الرئيسية لكل خوارزمية تتسع في فقرة. وبقية الكود موجودة لتلك الحالات.

الثاني أن المرجع البطيء أداة ممتازة. كل وحدة هنا تقريبًا تُختبر بمقارنتها بشيء أبسط: القوة الغاشمة للـ R-tree، وصيغة مغلقة للثقوب، و Haversine كحدّ معقول لـ Vincenty. وحين يختلف الاثنان في مدخل عشوائي، يقلّصه proptest إلى مثال صغير، ويظهر الخطأ غالبًا من أول نظرة.

الثالث خاص بـ Rust. الشجرة ذات روابط الأب والابن مزعجة مع الـ references ومريحة في arena مع الفهارس.

وإرجاع Boundary أو NoConvergence كنتائج صريحة علّمني شيئًا عامًا: حين يكون للخوارزمية مدخل لا تستطيع الإجابة عنه جيدًا، فصرّح بذلك في النوع (type) بدل إرجاع تخمين.

احصل على الكود

المصدر والمثال والاختبارات وقياسات الأداء على GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/geo-algos. المشروع برخصة MIT، ولا يستعمل أي بيانات خارجية.
