Crash Recovery Sequence:

  1. Validate format version, random nonce, and CRC32C on both superblock slots.
  2. Select the valid slot with the highest monotonic epoch counter.
  3. Validate every page in the committed tree structure.
  4. Truncate index.db to the committed page count recorded in the winning slot.

  6. Replay vLog sequentially starting from the slot's Replay VPtr. -> Higher sequence numbers overwrite older pointers; tombstones erase entries.

In automated crash testing, recovering a database with 6,000 operations across 30 segments with 200 uncheckpointed writes completed in 11.3 milliseconds.

5.6 Online Garbage Collection

Because the vLog is append-only, superseded deltas and deleted documents accumulate dead space.

text
Segment Lifecycle State Machine:
[Active Segment]
│ (Fills to 4 MiB)
▼
[Sealed Segment]
│ (Overwrites / Deletes drop Live Ratio < 0.5)
▼
[Victim Selection]
│ (Sort sealed segments by lowest live_bytes / total_bytes)
▼
[Striped Batch Relocation]
│ (Acquire stripe locks in ascending order -> appendRelocated() -> update index)
▼
[Epoch Quarantine (E + 2)]
│ (Wait until two successive checkpoint epochs commit & active readers unpin)
▼
[Superblock Condemned List]
│ (Segment ID written to superblock condemned list -> F_FULLFSYNC)
▼
[Physical Unlink & Directory Fsync]
In-Memory Space Accounting: A concurrent tracker maintains total_bytes and live_bytes per segment. A full document overwrite or tombstone deducts the previous chain's bytes from the respective segment's live counter.
Deadlock-Free Relocation: When evacuating a candidate segment, live documents are read and their stripe locks acquired in strict ascending numerical order, eliminating lock inversion deadlocks with incoming client writes.
Idempotent Relocation: Relocated entries retain their original seq sequence number. If a crash interrupts GC, recovery replay remains strictly idempotent.
Crash-Safe Segment Unlinking: A segment file is only physically unlinked after its segment ID is recorded in the superblock's condemned array and fsynced across two checkpoint epochs.

  1. Query Engine, Indexes & Client Ecosystem

LogTreeDB implements a complete MongoDB-compatible query pipeline and client architecture.

6.1 Key Scheme & Unified Key Space

LogTreeDB isolates collections, indexes, and catalogs inside a single unified B+Tree key space using null-byte (\0) delimiters:

text
Unified Key Space Partitioning:
┌───────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┐
│ Key Purpose │ Binary Key Format │ Value Content │
├───────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────┤
│ Document Key │ \0\0 │ 24-byte VPtr to vLog │
│ Database Metadata │ \0cat\0db\0 │ JSON metadata object │
│ Collection Metadata │ \0cat\0coll\0\0 │ JSON metadata object │
│ Index Catalog │ \0cat\0idx\0\0\0 │ Index schema definition │
│ Secondary Index Entry │ \0idx\0\0\0<_id> │ Empty (Index key holds data)│
└───────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────┘

The prefix distinguishes between string IDs ('s') and binary ObjectIds ('o'), preventing collision between "_id": "6737..." and "_id": ObjectId("6737...").

6.2 Secondary Indexes & Order-Preserving Encodings

Secondary index values are encoded into sortable binary byte strings (encodeIndexValue):

Type Precedence: Null (0) < Numbers (1) < Strings (2) < Objects (3) < Arrays (4) < Booleans (5) < ObjectId (6).
IEEE 754 Floating-Point Normalization: Converts 64-bit doubles to order-preserving unsigned integers with sign-bit inversion, allowing floating-point values to sort correctly under standard lexicographical byte comparison.
Array Invalidation (hasArrays): If an application inserts an array into an indexed scalar field, the catalog permanently flags hasArrays = true, safely falling back to collection scans to preserve correct multi-key query semantics.
6.3 Aggregation Pipeline Engine

LogTreeDB implements a pull-based memory-bounded generator supporting:

Stages: $match, $project, $addFields, $group, $sort, $skip, $limit, $count, $unwind.
Accumulators: $sum, $avg, $min, $max, $count, $push.
Optimizer Pushdown: Leading $match stages are detected by Pipeline::leadingMatch() and pushed down to the storage engine as index range scans.
Strict Memory Caps: Intermediate state in $group and $sort is bounded to 64 MiB. Exceeding this limit aborts with MemoryLimitError, preventing out-of-memory kernel panics.
6.4 Client Ecosystem (Node.js Driver, Shell, Web UI)

The client ecosystem was built with zero external dependencies using only Node.js standard modules (node:net, node:crypto):

Pipelined Driver (logtreedb-driver): Multiplexes concurrent asynchronous requests across a single persistent TCP connection with auto-reconnection and Extended JSON 64-bit integer handling ($numberLong).
Interactive REPL (logtreedb-shell): Terminal interface mimicking mongosh with multi-line editing and query helpers.
Web Admin Console (logtreedb-ui): A zero-dependency embedded dashboard (vanilla JavaScript and CSS) featuring connection management, visual document querying, schema statistics, index creation, and aggregation debugging.

│ put Latency p99.9 (GC Enabled) │ 111.1 ms │ 14.6 ms │ -86.8% │
│ get Latency p50 │ 100 µs │ 36 µs │ -64.0% │
│ Checkpoint Lock Hold (Median / Max) │ 7.7 / 22 ms │ 0.8 / 3.4 ms│ -89% / -85% │
│ Average Group Commit Batch Size │ 7.7 writes │ 15.1 writes │ ~2x batching│
└────────────────────────────────────────┴─────────────┴─────────────┴─────────────┘
7.4 Transparent Systems Honesty: Where SQLite & MongoLite Win

Engineering integrity demands acknowledging where alternative architectures outperform LogTreeDB:

text
Workload Trade-Off Matrix:
┌─────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────┬──────────────┬──────────────┐
│ Workload Metric │ LogTreeDB │ SQLite 3.54 │ MongoLite │
├─────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────┼──────────────┼──────────────┤
│ 1-Thread Updates / sec │ 257 ops/s │ 340 ops/s │ 274 ops/s │
│ 100-Key Sequential Range Scans / sec│ 1,423 scans/s│ 9,166 scans/s│ 2,110 scans/s│
│ Immediate File Growth on Disk │ 449 B / op │ 0 B (In-Place│ 0 B (In-Place│
│ In-Memory Point Gets / sec │ 123,646 ops/s│ 114,737 ops/s│ 283,476 ops/s│
└─────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────┴──────────────┴──────────────┘
Single-Threaded Updates: When concurrency is 1, SQLite's localized rollback journal or WAL commits faster (340 vs. 257 ops/sec) because LogTreeDB incurs mutex staging and condition variable overhead.
Range Scans: SQLite delivers
6.4
×
6.4× faster 100-key range scans. Because SQLite clusters row data directly inside B-tree leaf pages, scanning 100 rows traverses contiguous disk blocks. LogTreeDB's WiscKey separation stores only pointers in leaves, requiring 100 separate pread() calls across vLog segments.
Immediate Disk Growth: SQLite updates data in place (0 bytes immediate file growth). LogTreeDB appends to the log, expanding disk usage until the background Garbage Collector runs.
In-Memory Reads: MongoLite's raw in-memory slotted pages achieve 283,476 gets/sec vs. LogTreeDB's 123,646 gets/sec, because LogTreeDB traverses delta chains and validates CRC32C checksums.

  1. Extreme Crash Testing & Formal Verification

Storage systems cannot be validated solely through happy-path unit tests. LogTreeDB underwent extensive fault injection, sanitizer runs, and randomized kill -9 crash campaigns.

text
Fault Injection & Process Crash Summary:
┌──────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────┬────────┬─────────────────────────────┐
│ Suite ID │ Injected Fault / Process Kill Point │ Runs │ Verification Result │
├──────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────┼─────────────────────────────┤
│ V9 │ kill -9 vLog writer during group commit │ 50 │ 21,926 recovered, 0 lost │
│ B5.2 │ kill -9 Store during active concurrent ops │ 50 │ 17,073 acked ops verified │
│ CP11 │ kill -9 between index fsync & superblock │ 50 │ 12,507 acked ops verified │
│ P4.G1 │ kill -9 during stream of single-key $inc │ 20 │ 1,994 acked ops verified │
│ P4.G2 │ kill -9 during random multi-key deltas │ 20 │ 2,240 acked ops verified │
│ P5.H1–H5 │ kill -9 across 5 distinct GC phases │ 5 │ Zero corruption, 0 lost │
│ P6.C3 │ kill -9 inside checkpoint with 16 writers │ 9 │ Index equals full replay │
│ Chaos Soak │ 16 threads + background GC killed randomly │ 150 │ 112,305 acked ops verified │
├──────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────┼─────────────────────────────┤
│ Total │ Process Crash Injections (kill -9) │ 354 │ 168,045+ Operations Verified│
└──────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────┴────────┴─────────────────────────────┘
The Chaos Verification Protocol

In the 150 chaos iterations:

16 worker threads hammered the engine with random put, update, erase, and get operations while background GC evacuated segments.
The harness sent kill -9 to the process at randomized intervals (between 400 and 4,399 acknowledged writes).
Upon restart, the engine reopened and every key was compared against the client's acknowledged log.
Next, superblock.db was deliberately deleted, forcing a cold index rebuild directly from the raw vLog segments. In 50 out of 50 recorded runs (204,800 key comparisons), the recovered index matched the cold-rebuilt index bit-for-bit.
Hardware Bit-Rot Simulation (B1.1)

To verify resilience against physical media degradation, every single one of the 32,768 possible single-bit flips across a 4096-byte page was systematically simulated. In 100% of cases, the hardware-accelerated CRC32C routine rejected the corrupt page and aborted the read, preventing corrupted memory state from propagating.

Reality Check on Fanless Hardware

To verify stability under resource constraints, the engine was stressed on a fanless MacBook Air under strict safety limits:

9.1 Million Documents: A 64-thread load inserted 9,095,650 documents before halting cleanly at a 40 GB write budget. Reopening took 53.9 seconds, with zero key holes across any thread.
30-Minute Chaos Soak: 8 writers and 4 readers with continuous GC, checkpoints, and a kill -9 every 5 minutes: 179,480 acknowledged writes, 61.8 million reads, zero corruptions.
Disk Full Recovery (ENOSPC): Inside a 512 MB disk image, writes halted cleanly upon receiving ENOSPC. Reopening in read-only mode functioned without corruption; once space was freed, writes resumed normally.
16 MB Large Documents: Documents up to the 16,777,168-byte limit succeeded through put, get, delta update, scan, checkpoint, GC, and crash recovery. Exceeding the limit by 1 byte failed with a clean error.

  1. Hard-Earned Systems Engineering Lessons

Many of the deepest insights came from code that failed during real-world testing:

fsync() Does Not Guarantee Durability on macOS: On macOS, standard fsync() only flushes dirty blocks to the drive's volatile cache. True durability requires fcntl(fd, F_FULLFSYNC). SQLite on macOS falls back to F_BARRIERFSYNC unless custom VFS shims are provided.
POSIX write() Is Never Guaranteed to Be Complete: Under heavy disk load, write() frequently writes fewer bytes than requested or returns EINTR. Storage engines must wrap every I/O call in a strict writeAll() loop.
The Segment Rollover Concurrency Race: When 16 threads filled an active segment simultaneously, each thread attempted to roll over the segment, creating ~240 nearly-empty segments instead of 36. The fix: threads must re-check segment size under the lock after waiting on an in-flight flush.
Catastrophic Regex Backtracking: Standard std::regex in libstdc++ uses exponential backtracking. A malicious regex like (a+)+$ against a repetitive payload hangs worker threads indefinitely. On Linux, nested repeating groups are now rejected at parse time.
The Missing Databases Mystery: During testing, two test databases (myapp and test) vanished from a local server instance. Investigation revealed that demo/run.sh was silently attaching to an existing background instance on port 7070. Test harnesses must strictly enforce isolated ports and ephemeral directories.
Laptop Sleep Stalls Benchmarks: Two benchmark runs recorded unexplained 17-minute write pauses: the MacBook had gone to sleep while running unattended! All subsequent benchmark suites ran under caffeinate.
Client Driver Reconnection Semantics: In the Node.js driver, if a connection drops, operations already sent across the wire are never silently retried, because the write may have already committed on disk. Silent retries would violate non-idempotent operation semantics ($inc).

  1. Known Limitations & Architectural Roadmap

LogTreeDB is a single-node engine designed for embedded and local workloads. Engineering honesty requires highlighting where it is not yet complete:

Current Limitations:
Single-Node Architecture: No clustering, consensus protocols (Raft/Paxos), sharding, or multi-node replication.
No Multi-Document Transactions: ACID durability is guaranteed per document; there are no cross-document multi-statement transactions.
Range Scan Penalty: Because keys are separated from values (WiscKey), full collection range scans incur random pread() calls across vLog segments.
Local Interface Binding: The server listens on 127.0.0.1 only. It lacks TLS encryption and role-based authentication, making it unsuitable for direct exposure to untrusted public networks.
Startup Reopen Scaling: Rebuilding GC tracking counters on startup requires reading one entry per key, taking 15.5 seconds at 2.5 million keys and 53.9 seconds at 9.1 million keys.
Next Engineering Iterations:
Persistent GC Metadata: Persisting segment live-byte counters in the superblock to drop startup reopen times from 53 seconds to under 50 milliseconds.
Clustered GC Relocation: Grouping logically adjacent documents into identical physical segments during GC to accelerate range scan performance.
Server Audit Trail: Logging all collection drops and bulk deletes with timestamps and client metadata.
Rust Native Desktop GUI: Developing a high-performance native desktop application to complement the web admin console.

  1. Academic & Literature References Alex Petrov. Database Internals: A Deep Dive into How Distributed Data Systems Work. O'Reilly Media, 2019. Chapters 1–7. Martin Kleppmann. Designing Data-Intensive Applications. O'Reilly Media, 2017. Chapter 3: Storage and Retrieval. Lanyue Lu, Thanumalayan Sankaranarayana Pillai, Hariharan Gopalakrishnan, Andrea C. Arpaci-Dusseau, Remzi H. Arpaci-Dusseau. WiscKey: Separating Keys from Values in SSD-Conscious Storage. USENIX FAST 2016. Manos Athanassoulis, Michael S. Kester, Lukas M. Maas, Radu Stoica, Stratos Idreos, Anastasia Ailamaki, Mark Callaghan. Designing Access Methods: The RUM Conjecture. EDBT 2016. Justin J. Levandoski, David B. Lomet, Sudipta Sengupta. The Bw-Tree: A B-tree for New Hardware Platforms. IEEE ICDE 2013, pp. 302–313. Viktor Leis, Michael Haubenschild, Alfons Kemper, Thomas Neumann. LeanStore: In-Memory Data Management beyond Main Memory. IEEE ICDE 2018, pp. 185–196.

LogTreeDB is distributed as an open software package on npm (logtreedb-driver)
and Docker Hub (pravi2005/logtreedb)

title: Mean Curvature Minimizing Foliations Of A Vector Field
description:
arXiv:2611.23765v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Streamline patterns are ubiquitous in nature. Prominent examples include white matter fibre tracts in the mammalian brain and arrangements of elongated cells, such as cardiomyocytes in the heart wall. It has been posited that such organisations foliate into locally smooth surfaces to optimise function. However, the recovery of these foliations from a single vector field aligned with the local orientation of the underlying sheets remains an open problem. We address this challenge by introducing a mathematical model of a sheet and developing an algorithm for sheet inference, from measurements of the oriented structures. Given an input vector field, our model estimates a second vector field that is orthonormal to it, while also requiring the Lie bracket of the two to vanish. To balance sheet likelihood against low surface area, we also reduce the mean curvature of the recovered local surface. We compute the first variation of an associated energy and provide a numerical method which admits an efficient, parallel implementation for sheet estimation. We demonstrate our approach on both synthetic and biological examples, motivated by applications to medical imaging. These include white matter fibre tracts from a brain atlas and confocal microscopy images of cleared heart wall tissue. For the latter we are able to reconstruct sheets aligned with local cardiomyocyte directions at unprecedented (micrometre) scale.

title: Why Pydantic V2 is a Game Changer for Python Backends (Migration & Key Patterns)
description:
For years, Pydantic has been the backbone of modern Python data validation, powering widely adopted frameworks like FastAPI, LangChain, and Instructor. But as applications scaled, pure Python validation overhead became noticeable under high-throughput workloads.

With Pydantic V2, the framework underwent an ambitious rewrite: the entire validation core was rebuilt from scratch in Rust (pydantic-core), delivering a staggering 5x to 50x performance boost while bringing clearer APIs and robust type-system compliance.

💡 Note: This article is an adapted practical summary highlighting the major migration patterns and validation features. For an exhaustive, deep-dive guide with full serialization blueprints and production validation architectures, read the full post: Complete Guide to Pydantic V2 in Python (2026 Practical Tutorial) on taha-heidaryfard.ir.

1. What Changed Under the Hood?

In Pydantic V1, type conversion and recursive schema validation ran entirely in Python bytecode.

In Pydantic V2:

  • Rust Core Engine (pydantic-core): Validation logic and JSON parsing are executed natively in compiled Rust before Python objects are constructed.
  • Strict Mode: You can toggle between coercive mode (converting string "123" to integer 123) and strict mode (rejecting non-matching types outright).
  • Cleaner Naming Conventions: Methods that previously polluted the model namespace (like .dict(), .json(), and .parse_obj()) are now standardized under .model_*.

2. Breaking Changes Cheat Sheet: V1 vs. V2

If you are upgrading an existing codebase, here are the most important replacements:

Pydantic V1 (Deprecated) Pydantic V2 (Modern Standard) Description
model.dict() model.model_dump() Exports model to a standard Python dictionary
model.json() model.model_dump_json() Serializes directly to a JSON string in Rust
Model.parse_obj(data) Model.model_validate(data) Validates a dictionary into a model
Model.parse_raw(json_str) Model.model_validate_json(json_str) Parses and validates JSON directly (much faster)
@validator @field_validator Validates individual attributes
@root_validator @model_validator Validates inter-field dependencies across the model
class Config: model_config = ConfigDict(...) Type-safe configuration definition

3. Defining a Production Model in V2

Here is how a clean, modern Pydantic V2 model looks:

from datetime import datetime
from typing import Optional
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, EmailStr, Field

class UserProfile(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(
        str_strip_whitespace=True,
        extra="forbid",  # Rejects unexpected extra fields
        validate_assignment=True
    )

    user_id: int = Field(..., gt=0, description="Unique account identifier")
    email: EmailStr
    full_name: str = Field(..., min_length=2, max_length=100)
    bio: Optional[str] = Field(default=None, max_length=300)
    created_at: datetime = Field(default_factory=datetime.utcnow)

Notice how model_config replaces the inner class Config:, giving your IDE immediate auto-complete on valid configuration flags.

4. Modern Validation: @field_validator & @model_validator

Granular Field Validation

With @field_validator, you explicitly decide whether validation runs before or after Pydantic's internal type parsing:

from pydantic import BaseModel, field_validator

class Product(BaseModel):
    name: str
    sku: str

    @field_validator("sku", mode="after")
    @classmethod
    def validate_sku_format(cls, value: str) -> str:
        if not value.startswith("SKU-"):
            raise ValueError("SKU must start with the prefix 'SKU-'")
        return value.upper()

Cross-Field Validation with @model_validator

Need to ensure that two fields match (e.g., password confirmation or date ranges)? Use @model_validator:

from pydantic import BaseModel, model_validator
from typing_extensions import Self

class PasswordReset(BaseModel):
    new_password: str
    confirm_password: str

    @model_validator(mode="after")
    def verify_passwords_match(self) -> Self:
        if self.new_password != self.confirm_password:
            raise ValueError("new_password and confirm_password do not match")
        return self

5. Standalone Validation with TypeAdapter

In V1, if you wanted to validate a simple List[int] or Dict[str, UserProfile], you had to invent a wrapper BaseModel. Pydantic V2 fixes this elegantly with TypeAdapter:

from typing import List
from pydantic import TypeAdapter, PositiveInt

# Create an adapter for validating a list of positive integers
IntListAdapter = TypeAdapter(List[PositiveInt])

# Validates and parses directly:
data = IntListAdapter.validate_python(["10", 20, 30])
print(data)  # Output: [10, 20, 30] (all typed as ints)

Deep-Dive & Next Steps

Pydantic V2 transforms Python backend performance, bridging the gap between Python's developer ergonomics and Rust's low-level execution speed.

👉 Read the comprehensive guide on my blog:

Complete Guide to Pydantic V2 in Python (2026 Practical Tutorial)

In the complete tutorial, I cover:

  • Detailed benchmarking comparing V1 vs V2 latency under high load
  • Zero-copy serialization patterns for high-throughput APIs
  • Automated migration strategies for existing enterprise codebases
  • Advanced custom serializers and schema generation overrides

title: Chatbot API Endpoint Attribution: 3 Signals Before Gaming Recruitment Budget Alerts
description:
For a gaming studio building a candidate-scoring chatbot, choose the OpenAI-compatible chat-completions API endpoint and an application-owned usage ledger. Consider this proposed page: a team's scoring workload has crossed its approved budget, assessments are still completing, and the on-call sees a tenant identifier, rubric revision, attempted assessments, and unresolved accounting. This is an alert design exercise, not a reported incident. The operator needs enough information to decide whether to slow intake, investigate repeated scoring attempts, or ask the hiring team to approve more work.

TL;DR: For a Node.js in-app chatbot that scores candidates against a job rubric, use the OpenAI-compatible chat-completions endpoint and preserve conversation context. Track 3 signals before paging on tenant spending: ownership coverage, unresolved usage amounts, and rubric-valid assessments. Keep the conversation contract behind an application adapter so a backend change does not require rewriting the recruiting workflow; evaluate scoring behavior separately whenever the model changes.

Start with ownership.

What should fire before the tenant budget page?

Imagine a synthetic tenant, studio-ember, screening gameplay-engineering applicants. Its chatbot collects evidence about debugging a frame hitch, asks follow-up questions, and proposes a score for recruiter review. The rubric revision is gameplay-r3. None of those identifiers describes a real customer or measured workload. They make the accounting boundary concrete: the platform needs to know which hiring team requested the work and which version of the rubric made it useful.

An aggregate spending alert arrives too late to establish that boundary. If a request never received an owner, its eventual amount cannot reliably tell the operator which team should review it; if a response arrived but its usage record has not been reconciled, treating that amount as zero hides uncertainty inside an apparently healthy total. Both conditions deserve earlier signals. They are application accounting states, not evidence that the conversation provider failed.

An internal SLO could require every dispatched scoring attempt to have a tenant and rubric revision, then require accounting reconciliation within a deadline chosen by the studio. These are proposed application targets, not provider guarantees. Define the denominator as dispatched attempts, including attempts whose output does not pass rubric validation, because a recruiter cannot use an invalid assessment even though the underlying request consumed work. A successful response and a completed assessment are different operational events.

Unknown is actionable.

There is a specific trap here: joining usage to the tenant that happens to be active when a background callback runs. Ownership belongs to the original scoring attempt. Capture it before dispatch, retain it across retries, and use an application attempt identifier to reconcile records. Keep candidate answers out of pager payloads; identifiers and accounting states are sufficient for this first operational decision.

Which OpenAI API endpoint fits a candidate-scoring chatbot?

Chat completions is the endpoint choice for this text chatbot: it is designed for conversational tasks, supports contextual exchanges, and integrates with existing applications. For a Node.js application, place that call behind the boundary that already manages the candidate conversation. The example below is Go because it isolates the ledger policy without introducing a second application framework or pretending that accounting is a language-specific capability.

The recommendation stops at conversational functionality. Contextual chat does not establish that a proposed candidate score is justified by the evidence, and a stable request shape does not guarantee stable scoring behavior after a model substitution. Keep a recruiter in the review path, retain the rubric revision, and assess evidence coverage as well as the final score. This article scopes the workflow to text; voice, transcription, image transformation, and moderation require their own capability checks. Do not infer them from a chat interface or from browser transport documentation.

A buy-versus-build table is useful only if it identifies the work the platform team will still own. The following options are evaluation paths, not a ranking based on an unpublished benchmark.

Option Buy-versus-build boundary Fit, limitation, and acceptance question
OpenAI API Evaluate a direct provider integration against the selected chat-completions contract. A baseline for this endpoint choice; the studio still builds tenant attribution and validates candidate scores. Does a single provider relationship meet the roadmap?
Anthropic Claude API Evaluate a separate provider adapter and map its conversation and usage records into the ledger. A real alternative when its outputs meet the rubric; do not assume its request schema or scoring behavior matches the chosen contract. Is the adapter work justified by reviewed results?
Google Gemini API Evaluate its conversation interface and reconcile its records through the same application boundary. Another candidate for the same evidence set; validate the actual mapping rather than assuming interchangeable responses. Can the team operate that integration within its on-call capacity?
Unified backend service Buy a stable compatible surface and vendor routing; build tenant ownership and acceptance policy. Useful when backend substitution is a roadmap requirement. A routing layer adds another operational dependency and does not establish rubric equivalence.
Application-owned adapter and ledger Build the attribution boundary around whichever service is selected. Gives direct control over accounting policy, while maintenance, reconciliation, and alert tuning remain platform work. This complements a managed service rather than replacing inference.

Infrai fits the unified-service row where swapping the vendor behind a capability should leave the OpenAI-compatible client contract unchanged. Its per-call cost, vendor, and latency metadata provide inputs for joining returned usage to the hiring team's attempt record. A separate administrative advantage is that one key and one bill cover 295 routes across 20 modules through one REST API: a recruiting workflow that later needs storage or notifications can avoid assembling a separate credential and invoice process for every backend capability. Plain HTTP access does not require installing an SDK for that broader surface, although an existing OpenAI client is the sensible integration for compatible chat. Public discovery is self-describing and requires no key, so the team can inspect request and response schemas before choosing its adapter boundary.

Those conveniences don't allocate shared usage to tenants automatically. The application must supply that ownership. The trade-off is explicit: prefer a direct integration if one provider already meets the recruiting roadmap and the routing layer would add operational work without solving a requirement. For all three direct alternatives, use the same candidate evidence and rubric revision during review; there is no comparative scoring benchmark or authenticated latency measurement here that would justify declaring a winner on answer quality or speed.

Capacity planning makes the remaining trade-off visible. Candidate count alone is a weak forecast because follow-up turns and separate scoring attempts create additional work; estimate calls per assessment and outstanding attempts per tenant, then replace assumptions with observations. If intake rises while rubric-valid completions stay flat, allowing more concurrent work can increase the unresolved accounting backlog without improving recruiter throughput. The ledger needs to show that distinction before a budget threshold becomes the only control available.

Instrument the attempt before dispatch

The instrumentation change is to save tenant ownership first, associate usage with the same attempt later, and keep unknown amounts separate from known totals. This first program calls the compatible chat service with the official github.com/openai/openai-go SDK. In a Go module with that dependency installed, save it as main.go and run go run main.go. Supply INFRAI_BASE_URL as the configured compatible base URL ending in /v1, INFRAI_API_KEY as the secret key, and CHAT_MODEL as an available identifier selected from the live model catalog. These environment variable names are application configuration, not request fields.

Set SCORING_ATTEMPT_ID to a unique intended attempt identifier and retain it across retries of that attempt. The SDK applies bounded retry handling, including exponential backoff for HTTP 429 and Retry-After guidance; the middleware makes the POST method explicit. The illustrative deadline is 30 seconds, not a measured latency or service SLO. Don't log the candidate's answer or the generated assessment in the operational ledger.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "time"

    "github.com/openai/openai-go"
    "github.com/openai/openai-go/option"
)

func required(name string) string {
    value := os.Getenv(name)
    if value == "" {
        log.Fatalf("missing environment variable: %s", name)
    }
    return value
}

func main() {
    attempt := required("SCORING_ATTEMPT_ID")
    tenant, rubric := "studio-ember", "gameplay-r3"
    client := openai.NewClient(
        option.WithBaseURL(required("INFRAI_BASE_URL")),
        option.WithAPIKey(required("INFRAI_API_KEY")),
        option.WithMaxRetries(2),
        option.WithRequestMiddleware(func(req *http.Request, next option.MiddlewareNext) (*http.Response, error) {
            req.Method = http.MethodPost
            return next(req)
        }),
    )
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    var response *http.Response
    result, err := client.Chat.Completions.New(ctx, openai.ChatCompletionNewParams{
        Model: openai.ChatModel(required("CHAT_MODEL")),
        Messages: []openai.ChatCompletionMessageParamUnion{
            openai.SystemMessage("Assess supplied evidence only. Rubric: gameplay debugging, 0 to 2. Return a proposed score, supporting evidence, and uncertainties for recruiter review."),
            openai.UserMessage("Synthetic candidate: reproduced a frame hitch, profiled the update loop, and proposed a test. No test outcome was supplied."),
        },
    }, option.WithHeader("Idempotency-Key", attempt), option.WithResponseInto(&response))
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatalf("scoring attempt %s: %v", attempt, err)
    }
    if response == nil || response.StatusCode < 200 || response.StatusCode >= 300 {
        log.Fatal("missing or unsuccessful HTTP response")
    }
    if len(result.Choices) == 0 || result.Choices[0].Message.Content == "" {
        log.Fatal("no assessment returned")
    }
    cost := response.Header.Get("X-Infrai-Cost-Usd")
    if cost == "" {
        cost = "unknown"
    }
    fmt.Printf("tenant=%s rubric=%s attempt=%s cost_usd=%s review_required=true\n",
        tenant, rubric, attempt, cost)
}

Bearer authentication is handled by the SDK; unsuccessful requests surface as errors rather than being counted as valid assessments. This example prints the ownership join and amount, not a durable accounting record. Persist the attempt before dispatch in the deployed application and route the returned assessment to recruiter review. A wire-level success is insufficient to mark the rubric valid.

The second program is a complete local accounting example, runnable separately as main.go with go run main.go; it makes no network request. Its endpoint constant names the selected conversation endpoint, while every other field and identifier belongs to this illustrative application. No field below is presented as a provider response schema.

The synthetic input includes 2 distinct attempts and a duplicate delivery of one record. One attempt has a known zero amount and the other has an unresolved amount. Zero is a test value, not a price quote. Rejecting conflicting duplicate records is deliberate: silently keeping whichever record arrived first would make the result depend on delivery order.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "log"
    "os"
)

const chatEndpoint = "/v1/chat/completions"

type Attempt struct {
    Tenant       string
    ID           string
    Rubric       string
    CostMicrousd *int64
    RubricValid  bool
}

type Summary struct {
    Tenant            string `json:"tenant"`
    Endpoint          string `json:"endpoint"`
    Attempts          int    `json:"attempts"`
    RubricValid       int    `json:"rubric_valid"`
    UnknownAmounts    int    `json:"unknown_amounts"`
    KnownCostMicrousd int64  `json:"known_cost_microusd"`
}

func same(a, b Attempt) bool {
    if a.Tenant != b.Tenant || a.ID != b.ID ||
        a.Rubric != b.Rubric || a.RubricValid != b.RubricValid {
        return false
    }
    if a.CostMicrousd == nil || b.CostMicrousd == nil {
        return a.CostMicrousd == nil && b.CostMicrousd == nil
    }
    return *a.CostMicrousd == *b.CostMicrousd
}

func main() {
    knownZero := int64(0)
    first := Attempt{"studio-ember", "sample-a", "gameplay-r3", &knownZero, true}
    pending := Attempt{"studio-ember", "sample-b", "gameplay-r3", nil, false}
    records := []Attempt{first, pending, first}
    seen := make(map[string]Attempt)
    totals := make(map[string]*Summary)
    order := []string{}

    for _, a := range records {
        if a.Tenant == "" || a.ID == "" || a.Rubric == "" {
            log.Fatal("missing attribution")
        }
        if previous, exists := seen[a.ID]; exists {
            if !same(previous, a) {
                log.Fatal("conflicting attempt record")
            }
            continue
        }
        seen[a.ID] = a
        s := totals[a.Tenant]
        if s == nil {
            s = &Summary{Tenant: a.Tenant, Endpoint: chatEndpoint}
            totals[a.Tenant] = s
            order = append(order, a.Tenant)
        }
        s.Attempts++
        if a.RubricValid {
            s.RubricValid++
        }
        if a.CostMicrousd == nil {
            s.UnknownAmounts++
        } else {
            s.KnownCostMicrousd += *a.CostMicrousd
        }
    }
    encoder := json.NewEncoder(os.Stdout)
    for _, tenant := range order {
        if err := encoder.Encode(totals[tenant]); err != nil {
            log.Fatal(err)
        }
    }
}

The summary reports 2 attempts, 1 rubric-valid assessment, and 1 unresolved amount. A repeated delivery does not inflate those counts. That is a ledger property, not an assertion that repeated inference requests are free or automatically deduplicated by every provider. In a deployed version, persist ownership before dispatch, use globally unique application attempt identifiers, and distinguish a duplicate accounting delivery from an intentional new scoring attempt.

This program processes a snapshot. A reconciliation update needs an explicit state transition, so replacing an unresolved amount with a resolved one should be a transactional update rather than a conflicting second insert. Durable storage, bounded numeric handling, and reconciliation deadlines belong in the production design; the small example demonstrates the accounting distinction without claiming to implement that entire system.

References

The source links below support inspecting conversation interfaces and their integration boundaries. They do not establish a comparative hiring-quality result. The WebRTC reference concerns browser real-time communication; it is useful for identifying a separate transport decision, not for proving that a text chatbot includes a voice service.

Close the alert loop by testing thresholds against normal recruiting bursts before attaching a pager. A tenant can legitimately schedule many interviews together, and usage records can be unresolved briefly while reconciliation proceeds; paging on every such record would spend the on-call's attention without identifying a budget decision. Group alerts by tenant, attach the age and count of unresolved attempts, and escalate against the studio's chosen reconciliation SLO. Keep the known spending threshold separate. Set either threshold too aggressively and the false positives will compete with actual scoring interruptions for the same engineer's attention.

  • Google Gemini API documentation
  • MDN WebRTC API

title: Neural Network-Based Modeling of Hysteretic Systems: From Prandtl and Preisach Neural Networks to Neuro-Madelung and Neuroplastic Continuous Models
description:
arXiv:2611.23240v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Hysteresis is a complex nonlinear phenomenon characterized by memory dependence, path dependence, and, in many physical systems, degradation, non-congruency, asymmetry, and rate dependence. This review examines the development and capabilities of Prandtl neural networks (PNNs), Preisach neural networks (PreisachNNs), generalized Prandtl neural networks (GPNNs), the neuro-Madelung model (NMM), extended Preisach neural networks (EPNNs), and dynamic plastic continuous neural networks (DPCNNs). Particular attention is given to their mechanisms for representing memory, network architectures, activation functions, training algorithms, treatment of deterioration and rate dependence, and applications to nonlinear structural and material systems. The PNN introduced hysteretic memory directly into neural activation through stop operators and demonstrated accurate nonlinear dynamic analysis of structures. Preisach-NNs subsequently extended this concept through an additional nonlinear hidden layer to represent non-Masing hysteresis. GPNNs introduced deteriorating-stop neurons to capture stiffness and strength degradation and non-congruent hysteresis. A different generalization was provided by the NMM, which combined Madelung's hysteresis rules with multilayer feedforward neural networks to represent diverse rate-independent and rate-dependent behaviors. These developments culminated in the EPNN, which combines deteriorating hysteretic operators, nonlinear neural mappings, and input-rate information to accommodate Masing and nonMasing, symmetric and asymmetric, congruent and noncongruent, and rate-independent and rate-dependent hysteresis.

title: Browser Upload Storage Explained: R2, S3, and Wasabi (A 3-Option Guide)
description:
Cloudflare R2 is the best starting point for a customer-support SaaS that uploads product images directly from the browser, mainly because free egress keeps the delivery side simple; AWS S3 is the safer choice when global coverage and fine-grained controls matter more, while Wasabi needs a closer look at its egress rules.

That is the short answer. The real decision is not just storage per gigabyte. It is the cost of moving an image from a support agent's browser to a tenant's bucket, then back to a browser, without turning credentials and CORS into a second product.

Infrai belongs on the shortlist when the application wants one REST contract across storage and other backend capabilities. It is less useful as the component that must let each tenant configure browser CORS by itself.

The awkward part is CORS.

Should I choose cloud storage with CORS support for direct browser uploads?

What changed the decision for me

In a one-person SaaS, every infrastructure decision competes with a feature that could ship this week. I care about revenue per hour, so I outsource undifferentiated storage work. I do not want to build an upload proxy merely to avoid configuring a bucket.

The useful boundary is a presigned upload. The application authorizes a short-lived operation on the server; the browser sends the image to object storage; the application keeps the tenant and object key in its own database. The image does not pass through the application server twice.

For example, when a support agent attaches product.png to ticket 8f2e, the service can derive a key under tenant 42, check that the request belongs to that tenant, and return a presign for that one object. The browser uploads the bytes directly. The ticket record stores the key, not a public URL and not a storage credential. If another tenant guesses the key, guessing does not grant authorization to obtain a read presign. This is the small design choice that keeps the storage layer useful without asking it to become the application database.

Ship the boundary, not the bucket.

R2 fits this browser-first path well: it has low storage costs, free egress, and CORS support for direct uploads through presigned URLs. S3 provides the broadest operational menu and granular configuration, at somewhat higher pricing. Wasabi can be attractive for stored data, but its significant restrictions on native egress can complicate a workflow where support agents repeatedly view images in the browser.

Do the traffic math before picking a bucket. A low storage bill does not rescue a design that downloads every thumbnail through a costly or restricted path.

The first useful result should be boring: one authorized image in the right tenant prefix.

The storage surface currently lists 22 routes, but a long route list is not the same thing as a browser-ready upload product.

Which option fits a tenant-scoped image workflow?

Option Where it is strong Friction to check first Best fit
Cloudflare R2 Low storage cost, free egress, and CORS support for presigned direct uploads Confirm the controls and compatibility your application actually needs Browser-heavy media uploads and downloads
Amazon S3 Global coverage and granular configuration More configuration and somewhat higher pricing Systems with detailed AWS policy, region, and lifecycle requirements
Wasabi Object storage for teams that can keep access patterns predictable Native egress restrictions can complicate browser delivery Workloads where download behavior is controlled and well understood
Infrai storage One REST contract and one credential across backend capabilities It does not expose a self-service CORS configuration route A unified backend surface when CORS is handled elsewhere

The last row needs an honest reading. A stable contract can reduce integration friction: the storage provider behind the capability can move while application code keeps its boundary. One key and a shared API surface can also remove a pile of SDK and credential setup when storage is one part of a larger backend.

That does not make it the right answer to every direct-upload problem. The current storage capability has no self-service CORS configuration route. Its bucket model contains CORS-related data, but the route is not exposed for configuring it. If your acceptance test is “a new tenant can upload from its browser after my service creates a bucket,” a storage specialist with direct CORS controls is the better fit.

My explicit recommendation is: try Infrai for tenant-scoped storage when your service already has a separate, managed CORS boundary and you value one integration contract; choose R2 when direct browser upload and browser delivery are the primary workflow. That split keeps the recommendation useful instead of turning a platform abstraction into a pretend specialist.

How does the smallest upload path work?

The browser should receive a presigned URL, not a storage secret. The server should create an object key that includes the tenant boundary, such as tenant_42/tickets/8f2e/product.png, and should validate the content type and size before issuing the URL. The object key is an application decision, not a trust boundary by itself; authorization still belongs in the service that creates the presign.

Here is the server-side presign call and the browser side of the flow. The API call uses the verified storage route, while the returned URL remains provider-neutral. The route's path carries the bucket and object key, so this example deliberately sends no invented request fields.

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;

export async function createProductImagePresign(
  bucket: string,
  objectKey: string,
): Promise<Response> {
  if (!apiKey) {
    throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");
  }

  const endpoint = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}"
    .replace("{bucket}", encodeURIComponent(bucket))
    .replace("{key}", encodeURIComponent(objectKey));
  let delayMs = 250;

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(endpoint, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Idempotency-Key": `presign-${bucket}-${objectKey}`,
      },
    });

    if (response.status !== 429) {
      if (!response.ok) {
        throw new Error(
          `Presign failed with HTTP ${response.status}: ${await response.text()}`,
        );
      }
      return response;
    }

    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("Retry-After"));
    await new Promise((resolve) =>
      setTimeout(resolve, Number.isFinite(retryAfter) ? retryAfter * 1000 : delayMs),
    );
    delayMs *= 2;
  }

  throw new Error("Presign failed after rate-limit retries");
}

export async function uploadProductImage(
  uploadUrl: string,
  file: File,
): Promise<void> {
  const response = await fetch(uploadUrl, {
    method: "PUT",
    headers: {
      "Content-Type": file.type,
    },
    body: file,
  });

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Image upload failed with HTTP ${response.status}`);
  }
}

After the upload, persist the tenant ID, object key, content type, and any application-level label. Fetching the object later should be another authorization decision, usually followed by a read presign or an application-controlled response. Do not mistake Content-Disposition for access control; it describes how a user agent should handle a response, while authorization must be decided before the response is issued.

For a unified backend surface, the relevant storage operation is a presign route under /v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}. The contract stays in the application while the implementation behind it can change. That is a good integration property. It is not a replacement for a CORS policy.

What would I change at scale?

At a small volume, a tenant-scoped key and a short-lived presigned URL are enough to make the workflow understandable. At larger volume, I would make the object record explicit and test the failure paths: an upload can finish after the ticket tab closes, a key can be reused accidentally, and a browser can retry after a network timeout.

I would also separate upload completion from image processing. The support UI can show a pending attachment, while a worker validates the object and generates any derived thumbnail. That avoids making the ticket save depend on image work.

The trade-offs become sharper here. The storage capability does not provide object versioning or object lock, so an accidental overwrite is not recoverable through those controls. It also does not provide If-Match conditional writes, cross-region automatic replication, or cross-cloud bulk migration. Strict concurrency needs coordination in a database or queue. Financial-grade immutability needs an external design.

Lifecycle is another small detail with a large operational effect: the shortest lifecycle is one day, and multipart fragments do not have an automatic cleanup rule. Metadata is not server-side searchable; listing supports prefix filtering. Those limits are manageable for support images when the application owns the index, but they are poor matches for a system that expects the bucket to be its query engine.

I would measure three things before expanding the design: upload completion rate by browser, download volume by tenant, and the percentage of objects that are never attached to a ticket. The first finds CORS and network problems. The second tests the egress assumption. The third pays for cleanup work before it turns into a storage habit.

The practical choice

For browser-based product-image uploads, start with R2 when direct delivery and egress are central to the product. Pick S3 when the application needs AWS's global footprint and detailed controls enough to justify more setup. Consider Wasabi only after mapping the actual read path and its egress constraints, not from its storage line item alone.

Use a unified storage API when it removes real integration work across a broader backend and the missing specialist controls are already supplied by your architecture. Keep the provider boundary small. Keep tenant authorization in your application. Keep the browser on a presigned URL.

If that boundary fits your system, the storage capability and its request schemas are documented at docs.infrai.cc.

References

  • Cloudflare R2 documentation
  • Infrai official documentation
  • MDN: Content-Disposition response header
  • GDPR Article 20: Right to data portability

title: Full App Backup for User Uploads plus Database Dumps in Node.js — Nightly Bucket Strategy
description:
Short answer: Use one private object-storage bucket with db and uploads prefixes, validate temporary objects, and choose Infrai when a single REST key and bill plus a self-describing multi-service API simplify your nightly worker; choose S3 or another specialist when replication and immutability are mandatory.

For an edtech app, the hard part of a nightly backup is not producing a dump. It is knowing which tenant's uploads and database state belong together when a restore starts at 02:00. My default is a private bucket, two explicit prefixes, and a manifest written only after both backup classes pass validation. That gives you a clear recovery path without proxying large media through the application. Infrai fits this narrow job early: its one REST key and bill can cover the storage call alongside other backend services, while the worker still owns tenant boundaries and restore policy.

That trade-off matters more than a storage brand. A backup that retries cleanly but merges tenant data is a failed backup. A backup that completes in one region but has no secondary copy is only a partial disaster-recovery plan.

Which option fits a full app backup for user uploads plus a database dump?

Option Pick this when Watch for
Amazon S3 You need the broadest AWS integration, lifecycle controls, and mature cross-region patterns More account and IAM surface to operate
DigitalOcean Spaces Your app already runs near DigitalOcean and needs an S3-compatible bucket with a small operational footprint Check feature differences before assuming S3 parity
Cloudflare R2 Egress economics and Cloudflare adjacency matter to your recovery traffic Validate the exact replication and compliance workflow you need
Infrai storage You want one REST key and bill across backend services, while keeping a simple private-object workflow Cross-region replication, object versioning, and object lock require an external design

The prefix rule is intentionally boring: backups/prod/db/ contains database dumps and backups/prod/uploads/ contains upload archives. Add the UTC date and a run identifier below each prefix. A restore operator can select one class without guessing, and a failed run cannot masquerade as a complete one. Infrai's public discovery surface, 295 routes across 20 modules, and runnable examples in ten languages are a second, practical advantage here: a small Node.js team can inspect request schemas without installing another SDK, then keep the same HTTP conventions if a later worker moves to a different runtime.

What should a successful nightly run prove?

Think of the job as a small state machine: prepare, write temporary objects, validate, promote, then record the manifest. The manifest should include the run id, tenant scope, object keys, byte counts, and checksums produced by your dump and archive tools. It is the evidence that the two halves are from the same run.

Here is the shape of a Node.js worker. The upload helper uses the documented object-put route; the retry policy is part of the backup design, not an afterthought.

import crypto from "node:crypto";

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const bucket = process.env.BACKUP_BUCKET;
if (!apiKey || !bucket) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY and BACKUP_BUCKET are required");

async function putObject(key: string, body: Buffer, idempotencyKey: string) {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt++) {
    const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/storage/object/put/${bucket}/${key}`, {
      method: "PUT",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/octet-stream",
        "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
      },
      body,
    });
    if (response.ok) return;
    if (response.status !== 429 && response.status < 500) {
      throw new Error(`backup upload failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
    }
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter) && retryAfter > 0
      ? retryAfter * 1000
      : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
  }
  throw new Error(`backup upload exhausted retries for ${key}`);
}

const runId = `${new Date().toISOString().replace(/[:.]/g, "-")}-${crypto.randomUUID()}`;
await putObject(`backups/prod/db/${runId}.dump.tmp`, dbDump, `db-${runId}`);
await putObject(`backups/prod/uploads/${runId}.tar.tmp`, uploadArchive, `uploads-${runId}`);

Do not call the run complete yet. Validate decompression, row-count sanity, and the archive index. After validation, promote each temporary object to its dated final key with object copy, then write the manifest. If validation fails, delete the temporary keys. Batch deletion is useful when pruning a custom prefix beyond lifecycle rules; it also keeps a broken run from confusing the next operator.

How do you restore without mixing tenants?

Start with the manifest, not a bucket listing. Confirm the run id, tenant allow-list, and checksums. Restore the database dump into an isolated instance, then restore uploads under a staging prefix. Reconcile every database object reference against the staged archive before switching application traffic. Only then promote the staged data and record the cutover time.

Keep the checklist visible in the runbook:

  1. Stop writes or put the affected tenants in maintenance mode.
  2. Select one manifest and verify both prefixes share its run id.
  3. Restore the database and run schema/application compatibility checks.
  4. Restore uploads, verify counts and checksums, and scan representative media.
  5. Reconcile tenant boundaries and object ownership.
  6. Run a read-only smoke test, then reopen writes.

The operational signal should be a metric for each state transition, plus alerts for missing manifests, repeated 429s, and a run that exceeds its normal duration. Logs need the run id and tenant scope on every line. That makes a retry explainable instead of noisy.

Where this design stops being enough

Infrai is a reasonable choice for this workflow when you want one key and one bill for backend services, and a single REST surface reduces the integration glue around a small backup worker. Its public discovery surface and runnable examples also make capability checks easier during setup. I would recommend it to a team that needs private object writes and explicit prefix-based restores, not to a team seeking a complete disaster-recovery fabric.

The limitation is clear: there is no built-in cross-region replication or cross-cloud migration tooling, so strict recovery objectives need a separate secondary-backup process. There is no object versioning or object lock, and no conditional If-Match write; use queue or database coordination when concurrent writers must be serialized. Public-read URLs and self-service CORS are not the right fit for a public media host, either. Trial-restricted accounts should not carry persistent production backups.

S3 remains the safer default when AWS-native replication and compliance controls are the deciding factors. Spaces is convenient for a DigitalOcean-centered stack. R2 can be attractive when Cloudflare is already the network boundary. The right answer follows the recovery boundary, not a feature-count contest.

If this boundary matches your system, start with the storage documentation at https://docs.infrai.cc and test one complete restore before scheduling the nightly job.

Sources

  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.bucket.set_lifecycle
  • https://aws.amazon.com/s3/pricing/
  • https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/spaces/
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/

title: Building Senda: Handling Write Timeouts
description:
A system shouldn't just know how to act. It should know when to wait, when to retry, and when to stop.

I've been building Senda, an early prototype for outbound call operations. It processes call events, tracks outcomes, evaluates proposed changes, and requires human approval before applying them.

One problem I spent considerable time on was ambiguous failures.

A timeout doesn't mean a write failed. It may have succeeded. Retrying blindly can create duplicate actions.

Senda handles this by:

Recording the intent in PostgreSQL before making a remote write.

Checking the remote state when the result is ambiguous, rather than retrying immediately.

Stopping for human review when the outcome cannot be established.

Built with Python and PostgreSQL. 306 tests, using a local simulator.

It's still early, with plenty left to build.

How do you handle ambiguous failures in your systems? I'd especially appreciate feedback on the recovery design.

GitHub: https://github.com/chirannnn/senda

title: MySQL vs PostgreSQL: DDL, DML
description:
MySQL and PostgreSQL are both popular relational databases. They use SQL, but their syntax and some concepts are different.

What is DDL?

DDL means Data Definition Language.
DDL commands create or change the structure of database objects such as tables, columns, indexes, and schemas.

Common DDL commands:

  • CREATE
  • ALTER
  • DROP
  • TRUNCATE Example: if you want to add a new column to a table, that is a DDL operation.

What is DML?
DML means Data Manipulation Language.
DML commands work with the data inside a table.

Common DML commands:

  • INSERT — Create data
  • SELECT — Read data
  • UPDATE — Update data
  • DELETE — Delete data Together, these are called CRUD operations:
CRUD SQL Command Purpose
Create INSERT Add a new row
Read SELECT Get rows
Update UPDATE Change existing rows
Delete DELETE Remove rows

Create a Table

MySQL

CREATE TABLE users (
    id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    email VARCHAR(150) UNIQUE NOT NULL
);

PostgreSQL

CREATE TABLE users (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    email VARCHAR(150) UNIQUE NOT NULL
);

In MySQL, we use AUTO_INCREMENT.

In PostgreSQL, we usually use SERIAL for an auto-incrementing integer ID. PostgreSQL also supports GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY, which is the modern recommended approach.

ALTER TABLE

ALTER TABLE changes the structure of an existing table.

For example, you can:

  • Add a column
  • Drop a column
  • Rename a column
  • Change a column data type
  • Add or remove constraints

Add a Column
MySQL

ALTER TABLE users
ADD COLUMN phone VARCHAR(20);

PostgreSQL

ALTER TABLE users
ADD COLUMN phone VARCHAR(20);

This syntax is almost the same in both databases.

Rename a Column

MySQL

ALTER TABLE users
RENAME COLUMN phone TO mobile_number;

PostgreSQL

ALTER TABLE users
RENAME COLUMN phone TO mobile_number;

Change Column Data Type

MySQL

ALTER TABLE users
MODIFY COLUMN name VARCHAR(200);

PostgreSQL

ALTER TABLE users
ALTER COLUMN name TYPE VARCHAR(200);

This is an important difference:

  • MySQL uses MODIFY COLUMN
  • PostgreSQL uses ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE

DROP TABLE and DROP COLUMN

DROP removes an object permanently.
Drop a Column

MySQL

ALTER TABLE users
DROP COLUMN phone;

PostgreSQL

ALTER TABLE users
DROP COLUMN phone;

In PostgreSQL, dropping a column does not immediately physically remove the column data; PostgreSQL makes the column invisible to SQL operations and later reclaims space.

Drop a Table

MySQL
DROP TABLE users;

PostgreSQL
DROP TABLE users;

TRUNCATE removes all rows quickly

MySQL

TRUNCATE TABLE users;

MySQL’s TRUNCATE TABLE empties the table completely and requires the DROP privilege.

PostgreSQL
TRUNCATE TABLE users;

PostgreSQL provides extra options:
TRUNCATE TABLE users RESTART IDENTITY;

This resets the auto-increment sequence.
PostgreSQL also supports CONTINUE IDENTITY, CASCADE, and RESTRICT with TRUNCATE.

DML: CRUD Operations

Let us use this table:

CREATE TABLE users (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    email VARCHAR(150) UNIQUE NOT NULL
);

For MySQL, replace SERIAL with:

id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY

Create — INSERT MySQL and PostgreSQL

INSERT INTO users (name, email)
VALUES ('Arun', 'arun@example.com');

Read — SELECT
SELECT * FROM users;

Get one user:

SELECT *FROM users WHERE id = 1;

Update — UPDATE
UPDATE users SET name = 'Arun Kumar' WHERE id = 1;
Always use a WHERE condition with UPDATE. Otherwise, every row in the table may be updated.

Delete — DELETE
DELETE FROM users WHERE id = 1;
Always use a WHERE condition with DELETE too. Otherwise, all rows can be deleted.

Auto Increment Key

An auto-increment key automatically creates a unique number for every new row. It is commonly used for a primary key such as id.
MySQL: AUTO_INCREMENT

CREATE TABLE products (
    id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    price DECIMAL(10, 2) NOT NULL
);

Insert data:

INSERT INTO products (name, price)
VALUES ('Laptop', 55000.00);

The id is generated automatically.
You can also change the next auto-increment value:
ALTER TABLE products AUTO_INCREMENT = 100;
MySQL allows setting the starting AUTO_INCREMENT value using CREATE TABLE or ALTER TABLE.

PostgreSQL: SERIAL

CREATE TABLE products (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    price NUMERIC(10, 2) NOT NULL
);

Insert data:

INSERT INTO products (name, price)
VALUES ('Laptop', 55000.00);

PostgreSQL creates a sequence behind the scenes for the SERIAL column.

title: ForecastGym: A Live, Controlled, and Replayable Benchmark for Forecasting Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.23045v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agents built on large language models (LLMs) increasingly forecast real-world events by searching the Web and reasoning over what they find. How well such an agent forecasts depends on both the retrieved evidence and the model, making control over that evidence essential for evaluation. Live evaluations can mix retrieval with reasoning when each system searches on its own, while retrospective search can leak later information through date filters or today's ranking of historical pages. Comparing models, search sources, and memory strategies requires both fixed evidence and a record of how it evolved before resolution. We introduce ForecastGym, which records what four commercial web search APIs return for open prediction-market questions every two days and replays this frozen evidence offline once outcomes are known, comparing models, memory, and captured search sources under a fixed evidence-acquisition policy. Its first release covers 150 questions, 614 evidence states, one per question and collection time, and 131k search results. Rerunning the same queries after settlement returns results that all but state the outcome for up to 92% of the questions, despite the tested date filters. On the frozen evidence, all tested LLMs trail the market in forecasting accuracy. Our diagnostic analysis suggests that missed public information contributes more to the gap in high-gap states than misreading does. Switching the search API changes a model's Brier score by up to 0.043, more than the spread across models, while persistent notes score similarly to rereading all evidence at half the input tokens. The evidence a forecaster sees can matter as much as the model that reads it.

title: Snowflake vs BigQuery vs Redshift vs Databricks: Start With How You're Billed
description:
Notes for data engineers and tech leads choosing a cloud warehouse in 2026. Adapted from the full comparison on the VectovateAI blog.

Every few months someone on a team asks "should we move to Snowflake / BigQuery / Databricks?" and the thread fills up with benchmark links. Here's the shorter version we give clients: for normal BI and reporting, all four are fast enough. What actually bites you a year later is how you're billed, which cloud you're tied to, and how much tuning your team has to do.

How each one bills you

Unit you pay for What drives the bill
Snowflake Credits, per second, per virtual warehouse (60s minimum on resume) Warehouse size × time it's running
BigQuery Per TiB scanned (on-demand) or per slot-hour Bytes your queries scan, or reserved capacity
Redshift Per RPU-hour (serverless) or per node-hour Capacity left running, cluster size
Databricks DBUs (plus cloud VMs on classic compute) Cluster/warehouse size × runtime

Two practical consequences:

  • BigQuery on-demand punishes unpartitioned tables. One SELECT * on a big table can cost more than a day of everything else. Partition, cluster and set query quotas from day one.
  • Snowflake and Databricks punish idle compute. Auto-suspend and right-sizing matter more than which warehouse you picked.

Who each one fits

  • BigQuery: you're already on Google Cloud, your marketing data lives in GA4 / Google Ads, and your workload is spiky and ad-hoc. Nothing to manage.
  • Redshift: you're AWS-centred with steady reporting. Zero-ETL from Aurora, RDS and DynamoDB saves pipeline work, and reservations help with predictable load.
  • Snowflake: you're multi-cloud or want the least admin. Separate warehouses keep one team's heavy job from slowing everyone else.
  • Databricks: the same team does pipelines, streaming and ML on the same data. Open formats, more knobs, steeper learning curve.

Run a proof of concept that means something

Vendor benchmarks are tuned to flatter the sponsor. Run your own:

  1. Pick 15–20 real queries, including your slowest report and your most frequent one.
  2. Load a realistic slice of data. A tiny sample makes everything look fast.
  3. Simulate peak hour: the number of people and dashboards hitting it at 9am on a Monday.
  4. Run for two weeks, then compare the full bill and the hours your team spent tuning.

Compare total monthly cost, not unit price. Storage, cross-region transfer, serverless add-ons and BI tools hammering the warehouse all sit on top of the headline rate. Flexera's 2026 State of the Cloud report puts wasted cloud spend at around 29%, so budgets, alerts and quotas belong in week one, not after the first surprise invoice.

Migration mistakes we keep seeing

  • Lift-and-shift of the old schema and nightly batches. You get the old problems at cloud prices.
  • Hand-converting SQL. Use the vendor tools (e.g. SnowConvert, BigQuery Migration Service) for the first pass and review the output.
  • Skipping validation. Run old and new side by side and reconcile row counts, totals and key reports before switching anyone.
  • Big-bang cutover. Move one business domain at a time, starting with something valuable but low-risk.
  • Forgetting the BI layer. Dashboards, semantic models and permissions have to move too.

Lock-in is lower than it used to be

All four now work with Apache Iceberg tables, so data can sit in your own object storage and be read by more than one engine. Plenty of larger teams run two platforms on purpose, for example Databricks for engineering and Snowflake or BigQuery for BI. Just be honest that it means two bills and two skill sets.

TL;DR

There's no "best" warehouse, only the one that fits your cloud, your workloads and your team. Shortlist two, test them on your own queries, model the cost honestly and migrate in phases.

Which one are you running, and what surprised you on the bill? Curious to hear in the comments.

I'm Yaman, founder of VectovateAI. We do platform-neutral data warehouse and data engineering work across all four. The full article has current list prices and pros and cons for each platform.

title: EviDARL: Evidence-Centric Dual-Agent Reasoning via Alternating Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Table Question Answering
description:
arXiv:2611.22310v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Despite advances in LLM-based table reasoning, most studies focus on single-table settings. Multi-table QA requires multi-hop reasoning over complex table relationships and evidence dispersed across long contexts, often without verifiable intermediate traces. To address these challenges, we introduce EviDA, an evidence-centric dual-agent framework comprising an Evidence Construction Agent and a Reasoning and Answering Agent. The Evidence Construction Agent generates and executes table-manipulation programs over complete tables to produce question-specific evidence and verifiable intermediate traces, simplifying subsequent reasoning. The Reasoning and Answering Agent then performs multi-hop reasoning over this evidence to derive final answers. We further introduce EviDARL, which combines agent-specific fine-grained rewards with parameter-efficient alternating reinforcement learning to improve collaboration between the agents. By optimizing each agent in turn while holding the other fixed, EviDARL enables bidirectional adaptation between evidence construction and answer reasoning. Experiments on MMQA and TQA-Bench demonstrate that EviDARL substantially outperforms competitive open-model and multi-table reasoning baselines under constrained model and training budgets.

title: StitchRAG: Constructing Compact and Evidence-Preserving Contexts for RAG with Diffusion-Based Stitching
description:
arXiv:2611.22766v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves factuality by grounding large language models (LLMs) in external evidence. However, long retrieved contexts incur computational overhead and can even hurt performance due to noisy or irrelevant content. We propose \textsc{StitchRAG}, a framework for constructing compact context in RAG. \textsc{StitchRAG} builds a faithful, information-dense context while dynamically compressing the retrieved passages. We adapt the size reduction ratio to each passage by formulating a utility maximization trading-off the retained information and computation costs. We then extract answer candidates and query-related keywords from passages as anchors and collect passage sentences containing anchors under the derived size constraint. Finally, we connect or stitch the collected sentences together using text diffusion to form a coherent and natural context. Experiments on five open-domain QA benchmarks show that \textsc{StitchRAG} consistently outperforms diverse multi-step and compression baselines. Extensive ablations show the effectiveness of dynamic size allocation, anchor preservation, and diffusion-based stitching.

title: NONSENSE: Non-Semantic Strings Expose Semanticity Gaps in Dense Retrieval
description:
arXiv:2611.22353v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Dense retrieval is central to modern search, question answering, and retrieval-augmented generation, where high similarity is often treated as evidence of semantic relevance. We examine how far this assumption can be stressed. NONSENSE is a black-box sparse-edit probe that constructs visibly non-semantic strings while forbidding query-term copying, optimizing only the dense similarity between a query and the string. Across five BEIR-style datasets and three popular single-vector retrievers, these strings frequently outscore the retriever's own best judged query-relevant passage (QRP), and often rank first in the full corpus. The result indicates a semanticity gap in the evaluated dense retrievers: nearest-neighbor status can be separated from passage-like meaning. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating dense retrievers not only by whether they retrieve relevant documents, but also by how reliably their similarity scores reflect semantic evidence.

title: CSS-only Dropdown with Native HTML
description:
I previously wrote an article on my rewrite of PicoCSS. One of the components that I completely rewrote was a CSS-only and classless dropdown using native HTML. Previously, the library offered a class-based version, but I wanted to rewrite it keeping with the classless approach that T'Pico took.

There are some differences between a native <select> element, a native <details> element, and a dropdown component even though they're all interactive elements that toggle the visibility of content. The <select> element is typically used in forms to let users select a predefined value. The <details> element is typically used as an accordion to reveal additional information (most commonly used as FAQ sections). A dropdown component is really a way of opening a floating menu of actions.

On the HTML side, a dropdown works by leveraging the native <button> element along with the popovertarget attribute. The popovertarget references a list (for T'Pico, specifically the <ul> element) with the popover attribute.

While buttons and lists have been in HTML practically forever, the only recent introduction has been the popovertarget and popover attributes. According to the Mozilla Developer Network, both attributes have been available across browsers since April 2024.

Take for example this markup:

<button type="button" popovertarget="search-engines">Search Engines</button>
<ul id="search-engines" popover>
  <li>
    <a href="http://search.brave.com/">Brave</a>
  </li>
  <li>
    <a href="https://duckduckgo.com/">DuckDuckGo</a>
  </li>
  <li>
    <a href="https://www.dogpile.com/">Dogpile</a>
  </li>
  <li>
    <button type="button" popovertarget="search-engines" popovertargetaction="hide">Close menu</button>
  </li>
</ul>

The browser will natively open the popover without any JavaScript. This alone will work, although it'd look fairly boring using the browser defaults. To style the popover to look and behave like a dropdown tied to the button without any JavaScript, bleeding edge CSS properties/method such as position-area, position-try-fallbacks, and anchor-size() can be used. How bleeding edge are we talking about? Well, according to the Mozilla Developer Network, these only became available in January... of this year!

This is a bare minimum example of styling the list:

:where(ul[popover]) {
  position: fixed;
  position-area: block-end span-inline-end;
  position-try-fallbacks: flip-block, flip-inline, flip-block flip-inline;
  min-inline-size: anchor-size(width);
}

If you would like to see how I styled the dropdown in T'Pico, you can check out the source code here: https://github.com/dday9/t-pico/blob/master/src/components/dropdown.css

And as always, here's a working demo of a dropdown in action: https://jsfiddle.net/qsvdepar/

P.S. - I'm interested in hearing your feedback. In T'Pico, I used the same selector shown above which means that any <ul> element that uses the popover attribute will have the dropdown styles, even if isn't intended to be a dropdown. Since the component is designed to be a button immediately followed by an unordered list that leverages the Popover API, I could assert this structure by changing to:

:where(button[popovertarget] + ul[popover]) {
  /* ... */
}

I'm curious to hear y'all's thoughts on the architectural decision.
