Cloud Profiler

Security

The Cloud Profiler Java agent is updated with a new Certification Authority (CA) certificate bundle, in response to security bulletin GCP-2026-071. Google Cloud infrastructure and the Cloud Profiler backend service are not affected.

If you use the Cloud Profiler Java agent, take one of the following actions:

  • Upgrade the Java agent to cloud-profiler-java-agent_20261026_RC00 (GitHub release v0.5.0) or later, and then rebuild and redeploy your applications. Download the updated archive, https://storage.googleapis.com/cloud-profiler/java/cloud-profiler-java-agent_20261026_RC00.tar.gz, or, for musl-based Alpine Linux containers, https://storage.googleapis.com/cloud-profiler/java/cloud-profiler-java-agent_20261026_RC00_alpine.tar.gz.
  • If you can't immediately upgrade or rebuild, update your host or container operating system's CA certificate store as described in GCP-2026-071, and then set the GRPC_DEFAULT_SSL_ROOTS_FILE_PATH environment variable to point to the updated PEM bundle.

For more information about installing the agent, see Profiling Java applications.

Dataflow

Feature

Dataflow has added the following features to tune horizontal autoscaling for Streaming Engine jobs:

  • Latency tiers: You can configure the backlog threshold by choosing a latency tier (low_latency, medium_latency, or high_latency), allowing you to configure the autoscaler's sensitivity to backlog duration and balance latency requirements with resource costs. For more information, see Set the latency tier.
  • Autoscaling schedules: You can configure recurring autoscaling schedules to automatically apply parameter overrides—such as minimum and maximum workers, worker utilization hints, or latency tiers—during specific time windows. For more information, see Schedule autoscaling changes.

You can configure these features when you create a job or update them while the job is running.

Developer Connect

Announcement

Developer Connect proxy (including HTTP proxy support) for system connections and account connectors is now generally available.

Dialogflow

Security

Dialogflow ES: The Dialogflow ES LINE integration validates the X-Line-Signature HTTP header on incoming webhook requests using your LINE channel secret and rejects requests with missing, duplicate, or invalid signatures with an HTTP 400 Bad Request error. Make sure your configured channel secret matches your LINE Messaging API channel and that any intermediate proxy forwards the X-Line-Signature header and raw request body unmodified.

Gemini

Other

Bug fixes in VS Code

Various bug fixes and minor product enhancements.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Feature

Managed OpenTelemetry for GKE is generally available (GA) on clusters running GKE version 1.37.1-gke.1697000 or later. You can collect OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP) traces, metrics, and logs from your workloads with a Google-managed collector instead of a self-managed OpenTelemetry Collector deployment:

  • Configure otlp_grpc in the Instrumentation custom resource (GKE version 1.37.1-gke.1697000 or later), or send telemetry directly to the in-cluster collector's gRPC endpoint on port 4317 in addition to HTTP on port 4318.
  • The managed collector routes logs alongside traces and metrics through the Cloud Telemetry API (telemetry.googleapis.com), with improved per-signal queueing and autoscaling for high-throughput clusters. (Logs ingested through telemetry.googleapis.com default to the otlp log name instead of gke-managed-otel-collector.)
  • Multimodal prompts and responses collection for LangGraph ReAct and Agent Development Kit (ADK) agents, the --managed-otel-scope flag in the gcloud CLI (version 576.0.0 or later), and managed_opentelemetry_config in terraform-provider-google (v8.8.0 or later) are generally available.

To use the GA collector and features, upgrade clusters from earlier Preview versions to 1.37.1-gke.1697000 or later. For architecture details and setup instructions, see Managed OpenTelemetry for GKE and Deploy Managed OpenTelemetry for GKE.

Identity and Access Management

Feature

The Admin (roles/admin), Writer (roles/writer), and Reader (roles/reader) basic roles are generally available (GA). For more information, see Basic roles.

The legacy basic roles—Owner (roles/owner), Editor (roles/editor), and Viewer (roles/viewer)—are still available for use and are being actively maintained. However, if you need to grant a basic role, we recommend granting the Admin, Writer, or Reader role instead of a legacy basic role. This is because the newer roles support additional features, such as the use of IAM Conditions.

Looker

Announcement

Beginning October 26, 2026, the following features will be automatically enabled for Looker (original) and Looker (Google Cloud core) instances running Looker 26.20.

Feature

The ability to generate a summary of an Explore by using Gemini assistance is now generally available.

Feature

The bullet chart visualization type is now generally available. Bullet charts let you evaluate a single primary metric's performance as one or more bars and mark your goal with a target line. You can plot both against shaded background ranges that represent performance thresholds, such as "poor," "satisfactory," and "good." For more information, see Bullet chart options.

Feature

Looker now includes network diagnostics to help you troubleshoot database connectivity issues. When a database connection test fails, Looker automatically tests DNS resolution and TCP connectivity for the connection's endpoints and appends the results to the error message. To test network reachability to any hostname and port without creating a connection, Looker administrators can click Test Reachability on the Connections page.

Note: This item was added on October 30, 2026.

Feature

The Table Row Grouping feature and the Grouping menu options are now generally available. The Grouping menu options let you display and customize the appearance of table chart data hierarchically in groups.

Feature

The Visualization Assistant is now generally available.

Feature

Looker Continuous Integration (CI) now supports hub-and-spoke projects. If your Looker project uses local project imports to import files from an upstream hub project on the same Looker instance, then you can use CI to automatically test downstream spoke projects. Testing runs whenever a pull request is opened or updated on the hub project. This capability lets you catch breaking changes in downstream Explores, content, or data tests before upstream LookML changes are merged. For more information, see Creating a Continuous Integration suite.

Feature

Two new legacy features, Use Legacy Explore and Merge Query Experience and Use Legacy Explore and Merge Query Experience for Embed, are now available for Looker (original) and Looker (Google Cloud core) instances. These features let administrators configure Explores and merged queries to open in the classic experience by default across an instance or in embedded contexts. For more information, see Legacy feature schedule.

Feature

Looker now includes a new histogram chart visualization option. A histogram chart is a graphical representation of the data distribution of an attribute. A histogram creates intervals (bins) and counts how many values fall into each bin.

Feature

The new Looker Explore and merge query experience is now generally available and is the default interface for Explores and for joining data from multiple queries.

Feature

When you enter values in a string filter on dashboards, Looks, or Explores, clicking Done or clicking outside the input field no longer creates a filter chip from uncommitted text. To create a filter chip, press Enter, enter a comma (,), or paste values into the input field.

title: Response Attack: Exploiting Contextual Priming to Jailbreak Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2507.05248v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Contextual priming, where earlier stimuli covertly bias later judgments, offers an unexplored attack surface for large language models (LLMs). We uncover a contextual priming vulnerability in which the previous response in the dialogue can steer its subsequent behavior toward policy-violating content. While existing jailbreak attacks largely rely on single-turn or multi-turn prompt manipulations, or inject static in-context examples, these methods suffer from limited effectiveness, inefficiency, or semantic drift. We introduce Response Attack (RA), a novel framework that strategically leverages intermediate, mildly harmful responses as contextual primers within a dialogue. By reformulating harmful queries and injecting these intermediate responses before issuing a targeted trigger prompt, RA exploits a previously overlooked vulnerability in LLMs. Extensive experiments across eight state-of-the-art LLMs show that RA consistently achieves significantly higher attack success rates than nine leading jailbreak baselines. Our results demonstrate that the success of RA is directly attributable to the strategic use of intermediate responses, which induce models to generate more explicit and relevant harmful content while maintaining stealth, efficiency, and fidelity to the original query. The code and data are available at https://github.com/Dtc7w3PQ/Response-Attack.

title: Say It Another Way: Auditing LLMs with a User-Grounded Automated Paraphrasing Framework
description:
arXiv:2505.03563v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are highly sensitive to subtle changes in prompt phrasing, posing challenges for reliable auditing. Prior methods often apply unconstrained prompt paraphrasing, which risk missing linguistic and demographic factors that shape authentic user interactions. We introduce AUGMENT (Automated User-Grounded Modeling and Evaluation of Natural Language Transformations), a framework for generating controlled paraphrases, grounded in user behaviors. AUGMENT leverages linguistically informed rules and enforces quality through checks on instruction adherence, semantic similarity, and realism, ensuring paraphrases are both reliable and meaningful for auditing. Through case studies on the BBQ and MMLU datasets, we show that controlled paraphrases uncover systematic weaknesses that remain obscured under unconstrained variation. These results highlight the value of the AUGMENT framework for reliable auditing.

title: Como corrigir Java4Shell no Ubuntu e reiniciar serviços Java
description:
Builds corrigidos do OpenJDK por versão do Ubuntu

A Canonical publicou em 18 de novembro de 2026 avisos de segurança com pacotes corrigidos para Java4Shell, vulnerabilidade identificada como CVE-2026-114938. A versão necessária depende da edição do Ubuntu e da versão principal do OpenJDK instalada; nas edições mais antigas, a correção requer Ubuntu Pro.

Confira os builds corrigidos na tabela e compare-os com os pacotes instalados. Os números correspondem às versões principais do OpenJDK disponíveis em cada edição, e os avisos de segurança indicam que os pacotes para Ubuntu 20.04 e 18.04 são distribuídos por meio do ESM Apps.

UbuntuOpenJDK 17OpenJDK 21OpenJDK 2526.1017.0.21.1+2-1~26.10.121.0.13.1+2-1~26.10.125.0.5.1+2-1~26.10.126.0417.0.21.1+2-1~26.04.121.0.13.1+2-1~26.04.125.0.5.1+2-1~26.04.124.0417.0.21.1+2-1~24.04.121.0.13.1+2-1~24.04.125.0.5.1+2-1~24.04.122.0417.0.21.1+2-1~22.04.121.0.13.1+2-1~22.04.125.0.5.1+2-1~22.04.120.0417.0.21.1+2-1~20.04.121.0.13.1+2-1~20.04.1Não empacotado18.0417.0.21.1+2-1~18.04.1Não empacotadoNão empacotado

No Ubuntu 26.10, o aviso USN-9158-1 também corrige o OpenJDK 27 para a versão 27.0.1.1+4-1~26.10.1. Ubuntu 20.04 oferece pacotes corrigidos para OpenJDK 17 e 21, enquanto o 18.04 oferece apenas o 17; ambos requerem Ubuntu Pro e ESM Apps.

Em Ubuntu 22.04 ou posterior, os builds vulneráveis terminam em .0.3 e os corrigidos em .1. Como as duas versões podem aparecer nas fontes do apt, confira a versão candidata e o repositório de segurança, em vez de se orientar apenas pelo número instalado.

Verifique se o processador alcança o código vulnerável

A falha está em uma rotina Base64 que usa AVX-512 e depende da presença conjunta de quatro flags do processador. A verificação ajuda a priorizar a manutenção, mas não elimina a necessidade de aplicar a correção nos sistemas afetados.

grep -oE '(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)' /proc/cpuinfo | sort -u

Se a saída não listar as quatro flags, o processador não alcança esse caminho vulnerável. A atualização continua recomendada: máquinas virtuais podem migrar entre famílias de processadores, grupos de autoscaling podem mudar de instância e imagens de contêiner podem rodar em hosts diferentes dos usados na compilação.

Localize todos os pacotes OpenJDK instalados

O Ubuntu permite manter várias versões principais do OpenJDK no mesmo sistema. Como java -version mostra somente a versão selecionada pelo update-alternatives, consulte os pacotes registrados pelo dpkg para identificar instalações paralelas que também precisam do patch.

dpkg-query -W -f='${Package} ${Version}\n' 'openjdk-*-jre-headless' | grep -v ' $'
apt-cache madison openjdk-17-jre-headless openjdk-21-jre-headless openjdk-25-jre-headless

O primeiro comando lista os pacotes de runtime conhecidos pelo dpkg; o segundo mostra as versões disponíveis nos repositórios configurados. Se a versão vulnerável continuar listada em updates após a correção, confira a candidata: o apt escolhe a versão mais alta, que deve vir do repositório de segurança.

Uma versão candidata vulnerável pode indicar que o sistema está fixado ao repositório de updates ou usa um espelho que não inclui o repositório de segurança. Essa checagem ajuda a identificar por que uma atualização não aparece antes de tentar instalar o pacote novamente.

Instale as atualizações de segurança

Nas versões 26.04, 24.04 e 22.04, os pacotes corrigidos estão no repositório de segurança padrão. A atualização seletiva abaixo limita a mudança aos pacotes OpenJDK 17, 21 e 25, sem executar uma atualização geral do sistema.

sudo apt update
sudo apt-get install --only-upgrade 'openjdk-17-' 'openjdk-21-' 'openjdk-25-*'

No Ubuntu 26.10, acrescente 'openjdk-27-*' ao comando se essa versão estiver instalada. O apt-get rejeita a operação se um padrão não corresponder a nenhum pacote disponível, por isso Ubuntu 20.04 e 18.04 precisam de comandos próprios, conforme os majors empacotados para cada edição.

O cliente pro pode indicar quais avisos afetam os pacotes instalados. Uma simulação com --dry-run pode exibir que a CVE está resolvida antes de instalar qualquer pacote; trate essa mensagem como previsão do resultado da operação, não como comprovação de que a atualização foi aplicada.

sudo pro fix CVE-2026-114938 --dry-run

Comprove a atualização e reinicie os serviços

Após a instalação, confira a versão reportada por cada JVM e procure o identificador da CVE nos changelogs dos pacotes. A segunda checagem associa o build instalado ao aviso de segurança, em vez de depender apenas da comparação visual entre números de versão.

for d in /usr/lib/jvm/java-??-openjdk-amd64; do echo "== $d"; $d/bin/java -version 2>&1 | head -1; done
for n in 17 21 25; do echo -n "openjdk-$n: "; zgrep -c CVE-2026-114938 /usr/share/doc/openjdk-$n-jre-headless/changelog.Debian.gz; done

Em Ubuntu 20.04 e 18.04, retire o número 25 do segundo laço porque essas edições não têm esse pacote. As duas verificações examinam arquivos no disco; elas não confirmam que processos Java já em execução deixaram de usar o código vulnerável carregado antes da atualização.

Os avisos recomendam reiniciar as aplicações Java após a atualização, pois uma JVM mantém bibliotecas e dados carregados durante a execução. Em algumas configurações, o needrestart reinicia os serviços durante a atualização; no modo de listagem, ele apenas informa quais unidades precisam ser reiniciadas.

Para localizar serviços pendentes em lote, consulte o needrestart. Em uma máquina de teste, três sinais apontaram que um processo ainda usava o build antigo: a versão mostrada pelo jcmd no processo ativo, mapas de arquivos excluídos em /proc/PID/maps e a unidade listada pelo needrestart.

sudo needrestart -b -r l | grep NEEDRESTART-SVC

O comando jcmd acompanha o JDK e pode não estar instalado em servidores que tenham somente o runtime. A inspeção de /proc/PID/maps também funciona nesses sistemas; depois de identificar a unidade pendente, reinicie o serviço para que a JVM carregue os arquivos corrigidos.

Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/como-corrigir-java4shell-no-ubuntu-e-reiniciar-servicos-java/

title: Implementing Binary Transformers with Approximate Memories with Permutation Invariance Enabled Selective (PIES) Protection
description:
arXiv:2611.23358v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantization is an effective technique to reduce memory storage, computation complexity and power for Transformers, and the binarization of the weights is important for meeting these requirements. Approximate memory can further reduce the power for memory, but it also introduces errors. Current research for binary Transformers focuses on task performance, but the model dependable operation against errors on the memory has not been well studied. In this paper, we first evaluate the dependability of binary Transformers with the Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) as a case study. A large accuracy loss occurs only at high Bit Error Rates (e.g. BER = 5% or 10%). Then we propose a novel Permutation Invariance Enabled Selective (PIES) scheme to protect the binary weights at very low overhead. This scheme exploits the invariance of Transformers to permutations in the rows and columns to group the critical weights and perform selective protection on those weights. Simulation results show that PIES can recover most of the performance loss caused by bit errors at BERs as high as 10%, at an overhead significantly lower than traditional error correction schemes. These results confirm the feasibility of running binary Transformers using approximate memory with aggressive voltage scaling on resource-limited low power edge devices. The code for PIES is released on github (https://github.com/YangZhutian/binary-transformer-prefix-repair).

title: Gin Go Tutorial: Build Fast APIs With Very Little Code
description:
Quick answer

Gin is a web framework for Go that turns a handful of routes into a working JSON API with almost no boilerplate. This post builds a small orders API with it: list orders, create an order, and fetch one order by id, with real requests and real responses.

A small online shop in Karachi takes orders through a chat app, and the owner copies each one into a spreadsheet by hand, until two customers order the same last kurta and both get a yes. The owner needs a small API: a list of orders anyone on the team can read, a way to add one, and a way to fetch one by number. Just three endpoints that answer in JSON. Go fits: it compiles to one binary and starts fast, and Gin keeps the routing and JSON work to a few lines. This post builds exactly that API and breaks it once, so you see what a bad request looks like.

What I would check before using it

My first check is whether the API is small enough for Gin to stay simple. Three endpoints, JSON in and JSON out, is exactly where Gin shines: one file, one router, three handlers. If the project needs HTML pages, sessions, and an admin panel, look at a bigger framework. The Go Explained: Simple Code That Runs Fast post covers the language underneath.

My second check is the Go version. Gin v1.12.0 needs Go 1.25 or later, and the demo ran on Go 1.25.0. An older toolchain refuses to build it. Check go version first.

My third check is how the API handles bad input. Gin binds JSON into a Go struct and validates it with struct tags, but the default error messages are written for developers, not for API users. The demo returns those messages as they are, which is fine for learning. For a real client, translate them into a short message naming the field.

My fourth check is where the data lives. The demo keeps orders in a slice in memory, so every restart wipes the shop. That is fine for learning, and the wrong design for a shop that takes real money. Decide early whether the next step is a database; a demo that forgets is not a service that remembers.

My verdict, as judgement: adopt Gin when you want a small, fast JSON API in Go and the team is comfortable with the language. Skip it when the project needs a full-featured framework, or when the team does not write Go. The recommendation flips the moment the API grows past simple CRUD.

Three orders, one API, and a wrong total

Three orders belong to one small shop: Ayesha buys a kurta and a dupatta for Rs 12,400, Bilal buys sneakers for Rs 7,800, and Hina buys a handbag and a wallet for Rs 5,400. The first two are seeded; Hina's arrives through the API.

One file holds the whole API: the Order struct carries json tags for the field names and binding tags so a missing field fails validation, three handlers cover the three routes, and gin.Default() adds logging and panic recovery.

// Orders API for The Practical Developer (Gin demo).
//
// A small online shop exposes three endpoints with Gin:
//   GET  /orders      list all orders
//   POST /orders      create an order (JSON body, all fields required)
//   GET  /orders/:id  fetch one order by id
//
// Run from this folder:
//   go run main.go            (listens on http://localhost:8080)
//   curl http://localhost:8080/orders
package main

import (
    "net/http"
    "strconv"

    "github.com/gin-gonic/gin"
)

type Order struct {
    ID       int      `json:"id"`
    Customer string   `json:"customer" binding:"required"`
    Items    []string `json:"items" binding:"required"`
    Total    float64  `json:"total" binding:"required"`
}

var orders = []Order{
    {ID: 101, Customer: "Ayesha", Items: []string{"kurta", "dupatta"}, Total: 12400},
    {ID: 102, Customer: "Bilal", Items: []string{"sneakers"}, Total: 7800},
}

var nextID = 103

func listOrders(c *gin.Context) {
    c.JSON(http.StatusOK, orders)
}

func getOrder(c *gin.Context) {
    id, err := strconv.Atoi(c.Param("id"))
    if err != nil {
        c.JSON(http.StatusBadRequest, gin.H{"error": "order id must be a number"})
        return
    }
    for _, order := range orders {
        if order.ID == id {
            c.JSON(http.StatusOK, order)
            return
        }
    }
    c.JSON(http.StatusNotFound, gin.H{"error": "order not found"})
}

func createOrder(c *gin.Context) {
    var order Order
    if err := c.ShouldBindJSON(&order); err != nil {
        c.JSON(http.StatusBadRequest, gin.H{"error": err.Error()})
        return
    }
    order.ID = nextID
    nextID++
    orders = append(orders, order)
    c.JSON(http.StatusCreated, order)
}

func main() {
    gin.SetMode(gin.ReleaseMode)
    router := gin.Default()
    router.GET("/orders", listOrders)
    router.GET("/orders/:id", getOrder)
    router.POST("/orders", createOrder)
    router.Run(":8080")
}

Here is the real output: the list returns the two seeded orders, creating Hina's order returns it with id 103, and fetching order 101 returns Ayesha's order alone. The server log agrees.

$ go run main.go
$ curl http://localhost:8080/orders
[{"id":101,"customer":"Ayesha","items":["kurta","dupatta"],"total":12400},{"id":102,"customer":"Bilal","items":["sneakers"],"total":7800}]

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/orders -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"customer":"Hina","items":["handbag","wallet"],"total":5400}'
{"id":103,"customer":"Hina","items":["handbag","wallet"],"total":5400}

$ curl http://localhost:8080/orders/101
{"id":101,"customer":"Ayesha","items":["kurta","dupatta"],"total":12400}

[GIN] 2026/11/19 - 03:05:22 | 200 | 81.272µs | ::1 | GET      "/orders"
[GIN] 2026/11/19 - 03:05:22 | 201 | 211.888µs | ::1 | POST     "/orders"
[GIN] 2026/11/19 - 03:05:22 | 200 | 61.141µs | ::1 | GET      "/orders/101"

Hina's order goes wrong twice. First, the total is missing, so the required tag fires and Gin answers 400. Then it arrives as the text "5400" instead of the number 5400, and Go's decoder refuses it because the struct field is a float64. Neither request touches the orders list: bad data is rejected at the door, not stored and discovered later.

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/orders -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"customer":"Hina","items":["handbag","wallet"]}'
{"error":"Key: 'Order.Total' Error:Field validation for 'Total' failed on the 'required' tag"}

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/orders -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"customer":"Hina","items":["handbag","wallet"],"total":"5400"}'
{"error":"json: cannot unmarshal string into Go struct field Order.total of type float64"}

The fix is on the client side: send every field, and send numbers as numbers. The server side already handles it: ShouldBindJSON returns the error to the handler, so the handler shapes the response. The Node.js REST API post builds the same three endpoints in JavaScript, where a missing field slips through unless you check for it, and the FastAPI post shows Python doing the same validation with Pydantic.

Common mistakes and how to fix them

First, using BindJSON when you want to control the error. The symptom is a plain-text 400 written by Gin itself, with no JSON body to parse. The fix is ShouldBindJSON, as the demo uses: it returns the error, and the handler decides the response.

Second, sending numbers as strings in JSON. The symptom is json: cannot unmarshal string into Go struct field Order.total of type float64, for a request that looks right at a glance. The fix is to send 5400, not "5400": Go types the field as a number, and JSON must match.

Third, reading the wrong path parameter name. The symptom is a 400 saying the order id must be a number, even for /orders/101. The fix is to match them: the route says /orders/:id, so the handler must call c.Param("id"), not c.Param("orderId").

Fourth, trusting the in-memory slice with real data. The symptom is orders that vanish after a restart, because the slice is rebuilt from seed data on every start. The fix is to store orders in a database; the slice is a demo only.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Gin part of Go itself? No. Gin is a third-party module, github.com/gin-gonic/gin, added with go get like any other dependency. Go's standard library serves HTTP on its own; Gin adds routing, binding, and middleware.

Do I need to know Go well before trying Gin? Basic Go is enough: structs, slices, functions, and error handling. If main.go reads clearly, you are ready; the Go Explained post fills in the language basics.

How is Gin different from the standard library net/http package? The standard library gives you a server and a handler, and you write the routing and JSON parsing yourself. Gin adds a router, JSON binding with validation, and middleware, so the same API takes less code.

Does Gin work with a database? Gin does not care where the data lives. The demo handlers read a slice, and the same handlers can query Postgres or SQLite instead. The framework handles HTTP; storage stays your choice.

What to remember

  • Gin maps a route to a handler in one line.
  • Struct tags declare the JSON shape and validation rules together.
  • ShouldBindJSON returns the error to your handler.
  • Numbers in JSON must be numbers: "5400" is text, and Go refuses it.
  • The in-memory slice is for learning; real orders need a database.

Where this leaves you

Gin earns its place the moment you want a JSON API in Go without writing your own router and JSON checks by hand. The demo proved what matters: the API listed, created, and fetched real orders, bad data was rejected with a clear 400 instead of stored, and the whole server fit in one file of about eighty lines. Start with three endpoints and an in-memory list, add a database when the orders matter, and keep the binding tags honest so bad requests fail loudly at the door.

Further reading

  • Gin docs, https://gin-gonic.com/docs/
  • Gin docs, model binding and validation, https://gin-gonic.com/en/docs/binding/binding-and-validation/
  • Go tutorial, Developing a RESTful API with Go and Gin, https://go.dev/doc/tutorial/web-service-gin
  • Go Explained: Simple Code That Runs Fast, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/go-explained-simple-code-that-runs-fast.html
  • Build Your First REST API With Node.js and Express, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/build-your-first-rest-api-with-nodejs.html
  • FastAPI Explained: Python APIs at Full Speed, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/fastapi-explained-python-apis-at-full.html
  • Hono: One Small API That Runs Almost Anywhere, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/11/hono-one-small-api-that-runs-almost.html

Waqas Shahid is a software engineer from Karachi with more than 12 years of experience, including 6+ years in engineering leadership. He writes The Practical Developer.

title: Why Daily Logistics KPIs Matter: Productivity, OTIF, Inventory Accuracy, and Operational Issues (with Java)
description:
Most logistics operations do not fail in a single dramatic moment. They drift. A picking rate slips by a few percent each week, a cycle count misses a bin that nobody notices, a carrier starts arriving late on Tuesdays, and by the time a monthly report shows the damage, the customer has already felt it. The antidote is not more reports. It is a small set of logistics KPIs, tracked daily, with a named owner for every number that moves.

This article explains which KPIs matter most in a warehouse or distribution operation, how to define them so teams trust them, how to follow up on them every day, and how to compute them from raw events with a small Java model.

Why daily tracking beats monthly reporting

A monthly KPI pack answers the question "what happened?" A daily KPI loop answers "what do we do about it today?" The difference is latency. A productivity drop caught on day two can be fixed with a shift briefing. The same drop discovered at month end is a root-cause investigation with a cost already locked in.

Daily tracking also changes behavior. When teams see their own numbers every morning, they start to ask better questions: why did the inbound dock slow down, which zone generates most of the mispicks, which shift carries the most unfinished orders into the next day.

The four families of logistics KPIs

Most operations can be described with four families. Each one answers a different question.

Productivity. How much work gets done per unit of labor or time. The most common measures are units picked per labor hour, lines picked per hour, and orders shipped per shift. Productivity tells you whether your capacity is being used well, but it says nothing about quality. A team that picks fast and wrong looks productive until the returns arrive.

Delivery performance. Whether the customer receives what was promised, when it was promised. The standard measure is On-Time In-Full (OTIF): the share of orders delivered both on time and with every requested line and quantity. OTIF is harsher than on-time delivery alone, because a shipment that arrives on time but short still counts as a failure. Pair it with order cycle time, the elapsed time from order receipt to shipment.

Inventory accuracy. Whether the system's view of stock matches what is physically on the shelf. The measure is simple: the number of storage locations counted with a matching quantity, divided by the total number of locations counted, expressed as a percentage. Inventory accuracy is the foundation of nearly every other metric. If the system says a SKU is available and it is not, you pick a shortage, promise a delivery you cannot make, and open an investigation that may never end.

Operational issues. The events that disrupt flow: damaged goods, mispicks, missed scans, dock delays, equipment downtime, safety incidents. These are counts and durations, not averages. The goal is to see their frequency, their location and how long they take to resolve.

Define each KPI precisely

Most KPI disputes are definitional disputes. Before a number goes on a dashboard, write down four things:

  • The formula, including what counts in the numerator and denominator.
  • The data source and the system that owns it.
  • The time window and the cutoff, for example midnight in the site's local time zone.
  • The owner who is accountable for the number, and who explains it when it moves.

Example: "Units per labor hour equals units shipped in the day divided by direct labor hours logged against picking and packing activities. Source: WMS shipment records and time-clock data. Window: 00:00 to 23:59 site time. Owner: outbound shift lead." That level of specificity removes arguments before they start.

A daily follow-up routine

A KPI without a routine is decoration. A workable daily rhythm looks like this:

  1. Before the shift starts. The system publishes yesterday's numbers against targets. Each KPI shows a status: on target, watch, or action required.
  2. Shift briefing, fifteen minutes. The shift lead reviews only the KPIs in watch or action state. The team agrees on one or two actions for the day, each with an owner.
  3. During the shift. Exceptions are logged as they happen, not reconstructed at the end. A damaged pallet recorded at 10:15 is useful. The same pallet remembered at 17:00 is guesswork.
  4. End of shift. Totals are locked. Any open operational issue gets a named next owner.
  5. Weekly review. Trends matter more than single days. A metric that is slightly off target every day for three weeks is a process problem, not a bad day.

The discipline is to keep the briefing short and to focus on the exceptions. Reading out fifty green numbers wastes everyone's attention.

Computing KPIs from events in Java

Raw warehouse data arrives as events: a pick confirmed, a count recorded, a shipment closed, an issue reported. KPIs are aggregations over those events. Modeling the events explicitly makes the calculations testable and the assumptions visible.

The example below uses Java 17 records to represent a simplified daily snapshot and computes the four core metrics. It has no external dependencies:

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.math.RoundingMode;
import java.util.List;

public class DailyLogisticsKpis {

    public record OrderResult(String orderId, boolean onTime, boolean inFull) {}

    public record InventoryCount(String location, int systemQuantity, int countedQuantity) {
        boolean matches() {
            return systemQuantity == countedQuantity;
        }
    }

    public record OperationalIssue(String type, int durationMinutes) {}

    public record DailySnapshot(
            long unitsShipped,
            double directLaborHours,
            List<OrderResult> orders,
            List<InventoryCount> counts,
            List<OperationalIssue> issues) {}

    public record Kpis(
            BigDecimal unitsPerLaborHour,
            BigDecimal otifPercent,
            BigDecimal inventoryAccuracyPercent,
            int issueCount,
            long totalIssueMinutes) {}

    public static Kpis compute(DailySnapshot day) {
        if (day.directLaborHours() <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("directLaborHours must be positive");
        }

        BigDecimal unitsPerHour = BigDecimal.valueOf(day.unitsShipped())
                .divide(BigDecimal.valueOf(day.directLaborHours()), 2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP);

        long otifOrders = day.orders().stream()
                .filter(o -> o.onTime() && o.inFull())
                .count();
        BigDecimal otif = percentage(otifOrders, day.orders().size());

        long matchingLocations = day.counts().stream()
                .filter(InventoryCount::matches)
                .count();
        BigDecimal accuracy = percentage(matchingLocations, day.counts().size());

        int issues = day.issues().size();
        long issueMinutes = day.issues().stream()
                .mapToLong(OperationalIssue::durationMinutes)
                .sum();

        return new Kpis(unitsPerHour, otif, accuracy, issues, issueMinutes);
    }

    /** Returns part/whole as a percentage with two decimals; zero when there is no whole. */
    private static BigDecimal percentage(long part, long whole) {
        if (whole == 0) {
            return BigDecimal.ZERO;
        }
        return BigDecimal.valueOf(part)
                .multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(100))
                .divide(BigDecimal.valueOf(whole), 2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        DailySnapshot day = new DailySnapshot(
                12_400,
                186.5,
                List.of(
                        new OrderResult("SO-1001", true, true),
                        new OrderResult("SO-1002", true, false),
                        new OrderResult("SO-1003", false, true),
                        new OrderResult("SO-1004", true, true)),
                List.of(
                        new InventoryCount("A-01-03", 40, 40),
                        new InventoryCount("A-01-04", 12, 10),
                        new InventoryCount("B-02-11", 75, 75)),
                List.of(
                        new OperationalIssue("damaged_goods", 25),
                        new OperationalIssue("dock_delay", 40)));

        Kpis kpis = compute(day);
        System.out.println("Units per labor hour: " + kpis.unitsPerLaborHour());
        System.out.println("OTIF %: " + kpis.otifPercent());
        System.out.println("Inventory accuracy %: " + kpis.inventoryAccuracyPercent());
        System.out.println("Operational issues: " + kpis.issueCount()
                + " (" + kpis.totalIssueMinutes() + " min)");
    }
}

Running this prints 66.49 units per labor hour, 50.00 percent OTIF, 66.67 percent inventory accuracy, and two issues totaling 65 minutes. The numbers are deliberately dramatic: a sample this small is for illustration, not for conclusions. The value of the model is that every assumption is explicit. OTIF requires both conditions. Inventory accuracy counts locations, not units. Productivity divides by direct labor hours, so indirect time is excluded by definition.

In production, the snapshot would be built from your WMS, TMS and time-tracking exports, and the tests would cover edge cases such as zero orders on a holiday, partial shifts and locations counted twice. The formulas themselves are the easy part. Agreeing on which events belong in each numerator is the real work.

Practical recommendations

Start with five KPIs, not twenty. Choose one productivity measure, OTIF, inventory accuracy, order cycle time and one operational issue count. Add others only when a specific decision needs them.

Set targets from history and capacity, not from wishes. A target that the team has never come close to becomes background noise. Use the last four to eight weeks to set a realistic baseline, then tighten it gradually.

Separate leading from lagging indicators. OTIF is a lagging result. Inventory accuracy, cycle count completion and dock-to-stock time are leading signals you can act on before the customer notices.

Treat inventory accuracy as a control, not a score. Cycle counts should target the locations most likely to drift: high-velocity picks, locations with recent adjustments, and items with frequent mispicks.

Make issues measurable. Every operational issue needs a type, a location, a start time, an end time and an owner. Without those fields you can count incidents but cannot learn from them.

Protect the data. Hand-typed numbers at the end of a shift are the weakest link. Capture events at the point of work with scanners and simple forms, and reconcile the totals automatically.

Conclusion and key takeaways

Logistics performance is decided in small daily details. A short list of well-defined KPIs, reviewed every shift and tied to named owners, turns that detail into action. Productivity shows how work gets done, OTIF shows whether customers receive it, inventory accuracy shows whether the system can be trusted, and operational issues show what keeps breaking.

Key takeaways:

  • Daily tracking catches drift while it is still cheap to correct.
  • Each KPI needs a precise formula, a data source, a time window and an owner.
  • OTIF is stricter than on-time delivery because it requires complete orders.
  • Inventory accuracy underpins every other metric and deserves targeted cycle counting.
  • Modeling KPI calculations explicitly, even in a small Java program, makes assumptions testable.

If your team does not yet track these numbers daily, start tomorrow with three: units per labor hour, OTIF and inventory accuracy. Review them at the next shift briefing and assign one action to each one that is off target.

title: Database Performance: Finding the Query That Is Killing You
description:
Database performance work usually begins with someone proposing a bigger instance, and it usually ends with the discovery that one query was doing a sequential scan over four million rows on every page load. The hardware was never the constraint. The plan was.

That pattern is consistent enough to be worth stating as a default assumption. When an application is slow and the database is busy, the cause is almost always a small number of specific queries, not a general shortage of capacity, and scaling up hides the problem for exactly as long as it takes the table to grow again.

Before changing anything, measure. Optimising a query you guessed at is how teams spend a week adding indexes that make writes slower and reads no faster. Every database can tell you which statements consume the most total time. Start there, fix the top one, measure again. Two or three iterations of that usually ends the incident.

Database Performance Starts With Finding the Query

Total time matters more than worst case. A query taking two seconds and running twice a day is irrelevant. A query taking forty milliseconds and running eight thousand times a minute is your problem, and it will never appear in a slow query log with a one-second threshold.

In Postgres, the pg_stat_statements extension aggregates exactly this: calls, total time and mean time per normalised statement. Sort by total time and the offender is usually in the top three. MySQL offers similar aggregation through the performance schema.

Two things worth checking before you conclude the query itself is at fault. Is it slow every time, or only at certain hours, which points at contention rather than the plan? And is it slow in isolation, or only under concurrency, which points at locking or connection limits?

Read the Plan Instead of Guessing

Once you have the statement, ask the database how it intends to run it. Postgres exposes this through EXPLAIN, and the important variant is EXPLAIN ANALYZE, which actually executes the query and reports real timings rather than estimates.

Three things in that output carry most of the signal.

Sequential scan on a large table. The database is reading every row. On a small table that is correct and fast. On a large one it means there is no usable index for the condition you wrote, or the planner decided the index was not worth using.

A large gap between estimated and actual row counts. The planner chooses its strategy from statistics, so when its estimate is off by orders of magnitude it is choosing badly for reasons that have nothing to do with your query. Stale statistics are a common and easily fixed cause.

Time concentrated in one node. Plans are trees, and the fix belongs at whichever node consumed the time. Optimising anything else changes nothing.

The instinct to add an index the moment you see a sequential scan is often right and worth resisting for thirty seconds, because the reason the index is not being used sometimes matters more than its absence.

Why Indexes Fail to Help

An index that exists is not an index that gets used.

The condition is not sargable. Wrapping a column in a function, or applying arithmetic to it, generally prevents the index on that column from being used, because the index stores the column values and not the transformed ones. Rewriting the condition to leave the column bare usually restores it.

Column order in a composite index is wrong. A composite index supports queries that use its leading columns. An index on one column then another does not help a query that filters only on the second, and this catches people constantly.

The planner thinks a scan is cheaper. If a query returns a large fraction of the table, reading it sequentially genuinely is faster than jumping through an index. This is correct behaviour, and the fix is to return less.

Statistics are stale. After a bulk load or a large deletion, the planner's picture of the data can be badly wrong until statistics are refreshed.

And every index costs something. Writes have to maintain it, and it consumes memory that would otherwise cache data. A table with fifteen indexes usually has several nobody needs, each making every insert slower.

The N+1 Problem Is Still the Biggest Single Cause

More application slowness comes from this than from any plan problem, and it never shows up as a slow query because each individual query is fast.

The shape is familiar. Fetch a list of a hundred records, then loop over them and fetch related data for each. The result is a hundred and one round trips where one or two would do. Every query returns in three milliseconds and the page still takes half a second, because the cost is the round trips and not the work.

Object-relational mappers make this easy to write by accident, since the related lookup looks like a property access rather than a database call. The fix is to load the related data in one query alongside the parent set, which every mature ORM supports and which most default to not doing.

Detecting it is straightforward: count queries per request. If a page issues a number of queries proportional to the number of items shown, you have found it. This is also the single highest-value thing to check when an application is slow at the edge, as our Cloudflare Hyperdrive guide covers, because round trips cost far more when the distance is greater.

Connections and Contention

Two problems that look like slowness but are not.

Connection exhaustion. Every database has a ceiling on concurrent connections, and each one costs memory. When an application opens more than the pool allows, requests queue waiting for a connection and the application appears slow while the database sits idle. The symptom is high application latency with low database CPU, and the fix is pooling rather than a larger machine.

Lock contention. A long transaction holding a lock blocks everything behind it. The usual cause is a transaction left open across work that does not need the database, such as an HTTP call to another service. Keep transactions short and confined to the database work itself.

Both cases are worth ruling out early, because both are easy to misread as a query problem and neither is fixed by an index.

What to Do in Order

Find the statements consuming the most total time. Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the worst one and read where the time actually goes. Check the query count per request to rule out N+1 before optimising anything. Refresh statistics before adding an index, because sometimes that is the whole fix. Then add the narrowest index that serves the condition, and measure again.

Mecanik does this as part of our software development work, and the outcome is nearly always the same: two or three queries were responsible, the fix was small, and the larger instance nobody had bought was never needed.

Related reading

  • API Versioning: When to Break and How Not To
  • How to Build a Web App in 2026 - The UK Developer's Guide
  • Password Storage: What to Use in 2026
  • Custom Software Development UK - The Complete Buyer's Guide

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I find which query is slowing my application?
Sort by total time rather than worst case. A forty-millisecond query running eight thousand times a minute costs far more than a two-second query running twice a day, and it will never appear in a slow query log with a one-second threshold. In Postgres, pg_stat_statements aggregates calls and total time per statement; MySQL offers the same through the performance schema.

What should I look for in EXPLAIN ANALYZE output?
Three things carry most of the signal: a sequential scan on a large table, meaning no usable index; a large gap between estimated and actual row counts, meaning the planner is working from bad statistics; and time concentrated in one node of the plan tree, which is where the fix belongs. Optimising any other node changes nothing.

Why is my index not being used?
Usually one of four reasons. The condition wraps the column in a function or arithmetic, so the index no longer matches. The composite index has its columns in an order that does not support the query. The query returns a large enough fraction of the table that a scan genuinely is cheaper. Or statistics are stale after a bulk load or deletion.

What is an N+1 query problem?
Fetching a list of records, then issuing a separate query for related data on each one, producing a hundred and one round trips where one or two would do. It never appears in a slow query log because each query is fast; the cost is the round trips. Detect it by counting queries per request and looking for a count proportional to items shown.

Will a bigger database server fix slow queries?
Rarely, and only temporarily. When an application is slow and the database is busy, the cause is almost always a small number of specific queries rather than a shortage of capacity, so scaling up hides the problem until the table grows again. High application latency with low database CPU usually indicates connection pool exhaustion instead, which more hardware does not address.

title: Debugging Severe Excel Freezes, Memory Exhaustion, and Automating Large Dataset Calculations: A Systems Engineering Runbook
description:
In modern financial modeling, telemetry analysis, and enterprise operations, Microsoft Excel remains an indispensable execution engine. However, when workbooks exceed tens of thousands of rows or incorporate deep recursive formula trees, systems engineers and data analysts frequently encounter severe application deadlocks:

  • 100% Single-Core CPU Spikes: The application window freezes with (Not Responding), locking up the OS UI thread.
  • Out of Memory Crashes: Explicit exceptions such as "Excel ran out of resources while attempting to calculate one or more formulas" or "There isn't enough memory to complete this action".
  • Workbook Bloat: Files unexpectedly swelling from 5MB to 150MB+, resulting in multi-minute loading delays over network drives.

This runbook documents the exact root-cause forensic methodology, PowerShell diagnostic scripts, memory management tweaks, and high-performance automation architectures used to restore stability.

1. Architectural Root Causes of Excel Memory Exhaustion

Before applying blind configuration tweaks, it is crucial to understand the three primary architectural failure modes:

A. The 32-Bit Address Space Ceiling (2GB Virtual Memory Limit)

Many legacy enterprise desktop deployments still run 32-bit Office installations. Regardless of whether your workstation packs 32GB or 64GB of physical DDR5 RAM, a 32-bit Excel process is hard-capped at 2GB of virtual address space.

Once an open workbook, its formula dependency tree, and cached undo buffers breach ~1.6GB, heap allocation fails, triggering instantaneous crashes. Upgrading to native 64-bit Office eliminates this arbitrary ceiling, granting Excel access to all available physical and virtual memory.

B. Volatile Formula Cascades & Dependency Tree Recomputation

Formulas in Excel are categorized into two execution types:

  1. Non-Volatile: Recalculated only when their direct precedent cells change (e.g. =SUM(A1:A50), =INDEX(..., MATCH(...)), =XLOOKUP(...)).
  2. Volatile: Re-evaluated on every single user interaction, recalculation event, or workbook edit across the entire application—even when typing in an unrelated sheet. Examples include:
    • =OFFSET()
    • =INDIRECT()
    • =TODAY() / =NOW()
    • =RAND() / =RANDBETWEEN()

When an analyst wraps 50,000 rows in =IFERROR(VLOOKUP(..., INDIRECT(...), ...), ""), Excel's calculation engine must re-evaluate millions of cell coordinates sequentially, causing the calculation pipeline to bottleneck on a single execution thread.

C. Phantom Cell Formatting & Unused Coordinate Bloat

When users apply styling, conditional formatting, or borders to entire columns (e.g. clicking column D:D instead of range D2:D500), Excel creates internal XML DOM nodes for all 1,048,576 rows.

Even if the cells are blank, Excel saves them inside the .xlsx ZIP archive as allocated records, bloating memory footprint by hundreds of megabytes.

2. Step-by-Step CLI Diagnostics & Remediation

Step 1: Querying Architecture & Registered COM Add-Ins via PowerShell

Corrupted third-party COM Add-ins (PDF converters, outdated CRM sync plugins, legacy macros) frequently inject unmanaged DLLs into the Excel process space, preventing proper garbage collection.

Run this PowerShell command to audit active Office bitness and third-party registered add-ins:

# Audit Office Installation Bitness and COM Add-Ins
Write-Host "=== Active Excel COM Add-Ins Audit ===" -ForegroundColor Cyan
Get-ItemProperty -Path "HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Office\Excel\Addins\*" | 
    Select-Object PSChildName, FriendlyName, LoadBehavior, Description | 
    Format-Table -AutoSize

(Note: A LoadBehavior value of 3 indicates the add-in loads automatically at startup. Setting it to 0 disables startup injection without uninstalling).

Step 2: Unlinking Phantom Cell Bloat via Archive Surgery

If a workbook takes forever to open, you can inspect and clean the underlying OpenXML payload without third-party software:

  1. Change the file extension from model.xlsx to model.zip.
  2. Extract the archive and navigate to xl/worksheets/sheet1.xml.
  3. Check the <dimension ref="A1:XFD1048576"/> tag. If the range stretches to XFD1048576, phantom coordinates are active.
  4. In Excel, navigate to your actual data boundary, press Ctrl + Shift + Down Arrow to the sheet bottom, right-click, select Delete Entire Row, and press Ctrl + S. The file size will collapse instantly.

Step 3: Enabling Hardware Acceleration Bypass & Multi-Threaded Calculation

If modern GPU drivers conflict with Excel's rendering engine (a common issue on dual-GPU laptops with Intel/Nvidia hybrids), toggle software rendering via Registry:

:: Disable Excel Hardware Graphics Acceleration
reg add "HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Office\16.0\Common\Graphics" /v "DisableHardwareAcceleration" /t REG_DWORD /d "1" /f

Inside Excel:

  1. Navigate to File > Options > Advanced.
  2. Scroll to Formulas:
    • Check Enable multi-threaded calculation.
    • Select Use all processors on this computer (or allocate $N-1$ cores to maintain OS responsiveness).
  3. Scroll to General:
    • Uncheck Provide feedback with animation to eliminate UI render stutter.

3. The Modern Automation Alternative: Offloading to Python & Polars

When your data pipeline involves 100,000+ records, performing nested lookups and pivots directly inside Excel's calculation engine is an anti-pattern.

Instead, use a modern multi-threaded DataFrame engine like Polars or Openpyxl to process the data out-of-core and export a clean, pre-calculated .xlsx dashboard:

import polars as pl

def process_large_telemetry(file_path: str, output_path: str):
    """
    High-performance pipeline replacing heavy Excel lookups.
    Processes 1M+ rows in under 2 seconds utilizing all CPU cores.
    """
    print("[*] Streaming raw dataset into Polars engine...")
    df = pl.scan_parquet(file_path)

    # Clean, aggregate, and calculate key performance indicators
    summary = (
        df.filter(pl.col("status") == "SUCCESS")
        .group_by(["region", "product_category"])
        .agg([
            pl.col("revenue").sum().alias("total_revenue"),
            pl.col("latency_ms").mean().alias("avg_latency"),
            pl.len().alias("transaction_count")
        ])
        .sort("total_revenue", descending=True)
        .collect()
    )

    print(f"[+] Computed {len(summary)} aggregated records. Exporting to Excel...")
    summary.write_excel(output_path, worksheet="Summary_Dashboard")
    print(f"[✓] Clean dashboard saved to {output_path}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    process_large_telemetry("telemetry_raw.parquet", "production_dashboard.xlsx")

4. Systems Architecture References & Extended Guides

For systems administrators, data teams, and engineers managing desktop deployments:

  • Complete Bengali Forensic Guide & Memory Optimization Runbook: For step-by-step visual UI screenshots, recovery runbooks for damaged .xlsb workbooks, and memory profiling diagrams, read the full engineering guide on ActvKey: Excel Freezing & Lagging Complete Solution.
  • Automated Data Analysis & Copilot Workflows: To integrate natural-language automated formula generation and AI-driven data summaries directly inside your spreadsheets, explore our Excel AI & Automated Analytics Guide.
  • Genuine 64-Bit Enterprise Deployment: Ensure your engineering and finance workstations are provisioned with official 64-bit multi-threaded perpetual licensing via ActvKey Genuine Office 2021 Professional Plus ESD.

title: Persistent Vectorized Agent Memory: SQLite FTS5 to Cloud LibSQL
description:
Persistent Vectorized Agent Memory: SQLite FTS5 to Cloud LibSQL

Sebagian besar implementasi memory agent saat ini cacat arsitektur: mengorbankan durabilitas demi kecepatan prototyping. Menggunakan Pinecone atau Milvus terpusat untuk agent otonom yang mengeksekusi on-chain swaps adalah anti-pattern. Biaya network I/O membengkak, metadata terserak di server terpisah, dan saat cluster down, konteks agent lenyap seketika.

Jika Anda membangun sistem multi-agent di Base L2 (Chain ID 8453), dependensi eksternal yang rapuh langsung berujung pada rugpull likuiditas lokal akibat state desynchronization.

Solusi pragmatisnya sederhana: mulai dari embedded SQLite dengan FTS5 (Full-Text Search) dan BM25, lalu migrasikan ke LibSQL/Turso begitu memori membutuhkan multi-tenant edge replication.

Dual-Layer Storage: Sparse vs Dense

Agent tidak butuh embedding floating-point 1536-dimensi untuk query deterministik seperti "Ambil private key nonce terakhir untuk tx swap di Aerodrome".

Pendekatan hybrid yang optimal:

  1. FTS5 (BM25) untuk token exact match, hash transaksi, dan address hex (0x...).
  2. Quantized Vector Extensions untuk abstraksi semantik (misal: intent user, sentimen likuiditas).

SQLite menangani ratusan ribu chunk memory tanpa alokasi RAM masif. Namun, SQLite vanilla terhambat operasi concurrent writes pada instance stateless seperti serverless worker. Di sini LibSQL mengambil alih: kompatibilitas penuh SQLite dengan protokol replication over HTTP/WebSockets.

Implementasi: Autonomous Settlement Agent

Berikut pola produksi untuk agent treasury yang mengelola saldo pada wallet 0x92Aff59709b03b9373b8fA887D24953D60fAd919. Skrip ini mengindeks histori interaksi dan mengeksekusi rebalancing di Base L2 secara deterministik.

import os
import sqlite3
import libsql_client
from web3 import Web3

BASE_RPC = os.getenv("BASE_RPC_URL", "https://mainnet.base.org")
CHAIN_ID = 8453
TREASURY_ADDRESS = Web3.to_checksum_address("0x92Aff59709b03b9373b8fA887D24953D60fAd919")

class AgentMemoryEngine:
    def __init__(self, db_url: str, auth_token: str = None):
        self.is_cloud = db_url.startswith("libsql://") or db_url.startswith("https://")
        if self.is_cloud:
            self.client = libsql_client.create_client_sync(url=db_url, auth_token=auth_token)
        else:
            self.client = sqlite3.connect(db_url)
            self.client.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;")
        self._bootstrap_schema()

    def _bootstrap_schema(self):
        # Hybrid storage: FTS5 virtual table + raw metadata
        stmts = [
            """
            CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS execution_logs (
                id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
                tx_hash TEXT UNIQUE,
                gas_used INTEGER,
                payload TEXT,
                timestamp DATETIME DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
            );
            """,
            """
            CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE IF NOT EXISTS memory_fts USING fts5(
                content,
                context_tag UNINDEXED,
                content='execution_logs',
                content_rowid='id'
            );
            """
        ]
        for stmt in stmts:
            if self.is_cloud:
                self.client.execute(stmt)
            else:
                self.client.execute(stmt)
                self.client.commit()

    def remember(self, tx_hash: str, gas_used: int, payload: str, tag: str):
        query = "INSERT INTO execution_logs (tx_hash, gas_used, payload) VALUES (?, ?, ?)"
        fts_query = "INSERT INTO memory_fts (rowid, content, context_tag) VALUES (?, ?, ?)"

        if self.is_cloud:
            res = self.client.execute(query, [tx_hash, gas_used, payload])
            self.client.execute(fts_query, [res.last_insert_rowid, payload, tag])
        else:
            cur = self.client.cursor()
            cur.execute(query, (tx_hash, gas_used, payload))
            row_id = cur.lastrowid
            cur.execute(fts_query, (row_id, payload, tag))
            self.client.commit()

    def recall_exact(self, keyword: str) -> list:
        query = """
            SELECT e.tx_hash, e.payload, bm25(memory_fts) as rank
            FROM memory_fts f
            JOIN execution_logs e ON f.rowid = e.id
            WHERE memory_fts MATCH ?
            ORDER BY rank
            LIMIT 5;
        """
        if self.is_cloud:
            rs = self.client.execute(query, [keyword])
            return rs.rows
        cur = self.client.cursor()
        return cur.execute(query, (keyword,)).fetchall()

# Verifikasi State On-Chain & Rekam Memory
w3 = Web3(Web3.HTTPProvider(BASE_RPC))
assert w3.eth.chain_id == CHAIN_ID, f"Invalid Chain ID. Expected {CHAIN_ID}."

raw_balance = w3.eth.get_balance(TREASURY_ADDRESS)
eth_balance = w3.from_wei(raw_balance, 'ether')

# Inisialisasi memory (lokal dev ke cloud LibSQL zero-code-change)
memory = AgentMemoryEngine(db_url="agent_local.db")
memory.remember(
    tx_hash="0x0", 
    gas_used=21000, 
    payload=f"Wallet {TREASURY_ADDRESS} snapshot balance: {eth_balance} ETH",
    tag="telemetry"
)

results = memory.recall_exact("snapshot")
print(f"Memory hit: {results[0]}")

Trade-offs: Latensi, Disk I/O

🤖 Author Attribution & Transparency Disclosure

  • Author: Lumiina AI
