title: Conformally Calibrated Adaptive Computation in Neural Operators
description:
arXiv:2611.23440v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Selecting less computation in a neural operator need not reduce inference time. We study this gap using conformal calibration to choose Fourier modes or channel width per input subject to a fixed error budget. A triangle-inequality envelope bounds all candidates simultaneously; a direct-score rule handles non-monotone candidate errors and, with an input-independent score, calibrates a static baseline under the same marginal guarantee. Under frozen-model and exchangeability assumptions, both rules bound the probability of issuing a prediction outside the budget and abstain when calibration is infeasible. On Burgers and Darcy flow across three training seeds, mode selection reduces active spectral support without a measurable latency reduction, because full-grid transforms and channel mixing dominate the cost. Narrowing channels does reduce Darcy forward cost, but reference-based selection must first compute the dense prediction. An input-only binary width selector avoids that pass and runs at 0.52-0.95 times dense latency; yet static widths calibrated under the same rule are often as fast or faster, and on a separately generated 1,000-example test set they generally achieve higher coverage, while the selector falls below its 90% target in more than half of the settings. Adaptive computation in neural operators should therefore be judged by achieved coverage and complete runtime against a matched static comparator.

title: AWS us-east-1 Outage on November 15, 2026: What Happened to Sign-In and Network Load Balancers, and How to Design Around It
description:
On November 15, 2026, AWS reported connectivity issues in us-east-1 from 3:05 AM to 6:21 AM PST that affected 11 services, including IAM Identity Center sign-in and Elastic Load Balancing, where a subset of Network Load Balancers in a single cell of use1-az1 was affected. AWS has not published a root cause. The design lessons are to keep a break-glass sign-in path that does not depend on single sign-on, to spread load balancer targets across multiple Availability Zones, and to keep workloads already running in a second region.

Disclosure: Control Plane publishes this guide.

TL;DR

On Sunday, November 15, 2026, AWS us-east-1 had increased connectivity issues for 3 hours and 16 minutes, from the start time AWS gave (3:05 AM PST) to the last recovery (6:21 AM PST), according to the AWS Health Dashboard.

  • IAM Identity Center and AWS Sign Up were among 11 affected services, which also included Elastic Load Balancing, where a subset of Network Load Balancers (NLBs) in a single cell of use1-az1 was affected.
  • AWS fully mitigated the authentication issue at 5:20 AM PST. The NLB subset recovered last, at 6:21 AM PST.
  • AWS’s updates do not mention a cyberattack.
  • When IAM Identity Center sign-in fails, responders lose SSO access to the console and CLI, which slows incident response.
  • NLB nodes route to targets in their own Availability Zone by default, so targets in a single zone fail with that zone.
  • A second region that already serves traffic keeps users served when one region is impaired.
  • On Control Plane, a workload runs in every location of its Global Virtual Cloud (GVC), Control Plane’s set of locations across clouds, so when it runs in two or more locations and one fails, users are routed to the healthy ones.

What happened in AWS us-east-1 on November 15, 2026?

AWS gave these times in its resolved update on the AWS Health Dashboard, posted at 6:53 AM PST.

Time (PST) What AWS reported
3:05 AM Start of signup errors, authentication issues, and connectivity issues in us-east-1, per AWS’s resolved update. AWS lists 11 affected services, including IAM Identity Center and AWS Sign Up.
4:38 AM AWS posts its first update.
5:20 AM AWS fully mitigated the issue affecting authentication, and most AWS services observed full recovery.
6:10 AM End of the event window given in AWS’s resolved update.
6:21 AM AWS fully mitigated the underlying issue for a subset of customers using NLB in a single cell in use1-az1.
6:53 AM AWS posts its resolved update.

AWS’s resolved update gives 3:05 AM to 6:10 AM as the event window, and the same update says a subset of customers using NLBs in a single cell of use1-az1 had connectivity issues until 6:21 AM, 11 minutes later.

The 11 services AWS listed are IoT Device Management, CloudWatch, Connect, OpenSearch, Elastic Load Balancing, IAM Identity Center, Kiro, NAT Gateway, Sign Up, Step Functions, and VPC Lattice.

Why did a sign-in outage matter so much?

IAM Identity Center is the sign-in path for many organizations that use AWS single sign-on. When it is unavailable, engineers cannot use SSO to open the AWS Management Console. CLI sessions that depend on SSO-issued credentials cannot be refreshed. Credentials already issued keep working until they expire. The people who need to respond to an incident lose their usual way in.

An organization instance of IAM Identity Center is enabled in one primary Region. If that Region has a disruption, SSO access to accounts can be affected even when the workloads in those accounts run elsewhere. AWS supports replicating an organization instance to additional Regions so workforce users can keep reaching their AWS accounts, with permissions provisioned before the disruption, if the primary Region is disrupted. Replication needs a multi-Region customer managed KMS key and is not available with an Active Directory identity source. Management access and workload health are separate concerns, and each needs its own fallback.

AWS documentation recommends setting up emergency access to the console before a disruption occurs. One option is direct federation from your external identity provider to individual AWS accounts. Another is break-glass access that does not depend on that identity provider. AWS also recommends testing the configuration periodically, because you cannot create the required IAM roles if your access to create them is also disrupted.

On-call engineers often learn about an incident from alerts and then need to sign in to investigate. If sign-in fails, escalation steps that assume console access stall. Runbooks that fetch SSO tokens stall too.

This table maps each failure type to what it blocks and a workaround that does not depend on the failing component.

Failure What it blocks Workaround that does not depend on it
IAM Identity Center sign-in down New console and CLI sign-ins through SSO, so engineers cannot sign in to respond Emergency access through direct IAM federation, break-glass IAM users or roles with strong MFA, or a replicated IAM Identity Center instance in a second Region, set up and tested in advance
NLB cell in one AZ impaired Traffic to targets behind that NLB in that zone Targets registered in multiple AZs, or a new NLB with targets in multiple AZs as AWS advised
A regional service in us-east-1 impaired Anything homed only in that region Workloads already running in a second region, with DNS failover configured
Status and alerting hosted in the same region You cannot see or announce the incident Status page and alerting hosted outside the failing region

Authentication, load balancing, regional placement, and communication are four failure domains, and each needs a fallback that does not share the others’ dependencies.

What does a single-cell Network Load Balancer failure mean for your architecture?

AWS reported that a subset of customers using NLB in a single cell in use1-az1 had connectivity issues until 6:21 AM PST. Two AWS behaviors explain why that matters.

The first is how Availability Zones are named. An AZ ID such as use1-az1 identifies the same physical zone in every AWS account. Zone names such as us-east-1a are mapped randomly per account, so us-east-1a in one account may be a different physical zone from us-east-1a in another. To check whether your resources sat in the affected zone, compare AZ IDs. The VPC console shows the AZ ID for each subnet, and the AWS CLI describe-availability-zones command returns the mapping for your account.

The second is how Network Load Balancers route traffic. By default, each NLB node distributes traffic only across the registered targets in its own Availability Zone. Cross-zone load balancing is off by default for NLBs. You can turn it on at the load balancer level or per target group. AWS documentation states that an NLB is most effective when each enabled Availability Zone has at least one registered target.

The NLB has one IP address per enabled Availability Zone, and its DNS name resolves to those addresses. If the node in one zone is impaired and that zone holds your only targets, traffic to those targets stops. Healthy instances in other zones do not receive it unless they are registered and reachable through a working node.

AWS recommended that customers who needed immediate resolution create a new NLB with targets in multiple Availability Zones, and later recommended retrying any failed requests. Acting on that advice during an incident requires three things. You already have capacity running in other zones. You can update DNS records or upstream references quickly. You can sign in to make the change. The sign-in issue earlier in the same morning shows why the third point needs its own plan.

Register NLB targets in at least two Availability Zones. Decide per workload whether to turn on cross-zone load balancing. Watch target health and zonal health per zone so a zonal problem shows up before users report it. For an NLB with targets in more than one zone, you can turn on zonal shift and use it to move traffic away from one zone. Zonal shift is off by default.

How do you prepare for the next us-east-1 incident?

This checklist covers the six areas this incident touched, with a way to test each one.

Area What to have in place How to test it
Break-glass access Emergency access configured before any disruption, through direct IAM federation, break-glass IAM users or roles with strong MFA that do not depend on IAM Identity Center, or a replicated IAM Identity Center instance in a second Region Run a periodic sign-in drill using only the emergency path
Multi-AZ NLB targets and cross-zone settings Targets registered in two or more AZs for every NLB, with cross-zone load balancing set per workload Deregister targets in one AZ in a test environment and confirm traffic still reaches the others
A second region already serving traffic At least one more region running the workload and receiving production traffic Route part of real traffic to the second region on a schedule and confirm end-to-end behavior
DNS failover with health checks Route 53 health checks on endpoints in each region, with failover records and TTLs short enough for your recovery target Fail a health check on purpose and confirm DNS resolves to the healthy region
Status page and alerting outside the failing region Incident communication and alert pipelines hosted in another region or with a provider that does not depend on us-east-1 Send a test alert while simulating loss of us-east-1 and confirm it reaches on-call
Runbooks that do not need SSO Recovery steps that use the emergency access path and pre-provisioned resources Walk each runbook in a tabletop exercise without SSO

Route 53 health checks can monitor endpoints, and DNS failover records route traffic away from an endpoint that fails its check. Configure health checks and failover records in advance, because editing Route 53 records depends on Route 53’s management API in us-east-1. Failover only helps if the second region already has capacity and data it can serve. Schedule each drill in the checklist so every runbook has run at least once before an incident.

How does this compare with other cloud outages?

The November 15, 2026 incident lasted 3 hours and 16 minutes.

The cloud outage tracker records 63 major AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and Cloudflare incidents since January 2020, with a median duration of 5 hours and 57 minutes. By that measure, this incident was shorter than the median major incident across those providers.

Regional incidents happen on every large cloud. The useful response is design work: separate the sign-in path from the workload path, spread capacity across zones, and run in more than one region before you need to. Designing systems that survive the inevitable covers those patterns in more depth.

How Control Plane fits

Control Plane handles Day 2 operations for you, including autoscaling, built-in observability, and security. A Global Virtual Cloud (GVC) is Control Plane’s named set of locations across AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure regions, plus Kubernetes clusters you already run and your own servers. A workload runs in every location of its GVC, and by default every location serves traffic. When a workload runs in two or more locations and one fails, DNS routes users to the nearest location where the workload passes its readiness probes.

During the October 19 to 20, 2025 AWS us-east-1 outage, which lasted about 14 and a half hours, 20% of Control Plane customers had AWS us-east-1 in their GVC. Their workloads were active and running in healthy locations within 10 seconds, with no customer downtime, according to Control Plane’s internal incident telemetry. Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant.

Control Plane runs the workloads you deploy on it. It does not change how third-party SaaS, identity providers, or other organizations’ networks behave, so the break-glass and sign-in steps for AWS access still apply. For more on regional failures, read how companies stay online during AWS us-east-1 outages and how to keep your app online during an AWS region outage.

FAQ

These answers cover sign-in, load balancing, and regional design after the November 15, 2026 us-east-1 incident.

What happened to AWS us-east-1 on November 15, 2026?

AWS reported increased connectivity issues in us-east-1 from 3:05 AM to 6:21 AM PST, according to the AWS Health Dashboard. The incident affected 11 services, including IAM Identity Center sign-in and Elastic Load Balancing, where a subset of Network Load Balancers in a single cell of use1-az1 was affected. That NLB subset recovered last.

Was the November 15 AWS outage a cyberattack?

AWS’s updates do not mention a cyberattack. AWS described the event as increased connectivity issues.

How do I sign in to AWS when IAM Identity Center is down?

Use an access path you set up before the disruption. AWS documents replicating IAM Identity Center to an additional Region, direct IAM federation from your external identity provider to individual accounts, and break-glass access that does not depend on that identity provider. AWS recommends testing the setup periodically.

What is a break-glass account in AWS?

A break-glass account is an emergency IAM user or role, protected with strong MFA, that you use when normal sign-in paths such as IAM Identity Center are unavailable. Keep its credentials stored securely, limit who can use it, and test it on a schedule.

Are Network Load Balancers multi-AZ?

An NLB can span multiple Availability Zones, but by default each NLB node routes only to targets in its own zone. Cross-zone load balancing is off by default. Register targets in every enabled zone so the loss of one zone does not stop traffic.

What does use1-az1 mean?

use1-az1 is an Availability Zone ID in us-east-1 that refers to the same physical zone in every AWS account. Zone names such as us-east-1a are mapped randomly per account. Compare AZ IDs to check whether your resources were in the affected zone.

How do companies stay online during AWS us-east-1 outages?

They run workloads in at least two regions and use DNS failover with health checks to move traffic to the healthy region. They also keep an emergency sign-in path that does not depend on a single identity service. Status pages and alerting run outside the region they monitor.

Did AWS publish a root cause for the November 15 outage?

No. As of November 18, 2026, AWS has not published a root cause for the November 15 us-east-1 incident.

How long did the November 15, 2026 AWS outage last?

It lasted 3 hours and 16 minutes, from the start time AWS gave (3:05 AM PST) to the last recovery (6:21 AM PST). AWS’s resolved update lists 3:05 AM to 6:10 AM as the event window and reports that the NLB subset in use1-az1 had connectivity issues until 6:21 AM.

Should I move all my workloads out of us-east-1?

No. Run critical workloads in us-east-1 and at least one other region at the same time, with DNS failover and an independent sign-in path. A disruption in one region then affects a share of capacity, and the rest keeps serving.

title: Node.js Daily Property Changelog Watcher with 4 Incident Controls
description:
Run the watcher once a day, but page nobody merely because the page bytes changed. Fetch conditionally, extract only the changelog entries, compute a deterministic structural diff, and send a notification only after the new text passes a semantic near-duplicate check against recent property-management records. Keep the old snapshot until the notification succeeds. That is the decision rule.

TL;DR: treat scraping, change detection, semantic retrieval, and delivery as four separate incident controls. A fetch failure is not "no change," a rearranged navigation bar is not a new release, a high vector score is not proof that two records mean the same thing, and a successful diff is not useful if the notification disappears. The page that should fire is the one for a sustained inability to observe the source, not every ordinary content edit.

This design fits a Node.js service even though the reference implementation below is Go, because the important boundaries are HTTP semantics and persisted records rather than a framework-specific scheduler. The worker can be invoked by a Node.js cron process, a system timer, or a job queue; the same run contract applies: one source, one bounded execution, one durable outcome.

How should Node.js scrape a changelog page daily and notify safely?

Start with the failure modes, because they determine the state machine. If yesterday's fetch returned 200, today's request times out, and the worker records an empty body as the new baseline, tomorrow's successful request looks like a complete rewrite. If a consent banner changes on every request, a raw HTML hash creates daily noise. If notification delivery fails after the baseline advances, the only meaningful change is silently consumed.

Those are different incidents.

A useful run record therefore distinguishes unchanged, changed_and_sent, fetch_failed, parse_failed, and send_failed. Page on repeated inability to fetch or parse, because freshness is now unknown. Route a delivery failure to a retryable operational alert. Do not page on unchanged, and do not make every detected edit urgent; a changelog notification is usually work for daylight hours. Consider the concrete failure chain: a scheduled run starts, the origin stalls until the 45-second worker deadline, a careless implementation replaces the prior snapshot with an empty value, and the next healthy response appears to add every historical notice at once; retrieval then spends its latency budget comparing false additions, the delivery channel emits a wall of duplicates, and the on-call engineer receives a page for damage created inside the watcher. Preserving the accepted snapshot on every non-success path breaks that chain at its first link.

The scrape must also identify itself with a stable User-Agent, honor the site's access policy and terms, use a timeout, and avoid overlapping runs. Conditional requests make that courtesy concrete: send the stored ETag in If-None-Match and the stored modification time in If-Modified-Since. An origin may answer 304 Not Modified, but validators are optimizations, not the durable truth; the extracted canonical content remains the comparison boundary.

What page fired? It should be source_observation_stale, carrying the last successful observation time, consecutive failure count, and source identifier. A dashboard full of request counts will not answer whether the property operations team missed a policy change.

No page for ordinary edits.

Build a stable diff before asking for semantic similarity

HTML is presentation, so hash a canonical representation of the entries rather than the response body. Select the smallest stable container that owns the changelog, remove scripts, styles, navigation, timestamps such as "last viewed," and normalize whitespace. Preserve entry order only when order conveys recency. Store both the raw response and canonical text for a limited retention period so a parser regression can be investigated without immediately fetching a moving source again.

The structural diff is the first gate. Exact equality ends the run cheaply and predictably. Added or modified entries continue to retrieval, where each candidate is compared with a bounded window of recent records such as property notices, maintenance advisories, and lease-policy updates. Retrieval-augmented generation joins retrieved external context to generation; the useful idea here is narrower: retrieval supplies possible prior matches, while deterministic policy decides whether to notify. No generator belongs in the critical path unless the notification genuinely needs a summary.

A vector score is a ranking signal, not a universal meaning threshold. Embedding model, text length, chunking, and corpus all affect the score distribution. Calibrate on labeled pairs from this domain: duplicate wording, materially changed dates, different buildings with similar maintenance language, and unrelated notices that share boilerplate. The choice is explicit. A wider candidate set can improve recall but raises latency and creates more opportunities for false matches; a smaller set returns faster but may miss an older duplicate. Measure both on the same frozen evaluation set before changing the cutoff or candidate count.

This approach has limitations. It is a poor fit for a page that requires an interactive browser challenge, for a source whose terms prohibit automated access, or for a feed where every update must be acted on in seconds; use an authorized feed or publisher-supplied webhook in those cases. Daily polling also cannot prove that it observed a short-lived edit between runs, while semantic suppression can hide a meaningful change when protected fields are incomplete. The trade-off is acceptable only when the team can tolerate that observation interval and can route uncertain matches to review.

The four controls should leave these artifacts:

Control Durable input Success evidence Failure action
Fetch URL plus validators status and response hash retain baseline; retry
Extract raw response plus parser version canonical content hash retain baseline; alert after recurrence
Compare new entries plus retrieval corpus version candidates, scores, decision quarantine uncertain cases
Notify decision plus idempotency key delivery receipt retry without advancing baseline

Notice the order. Retrieval quality cannot rescue an unstable extractor, and a low-latency similarity query cannot compensate for losing the event after a delivery timeout.

Implement the run as a transactional handoff

Use a lease so two daily invocations cannot race. Persist a source record containing validators, the accepted canonical hash, snapshot location, last success time, and parser version. Persist notification attempts separately with an idempotency key derived from the source, canonical hash, and destination. The baseline advances only in the same durable transition that records successful delivery, or after an operator explicitly accepts a quarantined change.

The following Go sketch shows the control flow without binding the design to a scraping library, vector database, or messaging provider. A Node.js scheduler can execute this worker as a subprocess and treat its exit status as the run outcome; production implementations should back Store with transactions rather than process memory.

package watcher

import (
    "context"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "errors"
    "time"
)

type Snapshot struct {
    ETag, LastModified, Canonical, Hash string
}

type Candidate struct {
    ID    string
    Score float64
}

type Fetcher interface {
    Fetch(context.Context, string, Snapshot) (body []byte, next Snapshot, notModified bool, err error)
}

type Extractor interface {
    Canonicalize([]byte) (string, error)
}

type Retriever interface {
    Nearest(context.Context, string, int) ([]Candidate, error)
}

type Notifier interface {
    Send(context.Context, string, string) error
}

type Store interface {
    Load(context.Context, string) (Snapshot, error)
    CommitDelivered(context.Context, string, Snapshot, string) error
}

func Run(ctx context.Context, source string, f Fetcher, x Extractor, r Retriever, n Notifier, s Store) error {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 45*time.Second)
    defer cancel()

    old, err := s.Load(ctx, source)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    body, next, unchanged, err := f.Fetch(ctx, source, old)
    if err != nil {
        return err // Preserve the accepted baseline.
    }
    if unchanged {
        return nil
    }

    canonical, err := x.Canonicalize(body)
    if err != nil || canonical == "" {
        return errors.New("canonical extraction failed")
    }
    sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(canonical))
    next.Canonical, next.Hash = canonical, hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])
    if next.Hash == old.Hash {
        return nil
    }

    candidates, err := r.Nearest(ctx, canonical, 8)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    message := RenderDecision(canonical, candidates)
    key := source + ":" + next.Hash
    if err := n.Send(ctx, key, message); err != nil {
        return err // Retry with the same key; do not consume the change.
    }
    return s.CommitDelivered(ctx, source, next, key)
}

RenderDecision should apply a versioned policy, not improvise from a single score. For example, it can suppress a candidate only when calibrated similarity is above the reviewed threshold and protected fields such as property identifier, effective date, and notice type agree. A record saying "water shutoff on May 12" must not collapse into "water shutoff on May 19" because most tokens match. Put uncertain pairs in a review queue, and include the source excerpt and prior candidate in the notification so a human can verify the claim.

There is a small but important state issue in the sketch: if delivery succeeds and the commit fails, the next run may send again. The stable idempotency key makes that retry harmless only if the notifier enforces idempotency. If it cannot, persist an outbox row transactionally with the new snapshot, let a separate dispatcher deliver it, and mark the row sent after acknowledgment. This is the familiar transactional outbox boundary, and it is preferable to pretending a network call and a database commit are atomic.

Verify retrieval quality without hiding latency

Build a labeled corpus before tuning. For property management, include exact reposts, paraphrased maintenance notices, template-heavy notices for different buildings, date-only changes, unit-specific exceptions, and genuinely unrelated records. Split by time so near-identical records from one incident do not leak across training and evaluation. Report precision and recall at the actual operating threshold, then report p50, p95, and p99 end-to-end latency separately for fetch, extraction, retrieval, and notification.

No invented target helps here. The acceptable false-negative rate depends on what the notice controls, while the latency budget depends on the daily workflow. A legal-policy change may favor recall and human review; a low-impact amenity reminder may favor precision to prevent alert fatigue. Choose the threshold from labeled consequences, not from a pleasing round similarity score.

Fast is secondary.

Test the ugly paths. Replay a 304, a timeout, malformed HTML, a selector returning an empty string, reordered entries, duplicated delivery, retrieval unavailability, and a commit failure after delivery. Save fixtures from pages you are authorized to retain, strip personal data, and pin the parser version in every result. A canary run can execute a new extractor against the same stored responses without changing production state.

For observability, emit one structured run event with a correlation ID and stage durations, plus counters by terminal outcome. Track the age of the last successful canonical observation. That age is closer to the user-visible risk than a green process heartbeat.

Roll back the parser, policy, and corpus independently

Deploy extraction and semantic policy as separate versions. During a parser change, dual-run old and new extraction against stored raw responses and compare canonical hashes. During a threshold or embedding change, shadow the new policy on labeled and recent production candidates, record decisions without notifying, and inspect disagreements. Do not overwrite the old vectors until the new index is complete and queryable.

Rollback is then mechanical: stop the schedule, select the last accepted parser and policy versions, point retrieval at the prior complete corpus, and replay from the last delivered canonical hash. Keep notification idempotency keys through the entire replay window. If the source itself made a legitimate large rewrite, quarantine it for review rather than teaching the extractor to ignore broad changes.

Four independent controls make the watcher boring in the useful sense. The daily schedule is incidental; correctness comes from preserving evidence, separating failures, calibrating semantic decisions on property-specific records, and refusing to advance state before the change is durably delivered.

  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.html
  • https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/

title: Ampersand from Humans& now available on AI Gateway
description:
Ampersand from Humans& is now available on AI Gateway for free through November 13, 2026.

Ampersand is a model for group conversations. Humans& built Ampersand on Z.ai's open-weight GLM 5.3 and trained it with reinforcement learning in simulated group conversations that run for up to months of simulated time. Most chat models are built for one person asking a question and the model answering it. Ampersand is trained to take part in a conversation between several people. It reads every message, including the ones not addressed to it, and after each one it decides whether to reply or stay quiet.

It is designed to understand individual and shared goals, help people work through disagreements, and recognize when a contribution would be useful. That can mean asking a clarifying question, sharing relevant context, or waiting while people respond to one another.

For example:

Sam: Heads up, I'm out Friday, driving to my sister's. Alex: Have a good trip! Maya: Let's do the launch rehearsal Friday at 10 with all three of us. Ampersand: Quick flag, Maya: Sam said he's out Friday driving to his sister's, so a Friday 10am rehearsal with all three probably won't work. Might be worth picking a different time so everyone can make it.

Your application exposes these actions as caller-defined function tools. send_message delivers a contribution, while pass leaves the conversation quiet until the next human message. Your application executes both tools and records their results.

Call it through the AI SDK, the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API, or a coding agent. Use humansand/ampersand-v0.1 as the model name:

To use it in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and more, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup:

Then select humansand/ampersand-v0.1 in the agent. See the coding agents guide for details.

Try Ampersand in the model playground.

title: Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) no Jenkins: como mitigar e corrigir
description:
A vulnerabilidade Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) pode permitir execução remota de código antes da autenticação em controladores e agentes Jenkins quando o runtime e o processador atendem a requisitos específicos. Como o código vulnerável está no JDK usado pelo Jenkins, atualizar apenas o aplicativo não elimina a falha.

Quando o Jenkins fica exposto

São necessárias duas condições: uma versão afetada do OpenJDK — linha 17 a partir da 17.0.6 ou as linhas 21, 25 e 27 — e uma CPU com as instruções AVX-512 VBMI usadas pela intrínseca de decodificação Base64. Processadores recentes, como Intel Ice Lake ou posterior e AMD Zen 4 ou posterior, podem atender ao requisito.

O comando abaixo verifica no host as quatro flags relevantes. A presença de todas indica que o processador pode executar o caminho vulnerável; também é preciso confirmar qual versão do JDK está rodando com o Jenkins. Sistemas ARM64, como Graviton, e CPUs sem todas as flags ficam fora desse cenário.

grep -oE '(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)' /proc/cpuinfo | sort -u

Confira o JDK e a intrínseca

Em uma instalação com a imagem oficial, consulte a versão do Java diretamente no contêiner. As compilações Temurin 25.0.5+8 e 21.0.13+9 ainda são afetadas; as versões corrigidas começam em 25.0.5.1+2, 21.0.13.1+2 e 17.0.21.1+2. Compare a versão completa: um quarto campo numérico, por si só, não comprova a correção.

docker run --rm --entrypoint java jenkins/jenkins:lts-jdk25 -version

Para verificar o estado da intrínseca em um contêiner em execução, localize o PID do Jenkins e consulte a flag da JVM. O PID 7 foi usado no ambiente de teste; substitua-o pelo PID encontrado na sua instalação.

docker exec jenkins ps -eo pid,args
docker exec jenkins jcmd 7 VM.flags -all | grep UseBASE64Intrinsics

Antes da mitigação, UseBASE64Intrinsics pode aparecer como habilitada por padrão. Depois de aplicar a opção temporária e reiniciar o controlador, a consulta deve mostrar a flag desabilitada, com origem na linha de comando.

Mitigue até instalar o JDK corrigido

Enquanto a atualização não estiver disponível, desative a intrínseca vulnerável com -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics e reinicie o controlador para aplicar a opção. Em contêineres, passe-a por JAVA_OPTS; na instalação pelo chart oficial do Helm, acrescente-a a controller.javaOpts, sem apagar outras opções já definidas.

docker run -d --name jenkins -p 8080:8080 -p 50000:50000 \
-v jenkins_home:/var/jenkins_home \
-e JAVA_OPTS="-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics" \
jenkins/jenkins:lts-jdk21
controller:
javaOpts: "-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics"

Em instalações Debian ou Ubuntu, o serviço usa o JDK instalado pelo sistema e gerencia os argumentos da JVM com systemd. O drop-in abaixo preserva a opção headless; inclua também quaisquer outras opções que sua unidade já use, pois a linha substitui o valor de JAVA_OPTS.

sudo systemctl edit jenkins
[Service]
Environment="JAVA_OPTS=-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics -Djava.awt.headless=true"
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart jenkins

Atualize o runtime e confirme a correção

A correção definitiva é instalar uma compilação OpenJDK corrigida e reiniciar o Jenkins. As atualizações chegaram ao Ubuntu em 18 de novembro de 2026; em 19 de novembro, no Debian, as versões corrigidas estavam disponíveis apenas no sid. Em outras versões Debian, mantenha a mitigação temporária até a atualização do pacote.

No Ubuntu, atualize o runtime usado pelo Jenkins e repita a verificação para outros pacotes OpenJDK instalados, se houver. Confira tanto o pacote quanto a versão informada pelo Java antes de retirar a mitigação temporária.

dpkg -l 'openjdk-*'
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install --only-upgrade openjdk-21-jre-headless
dpkg -l openjdk-21-jre-headless | tail -1
sudo -u jenkins java -version

Em um JDK corrigido, UseBASE64Intrinsics pode continuar habilitada: o patch corrige a intrínseca, em vez de desativá-la. Portanto, confirme a correção pela versão instalada, não pelo estado da flag; depois, remova a opção temporária, que pode reduzir o desempenho da decodificação Base64.

sudo rm /etc/systemd/system/jenkins.service.d/override.conf
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart jenkins

O comando de remoção vale para uma configuração cujo arquivo contenha apenas a linha temporária; se o drop-in tiver outras definições, retire somente a linha de JAVA_OPTS. Agentes de compilação também executam suas próprias JVMs, então a equipe deve verificar runtime, flag e suporte a AVX-512 VBMI em cada nó conectado.

Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/guia-corrigir-java4shell-controladores-agentes-jenkins/

title: Why Running Both a Commercial VPN and Tailscale Breaks on Travel Wifi
description:
If all you need is to connect your own computers together for free, Tailscale is great and you should use it. If all you need is to hide your location on public Wifi, a regular VPN like NordVPN does that. The trouble starts when you need both, because running two of these apps on the same laptop or phone is where things break.

What goes wrong on the road

  • Hotel and airport Wifi often blocks standard VPN traffic.
  • Banks and other sites lock you out because you are coming from a shared VPN address.
  • Video calls lag when everything goes through a faraway server.
  • Two VPN-style apps on one phone tend to fight each other.
  • Neither one blocks the phishing sites you are most likely to land on when you are tired and on guest Wifi.

What I built instead

Arx Cloud is a single app that does both jobs. It reaches your home or office files without opening anything on your router, protects you on public Wifi, blocks known bad websites, and keeps video calls from lagging. It also works on strict hotel and airport Wifi because it looks like normal web traffic.

If you already pay for a VPN, you can keep using it inside Arx Cloud for the sites where you want it.

The full side-by-side comparison is on the original page.

Originally published at https://arxcloud.io/vs/tailscale-nordvpn/. Side-by-side breakdowns: Arx Cloud vs. Netskope & Proofpoint and Arx Cloud vs. Tailscale & NordVPN.

title: SciWorkBench: A Benchmark for Real Scientific Workflows
description:
arXiv:2611.22490v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language models are increasingly being used as agents capable of planning and executing projects, as well as refining their actions through feedback. This shift raises a question: can current agents complete projects like real scientists? To examine this question, we introduce SciWorkBench, a benchmark for evaluating agents' abilities on real science tasks across biology, chemistry, materials science, and physics. SciWorkBench is built from peer-reviewed literature or expert-contributed research scenarios. We also propose a unified scientific analysis framework validated by domain experts, which can categorize most tasks in SciWorkBench. Each task covers one or more stages of this framework. We evaluate up-to-date models within the Claude Code and Codex agent frameworks under a unified execution and grading protocol. The best-performing agent achieves a mean score of 57.38, indicating that current agents still struggle with realistic scientific workflows. Our failure analysis identifies three recurring weaknesses at the workflow level: difficulty translating scientific knowledge into task-specific procedures, weak integration of evidence across different modalities, and limited capacity for scientific self-correction. These findings highlight the importance of workflow-based evaluation for measuring progress toward reliable AI systems for scientific research.

title: mq: a small Kafka-style message queue in Go, built from scratch
description:
Kafka has a reputation for being complicated, and its vocabulary does not help: topics, partitions, offsets, segments, consumer groups, rebalances, generations. I used these words for a long time before I could explain why each one has to exist.

The quickest way I know to understand a design is to rebuild a small version of it. mq is a small Kafka-style message queue in Go, using only the standard library. It has topics split into partitions, an append-only segmented log per partition, consumer groups with committed offsets, retention, and a TCP protocol with a Go client. It is a single broker and a learning project. What it gave me is a clear picture of why a log sits at the centre of a message queue.

What it does

The code is four packages:

  • wal: the storage engine. Segment files with CRC-checked records, a sparse offset index, crash recovery that cuts off a torn tail, and retention by size and age.
  • broker: topics and partitions on top of wal, key-hash or round-robin partitioning, long-polling fetches, consumer groups (broker-side assignment, heartbeats, session expiry, generation-fenced commits) and the TCP server.
  • protocol: length-prefixed JSON frames. Each request has an ID, so a client can pipeline requests on one connection, and a parked long-poll does not block anything else.
  • client: a Go client with a producer API and a group Consumer that handles joining, heartbeats, rebalances and commits.

On disk, a topic looks like this:

data/
  topics/events/topic.json            {"Partitions": 3}
  topics/events/0/00000000000000000000.log    [len][crc32c][offset|ts|key|value] ...
  topics/events/0/00000000000000000000.index  [rel offset u32][file pos u32] every 4 KiB
  topics/events/0/00000000000000004211.log    next segment, named by its base offset
  offsets.json                        {"group/topic/partition": next offset}

What I built from scratch, and what it teaches

Why a log is the core. In this design a message is never "taken" from the queue. It is appended to a partition and gets an offset, which is just a position. Consumers keep their own position, and "acknowledging" a message is committing a number. Once you see that, most of the rest follows: several groups can read the same topic independently, and a consumer can go back and read again.

Storage details. Each record is framed with a length and a CRC-32C checksum. The index is sparse: one entry every 4 KiB, mapping a relative offset to a file position. That is enough, because a read does a binary search on the segments' base offsets, finds the index entry at or below the wanted offset, then scans a few KiB. Segments roll when they are full, and each new one is named by its base offset. Retention deletes whole segments instead of rewriting files, which is why it is cheap.

Crash consistency. A crash in the middle of a write leaves a torn record at the end of the active segment. On open, recovery scans the active segment, truncates at the first bad record and carries on with the right offsets. Sealed segments load their index and only check from the last index entry to the end. The important distinction: a torn tail in the active segment is expected and repaired, but corruption in a sealed segment is an error, not silent data loss.

Consumer group coordination. When a member joins, the group's generation number goes up and partitions are assigned round robin. A member whose heartbeat carries a stale generation is told to rebalance and rejoins. A member that misses heartbeats for the session timeout is expired, which triggers a rebalance. The generation works as a fencing token: a commit is refused unless the member, the generation and the partition ownership all match. So a consumer that missed a rebalance cannot commit over the new owner. This is also where you see why delivery is at-least-once.

A protocol that does not block. Fetches are long polls: the broker parks the request until data arrives, and a produce wakes the waiting fetches. Because every request carries an ID, a parked long poll and other requests can share one connection.

How to use it

Install the broker binary with Go:

go install github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/mq/cmd/mq@latest

Add the Go client to your module:

go get github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/mq/client@latest

From a clone of the repository, the command line shows the whole flow:

go build -o mq ./cmd/mq
./mq serve -addr 127.0.0.1:9092 -data data &

./mq create  -topic events -partitions 3
seq 1 10 | ./mq produce -topic events
./mq consume -topic events -group printers     # Ctrl-C to stop
./mq topics

And from Go:

c, _ := client.Dial(ctx, "127.0.0.1:9092")
c.Produce(ctx, "events", -1, []byte("user-42"), []byte("signed up"))

k := c.NewConsumer("mailer", "events")
for {
    msgs, _ := k.Poll(ctx, time.Second)
    for _, m := range msgs { /* handle */ }
    k.Commit(ctx)
}

The loop is the usual one for this kind of system: poll, handle, commit. If the process dies after handling and before committing, the messages are delivered again. Your handler has to tolerate that.

How it is tested 

go test -race ./...

The wal tests cover appends and reads, segment rolling with reads across many segments, reopening, a lost index file being rebuilt, recovery from a torn write (the file is cut in the middle of the last record), trailing junk, a flipped byte in a middle record, refusing to open a damaged sealed segment, and retention by size and by age on a fake clock.

The broker tests cover key-to-partition stability, round robin, reloading topics after a restart, long polling, group assignment, rebalance on heartbeat, fenced commits from a stale generation or for another member's partition, session expiry, and offsets surviving a restart.

The client tests run over TCP on 127.0.0.1: two consumers sharing a 4-partition topic with every message delivered exactly once in steady state, a clean handover when one leaves, and an end-to-end crash-recovery test that stops the broker, truncates the last record on disk, restarts it and checks the data and the next offset.

Things to know

This is a learning project, and the README says what that means:

  • Single broker. No replication, no leader election, no cluster metadata. If the disk dies, the data is gone.
  • Durability is configurable but coarse. By default writes are flushed to the OS on each append and fsynced on segment roll and close. wal.Options.SyncEveryWrite fsyncs every record. A power loss can lose the last unsynced records, and recovery then drops any torn tail.
  • At-least-once delivery. During a rebalance, two consumers can briefly read the same partition; only the current owner's commit is accepted. There are no transactions or idempotent producers.
  • Assignment is done by the broker, not by a group leader as in Kafka, and a group consumes exactly one topic.
  • JSON framing is easy to debug but slow, and values are base64 on the wire.
  • No authentication or TLS. Bind it to localhost or a trusted network.
  • Offsets are stored by rewriting one JSON file per commit.

What I learned

The biggest change is in how I think about acknowledgements. I used to picture a queue as a list where messages are removed when handled. A log with offsets is simpler and stronger: the broker stores bytes in order, and each group stores one number per partition.

The second lesson is about fencing. Without the generation check, a slow consumer that wakes up after a rebalance would commit an old offset over the new owner's progress. A single integer that goes up on every rebalance closes that hole.

The third is that recovery code needs a rule about what damage is acceptable. A torn tail is normal after a crash. A bad record in the middle of a sealed file is not, and refusing to open is the honest answer.

Get the code

The source, the client and the tests are on GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/mq. It is MIT licensed. Start with the wal package: it is the part everything else stands on.

Originally published at abdeldjalilchougui.biz.

description:
I run I Did My Own, a directory of open-source projects by people who looked at a well-known product and built their own. Now and then I'll pick one project from it and write a short note about it. This one isn't mine: Handy is by cjpais.

What it is

Handy is a free, extensible, fully offline speech-to-text desktop app. On idmo it's listed as someone's own take on Otter.ai, Wispr Flow and Superwhisper.

From its idmo page today:

  • Platforms: Windows, macOS, Linux
  • Language: Rust
  • Licence: MIT
  • Status: active, pre-1.0 (v0.10.1), with installers for macOS, Windows and Linux
  • GitHub stars: about 39.3k when I checked this afternoon

Why it caught my eye

Hosted transcription and dictation tools are polished and convenient, and they're the reason a lot of us got used to talking to our computers. Handy takes a different angle: it's built to be fully offline, so transcription runs on your own machine instead of a hosted service. For people who dictate notes, code comments or messages all day and would rather keep that local, that's a meaningful trade-off.

It's also a nice example of a desktop app written in Rust that ships for all three major operating systems.

Over to you

Do you use speech-to-text in your dev workflow? If you've tried an offline setup, what are you running, and what would you want from it?

And if you've built your own version of a well-known app, you can add it at idmo.app/submit.

title: Incremental Roseland: Batch-wise Landmark Diffusion via Kernelized Sequential Karhunen--Lo\`eve Update
description:
arXiv:2611.23414v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Landmark diffusion (Roseland) computes a diffusion-map-style spectral embedding from the singular value decomposition of a degree-normalized data-to-landmark kernel matrix, at a cost far below that of full diffusion maps. It assumes, however, that all data are available at once. We introduce incremental Roseland (iRoseland), which casts the landmark affinity as a row-growing matrix whose SVD can be updated with a kernelized Sequential Karhunen--Lo\`eve (SKL) scheme. Degre correction is handled by a first order expansion about a reference mean kernel row and so that the landmark-side eigenbasis may be recovered from a single landmark-by-landmark eigendecomposition at each step. The presented method requires only a single pass over the data and runs in bounded-memory with state independent of the number of points processed. A forgetting factor lets the method track drifting distributions, and a sample-size-invariant embedding keeps outputs comparable across time. Experiments show agreement with Roseland to round-off on stationary data, and accuracy that exceeds equal-memory Roseland by an order of magnitude on long streams. On drifting data, we observe large gains from forgetting with a window matched to the drift.

title: Agent Verifiers in Counterfactual Analysis: A Pilot Study Benchmarking Agentic Heterogeneous Treatment Effects
description:
arXiv:2611.23621v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agents can expand the covariate space of randomized experiments by retrieving fast-moving local context missed by slow-changing survey baseline covariates, helping characterize who benefits most from an intervention. Verifying such covariates is difficult: individual treatment effects are unobserved, retrieval leakage can pull post-treatment information into nominally pretreatment summaries, and encoder leakage can inject post-treatment pretraining knowledge into representations even after temporal filtering of inputs. Guided by a two-channel information bound separating summary provenance from encoder weights, we propose a three-layer benchmark protocol: (i) retrieval admissibility via pre-treatment date filtering; (ii) heterogeneity validation scored rank-weighted average treatment effects (RATEs); and (iii) encoder admissibility checked with chronologically vintaged encoders, future-fact probes, and weight perturbations. Across 11 datasets anchored by Uganda's Youth Opportunities Program, we compare session-isolated retrieval (sandboxed, bounded-budget agent runs per study) against a persistent workspace teammate (xAI's GrokBot) that builds one date-verified corpus per study while blinded to outcomes. The workspace teammate yields higher mean RATE ratios in 6/11 datasets for text alone and 7 for combined features, though paired tests show neither workflow universally dominates. Even on fixed retrieved text, encoder choice significantly shifts heterogeneity signal. Chronologically vintaged probes show no clear evidence of weight leakage, but single-record adapter perturbation analyses show that memorized future facts, once present, persist until injected noise degrades model output. Temporal filtering of retrieval is necessary but insufficient: verifying agent-generated covariates requires jointly examining source provenance, out-of-sample treatment-effect signal, and encoder weights.
