title: Securing a Node.js Modpack Control Plane Across Docker, WebSockets, SQLite, and Host Filesystems
description:
Anatomy of a Single-Process Control Plane: Express, Dockerode, WebSockets, and SQLite

A modpack control plane for friends and family rarely fails from a million-user surge. It fails when a heavy JVM garbage collection pause collides with a log stream, a SQLite write lock stalls an event watcher, or a coding agent like Claude Code wires an HTTP handler straight into the Docker socket without a boundary in between. Running the entire control plane as a single plain-JavaScript Node.js process—pairing Express, dockerode, ws, and built-in node:sqlite—strips away framework indirection and native build fragility while keeping every failure mode visible in one memory space.

Because Claude Code wrote most of the code while I owned the architecture, feature scope, manual review, and live server testing, single-process simplicity had to carry real structural weight. Without a compilation step rewriting line numbers or an ORM hiding SQL queries behind lazy proxies, runtime behavior stays readable—provided the process enforces hard boundaries around state, sockets, and the host filesystem.

Unidirectional Layering and Zero-Build JSDoc Type Checking

When AI generates endpoints quickly, the fastest way to rot a codebase is letting route handlers talk directly to dockerode or SQLite. If an Express route parses a body, queries a container, and writes a row in one function, testing a server start or crash state requires a live Docker daemon and a populated database—so developers skip writing tests, and subtle regressions slip into production.

Enforcing a strict one-way dependency chain—routes (parse and zod-validate only, zero business logic) to services (feature workflows) to docker, db, and storage adapters—isolates state transitions mechanically. Calling a service function in node:test against an in-memory or temporary SQLite database and a stubbed Docker client exercises actual branching logic without spawning containers. If a route handler imports a low-level adapter directly, test isolation collapses and every unit test turns into an integration hazard.

Pairing plain JavaScript with JSDoc annotations and tsc --checkJs in CI catches property typos, wrong return shapes, and nullability mismatches before runtime, while keeping stack traces pointed straight at the source file you wrote. A TypeScript build step introduces a source-map translation layer that can shift line numbers or mask runtime inspection; tsc --checkJs gives static type checking without rewriting the files executed by Node.js. However, JSDoc checking stops at type boundaries—if a zod schema accepts a wider string set than an internal enum assumes, type-checking passes while runtime logic hits an unexpected branch.

Built-In node:sqlite Versus Native Drivers on ARM64

Persisting server metadata, schedules, and crash history in SQLite avoids running a separate database daemon alongside game servers, yet native SQLite bindings frequently break on arm64 hosts when prebuilt binaries are missing and node-gyp attempts a C++ compilation against mismatched headers or toolchains. That build failure halts container image builds or deployment scripts before the application ever starts.

Using Node 24's built-in node:sqlite in synchronous mode with Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) eliminates external native add-on compilation completely. In WAL mode, readers append to or read from the WAL file while writers commit frames sequentially without blocking concurrent reads, and caching prepared statements by SQL text avoids re-parsing and re-planning identical statements on every call. If a single module owns the database connection and statement cache, connection lifecycle leaks and scattered pragma tweaks cannot happen across files.
Persistence Option Failure Mechanism Operational Verdict
Native C++ SQLite add-on Missing arm64 prebuilt binary triggers node-gyp build failure or ABI mismatch, aborting startup. Suboptimal for portable self-hosted control planes; avoid when built-in runtime support exists.
Built-in node:sqlite (synchronous + WAL + statement cache) Single-process synchronous writes can stall the event loop if large transactions or unindexed scans run during active log/WebSocket traffic. Optimal for low-to-moderate write concurrency on single-host Node 24 deployments.
External client-server DB (e.g., Postgres) Extra memory footprint and network/socket hops compete with JVM modpack heaps on constrained hosts. Excessive overhead for a personal modpack manager; use only if multi-node control plane scaling is required.

Synchronous node:sqlite stops working well when write volume or transaction duration grows large enough to block the Node.js event loop—for instance, writing thousands of high-frequency log lines per second into SQLite inside the request/event path will delay HTTP responses and WebSocket heartbeats. A common choice error is treating synchronous SQLite as free of I/O latency just because there is no network socket; large unbatched writes still flush pages and hold the event loop until complete. Decision rule: if state updates are discrete control-plane events on a single host using Node 24+, use built-in node:sqlite with WAL and prepared-statement caching; if high-volume telemetry ingestion or multi-writer concurrency saturates the event loop, move high-frequency streams out of synchronous SQLite writes into ring buffers or append-only log files.

Dockerode Event Watchers and Brokered WebSocket Log Streams

Shelling out to the docker CLI spawns child processes, allocates pipes, and parses text output that can change formatting across CLI versions—introducing subprocess overhead and fragile string parsing. Calling the Docker Engine API through dockerode keeps communication over a persistent socket or HTTP transport, returning structured objects for container inspection, stats, image pulls, and daemon events.

A background watcher subscribed to Docker events translates container state changes (such as non-zero exits or OOM kills) into persisted history and crash detection. Yet tying a watcher to a single process introduces a subtle coupling risk: if the control plane restarts while a modpack container is running or exiting, missed transient events can leave database state stale unless startup performs a reconciliation pass against dockerode container inspection.

Live console streaming exposes the sharpest throughput trap in a browser-based server panel. If every open browser tab opens its own upstream docker logs --follow stream for the same modpack container, opening ten tabs multiplies daemon log serialization, socket reads, and string decoding by ten—driving CPU and memory usage up even though the underlying container output is identical. Brokering WebSockets solves this mechanically: one upstream follow stream per container feeds an in-memory fan-out hub that pushes chunks to subscribed client sockets, while checking Origin headers and session cookies during the HTTP upgrade handshake blocks cross-site WebSocket hijacking before a socket is attached.

Brokering stops working cleanly if slow or stalled browser clients back up the fan-out path without flow control. When a client's TCP receive window fills and its WebSocket send buffer grows unbounded, retaining references to slow chunks increases Node.js heap memory until garbage collection thrashes or the process hits its memory limit. A typical choice error is broadcasting every raw log chunk unconditionally to every connected socket without checking buffered amounts or capping queue depth. Decision rule: if multiple clients can tail the same container log stream, broker a single upstream stream per container with per-client backpressure checks and bounded buffers; if a client's buffered output exceeds threshold or disconnects, drop/throttle that slow subscriber rather than stalling the upstream reader or inflating process heap.

Server-Rendered Views, CSP Nonces, and Path Canonicalization

Rendering pages with Express and Handlebars alongside a small esbuild bundle for interactive controls avoids heavy client-side framework overhead while keeping server-side control clear. Generating a fresh per-response Content Security Policy (CSP) nonce and attaching it to inline/bootstrapped script tags—without unsafe-inline—ensures that even if a modpack name, player message, or config value ever reaches HTML in a malformed way, an injected script tag lacking that request's random nonce is blocked by the browser's script-execution guard.

Host filesystem access carries the highest blast radius in a modpack manager because server directories hold world saves, configs, and potentially mounted secrets or adjacent host paths. If a file endpoint concatenates user-supplied relative paths onto a base data directory without canonicalization, sequences like ../ can walk outside the data root, and a symlink placed inside a modpack folder can point to a sensitive host file even when the lexical path looks contained. Resolving paths to their real filesystem target and verifying that the canonical path stays strictly inside the canonical data root prevents both lexical traversal and symlink escapes—provided the guard runs on every file operation (read, write, delete, rename, archive extract) rather than only on initial route entry.

  • Canonicalization before every I/O call: Resolve symlinks and relative segments first, then assert the resolved target sits inside the canonical data directory boundary; skipping re-verification across multi-step operations like renames or archive extractions allows escape windows.
  • Live verification alongside unit tests: Passing node:test suites without Docker proves service logic, while a live QA sweep against a running panel catches real socket upgrades, cookie/Origin rejections, CSP headers, and Docker API interactions that mocks cannot simulate.

Five Failure Scenarios in Production: Privilege Escalation, Log Backpressure, and Modpack Chaos

When you build a self-hosted control plane with an AI coding agent like Claude Code, code appears fast—sometimes faster than your threat model. In a plain-JavaScript Node.js panel using Express, dockerode, ws, and built-in node:sqlite, the happy path works on day one: a container boots, console lines stream into a browser tab, and server properties save cleanly. Real load is where assumptions get stress-tested. During live runs of heavy Minecraft modpacks for friends and family, five failure modes surfaced that expose what happens when architectural boundaries are loose or treated as optional.

1. Docker Socket Exposure and Privilege Escalation

Mounting /var/run/docker.sock into a Node.js control plane effectively hands root-equivalent control of the host to whatever code executes inside that process. If an unauthenticated or poorly scoped route accepts arbitrary container creation parameters—such as host bind mounts (/etc, /root, or /), privileged flags, or custom entrypoints—the causal chain is direct: an untrusted request reaches the Docker Engine API via dockerode, the daemon allocates a container with a host filesystem bind mount or elevated capabilities, and the attacker reads host secrets or spawns a root shell outside the container boundary. Even if the web panel itself runs as a non-root user inside its own container, access to the raw Docker socket bypasses container isolation because the daemon acts on behalf of the host.

Relying on dockerode over persistent socket/HTTP transports is still better than shelling out to the docker CLI, which spawns child processes, allocates extra pipes, and forces brittle string parsing on stdout/stderr. However, API ergonomics do not enforce authorization by themselves. Strict route-to-service layering helps keep raw dockerode calls out of HTTP handlers, while services enforce explicit allowlists on images, volumes, capabilities, and WebSocket upgrade origins and session cookies.

A common choice error is assuming that running the Node.js process as a non-root user protects the host when the Docker socket is mounted. Socket permissions only govern local Unix socket access; once opened, the daemon executes privileged lifecycle operations on the host. When a control plane cannot strictly constrain container parameters and socket access—or must expose multi-tenant self-service—use a dedicated container runtime proxy or separate daemon isolation rather than a raw host Docker socket. If you are testing this architecture and want to save your notes or come back to these failure modes later, signing in to a Google Account lets you keep your chat history in one place.

2. Path Traversal and Symlink Escapes During Modpack Extraction

Modpacks ship as sprawling zip archives containing nested configs, scripts, datapacks, and overrides. If extraction joins archive entry names onto a server data directory using naive string concatenation or regex checks for .., an entry like ../../../../etc/cron.d/pwn or a pre-existing symlink inside an extracted directory redirects file writes outside the intended data root. Physically, the file descriptor opens an inode outside the sandbox boundary, overwrites or exposes host files, and leaves stray files on the host filesystem even after the container stops.

Checking lexical paths before resolving symlinks fails because a symlink inside the target tree can point to an external directory while its lexical path still looks nested. Enforcing a path guard on every file operation—canonicalizing targets against the real filesystem path and verifying containment inside the canonical data root before reads, writes, deletes, renames, or archive extractions—closes that gap. Static type checking via JSDoc and tsc --checkJs catches wrong argument shapes at compile time, but it cannot prevent a string from resolving to a dangerous inode at runtime; runtime canonicalization has to do that work.

The typical mistake here is sanitizing only the incoming request path or only checking .. substrings. That stops sloppy inputs and fails on symlinked directories or multi-step archive entries. Canonicalize every target path to its real filesystem location and reject anything outside the canonical data root; if you need cross-directory sharing or host-level backups, move that into a controlled service step with explicit allowlists rather than weakening the path guard.

3. WebSocket Log Flooding and Backpressure

A modded game server under world generation, chunk loading, or tick lag can emit thousands of log lines per second. If every open browser tab opens its own upstream follow stream against the Docker daemon, each client multiplies socket reads, UTF-8 decoding, and string allocation across the single Node.js event loop. Worse, if a slow client connection stalls while chunks arrive faster than the TCP send buffer drains, unbounded per-client queues retain buffer references in the V8 heap. Heap usage climbs, garbage collection works harder to scan live references, and the Node.js process either slows to a crawl or gets OOM-killed.

Brokering one upstream follow stream per container into an in-memory fan-out hub solves the read multiplication problem: the daemon serializes and streams the log once per container, and the Node.js hub distributes frames to active subscribers. To protect memory under slow consumers, check subscriber buffered state and enforce bounded per-client queues—dropping or throttling lagging subscribers rather than letting queues grow without limit or blocking upstream reads.

A frequent choice error is treating WebSocket broadcast as "just ws.send(chunk) in a loop" without inspecting backpressure or connection health. A single brokered stream per server is optimal for personal and small-group panels on one host; if you ever need multi-node fan-out, durable log replay, or heavy search across gigabytes of logs, offload log persistence to rotating files or an external log pipeline instead of stuffing history into Node.js memory.
Failure Mode Underlying Mechanism Control Plane Mitigation
Docker socket privilege escape Unrestricted container config reaches Docker daemon via socket Strict service allowlists, origin/cookie upgrade checks, minimal mounts
Modpack archive traversal Unresolved symlinks or traversal paths escape data directory Real-path canonicalization and root containment check on every op
WebSocket log backpressure Per-tab streams + unbounded queues bloat V8 heap on slow clients One upstream stream per container, fan-out hub, bounded queues
SQLite write contention Synchronous writes or heavy loops block single-threaded event loop Built-in node:sqlite in WAL mode + cached statements + small writes
Crash-loop state drift JVM heap exhaustion or OOM kills collide with missed events Event watcher plus startup reconciliation against live container state

4. SQLite Write Contention on a Single-Threaded Event Loop

Using Node's built-in node:sqlite in synchronous mode with Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) avoids native node-gyp C++ compilation failures and ABI mismatches on arm64 hosts, and centralizing connection ownership with a prepared-statement cache keyed on SQL text avoids repeated SQL parsing and planning. Still, synchronous SQLite calls execute on the Node.js main thread. If code runs large multi-row transactions, unindexed scans, or high-frequency log inserts inside SQLite, disk page flushes and lock contention stall the event loop—delaying HTTP routes, health checks, and WebSocket heartbeats simultaneously.

WAL mode lets readers proceed concurrently with a writer, which helps read-heavy panel views, but single-writer serialization and synchronous I/O remain real constraints under bursty writes. Keep SQLite strictly for discrete control-plane state (servers, users, settings, audit/crash events), keep transactions compact, and never stream high-volume console logs into SQLite.

The classic mistake is reaching for a heavy external database like PostgreSQL on a small host where JVM heap memory is already tight, or conversely dumping high-frequency telemetry into synchronous SQLite. Use built-in node:sqlite with WAL and cached prepared statements for single-host control-plane state; move to an external database only when you actually have multiple control-plane nodes or concurrent writers that exceed single-host SQLite throughput.

5. Crash-Loop Recovery and Modpack Chaos

Modpacks are notoriously unstable: an oversized JVM heap allocation, a buggy mod tick loop, or an out-of-memory kill can crash a server container repeatedly right after boot. If your control plane relies solely on a live Docker event stream to record exits and crashes, a restart of the control plane itself can miss transient events, leaving the database claiming a server is starting or running when the container actually exited with code 137.

Pairing a background Docker event watcher with startup state reconciliation—inspecting live containers via dockerode when the panel boots and aligning persisted state—prevents stale UI states after restarts. Testing service logic with node:test against stubbed Docker clients and temporary/in-memory SQLite databases, backed by a live QA sweep script against a running panel, catches state-transition bugs before a bad modpack update hits real players.

A common choice error is trusting either the database row or the in-memory event listener as the single source of truth after a restart. Always reconcile persisted control-plane state against live Docker container inspection on startup; if a server enters rapid crash loops, surface exit codes and OOM status clearly and apply backoff or manual intervention rather than masking the failure with silent retries.

Filesystem Mediation, Modpack Pipelines, and Licensing Landmines

A modpack control plane looks benign right up until someone drops a 400 MB CurseForge or Modrinth archive into an upload field or edits a server's world directory through a web file manager. Behind a friendly browser UI, that single action hands an untrusted byte stream to a Node.js process that shares host storage with live JVM containers. When Claude Code scaffolds an archive extractor or a file route quickly, it almost always trusts path strings and stream lengths unless you force hard boundaries at the filesystem and licensing layers.

Path Canonicalization vs. Lexical Filtering: Why ../ Checks Fail

The most common bug in hand-rolled or AI-generated file services is filtering .. substrings or calling path.join(root, userInput) before opening a file descriptor. Lexical string normalization only inspects characters; it never touches inodes or directory entries on the underlying filesystem (ext4, XFS, or APFS).

Here is how a traversal or symlink escape actually executes:

  • Raw segment traversal: An attacker or malformed archive entry supplies ../../../../etc/cron.d/panel-job. Naive string concatenation resolves the target path outside the server data directory, allowing the kernel's openat syscall to create or overwrite a file on a completely different subtree once permissions allow.
  • Symlink indirection: Even if you strip .. from the requested path, a previously extracted or host-planted symbolic link inside mods/ or config/ may point to /etc or another server's world/playerdata. When the kernel traverses that symlink dentry during a read, write, rename, or archive extract, it redirects inode resolution to the external target.
  • TOCTOU races during extraction: If a check runs on a path before creating subdirectories or writing files, a concurrent request or nested archive entry can swap a directory for a symlink in the window between validation and the syscall, shifting where bytes land on disk.

Decision rule: If you expose any read, write, delete, rename, or zip/tar extraction against a server data folder, resolve the target against the canonicalized real path (fs.realpathSync) of the root directory on every operation and verify prefix containment with a trailing path separator—never rely on lexical checks or JSDoc types alone. Canonicalization is optimal for single-host Node.js file mediation because it enforces kernel-resolved boundary containment with zero external daemons. It stops working when untrusted users can race directory creation concurrently or when the control plane needs cross-volume bind mounts outside the data root; in those cases, move extraction into an unprivileged, disposable container with read-only host mounts rather than relaxing path guards in Node.

Archive Bombs, Disk Exhaustion, and World File Contention

Modpacks are notoriously uneven in shape: a lightweight client/server pack might be 18 MB of compressed JARs, while a heavy pack with bundled shader configs, custom dimensions, or pre-generated chunks can unpack to gigabytes of small files. A naive unzip loop that pipes an archive entry straight to disk without accounting for byte counts, entry counts, or live JVM writes creates physical and I/O failure modes.

During an archive bomb (a small compressed payload expanding into tens of gigabytes or millions of tiny files), compressed blocks feed the decompressor faster than disk write queues drain. Inode tables fill up or free filesystem blocks vanish; on a shared host where both the Node.js panel and Minecraft JVMs write to the same disk, block exhaustion stalls journal commits and forces JVM garbage-collection pauses or container eviction when host storage hits 100%.

World files introduce a second physical hazard: concurrent mutation. While a Minecraft server is running, chunks, region files (.mca), and level metadata are actively read and written by the JVM. Overwriting world/ or deleting dimension folders during a live tick loop corrupts chunk state or causes region file truncation and missing chunks on reload. Even when the server is stopped, copying or zipping a multi-gigabyte world directory synchronously or without byte/entry caps saturates disk read bandwidth and spikes memory buffers.
Approach Failure Mechanism Verdict
Unbounded stream extract to host disk Decompressed bytes or entry count exhaust disk blocks/inodes, starving host and JVM I/O Unacceptable; cap both total bytes and file count while streaming
Hot world overwrite/archive while container runs Concurrent JVM region/chunk writes collide with file mutations, corrupting world state Reject destructive world writes/restores unless container is cleanly stopped
Canonicalized guarded service + lifecycle gate Enforces byte/entry ceilings, real-path containment, and stopped-state checks before touching disk Optimal for self-hosted single-node panels

A typical AI choice error is treating "zip extraction" as a one-liner helper around a third-party archive library without tracking cumulative uncompressed bytes per archive or blocking world overwrites on running containers. Enforce hard byte budgets, maximum entry counts, and container-state preconditions inside the storage/modpack service layer—never inside Express route handlers.

Third-Party Mod Distribution and Licensing Landmines

Automated modpack ingestion crosses from systems engineering into legal liability the moment your tool fetches, caches, or redistributes third-party mods. Mod authors license their code and assets under varied terms—some use permissive open licenses, many use ARR (All Rights Reserved), and numerous platforms or individual authors explicitly set flags or terms prohibiting third-party distribution or automated scraping.

The mechanical risk is straightforward: if a control plane automatically downloads restricted mod JARs into a shared cache, bundles them into exportable server packs, or exposes cached mod binaries over a network endpoint without respecting distribution restrictions and platform APIs, the operator becomes the party distributing copyrighted binaries without authorization. Even for a private friends-and-family server, automated fetching that bypasses rate limits, API terms, or author distribution opt-outs turns a convenience feature into a compliance exposure.

Decision rule: If a modpack manifest or source marks a mod as restricted from third-party distribution or lacks permission for automated redistribution, fetch only via official APIs/workflows permitted by the source or require the operator to supply the local file manually—never silently mirror or re-host restricted binaries in a shared panel cache. Explicit manual drop-in for restricted mods is more tedious than full automation, and it stops scaling once dozens of users manage dozens of packs independently, at which point you should integrate official pack manifest resolvers and enforce strict per-pack isolation rather than building a public mod mirror.

Hardening the Control Plane: Guardrails, Isolation, and Operational Trade-offs

A plain-JavaScript control plane built around express, dockerode, ws, and node:sqlite—even when drafted rapidly with Claude Code and type-checked with tsc --checkJs—inherits root-equivalent blast radii the moment it touches /var/run/docker.sock, streams game-server console output, mutates modpack archives, and writes state to disk. Speed of generation does not remove physical bottlenecks; it compresses how quickly subtle race conditions, memory retention, and path escapes reach production.

Hardening a single-host control plane is not about bolting on heavy enterprise machinery. It is about placing explicit mechanical boundaries where data crosses trust zones, where byte streams hit storage or V8 heaps, and where container lifecycle state diverges from database rows.

Docker Daemon Exposure and Socket Proxying

Mounting /var/run/docker.sock into a Node.js process hands any reachable code path effective root control over the host daemon. If an HTTP route or WebSocket upgrade handler accepts arbitrary container configurations, bind mounts, privileged flags, or device passthroughs, an authenticated session—or a cross-origin browser tab—can instruct the daemon to mount the host root filesystem into a new container and read sensitive credentials or modify host binaries.

Routing calls through dockerode and enforcing strict service-layer allowlists prevents arbitrary image or mount specifications from reaching the daemon API, while validating Origin headers and session cookies on WebSocket upgrades blocks unauthorized browser-initiated connections. Still, a single application process holding raw daemon socket access remains one logic bug away from privileged container creation.

  • Direct daemon socket + permissive service specs: Fast to wire up, but any parameter leak in container creation or exec/attach paths lets an attacker escalate to host root via bind mounts or privileged flags.
  • Service-gated dockerode client on a single host: Optimal for a personal or small-group modpack panel because it eliminates shelling out to the docker CLI, keeps lifecycle transitions typed and testable, and restricts actions to predefined server records.
  • Socket proxy or isolated daemon: Necessary when multiple untrusted operators share a host or when the control plane itself should never hold raw daemon write authority; it adds network/proxy hop latency and operational complexity that a single-admin friends-and-family deployment usually does not need.

Decision rule: If you run a single-host panel for a trusted small group with strict service-layer allowlists and WebSocket origin/cookie checks, use a gated dockerode client; if untrusted users or multi-tenant boundaries exist, place a filtering Docker socket proxy or isolated daemon in front of the control plane.

Path Canonicalization vs. Lexical Filtering

Modpack management constantly moves files across mods/, config/, and world/ directories. Filtering .. substrings or calling path.join(root, userInput) fails because string manipulation never inspects kernel dentries, inodes, or directory entries on ext4, XFS, or APFS. A lexical check sees a clean string while the kernel resolves filesystem links underneath it.

The causal chain works in three distinct ways:

  • Raw traversal segments: A relative path like ../../../../etc/cron.d/panel-job escapes the server data directory, allowing openat to create or overwrite files outside the intended tree whenever process permissions permit.
  • Symlink indirection: Even when .. is blocked, a symlink sitting inside mods/ or config/ and pointing to /etc or another server's world/playerdata causes the kernel to follow the link during read, write, rename, or archive extraction syscalls, exposing or mutating out-of-bounds files.
  • Time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) races: Checking a path before creating directories or writing files leaves a window where a concurrent request or nested archive entry swaps a directory for a symlink between validation and the write syscall, redirecting the write to the symlink target.

On every read, write, delete, rename, or archive extract inside a server data folder, canonicalize both the data root and the resolved target with fs.realpathSync and verify prefix containment with a trailing path separator so /srv/data/server-10 cannot match /srv/data/server-1. That check is optimal for single-host Node.js file mediation, but it breaks down under heavy concurrent directory mutation or cross-volume bind mounts outside the canonical root. When extraction faces untrusted archives or concurrent races that lexical/realpath checks alone cannot serialize safely, move extraction into an unprivileged, disposable container with tight mounts rather than weakening path guards.

Archive Bombs, Disk Exhaustion, and Live World Mutation

Modpack archives behave erratically. A lightweight server pack might be an 18 MB bundle of JARs, while a heavy pack with shader presets, custom dimensions, or pre-generated chunks can expand to several gigabytes and tens of thousands of small files.

When an extraction stream decompresses faster than the underlying block device and filesystem journal can commit writes, dirty page buffers accumulate, disk queue depth saturates, and available blocks or inodes run out. On a host running both the Node.js control plane and heavy Minecraft JVMs on the same storage volume, 100% disk I/O saturation stalls journal flushes and storage writes—triggering severe JVM garbage-collection pauses, tick stalls, or container eviction.

Mutating a live world directory creates a different kind of damage. A running Minecraft server actively reads and writes region files (.mca), chunk data, and level state. Overwriting world/ or deleting dimension folders while the JVM tick loop is active collides with open file handles and ongoing writes, resulting in corrupted chunks, truncated regions, or missing terrain on reload. Reading or archiving a multi-gigabyte stopped world without size or throughput limits can likewise saturate disk read bandwidth and inflate memory buffers.

Decision rule: If an operation extracts an archive, enforce hard uncompressed byte and entry ceilings inside the storage service while streaming; if an operation overwrites, restores, or mutates world/ data, require the target container to be cleanly stopped first.

Brokered WebSocket Log Streams and Heap Backpressure

Minecraft servers emit dense console output during boot, world generation, and mod errors. Opening a separate upstream docker logs --follow stream for every browser tab wastes daemon connections and duplicates work, while a naive loop calling ws.send(chunk) on every log chunk ignores TCP and WebSocket backpressure.

When a client tab has a slow network connection or stalls while rendering DOM updates, its outbound socket buffer fills. Without per-client queue bounds and buffer monitoring, chunks accumulate in per-client arrays in the V8 heap. That retained memory increases garbage-collection pressure, stretches event-loop turn times, and can push the Node.js process into an out-of-memory (OOM) kill—or, if upstream reads block on a slow consumer, stall log delivery for healthy tabs.

Maintaining one brokered upstream follow stream per container into a fan-out hub with bounded per-client queues is optimal for a single-host control plane serving a small group of players: lagging subscribers get dropped or throttled rather than expanding V8 heap buffers or stalling upstream reads. It stops working well once you need multi-node fan-out, durable historical log search, or long scrollback replay, where external log storage is far better suited than in-memory Node.js queues.

SQLite WAL Contention and Crash-Loop State Drift

Node's built-in node:sqlite in synchronous mode with Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) avoids native node-gyp compilation headaches on arm64 hosts, and caching prepared statements by SQL string avoids repeated SQL parsing and query planning. WAL also lets readers proceed concurrently with a single writer, which fits a read-heavy control panel well on memory-constrained hosts where running PostgreSQL alongside large Minecraft JVMs wastes scarce RAM.

The catch is that synchronous SQLite calls execute on the main event-loop thread. Large multi-row transactions, unindexed scans, or high-frequency log inserts force disk flushes and write serialization that block incoming HTTP requests, health checks, and WebSocket heartbeats. Keep SQLite strictly for compact control-plane state—servers, users, configuration metadata, and discrete audit or crash events—and never turn it into a high-volume log sink.

State drift compounds these timing issues during crash loops. A modpack server hitting JVM heap limits, a runaway mod tick loop, or a kernel OOM kill (exit code 137) can restart repeatedly. If the control plane restarts mid-loop and relies only on a live Docker event listener, it misses prior exit events and can show stale database rows claiming a container is still starting or running. Relying solely on database rows misses live container state changes. The reliable pattern combines background Docker event watching with startup reconciliation via live container inspection in dockerode, surfacing exit codes and OOM signals with backoff or manual intervention instead of blind retry loops—verified through node:test unit suites with stubbed Docker clients and temporary SQLite databases alongside a live QA sweep against a running instance.
Failure Mode Underlying Mechanism Primary Guardrail Where It Breaks Down
Docker socket privilege escape Unrestricted container specs or unauthenticated/cross-origin upgrades over mounted socket Service-layer allowlists, origin/cookie checks, and socket proxy when untrusted Multi-tenant or untrusted operators sharing one daemon without a filtering proxy
Modpack path & archive escape Lexical filtering misses realpath symlinks, TOCTOU races, or archive bombs fs.realpathSync prefix check + stream byte/entry limits + stopped world gate Untrusted concurrent directory races or cross-volume bind mounts outside root
Log stream heap bloat Per-tab streams and unbounded per-client buffers retain chunks in V8 heap One upstream follow stream per container + bounded client queues with drop/throttle Multi-node deployments, durable log retention, or large log search
SQLite event-loop stalls Synchronous writes, large transactions, or log inserts block main thread WAL mode + SQL-keyed prepared statement cache + compact control-plane data only High-frequency telemetry/log writes or multi-writer concurrency
Crash-loop state drift Missed exit/OOM events during control-plane restarts leave stale status rows Docker event stream + startup live inspection + exit/OOM surfacing and backoff Ignoring exit codes (such as 137) or masking repeated failures with instant retries

title: Structured concurrency is finally leaving preview in JDK 28. Here's the API you'll actually use
description:
If you've been eyeing StructuredTaskScope but didn't want --enable-preview anywhere near production, the wait is almost over: JEP 543, Structured Concurrency, has been Targeted for JDK 28 since October 21. In the JDK 28 early-access docs the API no longer carries the preview mark.

It took a while. StructuredTaskScope has been in preview since JDK 21 and the API was reworked along the way: open() and open(Joiner) date from JDK 25, open(Joiner, UnaryOperator) from JDK 26 and open(UnaryOperator) from JDK 27. If you tried it in 21 and gave up, what you'll find now looks very different.

The idea, in one example

You start several subtasks inside a block, wait for them, and if one fails the others are cancelled. Nothing keeps running outside the try.

record CustomerView(Customer customer, List<Order> orders) {}

CustomerView loadView(long id) throws ExecutionException, InterruptedException {
    try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) {
        Subtask<Customer> customer = scope.fork(() -> customerRepo.find(id));
        Subtask<List<Order>> orders = scope.fork(() -> orderRepo.byCustomer(id));

        scope.join(); // if one fails, the other is cancelled and ExecutionException is thrown

        return new CustomerView(customer.get(), orders.get());
    }
}

open() with no arguments applies the most common policy: all succeed, or the first failure wins. If everything finishes, join() returns null and you read each result with get(). If one fails, join() throws ExecutionException with the original exception as the cause, and the subtasks still running are cancelled via interruption.

By default each subtask runs in an unnamed virtual thread. If you need something else, withThreadFactory lets you plug in your own.

Joiners decide when it's over

You change the policy by passing a Joiner to open. The factories in JDK 28:

  • awaitAllSuccessfulOrThrow(): the one from the example above; join() returns null.
  • allSuccessfulOrThrow(): join() returns a List<T> with every result.
  • anySuccessfulOrThrow(): the first successful result wins; it only fails if all of them fail.
  • allUntil(Predicate): returns every subtask and cancels when the predicate says so; failures don't make join() throw.

The first three have a variant that takes a Function<Throwable, R_X> so you choose which exception join() throws. That's what the third type parameter of StructuredTaskScope<T, R, R_X extends Throwable> is for.

A classic case: ask two replicas for the same thing, keep the fastest, and don't wait more than two seconds.

String fetchFastest(String key) throws ExecutionException, InterruptedException {
    try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open(
            Joiner.<String>anySuccessfulOrThrow(),
            cfg -> cfg.withTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2)))) {
        scope.fork(() -> mirrorA.fetch(key));
        scope.fork(() -> mirrorB.fetch(key));
        return scope.join(); // the first one to answer wins; the other is cancelled
    }
}

If the timeout fires, join() throws ExecutionException whose cause is a StructuredTaskScope.CancelledByTimeoutException. The config also has withName to name the scope.

If you already used the preview

The interface declaration, the join() signature and the Joiner names used here are the same in the JDK 27 preview and in the JDK 28 early access. So if your code compiles today with --enable-preview on JDK 27, chances are that moving to JDK 28 just means removing --enable-preview from javac and java.

One caveat: Targeted means the JEP is planned for JDK 28, and the early-access docs warn that the spec isn't final yet. Try your code on a JDK 28 build before taking anything for granted.

Check yourself in 2 minutes

Structured concurrency sits on top of virtual threads, and that's where most interview questions go. Three short challenges, no sign-up needed (they're in Spanish, the code isn't):

  • Virtual threads: scale, not speed
  • Pinning: when a virtual thread gets stuck
  • From ThreadLocal to ScopedValue

They come from NextPatch, a small daily habit I'm building for Java developers: a 45-second summary of one change between versions, then a 2-minute challenge.

Are you planning to use StructuredTaskScope once 28 ships, or are you sticking with CompletableFuture? I'm curious what's holding people back.

Originally published in Spanish on the NextPatch blog, with links to the JEP and the JDK 28 early-access javadoc.

title: ToolFlood: Beyond Selection -- Hiding Valid Tools from LLM Agents via Semantic Covering
description:
arXiv:2603.13950v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents increasingly use external tools for complex tasks and rely on embedding-based retrieval to select a small top-$k$ subset for reasoning. Prior work on attacking these systems competes for tool selection, assuming benign tools remain in the retrieved set; the robustness of the retrieval stage that produces this set is underexplored. This paper introduces ToolFlood, a retrieval-layer attack on tool-augmented LLM agents. Rather than altering which tool is chosen after retrieval, ToolFlood attacks retrieval itself: it injects a few attacker-controlled tools whose metadata is positioned to exploit the geometry of embedding space, so that these tools semantically span many user queries, dominate the top-k results, and push all benign tools out of the agent's context.
  ToolFlood uses a two-phase adversarial tool generation strategy. It first samples subsets of target queries and uses an LLM to iteratively generate diverse tool names and descriptions. It then runs an iterative greedy selection that chooses tools maximizing coverage of remaining queries in embedding space under a cosine-distance threshold, stopping when all queries are covered or a budget is reached. We provide theoretical intuition of retrieval saturation and show on a large catalog (ToolBench) that ToolFlood achieves up to a 95\% attack success rate with a ~1\% injection rate. The code is available at: https://github.com/as1-prog/ToolFlood

title: Your GPU is busy computing padding: cost lessons from fine-tuning on rented cards
description:
In the second post of this series I promised to write up how I rented cloud GPUs and burned money on them without doing the maths. In the third I said the promise still stood. Here it is.

Some context first. I'm building speech and language models for Crimean Tatar, a low-resource language (why, and where the data came from). ASR and TTS train fine on my 24 GB card at home. Full fine-tuning of the language model needs 141 GB or more, so that part runs on rented machines, which works like renting a car: you pay for the hours you have it, whether you're driving or standing on the hard shoulder with the bonnet up.

Over about a month and a half that came to a bit over $300. It wasn't one disaster but a series of iterations with different configurations until the recipe worked. Every mistake below is normal for real work, and I'm writing them down so they get cheaper for the next person, and for me.

I don't name base models, fine-tuning techniques, checkpoints or data sources. GPU classes, vendors and hourly prices are in, because a post about cost without them is useless.

The first run, in numbers

The first rental was an H200 with 141 GB at about $4.60/h, for a two-stage run that the estimate put at 9 to 11 hours and $33 to $40. I stopped it after 11.5 hours and $53, at 15% of stage 2, with about 46 hours still to go. Effective GPU yield over that time was roughly 3 to 4%. There were three independent causes, and any one of them would have blown the budget on its own.

Lesson 1: estimate cost on padded tokens, not on content

The biggest cause was padding. Our SFT conversations are short, median around 20 tokens, and every example was padded to seq_len = 1024. The attention mask and the loss mask make padding harmless for the result, but not for the bill: the matmuls still run over the full sequence, and most of what they compute is thrown away. It's like shipping one apple in a whole crate and paying for the crate. The estimate was based on content, 59M tokens, while the GPU processed 1.17B positions. That's the 20x miss.

What hurts is that the plan literally contained an assumption of about 1.2x padding overhead, and nobody tested it. Testing it takes a minute:

# what share of the compute you pay for is real tokens?
lengths = [len(tok(x).input_ids) for x in sample]   # a few thousand rows
useful = sum(lengths)
padded = len(lengths) * seq_len
print(f"useful share: {useful / padded:.1%}")        # ours: about 5%

The number that drives cost is steps × micro_batch × seq_len positions processed, divided by real throughput and multiplied by the hourly price, not "corpus size × epochs". If your median example is fifty times shorter than seq_len, no kernel optimisation will save you. The card is multiplying zeros and you're paying by the hour.

The fix was packing. We started packing short conversations into dense blocks, one after another, with a block-diagonal attention mask so packed neighbours can't see each other. There's one thing to watch here: some fast attention paths silently ignore a custom 4D mask, and then your packed examples do leak into each other. We checked that each conversation's logits inside a packed block match its logits computed alone. With that in place the useful share went from 5% to 99%, and stage 2, which the old way would have cost $331 to $413, came out at $14 to $17.

The left bar is an estimate, to be clear. We didn't finish the run the old way to find out.

Lesson 2: checkpoint by wall-clock, and not to a network disk

The second cause was checkpointing. We saved a full 46 GB checkpoint every 400 steps to a network volume, and training blocks while it writes, so the card simply stands and waits for the disk. About 600 GB got written over the run, and the GPU sat at 58 to 68% busy even before you count padding.

You do need checkpoints, because a crash without them sends you back to zero. But the frequency should be set in hours of work, weighing the cost of an hour against the chance of losing one, not in a step count picked by habit. A 46 GB checkpoint makes sense every few thousand steps, not every 400, and it should go to local disk where you can, with the copy to persistent storage happening later.

Lesson 3: feed the card

The third cause was the simplest. Two data loader workers were preparing batches on a 128-core machine, and with short examples the GPU finished a batch faster than the loader could prepare the next one. A fast card with a slow kitchen. Our rule of thumb since then is workers around a quarter of the vCPUs, and a look at GPU utilisation in the first ten minutes. If it isn't near full, something is wrong, and stopping costs less than continuing.

Lesson 4: "it works" and "it pays for itself" are different tests

The frustrating part is that before renting, the whole pipeline had passed a smoke test at home. That test proved the code was correct. It said nothing about throughput, because at home time is free and nobody looks at it. We ran the correctness test and skipped the economics test. There were also about 45 minutes and $3 lost to setup traps before the first training step, which is small, but it all counts.

Not everything was lost. Stage 1 did finish, and its weights were saved.

Lesson 5: rehearse the whole chain, not the pieces

With packing in place I started attempt two, and over September 1 and 2 we went through five machines in a row. Each one died before finishing.

One of them crashed at step 50 of 95, because a fresh change enabled an evaluation that needed about 160 GB on a 141 GB card. In run 1 that evaluation never had time to fire, so nobody had seen the problem. Another was killed by our own watchdog at step 80 of 95, four minutes before the end of the stage: it found a stale "run failed" marker left on the volume by the previous attempt and believed it. The fifth reached 65% of stage 2, ran 4.35 hours for $19.96, and crashed, and I'll come back to that one below.

Looking at those deaths together, I saw the pattern. The training loop itself never crashed. Not once. What crashed was everything around it: launch scripts, checks, watchdogs. Each piece had been tested on its own, but the chain as a whole had never been run end to end.

So now every rental is preceded by a full rehearsal at home, with the same chain, the same watchdogs and the same stage handover, but with a tiny model and for free. One rehearsal took 4.7 hours and caught 6 defects. The nastiest was in gradient accumulation: because of how a model wrapper handled it, the effective learning rate in stage 1 was 16x the configured one, and gradient clipping hid it, so the loss looked fine. In the cloud we would have paid for each of those six.

The stale marker also pointed at a whole class of bugs: stale state on persistent volumes. In a side benchmark, a script saw an old result file on disk, decided it had already downloaded the new one, and destroyed the machine along with the real result. Since then anything that signals run state is tied to a specific run ID.

Lesson 6: don't kill the machine, fix it in place

The most expensive thing in those two days wasn't a bug at all. It was a habit. On every error we did the same thing: destroy the machine, fix the code, start again on a fresh one. A fresh machine reinstalls the environment and re-downloads tens of gigabytes of weights while the meter runs. And when the machine goes, its logs go with it, so the root cause becomes a guess, and sometimes you pay for another machine just to reproduce it.

We wrote the rule down the same day: don't destroy, fix in place and restart the process on the same machine. Think of a flat tyre. You patch it at the roadside; you don't abandon the bike. Unfortunately the rule reached the code an hour too late. When the fifth machine crashed, the rescue script's first action was to lift the pre-shutdown pause, and the copy tool it relied on wasn't installed on the image. The machine was gone within minutes, logs included, and I still don't know why it crashed.

Once the rule was in, it paid off quickly. The next training ran both stages in one go for about $41 for the whole job, compared with $53 for 15% of stage 2 the first time. The run after that was the first real test of the rule: a short on-machine test found 3 defects for $1.50, we fixed them in place, and the whole job took 2.81 hours and $12.91 with zero crashes.

Lesson 7: your watchdog fails in both directions

The watchdog is a separate program that watches training, rescues results and shuts the machine down. Almost every mistake it made cost money, and it erred both ways.

On September 6 it was too quiet. A run on a B300 finished and the watchdog didn't notice, because it had broken silently twice that day. The machine sat with the finished result for 30 to 40 minutes at $7.89/h until I checked by hand. Since then we fire-drill the watchdog before every launch, triggering an event on purpose and confirming that the alert arrives, and I check the machine by hand near the end of the run. The same episode taught us that "run complete" doesn't mean "result safe". The result is safe once it's downloaded and verified.

On September 24 it was too strict. The watchdog sampled GPU utilisation every 5 minutes, and its last readings were 94, 0, 100, 0. The zeros landed on checkpoint saves, when the card is legitimately waiting on the disk. The average came out at 48% against a 50% threshold, so 28 seconds before the end of training it saved a checkpoint and destroyed the machine. The weights survived, all 51.6 GB, but the checkpoint's metadata files were zero bytes and we had to bring up a separate machine to rescue them. The flaw was in the logic itself: GPU utilisation alone can't tell a hang from a save, but the step counter can. The check now looks roughly like this:

# a hang is an idle card AND no progress, not just an idle card
hung = gpu_util_avg < 0.5 and step_now == step_at_last_check

A card is allowed to rest while it saves or finishes. A real hang is when the steps stop.

That left the question of where the watchdog lives. One that runs on the rented machine dies with that machine, which is exactly when you need it. Ours now runs at home and talks to the machine from outside.

Lesson 8: a hard dollar cap can kill a healthy run

Money had the same problem. The first rule was simple: hit the cap, rescue, destroy. On September 2 the watchdog, with a $36 cap, extrapolated from step 10 of 1,875 that the run would cost $35 to $38 and started rescuing a perfectly healthy job. We stopped it in time, but the lesson was clear. At step 10 an extrapolation knows almost nothing about real throughput, and a hard cap that fires later can kill a run that's almost done, taking everything you've already paid for with it. Now, near the limit, the system saves everything first and only then shuts down.

Lesson 9: a price list is not availability

A simpler mistake was trusting the price list. This is what we found once we started checking what was behind the prices:

vendor listed what we found
DigitalOcean MI300X 192 GB, $2.59/h not available in any region; new accounts start with a GPU quota of zero, raised via support; the available alternative was $3.80/h
RunPod MI300X, $2.39/h 12 create attempts out of 12 refused
Hostinger 192 GB card, $4.50/h paired with 16 GB RAM and 200 GB disk; we need about 315 GB for checkpoints alone
AMD Developer Cloud MI300X, $1.99/h available; the later versions trained there

No complaint at anyone here: a price list shows price, not stock or configuration. The first card didn't exist in any region, and the third came with less disk than our checkpoints alone take. Checking all of this cost under a cent, and since then we check that a card can actually be obtained before trusting a price.

Lesson 10: bill by machine lifetime, then check against the first minutes

The 20x miss wasn't our only accounting error. For the second version our report said $32, because it counted training hours only, while the balance said $41. The machine lived almost 9 hours, not 7, and paid for disks the whole time, so the listed $3.59/h for the card came out at about $4.60/h for the machine. You're billed for the machine's whole life, from creation to deletion, including setup, weight downloads and the final upload, not for the time the loss is going down.

So the estimate now starts from the real step count on the real packed block length, and the ETA gets re-checked against the first minutes of actual steps, because an estimate that has never been compared with real steps is a guess. Cost is counted from machine creation to deletion, disks included. For scale, version 3 on a B300 cost $79.31 for 123M tokens and version 4 on an MI300X about $41 for roughly 200M, and a training cycle now costs $10 to $12. On October 5 four launches failed at startup, at about fifty cents each: caught early, a failure costs pocket change instead of a run.

Lesson 11: measurement bugs are cheaper and more dangerous

The last group cost almost no money, but these bugs are sneakier. A rental mistake at least shows up on the bill; a measurement mistake produces a confident number that is simply wrong. Some appeared earlier in the series (1, 2, 3, 4), and here are the new ones.

Once the recogniser scored a WER near 100% on a book, and it looked like the data was garbage. The cause was the script: the recogniser output Latin and the book text was Cyrillic, so practically every word counted as an error. Before scoring, convert both sides to one script, and do it with the official transliterator, not by eye.

Another time two TTS samples out of two showed a pitch spike, and I started reworking data because of it. Out of 125 takes there were zero spikes. Generation is stochastic, and n = 2 is not a measurement. A related trap is repeating the wrong thing. A proper-name defect didn't show on 60 names in one sentence × 5 takes, although it appeared in about half of real sentences. With 4 names in 8 different sentences it showed at once, p = 0.0013. You have to vary the factor the defect depends on, not the one that's easiest to iterate.

The tooling made one of these mistakes for us. "Keep the last N checkpoints" deleted the best one, and two runs lost their best moment, so the best checkpoint by validation now lives outside the rotation.

The worst one was train/test overlap. 68% of the old dev text also appeared in training, so some version-3 numbers were inflated. That's an exam built from the homework problems: the grade says more about memory than about skill. We built a clean dev set from works that appear nowhere else in the data.

The checklist

Put together, the failure chart tells the story: at first nearly every run broke somewhere, and now failures are rare and cheap.

This is what I'd run through before renting a GPU now:

  • [ ] Measure the useful token share on a real sample. If it's far below 90%, pack.
  • [ ] Verify packing doesn't leak across examples, on the attention path you'll actually use.
  • [ ] Estimate from steps × batch × seq_len, then compare to the first minutes of real steps.
  • [ ] Checkpoint frequency in hours, to local disk; keep the best checkpoint outside rotation.
  • [ ] Data loader workers sized to the CPU count; GPU utilisation checked in the first ten minutes.
  • [ ] Full rehearsal of the whole chain at home with a tiny model.
  • [ ] No stale markers or result files on persistent volumes; state tied to a run ID.
  • [ ] Watchdog off the rented machine, fire-drilled before launch, hang = no steps, not low utilisation.
  • [ ] Near the limit: save first, shut down second.
  • [ ] On error: fix in place, keep the machine and its logs.
  • [ ] Confirm the card can actually be created before trusting its price.

A cheap cycle isn't a good cycle by default. One version with new data tied the previous one 6 : 5 in a blind comparison (the setup is described in the first post) and didn't ship. But that failure cost $10, not $53, and left full logs behind.

Where this leaves us

We're not stopping cloud training. We're in the data-collection stage now, and training will continue on rented machines, but each run is many times cheaper and doesn't break out of nowhere. The latest speech recogniser came out better than the previous one: more accurate on reference transcripts, and it won more often in the same blind comparison.

The bottleneck has moved. It isn't hardware or money any more; it's live conversational speech transcribed by people. We've learned to count GPUs. What the models are missing is living language.

Fifth post in the series.

Want to help? What the project needs most is native Crimean Tatar speakers. Listen to a short clip and say whether the machine transcribed it right. Read a page and mark which word is Turkish and which is ours. Write a dialogue with the real colour of the language. Record a few minutes of reading. No programming needed, just knowing your language well. Write to ai@ay.mw or on Telegram: t.me/ana_yurt_dev.

If you'd rather support the work financially: ko-fi.com/anayurt. After all of the above, every dollar now goes a lot further.

description: To create self-serve templates that bend—but don’t break—brand designers need to consider work through a marketing lens. Here’s how to set up editing guardrails and design layouts that flex and scale.

title: EEG2MCU: Sensing-to-Execution Co-Design for Wearable EEG Inference
description:
arXiv:2611.23619v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Wearable EEG inference is constrained not only by model size, but also by the channel-dependent sensing front end that must process high-dimensional inputs before compact downstream computation. We present EEG2MCU, a sensing-to-execution co-design framework that treats electrode count as a hardware design variable through task-aware montage selection. EEG2MCU retains a compact time-frequency representation and generates only the INT8 regions required by each first-layer tile, avoiding full input materialization. Halo reuse and access-aware placement across Flash, SRAM, and tightly coupled memory further reduce redundant generation and data movement. On a Cortex-M7 MCU, EEG2MCU reduces peak SRAM by 11.38x relative to the baseline, including a 1.71x reduction from the 62-to-19 electrode montage, while reducing latency by 2.57x and energy by 2.48x. It retains 94-96% of full-montage accuracy, demonstrating practical high-dimensional EEG inference under tight embedded-resource constraints.

title: MillBill: A Machining Agent with Geometric Feedback
description:
arXiv:2611.22565v2 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Turning a CAD model into a machining program requires both process knowledge and geometric precision. Language models can generate such workflows by writing geometry and toolpath code for each part, but this makes numerical execution part of the model's task. We introduce MillBill, an agent that separates machining decisions from their geometric execution and verification. Given a boundary-representation part, stock, and material, a locally hosted, mid-sized open model proposes operations and cutting parameters for indexed three-axis machining. A geometric harness generates toolpaths, simulates material removal, and returns feedback for plan refinement. Setup planning accounts for what the available cutters can physically reach, rather than visibility alone. We evaluate the resulting programs by the fraction of the target surface area within the specified tolerance after simulated machining. With Qwen3.8-27B, MillBill outperforms frontier-model approaches that construct their own geometry and toolpath workflows on the evaluated machining tasks. Code: https://github.com/kulibinai/millbill

title: AutoE2E: Don't speak - Language free end-to-end autonomy A Real-Time Driving Model for L2++ ADAS and L4 Robotaxis
description:
arXiv:2611.22374v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AutoE2E is an open-source end-to-end driving model developed by the Autoware Foundation Robotaxi Working Group. It introduces a temporal bird's-eye-view (BEV) architecture that combines multi-camera perception, HD-map information and route conditioning to predict future vehicle motion. The evaluated model uses a pretrained camera-BEV backbone, temporal feature fusion and a lightweight recurrent trajectory planner. It contains approximately 79.9 million parameters, of which approximately 1.45 million are trainable in the evaluated configuration. The v1.0 release provides model checkpoints, training and evaluation code, and DataModelConsole, a dashboard for visualizing and inspecting model experiments. On the KITScenes validation benchmark, the fine-tuned checkpoint achieves an average displacement error (ADE) of 0.745 m and a final displacement error (FDE) of 2.020 m at a three-second prediction horizon. The paper also reports preliminary real-vehicle research conducted with the Technical University of Munich's EDGAR platform, alongside ongoing collaboration with the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology. AutoE2E v1.0 is an early open research release. Its quantitative evaluation is open-loop, and the model has not yet demonstrated validated closed-loop autonomous driving. The release is intended to provide the autonomous-driving community with an inspectable baseline for further research, experimentation and collaborative development.

title: QDA: Closed-Loop LLM Quantization Design with Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.23388v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Post-training quantization is the standard way to serve large language models at low cost. However, the best quantization recipe differs across models and precisions. As a result, experts must redesign it for every new model, which is time-consuming and often sub-optimal. Fortunately, an LLM agent can take over this design by refining the recipe over rounds of building and evaluating candidates, so that more rounds lead to better recipes. However, evaluating one quantized reasoning model takes tens of GPU-hours, and combining methods from different codebases means porting each to the new architecture by hand. We present QDA, a system in which an agent designs the recipe for each model and precision. To make evaluation fast, QDA scores each candidate in minutes by its output KL divergence from the original model on reasoning traces that the agent never sees, and checks promising ones with long generations to catch failures such as repetition loops. To make building fast, QDA provides a library of public PTQ methods that are compatible with one another and with new model architectures. Across four reasoning models, QDA improves accuracy over the strongest public recipe by 0.9, 1.4 and 2.2 percentage points on average at W4A16, W4A8 and W3A16, using 64 GPU-hours per search. On the 320B-parameter MoE model GLM-5.3-Flash at NVFP4 W4A4, it recovers 98.3% of the FP8 model's accuracy, against 96.9% for the best vendor checkpoint. Every QDA checkpoint also runs on existing serving kernels with no inference overhead. We will release the library, the evaluator and the harness.

title: AllotNet: an Interpretable Mixture-of-Experts Choice Model for Moral Judgement in Humanitarian Aid Allocation, Validated against a Planted Synthetic Population
description:
arXiv:2611.23474v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Official development assistance fell by 23.1 per cent in 2025, and the decision of who is helped first when there is not enough for everyone is moving into software. A leading published machine-learning targeting system excluded 53 per cent of eligible households as deployed. If the rule of distribution ends up in code, it should carry the judgement of many cultures, and the machine should execute while a person judges. AllotNet is an interpretable mixture-of-experts conditional logit for the allocation judgements elicited by Allot, a pre-registered six-language instrument: eight linear taste experts over seven ethical criteria, weighted by a gate over participant context, with a damped residual, an encoder for household intake, an outcome head and a budget-constrained planner that builds a review queue and never rejects anyone. A model of human judgement has no answer key on real data, so we wrote one first: a planted synthetic population of 5.6 million sessions and 104 million responses (98 million usable choices), generated by the production code path from a ground truth hidden from the loss. All sixteen pre-specified checks passed: criterion ranking $\rho = 1.000$, hidden segments recovered (ARI 0.671), outcome head at 99 per cent of the noise ceiling, planner at 99.4 per cent of oracle. The caveats are reported with them: two checks are weaker than their titles, and a live-generation failure cost 260,712 seeds. The model has 23,550 parameters, is trained quantisation-aware for NVFP4 with its interpretable core in fp32 (welfare-rank parity $\rho = 0.9937$ at W4A16 on the shipped bundle; one parity threshold was relaxed post hoc), and ships as a 125 KB bundle with C11, Java, Rust and Python runtimes. Nothing has been trained on real data yet; at the study's real scale a hierarchical Bayesian mixed logit is the registered comparator.

title: What Do Learned 3D Models Add to Localization from Posed References?
description:
arXiv:2611.23697v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Localizing a query from a few posed reference images avoids building a 3D point map. We ask what the camera predictions of learned 3D models add to geometric estimation from the same references, and where failures arise. Across eight learned models and variants and five test sets, we compare reference budgets, swap pose components, and intervene on the references a model sees. At fine pose-error thresholds, geometric estimation with one additional reference is significantly more accurate than every model on two references on Cambridge and NAVER B1 and never significantly worse, alone or as a fallback behind a shared acceptance gate; with the same three references, the more accurate approach depends on the scene. The gain from the learned translation magnitude depends on reference selection: it improves seven of the eight models on 12-Scenes with the spread-out pairs we select, but none of the five we test with the two top-ranked retrieved references. Where retrieval also returns references from other locations, at NAVER Gangnam Station, models fail at different stages. A robust alignment brings Pi3X and MapAnything within 3.3 pp of adding references as needed. In controlled tests, aligning on the nearby references largely restores VGGT, Pi3X and MapAnything but not Depth Anything 3, and pose-conditioned Pi3X recovers only if the far poses are masked and left out of its input-pose normalization.

title: Distributed LLM Training Across Metros: Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText
description: Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText enables developers to efficiently train large language models across geographically distributed TPU slices by streaming parameter fragments instead of synchronizing full models at every step. This approach slashes cross-slice communication volume by over 60× and eliminates network stalls, allowing seamless multi-datacenter scaling without degrading model convergence or quality.
