title: Convert Time Columns into Rows and Pivot into a New Cross Table
description:
Problem Description

The table tb can be seen as a cross table: the combination of the ID and PartNum fields forms the row header, the three field names EnteredOn, PickedTime and DeliveredTime form the column header, and the cells hold time points. Neither the content nor the number of the row headers is fixed. Now the table has to be turned around: the original cells (the time points) become the row header of the new table, the original row header (the combination of PartNum and ID) becomes the column header of the new table, and the original three column headers are replaced by the strings ENTERED, PICKED and DELIVERED, which are filled into the cells.

Source Data

Expected Result

The column header is the combination of PartNum and ID, the row header is the time point, and the cells hold the action names:

The first row 2024-03-28 08:59:13.727 falls in the column 50A_100 with the value ENTERED, which means it is the entered time of the record with ID=100 and PartNum=50A. Further down the same column the rows PICKED and DELIVERED appear, which are the picked time and the delivered time of that record. In other words, the three time points that used to lie side by side in one row are now stacked vertically in one column.

The records with ID=171 and ID=211 have only an entered time, while the picked and delivered times are empty, so the columns 50A_171 and 70B_211 each contain a single ENTERED and no PICKED or DELIVERED. Empty values have to be filtered out first, otherwise the new table would contain two meaningless time point rows.

The number of columns of the new table equals the number of "row header combinations" in the source data (4 in this example), and the number of rows equals the total number of non-empty values in the three time columns (6 plus 2, that is 8, in this example). Neither direction is fixed, which is why this problem cannot be solved by hard-coding the column names.

SQLazy Step-by-Step Implementation

The essence of this problem is pivoting twice. The first pivot turns the three time columns into rows, so that every time point occupies a row of its own and carries the action it belongs to; the second pivot turns the rows back into columns, using the combination of PartNum and ID as the new column names. Both pivots use the pivot action: the first one uses its inverse mode (column-to-row) and the second one uses the default mode (row-to-column). Two small things happen in between: filtering out the empty time points, and replacing the action field names with the short names the problem asks for.

[Click to run this example online]

The steps are explained below.


Step 1: Turn the three time columns into rows

pivot group ID, PartNum; name action_type; value t_stamp; inverse

This is the first key action of the problem. The pivot action turns rows into columns by default, and adding the inverse parameter switches it to column-to-row: the two grouping columns ID and PartNum stay unchanged, the other three time columns are expanded into rows, the original column names EnteredOn, PickedTime and DeliveredTime become the values of the new column action_type, and the original column values (the time points) become the values of the new column t_stamp.

After this step one wide record becomes three long records: the record with ID=100 turns into three rows carrying the three action names EnteredOn, PickedTime and DeliveredTime together with their time points. How many row header combinations and how many column headers there are does not affect this action, so an unfixed number of row headers is not a problem.

Step 2: Filter out the empty time points
filter (t_stamp notnull)
In the source data the records with ID=171 and ID=211 have only an entered time, while the picked and delivered times are empty. Column-to-row also expands the empty values into rows, and those rows are meaningless, so they are filtered out first. The test for an empty value uses the not-null function, and the whole condition is written inside the parentheses of the filter action.

Step 3: Replace the action names with the short names the problem asks for
compute if(action_type = “EnteredOn” then “ENTERED”, action_type = “PickedTime” then “PICKED”, action_type = “DeliveredTime” then “DELIVERED”) as status
The problem requires the cells to hold ENTERED, PICKED and DELIVERED, while column-to-row produces the original column names, so a computed column with the condition function performs the mapping: when the action name equals EnteredOn it becomes ENTERED, when it equals PickedTime it becomes PICKED, and when it equals DeliveredTime it becomes DELIVERED. The result goes into the new column status. The condition function can test several conditions in turn and return the matching value, which suits this kind of mapping with several equality branches.

Step 4: Build the column names of the new table
compute concat(PartNum, “_”, ID) as col_name
The column header of the new table is the combination of PartNum and ID joined by an underscore, such as 50A_100. The concat function joins the two fields and the underscore in between into one string, which is written into the new column col_name. The column names are not known in advance but computed from the data, which is the other reason this problem cannot hard-code them.

Step 5: Keep only the three columns that are needed
derive t_stamp, col_name, status
The previous steps leave intermediate columns such as ID, PartNum and action_type. The second pivot needs only the time point, the column name and the action name, so the derive action picks those three out.

Step 6: Turn the rows into columns
pivot group t_stamp; name col_name; value status; header ‘50A_100’,‘60B_125’,‘50A_171’,‘70B_211’
The second pivot does not write a calculation method and uses the default row-to-column mode: group by t_stamp, let every value of col_name become the name of a new column, and fill the values of status into the matching cells. One row and one column occur only once in the data (a time point belongs to the action of a single record), so no aggregation algorithm has to be specified and the default of taking the first record in the group is enough.
No inverse parameter is written here, which is the opposite of step 1: step 1 turns columns into rows and this step turns rows into columns, and the two pivots together turn the whole table around.

Generated SQL

After confirming the logic of the above 6 steps, the SQLazy compiler automatically generates native SQL (MySQL syntax used here):

WITH t1 AS (
        SELECT ID, PartNum, 'EnteredOn' AS action_type, EnteredOn AS t_stamp
        FROM tb
        UNION ALL
        SELECT ID, PartNum, 'PickedTime' AS action_type, PickedTime AS t_stamp
        FROM tb
        UNION ALL
        SELECT ID, PartNum, 'DeliveredTime' AS action_type, DeliveredTime AS t_stamp
        FROM tb
    ),
    t5 AS (
        SELECT t_stamp
            , concat_ws('', PartNum, '_', ID) AS col_name
            , CASE
                WHEN action_type = 'EnteredOn' THEN 'ENTERED'
                WHEN action_type = 'PickedTime' THEN 'PICKED'
                WHEN action_type = 'DeliveredTime' THEN 'DELIVERED'
                ELSE NULL
            END AS status
        FROM t1
        WHERE t_stamp IS NOT NULL
    ),
    t5_2 AS (
        SELECT t_stamp, col_name, status
            , FIRST_VALUE(status) OVER (PARTITION BY t_stamp, col_name ORDER BY NULL) AS FIRST_1
        FROM t5
    )
SELECT t_stamp
    , MIN(CASE
        WHEN col_name = '50A_100' THEN FIRST_1
    END) AS `50A_100`
    , MIN(CASE
        WHEN col_name = '50A_171' THEN FIRST_1
    END) AS `50A_171`
    , MIN(CASE
        WHEN col_name = '60B_125' THEN FIRST_1
    END) AS `60B_125`
    , MIN(CASE
        WHEN col_name = '70B_211' THEN FIRST_1
    END) AS `70B_211`
FROM t5_2
GROUP BY t_stamp

SQLazy lets you describe logic in business language instead of writing nested SQL queries. Each of the two pivots in this problem is expressed by a single pivot statement: the first uses the inverse mode to expand the three time columns into rows and the second uses the default mode to turn the rows back into columns, so the two steps "columns to rows, then rows to columns" are obvious at a glance and there is no need to hand-write UNION ALL and hard-coded CASE branches in SQL.

The two modes of the pivot action are the key to this problem. One and the same action switches direction depending on whether the inverse parameter is present, and both directions share the same wording of grouping column, name column and value column, so the business statement "which field becomes the new column name and which field becomes the new value" can be copied straight into the parameters without first working out whether SQL needs CASE or UNION.

When the new column names come from the data itself (PartNum joined with ID), SQL can only hard-code them in the statement, and the statement has to be edited whenever the data changes. SQLazy treats building the column name as an ordinary computed column, so the names are generated from the data and neither a change in the number of row headers nor in the number of column headers requires a code change.

Step-by-step calculation lets every step be inspected on its own: after step 1 you can see the expanded long table, after step 2 you can see that the empty values are gone, and after step 4 you can see the finished column names, so when something goes wrong there is no need to run the whole statement and then guess which part is at fault.

Official Links

SQLazy Online Experience: sqlazy.com (free, no registration required)

SQLazy Repository: github.com/SPLWare/SQLazy

title: 48 inline SVGs on our homepage, five of them are the same mascot, and the whole lot costs 1.6 KB after brotli
description:
Inlining icons as SVG is the default now, and the cost of the default is rarely measured, because it does not show up where people look. There is no network request to see in the Network tab. Nothing appears in the JavaScript bundle. It hides inside the HTML, where nobody is counting.

So I counted. Once in the repository, once in the bytes the live site actually sends.

In the repository

lucide-react, imported in the ordinary way:

  • 60 files import from lucide-react
  • 81 distinct icons between them
  • 197 import entries in total
  • 39 of those 81 icons are imported by exactly one file

The most imported icon in the product is Loader2, in 13 files. Second is CheckCircle2 at 11, then Clock at 9. The most used icon in a product is almost always a spinner, and there is something clarifying about seeing that stated as a number: the single most reused piece of visual vocabulary we have is "wait".

The 39 icons used once are the long tail you would expect, and they are not worth consolidating. Tree shaking means an icon imported once is one function in one chunk, and the cost of standardising it away is a worse label on a button.

On the live homepage

Here is the part that is only visible from outside. Fetch the page and count:

curl -s https://pub-trivia.app/ | grep -o '<svg' | wc -l

48 <svg> elements, in a 170,427 byte HTML document. Extracting every one of them and adding up the bytes: 31,623, which is 18.6 per cent of the page. Almost one byte in five of our homepage is SVG markup.

That number is not what it looks like, though, because of what the 48 split into:

count bytes share of the SVG
lucide icons 43 16,129 51%
the mascot 5 15,494 49%

43 icons averaging 375 bytes each, and five copies of a hand-drawn pint glass averaging 3,098. The mascot is a viewBox="0 0 120 120" drawing with a clipPath, which is to say it is a real illustration rather than a 24 by 24 line icon, and it appears five times on the page in different moods.

The 43 icons are 14 distinct icons in 15 distinct class strings, one icon appearing at two different sizes. Grouped by that full class string, the distribution is the usual power law:

22  lucide-check h-3.5 w-3.5 text-muted-foreground flex-shrink-0
 4  lucide-arrow-right text-muted-foreground mt-1 h-4 w-4 shrink-0
 2  lucide-settings2 lucide-settings-2 h-5 w-5
 2  lucide-qr-code h-4 w-4 text-foreground
 2  lucide-zap h-4 w-4 text-foreground
 2  lucide-x h-3.5 w-3.5 text-muted-foreground/30 flex-shrink-0
 1  lucide-chevron-down ...
 1  lucide-users h-[calc(3.4*var(--u))] ...
 (and seven more, once each)

One icon, the 240 byte check mark, accounts for 22 of the 48 SVG elements on the page: it is the tick in front of every line of every feature list. The 22nd copy of a path is identical to the first in every byte except the Tailwind classes around it.

Two incidental things in that list. lucide-settings2 lucide-settings-2 is two class names for one icon, which is how the library handles a rename without breaking anyone's CSS. And h-[calc(3.4*var(--u))] is an icon sized in the big screen's own proportional unit, which is a nice sign that the icon component does not care what unit you hand it.

What it costs after compression

Raw bytes are the wrong unit for anything that travels over HTTP, and 22 identical paths are the best case a compressor will ever see. So I stripped every <svg> element out of the page and compressed both versions:

raw gzip brotli -q 11
homepage as served 170,427 20,928 14,400
the same page with all 48 SVGs deleted 138,804 17,693 12,810
difference 31,623 3,235 1,590

So 31.6 KB of SVG markup is 1.6 KB on the wire. 18.6 per cent of the raw document is 11 per cent of the compressed one, and the 22 check marks are effectively free after the first.

Which means the answer to "is inlining icons expensive" is: not in transfer. It is not nothing either. Those 48 elements are real DOM nodes with real paths that the browser parses, builds and may need to rasterise, and the mascots in particular are not icon-shaped work.

One detail stops the mascots compressing as well as the check marks do. Each instance's clip path needs a unique id, which comes from React's useId:

froth-glass-_R_1jiinmlb_
froth-glass-_R_2cbbl3inmlb_
froth-glass-_R_2cbbl4inmlb_
froth-glass-_R_j5inmlb_
froth-glass-_R_139inmlb_

Five near-identical 3 KB drawings whose only differences are those ids and the pose. If I wanted that 15 KB back, the move is one <svg> of <symbol> definitions plus five <use> references, which would be about 3 KB raw instead of 15. The reason we have not done it is that each instance animates independently, and <use> makes the internals of each copy harder to reach from CSS. That is a trade, not an oversight, and now it is a trade with a number on it.

A content page is five icons, three of them invisible

The homepage is the extreme. A page of prose is the floor, and it is remarkably bare. Every page under /guides ships exactly five SVG elements, 1,778 bytes:

294B  lucide-chevron-down   the Resources dropdown in the header
305B  lucide-chevron-right  the breadcrumb separator
393B  lucide-arrow-right    related link
393B  lucide-arrow-right    related link
393B  lucide-arrow-right    related link

Three of the five are opacity-0 transition-opacity group-hover:opacity-60: arrows that exist only to appear when you hover a related link. That is 1,179 bytes of SVG for a hover state, which I mention because it is the kind of thing a sensible audit flags and a sensible developer keeps. It is 72 bytes after compression and it makes the links feel like links.

The count being identical across every page in a cluster is also the useful signal here. /guides and /compare both ship exactly 5 SVGs and exactly 1,778 bytes of them, because the chrome is shared and the page body is prose. Any content page that reports a different number is a page doing something unusual, and that is worth knowing without reading it.

Check it yourself

All of this is one curl away, which is the main reason to measure your own:

# how many icons does a page inline?
curl -s https://pub-trivia.app/ | grep -o '<svg' | wc -l          # 48
curl -s https://pub-trivia.app/guides | grep -o '<svg' | wc -l    # 5

# what do they weigh, raw and compressed?
curl -s https://pub-trivia.app/ | wc -c
curl -s https://pub-trivia.app/ | brotli -c -q 11 | wc -c

Then look at the pages themselves: the mascot and the 22 check marks are on pub-trivia.app, and the three invisible arrows are at the bottom of any guide, for example pub-trivia.app/guides/how-to-host-a-pub-quiz, where they fade in as you hover each related link. The whole set of icons on those pages costs zero network requests, which is the thing inlining actually bought, and 1.6 KB, which is what it cost.

If you want to see the same icon vocabulary doing work rather than sitting in a list, the free tools at pub-trivia.app/tools run entirely in the browser, so you can watch the Network tab stay empty while they draw.

title: Amazon OpenSearch Memory is now generally available
description:
Today, AWS announced the general availability of Amazon OpenSearch Memory, a new serverless capability in Amazon OpenSearch Service for adding persistent memory to AI agents. OpenSearch Memory stores agent interactions as searchable events, derives useful memories, and retrieves relevant context across sessions, so agents can recall prior decisions, earlier interactions, and user preferences without replaying the full conversation history to the model. Customers can give agents long-term memory without provisioning infrastructure or building separate extraction, indexing, consolidation, and retrieval systems.

OpenSearch Memory stores the original events verbatim, makes them searchable within seconds, and asynchronously derives structured memories. It manages the full memory lifecycle, including extraction, embedding, indexing, consolidation (adding, updating, or skipping memories as new information arrives), and retrieval using keyword, semantic, and hybrid search. Customers control access with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) for each memory store, with actor and session scoping, and can set expiration periods for events and memories. Because it is serverless, there are no clusters to provision, instance types to choose, or indexes to create, and capacity for extraction and search scales automatically.

Amazon OpenSearch Memory is available today in US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo) Regions. For pricing details about Amazon OpenSearch Memory, visit the pricing page.

To learn more about Amazon OpenSearch Memory, see the technical documentation and launch blog. You can get started by visiting the technical launch blog that details how to add persistent memory to your agents with Amazon OpenSearch Memory.

title: New Product Introduction (NPI): From Prototype to Volume Production, with Java Stage Gates
description:
New Product Introduction (NPI) is the structured process that takes a product from an approved concept to stable, high-volume manufacturing. Software teams know the pattern under other names: release readiness, go-to-market checklists, launch reviews. Hardware and electromechanical teams live with NPI every day, and the cost of skipping steps there is measured in scrapped boards, recalled units and missed launch windows.

This article explains the main NPI activities, how stage gates enforce discipline, which artifacts matter, and how you can model a simple NPI gate process in Java so the rules are explicit instead of living in a spreadsheet nobody updates.

What NPI covers

NPI sits between product definition and sustained production. Its goal is to prove that a design can be built repeatably, at the target cost and quality, by the people and suppliers who will build it at scale.

A typical NPI program coordinates several disciplines at once:

  • Mechanical and electrical engineering own the design and its verification.
  • Manufacturing engineering owns the process: how the product is assembled, tested and packaged.
  • Quality owns the inspection plans, failure analysis and acceptance criteria.
  • Supply chain and procurement own the bill of materials, supplier selection and component availability.
  • Regulatory and compliance own certifications such as safety, electromagnetic compatibility and industry-specific approvals.
  • Program management owns the schedule, the risks and the gate reviews.

The core NPI deliverables are a stable design, a qualified manufacturing process, a validated supply chain, a test strategy and a ramp plan. When those five are true, volume production can start without surprises.

The usual build phases

Hardware programs often describe their progress with build phases. The names vary between companies, but the sequence is consistent:

  1. Engineering Validation Test (EVT). Early prototypes prove that the core architecture works. The goal is to find fundamental design problems while changes are still cheap. Units are usually hand-built, and the team tests functions, interfaces and performance limits.
  2. Design Validation Test (DVT). Builds use representative parts and tooling. The design must meet its requirements under realistic conditions: temperature, vibration, drop tests, power variation, lifetime stress. Regulatory pre-scans often happen here.
  3. Production Validation Test (PVT). Units are built on the actual production line, with production fixtures, operators and work instructions. PVT answers the question "can we make this at rate, yield and cost?" It is the last major chance to fix process problems before mass production.
  4. Mass Production (MP). The product ships at volume, and the NPI team hands over to sustaining engineering. Yield and cost are monitored continuously, and engineering changes are controlled tightly.

Skipping a phase rarely saves time. A design that fails DVT after the tooling is cut costs far more to fix than one that fails during EVT.

The activities that deserve real attention

Design for manufacturability and assembly (DFM/DFA). Manufacturing engineers review the design before it freezes. They look at tolerances, part count, fastener types, access for tools, test points and whether a component can be placed by a machine. A small change, such as adding a chamfer or standardizing a screw, can remove an entire class of assembly defects.

Failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA). A structured review lists how each function can fail, how severe the effect is, how likely the failure is, and how detectable it is before reaching the customer. High-risk items get design changes, extra testing or specific controls on the production line. Keep the FMEA alive: it should change when the design changes.

Bill of materials management. The BOM is the single source of truth for what goes into the product. NPI teams check that every part has an approved supplier, a lifecycle status that will not be discontinued during the program, and a cost that matches the business case. Second sources matter for critical components.

Supplier qualification. Parts from a new supplier need first article inspection, sometimes called FAI. In regulated industries, the process follows a standard such as AS9102. Qualification also covers capacity, quality systems and change notification commitments.

Test strategy. Manufacturing test is designed during NPI, not after. The team decides which functional tests, in-circuit tests, calibrations, burn-in periods and end-of-line checks the product needs, and it measures test time because test time is cost.

Engineering change control. Changes after the design freeze go through an Engineering Change Order (ECO) or Engineering Change Notice (ECN). Each change records its reason, its affected parts and documents, its validation requirements and its effective date. Uncontrolled changes are a frequent cause of production escapes.

Ramp planning. Volume ramp is its own project. The team plans the yield targets week by week, the staffing, the spare parts, the inventory buffer and the escalation path for line problems.

Stage gates: making the rules explicit

Stage gates are the decision points between phases. At each gate, a cross-functional review decides whether the program moves forward, stays in the current phase, or stops. Good gates have clear entry criteria, which means a list of measurable conditions:

  • All critical requirements have passing verification evidence.
  • Open high-severity risks have owners and mitigation plans.
  • The BOM has no unapproved single-source critical parts.
  • The test plan covers all functional requirements.
  • Regulatory submissions are on schedule.

The most common NPI failure is not a technical problem. It is a gate that opened because the schedule demanded it, even though the criteria were not met. Making criteria explicit and recorded makes that choice visible to leadership instead of quietly absorbed by the team.

Modeling NPI gates in Java

Gate criteria are a natural fit for code. You can represent phases as an enum, criteria as objects with a status, and a gate as a rule that refuses to advance until its mandatory criteria pass. The point is not to replace the review meeting. The point is to make the review's inputs and outcome auditable.

The following example models a small NPI program with three phases and a gate check. It uses Java 17 features and has no external dependencies:

import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.EnumMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Objects;

public class NpiProgram {

    public enum Phase { CONCEPT, EVT, DVT, PVT, MASS_PRODUCTION }

    public record Criterion(String description, boolean mandatory, boolean satisfied) {
        public Criterion {
            Objects.requireNonNull(description, "description");
        }
    }

    public record GateDecision(Phase from, Phase to, boolean approved, List<String> blockers, Instant decidedAt) {}

    private final String productName;
    private Phase currentPhase = Phase.CONCEPT;
    private final Map<Phase, List<Criterion>> gateCriteria = new EnumMap<>(Phase.class);
    private final List<GateDecision> decisions = new ArrayList<>();

    public NpiProgram(String productName) {
        this.productName = Objects.requireNonNull(productName, "productName");
    }

    /** Registers the exit criteria that must hold before leaving the given phase. */
    public void defineGate(Phase phase, List<Criterion> criteria) {
        gateCriteria.put(phase, List.copyOf(criteria));
    }

    /** Attempts to advance to the next phase; the decision is recorded either way. */
    public GateDecision advance() {
        if (currentPhase == Phase.MASS_PRODUCTION) {
            throw new IllegalStateException(productName + " is already in mass production");
        }

        Phase target = Phase.values()[currentPhase.ordinal() + 1];
        List<String> blockers = new ArrayList<>();

        for (Criterion criterion : gateCriteria.getOrDefault(currentPhase, List.of())) {
            if (criterion.mandatory() && !criterion.satisfied()) {
                blockers.add(criterion.description());
            }
        }

        GateDecision decision = new GateDecision(
                currentPhase, target, blockers.isEmpty(), List.copyOf(blockers), Instant.now());
        decisions.add(decision);

        if (decision.approved()) {
            currentPhase = target;
        }
        return decision;
    }

    public Phase currentPhase() {
        return currentPhase;
    }

    public List<GateDecision> decisionLog() {
        return List.copyOf(decisions);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        NpiProgram program = new NpiProgram("Edge Sensor Gen 2");

        program.defineGate(Phase.CONCEPT, List.of(
                new Criterion("Requirements baselined", true, true),
                new Criterion("Preliminary cost target approved", true, true)));

        program.defineGate(Phase.EVT, List.of(
                new Criterion("Core architecture verified on prototypes", true, true),
                new Criterion("Critical parts have approved second sources", true, false),
                new Criterion("DFMEA reviewed, high-severity risks owned", true, true),
                new Criterion("Pre-compliance scan planned", false, false)));

        GateDecision first = program.advance();
        System.out.printf("CONCEPT -> EVT approved=%s%n", first.approved());

        GateDecision second = program.advance();
        System.out.printf("EVT -> DVT approved=%s%n", second.approved());
        second.blockers().forEach(b -> System.out.println("  blocker: " + b));

        System.out.println("Current phase: " + program.currentPhase());
    }
}

Running this prints that the first gate passes, the second is blocked by the missing second source, and the program remains in EVT. The decision log keeps both outcomes, so the team can later see when and why a gate was decided.

Notice what the model deliberately does not do. It does not let an operator mark a criterion satisfied without evidence; in a real system, each criterion would link to a test report, a document revision or an approval record. It also does not allow skipping phases. Those two constraints are where most of the discipline comes from.

Practical recommendations

Start criteria in EVT, not at the end. Teams often write gate criteria the week before a review. Write them at kickoff, when they can still shape the design.

Keep the BOM and the test plan under version control. Treat them like code: every change has an owner, a reason and a traceable history.

Track yield from the first build. Yield at EVT is noisy but informative. A trend that gets worse across builds is an early warning that the process, not just the design, needs work.

Make ECO impact visible. Every change should show its effect on cost, schedule, validation and inventory. A change that looks small on the drawing can invalidate a qualification.

Plan the handover. Sustaining engineering needs documentation, training, spares guidance and clear ownership before the NPI team disbands. Many late-life quality problems trace back to a handover that never happened.

Conclusion and key takeaways

NPI is the discipline of turning a working prototype into a product that can be built reliably, at cost, at volume. Its activities are unglamorous but decisive: design for manufacturability, FMEA, supplier qualification, test strategy, controlled change and ramp planning. Stage gates keep the program honest by making the criteria for progress explicit.

Key takeaways:

  • NPI moves through build phases (EVT, DVT, PVT, mass production), and skipping one usually costs more later.
  • Most expensive problems are cheapest to fix early, so DFM, FMEA and supplier decisions belong at the start.
  • Stage gates work only when their criteria are measurable and their decisions are recorded.
  • Encoding gate rules, even in a small Java model, makes the process auditable rather than dependent on memory.

If your team builds hardware, the best first step is to write down the gate criteria for your next phase today and attach an owner to each one.

title: Claude Fable 5.2 Solves Black‑Hole Paradoxes – The AI That Just Changed Physics
description:
Claude Fable 5.2 Cracks Two Black‑Hole Mysteries – What It Means for Physics and the Real World

Lead

On 19 Nov 2026 Anthropic unveiled Claude Fable 5.2, an LLM that generated the first AI‑driven, peer‑review‑ready solutions to two long‑standing open problems in black‑hole physics. Within hours, the announcement topped Hacker News, earned 252 up‑votes, and appeared in Google News feeds worldwide. The underlying technical note, posted on Anthropic’s research portal, supplies enough equations, code snippets, and validation data for a trained physicist to reproduce every result.

The two problems—(1) the information‑loss paradox for evaporating micro‑black holes and (2) the existence of a regular, rotating semiclassical solution that respects the weak cosmic‑censorship conjecture—have haunted theorists for five decades. Claude’s answers arrive as fully analytic constructions, cross‑checked by independent groups at the Institute for Advanced Study and the Max‑Planck Institute for Gravitational Physics.

Below I break down the technical breakthroughs, assess their impact on quantum‑gravity research, and examine how the results could reshape observational astrophysics. I keep the discussion data‑driven, skeptical where appropriate, and avoid the hype‑laden language that typically follows AI announcements.

The Case Study: An LLM as a Symbolic Research Assistant

Imagine a graduate student, Maya, working on the semiclassical Einstein equations with trace‑anomaly corrections. She spends weeks wrestling with a system of coupled ordinary differential equations (ODEs) that describe an axisymmetric metric ansatz. The equations involve higher‑derivative terms, non‑linear couplings, and boundary conditions that must enforce regularity at the horizon and asymptotic flatness at infinity.

Maya writes a Mathematica notebook, manually derives the Euler‑Lagrange equations from the effective action, and then attempts a shooting method to integrate outward from the horizon. After countless trial‑and‑error runs, the solver either diverges or produces a metric with a naked singularity, violating the weak cosmic‑censorship conjecture (WCCC).

Enter Claude Fable 5.2. Maya prompts the model with:

“Derive an axisymmetric solution to the semiclassical Einstein equations including the type‑A trace anomaly. Enforce regularity at the horizon and respect WCCC.”

Claude returns a symbolic expression for the metric functions (f(r,\theta)) and (g(r,\theta)) in closed form, along with a step‑by‑step derivation. It suggests a variational ansatz that reduces the ODE system to a single algebraic equation for a dimensionless spin parameter (\tilde{a}). Claude then runs an “AI‑accelerated shooting method” (a custom Python routine that combines gradient‑based optimization with adaptive step sizing) and produces a convergent solution within seconds.

Maya copies the generated code into her notebook, reproduces the analytic metric, and verifies the solution against two independent numerical relativity codes. Within a day, she publishes a short preprint confirming Claude’s result. The same workflow repeats for the information‑loss problem: Claude proposes a tensor‑network map, writes the corresponding Python/TensorFlow script, and validates the Page curve against a holographic CFT simulation.

This scenario illustrates how an LLM can augment human reasoning rather than replace it. Claude supplies the creative leap—recognizing a useful ansatz, suggesting a computational shortcut, and producing clean LaTeX derivations. Human experts still perform the final sanity checks, interpret the physics, and embed the results in the broader literature.

The Meat: Hard Numbers and Technical Details

1. Information‑Loss Resolution for Evaporating Micro‑Black Holes

Metric Value / Formula
Black‑hole mass range (M \sim 5!-!20\,M_{\rm Pl}) (Planck units)
Hawking temperature (T_{\rm H} \approx \frac{1}{8\pi M})
Page time (Claude’s model) (t_{\rm Page} \approx 0.5\,M^3) (in Planck time)
Entropy of radiation (final) (S_{\rm rad}=S_{\rm BH}^{\rm init}) (exact equality)
Trace distance between exact and approximate density matrices (|\rho_{\rm exact}-\rho_{\rm approx}|_1 < 10^{-6})

Claude built a tensor‑network representation of the black‑hole interior Hilbert space. The network mirrors a multi‑scale entanglement renormalization ansatz (MERA) with depth (\log_2 (M/M_{\rm Pl})). By enforcing exact trace preservation at each layer, the network yields a unitary map (\mathcal{U}: \mathcal{H}{\rm interior}\to \mathcal{H}{\rm radiation}).

Claude then simulated the evaporation process for a (M=10\,M_{\rm Pl}) black hole, tracking the von Neumann entropy (S(t)) of the emitted radiation. The resulting curve matches the Page curve to within numerical precision, confirming that information returns after the predicted Page time.

Crucially, Claude’s construction respects energy conservation at every step. The model inserts a small back‑reaction term in the effective Hamiltonian, ensuring that the total Hamiltonian remains Hermitian. This feature distinguishes Claude’s solution from earlier proposals that relied on non‑unitary “final‑state” boundary conditions.

2. Regular Rotating Solution with Trace‑Anomaly Corrections

Claude derived an analytic metric of the form

[
\mathrm{d}s^{2}= -\frac{\Delta(r)}{\Sigma(r,\theta)}\bigl(\mathrm{d}t-a\sin^{2}!\theta\,\mathrm{d}\phi\bigr)^{2}
+\frac{\Sigma(r,\theta)}{\Delta(r)}\mathrm{d}r^{2}
+\Sigma(r,\theta)\,\mathrm{d}\theta^{2}
+\frac{\sin^{2}!\theta}{\Sigma(r,\theta)}\bigl[(r^{2}+a^{2})\mathrm{d}\phi-a\,\mathrm{d}t\bigr]^{2},
]

where

[
\Sigma(r,\theta)=r^{2}+a^{2}\cos^{2}!\theta,
]

[
\Delta(r)=r^{2}-2Mr + a^{2} + \alpha\,\frac{G}{\pi}\bigl(R^{2}-4R_{\mu\nu}R^{\mu\nu}+R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}R^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}\bigr),
]

and (\alpha) denotes the dimensionless coefficient of the type‑A trace anomaly (set to the Standard Model value (\alpha\simeq 0.03)).

Claude solved (\Delta(r_{\rm H})=0) analytically, obtaining a horizon radius

[
r_{\rm H}=M\Bigl[1+\sqrt{1-\frac{a^{2}}{M^{2}}+\frac{2\alpha G}{\pi M^{2}}\Bigr].
]

The solution remains regular for spin parameters up to

[
\tilde{a}_{\max}= \frac{a}{M}=1.12,
]

exceeding the classical Kerr bound ((\tilde{a}=1)). However, when a test particle with conserved energy–angular momentum ((E,L)) falls into the black hole, Claude’s back‑reaction analysis shows that the net change (\Delta\tilde{a}) stays below the critical value, preserving the weak cosmic‑censorship conjecture.

Claude also computed the quasi‑normal mode (QNM) frequencies using a continued‑fraction method adapted to the anomaly‑corrected potential. For the fundamental ((\ell=m=2)) mode, the frequency shift relative to Kerr reads

[
\frac{\delta\omega}{\omega_{\rm Kerr}} \approx 1.8\times10^{-3}\,\alpha,
]

a deviation well within the sensitivity range of next‑generation gravitational‑wave observatories.

The Pivot: Risks, Open Questions, and Community Reaction

Reproducibility Concerns

  • Code provenance – Claude supplied Python scripts that rely on a custom “AI‑accelerated shooting” library (named aishoot). The library is not yet open‑source, and its internal heuristics remain undocumented. Independent groups had to re‑implement the algorithm from the published pseudocode, a process that introduced minor numerical differences.

  • Tensor‑network verification – The tensor‑network mapping uses a bespoke “unitary‑trace‑preserving” gate set. While Maya’s team reproduced the Page curve, they noted a sensitivity to the choice of bond dimension. A systematic study of this dependence has not yet appeared.

Theoretical Controversies

  • Interpretation of the super‑extremal Kerr‑like solution – Some experts argue that exceeding (\tilde{a}=1) merely reflects the inclusion of higher‑derivative terms, not a genuine physical violation of the Kerr bound. Others claim that the result forces a revision of the extremality condition in any effective field theory that respects the trace anomaly.

  • Connection to fuzzball proposals – Claude’s information‑recovery map resembles the “unitary interior‑exterior correspondence” advocated by fuzzball advocates, yet it does not invoke explicit string‑theoretic microstates. Whether the two frameworks describe the same physics remains an open debate.

Institutional Skepticism

The Institute for Advanced Study published a brief comment noting that “Claude’s constructions represent an impressive synthesis of existing techniques, but the community must still assess whether the solutions survive beyond the specific models (AdS(_3)/CFT(_2) toy, type‑A anomaly) used in the derivation.”

The Max‑Planck Institute for Gravitational Physics echoed this sentiment, emphasizing the need for “independent verification of the back‑reaction calculations and a thorough stability analysis of the rotating metric.”

Outlook: From Theory to Observation

Gravitational‑Wave Tests

The analytic rotating solution predicts frequency shifts of order (10^{-3}) in the dominant QNM. Current LIGO‑Virgo detections achieve fractional uncertainties of a few percent for the ringdown phase, insufficient to resolve Claude’s effect. However, the upcoming Einstein Telescope (ET) and Cosmic Explorer (CE) target sub‑percent precision for high‑mass binary black‑hole mergers.

If ET or CE observes a systematic excess in the ((\ell=m=2)) mode frequency that correlates with inferred high spins ((\tilde{a}>0.9)), the data could provide the first empirical hint of trace‑anomaly corrections. Researchers can incorporate Claude’s corrected QNM formulas into Bayesian parameter‑estimation pipelines to test the hypothesis.

Black‑Hole Shadow Imaging

Claude’s metric modifies the photon‑sphere radius by

[
\Delta r_{\rm ph}\approx 0.001\,\alpha\,M,
]

a change far below the Event Horizon Telescope’s (EHT) current angular resolution (≈ 20 µas for M87*). Future space‑VLBI missions (e.g., the proposed Millimetron array) aim for sub‑µas resolution, potentially reaching the required sensitivity. Detecting such a minute shift would demand exquisite calibration and a robust model for plasma emission, making it a long‑term prospect.

High‑Energy Astrophysics

The unitary mapping for evaporating micro‑black holes suggests that Hawking‑like spectra from primordial black‑hole (PBH) evaporation could carry subtle correlations. Existing gamma‑ray telescopes (Fermi‑LAT, HESS) lack the spectral resolution to detect these correlations, but a dedicated MeV‑range interferometer might. Designing an experiment to measure the entanglement structure of PBH bursts lies far beyond current technology, yet Claude’s result provides a concrete theoretical target.

Closing Thoughts

Claude Fable 5.2 did not “solve” the black‑hole information paradox or rewrite the Kerr solution in a single stroke. Instead, it automated the discovery of two concrete, analytically tractable models that address long‑standing gaps in our understanding of quantum black holes. The models survive initial cross‑checks, inspire fresh lines of inquiry across holography, asymptotic safety, loop quantum gravity, and string theory, and generate testable predictions for forthcoming gravitational‑wave detectors.

The episode also demonstrates a new research workflow: an LLM proposes a mathematically sound ansatz, supplies executable code, and produces a polished derivation; human scientists verify, contextualize, and publish the findings. The community must remain vigilant about reproducibility, code transparency, and the limits of the underlying physical assumptions.

If the next generation of observatories confirms even a fraction of Claude’s predictions, the episode will mark a turning point—not because an AI “replaced” theorists, but because it augmented human creativity enough to crack problems that have resisted decades of manual effort. The true impact will unfold over the coming years, as physicists integrate these analytic tools into the broader quest for a complete quantum theory of gravity.

title: Render the answer summary as text instead of HTML
description:
The painting planner stores a surface selection such as Peeling or visible damage. The current choices are predefined, but the summary renderer still assigns labels and values with textContent. That keeps display data in the DOM as text. The distinction becomes more consequential if a later release allows custom room names or notes.

Keep the renderer’s contract small

The shared script clears the summary and uses a definition list. For each pair it creates a dt for the term and a dd for the answer. The browser handles text and markup differently. Building the nodes explicitly gives the renderer no reason to interpret a label as element syntax.

const term = document.createElement('dt');
const detail = document.createElement('dd');
term.textContent = label;
detail.textContent = value;
summary.append(term, detail);

Check semantics and replacement

For the current browser path, choose Interior, A few rooms and Peeling or visible damage. After finishing, scope to the summary and assert that the term Surface is followed by the selected text. Return to the question and revise the answer. Finish again and assert that there is still one Surface row. That exercises the clear-and-rebuild logic alongside the answer state.

For any future free-text variant, add a renderer test with a plain string containing angle brackets, such as Room . Assert that the complete value appears as text and that the dd contains no new elements. Keep this check at the output boundary. A future input length limit or persistence layer would have separate tests and would not change how the summary should display text.

Separately test that old rows are removed when the summary is rebuilt. It is possible to render perfectly safe text and still display a stale answer. The revision check should fail if a future change removes replaceChildren.

Perth Quotes painting planner is the live preview. Online enquiries are closed.

title: Pointing the OpenAI Python and Node SDKs at a model with fewer refusals
description:
Disclosure: I work on InterOdin, the API used in this tutorial. The pattern works for any OpenAI-compatible provider.

Security scripts often hit a wall with general-purpose models: a request to explain a malware sample from your own incident, or to draft a detection rule, comes back as a refusal. If your code already uses the official OpenAI SDK, you can switch the model behind it with a base URL and a key. This walkthrough uses Odin v1 through InterOdin, which serves both Chat Completions and Responses.

Install 

pip install openai     # Python
npm install openai     # JavaScript / TypeScript

Configure the client

Python:

import os

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.interodin.com/v1",
    api_key=os.environ["INTERODIN_API_KEY"],
)

completion = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="odin-v1",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Say hello in Romanian."}],
)
print(completion.choices[0].message.content)

TypeScript:

import OpenAI from 'openai'

const client = new OpenAI({
  baseURL: 'https://api.interodin.com/v1',
  apiKey: process.env.INTERODIN_API_KEY,
})

const completion = await client.chat.completions.create({
  model: 'odin-v1',
  messages: [{ role: 'user', content: 'Say hello in Romanian.' }],
})
console.log(completion.choices[0]?.message.content)

No code changes at all? Both SDKs read these environment variables:

export OPENAI_BASE_URL="https://api.interodin.com/v1"
export OPENAI_API_KEY="io-sk-your-key"

Responses API 

response = client.responses.create(model="odin-v1", input="Say hello in Romanian.", store=False)
print(response.output_text)

Responses is stateless here: send the full conversation in input on each turn.

What doesn't carry over

  • Images and files. Odin v1 is text-only. Images are replaced by a text note; a file in the newest message fails with 400 unsupported_content.
  • Hosted tools (file search, code interpreter, MCP) are removed from the request. Your own function tools run. Web search works on the Responses API only, billed per search.
  • previous_response_id, conversation and background: true return 400 unsupported_parameter, and stored responses can't be fetched, because nothing is stored.

Errors

The SDKs raise their usual exceptions: AuthenticationError for 401, RateLimitError for 429, and APIStatusError / APIError subclasses for the rest. Read the code field to tell insufficient_credits (402) apart from other errors. 429 and 5xx are retried automatically.

Billing is prepaid credits per token, with no subscription, and API prompts and completions are not stored. Fewer refusals does not mean no rules: the Acceptable Use Policy forbids illegal and harmful uses, so use it on systems and data you are authorised to work on.

The maintained version of this guide lives in the docs: https://docs.interodin.com/en/integrations/openai-sdk

title: How to Cut AI Coding Agent Token Spend by 90% With Local Log Surgery
description:
Most coding agent bills are not caused by complex reasoning. They come from streaming 1,500+ lines of node_modules and site-packages stack traces into every retry turn.

Where AI Coding Agent Tokens Actually Disappear

When you run an autonomous coding agent against a failing test suite, the real root cause is usually 5 to 15 lines of user code. Yet a standard terminal agent pipes the entire raw stdout and stderr of Jest, Vitest, Pytest, or Cargo straight into the LLM prompt.

A single failing Node.js or Python test regularly dumps 1,200 to 2,000 lines of internal framework frames from node_modules, site-packages, or .cargo/registry. Multiply that across 4 to 8 retry turns, and a routine one-line bug fix quietly consumes 38,000+ input tokens:

  • Framework stack frames repeat across every retry turn.
  • Syntax or indentation mistakes written directly to disk trigger extra LLM round-trips just to fix brackets.
  • Re-reading unchanged files between turns compounds prompt cache misses and latency.

Deterministic Log Surgery Before Any Prompt Leaves Your Machine

Instead of asking a frontier LLM to visually ignore 1,400 lines of traceback noise, a deterministic local harness can prune framework frames in sub-millisecond Rust memory before the API request is serialized.

In Kronumos, our local Rust Sub-Cortex intercepts command output, strips third-party stack frames, deduplicates repeated assertion blocks, masks secrets ([REDACTED]), and forwards only the exact failing user-code file, line number, and assertion delta:

Raw stderr captured: 1,482 lines (~14,200 tokens)
  -> Pruned 1,454 framework frames (node_modules/vitest, internal/modules)
  -> Scrubbed 2 env credentials in local memory
  -> Forwarded 28 surgical lines (~980 tokens)
Pinpointed: src/billing/calc.ts:84 (Expected 120, received NaN)

Stop Paying LLM Tokens for Syntax & Static Bug Checks

Another silent cost center is using an LLM to scan repositories or catch basic syntax issues. Running a local Tree-sitter AST pass for Rust, Python, TypeScript, JavaScript, and Go catches unguarded divisions, unhandled .unwrap() panics, and cross-file symbol coupling in milliseconds with zero LLM calls:

# Zero-LLM Tree-sitter AST static audit & blast-radius scan
kronumos hunt .
kronumos blast

# Test-verified autonomous fix loop with auto-rollback
kronumos --fix --auto-rollback

Combining 0-LLM static checks with local log surgery and transactional test verification cuts median task token spend from ~38,412 tokens down to ~2,512 tokens while keeping your git tree clean.

Quick Demo

Try It Yourself

Kronumos v1.3.0 runs natively on Linux, macOS, and Windows PowerShell (no WSL required) with Kronumos Cloud, OpenRouter BYOK, or offline Ollama:

  • Install Kronumos CLI
  • Try the Browser Workbench
  • Read the full guide on Kronumos

title: Building Resilient Web Applications: Beyond Offline Loading (Part 2)
description:
Making web applications useful when the backend is unavailable.

Introduction: Loading Offline Is Only the Beginning

In Part 1, we explored the challenges of building web applications for unreliable networks and low-bandwidth environments.

We discussed bandwidth, latency, browser storage, Service Workers, the Cache API, and how to make an application's shell available offline.

By the end, our Resilient Task Board could load its application shell after it had been installed and its required resources cached.

But there was still a problem.

The application could open offline, but could it actually do anything useful?

Imagine opening a task management application without an internet connection. The interface loads successfully, but your tasks are missing because the application still depends on an API request to retrieve them.

You try creating a task, and the request fails because the backend is unreachable.

We have improved availability, but we haven't solved data availability or offline interaction.

This is where the next layer of resilience begins.

1. Understanding the Difference Between Application Availability and Data Availability

An application can be available without its data being available.

Consider these two scenarios:

  • Application availability: The user can open the application, navigate its interface, and access its basic structure.
  • Data availability: The user can access relevant information even when the backend cannot be reached.

Caching HTML, CSS, and JavaScript helps with the first problem. It does not automatically solve the second.

For our Task Board, we need a way to store and retrieve tasks locally.

That brings us to IndexedDB.

2. IndexedDB: Giving the Browser a Local Database

In Part 1, we introduced three important browser storage technologies:

  • LocalStorage
  • Cache API
  • IndexedDB

Each serves a different purpose.

LocalStorage is useful for simple key-value data such as preferences. The Cache API is designed to store network requests and responses. IndexedDB, however, gives us a structured, asynchronous database inside the browser.

It can store JavaScript objects, create indexes, and support transactions.

For our Task Board, this makes IndexedDB a suitable place to store task records locally.

Think of it as a database available to the application even when the network is unavailable.

Why not LocalStorage?

Although LocalStorage can store serialized objects using JSON, it is synchronous and does not provide the structured querying, indexing, and transaction capabilities we need for a more substantial offline data layer.

IndexedDB is better suited to this job.

Designing our local data store

Our application already has a Task type. We can use that model to define the records stored locally.

For example:

export interface Task {
  id: number;
  title: string;
  description?: string;
  completed: boolean;
}

We can create an IndexedDB database and an object store for tasks.

const DB_NAME = "resilient-task-board";
const DB_VERSION = 1;
const TASK_STORE = "tasks";

export function openDatabase(): Promise<IDBDatabase> {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const request = indexedDB.open(DB_NAME, DB_VERSION);

    request.onupgradeneeded = (event) => {
      const db = (event.target as IDBOpenDBRequest).result;

      if (!db.objectStoreNames.contains(TASK_STORE)) {
        db.createObjectStore(TASK_STORE, {
          keyPath: "id",
          autoIncrement: true,
        });
      }
    };

    request.onsuccess = () => {
      resolve(request.result);
    };

    request.onerror = () => {
      reject(request.error);
    };
  });
}

A few things are happening here:

  • indexedDB.open() opens or creates the database.
  • DB_VERSION allows us to manage future database schema changes.
  • onupgradeneeded runs when the database is first created or its version changes.
  • createObjectStore() creates the equivalent of a collection or table for our task records.
  • keyPath tells IndexedDB which property identifies each record.

We now have a local database to work with.

Saving and retrieving tasks

Once the database is open, we can perform operations through transactions.

For example, retrieving all locally stored tasks:

export const getTasks = async (): Promise<Task[]> => {
  const db = await openDatabase();

  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const transaction = db.transaction(TASK_STORE, "readonly");
    const store = transaction.objectStore(TASK_STORE);
    const request = store.getAll();

    transaction.oncomplete = () => {
      db.close();
      resolve(request.result);
    };

    transaction.onerror = () => {
      db.close();
      reject(transaction.error);
    };

    transaction.onabort = () => {
      db.close();
      reject(transaction.error ?? new Error("Transaction aborted"));
    };
  });
};

Notice that we resolve the operation when the transaction completes, rather than assuming that an individual request succeeding means the entire transaction has committed.

That distinction matters when working with IndexedDB.

We can also save a task using a readwrite transaction and the object store's add() or put() method.

The important idea is that our application now has a local source from which it can retrieve data without depending on a network request.

3. Local-First Reads: Read From the Browser Before the Backend

Now that we have a local database, how should the application retrieve its tasks?

One approach is to always request data from the backend first and use IndexedDB only when the request fails.

But this still makes the user wait for the network whenever it is slow.

A better approach for our Task Board is a local-first read strategy.

The application reads from IndexedDB immediately, renders the available data, and then attempts to retrieve the latest data from the backend when connectivity is available.

The flow looks like this:

  1. The application requests tasks.
  2. It retrieves locally stored tasks from IndexedDB.
  3. The interface renders those tasks.
  4. It attempts to fetch the latest tasks from the backend.
  5. If the request succeeds, the local database is updated.
  6. The interface reflects the refreshed data.

This gives users a faster initial experience and allows them to see previously saved tasks even when offline.

There is an important distinction here: local-first does not mean the local database is always the source of truth.

In our architecture, MySQL remains the authoritative shared database. IndexedDB is the local copy used to support availability and interaction.

The two databases have different responsibilities.

Database Responsibility
MySQL Authoritative shared application data
IndexedDB Local data available to the current browser

This distinction becomes especially important when multiple users access the same application.

4. Offline Mutations: What Happens When Users Change Data?

Reading data offline is one challenge. Changing data offline is another.

Imagine a user creates a task while disconnected.

The browser cannot reach the backend, so the API request fails.

Should we simply display an error and ask the user to try again later?

That would mean the application is technically available offline but still not very useful.

Instead, we can allow the user to perform the operation locally and synchronize it with the backend when connectivity returns.

This is called offline mutation handling.

For example, when a user creates a task:

  1. Generate a unique identifier for the operation and a local identifier for the task.
  2. Save the task locally in IndexedDB.
  3. Record the operation as pending synchronization.
  4. Update the interface immediately.
  5. Attempt synchronization when the backend becomes reachable.
  6. Mark the operation as synchronized once the server confirms it.

The user does not have to wait for the backend before seeing the task appear.

Optimistic UI

This approach is closely related to a technique called optimistic UI.

Optimistic UI updates the interface before receiving confirmation from the server, based on the expectation that the operation will succeed.

For example, when a user marks a task as completed, the interface can immediately display it as completed.

But what if the request fails?

The application must have a recovery strategy. Depending on the operation and the application's data model, it can retain the pending change for retry or roll back the optimistic update.

Optimistic UI improves perceived responsiveness, but it does not guarantee that the server has accepted the change.

That distinction should never be ignored.

5. Building an Offline Mutation Queue

If users can perform several operations while offline, we need a reliable way to keep track of them.

This is where an offline mutation queue becomes useful.

Rather than sending an operation and forgetting about it when the request fails, we store it locally until the backend confirms that it has been processed.

A queue record might look like this:

interface PendingOperation {
  id: string;
  type: "CREATE_TASK" | "UPDATE_TASK" | "DELETE_TASK";
  payload: Record<string, unknown>;
  status: "pending" | "syncing" | "failed";
  createdAt: number;
  retryCount: number;
}

Each operation contains enough information for the application to attempt it again later.

For example, creating a task offline might produce this record:

const operation: PendingOperation = {
  id: crypto.randomUUID(),
  type: "CREATE_TASK",
  payload: {
    title: "Prepare workshop article",
    completed: false,
  },
  status: "pending",
  createdAt: Date.now(),
  retryCount: 0,
};

The operation is stored in IndexedDB alongside the locally available task data.

When connectivity returns, the application can process pending operations and send them to the backend.

A simplified synchronization flow looks like this:

User performs an action
        |
        v
Save change locally
        |
        v
Add operation to queue
        |
        v
Is backend reachable?
        |
    +---+---+
    |       |
   Yes      No
    |       |
    v       v
Send API   Keep operation
request    pending
    |
    v
Server confirms?
    |
  +---+---+
  |       |
 Yes      No
  |       |
  v       v
Mark as   Keep for
synced    retry/recovery

This gives us a controlled way to handle changes that cannot immediately reach the backend.

However, simply retrying every failed operation introduces another problem.

6. The Idempotency Problem: What If the Server Already Processed the Request?

Consider this scenario:

  1. A user creates a task.
  2. The browser sends the request.
  3. The backend creates the task successfully.
  4. The response gets lost because the network drops.
  5. The browser assumes the request failed.
  6. The application retries the request.

What happens?

Without additional protection, the backend may create the same task twice.

This is a classic distributed-systems problem: the client does not always know whether the server completed an operation when communication fails.

One solution is idempotency.

An operation is idempotent when repeating it produces the same intended result as performing it once.

For mutation requests, we can use an idempotency key: a unique identifier generated by the client and sent with the request.

For example:

POST /api/tasks
Idempotency-Key: 7c8f5d1a-...
Content-Type: application/json

The backend records the key and the result of processing the request.

If it receives the same key again, it can return the previously recorded result instead of creating another task.

This requires backend support. Generating an idempotency key in the browser alone does not prevent duplicate operations.

Retries without idempotency can create more problems than they solve.

7. Retry Strategies: Don't Attack the Backend

When a request fails, immediately retrying it repeatedly is usually a bad idea.

Imagine thousands of users reconnecting after a network outage and all their applications sending requests simultaneously.

The backend could become overwhelmed.

A better approach is to use exponential backoff.

Instead of retrying at fixed, very short intervals, the application progressively increases the delay between attempts.

For example:

Attempt Delay
1 1 second
2 2 seconds
3 4 seconds
4 8 seconds
5 16 seconds

In production systems, random jitter is often added to these delays to prevent many clients from retrying at exactly the same time.

We should also distinguish between temporary failures and permanent failures.

A temporary network error may justify another attempt. A validation error, such as an invalid task title, will not be fixed by repeatedly sending the same request.

Retries should be intentional, bounded, and based on the type of failure.

8. Conflict Resolution: What If Local and Server Data Differ?

There is one more problem we need to consider.

Suppose a user edits a task offline. Meanwhile, another user edits that same task on a different device and successfully saves the change to the backend.

When the first user reconnects, both versions exist:

  • The locally modified version.
  • The newer server version.

Which one should win?

This is a data conflict.

There is no universally correct conflict-resolution strategy. The right approach depends on the application and the importance of the data.

Some common strategies include:

Last-write-wins: The most recent update takes precedence. This is relatively simple, but it can silently overwrite meaningful changes.

Version-based conflict detection: Each record has a version number. The server rejects an update if the client is editing an outdated version, allowing the application to resolve the conflict.

Manual conflict resolution: The user is shown the conflicting versions and decides which changes to keep.

For a simple task board, last-write-wins might be acceptable in some situations. For financial transactions, collaborative documents, or other sensitive data, blindly overwriting changes would be a dangerous design choice.

Conflict resolution should be a deliberate product and engineering decision.

9. Putting the Architecture Together

Let's bring these concepts together.

Our resilient Task Board now has several distinct responsibilities:

Component Responsibility
Service Worker Intercepts requests and supports offline application loading
Cache API Stores application resources and selected network responses
IndexedDB Stores local application data and pending operations
React application Renders data and handles user interactions
Backend API Processes application operations and coordinates shared data
MySQL Stores authoritative application records

The overall data flow becomes:

  1. The Service Worker helps the application load.
  2. The React application retrieves locally available data from IndexedDB.
  3. The user interacts with the application.
  4. Changes are saved locally and recorded for synchronization.
  5. When the backend is reachable, pending operations are sent.
  6. The backend validates and processes operations, using idempotency protection where appropriate.
  7. Confirmed changes are reflected in the local database.

This is the foundation of a resilient, offline-capable application.

It is not enough to cache a page and call the application offline-ready. We must also think about the data, user actions, synchronization, and recovery.

10. Final Thoughts: Resilience Is an Architectural Decision

Building for unreliable networks requires us to change how we think about web applications.

Instead of assuming that every user action can immediately reach the backend, we design for the possibility that communication will be delayed or interrupted.

Instead of treating network failure as an exceptional situation, we make it part of the application's expected operating conditions.

And instead of leaving users uncertain about whether their actions were successful, we design clear states for pending, synchronized, and failed operations.

The key lessons from this series are:

  • Use the Service Worker and Cache API to support application availability.
  • Use IndexedDB for structured local application data.
  • Consider local-first reads to reduce dependency on network response times.
  • Use optimistic UI carefully to improve perceived responsiveness.
  • Queue offline mutations instead of losing user operations.
  • Implement idempotency to make retries safer.
  • Use sensible retry strategies and account for conflicts.

A resilient application is not one that never experiences network failure.

It is one that remains useful, communicates honestly with its users, and recovers gracefully when the network eventually returns.

The network may be unreliable. Your application doesn't have to be.

Explore the Project

Follow along with the Resilient Task Board repository, starting from the original version before the resilience improvements discussed in this series.

Further Reading

  • MDN: IndexedDB API
  • MDN: Cache API
  • MDN: Service Worker API
  • MDN: Background Synchronization API
  • MDN: HTTP Semantics

title: How to Align Modern Payment Platforms with PCI DSS Using MongoDB Enterprise Advanced
description:
Payment platforms operate in a demanding environment. They must protect payment account data and support the teams that authorize transactions, investigate suspicious activity, and resolve exceptions. The more people and systems that can see sensitive data, the harder it is to control exposure. And the more data is locked away, the harder it can be to use in legitimate workflows. So how can you set up the platforms to ensure they protect that data while also giving the right people access?

Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS), a global security standard managed by the PCI Security Standards Council, provides a framework for protecting payment account data, restricting access, securing networks, and monitoring activity. Meeting those objectives is not a database-only exercise. It depends on how the application handles data, how the database server protects and governs it, and how the underlying infrastructure is configured and operated.

While the fully managed MongoDB Atlas platform can provide a foundation for organizations pursuing PCI DSS compliance, with MongoDB’s infrastructure-level certifications supporting the infrastructure layer, some organizations opt for a self-managed architecture to maintain direct operational control over their infrastructure and internal security policies. For self-managed deployments, MongoDB Enterprise Advanced provides database security, governance, and encryption capabilities that can help support applicable PCI DSS objectives. Red Hat OpenShift provides configurable platform and network controls, while the MongoDB Controllers for Kubernetes (MCK) Operator manages MongoDB deployments on OpenShift.

Achieving alignment across this architecture requires a defense-in-depth model, which provides multiple overlapping layers of cybersecurity to protect data. While technical controls and reference architectures alone do not constitute formal compliance attestations, they provide the foundation needed to meet core PCI DSS objectives. The following sections walk through establishing this foundation across three complementary tiers—application, database, and infrastructure—before examining how they work together to protect sensitive payment workflows.

Start with the application layer

The application determines what payment data enters the platform, where it flows, and which business roles need it. In our reference payment service provider (PSP) demo, the application models two distinct workloads: high-throughput payment authorizations and post-transaction fraud investigations.  

This PSP demo application is designed to support deployment with either a fully managed MongoDB Atlas cluster or a self-managed MongoDB Enterprise Advanced deployment. Its core architecture, data models, and client-side encryption approach can be shared across both models, although configuration, integrations, and operational responsibilities may differ by environment. This dual compatibility gives organizations the flexibility to migrate workloads between cloud and on-premises environments as strategic needs evolve, eliminating infrastructure lock-in. Furthermore, it reinforces data sovereignty by allowing organizations to retain direct operational control over where cardholder data resides and how it is governed across hybrid architectures.

At the functional level, data minimization is enforced at the point of entry. Primary account numbers (PAN) are tokenized when downstream services do not need raw cardholder data, and sensitive authentication data (SAD) such as card verification value (CVV) never gets stored post-authorization. In addition, an isolated application programming interface (API) layer ensures that external clients never connect directly to the database tier.

These design choices reduce unnecessary exposure before data reaches storage. They also make the next layer more effective: The database can apply protection to the fields and workflows that genuinely need it, rather than compensating for an application that collects or shares too much.

Protect and govern data at the database layer

MongoDB Enterprise Advanced provides security capabilities for self-managed MongoDB deployments. One relevant capability is queryable encryption (QE). It allows selected fields to remain encrypted in the database while supporting defined query patterns over those fields. In practical terms, an authorized payment or investigation workflow can look up protected information, such as an account reference, without the database storing that value in plaintext. The client driver encrypts selected fields and decrypts query results using keys from the configured key management service (KMS), meaning the database engine processes only ciphertext for supported query patterns. QE is field- and query-specific, so teams can choose which data must be searchable and validate the supported patterns for their deployment.

Encryption works alongside access governance. MongoDB role-based access control lets administrators assign built-in or custom roles so that application services, analysts, auditors, and database operators receive only the permissions they need. MongoDB also supports IP-based authentication restrictions for database users. These controls help answer two different questions:

  • What may this identity do? 

  • From which network locations may it connect?

Database auditing can complement these protections by recording selected database activity for review and investigation. The value comes from connecting audit policy to the organization’s monitoring and response processes, not simply turning on logging in isolation.

Enforce the environment at the infrastructure layer

The database and application still need a tightly controlled environment. OpenShift provides platform controls that teams can configure to isolate workloads and govern their runtime. Those controls include role-based access for cluster and project operations, security context constraints for pod privileges, and NetworkPolicies to limit which workloads can communicate. For example, a policy can allow the payment API to reach MongoDB while denying unrelated workloads access to the database network path.

The MongoDB controllers for Kubernetes (MCK) operator manages the cluster’s deployment, while Ops Manager provides management capabilities such as automation, monitoring, and backup according to the deployment configuration. These tools help platform and database teams operate the deployment consistently; they do not replace the need to set restrictive policies, manage identities and keys, or review the resulting configuration.

The following high-level view shows how the layers work together:

Figure 1. Payment platform stack, from underlying infrastructure to business applications. 

As shown above, these components align into a defense-in-depth model. The stack builds upward from the host infrastructure and immutable operating system (RHEL OS) to the OpenShift container platform, establishing a hardened foundation. On top of this platform, the MCK operator provides persistence for the encrypted data, Ops Manager orchestrates data automation, and the business payment microservices run isolated at the application tier. This layered view helps teams map controls across each tier to meet PCI DSS requirements.

How the layers support PCI DSS objectives

Application-level tokenization and data minimization can reduce how much sensitive data the platform handles. Queryable encryption can protect selected fields while preserving supported lookup workflows. Database roles and IP restrictions can narrow access to the database, while OpenShift policies can further limit which workloads and network paths reach it. Auditing and operational monitoring help teams review activity and investigate events. The value, ultimately, occurs when this all comes together seamlessly.

As illustrated in Figure 2, the reference PSP demo organizes these controls into clear architectural boundaries:

  • Perimeter and access control: External entities (client devices, wallet systems, and merchant systems) communicate exclusively over HTTPS through the service gateway. Identity and access policies are enforced at the security gateway using standards such as OAuth, OIDC, and JWT backed by general identity and access management (GIAM), preventing direct access to data stores from untrusted networks.

  • Protected core processing: The core system coordinates payment workflows and integrates directly with a key management service (such as AWS KMS) and MongoDB EA. This design ensures that field encryption occurs before persistence and that the database engine handles only ciphertext for configured search patterns.

  • Event decoupling and specialized services: By routing events through an event bus (Kafka) to dedicated providers for fraud detection (FDS) and anti-money laundering (AML), the platform isolates investigative workflows from the core payment engine, supporting workload separation and least-privilege data access.

Figure 2. Reference view of a PCI DSS-aligned payment demo integrated with MongoDB Enterprise Advanced on OpenShift.

Together, these controls can support PCI DSS objectives such as protecting stored account data, restricting access based on business need, maintaining secure network boundaries, and monitoring access. With a self-managed MongoDB EA deployment on OpenShift, the organization remains responsible for the full cardholder data environment, including infrastructure configuration, identity and key management, operational procedures, and evidence.

The payment service demo application makes this layered approach tangible. Its payment and investigation workflows provide concrete context for demonstrating how queryable encryption can protect selected sensitive fields while supporting defined searches, how MongoDB roles and IP-based restrictions narrow database access, and how OpenShift policies can limit paths between the application and data tiers. MCK and the Ops Manager provide deployment and operational tooling for sensitive data, tailored to the organization’s needs. These layers offer a starting point for building a self-managed payment environment with controls across the stack.

The takeaway is straightforward: MongoDB Enterprise Advanced, MCK, and OpenShift can provide a practical foundation for running a payment application on infrastructure the same organization controls.
