title: Dive Shop Lahaina: Build a Local Business Data Audit With Python
description:
A local business website might show an address, contact details, service descriptions, and a list of activities.

But how do you know whether the information is complete, consistent, and still useful?

This is an interesting problem for developers working with local business websites.

A small business may appear in online directories, maps, social profiles, and travel listings. Over time, its information can change.

For example, someone researching a dive shop in Lahaina might find the correct business address but an outdated tour schedule.

Both pieces of information appear on the internet. Only one may be suitable for current use.

In this tutorial, we will build a lightweight local business data audit using Python, CSV, and Markdown.

We will use Dive Maui / Hawaiian Rafting Adventures in Lahaina, Hawaii, as a practical example.

No external APIs, databases, or paid tools are required.

1. What Are We Trying to Solve?

Local business information usually includes three important fields:

  • Name
  • Address
  • Phone number

These are often called NAP data.

For local SEO, consistent NAP information helps search engines and customers recognize the same business across different sources.

However, contact information is only part of the picture.

A complete review should also consider:

  • Business website
  • Contact information
  • Service descriptions
  • Current service availability
  • Geographic relevance
  • Source verification status
  • Last review date

The main challenge is separating confirmed information from information that still needs checking.

Our script will help organize that process.

It will not pretend to verify facts automatically.

2. Create a Simple Project Structure

We will start with three files.

local-business-audit/
|
|-- business.csv
|-- audit.py
|-- README.md

The CSV file stores business information.

The Python script checks the structure and reports missing values.

The Markdown README explains the purpose of the project.

This approach is useful for small datasets and can be expanded later.

3. Store Business Information in CSV

A CSV file is easy to create and can be opened in most spreadsheet applications.

For our example, create a file named business.csv.

business_name,address,city,state,postal_code,phone,service_status
Dive Maui / Hawaiian Rafting Adventures,1223 Front St,Lahaina,HI,96761,+18086617333,Needs current verification

These example contact details are drawn from Dive Maui's published business information.

The service status is deliberately marked as needing verification.

That distinction matters.

Some of Dive Maui's activity pages are marked unavailable following operational challenges connected to the 2023 Lahaina wildfires.

A valid business address does not prove that every service is currently operating.

This is an important principle for any local business dataset.

Do not treat historical service information as a confirmed current offering.

4. Read the CSV File With Python

Python includes a built-in csv module.

That means we can read our business file without installing an additional package.

Create a file called audit.py.

import csv

with open(
    "business.csv",
    newline="",
    encoding="utf-8"
) as file:
    reader = csv.DictReader(file)

    for business in reader:
        print("Business:", business["business_name"])
        print("City:", business["city"])
        print("Phone:", business["phone"])
        print("Status:", business["service_status"])

This script loads the CSV file and prints selected fields.

It is a simple first step, but it helps demonstrate how structured business information can be processed.

5. Check for Missing Information

A business record may contain empty values.

For example, a contact number could be missing, or a location might be incomplete.

We can add a function to identify those issues.

Replace the script with:

import csv

REQUIRED_FIELDS = [
    "business_name",
    "address",
    "city",
    "state",
    "postal_code",
    "phone"
]

def audit_business(business):
    missing = []

    for field in REQUIRED_FIELDS:
        value = business.get(field, "")

        if not value or not value.strip():
            missing.append(field)

    return missing


with open(
    "business.csv",
    newline="",
    encoding="utf-8"
) as file:

    reader = csv.DictReader(file)

    for business in reader:
        missing = audit_business(business)

        print(f"Business: {business['business_name']}")

        if missing:
            print("Missing fields:", ", ".join(missing))
        else:
            print("Required fields are populated.")

The script checks whether the required fields contain values.

However, there is an important limitation.

A populated field is not necessarily correct.

For example, a phone number might be present but outdated.

Our script checks completeness, not factual accuracy.

6. Add a Verification Status

A reliable local business audit should record whether information has been checked against an appropriate source.

We can use a separate field for this purpose.

For example:

business_name,nap_verified,services_verified
Dive Maui / Hawaiian Rafting Adventures,yes,no

In this example:

  • nap_verified indicates that the listed contact information has been checked.
  • services_verified indicates whether current service availability has been independently confirmed.

These values should be based on actual verification work.

Do not automatically mark a business as verified just because its fields are filled in.

For a more detailed project, you could add the review date and the name of the person performing the check.

7. Generate a Markdown Audit Report

Now we can turn our checks into a simple report.

The following script reads business.csv, identifies missing required fields, and creates audit-report.md.

import csv
from pathlib import Path

REQUIRED_FIELDS = [
    "business_name",
    "address",
    "city",
    "state",
    "postal_code",
    "phone"
]

def find_missing_fields(row):
    return [
        field
        for field in REQUIRED_FIELDS
        if not (row.get(field) or "").strip()
    ]

with open(
    "business.csv",
    newline="",
    encoding="utf-8"
) as file:
    businesses = list(csv.DictReader(file))

lines = [
    "# Local Business Data Audit",
    "",
    "This report checks data completeness.",
    "It does not independently verify accuracy.",
    ""
]

for business in businesses:
    name = business.get("business_name") or "Unnamed Business"
    missing = find_missing_fields(business)

    lines.append(f"## {name}")
    lines.append("")

    if missing:
        lines.append(
            "Missing fields: " + ", ".join(missing)
        )
    else:
        lines.append("All required fields are populated.")

    lines.append("")
    lines.append(
        "Service status: "
        + (business.get("service_status") or "Not recorded")
    )
    lines.append("")

Path("audit-report.md").write_text(
    "\n".join(lines),
    encoding="utf-8"
)

print("Audit report created.")

Run it with:

python audit.py

The output will be saved as a Markdown file.

This makes it easy to share the report internally, include it in documentation, or maintain it alongside other project files.

8. Think About Geographic Relevance

Local business data should identify the actual business location.

For example, Dive Maui lists its address as:

1223 Front Street, Lahaina, Hawaii 96761.

Nearby areas such as Kaanapali may be relevant to visitors researching local diving options.

However, being near a location does not automatically mean the business offers services throughout that area.

A business audit should distinguish:

Physical location: Where the business lists its address.

Target audience: People who may find the information relevant.

Verified service area: Locations the business actually confirms it serves.

These fields should not be treated as interchangeable.

If a campaign focuses on a seven-mile radius around a physical location, geographic filtering should use verified coordinates and an appropriate distance calculation.

A city name alone is not enough to confirm whether a point lies within that radius.

9. Avoid Turning Old Service Pages Into Current Claims

This is one of the most important lessons in the project.

Imagine that a dive shop website contains a detailed article about a boat diving trip.

The page describes the underwater location, explains the experience, and includes a price.

But a notice on the same page says the trip is currently unavailable.

A simple data scraper might collect the price and trip description while ignoring the notice.

That could produce an inaccurate business listing.

A better data model separates the service description from availability.

For example:

{
  "service": "Example guided boat dive",
  "historically_listed": true,
  "current_availability": "unverified",
  "requires_manual_review": true
}

This is an illustrative data structure, not a claim about the current status of a specific trip.

The key idea is simple.

A service can be documented without being available.

Automated systems should preserve that distinction.

10. A Real Local Example: Dive Maui

Dive Maui / Hawaiian Rafting Adventures is a family-run diving business based in Lahaina.

Its published website includes information about scuba activities, training, equipment rentals, and ocean experiences.

The business also explains that some previously offered activities are unavailable due to operational difficulties following the Lahaina wildfires.

This makes it a useful example of why local business data should be reviewed carefully rather than copied automatically.

Developers researching a dive shop in Lahaina can use the official Dive Maui website as a starting point for understanding the business's published information.

Current service availability should still be confirmed directly.

11. Ways to Improve the Audit

Our basic script is intentionally small.

Once the foundation is working, you could expand it with:

  • Phone number normalization
  • Duplicate business detection
  • Coordinate-based radius checks
  • Source URL tracking
  • Verification timestamps
  • Manual review flags
  • Change history between audits
  • Separate status fields for each service

These features would make the tool more useful for larger local business datasets.

However, additional automation should not create false confidence.

A script can identify missing information or inconsistent formats.

It cannot determine whether an unavailable ocean activity has resumed without reliable current evidence.

Final Thoughts

Local business data looks simple at first.

A business name, address, phone number, and website might seem like enough information.

But useful data also needs context.

Is the information current?

Has the source been checked?

Are services actually operating?

Does the stated service area match verified business information?

Python, CSV, and Markdown provide a lightweight way to organize these questions.

The code does not need to be complicated.

The important part is treating uncertainty honestly and keeping historical information separate from confirmed current facts.

That principle applies to dive shops in Lahaina, restaurants, repair businesses, and almost any other local service.

Good local data begins with clear records, careful verification, and fewer assumptions.

title: Teaching Language Models to Narrow Boolean Patent Searches from Search Feedback
description:
arXiv:2611.22270v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Patent prior-art searchers issue Boolean queries line by line, broadening to find relevant documents and narrowing until candidates can be screened. We distill 38,397 Japan Patent Office search reports into executable expert strategies, re-execute them, and evaluate generated strategies by citation recall and the smallest set containing each citation. Prompted models write valid, high-recall strategies but leave citations in sets too large to screen. We adapt a generator offline from scored rollouts in two forms: strategy-level learning from a screening-aware strategy score, and line-level learning from citation-preserving narrowing credit, which upweights the query lines keeping a found citation in a smaller set. On shared rollouts, line-level credit outperforms strategy-level scores on screening measures; iterated, it cuts the median citation-containing set from 768 to under 50 and places more citations in sets under 100 documents than experts, at lower recall. Strategy-level preference learning reaches near-complete recall; the two forms are complementary.

title: My first GitLab contribution: teaching gitlab-shell to explain its own errors
description:
Some error messages tell you exactly what went wrong. Others just shrug.

In gitlab-shell — the Go program that handles Git over SSH for GitLab — a failed JSON parse produced this, and only this:

parsing failed

No URL. No content type. Nothing about which request had just been parsed. If you were the operator staring at that log line, you knew something had failed and nothing else. Issue #888 in gitlab-shell asked for the obvious thing: when parsing fails, say what you were parsing.

I'm a high-school student in Tunisia, and that issue became my first contribution to GitLab.

The change

The fix itself is small. When the JSON parsing path in gitlab-shell fails now, it logs the request context before returning the error — the content type, and the URL it was talking to — using LabKit, GitLab's structured logging library.

One thing deliberately did not change: the returned error is still exactly parsing failed. Other code and other people's log searches match on that string, so the context goes to the logs, not into the error. The first version of my patch had loosened a couple of test expectations to make them pass; the review pushed back, the expectations went back to being strict, and I added a regression test for the new logging instead. That was round one.

What three rounds of review actually taught me

The automated reviewer on my merge request (!1664) was not a rubber stamp. It found real things, including one I should have caught myself.

Round two was a security catch. My first version logged the full request URL. URLs carry query strings, and query strings can carry tokens. The reviewer asked for the URL to be sanitized before it touched a log file — scheme, host and path only, with the query, fragment and any embedded credentials stripped. It was right, and it is the kind of mistake you only have to be taught once: a log line is a publication, and anything you would not paste in public does not belong in one.

Round three was about a test that could not fail. I had written an assertion that a sensitive string did not appear in the logged values — but the assertion ran against a list, in a form that would pass even if the string was there. A check that passes no matter what is worse than no check, because it gives you confidence you have not earned. The fix was to join the values into one string first, so the assertion could genuinely fail — and I verified that it does fail against the old code.

The part nobody warns you about

My fork's CI pipelines never ran. GitLab requires identity verification to run pipelines on my account, and verification wants a bank card, which I do not have. So the merge request carries a note from me explaining exactly that: the full test suite passes locally (31 packages), and the pipeline gap is an account limitation, not a code failure. Maintainers can run the pipeline on their side. If you are a young contributor without a card, this wall exists — it is not a rejection, and saying so plainly on the MR is better than staying silent.

Where it stands

After the third round, the automated review approved the merge request. It is now waiting on a human maintainer's review, which is where it should be — I am not claiming a merge that has not happened. Whatever the verdict, the three rounds already did their work:

  1. Error messages are written for the person who reads them at 3 a.m. Context is not decoration.
  2. Sanitize before you log. URLs, headers and tokens leak through helpfulness.
  3. A test that cannot fail is a lie you tell yourself. Make it prove it can fail first.

If you are looking for a first contribution of your own: pick the error message that annoyed you, in a project you actually use, and make it say what it knows

title: Amazon MSK Connect now supports restarting existing connectors
description:
Amazon MSK Connect (Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka Connect) now supports restarting both existing and newly created connectors and their tasks in place, enabling fast recovery for streaming data pipelines.

Amazon MSK Connect is a fully managed service that allows you to deploy, monitor, and scale Apache Kafka Connect connectors with Amazon MSK (Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka). Previously, recovering from failures required deleting and recreating the connector, resulting in downtime and operational overhead. With this feature, you can restart your connector and all its tasks in place, or selectively restart only the failed tasks, making recovery seamless. You can also restart connectors that have no failed tasks to recover from transient issues or to pick up changes in external systems or dependencies.

This restart capability is available at no additional cost through the Amazon MSK Console, AWS CLI, AWS SDK, and AWS CDK in all AWS Regions where Amazon MSK Connect is available. To learn more, visit the Amazon MSK Connect documentation. To get started, visit the Amazon MSK Console.

title: Travel Itinerary Retrieval Architecture: Node.js 3-Tier Latency Budgets for Planner RAG
description:
Short answer: give itinerary retrieval a 300 ms p95 contract, spend most of it on one high-recall pass, and reserve a small, explicit slice for reranking and context assembly. A travel planner feels slow when every candidate gets an expensive semantic lookup, so the architecture should narrow the set before it asks for richer signals.

How should a travel itinerary planner divide retrieval latency budgets?

Start with a deadline that the product can defend. For a B2B SaaS planner that watches travel policy pages and turns them into trip options, I use 300 ms p95 for retrieval, separate from model generation. That is a budget, not a benchmark claim. Your mileage may vary when the source corpus is remote or freshly indexed.

The request carries a destination, dates, traveler constraints, and a change token from the last itinerary. A cheap lexical filter removes stale or impossible documents. A vector pass then retrieves a few dozen candidates. A reranker scores that short list, and a context builder clips passages to the model's input limit. Each stage returns its elapsed time and candidate count; the caller can make a deliberate fallback when a slice is gone.

Here is a small Node.js skeleton. It uses generic HTTP boundaries so the same contract works with a self-hosted index or a managed service.

type Budget = { deadlineMs: number; spentMs: number };
type Candidate = { id: string; text: string; score?: number };

const elapsed = (start: number) => performance.now() - start;

async function retrieveItinerary(query: string, budget: Budget): Promise<Candidate[]> {
  const lexicalStart = performance.now();
  const lexical = await lexicalSearch(query, 60);
  budget.spentMs += elapsed(lexicalStart);

  if (budget.spentMs >= budget.deadlineMs) return lexical.slice(0, 8);

  const vectorStart = performance.now();
  const vector = await vectorSearch(query, 40);
  budget.spentMs += elapsed(vectorStart);

  const merged = mergeById([...lexical, ...vector]).slice(0, 40);
  if (budget.spentMs >= budget.deadlineMs) return merged.slice(0, 12);

  const rerankStart = performance.now();
  const ranked = await rerank(query, merged.slice(0, 20));
  budget.spentMs += elapsed(rerankStart);
  return ranked.slice(0, 8);
}

The important detail is the early return. It is an intentional quality trade: eight lexical matches are better than a timeout that leaves the planner with no answer. I log the branch, because a rising fallback rate points to a capacity or corpus problem rather than a prompt problem.

What fails when every retrieval stage gets the same deadline?

Uniform timeouts hide queueing. A vector request may be fast in isolation and slow under concurrent re-indexing; a reranker may have a stable median but a wide tail. If both receive 100 ms, the tail of the first consumes the second's share. Propagate one absolute deadline instead: deadline = requestStart + 300 and pass the remaining time to every dependency. For example, a request can leave the lexical stage with 210 ms remaining, spend 160 ms waiting for a busy vector shard, and arrive at reranking with only 50 ms. A per-stage timeout would still grant the reranker another 100 ms, quietly violating the user-visible contract. An absolute deadline makes the violation visible and lets the code return the already merged candidates instead of starting work it cannot finish.

Measure tails.

I also cap fan-out. Asking six regional indexes for twenty hits each creates 120 records to merge, deduplicate, and rerank. That work is CPU and memory pressure inside the API process, even when network calls are parallel. In practice, I start with two shards, 60 lexical hits, 40 vector hits, then measure recall before increasing either number.

Freshness creates another trap for a page-change product. An index that is ten minutes behind can return a beautifully relevant old policy. Store the source revision and fetched-at timestamp beside each chunk, and apply a freshness rule before ranking. If the rule rejects every candidate, report an empty result with a reason code; do not silently substitute unrelated travel advice.

A practical contract for quality, cost, and observability

Latency is only useful when paired with retrieval quality. Track recall@k on a small, labeled set of destinations, dates, and policy questions. Track p50 and p95 per stage, timeout fallbacks, duplicate rate after merging, and the percentage of context tokens that survive clipping. A single end-to-end number cannot tell you whether the lexical filter is too strict or the reranker is simply late.

Decision Helps Costs or risk
Lexical pre-filter Fast exact names, codes, and dates Misses paraphrases
Vector retrieval Better semantic recall Index and embedding work
Reranking top 20 Higher ordering precision Tail latency and compute
Freshness gate Prevents obsolete policy text Can produce fewer matches

Keep the instrumentation boring and structured. Emit one span per stage with candidate_count, elapsed_ms, deadline_remaining_ms, and fallback_reason. Sample full documents only in a protected debug stream; itinerary queries can contain passport or customer data. Redact query values in ordinary logs.

When is a simpler search path the right choice?

The catch is that a three-stage design is not suitable when the corpus is tiny, static, and already keyed by destination or booking code. In that case, a single indexed query is easier to operate and may leave more time for generation. Stick with the simpler path when its measured recall meets the product threshold and its p95 stays inside the same contract during an index rebuild.

Conversely, do not add a reranker just because semantic search is fashionable. If labeled tests show no meaningful gain for policy-change alerts, spend that slice on better chunk boundaries, source revision checks, or a warm connection pool. I am not sure which threshold will hold for your corpus; the experiment that resolves it is a replay of real itinerary queries with old and new page revisions, measured at the same concurrency as production.

The operational checklist is short: define the absolute deadline, bound fan-out, record candidate provenance, test stale revisions, and rehearse the fallback branch. Then load-test re-indexing and normal traffic together. A contract that survives that test is more valuable than a faster median on an idle laptop.

References

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Performance/now
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110

title: VIBRA: Backward-Compatible Cross-Modal Retrieval with Consensus Barycenters
description:
arXiv:2611.23606v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Backward-compatible retrieval enables a new encoder to query the gallery that an old model has already encoded, so that a cross-modal retrieval system can be upgraded without re-encoding billions of items. Existing compatible methods either fit the old query and stay near the accuracy of the old model, or run the old and the new encoder for every query. We propose VIBRA, which matches relevance on the old gallery, corrects the errors of a single model with the barycenter of several views, which is itself a query in the old space, and trains the new encoder to inherit this consensus, so that models absent at deployment still shape every query. We show that the barycenter gains margin over the average of its views exactly when their hardest irrelevant items differ, and we characterize the share of this gain that one encoder can reach. On five benchmarks with five upgrades among six CLIP, MetaCLIP and SigLIP2 backbones, VIBRA is the best compatible method in all 50 settings, improving Recall@1 by up to 5.6 points over the strongest baseline and by up to 18.0 points over the old model, while adding less than 1 ms to the latency of the new encoder.

title: Object Storage Download Links With Signed URLs and Attachment Filenames (and Why)
description:
Short answer: Keep the export private, set its content metadata, and return a short-lived signed URL whose response uses the requested attachment filename; choose a specialist when retention, residency, or public delivery is a hard requirement.

For an e-commerce export, keep the object private and hand the browser a short-lived signed URL with an attachment filename. That gives a customer a useful download without proxying CSV, PDF, or ZIP bytes through the Node.js app. The deciding constraint is trust: the app may authorize a download, but the storage provider still owns retention, deletion, and region controls.

I build around that boundary because every byte through a one-person SaaS API becomes another memory spike, timeout, and support ticket. The app should create the export and make the decision. Object storage should deliver it. Infrai is a concrete option here when its self-describing REST discovery can replace a storage SDK and the other backend adapters in the same export job, with a one key, one bill model that removes credential plumbing between those steps, a broad surface covering 295 routes across 20 backend modules, and documented capabilities that include runnable examples in 10 languages.

What the download flow needs to guarantee

Start with a private bucket and a key that is unguessable and stable enough to audit. A key such as exports/order-8421/2026-09-08.csv is easier to reason about than a public URL, but it is not an access policy. Authorization happens before the presign call, and the signed URL gets a short expiry.

Set metadata when the file is written. text/csv, application/pdf, and application/zip give browsers and native clients a reliable content type. If the signing implementation accepts response headers, set Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="orders-8421.csv" there. If it does not, put the intended filename in the object key or keep a tiny app-layer download endpoint that redirects after checking the session.

The filename is part of the product experience. A link named f3b7... is technically valid and still feels broken.

There is one more lifecycle detail. Export jobs often finish before a user chooses a final name. Write to a temporary key, then copy to the final key and delete the temporary object. That copy is a second write, so give it an idempotency key and record the final key in your database before returning the link.

How should Node.js handle a signed URL, attachment filename, and content disposition?

The smallest useful implementation has an upload and a presign call; set content metadata as part of the upload according to the capability schema. The exact request schemas are discoverable from the storage capability documentation; the paths below are the verified storage routes. This example keeps the API key in the environment and treats a rate limit as a normal control-flow case.

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

async function call(url: string, method: "PUT" | "POST", body: unknown, idempotencyKey: string) {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(url, {
      method,
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(body),
    });

    if (response.status === 429) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "1");
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, Math.max(retryAfter, 2 ** attempt) * 1000));
      continue;
    }
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`Storage request failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
    return response.json();
  }
  throw new Error("Storage request was rate limited too many times");
}

await call("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key}", "PUT", {
  content: "order_id,total\n8421,129.00\n",
}, "export-order-8421-upload-v1");

const signed = await call("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}", "POST", {
  expires_in: 900,
}, "export-order-8421-presign-v1");

console.log(signed);

The important behavior is the ordering, not a framework wrapper: metadata is attached before the link is issued, and retries cannot create duplicate writes. In production I would return only the signed URL and an application-approved filename from my own response, never the bucket credentials or a public object address.

Which storage option fits the trust boundary?

Infrai is a reasonable fit when the storage call is one piece of a broader backend workflow. Its discovery API is self-describing: a capability exposes its request and response schema plus runnable examples, so wiring storage into a new job means reading one endpoint instead of learning another SDK. The same key and REST surface can cover the adjacent job steps, which removes a separate credential and adapter from a small codebase.

That does not make it the default for every export system. Here is the trade-off I would put in a design review:

Option Good fit Boundary to verify
Infrai storage Private, app-authorized exports where one REST API and self-describing discovery reduce integration work No public URLs, object versioning, object lock, or cross-region automatic replication; lifecycle expiry is day-scale
Cloudflare R2 S3-shaped private delivery and Cloudflare-adjacent networking You still manage provider credentials, region policy, and the surrounding job integrations
Vercel Blob A Vercel-hosted app that wants a concise blob workflow Provider-specific controls and deployment coupling need review for regulated data
Amazon S3 Mature retention, versioning, object lock, and regional controls More IAM and service surface to operate for a one-person team

The catch is contractual and operational, not cosmetic. Infrai storage does not provide public or public-read ACLs, versioning/object lock, conditional If-Match writes, cross-region automatic replication, or self-service CORS configuration. It is not suitable for a static site, permanent public links, WORM retention, strict compare-and-swap concurrency, or browser direct uploads that require custom CORS rules. Stick with S3 when legal hold and object lock are hard requirements; use R2 when the delivery edge is the main concern; use Vercel Blob when the app is intentionally coupled to that platform.

Region and processor boundaries deserve their own checklist. Confirm where the bucket's data is processed, how deletion is audited, and which party is the processor in your contracts. A signed URL limits access; it does not change residency or erase an upstream retention obligation. Your mileage may vary by customer region, and I am not sure a single storage policy can satisfy every market without a separate regional bucket strategy.

What I would change at scale

At higher volume, I would move export state into a queue and persist {jobId, objectKey, filename, expiresAt} in a database. A worker writes the temporary key, copies it to the final key, and deletes the temporary object after the copy is confirmed. The download endpoint checks ownership, emits one presign, and logs the request ID. That keeps delivery simple while preserving a record of who authorized it.

I would also make deletion explicit. Lifecycle rules can clean up old exports, but a one-day minimum and no automatic multipart-fragment cleanup mean the queue still needs a janitor path. For regulated data, retention and deletion evidence belong in the database and provider audit logs, not in a filename convention.

This is a boring design. That is the point. Ship the export weekly, outsource byte delivery, and spend the saved revenue-per-hour on the checkout flow instead of another file proxy.

If this boundary matches your system, the storage discovery and schemas are at docs.infrai.cc.

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/
  • https://vercel.com/docs/vercel-blob
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/UsingMetadata.html
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Content-Disposition
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6266
  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.bucket.set_notification

title: PReMind: When Personal Memory Meets Visual Hazards
description:
arXiv:2611.23808v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Personalized vision-language assistants use visual observations and personal memories to provide advice tailored to the user. When the observed scene contains a physical hazard, personal context, such as allergies, medical conditions, or mobility constraints, can change what help is appropriate. Responding appropriately therefore requires recognizing the visible hazard and applying the relevant person's information. We introduce PReMind-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark that evaluates this combination across diverse hazards and personal-memory conditions. It separately measures memory access, grounding, abstention, and hazard response, and assesses joint success on interdependency cases. Existing models often satisfy one requirement while failing the other, and training only for safety or personalization leaves a gap in joint success. We therefore propose PReMind, a two-phase reinforcement learning framework that combines on-demand and forced-call interactions (memory always retrieved) to jointly train grounded memory use and hazard response. At 4B, PReMind raises joint success from 12.9% to 28.6% over its base on the interdependency set and improves hazard adequacy and correct abstention on the main test. Joint-success gains persist under forced-call evaluation and under a second LLM judge across three Phase II seeds; averaged over these seeds, joint success also improves on unseen hazard groups. These findings highlight the need to evaluate and train personal assistants to connect visual evidence with the relevant person's context.

title: How to Create an Effective API Test Plan: A Practical Guide for QA Engineers and Developers
description:
APIs are the backbone of modern applications. Whether you're building a microservices architecture, integrating third-party services, or developing a mobile application, APIs play a critical role in ensuring that different systems communicate correctly.

But here's a common problem: many development teams start API testing without having a clearly defined testing plan.

They write a few test cases, validate successful responses, check status codes, and move on. Unfortunately, this approach often misses important scenarios such as invalid inputs, authorization issues, integration failures, performance bottlenecks, and backward compatibility problems.

This is where an API Test Plan becomes essential.

In this article, we'll explore what an API test plan is, why it matters, what it should include, and how you can create one for your next API project.

What Is an API Test Plan?

An API test plan is a structured document that defines how an API will be tested throughout a development cycle or release.

It outlines:

  • What APIs and endpoints need testing.
  • Which testing approaches will be used.
  • What environments are required.
  • Which test data and tools will be used.
  • What risks need attention.
  • What conditions must be satisfied before releasing an API.

Think of it as a roadmap for your API testing activities.

Without a proper plan, testing can become inconsistent, resulting in missed scenarios and unexpected production issues.

Why Do You Need an API Test Plan?

A well-defined API test plan provides several benefits.

  1. Better Test Coverage

An API can have multiple endpoints, request parameters, authentication mechanisms, and response structures.

A testing plan helps ensure that important scenarios aren't overlooked.

  1. Early Detection of Defects

Testing shouldn't happen only after development is complete.

By defining testing activities early, teams can identify contract violations, validation issues, and integration problems before they reach production.

  1. Improved Team Collaboration

Developers, QA engineers, product managers, and DevOps teams can work with a shared understanding of testing responsibilities and release expectations.

  1. Reduced Production Risks

Identifying security vulnerabilities, performance issues, and backward compatibility problems before deployment helps reduce the chances of production failures.

10 Essential Components of an Effective API Test Plan

Let's look at the important sections every API test plan should cover.

  1. Testing Objectives and Scope

Start by defining what you want to achieve through API testing.

Identify:

  • APIs and endpoints included in testing.
  • API versions being tested.
  • Features covered in the release.
  • Integrations with external services.
  • Functional and non-functional testing requirements.

For example, if you're testing an e-commerce application, your scope might include product, customer, payment, and order management APIs.

Clearly document what is excluded from testing as well.

  1. Testing Approach and Methodology

Define the different types of API testing that will be performed.

Some important testing types include:

  • Functional Testing: Validates business logic and expected API behavior.
  • Negative Testing: Checks how APIs handle invalid inputs and unexpected requests.
  • Contract Testing: Ensures API requests and responses follow the defined specification.
  • Integration Testing: Validates communication between connected services.
  • Regression Testing: Ensures existing functionality continues working after changes.
  • Performance Testing: Measures response times, throughput, and stability under load.
  • Security Testing: Identifies authentication, authorization, and other security vulnerabilities.

Your testing approach should be based on the API's complexity, business requirements, and potential risks.

  1. Test Environment Configuration

A consistent test environment is essential for reliable results.

Document the environments where testing will happen, such as:

  • Local development.
  • Continuous Integration (CI).
  • QA or testing.
  • Staging.
  • Production smoke testing.

Also specify API base URLs, authentication configurations, database dependencies, external service mocks, and environment access permissions.

Keep sensitive credentials secure and avoid exposing production data in lower environments.

  1. Test Data Management

API testing requires different types of test data.

For example, when testing a user registration API, you should consider:

  • Valid user information.
  • Missing mandatory fields.
  • Invalid email addresses.
  • Duplicate usernames.
  • Boundary values.
  • Unauthorized requests.

Use synthetic or appropriately masked data wherever possible.

A good test data strategy makes test execution more repeatable and reliable.

  1. Entry and Exit Criteria

One of the most important parts of an API test plan is defining when testing can begin and when it can be considered complete.

Example entry criteria:

  • API specification is reviewed and approved.
  • Test environment is available.
  • Required test data is prepared.
  • Build deployment is successful.
  • Authentication credentials are configured.

Example exit criteria:

  • All critical test cases have been executed.
  • No unresolved critical or high-severity defects remain.
  • Positive and negative scenarios are covered.
  • Contract validation tests pass.
  • Performance requirements are satisfied.
  • Security checks meet agreed acceptance criteria.

Avoid vague statements such as "testing is completed successfully." Use measurable conditions instead.

  1. Risk Assessment

Not every API endpoint carries the same level of risk.

For example, a payment processing API requires more attention than a simple health-check endpoint.

Identify potential risks such as:

  • Unauthorized access to customer information.
  • Incorrect financial calculations.
  • Breaking changes in API responses.
  • Unexpected failures during high traffic.
  • Third-party integration failures.

Prioritize testing based on the likelihood and business impact of each risk.

This helps QA teams focus their efforts where they matter most.

  1. Test Coverage and Traceability

Define how you will measure API test coverage.

Useful coverage metrics include:

  • Percentage of API operations tested.
  • Positive and negative scenario coverage.
  • Request and response schema validation.
  • HTTP status code coverage.
  • Boundary value coverage.
  • Requirement-to-test traceability.

For example, every documented API operation should have appropriate positive and negative test scenarios.

Connecting requirements, API specifications, and test cases also makes it easier to identify gaps when an API changes.

  1. Tools and Technologies

Choose tools based on your testing requirements.

Some commonly used tools include:

  • Postman for API requests and functional validation.
  • REST Assured for Java-based API automation.
  • Pytest for Python-based testing.
  • Apache JMeter and k6 for performance testing.
  • OWASP ZAP for security testing.
  • Swagger and OpenAPI for API documentation and contract validation.

Your tool selection should support repeatable execution and integration with your development workflow.

  1. CI/CD Integration and Quality Gates

API testing becomes more effective when integrated into CI/CD pipelines.

Instead of waiting until the release stage, automate important checks throughout development.

A typical pipeline could look like this:

Pull Request

  • API specification validation.
  • Contract testing.
  • Functional smoke tests.

Merge to Main

  • Full functional testing.
  • Integration testing.
  • Regression checks.

Pre-Release

  • Performance testing.
  • Security testing.
  • Final quality assessment.

Define which failures should block a merge or deployment.

This ensures that API quality becomes part of the development process rather than a last-minute activity.

  1. Reporting and Defect Management

Finally, define how testing results will be reported.

Your plan should identify:

  • Test execution status.
  • Passed and failed test cases.
  • Defect severity and priority.
  • Outstanding risks.
  • Test coverage metrics.
  • Release readiness status.

Clear reporting helps stakeholders make informed release decisions.

Common Mistakes to Avoid When Creating an API Test Plan

Even experienced QA teams can make mistakes while planning API testing.

Here are some common ones:

  1. Testing only successful scenarios

Happy-path testing isn't enough. Include invalid inputs, missing parameters, unauthorized requests, and unexpected responses.

  1. Ignoring API contract changes

Changes in request or response structures can break existing consumers. Include contract validation and backward compatibility checks.

  1. Using unrealistic test data

Unrepresentative data can hide important defects. Include boundary values, invalid data, and different user roles.

  1. Not defining measurable exit criteria

Without clear release conditions, teams may disagree about whether testing is complete.

  1. Keeping testing separate from CI/CD

Manual-only testing can slow down feedback. Automate repeatable checks and integrate them into the development pipeline.

How API Test Planning Supports Shift-Left Testing

Shift-left testing means moving testing activities earlier in the software development lifecycle.

Instead of discovering problems just before production, teams validate API quality during development.

A well-defined API test plan supports this approach by establishing:

  • API contract validation before deployment.
  • Automated tests during pull requests.
  • Early detection of breaking API changes.
  • Continuous regression testing.
  • Consistent quality gates across releases.

When testing is planned around API specifications, developers and QA engineers can identify potential issues before they become expensive production defects.

Final Thoughts

An effective API test plan is more than a document. It's a practical framework that helps development and QA teams deliver reliable, secure, and maintainable APIs.

By defining testing scope, methodologies, environments, test data, risk priorities, coverage targets, and CI/CD quality gates, teams can make API testing more predictable and efficient.

If you're building or improving your API testing process, having a reusable template can save significant planning time.

Want a ready-to-use starting point?

Check out the detailed API Test Plan Template by Total Shift Left.

It includes fill-in sections for testing scope, environments, entry and exit criteria, risk assessment, coverage targets, test data, tools, CI quality gates, and reporting, along with a practical worked example.

Use it as a starting point and customize it for your next API release.

What does your API testing process look like? Do you maintain a formal API test plan, or do you manage testing activities directly through test cases and CI/CD pipelines?

title: Bigo Ads billing and top-up controls: a guide for mobile game studios
description:
Here is a working checklist on Bigo Ads for mobile game studios. It reflects what we see when companies expand into the UK in 2026.

Documents and entity details

Before you request an account, line up the basics: a legal entity name that matches the website footer, a working business email on your own domain, a privacy policy and terms page, a refund or cancellation policy where relevant, and a contact page with a reachable address. Reviewers on Bigo Ads compare these against the ad and landing page. Inconsistencies are the most common reason new accounts stall. Related reading: ad budget and ROAS calculator.

Billing and top-up controls

Decide who can add funds and who can change payment methods, and write it down. Use a single billing contact per account, keep invoices in one shared folder, and reconcile spend weekly against the platform's own report. If finance sits in another time zone, agree on a minimum balance trigger so campaigns never pause on a Friday night in the UK.

A 30-day launch outline

Week 1: account, billing, tracking and two landing pages. Week 2: three to five creative concepts at modest budgets. Week 3: cut the bottom half, duplicate winners into a second audience. Week 4: review cost per primary conversion against your target and decide to scale, hold or stop. Keep notes; the second market is far cheaper when the first one is documented.

Questions to ask a partner

If you work with an agency for Bigo Ads, ask how accounts are owned, how quickly appeals are handled, whether spend reports are shared in real time, and what happens to the account if you leave. Clear answers to those four questions matter more than a small difference in service fee.

What actually drives cost

The headline price on Bigo Ads is the auction, but total cost includes the account route (direct, agency or reseller), top-up fees, currency conversion, creative production and the time spent on appeals. For mobile game studios, the hidden line is usually wasted spend during the first two weeks while tracking and audiences settle. Budget for a learning period explicitly instead of judging the channel on day three.

Why Bigo Ads deserves a separate plan

Most teams copy their Meta or Google setup onto every new network. That rarely works for Bigo Ads. Audience intent, creative formats and review rules differ, and the cost of a mistake shows up as a disabled account rather than a weak campaign. For mobile game studios entering the UK, a short written plan per platform saves weeks: who owns the account, which payment method funds it, which landing pages are approved, and what result would justify scaling.

Common mistakes we see

  • Running the same creative on Bigo Ads that was built for another network.
  • Changing budget, audience and creative on the same day, which makes results unreadable.
  • Letting one freelancer own the only admin login.
  • Ignoring the policy centre until an ad is rejected.
  • Judging the channel before tracking has been verified.

Summary

Keep the plan small, written and measurable. Start with the basics above, review after 30 days, and expand what works.

Written by the PandaWM team in Hong Kong. PandaWM helps overseas-facing companies with GEO / AI search visibility, ad account opening and management on Facebook, Google, TikTok and about 20 smaller networks, multilingual websites, AiChatSale and a crypto payment gateway that serves overseas merchants only.

title: Localising Payment Flows for Central Asian Markets
description:
When you build checkout for a region where card penetration sits below 30 percent, the form has to start with mobile wallets and local bank transfers, not Visa/Mastercard tabs. Central Asia — Uzbekistan in particular — has its own mix of UZCARD, Humo, and phone-balance top-ups.

Field order matters

Western checkout forms put the card number first. For UZ users the card fields should sit below the wallet option, because most first-time deposits come from a mobile wallet. The heuristic: sort methods by historical conversion rate for the geo, not by global popularity.

const sortedMethods = methods
  .filter(m => m.supportedGeos.includes(geo))
  .sort((a, b) => b.conversionRate[geo] - a.conversionRate[geo]);

Handling sum validation

Minimum deposits vary per method and currency. A site like 888Starz publishes its method-specific limits openly, which lets you cross-check that your validator matches the operator's actual floor. Hard-coding limits leads to silent failures when the operator adjusts them server-side.

Currency display

UZS amounts run into the millions for modest sums. Use Intl.NumberFormat('uz-UZ', { style: 'currency', currency: 'UZS', maximumFractionDigits: 0 }) and always drop the decimals — no one pays 1.5 soum.

Takeaway

Localised payment UX is not about translating labels. It is about knowing which methods dominate, surfacing them first, and validating against the operator's real constraints rather than a static config file.

title: How can I test my API key?
description:
Send two requests before you trust it: one with no key at all, and one with a made-up key in the header the API documents. If the two answers differ, the API tells you whether a key reached it, and the answer to your real key means something. If the two answers are the same, a 401 cannot tell you whether your key arrived, and only a call that has to succeed proves the key works.

I sent exactly these two requests to six hosted memory APIs on 19 November 2026. Every request got a 401. Two APIs changed the message between the two requests, and four did not.

API (documented header) No key Made-up key in the documented header
Hindsight Cloud (Authorization: Bearer) "Authentication failed: API key required" "Authentication failed: Invalid API key format"
Mnemoverse (X-Api-Key) "Missing API key. Send X-Api-Key header." "This value does not have the shape of a Mnemoverse API key (mk_live_ followed by 32 lower-case hex characters)"
Letta Cloud (Authorization: Bearer) "Unauthorized" the same
Mem0 Platform (Authorization: Token) "Invalid API key. You can find your API key on https://app.mem0.ai/dashboard/api-keys." the same
Supermemory (Authorization: Bearer) "Unauthorized" the same
Zep (Authorization: Api-Key) "unauthorized" the same

Why a right key can still fail to arrive

An SDK sets the header for you. A proxy, a CI secret, a plain curl call or an MCP client configuration does not, and these six APIs alone use four ways to send a key: Bearer, Token and Api-Key in the Authorization header, and a separate X-Api-Key header. A key in a header the server does not read is, for the server, no key at all. At the four APIs that answer both requests the same way, that mistake looks exactly like a wrong key.

The two-minute check 

URL=https://api.vendor.example/v1/some-endpoint
curl -s -w ' %{http_code}\n' "$URL"
curl -s -w ' %{http_code}\n' "$URL" -H "Authorization: Bearer not-a-real-key"
curl -s -w ' %{http_code}\n' "$URL" -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY"

Put the header your vendor documents in the second and third lines. If the first two answers differ, the third one tells you what happened to your key: the "missing" message means the header was not read, the "invalid" message means the key arrived and was rejected, and a 200 means it works. If the first two answers are the same, a 401 on the third line proves nothing, so test the key with a request that has to succeed, such as listing your own resources.

Sources and method. The requests were sent on 19 November 2026 with curl from one machine, one at a time, with the made-up key probe-not-a-real-key-0000000000; the answers are quoted as the APIs returned them that day. The same requests on 17 November got the same answers. No accounts or keys were created. This article describes the APIs as of 19 November 2026.

I work on Mnemoverse; this comparison uses the same two requests for every API, Mnemoverse included.

title: User Acceptance Testing for Founders: Six Steps Before You Sign Off
description:
A feature can pass its tests and still fail the business.

That gap is exactly why user acceptance testing (UAT) deserves more attention during software handover.

For developers, passing functional tests may indicate that an implementation behaves as expected. For founders and operations leads, the question is different: can the people who will use this system complete their actual work with it?

This distinction becomes especially important when a company receives an MVP or SaaS product from an external development team. The build may be complete, but the business still needs to verify that the delivered product meets its requirements.

UAT provides a structured way to do that. Here are six practical steps I would follow before signing off.

  1. Define What the Software Must Prove

Don't begin acceptance testing with random clicks.

Start by translating the agreed requirements into observable acceptance criteria. A requirement such as "users can manage orders" is too broad to test reliably.

Break it into outcomes:

An authorised user can create an order.

Required customer and product information is validated.

The order can be updated according to business rules.

The correct status is displayed.

Relevant users can retrieve the order later.

Each criterion should describe an expected behaviour and a result that can be verified.

This also helps separate critical requirements from preferences. A missing function that blocks a core workflow should not be treated like a minor visual inconsistency.

I recommend maintaining a simple acceptance checklist linked to the relevant requirement or ticket. That gives testers and developers a shared reference rather than relying on memory or informal approval.

Watch out for: Requirements that describe screens or features but never define what successful business use looks like.

  1. Prepare Scenarios from Real Work

Acceptance scenarios should represent how people actually use the product.

A developer may know the intended workflow, but the operations team understands the exceptions, handoffs, and everyday decisions that happen around it.

Consider an inventory application. Testing whether a user can create a product record is useful, but it is only one part of the process. A more realistic scenario might include creating the record, updating stock, checking availability, and reviewing the resulting information.

Include both normal and exceptional conditions:

Missing required information

Invalid input

Duplicate submissions

Permission restrictions

Editing or cancelling an existing record

Recovering from an interrupted workflow

For each scenario, document the starting conditions, steps, and expected outcome.

Where possible, involve actual users or representatives of the teams who will operate the system. They often identify workflow gaps that aren't visible in a developer-led demonstration.

Watch out for: Testing only the happy path. Real users rarely operate software under perfect conditions all the time.

  1. Test Complete Workflows, Not Isolated Features

This is where I would spend particular attention during UAT.

Individual features can work correctly while the workflow connecting them remains broken.

A form might save successfully. A report might load. A notification might appear. But does the complete process work from the user's first action to the expected business outcome?

For a SaaS product, consider testing the journey from registration to account setup, subscription handling, and access to the correct features. For an internal operations tool, follow a request from submission through assignment, approval, completion, and reporting.

Check the transitions between modules, not just the modules themselves.

Also verify:

Data remains consistent across screens.

User permissions are respected throughout the workflow.

Status changes appear where expected.

Errors are understandable and recoverable.

Repeated actions don't create unintended duplicates.

Use an environment that resembles the intended operating environment as closely as practical. Configuration, integrations, roles, and realistic data can expose issues that a simplified demo environment hides.

UAT doesn't replace security, performance, or integration testing. Those need their own technical validation. But acceptance should establish that the integrated product supports the business process it was built for.

Watch out for: Declaring a workflow successful because every individual screen passed a separate test.

  1. Record Defects with Clear Evidence

A defect report should help someone reproduce the problem without having to guess what the tester meant.

"The dashboard is broken" isn't actionable enough.

A useful report includes:

Feature or workflow being tested

Steps to reproduce

Expected result

Actual result

Screenshot, error message, or relevant evidence

Severity and business impact

For example, "Order total is incorrect" needs more context. Which order? What inputs were used? What total was expected? What did the application display?

The business impact matters too. A layout issue and an incorrect financial calculation should not receive the same priority simply because both are defects.

I prefer a shared defect log that connects each issue to its test case and requirement. It makes discussions between developers, testers, and stakeholders more precise.

It also gives the team a record of what was found, what was fixed, and what remains unresolved.

Watch out for: Scattered feedback in chat messages, screenshots without context, and vague tickets that cannot be reproduced.

  1. Verify Fixes Through Retesting

A development ticket marked "resolved" is not proof that the original problem has disappeared.

After a fix is delivered, repeat the original test scenario. Confirm that the expected behaviour now occurs.

Then consider whether the change could have affected related functionality. This is where regression testing becomes important.

For example, changing how customer records are updated might resolve an editing issue but affect a report that uses the same data. Testing only the edited field could miss that side effect.

A practical defect lifecycle might look like this:

Reported
|
v
Under investigation
|
v
Fix delivered
|
v
Ready for retest
|
+---- Failed ----> Reopened
|
v
Verified
|
v
Closed

Keep the test result connected to the defect record. Where possible, note the build or release being tested so the team knows exactly which version was verified.

Not every fix requires repeating every test in the application. The scope of regression testing should reflect the risk and dependencies of the change. But important workflows deserve another end-to-end check.

Watch out for: Closing issues based only on a developer's status update.

  1. Make a Clear Acceptance Decision

UAT should end with a documented decision, not an assumption that the project is finished because the delivery date has arrived.

I would use three possible outcomes.

Accept: The agreed acceptance criteria have been met, and remaining issues do not prevent intended use.

Accept with conditions: The product can be accepted with known limitations, documented responsibilities, and agreed follow-up actions.

Defer or reject acceptance: Important requirements remain unmet, or unresolved defects make the product unsuitable for its intended purpose.

Record the decision alongside the test results, outstanding defects, and any conditions attached to acceptance.

Also review the handover requirements separately. Access credentials, deployment information, documentation, backups, third-party dependencies, ownership arrangements, and support responsibilities may all need verification.

This matters because UAT and operational handover are related, but they aren't identical. A product might pass its business acceptance tests while the organisation is still missing information needed to operate or maintain it.

If the project has contractual acceptance milestones or payment conditions, use the agreement as the reference for the formal decision.

Watch out for: Signing off because the team is tired, the project is late, or everyone wants to move on.

A Practical View of UAT Effort

The following is my rough, indicative view of where attention tends to go during a typical acceptance process. Actual effort depends on the product, scope, and risk.

  1. Define expectations ██████░░░░
  2. Prepare scenarios ███████░░░
  3. Test full workflows ██████████
  4. Record defects ███████░░░
  5. Retest fixes ████████░░
  6. Decide on sign-off ██████░░░░

I give end-to-end workflow testing the most attention because that is where separate features have to work together.

A Short UAT Checklist

Before accepting a build, I'd want to be able to answer these questions:

Are the acceptance criteria clear and agreed?

Do test scenarios reflect real business tasks?

Have complete workflows been tested?

Are defects documented with reproducible steps?

Have important fixes been retested?

Are remaining issues and conditions documented?

Has the acceptance decision been recorded?

Are operational handover responsibilities clear?

If several answers are still no, the project may need more validation before formal acceptance.

How KSoft Technologies Approaches User Acceptance Testing

At KSoft Technologies, our work involves helping founders and growing companies build, modernise, and scale software systems. We consider acceptance criteria, realistic workflow validation, defect resolution, and clear handover important parts of delivering software that supports actual business operations.

This is our own software engineering service, and the same principle guides the work: a build should be evaluated by how well it serves its intended users, not simply by whether development tasks are marked complete.

Final Thought

Founders don't need to become developers to make a responsible software acceptance decision.

They do need a clear understanding of what was promised, realistic scenarios that reflect how the business works, and evidence that the important workflows behave as expected.

UAT is not an obstacle to shipping. It's how you avoid confusing a finished build with a usable product.

I'm interested in how other teams handle this: Who owns the final acceptance decision in your projects—the product owner, operations team, founder, or a combination of them?

I'm writing from KSoft Technologies, where we work on software engineering and digital product delivery. Read the related guide to user acceptance testing.

title: Biologically-Inspired Spike Encoding and Optimization for Spiking Neural Networks
description:
arXiv:2611.23242v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer theoretical energy-efficiency advantages over conventional deep networks, but realizing these advantages on vision tasks requires sparse spike representations that naive rate-coding methods fail to provide. We combine biologically motivated spike-encoding schemes with two training improvements: Rouser adaptive-threshold surrogate gradients and Kronecker-Factored Approximate Curvature (K-FAC) second-order optimization. The spike encoding schemes experimented with are rate coding, latency coding, DVS-style delta modulation, and Difference-of-Gaussians (DoG) filtering. Experiments on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST demonstrate that biologically inspired encoders yield the largest accuracy gains in capacity-constrained regimes and serve as an effective parameter-efficiency lever. DoG and delta modulation encoders produce significantly sparser spike trains than rate coding. K-FAC yields modest but consistent accuracy improvements over Adam-trained baselines, and Rouser's learnable per-neuron thresholds improve Fashion-MNIST accuracy from 87.37% to 88.13% by enabling homeostatic firing-rate regulation. Biologically grounded pre-processing methods can help close the accuracy gap between SNNs and non-spiking baselines without increasing model size.

title: MobileWeave: Program-First Synthesis of Dependency-Linked Tasks for Training Mobile GUI Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.23860v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Native mobile GUI agents require large-scale training trajectories covering both individual app functions and multi-goal workflows within and across apps, which makes automatic task synthesis a promising way to scale training data. Existing synthesis pipelines, however, produce each task as free-form text, leaving implicit how its subgoals depend on one another. This matters because composition is a skill in its own right: a policy may complete each subtask of a workflow on its own, yet fail to chain these subtasks into the complete workflow. We present MobileWeave, which instead synthesizes every task as an executable program derived from the app implementations of a controllable simulator. MobileWeave abstracts each app into a typed capability graph with semantic types shared across apps, composes atomic programs into single- and cross-app composite programs through explicit value and object dependencies, and verifies each program by native execution, deriving both its instruction and its completion check from the same program. Trained on teacher trajectories collected for these tasks and on recovery supervision at the policy's own stalls, MobileWeave-8B improves its base model by 26.7 points on MobileGym and by 8.6, 21.3, and 17.6 points on AndroidWorld, AndroidLab, and MobileWorld, with comparable gains at 4B. Beyond these gains, we find that composition is learnable from task structure: explicit dependencies between subgoals act as a training signal that teaches a policy to compose skills it already masters. We release data, model, and code at https://maxxnotmarx.github.io/MobileWeave/ .

title: Every size on our big screen is one number times a CSS variable, and the variable is 1cqmin
description:
Our quiz product has two kinds of screen. There are the phones the teams hold, and there is one big screen the whole room looks at, which in practice is a laptop plugged into the pub TV or mirrored to it over AirPlay. We do not control that screen. We do not know its size, its aspect ratio, its scaling factor, or how far away the nearest table is sitting.

The same component also has to render inside a frame about 390 pixels wide, because the demo on our landing page is not a video or a screenshot. It is the real host screen, running, scaled down.

Two environments, one component, and the thing that made it work was giving up on absolute lengths almost entirely.

One unit, declared on the children

The whole stage is sized from a single custom property called --u:

export function StageFrame({ children, className = 'h-[100dvh]' }: {
    children: ReactNode
    className?: string
}) {
    return (
        <div
            className={`relative flex w-full flex-col overflow-hidden
                bg-background text-foreground
                [container-type:size]
                [&>*]:[--u:1cqmin]
                @max-3xl:[&>*]:[--u:1.8cqw] ${className}`}
        >
            {children}
        </div>
    )
}

On a wide screen, --u is 1cqmin: one per cent of the smaller dimension of the stage container. Everything inside is then written as a multiple of it:

<div className="grid shrink-0 grid-cols-2 items-center
    gap-x-[calc(2*var(--u))] gap-y-[calc(1.6*var(--u))]
    px-[calc(3*var(--u))] pt-[calc(2.4*var(--u))] pb-[calc(1.6*var(--u))]">

That is Tailwind arbitrary values, so it is verbose, but the property is the point rather than the syntax. A 1100 by 710 laptop stage and a 1920 by 1080 TV produce different values of --u, and every padding, radius, gap, badge and font size on the screen moves with it in exactly the same proportion. Nothing is ever almost right because one gap was in px.

Below 48rem, which is roughly a phone held upright, --u switches to 1.8cqw: a share of the width rather than the smaller dimension. On a tall narrow screen cqmin tracks the width anyway, but the multiplier bumps the whole scale up so the text is readable at arm's length instead of being sized for a room.

146 lengths and 47 multipliers

The five files that make up the big screen are 823 lines, and I counted what is actually in them:

  • 146 uses of var(--u), 145 of them a plain calc(k * var(--u)), and one where the multiplier is itself another custom property
  • 47 distinct values of k, from 0.4 to 40
  • the most common three are 2 (13 times), 1.2 (13 times) and 1.6 (12 times)

Forty-seven multipliers is more than a design system would allow and I am not going to pretend otherwise. There is no scale here, no 4-point grid, no named tokens. What there is instead is one dimension of freedom: every number on that screen is relative to the same thing, so the screen can be wrong at every size equally, which is a much easier bug to fix than being wrong at one size only.

The large end of the range is where it earns its keep. The podium area is calc(40*var(--u)) tall and the trophy inside it is calc(22*var(--u)) square. On a 13 inch laptop that is 284 and 156 CSS pixels; on a 55 inch TV at 1080p it is 432 and 237. Neither number is typed anywhere.

Why the variable is declared on the children

The detail that cost me the most time is in that [&>*] selector. The obvious thing to write is [--u:1cqmin] on the frame itself. That does not work, and the reason is in the container query spec: a container query length resolves against the nearest ancestor container, not against the element it is written on. The frame is the container. A cqmin declared there would be resolved against whatever container the frame itself is sitting inside, which on the landing page is a different box with a different size.

Declaring it on [&>*] means the value is computed one level down, where the frame is genuinely an ancestor container.

The same rule is the standing trap for anyone adding to this screen, so it is written at the top of the file: do not put anything inside the stage that is itself a container, because --u will silently start resolving against that instead.

Three places absolute lengths survive

An audit of the five files turns up exactly three kinds of length that are not multiples of --u:

  1. h-[100dvh] on the frame's default class, because the real stage fills the window and something has to say so.
  2. Icon sizes written as h-[1.1em] w-[1.1em]: ten elements, 20 declarations. These inherit from the font size next to them, which is itself a multiple of --u, so they scale, just one step removed.
  3. One single @3xl:max-w-[58cqw] on the quiz name in the lobby, which is a truncation limit rather than a size. It is a share of the container's width because what it is protecting against is a long name pushing the join instructions off the screen, and that is a width problem.

The one thing that is not proportional

Question text gets a font size chosen by how long the text is:

if (text.length > 200) return 'text-[length:calc(2.6*var(--u))] @3xl:text-[length:calc(3.2*var(--u))]'
if (text.length > 120) return 'text-[length:calc(3*var(--u))]   @3xl:text-[length:calc(3.8*var(--u))]'
return 'text-[length:calc(3.4*var(--u))] @3xl:text-[length:calc(4.4*var(--u))]'

Three tiers, two thresholds, both picked by looking at real text rather than derived from anything. This is the one place where the screen reacts to its content rather than its size, and it stays a multiple of --u so the two systems compose: a long question on a big TV is still bigger than a short question on a laptop.

The demo scales itself with a CSS division

The landing page needs the same stage at whatever width its column happens to be. The lazy version of this is to measure the container in JavaScript and set a transform. We did not want that, because a measured scale is wrong in the server HTML and then jumps when the page hydrates.

CSS can divide two lengths, as long as you are willing to be rude about it:

<div
  className="relative w-full overflow-hidden [container-type:inline-size]
             [--canvas-w:390] [--canvas-h:760]
             md:[--canvas-w:1100] md:[--canvas-h:710]"
  style={{ aspectRatio: 'var(--canvas-w) / var(--canvas-h)' }}
>
  <div
    className="absolute top-0 left-0 origin-top-left"
    style={{
      width: 'calc(var(--canvas-w) * 1px)',
      height: 'calc(var(--canvas-h) * 1px)',
      transform: 'scale(tan(atan2(100cqw, calc(var(--canvas-w) * 1px))))',
    }}
  />
</div>

tan(atan2(a, b)) is a / b. CSS will not divide two lengths directly, but atan2 takes two lengths and returns an angle, and tan turns that angle back into a unitless number. So the scale factor is "the width this thing actually has, divided by the width it was drawn at", computed by the browser, in the stylesheet, with no layout read.

The outer box's aspect-ratio comes from the same two numbers, so the frame reserves exactly the right height before anything renders. The inner stage is drawn at 1100 by 710 and squeezed to fit. Its own --u is then a share of the drawn size, which is fixed, which is why the scaled-down copy looks identical to the full size one instead of looking like a screen with a smaller font.

One nuance: the demo canvas is container-type: inline-size while the stage frame is container-type: size. The canvas only needs its own width for the 100cqw in that transform, and an inline-size container is cheaper, since a size container has to be layout-isolated in both axes.

See it

The host screen is the thing animating on pub-trivia.app, directly under the headline, at max-w-5xl on a laptop and max-w-[400px] on a phone. Two ways to check the claims in this post rather than take them:

  • Drag your browser window narrower and watch. Every gap, radius, badge and font size on that stage changes at the same time and in the same proportion, because they are all the same number times --u. Cross the phone threshold and the whole scale steps up at once.
  • View source on that page and search for atan2. You will find scale(tan(atan2(100cqw, calc(var(--canvas-w) * 1px)))) in the server HTML, with no JavaScript having run. Search for 1cqmin and you will find the unit declaration too.

The feature page for the same screen is pub-trivia.app/features/big-screen-display, and the leaderboard that shares its unit system is described at pub-trivia.app/features/live-leaderboard. If you want to put it on an actual TV, the free tier at pub-trivia.app/signup needs no card.
