title: Java4Shell: How to Check If You're Vulnerable (apt upgrade Misses Containers)
description:
You ran apt upgrade openjdk-17-jdk, java -version printed a new build, and you went to lunch. Your Keycloak container still runs its own JRE, your Jenkins agent image is pinned to last month's Temurin, and the vendor appliance in the corner has a JVM you have never seen a version string for.

Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) is a heap overflow in HotSpot's AVX-512 Base64 decoder. Calif, who found it, rates it 9.2 under CVSS 4.0 and lists Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate as pre-auth RCE in default configs. Oracle scores it 8.1 under CVSS 3.1, citing high attack complexity (Aikido). Patches shipped November 17, 2026.

Below: which Java 17, 21, 25 and 27 builds are affected, which are fixed, and four commands that find every JVM on a host or in a container image, including the ones java -version never sees.

Is it really the next Log4Shell?

Not in how easy it is to exploit. Log4Shell was one string in a User-Agent header. Here the overwritten bytes are a fixed pattern derived from the decoder, not attacker-chosen, and the Harness team didn't get code execution in their lab. With the default heap the write was silent across thousands of triggers; only after shrinking TLABs (-XX:TLABSize=2048 -XX:-ResizeTLAB) did they get a SIGSEGV in G1. Calif's own exploit is spray-and-retry heap grooming, and they say it is sensitive to RTT and jitter. On Lobsters someone called it "a nothingburger" next to Log4Shell, and the EPSS score quoted there was 0.00734.

I still think it's the worst JVM bug since Log4Shell, for two reasons.

First, the preconditions are boring. As a Lobsters commenter pointed out, Traefik, Envoy and HAProxy don't buffer requests by default, and Zen 4 shipped in 2022. And Base64 from strangers arrives before login all the time. Harness lists HTTP Basic headers, JWT segments decoded before the signature check, and SASL exchanges like Kafka SCRAM.

Second, and this is the Log4Shell part, the fix lives in every copy of the runtime. Log4Shell at least came down to one dependency in a pom.xml. Here you have to hunt down every JVM you ship, and most teams have no list of those.

Calif also says finding the bug took about an hour and the first working exploit two more, for under $200 in token costs. They're holding back the per-product chains until people have upgraded. Aikido had seen no confirmed exploitation in the wild as of November 18. I wouldn't bet on that lasting.

Which Java builds are affected

All of these need to be true:

  • an affected Java 17, 21, 25 or 27 build (Calif puts the start at 17.0.6)
  • x86-64 with AVX-512 VBMI: Intel Xeon Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids, Granite Rapids; AMD Zen 4 or newer
  • the JVM isn't already running with -XX:UseAVX=2 or -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics
  • attacker-controlled Base64 reaching java.util.Base64.Decoder

ARM64 is not affected. Graviton fleets can relax. EPYC Naples, Rome and Milan are AVX2-only, as one HN commenter noted, so older boxes are out of scope too.

According to Aikido, standard Java 8 and 11 are not affected, with one exception: Oracle lists its Java SE 8 Enterprise Performance Pack build (8u511-perf) as vulnerable.

Fixed builds, from Aikido's roundup:

Line Oracle fixed Temurin fixed Corretto fixed
17 17.0.21.1 17.0.21.1+2 17.0.21.1.2
21 21.0.13.1 21.0.13.1+2 21.0.13.1.2
25 25.0.5.1 25.0.5.1+2 25.0.5.1.2
27 27.0.1.1 27.0.1.1+4 27.0.1.1.4

EOL lines are affected and don't get their own fix. Move 18-20 to 21, 22-24 to 25, and 26 to 27. Red Hat is expediting RHEL 8, 9 and 10 builds. Zulu and Microsoft number their builds differently, Aikido has no fixed build numbers for Liberica yet, and distro packages carry their own versioning, so check each vendor's advisory and don't eyeball it against Oracle's table.

One Temurin gotcha: Adoptium publishes the binaries per platform as testing finishes, and the Docker Hub images only follow once every binary for that version is out. Your FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre rebuild may pull the old JRE for a while.

Check 1: does the CPU even have the instructions

This one is from Calif's writeup:

grep -m1 '^flags' /proc/cpuinfo | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E '^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$'

All four flags need to show up. If any are missing, this host can't hit the vulnerable path. But your autoscaling group can land the same image on a Sapphire Rapids node tomorrow, so don't treat a clean dev box as proof about production.

Check 2: every runtime on disk, including jlink'd ones

Every JDK, JRE and jlink-built runtime has a release file at its root. Reading those files covers bundled runtimes without executing anything:

sudo find / \( -path /proc -o -path /sys \) -prune -o -type f -name release -print0 2>/dev/null \
  | xargs -0 grep -H -E '^(IMPLEMENTOR|JAVA_VERSION|JAVA_RUNTIME_VERSION)=' 2>/dev/null

This is where the surprises turn up: /opt/<vendor>/jre, jpackage'd desktop tools, an IDE's bundled runtime, the copy your monitoring agent brought along.

Check 3: what's actually running

The binary on disk doesn't matter if the process still has the old one loaded. Harness's advice is to check the running process rather than trust the image tag. Finding processes by name misses custom launchers, so match on libjvm.so instead:

for m in $(sudo grep -l libjvm.so /proc/[0-9]*/maps 2>/dev/null); do
  pid=$(echo "$m" | cut -d/ -f3)
  echo "$pid $(sudo readlink /proc/$pid/exe) $(sudo grep -m1 -o '/[^ ]*libjvm.so' /proc/$pid/maps)"
done

For each hit, jcmd <pid> VM.version tells you the build, and jcmd <pid> VM.flags -all | grep -E 'UseBASE64Intrinsics|UseAVX' tells you whether the fast path is on. To see what a particular binary defaults to on this CPU:

/path/to/bin/java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -E 'UseBASE64Intrinsics|UseAVX'

UseBASE64Intrinsics true and UseAVX at 3 on a VBMI-capable host means you're exposed until you patch.

Check 4: container images, distroless included

Distroless images don't have a shell or find, so don't bother with docker exec. Export the filesystem and read the release file out of the tarball:

for img in $(docker image ls --format '{{.Repository}}:{{.Tag}}' | grep -v '<none>'); do
  cid=$(docker create "$img" true 2>/dev/null) || continue  # dummy cmd, never run; covers images with no CMD
  docker export "$cid" | tar -xOf - --wildcards --no-anchored 'release' 2>/dev/null \
    | grep -E '^(IMPLEMENTOR|JAVA_RUNTIME_VERSION)=' | sed "s|^|$img: |"
  docker rm "$cid" >/dev/null
done

For Kubernetes, kubectl get pods -A -o jsonpath='{..image}' | tr ' ' '\n' | sort -u gives you the image list to feed into the same loop.

Harness also published a runtime checker script that compares local JDKs against the advisory builds and checks the CPU and flags; exit code 2 means a JDK is still exposed. Their post shows it as curl | bash. Read it before you pipe it into a root shell on prod.

Stopgaps if you can't patch tonight

Calif lists both of these flags as workarounds and still tells everyone to update right away.

  • -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics forces the pure-Java decoder. This is the targeted fix. Harness notes it costs performance on Base64-heavy workloads.
  • -XX:UseAVX=2 turns off AVX-512 for the whole process. Red Hat recommends it, but it changes vectorization everywhere. An ARM64 JVM won't start with this flag, so don't bake it into a multi-arch image's JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS.

Strict Base64 validation in front of the decoder (length a multiple of 4, alphabet only, padding only at the end) is a backstop. Harness notes that a loose character-class check doesn't catch the inputs that overflow.

Switching to ZGC isn't a fix either. The only exploit discussed so far targets G1, but as one Lobsters commenter pointed out, the bug isn't in G1 and can still be used for denial of service under ZGC.

My order would be: internet-facing services that decode Base64 before auth (SSO, CI, artifact repos) first, then image rebuilds, then the appliances you'll have to open vendor tickets for.

Did your scan find a Java runtime you didn't know you were running? Where was it hiding? And if you think the Log4Shell comparison is overblown, make your case in the comments.

Sources

  • Calif, Java4Shell: Write once, RCE everywhere
  • Aikido, Java4Shell: pre-auth RCE flaw in Java 17 puts servers at risk
  • Harness, Past the end of the buffer: CVE-2026-114938
  • OpenJDK advisory: https://openjdk.org/groups/vulnerability/advisories/2026-11-17
  • Oracle CPU November 2026: https://www.oracle.com/security-alerts/cspunov2026.html
  • Discussion: Lobsters, Hacker News

title: Introducing Nonprofit: A Free Theme for Backdrop CMS
description:
Introducing Nonprofit: A Free Theme for Backdrop CMS

Building a professional website for a nonprofit organization should not require a complicated setup process or extensive custom development.

That's the idea behind Nonprofit, a free and open-source theme for Backdrop CMS, built with Tailwind CSS.

Why Nonprofit?

Backdrop CMS provides powerful tools for managing content, layouts, and configuration. However, creating a polished website often requires considerable time configuring these features.

Nonprofit aims to simplify that experience while preserving the flexibility that makes Backdrop CMS valuable.

Key Features

  • Modern, responsive design using Tailwind CSS
  • Flexible page layouts powered by Backdrop CMS
  • Content presentation using Views
  • Customizable theme settings
  • Sample content and configuration imports
  • A lightweight approach suitable for ordinary shared hosting

Simplifying Theme Setup

One of the most interesting parts of this project is its integration with Backdrop Theme Setup.

This reusable, JSON-driven PHP library helps theme developers configure their themes without manually recreating sample content and site settings.

It supports importing:

  • Sample content and taxonomy terms
  • Menu links
  • Views configurations
  • Layout blocks
  • Field configurations
  • Required modules and entity references

The library uses Backdrop's existing APIs and Configuration Management system rather than introducing a separate configuration framework.

The goal is to reduce repetitive setup work while keeping content management and presentation responsibilities clearly separated.

More Than Just a Theme

Nonprofit is also a starting point for a larger project: a Backdrop CMS distribution designed specifically for nonprofit organizations.

The long-term goal is to provide organizations with practical tools for managing their websites and operations, while keeping the system affordable, flexible, and accessible.

Get Involved

Backdrop CMS has a welcoming open-source community, and feedback from designers, developers, and nonprofit organizations is always valuable.

If you're interested in the project, I'd love to hear your thoughts, suggestions, and ideas for improvement.

Download and Explore Nonprofit

Nonprofit is free and open source. Explore the source code, try the theme, and share your feedback.

https://backdropcms.org/project/nonprofit

title: Safe to Omit, Worth Omitting? Keeping the Answer and Cutting Latency When an LLM Agent Skips Another's Message
description:
arXiv:2611.23570v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In multi-agent systems, a receiver agent often waits for a helper agent's message (text or its latent KV cache), which can improve performance but adds latency. We study when a receiver agent can skip the message safely (the final answer rarely changes) and beneficially (the time saved exceeds the cost of deciding). Our mechanism reads the receiver agent's confidence without the message and uses a finite-sample test to certify a threshold at which, with high probability, at most 5% of skipped answers change; if none passes, the system keeps communicating. We test it on OpenBookQA, ARC-Challenge, and MMLU-Pro with three Qwen model pairs, on cross-family agents, and on SQuAD and GSM8K. Four insights emerge. First, oracle headroom is weak evidence that messages help: control inputs without answer-specific content, matched to change answers as often as real messages, reproduce a median 76% of the oracle's gain. Second, whether a message can be skipped depends on how often and how predictably it alters the answer, not on its accuracy; every certified KV-cache path is less accurate than the receiver agent alone. Third, where text messages help, skipping keeps most of their gain: on unseen questions in the four such settings, the policies skip 59 to 80% and keep an estimated 76 to 95% of the gain. In two prospective tests with all rules fixed in advance, our mechanism skips a three-agent system's verifier on 39.9% of sealed questions, keeping 12.55 of its 12.80-point gain, and a 32B helper on 68.4% of held-out questions, keeping its whole gain. Fourth, safety does not determine efficiency: at batch size one, skipping text saves hundreds of milliseconds per query and skipping KV cache far less. Certification extends to SQuAD but not to GSM8K. In eleven tests on unseen questions, every certified policy we could test kept its change rate's 95% upper bound below 5% under our answer parsers.

title: Pluggable Subband-Decoupled Fusion and Unlabeled Capture Prototype Calibration: Bridging High-SNR Null-Subcarrier Regrowth and Low-SNR Coherent Preambles for Cross-Domain IoT RF Fingerprinting
description:
arXiv:2611.22812v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Zero-overhead physical-layer authentication at edge wireless access points (APs) is vital for securing resource-constrained Internet of Things (IoT) transceivers against credential cloning, yet cross-domain IEEE 802.11a/g radio frequency fingerprint identification (RFFI) faces an acute signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) crossover. Power-amplifier spectral regrowth on unpopulated null subcarriers resists indoor multipath at high SNR but decays quadratically below the thermal noise floor, whereas populated active in-band preambles survive low SNR yet degrade under severe multipath, causing static fusion to lose up to 44.7 percentage points (pp). To our knowledge, we propose the first RFFI framework that dynamically modulates active in-band waveforms and unpopulated null-subcarrier regrowth via a blind physical SNR gate: Pluggable Gated Subband-Decoupled Fusion with Unlabeled Capture-Aware Prototype Calibration (GSDF-CAPC). Avoiding the 20-35 dB subband gradient imbalance of joint training, GSDF pairs any frozen pretrained host backbone with a 46.3K null-subcarrier plug-in encoder (NS-Branch), fusing scale-standardized logits and gate-warped spherical embeddings under a source-calibrated lag-64 thermal-SNR gate with exact low-SNR fallback. Over unlabeled target AP captures, forward-only unbalanced optimal-transport calibration (UOT-CAPC) aligns shifted prototypes under packet-arrival skew and recovers parameter-free balanced Sinkhorn (U-CAPC) at equipartition. Across DataPort-WiFi, WiSig, and ORBIT MobRFFI, zero-retrain GSDF wins all 72/72 paired runs across eight backbones with 0.00 pp low-SNR loss, while edge IB-Host + GSDF (92.6K-93.3K active parameters, 1.82 ms single-core CPU latency) and timing-synchronized GSDF-STO / GSDF-Tri reach 57.50%-65.05% three-benchmark Macro-F1 (89.04%-100.00% over 5-10-packet IoT bursts).

title: Laravel Performance Tuning: How to Insert 100,000+ Records Efficiently (Beyond Eloquent)
description:
Stefan Bogdanescu

Founder & Senior Architect · 2026-07-15

If you've ever tried to insert 30,000 records using Eloquent and watched your script crawl along for 30+ seconds, you know the pain. The ORM that makes Laravel so productive for day-to-day development becomes a bottleneck the moment you need to move large volumes of data. In this guide, we'll cover practical Laravel bulk insert performance techniques that take you from minutes to seconds, using the tools Laravel gives you out of the box. For teams needing expert guidance on enterprise-scale architecture, a Laravel Agency can help design the right data pipelines from day one.

Why Eloquent Is Slow for Bulk Inserts

Eloquent models are expensive. Every time you call Model::create() or $model->save(), Laravel hydrates a full Eloquent model instance, fires events (creating, created, saving, saved), runs model validation, and casts attributes. For a single record, this overhead is negligible. For 100,000 records, it adds up fast.

The numbers: Inserting 100,000 records via Eloquent create() inside a loop takes roughly 90-120 seconds. Using the DB::insert() facade with a single batch query? Under 3 seconds. That's a 30-40x improvement with essentially zero additional complexity.

The DB Facade: Your First Step

Laravel's DB::insert() method lets you bypass the ORM entirely and send raw parameterized SQL directly to the database. Here's how you'd insert a batch of records:

$chunkSize = 500;
$records = [];

foreach ($data as $row) {
    $records[] = $row;

    if (count($records) >= $chunkSize) {
        DB::insert('INSERT INTO users (name, email, status) VALUES (?, ?, ?)', $records);
        $records = [];
    }
}

// Insert remaining records
if (!empty($records)) {
    DB::insert('INSERT INTO users (name, email, status) VALUES (?, ?, ?)', $records);
}

This approach avoids model hydration, event dispatching, and attribute casting entirely. The database receives a clean SQL statement with bound parameters, processes it, and moves on.

Transaction Wrapping for Integrity

When inserting large datasets, you want atomicity. If the process fails halfway through, you don't want orphaned records. Wrap your entire insert operation in a database transaction:

DB::transaction(function () use ($data) {
    foreach (array_chunk($data, 500) as $chunk) {
        DB::insert('INSERT INTO users (name, email, status) VALUES (?, ?, ?)', $chunk);
    }
});

Be mindful of transaction size. A single transaction holding millions of records can exhaust your database's transaction log. Stick to chunk sizes of 500-1000 records per batch, and consider using DB::beginTransaction() / DB::commit() manually with periodic commits for very large datasets.

Move Imports to the CLI

Web requests have hard timeout limits. Even with set_time_limit(0), you're fighting against proxy servers, load balancers, and good architectural practice. Heavy data imports belong in Artisan commands:

class ImportUsersCommand extends Command
{
    protected $signature = 'import:users {file}';

    public function handle()
    {
        $this->output->title('Starting user import...');
        $bar = $this->output->createProgressBar($totalChunks);

        DB::transaction(function () use ($data, $bar) {
            foreach (array_chunk($data, 500) as $chunk) {
                DB::insert('INSERT INTO users ...', $chunk);
                $bar->advance();
            }
        });

        $bar->finish();
    }
}

Running imports via the CLI gives you unlimited execution time, full access to Laravel's service container, and a progress bar for feedback. Pair this with Supervisor or Laravel Horizon for scheduled imports.

Raw PDO for Maximum Throughput

For truly extreme throughput, you can drop down to raw PDO and prepared statements. This gives you control over buffered queries and fetch modes:

$pdo = DB::getPdo();
$statement = $pdo->prepare('INSERT INTO users (name, email, status) VALUES (:name, :email, :status)');

foreach ($data as $row) {
    $statement->execute([
        ':name' => $row['name'],
        ':email' => $row['email'],
        ':status' => $row['status'],
    ]);
}

Pro tip: MariaDB and MySQL support LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE for CSV-based bulk imports. This is the fastest method available, often processing millions of rows per minute. Laravel's DB::unprepared() can execute this directly.

Summary

Bulk inserting data in Laravel doesn't have to be slow. Drop Eloquent for mass operations, wrap inserts in transactions, move heavy lifting to Artisan commands, and use raw SQL or PDO when you need maximum speed. These patterns are what separate hobby projects from production-grade enterprise systems.

Originally published at laravelcompany.com. More from our team: Laravel Mail and Laravel SEO.

title: How zkDatabase Works: From Data Sampling to Verifiable Query Results
description:
TL;DR: zkDatabase works by turning database operations into provable steps: data sampling, processing, storage commitments, lookup proofs, transformation proofs, and verifiable query results. The goal is to let an external verifier check that a data operation was correct without relying only on the database operator or exposing sensitive records.

Smart contracts and auditors increasingly rely on off-chain data for reserves, asset state, eligibility, and collateral; zkDatabase exists to make that reliance verifiable. It applies Zero-Knowledge Proofs so a data condition can be checked without exposing the raw data behind it.

Key Takeaways

  • zkDatabase works by proving database operations across a Verifiable Data Pipeline.
  • The core workflow includes data sampling, processing, immutable storage, lookup proving, and transformation proving.
  • Verifiable query results matter because institutions need to know whether a returned value came from a committed data state.
  • Zero-Knowledge Proofs allow verification without exposing the full dataset.
  • zkDatabase is best understood as a proof layer for institutional data workflows, not as a generic blockchain database.

How does zkDatabase work at a high level?

zkDatabase works by generating cryptographic proofs for database operations over committed data. A verifier checks the proof to confirm that the operation satisfied defined rules, rather than trusting a database export or operator statement.

The high-level pipeline is:

  1. Data is sampled from a source.
  2. Raw data is processed into a structured format.
  3. The data is committed into storage using cryptographic commitments.
  4. A lookup or query is executed against the committed state.
  5. A proof is generated for the query or transformation.
  6. A verifier checks the proof on-chain or in another verification environment.

This structure is why Orochi Network describes zkDatabase as part of Verifiable Data Infrastructure. The database is not only a place to store records. It is a system for producing evidence about records.

For a business-facing overview, see the companion article on zkDatabase as a provable database for institutions.

What is verifiable data sampling in zkDatabase?

Verifiable data sampling is the process of proving that data was collected from an approved source according to a defined method. It addresses the first trust point in the pipeline: where did the data come from, and was the sample authentic?

In institutional workflows, sampling can involve APIs, internal databases, custody systems, user inputs, application data, IoT devices, or third-party data sources. The key issue is not simply connecting to those sources. It is creating evidence that the sampled data is the data the workflow claims to use.

Without this step, a later proof can become misleading. A system may prove that a calculation was performed correctly over the wrong input. Verifiable sampling helps reduce that risk by tying the downstream proof to a more defensible input state.

This is important for stablecoin reserves, RWA collateral, fund NAV, and compliance-state checks. The verifier needs confidence not just in the final answer, but in the path from source data to answer.

What happens during verifiable processing and storage?

Verifiable processing turns sampled data into structured data while preserving proof continuity. Storage then commits that structured data into a tamper-evident state that future lookups and transformations can reference.

Processing matters because raw institutional data is often messy. Reserve records, custodian statements, asset metadata, eligibility fields, and chain events may have different formats. A proof system needs a defined structure before it can prove anything useful.

zkDatabase uses schemas and provable data types so records can be serialized, hashed, and included in cryptographic commitments. The storage layer can then anchor the state in a form that later operations can reference.

The result is a committed database state. A verifier does not need to inspect the whole database to verify every later query. The verifier can check whether a query result or state transition is linked to that committed state.

For more detail on proof architecture, see Orochi's Groth16 and zkDatabase architecture.

How do lookup proofs create verifiable query results?

Lookup proofs create verifiable query results by proving that a returned document exists in the committed database state and that the lookup operation was performed correctly. The verifier checks the proof instead of trusting a query response.

This is the heart of a provable database. That shift is why oracles, databases, and attestations aren't enough on their own for institutional data. In zkDatabase, a query result can be accompanied by proof that the result corresponds to a committed state.

For example, a stablecoin workflow might ask whether reserve data satisfies a threshold. A tokenized fund workflow might ask whether a NAV input was part of the approved dataset. A compliance workflow might ask whether an address belonged to an approved set at a timestamp.

In each case, the value of the lookup proof is the same: it connects the answer to the committed data state. The verifier can check the relationship without receiving the entire dataset.

What are transformation proofs in zkDatabase?

Transformation proofs verify that updates, inserts, deletes, or schema transformations follow approved rules. They help prove that the database state changed correctly, not just that a current record exists.

This matters because institutional data is not static. Reserves move. Collateral values update. Investors onboard and offboard. Compliance statuses change. Loans hit covenant checkpoints. A database that can prove only a static snapshot is less useful than one that can prove how the state changed over time.

Transformation proofs help create a chain of evidence across the data lifecycle. A verifier can reason about the state transition instead of relying only on a final report.

Operation What needs proof Institutional example
Insert New record was added correctly New custodian balance record
Update Existing record changed under approved rules Reserve composition update
Delete Record removal followed policy Expired eligibility credential
Transform Data format or schema changed correctly Raw custody file converted into reporting schema

This is where zkDatabase becomes more than a query tool. It can support a verifiable audit trail for data operations.

Why do verifiable query results matter for institutions?

Verifiable query results matter because institutional on-chain workflows often depend on private off-chain facts. If the query result is wrong, stale, or manipulated, the smart contract or reporting workflow can still execute as designed while relying on bad data.

The most important institutional use cases share a pattern:

  • Stablecoin issuers need reserve and redemption data to match token liabilities.
  • RWA platforms need ownership, collateral, and valuation state to match token claims.
  • Institutional DeFi protocols need collateral and eligibility data before execution.
  • Compliance teams need proof that a required condition was checked.

In all of these cases, the institution does not necessarily want to publish the full dataset. It wants to prove a specific condition about the dataset. Verifiable query results make that possible.

This is also why zkDatabase should be framed carefully. It proves properties of data operations. It does not guarantee that the institution's source data, legal structure, or governance model is sufficient. Those remain separate controls.

Where does zkDatabase fit after the query proof is generated?

After a query proof is generated, zkDatabase can make the result usable for smart contracts, auditors, counterparties, or internal risk systems. The verifier checks the proof and decides whether to rely on the result.

For an on-chain workflow, a supported verifier contract can check the proof before a transaction uses the data. For an audit workflow, the proof can become part of an evidence package. For a compliance workflow, the proof can show that a condition was checked without moving raw data into every downstream system.

This is the practical value of Verifiable Data. The proof turns a database answer into something that can be independently verified.

For an applied RWA view, see How zkDatabase can be applied to Real-World Assets.

What should technical teams take away from how zkDatabase works?

Conclusion: zkDatabase works by proving the data path from sampling to verifiable query results. It samples data, structures it, commits it, proves lookups, proves transformations, and lets verifiers check the resulting evidence.

For institutions, that means off-chain data can become a more reliable input to on-chain finance, reporting, and audit workflows. Orochi Network's role is to provide the Verifiable Data Infrastructure that helps turn sensitive database operations into proof-backed evidence.

View Technical Docs

Review how zkDatabase maps data sampling, storage commitments, lookup proofs, and transformation proofs into verifiable workflows.

FAQ: What should technical readers ask next?

How does zkDatabase work?

zkDatabase works by generating proofs for database operations over committed data states. It uses a Verifiable Data Pipeline that includes data sampling, processing, storage commitments, lookup proofs, and transformation proofs. A verifier can check whether a result is tied to the committed data state without seeing the entire dataset.

What are verifiable query results?

Verifiable query results are query outputs accompanied by cryptographic evidence that the result came from a committed database state and followed the expected lookup logic. They are useful when a smart contract, auditor, or counterparty needs to rely on a database answer without trusting only the database operator.

Does zkDatabase put all data on-chain?

zkDatabase does not require all raw data to be placed on-chain. The sensitive data can remain off-chain, while commitments and proofs allow verification of specific conditions or operations. This is important for institutions that need assurance without exposing customer data, reserve details, or proprietary records.

Why does zkDatabase use Zero-Knowledge Proofs?

zkDatabase uses Zero-Knowledge Proofs because institutions often need to prove statements about sensitive data without revealing the data itself. The proof can show that a condition was satisfied, such as membership, threshold coverage, or query correctness, while the underlying records remain private under the institution's access controls.

title: Node.js File Uploads: Presigned URLs, Proxy Backend, and Security (Fintech)
description:
Short answer: for browser file upload of fintech training artifacts, use a presigned URL when the browser can send bytes directly to private object storage; keep a proxy backend for content inspection or policy decisions that must happen before storage. Track both paths with the same retention record so cost, latency, and security are measurable instead of guessed.

The system has one job: accept a training artifact, preserve its chain of custody, and delete it according to a reproducible policy. A proxy path is browser -> Node.js -> storage. A direct path is browser -> storage, with Node.js authorizing the transfer and recording metadata. That small difference moves bandwidth, trust, and failure handling to different places.

Keep it private.

The first decision is about control, not a URL

Path Pick it when What you pay for operationally Main security control
Presigned URL Artifacts can be scanned after arrival and the browser needs low latency Upload state, CORS, and orphan cleanup Short expiry, private bucket, narrow key and size policy
Proxy backend Bytes need synchronous inspection, transformation, or a single egress point Application bandwidth, connection limits, and backpressure Stream validation before forwarding; never buffer unbounded bodies
Two-step quarantine You need direct transfer plus a gate before promotion A second state and scanner queue Write to quarantine, scan, then copy or mark approved

Cost follows byte movement. In a proxy design, every upload crosses the application network and competes with API traffic. Direct transfer usually lowers that contention, but it does not remove storage requests, failed retries, or abandoned multipart sessions. Latency follows the same shape: a nearby storage region can beat a distant application region, while a required scan can make a proxy the faster end-to-end choice because it rejects bad input early.

Should a web app use presigned URLs or a proxy backend for upload control?

Start with an application-level upload record. It should contain a random upload ID, tenant ID, expected byte count, content type, object key, retention class, and state (issued, received, quarantined, approved, or expired). The object key must not be derived from an untrusted filename. Keep the bucket private; a presigned URL grants a temporary operation, not a public link.

Here is a deliberately small Node.js authorization endpoint. It returns a generic storage URL produced by your storage adapter, so the rest of the application does not depend on an SDK. The adapter must enforce the same bucket, key prefix, method, and maximum size that the record contains.

import crypto from "node:crypto";

type UploadIntent = {
  uploadId: string;
  objectKey: string;
  contentType: string;
  maxBytes: number;
  expiresAt: string;
  uploadUrl: string;
};

export async function createUploadIntent(tenantId: string, contentType: string): Promise<UploadIntent> {
  const uploadId = crypto.randomUUID();
  const objectKey = `training/${tenantId}/${uploadId}`;
  const maxBytes = 50 * 1024 * 1024;
  const expiresAt = new Date(Date.now() + 10 * 60 * 1000).toISOString();

  const uploadUrl = await storage.presignPut({
    key: objectKey,
    contentType,
    maxBytes,
    expiresAt
  });

  await uploads.insert({ uploadId, tenantId, objectKey, contentType, maxBytes, expiresAt, state: "issued" });
  return { uploadId, objectKey, contentType, maxBytes, expiresAt, uploadUrl };
}

The browser uses the returned URL with the method and headers that were signed. After the request completes, the API performs a head check and compares the recorded byte count and checksum before moving the record to received. A 201 from your intent endpoint is not proof that the file arrived. That distinction prevents a support ticket from becoming a forensic exercise.

For a proxy, keep the same record and state machine. Stream the request, reject an announced or observed body above the limit, and cap concurrent streams per tenant. Return 413 for an oversized body, and emit a request ID that joins the API log to the storage log. I put the byte counter beside the stream, not in a later batch job; that is where a sudden 2 GB upload becomes visible.

What does the retention policy look like after upload?

Retention is a data contract, not a cleanup slogan. Store a policy version such as train-artifact-v3 with each upload. A worker can then calculate delete_at from the artifact's creation time and policy version, while a lifecycle rule in object storage provides a second, time-based backstop. AWS documents lifecycle management for expiring objects, and Google Cloud documents equivalent storage concepts; the exact rule syntax differs, so test it in a disposable bucket.

The quarantine path is useful when malware scanning or PII detection must precede approval. Direct upload still handles the bytes efficiently, but only the scanner can change quarantined to approved. A proxy is the better fit when that scan must happen before any durable object exists, or when regulation requires one controlled ingress address.

Measure a decision with the same fields on both paths: upload ID, tenant, byte range, storage region, elapsed milliseconds, retry count, final state, and retention policy version. Alert on issued records older than the URL expiry, quarantined records past their scan SLO, and multipart sessions with no progress. A dashboard that only counts HTTP 200 responses misses the abandoned half of the workflow.

My rule is boring and useful: compare p95 time-to-received, application egress bytes, scanner queue time, and rejected-byte rate for a week of representative artifacts. Your mileage may vary with enterprise proxies and browser CORS settings; a synthetic test from one laptop cannot settle that question. Also test expiry, tab refresh, duplicate completion, and a 413 response before launch.

This measurement takes more care than it first appears. For example, a direct upload can show a fast browser transfer while the quarantine scanner waits in a queue; a proxy can show higher request latency while rejecting a disallowed file before it reaches durable storage. Put both timestamps in the upload record, then report transfer time and approval time separately. Tag retries by cause (expired URL, client disconnect, policy rejection), and sample a few raw request IDs each day. That makes a cost or latency regression explainable: you can point to extra application egress, a slow region, or a scanner backlog instead of arguing from averages.

Measure twice.

When an upload fails, classify the boundary before changing the architecture. A browser-side CORS rejection is different from an expired signature, and both are different from a storage write that succeeded while the acknowledgement was lost. In the direct path, have the client send the upload ID back to the API after completion; the API can then perform its head check and safely accept a retry as an idempotent operation. In the proxy path, distinguish a client disconnect from an upstream timeout, and stop reading the request as soon as the policy limit is crossed. Record the first failure cause, not only the final retry status. A single artifact may produce three attempts: the first can fail at 8 MB because the tab was closed, the second can receive all bytes but miss its response, and the third can be rejected because the retention class changed while it was pending. Without per-attempt counters and a stable upload ID, those events collapse into one vague upload_failed metric. With them, an on-call engineer can decide whether to extend URL lifetime, tune connection pools, or fix a policy transition. The right response is often a small state-machine fix, not a wholesale move from direct upload to proxying.

The limits that should change your choice

The catch is that presigned URLs are delivery-simple, not policy-complete. They are a poor fit when every byte must be inspected synchronously, when clients cannot be trusted to reach storage, or when a single ingress point is a hard audit requirement. Stick with a proxy in those cases, accepting its throughput and scaling work.

Conversely, a proxy is not a free security upgrade. It enlarges the blast radius of a compromised app process and can turn a burst of large uploads into exhausted connections. Do not choose direct transfer for permanent public links, either; anonymous distribution is a separate access-control problem.

For this fintech workflow, I choose direct presigned transfer into quarantine, followed by a scanner and versioned retention policy. I choose a proxy only for the artifacts whose inspection or network boundary demands it. The decision is reversible when the upload record, metrics, and state transitions stay independent of the byte path.

  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/CORS

title: Natural Language Programming: Rethinking Language, Memory, and Cognition in the Era of Generative AI
description:
arXiv:2611.23106v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence is transforming the role of natural language in computational systems. In classical Natural Language Processing (NLP), language was treated as an object of computation: something to analyse, classify, translate, or generate. Large Language Models (LLMs) challenge this perspective, enabling natural language to function increasingly as an executable cognitive medium through which humans structure reasoning, orchestrate problem solving, and regulate hybrid human/AI workflows.
  This paper introduces Natural Language Programming (NLPg) as a theoretical and epistemological extension of traditional NLP. Rather than focusing on language understanding alone, NLPg conceptualises prompts as dynamic cognitive artefacts that externalise goals, constraints, assumptions, validation criteria, and intermediate reasoning states. Prompting is thus not merely a technical interaction technique, but a form of dialogic cognitive programming operating within distributed human/AI memory architectures.
  Building on theories of distributed cognition, extended mind, metacognition, and dialogic learning, the paper proposes the notion of Dialogic Working Memory, describing how prompts and conversational states function as temporary external memory structures supporting reasoning continuity and reflective regulation. We further map existing memory architectures (BTMA, SKGE, RMR) onto this framework, illustrating how episodic, semantic, and metacognitive layers support long-horizon conversational coherence.
  Finally, implications for computational linguistics and AI/mediated knowledge systems are discussed, suggesting a post symbolic and post interface paradigm in which natural language operates simultaneously as communication medium, executable specification, cognitive scaffold, and distributed memory architecture.

title: Large-scale Neuron Community Discovery Reveals Neuron-Sparse Behaviors in Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.23112v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: What reusable units of computation can we discover within a language model's neurons? Prior work has shown that individual forward passes can often be sparsified post-hoc to small groups of neurons, but it has been unclear whether these groups form coherent computational entities reused across inputs. We introduce neuron community discovery, an unsupervised method for finding neuron groups that recur across prompts and are causally necessary and sufficient, within the layers they span, for common computations. The method combines gradient-based attribution, a graph connecting neurons that are repeatedly attributed together, and community detection. Applied to Llama-3.1-8B using ten million prompts, it discovers thousands of candidate communities. We evaluate them on held-out prompts through three causal tests: community necessity, sufficiency within a layer subset, and layer necessity. These tests identify groups whose removal disrupts predictions and whose retention preserves predictions despite ablating the remaining MLP neurons in the tested layers. Discovered communities support functions like grammatical agreement, token-probability calibration, fixed phrases, in-context copying, addition, and multiplication. With communities capped at 128 neurons across all layers, 10.3% of held-out prompts have at least one layer's contribution explained on a neuron-sparse basis. Coverage remains 8.7% when requiring at least four layers and 3.3% when requiring at least twelve. These results show that small groups of existing neurons can provide reusable computational components across prompts, and that such groups can be discovered at scale.

title: TransFIRA+: Transfer Learning for Biometric Recognizability Assessment
description:
arXiv:2611.23442v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Biometric recognition in surveillance, video, and web imagery must contend with extreme variation in pose, blur, illumination, occlusion, and distance, where visual quality metrics fail to predict whether inputs are recognizable to the deployed encoder. Existing face image quality assessment methods rely on visual heuristics, curated annotations, or costly generative pipelines, leaving their predictions detached from the encoder's decision geometry. We introduce TransFIRA, a lightweight framework that grounds recognizability directly in embedding space. TransFIRA derives class-center similarity (CCS) and class-center angular separation (CCAS) from a pretrained encoder's embeddings and learns to predict them from images without quality annotations. Using predicted CCS for template weighting and CCAS>0 as a natural filtering threshold yields state-of-the-art face verification performance on BRIAR, raising TAR at $10^{-6}$ FMR from 0.085 with uniform averaging to 0.598. The predicted scores also reveal how image degradations affect encoder-specific recognizability. TransFIRA+ extends this framework to cross-camera multimodal person identification in untrimmed surveillance video. In this setting, body recognizability scores saturate within a narrow range, making direct weighting effectively uniform. We introduce a post-hoc sigmoid calibration that transforms these saturated scores into informative weights without retraining. After calibration, the BRIAR-trained TransFIRA predictor improves fused face and body identification on two unseen multi-camera datasets, outperforming detector-confidence weighting and uncalibrated CCS-rank weighting. Together, TransFIRA and TransFIRA+ demonstrate that encoder-grounded recognizability generalizes across biometric modalities and recognition settings.

title: Crypt: a vault that visibly rots, built with Kiro
description:
I built a vault that rots.

You seal it with a fake secret and a deadline. Then it starts to decay
in front of you. Fresh, then Dusty, then Cracked, then Rotting, then
Ghost. Open it while it is alive and the lid lifts and shows the secret.
Open it too late and the screen tells you the secret rotted away. It is
gone.

That is the whole thing. One flow. No login, no server, nothing stored
anywhere except your own browser.

The spooky look is not decoration. The worse the vault looks, the sooner
you have to open it. The design is the warning. That is the Costume
Contest fit: the haunting does real work.

How Kiro built it

I did not vibe-code this one. Kiro worked from a spec. Requirements
first, then design, then tasks, one at a time. Steering docs kept the
rules in place.

My favourite part is the boring part. Every time I save a file, a hook
runs node --check on the code. If I broke something, it tells me straight
away, while the fix is still small. The test harness is 24 out of 24
passing.

Try it

Live demo: https://skymiller1509-blip.github.io/crypt/
Repo: https://github.com/skymiller1509-blip/crypt

Tap "Make a 2 minute vault" and watch the whole decay in two minutes.
Or drag the Preview decay slider through all five stages.

One warning, and I mean it. Everything in the demo is fake data, and the
page says so on screen. Never type a real password into it.

title: SWIFT: Slow World, Instant Freshness, and Timely Action for Asynchronous Autonomous Driving
description:
arXiv:2611.23813v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Driving scenes keep changing during model computation, making both observation freshness and action-delivery time central to world-action planning. To retain rich generative world priors in autonomous driving without stalling real-time control, we present SWIFT (Slow World, Instant Freshness, and Timely action), a deployment-oriented asynchronous world-action system that moves world updates off the observation-to-action critical path. On a background GPU, a slow Video DiT streams surround-view history into read-only predictive world context, trained with a predictive span that covers both the update interval and background world computation. On a foreground GPU, a lightweight freshness carrier encodes current surround-view images into a gated key/value bank at every step, letting a fast Action DiT combine live visual feedback with the latest completed world context without waiting. On open-loop NAVSIM, SWIFT reaches 94.2 PDMS at 198.4 ms per decision with a trajectory scorer; on closed-loop Bench2Drive, it achieves an 80.30 Driving Score at 109.9 ms foreground latency. SWIFT further transfers to the Waymo E2E hidden test (8.0050 Rater Feedback Score) and nuScenes (0.54 m mean endpoint error, 0.03% mean collision rate). Across all four benchmarks, SWIFT achieves the best results among compared world-action methods, establishing a favorable accuracy-latency trade-off.

title: Go 1.28 will flag the error your rows.Next() loop forgets
description:
A for rows.Next() loop that stops early looks like a shorter result. Without rows.Err(), your service returns a truncated list with a 200. Go 1.28 adds a vet analyzer for that mistake. I ran it on a dozen of my Go services. It found nothing, and that is exactly the problem.

TL;DR: the Go 1.28 release notes, still a draft, announce two vet analyzers: scannererr for bufio.Scanner and sqlrowserr for database/sql. Both already exist in golang.org/x/tools. On a dozen of my Go services, sqlrowserr reported zero cases. Not because the code is clean: because it reads Postgres through pgx, and the analyzer only looks at database/sql. A manual grep found four rows.Next() without rows.Err(), one of them in production.

Source status: snapshot as of November 3, 2026. The Go 1.28 notes are a draft. The analyzers may change before the release expected in February 2027.

This article is for Go developers who read SQL results or streams line by line.

A loop that stops early looks like a shorter result

Here is the database/sql contract. rows.Next() returns true when a row is ready. It returns false when there are no more rows. It also returns false when an error happens during the read.

The documentation says it word for word: "Rows.Err should be consulted to distinguish between the two cases." Without that call, the two cases blur. A connection cut after row 40 of a 200-row result gives a list of 40 items. And err is nil.

Your HTTP handler then returns a 200 with 40 rows. The client sees nothing wrong. Neither do your tests, because they run against a local database that never drops. It is the same family of failure as the green test suite on a broken product: success and failure look alike. Go has others, such as January 31 plus one month giving March 3, with no error.

The damage depends on the loop. A truncated list in a web page is a quiet bug. A partial sum in a billing calculation is lost money. An incomplete security export is a hole in your audit. In my MFA article, the export handler calls rows.Err() for that reason.

bufio.Scanner has the same flaw. sc.Scan() returns false at the end of the file, and also on a read error. A line too long for the buffer stops the loop without a sound. Only sc.Err() tells the difference.

Go 1.28 adds two vet analyzers for this mistake

go vet is the static analyzer that ships with Go. The Go 1.28 release notes add two analyzers to it. I quote the draft as is:

The new scannererr analyzer checks for failure to handle scanner errors after a loop around bufio.Scanner.Scan, which may cause scanning or I/O errors to go unreported. The sqlrowserr analyzer performs a similar check for loops around sql.Rows.Next, so that iteration errors are correctly distinguished from a smaller result.

The page is labeled "DRAFT RELEASE NOTES". It states: "Go 1.28 is expected to be released in February 2027." Nothing is final. An analyzer can still change its name, its rule, or disappear.

I read the code of both analyzers in golang.org/x/tools. The sqlrowserr rule is simple. It looks for a call to Query or QueryContext on a sql.DB, sql.Conn, sql.Tx or sql.Stmt. The result must land in a local variable. That variable must be used in a loop that calls Next. If Err is never called on it, the analyzer reports.

It stays silent as soon as the variable leaves the function: passed as an argument, returned, stored in a field. The package documentation owns that choice: the goal is to catch the simple oversight, not to guarantee all error handling. To silence a deliberate case, _ = rows.Err() is enough.

scannererr follows the same logic for bufio.NewScanner. It ignores scanners built on a strings.Reader or a bytes.Buffer, because an in-memory read does not fail.

My lab: a dozen Go services, zero reports

One of my projects has a dozen Go services. They declare go 1.25.0 and all read Postgres through pgx, mostly through code generated by sqlc. I compiled the two analyzers into a small binary, then ran go vet -vettool on each module.

Result: zero reports, across the twelve modules, for both analyzers. One test package in one module did not compile, because a fake gRPC client was one method behind. The analyzer skipped it. Everything else was analyzed.

I would have liked to write that my code is clean. The real reason is elsewhere. None of these modules imports database/sql. The pgx.Rows type is a pgx interface, not the standard library's *sql.Rows. And the analyzer only looks at seven methods, all in database/sql.

To be sure, I wrote the same loop twice in a test module. One version with db.QueryContext from database/sql, one with pool.Query from pgx. Neither calls rows.Err(). The analyzer reports the first one:

std.go:10:15: sql.Rows "rows" is used in Next loop at line 16 without final check of rows.Err()

It says nothing about the second. So zero reports on my services means zero coverage, not zero bugs. The project's only bufio.NewScanner, in a test, does call scanner.Err(). There, the silence is deserved.

Zero reports means zero coverage, not zero bugs. The analyzer only looks at database/sql. My services read Postgres through pgx, and the grep finds four gaps there.

What the analyzer cannot see, I looked for by hand

I counted with grep. The twelve modules contain 118 calls to rows.Next() and 114 to rows.Err(). The code generated by sqlc always calls rows.Err() after the loop. The four gaps are in hand-written code.

Two are in integration tests, one of them reading a single row. A third is in a command that loads users to seed a database: a truncated list seeds fewer users, with no error at all. The fourth is in a production repository. Here is the code, identifiers renamed:

func (r *HistoryRepo) ListByCaseID(ctx context.Context, caseID string) ([]domain.Event, error) {
    rows, err := r.pool.Query(ctx,
        `SELECT id, event_type, title, created_at
         FROM case_events WHERE case_id = $1 ORDER BY created_at ASC`, caseID)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("list events: %w", err)
    }
    defer rows.Close()

    var events []domain.Event
    for rows.Next() {
        var e domain.Event
        if err := rows.Scan(&e.ID, &e.EventType, &e.Title, &e.CreatedAt); err != nil {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("scan event: %w", err)
        }
        events = append(events, e)
    }
    if events == nil {
        events = []domain.Event{}
    }
    return events, nil // rows.Err() is never read
}

This function returns the history of a case. If the connection drops halfway, it returns the first events and nil. The calling service builds the case view with a shortened history. The user sees a normal page, just shorter. No log, no alert.

This code is in one of my repositories anyway. It is exactly the oversight an analyzer should catch. And the pgx documentation is as clear as the standard library's. It says: "Callers should check rows.Err() after rows.Next() returns false to detect whether result-set reading ended prematurely due to an error."

The fix is three lines

For database/sql, add the check right after the loop:

for rows.Next() {
    // ...
}
if err := rows.Err(); err != nil {
    return nil, err
}
return ids, nil

For pgx, the same three lines work. pgx also offers helpers that do the check for you. pgx.CollectRows and pgx.ForEachRow call rows.Err() at the end of the loop, I checked their source. With db tags on the struct, the function above becomes:

rows, err := r.pool.Query(ctx, query, caseID)
if err != nil {
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("list events: %w", err)
}
events, err := pgx.CollectRows(rows, pgx.RowToStructByName[domain.Event])
if err != nil {
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("list events: %w", err)
}
return events, nil

For bufio.Scanner, it is if err := sc.Err(); err != nil after the loop. If you know the read cannot fail, write _ = sc.Err() with a comment. The analyzer goes quiet, and the reviewer understands it is a choice.

A test that fails when the loop stops early

An analyzer catches the oversight in the code. A test proves the consequence. With database/sql, the go-sqlmock library can simulate an error in the middle of the result with RowError. Here is the table test I ran on my two versions of the function:

func TestListIDs_StopsEarly(t *testing.T) {
    tests := []struct {
        name    string
        fn      func(context.Context, *sql.DB) ([]int64, error)
        wantErr bool
    }{
        {"buggy", listIDsBuggy, true},
        {"fixed", listIDs, true},
    }
    for _, tc := range tests {
        t.Run(tc.name, func(t *testing.T) {
            db, mock, err := sqlmock.New()
            if err != nil {
                t.Fatal(err)
            }
            defer db.Close()
            rows := sqlmock.NewRows([]string{"id"}).
                AddRow(int64(1)).AddRow(int64(2)).AddRow(int64(3)).
                RowError(1, errors.New("connection reset"))
            mock.ExpectQuery("SELECT id FROM things").WillReturnRows(rows)

            ids, err := tc.fn(context.Background(), db)
            if tc.wantErr && err == nil {
                t.Fatalf("got %d ids and no error, want an error", len(ids))
            }
        })
    }
}

The version without rows.Err() fails with the message got 1 ids and no error, want an error. Three rows in the result, one returned, no error. The fixed version passes.

With pgx, there is no official mock. Write a fake pgx.Rows whose Next returns false after one row and whose Err returns an error. The test must demand an error, not a list. In this lab, I only tested the database/sql version.

Run the analyzers today, without waiting for Go 1.28

Both analyzers are already in golang.org/x/tools v0.52.0. They have no ready-made command: the package's main.go carries a //go:build ignore. So you need a three-file module:

mkdir vet128 && cd vet128
go mod init vet128
cat > main.go <<'EOF'
package main

import (
    "golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/multichecker"
    "golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/passes/scannererr"
    "golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/passes/sqlrowserr"
)

func main() {
    multichecker.Main(scannererr.Analyzer, sqlrowserr.Analyzer)
}
EOF
go mod tidy
go build -o vet128 .

Then, in each module to check:

go vet -vettool=/path/to/vet128 ./...

The binary weighs about 9 MB. It needs Go 1.26 or newer, not Go 1.28. My local go vet, on Go 1.26.3, knows neither analyzer. gopls 0.22 already enables scannererr by default in the editor, but not sqlrowserr.

If you use pgx, add a grep until something better exists:

for f in $(grep -rl 'rows.Next()' --include='*.go' .); do
  n=$(grep -c 'rows.Next()' "$f"); e=$(grep -c 'rows.Err()' "$f")
  [ "$n" -gt "$e" ] && echo "$f next=$n err=$e"
done

It is crude. It compares files, not functions. It still found my four gaps in a few seconds.

The checklist

A rows.Next() loop without rows.Err() cannot tell the end of the result from a failure.

  • [ ] Call rows.Err() after every rows.Next() loop, with database/sql and with pgx alike
  • [ ] Call sc.Err() after every sc.Scan() loop over a file or a network stream
  • [ ] With pgx, prefer pgx.CollectRows or pgx.ForEachRow over hand-written loops
  • [ ] Compile scannererr and sqlrowserr into a multichecker and run it in CI
  • [ ] Know what your analyzer covers: sqlrowserr only sees database/sql
  • [ ] Compare your rows.Next() to your rows.Err() with a grep for non-standard drivers
  • [ ] Write a test where the read fails halfway and demand an error
  • [ ] Re-read the Go 1.28 notes at release time: the draft can change

The takeaway

An iteration error looks like a smaller result. That is the sentence from the Go 1.28 notes, and it is the whole point. The analyzer is coming, but it only covers database/sql. If you are on pgx, your tools are still code review and a grep.

Run the binary on your code this week. Then count your rows.Next() against your rows.Err(). The gap is your list of silent bugs.

Want a review of your database access code and your Go CI? See my Go backend takeover offer, or let's talk.

Sources: Go 1.28 release notes (draft) · sqlrowserr analyzer · scannererr analyzer · database/sql, Rows.Next and Rows.Err · bufio, Scanner.Err · pgx v5, Rows interface and CollectRows · multichecker package · go vet documentation · go-sqlmock, RowError

title: Designing a Currency Selector That Doesn't Annoy International Users
description:
A dropdown with 180 currencies is not a currency selector. It is a search problem disguised as a form field.

Smart defaults

Detect the user's likely currency from their IP-based geo, not from navigator.language (which reflects OS preference, not location):

const geo = headers['cf-ipcountry'] || 'US';
const DEFAULT_CURRENCY: Record<string, string> = {
  US: 'USD', GB: 'GBP', ES: 'EUR', MX: 'MXN', BR: 'BRL',
  IN: 'INR', AU: 'AUD', JP: 'JPY',
};
const suggested = DEFAULT_CURRENCY[geo] || 'USD';

Show the suggested currency pre-selected with a "change" link that opens the full list.

Searchable, not scrollable

When the full list opens, it should be a text input that filters as you type — matching both the code (EUR) and the name (Euro, евро):

function matchCurrency(query, currencies) {
  const q = query.toLowerCase();
  return currencies.filter(c =>
    c.code.toLowerCase().includes(q) ||
    c.name.toLowerCase().includes(q) ||
    (c.localName || '').toLowerCase().includes(q)
  );
}

Displaying amounts

Always format with Intl.NumberFormat for the selected locale, not by hardcoding $ or € symbols. A site like Oro7 that serves a Spanish-speaking audience needs es-MX formatting where the currency symbol follows the number, not precedes it.

Edge case: multi-currency accounts

Some platforms let users hold balances in several currencies. Display the active balance prominently and others in a collapsible section. Never auto-convert without confirmation — users are sensitive to exchange rates and want to see the rate before it applies.

Takeaway

Respect the user's location, let them search instead of scroll, and format amounts for their locale. Three rules, zero frustration.

title: Communicative On-Policy Distillation: Distilling Black-Box Teacher Capabilities through Communication for Long-Horizon Tasks
description:
arXiv:2611.23673v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a powerful paradigm for improving language-model agents on long-horizon tasks, yet its conventional formulation relies on teacher logits that text-only black- box models do not expose. To address this limitation, we introduce Communicative On-Policy Distillation (COPD), which uses natural-language communication as a medium for distilling a stronger model's capabilities into a smaller student. During task execution, the student au- tonomously decides when to consult a black-box teacher and formulates open-ended natural- language requests without predefined question templates or intervention schedules. Successful student-teacher interactions are retained as privileged references to supervise fresh adviser-free student rollouts through on-policy self-distillation, jointly with task-reward reinforcement learning. On CAMG-II, COPD achieves 2.46 times the gain of the strongest black-box OPD baseline. The capabilities it learns through communication generalize to Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2, improving task success without adviser access.

title: OCLDA-GS: Object-Centric Local Deformation-Aware Gaussian Streaming
description:
arXiv:2611.23416v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Streaming 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) allows for online reconstruction of dynamic scenes from multi-view videos for Free Viewpoint Video (FVV). Current time and storage efficient methods rely on selecting a subset of anchor Gaussians and neighborhood interpolation for fast streamable 3DGS. However, these methods can overlook object-specific motion and introduce inconsistencies near object boundaries. We propose OCLDA-GS, an object-centric streaming framework that dynamically reallocates object and motion-aware Gaussian anchors to allocate anchor Gaussian support for objects undergoing large motion while at the same time, restricting the gaussian neighborhood within object groups for more precise object boundaries. Furthermore, it estimates object-wise rigid transformations (e.g. a hand moving) and leverages these estimates to learn per-anchor local deformation correction for small deformations (e.g. wrinkles on a shirt). Then, we conduct experiments on three dynamic multi-view video datasets and demonstrate improvements over the previous baselines alongside improved quality between refinement timesteps. Under matched refinement budgets, our method improves PSNR over Instant Gaussian Stream (IGS) by 0.169 dB on N3DV, 0.202 dB on Meeting Room and +0.199 on Google Immersive, while reducing the mean PSNR drop between refinement timesteps by 9.2% and 13.8% in N3DV and Meeting Room, respectively.

title: Bringing the lake back to the lakehouse: Introducing the FILE type in Apache Iceberg
description:
by Sung Yun & Gaurav Soni, Google Cloud

The original promise of the data lake was simple: a single, universal home for all an organization’s data. Whether structured database exports, raw text documents, audio recordings, or high-resolution imagery, everything landed in object storage. But as data lakes grew into sprawling swamps lacking transactional guarantees and consistency, the industry pioneered the lakehouse.

Open table formats like Apache Iceberg brought order to the chaos, introducing data warehouse rigor—ACID transactions, snapshot isolation, partition evolution, and fast columnar pruning—directly to cloud storage.

Yet, in our collective rush to build the “house”, we quietly left the “lake” behind.

With the rapid rise of multimodal Large Language Models (LLMs), interest in processing unstructured data directly within the lakehouse has grown rapidly. Multimodal LLMs enable modern data warehouses and lakehouses to analyze unstructured inputs—such as raw images, audio, and documents—much like traditional structured data, without requiring complex, bespoke machine learning staging pipelines.

Because table formats were designed around structured rows and columns, unstructured media was left behind. Raw files were relegated back to external storage buckets, loosely connected to analytical tables through plain, unvalidated string URIs.

The Apache Iceberg community recently took a major step toward reuniting these two worlds by merging support for the new FILE data type into the Iceberg specification.

Limitations of using bare string URIs

Historically, platforms referenced external unstructured assets by storing simple string paths inside tabular columns. While straightforward, relying on plain string URIs introduces several operational challenges:

  • No file metadata in the table: A string path doesn't say what type a file is or how big it is. Engines guess types from file extensions, or make a separate call to object storage for each file.
  • Inconsistent engine behavior: Nothing marks a string column as a file reference, so every engine and team invents its own way of handling one, and what one writes, another can't reliably interpret.
  • No way to detect changes: If a file is replaced at the same path, the string stays the same, so nothing in the table shows that the bytes behind it have changed.

Addressing these operational bottlenecks required a structural shift in how table formats model unstructured assets.

Introducing the FILE type

In the specification slated for Iceberg v4, FILE is defined as a specialized nested type. Rather than treating external assets as opaque strings, it bundles the essential dimensional, transport, and integrity properties of unstructured data into a single schema element:

The native FILE type resolves these operational bottlenecks by storing essential file metadata alongside the reference in every value. Instead of storing an opaque path string, the column stores a structured reference containing standard attributes like uri, offset, size, content_type, checksum, and inline payload. Standardizing these properties gives query engines a single, predictable contract to handle common file management challenges:

  • Pay metadata fetch costs once: Writers capture file metadata such as size and content type once, in a standard format that any engine supporting the FILE type can read. Engines no longer have to make a separate call to object storage for each file every time they plan a query.
  • Detect stale metadata with checksums: Storing typed digests or ETags as checksum explicitly allows readers to detect when underlying files are modified or out of date, preventing silent asset drift.
  • Supply required metadata for LLM processing: The content_type attribute delivers explicit MIME metadata directly to multimodal LLMs and inference APIs, eliminating reliance on fragile file extension guessing.
  • Embedded micro-asset storage: Small binary payloads can be stored directly inside the inline field. The resolution rule allows engines to stream these co-located locally during columnar scans, bypassing the need to store an additional object entirely.
  • Govern structured and unstructured data side by side: The primary win lies in bringing structured business attributes and raw media assets into the exact same transactional table snapshot under unified governance.

Now that we know how and why the FILE type is structured as such, let’s take a look at it in action.

The FILE type in action: Native multimodal AI

Historically, tables pointed at unstructured files with plain string paths. Everything an engine needed to know about a file (what type it is, how big it is, whether it has changed) lived somewhere else: inside tables each team designed for itself, or only in object storage. Let’s look at an example where this breaks down. A claims application keeps policy data in the lakehouse, photos and documents in object storage, and file details in a side table that one team built and others had to find and join by path.

When multimodal AI processing happens (reading the bytes, calling a model, writing results back) the process breaks because of everything around it. Every engine has to guess file types from extensions, track down someone else's side table, or call object storage once per file. And when a file is replaced at the same path, nothing in the table changed, so nobody could tell.

Consider an auto insurer that uses this structure. Each claim pairs structured data (policy, amount, status, and the customer's written account of the accident) with evidence files: damage photos, repair-estimate PDFs, and recorded phone statements. They want to answer this question: "Which open claims have videos that aren’t zero bytes, and has any of that evidence changed since an adjuster reviewed it?"

Finding the videos becomes a filter on real metadata:

Consider how this simplifies an end-to-end multimodal workflow:

  • Every engine reads the same column: Teams using different engines can read the same data.
  • Filter on the real type: The job filters on content_type instead of guessing from extensions, and statistics lets engines skip data files that contain no data.
  • Changed evidence gets flagged: Comparing the checksum recorded at intake with the current object shows when a photo has been replaced.
  • Go straight to the bytes: Engines read the exact byte range from uri, offset, and size, and pass content_type to the multimodal model, with no side table and no extra metadata calls.

By elevating files from unmanaged external pointers to governed schema types, Iceberg transforms multimodal AI from a brittle multi-system coordination problem into a standard analytical query.

Ecosystem impact and looking ahead

The integration of the FILE type into the Apache Iceberg specification marks a major step forward for open lakehouse architectures. Rather than forcing organizations to rely on proprietary wrappers or fragmented storage systems to handle unstructured media, Iceberg establishes a portable, open standard.

With the specification finalized and targeted for adoption in the upcoming Iceberg v4 release, momentum now turns to native reader and writer implementations across the open source compute ecosystem—including Apache Spark, Trino, and DuckDB. As multimodal AI becomes an integral part of everyday enterprise workflows, standardizing the FILE type ensures that the open lakehouse remains the definitive, vendor-neutral foundation for structured and unstructured data alike.
